The Noble Sūtra of the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra) (Āryamahāparinirvāṇasūtra)

Toh 119 in the Kangyur is the Noble Sūtra of the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow, known in Sanskrit as the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and in Tibetan as Phags pa yongs su mya ngan las das pa chen po'i mdo. It is a major Mahāyāna sūtra recounting the final hours and teachings of the Buddha Śākyamuni as he approaches his passing into nirvāṇa between two śāla trees on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī river near Kuśinagara, surrounded by a vast assembly of monks and bodhisattvas. The text expounds on themes of central importance to Mahāyāna Buddhism, including the nature of nirvāṇa, the eternity and qualities of the Buddha, and the presence of buddha-nature in all sentient beings. As one of the most celebrated and extensive Mahāyāna sūtras, it belongs to the sūtra division of the Kangyur.

The Noble Sūtra of the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. First Section.

Homage to all buddhas and bodhisattvas.

Thus did I hear. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling between two śāla trees on the bank of the river Hiraṇyavatī, at Kuśinagara, the city of the mighty, surrounded by a great Saṅgha of fully ordained monks numbering some eighty thousand, seated before him, all together.

At that time, the Blessed One was drawing near to passing beyond sorrow into nirvāṇa on the fifteenth day of the middle spring month. Through the blessing of the Blessed One, his great voice pervaded all things, reaching to the very summit of existence, and became known to all sentient beings in their own individual languages, speaking these words: "Today the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, who loves the multitude of beings with great tenderness, who has become the refuge and protector of all sentient beings, who regards all sentient beings with equal care as a mother lioness regards her cub, who has become the refuge, the ally, the support, and the shelter of sentient beings — today passes beyond sorrow into nirvāṇa. If there are among ordinary persons any who have doubts or uncertainties, let them ask now: this is the final moment for asking and inquiring. Let them ask and entreat." And this voice became known everywhere.

At that time, in the early morning hours, the Blessed One cast forth from his mouth rays of light of many colors — blue, yellow, red, white, and crystal-clear — illuminating this great three-thousandfold world-system and all the world-systems of the ten directions. All sentient beings of the six classes who abide in those realms, the moment they were touched by those rays, were purified of all blameworthy afflictions.

At that time, ordinary persons who saw and heard such a sign were stricken and tormented by a great grief, and all at once they beat their breasts and wept, crying out: "Alas! O you who have been like the most loving of parents! Oh no, oh no! Can it be that you are passing into nirvāṇa?" And striking their heads and chests with their palms, they beat their breasts in lamentation. Some trembled throughout their bodies, their hair standing on end, and wept with voices broken with sobbing.

At that time this great earth, and the mountains and the ocean, were all shaken and stirred in a tremendous upheaval.

Then those sentient beings, encouraging one another and seeking to dispel their grief, spoke thus: "Friends, do not sorrow! Let us go quickly to Kuśinagara, the city of the mighty, to where the Tathāgata is. Let us bow our heads to the feet of the Tathāgata and entreat him: may the Tathāgata not pass beyond sorrow, may he remain in the world for one full eon, or until one eon has nearly passed." So they spoke.

And some, grasping one another's hands, said: "The world is empty! Because the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, unwholesome actions have arisen in the world. Friends, the Tathāgata will surely pass beyond sorrow before long — let us go quickly." So they spoke.

Others said: "The world is empty! The world is empty! From this day forward we have no protector, no refuge — we have become destitute. Today we have been utterly separated from the unsurpassed Blessed One. Henceforth, to whom shall we address our doubts and uncertainties?" So they spoke.

At that time, a great number of senior monks, among them the venerable Mahākātyāyana, the venerable Bakula, and the venerable Ānanda and others —

touched by the light of the buddha, their entire bodies trembled and shook beyond all bearing, their minds became intoxicated, and they cried out in lamentation, overwhelmed by manifold sufferings of that kind.

At that time, there were also some eighty thousand fully ordained monks — all of them arhats: masters of their minds, who had accomplished what was to be done, who had thoroughly abandoned all afflictions, whose every faculty was completely tamed, who were mighty as great nāga kings, possessed of the wisdom of emptiness, who had at last attained their own highest good, surrounded by sandalwood groves as by sandalwood, surrounded by lions as by the lion-king — endowed with immeasurable virtues of that kind, and all of them true sons of the buddha. These monks too had been dwelling and had set out at the early morning hour just after the sun had risen. While using their tooth-cleansing sticks, they were touched by the light of the buddha and said to one another: "Friends, go quickly — rinse your mouth and wash your hands." The moment those words were spoken, the hairs of their bodies all stood on end, and the blood suffusing their bodies all the way to the skin became like flower petals; their eyes filled with tears and they experienced great suffering.

All of them — for the sake of benefit and happiness for all sentient beings, so as to practice yoga on the ultimate emptiness of the Great Vehicle, so as to teach what the Tathāgata had taught in his compassionate skillful means, so as never to interrupt the continuous teaching of Dharma in its manifold aspects, and so as to tame all sentient beings completely — went quickly to where the Blessed One was, and with the crowns of their heads bowed down at the feet of the buddha. They circumambulated him a hundredfold and then a thousandfold, joined their palms together, and stood to one side.

At that time there were also some sixty thousand fully ordained nuns — among them the daughter of Kuntala, the nun Śrībhadrā, the nun Priyadarśanā, the nun Sāgaramatī, and others — all of them arhats with defilements exhausted: masters of their minds, who had accomplished what was to be done, who had thoroughly abandoned all afflictions, whose faculties were completely tamed, whose dignity was supremely great like that of mighty nāgas, and who were possessed of the wisdom of emptiness. In the early morning hour, at the very first rising of the sun, the hairs of their bodies all bristled and stood on end, the blood suffusing their bodies all the way to the skin became like flower petals, their eyes filled completely with tears, and they experienced great suffering.

They too — for the sake of benefit and happiness for all sentient beings, so as to practice yoga on the ultimate emptiness of the Great Vehicle, so as to teach what the Tathāgata had taught in his compassionate skillful means, so as never to interrupt the continuous teaching of Dharma in its manifold aspects, and so as to tame all sentient beings completely — went quickly to where the Blessed One was, bowed the crowns of their heads at the feet of the buddha, circumambulated him a hundredfold and then a thousandfold, joined their palms together, and stood to one side.

Among those nuns there were some who were bodhisattvas — like nāgas among human beings, having thoroughly entered the ten grounds, abiding in imperturbability; and though they displayed the body of a woman for the sake of taming sentient beings, they were ever devoted to the four immeasurables, and through mastery of mind they were in truth nothing other than emanations of a buddha's body.

At that time there were also bodhisattvas and great beings (mahāsattvas) as numerous as the grains of sand in a single river Gaṅgā — who, like nāgas among human beings, had thoroughly entered the ten grounds and abided supremely in imperturbability, and who through skillful means displayed the body alone — among them the bodhisattva Sāgaraśrī and the bodhisattva Akṣayamati and others —

Led foremost by those bodhisattvas and great beings, all of them showed reverence toward the Great Vehicle, were firmly established in the Great Vehicle, were supremely skilled in the Great Vehicle, were supremely devoted to the Great Vehicle, and were supremely dedicated to guarding the Great Vehicle. They were in profound harmony with the minds of all beings in the world. They pledged themselves by solemn vow to liberate in the future those not yet liberated. Throughout the past, over the course of innumerable aeons, they had perfectly guarded their moral discipline, fully upheld right conduct, and liberated those not yet free. They sustained without interruption the lineage of the Three Jewels, and in times to come they would turn the wheel of Dharma. Adorned with great adornments, they were endowed with such boundless qualities as these, and they looked upon every sentient being with the same feeling as one would have toward an only child.

These bodhisattvas too, in the early morning, the moment the sun had just risen, were touched by the light of the buddha, and the hairs of their bodies all stood on end. Their bodies, suffused throughout with flushing blood, became like flesh upon a lotus flower, and their eyes filled completely with tears, so that they experienced a welling of deep emotion.

And they, for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, and in order to accomplish the practice of yoga upon the ultimate emptiness of the Great Vehicle, and in order to demonstrate the teaching that the Tathāgata had spoken with skillful intent, and in order to expound the Dharma continuously in its many and various aspects, and in order to fully tame all sentient beings — for all these reasons, they swiftly went and came to the place where the Blessed One was. They bowed their heads to the feet of the buddha in homage, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, then with palms pressed together, together with their retinues, respectfully took their places to one side.

At that time there were also laymen (upāsakas) who kept the five precepts in their fullness, as numerous as the grains of sand in two rivers Gaṅgā, led foremost by the layman King Radiance of Unsullied Renown and the layman Excellent Qualities and others. All of them were supremely devoted to the antidotal teachings, and the antidotal teachings upon which they so ardently reflected were these: suffering and happiness; permanence and impermanence; purity and impurity; self and no-self; the definite and the indefinite; taking refuge and not taking refuge; sentient being and non-sentient being; the lasting and the non-lasting; bliss and the absence of bliss; the conditioned and the unconditioned; annihilation and the absence of annihilation; the transcendence of sorrow and the non-transcendence of sorrow; the superior and the non-superior — and so forth. Such were precisely the antidotal teachings upon which they were supremely devoted to reflection.

Furthermore, all of them were devoted to hearing the unsurpassed Great Vehicle, were able to teach others precisely as they themselves had heard, perfectly guarded their moral discipline, were devoted to the Great Vehicle like someone tormented by thirst, were themselves utterly satisfied yet also satisfied others who were tormented by thirst, entered deeply into unsurpassed wisdom, were devoted to the Great Vehicle, were supremely dedicated to protecting the Great Vehicle, were in profound harmony with the minds of all worldly beings, rescued those not yet rescued, liberated those not yet liberated, sustained without interruption the lineage of the Three Jewels, would in the future turn the wheel of Dharma extensively, were adorned with great adornments, were devoted to the taste of the profoundly deep mind, were perfectly pure in moral discipline — all of them endowed with such qualities as these. They had aroused in their minds the thought of great compassion toward all sentient beings and looked upon them without distinction, just as one would an only child.

At the early morning hour, just as the sun rose, its rays touched them and they entered into the Tathāgata's presence for the purpose of making offerings. Each one of them, from their own quarters, had arranged many hundreds of fragrant wooden thrones — namely, thrones of sandalwood, of aloe wood, of red sandalwood, of fragrant divine wood, and so forth. Those woods were beautiful with fine carvings and adorned with the seven precious substances; they shone and gleamed with intense brilliance, like an artist spreading pigments of many colors, and through the blessing of the buddhas they were endowed with the colors blue, yellow, red, and white — such that the sight of them would bring sheer joy to multitudes of beings. And upon those many kinds of fragrant wood thrones, yet further adornments were applied: various kinds of perfume pouches, saffron, aloe wood, costus, and the like were lavishly rubbed on, and the thrones were scattered and adorned with flowers of many kinds — blue lotuses, white water lilies, red lotuses, and white lotuses, and so forth. Furthermore, draped over those thrones were banners of five colors, exceedingly soft and beautiful, spread out in the manner of divine garments of kauśeya silk or fine linen.

Those fragrant wooden thrones were mounted on chariots of precious gems, and from those gem-encrusted chariots there issued lights of many colors — blue, yellow, red, and white. The yokes, axle-beams, and other fittings of the chariots were adorned with the seven precious substances, and each chariot was drawn by four horses. Those horses were swift as the wind. Arrayed before each chariot were some fifty victory banners of the seven precious substances, covered overhead with a net of gold. Spread above each of those precious gem chariots were some fifty precious gem parasols. Each chariot was also hung with garlands of flowers — blue lotuses, white water lilies, red lotuses, and white lotuses — their petals made of gold and their stamens fashioned from vajra crystal. Within those golden flowers, dark bees hovered and played.

Furthermore, from those flowers there issued sounds exceedingly lovely and melodious, as well as sounds that were other than that — the sounds of impermanence, of suffering, of emptiness, and of no-self. And beyond those, there sounded the proclamation of the prior practices of bodhisattvas, and the sounds of various kinds of music were heard — songs, dance, flutes, nine-stringed lutes, cymbals, bells, and drums. Beyond those musical sounds there also arose a voice calling out: "Ki hud! Ki hud! The worlds are emptied!"

Before each chariot there stood an attendant holding a small throne fashioned from the four precious gems, and upon those small thrones were heaped flowers of many kinds — blue lotuses, white water lilies, red lotuses, white lotuses, saffron, ointments, incense, and other excellent and supremely fine offerings, all arranged in place. The offerings of various foods that the lay practitioners had set out for the buddhas and the Saṅgha were all prepared by burning sandalwood and fragrant aloe wood and stirring those foods with water endowed with the eight qualities. Those foods were endowed with the six tastes — cold, sour, sweet, hot, salty-pungent, and astringent.

Furthermore, those foods possessed three qualities: they were soft and tender, clean and pure, and prepared in accordance with the Dharma. Having arranged such various and manifold offerings as these, the lay practitioners came to the foot of the śāla tree, the place where the Great One would pass beyond.

Moreover, the ground had been spread over with golden sand, and upon it were laid divine garments of kācalinda cloth, and silks and fine fabrics were strewn across it, extending in all directions for a full twelve leagues around. Thrones of lion-seat fashioned from the seven precious gems were arranged for the Buddha and the Saṅgha to rest upon, and the height of those thrones was equal to that of Mount Meru. Above those thrones precious canopies were raised, and from them many kinds of garlands were hung. Upon the śāla trees themselves banners and pennants of many kinds were hung, and parasols were spread, and the branches of those trees were anointed with scented oil perfumed with various kinds of incense. And the spaces between the trees were filled to overflowing with flowers of many kinds.

Each of those lay practitioners resolved within their minds: "If ordinary beings are hungry, we shall give them food. If they are thirsty, we shall give them drink. If they wish for garments, garments. If they wish for medicine, medicine." Thus they gave to all ordinary beings whatever was wished for, and that giving was free from the minds of attachment, aversion, delusion, and agitation. Nor did they act out of any thought for worldly wealth and enjoyment; it was solely for the sake of unsurpassed, perfectly pure awakening.

Those lay practitioners, resting steadfastly in unsurpassed awakening, then reflected within their minds: "The Tathāgata will accept these our offerings and then pass beyond nirvāṇa." At that thought, the hairs on all their bodies stood on end, and their bodies, suffused with blood, became like a piece of flesh laid bare of skin. Their eyes filled with tears. Their minds were tormented by great suffering. Each and every one of them packed up the offerings they had individually arranged — the fragrant wood, the victory banners, the pennants, the parasols, and the foods — loaded them onto jeweled carriages, went to where the Buddha was, and arrived before him. They prostrated at the feet of the Buddha with their crowns touching the ground, and with the offerings they had arranged they made offerings to the Tathāgata. They circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and then cried out with their voices and wept. The sound of their weeping shook heaven and earth. They beat their breasts and wailed, tears streaming down like rain, and said to one another, sobbing: "Oh! Oh! Friends, the world is empty! The world is empty!" Having said these words, they prostrated their bodies before the Tathāgata and addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Out of loving kindness for us, may the Tathāgata accept this last inner offering that we have arranged. Please accept it." The Blessed One, knowing the time, said nothing and did not accept it. And so even though they beseeched him in this same way three times, he did not grant acceptance.

Those lay practitioners, finding that things had not turned out as they had hoped, were tormented by grief and stood there in silence. Their condition was like that of parents deeply devoted to their only child, when that child is suddenly struck by illness and dies and is carried away to the charnel ground, and they are tormented by the most intense grief. Just so were those lay practitioners tormented by grief. They set down all the offering articles in one place and stood to one side in silence.

At that time, there were also laywomen as numerous as the grains of sand of three Ganges rivers, perfectly guarding the five precepts, endowed with proper conduct, such as the laywoman Jīvanaśrī and the laywoman Śrīmālā.

Led foremost by the laywoman Viśākā, all eighty-four thousand laywomen perfectly upheld the sacred Dharma. In order to tame countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, they appeared in female form while thoroughly condemning the ways of household life. They had come to regard their own bodies as being like a venomous serpent. They understood the body to be perpetually devoured by countless worms, utterly foul, and bound fast by desire. They saw this body as dreadful as a corpse, as impure, understanding that it ceaselessly leaks from its nine openings. They understood this body to be like a fortress, wrapped round with flesh, skin, sinew, and blood vessels, with the hands and feet as its watchtowers, the eyes as its arrow-slits, the head as its central hall, and the mind, like a king, dwelling within. They understood that this body, resembling a fortress, is utterly abandoned by the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while ordinary deluded beings remain attached to it. They understood that the demons of attachment, aversion, and delusion dwell within it. They understood this body to be without essence, like a plantain shoot, or an eraṇḍa plant, or a water bubble, or a water-reed. They understood this body to be impermanent, shifting moment by moment, like a flash of lightning, or a swift-flowing current, or a magical illusion, or a mirage, or a line drawn on water. They understood this body to be changeable and transient, like a tree standing on a crumbling riverbank. They understood this body to endure not for long, becoming food for jackals, foxes, flesh-eating birds, owls, vultures, crows, hyenas, and hungry dogs; and they had come to understand that no wise and discerning person would hold affection and attachment for it. They understood that even if one were to pour the waters of a great ocean into the hollow of a hoof-print, it might fit, yet the impermanence, impurity, and foulness of this body are not easy to fully express. To roll up this great earth into a mustard-seed or reduce it to fine dust is easier, they knew, than fully describing the faults and flaws of this body. Therefore, having abandoned it entirely, as one spits out saliva, and by means of that very cause and that very condition, these laywomen applied themselves constantly to the practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. They were devoted to hearing and upholding the sūtras of the Great Vehicle, and having heard them, they were able to expound them extensively to others. They upheld their former aspirational prayers. They utterly condemned the female body, knowing it to be profoundly defective and realizing it to be without essence. Their minds were perpetually engaged in yogic practice. Likewise, through correct contemplation, they fully severed the stream of endless cyclic existence. Their devotion to the Great Vehicle was like that of one tormented by thirst. Having themselves been thoroughly satisfied, they brought deep satisfaction to others as well. They were full of enthusiasm for the Great Vehicle, guarding it with utmost care. Though appearing in female form, they were bodhisattvas through and through. They were all deeply aligned with the wishes of the world, liberating the unrescued, freeing the unfree, and sustaining without interruption the lineage of the Three Jewels. In the future they would turn the wheel of Dharma. They were adorned with great ornaments, perfectly guarding their ethical conduct, and endowed with immeasurable qualities such as these. They aroused the mind of compassion toward all sentient beings, regarding them without duality, as equal and utterly non-different from an only child. These laywomen too, in the early morning when the first rays of the sun appeared and the light touched them, said one to another: "Today we shall set out for the place of the twin śāla trees."

The laywomen arranged their offerings with preparations twice as fine as those made before, and came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, touching their heads to the ground, and circumambulated him a hundred thousand times. Then they addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, out of love for us, may the Tathāgata accept these offerings we have prepared for the Buddha and for the Saṅgha together with the monks." But the Blessed One said nothing, and he did not consent to receive them. The laywomen, finding that things had not gone as they had hoped, were stricken with sorrow and withdrew to one side.

Now at that time there were also others — Licchavi men, women, boys, girls, wives, and retinues, in numbers as countless as the grains of sand in four great Ganges rivers, who dwelt in the city of Vaiśālī; and likewise members of the royal lineage of Jambudvīpa together with their royal entourages. All of them, for the sake of the Dharma they desired, guarded their moral discipline completely, possessed of proper conduct, and devoted themselves to study under others. Those who were absolutely resolute in cutting off and thoroughly rebuking whoever denigrated the sacred Dharma, these very ones pledged to one another, saying: "Let the true Dharma — profound beyond measure, like a treasury of gold, silver, and precious jewels, like nectar inexhaustible — remain long in the world, and may we ourselves always apply ourselves to it diligently. If there is anyone who abuses authority over the Dharma as spoken from that very mouth, or who defames it, we shall cut out that person's tongue. Furthermore, if any who have gone forth from home into homelessness should fall away from their moral discipline, we shall reduce them to the status of householders and put them to work. And if there is one who applies himself diligently to the sacred Dharma, we shall serve and honor him as we would our own parents. And if there is one within the Saṅgha who is diligent in the practice of the sacred Dharma, we shall rejoice with him and also lend him our support." So they pledged. They were forever eager to hear the sūtras of the Great Vehicle, and upon hearing them they would teach them extensively to others. Such were the qualities with which they were endowed. Among these were the Licchavi youth Pure Stainless Essence, the Licchavi youth Mindfully Purified, the Licchavi youth Ever Stainless Pure Virtue, and others of their kind. These said one to another: "Friends, let us quickly go to where the Tathāgata is, and set out to make offerings of every kind in full and magnificent array."

Then each of those Licchavīs arranged eighty-four thousand woolen oxen, eighty-four thousand jeweled chariots drawn by four horses, eighty-four thousand wish-fulfilling precious jewels, and also eighty-four thousand measures of sandalwood and aloe-wood compacted together. Before each of those woolen oxen they also arranged victory banners, pennants, and canopies of precious jewels. Even the smallest of the canopies covered a full league in all directions around. Even the shortest of the pennants trailed a length of thirty-two leagues. Even the lowest of the jeweled victory banners stood a hundred leagues in height. Having arranged such offerings, they came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the feet of the Buddha and circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and then addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, we offer these offerings to the Buddha and to the Saṅgha of monks; may the Tathāgata, out of compassion for us, accept these offerings." But the Tathāgata said nothing, and did not consent to receive them.

The sons of the Licchavīs found that things had not gone as they had wished, and they were overwhelmed with grief. By the blessing of the Blessed One, they rose up from the ground to the height of seven palm trees and remained in the sky above, silent and still.

At that same time, there were also great ministers, householders, and merchants as numerous as the grains of sand in five Ganges rivers, all deeply devoted to the Great Vehicle and following a different teacher, and there was among them one who had disparaged the true Dharma. Their coming was subdued entirely, as hail falls upon grass and trees — precisely thus. Led first by the merchant Sunlight, the merchant Protector of the World, the merchant Protector of the Dharma, and others, they each separately arranged offerings that were fully five times greater than those arranged before. They came to the place between the two sāla trees where the Tathāgata lay, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, we offer these offerings to the Buddha and to the Saṅgha of monks; may the Tathāgata accept them." But the Tathāgata said nothing, and did not consent to receive them. Those merchants, finding that things had not gone as they had wished, became tormented with great grief, and by the blessing of the Blessed One they rose from the ground to the height of seven palm trees and remained in the sky above, silent and still.

At that time there also arrived the king of Vaiśālī together with his queens, and furthermore all the petty kings of Jambudvīpa apart from King Ajātaśatru, along with all the inhabitants of every city, every region, and every village — led first by King Candraprabha Vimala and the other kings, each accompanied by his own fourfold army. Each of those kings came with a retinue of eight hundred thousand. The army consisted of elephants and cavalry: the elephants had six tusks, and the horses were fleet as the wind. The offerings they had arranged surpassed the previous ones by more than sixfold. Even the smallest of the jeweled canopies covered an area eight leagues across in all directions. Even the shortest of the pennants trailed a length of sixteen leagues. Even the smallest of the jeweled victory banners stood thirty-six leagues in height.

All those kings abided in the true Dharma and utterly condemned every false teaching; they honored the Great Vehicle, they were deeply devoted to the Great Vehicle, they loved all sentient beings as one loves an only child, and the fragrance of the food they had set out wafted to a distance of four leagues. In the early morning hour, bearing all manner of offerings, they went to where the Tathāgata lay between the two sāla trees, and then addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, we offer these offerings to the Buddha and to the Saṅgha of monks; may the Tathāgata, out of compassion, accept this final offering of ours." But the Tathāgata, knowing the right time, did not consent to receive them. Those kings too, finding that things had not gone as they had wished, became tormented with great grief, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, there gathered also a number of royal consorts as numerous as the grains of sand in seven Ganges rivers — all of them except one, who was solely a consort of Ajātaśatru. Appearing in female form in order to tame sentient beings,

they constantly applied themselves with body and engaged in practice, familiarizing and habituating the mind with the teachings on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and so forth. They were first led on by the royal consort Lovely in the Three Realms, and by the royal consort Qualities of Desire, and the rest. All of them abided in the holy Dharma, completely guarding their moral discipline, endowed with proper conduct, and loving each and every sentient being exactly as though each were their only child. They said to one another: "Let us too swiftly go to where the Buddha dwells."

The offerings arrayed by the royal consorts exceeded those of the preceding group sevenfold and more: flowers, incense, jeweled victory banners, silk pennants, parasols, and the finest foods. Even the smallest of the jeweled parasols was wide enough to cover a circumference of sixteen leagues in all directions. The shortest of the pennants measured some thirty-six leagues in height. The lowest of the jeweled victory banners stood some sixty-eight leagues tall. The fragrance of the food offerings spread and wafted for a distance of eight leagues. Having arranged such offerings as these, they proceeded to where the Tathāgata was. They bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him many hundreds and thousands of times, and then addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Blessed One, we have arranged these offerings and present them to the Buddha and to the Saṅgha of monks. Out of compassion for us, may the Tathāgata accept this last of our offerings."

But the Tathāgata, knowing the right time, said nothing and did not consent to receive them. The royal consorts, finding that things had not gone as they had wished, became tormented with overwhelming grief. Tearing their hair, beating their chests, and wailing, they became as those who have lost a dearly beloved child, and withdrew to one side without uttering a word.

At that time, among the goddesses (suras) as numerous as the grains of sand in eight Ganges rivers, the one called Wide-Eyed Goddess spoke first and said: "Friends, do you see? Look! Do you see how the great assembly has laid out all manner of diverse offerings and is presenting them to the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha of monks? Let us too arrange offerings and, having made offering to the Tathāgata, beseech the Tathāgata — after he has received them — to remain and not pass into nirvāṇa. Friends, it is exceedingly rare for a buddha, the Blessed One, to appear in the world, and it is exceedingly rare to be able to arrange and present a last offering. If the Blessed One passes into nirvāṇa, the world will be left empty."

Now those goddesses desired the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), were devoted to hearing the Great Vehicle, and having heard it were capable of teaching it extensively to others. They were as though parched with thirst for the Great Vehicle, and just as one who is deeply satisfied can still satisfy others who are parched, so too did they satisfy others. They protected the Great Vehicle. When there were those who had entered another path and who disparaged the Great Vehicle out of jealousy, these goddesses crushed them utterly, as hailstones crush grass. They completely guarded their moral discipline and were endowed with proper conduct. They were supremely skilled in winning the minds of all the world. They tamed those who were untamed and liberated those who were unliberated. In times yet to come, they would turn the wheel of Dharma and sustain the unbroken lineage of the Three Jewels. They applied themselves with diligence to the Great Vehicle, and

adorned with great ornaments, endowed with immeasurable qualities of that kind, and loving toward all sentient beings exactly as one loves an only child — these divine daughters, too, in the early morning when the sun first rose, each set out various divine fragrant trees, which surpassed the fragrant trees of humans, and whose fragrance, pervading the human world, dispelled every disagreeable smell. They mounted white palanquins draped with white parasols and drawn by four white horses. Over each palanquin they raised a white canopy, and around the edges of each canopy golden bells were hung. They arranged all manner of incense, flowers, jeweled victory banners, pennants, parasols, excellent and exquisite food and drink, and various kinds of music. They set down lion thrones whose four legs were fashioned from deep-blue lapis lazuli, whose backs were fitted with cushions of seven kinds of precious stone, and before each of which stood a golden footstool. On lamp-pillars made of seven kinds of precious stone, lamps blazed with all manner of precious jewels. The entire ground was strewn with divine flowers in this fashion. Having arranged all of this, these divine daughters arrived with aching hearts, tears streaming down their faces. Yet even in their great suffering, for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings — so that the Great Vehicle, the ultimate truth endowed with emptiness, might be made manifest, so that what the Tathāgata intended and taught might be openly demonstrated, and so that the unbroken stream of teaching the various Dharmas might not be cut off — they came before the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, out of your compassion for us, please accept this last of the offerings we have arranged." The Blessed One, knowing the right time, said nothing and did not accept. The divine daughters, their hope unfulfilled, were grieved at heart and, without a word, withdrew to one side.

Then, at that time, as many yakṣa kings (yakṣas) as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges rivers arrived from the four directions — led first by the yakṣa king Ngalsopos and others — and said to one another, "Come, friends, let us go quickly to where the Buddha is!" Having arranged offerings surpassing even those of the nāgas, they came before the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, out of your compassion for us, please accept this last of the offerings we have arranged." To this the Blessed One said nothing and did not accept.

At that time, as many nāga kings (nāgas) as there are grains of sand in nine Ganges rivers arrived from the four directions — led first by the nāga king Jokpo, the nāga king Gawos, and the nāga king Nyegawos and others. These nāga kings too, in the early morning when the sun first rose, arranged offerings of worship surpassing those of gods and humans, came before the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, out of your compassion for us, please accept this last of the offerings we have arranged." The Tathāgata, knowing the right time, said nothing and did not accept. The nāga kings too, their hope unfulfilled, were grieved at heart and withdrew to one side.

The yakṣa kings, their hope likewise unfulfilled, were grieved at heart and withdrew to one side.

Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in twenty Ganges rivers, garuḍa kings led by one named Conqueror of Opponents came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in thirty Ganges rivers, gandharva kings led by the greatly powerful one came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in forty Ganges rivers, kinnara kings led by one named the Greatly Seeing came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in fifty Ganges rivers, great serpent kings led by one named the Very Greatly Seeing came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in sixty Ganges rivers, asura kings led by Khābibili came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in seventy Ganges rivers, tānapā kings led by Stainless Flowing Water, Vātidatā, and others came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in eighty Ganges rivers, rākṣasa kings led by one named the Terrifying came forward first. All of these had completely abandoned wicked and non-virtuous minds; they refrained from eating human flesh; toward those who were their enemies and adversaries they gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion; and even their unpleasant forms all became beautiful and fair through the blessing of the Buddha. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in ninety Ganges rivers, gods of the forest groves led by one named Delighting in Fragrant Incense came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in a thousand Ganges rivers, vidyādhara kings led by one named the Great Miraculous Power came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in one hundred thousand Ganges rivers, prabhāsana kings led by one named the Greatly Seeing came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in ten million Ganges rivers, the goddesses of desire — Lampā, Urvaśī, Tilottamā, Miśrakeśī, and others — came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in a hundred million Ganges rivers, earth-dwelling hungry ghost kings led by one named White Wing came forward first. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in one billion Ganges rivers, the sons of the gods and the god-kings were led forward first by the protectors of the four directions. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in one billion Ganges rivers, the river gods filled the area around the śāla trees to overflowing with flowers — both those in season and those out of season — gathered from the four directions. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in one billion Ganges rivers, the gods presiding over wind and rain thought to themselves: when the Tathāgata has entered into nirvāṇa and lies at rest, we shall send down great rain, so that any fires lit in due time may be extinguished, and those among the assembled retinue who are afflicted by heat may be thoroughly cooled. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in twenty Ganges rivers, great fragrant bulls — the bull king Lāhu, the bull king the Golden One, the bull king Sweet Flavor, the bull king Indigo Eye, the bull king the Fragrant One, and others — came forward first. All of these revered the Great Vehicle and were devoted to the Great Vehicle alone. Knowing that the Buddha, the Blessed One, would pass into nirvāṇa before long, each of them brought forth immeasurable and incalculable fine lotuses, came before the Buddha, the Blessed One, bowed their heads in homage, and stood to one side. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in twenty Ganges rivers, lion kings among wild animals led by one named Lion's Roar came forward first; having bestowed fearlessness upon all sentient beings, each of them took flowers and fruits, came before the Buddha, bowed at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in twenty Ganges rivers, bird kings — geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, kalandakas, and

guyas, jīvaṃjakas, and kalandakas — each of them took flowers and fruits, came before the Buddha, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, and stood to one side. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in twenty Ganges rivers, water buffalo, cattle, sheep, and similar animals came before the Buddha; and all the ponds of finest grass in the city of Kuśinagara, together with every manger and trough, became spontaneously filled with fragrant milk rich in colour and taste, and they stood to one side. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in twenty Ganges rivers, sages dwelling on the four continents, led first by one named Patient Sage, each of them took flowers, incense, sweet fruits, and the like, came before the Buddha, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated three times, and then addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, out of compassion for us, please accept this, our last inner offering." But the Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, said nothing and did not consent to accept it. The sages, finding things not as they had wished, were pierced with grief and sorrow of heart, and stood to one side. The bee king of Jambudvīpa, named Melodious Sound, came forward first, and all the bees, taking flowers of many varieties, came before the Buddha, bowed at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated once, and stood to one side. At that time, all the monks and nuns dwelling in Jambudvīpa assembled there — all save two alone: Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda. Furthermore, immeasurable and incountable world-realms — as many as grains of sand in the Ganges — led by Mount Meru, king of mountains, together with all the mountains of Jambudvīpa and the other mountains: each of those mountains was richly adorned with dense forests, with trees whose foliage and branches hung so thickly that they screened out the light of the sun, with blossoms of many varieties in full bloom, and on every side with streams and springs utterly pure and fragrant. They were filled throughout with gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, great serpents, vidyādharas, sages, and the like, all making music of many kinds. Those gods and sages came before the Blessed One, bowed their heads at the feet of the Buddha, and stood to one side. Furthermore, as many as grains of sand in incalculable Ganges rivers, the gods of the four great oceans, and the gods of all the rivers, possessed of great majesty and supernatural power, laid out offerings surpassing all that had come before, and by the radiance of the gods' bodies, the splendour of their music, and the light of their lamps, they caused even the light of the sun and moon to be invisible. They scattered campaka flowers on the bank of the river Hiraṇyavatī, came before the Buddha, bowed at the feet of the Buddha, and stood to one side. At that time, all the śāla-tree groves of the city of Kuśinagara turned white, and in the sky above there arose of themselves magnificent palaces of seven precious jewels, with turrets and painted designs, adorned with beauty, adorned all around with jewels of many kinds, and before those palaces there spontaneously appeared from springs, ponds, and pools lotus flowers blooming — just like the renowned grove called Most Delightful in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three gods in the north, called Uttarakuru. At that time, all the śāla-tree groves were adorned in manifold ways and became exceedingly beautiful.

At that time, all the gods, humans, asuras, and all other beings understood that this was a sign of the Tathāgata's passing into nirvāṇa, and every one of them became tormented with grief and fell into sorrow.

At that time, the kings of the Four Great Kings and Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, said to one another: "Friends, behold how the gods, humans, asuras, and all beings of the world are preparing offerings and making offerings to the Tathāgata. Let us likewise make offerings. If we make offerings at the very last moment, we shall certainly perfect the perfection of generosity (pāramitā)." And so it was spoken.

Then the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings prepared offerings far exceeding those made before, which were as follows: the flowers māndārava and great māndārava, the flowers kacilika and great kacilika, the flowers mañjūṣaka and great mañjūṣaka, the flowers santānika and great santānika, the flowers "pleasing" and great "pleasing," the flowers "all-good" and great "all-good," the flowers "timely" and great "timely," the flowers "fragrant city" and great "fragrant city," the flowers "supremely joyful" and great "supremely joyful," the flowers "wish-fulfilling" and great "wish-fulfilling," the flowers "fragrant intoxication" and great "fragrant intoxication," the flowers "all-fragrant" and great "all-fragrant," the flower known as "divine golden petals," the flower known as "nāga," the flowers of the pāricitra tree, the flowers of the kovidāra tree, and also various kinds of delicious food of many flavors. Carrying these, they came to where the Buddha was, and bowed their heads in prostration at the feet of the Blessed One. The light of the gods outshone even the light of the sun and moon. Having laid out these articles of offering so as to make offering to the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata, knowing the time, said nothing and did not accept.

At that time the gods, seeing that things had not gone as they had hoped, were tormented with grief and withdrew to one side.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, and the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three prepared offerings far surpassing those made before, with the same flowers as before, but now most excellently fragrant with sweet perfume. They also prepared the great palace called "Victor of Immeasurable Mansions" and the smaller immeasurable mansions, and came to where the Buddha was, and bowed their heads in prostration at the feet of the Blessed One. They addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, we have the deepest faith and devotion in the Great Vehicle. Out of compassion for us, may the Tathāgata please accept these offerings." The Blessed One, knowing the time, said nothing and did not accept.

The Noble Sūtra of the Great Passing into Nirvāṇa. Second Fascicle.

Then Śakra and his retinue of gods, seeing that things had not gone as they had hoped, were tormented with grief and withdrew to one side.

Through all six levels of the heavens of the desire realm, the articles of offering that had been arranged included victory banners of precious jewels, pennants, and canopies, each one more magnificent than the last. Even the smallest of the jeweled canopies covered all four continents. Even the shortest of the pennants encircled all four oceans. Even the lowest of the victory banners reached up to touch the Heaven of Wielding Others' Emanations (Paranirmitavaśavartin), and when moved by the wind they gave forth sweet and melodious sounds.

They arranged food and drink of the most excellent and varied kinds, then came to where the Blessed One was. They prostrated with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed him thus: "Blessed One, out of compassion for us, please accept this, the last of our offerings." But the Tathāgata, who knows the right time, said nothing and did not accept it.

Then the gods too, their hopes unfulfilled, were tormented with grief and withdrew to one side.

Beyond all of these — at the very summit of existence — the gods of the Brahmā realms (Brahmaloka) had also assembled. At that moment, Brahmā, King of the gods, and the gods of the Brahmā realms illuminated all four continents with their light, causing even the light of the sun and moon in the desire realm to disappear. They too, each carrying jeweled victory banners, pennants, and canopies — even the shortest of the pennants stretching from the Brahmā realm all the way down to touch the śāla grove — came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed him thus: "Blessed One, out of compassion for us, please accept this, the last of our offerings." But the Tathāgata, who knows the right time, said nothing and did not accept it. The gods of the Brahmā realms, their hopes unfulfilled, were tormented with grief and withdrew to one side.

Then Vemacitrin, king of the asuras (demigods), arrived together with a retinue of countless asuras. The radiance of their bodies surpassed even that of the Brahmā gods. Carrying jeweled victory banners, pennants, and canopies — even the smallest of the canopies covering a thousandfold minor world system — and bearing the most exquisite and excellent foods, they came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed him thus: "Blessed One, out of compassion for us, please accept this, the last of our offerings." But the Tathāgata, who knows the right time, said nothing and did not accept it. The asuras, their hopes unfulfilled, were tormented with grief and withdrew to one side.

Then Māra the Evil One (Skt. Māra pāpīyas), king of māras in the desire realm, arrived together with a retinue of innumerable divine daughters. He opened the gates of the hells, rained down cooling and purifying water upon them, and commanded those within, saying: "You and all the others can do nothing else — so with one-pointed mind, recollect the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, and rejoice in the offerings being made to him. You will thereby attain lasting and perfect happiness."

Then Māra the Evil One, with a cooling rain, extinguished the weapons of the hell beings and the raging fires that cause suffering there. Through the blessing of the Buddha, the host of Māra's retinue also gave rise to this thought in their minds. All of them laid aside their swords, bows and arrows, armor, spears, iron hooks, iron mallets, battle-axes, wheels, lassos, and every other weapon, and arranged offerings surpassing those of gods and humans. Carrying canopies — even the smallest of which covered a middling thousandfold world system — they came to where the Buddha was.

They prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, touching their crowns to the ground, and then addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, we too have profound faith and devotion toward the Great Vehicle, and we wish to protect the Great Vehicle. Blessed One, if a son or daughter of good family should uphold this Great Vehicle for the sake of gain and fame, or to instill fear in others, or to deceive others, or for wealth and material goods, or merely to win the affection of others — whether truthfully or untruthfully — at that time, in order to dispel that person's fears, we offer this secret mantra:

Cyog kye, ta ta la cyog kye, lo ha le, ma hā lo ha le, ala cala tala svāhā.

We offer this secret mantra for those who have lost their minds, for those who are frightened and fearful, for those who teach the Dharma, for those who do not obstruct the authentic Dharma, for taming non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), for protecting our own bodies, for protecting the authentic Dharma, and for protecting the Great Vehicle. Whoever holds this mantra in mind will be freed from the fear of being trampled by a wild ox. Even if one is in a wilderness or forest, or in a deserted and dangerous place, one will have no fear. One will be liberated from the fears of water, fire, lions, tigers, wolves, enemies, and royal punishment. Blessed One, whoever holds this mantra in mind will be freed from all those fears and more. Blessed One, we will protect and shelter whoever holds this mantra just as a turtle conceals its six limbs within its shell. Blessed One, we do not speak these words out of deception or guile — we genuinely bestow our power and might upon whoever holds this dhāraṇī mantra. Blessed One, out of love for us, please accept this, the last of our inner offerings."

Then the Blessed One spoke to Māra the Evil One: "The food offerings you have presented I do not accept. I accept this mantra for the benefit and happiness of all beings and the four assemblies." Having said this, the Blessed One spoke no further and did not grant acceptance of anything else. When this same request had been made three times and still not accepted, Māra the Evil One, finding that things had not gone as he had hoped, was tormented in his mind with grief and withdrew to one side.

At that moment the great lord who governs gods, Śakra (Indra), also arrived together with a retinue of innumerable, immeasurable gods, bearing offerings. The offerings he brought surpassed those of Brahmā, of Śakra himself, of the four protectors of the world, of gods, humans, asuras, the eight classes of non-humans, and all other beings — just as a piece of crystal placed next to charcoal makes everything else invisible by its brilliance, so that all were unseen. Carrying canopies of precious jewels — the smallest of which covered an entire great trichiliocosm along with its offerings and more — they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One with their crowns touching the ground, circumambulated him countless times, and then addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, when we present this, the last of our inner offerings, it is as though a bee were offering a gift, or as though a single handful of water were poured into the great ocean, or as though the light of a single small lamp were held up against a thousand suns, or as though a single flower were picked up in the season when summer blossoms are at their fullest and placed amid a multitude of flowers, or as though a single mustard seed were presented to Mount Meru, the king of mountains — like the ocean, and the sun, and

the multitude of flowers, and Mount Meru — just as a mustard seed is of no benefit to Mount Meru, so too, Blessed One, are these offerings of ours. Even if this entire great trichiliocosm were filled with incense, flowers, music, banners, parasols, and victory standards and presented as an offering, it would not be worth speaking of as adequate recompense. And why is that? Because the Tathāgata, for the sake of the many beings, took on vast suffering in the births of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals. Therefore, Blessed One, please accept these offerings out of your compassionate love for us." Thus they supplicated him.

At that time, in the east, beyond world-realms as innumerable and immeasurable as the grains of sand in countless Ganges rivers, in a buddha-field called Melodious Sound of Pleasing Fragrance, there dwelt the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha named Equal to Space — one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, a tamer and guide of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, a blessed buddha. At that moment that buddha spoke these words to his great personal attendant: "Noble son, go now from here to the western world-realm called Endurance, where the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha named Śākyamuni — one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, a tamer and guide of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, a blessed buddha — will not long from now pass into complete nirvāṇa. Noble son, take this food from this world-realm, this fragrant food of supremely sweet scent that is pleasing and a source of happiness, and offer it to that Blessed One. Having been fed that offering, that Blessed One will pass into complete nirvāṇa. Noble son, go, prostrate to him, and the time has also come to ask whatever questions still give you doubt."

Then the great bodhisattva named Immeasurable Body rose from his seat, bowed his head to the feet of the buddha, circumambulated him three times, and together with innumerable and immeasurable bodhisattvas, set out from that buddha-field and arrived in the world-realm of Endurance. At that moment, the great trichiliocosm trembled in six ways. Within the assembly, Brahmā, Śakra (Indra), the protectors of the four directions, the māra of evil deeds, the great lords of power, and others, upon seeing the earth tremble, were struck with such terror that their skin stood on end and their tongues nearly dried up in fright. They scattered in all directions, and even the radiance and splendor of their bodies became invisible.

Then Mañjuśrī, appearing as a youth, rose from his seat and said these words to those gathered in the assembly: "Noble sons, do not be afraid. Have no fear. And why is that? To the east, beyond world-realms as innumerable and immeasurable as the grains of sand in countless Ganges rivers, in a world-realm called Melodious Sound of Pleasing Fragrance, there dwells the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha named Equal to Space, one endowed with the thirty-two major marks. There, the bodhisattva named Immeasurable Body, together with a retinue of innumerable bodhisattvas, is coming to this world-realm to make offerings to the Tathāgata. It is the splendor and blessing of that bodhisattva that has caused even the radiance of your own bodies to become invisible. Therefore, have no fear — give rise to great joy!"

At that moment, all the assembled retinues, from a great distance, beheld that buddha together with his vast entourage — and the seeing was just as one sees one's own reflection in a clear, bright mirror. Then Mañjuśrī again spoke these words to the many assembled retinues: "Just as you behold this buddha, so too, through the blessing of the Tathāgata, you may likewise behold immeasurable buddhas, as numerous as could be counted, dwelling in the ten directions."

At that moment, the many assembled retinues said to one another in alarm: "Gone! Gone! The world is empty! The world is empty! The Tathāgata will before long pass completely into nirvāṇa!"

At that moment, all the many assembled retinues beheld the bodhisattva Immeasurable Body together with his retinue, and the sight was this: from each and every pore of that bodhisattva's body there issued forth a great lotus flower, and upon each of those lotuses there were as many as seventy-eight thousand cities. Each of those cities was equal in breadth and extent to Vaiśālī, adorned with walls and moats fashioned of the seven precious substances, and lined with seven rows of precious jewel palā trees. All the people dwelling therein enjoyed supreme happiness and wellbeing. The raised platforms of those cities were made of Jambū River gold, and between each raised platform stood trees of the seven precious kinds in manifold varieties, laden abundantly with flowers and fruit. When a gentle breeze moved through them, the sound that arose was exceedingly beautiful — like what is called divine music — and whoever among the people dwelling there heard it experienced a supreme and exquisite happiness. The moats were filled entirely with pure, fragrant water resembling vaiḍūrya, and upon those waters were boats fashioned of the seven precious substances. People sported and bathed upon those boats, rejoicing with one another and experiencing great delight. And there, too, lotuses of every hue bloomed in those waters — blue utpala lotuses, white kumuda lotuses, pink padma lotuses, and pure white puṇḍarīka lotuses — each as wide as a chariot wheel.

On either side of the moats there were many pleasure groves, and within each pleasure grove there were five ponds fed by springs. Within those ponds, too, there bloomed outstanding blossoms of utpala, kumuda, padma, and puṇḍarīka, of great size equal to a chariot wheel, with a fragrance supremely sweet and utterly pleasing, the waters brilliantly clear and gentle, with geese, ducks, and other birds swimming and at play.

Within those pleasure groves there were also palatial jeweled halls, each four leagues in breadth and extent. The walls of those palatial halls were made of four precious substances — gold, silver, vaiḍūrya, and crystal — and their latticed screens were likewise made of gold. The floors were laid with coral and spread with golden sand. Before those palatial halls there were cascading waterfalls, springs, and ponds fashioned of the seven precious substances, and each pond had a staircase of eighty-four steps of gold. The banks of those waters were made of Jambū River gold, and they were equal to the Park of Joy called Sudharmā in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

Within each of those cities there were as many as eighty-four thousand kings, and each of those kings had a queen and an inconceivable number of palace retinues. Together with them, they sported and rejoiced.

All the people dwelling there sported and rejoiced, each in their own abode. And the sentient beings dwelling there heard no other sound in their ears but the sole sound of the unsurpassed Great Vehicle.

Within each of those flowers there was a lion throne. The four legs of each throne were fashioned of deep blue lapis lazuli, and upon them were spread utterly soft white garments that transcend the three realms. Upon each of those thrones sat a king, taming sentient beings through the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. Among those sentient beings, some would copy out sūtras of the Great Vehicle into volumes, carry them, hold them, read them, recite them, diligently practice in accordance with what had been taught, and bring their understanding to full comprehensiveness.

At that time, the bodhisattva Immeasurable Body, in whose own body he had arrayed an immeasurable number of sentient beings, had those beings forsake their worldly pleasures, and together they all cried out, "Alas, alas! The world is empty! The Tathāgata will before long pass fully into nirvāṇa!"

At that time, the bodhisattva Immeasurable Body, surrounded by an immeasurable retinue of bodhisattvas, having displayed such miraculous powers, took up immeasurable and manifold offerings together with fragrant food — for whoever was touched by the fragrance of that food would have all the stains of affliction utterly pacified — and by the blessing of that bodhisattva, every being in the entire assembly witnessed those miraculous displays.

The bodhisattva Immeasurable Body was of a vast and immeasurable form: being equal to space itself, no one other than the Buddha, the Blessed One, was able to perceive the limits of that bodhisattva's body.

Then the bodhisattva Immeasurable Body, together with his retinue, having prepared offerings even more abundant than before, went to where the Buddha was, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and with palms pressed together in reverence, addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, out of compassion for us, please accept these offerings." The Tathāgata, knowing the proper time, said nothing and gave no indication of acceptance, and so the bodhisattva Immeasurable Body with his retinue withdrew to one side.

It should be understood in the same way that from all the buddha-fields of the southern, western, and northern directions, an immeasurable number of bodhisattvas named Immeasurable Body likewise arrived, each having prepared offerings even more abundant than before, went to where the Buddha was, and then withdrew to one side.

At that time, in that auspicious and merit-filled place between the two śāla trees, not even the tiniest space remained in a radius of thirty-two leagues in all directions, so completely was it filled by the assembled retinues. The bodhisattvas with their retinues who had gathered from the four directions occupied a space no greater than the tip of a blade of grass, the tip of a needle, or a single fine particle of dust. Every bodhisattva from buddha-fields as numerous as the finest atoms in the world-realms of the ten directions had assembled there, and every member of the retinue dwelling in Jambudvīpa had assembled as well — with only two exceptions: Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda. King Ajātaśatru with his retinue, a serpent so venomous that a mere glance from it could kill, bubbles, poison, and those engaged in the sixteen classes of utterly wicked and sinful actions — these alone were absent; all others had assembled.

The rākṣasas, the dānavas,

the asuras (demigods), and all the rest had cast aside their malicious intentions and had arisen in each other's minds feelings of love and tenderness, as though for a father, a mother, or a sibling. Every sentient being dwelling in the great trichiliocosm (the vast three-thousandfold world-system) had likewise given rise to a mind of loving-kindness for one another — all save one: those given over to wrong desire. At that time, by the blessing of the buddha, every part of the ground throughout the great trichiliocosm became smooth and level. Ravines, sand, gravel, stones, thorned trees, and poisonous grasses were gone, and the whole was adorned with a great wealth and variety of precious jewels, becoming like the realm of Sukhāvatī, the world-realm of Amitāyus, the buddha of the western direction. At that time, all the many assembled maṇḍalas of the retinue could see the world-realms of the ten directions, as numerous as the finest atoms, with perfect clarity — just as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a bright mirror.

Then from the mouth of the Tathāgata there issued five rays of light. They illuminated all the many maṇḍalas of the retinue, and overpowering and subduing the radiance of those assemblies' own bodily light, the rays re-entered through the Tathāgata's mouth. At that time, the gods, humans, asuras, and all others in the retinue witnessed those rays of the buddha's radiance re-entering through his mouth, and all were struck with fear, their entire bodies' hair standing on end. They said to one another: "The Tathāgata has emitted rays of light and drawn them back in — this is not without cause, not without condition. Having performed all his deeds in the ten directions, this is surely the sign that he will finally pass into complete nirvāṇa."

"Alas, alas! The Tathāgata, with the four immeasurable states of mind, has not accepted the offerings of the gods and humans. From this day forward, the sun of primordial wisdom shall set, and the supreme vessel of Dharma shall sink. Alas, how wretched! The world is afflicted with great suffering!" Having spoken thus, they beat their chests with their fists. Crying aloud in lamentation, their bodies trembling unbearably, blood began to seep from their pores.

At that time, there was assembled in that retinue a layman named Cunda, a carpenter from the city of Pāvā, together with his retinue of fifty peers. Desiring that beings of the world might obtain the fruit of virtue, he rose from his customary posture of composure, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, and, turning toward where the Blessed One was, joined his palms and shed tears. Bowing with his head to the feet of the buddha, he addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, please accept this, our final offering — and do so for the sake of liberating incalculable sentient beings. Blessed One, from this day forward we are without protector, without refuge, without ally, without support, without dwelling place. In our utter destitution, we offer the Tathāgata but a humble meal in the time before the final moment arrives. Blessed One, out of compassion, please accept this, our last offering, and only then proceed to pass into complete nirvāṇa. Blessed One, it is like a person of the warrior class, a brahmin, or even an outcast who, impoverished, travels to another land, takes up farming, tills the soil, levels the field, makes the earth even, clears it of stones, and removes the ridges from the field — but lacking all else, waits only for the rain from above. Blessed One, 'tilling the soil' is an analogy for the seven bodily and verbal actions."

"'Leveling the ground of the field' is an analogy for wisdom. 'There being no stones and no ridges in the field' is an analogy for the afflictions. Blessed One, we too have subdued our craving, we have tilled the field, yet if the ridges of the field are not removed, we can only hope for the nectar-rain of the Tathāgata. We four are the impoverished ones of noble family. We are impoverished and destitute in the precious Dharma of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Therefore, out of compassion, please remove the suffering of our poverty and destitution, and please liberate the measureless number of sentient beings utterly tormented by suffering. Our offering is exceedingly humble, yet if it is accepted as the alms-round of the Tathāgata's great retinue, then, Blessed One, we have no protector, no refuge, no ally. Please look upon us with compassion, as one would a creature seized by Rāhu."

Then the Blessed One, the omniscient one, the unsurpassed tamer of persons who must be tamed, declared these words to Cunda:

"Excellent! Excellent! I shall rain down upon your body the unsurpassed Dharma-rain, removing your poverty and destitution, and cause the sprout of Dharma to grow. You now wish to attain, in this very life, the individual perfect knowledge of vitality, radiance, strength, well-being, and unobstructedness. I shall always grant you the individual perfect knowledge of vitality, radiance, strength, well-being, and unobstructedness. Why is this? Cunda, because from the giving of this gift of food, two fruits of equal excellence will be obtained. What are these two? First, after this meal is eaten, unsurpassed perfect awakening is attained; and second, after this meal is eaten, complete nirvāṇa is reached. And by my accepting this, your last inner offering, your perfection of generosity is brought to complete fulfillment."

Then Cunda addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, according to what you have said — that the two fruits of giving a gift are of equal excellence — this is not so. Why? Because the former gift that was received was given when the afflictions had not yet been exhausted and the wisdom of omniscience was not yet complete, and it did not bring the sentient being's perfection of generosity to fulfillment. The gift received afterward, given after the giving, was given when the afflictions were exhausted, the wisdom of omniscience was fully complete, and it does bring the sentient being's perfection of generosity to fulfillment. The former gift was received by a sentient being. The latter gift is received by the God of gods. The former gift was received by a body mixed with food, a body accompanied by afflictions, a body subject to hunger, an impermanent body. The latter gift is received by a body free from afflictions, a vajra-like body, a dharmakāya, a permanent body, a body without limit. How then can you say the fruits of these two gifts are of equal excellence? The former gift received was one whereby the perfection of generosity through to the Perfection of Wisdom were not yet brought to complete fulfillment — whereby only the eye of flesh was obtained and not the eye of a buddha, through to the eye of wisdom, which had not yet been obtained. The latter gift received was one whereby the perfection of generosity through to the Perfection of Wisdom are fully complete, and one is endowed with the eye of a buddha, through to —"

the eye of wisdom — how then can you say the fruits of these two gifts are of equal excellence?"

The Blessed One replied: "The former gift received was one where, immediately upon receiving it, a request was made on the spot, and through that very request the recipient obtained long life, good complexion, strength, happiness, and discernment.

The latter gift received was one where no request was made, no asking at all, and the five fruits did not arise — so why do I say the fruits of these two gifts are of equal excellence?

Noble son, a Tathāgata, through immeasurable, endless, and countless aeons, is not a body that requires food, not a body joined to afflictions, not a body that is the last of a conventional series — he is a permanent body, a dharmakāya, a vajra body.

Noble son, one who has not seen the nature of a buddha has an afflicted body, a body that requires food, a body that is the last of a conventional series.

At that time, the bodhisattva received almsfood, entered meditative absorption in the vajra-like samādhi, and right upon receiving that alms-round offering, beheld the nature of a buddha and fully and perfectly awakened to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. Therefore I say the fruits of these two gifts are of equal excellence.

When the bodhisattva first arose, he vanquished the four māras, and likewise as I approach passing into nirvāṇa I have vanquished the four māras — therefore I say the fruits of these two gifts are of equal excellence.

At the time of that bodhisattva, the twelve branches of scripture had not yet been taught at length; yet all of them had already been understood in his mind. Now, as I approach passing into nirvāṇa, I open them out and teach them extensively to sentient beings — therefore the two gifts are of equal excellence.

Noble son, the body of the Tathāgata does not receive almsfood for immeasurable and countless aeons — yet I have spoken these words to the hearers: 'Long ago, the Tathāgata received the milk-porridge offered by the cowherd women Nandā and Nandapalā, and having received it, fully and perfectly awakened to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. Now he does not receive solid food again. For the sake of this great assembly gathered here, he has accepted this, your final offering — yet in the ultimate sense there is no reception at all.'

At that time, when the members of that great assembly saw the Blessed One accepting Cunda's offering, all rejoiced and delighted, and with one voice said to Cunda: 'Excellent! Most excellent! Your name has fallen aptly upon you. The name Cunda means one who is skilled in the ultimate, and today you have undertaken a great purpose — therefore from that purpose the name Cunda has been given. In this very life you have obtained great renown and great benefit, and your aspirations have been entirely fulfilled. How wonderful! Cunda, though born among humans, you have obtained the supreme happiness that is so very difficult to find. Excellent!

Cunda, like the udumbara flower that is exceedingly rare in the world, a buddha's appearance in the world is likewise exceedingly rare. Even to encounter a buddha and give rise to faith is exceedingly difficult. To hear the Dharma is exceedingly difficult. To prepare offerings and present them to a buddha at the time of his passing into final nirvāṇa is exceedingly difficult.

We pay homage to Cunda! We pay homage to Cunda! You have fully completed the perfection of generosity — full and utterly pure like the moon of the fifteenth day of the autumn month. Just as when the moon is veiled by clouds or haze all people yearn to gaze upon it, so do we and all others gaze upon you with that very longing. By the Blessed One's acceptance of your final offering, your perfection of generosity has been brought to complete fulfillment. Cunda, we pay homage to you!'

Therefore you are like the full moon in all its completion, and there is no sentient being who does not gaze upon you. We pay homage to you, Cunda! Though you have obtained a human body, your mind is like the mind of a buddha — Cunda, you are truly a son of a buddha, no different from Rāhu (the eclipse-demon who seizes the moon).

Then those in the assembly spoke these verses:

You were born among human beings,
yet you stand supremely higher than the six classes of gods.
All of us, your entire retinue,
bow to you and offer our prayers.

The Blessed One, the noblest hero among men,
has declared that he will pass into final nirvāṇa.
For the sake of your compassion toward us,
please petition the Blessed One to remain.

Please remain long in this world
and, for the benefit of an immeasurable retinue,
teach the unsurpassable, supreme Dharma
that is praised by the wise.

If you do not make this petition,
we, these human beings, cannot go on living.
Therefore, please, we beseech you —
petition the Teacher who turns the wheel.

At that moment Cunda was filled with great joy and delight toward the Teacher who turns the wheel. Just as a person whose father and mother have died is suddenly restored and revived — just so did Cunda become filled with extraordinary joy. He touched his head to the feet of the Blessed One and spoke these verses:

Excellent — may there be happiness and well-being!
A human body has been well obtained.
Attachment, aversion, and delusion have been cleared away.
The three lower destinies have been utterly abandoned.

Excellent — there is happiness and well-being!
I have beheld a mountain of precious gold
and met the Teacher who turns the wheel.
I have no fear of being born in the animal realm.

A buddha is as rare as the udumbara flower (uḍumbara),
and an encounter is exceedingly difficult to come by.
Yet through this encounter, roots of virtue have been planted,
and the sufferings of the hungry ghosts have been completely vanquished.

Other things, too, that are completely vanquished
are all the ranks of the asuras.
More difficult than a needle-tip catching a mustard seed
is the arising of a buddha — so rare is it.

I have completed the perfection of generosity.
I am freed from the continuum of gods and humans.
Untainted by the conditions of the world,
like a lotus unsullied by water —
having thoroughly abandoned existence to its limit,
I am fully liberated from the stream of saṃsāra.

Obtaining a human body is exceedingly difficult.
Encountering the arising of a buddha is difficult.
Just as within a great ocean
a blind sea-turtle might arise
and chance to put its head through a hole in a wooden yoke —
so difficult is the arising of a buddha.

By this offering that I have presented,
may I attain the unsurpassable fruit.
All the afflictions without exception,
being without substance, have been wholly vanquished.

As for myself here and now,
I have no longing for the bodies of gods or humans.
And even if I were to obtain such a birth,
