I would have no delight or desire in it.

Blessed One, through your acceptance of my offering,
my joy is beyond measure.
Just as from the eraṇḍa flower
the fragrance of fine sandalwood arises,
so am I one like the eraṇḍa —
through the Blessed One's acceptance of my offering,
like the sweet fragrance of fine sandalwood,
for that reason I am filled with extraordinary joy.

I have directly obtained the fruit.
I have reached the supreme unsurpassable state.
Brahmā, Śakra (Indra), and the gods
have all come and make offerings to me.

All the world together
has given rise to great suffering and grief,
understanding that the Blessed One who dwells among them —
the buddha, the Bhagavān — is about to pass into final nirvāṇa.

With one voice, all together in great proclamation:
"There is no ruler of the world any longer!"

Please do not abandon all sentient beings;
look upon them as your own children.
Blessed One, teach the unsurpassable Dharma
to the Saṅgha and your retinue.

Just as in the midst of a great ocean
a mountain of jewels and a Mount Meru shines —
so too, Blessed One, cut through what is not known,
dispel the darkness of ignorance.
Just as clouds parting in the open sky
bring cool relief throughout the expanse —
so too, Blessed One, may you utterly remove

all afflictions utterly removed —
just as the sun rising in the sky
shines everywhere without a cloud.

Yet now these sentient beings
weep so deeply that their eyes are swollen.
The roaring torrent of saṃsāric suffering
has swept all who wander in cyclic existence into distraction.

Therefore, buddha, Blessed One —
to awaken faith in beings
and to sever the suffering of cyclic existence —
we implore you: remain in the world for a long time.

The Blessed One then spoke to Cunda:

So it is, so it is. Just as you have said. A buddha, a Blessed One, appearing in the world is extraordinarily rare — like the udumbara flower. That faith should arise upon meeting a buddha is even rarer still. To offer worship to a Tathāgata on the very eve of his passing into final nirvāṇa, and thereby to perfect the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā) — this is rarer still. Cunda, do not grieve; be joyful instead. The Tathāgata has accepted this final material offering, and by it the perfection of generosity is perfectly fulfilled. That is enough — do not petition the Blessed One to remain long in the world. You must know that all the domains of activity of the buddhas are impermanent, and that the defining characteristic of all conditioning factors is just such a nature. Know this to be so.

Then the Blessed One spoke these verses to Cunda:

All that inhabits the world —
whatever is born must die.
Even a sage whose years are beyond counting
must in the end come to exhaustion.

Where there is flourishing, there is decline;
where there is meeting, there is parting.
Youth too is impermanent —
even the bloom of prime is seized away by illness.
Life too is seized away by death.
There is nothing at all that is permanent.

Even mighty kings who reign supreme,
whose gifts and power are unmatched —
all of them undergo change and transformation,
and life's vital breath is no different.

The wheel of suffering has no end;
the stream of wandering in cyclic existence never ceases.
Nothing in all three realms is permanent.
Nothing in all of conditioned existence is happiness.

The things that constitute conditioned existence —
all of them are empty, without substance,
subject to destruction, undergoing change and transformation,
ever attended by misery and fault,
full of faults and subject to ruin,
perpetually afflicted by old age, sickness, and death.
The phenomena of conditioned existence are boundless,
accompanied by the enemy of change and transformation.
Afflictions permeate them utterly —
like a silkworm in its cocoon.
What wise and discerning person
would find delight or attachment in that?

This body is a heap of suffering,
altogether impure and defiled,
bound by faults and riddled with wounds —
never, from the beginning, a source of benefit.
From the body of a god above
down to the body of a human here below —
all of it is just the same.
Therefore, since all objects of desire are impermanent,
I have no attachment to them.

If one resolves well to abandon desire,
one will come to know the true nature of reality.
To sever all conditioned existence completely —
today, now, I pass utterly into nirvāṇa.
I have crossed to the other shore of conditioned existence,
gone utterly beyond all suffering.
Therefore what I attain this day
is unsurpassable bliss, and nothing else.

By reason of its causes and conditions,
one arrives at the limit that is free of conceptual elaboration.
Having severed all bondage entirely,
today, now, I pass utterly into nirvāṇa.

For me there is no old age, no illness, no death.
The measure of this life is inexhaustible.
This passing into nirvāṇa today
is like the dying down of a great fire.

Cunda, do not be confused about this.
Contemplate the qualities of the Tathāgata,
and this buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha)
as immovable as Mount Meru.
I enter nirvāṇa
and will experience supreme bliss.
This is the very nature of all buddhas.
Therefore do not weep.

Then Cunda addressed the Blessed One in these words:

So it is, so it is. Just as the Blessed One has declared —

My wisdom, which I seek to employ, is exceedingly small — like a tiny bee — and so how could I possibly comprehend the profound meaning of the Tathāgata's passing utterly into nirvāṇa? Blessed One, I have now become equal to the great bodhisattvas — the great beings who, like a great river, have utterly crossed beyond all afflictions and defilements — such as Mañjuśrī in his youth and the rest. Blessed One, just as a newly ordained novice who has not yet received full ordination is nevertheless counted among the Saṅgha, so too have I, through the blessing of the buddhas and the bodhisattvas, come to be counted among those great bodhisattvas. Therefore I beseech the Tathāgata to remain in the world for a long time and not to pass into nirvāṇa. Blessed One, just as one who is not hungry has no need to eat again, so too, being like that, I beseech you to remain in the world for a long time without passing into nirvāṇa.

Then Mañjuśrī the Youthful spoke to Cunda in these words:

Cunda, you ask that the Tathāgata remain in the world for a long time and not pass utterly into nirvāṇa, saying that just as someone who is not at all hungry would find it repulsive to eat again. Rather than speaking in such a way, you should thoroughly comprehend the defining marks of formations. If formations are examined in that way, one will come to abide in the meditative absorption of emptiness. Those who desire the true Dharma should train in precisely this manner.

Cunda then spoke to Mañjuśrī:

The Tathāgata is the supreme one among gods and humans. Since he is supremely excellent, surely the Tathāgata is not a formation? If he were a formation, he would be subject to arising and ceasing — like a water bubble on water, arising immediately and immediately disintegrating. Revolving in saṃsāra is like the wheel of a cart, and all formations are just like that. Now, as I have heard before, the lifespan of the gods is said to be extremely long — so why is it that the Blessed One, the god above gods, has so short a lifespan that he does not remain even a hundred years? Consider, for instance, the chief of a village who has come to power: through his authority and might he subdues his opponents, but when at last his merit is exhausted and he falls into poverty, everyone despises him, tramples on him, and puts him to work. Why so? Because his splendor and power have diminished. If that were so, then the Blessed One would also be like formations. But if he were like formations, it would not be fitting to call him the god above gods. Why? Because formations are subject to birth and death. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, I do not regard the Tathāgata as being like formations. Does Mañjuśrī speak with knowledge, or is it that without knowing he says the Tathāgata is like formations? If the Tathāgata were indeed like formations, then the Tathāgata — who is the god above gods in the three worlds, the sovereign king of the Dharma — could not properly be so designated. Consider, for example, a king who has a great champion wrestler capable of defeating a thousand opponents, one whom no one can overcome — that man is called the wrestler who cannot be defeated. The king honors that wrestler, and others bestow gifts upon him more abundantly than anyone else. Now, when it is said that this wrestler cannot be defeated, it does not mean that he is undefeatable by physical strength alone; rather, because he surpasses thousands of opponents through many diverse skills, he is given the designation "the wrestler who cannot be defeated." The Tathāgata is just like that. The māra of afflictions and —

the māra of the aggregates, the māra of the divine son, and the māra of the lord of death — having utterly vanquished all of these, the Tathāgata is declared supreme within the three realms. It is just as with that one wrestler who is capable of defeating a thousand opponents. Therefore, because the Tathāgata likewise possesses immeasurable and manifold qualities, the Tathāgata is designated "the perfectly and completely awakened buddha."

Mañjuśrī, it is not appropriate to conceive of the Tathāgata as being in conformity with formations through conceptual thought. Consider this example: a wealthy householder's son is born, and a fortune-teller examines him and determines, "He will be short-lived." The moment the parents hear this, knowing that the child will not be a source of honor for the family line, they do not cherish him; they regard him as worth no more than a blade of grass. For as long as that short-lived child lives, neither renunciants nor brahmins, nor any boys or girls of any age, treat him with respect.

Now, if the Tathāgata were in conformity with formations, then all the gods, humans, and sentient beings that dwell throughout the world would likewise treat him with no respect, and the true Dharma that the Tathāgata has taught — which is unchanging and unshifting — would come to have no one to uphold it. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, it is not appropriate to say that the Tathāgata conforms to formations.

Mañjuśrī, consider this further example: a destitute woman with no home, no support, and no refuge, afflicted by illness and tormented by hunger and thirst, wanders until she enters someone's house and gives birth there. The householder does not let her stay but drives her away. Though she has only just given birth, she takes her infant in her arms and sets out for another land. Along the way she is tormented by wind, rain, and hail; she encounters gnats, mosquitoes, and venomous serpents; and when the Ganges river blocks her path, though that river is exceedingly deep and swift, she clutches her infant to her breast and plunges in. Both mother and child then sink beneath the waters.

By the merit of the love and affection she bore toward her child, she was reborn, the very instant of her death, as a god in the Brahmā heaven.

Mañjuśrī, sons of good family, for the sake of protecting the sacred Dharma, one should not say of the Tathāgata either that he conforms to formations or that he does not conform to formations. I myself am obscured by delusion, lacking the eye of wisdom, and cannot fathom the sacred Dharma of the Tathāgata, which is inconceivable. Therefore one should not say definitively that the Tathāgata is conditioned or that he is unconditioned. Nor should one, through right view, say definitively that the Tathāgata is unconditioned. Why? Because he gives rise to qualities that make all sentient beings virtuous, and because of his compassion for the many beings throughout all destinies.

Just as that destitute woman, when crossing the Ganges, thought lovingly of her child and gave up both body and life, so too, sons of good family, a bodhisattva who is a protector of the Dharma should, even at the cost of body and life, never say of the Tathāgata that he conforms to the conditioned, nor that he conforms to the unconditioned.

The Noble Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra. The Third Fascicle.

Thus, by declaring that the Tathāgata conforms to the unconditioned, one comes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening — just as that destitute woman was reborn as a god in the Brahmā heaven. Why? Because of protecting the Dharma. And what is protecting the Dharma? It is declaring, "The Tathāgata is unconditioned."

Sons of good family, that person does not hope for liberation — rather, liberation comes to them on its own. Just as that destitute woman did not hope to be reborn in the Brahmā heaven,

yet she was born as a god in the Brahmā heaven. Mañjuśrī, consider this further example: a person who had gone a long way as a traveler on a road grew weary along the way and lay down to rest in another person's house. That house then caught fire and blazed up. Seized with terror and fright, the person thought, "I will surely die." Yet because he possessed a sense of shame and modesty, he wrapped his body in his clothing. At the moment of his death, he was reborn as a god in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. After that, he was born eighty times as a king in the realm of Great Brahmā. Then, for a full thousand years, he was born among humans as a wheel-turning king. That person was never born in any of the three lower destinies; instead, from one life to the next, he was born in ever higher and more blissful states. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, those sons of good family who possess shame and modesty will not look upon the Buddha, the Blessed One, as conforming to the conditioned. Mañjuśrī, it is the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) with their mistaken views who say that the Tathāgata conforms to the conditioned. The monks who guard their ethical conduct will not regard the Tathāgata in that way — as something conditioned. If one were to say, "The Tathāgata is conditioned," that would be speaking falsely. Know that such a person will be reborn in the hells immediately upon dying — just as a person who remains inside a burning house. Mañjuśrī, since the Tathāgata is truly possessed of the nature of the unconditioned, one must not speak of him as conditioned.

Mañjuśrī, from this day forward, as you wander in saṃsāra, abandon wandering there in ignorance and seek true primordial wisdom. The Tathāgata is unconditioned. Whoever sees the Tathāgata in exactly this way will swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, endowed with the thirty-two major marks.

Then Mañjuśrī, the Crown Prince, said to Cunda: "Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, you have now manifestly brought about the cause of a very long life. To regard the Tathāgata as one possessed of the nature of permanence, as one whose nature is unchanging and unshifting, as one whose nature is unconditioned — that is excellent. It is excellent that you did not describe the Tathāgata as bearing the defining marks of something conditioned. Just as that person who was scorched by fire, possessing shame and modesty and having wrapped his body in his clothing — through the virtue of that intention he was born as a god in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, became a king in the realm of Brahmā and a wheel-turning king, and was always born in pleasant states and never in the lower destinies — in the very same way, because you did not describe the Tathāgata as bearing the defining marks of something conditioned, in the future without any doubt you will certainly attain the thirty-two major marks, the eighty minor marks of excellence, the eighteen unshared qualities, boundless life, non-abiding in saṃsāra, supreme bliss, and before long you will attain perfect and complete awakening. This will be explained in detail by the Tathāgata himself. Let the two of us, then, refrain from describing the Tathāgata as bearing the defining marks of something conditioned."

"Now, let us set aside this matter of the conditioned and the unconditioned for the moment, and quickly offer whatever alms food is available. This act of giving will be foremost among all acts of giving. To the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who have come a long way and are weary, with a pure and wholehearted mind, quickly offer whatever they wish. This will become the seed for the complete perfection of your perfection of generosity (pāramitā). Cunda, whoever at the final moment of their life makes an offering — however much they are able — to the Buddha and the Saṅgha,

whether little or much, whether sufficient or insufficient — make offerings to the Tathāgata at the very moment of his passing into nirvāṇa."

Then Cunda spoke to Mañjuśrī: "Why do you say, with such attachment to alms, that one should offer much or little, sufficient or insufficient, in due season?"

Mañjuśrī replied: "Cunda, if the Tathāgata endured austerities for six full years, why would he be impeded for even a single instant now? Cunda, do you think that the Tathāgata, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, will actually accept this alms food? Know this: the body of the Tathāgata is assuredly the dharmakāya — it is not a body sustained by food."

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to Mañjuśrī: "It is so, it is exactly so — just as Cunda has said. Cunda, excellent indeed! You are endowed with supreme and great primordial wisdom, and you have understood well the profoundly deep sūtras of the Great Vehicle."

Mañjuśrī then said to Cunda: "You have understood the Tathāgata as unconditioned. Since the lifespan of the Tathāgata's body is immeasurably long, if you understand it in precisely this way, the Tathāgata will rejoice in you."

Cunda replied: "It is not only in me that he rejoices — he rejoices in all sentient beings."

Mañjuśrī said: "The Tathāgata rejoices in you, in me, and in all sentient beings alike."

Cunda said: "Mañjuśrī, do not say that the Tathāgata rejoices. The word 'rejoicing' implies a perverse perception. Whatever involves a perverse perception is saṃsāra. Whatever is saṃsāra belongs to the conditioned. Therefore, Mañjuśrī, one should not regard the Tathāgata as conditioned. If one were to say that the Tathāgata is conditioned, then both you and I, my friend, would be acting in error. Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata has no intention of attachment. To intend with attachment is like a cow that, even while hungry or thirsty and searching for grass and water, immediately turns back to look for her calf, whether she has had enough or not. The Blessed One, the buddha, has no such intention — he regards all beings as though they were beings seized by Rāhu. Such an intention as that is the domain of the wisdom of the buddhas.

"Mañjuśrī, consider this example: to hope that a donkey-drawn cart can match a chariot drawn by the finest horses of a great king is entirely without foundation. Similarly, both you and I, my friend, are just like that — to hope to fathom the limits of the Tathāgata's profound intention is equally without foundation.

"Mañjuśrī, consider this further example: a lord among garuḍas soars countless leagues up into the sky above, and then looks down upon the ocean below. All the beings that dwell in the water — fish, turtles, crabs, sea monsters, nāgas, and every other kind of creature that inhabits the water — he sees clearly, just as a reflection appears in a bright mirror. This cannot be measured by those of small understanding. In the very same way that these beings cannot be perceived by those who have not soared aloft, so too both you and I, my friend, are like that — the wisdom of the Tathāgata cannot be fathomed."

Mañjuśrī then said to Cunda: "It is so, it is exactly so — just as you have said. It is not that I myself have not understood these points, but rather I have been teaching them for the sake of you and the bodhisattvas."

At that moment the Blessed One released from his mouth rays of light in many colors, and those rays illuminated the entire body of Mañjuśrī. The instant that light touched Mañjuśrī, he understood the nature of things exactly as they are, and he said this to Cunda: "The Tathāgata has shown this sign — it is certain that before long he will pass fully into nirvāṇa. The time has come for you to offer to the Blessed One and the great Saṅgha the final meal of offerings you have prepared within your home. Cunda, you must understand that the Tathāgata's sending forth these rays of light in many colors is not without cause and condition."

When Cunda heard these words, he sat in silence.

The Blessed One then declared to Cunda: "The time has come for you to present the offerings you have prepared to the buddhas and the Saṅgha. The Tathāgata will pass into nirvāṇa." He declared this in the same manner two and three times.

At that moment, the instant Cunda heard the Blessed One speak these words, he let out a great cry of weeping and lamented aloud: "Alas, alas — the world is empty!" And he called out to those gathered in the assembly: "Let us all prostrate with the five limbs of our bodies to the ground, and together in one voice beseech the Blessed One not to pass into nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One declared to Cunda: "Do not weep, and do not let your heart be utterly consumed with anguish. Regard this body of mine as like a plantain tree, or a mirage, or a water bubble, or an illusion, or a city of gandharvas (fragrance-eaters, beings who feed on scent), or unfired clay, or a flash of lightning, or a line drawn on water, or a prisoner being led to execution, or a ripened fruit, or rotting flesh, or a thread whose fibers are exhausted, or like a wooden pestle. Regard the formations (saṃskāras) as food mixed with poison. Regard all conditioned phenomena as having the fault of many flaws."

Then Cunda said to the Blessed One: "If the Tathāgata has no wish to remain long in the world, how could I not weep? Alas, alas — the world is empty! Blessed One, out of compassion for us and for all sentient beings, we beseech you to remain long in the world and not pass into nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One declared to Cunda: "Do not say that I should remain long in the world out of compassion for you — it is out of compassion for you and for all beings that I am passing fully into nirvāṇa. Why is that? This too is the nature of reality (dharmatā) of all buddhas, and conditioned things are the same."

The Blessed One then spoke this verse:

All phenomena that are conditioned
are by their very nature impermanent.
Having arisen, they do not remain —
therefore perfect pacification is bliss.

"Cunda, you must understand that all conditioned things are mixed together, that all phenomena are without self, that they are impermanent and do not endure long. This body is extremely full of faults — regard it as like a water bubble — and therefore do not weep."

Then Cunda said to the Blessed One: "It is so, it is exactly so — just as the Blessed One has said. I understand that the Tathāgata's passing into nirvāṇa is a display of skillful means, yet even though I do not grieve, I cannot bear it. And yet, when I reflect on it deeply, joy and delight also arise."

The Blessed One declared to Cunda: "Excellent, most excellent! It is good that you understand that the Tathāgata has shown his passing into nirvāṇa in a manner suited to sentient beings. Cunda, listen well."

It is like this: just as the bird called the sanderling gathers at a lake called the Cool Lake during the heat of summer, so too the Blessed One is like that, and has gone to that very place. Cunda, without speculating as to whether the Tathāgata's lifespan is long or short, know that all phenomena are like illusions, and that the Tathāgata, through skillful means, does not cling to anything whatsoever. Why is this? Because such is the nature of reality of a buddha.

Cunda, the fact that the Tathāgata has accepted this last meal offering you have arranged is in order to liberate you from the river of saṃsāra. As for any being — whether a god, a human, or any other being in the world — who arranges a last meal offering and presents it to me, that being will attain the fruit of immovability and will perpetually experience happiness. Why is this? Because I am the field of merit for all sentient beings. If you also wish to become a field of merit for sentient beings, then without delay, quickly present the meal offering you have prepared.

Then Cunda, with the aspiration to liberate all sentient beings, bowed his head and spoke to the Blessed One with tears streaming down his face, saying: "Most excellent! Blessed One, if I am truly to become a field of merit, let me speak. We who are śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot fathom whether the Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa or does not pass into nirvāṇa, since our wisdom is like that of a gnat in comparison to his. Therefore we cannot reckon whether the Tathāgata passes into complete nirvāṇa or does not."

Then Cunda together with his retinue, weeping with tears streaming down their faces, circumambulated the Tathāgata, scattered incense and flowers, made offerings, and then rose from their seats alongside Mañjuśrī and went to prepare the meal offering.

The very moment they had gone, the earth shook in six ways, all the way up to the Brahmā world. There are two kinds of earth-shaking: ordinary trembling and great trembling. A slight motion is called an ordinary trembling; a great motion is called a great trembling. A quiet sound is called an ordinary trembling; a loud sound is called a great trembling. When only the earth moves, it is called an ordinary trembling; when mountains, waters, trees, oceans, and everything else move, it is called a great trembling. When movement occurs in one direction it is called an ordinary trembling; when there is a revolving motion in all directions it is called a great trembling. When only the ground stirs, it is called an ordinary trembling; when the ground stirs and the minds of all sentient beings are also moved, it is called a great trembling. When the bodhisattva who had dwelt in the highest realm descended from the heavens and came to Jambudvīpa, that was a great trembling. The first birth, the going forth into renunciation, the attainment of unsurpassable complete and perfect awakening, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the passing into complete nirvāṇa — each of these is a great trembling. Now the Tathāgata is passing into complete nirvāṇa, and therefore the earth also trembles greatly.

Then gods, nāgas, gandharvas (Skt. gandharva), asuras, garuḍas (Skt. garuḍa), kinnaras (Skt. kinnara), great serpents (Skt. mahoraga), humans and non-humans, and all such beings — the moment they heard this, the hairs on their bodies stood on end. All of them wept in every direction and with one voice chanted these verses:

We prostrate and beseech you, O Helmsman.
Now that the Great Sage has abandoned us,
we are left without refuge or protector.
The Blessed One has gone into nirvāṇa
and we sink into an ocean of suffering.
Despondent and tormented by grief,
we are like calves that have not yet lost their mothers.

The destitute have no protector, no refuge.
Like one who is gravely ill
and lacks a skilled physician,
they crave food to their heart's desire.
Sentient beings are tormented by the sickness of affliction,
constantly harmed by wrong views.
Bereft of the skilled physician of Dharma,
they seek the poison of nihilistic views.
Therefore, O buddha, Blessed One,
we beg you, do not abandon us.
For example, if a king is absent,
all his people go hungry.
We too are in just such a state,
losing both the taste of Dharma and our refuge.

Hearing that the buddha has passed into nirvāṇa,
our minds have grown confused and dazed,
like the great earth violently shaking
and all directions reeling and disrupted.
The sage has gone to nirvāṇa:
the sun of buddhahood has fallen to the ground,
the waters of Dharma have dried up,
and without doubt we shall perish.

When the Blessed One passes into nirvāṇa,
the anguish of suffering that burns sentient beings
is like the child of a merchant
who has just lost both father and mother.
Now that the Blessed One has passed into nirvāṇa,
if he no longer remains among us,
then we and all sentient beings
shall be left without protector or refuge.

When the Blessed One passes into nirvāṇa,
even down to those born in animal realms,
all will be downcast with suffering and anguish,
tormented and uttering cries of lamentation.

Here and now we cannot find relief from grief.
That we have been forsaken by the Tathāgata
is like saliva spat upon the ground.
For example, when the sun rises,
its rays blaze forth in every direction,
illuminating everything everywhere,
and all darkness is utterly dispelled.
So too the miraculous light of the Tathāgata
has cleared away our afflictions.
And dwelling in the midst of his retinue,
he was like Mount Meru, king among mountains.

Blessed One, for example, if a king has sons of fine form, handsome and exceedingly beautiful, he loves them deeply and trains them from an early age in all manner of arts, and then, once they have absorbed this training, he entrusts them to an executioner with the command: "Put them to death."

Blessed One, we too have become sons of the Dharma. If the Blessed One were to teach and guide us, we would come to possess right view. We therefore beseech you not to abandon us. If you were to utterly forsake us, would that not be like a king abandoning his sons? We beg you to remain in the world for a long time without passing into nirvāṇa.

Blessed One, for example, a man who has trained thoroughly in the arts may come to be frightened by those very arts. Likewise the Blessed One, having comprehended all phenomena within himself, has come to be overawed by the Dharma itself. If the Tathāgata were to remain long in the world and teach a Dharma like nectar, satisfying all to the full, then there would be no fear that any sentient being would fall into the hells.

Blessed One, for example, a man is seized in the midst of some work he was doing, cast into prison, and someone comes to him and asks: "What are you doing here?" He replies: "I am enduring very great suffering here; if I could be freed from this, I would be utterly happy." Blessed One, you are just like that. You have performed austerities (Skt. duṣkara) on our behalf, and if we are not liberated from the afflictions of cyclic existence, how could the Tathāgata be at ease?

Blessed One, for example, a highly skilled physician teaches the secrets of medicine to his own son but does not teach them to other students. Blessed One, you are just like that: the exceedingly profound heart of what you have taught with intent you have revealed to Mañjuśrī alone, and have not revealed it to us. The Tathāgata, like that physician, teaches only his own son and not other students — yet surely the Tathāgata is not one who would be jealous regarding any of the Dharmas.

If that physician withheld his teaching from everyone else out of a mind of partiality and aversion, it would be a different matter — but since the Tathāgata's mind is free of partiality and aversion, why has he not taught us? Blessed One, we beseech you: remain long and do not pass into nirvāṇa.

Blessed One, consider this example: whether old or young, a person afflicted by illness who abandons the good road and takes instead a treacherous path full of ravines and precipices will suffer greatly. If someone else sees this and, moved by compassion, shows that person a safe and level road free of danger, the sufferer is set on the right way.

Blessed One, we are just like that person. In this analogy, "the young one" stands for one who has not yet generated the Dharma body. "The old one" stands for the great afflictions. "Being ill" stands for not being liberated from cyclic existence. "The path beset with precipices" stands for the twenty-five existences.

Blessed One, please show us the true path of the nectar of deathlessness, and remain in this world for a long time without passing into nirvāṇa.

Then the Blessed One declared to the assembly of monks: "You monks, do not weep and wail like foolish ordinary beings or like gods and humans. Instead, apply yourselves diligently to the establishment of mindfulness." At that moment, when the gods, humans, asuras, and the rest heard the Blessed One declare, "Do not weep," it was like someone whose child has just died and who is told immediately upon the child's death, "Do not weep."

Then the Blessed One spoke in verse to that great assembly:

Take heart and be gladdened, each of you,
and do not give way to great grief.
This is the very nature of all buddhas:
therefore he remains in silence, saying nothing more.
Be devoted to heedful conduct,
and guard the mind with true mindfulness.
Thoroughly abandon what is not Dharma,
take heart, and be joyful.

Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, if any of you have doubts or uncertainties, ask about them all — put your questions now. Whatever doubts you have — about emptiness and non-emptiness, permanence and impermanence, suffering and non-suffering, existence and non-existence, coming and going, arriving and not arriving, continuity and discontinuity, annihilation and permanence, sentient beings and non-sentient beings, being and non-being, truth and untruth, the correct and the incorrect, cessation and non-cessation, the secret and the non-secret, duality and non-duality, and other such matters — whatever doubts have arisen about any of these things, now is the time to ask. Whatever questions you ask, the doubt behind them will be resolved. I have already taught you a Dharma like the nectar of deathlessness, and from the very first this was intended to bring you to the complete passing beyond sorrow. Monks, it is extremely rare for a buddha to come into the world. It is extremely difficult to obtain a human body. It is extremely difficult to meet a buddha and give rise to faith. It is extremely difficult to endure what is hard to endure. And it is extremely difficult to perfect and maintain one's moral discipline without losing or degrading it, so as to attain the fruit of arhatship — it is as rare as finding the fruit of the udumbara flower or the seed grain of the śāla tree. Monks, you have freed yourselves from the eight states of non-leisure, you have obtained this difficult-to-obtain human body, and having met with me, do not let this opportunity be wasted. In former times I practiced countless and varied hardships, and through them I have now come to be endowed with such supreme skillful means. It was for your sake and for the sake of beings like you that throughout measureless ages I gave away my limbs — my arms, my legs, my head, my eyes, my feet, my marrow. Therefore, do not be heedless. Monks, one who is adorned with the citadel of the precious true Dharma, endowed with various precious qualities, and perfect in moral discipline —"

"— should be thought of as the foundation of meditative absorption and wisdom, and as its embankment and its watch-post. Yet beneath the very shadow of a citadel such as the precious Dharma of a buddha, you are the sort of people who take up what is counterfeit and deceptive. It is as if merchants who have reached an island of true jewels were to take gravel and pebbles and return home with those. You are just like them: having reached an island of jewels, you take up illusory goods. Monks, do not generate a mind of contentment through a spirit of timidity. You have gone forth, yet you do not turn your hearts toward the Great Vehicle. Monks, you wear robes dyed in ochre, yet your minds have not grown attached to the perfectly pure Dharma of the Great Vehicle. Monks, you go about wandering for alms, yet you have not tasted the Dharma-food of the Great Vehicle. Monks, you have shaved your hair and beard, yet you have not made the true Dharma the means of freeing yourselves entirely from affliction. Monks, here and now, in this entire assembly, I reveal and show you these things through genuine speech. The defining marks of the Tathāgata's Dharma are true and unerring. Therefore, with a courageous and resolute mind, strive earnestly to destroy all affliction. If the sun of wisdom endowed with the ten powers were to set, you too would be covered by ignorance. Monks, consider: just as the trees and plants that grow on the great earth and on mountains become useful to sentient beings, so too is my Dharma — it gives rise to the taste of Dharma like a supremely wholesome nectar, and it becomes medicine for the many and varied diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings.

"Here and now I have spoken with care for all sentient beings and for the retinue of four kinds who have become my children, and I settle them in the heart of what I have spoken with care, and resting myself in that, I pass into complete nirvāṇa. What is called 'the heart of what I have spoken with care'? Consider the letter 'i' — if you place three dots in a vertical column, it does not become the letter 'i'; but if you arrange them in three horizontally, as in the eye of a great sovereign, it becomes the letter 'i,' and it is not the same as the three dots kept separate. I too am like that: the Dharma of liberation does not pass into nirvāṇa; the body of the Tathāgata does not pass into nirvāṇa; the Perfection of Wisdom does not pass into nirvāṇa; nor does nirvāṇa consist in the three Dharmas being separated from one another. Abiding in these three Dharmas, it is for the sake of sentient beings that this is called 'passing into nirvāṇa,' just as in the world the letter 'i' is known as such."

At that moment the monks heard the Blessed One, the Buddha, declare that he would definitively pass into complete nirvāṇa, and they were overcome with grief. The hair of their entire bodies stood on end, and with eyes full of tears they bowed their heads to the feet of the Buddha, circumambulated him countless times, and then addressed the Blessed One in these words:

"Blessed One, you have taught so well: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. Blessed One, just as, among all the tracks of wandering beings, the track of the bull elephant is supreme, so too is the perception of impermanence — it is supreme among all perceptions. Whoever applies diligent and earnest effort to it will cause all the desires of the desire realm, the desires of the form and formless realms, and all the perceptions of ignorance, pride, and impermanence to cease entirely. Blessed One, if the Tathāgata is separated from the perception of impermanence, then it is not fitting that he depart now into complete nirvāṇa."

"But if he is not separated from it, then why did he apply diligent effort to impermanence and become separated from the desires of the three realms, from ignorance, from pride, and from the perception of impermanence?" So it was declared.

"Blessed One, consider, for example, how farmers in the autumn season plow their fields and clear the fields entirely of weeds. The perception of impermanence is just like that: it clears away the desires of the desire realm, the desires of the form and formless realms, ignorance, pride, and the perception of impermanence down to their very roots.

Blessed One, consider further: among all the methods of plowing, the autumn plow is the best. Among all tracks, the track of the bull elephant is supreme. And among all perceptions, the perception of impermanence is supreme.

Blessed One, consider also: when a great king is at the time of his passing, he first issues a proclamation to all four borders and grants freedom to all prisoners, so that they may spend their remaining time alive in liberty. The Tathāgata likewise has liberated all sentient beings from the ignorance that lacks wisdom and that covers them completely, and has set them free — and yet it is fitting that he pass into nirvāṇa only after doing so. Why, then, would the Tathāgata abandon us before we are liberated and pass into complete nirvāṇa?

Blessed One, consider: a person seized by a hungry ghost (preta), upon meeting an expert spell-caster, is freed from it by the power of the spell. The Tathāgata likewise removes the hungry ghost of ignorance through the hearers, and sets beings at ease in the Dharma of the Perfection of Wisdom, liberation, and so forth — just as in the world the letter A is renowned as the first of all letters.

Blessed One, consider: a bull elephant of perfume-wood, when bound by men, will not be tamed even if a skilled trainer is present — but once the binding rope is cut, it goes wherever it wishes. In the same way, so long as we are not fully freed from the bondage of the fifty-seven afflictions, why would the Tathāgata abandon us and pass into nirvāṇa?

Blessed One, consider: one struck by a fever, upon meeting a skilled physician, recovers at once. I too am like that: afflicted by many burning fevers of wrong dying, I have met the Tathāgata and yet my illness is not cured, and I have not attained the unsurpassed and permanent bliss. Why, then, would the Tathāgata abandon me and pass into nirvāṇa?

Blessed One, consider: a madman, because he has lost his senses, does not know near from far, and acts improperly and indecently toward his mother, his daughter, and his sister, speaking without shame and lying down upon filth. When a skilled physician administers medicine and makes him vomit up the alcohol he had drunk, immediately his senses return, and a mind of conscience and shame arises in him, and he feels remorse, thinking: 'Alcohol is the root of all evil and all non-virtue; whoever abandons it completely will abandon all evil as well.'

Blessed One, we too are like that. We have wandered in saṃsāra since beginningless time, intoxicated by desire and attached to the five objects of desire: we have conceived of those who are not our mothers as our mothers, those who are not our sisters as our sisters, those who are not our daughters as our daughters, those who are not sentient beings as sentient beings — and so we have wandered in saṃsāra, experiencing suffering, just as the madman lies upon vomit. The Tathāgata has administered to us the medicine of the Dharma, and we have vomited up the alcohol of the afflictions — yet we have not fully recovered. Why, then, would the Tathāgata abandon us and pass into nirvāṇa?

Blessed One, consider: if someone claims that a certain tree is hard and has heartwood, that would be incorrect. Blessed One, ordinary beings are likewise: they hold to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and living being —"

— and to "possessor of vitality," "lord of vitality," "consciousness," "seer," "agent," and "doer" as truly and genuinely real — that too would be incorrect. We likewise apply ourselves diligently to the perception of no-self.

Blessed One, consider: a bee is in no way needed at all, and the body too is like that — it has no self, no owner. Blessed One, just as a flower with seven petals has no fragrance within it, so too this body has no self and no owner. And so we, with a mind of that very kind, apply ourselves diligently to the perception of no-self.

As the Blessed One has taught, there is no self and no mine in any phenomenon whatsoever. "Monks, apply yourselves diligently in that very manner. By applying yourselves in that way, pride will be utterly relinquished" — so it was taught. And so, having relinquished pride in accordance with that teaching, we implore the Blessed One to pass into nirvāṇa.

Blessed One, consider: there is no traceable path left behind by a bird that flies through the sky. In the same way, one who applies oneself diligently to the perception of no-self gives no grounds for saying that views remain.

Then the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Excellent! Most excellent! You have cultivated well the perception of no-self."

Then the monks addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, we apply ourselves not only to the perception of no-self, but also — beyond that — to the perception of suffering, of emptiness, of impermanence, and of no-self. Blessed One, consider: a madman whose mind has become disordered thinks that he is circling among mountains, rivers, crags, trees, houses, the sun, the moon, and the stars. Blessed One, if a person does not apply himself diligently to the perceptions of suffering, impermanence, and no-self and so forth, that person will not be called a noble one, and, through heedlessness, will wander endlessly in saṃsāra. Blessed One, for that reason we apply ourselves very diligently to those perceptions."

At that time the Blessed One declared to the monks: "Listen well and take it deeply to heart. In using the analogy of the madman, you have grasped only the words and letters; you have not understood the meaning. What, then, is the meaning? Just as the madman perceives himself as circling around the sun, the moon, and so forth when he is not circling at all, so too is the case with ordinary beings: covered over by defiled ignorance in its entirety, they give rise to inverted minds. They perceive a self as having no self, the permanent as impermanent, the utterly pure as utterly impure, and bliss as suffering. Covered over by defilement in their entirety, they give rise to such perceptions, yet fail to penetrate the actual meaning — just like that madman, who gives rise to the perception of circling in what is not actually a place of circling.

The word 'self' means 'buddha.' The word 'permanent' means 'dharmakāya.' The word 'bliss' means 'nirvāṇa.' And 'utterly pure' means 'Dharma.'

Why, then, do you monks say that perceiving a self is arrogance and leads to wandering in saṃsāra? According to what you say, we too apply ourselves diligently to the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, and no-self — but that is altogether without real purpose. Since applying yourselves to those three has no genuine meaning, I will now teach what surpasses those three improper objects of diligent application. To grasp bliss in what is suffering, and to grasp suffering in what is bliss — those are inverted phenomena. To grasp permanence in what is impermanent, and

to grasp impermanence in what is permanent — that is an inverted phenomenon. To grasp self in what is selfless, and to grasp no-self in what has a self — those are inverted phenomena. To grasp purity in what is impure, and to grasp impurity in what is utterly pure — those are inverted phenomena. No person knows how to apply themselves properly and correctly to these four inverted phenomena.

Therefore, monks, generate the perception of bliss with regard to phenomena that are suffering. Generate the perception of permanence with regard to the impermanent. Generate the perception of self with regard to the selfless. Generate the perception of purity with regard to the impure. For there exists in the world permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity. And beyond the world as well there exists permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity. Worldly phenomena can be spoken of, yet they are without meaning. What transcends the world can likewise be spoken of, and it also has meaning. Why is this? It is because worldly phenomena, being accompanied by the four inversions, do not comprehend the meaning. How so? Through inverted perception, inverted mind, and inverted views — these three inversions — worldly beings see bliss as suffering, see the permanent as impermanent, see the self as selfless, and see the utterly pure as impure. This is what is called inversion. Because of inversion, worldly beings know words but do not know the meaning.

What, then, is the meaning? No-self means saṃsāra. Self means the Tathāgata. Impermanence means śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Permanence means the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata. Suffering means all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Bliss means complete nirvāṇa. Impurity means conditioned phenomena. Utter purity means the authentic Dharma of buddhas and bodhisattvas — and therefore it is called non-inverted. Thus one who is non-inverted knows both the words that are spoken and the meaning. Whoever wishes to fully abandon the four inversions should, in just this way, come to know permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity.

Then the monks addressed the Blessed One with these words: As the Blessed One has declared — that by overcoming the four inversions one should come to understand permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity — the Tathāgata himself is free of the four inversions and has understood permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity. If the Tathāgata has understood permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity in this way, then why, without first showing us how to fully abandon our four inversions, did he leave us behind and pass into nirvāṇa — remaining for only a single aeon or half an aeon? If the Tathāgata became our Teacher out of compassion for us, then we too would receive it with single-pointed minds, bowing our heads, and apply ourselves diligently. But if the Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa, we too shall dwell together with these afflicted bodies, practicing the holy life, and we too shall pass into nirvāṇa in the wake of the Blessed One.

At that point the Blessed One again declared to the monks: Do not speak thus. I have entrusted all the supreme, authentic Dharma to the great Kāśyapa. The great Kāśyapa shall become your dwelling and support, just as the Tathāgata has been the dwelling and support of all sentient beings.

The great Kāśyapa shall likewise become a dwelling and support for all of you and everyone else. Consider the following example: when a great and powerful king is about to go into seclusion, he entrusts all the affairs of the realm to his great minister. In the same way, the Tathāgata has entrusted all of the supreme Dharma to the great Kāśyapa.

You monks are not right to apply yourselves again and again to the perceptions of impermanence and suffering. Consider this example: in the summer season, when a vaiḍūrya jewel falls into a great lake while people are sporting on a raft, all those who are unskilled dive into the water and each pulls out mud, stones, grass, wood, and gravel, thinking they have found the vaiḍūrya jewel, and they emerge with joy — yet from the very beginning they know it was not the right thing. Meanwhile, because the jewel is in the water, by the power of the jewel the water becomes completely clear, and everyone can see that the precious jewel lies at the bottom, just as one sees the moon reflected in the sky above. At that time, the one among that company who is skilled in means enters the water calmly and retrieves the jewel.

Monks, your applying yourselves to the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and impurity is like those many people each pulling out mud, stones, grass, wood, and gravel and thinking they have found the precious jewel. You too must become thoroughly skilled in means, and wherever you dwell, apply yourselves with skill to the perceptions of self, permanence, bliss, and perfect purity. Your former diligent application to the mere signs of these four qualities of the Dharma was entirely inverted. When you meditate correctly, just as it truly is, upon these perceptions, applying yourselves rightly to them — just as the one skilled in means retrieves the precious jewel — so too you must diligently cultivate the perceptions of self, permanence, bliss, and perfect purity.

Then the monks spoke to the Blessed One with these words: The Blessed One previously taught, "All phenomena are without self — apply yourselves accordingly. If you do so, the perception of self will be abandoned. Once the perception of self is abandoned, you will be free of pride. Once free of pride, you will pass beyond sorrow." What is the meaning of what you said?

Then the Blessed One declared: Excellent! Most excellent! You have asked this matter well, in order to resolve our doubt. Consider this example: there was once an ignorant king of little understanding, and he had a physician who was likewise ignorant and foolish. The king, failing to recognize this, bestowed great favour upon that physician. That foolish physician prescribed milk as medicine for every illness. Not knowing what had originally caused any illness, and not being skilled in administering milk as medicine, he gave milk as medicine for all disorders of wind, phlegm, and bile alike. The king could not discern the physician's true competence, nor distinguish whether the milk was good or bad.

Then a skilled physician arrived from another land, one endowed with the eight branches of medical knowledge, thoroughly expert in healing all diseases, and fully conversant with every form of examination. At that time, the unskilled physician did not seek to ask questions of that skilled physician or to learn from him. Instead, he gave rise to a mind of pride. The skilled physician, relying upon the unskilled one and taking him as his teacher,

in order to learn the secret methods of medical examination, he petitioned the unskilled physician, saying: "I beg you to accept me as your student and to demonstrate and explain the methods of examination." Upon this request, the unskilled physician made the following declaration to the skilled one: "If you will serve me for forty-eight years, I will teach you all the methods of examination." Then the skilled physician replied: "I will do exactly as the unskilled one has said. I will serve you for however long it takes." And so the unskilled physician led the new physician to the royal palace. When they arrived before the king, the new physician spoke at length with the king about the various methods of examination, about many other arts, about the governance of the realm, and about the means of curing the sick, saying: "Great King, please take all of this to heart." At that time, upon hearing these words, the king recognized that the old physician was unskilled and banished him from the land. He then showed even greater respect and honour toward the new physician.

At that time the new physician thought to himself, "The moment has come to instruct this king," and so he addressed the king thus: "Great King, if you would be so gracious as to attend to me, please grant me one request." The king replied: "From my right hand to every limb and member of my body — ask for whatever you wish, and it shall all be given." The physician then made his request: "Although you have granted me the asking of every limb and member of the royal body, I am not bold enough to ask for much. My single request is this: please issue an edict henceforth throughout the land, proclaiming that no one among the king's subjects is to offer milk as a medicinal treatment in the manner of the old physician. Why so? Because that medicine is poisonous and has caused many deaths. If anyone is found administering that medicine, let it be proclaimed that his head and limbs shall be cut off." Having issued this edict, the use of milk as medicine was stopped, untimely deaths ceased, and all became well and happy. "This is the request I ask you to grant."

Then the king said: "This request of yours will be of the greatest benefit. From this day forth, if any subject of the realm should be found administering milk as medicine, permission shall not be given. If anyone administers milk, let it be proclaimed that the chief of his limbs — his head — shall be cut off." And so the edict was issued.

Then the skilled physician compounded medicines of many flavours — hot, cold, sour, sweet, bitter, and the like — and whenever he treated a disease, there was none that was not cured. Then, before long had passed, the king himself was struck by illness and summoned the physician, saying: "I have fallen into great suffering from sickness — how am I to be cured?" The physician examined the king's illness and it appeared that milk was needed as medicine, so he addressed the king: "For the king's illness, when treated by appropriate means, I would prescribe milk as medicine. I must confess that what I said before — that milk ought not be given as medicine — has turned out to be false. There is nothing better than milk as medicine, and since the king's illness has arisen from heat, administering milk as medicine would be good." The king replied: "Physician, are you perhaps out of your senses? You say that milk is beneficial for this illness brought on by heat? Previously you yourself said that milk contains poison — how then am I now to drink it? Are you deceiving me? You had the old physician — who had praised milk — expelled on the grounds that his medicine was poisonous, and now after all that you say that milk is good medicine for a sick person. My old physician must surely have been more skilled than you."

Then the physician again addressed the king, saying: "Great King, please do not speak thus.

Consider, for example, how a woodworm's trail can serve as a letter. The worm itself does not know whether it is a letter or not, but when a wise and discerning person sees it, they recognize it as a letter — and no one finds that surprising. Great King, the earlier physician was just like this: not understanding illnesses, he prescribed milk as medicine for all cases without distinction — just as the worm's trail becomes a letter. The earlier physician understood neither the good and bad qualities of milk nor whether it was appropriate or inappropriate.

The king said: "How is it that the earlier physician did not know this?" The physician replied: "Milk, Your Majesty, can be both a poison and a nectar. How can it be both? If a cow has not been given bad fodder and dry grass, has not eaten straw, if her calf is well tamed and gentle, if she lives not on a high mountain or in dense forest, if she is given clean flowing water to drink and is not driven too hard, if she does not live with a bull or share a herd but feeds and drinks at her ease, and moves about and rests peacefully — the milk of such a cow benefits the ill and is therefore called nectar. Any other milk is called poisonous."

When the Great King heard these words he said: "Physician, excellent! Most excellent have you spoken! From now on I shall know both the good and bad qualities of milk and what is appropriate or inappropriate." The physician then administered milk as medicine, the illness was cured, and a proclamation was issued to all the people of the realm: "From this day forward, take milk as medicine." When the people heard this, they all cried out in anger: "Has our Great King been seized by a hungry ghost? Has he gone mad? What has come over him? We have been deceived — he is telling us to take milk as medicine." All the people of the realm, full of anger, came before the king. To them the king declared: "Do not reproach me. Whether milk is appropriate or inappropriate as medicine is a matter of this physician's diagnosis — I am not at fault." Then the Great King and all the people of the realm became thoroughly pleased and satisfied, and they showed the physician great honour and respect. Milk was administered as medicine to all the sick, and their illnesses were healed.

Monks, you should likewise understand the Tathāgata — the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the unsurpassed one, tamer and guide of persons, teacher of gods and human beings, the Blessed One — as being like a great physician who came into the world, subdued all the physicians who were tīrthikas with wrong views, and declared to every king: "I am the physician." In order to discipline the tīrthikas he taught: "There is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-force, no vital essence, no agent of life, no awareness, no sight, no act, no doer."

Monks, when tīrthikas speak of a self it is just like the worm's trail becoming a letter — similar to that. Therefore the Tathāgata taught no-self within the Dharma of the buddhas, and he did so in order to discipline sentient beings, knowing the right time. Yet his teaching of no-self does so with cause and condition present; and his teaching that a self exists is like the skilled physician who knows when milk is appropriate and when it is not as medicine — it is not at all like the grasping at a self held by childish and base persons. The grasping at a self held by childish and base persons — is it the size of a thumb,

or as small as a subtle particle — that is what they grasp at. The Tathāgata's use of the word "self" is not like that. Therefore, although he declared that all phenomena are without self, in ultimate truth they are not without a self. What is called "self" is that phenomenon which is true, which truly and permanently abides, which is a lord and master, which is unchanging and unmoving — that is called "self." It is just as the great physician is skilled regarding milk as medicine. The Tathāgata is likewise: for the sake of ordinary persons he declared that in all phenomena a self truly exists. Therefore, you and the rest of the fourfold assembly should, in just this manner, diligently apply yourselves to all phenomena.

The Fourth Fascicle. The Blessed One then spoke further to the monks, saying this: "Monks, whatever doubts you have regarding the Vinaya (monastic discipline), ask whatever you wish about them, and I will teach and explain so as to set your minds at ease. I have directly realized that all phenomena are emptiness by essential nature. Monks, you should not think that the Tathāgata has done nothing more than realize all phenomena as emptiness by intrinsic nature. Monks, now is the time to ask whatever doubts you have about the Vinaya."

Thereupon the monks addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Blessed One, we lack wisdom and do not have the capacity to put questions and supplications to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha. Why is this? Because the domain of conduct of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, his meditative absorption is inconceivable, and what the Teacher has taught is also inconceivable. We are of feeble wisdom and do not have the capacity to put questions and supplications to the Tathāgata."

"Blessed One, by way of example: there was an elderly man, one hundred and twenty years old, bent with age, always sick and without the strength to make effort, frail, and no longer in command of his own life. Wishing to pursue some business in another land, a wealthy man entrusted him with hundreds of thousands of gold coins, saying: 'I am entrusting you with these precious jewels. After ten or twenty years, when I return, give them back to me.' That old man took the jewels, but before long he died of illness. His lineage was broken, and everything he had been entrusted with was scattered and lost. When the owner of the wealth returned, there was no one from whom to recover them. Likewise, that foolish man whom he had entrusted — since no one had examined whether it was fitting or not to entrust him — when the owner came back from the other land, all the jewels were scattered and could not be recovered.

"Blessed One, we hearers (śrāvakas) are like that. Although we have heard the Tathāgata again and again earnestly teaching the Vinaya, we are unable to hold it, to retain it, or to keep the Dharma lasting long — just as the old man received what was entrusted to him by another. Since we lack wisdom, there is nothing that we can even ask or inquire about regarding the Vinaya."

The Blessed One then declared to the monks: "If you ask me today, it will be for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings. Therefore ask whatever you wish."

Thereupon the monks addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Blessed One, take for example a man in the prime of his life, twenty-five years old, in full vigor of youth, endowed with a handsome form, with abundant wealth, precious jewels, gold, silver, and beryl in great plenty, and surrounded by a retinue of father, mother, wife, and children. Suppose someone entrusted him with wealth and precious jewels,

and said to him: "I have business to attend to and must travel to another land. I entrust these jewels and precious things to you. When I return, please give them back."

The young man guarded them as carefully as if they were his own possessions. Later, that man fell ill, and gathering all those close to him around him, he gave this instruction: "These precious jewels were entrusted to me by a certain elder. When he comes to reclaim them, return them to him."

A wise and discerning person, upon inquiring whether the things had been entrusted or not, would recover all the jewels as soon as the other returned.

In just the same way, Blessed One, if this precious Jewel of the Dharma is entrusted to those who are joyful or to monks, it will not endure for long. Why is that? Because the great Kāśyapa and all the śrāvakas are impermanent, just as the elder who received another's wealth on trust will eventually give it back. Therefore, if this supreme precious Jewel of the Dharma is entrusted to bodhisattvas, then, because bodhisattvas are skilled in questioning and in giving answers, this precious Dharma will endure long and will spread vastly for immeasurable eons, bringing benefit to sentient beings — just as wealth and precious jewels entrusted to a man in the prime of youth will remain secure. For this reason, it is the great bodhisattvas who have the power to request and to beseech. As for us, our wisdom is like that of insects — we do not have the capacity to request the Tathāgata's profoundly deep Dharma.

Having said this, they fell silent.

Then the Blessed One spoke words of high praise: "Excellent! Excellent!" And he said: "Monks, you have well attained the mind of one without defilement, the mind of an arhat. I too have considered this: by these two conditions, if this Great Vehicle is entrusted to bodhisattvas, the sacred Dharma will endure long."

Then the Blessed One declared to the sons and daughters of noble families assembled in the midst of the retinue: "My lifespan is immeasurable, and my individual perfect knowledge is likewise inexhaustible. Ask whatever you wish concerning the Vinaya and the Abhidharma, freely and as you desire." He repeated this invitation two and three times.

At that time, in the midst of the assembled retinue, a great bodhisattva who resided in the city called Tāla — a young man of brahmin lineage named the Great Kāśyapa — arose from his seat, inspired by the blessing of the Buddha. He arranged his outer robe over one shoulder, circumambulated one hundred thousand times, knelt upon his right knee, joined his palms together, and addressed the Blessed One in these words: "If the Blessed One would grant me permission to ask, and having asked, to receive a prophecy in response, then I shall inquire of the Tathāgata on one matter."

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "You may ask the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha whatever you wish, and I shall prophesy concerning each thing asked, so that your mind will be satisfied and free of doubt."

Then the great bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, since out of compassion you grant me leave to ask — my wisdom is like that of an insect, while the qualities of the Tathāgata are supremely lofty, and you are fully surrounded by an indestructible retinue like that of a beast of prey, like a lion. The body of the Tathāgata is likewise indestructible, like a vajra, with a hue resembling vaiḍūrya gemstone, and you are encompassed by a boundless ocean of gnosis and wisdom.

The great bodhisattvas and other beings dwelling in the midst of this assembly likewise possess supreme and limitless qualities beyond measure. How could I dare to ask questions here in the midst of this assembly, which is like a herd of great fragrant elephants? Yet by the blessing of the Buddha and by the power of the wholesome roots of this vast retinue, I wish to ask a little. And so he addressed the Blessed One in verse:

What is it that makes life long,
and how does one attain a body indestructible as a vajra?
Through what causes and conditions
does one also attain the power of supreme stability?

How does one, through this very sūtra,
at last arrive at the perfection of the far shore?
Whatever the Blessed One intends —
please declare it to sentient beings.

How does one attain true greatness
and become a support and refuge for all?
Without being an arhat,
one is yet equal to an arhat.

How do the māras of the gods
seek to create obstacles? Please tell us.
How are the words of the Blessed One
and the words of māras to be understood and distinguished?

How do those who steer the rudder
joyfully speak the ultimate truth,
and yet, while truly endowed with virtue,
display the four inversions?

How does one perform virtuous action?
O Great Sage, please explain.
How do bodhisattvas
come to see even what is hard to see?

How does one take in the full meaning,
and yet grasp only half of it?
How does one conduct oneself in conformity with the noble ones,
stage by stage, as it were —

like Kaliṅga, like sun and moon,
like the pole star among the great stars?
How does one, without having aroused the mind,
still be called a bodhisattva?

How does one attain a fearless mind
in the midst of the assembly,
and be free of all blemish,
like the golden river of Jambudvīpa?

How does one in this turbid world
remain unattached, like a lotus?
How does one, though surrounded by afflictions,
not become tainted by them —

like a skilled physician who cures diseases
yet does not contract the illness?
How does one become like a captain
upon the great ocean of saṃsāra?

How does one utterly abandon saṃsāra,
like a snake shedding its skin?
How is it that, like a wish-fulfilling divine tree,
one becomes so for the Three Jewels —

and when there is no family of the three vehicles,
for what purpose were they taught?
For example, just as pleasure has not yet arisen,
how can one be said to experience pleasure?

How do bodhisattvas
attain an indestructible retinue?
How does one become an eye for leaders
who are blind and bewildered?

How does one who has many heads teach —
O Great Sage, please explain.
How do those who speak the Dharma arise
like the days of the waxing moon?

How does one who has reached the end
demonstrate the passing into nirvāṇa?
How does one who is courageous and diligent
show the path to humans, gods, and māras?

How does one know the characteristics of phenomena
and experience the bliss of Dharma?
How are bodhisattvas
entirely free from illness?

How does one who teaches with intention
reveal what was spoken for the sake of ordinary beings?
What is the meaning of having reached the end,
and how is one who has not yet reached it described?

If it is taught to cut doubt,
why is it not stated as a single definitive answer?
How does one draw near
to the supreme, unsurpassed awakening?

On behalf of the bodhisattvas,
I ask this of the Tathāgata:
Please teach those who are holy
the deeply profound conduct.

If the nature of bliss pervades
all phenomena in all their aspects,
then let the supreme Great Sage
separately analyze and teach it.

You who are the supreme two-footed being, like a physician,
the support and refuge of ordinary people —
though I have begun to ask of the aggregates,
the wisdom that would seek them out is not in me.

In the same way, even a diligent bodhisattva
is unable to know
the domain of the buddhas,
which is supremely profound.

At that moment the Blessed One praised bodhisattva Kāśyapa, saying: "Excellent! Excellent!" And then he said: "Son of good family, although you have not yet attained the gnosis of omniscience, your asking and inquiring into the essence of the supremely profound is not in the least different from asking with the gnosis of omniscience. Son of good family, long ago, at the time of awakening to full and perfect enlightenment beneath the tree of awakening, bodhisattvas arrived from immeasurable and innumerable buddha-fields, as many as the grains of sand in the Gaṅgā river, and the variety of words, the meanings, and the qualities with which they asked me about the supremely profound were exactly like these and no different. Whoever asks in such a way acts for the benefit and the happiness of immeasurable sentient beings."

Then bodhisattva Kāśyapa said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, since I lack wisdom, I do not have the power to ask about such a supremely profound matter. Blessed One, it is like this: bees do not have the power to fly to the far shore of the ocean, nor the power to traverse the entire expanse of the sky. In just the same way, I do not have the power to ask about such a supremely profound matter — the nature of the ocean of the Tathāgata's gnosis, which is like space. Blessed One, it is as if a precious jewel from the crest ornament of a king were entrusted to a minister who guards the treasury; that minister would receive it on the crown of his head and guard it with the utmost care. In just the same way, I receive on the crown of my head this profound and vastly extensive meaning spoken by the Tathāgata, and I devote great effort to guarding it. Why is that? Because I do so for the sake of accomplishing the supremely profound wisdom."

Then the Blessed One spoke to bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, listen very carefully. I will explain to you the karma that extends the life-span of the Tathāgata. When a bodhisattva hears the causes and conditions of that karma, his life will become long. Therefore listen very carefully. Whatever karma serves as a cause for awakening — that is to be grasped carefully and listened to; and having heard it, one should teach it extensively to others. Son of good family, I myself in former times applied great effort to accomplishing those very karmas, and swiftly I attained complete and perfect unsurpassed awakening. This too I will explain to you in detail. Son of good family, it is like this: when a crown prince brings joy to a king by being born, the king, out of love and remembrance, visits all the places where the child was born. In just the same way, a bodhisattva who wishes for long life should in the very same way guard and protect all sentient beings as though they were his own children, generating loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and great equanimity, and should uphold the precept of not taking life. One should apply oneself to virtuous qualities and establish all sentient beings in the path of the five precepts and the ten virtuous actions. Furthermore, one should liberate all sentient beings who suffer in the hells, among hungry ghosts, among animals, in the realm of asuras, and throughout all their existences — freeing those who are not yet free,

leading those who have not yet reached the far shore to reach it, and guiding those who have not yet passed beyond sorrow to pass beyond sorrow, and filling those who are afraid with ease and joy. Through such causes and conditions of action, a bodhisattva will gain long life and attain the power of wisdom, and in whatever existence the consciousness passes, rebirth will occur among the gods of the high realms. Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, the meaning of what has been said — that a great bodhisattva should generate the perception of regarding all sentient beings as equal to an only child — is so very profound that I do not understand it. Blessed One, it seems improper that a Tathāgata should have said that a great bodhisattva should generate the perception of regarding all sentient beings with an evenminded love as though they were an only child. Why so? Among those who have entered the teaching of the Tathāgata, there are some who have broken their moral discipline, some who act improperly, and some who actually damage the sacred Dharma — how, then, can one generate the perception of regarding even these as though they were an only child?"

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: "That is indeed so. That is indeed so. I myself regard all sentient beings as my son Rāhula."

Kāśyapa then said to the Blessed One: "Formerly, on the fifteenth day of the month, when a fully purified Saṅgha was performing the restoration ceremony, a certain immature youth — one whose body, speech, and mind had not been tamed — listened to the Saṅgha's restoration ceremony from a secluded place, and Vajrapāṇi, through the blessing of his buddha-power, struck him to dust with his vajra club. Blessed One, since Vajrapāṇi in his great anger separated that youth from his life, why did the Tathāgata say that all sentient beings are like his son Rāhula?"

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: "Do not speak thus. That youth too was merely an emanation, not a real human being — he appeared in order to remove those who had broken their moral discipline from within a fully purified Saṅgha. Vajrapāṇi likewise was merely an emanation. Kāśyapa, even toward those who harm the sacred Dharma, who are driven by wrong craving, who take life, who hold wrong views, and who have broken their moral discipline — toward even these I generate great compassion and regard them as I regard my son Rāhula. Son of good family, take the following example: when ministers of a king have committed an offense and violated the law, the king does not release them but applies whatever penalty the law prescribes. A Tathāgata is not like that. When there are those who have fallen away from the teaching, he performs the act of expulsion, the act of reprimand, the act of suspension, the act of formally raising the offense, the act of rendering invisible, the act of pacification, and the act of abandoning wrong views. Son of good family, in this way the Tathāgata performs the work of fully taming those who disparage the Dharma, and he reveals to those who conduct themselves badly the ripened fruit of their karma. Son of good family, know it in this way: the Tathāgata is one who grants fearlessness even to wicked sentient beings. If he sends forth even one, two, or five rays of light, all sentient beings touched by them will wholly abandon their misdeeds. Therefore the Tathāgata is endowed with immeasurable power of that kind. Son of good family, if you wish to see for yourself what you have not yet seen — the qualities you have not yet beheld — I shall show you a portion of it."

After my passing into nirvāṇa, know that any person — in whatever region there are monks who possess moral discipline, whose conduct is unblemished, who guard the sacred Dharma, and who, seeing those who conduct themselves in ways contrary to the Dharma, expel them and punish them with penalties — that person obtains merit that is immeasurable and incalculable.

Son of good family, consider this example: a king who conducts himself only in unwholesome ways falls ill, and a neighboring king, hearing that things have come to such a pass, raises an army in order to be rid of that ailing king. If the ailing king, frightened by the weakness of his own power and forces, abandons non-virtue and strives toward virtue, then that opposing king who advanced against him obtains immeasurable merit.

In just the same way, monks who uphold the Dharma likewise obtain immeasurable merit if, by expelling and penalizing those persons who conduct themselves contrary to the Dharma, they bring them into the practice of wholesome qualities.

Son of good family, consider this further example: if a poisonous plant springs up in a householder's garden, as soon as the householder recognizes it as poisonous he eradicates it from the root.
