Likewise, if a gray hair appears on the head of a young man, feeling ashamed he pulls it out from the root at once, ensuring that no more will grow. A monk who upholds the Dharma is like that: when he sees a monk whose moral discipline has degenerated conducting himself in ways contrary to the sacred Dharma, he must expel that monk from the community and impose a penalty. A monk of good character who sees those whose precepts have degenerated and neither expels them from the community nor penalizes them — know that such a monk is an enemy of the Dharma taught by the Buddha. But one who does expel them and impose penalties is a true and genuine attendant-śrāvaka of mine.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One and said: "As the Blessed One has taught, that he looks upon all sentient beings as a son — as his own child Rāhula — such a statement seems improper. Blessed One, if one person raises a weapon and strikes at the Buddha, and another person anoints the body of the Buddha with a sandalwood fan, and the Blessed One regards both with equanimity, then why did you say that those whose precepts have degenerated are to be cut down with penalties? If those whose precepts have degenerated are to be penalized, that contradicts your earlier teaching."

The Blessed One then spoke to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, consider this example: a king or great minister has two, three, or four sons who are handsome in form and sharp in wisdom. He goes to a learned teacher, an expert instructor, and makes this request: 'I entrust these sons of mine to you — please train them in deportment, classical learning, the arts, letters, arithmetic, and reckoning. Even if three of the four sons should die under the rod, so be it; do whatever it takes to train the one remaining. If three of them die, I will hold no grievance against you.' Kāśyapa, what do you think? Does the father of that child and that teaching master incur the fault of killing? The answer came: 'No, Blessed One.' And why not? Because it is done with the thought of love, wishing them to acquire training — and not with ill will; therefore immeasurable merit is obtained.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata is just like that: he looks upon even those whose precepts have degenerated as though they were his only child. The Tathāgata has entrusted the unsurpassed sacred Dharma to kings, great ministers, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, and in doing so he has directed that among kings and those four assemblies, those who have entered into the training shall, through heightened moral discipline —

— meditative absorption, and wisdom attain these through encouragement. Whoever among the three trainings does not train, but instead is lazy, allows their moral discipline to degenerate, and makes the Dharma unsuitable, shall be punished with punishment by the king, the great ministers, and the four assemblies. Son of good family, would that king and those four assemblies incur the fault of blameworthy wrongdoing?" "No, Blessed One." The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, if that king and those four assemblies would not become guilty, then what need is there even to speak of the Tathāgata? Son of good family, the Tathāgata, with an equanimous mind, regards all sentient beings as though they were his only child. One who thinks in this way is called a bodhisattva who, with an equanimous mind, perceives all sentient beings as though they were his only child.

Son of good family, a bodhisattva who diligently applies himself to that practice in this way will attain long life and will come to know his former existences.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then again addressed the Blessed One in these words: "As the Buddha has said, a bodhisattva who diligently cultivates equanimous mind and perceives all sentient beings as though they were his only child will attain long life — it does not seem fitting that the Tathāgata would say such a thing. Why so? Consider this: a certain learned person, skilled in teaching many aspects of Dharma in service to the wise, who is endowed with wisdom, comes to his house and strikes his parents with sticks and stones. Parents are a field of merit; they render only benefit and happiness, and are exceedingly difficult to encounter — they are worthy of veneration. If one harms and injures them, this contradicts and conflicts with what a seeker of Dharma should say and do. The Tathāgata is just like that: if a bodhisattva diligently cultivates equanimous mind and, by perceiving all sentient beings as though they were his only child, attains long life and comes to know his former existences — and does not pass away, but abides constantly in the world — then why did the Blessed One's own life span become extremely short, no different from that of an ordinary person? Could it be that the Tathāgata regarded all sentient beings as though they were enemies? Blessed One, what former wrongdoing did you commit, and how many vital faculties did you separate from life, that your own life span became so extremely short, not even reaching a hundred years?"

The Blessed One then declared to Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, why have you spoken such disrespectful words in the presence of the Tathāgata? The life span of the Tathāgata is the supreme and most excellent of all life spans. It is also the supreme and most excellent among all permanent phenomena.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again asked the Blessed One: "What, then, is meant by saying that the Tathāgata's life span is long?" The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, there are eight great rivers: the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Śalā, the Alilabaratā, the Mahā, the Sindhu, the Pakṣu, and the Sītā — these eight great rivers, together with all other streams, flow down into the great ocean. Kāśyapa, in just the same way, all the rivers of vital life of every being — gods and all others, those dwelling on earth and in the sky — flow down into the ocean of the Tathāgata's life span. Therefore the Tathāgata's life span is immeasurable.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, consider this: from the lake called Anavatapta (Skt. Anavatapta), four great rivers flow forth. The Tathāgata likewise is the source from which all life arises.

Kāśyapa, consider this: among all permanent phenomena, space is supreme. The Tathāgata likewise is supreme among all that is permanent."

is supreme. Kāśyapa, consider this: among all medicines, the essence of butter is supreme. In just the same way, the Tathāgata is supreme in life span among all sentient beings.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "If the Tathāgata's life span is such, it would be fitting that he remain for one full eon, or for just short of one eon, and continuously pour down the rain of the holy Dharma."

The Blessed One declared: "Kāśyapa, do not give rise to the perception that the Tathāgata is subject to cessation or exhaustion. Kāśyapa, even a monk, a nun, a layman, a laywoman, or even a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika) who possesses the five superknowledges and has attained mastery can, for the span of an eon or just short of an eon, gain power over walking, standing, sitting, and lying down through the sky. Flames blaze from the left side of the body, water flows from the right side, smoke billows from the upper body, and one can transform into what appears to be a great mass of fire. And if one wishes to remain alive for as long as desired, one abides at will and gains mastery over the length of one's life. If even one who has only attained the five superknowledges possesses such miraculous power, what need is there to speak of the Tathāgata, who has obtained the power to govern all phenomena? What need is there to speak of remaining for half an eon, or one eon, or a hundred eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or an immeasurable number of eons? Therefore, understand the Tathāgata as one whose nature is permanent, who abides with a permanent body, whose nature is unchanging. The Tathāgata's body is an emanation body (nirmāṇakāya); it is not a body sustained by food. For the sake of liberating sentient beings, it was shown in a form resembling a poisonous tree, and therefore understand that the passing into nirvāṇa that was shown was a display. Kāśyapa, therefore understand the Tathāgata as one whose nature is permanent and unchanging. You and those like you should apply yourselves with the utmost and tireless diligence to the ultimate. Having done so with such diligence, explain it widely to others."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "What difference and distinction is there between transcendent phenomena and worldly phenomena? If, as the Buddha has said, the Buddha too has the nature of permanence and is unchanging, then Brahmā, the god of the worldly realm, is also permanent, and Śakra, the ruling deity, is also permanent and unchanging. The self that is spoken of as being of unchanging nature is also permanent, intrinsic nature is also permanent, and subtle particles are also said to be permanent. If this is so and the Tathāgata too has the nature of permanence, why does the Tathāgata not openly demonstrate permanence? If permanence is not openly demonstrated, what difference and distinction can there be? From Brahmā down to subtle particles and intrinsic nature, those who claim permanence have not openly demonstrated it either."

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Consider this example. A certain householder owned many cows of various colors, and he entrusted them all together to a cowherd, who drove them to wherever grass and water were to be found and kept them alive. This was not for the sake of ordinary curds and milk alone, but for the sake of obtaining the essence of butter. Later, when the householder died, the cows were driven off by thieves. Those thieves, having no women among them, milked the cows and each drank the milk separately. Afterward, the thieves said to one another: 'In the past, that great householder kept all these cows not merely for curds and milk, but solely for the sake of the essence of butter. Now, what method shall we use

to obtain the essence of butter,' and they deliberated together. Now, the essence of butter is the finest of all savory things in the world, yet even if milk is available, they said, there is no vessel in which to pour it. Then they discussed it again, saying, 'We have a leather bag, so let us pour it into the bag.' But even though a place for pouring was available, since they did not know the method of curdling and churning, they were unable to obtain even ordinary cream, let alone plain butter, still less the essence of butter. Those wicked thieves, in their desire for the essence of butter, added water again and again, and thus everything from the milk to the essence of butter was corrupted. Foolish people are just like this. Whatever small measure of virtue they possess comes from the holy Dharma of the Tathāgata. Why is that? After the buddha, the Blessed One, passed completely into nirvāṇa, stealing from the virtuous Dharma of the Tathāgata the portions belonging to moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom is like those thieves stealing the cows. Foolish people, though they may obtain a measure of moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom, yet having no skill in the methods of application, are unable to achieve liberation and to teach it. For this reason, not being able to attain enduring moral discipline, enduring meditative absorption, enduring wisdom, or liberation up to its fullness, is comparable to those thieves who, lacking skill in method, fail to obtain the essence of butter. Just as those thieves, in their desire for the essence of butter, added water, so too base people are like them: desiring liberation, they say that nirvāṇa is self, sentient being, life-force, person, Brahmā, a sovereign deity, subtle particles, the intrinsic nature of the world, moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or the sphere without perception. But they neither attain true liberation nor transcend suffering, just as those thieves did not obtain the essence of butter. Base people, through the causes and conditions of having practiced a little celibacy and shown some reverence to their parents, are born as gods in the higher realms and experience a small measure of pleasant enjoyment — this is like those thieves diluting the milk with water. Base people do not understand that they have been born as gods in the higher realms through the causes of practicing a little celibacy and showing some reverence to their parents. Furthermore, they do not know moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, or how to take refuge in the Three Jewels. Because of this ignorance, though they speak of permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity, they do not understand even that. Therefore, the Tathāgata came into the world and taught and explained permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity. Just as when a wheel-turning king (Skt. cakravartin) appears in the world, the force of his merit causes the wicked thieves to flee and scatter in all directions, and since the cows have not perished, the wheel-turning king entrusts them to a skilled cowherd, and through the skill of that cowherd the essence of butter comes to be present once more, and because the essence of butter is present all sentient beings are freed from the suffering of illness — in the same way, when the king who turns the wheel of Dharma came into the world, base people became unable to teach moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom, and they fled and scattered. Then the Blessed One, for the benefit of sentient beings, taught and explained to the great bodhisattvas both worldly Dharmas and transcendent Dharmas, and thus the great bodhisattvas, great beings, came to obtain what is like the essence of butter.

Furthermore, the way in which countless, immeasurable sentient beings are to obtain the Dharma that is like the nectar of the unsurpassable is as follows: it is the qualities of the Tathāgata — permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity. For this reason, son of good family, know that the Tathāgata is endowed with the quality of permanence and unchangingness. This is unlike what worldly, base people say when they claim that Brahmā and the other gods possess the quality of permanence. In brief, the quality known as permanence belongs to the Tathāgata alone and not to any other phenomena. Kāśyapa, therefore, one should understand the body of the Tathāgata accordingly.

Kāśyapa, whatever sons of good family or daughters of good family always apply themselves with one-pointed mind to these two words — "the buddha is permanent" and "the buddha abides" — know that such a person follows after me and has arrived at the place where I have gone. Kāśyapa, whatever son of good family applies himself to these two words — if he has abandoned conceptual signs, know that the Tathāgata has resolved to pass into nirvāṇa. Son of good family, the meaning of passing into nirvāṇa is itself the nature of reality of a buddha.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, what is the meaning of what is called the nature of reality? Blessed One, since I do not understand the meaning of what the nature of reality is, I ask the Tathāgata, out of compassionate care, to explain it in full.

What is called the nature of reality is utterly free of body, and what is free of body is nothing whatsoever. If it is nothing whatsoever, how can what is called body be established? If body were to be established, then the nature of reality too would not be present in the body. And if the nature of reality were not present in the body, how is it to be established? How am I to understand these matters?

With this the Blessed One declared to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: Son of good family, you should not negate the nature of reality in this way. In the nature of reality there is no negation. Son of good family, take for example the gods of the sphere of non-perception: though they possess the aggregate of form, because they have no perception of form it would be inappropriate to ask of those gods how they dwell, how they enjoy bliss, how they engage in perception, and how they hear and see. In the same way, son of good family, the domain of the Tathāgata is not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Son of good family, one should not say that the body of the Tathāgata is subject to cessation. Son of good family, cessation is a domain of buddhas and is not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Son of good family, you should not speculate or conjecture about where the Tathāgata dwells, where he moves, what he perceives, and what he enjoys. Son of good family, these matters are not something to be known and understood by you and those like you, for the dharmakāya of a buddha and the manifold skillful means are inconceivable.

Son of good family, moreover, always be mindful of and apply yourself to the buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. These three things — the Dharma in its threefold aspect — have the defining characteristic of non-differentiation, the defining characteristic of non-impermanence, and the defining characteristic of non-transformation. Whoever perceives these three Dharmas as separate — such a person does not truly take refuge in the three refuges, is said to lack moral discipline, and is incapable of attaining even the awakening of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. But whoever applies himself with a perception of permanence to that which is inconceivable — such a person is the proper basis for going for refuge.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: because a tree exists, there is a shadow. The Tathāgata is like this — because he possesses a permanent Dharma, there exists a proper basis for going for refuge; but he is not impermanent. Whoever says of the Tathāgata that he is impermanent — such a Tathāgata would not be a proper basis for going for refuge for gods and men of the world together.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, consider this: when the sky is overcast, a fruit tree is present and yet there is no shadow."

The Blessed One declared: "Kāśyapa, one must not say that the tree is present and yet has no shadow — it is simply that it cannot be seen with the eye of flesh. Son of good family, the Tathāgata is like this: he abides permanently by his very own intrinsic nature, unchanging and without transformation. But because one lacks the eye of wisdom, one cannot see him — just as at the time of an overcast sky one cannot see the shadow of the tree. Ordinary beings, after the buddha passes into nirvāṇa, may say that the Tathāgata is possessed of the quality of impermanence — and those who say that the Tathāgata is separate and distinct from the Dharma and the Saṅgha will not come to be among those who go for refuge to the three refuges. It is as if, because your mother and father are separately individual, one were to call them impermanent."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, it is a wondrous thing that I will come to recall that the buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are permanent — and that this memory will extend back through seven generations of ancestors. Blessed One, I will habituate myself to contemplating the inconceivable nature of the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; and having myself become accustomed to this, I will also teach its meaning widely to others. Those who do not have faith in this have long been cultivating the meditation on impermanence — and toward such persons I will act as a mother or as hail."

Then the Blessed One declared to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Excellent! Excellent!" And he said: "You are one who guards and fully upholds the true Dharma. By thus guarding the Dharma, and through the roots of virtue that do not deceive sentient beings, through that very condition you will come to have long life and knowledge of your former abodes."

This is the first chapter, called "The Chapter on the Life-span," from the noble sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa.

Then the Blessed One spoke to Kāśyapa as follows: "Son of good family, what is called the body of the Tathāgata is a body that abides permanently, an indestructible body, a vajra body — not a body that depends on food, but the dharmakāya."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, such bodies as you have described I have not seen. What I have seen is a body that is impermanent, destructible, made of dust, and dependent on food. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata has departed into complete parinirvāṇa."

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: "You must not look upon the body of the Tathāgata as though it were without essence or subject to destruction, like the body of an ordinary being. Son of good family, you should understand it in this way: the body of the Tathāgata is stable for immeasurable aeons, it has essence and is indestructible, it is not like the body of gods or humans, it is not a body subject to destruction, it is not a body dependent on food."

The body of the Tathāgata is a body that is not-body — not arising and not ceasing; not aggregated; not made; immeasurable; infinite; without trace; without consciousness; without form; ultimately perfectly pure; unshaking, without sensation; without formations; without abiding; unmade; without savour; unmixed; not compounded.

Not karma, not result, not conduct, not cessation, not mind, not countable, inconceivable, immeasurable, not fully known, separated from mind, yet also not separated from mind, without equality with mind, yet also not without it, without going and coming, yet also not without going and coming, indestructible, undiminished, uncut, not cut off, not arisen, not ceasing, without a lord, yet also not without a lord, neither existent nor non-existent, without feeling, without conceptual thought, without syllable, yet also not without syllable, not meditative absorption, yet also not without meditative absorption, without anything to behold, yet manifest and apparent, without abiding, yet also not without abiding, without support, yet also not without support, neither darkness nor light, neither at peace nor unpeaceful, not grasping at anything whatsoever, not releasing, perfectly pure, stainless, without dispute, with all dispute cut off, abiding without abiding, not grasping, not a phenomenon of falling, yet also not a non-phenomenon, not a field of merit, yet also not not a field of merit, inexhaustible and without exhaustion, free from all exhaustion, empty of emptiness itself, not permanently abiding, not cut off by a stream of moments, without the stain of turbidity, without syllable, separated from syllable, not sound, not spoken, not something cultivated through habituation, not expressible, not something inferred, not one, not many, not form, not a sign, yet adorned with excellent marks, not bold, not fearful, without peace, not at peace, not tormented, not something to be seen as free from torment, without sign. The Tathāgata, though he has acted for the benefit of all sentient beings, is without the act of having benefited sentient beings; though he liberates sentient beings, there is no liberation; though he causes sentient beings to fully awaken, there is no full awakening. He teaches the Dharma truly and just as it is, in non-duality, immeasurable, equal to what is unequal, equal to space, in harmony with formlessness and the unborn, uninterrupted, impermanent, yet though always moving in the single vehicle, sentient beings perceive it as three. Unchanging, irreversible, with all afflictions (kleśas) utterly severed, non-contentious, not singular, not a defining characteristic, yet abiding in defining characteristics, not assembled, not dispersed, not long, not short, not round, not square, not the aggregates, not the sense bases, not the elements, yet also not other than the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, not increasing, not decreasing, not good, not bad.

The body of the Tathāgata is thus endowed with immeasurable qualities beyond measure: without knowing, yet also without not-knowing; without seeing, yet also without not-seeing; not conditioned, not unconditioned; not the world, yet also not other than the world; not made, yet also not unmade; not abiding, yet also not non-abiding; not the four great elements, yet also not other than the four great elements; not a cause, yet also not without cause; not a sentient being, yet also not without sentient beings; not an ascetic, not a brahmin; like a lion, a great lion; not a body, yet also not a non-body; inexpressible, separated even from the defining characteristic of a single dharma, not to be estimated or counted. At the moment of passing into nirvāṇa, not passing into nirvāṇa. Such is the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, endowed with immeasurable and supreme qualities of this kind.

Kāśyapa, this is known by the Tathāgata alone; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Kāśyapa, such is the body of the Tathāgata, endowed with immeasurable qualities — it is not a body nourished and sustained by food. Kāśyapa, given that the body of the Tathāgata is endowed with true qualities of this kind, how could there be in it illness, suffering, insubstantiality, or instability like an unfired clay pot? Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata displayed illness and suffering for the sake of taming sentient beings.

Son of good family, you should understand it in this way: the body of the Tathāgata is a vajra body. From this day forward, you should hold this meaning one-pointedly in mind, and you should not think of it as a body of food. Teach others as well that the body of the Tathāgata is the dharmakāya.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, if the Tathāgata is endowed with such qualities, how could there be illness, impermanence, or decay? From this day forward I shall contemplate the body of the Tathāgata as permanent and the dharmakāya as supremely blissful, and I shall teach others likewise. Blessed One, since the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is indestructible like a vajra, I do not seek what has arisen from causes.

The Blessed One then declared to Kāśyapa: It is through the cause and condition of protecting and upholding the sacred Dharma that one comes to be endowed with a vajra body. Kāśyapa, it is through the cause and condition of my having guarded and protected the Dharma in former times that I have come to be endowed with a vajra body, abiding always, indestructible.

Son of good family, one who protects and guards the sacred Dharma does not grasp at the five precepts, does not keep the code of conduct, but takes up weapons — swords, bows and arrows, spears, and the like — and protects monks whose monastic discipline is perfectly pure. Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: But Blessed One, is not a monk who has set aside his guarding role and dwells in a solitary place — a charnel ground or at the foot of a tree — a true monk? Will one who follows the way of protection be called a householder who grasps at a head?

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: Do not say "a householder who grasps at a head." Wherever a monk may dwell, if he takes only what is needed for bodily subsistence, reads and recites the sūtras, applies himself to meditation, and, when there are those who ask about the Dharma, teaches them generosity, moral discipline, the accumulation of merit, few desires, contentment, and other Dharma topics of various kinds — yet he does not roar the lion's roar, he is not surrounded like a lion, he cannot tame those who practice the depraved Dharma. Such a monk can accomplish neither his own benefit nor the benefit of others; he is heedless and lazy. Know that even though he guards moral discipline and practices celibacy, he can accomplish nothing whatsoever.

As for a monk who has abundant necessities of life and perfectly guards his moral discipline, who roars the lion's roar, reciting the nine divisions of the sacred Dharma — sūtras, prose and verse mixed compositions (geyas), prophecies, verses, intentional utterances, birth stories, accounts of wonderful events, narratives of origins, and marvellous events, accounts of realization, extensive discourses, and definitive teachings — and teaches them widely to others, for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, proclaiming thus from the Nirvāṇa Sūtra: "Monks are like servants —

cattle, sheep, and other such improper possessions are not permitted to be kept" — and proclaiming further that any monk who keeps such uninspected possessions should be punished with a penalty, and citing as well other sūtras in which the Tathāgata declares that monks who kept such uninspected possessions were penalized by a certain great king and reduced to the status of laypeople — when a monk roars the lion's roar in this manner, those of bad moral discipline, upon hearing such words, give rise to aversion and kill that Dharma-teacher. Yet even if that Dharma-teacher's life is cut short in this way, he is still called one who upholds moral discipline and works for the benefit of self and others. For this reason I permit kings, great ministers, and laypeople to protect Dharma-teachers. Whoever wishes to protect the sacred Dharma should train in this way. Kāśyapa, one who has broken moral discipline and does not protect the Dharma is called a householder with a shaved head — that epithet does not apply to one who guards moral discipline.

The Fifth Fascicle.

O son of noble family, far beyond the past, across a limitless, boundless, and innumerable expanse of aeons, in this very city of Kuśinagara, there arose a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha named the Blessed One "Joyfully Arisen" — endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer and guide of persons, Teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One. At that time and in that era, this world-realm was exceedingly vast, utterly pure, its human population great, its people happy and untroubled by want of food and drink — just as the bodhisattvas of the world-realm of Sukhāvatī are. That Blessed One Buddha dwelt in the world for a measureless duration, accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, and then passed into complete nirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees. After that buddha had passed into nirvāṇa, the sacred Dharma remained for more than forty times ten thousand years beyond measure.

At that time there was a monk named Guṇamati who guarded his moral discipline with the utmost care. He had a vast retinue, and he roared the lion's roar before his assembly, being supremely skilled in teaching the nine divisions of the sūtras in great detail. He proclaimed to the monks that keeping servants, male or female, cattle, sheep, and other such improper possessions was not permitted. At that time the very many monks of broken moral discipline, upon hearing this proclamation, all gave rise to minds of aversion and, taking up weapons, closed in upon that Dharma-teacher. At that time the king of that land, named Guṇavān, upon hearing what had occurred, went immediately to where the Dharma-teacher was in order to protect the Dharma. He arrayed himself against those monks of broken and corrupt moral discipline, fought them, and freed the Dharma-teaching monk from those obstacles. At that time there was not a single wound on the king's body — not even a scratch the size of a sesame seed — from swords, arrows, spears, or any other weapon. At that time the monk Guṇamati said to the king: "Excellent! Excellent! O king, you have truly guarded the sacred Dharma in the right way. In time to come you shall become an immeasurable vessel of the Dharma." That king, his mind filled with great joy upon hearing the Dharma at that moment, passed away immediately thereafter, and was born in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, where he became that buddha's supreme attendant. The king's retinue, who had entered into battle and were wounded,

rejoiced and felt sympathetic gladness, and in every respect became irreversible from the awakening mind (bodhicitta). When they passed away, they were all born in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya. The monk Guṇamati, too, when he later passed away, was likewise born in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, where he became the lowest among that Blessed Buddha's śrāvaka Saṅgha. Therefore, when the sacred Dharma is declining and nearing its end, one must guard and protect it in just that way.

Kāśyapa, at that time, in that age, the king was none other than myself. The monk who taught the Dharma was the buddha known as Kāśyapa. Kāśyapa, by guarding the sacred Dharma, one gains results such as these, boundless and immeasurable. It was through that cause and that condition that I have come to be adorned throughout with a dharmakāya, the truth body, beautified with manifold major marks and excellent minor marks of every kind, together with an indestructible body that has arisen spontaneously.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, the permanence of the Tathāgata's body is like an inscription carved in stone."

The Blessed One then spoke to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa as follows: "Therefore, son of good family, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen must arouse the utmost diligence and guard the sacred Dharma. The fruit of guarding the sacred Dharma is vast and immeasurable. Son of good family, therefore lay Dharma-protectors should take up weapons in hand and guard and protect the Dharma-preaching monks.

One should not be called a person of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) merely for keeping the five precepts of moral discipline. Yet even if one does not keep the five precepts, if one guards the sacred Dharma, that is called the Great Vehicle. To guard the sacred Dharma, one should take weapons in hand and protect the Dharma-preacher."

Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One again: "Blessed One, if a monk associates with and relies upon laymen who bear weapons in the manner described, should he be called a Teacher, or should he not? Does such conduct constitute the keeping of moral discipline, or its violation?"

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: "Do not think that those people have violated moral discipline. Son of good family, after I have passed completely into nirvāṇa, in this turbid world the regions will fall into strife, and people will plunder one another, bringing the threat of famine. At that time, many will struggle to go forth into the monastic life out of destitution, and those people shall be called shaven-headed impostors. Among these shaven-headed impostor individuals, those monks who uphold moral discipline, who possess proper conduct, who are fully pure, and who guard the sacred Dharma — these will be expelled, killed, and harmed.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One: "How should monks who uphold moral discipline and fully maintain the sacred Dharma travel through towns and regions in order to tame sentient beings?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, therefore I permit those who uphold moral discipline to associate with and rely upon armed householders. If a king, minister, householder, layman, or any other person takes up weapons for the sake of protecting the Dharma, that too is called keeping moral discipline. Although they bear weapons, because they do not take life, such a one is called the supreme keeper of moral discipline."

Kāśyapa then asked further: "Blessed One, a Dharma-protector endowed with right view who teaches the Mahāyāna sūtras extensively is like a precious royal parasol, like a vessel of butter oil,

he never exercises control over grain, produce, and fruits of various kinds. He does not rely upon a king, minister, or householder merely for the sake of gain and honor. Toward his donors he harbors no thought of living by deceit and guile. Because he is endowed with proper conduct, he tames unruly persons whose moral discipline has degenerated, and such a one is called a teacher who upholds moral discipline and protects the Dharma. Because he is a genuine spiritual friend to many sentient beings, his mind is vast and wide as the ocean.

Kāśyapa, if a monk teaches Dharma to others for the sake of gain and honor, then all those who belong to that person's retinue will likewise teach Dharma for the sake of gain and honor, and that person causes even his own monastic Saṅgha to become corrupt. Kāśyapa, there are three kinds of Saṅgha: the Saṅgha of those whose moral discipline has degenerated and who wear armor, the Saṅgha of the dull and deluded, and the Saṅgha of the utterly pure.

The Saṅgha of those whose moral discipline has degenerated and who wear armor is easy to destroy, whereas the Saṅgha that upholds moral discipline and is utterly pure cannot be destroyed by the circumstance of gain and honor.

Now, what is the Saṅgha of those whose moral discipline has degenerated and who wear armor? It is this: if a monk, though himself guarding moral discipline, relies upon those whose moral discipline has degenerated for the sake of gain and honor, sitting with them, going about with them, staying with them, consorting with them, befriending one another, and performing actions in concert with them, such a one is called both one whose moral discipline has degenerated and a member of the armored Saṅgha.

What then is the Saṅgha of the dull and deluded? It is a monk who dwells at the forest's edge, whose faculties are dull, who is sluggish and foolish, who has few desires and goes on alms rounds, and who on the day of the restoration ceremony and at the times when the formal proceedings arise, regards those of his vicinity who have become attendants as pure and admits them to confession, while when he sees those of his vicinity who are not pure, whose moral discipline has degenerated, he regards them as pure and admits them to confession without excluding them, and then together performs the restoration ceremony and the proceedings arising from the Vinaya with them — such a one belongs to the Saṅgha of the dull and deluded.

What then is the Saṅgha of the utterly pure? It is a monastic Saṅgha that cannot be divided or destroyed even by a hundred thousand ten-million māras. Such a one is a bodhisattva Saṅgha, pure by its very intrinsic nature. If one tames the previously mentioned two kinds of Saṅgha and brings them within the Saṅgha of the utterly pure, such a one is called the unsurpassed great master who protects the Dharma.

One who is skilled in the Vinaya is supremely expert in the heavy and light characteristics of moral discipline for the sake of benefiting and taming sentient beings, and makes no effort to investigate what is not within the domain of moral discipline, but examines and comes to know what pertains to the domain of moral discipline.

In that regard, how is it that bodhisattvas, for the sake of taming sentient beings, constantly and without fixed time enter into cities, frequenting even desolate places and the dwellings of courtesans, and even residing together with them for many years — something that śrāvakas must not do? This is called taming for the sake of the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.

What is to be understood as heavy? There are four matters concerning which the Tathāgata prescribed moral discipline from one case, saying, "From this day forward, do not transgress this" — these are like the four root cases, the violations for which the Tathāgata has prescribed that those who go forth are not permitted to act. If one does so deliberately, that person is not a renunciate and not a son of the Śākyas. These are called the heavy.

What then are the light? If for a light matter one is urged up to three times and then the transgression is relinquished, that is called a light matter. Whatever does not arise from moral discipline, that which has been taught as not being part of the conduct of the wholly impure, is not to be practiced alongside such impure conduct.

That which arises from the Vinaya is the thorough training in moral discipline, the not relying on those whose moral discipline has degenerated, and the arising of a mind of great joy upon seeing one who inclines toward and walks in accordance with moral discipline. One who knows all that is to be done as the Dharma of the buddhas and is supremely skilled in teaching it — such a person is called a master of moral discipline. One who is thoroughly versed even in a single syllable, or who holds the sūtras with great mastery, is likewise the same.

Therefore, son of good family, the Dharma of the buddhas is immeasurable and inconceivable, and the Tathāgata too is inconceivable.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One: "It is so, it is indeed so. Just as the Blessed One has declared — the Dharma of the buddhas is inconceivable, and the Tathāgata is inconceivable. Therefore the Tathāgata is permanent, indestructible, and unchanging. I myself shall apply myself to this with great diligence, and I wish to teach these very meanings extensively to others as well."

Then the Blessed One gave the bodhisattva Kāśyapa the word "Excellent! Excellent!" and spoke these words: "The body of the Tathāgata is a vajra body, an indestructible body. Bodhisattvas should train in this and come to see and know it as such. Whoever directly cognizes and sees it in this way — that is called seeing the Tathāgata's vajra body, the indestructible body, just as one sees a reflection in a mirror."

This is the second chapter, called "The Vajra Body," from the Great Sūtra of the Great Passage Beyond Sorrow (Mahāparinirvāṇa).

Then the Blessed One again spoke these words to Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, you should hold the name, the words, and the qualities of this sūtra well. Whatever son or daughter of good family merely hears the name of this sūtra — for them there is no occasion to be reborn in the four lower states of existence. Why is that? It is because I declare this sūtra to be the qualities accomplished by immeasurable, incalculable buddhas, Blessed Ones."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, what is the name of this sūtra? How should bodhisattvas, great beings, hold it?"

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "The name of this sūtra is 'The Great Passage Beyond Sorrow' — good at the beginning, good in the middle, good at the end; its meaning is excellent, its words are excellent; it is unmixed, thoroughly pure, wholly and purely the conduct of brahmahood, a precious treasury like a vajra, undiminished. Listen to it very well, and I shall explain it to you."

"Son of good family, the word 'great' in the name means 'permanent.' For example, just as the eight great rivers all flow into the ocean, so too does this sūtra — having subdued all afflictions and all the hosts of māras — ultimately release body and life into the great passage beyond sorrow. Hence it is called the Great Passage Beyond Sorrow.

"Son of good family, consider the example of a skillful physician whose excellent compendium of medical treatments contains all medical treatments gathered together. In the same way, son of good family, all the profound aspects of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata are gathered into the Great Passage Beyond Sorrow. Hence it is called the Great Passage Beyond Sorrow.

"Son of good family, consider this example: farmers who have sown seeds in their fields during the summer always carry hope in their hearts, and when the fruit comes to hand, all their hoping comes to rest.

Son of good family, all sentient beings are likewise: one who meditates on other sūtras always hopes for this taste of the Dharma. Yet when one has heard this Great Passage Beyond Sorrow, all hope for the taste of the Dharma from other sūtras comes to rest — and this is because this Great Passage Beyond Sorrow liberates all sentient beings from conditioned existence.

Son of good family, consider this example: among all kinds of tracks, the track of the bull elephant is supreme. Likewise, this sūtra surpasses all other sūtras in meditative absorption.

Son of good family, consider this example: among the things plowed in a field, autumn sowing is supreme among field crops. Likewise, this sūtra is the supreme of all sūtras.

Son of good family, consider this example: among medicines, butter essence is supreme. Likewise, this Great Passage Beyond Sorrow is supreme, for it pacifies the minds of all sentient beings tormented by their afflictions.

Son of good family, consider this example: butter and cream possess eight kinds of flavor. Likewise, this Great Passage Beyond Sorrow also possesses eight flavors. What are the eight? Permanence, stability, bliss, coolness, freedom from aging, freedom from death, freedom from stain, and perfect peace — these are called the eight flavors. Because it possesses these eight flavors, it is called the Great Passage Beyond Sorrow.

A bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in this fully and continuously — it is that very one who demonstrates the passage beyond sorrow. Such a one is called the Great Passage Beyond Sorrow.

Kāśyapa, whatever son or daughter of good family wishes to pass beyond sorrow through this Great Passage Beyond Sorrow should train in this way: know that the Tathāgata is possessed of the quality of permanence and abiding, and know that the Dharma and the Saṅgha are likewise.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa said this to the Blessed One: "How wondrous, Blessed One! The qualities of the Tathāgata are inconceivable, the Dharma and the Saṅgha are inconceivable, and this Great Passage Beyond Sorrow is also inconceivable. Whoever studies this sūtra attains the true gateway of the Dharma and may be called a skilled physician. Those who do not study it I regard as blind, lacking the eye of wisdom, utterly covered over by ignorance."

This is the third chapter of the noble sūtra the Great Passage Beyond Sorrow, entitled "Proclaiming the Qualities of Its Name."

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, who expounds and teaches the Great Passage Beyond Sorrow should be skilled in these four defining marks. What are the four? Acting properly toward oneself, conducting oneself properly toward others, answering questions just as they are asked, and being skilled in dependent origination.

"What is acting properly toward oneself? The Blessed One, the Buddha, having observed dependent origination, taught it. Consider the example of a monk who, upon seeing a great mass of fire, thinks: 'I would sooner enter that great mass of fire and be burned.' He does not disparage the twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata and the essential meaning of the interpretive teachings by saying: 'This was taught by the evil Māra.' To whatever extent one speaks of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha as impermanent, one deceives oneself and deceives others as well. Rather: I would sooner have my tongue cut off with a sharp sword than say that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are impermanent."

One should not believe those who speak in that way, but instead one should arouse a mind of compassion toward them. Holding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha to be inconceivable, and regarding one's own body as like a great mass of fire — this is called acting rightly toward oneself.

Now, what is meant by acting rightly toward others? Once, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma, a woman arrived carrying a nursing infant at her breast. She came to where the Blessed One was, paid homage at the feet of the Buddha, and sat to one side, keeping in mind her intention to make a request of the Buddha. At that moment, knowing this already, the Blessed One spoke to the woman thus: "You have thought of your child with affection and have stirred much butter. Have you come intending to ask something, or not knowing whether to ask?"

The woman then addressed the Blessed One: "It is wonderful! The Blessed One knows just as I had it in my mind. May the Blessed One tell me whether the butter I have offered is much or little. Blessed One, I fear that this bit of butter I gave today, without making a request, may become an obstacle to my life. Therefore may the Tathāgata instruct me."

The Blessed One replied: "The butter that your child has consumed has, from this very moment, become of the highest benefit for his life and body."

Upon hearing these words of the Blessed One, the woman was filled with great joy and spoke again: "I rejoice that the Blessed One has spoken truly! It is excellent that the Blessed One, for the sake of taming sentient beings, has distinguished and taught what should be requested and what need not be requested, and has furthermore taught that all phenomena are without self and are impermanent. Had the Blessed One spoken of permanence at the outset, this retinue gathered to be disciplined would have said, 'This teaching accords with the non-Buddhists,' and would have rejected it."

The Blessed One then said to the woman: "When your child is born and has just learned to run, he also needs food that is easy to digest, and the butter given earlier is no longer sufficient. My own śrāvakas in their immediate circle are likewise like your young child — they cannot digest this teaching of permanence. That is why I first taught suffering, impermanence, and so forth. For those among my śrāvakas' immediate circle who are endowed with good qualities and are able and diligent in practicing the sūtras of the Great Vehicle, I have taught in this very sūtra the six flavors. What are the six flavors? Suffering is like a sour flavor. Impermanence is like a salty flavor. Selflessness is like a bitter flavor. Bliss is like a sweet flavor. Self is like a pungent flavor. Permanence is like an astringent flavor. In the world there are three flavors: impermanence, selflessness, and the absence of bliss. Affliction is like wood, and wisdom is like fire; by their cause and their condition, what becomes the food of nirvāṇa is permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity — and those who have become the immediate circle taste that flavor."

Then the Blessed One spoke again to the woman: "If you need to attend to your affairs and go elsewhere, send the wayward child away from the household and entrust the treasure of jewels to the capable son."

The woman replied: "As the noble one commands — I will show the treasure of jewels to the capable son, but not to the bad one."

The Blessed One then said: "I too am like that. When I pass into complete nirvāṇa,

The Tathāgata, with deliberate intent, taught the unsurpassed treasury of Dharma without displaying it to the śrāvakas of the immediate circle — just as you did not show the treasury of jewels to the wayward child. Entrusting and commending it to the bodhisattvas is just as you entrusted the treasury of jewels to the capable son. Why is that? The śrāvakas of the immediate circle, holding the perception that birth and transition occur, think: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, has truly passed into nirvāṇa" — yet I have not truly passed into nirvāṇa. It is like this: you have gone on a long journey and have not yet returned, and your wayward child says you have died when you have not. The bodhisattvas, on the other hand, say: "The Tathāgata is permanent, unchanging, and immutable" — just as your capable son says that you have not died. For this reason I have entrusted the treasury of Dharma taught with unsurpassed intent to the bodhisattvas.

Son of good family, whatever sentient being holds the buddha to be permanent, stable, unchanging, and immutable — know that in that very abiding the buddha dwells. Such beings are rightly called those who truly proclaim to others.

Now, as to how one answers in accordance with what was asked: if a person were to say to the Buddha, the Blessed One, "Without giving any wealth or material goods whatsoever, I would be renowned by the name of a great benefactor" — the Blessed One would reply to him thus: "Those śramaṇas and brahmins and the like who are of few desires and contentment, who do not keep or seek unsolicited requisites — giving them a male servant, a female servant, or a hired worker; giving a woman to one who practices celibacy; giving meat and wine to one who has renounced meat and wine; giving food to one who does not eat after midday; giving flowers and incense to one who does not handle flowers and incense for adornment — such acts will be universally renowned by the name of generosity, and not even the slightest amount of wealth or material goods will be diminished. This is what is called answering in accordance with what was asked."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, although it would be improper to give meat to one who does not seek it, why do I say this? Because I see those who do not seek meat as endowed with eight great qualities."

The Blessed One said to Kāśyapa: "Excellent! It is excellent that you understand my intent. Those bodhisattvas who guard the Dharma should understand it thus. Son of good family, from this day forward I do not permit those of the immediate śrāvaka circle to eat meat. Even if a faithful donor gives it, one should cultivate the perception of it as being like the flesh of one's own child."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: "Blessed One, why does the Tathāgata not permit the seeking of meat?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, eating meat severs the seed of great compassion."

Kāśyapa asked: "Did not the Blessed One previously permit the eating of meat that is pure in three respects?"

The Blessed One replied: "Kāśyapa, permitting the eating of meat pure in three respects was taught as a gradual method for cutting off the habit."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Why is the eating of the ten kinds of uninspected meat and the nine kinds of inspected meat not permitted?"

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: "That too was taught for the purpose of cutting off the habit — in short, it was taught in order to lead toward the complete abandonment of meat."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then said:

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, why did the Tathāgata declare fish to be a permitted food?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, I never declared fish and the like to be permitted foods. What I declared to be permitted foods were sugarcane, rice, barley, buckwheat, millet, and other grains, sesame, milk, yogurt, butter, oil, and the like. And although I did permit wearing many kinds of garments, even that permission was given only for the purpose of covering the body and changing appearance — how much less, then, could attachment to fish be acceptable. As for what Kāśyapa has said — that if the Tathāgata does not permit the seeking of meat, then by the same reasoning the five kinds of flavors, namely milk, yogurt, fresh butter, clarified butter, and sesame oil and the like, and garments of silk, necklaces, sandals, and vessels of gold and silver, should also not be permitted — the Blessed One replied: Son of good family, that view is not in accord with the view of the naked ascetics. Rather, the Tathāgata, having considered separately those who are bound by moral discipline, taught accordingly; and because the intention differed, the eating of meat pure in three respects was permitted. Because the perception differed, ten kinds of meat were prohibited. And because the perception differed, meat from animals that died naturally and all such meat was not permitted for eating. Kāśyapa, from this day forward, I declare that those who have become my close attendants must not eat any meat whatsoever."

Kāśyapa, those who eat meat — whether walking, staying, sitting, or lying down — cause fear and terror in every sentient being their scent reaches. It is like this: when a person reeks of the smell of a lion, everyone is afraid and terrified. Son of good family, it is like a person who has eaten garlic — on account of the smell, everyone finds them disagreeable and keeps away, to say nothing of drawing near to them. Those who eat meat are just the same: when the smell of meat reaches sentient beings, they become frightened, and the perception of mortal danger arises in them. Every creature dwelling in water, dwelling on land, or moving through the sky flees and runs away, saying, "This is our enemy." Therefore bodhisattvas do not strive to eat meat. They may demonstrate eating meat in order to liberate sentient beings, and they may appear to eat it, but in reality they do not eat it. Son of good family, so it is that a bodhisattva does not even eat pure food — how much less need it be said that they would eat meat.

Son of good family, after I have passed completely into nirvāṇa, when a measureless hundred of years have passed, noble ones who have arisen through the four noble paths will likewise pass into nirvāṇa, and the true Dharma will decline. When people treat images as Dharma, there will be monks who affect the appearance of those who uphold the Vinaya, and who recite and chant the sūtras only a little; who are attached to food for the sustenance of the body, who wear coarse and rough garments, whose complexion has become dark, who have lost their splendor, who raise cattle and sheep, who carry loads of wood and grass, who let their hair and nails grow long. Though they wear the ochre robe, they are like hunters — with downcast eyes and slow steps, like cats stalking mice. They constantly declare, "I am an arhat," yet they are tormented by illness, suffering, sleep, and impurity. Outwardly they affect good conduct, but inwardly their minds are overwhelmed by jealousy and desire, making them no different from brahmins of wrong views and the like. Though not true ascetics, they present themselves in the form of ascetics, cultivate wrong views, and slander the true Dharma as well. Those persons render improper the moral discipline, the Vinaya, the conduct, and the teaching of the fruit of liberation as established by the Tathāgata; they render improper the teaching to abandon uninspected phenomena; they render improper even the profoundly intended teachings. Then, composing sūtras and Vinaya teachings of their own invention,

They would say, "The Tathāgata has permitted us to eat meat," write it down, argue with one another claiming it was spoken by the Buddha, and each one proclaim, "I am an ascetic, a son of the Śākyas."

O son of good family, at that time there will also be other monks who stockpile large quantities of grain, handle and consume fish, carry vessels of butter, precious parasols, and sandals, depend upon kings, ministers, and householders, study and practice astrology, reading of omens, divination, and medicine; keep male and female servants, and use gold, silver, musāragalva, sphatika crystal, crystal cloth, pearls, coral, shells, and various kinds of ornamental chains and fruit of every variety. They will also engage in sports and games, archery, the crafting of written texts, plowing and cultivating fields, casting spells, combining mantras with medicines, and songs, dancing, music, and the offering of incense and flowers. They will study and practice the application of eye-salves and collyrium, and every manner of craft and trade.

Any monk who has abandoned these non-virtuous things is to be understood as a true companion of mine. Then Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One, saying: Blessed One, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who depend on donors for their livelihood, when they go for alms and are offered food mixed with meat, how should they proceed? How should they examine it?

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: Separate the meat from the food, wash it with water, and then eat. If the alms-bowl has been touched by meat but carries no smell or taste of it, there is no fault in using it. If, when going for alms, meat comes in great quantity, it should not be accepted. If meat is visible within the food, do not eat it. If one does eat it, there is a transgression. Were I to explain in full this matter, together with the prohibition against eating meat that I have set forth, there would be no end to it; and since the time of my passing into nirvāṇa has come, I have spoken only in part.

These, then, are called the answers to the questions put.

Now, Kāśyapa, in what way is one to be considered learned in the meaning of dependent origination? It is like this: when the fourfold retinue came into my presence and asked the Blessed One why, from the time the Tathāgata first fully awakened, he did not teach this exceedingly profound doctrinal text to the utterly vanquished royal host, whereas at some times he taught it as utterly profound, at other times as not profound, at some times called it degenerate, and at others said it was not degenerate, and asked in what case one should speak of a transgression, and what is meant by the Vinaya of individual liberation (prātimokṣa)?

The Blessed One declared: Individual liberation (prātimokṣa) means knowing contentment, being endowed with proper conduct, hoarding absolutely nothing, and maintaining a completely pure livelihood. A transgression is a falling in regard to the four classes of tantra. Furthermore, a transgression means falling into the hells or all the way to the realm of ceaseless torment; and the swiftest of descents is like the fall of violent rain, beyond any reversal. Even hearing of it alone causes fear and terror, so that one will be diligent in guarding moral discipline, maintaining the restraint of conduct, knowing contentment, and refraining from accepting any uninspected material goods.

Furthermore, a transgression means generating the realms of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts. Because of this meaning, it is called a transgression. And further, individual liberation means the complete abandonment of all unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.

The Vinaya (monastic discipline) enters into the profoundly deep meaning of moral discipline and the sūtras, and does not permit the acceptance of any uninspected material goods or uninspected causes and conditions. Furthermore, it does not permit the practice of the four defeats, the thirteen remainders of the Saṅgha, the two undetermined cases, the thirty rules entailing forfeiture and confession, the ninety-one downfalls, the four individually confessed rules, the many trainings, and the seven rules of extremely peaceful settlement, and so forth. For some individuals there is even the complete breakdown of all moral discipline. The term "all" here refers to everything from the four defeats up through the seven rules of extremely peaceful settlement.

For some individuals, having denigrated the profoundly deep authentic Dharma and become ones with distorted craving, they seize upon all defining characteristics and conceive of them as complete even in the absence of causes and conditions, while proclaiming, "I myself am sharp-facultied and endowed with wisdom." They conceal and hide every serious and light misdeed, just as a turtle draws in its six limbs. Such ones who commit misdeeds feel no remorse for a long time, and because they feel no remorse, the misdeeds grow and multiply day and night. Those monks in whom offenses have arisen never feel remorse, and so the offenses pervade them entirely. It is for this reason that the Tathāgata, knowing these matters, established the rules gradually rather than all at once.

At that time, sons and daughters of noble family addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Since the Tathāgata knew this, why did he not establish the rules from the beginning? Has the Blessed One not sent sentient beings to the avīci hells? For example, when many people travel to another region and a road guide leads them astray so that they wander off the path and enter upon what is not the path, those people do not realize they have been led astray but think it is the road; there is then no occasion to ask others whether or not it is the path. Just so, sentient beings are led astray by the Buddha's teachings, and when they do not see what is truly correct, the Tathāgata then shows them the true path from the beginning, saying, 'Monks, this is a breach of moral discipline; this is the guarding of moral discipline.' Since the establishment of moral discipline is appropriate, why did the Tathāgata — who is perfectly and completely awakened, who knows and sees the true path, who is like a god among gods, and who is supremely skilled in presenting the qualities and aims of the ten virtuous actions — why did he not establish this moral discipline from the beginning?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of noble family, it is true that the Tathāgata teaches sentient beings the qualities of the ten virtuous actions. However, the Tathāgata looks upon all sentient beings as he would upon his own son Rāhula. Why then do you say that the Blessed One has sent sentient beings to the hells? When I see that some individual has acquired the causes for falling into the avīci hells, I nonetheless remain in the world for a full eon or for the remainder of a full eon for the sake of that individual. Since I am endowed with great compassion toward all sentient beings, I — who regard all as my own children — would I then send sentient beings to the hells? Son of noble family, consider this example: in this royal domain, those who wear stitched garments, if there is a hole torn in the cloth, mend it with a patch at once. The Tathāgata is similar: when he sees even a single cause or condition that would lead a sentient being to fall into the avīci hells, he protects that being through the moral discipline of virtue. Son of noble family, consider further:

Consider this example: a wheel-turning king (cakravartin) first tames sentient beings through the teaching of the ten virtues. Afterward, should there be those who engage in non-virtue, he punishes them with whatever penalty is fitting. Having imposed the penalty for their offense, he then causes them to live by the law of the primordial royal order. Son of noble family, I am similar to this: even though the teaching exists, what was not established at the outset — should monks behave in ways contrary to the Dharma — is now established with whatever rules are fitting. In this way, those who have devotion to the Dharma will come to have devotion toward the Teacher as well. It is for this reason that the assembly came to see the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.

Consider further: the precious wheel of the wheel-turning king is inconceivable. The Tathāgata likewise is inconceivable; the Dharma and the Saṅgha are likewise inconceivable; the teaching of the Dharma and the hearing of the Dharma are likewise inconceivable. This is what is called being skilled in dependent origination.

A bodhisattva who is skilled in analyzing the meaning of these four aspects of defining characteristics is called one skilled in the meaning of dependent origination within the Great Vehicle's great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "I acting rightly with respect to myself" — this refers to attaining the great nirvāṇa. "Others acting rightly with respect to others" refers to my teaching the monks that the Tathāgata is permanent, unchanging, and unshifting. "Answering what was asked" refers to the fact that, because Kāśyapa asked, I taught the bodhisattvas, the great beings, the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen extensively on the meaning of what is profound. The meaning of dependent origination is this: śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not know this meaning, which is so very profound — they speak of it in syllables, like the letter "i," by means of three dots — and those who have not heard the essence of what I taught with the great wisdom of liberation and the passing into nirvāṇa, I have today laid out and taught distinctly to the śrāvakas, thereby opening the eye of wisdom.

Now, if someone should say, "These four aspects of what exists are one — would that not be false?" — one should respond to that person thus: "Space is utterly empty, unmoving and undisturbed; what distinction could there then be among the four aspects? Would it be right to call that false? No, Blessed One. These many words all have a single meaning: that is, the meaning of emptiness." The acting rightly of self and other, the answering of questions, and the meaning of dependent origination are likewise the same — they are not separate from or different from great nirvāṇa.

Then the Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Son of noble family or daughter of noble family who says this — 'The Tathāgata is impermanent' — if asked, 'How is he impermanent?' — as the Blessed One has taught, nirvāṇa is called the cessation of all afflictions. Just as when a fire dies there is nothing whatsoever left, the cessation of all afflictions is likewise like that — and if that is what is called nirvāṇa, why then speak of the Tathāgata as one whose nature it is to abide permanently, unchanging and unshifting?

"Or again, as the Blessed One has taught, nirvāṇa is called freedom from existence. If in nirvāṇa there is no existence whatsoever, how then can the Tathāgata be said to be one whose nature it is to abide permanently, unchanging and unshifting? It is like worn-out and tattered cloth — when it has perished, there is nothing whatsoever. Nirvāṇa is similar: if with the cessation of all afflictions there is nothing whatsoever that can be called an existing thing —"

"And why, then, speak of the Tathāgata as one whose nature it is to abide permanently, unchanging and unshifting? As the Blessed One has taught, freedom from desire and perfect peace is called passing beyond sorrow — nirvāṇa. It is like a man whose head has been cut off: one says that he has no head. Just so, freedom from desire and perfect peace is like that — empty, with nothing whatsoever — and this is called nirvāṇa. Then again, why speak of the Tathāgata as one whose nature it is to abide permanently, unchanging and unshifting?"

And the Blessed One further declared this in verse:

Just as iron that is blazing hot,
when struck with a hammer, gives off sparks,
and once they scatter, they are gone at once —
their whereabouts cannot be known.

So too, one who is perfectly liberated
bears a characteristic like to that:
having utterly abandoned all desire,
having crossed beyond the swamp of existence,

having attained the abode of the unmoving —
the place reached cannot be known.

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One was asked again: "Why then speak of the Tathāgata as one whose nature it is to abide permanently, unchanging and unshifting?"

The Blessed One replied: "Kāśyapa, any person who speaks in that way speaks wrongly. Kāśyapa, you yourself must not give rise to a perception of cessation and extinction with respect to the Tathāgata himself. Kāśyapa, the cessation of afflictions is not designated as 'a thing.' Why? Because it is consummate, it is called permanent. This word is perfect peace — it is supreme. All marks, without remainder, are exhausted. This word is pure, permanent, stable, irreversible. Therefore nirvāṇa is called permanent and stable. The Tathāgata likewise is such — permanent, stable, and unchanging. What is called impermanent is the afflictions. 'Scattering apart and becoming nonexistent, with no place to be found' means that the Tathāgata, with all afflictions ceased, does not abide in the five streams of consciousness. Therefore the Tathāgata is one whose nature it is to abide permanently, unchanging and unshifting.

"Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the Teacher of the buddhas is the Dharma. Therefore the Tathāgata too shows veneration and homage. Because the Dharma is permanent, the buddhas too are permanent."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One again, saying: "If, because the fire of the afflictions has been extinguished, the Tathāgata too is extinguished, then the Tathāgata does not abide permanently. It is like iron that has been heated to a red glow — when it cools, it cannot be found. The afflictions of the Tathāgata are similar: when they are at peace, the place of peace too cannot be found. Furthermore, it is like iron: when its heat and redness have cooled and ceased to exist — so too the Tathāgata is like that: cooled and without permanence, for when the fire of the afflictions is extinguished and he has entered into complete nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata is impermanent."

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, what is called 'iron' refers to inferior bellows-work — and inferior bellows-work, even if the afflictions cease, produces them again immediately afterward, and so is called impermanent. The Tathāgata is not like that: because once ceased, he does not arise again, he is called permanent."

Kāśyapa said: "But just as iron, after its red glow has cooled, when fire is applied again afterward becomes red once more — if the Tathāgata is like that, then the afflictions would arise again, and because the afflictions arise again, he would be impermanent."

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: "You must not say that the Tathāgata is impermanent. Why? Because the Tathāgata is permanent. Son of good family, consider: even when wood is burned, there is still ash. When the afflictions are extinguished, nirvāṇa exists —"

— like the example of a worn garment, a severed head, or a broken vessel, and so on. Those things still bear their respective names: "worn garment," "severed head," "broken vessel." Kāśyapa, though iron cools, it can become hot again afterward. The Tathāgata is not like that: having cut off the afflictions and become utterly cool at the end, the fire of the afflictions will never arise again. Kāśyapa, know that the immeasurable multitude of sentient beings is like that iron, and that I, through the fire of undefiled wisdom, burn away those sentient beings' defilements.

Then Kāśyapa said: "Excellent! Excellent! Today I have heard rightly that the Tathāgata is indeed permanent."

The sixth fascicle.

The Blessed One spoke to Kāśyapa: "Consider, for example, a wheel-turning king who goes outside his palace to take a stroll. Even though he is absent from the midst of his great retinue, it would not be right to say that the wheel-turning king has died. Son of good family, the Tathāgata is likewise: even though he is not manifest in this world-realm of Jambudvīpa and has entered into nirvāṇa, one must not say that he is impermanent. The Tathāgata arose from immeasurable afflictions, yet having entered nirvāṇa, he dwells in the abode of perfect bliss, wanders amid the flowers of the branches of awakening, and lives in perfect ease."

Then Kāśyapa said: "Blessed One, you have said, 'I crossed over the ocean of afflictions long ago.' If the Blessed One has indeed crossed over the ocean of afflictions, then why was a son born to Rāhulā — like a son born to one who grasps at fame? It therefore seems as though the Tathāgata has not yet escaped the great ocean of afflictions and defilements. Blessed One, I ask you to explain to me the cause and condition of this."

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: "You must not say: 'If the Tathāgata crossed over the ocean of afflictions long ago, then why was a son born to Rāhulā like Rāhula? — and so the Tathāgata is no different from one who has not crossed over the great ocean of afflictions and defilements.' Do not speak in that way. Son of good family, the great and complete nirvāṇa is an establishment of great meaning, so listen with thorough and careful attention, teach it extensively to others as well, and give rise to neither doubt nor fear.

When a bodhisattva, a great being, dwells in the great complete nirvāṇa, he is as lofty and vast as Mount Meru, king of mountains. Even if he were placed inside a single mustard seed, the sentient beings dwelling on Mount Meru would not perceive one another's presence nor know of one another's movement. Only those of the disposition that can be tamed would, by the bodhisattva's power, see Mount Meru placed inside that mustard seed and then restored to its place.

Son of good family, furthermore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, dwells in the great complete nirvāṇa, even if this entire great trichiliocosm were placed inside a single mustard seed, the sentient beings dwelling therein would not perceive one another nor know of one another's movement from place to place. Only those of the disposition that can be tamed would know that the bodhisattva had placed this great trichiliocosm inside the mustard seed and then restored it to its place.

Son of good family, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, dwelling in the great complete nirvāṇa is capable of placing this great trichiliocosm into a single pore of a hair and then restoring it — in its full expanse — to its former place.

Son of good family, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, dwelling in the great complete nirvāṇa is capable of taking up this great trichiliocosm and placing it on the tip of a needle, or of hurling it to another buddha-field altogether — and throughout this, not a single sentient being dwelling therein would know from where they had come or where they had gone. Only those of the disposition that can be tamed would know, from the moment of their being taken up to the moment of their restoration to their former place.

Son of good family, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, dwelling in the great complete nirvāṇa is capable of taking up with the right hand all the world-systems of the great trichiliocosms of the ten directions, spinning them like a potter's wheel, and hurling them to a distance equal to as many atoms as there are world-systems — and the sentient beings dwelling therein would not perceive even the slightest movement, neither going nor coming. Only those of the disposition that can be tamed would know, from the moment of their being taken up to the moment of their being brought back to their former place.

Son of good family, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, dwelling in the great complete nirvāṇa is capable of placing within his own belly all the immeasurable buddha-fields of the ten directions — and the sentient beings dwelling therein would neither crowd one another nor feel crowded, would not know of going or coming or remaining. Only those of the disposition that can be tamed would know, from the moment of this taking place to the moment of their restoration to their former place.

Son of good family, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, dwelling in the great complete nirvāṇa is capable of placing all the world-systems of the ten directions within a single atom — and the sentient beings dwelling therein would neither crowd one another nor feel crowded, and would not know of going or coming. Only those of the disposition that can be tamed would know, from the moment it is seen to be so until the moment of their return to their place.

Son of good family, thus it is that a bodhisattva, a great being, dwelling in the great complete nirvāṇa displays an immeasurable array of such miraculous displays of higher knowledge — and for this reason it is called the great complete nirvāṇa.
