Now, when this bodhisattva, this great being, displays these immeasurable miraculous shows of higher knowledge, and when no sentient being is able to gauge or comprehend them — how then could you understand that the Tathāgata has given birth to a son named Rāhula simply because he was drawn toward the realm of desire? Son of good family, it is because he has long dwelt in this great complete nirvāṇa and has displayed manifold miraculous shows of higher knowledge — appearing in hundreds of forms in hundreds of suns and moons, and in hundreds of Jambudvīpas throughout the great trichiliocosm — just as it is taught in detail in the sūtra of the meditative absorption known as "Going Heroically." Though I show this great trichiliocosm's Jambudvīpa my full passing into nirvāṇa, in the end I have not truly and finally passed into nirvāṇa. And though I show my entry into the womb of a mother here in Jambudvīpa, it is in order that the father, the mother, and the world might conceive of me as their son — for my body is not ultimately born from a gathering of desire. I have, for an immeasurably long time across countless eons, utterly abandoned desire; therefore this body of mine is a dharmakāya — and yet I have displayed, in accordance with worldly convention, an entry into the womb.

Son of good family, here in Jambudvīpa, in the Lumbinī Grove, I was born from the womb of my mother, the goddess Māyā — and immediately upon birth I took seven steps toward the east and said these words: "Among gods, humans, and asuras, I am the highest, the most excellent, the foremost." And upon seeing this, the father and mother, and all the gods and humans of the world, were filled with joy, and in their minds arose a sense of wonder and amazement.

All people regarded me as a mere infant. And yet this body of mine has been free, from immeasurable eons past, from any such qualities of affliction. The Tathāgata's body is the dharmakāya — it is not a body made from flesh and blood, sinew and tendon, bones and limbs — and yet, in accordance with worldly convention, I displayed the body of a newborn child.

Taking seven steps toward the south, I manifestly revealed to immeasurable sentient beings the unsurpassable field of merit. Taking seven steps toward the west, I displayed this as the final body — one in which birth is exhausted, and there is no more aging or death. Taking seven steps toward the north, I displayed liberation from all the wandering of existence in saṃsāra. Taking seven steps toward the east, I manifestly revealed myself to be the Teacher of sentient beings. Taking seven steps each toward the four intermediate directions, I displayed the complete and perfect awakening of the Tathāgata — having utterly vanquished the various kinds of affliction and the four māras. Taking seven steps in the upward direction, I displayed one who is unstained by any and all impure things, become like the sky. Taking seven steps in the downward direction, I extinguished the fires of the hells with a rain of Dharma, so that those sentient beings would experience great bliss — and to those of corrupt moral discipline I displayed this as a hailstorm and a storm of thunder.

Having been born in Jambudvīpa and seven days having passed, I displayed the cutting of hair, and all people regarded me as a newborn infant. When the hair was first cut, there is no one in the world — no god, human, māra, Brahmā, brahmin, or any other — who is able to see even the uṣṇīṣa mark atop my head; how much less could anyone take up a blade and cut my hair? To take up a blade and shave the crown of my head is simply impossible. Yet I, for a very long time, throughout immeasurable eons, have worn my hair and beard cut short — and even now, I have displayed the cutting of hair in accordance with worldly convention.

From the very moment of my birth, my father and mother, wishing to present me to the gods, carried me into a shrine of the gods and presented me to the great lord of the gods who rules over them. When the great lord of gods saw me, he joined his palms together in reverence and, making obeisance, stood respectfully to one side. For a very long time, throughout immeasurable eons, I have abstained from entering into divine shrines — and yet this too I displayed in order to accord with worldly convention.

I also displayed in Jambudvīpa the piercing of the ears. No sentient being whatsoever can truly pierce my ears — and yet this too I manifestly displayed in order to accord with worldly convention. Lion-shaped earrings were fashioned from precious jewels and placed upon my ears — and yet for throughout immeasurable eons I have entirely abandoned all adornments and ornaments. This too I displayed in order to accord with worldly convention.

I also attended a school of letters and studied writing and arithmetic. Throughout immeasurable eons, endowed as I am with all excellence, were one to examine the three realms, there is no sentient being whatsoever who could serve as my teacher — and yet this too, entering a school of learning, I displayed in order to accord with worldly convention.

Therefore, one speaks of a Tathāgata, a perfectly complete buddha. I displayed the training in elephant riding, the taming of horses, the overcoming of opponents in strength, and the cultivation of various kinds of athletic skill. I also displayed in Jambudvīpa the role of a regent, and sentient beings, taking me for a regent, saw me thoroughly enjoying the five objects of desire. For throughout immeasurable eons I have entirely abandoned the pleasures of the five objects of desire — and yet this too I displayed in order to accord with worldly convention.

When the astrologers examined my marks, they declared that if I did not go forth into renunciation, I would become a wheel-turning king —

and would rule over Jambudvīpa — and all sentient beings believed this. But I had long since relinquished the methods of a wheel-turning king through immeasurable eons, and had entered instead upon the role of a king who turns the wheel of Dharma. In Jambudvīpa I displayed renouncing many women and the five objects of desire, beholding old age, sickness, and death, and seeing an ascetic — and so all sentient beings said: "Surely the regent Suyaśas has at last gone forth into renunciation." Yet I had already gone forth and cultivated the path throughout immeasurable eons; this too I displayed merely to accord with worldly convention.

In Jambudvīpa, I displayed going forth from home into homelessness, receiving full ordination, and applying myself with great diligence to the path — attaining in sequence the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and finally the fruit of arhatship — so that ordinary beings would think: "Attaining the fruit of arhatship is not so difficult; it is rather easy." Yet I had already attained the fruit of arhatship innumerable eons ago; I displayed this too in order to tame sentient beings.

At the seat of awakening, I displayed sitting on the grass I had spread there, subduing the hosts of Māra. Ordinary beings thought: "It is only now, at the seat of awakening, that he is subduing the hosts of Māra." But I had already subdued every Māra innumerable eons before; I displayed the subduing of Māra in order to tame sentient beings who were yet untamed.

I also displayed the elimination of great and small bodily impurities, and the movement of breath in and out — so that ordinary beings would think: "He has great and small bodily impurities, and inward and outward breathing." This body of mine is the fruit of merit, and is therefore free from such inattentiveness as involves great and small impurities and inward and outward breathing; yet I displayed even this in order to accord with worldly convention.

I also displayed accepting food given by opponents — even though there is in this body of mine no inattentiveness born of hunger or thirst. Yet this too I displayed in order to accord with worldly convention.

Furthermore, I displayed lying down and sleeping in conformity with ordinary beings. I have possessed, throughout immeasurable eons, the most profound wisdom and have been utterly free from the three states of existence — yet I displayed walking, standing, moving about, carrying a load on the head, carrying a load on the back, carrying a load on the side, having sores, bathing, washing the feet, washing the hands, washing the face, rinsing the mouth, and chewing a tooth-stick — so that ordinary beings would think: "He has all of these." In truth, this body of mine has none of them. My feet are utterly pure like lotuses, and my face has the fragrance of the unsullied blue lotus flower — yet ordinary beings think of me as a person. In reality, inwardly I am not a person.

I also displayed wearing stitched cloth, rinsing it, mending it, and walking about — yet I had long since ceased to need clothing. Ordinary beings thought: "Rāhula is his son, King Śuddhodana is his father, Māyādevī is his mother; he enjoyed worldly pleasures and then abandoned all these things, went forth into renunciation, and applies himself diligently to the path." Others thought: "He is the eldest regent-son of a great king, belonging to the noble Gautama lineage, and has renounced all worldly happiness to seek the Dharma that transcends the world." But I have long since entirely abandoned all the objects of worldly desire; all of this was merely a display.

O son of good family, even though I repeatedly display passing into nirvāṇa in this Jambudvīpa —

it is not a final, complete passing into nirvāṇa. Ordinary people think: "The Tathāgata has truly and finally ceased to exist." Yet the Tathāgata does not come to an end; know him to be one whose nature is to abide permanently, unchanging and unshifting.

O son of good family, what is called the great nirvāṇa is the dharmadhātu, the basic space of phenomena, of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

Furthermore, I displayed appearing in this world in Jambudvīpa, and ordinary people think: "He has only now attained awakening." Yet I displayed an awakening in Jambudvīpa at the very beginning of the world — even though, for countless eons, I had already accomplished every act that needed to be accomplished.

I also displayed in Jambudvīpa the appearance of one who had not restrained his ethical conduct and had broken all four root precepts. Ordinary people thus think that I had truly broken my ethical conduct — yet in reality, throughout countless eons, there has never been any lapse in my keeping of the precepts.

I also displayed appearing in Jambudvīpa as one with wrong craving. All ordinary people think of me as truly having wrong craving — yet I do not truly have wrong craving. For if I did have wrong craving, how could I have attained awakening to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?

I also displayed in Jambudvīpa the appearance of one who had caused a schism in the Saṅgha. Ordinary people think that I truly created a schism in the Saṅgha — yet when I look out upon all the world with its gods and humans, I do not see anyone who could truly cause a schism in the Saṅgha.

I also displayed in Jambudvīpa the appearance of one who protects the sacred Dharma. Ordinary people, thinking me to be a guardian of the Dharma, are all filled with wonder. But this is simply the nature of reality of the buddhas — and so one should not be astonished at it.

I also displayed in Jambudvīpa appearing in the body of the wicked māra. Ordinary people truly think of me as the wicked māra — yet throughout countless eons I have been entirely free from all acts of māra, pure as a lotus, untainted by anything.

I also displayed in Jambudvīpa attaining buddhahood in the body of a woman. Ordinary people think: "How wondrous! A woman has attained awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment!" Yet the Tathāgata never truly takes on a female body; it is only displayed in female form in order to train immeasurable sentient beings. Out of affection for all sentient beings, he displays a vast variety of forms and appearances.

I also displayed in Jambudvīpa taking birth in the four lower states of existence along the path of karma. I have long since severed the stream of transmigration through those states — yet to train the sentient beings dwelling in those realms, I displayed birth there as well, through the power of karma.

I also displayed in Jambudvīpa appearing as the divine king Brahmā. This was done in order to bring those who revere Brahmā into the true Dharma. In truth I am not actually Brahmā — yet ordinary people think of me as the true divine king Brahmā. In the same way, I have displayed appearing in divine form as various other gods.

I also displayed in Jambudvīpa going to the dwelling of a woman who sells snakes. In truth, there is not in me even a perception of desire; I am pure and untainted as a lotus, unaffected by anything. Yet for the sake of teaching the sacred Dharma at crossroads to sentient beings overwhelmed by desire,

In me there is not even a mind of attachment or desire, yet ordinary people think of me as one who comes under the sway of women. I also displayed in this Jambudvīpa going about among the caste of those who wear blue garments, and this was in order to bring those who had become servants into the true Dharma. Know well that in me there is in truth no karma of falling into the station of those who wear blue garments. I also displayed in this Jambudvīpa appearing as something like a teacher, and this was in order to bring millions of young boys and girls into the true Dharma. I also displayed in this Jambudvīpa drinking wine, residing in royal courts, and engaging in contest and rivalry for the sake of victory or defeat, and all of this was in order to tame and liberate those sentient beings. Although I possess no such bad karma, ordinary people think of me as one who also performs such actions. I also displayed for a long time in charnel grounds in the body of a vulture, and this was in order to liberate all birds. Ordinary people truly think of me as a vulture, yet though I have long since been free of any such karma, I displayed even that form in order to liberate beings of the bird kind.

I also displayed in this Jambudvīpa the body of a householder, in order to tame and bring countless sentient beings into the sacred Dharma. Beyond this, I appeared as a king, as ministers, as princes, and as great counselors, and in each of these roles I was foremost and supreme, entering into the ways of kingship so that the sacred Dharma might be diligently upheld. I also appeared in this Jambudvīpa when an age of pestilence arose, and I healed the many sentient beings tormented by disease with medicine, and afterward taught the sacred Dharma and established them in unsurpassable awakening; yet ordinary people think that a true age of pestilence had arisen. Furthermore, when an age of famine arose in this Jambudvīpa, I gave those beings food and drink according to their every wish, and then first taught the sacred Dharma and established them in unsurpassable awakening. Furthermore, when an age of war and weapons arose in this Jambudvīpa, I taught the sacred Dharma amid it, caused them to abandon the holding of enmity toward enemies, and established them in unsurpassable awakening.

Furthermore, to those who cling to permanence I taught the perception of impermanence; to those who perceive happiness I taught the perception of suffering; to those who perceive a self I taught selflessness; and to those who perceive utter purity I taught the perception of impurity. For any sentient being who clings with attachment to the three realms, I teach the sacred Dharma and cause that being to abandon that abode. In order to tame and liberate sentient beings, I teach the supreme and sacred Dharma as though it were medicine. In order to cut down every tree of affliction entirely, I cause to grow the supreme tree of Dharma-medicine. In order to tame and liberate those who are non-Buddhists, I teach the true Dharma. Although I display openly as the teacher of all sentient beings, from the very beginning I do not think of myself as "the teacher of sentient beings." I also display openly the going among the lowly and base in order to liberate them, and this is for the sake of teaching the Dharma — it is not that a body of that kind is taken up through bad karma. The Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha, abides in ease in the great and complete nirvāṇa in just this way. Therefore he is said to be ever-abiding, possessed of unchanging qualities.

Just as it is with Jambudvīpa, so likewise it extends in the same way to the eastern continent of Videha, the western continent of Godānīya, and the northern continent of Uttarakuru. And just as it is with the four continents, so too it is the same with the great trichiliocosm, the world-system of the three-thousandfold great thousand worlds.

The twenty-five existences are as extensively taught in the sūtra known as the Courageous Progression. For that reason it is called the great and complete nirvāṇa. A bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in ease within the great and complete nirvāṇa has no fear in displaying such miraculous powers of direct knowledge. Kāśyapa, for that reason do not say to Rāhu that he is a son of the Buddha. Why is that? Because I have been utterly free from craving for existence throughout immeasurable eons in the past — therefore the Tathāgata is said to be ever-abiding, unchanging, and unaltered.

Kāśyapa then asked: Why is the Tathāgata called one who possesses the quality of ever-abiding? As the Blessed One himself taught, just as a butter-lamp that has gone out has no location and no direction, so too the Tathāgata is like that — did you not teach that upon passing into nirvāṇa there is likewise no location and no direction?

The Blessed One spoke to Kāśyapa: Son of good family, do not say that — that just as a butter-lamp, upon going out, has no location and no direction, so too the Tathāgata is like that, and upon passing into nirvāṇa has no location and no direction.

Son of good family, consider this example. When a man or a woman lights a butter-lamp, they fill a vessel — large or small — with butter and light it. As long as there is butter, the light exists. If the butter is exhausted, the light ceases to exist. The cessation of the light is like the exhaustion of the afflictions. Though the light burns out and disappears, the vessel of the butter-lamp does not thereby cease to exist. The Tathāgata is likewise: though the afflictions are exhausted and gone, the dharmakāya ever remains.

Son of good family, what do you think — do the light and the vessel of the butter-lamp both disappear at once?

Kāśyapa replied: No, Blessed One. They do not disappear simultaneously, yet they both seem impermanent. If the dharmakāya is like the vessel of the butter-lamp, then since the vessel of the butter-lamp is impermanent, the dharmakāya too would be impermanent in the same way.

Son of good family, do not speak like that. What is known in the world as a vessel, and what is called the unsurpassed vessel of Dharma of the buddha, the Blessed One — though the vessel is impermanent, the Tathāgata is not. The passing beyond sorrow of all phenomena is permanent; and because it is the essential nature of the Tathāgata, it is called permanent.

Furthermore, son of good family, the term "the butter-lamp going out" applies to the nirvāṇa of the arhat. Because all the afflictions of desire have been eliminated, it is like a butter-lamp going out. The once-returner still has desire, and because of that desire it would be incorrect to call him one whose butter-lamp has gone out. Therefore I previously spoke of it as being like a butter-lamp going out in order to negate signs — but the great and complete nirvāṇa is not like a butter-lamp going out.

The non-returner is not one who returns again and again. They do not return to the twenty-five existences, and because they do not take up a coarse body, a body with worms, or a body with afflictions, they are called non-returners. Taking up a body again is called returning; not taking up a body is called not returning. When there is going and returning, it is called returning; when there is no going and no returning, it is called not returning.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words.

"Blessed One, it is not the case that what the Blessed One, the buddha, has spoken carries a hidden meaning, a concealed essence. Why is that? It is true that the Tathāgata speaks with a hidden intent, but there is no concealed essence to what is spoken with hidden intent. Consider, for example, a magician who fashions a wooden automaton in the shape of a man. That wooden man can be seen by everyone, yet its stretching, contracting, bowing, and bending cannot be effected from within. The Dharma of a buddha is not like that. If it is to be seen and known by all sentient beings, then why does the Blessed One say that the Tathāgata speaks with hidden intent and that there is a concealed essence?"

The Blessed One then declared to Kāśyapa, "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, it is just as you have said. Truly, in the Tathāgata there is no concealed essence to what is spoken with hidden intent. Why is that? It is like this: the autumn moon, appearing in the open sky with brilliant clarity and completely unobscured, is seen by all people. Similarly, the word of the Tathāgata is likewise utterly clear and perfectly pure. It is only because foolish and ignoble persons do not understand it that it is called 'spoken with hidden intent and concealed essence.' For the wise and discerning who comprehend it, it is not called secret.

"Noble son, consider this example: a person who has accumulated great quantities of gold and silver, beyond all measure of weight, yet acts with miserliness and gives nothing to the destitute — because they hoard by concealment, their treasury is called hidden. The Tathāgata is not like that. Having accumulated immeasurable precious sacred Dharma over immeasurable eons, and without any miserliness always giving it to all sentient beings — why should one say that the Tathāgata has a concealed essence in what is spoken with hidden intent?

"Noble son, consider this example: a person whose faculties are incomplete — missing one eye, one hand, or one foot — conceals themselves from others out of shame, and that is called keeping secret. The Tathāgata is not like that. Since all the sacred qualities are perfectly complete and without deficiency, the Tathāgata lets all people see them — so why should one say that the Tathāgata has a concealed essence in what is spoken with hidden intent?

"Noble son, consider this example: a poor man burdened with many debts is afraid of his creditors and hides from being seen — and that is called keeping secret. The Tathāgata is not like that. Having no attachment even to worldly phenomena with respect to any sentient being, and having attachment to the Tathāgata for supramundane phenomena in regard to sentient beings, the Tathāgata does not conceal them. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as equal to an only child, and discloses and teaches the unsurpassed Dharma.

"Noble son, consider this example: a wealthy householder who has only one child, greatly cherishing and loving that child, displays all the precious things he possesses. The Tathāgata likewise is just the same, looking upon all sentient beings as equal to an only child.

"Noble son, consider this example: in the world, people cover with clothing the marks of male and female bodies that they find displeasing — and that is called keeping secret. The Tathāgata is not like that. Having gone far beyond the senses and transcended the senses, there is nothing hidden or concealed.

"Noble son, consider this example: brahmins do not wish the warrior caste (kṣatriyas) and the outcaste class to hear all the learned sciences of sacred speech. Why? Because in the sciences of sacred speech there are defects and faults.

The sacred Dharma of the Tathāgata is not like that. From beginning to end and throughout the middle, it is virtuous, and it is not fitting to call it secret.

Noble son, consider this example: a householder has only one son, whom he loves and cherishes deeply. He brings the boy to a teacher and has him begin his studies. But fearing that the child might be slow to learn, the householder, out of love, takes him home and applies diligent effort day and night — teaching him the elementary letters and showing him those, but not showing him the great learning. Why? Because the boy is young, his strength is not yet complete, and so he does not have the capacity to master it. Noble son, if that householder has the boy study only the elementary letters, will the boy thereby come to know and understand the great learning?

The reply came: No, Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: Did that householder keep it secret from his son?

The reply came: No, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said: And for what reason? It was not shown because the boy was young and lacked the capacity to master it — but it was not withheld because of miserliness in order to keep it secret. Why? Because if one withholds something with a mind of miserliness, that may be called secrecy. But the Tathāgata is not like that, and so it is not fitting to say that the Tathāgata has a hidden core to what he teaches.

The Blessed One declared: Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, it is just as you have said: when something is withheld with a mind of aversion, jealousy, or miserliness, that may indeed be called secrecy. But since the Tathāgata harbors no aversion, jealousy, or miserliness, it is not fitting to say that the Tathāgata has secrets.

Noble son, the householder stands for the Tathāgata. The only son stands for all sentient beings, for the Tathāgata looks upon all sentient beings as he would an only child. The son who is learning stands for the disciples who are close attendants, the śrāvakas. The elementary letters stand for the nine categories of scripture. The great learning stands for the vast sūtra collections of the Great Vehicle. Because the śrāvakas lack the strength of wisdom, the Tathāgata taught the nine categories of scripture — the equivalent of the elementary letters — but did not teach the vast sūtra collections of the Great Vehicle, the equivalent of the great learning.

Noble son, if the householder's son has come to full strength and has the capacity to master it, yet the great learning is still not taught to him, then that may be called secrecy. Likewise, if a śrāvaka were to gain the capacity to master the great learning of the Great Vehicle, and yet the Tathāgata withheld it out of miserliness and did not teach it, then it would be fitting to say that the Tathāgata has a hidden core to his teaching. But the Tathāgata is not like that. Therefore the Tathāgata has no hidden core to his teaching.

Just as that householder first showed his son the elementary letters and afterward taught him the great learning, so too the Tathāgata is the same: he first taught his close attendants the nine categories of scripture — the equivalent of the elementary letters — and afterward teaches the great learning. And that great learning is this: the Tathāgata is possessed of a nature that abides permanently, unchanging and unwavering.

Noble son, consider also this further example: in the summer season, a great rain cloud arises and a great rain falls. Those farmers who have sown many seeds in their fields will obtain abundant harvests, while those who have sown few seeds will obtain small harvests. In this, the fault lies not with the nāga king who brings the rain, nor does the nāga king withhold anything in secret. The Tathāgata is likewise:

By sending down the great rain of the Dharma — the great nirvāṇa — those sentient beings who have cultivated wholesome fruit will come to obtain the sprouts and fruit of wisdom. Those who lack wholesome seeds obtain nothing at all, and that they obtain nothing is not the fault of the Tathāgata. Nor, in truth, does the Tathāgata withhold anything in secret.

Kāśyapa then asked: If I understand correctly that the Blessed One's teachings contain no hidden essence beyond what is intended, then when the Blessed One said that the great learning is possessed by the Tathāgata of a nature that abides permanently, unchanging and unwavering, would it not be improper to say so? For what reason? Because the Blessed One previously spoke this verse:

When even the Tathāgata, and the solitary buddhas,
and the companions of the hearers (śrāvakas)
must cast off this impermanent body,
what need is there to speak of the base-born and lowly?

And now here you say "abides permanently, unchanging and unwavering." What then is the meaning of this?

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, I spoke that verse in order to teach the companions who are hearers by means of partial letters. Let me give another example. When the great king Prasenajit's mother passed away, the king was overwhelmed with grief, weeping and lamenting, his heart transfixed. I came to where he was, and knowing full well what had befallen him, I asked: "Great king, why are you so stricken with grief and despair?" The king replied: "My great queen has passed from this life. If anyone could restore my mother's life, I would offer them my kingdom, my elephants, my horses, the seven precious things, and even my own body and life." I then said to that king: "Great king, do not let your mind be tormented by grief. All sentient beings, when their life is exhausted, die. Even buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and hearers must cast off the body — what then need be said of the base-born and lowly?" Noble son, I spoke those verses of partial letters in order to dispel that king's grief.

But now I have taught the great learning to the companions who are hearers, declaring: the Tathāgata abides permanently, unchanging and unwavering. If any person were to say that the Tathāgata is impermanent, why would that person's tongue not be cut out?

Kāśyapa then asked again: Blessed One, did you not also speak this verse:

Desiring nothing whatsoever,
knowing the measure of what is received,
like a bird in flight through the sky —
its trail cannot be traced by anyone.

What is the meaning of this? What is meant by "desiring nothing whatsoever" within this assembly? What is meant by "knowing the measure of what is received"? And who is like a bird flying through the sky, leaving no trace? And in which direction has such a one gone?

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Desiring nothing" refers to precious jewels. Noble son, there are two kinds of wealth: conditioned and unconditioned. Conditioned wealth pertains to the conduct of hearers. Unconditioned wealth pertains to the conduct of the Tathāgata.

Noble son, the Saṅgha too is of two kinds: conditioned and unconditioned. The conditioned Saṅgha refers to the hearers. The Saṅgha of hearers is without wealth. Why without it? Because they do not accumulate male servants and female servants, nor stores of unlawful goods, storehouses, grain measures, sesame, lentils, legumes large and small, and the like.

Now if someone were to say that the Tathāgata permitted the keeping of male servants, female servants, workers, and so forth —

Such a one's tongue would become mute and dumb. My hearers (śrāvakas) are also called "those who do not accumulate," and they are also called "those who know the measure of food." One who is attached to food is called "one who does not know moderation," and one who is unattached to food is called "one who knows moderation." The phrase "not falling away afterward" means drawing near to unsurpassed awakening. Such a person has gone forth as I have taught, yet there is no place to which one has arrived.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked further: If even the conditioned Saṅgha is described as "not accumulating," what need is there to say anything about the unconditioned Saṅgha? And if the Tathāgata is described in the same way, who could accumulate more than the Tathāgata? If "accumulating" were to refer to keeping secrets or concealing things, that would not be fitting for the Tathāgata, since the Tathāgata has no miserliness in speech and therefore cannot be said to have secrets. As for "not falling away afterward," this refers to nirvāṇa. Nirvāṇa is free from sun and moon, stars and planets, cold and heat, wind and rain, birth and aging, sickness and death, and all twenty-five modes of existence; it is free from grief, suffering, and affliction.

Thus nirvāṇa is the permanent, unchanging, and unshifting abode of the Tathāgata. It is for this cause and these conditions that the Tathāgata passed into the great parinirvāṇa at the foot of the śāla trees.

The Blessed One declared: The name "Great Kāśyapa" signifies one who is by nature vast and wide. For example, one who is able to live for a measureless number of years is called a great person. If such a one abides in the sacred Dharma in ease and contentment, he is called foremost among human beings. When I taught the eight qualities of a great person, it is possible that a single individual may attain them, or that all may attain them. If a single person possesses all eight, that one is called supreme and foremost.

"Passing beyond sorrow" means being free from the fault of wrongdoing. Noble son, take the example of a person who is struck by a poisoned arrow. That person experiences the great pain of illness. If such a person meets a skilled physician, the physician treats him with excellent medicine, and he is freed from the pain of illness and becomes entirely well. That physician then travels through villages, towns, and their outskirts, and wherever there are those suffering from wounds, he heals them all and frees them from their pain.

Noble son, the Tathāgata is like that physician. Having attained full awakening, he became the king of physicians. Throughout immeasurable eons in Jambudvīpa, for sentient beings tormented by suffering — those pierced by the thorn of the afflictions of attachment, aversion, and delusion, experiencing great pain — he healed them with the medicinal Dharma of the sūtras of the Great Vehicle, like nectar. And in other directions and other places as well, he showed those pierced by the thorns of afflictions how to fully awaken, and healed them too. For this reason, he is called the great complete parinirvāṇa.

The great complete parinirvāṇa is a state of perfect liberation. Because the Tathāgata manifests his form wherever sentient beings are to be tamed, and because of this profoundly deep and perfectly real meaning, it is also called the great complete parinirvāṇa.

Then once more the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, is the physician of the world able to heal all the illnesses of sentient beings?

Noble son, illness in the world is of two kinds: those that can be healed and those that cannot be healed. Those that can be healed: when treated by a physician, the patient recovers. Those that cannot be healed: even when treated by a physician, the patient does not recover.

Kāśyapa asked again: Blessed One, you have declared that the Tathāgata healed sentient beings in Jambudvīpa. If he healed them, why do so many sentient beings remain who have not passed beyond sorrow? And if not all attained it, why did you declare that the Tathāgata healed all and then departed to another realm?

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, sentient beings in Jambudvīpa are of two kinds: those who have faith and those who do not. Those who have faith are fit to be healed. Why is this? Because they will certainly pass beyond sorrow and be without fault, I declared that I healed all sentient beings of Jambudvīpa. Those who have no faith are called those of wrong craving. Those of wrong craving are not fit to be healed. Since all except those of wrong craving have been healed, there is no fault in passing beyond sorrow.

Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, what is this passing beyond sorrow?

Noble son, passing beyond sorrow means liberation.

Kāśyapa asked again: Is this liberation endowed with form, or is it without form?

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, for some it is with form, and for some it is without form. Without form is the liberation of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. With form is the liberation of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Therefore, noble son, liberation is both with form and without form. The Tathāgata declared it to be without form to the immediate disciples of the śrāvakas.

Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, if śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have no form, in what do they abide?

Noble son, consider the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: they are both with form and without form, and so I declared them to be without form. Now if someone were to object and say, "If the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are without form, how do they abide, move, depart, and arrive?" — the answer is that these matters lie within the domain of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and are not known to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Liberation is similar: it is both with form and without form, and so it is said to be without form. It is both with perception and without perception, and so it is said to be without perception. These matters lie within the domain of the buddhas and are not known to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.


The Seventh Fascicle.


Then once more the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, out of your compassion for us, please explain at greater length the meaning of liberation in the great complete parinirvāṇa.

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, true and perfect liberation means complete freedom from all the bonds by which one is bound. One who is thus truly liberated, being completely free from all bonds, neither takes birth nor gathers conditions. Consider, for example, how a child arises from the coming-together of a father and a mother. True and perfect liberation is not like that; therefore that liberation is called unborn.

Kāśyapa, consider how clarified butter is pure by its own nature. The Tathāgata is likewise: he did not arise through the condition of a father and mother coming together.

Yet, being pure by its very nature, the Tathāgata displayed a father and a mother for the sake of taming ordinary beings. True and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata himself, and in the Tathāgata's liberation there is no duality, no division.

Consider, for example, how in the summer season, when a seed is planted and moistened by heat and moisture, it immediately sprouts and grows. True and perfect liberation is not like that.

Furthermore, liberation means being empty and nonexistent. That which is empty and nonexistent is liberation. Liberation is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is not made empty or nonexistent; he is not something fabricated or constructed. Things that are fabricated, such as castles, towns, houses, granaries, and barns — true and perfect liberation is nothing like those. Therefore liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is an unconditioned phenomenon (dharma). Conditioned things are like clay vessels — they are subject to destruction. Liberation is not like that. True and perfect liberation is the unborn, the unceasing. Therefore liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata likewise neither arises nor ceases, neither ages nor dies, neither deteriorates nor decays — he is not a conditioned phenomenon. For this reason the Tathāgata, having passed into nirvāṇa, is said to be without aging and without death.

What does this mean exactly? "Aging" refers to change and transformation — the whitening of hair and the appearance of wrinkles on the face. "Death" refers to the dissolution of the body and the passing away of the life force. None of these things are present in liberation; because they are absent, it is called liberation. In the Tathāgata there are no conditioned phenomena such as hair turning white or wrinkles forming on the face. Therefore the Tathāgata has no aging. Because there is no aging, there is no death either.

Furthermore, liberation means freedom from illness. "Illness" refers to the four hundred and four diseases, as well as harm to the body caused by other adverse conditions. Because none of these are present, it is called liberation. That which is wholly free from illness is true and perfect liberation. True and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata. Since the Tathāgata is without illness, the dharmakāya is likewise without illness. It is by being thus free from illness that one is called a Tathāgata.

"Death" refers to the dissolution of the body and the passing away of the life force. Because there is no death in him, he is like refined gold. Refined gold is true and perfect, utterly pure liberation. True and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata. Thus the Tathāgata is endowed with such a fullness of qualities — so why should the Tathāgata be called impermanent? If one were to say that the Tathāgata is impermanent, that position is untenable. His body is like a vajra — how could it be impermanent? Therefore one must not say that the life of the Tathāgata is exhausted. The Tathāgata is utterly pure, stainless. The body of the Tathāgata is unstained by the womb; like the white lotus flower, the pundarīka, it is pure by its own nature. The Tathāgata's liberation is likewise. That very liberation is the Tathāgata. Therefore the Tathāgata is utterly pure and without stain.

Furthermore, liberation means the complete and total exhaustion of every last wound of defilement (āsrava), leaving nothing remainder. The Tathāgata is likewise — he is entirely without the wounds of defilement. Furthermore, liberation means freedom from dispute.

For example, a person who is hungry and sees food becomes intensely attached to it. Liberation is not like that.

Furthermore, liberation is called peaceful bliss. When base flatterers say of a great sovereign that he dwells in blissful peace, those words are false and untrue. True blissful peace is ultimate liberation. Ultimate liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is supreme bliss. For example, a place full of many enemies is not bliss. A place free of enemies is called supreme bliss. Liberation, too, is free of fear, and so it is called supreme bliss. Therefore supreme bliss is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata. What is called the Tathāgata is Dharma.

Furthermore, liberation is called without equal. As for being without equal — kings, for instance, have peers who are equal to them in territory and realm, and so they are considered equals. Liberation has nothing of that kind. Without equal — for example, a wheel-turning king (cakravartin) has no equal. Liberation likewise has no equal. Having no equal is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata, the wheel-turning king of the Dharma wheel. Therefore the Tathāgata has no equal; there is no basis for saying that the Tathāgata has a peer.

Furthermore, liberation is called free from sorrow. As for having sorrow — kings, for example, feel sorrow out of fear of their enemies' attacks. Liberation has no such thing. For example, when all enemies have been vanquished, there is no sorrow or anxiety for that person. Liberation likewise has no sorrow or fear. Free from sorrow and fear is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called free from grief and aging. For example, if a woman hears the evil news that her only son who had gone to another land has died, she will be tormented with grief. Then if she hears that he has not died, joy arises in her instantly. Liberation has none of those things — the absence of grief and joy alike is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called free from dust and stain. For example, in spring when the sun sets, the wind rises and dust is stirred up. Liberation has none of those things whatsoever. Freedom from dust is the simile for true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

For example, the precious jewel set in the top-knot of a wheel-turning king is without stain. Liberation likewise is without stain. Freedom from stain is liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

For example, refined gold that is unmixed with sand is called a true jewel, and when a person finds it, he regards it as a treasury of wealth. Liberation itself is like a true jewel. The true jewel is the simile for true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

For example, a broken clay pot makes a disagreeable sound. A vajra jewel vessel is not like that. True liberation likewise is without disagreeable sound. The vajra jewel vessel is the symbol of true liberation.

True liberation is the Tathāgata. Therefore the body of the Tathāgata is indestructible.

As for disagreeable sound, it is like this: the fruit of the eraṇḍa plant, dried in the fierce heat of the summer sun, tormented by that heat, emits a sound. In liberation, nothing of that kind exists. Like the vajra jewel vessel, there is no disagreeable sound of breaking. Even if hundreds and thousands and countless people were all to shoot arrows at it simultaneously, it would not be destroyed, and there would be no disagreeable sound of breaking. The absence of disagreeable sound of breaking is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

It is like this: when a poor man is seized for another's debt, he is bound with iron chains and with rope, and starved, and made to suffer. In liberation, nothing of that kind exists, and there is no debt either. It is like this: a wealthy merchant possesses wealth and precious goods beyond count, and has power and mastery, and has no debt. Liberation likewise is similar: it possesses abundant precious wealth of Dharma and has power and mastery, and thus has no debt. Freedom from debt is the simile for true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation means freedom from being tormented. It is like this: in spring, going out in fierce heat; in summer, eating sweet food; in winter, being touched by cold. In true liberation, nothing of that kind — nothing disagreeable — exists at all. Freedom from being tormented is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

As for being tormented, it is like this: if a person eats fish to satiety and then drinks milk afterward, that person is not far from death. In true liberation, nothing of that kind exists. But if that person were to find something like a medicinal nectar, the illness would be healed and he would survive. True liberation is just like that. The medicinal nectar is the name for true liberation. That true liberation is the Tathāgata — so how could one speak of it as tormenting or not tormenting?

It is like this: childish, lowly people who have come under the power of pride think to themselves, "Among all sentient beings, there is nothing that can kill me," and so they take hold of tigers, snakes, and vicious insects. Such a lowly person is not far from the end of his life, and one should know that sudden death will come to him. In true liberation, nothing of that kind exists.

Freedom from torment is like this: the precious jewel gem of a wheel-turning king is able to tame ninety-six types of vicious insects and vermin, and the mere fragrance of that precious gem causes all that is venomous to disappear. True liberation is likewise similar: it has gone far from the twenty-five modes of existence. Freedom from venom is the simile for true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, freedom from venom is like space. Liberation too is like that. Space is the name for true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

As for being burned, it is like this: when fire is set to dry grass, it blazes and is consumed. In true liberation, nothing of that kind exists.

Furthermore, freedom from being utterly tormented is like this:

The sun and moon do not cause scorching torment to sentient beings. Liberation is likewise similar: it does not cause scorching torment to any sentient being whatsoever. Freedom from scorching torment is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is said to be of unshakable nature, like the presence of loving-kindness and the absence of aversion. In true liberation, nothing of that kind exists. What is called unshakable is like a wheel-turning king: there is no one who could become a companion equal to such a king, and there is no ground for saying that such a companion exists. Liberation is likewise similar: nothing else can become its companion, and there is no ground for saying that any companion exists. That the king has no companion — that is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is Dharma itself.

Furthermore, what is called unshakable is this: for example, a white garment can easily have its color changed. Liberation is not like that. For example, there is no ground for saying that the flower called the blue lotus has a smell or that it has a blue color — and yet the blue lotus is what it is. Liberation is likewise similar: there is no ground for saying that it has a smell or that its hue is otherwise than it is. Therefore liberation itself is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is wondrous. It is like this: a lotus born in water is nothing to marvel at. But if a lotus were born from within fire, that would be wondrous and astonishing, and all who saw it would be filled with joy. True liberation is likewise similar: all those who see it are filled with profound joy in their minds. What is called wondrous is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is the dharmakāya, the truth body.

Furthermore, what is called wondrous is this: for example, an infant just born, while still toothless, grows greatly on mother's milk and then teeth arise anew. Liberation is not like that: there is nothing in it that can be called arising or non-arising.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is empty, peaceful, and without indeterminacy. Indeterminacy applies to one who holds wrong craving; at the root, there is degeneration, and there is no ground for saying that such a one cannot change and will not attain awakening. Why is that? If that person were to generate completely pure faith in the noble Dharma of the buddhas, that person would be made free of wrong craving. And even if one were to become a layman, one would be made free of wrong craving. And if the unwholesome fault of degeneration at the root were removed, full and manifest awakening would be attained. Therefore there is no ground for saying that such a one will ultimately not change and will not attain manifest awakening. In true liberation, there is no such thing as obstruction or the negation of such qualities. Furthermore, what is called empty and peaceful is the dharmadhātu, the basic space of phenomena. That very dharmadhātu, just as it is, is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, when what is called wrong craving is stopped and utterly extinguished, one no longer speaks of such a person as one who holds wrong craving. Now, who is it who is called one who holds wrong craving? One who holds wrong craving is one who has severed all roots of virtue, who does not abide in any virtuous dharma, and in whom not even a single instant of virtuous mind arises. In true liberation there are none of those conditions whatsoever. Because there are no such conditions whatsoever, it is true liberation. True liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is immeasurable.

To illustrate: a heap of sesame seeds can be measured and counted. True liberation is not like that. The great ocean, by contrast, is immeasurable and cannot be fathomed. Liberation is likewise — immeasurable and unfathomable. That which is immeasurable is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is without limit. Just as the karmic maturation of all sentient beings is vast beyond measure, liberation is likewise — its ripening is without limit. Ripening without limit is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is vast and wide. The great ocean, for example, has no equal. Liberation is likewise — it has no equal. That which has no equal is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is the supreme unsurpassed. Space, for example, is supremely lofty and without equal. Liberation is likewise — unsurpassed in its supreme loftiness. That which is lofty and without equal is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is without fixed abode. Just as all other animals do not abide in the place where the lion, king of beasts, dwells, liberation is likewise — it has no fixed abode. Having no fixed abode is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is unsurpassed. Just as the north is the foremost of all directions, liberation is likewise — unsurpassed. The unsurpassed is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is unsurpassed even beyond the unsurpassed. Just as the north is unsurpassed even beyond the unsurpassedness of the east, liberation is likewise — unsurpassed beyond the unsurpassed. The unsurpassed beyond the unsurpassed is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is of a permanent nature. Gods and humans, for example, possess bodies that are subject to decay and transference of life — they are impermanent, not permanent. Liberation is not like that; it is not impermanent. That which is not impermanent is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation has a firm and solid core. Acacia wood, sandalwood, and aloe wood are by nature hard and solid. Liberation is likewise — by nature hard, solid, and firm. That which is by nature firm and solid is true liberation, and true liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is said to be not hollow. Reeds and bamboo, for example, are hollow inside and therefore have a hollow core. Liberation is not like that. Therefore, know that liberation itself is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is that which is not stained by anything. When a wall has not been plastered smooth on the outside, insects and small creatures dwell and move about upon it. But if it is coated with plaster and painted with designs, the insects depart on smelling the scent of the pigments and no longer remain there.

Not dwelling in that way is liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is said to be without limit or boundary. A city, for example, has its boundaries and limits, but liberation is not like that. Space, for example, is without limit, and liberation is likewise without limit. Therefore, liberation itself is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is said to be beyond sight. Just as in the empty sky it is extremely difficult to follow a bird's trail with the eye, that extreme difficulty of being seen is the analogy for perfect liberation. And perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called very profound. Why is that? Because none of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas are able to enter into it. That into which they are unable to enter is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called very profound is that which buddhas and bodhisattvas hold in the highest reverence. Just as the most senior children show the deepest reverence and respect toward their parents, and that merit is extraordinarily profound, so that profundity of merit is the analogy for perfect liberation. And perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is not seen even when looked for. Just as a person cannot see the top of their own head, so too liberation cannot be seen even when looked for — not by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Not being seen even when looked for is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is without a dwelling-place or support. Space, for example, has no dwelling-place or support, and liberation is likewise. The expression "dwelling-place and support" is the analogy for the twenty-five modes of existence. Having no dwelling-place or support is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is nothing that can be taken up. The fruit of a mango tree on its branch, for example, is something that can be reached for and grasped. Liberation is not like that — it is nothing that can be reached for or grasped. Not being something that can be reached for or grasped is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is nothing that can be seized. An illusion, for example, cannot be seized, and liberation is likewise — it cannot be seized. Not being something that can be seized is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is without a physical body. A person, for example, by having a body is subject to scabies, leprosy, wasting disease, madness, and the like. Perfect liberation has none of such diseases. That which is free from those diseases is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is of a single taste. Just as milk is of a single taste, liberation is likewise — it is of a single taste. Being of a single taste is liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is thoroughly pure. Just as unmuddied water is utterly pure and clear, liberation is likewise — thoroughly pure and clear. Being thoroughly pure and clear is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is of a single taste. Just as rain falling from the sky is pure and of a single taste, liberation is likewise — pure and of a single taste. Being pure and of a single taste is perfect liberation.

Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is utterly luminous. Just as a full moon is unobscured by clouds or mist, liberation is likewise — free of clouds and mist. Being free of clouds and mist is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is supremely peaceful. Just as a person who has recovered from a burning fever is at peace, liberation is likewise — supremely peaceful. Being supremely peaceful is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is equanimity. In a wild and desolate place there are venomous snakes and wolves and the like, all with murderous intent. Liberation is not like that — it has no murderous intent. Having no murderous intent is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called equanimity: just as parents have an even and impartial mind toward their children, liberation is likewise — of an even mind. Being of an even mind is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is without another abode. Just as a person who dwells in an exceedingly fine and perfectly pure dwelling has no need of any other abode, liberation is likewise — without another abode. Being without another abode is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is contentment. Just as a person who is hungry and encounters delicious food eats without knowing when to stop, liberation is not like that. It is like one who has drunk warm milk-porridge and desires nothing more. Desiring nothing further is the example of perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is complete severance. Just as a person who cuts the rope that binds them becomes free from bondage, liberation is likewise — it severs all bonds of doubt. Thus, severing doubt is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the gone-beyond (pāramitā). A river has a near bank and a far bank. Liberation is not like that — there is nothing called a near bank, yet there is what is called the far bank. The far bank is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is utter silence. Just as the ocean gives rise to many sounds and roaring when great waves arise, liberation is not like that. And so liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is delicious and sweet. Just as when āmalaka fruit is added to a compound medicine it makes the taste pungent, liberation is not like that — it has a flavor that is wholly refreshing and sweet. Having a wholly refreshing and sweet flavor is the example of perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the dispelling of all afflictions. Just as a skilled physician compounds various medicines and is expert at healing the sick, liberation is likewise — it dispels all afflictions entirely. Dispelling all afflictions is the example of perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is without constriction. Just as a small house is confining and cannot hold many people, liberation is not like that — it can hold many.

Holding many is the example of perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the stilling of desire and is unmixed with attachment. As an example, a woman is one in whom attachment is abundant. Liberation is not like that, and such liberation is the Tathāgata. Thus the Tathāgata is entirely free from all the afflictive defilements — attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, and the rest.

Furthermore, liberation is without craving. Craving has two aspects: the craving of hungry ghosts and the craving for Dharma. In perfect liberation there is no craving of the hungry-ghost kind, yet out of loving care for sentient beings there is the craving for Dharma. Thus the craving for Dharma is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is free from self and what belongs to self. Such liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.

Furthermore, liberation is cessation — the exhaustion of all clinging to continued existence, gone far away from it. Such liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.

Furthermore, liberation is protector and refuge, saving one from all fears. Such liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.

Liberation is like a dwelling place. Whoever abides in it seeks no other dwelling. Just as a person who relies on a king seeks no other residence — yet dwelling with a king is subject to change — abiding in liberation undergoes no change. That which undergoes no change is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.

Furthermore, liberation is like a place of safety and support. Just as a person who goes into a wild and desolate region feels fear or anxiety, liberation is not like that — there is no fear and no anxiety. The absence of fear and anxiety is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, that which is called liberation is fearlessness. Just as the lion king is not frightened by any wild beast, liberation is likewise — it is not frightened by any host of māras. Fearlessness is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is non-deviation. Just as on a narrow path two people cannot walk side by side, liberation is not like that — and such liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, deviation is like a person who, frightened by a tiger, leaps into a pit. Liberation is not like that, and such liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, non-deviation is like someone who abandons a broken and small boat, boards a fine vessel, crosses the ocean safely, and arrives at a place of happiness. Liberation is likewise — the mind is supremely at ease. That supreme ease of mind is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, that which is called liberation is being extracted from causes and conditions. Consider: from the condition of milk comes curds; from the condition of curds comes butter; from the condition of butter comes the essence of butter. In perfect liberation there is no cause whatsoever. Being without cause is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the subduing of pride. Just as a great king is proud before lesser kings, liberation is not of that kind —

Thus liberation is the Tathāgata. And the Tathāgata is the Dharma.

Furthermore, liberation is the taming of the heedless. The heedless are those of many desires. In liberation these are absent. Being free of these is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the dispelling of ignorance. Just as medicine that is free of impurities is supreme — like the essence of butter — so too is liberation: having removed the impurity of ignorance, it is endowed with perfect knowledge. Being endowed with perfect knowledge is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is utter solitude — singular, without duality, like a wild yak bull alone in a remote wilderness, without companion. Liberation too is like that: singular and without duality. Being singular and without duality is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is endowed with a hard core. Reed, marsh grass, and medicinal herb are all hollow within, yet fruit is hard. All the gods and humans of the world, save the Buddha, the Blessed One, are neither hard nor stable. Perfect liberation is that which has gone far from every stream of conditioned existence. Thus liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the generation of higher knowledges (abhijñā). Perfect liberation is like that as well. Thus that liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the abandonment of all conditioned existence. It is like a person who has eaten to excess and vomits — liberation likewise abandons all conditioned existence. The abandonment of all conditioned existence is perfect liberation, and perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is infallible. Just as the fragrance of the pāśika flower is absent from each of its seven petals, so too is liberation. Thus liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is like the water element. The water element is supreme among the four great elements: it moistens and nourishes all plants and fruits. Liberation too is like that: it moistens all births. Thus liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called entrance. Just as where there is a door there is entry, and where there is a source of gold there is gold, so too liberation: it brings those who cultivate selflessness to enter. Thus liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is virtue. Just as a student who follows a teacher and heeds instructions is called virtuous, so too is liberation. Thus liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is a Dharma that transcends the world — it is the summit of all phenomena. Just as among all things with flavor, butter and milk are supreme, so too is liberation. Thus liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is called immovable. Just as a stone threshold cannot be moved by the wind, so too is perfect liberation. Thus liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is without turbulent waves. Just as the waters of the ocean surge with great waves, liberation is not like that. Thus liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is like a royal palace. Liberation too is like that. Thus liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is useful for every purpose. Just as the gold of the Jambū River is useful for every purpose and no fault or blemish can be imputed to it, so too is liberation: it is without fault or blemish. That which is without fault or blemish is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is the abandonment of the conduct of a servant and a slave. Just as a great person does not perform the deeds of a servant, so too is liberation: it is the complete relinquishment of the five aggregates. The complete relinquishment of the five aggregates is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is consummation. Just as one who has been cast into prison, when released from it, first bathes thoroughly and then goes home, so too is liberation: it is final and complete purity. Final and complete purity is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is ease without contrivance. Ease without contrivance comes from expelling all that belongs to attachment, aversion, delusion, and so forth. Just as a person who, without being aware of it, has been seized by a venomous snake is given an emetic to remove the poison — and when they vomit, the poison is gone and the body is at ease — so too is liberation: by expelling all the virulent poison of the afflictions, the body becomes at ease. This is called ease without contrivance. Ease without contrivance is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, what is called liberation is the cutting of the venomous snake of the four kinds of affliction. The cutting of the afflictions is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the relinquishment of all existence, the cessation of all suffering, the attainment of all happiness, the complete severing of all attachment, aversion, and delusion, and the uprooting of all the roots of the afflictions. The uprooting of the roots of the afflictions is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is the complete severance of all conditioned phenomena and the bringing forth of all undefiled phenomena, the cutting of all continuity — namely: it cuts only what grasps and clings, whether as "self," as "no-self," as "neither self" or "neither no-self," but it does not cut the view of self. For the view of self is the nature of a buddha. The nature of a buddha is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is an emptiness that is not empty. What is called "the emptiness that is empty" means having nothing whatsoever. Having nothing whatsoever is like the so-called liberation of the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) naked ascetics and the like. The naked ascetics are devoid of perfect liberation, and therefore theirs is called "the emptiness that is empty." Perfect liberation is not like that — it is an emptiness that is not empty. The emptiness that is not empty is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is non-empty.

Consider, for example, a vessel that holds water, butter, cream, wine, or honey. Even when the water, butter, cream, wine, or honey is absent, one still designates it as a vessel for water and so forth. Yet to that vessel, neither "empty" nor "non-empty" can rightly be applied. To call it "empty" would be inappropriate, for one cannot then designate it as having form, scent, taste, and texture. To call it "non-empty" would also be inappropriate, for there is none of the water and so forth within it.

Liberation is similar to this. To it, neither "form" nor "not form," neither "empty" nor "non-empty" can rightly be applied. If it were called "empty," then it could not rightly be designated as permanent, blissful, self, and pure. But to call it "non-empty" — permanent, blissful, self, and pure — by whom would those qualities be experienced? Therefore, to it, neither "empty" nor "non-empty" can rightly be applied.

That is to say: because the twenty-five modes of existence, all affliction, all suffering, all signs, and all conditioned formations (saṃskāra) are absent, liberation is like the vessel in which there is no cream — and so it is called "empty." As for being called "non-empty": its true form — permanent, blissful, self, and pure — is immovable and unchanging, just as the vessel is called "non-empty" by virtue of possessing form, scent, taste, and texture. Therefore liberation is like that vessel.

Yet the vessel, when it meets with conditions, can be broken. Liberation is not like that — it is indestructible. What is indestructible is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, liberation is free from desire. By way of example, a person possessed of a desirous mind may aspire to become Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, or the king of Brahmā (Brahman), or a sovereign king. Liberation is not like that. When one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, there is no desire, and there is no doubt. Freedom from desire and doubt is perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata. If one were to say that in liberation there is desire and doubt, that has no basis whatsoever.

Furthermore, liberation is the thorough severing of all craving for existence, all signs, all bonds, all affliction, all saṃsāra, all causes and conditions, and all fruits of karmic maturation. Such being the case, liberation is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is nirvāṇa.

All sentient beings, fearing the afflictions of saṃsāra, incline toward the Three Refuges. It is like a deer that is frightened by a hunter: when it escapes from an obstacle it makes a single leap — that is one going for refuge. In this way, making three leaps is the simile for going for the Three Refuges. By making three leaps, one comes to ease and wellbeing.

Ordinary beings are just like this: frightened by the hunter of the four māras, they incline toward and go for the Three Refuges. By turning to the Three Refuges, they come to ease and wellbeing. Whoever comes to ease and wellbeing has attained perfect liberation. Perfect liberation is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is nirvāṇa. Nirvāṇa is inexhaustible. What is inexhaustible is the intrinsic nature of the buddha. The intrinsic nature of the buddha is certainty. What is certainty is the unsurpassed, perfectly complete buddha.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa said this to the Blessed One:

The Blessed One then declared to Kāśyapa: "Noble son, nirvāṇa, the intrinsic nature of the buddha, certainty, and the Tathāgata — if these are one in meaning, why then did I teach the Three Refuges?" The Blessed One replied: "Noble son, sentient beings, frightened by saṃsāra, turn and go to the Three Refuges. By taking the Three Refuges, they should understand that this itself is the intrinsic nature of the buddha, certainty, and nirvāṇa.

"Noble son, some phenomena share one name yet have different meanings. Other phenomena differ both in name and in meaning. Those that share one name yet have different meanings are these: 'the buddha is permanent,' 'the Dharma is permanent,' 'the Saṅgha of monks is permanent,' 'passing beyond sorrow,' and 'space is permanent' — these are said to share one name yet have different meanings.

"Those that differ both in name and in meaning are these: 'buddha' means one who experiences; 'Dharma' means what does not experience; 'Saṅgha' means harmony; 'passing beyond sorrow' means complete liberation; and 'space' means that which is neither virtue nor non-virtue and is unobstructed — these are said to differ both in name and in meaning.

"Noble son, the Three Refuges are likewise: they differ both in name and in meaning. Among them there is nothing whatsoever that can be called 'one.'

"For this reason, the next day I said to the matriarch Gautamī: 'Gautamī, do not make offerings to me — make offerings to the Saṅgha. By making offerings to the Saṅgha, it is called making offerings to the Three Jewels.'"

Then the matriarch spoke thus: "Within the Saṅgha, there is neither a buddha nor the Dharma — why then does making offerings to the Saṅgha become making offerings to the Three Jewels?"

To this I replied: "Acting in accordance with what I have taught is making offerings to the buddha. Desiring complete liberation is making offerings to the Dharma. Accepting the Saṅgha is making offerings to the Saṅgha. Therefore, noble son, it is not right to call the Three Jewels 'one.'

"Noble son, the Blessed One at certain times teaches 'one' as 'three,' and at certain times teaches 'three' as 'one.' Therefore the domain of activity of the buddhas is beyond the comprehension of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

Kāśyapa then asked again: "Blessed One, when the Blessed One said 'ultimate ease is nirvāṇa,' what is the meaning of that? Nirvāṇa, it is said, is equanimity with regard to the body and equanimity with regard to gnosis. If there is equanimity toward body and gnosis, who then experiences the ease?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, consider the example of a person who has eaten to excess and, suffering from indigestion, goes outside, vomits, and returns. His companions ask him: 'How is your discomfort — are you better?' He replies: 'I am better; there is no more discomfort.'

"The Tathāgata is likewise: having finally parted from the twenty-five modes of existence and passed fully into nirvāṇa, having reached the state of perfect ease — there is no movement, no exhaustion, and nothing to be called cessation. Because all feelings have been severed, it is said that there is no experience of ease as a feeling. The absence of any such felt experience is what is called permanent ease. For anyone to say that the Tathāgata experiences ease as a feeling — that has no basis. Therefore, ultimate ease is nirvāṇa. That nirvāṇa is perfect liberation. And perfect liberation is the Tathāgata."

Kāśyapa then asked again: "Is liberation that which is unborn and unceasing?"

"Just so, just so."

"Son of good family, that which is unborn and unceasing is perfect liberation. And just so, perfect liberation is the Tathāgata."

Kāśyapa asked again: "If that which is unborn and unceasing is perfect liberation, then space too has the characteristic of being unborn and unceasing — would space also be the Tathāgata? And would the Tathāgata then not be perfect liberation?"

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, it is not so. Why is it not so? Son of good family, consider this: the kalandaka bird and the jīvañjīvaka bird have voices of exceeding beauty, yet they are not in any way comparable to the cry of a crow. The crow's call, Blessed One, is exceedingly unpleasant, and it cannot compare to the jīvañjīvaka bird — no, not even in a thousand ways."

Kāśyapa continued: "The kalandaka and similar birds have voices of great beauty and bodies of remarkable appearance — why then has the Tathāgata used the crow as an illustration? To take a mustard seed as an analogy for Mount Meru would be such a comparison, and the same applies to the Blessed One and space. The song of the kalandaka bird is fitting as an analogy for the speech of the buddha, the Blessed One — but the cry of the crow is not fitting as an analogy."
