Then the Blessed One spoke thus to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Excellent! Excellent! You are deeply skilled in the meaning of what is profound. The Tathāgata, on certain occasions, looking to causes and conditions, has also described space as an analogy for perfect liberation. And just so, perfect liberation is the Tathāgata. Perfect liberation — perfectly and completely — cannot be created by any god or human within this world together with its gods. Space is not, in the strict sense, a proper analogy, yet for the purpose of taming sentient beings, even what is not a proper analogy is employed as one. Therefore, know that liberation itself is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata itself is liberation. Liberation and the Tathāgata are non-dual and without distinction.

"Son of good family, when we say 'not a proper analogy,' what is meant is this: things that are uncreated are, strictly speaking, not fit to be drawn as analogies for one another, yet in the context of certain causes and conditions, such analogies are permissible. In the sūtras as well it is said: 'His face is like the full moon,' and 'A white wool-clad elephant is like a snow mountain.' It is not correct to say the full moon is his face, nor is it correct to say a snow mountain is a white wool-clad elephant. Son of good family, while it is not strictly fitting to use analogies for perfect liberation, analogies are shown for the purpose of taming sentient beings. And it is just the same that, through many analogies, one comes to understand the nature of reality of phenomena."

The eighth fascicle.

Kāśyapa then asked: "For what reason has the Tathāgata spoken of these in two aspects?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, consider this: if a man were to take up a sword and approach with an intention of aversion, coming to kill the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata neither became angry nor changed countenance — would that man then have committed the action without interval of killing a Tathāgata?"

"He would not, Blessed One."

"Blessed One, why is that?"

"Because the body of the Tathāgata cannot be destroyed. And how is that? The body of the Tathāgata has no physical aggregates; it is endowed with nothing other than the nature of reality. Since the nature of reality of phenomena cannot be destroyed, how could that person ever destroy the body of a buddha? Yet, because of the evil mind he bears, he would indeed become a being carrying the karma of the most heinous act without interval."

Through that, one comes to understand the nature of reality of phenomena.

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, what you asked before accords well with what I have taught. Noble son, consider this example: a wicked man comes to bring a meal to another man who is working in a field, intending to kill him. Having sharpened his sword and set out, the victim becomes aware of the danger and hides inside a pile of grain-sacks. The wicked man, sword in hand, circles around the pile of grain-sacks, strikes it with his sword, and thinks to himself, 'That one is done for!' — and so a mind of joy arises in him. Later, his mother emerges from inside that pile of grain-sacks. When she returns home, what do you think? Has that man committed the most heinous act without interval?"

"Blessed One, it is by no means certain."

"Why is that?"

"To say that he has committed a wrong, his mother's body was not destroyed. If her body was not destroyed, how could it be right to say that a wrong was committed? Yet to say that no wrong was committed, he harbored the thought 'That one is done for!' and even gave rise to a mind of joy — so how could that be right either? That man did not complete the most heinous act without interval, yet he did perform a deed of the kind that is without interval. Through such causes and conditions, one comes to understand the nature of reality of phenomena."

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, through such causes and conditions, I have taught examples of liberation using various skillful means and similes. Though one might demonstrate through examples as numerous and limitless as can be counted, in truth no perfect example can be fashioned. In the context of certain causes and conditions an example is fitting, while in the context of other causes and conditions an example is not fitting. Therefore liberation is endowed with immeasurable qualities of such a kind — it is entry into nirvāṇa. The passing beyond sorrow, and the Tathāgata as well, are equally endowed with immeasurable qualities of such a kind. Being endowed with immeasurable qualities of such a kind and being utterly perfect, it is called the Great Nirvāṇa."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I have sought from the very beginning the place where the Tathāgata has come — yet it is a place not to be found by searching. Since it cannot be found by searching in that way, I understand that even the measure of his lifespan likewise cannot be found by searching."

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, you indeed hold and guard the authentic Dharma with great care. Whatever noble sons or noble daughters who wish to cut the bonds of thorough affliction should likewise hold and guard the authentic Dharma in this way.

"Noble son, through this profoundly deep sūtra of complete nirvāṇa, four types of persons who guard the authentic Dharma, establish the authentic Dharma, are able to contemplate the authentic Dharma, and show compassion for the world with all that is in it — these will become a support and refuge for the world with all that is in it, and will bring benefit and happiness to many gods and humans.

"Who are these four types of persons? The person who has transcended the ordinary world while still bearing the defining marks of affliction is called the stream-enterer (Skt. srotāpanna) — this is the first. The once-returner (Skt. sakṛdāgāmin) is the second. The non-returner (Skt. anāgāmin) is the third. The arhat is the fourth. When these four types of persons appear in the world, they show compassion for the world with all that is in it, become a support and refuge for the world with all that is in it, and bring benefit and happiness to many gods and humans."

Now, what is meant by "bearing the defining marks of affliction"? Here, a person who fully maintains and guards moral discipline, whose conduct is unimpaired, who establishes the genuine Dharma correctly, and who, having heard it from a buddha exactly as it was spoken, is learned in both letter and meaning and expounds it at length to others — this is as follows: such a person teaches at length the qualities of the eight great beings, beginning with having few desires, having many desires, and awakening, and so forth. When faults arise, such a person makes those who have committed them confess and feel remorse, and then purifies those faults. Such a person is also highly skilled in the skillful means, conduct, and the Dharma spoken with intentional meaning that belong to the bodhisattvas. That person is not one of the eight great beings, but rather what is called an ordinary childlike being. The eight great beings are not called ordinary childlike beings; they are called bodhisattvas, not buddhas. The second of the two persons is called the stream-enterer.

The once-returner either finds the genuine Dharma, holds the genuine Dharma, or, upon hearing the Dharma from a buddha, writes it down in books exactly as heard, retains it, reads it, recites it, and expounds and explains it at length to others. However, this person, after hearing the Dharma, does not write it down, does not retain it, does not hold it, and does not explain it to others. There is no occasion for this person to say that the Buddha permitted the holding of uninvestigated property such as male and female servants and the like. This is called the second person. That person has not attained the ground of either the second or the third, nor is such a person called a prophesied bodhisattva.

The third person is called the non-returner. The non-returner has no occasion to disparage the genuine Dharma, to say that the Buddha permitted the holding of uninvestigated property such as male and female servants and workers and the like, to learn and hold the texts and sciences of non-Buddhists, to become obscured by manifest afflictions, to become covered and shrouded by underlying afflictive tendencies, to genuinely conceal and hide the authentic relics of the Tathāgata, to be harmed and injured by many kinds of external illness, to be seized by the four kinds of virulent poison, or to assert the existence of a self and the like — but there is occasion for this person to assert no-self. There is no occasion to assert attachment to worldly phenomena, but there is occasion to teach the Great Vehicle without interruption and without obstacle. There is no occasion for the body one has assumed to be devoured by eighty-four thousand parasites, but there is occasion for attachment to be completely abandoned, so that even in sleep as a young person no impure emission occurs. And there is no occasion to be frightened and terrified when performing the acts of dying. As for what is meant by "non-returner": that person does not return again into the faults and defects enumerated above, nor becomes tainted by them. Even if such a person does take rebirth and is born again, that one is called a bodhisattva, and having also received a prophecy, will without great delay awaken to the unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. This is called the third person.

The fourth person is called the arhat. The arhat has cut off all afflictions, has laid down the burden, has accomplished what had to be done, has thoroughly found one's own benefit hereafter, abides perfectly on the ten grounds, wields mastery over primordial wisdom, manifests various forms and aspects of appearance in accordance with whatever ordinary beings aspire to, and, for those who wish to fully awaken, manifests full awakening.

It is because one possesses such qualities, immeasurable and without limit, that one is called an arhat.

Therefore, when these four great persons appear in the world, out of loving care for all those who dwell in the world, they become a refuge and support for the world's inhabitants, work for the welfare and happiness of the many — gods and humans alike — and become supreme among gods and humans, become foremost, become most excellent. It is just as one who has gone for refuge in all the Tathāgatas becomes most excellent among human beings.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, I myself do not dwell in or rely upon these four persons. For what reason? Because the Blessed One, in a sūtra spoken earlier in reply to a question from the householder Kuśīla, declared: 'Kuśīla, should someone come disguised in the likeness of a buddha — in order to destroy and lead astray gods, māras, Brahmā, and the rest — adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor marks, with a halo of light filling a fathom on all sides, a face like the full moon, the ūrṇā hair between the brows either white as snow or gleaming like a conch shell, then you must discern whether that one is genuine or not. Having discerned and understood, tame that one.' Now, Blessed One, if māras and the like are able to display and conjure even the body of a buddha, how much more need be said of their displaying the bodies of the four persons — the arhat and the rest — traveling through the sky, lying down, sitting, emitting water from the left side of the body and fire from the right, or showing smoke billowing from the body so that it appears like a mass of flames. For these very reasons of cause and condition, even if such appearances occur, faith does not arise in me; and even if there be a teacher, I do not think to treat them as proper, to honor them with reverence, or to regard them as a refuge and support."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, if I myself have doubts about a teaching, I do not accept it — how much less should those others do so. Therefore, examine carefully and deeply whether something is virtuous or non-virtuous, to be done or not to be done, and then internalize it thoroughly. If you act in this way, you will experience happiness for a long time."

"Son of good family, consider this example: a dog-thief comes to a house; a maidservant keeping watch over the house notices him and says to him, 'Get out quickly! If you do not flee, you will be killed.' Hearing those words, the dog flees and does not return. In the same way, when you are disciplining the evil māra, say to him: 'Wicked māra, do not display yourself in such a form! If you do, you will be bound with the five bonds.' If the māra hears those words, he will flee and not return — just as the dog-thief did not return."

Kāśyapa then asked again: "Blessed One, you declared to the householder Kuśīla that one who disciplines māra in such a way is 'close to complete and perfect nirvāṇa.' Then why did the Blessed One say that the four persons are to be regarded as refuge and support? Are the four persons fit to be relied upon with certainty as teachers?"

The Blessed One answered Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, what I have said is consistent with that — it is just so. Son of good family, I taught the disciplining of māra for those who have the eyes of a śrāvaka; I did not teach it for persons who strive earnestly in the Great Vehicle. A person who is a śrāvaka, even one who has attained the eye of miraculous vision, is said to have the eye of flesh. But one who studies the Great Vehicle, even if they have only the eye of flesh, is said to have the eye of a buddha. Why? Because the sūtras of the Great Vehicle are called the vehicle of the buddhas."

The vehicle of the buddhas is the supreme and most excellent of all vehicles. Son of good family, consider this analogy. A brave man of great martial skill is always accompanied and supported by those who are not timid soldiers. That brave man teaches those soldiers: "Hold the bow in this manner. Release the arrow in this manner. Learn to wield the spear and the sling, and catch hold of the lasso in this manner." Furthermore, he instructs them: "Engaging in battle is like walking on the edge of a blade, yet do not give rise to thoughts of fear or terror. Instead, generate a thought that utterly despises the enemy — whether gods or humans — and give rise to the thought: 'I am exceptionally brave and skilled.' At intervals, when weaker soldiers act the part of warriors, taking up bows, swords, and various weapons to come to the battlefield, if they then call out loudly, do not act as though you are frightened or terrified by them. Once the soldier knows that you are not afraid, he will immediately scatter and flee like a thieving dog."

Son of good family, the Tathāgata likewise says to the śrāvakas: "Do not be frightened by the evil māra. Even if the evil māra manifests in the form of a buddha and comes before you, subdue the hordes of māra with utterly steadfast and vigorous diligence. At that time, māra, overcome with grief and displeasure, will go away."

Son of good family, consider another analogy. Just as a warrior of great bravery needs no instruction from another, so too is the one who strives earnestly in the Great Vehicle: upon hearing sūtras of profound depth in their many varieties, the mind becomes greatly delighted and overjoyed, and no fear or terror arises. Why? Because a person who studies the Great Vehicle has paid homage to, venerated, and made offerings to hundreds of thousands and countless buddhas of the past. Therefore, even if hundreds of thousands and countless hordes of māra were to harm or attack such a person, fear and terror would never arise in them.

Son of good family, consider this analogy. If a person obtains the medicine called "agada," they have no fear of any venomous snake or other such dangers, because the power of that medicine can subdue all poisons. The sūtras of the Great Vehicle are likewise: they give rise to no fear of any malevolent māra, and can tame them so that they do not rise again.

Son of good family, consider yet another analogy. A venomous nāga, when it kills another being, does so sometimes merely by looking with its eyes, and sometimes merely by its breath — and the being dies. For this reason, all creatures — lions, tigers, leopards, wolves, dogs, and the rest — are frightened of it. There is not one among those wild beasts that does not die from merely hearing its sound or being touched by its body. But a person who is supremely skilled in mantra can, through the power of mantra, subdue the venomous nāga, the garuḍa, the enraged wild elephant, the lion, the tiger, the leopard, and all the rest — even to the point of being able to ride and direct them. Those wild beasts, by the mere sight of that one skilled in mantra, become tame of their own accord.

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are similar to those animals: upon seeing the evil māra, they all become frightened and terrified. The evil māra, for his part, has no thought of fear or terror toward them and performs the works of māra freely. Those who study the Great Vehicle, by contrast, are like the mantra master: when they see how śrāvakas have been frightened by māra and lose faith and conviction in the Great Vehicle, they first subdue the ranks of māra through skillful means and bring them all to submission, and then, after that, they teach and expound the holy Dharma in its many varieties. When śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas see those māras thus subdued in this way, they initially take fright, but then they generate faith and conviction in the supreme and unsurpassed holy Dharma of the Great Vehicle.

They declared: "From this day forward, we shall cause no more hindrances or obstacles to this holy Dharma."

Furthermore, good son, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas feel fear and terror in the face of the afflictions. Those who study the Great Vehicle, however, feel no such fear or timidity. Those who apply themselves earnestly to the Great Vehicle possess power of that kind. It is for this reason that what was taught and explained earlier was done so in order that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas might tame the māras — it was not for the sake of the Great Vehicle. This most profound sūtra of the Great Vehicle on nirvāṇa is wondrous and extraordinary: there is no one capable of taming it. As for the person who listens to and hears it, holds faith in it and retains it, and trusts that the Tathāgata possesses the quality of permanence — such a person is exceedingly rare, like the udumbara flower. Once I have passed into nirvāṇa, whoever hears this most profound sūtra of the Great Vehicle and gives rise to a mind of faith — know that such a person will not fall into the lower realms for a hundred thousand aeons in the time to come.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Good son, after I have passed into nirvāṇa, countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings will slander and disbelieve this holy sūtra on the complete passing into nirvāṇa."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: "Blessed One, if sentient beings were to attend upon and venerate this sūtra for a long time after the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa, what kind of person, endowed with great virtue, would be able to liberate those who slander the Dharma?"

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: "Good son, for forty years after my passing into nirvāṇa this teaching will flourish widely throughout this world of Jambudvīpa, and then it will sink beneath the earth. Good son, consider this example: in a place where there are sugarcane, rice, molasses, milk, butter, and the essence of butter, the sentient beings who dwell there regard that taste as the supreme and finest of all tastes. Yet some of them eat nothing but millet and barley seeds, and they say: 'There is nothing more excellent than our food.' This is the karmic maturation of the deeds of beings of little merit. Those who are fortunate and endowed with merit never even hear of millet and barley seeds; they eat nothing but rice, sugarcane, molasses, and the essence of butter. This holy sūtra on nirvāṇa is just like this: those of dull faculties, of little merit, and without good fortune have no wish to hear it. Just as those of little merit have no desire for rice and molasses and the like, so too both vehicles of lesser scope are like that — they have no desire for this holy sūtra of the Great Passing beyond Sorrow. As for the ordinary person who is eager to hear this sūtra, who when they hear it rejoices greatly and does not slander it — they are like the fortunate sentient being who eats rice and the rest.

Good son, consider another example: a king who dwells in a very wretched and desolate mountain retreat, where sugarcane, rice, and molasses are available but scarce. Fearing their exhaustion, he restrains his wish to eat them and eats nothing but millet and barley seeds. Another king hears of this and, moved by kindness, loads rice, molasses, and the like onto carts and sends them as a gift. That first king then distributes and gives them to everyone, and only after that does he eat. Having eaten, they all rejoice, saying: 'Thanks to that king, we have eaten food we had never tasted before.' Good son, the fourth kind of person is likewise like this — a great caravan leader in the unsurpassed great Dharma.

Of those four kinds of persons, one of them, in some other region, sees that countless bodhisattvas are studying this sūtra of the Great Vehicle, or copying it into manuscripts, or having others copy it into manuscripts — whether for the sake of gain, honour, and renown, or for the sake of mastering the Dharma, or for the sake of having a support and a place of residence, or merely for the purpose of sending and exchanging it for other sūtras — yet sees that those bodhisattvas are unable to teach and expound it extensively to others. For the sake of those bodhisattvas, that person conveys this supreme sūtra to that region, gives it to them, causes them to arouse the mind of unsurpassable awakening, and establishes them on the path to awakening. Those bodhisattvas, having heard this sūtra, then teach and expound it extensively to others, and countless sentient beings come to taste the flavour of the Dharma of this Great Vehicle sūtra. That is how, through the power of that one bodhisattva, the sūtra comes to be heard by those who had not heard it before — just as, through the power of that one king, all came to taste food they had never tasted before.

Good son, furthermore, know that the place where this sūtra of the Great Passage into Nirvāṇa abides is like a vajra, and know that the person who dwells there is likewise like a vajra. Whoever listens to this sūtra will be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and whatever aspiration one holds will be fulfilled. Monk, you must hold firmly everything I have spoken here. As for any sentient being who is unable to listen to this sūtra, know that person to be a most fitting object of compassion — for that person is unable to hold the meaning of this supremely profound Great Vehicle sūtra.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One and said: Blessed One, for forty years after the Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa, this Great Vehicle sūtra will spread widely throughout Jambudvīpa. After that it will sink beneath the earth, and only after a very long time will it emerge again.

The Blessed One declared: Good son, this sacred Dharma of mine, except for the last eighty years, will for the preceding forty years rain down as a great shower of Dharma upon this Jambudvīpa.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One and said: Blessed One, when this sūtra is at the time of the decline of the sacred Dharma — when pure moral discipline has deteriorated, when what is not Dharma increases and proliferates, when there are no sentient beings who act in accordance with what is proper — may the Tathāgata, out of compassion for ordinary beings, please disclose and teach this openly, so that bodhisattvas who hear it may hold it. And by holding it in mind, may they become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Thereupon the Blessed One declared to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: Excellent! Most excellent! Good son, it is good that you have asked about these matters. Good son, any sentient being who arouses the mind of awakening toward buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in the Gaṅgā river — if in this degenerate age that person holds and retains this sūtra, they do not slander it.

Good son, any sentient being who arouses the mind of awakening toward buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in one Gaṅgā river — in this degenerate age, that person will not slander this Dharma, and will come to have faith and devotion toward this sūtra, yet will be unable to expound it extensively to others or teach it.

Good son, any sentient being who arouses the mind of awakening toward buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in two Gaṅgā rivers — in this degenerate age, that person will not slander this Dharma, and will come to have faith and devotion, to hold and retain it, to read and recite it, yet will be unable to teach it extensively to others.

Any sentient being who arouses the mind of awakening toward buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in three Gaṅgā rivers — in this degenerate age, that person will not slander this Dharma, and will come to hold and retain it, to read and recite it, and to write it down in a volume; and though they may teach it to others, they will not understand its profound meaning.

Any sentient being who arouses the mind of awakening toward buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in four Gaṅgā rivers — in this degenerate age, that person will not slander this Dharma, and will come to hold and retain it, to read and recite it, and to write it down in a volume; and that person will be able to teach others one sixteenth of its profound meaning. They will teach and expound it, yet even so they will not know it completely.

Any sentient being who arouses the mind of awakening toward buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in five Gaṅgā rivers — in this degenerate age, that person will not slander this Dharma, and will come to hold and retain it, to read and recite it, and to write it down in a volume; and that person will also be able to teach others eight sixteenths of its profound meaning.

Any sentient being who arouses the mind of awakening toward buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in six Gaṅgā rivers — in this degenerate age, that person will not slander this Dharma, and will come to hold and retain it, to read and recite it, and to write it down in a volume; and that person will also be able to teach others twelve sixteenths of its profound meaning.

Any sentient being who arouses the mind of awakening toward buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in seven Gaṅgā rivers — in this degenerate age, that person will not slander this Dharma, and will come to hold and retain it, to recite and read it, and to write it down in a volume; and that person will also be able to teach others fourteen sixteenths of its profound meaning.

Any sentient being who arouses the mind of awakening toward buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in eight Gaṅgā rivers — in this degenerate age, that person will not slander this Dharma, and will come to hold and retain it, to read and recite it; they will urge others to write it down in a volume; they themselves will listen to and retain it, and will urge others likewise to listen to it, retain it, read and recite it, and take it to heart; out of love for the world, they will guard it carefully and make offerings to the sūtra, and will equally urge others to make offerings, to pay homage, to render reverence, to show respect, to bow before it, and to read and recite it. Such a person will come to a complete and thorough understanding of the profound meaning, which is this: the Tathāgata is endowed with the quality of permanently abiding — unchanging, ultimately blissful; they will expound extensively that sentient beings possess the nature of a buddha; they will be thoroughly skilled in the treasury of the Tathāgata's Dharma; and by making offerings to those buddhas, they will come to understand the holding, retaining, protecting, and establishing of these unsurpassed and genuine Dharmas.

Whoever arouses the mind of awakening toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment — that person will, in a future time, hold, retain, and protect these genuine Dharmas, and it should be understood that they will certainly come to know the establishing of the genuine Dharma. Therefore, you too, in this coming degenerate age —

it should be understood that they will protect the genuine Dharma. And why is this? It is because those who arouse the mind of awakening will certainly, in a future time, be able to guard and hold these unsurpassed and genuine Dharmas.

Noble son, monks of poor moral discipline, upon hearing that I have passed into nirvāṇa, will feel no grief. They will say: "Now that the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, we are satisfied. While the Tathāgata dwelt in the world, he was an obstacle to our gains; but now that he has passed into nirvāṇa, there is no one to obstruct or take away our gains. Since there is no one to obstruct or take them, we shall obtain gains in abundance. While the Tathāgata dwelt in the world, moral discipline was extremely strict; but now that he has passed into nirvāṇa, everything will become lax. Even wearing the monastic robe on one's body will amount to nothing more than playing at the appearance of the Dharma. Now it is worn out and tattered — like a tattered banner on a stick." Anyone who speaks in such a way slanders and debases this sūtra. Noble son, you must take this to heart.

Whatever sentient being possesses an abundance of qualities beyond measure will have faith and confidence in this Great Vehicle sūtra. Having gained that faith, they will hold and retain it; and if they then teach and explain it in full to other sentient beings who are eager to hear it, that person, by the mere act of hearing it, will be purified of all non-virtuous karma accumulated over countless and immeasurable past eons.

But whoever lacks faith in this sūtra, whoever has no confidence in it — in this very life they will be tormented and caused to suffer by illnesses of every kind; they will be reproached and reviled by many people; and after death they will be despised and scorned by all. Their appearance will be ugly; they will be utterly destitute of the necessities of life; whatever small thing they obtain will be of poor and coarse quality; and wherever they are born they will always be poor and of inferior birth. They will be born in a lineage that slanders the genuine Dharma and holds wrong views. When the time of death comes, they will be born in a land torn by strife, or will meet with weapons, or will encounter a king who acts without justice, or will encounter enemies, or will fail to meet spiritual friends and companions even when they exist. They will find no necessities for life whatsoever; and even if they obtain a little, they will always be utterly tormented by hunger and thirst. They will associate with and rely on base and inferior people; kings and ministers too will want nothing to do with them; and even if they teach and explain without departing from the meaning, no one will have confidence in them or accept what they say. Such a person will not be born in a good and virtuous state. Just as a bird with broken wings cannot fly, that person likewise will not, in a future time, be born in a good state among gods or humans.

Now, if any person has confidence and faith in this Great Vehicle sūtra, then even if their present body is ugly and unattractive, through the power of the virtues of this sūtra they will come to be reborn with a beautiful form, endowed with splendor and might, with their radiance increasing and flourishing. All gods and humans dwelling in the world will find them pleasing and will wish to behold them; they will render them honor, respect, and offering, and will be loath to let them go. Kings and ministers, relatives, and retinues will have faith and confidence in whatever they say and teach.

If any attendant among my śrāvakas wishes to engage in the most excellent and supreme purpose, they should expound and teach this Great Vehicle sūtra in full to all those dwelling in the world.

Noble son, consider the following example: dew, however much it may wish to remain for a long time, cannot outlast the rising of the sun — the moment the sun rises, even whatever remains vanishes without a trace. Noble son, it is exactly the same with all the non-virtuous karma of those sentient beings:

— they cannot outlast the rising of the great sun of nirvāṇa. The very moment that sun rises, all their non-virtuous karma will melt away and be purified.

Noble son, here is another example. When a person has gone forth, shaving their hair and beard and wearing the robes, even if they have not undertaken the ten precepts of a novice, should a single householder invite the entire Saṅgha and that person — though they have not undertaken the precepts — is included among those invited as guests of the Saṅgha, then, although they have not undertaken the precepts, they still count as part of the Saṅgha.

Noble son, in exactly the same way, any sentient being who arouses the intention to study this Great Vehicle sūtra of nirvāṇa — who resolves to have it copied into a volume, to carry it, to hold it, to read it, or to recite it — that person too is like one who, though not yet fully accomplished, has reached the tenth ground. They are to be counted among those of the tenth ground.

If any sentient being — whether or not they have become an attendant of the Buddha — who, out of fear born of attachment, or for the sake of profit and gain, hears and listens to even a single verse of this sūtra and does not disparage it, that person is to be understood as one who is close to and approaching unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening.

Noble son, given such causes and conditions, were anyone to say of the four great beings what the Buddha has declared is not what the Buddha has declared, that would simply be impossible. Therefore, I have declared the four great beings to be, as it were, the support and foundation of the world.

Noble son, you should therefore make offerings to these four beings. The assembly then addressed the Blessed One: Blessed One, how should we seek out and make offerings to these four great beings?

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: To any person who guards and upholds the sacred Dharma, you should make supplication, and offer up even your body and your life as an act of homage. I have also said the same in other Great Vehicle sūtras:

Whoever knows the sacred Dharma,
whether old or young,
should honor them, pay homage, and make obeisance,
as to a father or a brahmin.

Whoever knows the sacred Dharma,
whether old or young,
should honor them, pay homage, and make obeisance,
as the gods worship their sovereign lord.

Then once again the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One: Blessed One, it is as you have declared — making offerings to one's teacher and preceptor is indeed as you have said. But please explain this at greater length. If a teacher who possesses moral discipline were to inquire about something not previously heard from a younger person, should one then pay homage to that person? And if one did pay homage to them, could one still be called a guardian of moral discipline? And conversely, if a younger person who possesses moral discipline were to inquire about something not previously heard from an elderly teacher whose moral discipline has deteriorated, should one also pay homage to that person? And if a person who has gone forth were to inquire about something not previously heard from a householder, should one also pay homage to that householder? You have also declared that one who has gone forth should not bow down to a householder. Yet by the Buddha's Dharma, the young and junior should show respect and pay homage to their senior teachers. Why is that? Because those senior teachers have received full ordination earlier, and therefore one should show respect and bow down to them — so you have also declared.

Yet according to what the Blessed One has declared, one whose moral discipline has deteriorated does not truly enter into the Buddha's Dharma. You have declared such a person to be like weeds or grass in a field of good crop. But elsewhere the Blessed One has declared that if someone knows the sacred Dharma, whether old or young, one should honor them just as the gods honor their sovereign lord and king. How are these two meanings to be understood? Is there not a contradiction in what the Tathāgata has declared?

According to what the Blessed One has declared, in another mode the Blessed One declared that a monk who upholds moral discipline has no fault — why did the Blessed One say this? As for the declaration in other sūtras that those whose moral discipline has deteriorated are cut off by punishment, that too is not of definitive meaning.

The Blessed One then declared to Kāśyapa: Son of good family, I spoke those verses for the sake of bodhisattvas striving in the Great Vehicle in the time to come — not for the sake of the śrāvaka community. Son of good family, as I declared before, when the sacred Dharma is in decline and those of corrupt conduct are active, when those of corrupt discipline arise and act contrary to the Dharma, when no noble ones (āryas) at all appear openly, when servants — both male and female — and uninspected property are being held and used: at such a time, one among the four types of persons will appear — one who, having shaved hair and beard and gone forth into renunciation, exerts effort on the path. This person, observing individual monks holding servants — male and female — and laborers, holding uninspected property, not knowing what has and has not been examined, not knowing what is and is not in accord with the Vinaya, and yet seeing all this, in order to train those monks will outwardly conform his conduct to theirs, while within his own conduct is discordant. He is profoundly aware of his own domain of practice and of the sphere of the buddhas' conduct, and even when he sees faults and defeats incurred by opponents, he says nothing — he raises no objection. Why is this? Because he has appeared in the world in order to protect and establish the sacred Dharma — therefore he says nothing and raises no objection. Son of good family, in this way, because that person acts for the protection of the Dharma, even though faults are present, one should not say that his moral discipline is broken.

Son of good family, consider this analogy. A king falls gravely ill and dies, and his heir is young and incapable of managing the affairs of state. At such a time, it happens that an outcast, enormously wealthy with great treasure and abundant possessions, with a very large retinue, grows proud of his power, seizes the royal throne by force, and installs himself as king. The householders, brahmins, and others who live in that land mostly scatter and flee to other regions. Even those who remain there have no wish to look upon that great king. If householders, merchants, brahmins, and the like cannot bring themselves to abandon the land, it is as though they will simply die in the very place where they were born, like trees fixed in their own ground. The outcast king, recognizing that many of the country's people have scattered and fled, then stations other outcasts at all the roads and marketplaces, and for seven days has drums beaten, proclaiming: "O brahmins! Whoever among you consecrates me by pouring empowerment upon my head — I will give half the kingdom!" Yet not a single brahmin came forward. Each said to the other: "It is impossible that one of brahmin lineage would perform such a service as this."

The outcast king then declared further: "If not even one of you brahmins will become my officiating priest, I will place you brahmins together with the lowborn outcasts, treat you as equals, and make you perform the same labors. But if you consecrate me by pouring empowerment upon my head, I will give half the kingdom. I bind this word with a pledge that it is no lie. I will also divide and bestow the ambrosia of immortality of the Thirty-Three Heaven." At that time, a young brahmin's son — very young, celibate, bearing the mark of the topknot, and highly skilled in mantra and ritual — went to where the king was and addressed the great king, declaring: "I will perform this for Your Majesty."

The king was overjoyed and appointed that young brahmin to perform the head-consecration empowerment. When the other brahmins heard this, they all reviled the youth, saying: "You are a brahmin — why do you make yourself the ritual master of that lowborn outcaste?" At that time the king gave the young man half the kingdom, and together they assumed the governance of the realm.

After some time had passed, the young man addressed the king with these words: "If I leave my home and come to serve as Your Majesty's teacher, I will instruct and train the king in mantra, craft, and related arts, yet the king does not think of me as someone close." The king replied: "How could I not think of you as someone close?" The young man said: "Your Majesty has not yet sought that elixir of immortality promised to you long ago." The king replied: "Excellent! Excellent! Great teacher, I had not sought it — forgive me. Since the teacher wishes it, please accept all of it." Then the young man took the medicine the king gave him, went home, and drank it together with the chief ministers. After they had drunk it, they felt greatly at ease. The ministers then reported to the king, saying: "Teacher, there is indeed a deathless medicine — it is like ambrosia." When the king heard this, he said to the teacher: "Great teacher, will you not give a portion of this ambrosia that the chief ministers desire?"

Thereupon the young man mixed poison into it and gave it to the king. The moment the king swallowed it, the poison took hold, he lost all sensation, and he collapsed as though dead. Then the young brahmin consecrated a regent as king, and declared: "It is not right that outcasts and the like sit by birth-right upon the lion throne. I have never heard from ancient times that a lowborn outcaste may be king. Since there is no custom by which a lowborn outcaste may be king and hold sovereignty over subjects, you shall be king. Rule the kingdom by the law of righteousness." After all this was done, the young man gave the outcaste a restorative medicine and brought him back to his senses. Once he had recovered, he was expelled from that land. Even though the young man had done all these things, he did not transgress brahmin law. The householders and brahmins and others who witnessed what had happened were filled with wonder and admiration, and all praised and extolled him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble man, you have rightly expelled this lowborn outcaste."

Sons of the lineage, in just the same way are the bodhisattvas who, after my complete passing into nirvāṇa, guard and uphold the sacred Dharma. Through skillful means they carry and make use of all the requisites of monks who are degenerate in ethical conduct in name only and who have not been scrutinized, and they associate in ways befitting those acts. At such times, if certain individuals punish monks who are sinful and who have violated their ethical discipline many times over, the bodhisattva steps into their place, showing them service, reverence, and homage, offering all four kinds of requisites — or, if that is not suitable, offering sūtras and all the requisites of livelihood. And should he himself lack the means, he solicits from patrons by various methods and makes the offering. Thus he carries and makes use of all eight kinds of unsolicited requisites. And why? Because that individual's disciplining of sinful monks is just like the young brahmin's disciplining of the lowborn outcaste. Accordingly, when a bodhisattva renders service, reverence, or homage to such an individual, or carries the eight unsolicited requisites, there is no wrongdoing. And why? Because that bodhisattva expelled the sinful monks in order to bring great wellbeing to the pure Saṅgha.

— for the sake of bringing benefit and wellbeing to all gods and humans in the world, through the wide propagation of the sūtras of the Great Vehicle.

Noble son, for that reason and on account of those conditions, I taught in the sūtras those two verses. Bodhisattvas, too, praise and extol one who is a guardian of the true Dharma, just as householders, brahmins, and others praised the young brahmin, saying "Excellent! Excellent!" One who is a bodhisattva guarding the Dharma must act in exactly that manner.

Now, if someone, upon seeing that guardians of the Dharma are working alongside monks of broken ethical conduct, takes that as a fault, that person should know that the harm is to himself — for the one guarding the Dharma, there is no fault. Noble son, any monk who, having fallen into ethical failure, comes under the sway of pride, concealing his transgression and feeling no remorse — that person is to be called one who has truly broken his ethical conduct. But the bodhisattva, the great being, who may show signs of lapse while guarding the Dharma, should not be said to have broken his ethical conduct. And why? Because he is not under the sway of pride — he has openly confessed and disclosed his transgression.

Noble son, for that reason I taught in the sūtras these verses of definite import:

One who knows the true Dharma,
whether elder or young,
should be served, honored, and reverenced,
bowing down to him with joined palms —
as brahmins revere the fire deity,
as the thirty-three gods
honor Śakra, the Mighty Lord.

For that reason and on account of those conditions, I did not teach these verses for those of the śrāvaka vehicle, but taught them solely for the bodhisattvas.

Then again, the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "If the great bodhisattvas, the great beings, appear to be lax in their ethical conduct in this way, would it be right to say that their originally undertaken ethical conduct has been impaired?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, do not say such a thing. And why? The ethical conduct originally undertaken does not become impaired any more than conduct that has been well undertaken and maintained. And even if it should become impaired, one immediately feels remorse, confesses openly, and through that confession it is completely purified.

Noble son, consider this analogy: it is like the headwork of an irrigation channel. If it develops a breach, water leaks out. And why? Because it has not been repaired. But if that breach is mended, the water does not leak to the outside.

The bodhisattva is just like that: even while experiencing a lapse in ethical conduct, he simultaneously performs the restoration ceremony, the acts arising from the rules, and the acts of the Saṅgha — and his ethical conduct is not impaired. He is not like the irrigation channel with a breach. And why? If there were no one with fully pure ethical conduct, the Saṅgha would decline, and pride and laziness would arise again and again. But if there is one with fully pure ethical conduct, even the ethical conduct undertaken at the time of full ordination is not impaired.

Noble son, laxity with respect to the vehicle may be called laxity, but laxity with respect to ethical conduct should not be called laxity. When great bodhisattvas, great beings, in this Great Vehicle are free from minds of pride and laziness, that itself is called ethical conduct — they wash themselves with the water of the Great Vehicle for the sake of guarding the true Dharma. Therefore, even if a bodhisattva appears to show a lapse in ethical conduct, it should not be called laxity.

Then once more the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, though there may be four kinds of persons within the Saṅgha, when it is as difficult to discern whether they are ripe or unripe as it is to tell a ripe mango fruit from an unripe one, how is one to distinguish between those who have broken their ethical conduct and those who have not?"

The Blessed One declared:

Noble son, this is easy to discern by means of this great sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa. And how is it discerned by means of this great sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa? Consider, for example, how farmers sow grain and weeds together in a field, then remove the wild weeds and other growth. When they examine it with a fleshly eye they call the field ripe, and once the grain has matured they separate the grain from the grass and weeds. In the same way, the Saṅgha can become blemished through eight kinds of unexamined things. Yet when these are removed, even examination with a fleshly eye reveals it to be thoroughly pure. When those who have broken ethical conduct and those who guard it commit no transgression, it is difficult to discern them by examination with a fleshly eye. But when a transgression has openly occurred, it is easy to know — just as wild weeds are easy to recognize and discern. The Saṅgha is similar: the eight unexamined things are to be abandoned like a venomous snake, and then that Saṅgha is called the thoroughly pure noble Saṅgha, a field of merit worthy of offering by gods and humans, in which the fruit of thorough purity will ripen. This is not something those with fleshly eyes can perceive.

Noble son, consider further: in a grove of kālaka trees, the kālaka trees are extremely numerous, while there is only a single cintaka tree. The fruit of the kālaka and the cintaka are similar, and since they cannot be distinguished, when the fruit has ripened, a woman gathers them all together. In that grove, roughly one tenth of the fruit is cintaka fruit, while more than nine tenths is kālaka fruit. The woman, not knowing this, gathers them together and sells them at market. Small foolish children, not knowing the real nature of the fruit, buy the kālaka fruit and eat it, and immediately upon eating it they die. Wise and discerning people, upon hearing what has happened, ask the woman: "Where did this poisonous fruit come from?" The woman names the direction and place from which she came. Then everyone proclaims to one another: "In that place and direction there are abundant kālaka trees, and there is only a single cintaka tree," and they go their way.

Noble son, those within the Saṅgha who practice the eight unexamined things are just like this. Among the Saṅgha, those who practice the eight unexamined things are extremely numerous, while those who guard ethical conduct fully and do not practice the eight unexamined things are just a few. Those who know that a person carries and practices things contrary to the Dharma nonetheless work alongside them and do not part from them — just as in a grove of kālaka trees a single cintaka tree grows. When a lay practitioner sees such persons practicing many things contrary to the Dharma and receiving no offerings or acts of reverence, and intends to make an offering to such a person, he should first ask that person: "Venerable one, do you practice the eight unexamined things? Has the Buddha permitted this?" If the person says the Buddha has permitted it, then ask: "Is it proper or improper to join with such a person in the restoration ceremony, in petitions, in formal acts of request, and in acts of Dharmic procedure?" When the lay practitioner asks this and the monastics say: "The Blessed One, out of compassion, has permitted us to carry and practice these eight unexamined things," then the lay practitioner should reflect: "From the monks of a single monastery, some say that gold and silver and the like have been permitted by the Buddha, while others say they have not been permitted." One should not dwell together with those who say it is permitted and those who say it is not permitted. One should not join them in the restoration ceremony or in acts of Dharmic procedure.

"When young, one would not even drink from the same water source, nor share the requisites of livelihood in common." If they say this, then ask: "Why do you say that the Buddha has permitted it? Whatever the Blessed One has permitted the gods to enjoy and keep among themselves is not fitting for you, the Saṅgha, to enjoy. And if you do enjoy it, you are not fit to participate in the restoration ceremony, in the rite of going forth from the community, in formal requests, in petitions, or in the acts of Dharmic procedure performed by the Saṅgha. And if you do perform the restoration ceremony, the going forth, formal requests, petitions, and acts of Dharmic procedure together with the Saṅgha, then immediately upon death you will fall into the hells — just as parrots die from eating the kāla fruit."

Son of good family, consider further this example: in a town or marketplace, a medicine seller who sells good mountain-grown medicinal herbs will have many buyers. If another person sells a similar medicine, but everyone is unaware of this, and all come to the medicine seller's stall seeking medicine and ask, "Do you have mountain-grown herbs?" — then that medicine seller, taking some similar herb, says falsely, "This is mountain-grown medicine," and sells it. Because the buyers cannot distinguish it with their physical eyes, they think to themselves: "I have obtained and purchased fine mountain-grown medicine."

The ninth fascicle.

Kāśyapa, within the Saṅgha of śrāvaka monastics there exist what are called the Saṅgha in name only, the authentic Saṅgha, and the harmonious Saṅgha. Whether that Saṅgha upholds moral discipline or whether its discipline is impaired, one should equally offer it homage, reverence, prostrations, and the like. The failure of the lay practitioner to distinguish is like a person failing to distinguish genuine mountain-grown medicinal herbs. Who upholds moral discipline and who has impaired it, who constitutes the authentic Saṅgha and who the Saṅgha in name only — one who possesses the divine eye knows and discerns this.

Kāśyapa, if a lay practitioner truly knows that a monk has impaired his moral discipline, he should not pay that monk service, prostrations, offerings, and the like. If one truly knows that a particular person engages in the eight unexamined things, one should not extend to him respectful attendance, provision of offerings and supplies, prostrations, homage, and the like. If there is someone within the Saṅgha whose moral discipline is impaired, merely wearing the ochre robe is not sufficient reason to offer him prostrations, homage, and the like.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa once more addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Excellent! Excellent! Blessed One, the Tathāgata has spoken rightly and truly, and I wish to hold it in mind. Just as a vajra differs from other precious stones — so, Blessed One, as you have taught, monks should abide in these four principles of the Dharma. What are the four? Abiding in the Dharma rather than in the person; abiding in the meaning rather than in the words; abiding in primordial wisdom rather than in ordinary consciousness; and abiding in the definitive meaning rather than in the interpretable meaning. One should seek to understand these four principles of the Dharma, not the four types of persons."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, 'abiding in the Dharma' means the great parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata. The Dharma of the buddhas is the nature of reality of phenomena. That which is called the nature of reality is the Tathāgata himself. Therefore the Tathāgata is permanent and unchanging. Whoever says that the Tathāgata is impermanent is one who neither sees nor knows the nature of reality. And if one does not see and does not know the nature of reality, one does not abide in it or rely upon it.

If the four types of persons described above appear in the world and guard and uphold the sacred Dharma, one should know and recognize them, and one should abide in and rely upon them. Why is this? Because those individuals are supremely skilled in the profound meaning that the Tathāgata intended and taught, and they know that the Tathāgata is permanent and unchanging. There is simply no ground for saying that the Tathāgata is impermanent, or that he possesses the nature of change and transformation. Those four types of persons are themselves called "Tathāgata." Why is this? Because those individuals both know what the Tathāgata intended and taught, and are also capable of teaching it to others.

If a person both knows the profound meaning that the Tathāgata intended and taught, and knows that the Tathāgata possesses the nature of permanence and unchangingness, there is no ground for that person to say "the Tathāgata is impermanent" merely for the sake of material gain or reputation. One should abide in and rely upon such a person as well — how much more so upon the four persons themselves. "Abiding in the Dharma" means abiding in the nature of reality. "Not abiding in persons" means not abiding in śrāvakas. The nature of reality is the Tathāgata. The śrāvaka is the conditioned. The Tathāgata is permanent. The conditioned is impermanent.

Son of good family, if a person of degenerate moral discipline says, for the sake of gain or reputation, "The Tathāgata is impermanent, subject to change and transformation," one must not abide in that person.

Son of good family, this is called "the definitive meaning." Now, what is meant by "abiding in the meaning and not in the words"? The meaning is the direct realization of the meaning. That which is called "the directly realized meaning" is the inexhaustible. The inexhaustible is what is consummate and excellent. The meaning of what is consummate and excellent is the Tathāgata abiding forever, unchanging, without transformation. The meaning of the Tathāgata abiding forever, unchanging, without transformation, is the permanence of the Dharma. The meaning of the permanence of the Dharma is the permanence of the Saṅgha. This is called "abiding in the meaning and not in the words."

Now, what are the words in which one must not abide? They are these: the learning systems of the world that are filled with elaboration; the innumerable sūtras that the Blessed One spoke for those who are acquisitive without limit or contentment, who live by deceit and act with cunning, who feign proper conduct for the sake of gain and fame, and who rely upon householders. Furthermore, if someone says, "The Blessed One, the Buddha, permitted monks to keep and use the following: male servants and female servants, uninvestigated goods, gold, silver, precious stones, grain, rice, storehouses, cattle, sheep, wool, elephants, horses, and the like — to use and trade in them," or says, "When a time of famine came, out of compassion for his sons, the Blessed One said, 'Monks, you may keep and use surplus provisions,'" or says, "I have taken this cloth, and having rendered it fit for food, it is permissible to eat it even without receiving it formally" — even if such statements appear in sūtras, one must not abide in those words.

Now, what is meant by "abiding in wisdom and not in consciousness"? Wisdom is the Tathāgata. Any śrāvaka who does not fully abide in the qualities of the Tathāgata — that is consciousness, and one must not abide in it. Whoever knows the Tathāgata himself to be the dharmakāya, the truth body — that is authentic wisdom, and one should abide in it. Whoever knows the body that the Tathāgata presents as a skillful means to be something composed of aggregates, elements, and sense sources, sustained by food — that is consciousness, and one must not abide in it. And whether this is taught through speech or derived from texts and learned traditions, one must not abide in it.

One abides in sūtras of definitive meaning and does not abide in sūtras of provisional meaning. What is meant by this? Sūtras of provisional meaning are those such as the following: when those who belong to the śrāvaka vehicle hear of the Blessed One's profoundly deep meaning, they give rise to doubt and astonishment, for they do not know that from the profound, essential meaning there arises a vast ocean of primordial wisdom. As an analogy, a small child who understands nothing and makes no distinctions — this is called provisional meaning. Definitive meaning, on the other hand, is when the authentic primordial wisdom of a bodhisattva enters an unobstructed wisdom just as intended — as an analogy, a great person for whom nothing is unknown. This is called definitive meaning. Furthermore, the śrāvaka vehicle is called provisional meaning. The unsurpassed Great Vehicle is called definitive meaning. Whoever says that the Tathāgata is impermanent, subject to change and alteration, speaks provisional meaning. Whoever says that the Tathāgata is permanent, not subject to change or alteration, speaks definitive meaning. Whatever is understood and realized through the teachings of the śrāvaka vehicle is provisional meaning. Whatever is comprehended and known through the teachings of the bodhisattva vehicle is definitive meaning. Whoever says that the Tathāgata requires nourishment through food speaks provisional meaning. Whoever says that the Tathāgata is permanent, abiding, unchanging, and unalterable speaks definitive meaning. Whoever says that the Tathāgata's passage into nirvāṇa is like a fire dying out when the wood is exhausted speaks provisional meaning. Whoever says that the Tathāgata has entered into the very expanse of the dharmadhātu speaks definitive meaning.

In short, one must not abide in the Dharma of the śrāvaka vehicle. Why? Because the Tathāgata taught the śrāvaka vehicle as a preparatory method for liberating ordinary beings. It is like a householder teaching a young child only half the alphabet. Noble son, the śrāvaka vehicle is comparable to a field that has just been freshly plowed — since it yields no fruit, one must not abide in it. Therefore the śrāvaka vehicle is called provisional meaning, and one should abide in the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. Why? Because the Tathāgata, as a preparatory method for liberating ordinary beings, taught the Great Vehicle — and therefore it is called definitive meaning, and one should abide in it. In this way one should thoroughly comprehend and know the four modes of abiding of this kind.

Furthermore, as for abiding in the meaning — "meaning" is the authentic. The authentic is luminosity. Luminosity is the unshrunken. The unshrunken is the Tathāgata. And further: luminosity is primordial wisdom. The authentic is that which permanently abides. The permanent Tathāgata is one who abides in Dharma. "Dharma" here means that which is permanent, without limit, inconceivable, ungraspable, and unbounded — and which is fit to be beheld. If someone says it cannot be seen, one must not abide in that person. Therefore one abides in Dharma and not in persons.

If someone says with very fine words that it is impermanent, one must not abide in those words. Therefore one abides in the meaning and not in words.

The Saṅgha that abides in primordial wisdom is permanent, unconditioned, unalterable, and does not hold to the eight unexamined things. Therefore one abides in primordial wisdom and not in consciousness.

There are also some who say: "Created by consciousness, experienced by consciousness — there is no harmonious Saṅgha." Why? Because "harmonious" means that there is nothing whatsoever. Since there is nothing whatsoever, of what could one say "permanent"? Therefore one does not abide in consciousness.

What then is abiding in the definitive meaning? "Definitive meaning" means contentment: never sustaining oneself through deception, never embellishing one's conduct, never entertaining conceit, never clinging to gain and fame, and never becoming attached to the Dharma that the Tathāgata taught as a preparatory method. That is what is called the definitive meaning. Whoever abides in that is said to abide in the ultimate truth. Therefore one abides in the definitive meaning.

What then is not abiding in the provisional meaning? The provisional meaning refers to what is taught in the sūtras: "All is subject to affliction; all is impermanent; all is suffering; all is empty; all is without self." This is what is called the provisional meaning. Why? Because not understanding those very meanings causes many beings to fall into the boundless hells. How is that? Through clinging and attachment one fails to directly realize the meaning. Some take it that the Tathāgata taught, "All that is subject to affliction — nirvāṇa too is subject to affliction; all that is impermanent — nirvāṇa too is impermanent," and one must understand this at length through suffering, emptiness, and selflessness as well. Therefore one should not abide in sūtras of the provisional meaning.

Now, if someone were to say, "Because the Tathāgata is deeply skilled in time and measure out of loving concern for all sentient beings, he who is skilled in time speaks of the light as heavy and the heavy as light. Understanding this, the Tathāgata knew that there was a lay attendant whose patron, moved by faith, provided him with all the requisites he desired. To that person, the Blessed One did not permit the holding and use of any of the unexamined things such as male servants, female servants, gold, silver, and jewels, the conducting of trade, and so forth. Yet when there was a lay attendant who had no patron to provide him with the requisites for a livelihood, and famine had come and alms could not be found, in order to establish and protect the proper Dharma, the Tathāgata did permit my attendants to hold and use male servants, female servants, gold, silver, vehicles, dwellings, grain and rice, trade goods, and the like. And even though he permitted the holding and use of such things, a patron endowed with great faith must by no means be absent" — if someone were to speak thus, one should not abide in those words. And even if the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, or the sūtras were to say something in accord with this, one should not abide in those three baskets of scripture either.

"I taught these four grounds of abiding for beings with the eye of flesh, not for those with the eye of wisdom. For that reason I have taught these four grounds of abiding."

"Dharma" means the dharmatā, the nature of reality, of all phenomena. "Meaning" means the Tathāgata, who is permanent and unchanging. "Primordial wisdom" means knowing that the nature of the buddha is present in all sentient beings. "Definitive meaning" means understanding all sūtras of the Great Vehicle.

Then once again the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One, saying, "Blessed One, should we not abide in the four kinds of persons mentioned earlier by the Blessed One?" The Blessed One replied, "Indeed it is so. Indeed it is so."

"Son of good family, one should not abide in what the Blessed One has described in that way. And why not? Because there are four kinds of māra. What are the four? They are those who hold sūtras and Vinaya taught by māra."

Then once again the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One, saying, "Blessed One, since you have said there are also four kinds of māra, how are we to distinguish what is taught by māra from what was spoken by the Buddha? For there are ordinary beings who follow māra, and there are also those who follow what the Buddha has taught. How are we to recognize which is which?"

The Blessed One then declared to Kāśyapa, "After seven hundred years have passed following my complete nirvāṇa, the wicked māra will damage and corrupt the sacred Dharma. Just as a hunter wears a covering of saffron-colored cloth, so too will the wicked māra appear in the form of a monk, in the form of a nun, in the form of a male lay practitioner, and in the form of a female lay practitioner. And beyond these, he will take on emanation forms ranging from stream-enterers all the way up to arhats, and will also appear in the form of a buddha. The king of māra, with his defiled body, will manifest as an undefiled body, and will damage and corrupt my sacred Dharma.

"When the wicked māra acts to corrupt the sacred Dharma, he will say things such as these: 'The bodhisattva previously became invisible from Tuṣita heaven and was born from the union of his father and mother in the palace of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu.' He will say: 'This person was born in the human lineage, present in the world, and it is impossible that all the assemblies of gods and humans should venerate and pay homage to him.' And further he will say: 'Previously he engaged in many austerities and, having given gifts such as his head, his eyes, his bones, his limbs, his lands, his kingdoms, his wives, his sons, and so forth, he then fully awakened to buddhahood — and by that cause and through those conditions, those present in the world, namely gods, humans, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and great serpents (nāgas) and the rest, came to venerate and pay homage to him.' If such things appear in a sūtra or in the Vinaya, know that this is taught by māra.

"Son of good family, when in a sūtra or the Vinaya the following is found — that the Tathāgata awakened long ago, and that he demonstrated his awakening in order to liberate sentient beings, and that following worldly convention he showed himself as born from the union of father and mother — when a sūtra or Vinaya contains such a statement, know that this is truly the Tathāgata. Whoever follows what is taught by māra belongs to the party of māra. Whoever follows the sūtras and Vinaya taught by the Buddha should be known as a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, if one does not believe that from the moment of the Tathāgata's birth he walked seven steps in each of the ten directions, then one has entered upon what is taught by māra. But when one says that the Tathāgata appeared in the world and walked seven steps in each of the ten directions as a display of skillful means by the Tathāgata, then that is the sūtra and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata. Whoever follows what is taught by māra is called one who belongs to the party of māra. Whoever follows the sūtras and Vinaya taught by the Buddha is called a bodhisattva."

Regarding this: when the bodhisattva had just been born and the royal father led him to pay reverence at the shrine of the gods, the gods, upon seeing him, immediately prostrated to him. For that reason he is called a buddha. Regarding this, if someone contends thus: "The gods came first; the Buddha came later, so why should the gods bow down and show reverence to the Buddha?" — one should know that this is what is taught by māra the evil one. But when the sūtras and Vinaya say that when the Blessed One Buddha went to the shrine of the gods, Maheśvara the great lord, Mahābrahmā the great Brahmā, Śakra the lord of the gods, and all the other gods joined their palms together and, with full reverence, prostrated at his feet — this is what is taught by the Buddha. Whoever follows what is taught by māra is called one who belongs to the party of māra. Whoever follows what is taught by the Buddha is called a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, when sūtras and Vinaya say that while the bodhisattva served as regent, he sought queens from the four directions with a mind of desire and, within the palace, freely enjoyed the five objects of desire — if such a statement appears in a sūtra or Vinaya, that is what is taught by māra. But when sūtras and Vinaya say that the bodhisattva, having long since completely relinquished desire and the allure of a retinue of consorts, and having cast aside even the five objects of desire of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three as one spits out saliva — to say nothing of human desires — shaved his head and beard, and went forth from home into homelessness, and then applied himself earnestly to awakening — if such a statement appears in the sūtras and Vinaya, that is what is taught by the Buddha. Whoever follows the sūtras and Vinaya taught by māra is called one who belongs to the party of māra. Whoever follows the sūtras and Vinaya taught by the Buddha is called a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, if a sūtra or Vinaya says: "Formerly, when the Blessed One Buddha dwelt in Prince Jeta's Grove, he, out of great compassion and loving care for sentient beings, permitted the monks to keep and make use of male slaves, female slaves, hired laborers, cattle, goats, sheep, woolen elephants, horses, donkeys, mules, birds, dogs, pigs, and the like; gold, silver, vaidūrya, pearl, crystal, asmagarbha, musāragalva, crystal cloth, iron, copper, and copper vessels of various sizes, and other goods not sanctioned by the Vinaya; to plow fields; to engage in trade; and to store and use grain and the like" — if such a statement appears in a sūtra or Vinaya, that is what is taught by māra.

But regarding this: formerly, when the Buddha dwelt in Prince Jeta's Grove in the place called the hungry ghost Dālilā, the Blessed One, for the sake of a brahmin named Qualities and in order to utterly defeat King Army, declared: "A monk should not hold or make use of gold, silver, vaidūrya, crystal, pearl, musāragalva, coral, asmagarbha, crystal cloth, male slaves, female slaves, hired laborers, boys, girls, cattle, sheep, woolen elephants, horses, donkeys, mules, birds, dogs, pigs, iron, copper, large and small copper vessels, and other unsanctioned goods, nor thrones, bedding,

various articles of livelihood, houses and dwellings, farming, trade goods, waving a cloth to agitate food, waving a cloth to sift flour, winnowing rice, mantras for bodily sustenance, rituals for taming hawks, reading stars, casting divination, reading a husband's physiognomic signs, dispelling nightmares, and examining by the sixty-four branches of expertise to determine whether this will become a boy or a girl, whether it will not be a boy or will not be a girl; likewise the eighteen branches of traditional knowledge, mantras, crafts of various kinds, speaking endless worldly treatises, and compounding powdered incense, ointments, and various fumigants; various garlands of flowers, rituals for dressing hair, duplicity, deception, trickery, insatiable craving for gains, delight in gatherings and chatter and tales, delight in fish and meat, compounding poisons, compounding medicines for removing moles, compounding anointing butter preparations, making precious parasols and shoes and the like, fans and gift-boxes and paintings and the like, measures of rice, various types of beans, varieties of fruit and so on; relying on kings, princes, ministers, and great officials; relying on women; laughing out loud and boisterously in company; falling entirely silent in company; doubting among the Dharmas; speaking falsehood; falsely declaring this good, that bad, this virtuous, that non-virtuous; dressing in fine robes and preening and the like — engaging and acting in all these various uninvestigated pursuits; praising oneself in front of faithful donors; selling liquor in uninvestigated places; constantly going about trading serpents with serpent-women — all such things have not been declared by me as permitted for monks. Nor are these permitted to remain within the company of monks. They are to be returned to the status of laypeople and put to work accordingly. It is like wild grain growing up within a cultivated field: it is cleared out and removed without exception."

Know that the sūtras and Vinaya taught in this way are what the Tathāgata has proclaimed. Whoever follows that which is taught by māra is counted among the party of māra. Whoever follows that which is taught by the Buddha is called a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, it is said: a bodhisattva goes to the shrines of worldly gods in order to pay homage to those gods. For instance, he goes to the god Brahmā, the Great Sovereign (Śiva), Yugasela, Kātyāyana, and so forth. Yet going there is not the same as going in order to discipline the gods. There is simply no basis for that claim.

Moreover, it is said: a bodhisattva, being unable to excel tīrthikas in their scriptural learning, ascetic practices, conduct, speech and discourse, the arts, and the resolution of disputes and arguments, is therefore not shown respect by boys, girls, great officials, and the like. And since he does not know how to compound medicines and the like, he is called a Tathāgata. But if he did know, would he then be said to have wrong views and mistaken understanding? Furthermore, the Tathāgata regards enemies and friends with equal consideration. Whether struck with a weapon or anointed with perfumed unguents, he holds no thought of benefit or harm toward either, abiding in the middle. He is therefore called Tathāgata — "thus-gone." Should such a passage appear in a sūtra or the Vinaya, know that it is taught by māra.

Now, as for what is said: a bodhisattva, by such skillful means, goes to divine shrines and —

going forth from the Dharma of non-Buddhist adherents and demonstrating engagement in study; demonstrating conduct, austerity, and knowing contentment; demonstrating study in a school of letters so as to master all the arts of word and expression; demonstrating the reconciling of those who have fallen into dispute and quarrel; and demonstrating excellence and supremacy over the many in a great retinue — princes and princesses, queens, palace servants, householders, merchants, brahmins and the like, kings, great ministers, and the poor — and demonstrating that these very ones offer service and reverence. In such ways and more, many different aspects of things are demonstrated. Yet even while abiding in those views, attachment does not arise — just as a lotus is not soiled by dust and grime. And to liberate the many beings, one engages in such manifold skillful means in accordance with the ways of the world. Should such a passage appear in a sūtra or the Vinaya, know that it has been taught by the Tathāgata. And whoever follows what is taught by māra is to be counted among the faction of māra. Whoever follows what is taught by the Buddha is a great bodhisattva.

Now, there are those who say: "The Tathāgata taught us sūtras and Vinaya, and among unwholesome phenomena, the weighty and the light, and those intermediate between them as transgressions, are heavy by their inherent nature. Therefore we do not transgress the Vinaya. We have long endured with patience. But if you do not trust in these teachings, then, as we say, we have set aside our Vinaya and will follow yours. Your Vinaya is taught by māra, whereas our sūtras and Vinaya were established by the Buddha. The nine limbs of scripture that the Tathāgata formerly spoke were all definitively taught within our nine sūtras and our Vinaya; but of the vastly expanded sūtras we have not heard even a single word or a single syllable. The sūtras and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata are beyond measure — so there is no such thing as 'vastly expanded sūtras,' and from among those we have never heard that there are ten categories of scriptural scripture.
