If such a thing does exist, know that without doubt it was composed by Devadatta. That wicked Devadatta, in order to destroy wholesome Dharma, composed vastly expanded sūtras; and since our sūtras are taught by māra, we do not trust them." Why do they say this? "Because words such as these — destroying the Dharma and disparaging one another — come from your sūtras, not from ours. From our own sūtras and Vinaya, taught by the Tathāgata, there comes in secret this statement: 'After I have passed into complete nirvāṇa, in a degenerate age, inauthentic sūtras and Vinaya called vastly expanded Mahāyāna sūtras will appear.' Thus it is said that in a future time such wicked monks will arise. And I too have spoken thus: that there exist vastly expanded sūtras apart from the nine limbs of scripture. Thus whoever understands the meaning of this truly comprehends the sūtras and Vinaya in an utterly correct way; such a one has abandoned all phenomena not yet examined — pure and clear like a fish in the water of the moon, as I have said. But as for those who say: 'Even from each individual sūtra taught by the Tathāgata, meanings as numerous as the grains of sand of the Ganges River arise' — they have not said this, and therefore this is simply not valid. And if it does exist, why was it not taught in our Vinaya?"

"It was not taught in this way; since it has not arisen, we do not believe in it." When someone speaks thus, that person should be understood to have committed a very grave offense. Yet that same person may also say: "As for those sūtras and the Vinaya, I shall uphold them." Why so? Because they lead to contentment, to few desires, to cutting through mental afflictions, to wisdom, and to being a cause of the wholesome phenomena that bring liberation. Even if one speaks thus, such a person is still not my intimate companion.

On the other hand, someone who says: "The Tathāgata taught the vastly expanded sūtras in order to liberate the many beings," — that person should be recognized as a true and genuine intimate companion of mine.

As for one who does not accept the vastly expanded sūtras, that person is not my intimate companion, has not gone forth through the Dharma of the buddha, and should be known to belong to the assembly of tīrthikas with wrong views.

Whatever sūtra or Vinaya contains the declaration: "This was taught by a buddha" — that is indeed taught by a buddha. Whatever does not contain this is taught by Māra. Whoever follows what is taught by Māra is called a member of Māra's retinue. Whoever follows what is taught by a buddha is called a bodhisattva.

Noble son, there are also those who say: "The Tathāgata is not made up of limitless qualities; impermanent, he changes and passes away. He is said to be without self because he has obtained empty phenomena. This is not in accord with the world." Any sūtra or Vinaya from which such words arise is taught by Māra.

On the other hand, whatever is found in sūtra or Vinaya declaring: "The Tathāgata, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, is inconceivable, formed from immeasurable and innumerable qualities, and therefore is permanent, abiding, unchanging, and unshifting" — that is taught by a buddha. Whoever follows what is taught by Māra belongs to Māra's party. Whoever follows what is taught by a buddha is called a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, there are some who say: "Monks, no one has individually incurred a root defeat, and yet all have incurred a root defeat — they have become like a palmyra palm tree whose crown has been cut off." Even so, that monk has not incurred a root defeat. Why? Because I declared: "If one falls into even a single one of the four root defeats, one cannot return, just as a broken stone cannot be mended." As for one who says "The teacher has attained superhuman states," that person has incurred a root defeat. Why? Because if one, having truly attained nothing whatsoever, pretends to have attained it through deception and guile, that person is said to have fallen from the human condition — that is a root defeat.

This is how it is. A monk who has few desires, is content, guards his ethical discipline, is utterly pure, and dwells at the forest's edge — suppose a king or a great minister comes to him and, thinking "this monk will become an arhat," approaches him, pays him reverence, venerates him, and prostrates to him, then says: "Great teacher, in this very next life this body of yours will awaken to the highest, perfect, complete awakening." That monk then says to the king: "Great king, I have not truly attained the fruit of the ascetic life. Therefore, great king, please do not say to me, 'You have attained the fruit of the ascetic life.' Great king, please do not declare to me the teaching of one without contentment. As for those without contentment, even should they praise you up to the point of saying, 'You have manifestly awakened to the highest, perfect, complete awakening,' he does not answer and says nothing whatsoever."

"And if I too were to give no answer and say nothing whatsoever, the Blessed One, the buddha, would condemn me for that. One who conducts oneself with contentment is praised and extolled by all the buddhas. Therefore I am always glad to dwell in contentment. Contentment means this: even should the king say to me, 'You have attained the fruit,' when I have not attained the fruit, I do not desire that — this is what is called contentment."

At that point the king says: "Great teacher, you have truly attained the fruit of the arhat and are not different from a buddha." When he says this, the king then proclaims throughout all the subjects of his realm, all his queens, and all the retinue of his palace attendants: "This monk has attained the fruit of the ascetic life." When all who hear these words develop toward that monk a mind of very deep faith, wishing to make offerings, to show respect, and to render service, then because that monk is truly living a pure and holy life (brahmacarya), by that cause and condition all those who rejoice in him acquire great merit, while the monk himself does not incur the fault of a root defeat (pārājika). Why is that? Because in the minds of others there arises, of their own accord, joy, faith, praise, and the wish to make offerings. Thus there is no fault at all for that monk. And if anyone were to say that there is a fault in this, it should be understood that such a sūtra was taught by Māra.

Furthermore, monks, from a profound sūtra spoken by the buddha with hidden intent, the teaching goes: "All sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Because they possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha, by cutting through measureless defilements they will manifestly and perfectly awaken to the highest, perfect, complete awakening — with the sole exception of those who have wrong craving." If a king or a great minister were then to ask: "Monk, will you awaken, or will you not? Do you possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha?" — one should reply as follows: "As for the intrinsic nature of a buddha in my body, it is certainly present; the only thing uncertain is whether or not I will be fully accomplished as a buddha." The king says: "Venerable one, if one does not perform the deeds of wrong craving, it is absolutely certain and without doubt that one will be accomplished." The monk replies: "It is just as the great king has said. In that certain sense, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is indeed present." Even though the monk says this, it does not become a root defeat.

Furthermore, monks, when one goes forth into renunciation and thinks to oneself: "I will ultimately and without fail manifestly awaken to the highest, perfect, complete awakening" — even if that person has not yet attained the highest awakening, they will obtain merit that is measureless, boundless, and incalculable. If someone were to say that a root defeat arises for them — well then, consider this: there is not a single monk who has gone forth without such a thought having arisen. Why is that? I myself, for eighty million world-ages (kalpas), abandoned all things that had not been examined, and by living the conduct of few desires and contentment, I devoted myself with diligence to the unsurpassable collection of Dharma teachings of the Tathāgata. Knowing for certain that the intrinsic nature of a buddha was present in my own body, it is for this reason that, upon manifestly awakening to the highest, perfect, complete awakening, I came to be called "buddha," one who is endowed with great compassion. Whatever sūtra or Vinaya teaching speaks in this way is to be recognized as taught by the buddha.

Whoever does not follow this teaching is to be called one who belongs to the class of māras. Whoever does follow this teaching is to be called a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, there are those who say the following: there are no four defeats, no thirteen remainders for the Saṅgha, no two indeterminate rules, no thirty rules entailing forfeiture, no ninety-one transgressions, no four rules to be confessed individually, no many trainings, no seven rules for the complete pacification of disputes, and so on. There are no grave offenses, no five acts of immediate retribution, and nothing at all called wrong craving. If monks who transgress these and similar rules fall into the hells, then all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) by comparison are born as gods of the higher realms. Why is this? Because there is no such thing as a breach of moral discipline for non-Buddhists and the like. Therefore the Tathāgata taught what is called moral discipline for the purpose of training persons. As the Buddha himself declared: "My monks, if any of you wishes to engage in unchaste conduct, set aside the Dharma robes and, wearing the clothes of a householder, engage in unchaste conduct." Beyond that, some think: "This engaging in unchaste conduct is not a fault exclusive to us alone — even during the lifetime of the Tathāgata, monks engaged in unchaste conduct and still attained liberation, and there have always been those who were reborn as gods of the higher realms after death; this conduct was not ours alone. Some transgressed the four defeats, some transgressed the five precepts of moral discipline, some performed all manner of unexamined and improper actions, and yet attained genuine liberation." And the Tathāgata did declare that if one commits a single offense, one falls into the hells for eight hundred billion years reckoned by the days and months and years of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three — yet that too was spoken by the Tathāgata solely for the purpose of training persons. So they say: there is no distinction at all in weight between a defeat and an ordinary offense. When they say that the holders of the Vinaya are falsely claiming that the Buddha established these rules, that is not the teaching of the Buddha. One should understand that such speech belongs to the sūtras and Vinaya of māras.

As for those who say the following: "One who abides in moral discipline, if they breach it even in the slightest minor offense, will experience immeasurable suffering — knowing this, one must guard one's body with extreme care, just as tortoises withdraw their six limbs" — but also those holders of the Vinaya who say: "No matter what breach of moral discipline occurs, no unwholesome fruit will ripen" — one should not associate with such a person. As the Blessed One declared in verse:

Whoever transgresses even a single Dharma,
that one is a speaker of falsehood.
Not seeing the world beyond,
there is no evil they will not commit.

Therefore one should not associate with such a person. Since my Buddha's Dharma is in this way perfectly pure, it goes without saying that grave offenses, the remainders for the Saṅgha, and defeats are to be reckoned as blameworthy. Therefore those rules of Dharma should be guarded with great care. If they are not guarded, what else could one call "moral discipline"? I have also declared in the sūtras: from the transgression of the four defeats down to the slightest minor offense — if breached, it is to be cut by the penalty. This I have declared.

For ordinary persons, if moral discipline is not guarded, how could the intrinsic nature of a buddha ever be seen? Although the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present in all sentient beings, it can be seen only through the guarding of moral discipline. By seeing the intrinsic nature of a buddha, one will manifestly awaken to the highest, perfect, complete awakening.

Among the nine branches of the sūtra scriptures, there is none more extensive than the sūtra genre itself.

Yet I have not declared that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists. Although it is not declared in those sūtra scriptures, it is to be understood as truly existing. And whoever speaks in these words is to be understood as a true and proper attendant of mine.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "The Blessed One has declared that the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present in all sentient beings. If one has not heard this from the nine branches of the sūtra scriptures, and now teaches and declares it as existing, would that not constitute a defeat?"

The Blessed One declared: "It is as you have said — it would not constitute a defeat. Son of good family, consider this example: if a person were to say, 'Within the ocean there are the seven precious substances — but not an eighth,' they would incur no offense. Likewise, even if one were to say, 'The intrinsic nature of a buddha does not exist,' having not found it spoken of in the nine branches of the sūtra scriptures, one would incur no offense. Why is that? Because the Blessed One has declared the intrinsic nature of a buddha to exist in the ocean of wisdom of the Great Vehicle, and it is not known or seen by the two vehicles. Therefore, even to say it does not exist incurs no offense. For this domain of knowledge is known by the buddhas alone; it is not the domain of knowledge of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Son of good family, if a person has not heard of the profoundly deep tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature), they will not know that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists. And what is this profoundly deep essence? It is this: the expansive sūtra scriptures of the Great Vehicle. Son of good family, certain non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) proclaim a self as eternal, while others proclaim no-self as annihilation. The Tathāgata is not like that. He teaches that a self exists, and he also teaches that there is no-self — and therefore it is called the Middle Way. In that regard, whoever declares, speaking from what the Buddha has taught as the Middle Way, 'The intrinsic nature of a buddha is present in all sentient beings, but because it is veiled by afflictions it is neither known nor seen — therefore one must diligently apply the means of cutting through afflictions,' whoever speaks in these words is to be understood as one who has not fallen from the four defeats. But whoever does not speak in these words is called one who has fallen from the four defeats.

In this regard, if someone were to say, 'I have manifestly awakened to the highest, perfect, complete awakening — and why? Because the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists, and one who possesses the intrinsic nature of a buddha will without any doubt manifestly awaken to the highest, perfect, complete awakening; therefore I have manifestly awakened to awakening,' that person is to be understood as having incurred a defeat. And why? Because although the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists, if one has not applied diligent effort to the means of its realization, it will not be seen. Not being seen, one will not awaken to the highest, perfect, complete awakening.

Son of good family, therefore the qualities of a buddha are profoundly deep and inconceivable."

Then once again the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, if a king were to ask, 'In what way have certain monks fallen from the Dharma proper to a human teacher?' — what should one say in reply?"

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "A monk who, for the sake of gain and alms, lives by deceit and pretense, thinking to himself, 'By this the people of the world will recognize me as a monk' — and who thus harbors in his mind

thinking, 'How shall I gain great wealth and renown?' — those foolish, deluded monks, night and day, think to themselves: 'Even though I have not attained the fruit of the contemplative life, those who inhabit the world will regard me as one who has attained the fruit of the contemplative life. All laymen and laywomen and the rest will say of me, "He is a noble one, a man of merit."' And all this is not for the sake of the Dharma, not out of desire for what is good, but only for gain and renown. Conforming his conduct, wearing the saffron robe, carrying his alms bowl, abiding impeccably in the outer forms of the precepts, he disguises himself as though he were an arhat, so that the people of the world will say: 'This monk is supremely excellent — he applies himself diligently to austerity and the qualities of perfect peace.' Praised in this way, and through that cause and condition, he comes to have many disciples and a large retinue. All of them offer him robes, alms, bedding, and medicines for illness in abundance, and many women attend upon him with service and reverence. If a monk or nun thinks in this way, that person is said to have fallen from the Dharma proper to a human teacher.

Now, regarding those monks who, for the sake of establishing the supreme and holy Dharma, abide in the outer forms of the precepts though they are not arhats — if others think of them as arhats, such a monk is a truly virtuous monk, a peaceful monk, a good monk, and in countless beings faith will arise. Through that cause and condition, countless monks will enter their retinue, and monks whose discipline has degenerated, as well as laypeople, will come to abide in the restraint of moral discipline. Through that cause and condition, the holy Dharma will long endure; the unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgatas will spread and expand; countless beings will be liberated through the greatly and thoroughly expansive Dharma of the Great Vehicle; and one will become supremely skilled in both the weighty and the light matters of the sūtras and the Vinaya spoken by the Tathāgata. Such a monk will say this: 'I possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha — and, as the sūtra called the Tathāgatagarbha declares, I will without doubt attain complete and perfect awakening, and the defilements of countless beings will be exhausted.' And to countless laypeople he will likewise say: 'You too possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha. If we abide on the ground of the Tathāgata's awakening, we will attain highest, perfect, complete awakening, and the defilements of countless beings will be pacified.' Even though he speaks in this way, that person is not one who teaches the Dharma proper to a human teacher — he is to be called a bodhisattva. Even for the minor fault of an offense committed without deliberate wrongdoing, such a person falls into the hells and experiences suffering for eight hundred thousand years counted by the years, months, and days of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three — how much more, then, for one who deliberately commits a grave and heavy sin. Therefore it is taught in the Great Vehicle: 'If a monk in the Great Vehicle commits a grave offense, one should not associate with him.' Now, what constitutes a grave offense according to the sūtras of the Great Vehicle? If a single householder were to build a temple enshrining an image of the Buddha and were to offer a garland of flowers to the Buddha, and a monk were to take the thread on which that garland was strung without asking — that is a grave offense, whether he knew it to be so or not. Likewise, if with a mind of desire one were to destroy a stūpa of the Buddha, that too is a grave offense, and one should not associate with such a person.

If a king or minister, upon seeing a stūpa in ruins, were to have it repaired — whether in order to make offerings to the relics or to restore what had fallen into disrepair — and were to find precious objects inside the stūpa and then place them in the keeping of a monk, and that monk were to claim authority over them and use them for his own purposes, then that monk is one who has fallen from the robe. He becomes a source of quarrel and conflict, and lay practitioners should neither attend upon him, nor offer him worship, nor show him reverence. That monk is to be called "one lacking the faculties," or "one of double marks," or "one of indeterminate sex." The reason he is called "one of indeterminate sex" is this: when he is seized by desire for a woman, he becomes a woman, and when he is seized by desire for a man, he becomes a man. Such a monk is called "one of degenerate faculties" — he is to be called neither man nor woman, neither one who has gone forth nor a householder — and no attendance, offering, or reverence is to be shown to him.

According to the teaching of the Buddha, the conduct proper to a contemplative (śramaṇa) is this: with a mind of compassion, to be a protector and refuge for sentient beings, and to bestow fearlessness upon all, down to the smallest ant — that is called the conduct of a contemplative. To refrain completely from drinking the maddening fluid of alcohol, and to abandon entirely everything down to that which has an unwholesome smell — that is called the conduct of a contemplative. To speak no falsehood, and not even to entertain in one's mind the thought of speaking falsely, even in a dream — that is called the conduct of a contemplative. To be entirely without a mind of attachment, even in a dream — that is called the conduct of a contemplative.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "If a monk were to engage in unchaste conduct during a dream, would his ethical discipline thereby be broken?"

The Blessed One declared: "It is not so. A monk of genuine virtue regards unchaste conduct as utterly defiling, and does not, even for an instant, give rise to the perception of anything pure in it. If a monk has abandoned the perception by which a woman disturbs the mind and yet dreams of engaging in unchaste conduct, he gives rise immediately upon waking to a mind of intense remorse. When a monk is on alms round and a time of famine has come, if he finds some meat, he perceives it as no different from eating the flesh of his own child. If a mind of attachment arises, he abandons it right away.

These categories of teaching are to be understood as the sūtras and Vinaya spoken by the Buddha in accordance with the Buddha's teaching. Whoever follows what is taught by māra belongs to the ranks of māra. Whoever follows what is taught by the Buddha is called a bodhisattva.

In this regard, if someone were to say: 'The Tathāgata has permitted going forth for all of the following — one who always stands on one leg, one who remains silent and says nothing, one who leaps into water, one who leaps into fire, one who leaps from a cliff, one who is shameless before others, one who drinks poison, one who eats nothing, one who sleeps in the ashes, one who binds his own limbs, one who kills sentient beings, one who possesses spells, one of outcaste birth, one lacking faculties, one of double marks, one of indeterminate sex, one whose faculties are incomplete, and all the rest' — that is the teaching of māra.

As for what the Blessed One formerly permitted as exceptional allowances: the five preparations made from cow's milk, sesame oil, honey and the like, garments of the kauśeya type, sandal-wood fragments to wear, and similar articles — those he did permit. But if, going beyond these, someone were to say: 'He also permitted the wearing of the mahāliṅga garment,' or 'He permitted the eating of all seeds whatsoever,' or 'The Buddha taught that all grass and trees and the like possess life, and then passed into nirvāṇa' — such statements are the teaching of māra.

When such things appear in the sūtras and Vinaya, know that they are the teaching of māra. The Buddha never permitted standing constantly on one leg; what he did permit was going, staying, sitting, and lying down for the sake of the Dharma. What he did not permit was consuming poison, abstaining from food, burning the body with the five forms of heat, binding the limbs, killing sentient beings, practicing spells and incantations, making sandals from candle-wicks or from the teeth of cattle, using seeds as food, holding that grass and trees possess life, and wearing the mahāliṅga garment. If someone says: 'The Blessed One permitted these things,' then know that person belongs to the company of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and is not a true disciple of the Buddha. What the Buddha did permit were the five preparations made from cow's milk, sesame oil, honey and the like, garments of the kauśeya type, and sandals with a strap. The Buddha declared that the four great elements are without life. Whatever has arisen in the sūtras and Vinaya in this way is called the teaching of the Buddha. One who follows what the Buddha has taught is truly my genuine disciple. If one does not follow what the Buddha has taught, that person is counted among the ranks of māra. If one enters into the sūtras and Vinaya of the Buddha's teaching, know that such a person is a great bodhisattva. Noble son, this detailed account that I have now explained to you is the distinction between what māra teaches and what the Buddha taught.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then again asked: Blessed One, I sought from the very beginning the defining characteristic that distinguishes the teaching of māra from the teaching of the Buddha, and through this I shall come to understand the profound Dharma of the Buddha.

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, one who thus discerns and clearly understands such distinctions may be called learned and endowed with wisdom. Noble son, suffering cannot properly be called the noble truth. Why is that? For if suffering were to be called the noble truth of suffering, then even cattle, sheep, donkeys, horses, and the beings of the hell realms would possess the noble truth. Noble son, one who thinks of the supremely profound and exalted dharmakāya — the domain of the Tathāgata, permanent, stable, and immutable — as a body sustained by food, and thus conceives it not to be the dharmakāya, and who does not know the qualities, splendor, and greatness of the Tathāgata, is called one in suffering. Why is that? Because of not knowing, such a person sees Dharma as what is not Dharma, and sees what is not Dharma as Dharma. Therefore that person will without fail fall into the lower realms, wander in cyclic existence, give rise to all manner of afflictions, and experience great suffering.

Now, one who knows that the Tathāgata is permanent, stable, immutable, and unchanging — or even one who merely hears the two words 'permanent' and 'stable' enter their ears — is reborn in the higher realms, and later, upon liberation, will come to comprehend and realize that the Tathāgata is permanent, stable, immutable, and unchanging. Through that comprehension and realization, such a person will say: 'By realizing this meaning before, I attained liberation. From beginningless time, through not knowing and not realizing, I wandered in cyclic existence without end — and this I have now come to know through authentic primordial wisdom.'

The tenth fascicle.

Knowing through authentic primordial wisdom in this way is called cultivating suffering, and it becomes of great benefit and happiness. One who does not understand things in such a manner will, even through great effort, fail to bring about benefit and happiness.

That, then, is knowing suffering — and it is called the noble truth of suffering. If one does not apply diligent effort in that manner, it is merely called "suffering" and is not the noble truth of suffering.

The noble truth of the origin of suffering is this: when authentic primordial wisdom does not arise with respect to authentic Dharma, one holds and makes use of uninvestigated things — servants, both male and female, and the like — and one speaks of what is not Dharma as authentic Dharma, thus causing the genuine Dharma not to exist and not to endure for a long time. Through that cause and that condition, one does not know the nature of reality of phenomena. Through not knowing, one revolves in cyclic existence, and through experiencing much suffering one may be born in the higher realms, but one is not liberated through authentic liberation. Whereas one who possesses profound wisdom and who does not destroy the genuine Dharma — through that as cause and condition — is born in the higher realms and is liberated through authentic liberation.

If one does not know the noble truth of the origin of suffering, and one says: "The genuine Dharma is impermanent, unstable, subject to change" — then through that as cause and condition one will revolve in cyclic existence for countless eons and will experience much suffering.

If, however, one knows the genuine Dharma to be permanent, stable, unchanging, and unshifting, that is knowing the origin, and it is called the noble truth of the origin. If one does not apply diligent effort in that manner, it is merely called "the origin" and is not the noble truth of the origin.

The noble truth of the cessation of suffering is this: one should not cultivate emptiness repeatedly and diligently and call that virtue. Why? Because doing so would cease all phenomena and destroy the genuine scriptural collection of the Tathāgata. To study and apply diligent effort in the way taught here is to cultivate emptiness. Cultivating the cessation of suffering means turning back from all tīrthikas (non-Buddhist adherents).

If one were to hold that cultivating emptiness is the truth of cessation, then any tīrthika who cultivates a doctrine of emptiness would likewise possess the truth of cessation — but that cannot be so.

Here, whoever says: "The tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature) exists; although it is not presently seen, if all afflictions are removed it will be realized" — or whoever, even for just an instant, arouses the mind toward this — through that as cause and condition will attain mastery over all phenomena.

But whoever cultivates the tathāgatagarbha in the mode of self, as emptiness, or as the absence of peace — that person will wander in cyclic existence experiencing suffering for incalculable births. On the other hand, whoever does not cultivate it in that erroneous manner will swiftly be cleansed, even of afflictions. Why? Because it is through knowing the secret of the tathāgatagarbha that this is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

Whoever applies diligent effort in this manner is my close attendant. Whoever does not apply diligent effort in this manner cultivates in a meaningless way, and that is not the noble truth of cessation.

The noble truth of the path is as follows. With regard to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and authentic liberation, certain sentient beings, with a mind of perverse understanding, hold this view: "There is no Buddha, no Dharma, no Saṅgha, and no authentic liberation — one wanders in cyclic existence as in an illusion." Through that as cause and condition, one will revolve through the three states of existence and will experience great suffering for a long time.

Whereas whoever arouses the mind as follows: that the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and —

authentic liberation is permanent, stable, immutable, and unchanging — whoever thinks this, even for a single instant, will gain the power to have merit arise according to their wishes for a boundless number of lifetimes. And why is this? Even I myself, in former times, through the four perversions, took what is not the Dharma to be Dharma, and so experienced a boundless ripening of non-virtuous karma. Now, because that kind of perverse view has ceased, I have become fully and perfectly awakened to complete enlightenment. This is called the noble truth of the path.

With regard to this: whoever says "The Three Jewels are impermanent" and cultivates that view cultivates to no purpose — that is not the noble truth of the path. Whoever cultivates those teachings as permanent and stable is called a close attendant of mine. Such a one is said to truly see the Four Noble Truths and to be diligently cultivating the Four Noble Truths.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then petitioned the Blessed One: "I too have long sought the Dharma with which to be most diligent in the Four Noble Truths."

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, the four perversions are as follows. To produce the perception of suffering with regard to what is not suffering — this is called a perversion. What is without suffering is the Tathāgata. To produce the perception of suffering with regard to the Tathāgata is to regard the Tathāgata as impermanent, as something that changes and passes away. Whoever says that the Tathāgata is impermanent — that is suffering of grave transgression. Whoever says, 'The Tathāgata, abandoning a body of suffering, has passed into nirvāṇa like a fire that has consumed its fuel and gone out' — that is to produce the perception of suffering with regard to what is without suffering, and is called a perversion.

"If someone were to object: 'But you have declared the Tathāgata to be permanent — is that not the view of a self? And if it is the view of a self, will that not become a transgression beyond measure? Therefore surely it is right to say that the Tathāgata is impermanent.' Whoever speaks thus — 'I' is a word for bliss, and to say 'the Tathāgata is impermanent' is suffering. If one asks why what is suffering could become bliss: to perceive bliss as suffering is a perversion, and to perceive suffering as bliss is also a perversion. Bliss is the Tathāgata; suffering is to say the Tathāgata is impermanent. If someone says the Tathāgata is impermanent, that is what is called perceiving bliss as suffering. That the Tathāgata is permanent — that is bliss. If, as I have taught, the Tathāgata is truly permanent, why would he pass into nirvāṇa? And if the Tathāgata is not suffering, why did he abandon the body and enter nirvāṇa?' — to produce the perception of suffering in regard to bliss in this way is called a single perversion.

"To produce the perception of permanence with regard to the impermanent, and to produce the perception of impermanence with regard to the permanent — these too are called perversions. The impermanent is failing to cultivate emptiness. Failing to cultivate emptiness leads to a short life. But if someone then says, 'Though one has not cultivated emptiness through which peace arises, one will still have a long life' — that is called a perversion, and these are two perversions. To produce the perception of self with regard to what is without self, and to produce the perception of no-self with regard to what has a self — these too are perversions. Worldly people assert that a self exists, and some assert that a self exists even within the dharmas of a buddha. Worldly people may assert the existence of a self, yet —"

since a buddha's intrinsic nature does not exist in that way, to produce the perception of self with regard to what is without self is called a perversion. The self that exists within the dharmas of a buddha is the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Worldly people say that there is no self in the dharmas of a buddha — and therefore to produce the perception of no-self with regard to what has a self is called a perversion. And if one were to say with certainty that there is no self in the dharmas of a buddha, then the Tathāgata's declaration to his attendants, "Cultivate the perception of no-self," would also be called a perversion. These are the three perversions.

To produce the perception of the impure with regard to what is pure, and to produce the perception of the pure with regard to what is impure — these too are perversions. What is pure is the body of the Tathāgata, who is permanent and abiding — not a body commingled with food, not a body afflicted by mental afflictions, not a body of flesh and blood, not a body framed together by veins, sinews, and bones. Therefore, if someone says, "The Tathāgata is impermanent, having a body commingled with food, a body framed by veins, sinews, and bones up to the marrow, and the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and liberation will also cease and be extinguished" — that is called a perversion.

To produce the perception of the pure with regard to what is impure: if someone says, "In this body of mine there is not even a trace of impurity; since there is no impurity, I shall certainly arrive at a state of utter purity — and the Tathāgata's teaching to practice meditation on impurity with earnest effort is a lie" — that is called a perversion. These are called the four perversions.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "We have now arrived at right view, having formerly held wrong views. Blessed One, does there exist something called 'self' in the twenty-five existences, or does it not?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, the meaning of the word 'self' is the meaning of tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature). That the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists in every sentient being — this is what is meant by the word 'self.' Yet the meaning of this 'self' has been veiled since beginningless time by limitless defilements, and therefore sentient beings have not been able to see it.

"Noble son, consider this example. A poor woman has a treasure of gold within her house, yet no one at all knows it is there. Later, a man of great skill in means comes to the poor woman and says: 'Young woman, are you able to work as my servant for wages?' The woman replies: 'I am not able to do so. But if you can show my son a hidden treasure of gold, I will do your bidding.' The man says: 'I am highly skilled in means, so I know where the hidden treasure of gold belonging to your son is, and I shall show it to you.' The woman says: 'If no one in my household, great or small, knows of it, how could you know?' The man says: 'I know it without any doubt.' The woman says: 'I wish to see it right now — show it to me.' Then the man entered her house, dug up the treasure of gold, and showed it to the woman. When she saw the treasure, she was filled with great joy; a perception of wonder and amazement arose in her, and she paid reverence to that man.

"Noble son, the buddha-nature in every sentient being is just like that. That all sentient beings fail to see it is like the poor woman's failure to see the treasure of jewels. Noble son, I see that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists in all ordinary beings, yet it is veiled by defilements —

just as the poor woman's failure to see the treasure of gold was demonstrated. Noble son, in the same way the Tathāgata, too, reveals to all sentient beings the precious treasure of perfect awakening — and that is the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Ordinary beings, upon seeing such things, give rise to a mind of great joy, and they honor and pay reverence to the Tathāgata, drawing near to him. The skillful man is the analogy for the Tathāgata. The poor woman is the analogy for the limitless multitude of ordinary beings. The treasure of gold is the analogy for the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Noble son, here is yet another example. Suppose a woman who is nursing a small infant finds that the child falls ill. That woman, stricken with deep grief, goes in search of a physician. The physician prepares a compound medicine of ghee, milk, and sugar — three ingredients mixed together — applies it to the child, and gives the woman the following instruction: 'Once you have given this medicine to the child, do not let him nurse until the medicine has been absorbed.' So then, in order to prevent the child from nursing, the woman smears her breast with bile and says to the child: 'My breast has been smeared with poison — you must not nurse.' Tormented by thirst, the child desires to nurse, but the moment he tastes the bitter flavor he finds he cannot drink. When the medicine has been absorbed, the woman washes her breast clean and calls out: 'Come here, child — now you may nurse.' But the child, though tormented by thirst, has already tasted the bitter flavor before, and even though he is called, he cannot bring himself to come. Then the mother speaks to him again: 'Earlier you took the medicine, and because it had not yet been absorbed, I could not let you nurse, and so I smeared it with something bitter. Now your medicine has indeed been absorbed, and the bitter taste has been washed away — there is no more bitterness now.' At that, coaxed over by the mother, he is at last able to drink.

Noble son, the Tathāgata is just the same. In order to liberate all sentient beings, he teaches them to apply themselves diligently to the Dharma of selflessness. Through diligent application to it, the notion called 'self' is no longer present, and they pass fully into nirvāṇa. Furthermore, in order to remove the wrong views of worldly non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), in order to teach that he transcends the doctrines of worldly tīrthikas, and in order to show that the view of self held by worldly tīrthikas is not correct, he teaches that through meditation on the Dharma of selflessness one comes to have a completely purified body. Just as that woman smeared her breast with bile for the sake of her child, so too the Tathāgata is just the same: in order that people may meditate on emptiness, he declared that all phenomena are without self. And just as that woman, after washing her breast, called her child and let him nurse, in the same way my revelation of the tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature) is just like that. O monk, you too should have no fear. Just as the mother called her child and let him nurse freely at her breast, so too, O monk, you must make a proper distinction: the tathāgatagarbha is not something to be done away with.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: 'Blessed One, there is in truth no such thing as a self. Why is that? A newborn infant, just at birth, makes no distinction whatsoever and has no such seeking. If there were truly a self, then from the very moment of birth it would be fitting that he distinguish and seek after everything. Therefore it is clearly evident that there is no self. And if a self did truly exist, it would be unreasonable for it to cease after taking a single birth. Moreover, if all beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha and it is something permanent, then it would likewise be unreasonable for it to be destroyed.'

'If it does not have the defining mark of being subject to destruction, then why do the kṣatriya class, brahmins, low castes, outcaste peoples, animals, and so forth exist as distinct and various kinds, with the karmic maturation of their actions being so diverse, discordant, and arising from different causes? And if what is called "a self" were truly certain to exist, then all sentient beings would be without distinction of good or bad — they would all be of the same kind. It is therefore evident that what is called "the intrinsic nature of a buddha" is not a permanent phenomenon. But if the intrinsic nature of a buddha were indeed permanently fixed, then why would he teach and speak of killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, lying, slander, harsh speech, idle chatter, attachment, aversion, and wrong views, and all the rest? If what is called "the nature of a self" were permanent, then why would drinking wine cause one to become intoxicated and lose mindfulness? If the nature of what is called "a self" were permanent, then the blind would also be able to see forms, the deaf would also be able to hear sounds, the mute would also be able to speak, and the lame would also be able to walk. If the nature of what is called "a self" were permanent, then it would be unreasonable for one to come to harm from water, fire, precipices, poisons, weapons, and savage wild animals. If what is called "a self" were permanent, then it would be unreasonable that what one knew before should be forgotten later. And if nothing were forgotten, why would one ever say such things as, "I did not see this person before," and the like? If what is called "a self" were permanent, then all the things one did in youth, in the bloom of one's years, and in old age and decline, and indeed everything one has ever done, should never be forgotten but should be remembered. And if what is called "a self" were permanent, where does it reside? Does it reside in saliva and mucus? Does it reside in blue, yellow, red, and other colors? If what is called "a self" were indeed permanent, it would be fitting that it permeate everywhere, just as sesame oil pervades a body rubbed with it — in which case it would be fitting that when the body is cut, the self should also be cut and severed. The Blessed One then declared to Kāśyapa: Noble son, consider this analogy. A king had a wrestler, and in the course of a wrestling match that wrestler happened to have a single vajra-gem. While straining against another wrestler, that wrestler's opponent struck him on the head, and in the heat of the match the gem sank beneath the skin. Not knowing where the gem had gone, and because a wound had appeared, the wrestler summoned a physician. A highly skilled physician, knowing that the gem had gone beneath the skin and that it was because of this that the wound had appeared, did not apply medicine to the wound itself, but instead said: "Great strong one, where is the gem from your wrestling match?" The wrestler was alarmed and said to the physician: "It seems fitting that my wrestling gem has not gone anywhere — and if it is not there, is this not some illusion?" And he was utterly grief-stricken. Then the physician cheered him up and said: "Do not grieve like this. When you were straining in the match, the gem sank beneath the skin, and only a reflection of it is appearing on the outside. When you were exerting your strength you generated aversion, and by the power of the gem it sank beneath the skin without your feeling it." Even as he said this, the wrestler did not believe it and said: "Physician, do not deceive me. If it had truly sunk beneath the skin it would be utterly filthy with pus and blood — it would be fitting that it would come back out. And if it had gone inside the body of its own accord, it would not be fitting that you should be able to see it." Then the physician held up a mirror, and within the mirror the gem appeared, shining with clarity. Upon seeing this the wrestler was filled with a sense of wonder and amazement. Noble son, all sentient beings are just the same as this. Because they have not attended upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), even though they possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha, they are unable to see it. Through attachment, aversion, and —'

delusion covers and overwhelms sentient beings, so that they are born and fall into all manner of states: the hells, the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, the asura realm, the outcast class, the low castes, the warrior-noble caste, the brahmin caste, and so on in their many varieties. And because the mind generates karma of many different kinds, even when a human body is obtained, one may be born deaf, blind, mute, or feeble-minded, and one experiences the ripened fruit of the twenty-five modes of existence. Because the mind is obscured by attachment, aversion, and delusion, one does not know the intrinsic nature of a buddha — just as the wrestler did not know that the precious gem had sunk into his flesh and thought he had lost it. Ordinary beings are just the same: not knowing how to attend upon a spiritual friend, and not knowing the profoundly secret tathāgatagarbha, they meditate on and apply themselves diligently to selflessness. Yet it is like this: those who are not noble ones may speak of selflessness and yet not know the true defining characteristic of what is called the self. My own attendants are like this as well. Not knowing how to attend upon a spiritual friend, they do not know how to meditate on selflessness; they do not know the basis of selflessness; they do not know its defining characteristic. And if they do not know the defining characteristic of selflessness, what need is there to speak of knowing the true defining characteristic of the self?

Noble son, it is in this very way that the Tathāgata has proclaimed that the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present in all sentient beings — just as the skilled physician revealed the vajra gem within the wrestler's flesh. Ordinary beings are covered and overwhelmed by afflictions without measure, and so they do not know the intrinsic nature of a buddha. But when, at last, the afflictions are exhausted, it becomes clearly and directly realized — just as the wrestler saw the precious gem shining within the bright mirror.

Noble son, the tathāgatagarbha is thus immeasurable and inconceivable.

Noble son, here is another illustration. On the Himalayan range there is a medicinal herb called Sweet Wellbeing. Its flavor is supremely sweet, yet because it grows deep within a dense thicket it cannot be seen. One knows it is present in that place only by its fragrance. In a past age, a wheel-turning king (cakravartin), desiring that herb, had wooden troughs set up throughout the Himalayan range and collected the herb's exudate. When the herb ripened its essence flowed out like water into the ground, and from there it flowed further into the wooden troughs, and that flavor was true and pure. After that king had passed, the flavor of the herb became, in some places, sour; in some places, salty; in some places, sweet; in some places, bitter; in some places, hot; and in some places, astringent. Thus that single flavor, depending on where it flowed, became differentiated into many kinds — yet the true flavor of the herb remained in the mountain.

Similarly, a full moon, through the demerits of those with little merit, is put to labor under great hardship and cannot be obtained even by digging earnestly into the earth. But if noble kings were to appear in the world, through the condition of their merit, that true flavor of the herb would be fully obtained.

Noble son, the flavor of the tathāgatagarbha is just the same. Covered by the dense thicket of defilements, ignorant sentient beings are unable to see it. The single medicinal flavor is the simile for the intrinsic nature of a buddha. And the way that single flavor, under the power of defilement, becomes diversified into many flavors illustrates the following: beings in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, gods, humans, males, females, those of indeterminate sex, the warrior-noble caste,

brahmins, and those of low caste and outcaste birth, and so on. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is supremely indestructible, and therefore it cannot be killed. If it were killed, that would mean the intrinsic nature of a buddha had been made nonexistent. But the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not something that can by its own nature be made nonexistent — there is no basis upon which it could be made nonexistent. That which bears the name "self" is none other than the secret essence of the Tathāgata. This secret essence, then, cannot be destroyed or made nonexistent by anyone whatsoever. And although it cannot be made nonexistent, it cannot yet be seen. If one fully awakens to unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening, one will then know and realize it — and for that reason, it cannot be killed.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: If it cannot be killed, does that mean there is also no such thing as non-virtuous action?

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: In truth, killing does exist. Why is that? Noble son, the buddha-nature of sentient beings resides within the five aggregates. If the five aggregates are destroyed, that is called taking life. If life is taken, one falls into a lower realm. Through the causes and conditions of karma, beings cycle in saṃsāra with the various characteristics of warrior nobles, brahmins, those of low caste and outcastes, males, females, those of indeterminate sex, and the twenty-five modes of existence and so forth. Those who are not noble ones grasp at the notion of "self" under various characteristics — as something great, as something small, as a sesame seed, as a louse, as a bean, or no larger than a thumb — and to grasp at it under the false characteristics of an illusion is not correct. The characteristic of self that transcends the world is called the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and to grasp at self in that way is said to be supremely excellent.

Noble son, consider further this example: a man supremely skilled in the knowledge of treasure-sites takes a sharp pick and digs. He can dig through rocks, gravel, and boulders without obstruction. But if he strikes a vajra (diamond), he can go no further at all. A vajra cannot be pierced or cut by any weapon whatsoever. Noble son, the buddha-nature of sentient beings is just like that. Every opponent in the world — gods, evil māras, humans, and all beings of the world together — cannot destroy it. The characteristic of the five aggregates is that they are conditioned. The characteristic of the conditioned is that it is like rock or gravel — it can be pierced and cut. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is like a vajra — it cannot be destroyed. Therefore, to destroy the five aggregates is called taking life.

Noble son, know that the Dharma of a buddha is in this way inconceivable.

Noble son, the vast and extensive sūtras (mahāsūtras) are like ambrosia and they are also like poison.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: For what reason has the Tathāgata said that the vast and extensive sūtras are like ambrosia and also like poison?

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, do you wish to understand the true meaning of the tathāgatagarbha?

Kāśyapa said: I wish to realize what the meaning of the tathāgatagarbha is.

Then the Blessed One spoke in verse:

Some who drink ambrosia
die early, perishing before their time.
Some who drink ambrosia
live long and dwell there always.
Some survive by drinking poison.
Some die through the condition of poison.
The sūtras of the Great Vehicle
are like the unobstructed radiance of primordial wisdom.
The sūtras of the Great Vehicle

are mixed with medicine and with poison. Just as butter, molasses, ghee, and the like, when drunk and digested, become medicine, yet when undigested are called poison, so too the extensive sūtras are the same: for the wise they become ambrosia, but for the foolish, those who do not know the intrinsic nature of the buddhas, they become poison. The ambrosia of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Great Vehicle — just as all the tastes of fermentation become the finest milk, so likewise those who apply diligence, through the power of the Great Vehicle, pass fully into nirvāṇa and become kings among the supreme assembly of human beings. Kāśyapa, you and any sentient being who knows the intrinsic nature of the buddhas will, through the taste of the supreme unsurpassed nectar, become free from birth and death.

Kāśyapa, know this and realize the Three Jewels. The defining characteristic of the Three Jewels is precisely what is called the defining characteristic of the self. Whoever directly realizes the identity of self and the intrinsic nature of the buddhas will thereby realize the tathāgatagarbha. One who knows self and what is one's own has transcended the world. The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are supremely unsurpassed and excellent. These verses I have spoken convey this very meaning of the defining characteristic.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One in verse:

If I realize nothing at all
of the three refuges,
how can I take refuge in them
without the supreme fearlessness?
If I do not realize the Three Jewels,
how am I to act without a self?
If one takes refuge in the Buddha,
one will attain perfect happiness.
Let the Victor teach me
how to take refuge in the Dharma.
How does one attain great sovereignty,
and what is it that does not come under sovereignty?
How does one take refuge in the Saṅgha
and thereby attain unsurpassed happiness?
When one speaks words of happiness,
one will be fully awakened in the future.
If that is not accomplished in the future,
how does one turn to the Three Jewels?
I did not seek this before of my own accord,
yet because of compulsion I will seek it —
how then, without being pregnant,
does one give rise to the perception that one is giving birth to children?
If one is certainly carrying a child in the womb,
that is called having a child.
And if there is indeed a child in the womb,
it will certainly emerge before long.
That is the meaning of a child,
and it is the same for sentient beings.
As the Blessed One has taught,
the foolish cannot understand it.
Because they neither realize nor know it in this way,
they circle round and round in saṃsāra again and again.
Laypeople who are only so in name
do not seek the true meaning.
Please explain it extensively and in detail,
and please cut through my doubt.
Blessed One of great primordial wisdom,
please, out of loving compassion,
explain expansively the Tathāgata's
secret jewel-heart.

The Blessed One replied:

Kāśyapa, know this —
whatever the secret heart may be,
I will explain and reveal it fully
and cut through your doubt.
Listen and examine it well.
You, among bodhisattvas,
will come to be called by the name and title
of the seventh buddha to arise.
One who takes refuge in the buddhas
is a true lay practitioner
and will never take refuge
in any other gods.
One who takes refuge in the sublime Dharma
is free from the mind that harms and kills.
One who takes refuge in the Saṅgha
will not turn to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
One who takes refuge in the Three Jewels
will attain fearlessness.
Kāśyapa, by taking refuge in the Buddha,
I take refuge in the three,
and this I call the true path
within the domain of activity of the buddhas.
The defining characteristic of the Three Jewels is identical —

possessed of great primordial wisdom.
My own nature and the nature of the buddhas
are nondual, without distinction.
This path of praising the buddhas
is the abode of happiness for those who seek the true,
and because the buddhas know and see all things,
they shall be praised by countless buddhas.
I too incline toward and enter
the unsurpassed path of praising the Sugata —
that path which is the supreme nectar, the most holy,
unequaled anywhere in conditioned existence.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: Noble son, do not divide the Three Jewels as śrāvakas or low-born householders do. In the Great Vehicle, there is no defining characteristic that distinguishes the Three Jewels as separate. Why is that? Because within the very essential nature of the buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha are present. It is for the purpose of guiding śrāvakas and low-born householders that the Three Jewels are distinguished and taught as separate.

Noble son, those who wish to follow worldly teachings distinguish among the three objects of refuge as if they were different. But bodhisattvas think in this way: through this very body having taken refuge in the buddha, this very body itself will fully awaken. And once one has fully awakened and become a buddha, there is no longer any practice of paying homage, showing reverence, making offerings, or prostrating to the buddha. Why is that? Because the Blessed One, the buddha, has equally made himself a refuge for all sentient beings.

Whoever tends to the reliquary of the body of Dharma should reverently prostrate before the stūpas of the buddhas. Why? For the purpose of guiding ordinary beings. Furthermore, sentient beings generate the perception of my body as though it were a stūpa, and they make prostrations and offerings to it. In doing so, those sentient beings also thereby make the dharmakāya a place to which they can turn for refuge. All sentient beings dwell in what is untrue and in wrong teachings; therefore, I have gradually taught the true Dharma.

Moreover, for those who have taken refuge in what is not the true Saṅgha, he also creates a condition by which they come to take refuge in the true Saṅgha. And to those who divide the Three Jewels as separate, he also teaches that the place of refuge is one, and that the threefold distinction has no ultimate difference. For those who are like the blind wandering in darkness, he appears as an eye. Furthermore, he thinks to himself: I should also establish the true place of refuge in the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Noble son, in this way, bodhisattvas, great beings, perform the deeds of a buddha on behalf of immeasurable unruly sentient beings as well as those who are learned and wise. Noble son, consider the example of a man who goes to the battlefield and thinks: I am supreme, and all these armies depend on me alone. Likewise, consider a young regent who thinks: I have subdued all the princes, I have become master of all the domain and power of the great king, and all the princes follow me — therefore I shall not give rise to any weak intentions. As it is with the king and the prince, so too it is with the great minister. Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, also thinks in exactly the same way: how may these three things come to be of one nature with me? Noble son, these three things I have taught are nirvāṇa.

The Tathāgata is the supreme being without equal. Just as among all the limbs and branches of the human body the head is supreme and is nothing other than that, so too the buddha is similarly supreme and foremost — not the Dharma and the Saṅgha. For the sake of liberating worldly beings, the various characteristics have been taught distinctly, like the separate rungs of a ladder. Therefore you should not, like a foolish child, grasp the Three Jewels as having separately distinct characteristics. Because you have entered the Great Vehicle, your faculties are sharp — like a keen-edged sword.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked the Blessed One: I ask this of the Blessed One with full understanding, not out of ignorance. I have entered into this inquiry on behalf of those bodhisattvas who are courageous yet of dull faculties, in order to clarify the domain of the pure and stainless conduct. Furthermore, I have entered into this inquiry in order to open and present the wondrous and extraordinary things that the Tathāgata reveals to bodhisattvas, and to praise the vast and extensive Mahāyāna sūtras. Since the Tathāgata has taught this so well with great compassion, I too wish to abide in it. That which shows the thoroughly purified domain of the bodhisattvas' conduct is precisely this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa. Blessed One, I shall also teach this secret essence of the Tathāgata extensively to all sentient beings, and cause them to rightly understand the meaning of going for refuge to the Three Jewels. In this regard, any sentient being who has faith and confidence in this noble sūtra of the great nirvāṇa will be one who has understood and grasped the meaning of going for refuge to the Three Jewels. Why is this so? Because within this secret essence of the Tathāgata, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present. Whoever teaches and expounds this sūtra but says that the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not present in that person's body — such a person is no other than one who does not go for refuge to the Three Jewels. Why? Because in a future time this very body of mine will become the Three Jewels, and hearers, solitary buddhas, and all other ordinary beings besides will rely upon me and render service, honor, and veneration. Noble son, for that reason, one should train properly in the Mahāyāna sūtras.

Kāśyapa then further asked: The intrinsic nature of a buddha is inconceivable, and in just the same way the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor marks are also inconceivable.

The Blessed One then declared to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: Excellent! Most excellent! Noble son, since you are endowed with profound wisdom, I too shall teach you well concerning entry into the essence of the Tathāgata. If what is called the self were a permanent and enduring phenomenon, one could never be freed from suffering. If there were no such thing as a self, then the holy life of pure conduct would be entirely without benefit or purpose. If one claims that all phenomena are without a self, that view is annihilationism. If one insists on asserting a permanent, enduring self, that view is eternalism. If one views all formations as impermanent, that too falls into the view of annihilationism. If one views formations as permanent, that likewise becomes the view of eternalism. If one says that all is suffering, that too is the view of annihilationism.

If one says that all is bliss, that too is the view of eternalism. If one insists with great emphasis that all phenomena are permanent, one falls into the view of annihilationism. If one insists with great emphasis that all phenomena are annihilated, one falls into the view of eternalism. Consider, for example, a caterpillar making its way into a hollow: it releases its front legs before releasing its hind legs. Insisting upon permanence or annihilation is just like that — it depends upon the conditions of annihilation and permanence in turn.

Seeing the matter in this light: to insist upon other phenomena as being of the nature of suffering is non-virtue. To insist upon other phenomena as being of the nature of bliss is called virtue. To insist upon other phenomena as being without a self is to be on the side of thorough affliction. To insist upon other phenomena as being of the nature of permanence is called the secret essence of the Tathāgata, for nirvāṇa is without location or support. To insist upon other phenomena as being of the nature of impermanence is to hold that material things and goods exist. To insist upon other phenomena as being of the nature of permanence is the buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and perfect liberation. Therefore one should understand that the intrinsic nature of the buddha is the Middle Way, entirely free from both extremes.

When the true Dharma is taught, those who are immature and foolish entertain doubt about it. For example, when the weak and sick drink butter, their bodies become light and they feel joy. The phenomena of existence and non-existence, likewise, are not severed in a single intrinsic nature. For example, just as the four great elements are mutually discordant in their natures and each serves as the antidote to the other, a skilled physician understands this fully in accordance with whichever element is predominant. Noble son, the Tathāgata is similar: like a physician to all sentient beings, he knows the various natures of thorough affliction in all their different forms and clears them away entirely, and he teaches the secret essence of the Tathāgata — the intrinsic nature of the buddha, utterly pure, unchanging, and unshifting.

If one says it exists, among those of the type who are unfit — the wise and discerning who are attached — if one says it does not exist, one becomes a speaker of falsehood. If one says it exists, among those of the type who are unfit — the noble ones who say nothing — there is yet another type who speak frivolously and disputatiously, wishing to realize the true nature of reality. Those who are immature and foolish speak frivolously and argue, and thus do not know the secret essence of the Tathāgata.

If one says it is suffering, immature and foolish persons will think: "This body is impermanent." If one says all is suffering, they will not know that the body possesses the intrinsic nature of bliss. If one says it is impermanent, immature and foolish persons will think "all bodies are impermanent" and will grasp at this as though taking unfired clay vessels. But the wise and discerning make a distinction and do not say that everything without exception is impermanent. Why so? Because within one's own body there exists the seed of the intrinsic nature of the buddha.

If one says there is no self, immature and foolish persons will grasp at the idea that all the qualities of the buddha are without a self. But the wise and discerning understand that "no-self" is nothing more than a conventional label, a mere designation, and they distinguish this analytically as being without ultimate truth. Understanding in this way, they raise no doubt about it.

If one says that the essence of the Tathāgata is empty, when immature and foolish persons hear this, they will give rise to a view of annihilation or nihilism. But the wise and discerning distinguish the Tathāgata as permanent, unchanging, and unshifting. If one says that liberation is like a magical illusion, immature and foolish persons will grasp at the idea that those who have attained liberation possess qualities of Māra. But the wise and discerning make a distinction — as a lion stands alone among men — and distinguish the Tathāgata, the singular one, as permanent, steadfast, unchanging, and unshifting.

If one says that formations arise through the condition of ignorance, when immature and foolish persons hear this, they will fail to distinguish the two phenomena of knowledge and ignorance as non-dual. But the wise and discerning realize their non-duality by nature.

That which is non-dual is reality itself.

If one says that consciousness arises through the condition of formations, immature and foolish persons will grasp at formations and consciousness as two. But the wise and discerning realize their non-duality by nature. That which is non-dual is reality itself.

If one says that among the ten virtues and ten non-virtues, these belong to the category of what is to be done and these to the category of what is not to be done, these lead to the path of higher realms and these are causes of the lower destinies, these are white phenomena and these are black phenomena — immature and foolish persons will grasp at duality. But the wise and discerning realize their non-duality by nature. That which is non-dual is reality itself.

If one says that all phenomena are suffering and one should apply oneself diligently to that teaching, immature and foolish persons will grasp at duality. But the wise and discerning realize their non-duality by nature. That which is non-dual is reality itself.

If one says that all formations are impermanent, or that the tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature) too is impermanent, immature and foolish persons will grasp at duality. But the wise and discerning realize their non-duality by nature. That which is non-dual is reality itself.

If one says that all phenomena are without self, and that therefore the tathāgatagarbha too is truly without existence, immature and foolish persons will grasp at duality. But the wise and discerning realize their non-duality by nature. That which is non-dual is reality itself.

Self and no-self are by nature non-dual. The meaning of the tathāgatagarbha has thus been praised by the Blessed One, the Buddha, in an immeasurable, boundless, and limitless way, and I too have taught it extensively in all the sūtras endowed with qualities.

The eleventh fascicle begins here.

O son of good family, just as you have understood that "self" and "no-self" are by nature non-dual, take that to heart and bear it on the crown of your head. O son of good family, take this sūtra firmly to heart and keep it in mind. I myself have previously taught in the great sūtras of the noble Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) that self and no-self are non-dual by way of their defining characteristics.

It is like this: from milk arises curds, from curds arises butter, from butter arises clarified butter, and from clarified butter arises the essence of butter. In this way, whether the nature of curds arises from milk, or from the curds themselves, or from somewhere else — this same reasoning should be understood in detail right up to the essence of butter. If it arose from somewhere else, it would be made by something other, and if made by something other, then all sentient beings would not have come from milk. If it did not arise from milk, then milk would be entirely unnecessary. If it arose from the curds themselves, that too does not hold — for if the essence of butter were to come about, it would arise in a continuous sequence. If it arose in a continuous sequence, it would not have arisen all at once. And if it did not arise all at once, the five flavors would arise simultaneously — yet they do not arise simultaneously, and certainly they did not come from somewhere else entirely. Therefore, while the characteristic of curds — a great sweet flavour — is already present in the milk, it cannot transform on its own. In the same way, one should understand this in full detail right up to the essence of butter.

Through the cause and condition of eating grass and drinking water, the animal's blood is formed, and from the blood milk is produced. If sweet grass is eaten, the milk will be sweet. If bitter grass is eaten, the milk too will be bitter. On snowy mountains there is a grass called the rich grass, and if it is eaten, the result is the essence of butter alone — it does not appear blue, yellow, red, white, or black.

When other grasses are eaten, the taste and colour of the milk will also differ, in accordance with those causes and conditions.

The foolish ordinary being produces two characteristic marks through the cause and condition of karma rooted in knowledge and ignorance. If ignorance is reversed, that is called knowledge. In the same way, all phenomena have no two defining characteristics called virtue and non-virtue.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, what is the meaning of the statement you have made that curds exist within milk? Blessed One, if the intrinsic nature of curds is certainly present within milk, yet is so subtle it cannot be seen, why did you say that curds arise through the condition of milk? If phenomena did not exist from the beginning, then it would be fitting to say they are born. But if something was already there before, why do you declare it to be born? If the intrinsic nature of curds is certainly present within milk, then by the same reasoning, milk would also have to be present within all trees and plants. And likewise, trees and plants would have to be present within milk. But if you say that curds are certainly absent from milk, then why does no rabbit's horn arise from it? And if poison is poured into the milk and one drinks the curds produced from it, one dies — therefore it is equally not fitting to say that the intrinsic nature of curds is certainly absent from milk. And if you say that curds arise from something other than milk, why do curds not arise from water? Therefore it is not fitting to say that curds arise from something wholly other."

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, it is not fitting to say simply that curds are definitely present within milk, nor that curds are definitely absent from milk, nor that they arise from something entirely other. If one says that curds are definitely present in milk, why would the substance and the taste still be distinct? Therefore it is not fitting to say that the intrinsic nature of curds is definitely present in milk. And if one says that curds are definitely absent from milk, why does no rabbit's horn arise from milk? And if poison is poured into the milk and one drinks the curds, one dies — therefore it is equally not fitting to say that the intrinsic nature of curds is definitely absent from milk. And if one says they arise from something other than milk, why do curds not arise from water? Therefore it is not fitting to say that curds arise from something wholly other.

"Son of good family, from the eating of grass comes blood, and from blood comes milk, which is produced through the merit of sentient beings. Although milk has thus arisen from grass and blood, it is not fitting to call it 'two.' It is to be called 'arisen from cause and condition.' The same should be understood in full detail right up to the essence of butter.

"Thus what is called the curds of milk — curds are designated through causes and conditions, while not appearing as milk. From what causes and conditions do they arise? They arise from warmth and sourness. Therefore, from what arises through cause and condition right up to the essence of butter, the same should be understood in full detail. Therefore it is not fitting to say that the intrinsic nature of curds is definitely absent from milk and that they arise from something else — there is no basis for such a claim.

"Son of good family, knowledge and ignorance are likewise similar. When accompanied by complete affliction, it is called ignorance. When accompanied by virtuous phenomena, that same thing at that time is called knowledge. Therefore in what I have taught, there are no two defining characteristics. It is for this very reason, through that cause and that condition, that I previously spoke thus: on snowy mountains there is a grass called the rich grass, and when it is eaten, everything becomes the essence of butter — similarly, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is just like this.

"Son of good family, just as sentient beings with little merit do not see the rich grass, so too is the intrinsic nature of buddhahood — because it is covered over by complete affliction, sentient beings do not see it."

Here is an analogy: although the ocean has one taste — the taste of salt — within it there is also the taste of excellent water, the taste of milk. Just as the snowy mountains possess many good qualities and only the finest medicinal herbs grow there, yet on them too poisons do grow. The bodies of ordinary beings are likewise: they contain the four deadly serpent venoms, yet within them there also exists something like a sovereign medicinal herb — that is the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, which is not a conditioned phenomenon, but has become covered over by complete affliction.

Whether it be someone of the warrior class, the brahmin class, the merchant class, or the common class, if they clear away all afflictions, they will behold the intrinsic nature of buddhahood and will fully awaken to unsurpassed awakening.

Here is another analogy: when clouds gather in the sky above and thunder rolls, flowers bloom on all the tusks of yak-bulls. But if the thunder does not roll, the flowers do not bloom, and there is nothing to be named. The intrinsic nature of buddhahood in sentient beings is just like this: if it is covered over by complete affliction, it cannot be seen.

Therefore I have taught that sentient beings are without self. But whoever hears this sūtra collection of the Great Nirvāṇa will behold this intrinsic nature of buddhahood — just like the flowers on the tusks of yak-bulls. Even if one hears all the meditative absorptions of other sūtra collections, if one has not heard this sūtra, one will not see the genuine tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature), just as when the thunder does not roll, the flowers on the tusks of yak-bulls cannot be seen.

If one does hear this sūtra, one will come to understand the innermost heart of what all the Tathāgatas intended when they taught.
