What is called the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is illustrated by the analogy of beholding the flowers on the tusks of yak-bulls when thunder rolls in the sky above. If one hears this sūtra, one will come to understand that all immeasurable sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

Therefore the Great Nirvāṇa is called the innermost heart of what the Tathāgata intended and taught. The arising of the dharmakāya is like the blooming of flowers on the tusks of yak-bulls when thunder rolls. Because such a vast and great purpose arises and comes into being, it is called the Great Nirvāṇa.

Whatever son or daughter of good family applies themselves with great diligence to this Great Nirvāṇa — they repay the kindness of the Buddha, and are called genuine attendants of the Buddha.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "It is utterly wonderful! Blessed One, what is called the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is extremely profound and extremely subtle, difficult to see and difficult to enter into — it is not something to be understood by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, so it is, so it is — it is just as you have said."

Then again the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "In what way is the intrinsic nature of buddhahood so profound, so difficult to see, and so difficult to enter into?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, here is an analogy. A blind person, wishing to heal their eyes, went to a skilled physician. The physician took a golden blade, cut away the cataract film over the eye, then held up one finger and showed it — and the blind one said, 'I do not see it.' When two or three fingers were shown, they said, 'Now I see it just a little.'"

Son of good family, had this great sūtra of mahāparinirvāṇa not been taught, bodhisattvas who have completed the immeasurable perfections and who dwell on up through the ten grounds would still not see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood — and that is just like the blind person in the analogy. Once the Tathāgata taught it, they came to see just a little. The great bodhisattvas, having seen in this way, spoke thus: "How utterly marvelous! Blessed One, we have wandered in saṃsāra for countless eons and have been thoroughly deceived by no-self."

Son of good family, thus even bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten grounds do not see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood with clarity — to say nothing, then, of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas seeing it.

Son of good family, here is another analogy. When a bird soars high up into the lofty sky, one cannot easily discern whether what one sees is a bird or the sky itself — only upon careful examination does one finally distinguish it. Likewise, a bodhisattva dwelling on the ten grounds understands and sees the tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature) only in a partial way, and their seeing is just like that. How much less, then, do śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas understand and see it.

Son of good family, it is like a person intoxicated with drink who walks along a road and cannot easily see the road clearly before them. A bodhisattva dwelling on the ten grounds is similarly — they understand and see the tathāgatagarbha only partially.

Son of good family, it is like a person who has gone into a remote wilderness and, tormented by thirst, searches for water. They see a kingfisher perched on a tree, and because they are tormented by thirst, they cannot discern whether it is the tree or the water. Only upon careful examination do they finally know it to be a kingfisher in a tree. A bodhisattva dwelling on the ten grounds who sees and understands the tathāgatagarbha within their own body is similarly — their understanding is not clear and easy.

Son of good family, it is like a very weak prince who plays and plays through the night until dawn, and when morning comes cannot easily see and understand everything with clarity. A bodhisattva dwelling on the ten grounds who sees the tathāgatagarbha within their own body is similarly — they do not understand it clearly.

Son of good family, it is like a minister dispatched by a king who travels through the dark of night and, by a flash of lightning, sees a herd of yaks. He thinks to himself: "Is that yaks? Or a forest? Or clouds? Or buildings?" He believes them to be yaks, yet has no certainty. A bodhisattva dwelling on the ten grounds is similarly — they do not clearly understand the tathāgatagarbha within their own body.

Son of good family, here is yet another analogy. Monks who observe moral discipline, when they examine water that is declared free of living creatures, cannot easily discern whether the movement they see in the water consists of living creatures or particles of dust. After examining it for a long time, they come to know it is dust, yet they do not understand it with certainty. A bodhisattva dwelling on the ten grounds is similarly — they do not easily or clearly understand the tathāgatagarbha within their own body.

Son of good family, it is like someone who is drowsy and —

the sky being unclear, someone sees from a great distance a small child and cannot make out whether it is an animal, a bird, a human, or what it might be. After examining it for a long time, they come to see that it is a child, yet they do not understand this with clarity. A bodhisattva dwelling on the ten grounds likewise sees the tathāgatagarbha within their own body, yet they do not understand it with clarity.

Son of good family, here is another analogy. Suppose a person, in the darkness of the night, sees painted on a wall an image of a bodhisattva, and wonders: "Is this the form of a bodhisattva? Is it the form of the Sovereign Lord (Śiva)? Is it the form of the Great Brahma? Or is it simply cloth of a different color?" After examining it for a long time, they come to know it is the form of a bodhisattva, yet they do not understand this with clarity. A bodhisattva dwelling on the ten grounds likewise sees the tathāgatagarbha within their own body yet does not understand it with clarity.

Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is thus profoundly deep, and because it is difficult to see and difficult to realize, only a buddha alone realizes it; śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot come to realize it.

Son of good family, the learned and wise should therefore examine and analyze the tathāgatagarbha in just this manner.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One, saying: Blessed One, if the intrinsic nature of a buddha is so profound and so difficult to see, how could those who have fleshly eyes ever come to see it?

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: Son of good family, take the analogy of the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception — even they cannot realize it through either of the two vehicles, yet they realize it through trusting in the scriptural authority of the sūtras. Son of good family, it is the same for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: relying upon the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, they come to realize that the tathāgatagarbha exists within their own bodies. Son of good family, therefore you should apply yourselves with diligence to the practice of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is known by a buddha alone; it is not known by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then again asked the Blessed One: The ignoble and the foolish, those who are not noble ones (āryans), claim that a self exists in all sentient beings.

The Blessed One replied: Here is an analogy. A prince and a poor man became friends and would visit each other's homes. The poor man, upon seeing that the prince possessed an exceedingly fine sword, developed a feeling of longing for it. Later, the prince took the sword and went away to another region. The poor man subsequently, while sleeping in someone else's house, cried out in his sleep with the words "sword, sword!" One of the people present there heard him call out those words, seized him, and brought him before the king. The king then asked the man: "What is this about you saying 'sword, sword'?" The man explained the matter to the king in full detail, saying: "Even if the king were to cut my body, my limbs, and my extremities into pieces, the sword is not mine. I previously was a friend of a certain great prince, and I saw with my own eyes that the prince had a fine sword; but as for touching it with my hands — that I could not do, let alone deliberately taking it for myself." The king then said: "You say you saw this sword — then what was its shape like?" He replied:

"Great King, what I saw was something resembling a rainbow."

When the king heard those words, he laughed and said: "Do not grieve — go wherever you are happy. If a sword of that description does not exist in my treasury, then as for the prince you speak of having seen it — what need is there even to mention that? After that, the king addressed his ministers: "Have any of you seen a sword of that description?" Before long, he too passed away. Then a successor king was consecrated and invested with royal authority, and he likewise asked the ministers: "Did any of you previously see a sword of that description in the treasury?" The ministers replied: "Your Majesty, we did see it previously." He asked again: "If you saw it, what was the shape of that sword like?" They answered: "Your Majesty, we saw something resembling a rainbow."

The king declared: "There could not be a sword of that description in my treasury." And so through four successive reigns the sword was sought, yet its source was never found. Then, after many years had passed, the prince who had formerly fled returned from another land, assumed the kingship, and gained royal authority. He too addressed his ministers: "Have you seen that sword?" The ministers replied: "Your Majesty, we have indeed seen it." He asked: "Since you have seen it, what was the shape of that sword like?" Some of the ministers said: "Your Highness, it was exceedingly bright — it resembled a blue lotus flower." Others said: "It resembled a rainbow." Others said: "Its color was red, resembling a heap of fire." Others said: "It resembled a black serpent." At that, the king laughed and declared to the ministers: "You have not truly seen my sword."

Noble son, the bodhisattva, the great being, is just like this. Having appeared in the world, he teaches the true defining characteristic of what is called "self," and the moment he has taught it he is gone — just as the prince, holding that fine sword, fled to another land. All the foolish and confused assert: "There is a self! There is a self!" Yet such talk of a self resembles nothing so much as the poor man who, sleeping in another's house, blurted out "sword, sword" in his sleep. If śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are asked what the defining characteristic of "self" is as it pertains to sentient beings, some will say: "The defining characteristic of a self-view and of what is called no-self is something about the size of a thumb." Others will say: "It is something about the size of a barleycorn." Others will say: "It is something about the size of a sesame seed." And others will say: "The defining characteristic of self dwells in the mind, blazing and luminous like the sun." Thus ordinary people do not know the defining characteristic of what is called "self" — just as the ministers did not know that fine sword. Since the foolish and confused do not understand the defining characteristic of "self" as the bodhisattva has taught it, they make various distinctions and hold them as the defining characteristic of "self" — which is just like answering the question "What was the shape of the sword like?" by saying "It resembled a rainbow."

In this way, the ignoble and foolish generate without interruption a stream of wrong views. And it is in order to sever those wrong views that the Tathāgata taught no-self — just as the successive princes said to their ministers: "There is no sword of that kind in my treasury." Noble son, when the Tathāgata today teaches what is called "self," that is to be understood as the nature of a buddha. And that nature of a buddha, within the Dharma taught by a buddha, is like a sword exceedingly bright and pure.

Noble son, that which the ignoble and foolish call "well spoken" does not enter into the supreme Dharma of a buddha. Whatever is well analyzed and followed in accordance with the teaching — that is to be understood as resembling the form of a bodhisattva.

Noble son, however many different ways of speaking there are — the science of spells, the treatises victorious over words, letters, and all the rest — these were all taught by the Buddha, not by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "How is it that the Tathāgata taught the syllable-mothers?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, by teaching the half-syllable syllable-mothers of old, one comes to retain treatises, sciences of spells, victory through words, sounds, languages, and the like. Through learning the syllable-mothers, the ignoble and childish then come, on that basis, to understand Dharma and what is not Dharma, and so forth.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again asked the Blessed One: "What is the meaning of the word 'syllable'?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, the fourteen elements of the syllable — these are called the meaning of 'syllable.' The word 'syllable' denotes nirvāṇa: because it is permanent, it does not leak. What does not leak is inexhaustible. What is called inexhaustible is the vajra body of the Tathāgata. Therefore the fourteen syllable elements are the syllable-mothers.

"Among them, the letter A signifies the indestructible. What is indestructible is called the Three Jewels — it is like a vajra. Furthermore, the letter A signifies the undefiled. What is undefiled is called the Tathāgata: the Tathāgata, from whom nothing leaks through any of the nine orifices, is therefore called 'without defilement.' Having no nine orifices, nothing leaks; what does not leak is permanent. What is permanent is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata, being unconditioned, is undefiled. Furthermore, the letter A is called 'the assembly of qualities.' The assembly of qualities is the Three Jewels, and therefore it is called A. As for the letter A in this context: it bears the meaning of 'master.' What is the meaning of 'master'? One who is renowned in the world as 'noble.' And what is that which is called 'noble'? 'Noble' means: without attachment, of few desires, knowing contentment, utterly pure, and liberating sentient beings who revolve in cyclic existence through the three realms — such is what is called 'noble.' Furthermore, the letter A signifies 'endowed,' meaning one who strictly guards moral discipline and is inclined to a conduct of virtue. Furthermore, the letter A signifies the one who, following the conduct of the noble ones, learns how to walk, stand, move, and stir; to pay reverence to the Three Jewels and to one's parents; to make offerings, show respect, perform service, and make prostrations; and who also trains in the Great Vehicle. Noble son, you and the others who hold the vow of moral discipline, along with the great-spirited bodhisattvas, are called 'noble.'

"Furthermore, the letter Ā signifies teaching and training: just as the Tathāgata has shown that these things are proper to be done and these things are not proper to be done, one who does not perform what is contrary to Dharma is called 'noble' — and therefore it is called Ā.

"As for the letter I: it signifies the vast brahmacarya (the divine practice of purity) of the Dharma of a buddha, which is luminous and stainless like a fully risen moon. One explains that these things are proper for you and others to do, these things are not proper to do, this is the meaning, this is not the meaning, this was spoken by the Buddha, this was taught by Māra — and therefore it is called I.

"As for the letter Ī: it signifies the Dharma of a buddha, which is exceedingly profound and subtle, difficult to fathom, and which the great sovereign of the gods —"

— just as Brahmā the Great rules through Dharma. And whosoever holds it in mind is called a guardian of the Dharma. Furthermore, those who exercise rule are the four protectors of the world, and these four rulers have authority to guard, hold, teach extensively, and expound this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra. Furthermore, the letter Ī signifies the authority to teach the Dharma to ordinary people. Furthermore, the letter Ī signifies that which is taught for the sake of bringing beings under its sway — and what is that? It is this: applying oneself diligently to the sūtras of great extent. Furthermore, the letter Ī signifies that, just as impurity is removed, so too miserliness and jealousy are utterly cut away, and all things are rendered auspicious — and therefore it is called Ī.

As for the letter U: it signifies the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, which among all sūtras is supreme, excellent, and the highest above the highest. Furthermore, the letter U signifies the nature of the Tathāgata, which no śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha has ever heard before — just as, among all the continents, the melodious sound of the north is the most excellent and supreme. If a bodhisattva were to listen to this sūtra or hold it in mind, that bodhisattva would become supreme among all sentient beings, would become foremost, would become the most excellent. Therefore this sūtra is the foremost of all, the most excellent and supreme, and for that reason it is called U.

As for the letter Ū: just as fresh milk is the most superior of all flavors, so too the nature of the Tathāgata is like that — it is the foremost, the most excellent, and the supreme among all sūtras. Whoever slanders or belittles this sūtra should be known as no different from an animal. Furthermore, the letter Ū signifies that a person who lacks the wisdom of right mindfulness, and who slanders and belittles the secret essence taught by the Tathāgata — that person is to be known as a being who is deeply pitiable, for that person is bereft of the teaching on the selflessness of the Tathāgata's secret essence, and therefore it is called Ū.

As for the letter E: it signifies the nirvāṇa that is the nature of reality of the buddhas, and therefore it is called E. Furthermore, the letter E signifies the meaning of the Tathāgata.

As for the letter AI: whether the Tathāgata goes or stays, whether he is active or still, whether he moves and stirs in every way — in all of this he never fails to act for the benefit and well-being of ordinary people, and therefore it is called AI.

As for the letter O: it signifies the meaning of mental affliction. Mental affliction is what is called "possessing defilements." The Tathāgata has utterly severed all mental afflictions, and therefore it is called O.

As for the letter AU: it signifies the meaning of the Great Vehicle, the consummate meaning of the fourteen syllables. The Great Vehicle sūtras are likewise: they are the consummate and most excellent among all sūtras, and therefore it is called AU.

As for the letter AṂ: it removes all impure things that have not been examined, and through the teaching of the Buddha enables one to relinquish all precious things such as gold and silver — and therefore it is called AṂ.

As for the letter AḤ: it signifies the meaning of the supreme vehicle. Why is this? Because this Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, is the foremost, the most excellent, and the supreme among all sūtras, and therefore it is called AḤ.

As for the letter KA: it signifies the arising of compassion for all sentient beings — just as a rāhu (the eclipse-seizing demon) regards beings as its own children and turns toward virtue — and therefore it is called KA.

As for the letter KHA: it signifies one who is not a spiritual friend. One who is not a spiritual friend is a blemished and impure one —

one who has no faith in the tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature) — and therefore it is called KHA.

As for the letter GA: it signifies the essence. The essence means the secret essence of the Tathāgata — namely, that all sentient beings possess the nature of a buddha — and therefore it is called GA.

As for the letter GHA: it signifies the sound of the Tathāgata's permanence. How is the Tathāgata the sound of permanence? It is like this: the Tathāgata is permanent, stable, unchanging, and unshifting — and therefore it is called GHA.

As for the letter NGA: it signifies the defining characteristic of the dissolution of all conditioning factors — and therefore it is called NGA.

As for the letter CA: it signifies the purpose of cultivation. The taming of all sentient beings is what is called the purpose of cultivation — and therefore it is called CA.

As for the letter CHA: it signifies that the Tathāgata shelters and covers all sentient beings like a great canopy — and therefore it is called CHA.

As for the letter JA: it signifies perfect liberation, which is without the characteristic of aging — and therefore it is called JA.

As for the letter JHA: it signifies being bound by afflictions on every side, which is like a dense forest — and therefore it is called JHA.

As for the letter NYA: it signifies the meaning of wisdom. Because one knows the nature of reality as it truly is, it is called NYA.

As for the letter ṬA: it signifies that in Jambudvīpa the Tathāgata appeared with only half his body revealed and taught the Dharma — which is like a half-moon — and therefore it is called ṬA.

As for the letter ṬHA: it signifies that the dharmakāya is perfectly complete, like a full moon — and therefore it is called ṬHA.

As for the letter ḌA: it signifies foolish monks who do not understand permanence and impermanence, and who are like small children — and therefore it is called ḌA.

As for the letter ḌHA: it signifies one who is ungrateful toward a teacher and is like flesh consumed by the body — and therefore it is called ḌHA.

As for the letter ṆA: it signifies that which is not the purpose of the noble ones, being like tīrthikas — and therefore it is called ṆA.

As for the letter TA: it signifies the occasion when the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "O monks, abandon fear and dread — I will teach you the true Dharma." This is why it is called TA.

As for the letter THA: it signifies the meaning of foolishness and delusion. Sentient beings, seized by saṃsāra and spinning within it, are like silkworm grubs or bubbles — and therefore it is called THA.

As for the letter DA: it signifies the giving of a great gift — namely, the Great Vehicle — and therefore it is called DA.

As for the letter DHA: it signifies the praising and extolling of qualities, in this way: the Three Jewels are like Mount Meru, the king of mountains — supremely excellent, high, vast, and great, never toppling or falling — and therefore it is called DHA.

As for the letter NA: it signifies that the Three Jewels are utterly firm, like the pivoting post of a door, immovable — and therefore it is called NA.

As for the letter PA: it signifies a perverted meaning. If someone says, "The Three Jewels will be exhausted and cease to exist," one should understand that such a person has deceived themselves — and therefore it is called PA.

As for the letter PHA: it signifies a worldly obstructor. If someone says, "When the cosmic dissolution comes upon the world, the Three Jewels too will cease to exist," that person is utterly foolish and without wisdom, and exercises power over what is noble — and therefore it is called PHA.

As for the letter BA: it signifies the ten powers of a buddha — and therefore it is called BA.

As for the letter BHA: it signifies carrying a heavy burden — bearing the unsurpassed and true Dharma upon one's shoulders with patience. One should understand that such a being is a great bodhisattva — and therefore it is called BHA.

As for the letter MA: it signifies the extremely strict and austere Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra of the Great Vehicle — the great passing beyond sorrow — and therefore it is called MA.

As for the letter YA: it signifies that bodhisattvas teach the Dharma of the Great Vehicle to sentient beings in every place — and therefore it is called YA.

As for the letter RA: because one has utterly destroyed attachment, aversion, and delusion and teaches the true Dharma, it is called RA.

As for the letter LA: those who follow the vehicle of the hearers (śrāvakas) remain in a state of change, whereas the Great Vehicle is the teaching that does not waver. Because one abandons the vehicle of the hearers and strives in the unsurpassed Great Vehicle, it is called LA.

As for the letter VA: because the Blessed One, the buddha, rained down a great shower of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings — encompassing the worldly sciences, letters, treatises, and the like — it is called VA.

As for the letter ŚA: because one has utterly abandoned the five kinds of thorns, it is called ŚA.

As for the letter ṢA: it signifies the complete fulfillment of meaning. Whoever hears this sūtra of the great passing beyond sorrow — this sūtra of great purpose — is as one who has heard and holds all the sūtras of the Great Vehicle. Therefore it is called ṢA.

As for the letter SA: because the true Dharma is taught to sentient beings, causing their minds to become glad, it is called SA.

As for the letter HA: it signifies the mind's great rejoicing. Marvellous indeed is the Blessed One — how wonderful that he is free from all formations! "Oh! The Tathāgata has passed fully beyond sorrow" — this exclamation of astonishment is called HA.

As for what is called KṢA: it pertains to the domain of Māra. Because innumerable māras are unable to destroy the secret essence of the Tathāgata, it is called KṢA. Furthermore, KṢA also signifies what is taught in accordance with the ways of the world — showing the relationships between parents, spouse, and children — and therefore it is called KṢA.

Now, the four syllables RI, RĪ, LI, and LĪ have four meanings. These are: the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the antidotal Dharma. Regarding the antidotal Dharma: even though someone — like Devadatta (lha sbyin) — creates a schism in the Saṅgha by worldly means, or displays various forms and appearances in order to undermine moral discipline, a wise person endowed with wisdom will see through it and feel no fear. Since this is merely engaging with worldly convention, the syllables RI, RĪ, LI, and LĪ are so called.

Through the breath, the organ of taste, the length and shortness of the nasal breath, and the act of drawing forth, one comes to know the meaning from the sound that follows. These also differ in form depending on the tongue and the teeth.

In this way, the meaning of the letters brings about a complete purification of the verbal karma of sentient beings. Yet the buddha-nature within sentient beings does not become pristinely pure for the first time by virtue of the letters. Why is that? Because it is by nature pure from the very beginning. Although it dwells within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, it is not like the aggregates, elements, and sense bases. Therefore sentient beings should take refuge in the bodhisattvas. Because of the buddha-nature, one should view all sentient beings without distinction.

Thus, incomplete letters are the root of sūtras, treatises, speech, and mastery through words. The meaning of an incomplete letter is the root of all afflicted speech — therefore it is called an incomplete letter. A complete letter is the root of all virtuous Dharma speech. For example, in the world, a person who does what is sinful and unwholesome is called "incomplete" or "half." One who practices all that is virtuous is called "complete." In this way, all sūtras, treatises, and speech have incomplete letters as their root.

Now, if someone were to say that even the Tathāgata and true liberation fall under incomplete letters, that is not so. Why? Because they are free from letters altogether. Therefore the Tathāgata is unobstructed and unattached with respect to all phenomena, and is perfectly and truly liberated.

Then, as for who it is that has understood and knows the meaning of the letters —

One who knows that the Tathāgata came into the world and made incomplete letters to be no more is called one who understands and has realized the meaning of the letters. One who follows the meaning of incomplete letters does not know the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata.

Now, what is the meaning of "letterless"? One who keeps company with and engages in unwholesome phenomena is called "letterless." Furthermore, "letterless" also applies to one who keeps company with and engages in wholesome phenomena yet does not know whether the Tathāgata is permanent or impermanent, eternal or non-eternal; who does not know the Dharma and the Saṅgha; who does not know what is Vinaya and what is not Vinaya, what is sūtra and what is not sūtra, what has been taught by māra and what has been taught by a buddha; and who cannot make distinctions. Such a one is said to have entered into the meaning of "letterless."

Thus I have also explained the following of the meaning of the letterless. Therefore, son of good family, abandoning incomplete letters, you should become highly skilled in complete letters.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, we shall become highly skilled in the enumeration of letters. Having met the Teacher, the unsurpassed one, we shall act in accordance with the word of the Tathāgata as taught."

The Blessed One declared to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Excellent! Excellent! Those who wish to practice the sublime Dharma should train in precisely this way."

Then the Blessed One spoke again to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, consider how among birds the kalandaka and the śārika, wherever they go, never part from each other but always remain together. In just the same way, suffering, impermanence, and selflessness are like those birds — they never part from one another.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that suffering, impermanence, and selflessness are said to be like the śārika and the kalandaka?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, the phenomena of suffering are one thing, the phenomena of happiness another; the phenomena of permanence are one thing, the phenomena of impermanence another; the phenomena called 'self' are one thing, the phenomena of selflessness another. As an example, rice is different from barley, and barley is different from beans and sugarcane. Yet from the first sprouting of a seedling up through the leaves and flowers, all such things are impermanent. Once the fruit has ripened and is fully enjoyed by a person, it is called 'permanent.' Why? Because by its defining characteristic it is genuinely and truly so."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if those things are permanent in that way, is the Tathāgata then similar to them?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, do not speak in that way. Why? If one were to say that the Tathāgata is like the king of mountains, Mount Meru, then when the eon is destroyed and Mount Meru collapses and crumbles, would the Tathāgata also perish at that time? Son of good family, you should not ask about such matters. Son of good family, among all phenomena, apart from nirvāṇa, not a single phenomenon is called permanent. It is only conventionally that the fruit is said to be permanent."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, excellent! Most excellent! It is just as the Blessed One has said."

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "It is so. It is exactly so. Son of good family, even if one has applied oneself with great diligence to the meditative absorption of all sūtras and the like, but has not heard the great complete nirvāṇa, one will declare that all things are impermanent. Yet one who has heard this sūtra — even while still with afflictions — becomes like one who is free from afflictions.

and will act for the benefit and happiness of all the world, gods and humans alike. And why is this? It is because, through realizing that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within one's own body, one is said to be permanent.

Son of good family, here is another example. The mango tree before its flowers have appeared is said to be impermanent. But once the fruit has manifested and come to serve a beneficial purpose, it is said to be permanent. And so it is, son of good family: even if one has cultivated the meditative absorption of all sūtras, yet has not heard this great complete nirvāṇa, one will declare that all things are impermanent. But one who has heard this sūtra — even while still with afflictions — becomes like one who is free from afflictions, and will act for the benefit and happiness of all gods and humans. And why is this? It is because, through realizing that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within one's own body, one is said to be permanent.

Son of good family, here is yet another example. A lump of gold while being melted in the fire is said to be impermanent. But once it has been melted and become gold, serving a beneficial purpose, it is said to be permanent. And so it is, son of good family: even if one has cultivated the meditative absorption of all sūtras, yet has not heard this great complete nirvāṇa, one will declare that all things are impermanent. But one who has heard this sūtra — even while still with afflictions — becomes like one who is free from afflictions, and will act for the benefit and happiness of all gods and humans. And why is this? It is because, through realizing that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within one's own body, one is said to be permanent.

Son of good family, here is yet another example. Sesame seeds while being pressed for oil are said to be impermanent. But once they have been pressed and become oil, serving a beneficial purpose, they are said to be permanent. Son of good family, even if one has cultivated the meditative absorption of all sūtras, yet has not heard this sūtra of the great complete nirvāṇa, one will declare that all things are impermanent. But one who has heard this sūtra — even while still with afflictions — becomes like one who is free from afflictions, and will act for the benefit and happiness of all gods and humans. And why is this? It is because, through realizing that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within one's own body, one is said to be permanent.

Son of good family, here is yet another example. All rivers flow into the ocean. Likewise, the meditative absorptions of all sūtras flow into this sūtra of the Great Vehicle, the great complete nirvāṇa. And why is this? Because in the end, the intrinsic nature of a buddha has been well proclaimed within it.

Son of good family, therefore I have taught that some things are permanent and other things are impermanent. You should understand this to apply in the same extensive way, all the way through to selflessness.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Tathāgata is free from the sorrow of longing. It is beings of the heavenly realms who have such sorrow of longing — the Tathāgata is not a heavenly being. The sorrow of longing belongs to humans — the Tathāgata is not a human. Those subject to the sorrow of longing are the twenty-five modes of existence — the Tathāgata is not the twenty-five modes of existence. Since the Tathāgata is free from the sorrow of longing, why then has it been proclaimed and taught that the Tathāgata has the sorrow of longing?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, the gods of the realm of non-perception are called 'without perception.' If there is no perception, there is no vital life-force either. And if there is no vital life-force, how could there be any aggregates, elements, or sense bases? Therefore it is not proper to say that the life-force of the gods of non-perception abides here in this place. Son of good family, take the example of a tree-deity: though it dwells in a tree, it is not proper to say that it dwells definitively in the branches, the twigs, the trunk, or the leaves; yet though its dwelling-place is indefinite, it is not proper to say that it does not exist. The life-force of the gods of non-perception is similar to this. Son of good family, the qualities of a buddha are likewise —

profoundly deep and difficult to realize. Although the Tathāgata has no grief or suffering born of longing, in order to arouse great compassion for sentient beings he displays the appearance of grief born of longing, and he looks upon sentient beings as though they were his own child — like Rāhu holding the moon. Furthermore, son of good family, the life-force of the gods of non-perception is known only to a buddha alone; it is not something others can realize or understand. The same holds true for the gods of the sphere neither of perception nor of non-perception. Kāśyapa, the intrinsic nature of a Tathāgata is utterly pure and without attachment. If it were like an emanation, how could there be any grief or suffering born of longing? Yet if the Tathāgata had no grief, how would he work for the benefit of all sentient beings and cause the Dharma of the buddhas to spread wide? And if he had none, why is it said that he looks upon all sentient beings as his own child, like Rāhu holding the moon? For if he did not truly look upon all sentient beings as his own child, like Rāhu holding the moon, then that very statement would be false.

Therefore, son of good family: a buddha is inconceivable; the Dharma is inconceivable; the buddha-nature of sentient beings is inconceivable; and the lifespan of the gods of non-perception is inconceivable. The question of whether there is grief in the Tathāgata or whether there is no grief falls within the domain of the buddhas; it is not something śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can know.

Son of good family, consider this example: to empty space nothing clings — not a house, not even the finest particle. Yet it is also untenable to say that a house does not rest on space. Therefore it is not right to say either that a house rests in space or that it does not rest in space. Ordinary childish people do say that a house rests in space, but in truth space has no resting place. Why? Because it abides by its own intrinsic nature. Son of good family, mind is similar: it is not right to say either that it rests in the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, or that it does not rest in them. The life of the gods of non-perception is likewise, and in the same way the Tathāgata's grief is likewise.

If there is no grief, why is it said that he looks upon sentient beings as his own child, like Rāhu holding the moon? And if there is, why is it said that by nature he is like empty space? Son of good family, consider a skilled conjurer who creates houses, slayings, healings, captivities, releases, and diverse things — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, all manner of precious gems, forests, fruit-trees, and the rest. In all of these there is no reality, no true nature. The Tathāgata is similar: he displays grief and so forth in conformity with the world, but they are not real. Son of good family, when the Tathāgata has passed utterly into nirvāṇa, how could there be grief or suffering in him? One who thinks that the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa and is impermanent should be understood to be a person who is himself bound by grief. Conversely, one who thinks that the Tathāgata has not passed into nirvāṇa and that he abides permanently, unchangingly — that person is free of grief; yet such a person has no knowledge of whether the Tathāgata has grief or is without grief.

Furthermore, son of good family, consider this example: a person of the lowest capacity does not know the qualities of a person of middling or superior capacity; a person of middling capacity does not know the qualities of one of superior capacity; a person of superior capacity knows the qualities of the superior, and also knows the qualities of the middling and the lowest. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are similar:

they know only as much as they themselves can know. The Tathāgata is not like that: he is known by himself and known by others as well. For this reason the Tathāgata is called "wisdom without obstruction."

Appearing to the world in a manner likened to an illusion, he teaches those with the eyes of flesh, who suppose that what is shown is a true and real thing. There is no basis on which they could come to know the Tathāgata's unobstructed wisdom. Whether there is grief or no grief is known by the buddha alone. Therefore the quality of having a self belongs to one class, and the quality of having no self belongs to another — like the starling and the kalandaka bird.

Furthermore, son of good family, the Dharma of the buddhas is comparable to a starling and a kalandaka going together. The starling and the kalandaka, when summer rains cause the rivers to flood, fly straight to wherever water is to be found, to a high and secure place, in order to lay their eggs and raise their young. The Tathāgata's coming into the world is just like that: just as the starling and the kalandaka and the rest place their young in a high, safe place, so too the Tathāgata, having accomplished every deed for sentient beings, passes into complete nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, the quality of suffering belongs to one class, and the quality of happiness belongs to another. All formations are suffering; nirvāṇa is happiness. In the ultimate sense, all formations are subject to destruction.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that sentient beings who have attained the passing beyond sorrow can be called supremely happy?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, as I have taught, all that is assembled among formations consists in aging and death."

One who is heedful and practises heedfulness
abides in a place that is like nectar.
One who is without heed and is heedless
abides in a place of death.

Those who practise heedfulness
attain the abode of the deathless.
Those who are without heedfulness
walk forever on the path of death.

Whatever is without heedfulness is called a conditioned phenomenon, and every conditioned phenomenon is the supreme form of suffering. Whatever is heedful is called nirvāṇa, and nirvāṇa is called nectar — the supreme happiness. If one enters into formations, that is called the abode of death, and it becomes the supreme form of suffering. If one reaches nirvāṇa, that is called the deathless, and one will taste the supreme happiness. If one is heedful, then even though many formations have assembled, they are called permanent, happy, deathless, and indestructible.

Now, what is heedlessness and what is heedfulness? Those who are not noble ones, those of common stock and low birth, are heedless — possessing the quality of being accompanied by death. Noble ones who have transcended the world are possessed of heedfulness — free from aging and death. Why? Because they have entered nirvāṇa, which is supreme happiness. Therefore the quality of suffering belongs to one class, and the quality of happiness belongs to another. The quality called "self" belongs to one class, and the quality called "no-self" belongs to another — just as people walking on the ground, when they look for the tracks of birds in the sky, cannot see them.

The Twelfth Fascicle.

Son of good family, sentient beings are just like that: they lack the eye of higher vision, and bound by afflictions, they do not see that within themselves the nature of a buddha exists. For this reason I have taught the doctrine called "no-self." Why? Those who lack the eye of higher vision do not rightly know the true meaning of what is called "self";

they grasp at something inferior as "self," and under the power of afflictions they conceptualize conditioned things, calling them "impermanent." Therefore I have taught that the quality of permanence belongs to one class and the quality of impermanence belongs to another. On this there is the following verse:

Those who are courageous and capable of effort,
Whether seated on a mountain peak
Or dwelling in a plain or solitary place,
Are always seen by the childish and ignoble.
Having reached the ground of great primordial wisdom
And ascended to the unsurpassed platform,
By dispelling all one's own sorrow
One beholds the sorrow of all sentient beings.

The Tathāgata, having overcome the boundless afflictions of sentient beings and abiding on the mountain of primordial wisdom, sees that all ordinary beings are forever tormented and oppressed by measureless afflictions.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Blessed One, it does not seem to be as the Blessed One has expressed it in verse. Why? In nirvāṇa there is nothing that could be called 'sorrow,' and there is no joy either. Why then did you say that it resembles ascending to a platform of wisdom, reaching a place like a mountain peak, and beholding all sentient beings?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, the platform of wisdom refers to nirvāṇa. The one free of sorrow is the Tathāgata. The one possessed of sorrow refers to the childish and ignoble. The childish and ignoble are possessed of sorrow; the Tathāgata is free of sorrow. 'The peak of Mount Meru' signifies perfect liberation. Whoever strives and applies diligence is like Mount Meru — unshakeable and immovable. 'The ground' refers to the conceptualization of conditioned things: the childish and ignoble, dwelling on that ground, conceptualize conditioned things. Those who are wise and possessed of wisdom have fully awakened: having abandoned existence, they are called Tathāgata because they are permanent. The Tathāgata, out of loving concern for the measureless ordinary beings who are pierced by the thorn of existence, is described as having sorrow."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, if the Tathāgata has sorrow, then it would be inappropriate to designate him as a perfectly and completely awakened buddha."

The Blessed One said to Kāśyapa: "Even so, it is not without meaning. The Tathāgata manifests birth among whichever ordinary beings are to be tamed, and in whatever manner they are to be tamed. Though he manifests birth, in truth he has no birth. Therefore the Tathāgata is one whose nature is permanent and abiding — like the kalandaka bird and the śārika bird.

Son of good family, consider further this analogy. When people see the moon obscured by clouds and no longer visible, they think the moon has set — yet in truth the moon does not set. When it rises over another continent, the beings dwelling there think the moon has risen — yet in truth the moon does not rise. Why? Because it is obscured and hidden by Mount Meru; there is no such thing as the moon rising or setting. The Tathāgata, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, is just the same. Coming into the great trichiliocosm, he manifests a father and a mother in Jambudvīpa, and ordinary beings think, 'The Tathāgata has appeared in Jambudvīpa.' He also manifests nirvāṇa in Jambudvīpa, and although the Tathāgata does not truly pass into nirvāṇa, sentient beings think, 'The Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa' — just as in the analogy of the setting moon."

Noble son, the Tathāgata himself has in truth no birth and no cessation — yet he shows birth and cessation in order to tame sentient beings.

Noble son, consider an analogy. When the moon appears full in some world-systems, it appears as a crescent in others. When it appears as a crescent in these world-systems, it appears full in others. When the people of Jambudvīpa first see the moon rising, they say "It is the first day of the month" and form the perception of a new moon. When they see the moon full and swelling, they say "It is the fifteenth day of the month" and form the perception of a full moon. In truth, the moon itself has no waxing or waning — yet through the power of Mount Meru there appears to be waxing and waning.

Noble son, the Tathāgata is just the same. In this Jambudvīpa he shows a first birth and he shows nirvāṇa. Showing that first birth is like the new moon. When all see the young one newly born and taking seven steps, they think of him as the moon on the second day. Then, when the young one is shown entering upon learning, they think of him as the moon on the third day. When the going forth (pravrajyā) is shown, they think of him as the moon on the eighth day. When he sends forth the great light of primordial wisdom (jñāna) and tames countless sentient beings and many māras, they think of him as the full moon on the fifteenth day. And further, when he who is perfectly adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor marks shows nirvāṇa, they think of him as the waning moon.

In this way, sentient beings do not all see the same thing. Some see the moon as a crescent, some see it as full, some see it as waning — yet in truth the intrinsic nature of the moon knows no waxing or waning; it is always full and complete. The Tathāgata is just the same, and therefore he is called permanent, stable, and unchanging.

Noble son, here is yet another analogy. When the moon is full, it appears wherever there are cities, or villages, or mountains, or pastures, or rivers, or wells, or ponds, or hollows — it appears in every place. And whether a sentient being travels one league or up to a hundred thousand leagues, that person sees the moon in just the same way. Foolish and confused people then wonder: "When I was at home I saw this moon; now here in this remote wilderness I see it too — is it the same moon I saw before, or is it not?" They even deliberate about its size. Some say, "It is about the size of a copper bowl." Some say, "It is about the size of a chariot wheel." Some say, "It is forty-nine leagues across." Although all see the light of the moon, some see it as a round, golden bowl. In this way, even though the intrinsic nature of the moon is one and the same, sentient beings of different kinds perceive it as appearing in many different ways.

Noble son, the Tathāgata is just the same. When he has appeared manifestly in the world, some gods and humans think, "The Tathāgata dwells before me alone." Some sentient beings think, "The Tathāgata appears before me alone." Some sentient beings who are deaf or mute think, "The Tathāgata too must be deaf or mute." Sentient beings who speak many different and mutually unintelligible languages each think, "The Tathāgata speaks in my own language." Each one thinks, "He has come to my house alone and accepted my offerings alone." Some sentient beings see the body of the Tathāgata as measurelessly vast and wide. Some see his body as extremely small. Some see him as having the form of a śrāvaka.

Some see him as having the form of a pratyekabuddha. Some non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) think, "The Tathāgata has gone forth through our own doctrine and entered our path of training." Some sentient beings think, "The Tathāgata has come into the world for my sake alone."

The true nature of the Tathāgata is like the moon: it is the dharmakāya, the unborn body, the body of skillful means. Like the moon, it shows birth in all places and in all modes of prior karma without measure, in accordance with the ways of the world. Therefore the Tathāgata is permanent, stable, unchanging, and unaltering.

Moreover, son of good family, when an asura (demigod) such as Rāhu covers the moon with his hand, people of the world say, "The moon has died." Yet in truth the king of the asuras has not killed the moon — he has merely obscured its light. The moon itself has not waned or diminished; covered by the hand, it simply cannot be seen. When the hand is withdrawn, people of the world say, "The moon has been born again," and they say, "This moon has even experienced suffering." Yet even if a hundred thousand asuras were to gather, they could not harm the moon.

The Tathāgata is just like this. Although some sentient beings arouse a malicious mind toward the Tathāgata — drawing blood from the body of a buddha, committing the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya), or acting out of wrong craving — even these things are shown only so that future sentient beings who would destroy the Saṅgha and the Dharma and act improperly might be tamed. For even if a hundred thousand māras were to gather, they could not draw blood from the body of the Tathāgata. Why? Because the body of the Tathāgata has no flesh, no blood, no tendons, no sinews, no bones. The Tathāgata in truth undergoes neither disturbance nor destruction. Sentient beings, however, think: "The Dharma and the Saṅgha are being destroyed, and the Tathāgata too will cease to exist." The Tathāgata's true nature neither changes nor is destroyed; yet this too is shown in accordance with the ways of the world.

Moreover, son of good family, consider this example: if two people fight and one is stabbed with a weapon, and blood flows from the body or death results, yet the one who struck had no intention to kill, then the defining characteristic of that act is light and not grave. Likewise, since the Tathāgata has from the very beginning no intention to kill, even if blood were to flow from his body, the defining characteristic of that act is light and not grave. In this way the Tathāgata has shown the ripening of karmic results in order to tame future sentient beings.

Moreover, son of good family, consider this example: a skilled physician exerts diligence and teaches medicine to his son. "This is the medicine of roots," he says, "this is the medicine of fragrance, this is the medicine of color — learn to know them well in all their various and distinct kinds." The son, just as his father instructed him, applies himself diligently and becomes learned in medicine. Later, when that physician has passed away and died, the physician's son recalls: "My father taught me, saying: these are the medicines of roots, of stalks, of flowers, of colors."

The Tathāgata is just like this. In order to tame sentient beings, he established moral discipline and taught: "This is moral discipline. These are the five acts of immediate retribution. These are the acts of usurping and consuming authority over the sacred Dharma. This is the act of wrong craving — do not commit it." These things too were taught for the sake of beings of future times.

Therefore, monks, after the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, these are the sūtra collections of profound meaning. These are the Vinaya teachings proclaimed with the defining marks of what is weighty and what is light. This is the Abhidharma (Skt. abhidharma), the elaborated exposition of Dharma terms. Just as the skilled physician showed medicines to his son, so did he make all of this directly evident.

Furthermore, son of good family, people in the world perceive that the moon dies once in six months. The gods of the higher realms, however, see the moon die in a single moment. Why is this? Because a day of the gods is long, while a day of humans is short.

Son of good family, it is the same with the Tathāgata. Gods and humans think that the Tathāgata's lifespan is very short — just as gods and humans see the moon die in a single instant. The Tathāgata, moreover, in a single moment reveals many hundreds of thousands of nirvāṇas, and thereby shows the conquest of the māra of afflictions, the māra of the aggregates, the māra of the Lord of Death, and the māra who is a son of the gods — and so on. Thus many hundreds of thousands of divine māras come to know that the Tathāgata has passed into complete nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, he reveals many hundreds of thousands of previous actions, causes, and conditions in forms as varied as the defining characteristics of the world. In this way, because it is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable, the Tathāgata is permanent, abiding, and unchanging.

Son of good family, consider the following simile: the bright moon is wished to be seen by all beings, and so it is called "delightful to behold." Sentient beings, bound by attachment, aversion, and delusion, are not called "delightful to behold." But the Tathāgata, being utterly pure, stainless, supreme, and most excellent, is called "delightful to behold." Those who are devoted to the Dharma take no pleasure in worldly sights. Those who are unvirtuous do not even wish to see him. Therefore the Tathāgata is like the bright moon.

Son of good family, consider further the following simile: it is like the rising sun, which differs according to the three seasons — spring, summer, and winter. In winter the days are short; in summer the days are long; in spring they are neither long nor short.

The Tathāgata is likewise. In this great trichiliocosm world-system, he shows a very short lifespan, and he also shows a very short lifespan to the śrāvakas, so that all of them think the Tathāgata's lifespan is very short — just like the winter sun. To the bodhisattvas he shows a lifespan of one eon or just short of one eon, which is neither long nor short — just like the spring sun. The buddhas themselves behold the buddha's lifespan as immeasurable — just like the summer sun.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata revealed in the world the widely expansive Mahāyāna sūtra collections that he taught, and let fall a great rain of Dharma. Whoever in times to come guards, upholds, expounds, and teaches these sūtra collections and thereby acts for the benefit of sentient beings — know that person to be a true bodhisattva. This is comparable to rain falling in the summer season.

When śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas hear this teaching revealed with the Tathāgata's intended meaning, they are like the winter season — encountering great cold and frost. When bodhisattvas hear this teaching, proclaimed with the Tathāgata's intended meaning, revealing that the Tathāgata is permanent and unchanging, it is like the spring season, when all sprouts burst forth.

In the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata there is no such thing as "long" or "short." Though these are taught for the sake of worldly beings, that is the genuine nature of reality of a buddha.

Moreover, son of good family, consider this analogy: all the stars are invisible during the day. Foolish people think the stars have set and are gone. In truth they have not disappeared; they are simply not visible because of the light of the sun. The Tathāgata is similar: that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not see him is just like worldly people not seeing the stars in the daytime.

Moreover, son of good family, consider this further analogy: when the sun and moon are not visible on a misty evening, foolish and confused people think the sun and moon have gone and ceased to exist. In truth, the sun and moon have not ceased to exist. Likewise, when the sacred Dharma of the Tathāgata appears to have vanished and the Three Jewels are no longer visibly manifest, it is similar — they have not in truth gone away and ceased to be forever. Therefore, know that the Tathāgata is permanent, unchanging, and immutable. Why is this? Because the true nature of the Three Jewels is unstained by any defilement.

Moreover, son of good family, consider this analogy: on a moonless night, when a single bright star rises in the east, it shines very clearly, and then immediately sets again. When worldly people see this, they say it is an ill omen. A pratyekabuddha is similar: arising in a world without a buddha, when ordinary beings see him they all think, "The Tathāgata has truly passed into nirvāṇa," and they grieve. But in truth the Tathāgata has not ceased to be — just as the sun and moon have not disappeared, they are merely not visible.

Moreover, son of good family, consider this analogy: when the sun rises, darkness vanishes at once. The sūtra collection of the Great Parinirvāṇa is similar: when it arises in the world, if it reaches the ears of sentient beings, it dispels all non-virtue and all heinous sinful deeds without interval. The domain of practice of this profound Great Parinirvāṇa is inconceivable, for the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata has been perfectly taught therein. Therefore, sons and daughters of good family, generate the mind that holds the Tathāgata to be permanent, unchanging, and immutable; that the sacred Dharma is a stream that never breaks; and that the Saṅgha, likewise, shall never cease to be.

Therefore, one who applies diligent and earnest effort to this sūtra collection with great skillful means will, before long, attain unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening.

Accordingly, this sūtra collection may also be called "Spontaneously Accomplished with Measureless Qualities," and also "Awakening that Is Inexhaustible" — and because it is inexhaustible, it is designated the Great Parinirvāṇa. Because it is supremely luminous, it is equal to the summer sun. Because its assembly is boundless, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.

Son of good family, consider this: the light of the sun and moon is the foremost of all lights. The light of the Great Parinirvāṇa is similar — it is supreme among all the lights of sūtra meditative absorptions, and no other light of sūtra meditative absorption can approach it. Why is this? Because the light of this Great Parinirvāṇa penetrates into every pore of sentient beings, and even if a sentient being has not yet given rise to the awakening mind, it causes that being to form the cause for awakening. For this reason it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, as the Blessed One has declared, if the light rays of the Great Parinirvāṇa penetrate into every pore of all sentient beings, and thereby become a cause for awakening even in those beings who have not yet given rise to the awakening mind — this, I venture to say, cannot be right. Why? Blessed One, if those who have committed the four defeats, who have performed the five acts of immediate retribution, or who have engaged in the karma of wrong craving were to become a cause for awakening simply by being touched by those light rays, then what distinction could there possibly be between them and those who guard their moral discipline and who have accumulated collections of virtue and the like? And if there were no distinction, why would the Tathāgata have taught the four qualities in which a Tathāgata abides? Blessed One, as the Blessed One has declared, if any sentient being who hears this Great Parinirvāṇa sūtra with their very ears will have all afflictions dispelled — then why did the Tathāgata previously state that certain persons had in former times given rise to the awakening mind before buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet even after hearing the Great Parinirvāṇa, had still not come to understand its meaning? If they do not grasp its meaning, how could all afflictions be severed?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, with the sole exception of those with wrong craving, if other sentient beings hear this sūtra, it will become for all of them a cause for awakening. When the light rays of the sound of the Dharma enter into their pores, they will without fail attain unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. Why is this? Any person who attends, makes offerings to, and pays homage to immeasurable buddhas — such a person will then come to hear this Great Parinirvāṇa sūtra. Those of small merit will not come to hear it. How is this so? Those endowed with great qualities will come to hear this great matter, while those who are weak and of small capacity will not. Now, this 'great matter' refers to the profound secret essence of all buddhas — the buddha-nature itself. Therefore it is called the great matter."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then again addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that those who have not given rise to the awakening mind become a cause for awakening?"

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Someone who, after hearing this Great Parinirvāṇa sūtra, thinks 'I have no need to give rise to the awakening mind' and thereby disparages the sacred Dharma — such a person will in a dream see the form of a demon (rākṣasa) and will be gripped by intense terror. That demon will say, 'Son of good family, if you do not now give rise to the awakening mind, I will cut the thread of your living breath.' Filled with fear, that person will awaken from the dream and will give rise to the awakening mind. When that person passes away, even if they fall into one of the three lower destinies, or are born among humans or as a god in the higher realms, the stream of their awakening mind will never be severed — and because of that recollection, such a person should be understood to be a great bodhisattva. It is in this way — through the power and force of the Great Parinirvāṇa — that one who has not given rise to the awakening mind becomes a cause for awakening. Son of good family, this is called the cause and condition of a bodhisattva's giving rise to the awakening mind; it is not a matter of being without cause and condition. Therefore this sublime sūtra of the Great Vehicle was authentically declared by the awakened ones.

"Son of good family, here is another analogy. When great rain clouds cover the sky above and a great rain falls — if a dry tree, or a rock, or

it flows down to every high mountain and rocky place where water would not otherwise reach, and all the low-lying hollows and valleys fill completely with water — becoming a benefit for all the countless sentient beings. This sublime sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is just the same: even though the great rain of Dharma falls upon all sentient beings, those with perverted craving alone have no ground in which the awakening mind can arise.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: a burnt seed, though soaked through by rain for a hundred thousand aeons, will never sprout — there is simply no ground in which it can grow. Those with perverted craving are exactly the same: even though they come to hear this sublime sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa in its entirety, the sprout of the awakening mind will not grow in them — there is no ground in which it can arise. Why is that? Because such a person has utterly destroyed every wholesome root and has become like a burnt seed; therefore the root and sprout of awakening cannot grow.

Son of good family, here is yet another analogy. Take a precious gem of the water-clearing kind: if it is placed in muddy water, by the power of the gem the water becomes clear. But if it is placed in mire, it will not become clear. This sublime sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is just the same. If it is brought among beings who are like muddy water — those who have committed one of the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya) or in whom one of the four root defeats (pārājika) has arisen — it is possible that they will be purified and that the awakening mind will arise in them. But if those with perverted craving, who are like a pit of mire, are left with it for a hundred thousand years, they will never be purified, nor will the awakening mind possibly arise. Why is that? Because those with perverted craving have destroyed every wholesome root and have thus become unfit vessels. Indeed, even if such a person were to listen to or hold this sublime sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa for a hundred thousand years, they would be unable to arouse the awakening mind. Why? Because they are entirely without a virtuous mind.

Son of good family, here is yet another analogy. Among all medicinal plants there is one called the King of Medicines — the supreme and most excellent of all medicines. Whether it is combined with a cloth, or mixed with honey, or blended with butter, or stirred into water, or stirred into milk, or applied as a powder, or made into pills, or rubbed in as a salve, or burned as incense, or applied to the eyes — even merely seeing it or touching it cures every disease of sentient beings. Yet that medicinal plant never thinks: "If beings take my roots, they will not gather my leaves," or "If they gather my leaves, they will not take my roots," or "If they take my trunk, they will strip my bark," or "If they strip my bark, they will not gather my trunk." It has no such thoughts at all. And yet for all that, it is able to remove all the painful diseases of sentient beings.

Son of good family, this sublime sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is exactly the same: it eliminates all four root defeats and all five acts of immediate retribution, and all unwholesome actions, whether outer or inner, of every sentient being — and even those who have not yet aroused the awakening mind will, through its power, come to arouse it. Why is that? Because this sūtra too is like a king among all sūtras, just as the King of Medicines is the king among medicines. Whether one diligently applies oneself to this Great Parinirvāṇa or does not, if one hears that this sūtra's name exists and upon hearing it immediately gives rise to faith and trust, it will eliminate every disease of affliction. Yet those with perverted craving cannot be established with ease in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Just as the King of Medicines, though it heals every illness, cannot reverse the coming of inevitable death.

Noble son, here is another analogy. When those whose hands have open wounds grasp poison, the poison enters within. But one who has no wound, even grasping it, the poison does not enter within. Those with perverted craving are likewise: because there is no cause for awakening, they resemble grasping poison with an unwounded hand — it does not enter within. The wound stands for the cause of unsurpassed awakening. The poison stands for what is like the ultimate medicine. The absence of a wound stands for one like those with perverted craving.

Noble son, here is another analogy. A vajra is not crushed by anything; though it can pierce and shatter everything, it can itself be crushed by a tortoise shell and a deer's horn. This sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise: though it brings measureless sentient beings easily onto the path of awakening, those with perverted craving it cannot cause to generate the cause of awakening.

Noble son, here is another analogy. Plants such as grass, reeds, trees such as the śāli rice plant, and creepers — though their stalks and branches are cut, they immediately regrow. They are not like the tāla palm, which, once cut, does not grow back. Those sentient beings are likewise: even if they have committed the four root downfalls that entail defeat, or have performed the five acts of immediate retribution, yet upon hearing this sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa the cause of awakening can still arise again in them. Those with perverted craving are not like that: even if they hear or attend to this holy sūtra, the cause of awakening cannot arise.

Noble son, here is another analogy. When trees such as the banana and the cane are cut, it is as though their seeds have been burned — they do not grow back. Those with perverted craving are likewise: even though they hear this sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa, no cause of awakening arises — this is like a burned seed.

Noble son, here is another analogy. When a great rain falls, it does not cling to empty sky. This sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa is likewise: though it rains down the Dharma rain everywhere, it does not cling to those with perverted craving. In the body of one with perverted craving it is as though a vajra were driven in throughout — nothing whatsoever can take hold.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Blessed One has also declared in a verse:

Not seeing the wholesome, one does not act wholesomely.
Seeing the unwholesome, one commits what is unwholesome.
Fearing that and falling away from it
is like dreading a bad road's precipice."

He then asked: "Blessed One, what is the meaning of these words you have spoken?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, 'not seeing' means not seeing the nature of a buddha. 'The wholesome' means unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. 'Does not act' means not serving and honoring a spiritual friend. 'Seeing' means seeing as though cause and effect did not exist. 'The unwholesome' means denigrating the extensively taught sūtras of the Great Vehicle. 'Commits' means those with perverted craving claim that the extensive teaching does not exist. Therefore, those with perverted craving have no mind inclined toward or striving in the wholly pure wholesome Dharmas. As for what Dharma is called 'wholesome,' that is nirvāṇa. To be inclined toward and striving in nirvāṇa means to apply oneself diligently to the conduct of the noble ones. Those with perverted craving do not follow the conduct of the noble ones, and so they are unable to be inclined toward or to strive in nirvāṇa. 'One should fear that' refers to the denigration of the holy Dharma. By whom should it be feared? By the wise, those possessed of wisdom. Why? Because through denigrating the Dharma the mind of virtue is absent, for there is then no means of engagement. 'The bad road's precipice' refers to the conditioning formations."

Kāśyapa then asked again: "Blessed One, in what you have declared, what are 'the things that are seen'?"

"What things will become virtuous,
What is the ground of fearlessness,
As a king travels the path of ease" —
what is the meaning of these words?

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, 'the things that are seen' refers to confession of wrongdoing. From the beginning of saṃsāra, whatever non-virtuous and unwholesome acts one has done — all are confessed, and one arrives at a place of no return. Therefore that ground is fearless. For example, when a king sets out upon a road, bandits and the like flee and scatter at the sight of him. Likewise, when non-virtuous and unwholesome acts are confessed and disclosed, all of them are purified.

"Furthermore, 'the things that are done are not seen' refers to those with perverted craving who, though they have performed non-virtuous and unwholesome deeds, do not see them. Those with perverted craving, swollen with the arrogance of pride, perform many non-virtuous and unwholesome acts yet feel no dread or fear from the very beginning. Therefore they do not attain nirvāṇa — this is like monkeys grasping at the reflection of the moon in water.

"Son of good family, even if immeasurable sentient beings, all at the same moment, were to awaken to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening, even those Tathāgatas could not rightfully enable those with perverted craving to attain awakening. Therefore this is called 'not seeing the things that are done.'

"Furthermore, as for 'not seeing what has been done by another' — it is not seen because it has been done by the Tathāgata. Even though the Tathāgata reveals and teaches the buddha-nature to ordinary beings, those with perverted craving, spinning endlessly in saṃsāra, will not come to know or see it. Therefore this is called 'not seeing what the Tathāgata has done.'

"Furthermore, when at last the Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa, those with perverted craving grasp at it as genuine impermanence — seeing it as like a lamp and its oil being extinguished. Why? Because such a person does not diminish their non-virtuous and unwholesome karma.

"When a bodhisattva dedicates the virtuous acts they have performed toward unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening, those with perverted craving mock and doubt him. Yet the bodhisattvas dedicate even those very beings toward the attainment of unsurpassable awakening. Why? Because such is the nature of reality of the buddhas.

From milk comes curds in time;
Evil deeds do not ripen at once.
Like fire-embers covered by ash,
A fool who scorns them will be burned.

"Those with perverted craving are said to be without eyes. Therefore they do not see the path of the arhat (Skt. arhat). The arhat does not travel the bad road and precipice of the path of saṃsāra. Those who are without eyes, by denigrating the vast and extensive teaching, do not cultivate a mind of loving-kindness as the arhat does. Those with perverted craving who do not cultivate the vast and extensive teaching are likewise the same.

"There is a person who says: 'I have no faith in the sūtra collections of the śrāvakas (Skt. śrāvaka), but I have faith in the Great Vehicle, and I recite it, read it, expound it, and explain it. Therefore I am a bodhisattva. Since the buddha-nature exists in all sentient beings, within the body of sentient beings there also exist the ten powers, the thirty-two major marks, and the eighty excellent minor marks. What I say and what the Buddha has said are not different. You and I together will overcome immeasurable afflictions — just as a water-vessel, when broken, by destroying all afflictions one will behold unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening.' Even though such a person teaches and explains in this way,

he does not genuinely believe that the buddha-nature truly exists within sentient beings, and he teaches in the manner of written words merely for the sake of benefit and happiness. One who teaches in that way is called a wrongdoer. And a wrongdoer is one for whom the fruit does not ripen quickly, just as milk does not quickly turn to curds.

Consider, for example, a royal messenger who is supremely eloquent and endowed with skillful means: when the king dispatches him with a command to a foreign land, even at the cost of his life and limb he does not conceal the king's command. A wise and discerning person is similarly: even at the cost of life and limb, not looking to his own safety amidst childish and lowly people, he proclaims and teaches this extensive Great Vehicle — the Tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature), which is the intrinsic nature of a buddha present in all sentient beings.

Noble son, there are certain people of wrong desire who dress themselves up as arhats. Dwelling at the margins of the teaching, they slander and disparage the sūtras of the extensive Great Vehicle, and childish, lowly disciples take them to be genuine arhats or great bodhisattvas. Such a wrongdoing mendicant, though he dwells at the margins of the teaching, renders those marginal Dharmas improper. When he sees others gaining offerings and honor, jealousy arises in his mind, and he says: "These sūtras of the extensive Great Vehicle were taught by the Māra of evil deeds, and the Tathāgata, too, is impermanent." In this way he destroys the true Dharma and corrupts the Saṅgha. Furthermore, he says: "What was spoken by the evil Māra of evil deeds was not spoken in accordance with virtue," and in this way he speaks of sinful and non-virtuous phenomena. Yet even though he commits such wrong deeds, just as milk does not immediately turn to curds, the ripening does not come at once. Like one who scorns a fire concealed beneath its own ash, he exults for a time above it. Such a person is called one of wrong desire.

Therefore this noble sūtra of the extensive Great Vehicle is definitively and utterly pure. Just as a precious jewel placed in turbid water clears and purifies the water, so too is this sūtra of the Great Vehicle.

Noble son, here is another analogy: when lotus blossoms are touched by the rays of the sun, they immediately open.
