So too are all sentient beings: if they behold the great nirvāṇa that is like the sun, those who have not yet aroused the mind will arouse it and it will become a cause for awakening. Therefore, when the light of nirvāṇa enters the pore of a single hair, it will become a supreme cause.

Thus have I spoken. One of wrong desire, though the buddha-nature is present within, is entirely bound by immeasurable impure defilements and does not attain liberation — just like the cocoon of a silk-worm wrapped in its own thread. Through the condition of such karma the cause of awakening does not arise, and the wandering in saṃsāra becomes endless and without limit.

Noble son, here is yet another analogy: the blue lotus, the red lotus, the water lily, and the white lotus all arise from the midst of mud and filth, yet they are unstained by the mud. Any sentient being who diligently applies himself to this noble sūtra, this Great Discourse on Great Nirvāṇa, is likewise: though accompanied by afflictions, he is unstained by those afflictions. Why is that? Because he comes to know the defining characteristics of the Tathāgata's nature.

Noble son, consider a region where an exceedingly cool breeze blows: any sentient being afflicted by heat, when that breeze touches the pores of his body, is relieved of that affliction. This Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Discourse on Great Nirvāṇa, is also like that. It enters the pores of all sentient beings and becomes a cause for awakening — with the sole exception of those of wrong desire. Why? Because they are not vessels for the Dharma.

Noble son, consider further this example: a skilled physician, expert in the eight branches of medical knowledge, is able to cure all diseases — yet not in the case of one whose time of death has inevitably arrived. All the meditative absorptions (samādhis) of the sūtras are likewise: they are capable of curing the disease of affliction by attachment, aversion, and delusion in all sentient beings, and of drawing out the thorn of affliction — yet not in the case of one who has incurred the four defeats or committed the five acts of immediate consequence.

Noble son, consider further: physicians even more skilled than the eight branches of knowledge are able to dispel all the suffering of illness in sentient beings — yet not in the case of one whose death has come without doubt. This Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Discourse on Great Nirvāṇa, is also like that: it abandons all the afflictions of sentient beings, establishes them with ease on the path toward becoming a cause for the Tathāgata's complete purification, and arouses the awakening mind in those who have not yet aroused it — yet not in the case of one who is destined to die with wrong desire.

Noble son, consider further: a skilled physician is able to restore sight to those who have gone blind through eye disease — enabling them to see the sun, the moon, fire, stars, and all visible forms — yet not in the case of one who has been blind from the very beginning. This Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Discourse on Great Nirvāṇa, is also like that: even those who follow the vehicle of hearers and pratyekabuddhas can gain the eye of wisdom and be established in the boundless and unlimited sūtras of the Great Vehicle; and even those who have not aroused the awakening mind, who have incurred the four defeats or committed the five acts of immediate consequence, can be made to arouse the awakening mind toward awakening — yet not those who have been blind from the very beginning and are possessed of wrong desire.

Noble son, consider further this example: a supremely skilled physician endowed with the eight branches of medical knowledge, wishing to cure all the diseases of sentient beings, compounds many kinds of medicine — emetics, purgatives, ointments, fumigants, nasal preparations, powders, pills, and the like. If a certain poor person refuses the medicine even so, out of compassion for him the physician brings him home, administers the medicine by force, and restores him to health. If a woman in childbirth cannot deliver the afterbirth, he administers medicine to her, so that the afterbirth comes and the child is born easily and well. This Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Discourse on Great Nirvāṇa, is also like that: in whatever place it dwells, there it pacifies the immeasurable afflictions of sentient beings; and even those who have incurred the four defeats, committed the five acts of immediate consequence, and have not aroused the awakening mind, come to arouse it — with the sole exception of those of wrong desire.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, those who have incurred the four defeats and committed the five acts of immediate consequence are like a palm tree that has been cut at its crown and will not grow again. Since they have not aroused the awakening mind toward awakening, how can they become a cause for awakening?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, if in a dream those sentient beings were to fall into a hell realm and experience great suffering, remorse would arise in their minds, and they would think: 'Alas! Why have I come to experience such evil? If only I could be freed from this evil — I would without doubt arouse the awakening mind toward awakening. What I am experiencing right now is indeed the very depth of suffering.' Then, waking from the dream, they would come to understand that the sacred Dharma bears great fruit. Just as a young child, from birth onward until it has grown large, constantly thinks: 'That physician is supremely skilled in medicine. While I was still in my mother's womb, he gave medicine to my mother, and through the power of that medicine I came to dwell at ease —

and I too have come to live and thrive. How wonderful! My mother endured great suffering for the ten months of her pregnancy. After I was born, she freed me from the discomfort of being soiled, brought me into contact with the ease of being clean, wiped away even the smallest impurities of excrement and urine, suckled me at her breast, nourished this body of mine, and cared for me greatly. Therefore, in order to repay her kindness, I shall care for her greatly and make offerings to her in a way that accords with her heart.' With such thoughts does a child's mind dwell.

Even if, at the very end of one's life, one has committed the four defeats or perpetrated the five acts of immediate consequence, if one calls to mind this Great Vehicle sūtra, the great nirvāṇa, that person will be caused by this sūtra to make a cause for awakening — whether they are reborn in hell, in an animal realm, among hungry ghosts, among gods, or among humans — excepting only those possessed of wrong craving.

Son of good family, here is another illustration. A skilled physician, or the son of a skilled physician, is expert in medicine surpassing all others, deeply versed in antidotes to poisons, and also skilled in healing mantras. By the power of his mantras and medicines, he renders even a virulent snake, a nāga, or other deadly things free of venom. Now, if medicine is applied to a shoe, and that shoe then comes into contact with a virulent snake and the like, the venom is stilled — but this does not apply to what is called the great nāga of wrong craving. This Great Vehicle sūtra, the great nirvāṇa, is likewise: for sentient beings who have committed the four defeats or perpetrated the five acts of immediate consequence, it purifies those evils and transgressions and establishes them on the path to awakening. Just as medicine smeared on a shoe stills the poison, so too this sūtra, even for those who have not yet aroused the awakening mind, causes them to arouse it and establishes them easily on the path to awakening. Through the power of this sūtra of the Great Vehicle, the great nirvāṇa — which is like medicine — all sentient beings are brought to ease, excepting only those possessed of wrong craving, who are like the great nāga.

Son of good family, here is yet another illustration. A person might compound a poison and smear it on a great drum, then beat that drum in the midst of a large crowd. Even if those who hear the sound have no wish to hear it, all who do hear it, though they may die, will not die suddenly — with the sole exception of those possessed of wrong craving. This Great Vehicle sūtra, the great nirvāṇa, is likewise: wherever its sound is heard amid a great gathering of conditioning factors, all the mental afflictions of attachment, aversion, and delusion will be purged. Even without any deliberate reflection or intentional thought about it, through the power of the great nirvāṇa, all afflictions will be stilled. Those who have committed the four defeats and perpetrated the five acts of immediate consequence — if they hear this sūtra, it will become a cause for their unsurpassed awakening, and their afflictions will be wholly swept away, so that they do not die suddenly, excepting only those possessed of wrong craving.

Son of good family, here is yet another illustration. When darkness falls, all activity ceases, and even what remains unfinished must wait until the following day. The study of the Great Vehicle is likewise. Though one may be diligent in the meditative absorption of every sūtra, upon hearing this sūtra — the great nirvāṇa, like the sun, which the Tathāgata taught with deep intent — one immediately takes up the work of awakening and dwells at ease in the sacred Dharma.

Consider, for example, the rain: it brings forth the germination of every seed, the ripening of every fruit, and the removal of drought and famine, making all things abundantly available. This immeasurable rain of Dharma from the tathāgatagarbha is likewise: it dispels the eight kinds of burning affliction, and by the appearance of this sūtra in the world it causes all fruits to ripen —

bringing benefit and well-being to all, and causing ordinary beings to behold the intrinsic nature of a buddha — just as, in the Puṇḍarīka Sūtra, eight thousand hearers received a prophecy and thereby attained the great fruit.

Consider, further, one who is possessed of wrong craving: just as a farmer who has done his work in the harvest season stores it away for winter and does nothing else thereafter, such a one similarly exerts no effort toward virtuous Dharma.

Son of good family, here is another example. Suppose a skilled physician hears that the son of an enemy has been poisoned. He prepares a fine medicine and dispatches a man with these words: "Take this medicine and deliver it to him." Now, even if that very messenger, while on the road, should encounter a hungry ghost, the power of the medicine will cause it to flee and run away. And if you are delayed in delivering it, I myself will go in your stead, so that the sick man does not suddenly die. If the sick man then meets either that messenger or the physician himself, the power of the medicine will free him from the suffering of illness and he will be at ease.

This Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Nirvāṇa, is likewise. Whether it be a monk, or a nun, or a layman, or a laywoman, or even a non-Buddhist adherent — whoever carries this sūtra, retains it, reads it, recites it, takes it to heart, teaches and expounds it extensively to others, copies it into a manuscript himself, or has others copy it: all of these become causes of awakening for each and every one of them. If those who have violated the four defeats, who have committed the five heinous crimes, who have been possessed by hungry ghosts, or who have been harmed by malevolent forces hear this sūtra, all their misdeeds will be purified — just as the sight of that skilled physician causes hungry ghosts and the like to flee and run away. Therefore, such a person is to be known as a true bodhisattva, a great being. And why? Because they have merely heard the Great Nirvāṇa and have contemplated the permanence of the Tathāgata. If the mere hearing of it brings such a result, what need is there to speak of copying it into a manuscript, carrying it, retaining it, reading it, or reciting it? Know that all who do so — except those possessed of wrong craving — are bodhisattvas, great beings.

Son of good family, here is yet another example. A deaf person cannot hear any sound at all. One possessed of wrong craving is likewise: even if they make an effort to hear this sublime sūtra, they do not hear it. And why? Because they lack the cause for hearing.

Son of good family, here is yet another example. A skilled physician who fully understands every method of examination and knows mantras without measure said this to a king: "Great King, Great King, you have a disease that will certainly bring death." The king replied: "You have not examined my interior — how do you know I have a disease that will certainly bring death?" The physician said: "If you do not believe me, take this purgative medicine and the disease will come out and you will see it for yourself." Yet the king could not bring himself to take the medicine. Then that physician, through the power of his mantras, caused a boil to form on the king's lower back, and from it worms and blood emerged. When the king saw what had happened, he was greatly alarmed. He praised the physician with the words "Excellent! Excellent!" and said: "Formerly I did not heed your words, yet now you have done my body the greatest benefit." Thereafter he honoured that physician as if he were his own father and mother.

This Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Nirvāṇa, is likewise. Whether a sentient being is governed by desire or is free from desire —

it quells all their afflictions. Whatever sentient being dreams of this sūtra and, in that dream, makes offerings and pays homage to it, they do so just as the great king honoured the skilled physician. And just as the skilled physician cannot heal one who is certain to die, so too this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa cannot heal one who clings to wrong views.

Noble son, here is yet another example. A skilled physician, learned in the eight branches of medical knowledge, may be able to cure every disease, yet he cannot cure a disease that will certainly prove fatal. Buddhas and bodhisattvas are likewise: although they can heal all the moral faults of sentient beings in existence, they cannot heal those who cling to wrong views, who are like patients with a fatal disease.

Noble son, here is yet another example. A skilled physician, having mastered the eight branches of medical knowledge and perfected every aspect of medicine and medical science, comprehending all things, first teaches his son about the medicines that arise from water, from dry land, and from the mountains. Once the son has learned these, the father then teaches him the eight branches of medical knowledge, and thereafter he also teaches him the supreme secret examination that goes beyond them. The Tathāgata, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, is likewise. He first taught the monks who are like sons every means of removing all afflictions, and set them to applying themselves diligently to the perception of the body as insubstantial and in need of purification — and this is comparable to teaching about water, dry land, and rocky mountains. By "water" is meant the teaching that the sufferings experienced in the body are like water bubbles. By "dry land" is meant the teaching that this body is insubstantial, like a plantain tree. By "rocky mountains" is meant the teaching of meditating on the perception of no-self amid the afflictions — and therefore one says of the body that it is without self. In this way the Tathāgata taught the attendant monks the nine classes of sūtra, and caused them to understand; then, following that, he revealed the tathāgatagarbha (buddha-nature), and — in the manner of speaking to sons — declared: "The Tathāgata is permanent." In this way the Tathāgata's teaching of this Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Nirvāṇa, becomes a cause of awakening for all sentient beings, whether they have generated the awakening mind or have not yet generated it — with the sole exception of those who cling to wrong views.

Noble son, this Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Nirvāṇa, is boundless, limitless, and inconceivable. Therefore it is like the most excellent and supreme of skilled physicians, the foremost, the king of all sūtras.

Noble son, here is yet another example. A great ship ferries people from this shore of the ocean to the far shore, and from the far shore back to this one again. The Tathāgata, the perfectly and fully awakened buddha, is likewise: embarked in the precious vessel of the Great Nirvāṇa, he completely liberates sentient beings, and wherever they are to go he conveys them there and causes them to behold the form of the Tathāgata. Therefore the Tathāgata is like the captain of a ship. And just as even a raft, so long as it holds together, enables beings to cross the ocean, so too the Tathāgata, who perpetually labours to liberate the multitude of sentient beings, is just the same.

The Thirteenth Fascicle.

Noble son, here is yet another example. Those who have boarded a ship to cross the great ocean — if they have the wind, they will reach the far shore, however immeasurably distant, in a single instant. But if they have no wind, they may remain there for immeasurable years without ever advancing from their place.

But if the ship were to sink, those aboard would perish. Just so it is with sentient beings who have boarded the ship of formations on the great ocean of cyclic existence amid delusion. If they encounter the fierce wind of great nirvāṇa, they will swiftly arrive at unsurpassed and perfect awakening. But if they do not encounter it, they will wander in cyclic existence for immeasurable aeons, and they may fall into rebirth as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.

Noble son, here is yet another example. Those who have been long at sea on a great ocean, lacking wind, think to themselves: "We will surely perish." But then, should a fierce wind arise and carry them beyond the ocean just as they wished, they cry out: "The wind has satisfied us utterly! We have safely escaped the perils of the ocean." In the same way, sentient beings who have long wandered the ocean of cyclic existence amid delusion, tormented by suffering, and who have not encountered the wind of great nirvāṇa, think to themselves: "We will surely fall into rebirth as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals." But then, should they encounter the wind of great nirvāṇa and be established, just as they wished, in unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening, they understand for the very first time that this is truly real. A perception of wonder and astonishment arises, and they say: "Before now I had never heard of this secret heart-essence of the Tathāgata." And so pure and unwavering faith arises in their minds toward the sūtra of great nirvāṇa.

Noble son, here is yet another example. When a snake sheds its skin, would you call that snake dead? The answer was given: "No, Blessed One." The Blessed One said: Noble son, the Tathāgata is just the same. When the Tathāgata, through skillful means, has shown the laying aside of the body, how could the Tathāgata be called impermanent on that account? The answer was given: "No, Blessed One." The Tathāgata's laying aside of the body here in Jambudvīpa through skillful means is like a snake shedding its skin. Therefore the Tathāgata is said to be permanent and abiding.

Noble son, here is yet another example. A skilled goldsmith beats gold into various implements according to his wish. The Tathāgata is just the same. In the twenty-five modes of existence the Tathāgata manifests various physical forms and thereby draws ordinary beings out from cyclic existence. Therefore the Tathāgata is said to be of immeasurable form. Though displaying various forms in this way, the Tathāgata is nonetheless said to be permanent, abiding, unchanging, and unaltering.

Noble son, here is yet another example. The mango tree and the rose-apple tree (jambu) transform three times in a single year. At one time they burst forth abundantly with flowers and so forth; at another time they burst forth abundantly with leaves and so forth; and at yet another time all the leaves fall away and the tree stands as if bare and dry. Noble son, what do you think — is the tree truly withered and dead at that time? The answer was given: "No, Blessed One." The Blessed One declared: Noble son, the Tathāgata is just the same. In the three worlds the Tathāgata shows three kinds of body: at one time the first birth is shown, at another time the body reaching its full maturity is shown, and at yet another time nirvāṇa is shown. But the body of the Tathāgata is not impermanent.

The bodhisattva, the great being Kāśyapa, praised the Blessed One with the words "Excellent! Most excellent!" and then declared, in accord with what the Blessed One had taught: "The Tathāgata is permanent, stable, unchanging, and unalterable."

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, what the Tathāgata has taught through his intended meaning is exceedingly difficult to understand. Consider this analogy. A great king once commanded his ministers, "Bring the saintapa." Now, the word "saintapa" is a single name applied to four different things: salt, a vessel, water, and a horse — these four things share this one name. A wise minister, understanding this, would reason as follows: if the king intends to bathe and gives the command "Bring the saintapa," the minister offers water. When the king is engaged in eating and gives the command "Bring the saintapa," the minister offers salt. When the king has finished eating and is about to drink to quench his thirst and gives the command "Bring the saintapa," the minister offers a vessel. And if the king is preparing to travel and gives the command "Bring the saintapa," the minister brings a horse and leads it forward. In this way a wise minister is skilled in the four instructions of the king.

This sūtra of the Great Vehicle is just the same: there are four kinds of impermanence, and those who are deeply skilled in the Great Vehicle must be thoroughly expert in them.

When the buddha, the Blessed One, appeared in the world and taught sentient beings that the Tathāgata had passed into nirvāṇa, skilled persons understood that the Tathāgata was teaching impermanence to those who clung to permanence — and this was in order to lead the monks to apply themselves earnestly to the characteristic of impermanence.

Furthermore, when he taught that at a certain time the true Dharma would perish, skilled persons understood that the Tathāgata was teaching suffering (duḥkha) to those who clung to what is blissful — and this was in order to lead the monks to apply themselves earnestly to the characteristic of suffering.

Furthermore, when he taught in these words, "I am afflicted by illness and pain, and the Saṅgha too will disintegrate," skilled persons understood that the Tathāgata was teaching selflessness to those who clung to a self — and this was in order to lead the monks to apply themselves earnestly to selflessness.

When at a certain time he taught thus, "What is called emptiness is true and complete liberation," skilled persons understood that the Tathāgata was teaching complete liberation — and they understood that the twenty-five modes of existence are absent in it. This was in order to lead the monks to apply themselves earnestly to emptiness. And so it is that for true and complete liberation, "emptiness" is taught.

It is also called "the unmoving, the motionless." Since there is no suffering in that liberation, it is called "the unmoving."

True and complete liberation is called "the signless," because it is free from signs — because form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and so forth are absent in it.

True and complete liberation is permanent, unchanging, and unalterable. Since liberation is free from impermanence, from distress, and from alteration, liberation is therefore permanent, stable, unchanging, and cool.

Now, if it were taught that the nature of the Tathāgata exists in all sentient beings, a skilled person would understand it thus: the Tathāgata has taught the Dharma under the name of permanence in order to lead the monks to apply themselves earnestly to the truly permanent Dharma.

Monks, know that one who thus follows and trains diligently is truly my genuine attendant. One who is skilled in the essential import of what the Tathāgata has taught through his intended meaning is like the wise minister of that great king who understood the king's intention.

Noble son, if even that great king possessed words spoken with a hidden intent, how much more so the Tathāgata. Noble son, for this reason, what the Tathāgata has spoken with a hidden intent is extremely difficult to understand. A wise and discerning person will come to know this profound Dharma that I have taught with a hidden intent, but foolish and dull-witted people in the world will not come to know it.

Furthermore, noble son, consider this example: when a great blight strikes the śāl tree, the kaṇikāra tree, and the aśoka tree, flowers and fruits no longer grow. All water-born plants likewise fail to yield oil even when pressed to the limit, and all medicinal plants lose their potency.

Noble son, this Mahāyāna sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa is the same. When I pass into nirvāṇa, sentient beings will not venerate it, and its splendor will diminish. Why is that? Because those sentient beings do not understand what the Tathāgata has taught with a hidden intent. And why is that? Because sentient beings have scant merit.

Noble son, furthermore, when the authentic Dharma of the Tathāgata is on the verge of ruin and destruction, at that time and in that age there will be many monks who engage in evil conduct. Not understanding the essential import of what the Tathāgata has taught with a hidden intent, they will be lazy and lax, and will be unable to read, recite, explicate, and teach the authentic Dharma of the Tathāgata. They are like foolish thieves who, discarding genuine jewels, carry away mere chaff instead. In the same way, not understanding the essential import of what the Tathāgata has taught with a hidden intent, they will be negligent toward this sūtra and will not arouse diligence. Alas, in a future time such beings will fall into a great abyss of terrible dread. Alas, those sentient beings will not exert themselves with regard to this Mahāyāna sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa. It is only bodhisattvas, great beings, who will enter into the true and genuine meaning of this sūtra, without clinging to the letter or the word, following after it and not contradicting it, and who will likewise teach it to sentient beings.

Noble son, furthermore, consider this example: some dishonest milk-sellers, wishing to make their milk go further, add two or three parts water and sell it to another milk-dealer. That dealer then adds two or three parts water to it and sells it to people living near the town. Those people add two or three more parts water to it and sell it to people living in the town. Those buyers then add two or three more parts water to it and sell it at market. At that time, a man setting out for the wedding of his son's bride sends someone to the market to buy good milk. The buyer, encountering that milk, knows full well it has been diluted with a great deal of water, yet pressed by urgent need he buys it at high price. He returns home and boils it into a porridge, and there is no taste of milk. And yet, though it lacks the taste of milk, it still surpasses the taste of water by many hundreds and thousands of times. Why? Because a taste transformed by milk is superior to any other taste.

Noble son, eighty years after I pass into nirvāṇa, before the authentic Dharma has yet fallen into ruin, at that time and in that age this sūtra will spread very widely throughout this Jambudvīpa. At that time, wicked monks will compile extracts from this sūtra and arrange it into many partial fragments, thereby stripping the authentic Dharma of its color, its scent, and its savory taste. Those evil ones may indeed read or recite this sūtra, but they will have emptied it of the profound meaning that the Tathāgata taught with a hidden intent.

They took worldly expressions that were meaningless and placed what had been stated earlier at the end; what had been stated later they placed at the beginning; what had been stated at the beginning and at the end they placed in the middle; and what had been stated in the middle they placed at the beginning and at the end.

In this way, those wicked monks are companions of Māra. They say that all things that have not been examined are permitted by the Tathāgata to be held and practiced. Just as one adulterates milk by adding water along with buttermilk and so forth, so too those wicked monks are the same: by adding worldly words and settling it corruptly in a fixed form, they caused the many to be instructed in what is not correct, to transcribe it incorrectly into books, to engage in incorrect transcription, and rendered it unworthy of reverence, praise, veneration, and honor.

Those wicked monks, unable to teach even a little of this sūtra on account of gain and fame, how much less could they teach it in full extent? Just as a poor milkmaid sells milk from one vessel to another until it loses all taste, so too with this Great Vehicle sūtra, the Great Mahāparinirvāṇa — it becomes diluted and loses its taste. Yet even though it loses its taste, it still surpasses all other tastes, just as the taste of milk, though depleted of other tastes, remains superior to all others. Why is that? Because this Great Vehicle sūtra, the Mahāparinirvāṇa, is supreme and most excellent among all śrāvaka sūtras, just as milk with all its taste is supreme and most excellent. Therefore it is called the Great Mahāparinirvāṇa.

Noble son, furthermore, there is no noble son or noble daughter who does not desire to be rid of a woman's body. Why is that? Because all women are the abode of every evil.

Noble son, furthermore, consider this example: the urine of a fly cannot moisten this great earth. So too the insatiable attachment called "woman" is the same: even if every man who could be rolled into a ball the size of a mustard seed from all this great earth were to engage in unchaste acts with a single woman, she would have no sense of satisfaction. Even if men equal in number to the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā were given to a single woman to engage in unchaste acts with her, she would have no satisfaction or weariness.

Noble son, consider this example: into a great ocean, all rains and all flowing rivers pour, yet that ocean is never filled or satisfied. A woman is by her very nature the same, so that even if everything that exists were to become male and engage in unchaste acts with a single woman, she would feel no satisfaction or weariness.

Noble son, furthermore, consider this example: the aśoka tree, the pāṭala tree, the kañcana tree — when their flowers bloom in summer, the bees gather their fragrance and their pollen without ever being satisfied. A woman's attachment to men is the same — she knows no weariness.

Noble son, therefore, noble sons and noble daughters who listen to this Great Vehicle sūtra, the Mahāparinirvāṇa, will constantly reproach womanhood and seek a male body. Why is that? Because this Great Vehicle sūtra possesses the marks of a man (puruṣa). That is to say, it is of the nature of a buddha. Whoever does not know the nature of a buddha lacks the marks of a man. Why? Because they do not know that they themselves possess the nature of a buddha. Whoever does not know the nature of a buddha — that one, I declare, is called a woman. Whoever knows the nature of a buddha — that one, I declare, is said to possess the marks of a man. Therefore, whatever woman comes to know that she herself possesses the nature of a buddha — that one is called a man.

Sons of the lineage, know that this Great Vehicle sūtra of the complete passing beyond sorrow is a mass of merit that is immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable. Why is that? Because it expounds the secret essence of the Tathāgata. Therefore, if sons of the lineage or daughters of the lineage desire to swiftly come to know the secret essence of the Tathāgata, they should apply themselves with earnest and diligent effort to this sūtra.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One and said: So it is, so it is indeed. Just as the Blessed One has declared, I too, having realized the secret essence of the Tathāgata, possess the marks of a man. It was through the Tathāgata's urging that I came to certain realization.

The Blessed One declared: Excellent! Son of the lineage, it is well that you have spoken thus in accordance with the ways of the world.

Kāśyapa said: But I do not follow worldly conventions, Blessed One.

The Blessed One then said to Kāśyapa: Excellent! Most excellent indeed! The understanding you possess knows the supremely profound and difficult-to-know flavor of the unsurpassed Dharma — just as bees, without harming the color of a flower, taste only its sweetness.

Son of the lineage, consider further this analogy: a fly's urine cannot moisten this great earth. Similarly, when this sūtra spreads in the future, and the sublime Dharma draws near to its destruction, this sūtra will first disappear from this land. Know, therefore, that it is a sign that the sublime Dharma is declining.

Son of the lineage, consider further this analogy: when autumn has passed, winter comes on, and in the winter season rain falls without cease. Likewise, this Great Vehicle sūtra of the complete passing beyond sorrow will spread extensively for the sake of the bodhisattvas of the southern direction, filling every place with a rain of Dharma. But when the sublime Dharma nears its destruction, it will disappear into the earth in the land of Kashmir without perishing there — some will have faith in it, others will not. Then all the other Great Vehicle sūtras, rich with the taste of ambrosia, will also sink into the earth. Once this sūtra has disappeared, all the other Great Vehicle sūtras will likewise disappear and cease to exist.

However, if bodhisattvas and others who are like the king of elephants among men — beings in whom the full excellence of this sūtra remains undimmed — are present, they will know that the unsurpassed sublime Dharma of the Tathāgata will not long remain absent.

Then the youthful Mañjuśrī addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, the venerable one now has a doubt. May the Blessed One please resolve that doubt.

The Blessed One declared: Speak whatever doubt you have, and I will dispel your doubt.

Mañjuśrī said: When one seeks and then sees the intrinsic nature of a buddha, one says the Tathāgata is permanent. But if it is only upon seeing the intrinsic nature of a buddha that one calls it permanent, does that not imply that before it was seen it was not permanent? And if something is impermanent from the very beginning, it would follow that it remains impermanent ever after as well. Why so? Because it is like things of the world — something that did not exist from the beginning, if it comes to exist, will again cease to exist. All conditioned things are impermanent. In that case, buddhas and bodhisattvas, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and all the rest would be no different in this regard.

Then the Blessed One spoke in verse:

What had a beginning does not exist now.
What had no beginning does exist now.
All phenomena of existence in the three times
are not of that kind.

"Son of good family, for this reason, buddhas and bodhisattvas, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are both different and not different."

Mañjuśrī then addressed the Blessed One: "Excellent! Excellent! It is just as the noble one has declared. I too understand it thus: that buddhas and bodhisattvas, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are indeed both different and not different."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "As the Blessed One has taught, that there is no difference among buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas — may the Tathāgata please explain this extensively and teach it for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, listen carefully, attend to it well, and hold it in mind; I shall explain it to you in full."

"Son of good family, it is like this. Consider a householder or a householder's son who owns many cows of various breeds and coat colors. He sets them to pasture in a meadow, and then, when the time of the seasonal rains arrives, all the cows are milked and the milk is poured together into a single vessel. Seeing that all this milk, coming from cows of different colors, becomes uniformly white, he is struck with wonder and amazement. He thinks: 'How remarkable that these cows, though of different coat colors, have produced milk of a single uniform color. This milk becoming one in color must arise through the karmic maturation of sentient beings.' "

"Son of good family, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are likewise. Their converging into the single intrinsic nature of a buddha is like that milk. Why so? Because they converge in the undefiled. Ordinary persons say that buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are different. Even uninformed śrāvakas and novices may doubt, wondering why the three vehicles should not be different from one another. Yet they will later come to realize for themselves that all three vehicles converge in the intrinsic nature of buddhahood — just as that person comes to know through the power of karmic causes and conditions that the milk has become one in color."

"Son of good family, here is another example: take gold ore. When the impurities are removed and cast away, and it is smelted, pure gold emerges, and its value is beyond measure."

"Son of good family, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are likewise. All converge in achieving the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. Why so? Because the afflictions are completely removed. This corresponds to the gold ore being smelted and the impurities cast away."

"Therefore all sentient beings converge in the single intrinsic nature of buddhahood and are not different. Having heard the essential purport that the Tathāgata expressed with this intention in former times, when one fully awakens later, one will know it for oneself — just as that householder came to understand that the milk of the cows had become one in color. Why so? Because immeasurable afflictions without exception have been removed."

"Therefore, that all sentient beings converge in the single intrinsic nature of buddhahood and are not different — this is the essential purport that the Tathāgata formerly expressed with this intention. Just as one who has heard this essential purport will later, at the time of full awakening, come to know it for oneself, like the householder who understood that the milk had converged into one — why so? Because immeasurable afflictions without exception have been removed."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, if all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, what distinction can there be between a buddha and a sentient being? To speak thus would become a fault. Moreover, if all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, why did Śāriputra and those like him attain nirvāṇa through a lesser nirvāṇa, the pratyekabuddhas attain nirvāṇa through an intermediate nirvāṇa, and the bodhisattvas attain nirvāṇa through a great nirvāṇa? If these and the others are unified in the single intrinsic nature of buddhahood, why did the Tathāgata not attain complete nirvāṇa through the nirvāṇa of a Tathāgata?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, the passing into nirvāṇa attained by the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is not that attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, the great complete nirvāṇa is called the spiritual friend. Even if there were no buddha present in the world, it would still be possible for the two vehicles to attain their respective two nirvāṇas."

Kāśyapa asked again: "What is the meaning of what the Blessed One has just said?"

The Blessed One declared: "For immeasurable, incalculable, and innumerable eons, a buddha, a Blessed One, appears in the world on occasion, and distinguishes and teaches the three vehicles. Son of good family, when you asked what distinction there is between bodhisattvas and the two other vehicles — that very meaning, that I had formerly expressed through the intention of the Tathāgata, I have now explained at length from this great complete nirvāṇa, saying that arhats have no spiritual friend. Why so? Because arhats have attained the great complete nirvāṇa. Therefore, because the great complete nirvāṇa ultimately becomes bliss, it is called the great complete nirvāṇa."

Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I have now grasped from the very beginning the meaning of there being distinction and of there being no distinction, as the Blessed One has taught. And why? Because bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all the rest — it is my wish that they will all arrive, in the time to come, at the great complete nirvāṇa. Just as all rivers flow into the ocean, so all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas — I would call them permanent; they are not impermanent. Therefore there is distinction, and yet there is also no distinction."

Kāśyapa again asked: "What is the distinction in terms of defining characteristics?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, śrāvakas are like milk. Pratyekabuddhas are like curds. Bodhisattvas are like butter or clarified butter. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are like the essence of butter. Therefore in this great complete nirvāṇa, four distinct defining characteristics have been explained."

Kāśyapa again asked: "What is the defining characteristic of all sentient beings?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, take for example milk that has just come from a newborn calf — it is mixed with blood. Likewise, the defining characteristic of childish, common beings mixed with afflictions is similar to that."

Then Kāśyapa again said: "The one who dwells in the city of Kuśāgāra, named Prabhāpāla, of low birth, whom the Blessed One has prophesied — you have prophesied that he, by merely arousing the awakening mind, will swiftly reach, in this world-realm, unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening, counted among a thousand buddhas. And the venerable Śāriputra —

and Maudgalyāyana and the others will swiftly realize complete and perfect awakening" — you have not given that prophecy. The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, certain śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, by the power of their aspiration, will abide in the world for a long time, uphold the sacred Dharma for an extended period, and then realize unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening. Those who have made the aspiration to attain it swiftly will be prophesied to attain it swiftly. Son of good family, consider further this example: a merchant takes hold of a priceless precious jewel and comes to the market to sell it. When foolish people who do not know the value of the jewel see it, they mock, disparage, and scorn it. Even when the owner of the jewel says, 'This is a priceless precious jewel,' they scorn it still. Among themselves they say, 'This is not a true precious jewel — it is a mere piece of glass.' Son of good family, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are just like that. If they hear a prophecy that someone will attain awakening swiftly, they become lazy and complacent, and their mocking and disparagement is just like the foolishness of those who do not recognize a genuine precious jewel. In future times, monks will be unable to apply diligent effort to virtuous qualities; driven by poverty and preoccupied with obtaining food and drink, they go forth into renunciation merely to sustain the body, and, with distracted minds, they live by deceit. If the Tathāgata were then to give the prophecy that śrāvakas will attain awakening swiftly, those monks would mock and disparage, saying, 'Though their moral discipline is entirely degenerate, they have obtained the Dharma of a superior person.' Therefore, whoever has aroused the aspiration for swift attainment is given the prophecy of swift attainment, while those who guard and uphold the sacred Dharma are given the prophecy of long duration.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again asked the Blessed One: "How do bodhisattvas, great beings, attain the irreversible retinue?" The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "When a bodhisattva applies diligent effort to guarding and upholding the sacred Dharma, by that cause and that condition he will attain the irreversible retinue."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again asked the Blessed One: "By what cause and by what condition do sentient beings find their mouths and lips parched?" The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Whoever does not know how to regard the Three Jewels as enduring — by that cause and that condition their mouths and lips are perpetually parched. There will be people who cannot distinguish and do not discern the six kinds of flavor: sweet, cold, hot, sour, bitter, and salty, and so forth. All sentient beings, through their foolishness and being under the sway of delusion, do not know the Three Jewels as permanent — and for that reason their mouths and lips are perpetually parched.

Son of good family, consider further: any sentient being who does not know the Tathāgata as truly permanent is to be understood as blind. Any sentient being who knows the Tathāgata as truly permanent — though that person has physical eyes, I declare they are endowed with divine sight. Son of good family, consider further: whoever knows the Tathāgata as truly permanent is one who has long attended to this sūtra with diligence, and is to be understood as endowed with the divine eye. Even one who is endowed with the divine eye, if they do not know the Tathāgata as truly permanent, is called one who has only physical eyes — for such a person knows neither the limbs and joints of their own body, nor can they make others understand them. Therefore they are called one with physical eyes only.

Son of good family, consider further: the Tathāgata is at all times the father and mother of all sentient beings.

Why is this so? When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with a single voice to all sentient beings of various kinds — those with two legs, those with four legs, those with many legs, and those with no legs — each and every one of those different kinds understands it individually, and each one thinks to themselves, "The Tathāgata is teaching the Dharma to me alone today." For this reason, he is called one who is like a father and mother.

Son of good family, consider further: a baby, from the moment of birth until the age of sixteen months, strives to speak, yet is not able to be understood or to communicate. Its father and mother, in order to teach it to speak, repeat back whatever the infant says. Now tell me — does this mean that the father and mother of that child are themselves unable to speak and have some deficiency? The answer was: No, Blessed One.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the Tathāgata is just like that. Following the various kinds of sentient beings, he teaches the holy Dharma in various kinds of speech. In order to guide beings to the sacred Dharma, he shows various kinds of deportment as is fitting. When the Tathāgata speaks in a manner suited to those beings, does this in any way indicate incapacity on his part? The answer was: No, Blessed One. It is because the speech of the Tathāgata is like the roar of a lion — following the various kinds of worldly beings, in various kinds of speech, he teaches the holy Dharma to sentient beings.

This is the fourth chapter, the chapter on buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha), from the Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa of the Noble Ones.

Then at that moment, from the mouth of the Blessed One there radiated lights of various colors — blue, yellow, red, white, tawny, and purple — illuminating the entire body of Cunda. The moment those lights touched Cunda's body, he and his retinue took up abundant food and went quickly to where the Buddha was, carrying abundant and excellent articles of offering in order to make a final offering to the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha of monks.

At that time, certain gods of great splendor surrounded him on all sides and appeared before him, and they commanded Cunda: "Cunda, wait a moment with your offering."

At that time, the Tathāgata again radiated immeasurable and incalculable lights of various kinds, causing them to shine upon the bodies of the gods. The moment those divine retinues were touched by that light, the gods too opened their minds and were allowed to present their offerings.

At that time, all the gods and humans, each taking up various kinds of offerings, drew near before the Buddha, knelt on one knee, and beseeched the Tathāgata thus: "Blessed One, please be so gracious as to have this Saṅgha of monks accept our offerings."

The monks of the Saṅgha, being aware of the proper time, took up their bowls and remained in their conduct with one-pointed mind.

At that time, Cunda set up many lion-throne seats for the Buddha and the Saṅgha to sit upon, adorned them with banners, victory standards, and parasols, and arrayed them with incense, flowers, and garlands.

At that time, this great trichiliocosm world-system, adorned with these ornaments, became like the world-system of Sukhāvatī in the western direction.

Then Cunda came before the Buddha, overwhelmed by great sorrow and grief at the thought of losing him, and besought the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, out of compassion, please remain for one eon or until the end of an eon."

The Blessed One then declared to Cunda:

"If you wish me to remain long in this world, then quickly offer the articles for this final offering and perfect the perfection of generosity."

At that moment, all the bodhisattvas, the great beings, together with gods, humans, and all the rest, spoke with one voice, saying: "How wonderful! Cunda, because your merit is great and complete, the Tathāgata has accepted your final offering. As for us, lacking such merit, even the offerings we arrayed have come to nothing." So they said.

Then, in order to fulfill their hopes and aspirations, the Blessed One emanated from each pore of his body countless emanation buddhas. Each of those buddhas, in turn, was encircled by an immeasurable retinue of monks, and the Blessed One together with those innumerable retinues of the Saṅgha showed that they too accepted the offerings. The Blessed One Śākyamuni likewise accepted Cunda's offering. At that time, the alms-bowl of rice that Cunda had offered — a measure of eight dreys by the standard of the central land — through the blessing of the Blessed One was sufficient to satisfy every one of those gathered assemblies with food. When Cunda saw this, a great joy arose in him, and all those assembled circles of the retinue were likewise filled with great joy.

Then, through the blessing of the Blessed One, it arose in the minds of each one of those assembled circles that the Tathāgata, having accepted their final offering, would before long pass into nirvāṇa. Thinking thus, a mixture of grief and joy arose in their hearts.

At that time, though the ground of that grove was very small and cramped, through the blessing of the Tathāgata, even in a space no larger than the point of a needle, immeasurable blessed buddhas sat with their retinues, accepted alms-food, and all that food was seen to be inexhaustible.

Then all the gods, humans, asuras, and the rest burst into tears and wept, saying: "The Tathāgata has accepted our final offering, and having accepted it will pass into nirvāṇa. After this, to whom shall we make offerings? Now that our unsurpassable helmsman is gone from us, we are left blind."

Then the Blessed One, to gladden and encourage those assembled circles, spoke in verse:

Do not grieve, you who are here assembled.
Such is the nature of a buddha, and so it is —
even after I have passed into nirvāṇa
I shall, for countless immeasurable eons,
dwell always in the highest bliss,
abide always in supreme happiness.
Listen carefully, all of you:
My passing into nirvāṇa I shall now explain.
Having no perception of food,
I am free from the faults of hunger and thirst.
Today I have set forth an aspiration
of devoted care for you and all the rest,
that every one of these assembled circles here
may attain supreme happiness.
Hear this and take it carefully to heart:
the phenomena of buddhahood are permanent.

When on some day a crow and an owl
make their nest together in a single tree
and those two become as siblings to each other —
on that day I shall pass into nirvāṇa.
Yet the Tathāgata beholds all beings
as Rāhu beholds the moon —
he who has become the chief of every migrating being,
why should he pass into complete nirvāṇa?

When on some day a snake and a mongoose
make their home together in a single burrow
and those two become as siblings to each other —
on that day I shall pass into complete nirvāṇa.
Yet the Tathāgata beholds all with a gaze
as Rāhu beholds — surveying everything —
he who has become the chief of all sentient beings —

why should he pass into complete nirvāṇa?

If the seven petals of a flower were to take on the fragrance of kāśika cloth,
or if a cintā fruit were to grow from a kālaka tree —
on that day I shall pass into nirvāṇa.
Yet the Tathāgata beholds all beings with a gaze as Rāhu beholds —
why then, having utterly relinquished compassion,
should he pass into complete nirvāṇa?

If those who are bound by wrong craving were, at their very core, to awaken to buddhahood
and come to abide in the highest bliss —
then on that day he shall pass into nirvāṇa.
Yet the Tathāgata beholds all beings with a gaze as Rāhu beholds —
why then, having utterly relinquished compassion,
should he pass into complete nirvāṇa?

If all ordinary beings were simultaneously to awaken,
every fault and flaw entirely abandoned —
then on that day he shall pass into nirvāṇa.
Yet the Tathāgata beholds all beings with a gaze as Rāhu beholds —
why then, having utterly relinquished compassion,
should he pass into complete nirvāṇa?

If the urine of a tiny insect could destroy this great earth,
leaving mountains and every land entirely gone,
or fill the great ocean to overflowing —
then on that day shall he pass into nirvāṇa.
Yet he who beholds all with a mind of compassion, gazing as Rāhu gazes,
he who has become the chief of all migrating beings —
why should he pass into complete nirvāṇa?

Therefore, you and all those with you: cultivate devotion to the sacred Dharma.
Do not be tormented by grief; do not give way to weeping and lamentation.
Whoever practises what is true and genuine — meditate on the Tathāgata as permanent.
Understand likewise that the sacred Dharma itself is unchanging and abides forever.
Furthermore, cultivate the perception that the Three Jewels abide permanently.
To one who guards this with the utmost care, it is as though flowers bloom on a dry tree by the power of a mantra.
That one, with respect to the Three Jewels — let the fourfold retinue hear this well —
having heard it and rejoiced exceedingly, should arouse the mind of awakening.
Whoever takes hold of the Three Jewels as truly and ultimately permanent —
that one is the supreme among the aspirational prayers offered by many buddhas.

As for any monk, or nun, or male lay practitioner, or female lay practitioner who makes such an aspirational prayer — the supreme aspirational prayer of the Tathāgata — they are not foolish, not deluded: they should be known as worthy of veneration. Through the power of that aspiration, the fruit of virtue ripening, they will become the supreme among the world's finest, like an arhat. Whoever does not understand the Three Jewels to be truly permanent should be known as being of inferior lineage. Whoever understands these three aspects of the Dharma to be truly permanent will, by the condition of the truth of the Dharma, be parted from suffering and become supremely blissful, free from harm, and free from all obstacles.

At that time, the assembly of gods, humans, asuras, and the rest, having heard those very words thus spoken, gave rise to a mind of great joy and delight. Their minds became exceedingly tame and content; their minds became utterly cleansed of all obscurations; their minds became free of high and low. Radiant with splendor and serene, their faces lit with a gentle smile, they understood the Tathāgata to be truly permanent, and thereupon they made offerings of many kinds with divine substances: divine flowers, incense, powder, ointments, and divine music — offering fully with all of these.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, do you see this wondrous and marvelous maṇḍala of assemblies?"

Kāśyapa replied: "I do, Blessed One. I see the Tathāgata — immeasurable, beyond reckoning — receiving the offerings of his many great retinues."

He also saw that the bodies of the many buddhas were exceedingly great, yet the thrones on which they sat were no larger than the tip of a needle — and although surrounded by vast retinues, none pressed or crowded against another.

He also saw those many great retinues giving rise to great aspiration and reciting thirteen verses.

He also saw that each of those maṇḍalas of retinues thought to itself, "The Tathāgata is receiving my offerings alone."

Even if the offerings presented by Cunda were to be divided into the finest particles, and even a single such particle were offered to each buddha, there would still not be enough to go around — yet through the blessing of the Tathāgata, all would become sufficient and complete.

Then the great bodhisattvas, Mañjuśrī the Ever-Youthful and the rest, perceived these wondrous and marvelous things. This too was revealed by the Tathāgata as a skillful means, so that the retinues of śrāvakas, asuras, and the rest might know that the Tathāgata is by nature permanent.

Then the Blessed One said to Cunda: "Do you regard what you have seen as wondrous and marvelous?"

Cunda replied: "It is so, Blessed One. Formerly I saw measureless, innumerable buddhas, each adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor marks of excellence. Now, however, all have assumed the supreme form of great bodhisattvas, while a single buddha sits like a medicinal tree, surrounded and attended by the great bodhisattvas. This too I have seen."

The Blessed One said to Cunda: "The measureless buddhas you saw before were none other than my own manifest emanations, displayed for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings and to bring them joy. Those great bodhisattvas, too, are of inconceivable conduct — they are nothing other than the deeds of immeasurable buddhas. You, Cunda, are yourself endowed with the conduct of a great bodhisattva; established perfectly on the ten grounds, you are complete in the conduct of a bodhisattva."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the Blessed One: "It is so. It is exactly so. It is just as the Blessed One has declared. This Cunda is endowed with the conduct of all bodhisattvas, and we rejoice in this."

The Tathāgata taught the great Mahāyāna sūtra, the Great Nirvāṇa, in order to shed a great light for the measureless beings of future generations yet to come.

Kāśyapa asked: "Among all the sūtras the Blessed One has taught, has the Blessed One's teaching conveyed a meaning with remainder, or a meaning without remainder?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, what I have taught has both a meaning with remainder and a meaning without remainder."

Then Cunda said to the Blessed One: "As the Blessed One has declared, giving away all one's material possessions in generosity is to be praised and extolled, though it is not to be disparaged — what, then, is the meaning of what the Blessed One has said? What is the distinction between one endowed with moral discipline and one of corrupt moral discipline?"

The Blessed One declared: "With a single exception, I praise and extol all other forms of giving."

Cunda asked: "What is the one exception?"

The Blessed One replied: "It is that which in this sūtra is described as corrupt moral discipline."

Cunda then asked further:

"Blessed One, what is the meaning of this?"

The Blessed One declared: "The term 'one of corrupt moral discipline' is to be applied to one who holds wrong views. All other forms of giving are praised and extolled, and will yield a great fruit."

Cunda asked again: "What is meant by 'one who holds wrong views'?"

The Blessed One declared to Cunda: "Any monk, nun, layman, or laywoman who speaks harmful words and slanders the sacred Dharma, and who — even having committed blameworthy actions — feels no remorse, no shame, and no scruple: such a person is said to have fallen onto the path of wrong views. Likewise, one who knows by their own conscience that they have transgressed one of the four root precepts or committed one of the five acts of immediate consequence, and who — even having committed such grave blameworthy acts — from the very beginning feels no fear, no shame, no scruple, who feels no remorse and makes no confession, who has no love or cherishing for the sacred Dharma, who has no mind settled in Dharma, but who instead disparages and slanders and heaps many faults upon others: such a person too is said to have fallen onto the path of wrong views. Furthermore, one who declares that there is no Buddha, no Dharma, no Saṅgha — that person too is said to have fallen onto the path of wrong views. Apart from these alone who hold wrong views, all other ordinary beings are praised and extolled."

The fourteenth fascicle.

Then Cunda again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, what is the meaning of 'corrupt moral discipline'?"

The Blessed One declared: "One who has transgressed the four root precepts, who has committed the five acts of immediate consequence, and who utterly slanders the sacred Dharma — that is what is called corrupt moral discipline."

Cunda then asked: "Does one with corrupt moral discipline in that way have any chance of liberation?"

The Blessed One declared: "Given the appropriate causes and conditions, there is indeed a chance of liberation. If such a one still wears the monastic robe and has not yet entirely abandoned it, and if they are endowed with a mind of shame, scruple, and fear, and are filled with deep remorse — thinking: 'Alas, why did I commit this great blameworthy act? Alas, why did I perform this deed that will bring me suffering?' — and if, having given rise to such a mind of deep remorse, they also generate a mind of protecting the Dharma and of settling in the Dharma, and they make offerings to those who uphold and preserve the Dharma, and they request the recitation and reading of the sūtras of the Great Vehicle, and they make supplications, and they themselves receive, uphold, read, recite, and penetrate them to the depths, and widely teach and expound them to others — such a person shall not be called one of corrupt moral discipline. Why is this? Noble son, it is like this: when the sun rises, the darkness of mist and fog that was invisible becomes entirely dispelled. The appearance of this great sūtra of the complete passing beyond sorrow (nirvāṇa) in the world is just the same — it has the power to dispel all blameworthy deeds committed by sentient beings throughout immeasurable eons. Therefore those who have taken refuge in the sacred Dharma through this sūtra will obtain a great fruit, and those of corrupt moral discipline will be able to attain liberation. This is why it is taught thus. As for one who has slandered the sacred Dharma and yet feels deep remorse and makes confession, and who having taken refuge in the Dharma calls to mind all the non-virtuous deeds they have committed — it is as with a person who has committed the act of killing a human being and in whom a mind of great fear arises, or in whom a mind of utter shame and scruple arises —

thinking that aside from the sacred Dharma there is nothing else, anywhere, that could serve as refuge and ally. When such a person takes refuge in the sacred Dharma in the very manner it has been taught and proclaimed, and one makes a gift to that person, one will obtain immeasurable merit and become a worthy object of veneration for the world. But if someone who has committed the blameworthy acts described here goes for a month, or up to fifteen days, without generating a mind of taking refuge, confessing, or feeling remorse, and one makes a gift to such a person, the result will not be great. It is the same for one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya): if a mind of remorse has arisen, and one possesses inwardly a mind of shame and scruple, thinking, "Because I have committed non-virtuous deeds I will experience great suffering," and one then turns to the sacred Dharma as protector and refuge and takes up its upholding — then, even for one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, this is no longer as if those acts were done without remedy. If one then makes a gift to such a person, one will obtain immeasurable merit. And if one has committed acts of immediate retribution and yet generates a mind to guard and take refuge in the sacred Dharma, and one makes a gift to that person, the merit that accrues is beyond all telling.

Noble son, listen further: here is another illustration. Reflect very carefully on those who have committed great blameworthy acts — I shall set it out fully and explain it to you. Let them give rise to this thought: "What is called the sacred Dharma is the very essence of the Tathāgata. Therefore it must be guarded, protected, and upheld." If one makes a gift to a person who holds that thought, one will obtain the supreme fruit of merit.

Noble son, consider this example. A pregnant woman near the time of giving birth was in a land struck by famine and unrest, and she fled to another land where there was a shrine to a deity. There she gave birth to her child. Later, hearing the news that the unrest in her own land had quieted and the harvests were excellent, she took her child in her arms and set out to return home. Along the way a great river roared in flood, and she could not cross it with her child in her arms. She thought to herself: "It is better that both my child and I should die together than that I abandon my child and cross alone." And so, thinking only of saving her child from the water, she entered the current, and both mother and child perished in the river. The moment she died, she was reborn as a god in the higher realms, for though that woman was by nature rough and fierce, because she had thought with love for her child she was reborn as a god in the higher realms.

In the same way, even those who have broken the four root precepts and committed the five acts of immediate retribution, if they generate a mind to guard and protect the sacred Dharma — though they have previously performed non-virtuous deeds, through their having upheld the Dharma they become in this world a supreme field of merit without equal. Therefore, one who guards and protects the Dharma is endowed with the supreme and boundless fruit.

Then the venerable one asked again: "Blessed One, if those of wrong craving feel very deep remorse, possess shame, and with reverence make offerings and praises to the Three Jewels — if one makes a gift to such a person, will one obtain a great fruit?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, do not speak in that way. Noble son, consider this example. A man ate a mango fruit and cast the seed on the ground. He thought: 'There is certainly still sweetness inside this fruit.' He broke open the seed and tasted it —

it was so extremely bitter that he felt regret over the fruit and, suspecting there was nothing left in it at all, broke the seed and planted it in the ground. Wishing for it to grow, he watered it regularly with ghee and milk and other such things and attended to it with great care. Now, what do you think — would it grow?"

The reply came: "No, Blessed One. Even if a rain of the most supreme and unsurpassable nectar were to fall from the sky, it would not grow."

"Noble son, one of wrong craving is just like that. When the roots of virtue have been utterly burned away, what unwholesome action could serve as a basis for their purification? Noble son, if a wholesome mind has arisen, then one should not call that person one of wrong craving. Noble son, not all gifts that are given bear the same fruit upon maturation. Why is this? The ripened fruit of a gift given to śrāvakas and the fruit of a gift given to pratyekabuddhas are different from one another, and a gift given to a Tathāgata alone yields a supreme and unsurpassable fruit. Therefore it is not the case that all acts of giving are equal in their fruit."

The venerable one asked again: "For what reason did the Tathāgata speak this verse in the way he did?"

The Blessed One declared to him: "My speaking of that verse was not without cause and condition. In former times, here in Rājagṛha, a layworshiper of very little faith gave a gift to a naked tīrthika and then asked me about the meaning of giving. It was on account of that cause and that condition that I spoke those verses. Furthermore, I spoke them with the great bodhisattvas in mind, in order to reveal the essential point of what was taught for their sake. As for the meaning of that verse: the word 'all' refers to 'all' in a partial sense only. The great bodhisattvas, as the foremost among human beings, gather together those who guard their ethical discipline and supply whatever they need, while those of corrupt ethical discipline they utterly cast aside, like the corpse of a dead field animal or a wild jackal."

"Furthermore, noble son, I once spoke these verses:

All the rivers that flow
assuredly have their bends and turns.
All that belongs to the forest grove
will certainly become wood — there is no doubt.
All that women speak
is assuredly tinged with deceit.
All those who hold power
will without doubt possess abundant wealth."

Then the great bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the ever-youthful, rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and spoke these verses in reply:

"Not all the rivers that flow
assuredly have bends and turns.
Not all that belongs to the forest grove
is assuredly wood throughout.
Not all that women speak
is assuredly tinged with deceit.
Not all those who hold power
are assuredly possessed of abundant wealth."

"Therefore, Blessed One, the meaning of what you have taught is one that involves something beyond the obvious. Out of your compassion for us, please reveal its cause and condition. Why do we ask? Blessed One, in this great trichiliocosm, in the western continent called Godānīya, there is a river known as the Sāpakā — dark as a line of ink, it flows into the western ocean. The defining characteristics of that river have not been spoken by the Blessed One in any other sūtra, yet here in this most extensive sūtra the Tathāgata has declared something that goes beyond all others. May the Blessed One please cause the bodhisattvas as well to understand these matters."

"Blessed One, consider the analogy of a person who knows raw gold ore but does not know refined gold. The Tathāgata is similar: though he comprehends all phenomena in his mind, what he has taught and spoken still carries a remainder beyond what has been expressed. Whatever the Tathāgata has spoken with that remainder is nevertheless spoken with skillful means and with a deeper intent. Every statement that all forests are definitely trees also carries a remainder, for forests made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and other precious substances of many kinds are also called forests. Every statement that all women are definitely deceitful also carries a remainder, for there are some women who fully guard their ethical conduct, who are endowed with good qualities, and who are possessed of loving-kindness and compassion. Every statement that all those with power are endowed with wealth also carries a remainder, for among those with power, a wheel-turning king who is a Tathāgata, the Dharma-king, does not fall within the class of Māra, the lord of death, and cannot be destroyed by him. Brahmā, Indra (Śakra), and others do indeed possess power, yet they are impermanent. That which is permanent, unchanging, and unshifting is what is truly called 'possessed of power,' and this refers to none other than the complete nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle."

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, you speak with tremendous eloquence. Yet wait a moment and listen steadily. Mañjuśrī, consider a householder tormented by illness, greatly weakened, who encounters a skilled physician. That physician compounds a medicine with the drug aconite, and the patient, being hungry, wishes to eat a great deal. The physician says to him: 'If you want to take the medicine, it could be given in large quantity, but you are weak and frail and cannot digest it, so it must not be given in large quantity. Therefore this aconite medicine may be called nectar, and it may also be called poison — if it is drunk in large quantity and not digested, it is called poison.' Noble son, do not think that what was said by that skilled physician is contradictory, mistaken, or without the power of medicine.

"Noble son, the Tathāgata is likewise. For the sake of taming kings, queens, princes, great ministers, conquering kings, princes, queens, and the arrogant courtiers of the palace, and in order to inspire fear and dread in them so that they might be disciplined, the Tathāgata spoke, like that skilled physician, these verses:

All flowing rivers
certainly contain bends, without fail.
All that belongs to forests
is certainly wood, beyond doubt.
All women who are mentioned
are without exception certain to be sly and guileful.
All those possessed of power
are without doubt possessed of wealth.

"Mañjuśrī, you should understand it thus: in what the Tathāgata has spoken there is no error. This great earth may shift and reverse, yet in what the Tathāgata has spoken there is no error. Therefore everything spoken by the Tathāgata carries a remainder."

Then the Blessed One praised the youthful Mañjuśrī with the words: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, having long ago deeply understood this meaning, out of affection for all and in order to bring all sentient beings to gnosis, you have done well to ask the Tathāgata at length about the meaning of these verses."

Then the youthful Mañjuśrī once again presented a verse before the Buddha:

When another from a foreign land has spoken —

One does not turn back merely for the sake of following along —
Do not examine what others have done or left undone.
Rather, examine most carefully your own self —
What virtue and non-virtue you yourself practise.

The Blessed One declared this teaching-medicine in just those words. If it was not rightly taught, then please, Tathāgata, out of loving concern, rightly explain why one who follows along with and does not contradict what another, an outsider, says. For why is this? The Blessed One has taught in many ways that all ninety-five students of the outer schools will go to the lower realms, while the attendants of the śrāvakas will all go to the right path. And yet a person who guards ethical discipline fully, whose conduct is extremely restrained, who guards the sense faculties — such a person is also one who is deeply devoted to the great Dharma and who practises the path of virtue. Why then, Blessed One, did you say in the ninth sūtra that when an outsider slanders another, one should revile and mock him? With what intention did you speak the meaning of those verses?

The Blessed One then declared to Mañjuśrī: Noble son, that verse which I spoke was not spoken for the sake of all sentient beings in general. At that time it was spoken solely for the sake of King Ajātaśatru. A buddha, a Blessed One, does not teach anything arbitrarily, without cause and condition. It is because cause and condition were present that it was spoken in just those words. Noble son, King Ajātaśatru had slain his father and then came to where I was, wishing to be tamed, and he asked me this: "How is it that the Buddha, the Blessed One, is said to be omniscient, and yet is not omniscient? For if he is omniscient, then someone like Devadatta, who throughout countless former lives with malicious intent did harm to the Tathāgata — why did the Tathāgata permit him to go forth into renunciation?" Having been asked this, noble son, it was because of that cause and that condition, on account of that king, that I spoke the verse thus:

When another from a foreign land has spoken,
One does not turn back merely for the sake of following along.
Do not examine what others have done or left undone.
Rather, examine most carefully your own body —
What virtue and non-virtue you yourself practise.

The Blessed One then declared: Noble son, the great king, having committed the heinous and boundless transgression of killing his father, instead of feeling deep remorse, confessing, and purifying himself completely — why did he enter into seeking out the faults and flaws of others? Noble son, it was for that king's sake, and for that reason, that I spoke those verses. Furthermore, noble son, those verses were also spoken for the sake of those who, though they guard ethical discipline fully and are endowed with proper conduct, fall into seeking out the faults of others. As for any person who, taught and corrected by an outsider, abandons non-virtue completely and also turns others away from non-virtuous action — that person is truly my own genuine attendant.

Then the Blessed One spoke a verse to Mañjuśrī:

There is no one at all who is unafraid of weapons.
All beings cling to life and breath.
Taking one's own body as the measure,
Neither harm nor kill another.

Then the youthful Mañjuśrī once again presented a verse before the Blessed One:

Not everyone fears weapons —
Not everyone clings to life.
Taking one's own body as the measure,
Strive to practise virtue.

This statement in which the Tathāgata expressed the meaning of the Dharma in words has not reached the ultimate extent. Why is this? Because an arhat, and —

a wheel-turning king's precious queen, his precious elephant, his precious horse, and his precious minister — there is no place where the sharp weapons of gods or asuras could kill them. A courageous hero, a woman endowed with water, the king of horses, the king of beasts, and a monk who guards his moral discipline — even when a weapon is visibly present before them, they feel neither fear nor terror. Therefore this verse spoken by the Tathāgata is also incomplete. And the phrase "Taking one's own body as the measure" is likewise incomplete. Why is this? If arhats were to take others as the measure with reference to themselves, they would have the perception of self and the perception of a living soul. But if there were the perception of self and the perception of a living soul, they would be protecting themselves — and even foolish, ignoble persons would come to see the arhats, and all would become practitioners of yoga.
