If that were the case, it would be a wrong view. And if it were a wrong view, immediately upon death they would be reborn in a hell realm. Furthermore, there is absolutely no occasion for arhats to ever generate a mind wishing to kill any sentient being. And there is no sentient being, however innumerable, capable of killing an arhat.

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, what is called "the perception of self" — the arising of a mind of great compassion toward sentient beings, free of any thought of killing — this is the equanimity of mind that belongs to the arhats. Do not think that the Blessed One has spoken something contradictory without cause or condition. Long ago, here in Rājagṛha, a hunter killed many mountain game and invited me, saying "Come eat the meat." At that time I accepted the invitation, but holding in mind an intense love toward all sentient beings — as the planet Rāhu holds the moon — I spoke these words in verse:

May you live an exceedingly long life
and dwell long in this world.
Holding to the teaching of non-killing,
may you become like the lifespan of a buddha.

And this verse also was spoken:

There is no one at all who is unafraid of weapons.
All beings cling to life and breath.
Taking one's own body as the measure,
Neither harm nor kill another.

Then the Blessed One gave praise to the youthful Mañjuśrī, saying "Excellent! Excellent!" and said: It is excellent that you have asked the Tathāgata such a profoundly deep meaning on behalf of the bodhisattvas, the great beings.

Then Mañjuśrī presented this verse before the Blessed One:

Just as one honours one's mother and father
and follows them with reverence,
so too those who take up such practice
fall into the hell of uninterrupted torment.

Then the Blessed One spoke this verse in reply to Mañjuśrī:

Attachment is called "the mother,"
ignorance is called "the father."
To follow them with reverence
is to fall into the hell of uninterrupted torment.

Then the Blessed One once again spoke in verse to the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:

All that is governed by another is called suffering.
All that is governed by oneself has power and ease.
All pride and arrogance, backed by force, brings fierce anger.
All that is virtuous and gentle has love and compassion for all.

Then the great bodhisattva, the youthful Mañjuśrī, again addressed the Blessed One thus: This too that the Tathāgata has spoken has not reached the ultimate extent of meaning. Blessed One, out of your loving care, please teach the causes and conditions for this. Why is this? Consider, for instance, when the sons of a householder are learning from a teacher — are they not under the teacher's authority?

Even if one is under the teacher's authority, the purpose of learning is not accomplished. And if one is not under the teacher's authority, it is likewise not accomplished. And if one is under one's own authority, learning is also not accomplished. Therefore what the Tathāgata has said still has remainder. Blessed One, consider further this example: princes who have learned nothing and know nothing may be under their own authority, yet through their foolishness and ignorance they suffer perpetually. Thus, to say that such a prince is under his own authority yields no accomplished purpose, and to say he is under another's authority likewise yields no accomplished purpose. Therefore the meaning of what the Blessed One has taught still has remainder, and so it is not fitting to say without qualification that all that is governed by another necessarily brings suffering, nor is it fitting to say that all that is governed by oneself necessarily brings ease. And to say that all pride and arrogance necessarily brings fierce anger — this too still has remainder. Blessed One, consider, for instance, women of good family who, through the force of their own pride, go forth into the religious life. Once entered upon training, they fully guard their moral discipline and keep their conduct extremely restrained, applying themselves diligently with undistracted senses. Therefore it is not fitting to say that all defilements arising from pride necessarily bring fierce anger. Moreover, to say that all that is virtuous and gentle necessarily has loving-kindness and compassion — this too still has remainder. Consider, for instance, a person who has committed a defeat, yet has not discarded the religious robes. Though his outward conduct be extremely restrained, when the Dharma-protectors see him they are averse and expel him. When he passes from this life he falls into a hell state. And if a monk has committed a defeat, those same Dharma-protectors will drive him out and reduce him to the status of a layman. Therefore it is not fitting to say that all who are virtuous and gentle necessarily have loving-kindness.

Then the Blessed One declared to Mañjuśrī: It is because causes and conditions are present that the Tathāgata has spoken in this way with remainder. Furthermore, Blessed One — it was because causes and conditions are present that the following was said. Here in Rājagṛha there was a woman named Śintuwa Zangmo who, on the road to her parents' home, came to a crossroads and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and said these words: "All women are without power and without authority. All men are unobstructed in their power." Having understood the intention of that woman, the Tathāgata then spoke these verses for her sake.

Mañjuśrī spoke in verse:
All sentient beings without exception,
each one depends on food and drink.
All those who possess power —
in their minds there is no jealousy.
All who depend on the conditions of food and drink
come to experience the suffering of illness.
All whose conduct is utterly pure
come to experience supreme ease.
Blessed One, does not the one who receives alms and offerings from the noble one — does the Tathāgata not also incur such dependency?

To this the Blessed One replied to Mañjuśrī in verse:
It is not the case that all sentient beings
depend on food and drink.
It is not the case that all those who possess power
are without any mind of jealousy.
It is not the case that all, through the force of food,
are afflicted by illness.
And it is not the case that all whose conduct is pure
experience ease.

Mañjuśrī, if you were to fall ill, then it would likewise follow that I too would fall ill. Why is that? Because arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas —

the Tathāgata in truth eats nothing at all. He displayed the acceptance of offerings from countless ordinary beings solely in order to tame those on the other shore, to bring the perfection of generosity to complete fulfillment for those beings, and to liberate sentient beings from the hells, from the realms of animal birth, and from the world of the Lord of Death.

Now, if anyone were to think that the Tathāgata practised the most severe austerities for six years and that his body thereby became greatly weakened and emaciated, that view is not correct. The buddha, the Blessed One, liberated from conditioned existence, is unlike the lowborn and the ignoble. Why then would his body become frail and thin? The buddha, the Blessed One, through the most earnest application of diligence, would attain a vajra-like body. He is not like those in the world who possess bodies with imperfections, and my attendants likewise — by inconceivable means — are not dependent on food.

As for the verse "all those who possess power are without any mind of jealousy" — that too carries a remainder. For in the world there are certain human beings in whom, throughout a single lifetime, there is no mind of jealousy and yet who also have no power whatsoever.

As for the verse "all illness arises from food" — that too carries a remainder. For some people, illness arises from a sudden affliction that was not caused by food at all — such as being pierced by a thorn, or being struck by a weapon, and so forth.

As for the verse "all whose conduct is pure experience ease" — that too carries a remainder. For in the world there are tīrthikas who live in complete brahmacharya and yet experience much suffering.

Therefore, everything the Tathāgata has spoken also carries a remainder. It is not the case that the Tathāgata spoke these verses without cause and condition; he spoke them as having a cause and having a condition. In former times, in the land of Hudaya, a brahmin named Yakṣa came to where I was staying. Wishing to uphold the fourfold precepts of the eightfold observance, I at that time spoke those verses to him.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One thus: Blessed One, what is meant by "that which is without remainder," and what is meant by "all phenomena"?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, the expression "all" refers to everything apart from the phenomena of the side of awakening and from enthusiasm for virtuous phenomena — and that too may be called "without remainder." All other phenomena may be called "with remainder" and may also be called "without remainder," so that sons of good family who are devoted to the Dharma may understand the meaning of "with remainder" and "without remainder."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa was filled with great joy and delight, and he again addressed the Blessed One thus: How wonderful! Blessed One, you look upon all sentient beings with the same equanimity as a father looks upon his son Rāhu.

Then the Blessed One said to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: Excellent, excellent! It is well that you have understood this exceedingly profound meaning.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then again addressed the Blessed One: Blessed One, I pray that you set forth whatever virtues and merits are obtained from this Great Vehicle sūtra of the passage beyond sorrow.

The Blessed One replied to Kāśyapa: Son of good family, the mass of merit obtained merely from hearing the name of this sūtra is something that no śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha can express — only the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, can do so. And why is that? Because it is the domain of the buddhas, being beyond conceptual measure.

As for one who holds it, upholds it, reads it, or recites it —

— or who studies it intently, or who copies it in a manuscript, or who commissions its copying — needless is it even to speak of these, for at that very moment all those dwelling in the world, gods (devas), humans, asuras, and all the rest, will with one voice offer this verse before the buddhas:

The buddhas are inconceivable,
and likewise the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Therefore we beseech you:
please remain a little while longer.

Venerable Great Kāśyapa,
and likewise Ānanda and the rest —
both these central figures of the retinue assembly —
we pray you too to remain for a time.

The lord of the middle land, Aṅga,
the great king Ajātaśatru,
who holds deep devotion to the Buddha —
he too is not yet present here.

Therefore, Tathāgata, out of loving care,
please remain a little while longer.
Among this vast assembly of the retinue,
we pray you to dispel our doubts.

Then the Tathāgata spoke these verses to the great assembly:

My eldest son in the Dharma,
known as Great Kāśyapa,
and Ānanda, supreme in diligent effort —
they shall resolve the doubts of all.

Listen well, all of you.
From Ānanda's extensive learning
a thorough understanding will arise
of what is permanent and what is impermanent.
Therefore, do not be unhappy or distressed.

Then all those many circles of the retinue made offerings of various kinds to the Blessed One, and each of them gave rise to the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas, as many as the sands of the Ganges, became established on the first ground.

At that time the Blessed One gave a prophecy to Mañjuśrī the youthful, to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa, and to Cunda, and spoke these words: Sons of good family, attend to my words with great diligence and be heedful. I am now afflicted with pain throughout my back, and I intend to lie down as a small child might lie down when ill. You, Mañjuśrī and the others, teach the Dharma of the Great Vehicle in full to the fourfold assembly. These very teachings I now entrust entirely to you. Likewise, Kāśyapa and Ānanda, I entrust these true teachings to you as well.

With those words, the Tathāgata, in order to tame ordinary beings, lowered his right side as one who is ill and lay down to rest.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One: Blessed One, the Tathāgata is entirely free from all the flaws of suffering through illness, and he is without fear. It is all sentient beings, Blessed One, who are caused to fall ill by four poisonous thorns: attachment, aversion, delusion, and pride. When these causes of illness are present, many sicknesses arise — heat from desire, chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, numbness throughout the body, heart disturbance and forgetfulness, fever and confusion, skin disease, burning and aching eyes and ears, pain in the back, abdominal swelling, madness, emaciation and wasting, torment by the hungry ghosts, and so forth — the many diseases of body and mind. Since you, the Blessed One, are without any of these, why then, Tathāgata, do you regard your own life span and say, "I am afflicted with back pain — Mañjuśrī, teach the Dharma to the great assembly"?

Those who do not fall ill through causes and conditions of either kind are those who bear loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, and who give medicine to the sick and offer it freely to the poor.

The Tathāgata, for countless eons in the past, applied himself with great diligence to the path of awakening, and constantly through pleasant speech worked for the well-being of sentient beings so that they would not suffer — and he freely gave all manner of medicines to the sick. Why then, it is asked, has he fallen ill like this today?

The Blessed One replied: In the world, sick people sometimes sit up and sometimes lie down; sometimes, being uncomfortable, they ask for food and drink; sometimes they give instructions to their attendants about their teeth-cleaning and their tasks, saying, "This is how it should be done." If the Tathāgata were to remain completely silent and simply lie resting, why would he not be teaching the śrāvakas, his close disciples, about the perfection of moral discipline, about meditative concentration, liberation, meditative absorption, and the practice of right effort? Why would he not be teaching these profoundly deep sūtras of the Great Vehicle? And why would the Tathāgata, through his boundless skillful means, not be showing the great Kāśyapa — who among human beings is like a king of elephants — and the great beings the non-regression from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening? Why would he not be teaching that those monks who are unruly should be disciplined with penalties for grasping at all things without investigation? Blessed One, since you are in truth not ill at all, why do you remain silent and lie with your right side inclined?

When bodhisattvas give medicine as a condition for the relief of the sick, they dedicate every root of virtue, sharing it equally with all sentient beings and dedicating it to the wisdom of omniscience, thereby fully clearing away the afflictive obscurations, the karmic obscurations, and the ripening obscurations of all sentient beings.

What is called the afflictive obscuration (kleśāvaraṇa) is this: the affliction of being bound up by attachment, aversion, delusion, and the enwrapping of wrathfulness; jealousy; miserliness; deception; pretense; shamelessness; lack of conscience; pride; exaggerated pride; pride surpassing pride; the conceit of "I am"; perverse pride; presumptuous pride; pride of inferiority; heedlessness; arrogance; resentment; quarrelsomeness; wrong livelihood; crafty pretense through guile and deceit; seeking gain through gain; seeking through what is contrary to Dharma; seeking in excess; disrespect; failure to act according to instruction; reliance on unwholesome friends; attachment to gains without weariness; being so tightly bound by bondage that it is difficult to be freed; coveting base desires; clinging with base attachment; the view of the transitory collection (the notion of a self in the aggregates); the view of existence (eternalism); the view of non-existence (nihilism); distraction and agitation; elation; sleep; laziness; displeasure; attachment to food and drink; dullness of mind; focusing the mind on other things; attending to unwholesome things; conduct of body and speech that is corrupt; delight in much talking; dullness of the faculties; lying in one's every utterance; thoughts of desire; thoughts of aversion; and being entirely covered over by thoughts of harm — this is called the afflictive obscuration. Then there is the karmic obscuration of the blameworthy deeds of the five acts of immediate retribution (pārājika). And birth in hells as a sentient being, birth as an animal, birth as a hungry ghost, disparagement of the holy Dharma, and birth among those who hold wrong views — these are called the ripening obscuration. These three kinds of obscuration are called the great illness. Now, bodhisattvas who, throughout immeasurable eons, conduct the conduct of awakening, give the gift of healing medicine to all who are sick and make this aspiration:

May all sentient beings be utterly freed from illness and attain the vajra body of the Tathāgata. May I become the supreme king of medicine for all boundless sentient beings and dispel every malady. May all sentient beings obtain the medicine agada, and through the power of that medicine may every poison be dispelled. Moreover, may all sentient beings be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and may they swiftly find the unsurpassed medicine of buddhahood and have every thorn of affliction removed. Moreover, may all sentient beings, through the arousing of the most vigorous diligence, possess the mind of the Tathāgata — vajra-like — become the supreme medicine, heal every illness, and be free from any perception of quarrel and conflict. Moreover, may sentient beings become a great medicinal tree and dispel every malady. Moreover, may all sentient beings have the poisonous thorns extracted and attain the unsurpassed rays of light of the Tathāgata. And moreover, may all sentient beings enter the supremely profound Dharma treasury of the great medicine of the Tathāgata's wisdom.

Such is the aspiration they make.

O Blessed One, the bodhisattva thus makes that aspiration for a hundred thousand immeasurable, incalculable, innumerable eons, striving to free all sentient beings from illness. Why, then, does the Tathāgata declare that he is ill?

The Blessed One replied: Furthermore, O Blessed One, there are certain sick persons in the world who cannot sit up, stand, or walk, who cannot even eat or drink. They cannot teach or instruct their children, and they cannot manage the affairs of their livelihood. At that time their father and mother, wife, children, retinue, relatives, and friends all come to regard them as certain to die.

O Blessed One, likewise the Tathāgata is similar to such a person. He lies down on his right side and remains completely silent, so that the foolish people here in Jambudvīpa come to think: "The Tathāgata, the perfectly complete buddha, has surely passed into nirvāṇa" — and they generate the perception that cessation is exhausted. Yet the Tathāgata himself has not ultimately passed into nirvāṇa at all. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is permanent, unchanging, and unshifting. It would be improper to say "I have lain down for such-and-such a cause and condition."

O Blessed One, furthermore there are sick persons in the world who are utterly emaciated and wasted, lying flat on their backs or on their sides, unable to rise. At that time even their attendants develop an aversion toward them and come to regard them as certain, without doubt, to die. The Tathāgata is similarly regarded with aversion by the ninety-five kinds of tīrthikas, who perceive him as passing into nirvāṇa. These tīrthikas say: "We and others are made permanent by such dharmas as the self, the lord, time, atoms, and so forth — we are without change or shift. But the ascetic Gautama has been seized by impermanence and has come to be subject to change and shifting." Therefore, O Blessed One, it would be improper for him to lie down in silence.

O Blessed One, furthermore there are sick persons in the world in whom the four great elements (mahābhūtas) have become impaired and unequal, and they have grown extremely wasted and emaciated. Because of this they cannot rise, sit, or stand at will, and they must simply lie down. The Tathāgata, however, is not one in whom the four great elements are impaired or unequal; he is possessed of the full power of his body and is not weakened. O Blessed One, the strength of ten small bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single great bull elephant.

The strength of ten great blue bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single great blue bull elephant of the highest rank. The strength of ten of those highest-ranking great blue bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single tame bull elephant. The strength of ten tame bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single wild bull elephant. The strength of ten wild bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single two-tusked bull elephant. The strength of ten two-tusked bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single four-tusked bull elephant. The strength of ten four-tusked bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single white bull elephant of the Snow Mountains. The strength of ten white bull elephants of the Snow Mountains does not equal the strength of a single fragrant-wood bull elephant. The strength of ten fragrant-wood bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single blue bull elephant. The strength of ten blue bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single yellow bull elephant. The strength of ten yellow bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single red bull elephant. The strength of ten red bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single white bull elephant. The strength of ten white bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single bull elephant called Mountain. The strength of ten bull elephants called Mountain does not equal the strength of a single utpala bull elephant. The strength of ten utpala bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single kumuda bull elephant. The strength of ten kumuda bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single puṇḍarīka bull elephant. The strength of ten puṇḍarīka bull elephants does not equal the strength of a single human champion. The strength of ten human champions does not equal the strength of a single Pārgana warrior. The strength of ten Pārgana warriors does not equal the strength of a single mighty eight-armed being. The strength of ten such mighty beings does not equal the strength of a single joint in the body of the bodhisattva on the tenth ground.

In all ordinary beings, the bones and joints do not touch and connect with one another. In a champion of great strength, the bones and joints do touch one another. In a Pārgana warrior, the bones and joints are connected to one another. In a mighty being, the bones and joints are connected in a continuous chain, one to the next. In a bodhisattva, the bones and joints are knotted together like a coiled dragon, and therefore that one's strength is supremely great.

When the world first arose and was established, resting firm at the diamond-boundary, there appeared the vajra throne at the heart of the seat of awakening, the awakening maṇḍala at Vajrāsana, and the bodhisattva sat upon that seat. At that very moment the ten powers were attained.

The Tathāgata is not like a small child. A small child is foolish, without understanding, unable even to speak properly, and so can lie down sprawling however it wishes without anyone taking offense. The Tathāgata, however, is possessed of great primordial wisdom, illuminating all with his radiance. Among humans he is like a nāga: endowed with great splendor, having fully accomplished great miraculous power, he is the unsurpassed great sage who has entirely severed the web of doubt, who has drawn out the thorn of desire, whose conduct is supremely beautiful, who is master of all comportment, and who is utterly without fear. Why then should he lie down on his right side, causing all the gods and humans of the world to be displeased and tormented with suffering?

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the following verses before the Blessed One:

O Gautama of great qualities,
please rise and teach the true Dharma.
You are not like a small child
nor like a sick person lying down.
Gods and humans — steer the Teacher's course!
This one who lies slumbering beneath the lord of trees:
upon seeing this, what foolish, ill-bred child

would say he will surely pass into nirvāṇa? One who does not understand that the vast sūtras were taught with the intention of conveying the profound domain of the buddhas' activity is like a blind person who cannot see the path. Great bodhisattvas such as the youthful Mañjuśrī, who realize the profound meaning, are like those who are accustomed to wide open spaces. The Blessed One, who has gone beyond in the three times, has become the foremost embodiment of great compassion. Where now is that great compassion? If you possess no compassion, it would not be fitting to call you a buddha. If you have passed into nirvāṇa, it would not be fitting to call you permanent. O unsurpassed Blessed One, grant us our request: for the happiness of all beings, please tame the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

Then the Blessed One, whose mind was thoroughly familiar with great compassion and who knew the individual thoughts of each sentient being, arose from his resting in order to accomplish their ultimate benefit and happiness. He sat upright in the cross-legged posture. At that moment his body color shone brilliantly and radiantly, luminous as refined gold. His face was supremely beautiful, like the full moon. His body, utterly clear and pure, without the slightest stain or turbidity, emitted great rays of light that filled the entire expanse of space. With light far surpassing a hundred thousand suns, he illuminated all sentient beings in the buddha-realms in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, bestowing upon them the radiance of great primordial wisdom, and completely dispelling the darkness of ignorance. Moreover, he established hundreds of thousands of ten millions of sentient beings in the irreversible awakening mind.

At that moment, the Blessed One, undaunted like the king of lions, his body fully adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and the eighty minor marks of excellence, emanated from each pore of his body a single lotus. Each of those lotuses had a thousand petals. The petals themselves were of gold, the stalks of beryl, the anthers of vajra, and the base of crystal, and each lotus was as wide as a chariot wheel. From each of those lotuses there arose lights of many colors: blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and the color of crystal. These lights, one by one, reached the Avīci great hell, the hell of Perception, the hell of Black Lines, the hell of Assembly, the great hell of Wailing, the great hell of Great Wailing, the hell of Burning, and the hell of Intense Burning. The sentient beings born in these eight hells were being perpetually tormented by manifold sufferings — burning, boiling, scorching smoke, and being beaten with hammers, and the like — but the moment those lights touched them, all those sufferings were utterly and completely purified without remainder, and they came to experience profound bliss and a most refreshing coolness.

From those rays of light there rang out this sound, proclaiming the essence of what the Tathāgata had taught with intention: "O sentient beings, each and every one of you possesses the nature of a buddha!" Upon hearing those words, those sentient beings immediately passed from that life and were reborn as gods in the higher realms or as humans.

As for the eight cold hells, these are as follows:

The hell of Apāpa, the hell of Atata, the hell of Alala, the hell of Aṭaṭa, the hell of Utpala, the hell of Paduma, the hell of Kumuda, and the hell of Puṇḍarīka. The sentient beings born in these places experience constant and tremendous suffering: their bodies are split apart, shattered, and cut into pieces. Yet the moment those rays of light touched them, all that suffering was utterly and completely purified without remainder. They were warmed and soothed, and from those rays of light there rang out this sound, proclaiming the essence of what the Tathāgata had taught with intention: "O sentient beings, each and every one of you possesses the nature of a buddha!" Upon hearing those words, those sentient beings immediately passed from that life and were reborn as gods in the higher realms or as humans.

At that very time, all the hells of the sentient beings throughout this Jambudvīpa and throughout all the other world-systems became utterly empty, and there was no more experience of suffering — with the sole exception of those who had reviled the vast sūtras of the Great Vehicle.

As for those beings born in the realm of hungry ghosts (pretas), tormented by hunger and thirst, their bodies wrapped and ensnared by their own tangled hair, who for hundreds and thousands of years had not even heard the word "water" — the moment those rays of light touched them, they were freed from the torment of hunger and thirst. And from those rays of light there rang out this sound, proclaiming the essence of what the Tathāgata had taught with intention: "O sentient beings, each and every one of you possesses the nature of a buddha!" Upon hearing those words, those sentient beings passed from that life and were immediately reborn as gods in the higher realms or as humans, and the realm of hungry ghosts too became utterly empty — with the sole exception of those who had reviled the vast sūtras of the Great Vehicle.

As for the sentient beings born in the animal realm, preying upon one another, devouring and harming each other — the moment those rays of light touched them, their minds of evil were pacified. And from those rays of light there rang out this sound, proclaiming the essence of what the Tathāgata had taught: "O sentient beings, each and every one of you possesses the nature of a buddha!" Upon hearing those words, those sentient beings passed from that life and were immediately reborn as gods or as humans.

The Noble Great Sūtra of the Utter Passing into Nirvāṇa, the Fifteenth Section.

At that very time, the animal realm too became utterly empty — with the sole exception of those who had reviled the sacred Dharma.

Upon every single lotus flower there sat a buddha, each surrounded by halos of light extending a fathom in every direction, blazing brilliantly like refined gold, of incomparable beauty and surpassing loveliness, their bodies magnificently adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great being and the eighty minor excellent features. Some of those buddhas sat; some stood; some reclined; some remained at rest; some roared like thunder; some let fall rain; some sent out flashes of lightning; some caused wind to blow; some blazed with their bodies like masses of flame. Some manifested mountains of the seven precious substances, and lotus ponds, and pools, and springs, and rivers, and forests. Some manifested lands, villages, towns, and cities made of the seven precious substances. Some manifested oxen, horses, lions, tigers, wolves, peacocks, garuḍas, and the like. Some manifested a vision of the world as seen by beings dwelling in Jambudvīpa, filled with nothing but hells, animals, and hungry ghosts. Some manifested the six successive levels of abode within the desire realm.

Some manifested to the Blessed One the many faults of the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases. Some taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. Some manifested dependent origination. Some manifested how all karma and mental afflictions arise from causes and conditions. Some manifested self and no-self. Some manifested the two qualities of suffering and happiness. Some manifested permanence and impermanence. Some manifested purity and impurity. Some Blessed Ones manifested the six perfections to the bodhisattvas. Some manifested the qualities of bodhisattvas. Some manifested the qualities of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Some manifested the qualities of the śrāvakas. Some set forth the single vehicle and taught it. Some manifested the full awakening of the three vehicles. Some Blessed Ones manifested water flowing from the left side of their bodies and fire blazing from the right. Some manifested birth, the going forth into renunciation, the entering upon the essence of awakening, the turning of the wheel of Dharma at the foot of the awakening tree, and the passing into complete nirvāṇa. Some Blessed Ones roared with the lion's roar, and manifested members of their assemblies attaining the first, second, third, and fourth fruits. Some also manifested the immeasurable causes and conditions that lead out from saṃsāra.

At that time, in this Jambudvīpa, all sentient beings who were touched by that light were transformed: the blind came to see, the deaf came to hear, the mute came to speak, the lame became able to walk, the impoverished came to possess wealth and enjoyment, the miserly became capable of generosity, those filled with aversion came to possess a mind of loving-kindness, and those without faith came to have faith. In this way, throughout all the world-systems, there was not even a single sentient being engaged in non-virtuous conduct — with the sole exception of those possessed of wrong craving.

At that time all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, great serpents, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, humans, and non-humans, with one voice spoke these words: "Most excellent! Most excellent! The peerless Blessed One acts for the benefit and happiness of all — most excellent!" Having thus spoken, they rejoiced and were filled with delight, and some sang songs, some danced, some stirred their limbs, and scattered before the buddha and the Saṅgha manifold varieties of flowers — flowers of divine substance: utpala flowers of divine substance, kumuda flowers of divine substance, lotus flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, māndārava flowers of divine substance, great māndārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, great mañjūṣaka flowers, sandalwood and great sandalwood, lochanī and great lochanī, fragrant flowers and great fragrant flowers, delightful flowers and greatly delightful flowers, joy-inspiring flowers and greatly joy-inspiring flowers, beautiful flowers and supremely beautiful flowers. They also scattered in abundance many divine incenses — divine liquid incense, aloeswood, sandalwood, saffron, compounded incense, ocean-shore heaped incense, and others. They offered furthermore divine banners of precious jewels, pennants, and parasols; and also divine musical instruments — flutes, lutes with many strings, lutes with nine strings,

— and drums and other instruments — they made offerings in abundance, and then, in the presence of the buddha, they spoke these verses:

We bow down to you with earnest, joyful effort,
to the supreme among bipeds, perfectly and completely awakened without superior,
whom even the retinue of gods and humans cannot fathom.
You, Gautama, bull among the herd, have realized it utterly.

In ages past, for our sake, O Blessed One,
you performed austerities for immeasurable eons.
For what reason, having wholeheartedly committed yourself,
do you now intend to pass beyond sorrow in complete nirvāṇa?

The innermost secret of the Tathāgata —
all beings throughout every realm know it not.
Because of this, it is supremely difficult to arise.
They revolve throughout saṃsāra and fall into the lower realms.

Even the arhats proclaimed by the Blessed One —
all of them too enter into nirvāṇa.
So who among childish, base people will come to understand
the profound domain in which buddhas move?

Yet teach the Dharma, rich and sweet, to all beings,
for the sake of clearing away the afflictions of all beings.
Whoever tastes these nectars
shall never again take on birth, aging, sickness, or death.

The Blessed One has thoroughly healed
countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings,
those utterly tormented and afflicted by illness —
every last one, leaving none behind.

Because the Blessed One long ago abandoned sickness,
you have become the seventh among the final buddhas.
Here today, having rained down the Dharma everywhere,
moisten in us the seeds of virtue.

Thus the retinue of gods, humans, and all the rest
spoke these words and fell silent.

When these verses were offered, all the buddhas dwelling upon their lotus thrones, from Jambudvīpa to the realm of purity, heard them all.

Then the Blessed One praised the bodhisattva Kāśyapa, saying: "Excellent! Excellent!" And he continued: "Son of good family, because you possess such profoundly deep primordial wisdom, no māra and no tīrthika is able to destroy you. Son of good family, dwelling in such perfect ease as you do, you cannot be shaken by the winds of any wrong view. Son of good family, the analytical insight and confidence you have attained is such that, through having made offerings to immeasurable past blessed buddhas as numerous as the grains of sand in the Ganges, you came to ask these very questions of Tathāgatas, arhats, fully and completely awakened buddhas. Son of good family, throughout immeasurable, boundless, incalculable eons, over tens of millions of hundreds of thousands of eons, I was so weary from being separated from illness in its very substance that I utterly abandoned lying down in sleep.

"Kāśyapa, in a past era beyond immeasurable and incalculable eons, at that time there was a fully and completely awakened buddha, an arhat, a Tathāgata by the name Unsurpassed Victor — endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer and guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a blessed buddha — who appeared in the world and, for the śrāvakas, expounded at length this sūtra collection of the Great Vehicle, the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, opening it up, teaching it, and making its meaning understood.

"At that time I too had become a śrāvaka of that buddha. I took up this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, reading it, reciting it, penetrating its meaning, copying it into a volume, widely opening and teaching it to others, and engaging in all such activities. That same root of virtue I dedicated to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect awakening.

"Son of good family, from that time until now, I have never experienced falling into the lower realms through the karma of sinful afflictions."

I have never taken on a body born of wrong craving through denigrating the sacred Dharma, nor a body that is stunted, lacking faculties, or hermaphrodite. I have never performed any of the actions without interval: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, destroying a stūpa, creating a schism in the Saṅgha, drawing blood from the body of a buddha with malicious intent, or performing any of the four actions entailing a root downfall. From that time until now, my body and mind have been thoroughly at ease and have never been tormented by suffering. Kāśyapa, truly I am entirely free of all illness. And why is that? Because the Blessed One, the buddha, long ago abandoned all illness completely.

Kāśyapa, ordinary beings, because they do not understand the intended meaning of what was taught in drawing upon the extensively expanded Great Vehicle, think: "The Tathāgata truly has illness." Kāśyapa, although it is said that "the Tathāgata is a lion among human beings," the Tathāgata is not in truth a lion. You should understand that when such words were spoken, they were spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention. Kāśyapa, although it is also said that "the Tathāgata is a great nāga among human beings," I have in truth abandoned all such actions for immeasurable eons.

Kāśyapa, some say that "the Tathāgata is a human being" and others say "the Tathāgata is a god." Yet in truth the Tathāgata is neither human nor god, neither yakṣa nor gandharva, neither asura nor garuḍa, neither kinnara nor great serpent. He is not a self, not a life-force, not a living soul, not a procreative power, not a lord of procreation. He is not something made, nor something unmade. He is not a sentient being, nor a non-sentient being. He is not the Blessed One, not a śrāvaka, not one who speaks, not one who does not speak. You should understand that all such statements were made by the Tathāgata with a specific intention.

Kāśyapa, it is also said that "the Tathāgata is like the ocean" and "the Tathāgata is like Mount Meru." Yet in truth the Tathāgata does not taste of salt, nor is he like a mass of rock. You should understand that such words too were spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention.

Kāśyapa, it is also said that "the Tathāgata is like the puṇḍarīka." Yet in truth the Tathāgata is not a puṇḍarīka. You should understand that this too was spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention.

Kāśyapa, it is also said that "the Tathāgata is like a father and mother." Yet in truth the Tathāgata is not a father and mother. You should understand that this too was spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention.

Kāśyapa, it is also said that "the Tathāgata is a great caravan leader." Yet in truth the Tathāgata is not literally a great caravan leader. You should understand that this too was spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention.

Kāśyapa, it is also said that "the Tathāgata is like a merchant." Yet in truth the Tathāgata is not literally a merchant. You should understand that this too was spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention.

Kāśyapa, it is also said that "the Tathāgata has conquered Māra." Yet in truth the Tathāgata harbors no ill will toward anyone; it was said in that way for the sake of taming those who needed taming. You should understand that this too was spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention.

Kāśyapa, it is also said that "the Tathāgata heals malignant tumors." Yet in truth the Tathāgata is not literally a physician who heals tumors. You should understand that this too was spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention.

Kāśyapa, as I have already taught above —

Any son or daughter of good family who has thoroughly purified the actions of body, speech, and mind — even though they may have friends and companions at the final hour of death, if their body is burned in fire, or cast into water or into a charnel ground, and eaten by foxes, dogs, wolves, and the like, nevertheless their consciousness will take birth in the higher realms. Thus their mind has neither gone nor come, nor is there any place to which it has departed. It is simply a continuum of successive moments that are similar to one another, before and after; there is no separation. This is what was said, and you should understand that it too was spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention.

Kāśyapa, in the same way, when it is said "I am now ill" — that too was spoken by the Tathāgata with a specific intention. Therefore, since one who holds a view of a real self is afflicted with self-conceit, I directed Mañjuśrī to teach the Dharma to the four assemblies.

Kāśyapa, in truth the Tathāgata, the fully and perfectly awakened buddha, does not fall ill. He does not lie down on his right side, and he does not pass away into nirvāṇa at the end. Kāśyapa, this great parinirvāṇa is a profoundly deep meditative absorption of the buddhas; it does not lie within the sphere of activity of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Kāśyapa, you asked me earlier: "Why does the Tathāgata sleep and not rise? Why does he not take food? Why does he not give instructions to the assembly, or display the activities of livelihood?" Kāśyapa, it is like this: in space itself there is no sitting and no standing, no desire for food or drink, no giving of instructions to the assembly, no display of the activities of livelihood. There is no coming, no going, no birth, no cessation, no aging, no youth, no arising, no passing away, no speaking, no walking, no liberation, no bondage. There is no utterance of "self," no utterance of "other," no liberation of self, no liberation of other, no wellness, no illness.

Son of good family, the Blessed One, the buddha, is likewise: being like space, how could there be suffering through sickness?

Kāśyapa, in the world there are three kinds of illness in persons that are exceedingly difficult to cure. What are they? Disparagement of the Great Vehicle, commission of the five heinous crimes (anantarya), and holding perverted craving. These three kinds of illness are exceedingly difficult to cure in the world; śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas alike are unable to cure them.

Son of good family, consider, by way of example, an illness that is certainly fatal and difficult to heal: whether or not there is a nurse and wish-fulfilling medicine, the illness is such that it definitely cannot be cured, and the person will assuredly die.

Son of good family, those three kinds of persons are similar to that. Even if a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a bodhisattva teaches the Dharma or does not teach it, those persons will not generate the awakening mind directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Without having heard the Dharma, those who would generate the awakening mind cannot be led to generate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Kāśyapa, consider, by way of example, one whose illness can be healed: if they have a nurse and wish-fulfilling medicine, they will recover. If they lack all three, they will not recover. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are similar to that: if they hear the Dharma from a buddha or bodhisattva, they will immediately generate the awakening mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; without having heard the Dharma they will not generate the awakening mind.

Kāśyapa, consider further the example of a patient who, even though attended by a nurse and having wish-fulfilling medicine —

— does recover nonetheless. Likewise, there is a certain type of person who is similar to that: whether they have met a śrāvaka or not, whether they have met a pratyekabuddha or not, whether they have met a bodhisattva or not, whether they have met a Tathāgata or not, whether they have heard the Dharma or not — such a person will still attain manifest, unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Here is an example: if any person — for their own sake or for another's sake, out of fear, or for gain and fame, or out of deceitfulness, or with intent to deceive others — were to write out this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's Great Nirvāṇa, or have it copied, or carry it, or hold it, or read it, or recite it, or venerate it with reverence, or teach and expound it to others — Kāśyapa, these five types of person engage with this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's Great Nirvāṇa as though it were something defective. The Tathāgata does not do so. What are the five? They are as follows.

The first is the person who has cut off the three fetters of affliction, attained the fruit of stream-entry, and will never again be born in the hell realm, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, but will turn back after at most seven lives among gods and humans, and having cut off all suffering will enter nirvāṇa. Kāśyapa, this is called the first person who engages faultily. After eighty thousand future aeons have passed, they will attain manifest, unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Kāśyapa, the second is the person who has cut off those same final three fetters and has further attenuated attachment, aversion, and delusion, attaining the fruit of once-return. They return once, and having completely cut off suffering they enter nirvāṇa. Kāśyapa, this is called the second person who engages faultily. After sixty thousand aeons have passed, they too will attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Kāśyapa, the third person has cut off the final five fetters and, attaining the fruit of non-return, does not return, and having cut off all suffering enters nirvāṇa. This is called the third person who engages faultily. After forty thousand aeons have passed, they will attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Kāśyapa, the fourth person has completely cut off attachment, aversion, and delusion, attaining the fruit of arhatship, and enters nirvāṇa with no afflictions remaining whatsoever. This person, however, is not one who practices in solitude like a rhinoceros horn. This is called the fourth person who engages faultily. After twenty thousand aeons have passed, they will attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Kāśyapa, the fifth person has also completely cut off attachment, aversion, and delusion, attaining the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, and enters nirvāṇa with no afflictions remaining whatsoever. This one practices in solitude, like a rhinoceros horn. This is called the fifth person who engages faultily. After ten thousand aeons have passed, they will attain manifest, unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Kāśyapa, these are called the five persons who engage faultily. The Tathāgata does not do so.

From the noble sūtra, the Great Nirvāṇa.

This concludes the fifth chapter, called "Questioned by the Great Assembly."

Then the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: Sons of good family, great bodhisattvas should take to heart five modes of conduct found in this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle. What are the five? Noble conduct, holy conduct, divine conduct, childish conduct, and faulty conduct. Sons of good family, great bodhisattvas should be extremely diligent in regard to these five modes of conduct. There is yet one further mode of conduct: the conduct of the Tathāgata. That too is this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle.

Kāśyapa, how does a great bodhisattva engage in noble conduct? If a great bodhisattva hears this sūtra of nirvāṇa from a śrāvaka or from a Tathāgata and generates faith, having generated faith they should reflect thus: The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have a path without equal, and there is a great and true Dharma by which the great assembly practices correctly. Furthermore, there exists this vast sūtra of the Great Vehicle. I too should have faith and devotion toward it. In order to seek the sūtra of the Great Vehicle, I should give away entirely my beloved wife and children, my retinue, my dwelling place, gold, silver, and jewels, fine ornaments, flowers, incense, music, male servants and female servants, workers, boys and girls, oxen, horses, chariots, cattle, sheep, birds, dogs, pigs, and the like. And they should further think: A household life lived in utter squalor is like a prison, and all mental afflictions arise from within it. The going forth is exceedingly open, like the sky, and all virtuous qualities arise and grow through it. A householder cannot reach the far shore of a complete livelihood. Therefore, for the sake of living the holy life, I shall shave my head and beard, go forth from home into homelessness, and diligently apply myself to awakening. Having resolved thus, they then definitively go forth and diligently apply themselves to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

When the bodhisattva goes forth in this way, Māra the Evil One is filled with great distress and says: Yet another bodhisattva will contend with me! Sons of good family, how could such a bodhisattva contend with others? At that time the bodhisattva goes to the dwelling place of the Saṅgha and, finding either a Tathāgata or one who lives according to the Tathāgata's way of conduct — whose faculties are pacified, whose mind is gentle and serene, who is completely pure and wholly at peace — approaches them, requests the going forth, shaves their head and beard, and dons the saffron-colored Dharma robe. Having thus gone forth, they guard their moral discipline completely, with conduct that is unimpaired and beautiful. They refrain from transgressions and, even for the slightest offense, they give rise to a mind of fear. Their resolve to guard moral discipline is as firm as a vajra.

Sons of good family, consider a man who enters the ocean holding a plank. From within the ocean a demon (rākṣasa) approaches him and demands the plank. The man hears these words and thinks: If I give away this plank I will certainly sink into the water and die. He then says to the demon: You may kill me if you wish, but this plank is not something I should give away. The demon speaks again:

He did not give it. The demon said: If you will not give the whole, will you not give half? He did not give that either. The demon said again: If you will not give half, then give a third. He did not give that. The demon said again: If you will not give a third, then give a palmful. Still he did not give it. The demon said again: Since you will not give even a palmful, I am tormented by terrible hunger and consumed by suffering — please grant me just a particle of it. The man replied: Your request is not great; it is exceedingly small. Nevertheless, I have not yet crossed the ocean, I do not know whether the far shore is near or far, and if I were to give it to you, I would be left gasping for breath. How would I ever escape the perils of the ocean? I would die in the water.

Sons of good family, the way in which a bodhisattva, a great being, guards and protects moral discipline is exactly like this. Just as the man crossing the ocean guards his plank, so too, when the bodhisattva is protecting moral discipline, the unruly afflictive demons say to him: Believe what we tell you — we are not deceiving you. Even if you have broken all four root defeats, if you keep the rest of the moral discipline, that very cause and that very condition will bring you to the blissfully pleasant nirvāṇa. But the bodhisattva does not follow those words. The afflictive demon says again: If you do not wish to break all four root defeats, then even without keeping the remaining rules of the Saṅgha, that very cause and that very condition will bring you to the blissfully pleasant nirvāṇa. But the bodhisattva does not follow those words. The afflictive demon says again: If you do not wish to break the remaining rules of the Saṅgha, then even if you break the rules concerning the grave offenses, that very cause and that very condition will bring you to the blissfully pleasant nirvāṇa. But the bodhisattva does not follow those words. The afflictive demon says again: If you do not wish to break the rules concerning the grave offenses, then even if you break the rules concerning the transgressions requiring abandonment, that very cause and that very condition will bring you to the blissfully pleasant nirvāṇa. But the bodhisattva does not follow those words. The demon says again: If you do not wish to break the transgressions requiring abandonment in that way, then even if you break the ninety transgressions, that very cause and that very condition will bring you to the blissfully pleasant nirvāṇa. But the bodhisattva does not follow those words. The demon says again: If you do not wish to break the ninety transgressions, then even if you break the rules concerning acts of wrongdoing, that very cause and that very condition will bring you to the blissfully pleasant nirvāṇa. But at that point the bodhisattva thinks to himself: If an act of wrongdoing arises in me and I do not confess and disclose it, I will not reach the far shore of saṃsāra, nor will I attain nirvāṇa. And so, even from youth, the bodhisattva, the great being, guards and holds even acts of wrongdoing with a mind firm as a vajra. The bodhisattva, the great being, is supremely steadfast and unwavering in protecting the four root defeats and in protecting against acts of wrongdoing — these two he holds as one.

If the bodhisattva guards in this way, it is called possessing the five branches of moral discipline. They are as follows: the moral discipline of thoroughly purifying the essential nature of the bodhisattva's actions; the moral discipline of thoroughly purifying the retinues of the earlier and later times; the moral discipline of thoroughly purifying one's thoughts by not entertaining unwholesome thoughts; the moral discipline of thoroughly purifying mindfulness by guarding and maintaining genuine mindfulness; and the moral discipline of dedicating everything toward the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the moral discipline of the bodhisattva, the great being, has two aspects: the moral discipline received as it is correctly taught in the world, and the moral discipline of the true Dharma that is attained. If the bodhisattva attains the moral discipline of the true Dharma, he will never commit any wrongdoing. The moral discipline received as it is correctly taught in the world is obtained through making a formal request and through the performance of the fourfold act.

Furthermore, son of good family, moral discipline also has two aspects: the moral discipline that is weighty by its very nature, and the moral discipline that prevents one from being disgraced by the world. The moral discipline that is weighty by its very nature consists of the four root defeats. The moral discipline that prevents one from being disgraced by the world consists in the following: not engaging in trade; not manipulating measures of volume and weight, and not falsifying scales; not deceiving others; and further, not relying on one's lineage or power to plunder the wealth of others; and further, not binding others with harmful intent and ruining what they have done, rendering it worthless; not sleeping while a lamp or fire is burning; not doing the work of a householder or farmer; not engaging in wrong livelihood and such improper activities; and further, not keeping oxen, horses, carts, cattle, sheep, female elephants, donkeys, birds, dogs, monkeys, peacocks, parrots, Śārikas, cuckoos, parrots of another kind, tigers, leopards, cats, pigs, and other such ferocious and dangerous wild beasts; not keeping or supporting boys, girls, men, women, male slaves, female slaves, or hired workers; and further, not keeping gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, asmagarbha, musāragalva, coral, crystal cloth, necklaces, and the like among precious things; not keeping bronze vessels, earthenware vessels, iron vessels, copper kettles, small vessels, soft cushions, and beyond those, not keeping millet, rice, barley, wheat, beans, sesame, fermented foods, or unfermented foods and the like; always eating only once and not taking food again and again; always going on alms rounds; performing the duties of food service within the Saṅgha; always being content; not going when invited as a houseguest to someone's home; not eating meat; not drinking fermented beverages that cause intoxication; not eating the five types of pungent roots and the like — foods that are pungent and malodorous. Thereby his body is free from malodorous smell, and he will always be honored, attended upon, revered, and praised by all gods and humans who dwell in the world; knowing moderation in food, not keeping leftovers; even when accepting robes given by a donor, accepting only what is fitting; going wherever one goes always inseparably accompanied, like a bird with its wings, by the three Dharma-robes and the alms bowl; and further, not keeping root fruits, trunk fruits, seeds from joints, seeds from nodes, or seed-fruits; and further, not keeping treasure troves of precious things, gold, silver,

not lying on or keeping beds, food, drink, granaries, storehouses, dress robes, or high seats; not sitting on seats made of ox-wool with ivory legs, on golden seats, or on seats furnished with many kinds of upholstery; and further, not keeping any soft seat made of grass; not sitting on ox-wool cushions or horse-hair cushions; not spreading excessively soft robes; not placing two cushions upon a seat; and further, not keeping fine cushions or stuffed cushions; never watching the fighting of yaks, the fighting of horses, the fighting of chariots, the fighting of armies, the fighting of men, the fighting of women, the fighting of bull elephants, the fighting of rams, the fighting of water-buffaloes, the fighting of birds, or the fighting of quail and the like; not watching deliberately staged battles; and further, not listening to the blowing of conch shells, the beating of drums, flutes, lutes, lutes with many strings, gongs, horns, or nine-stringed instruments and the like — save for music offered in worship to the buddhas; not playing or watching games such as throwing cowry shells, casting dice, the lion-game with forfeit pieces, spreading ox-wool fleeces, spinning tops, board games, ball games, stone-throwing, chess, and all manner of diversion games; never reading omens or signs — omens of the hand, the foot, the face, or the eyes; not using the fingernail as a mirror; not making incisions on grass, sticks, pots, or skulls for the sake of divination and signs; not gazing at stars and the like, except for the purpose of warding off sleep; not acting as a royal messenger, carrying words from this side to the far side and words from the far side to this side for the sake of royal messages; not living crookedly through cunning and deceit; and further, not speaking of talk of kings, ministers, thieves, enemies, food, drink, regions, famine, dangers, happiness, and the like.

Sons of good family, these are called the moral discipline of a bodhisattva, a great being, that is not to be censured by the world.

Sons of good family, for a bodhisattva, a great being, there is no distinction between keeping moral discipline that has been formally established and keeping moral discipline that is weighty by its very intrinsic nature.

Sons of good family, when a bodhisattva, a great being, thus perfectly guards moral discipline, he makes this solemn vow: "Better that this body of mine leap into a deep pit of blazing fire than that I, by violating the moral discipline established by the buddhas of the past, the future, and the present, commit an act of unchastity toward a daughter of the warrior class, a brahmin woman, or a laywoman." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow: "Better that my body be wrapped and bound by iron heated to a fierce blaze than that this body, its moral discipline broken, should ever put on a robe given in faith by a generous donor." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that a lump of molten iron be swallowed down my throat than that this mouth, its moral discipline broken, should ever eat food given in faith by a generous donor." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that this body of mine lie upon iron heated to a fierce blaze than that this body, its moral discipline broken, should ever lie upon a seat or bed given in faith by a generous donor." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that three hundred spear-blades be thrust into this body of mine than that

this body, its moral discipline broken, should ever drink medicine for illness given in faith by a generous donor." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that this body of mine be boiled in a great cauldron of intensely boiling copper than that this body, its moral discipline broken, should ever dwell in a residence built in faith by a generous donor." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that this body be beaten from head to foot with iron hammers until it is reduced to dust than that this body, its moral discipline broken, should ever desire the reverence and homage of nobles, brahmins, and householders." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that both eyes be gouged out with intensely hot iron skewers than that I should, with a mind of attachment, gaze upon the beautiful form of another." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that the faculty of hearing be pierced through with many needles than that I should, with a mind accompanied by attachment, listen to pleasant sounds." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that the nose be cut off with a sharp blade than that I should, with a mind of attachment, smell a sweet fragrance." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that the tongue be cut off with a sharp blade than that I should, with a mind of attachment, be attached to a delicious taste." Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, also makes this solemn vow in these words: "Better that this body of mine be hacked limb from limb with a sharp axe than that I should, with a mind accompanied by attachment, be attached to the many objects of touch."

Why is this so? Because by that cause and through those conditions, yogins are reborn in the hells, in the animal realm, and in the world of the Lord of Death.

Kāśyapa, thus it is that the bodhisattva, the great being, is said to guard moral discipline completely.

When the bodhisattva, the great being, has guarded moral discipline with great care, he makes this aspiration on behalf of all sentient beings: "By this cause and through these conditions, may all sentient beings come to possess moral discipline that is most carefully guarded, moral discipline that is perfectly pure, moral discipline that is supremely wholesome, moral discipline that is unimpaired, moral discipline that is irreversible, moral discipline of the Great Vehicle, moral discipline of irreversibility, moral discipline united with the mind, moral discipline carried to its completion, and moral discipline that is the perfection fulfilled."

Sons of good family, when the bodhisattva, the great being, thus thoroughly purifies and refines moral discipline, he comes to abide from the very outset on the unshakeable ground. Why is it called the unshakeable ground? Because when the bodhisattva abides on the unshakeable ground, he cannot be shaken, cannot fall, cannot be turned back, and cannot be destroyed.

Sons of good family, consider, for example, Mount Meru, the king of mountains: even the most violent and fierce gale-force winds cannot shake it, cannot topple it, cannot destroy it. So too it is with the bodhisattva, the great being, who abides there: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and objects of touch cannot shake him; he will not fall into the hells, into the animal realm, or into the world of the Lord of Death; he will not turn back toward the ground of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;

and the winds of the many wrong views cannot shatter him or cause him to live in distorted ways.

Sons of good family, furthermore, "unshakeable" means: he is not shaken by attachment, aversion, or delusion. Furthermore, "he cannot fall" means: he does not fall into the four root defeats. Furthermore, "he cannot be turned back" means: he does not turn back from moral discipline to the household life. Furthermore, "he cannot be destroyed" means: he is not shattered by contradicting the sūtras of the Great Vehicle.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, is not shaken by the māra of the afflictions. He will not fall through the māra of the aggregates. Although, from the very heart of the path up to the moment of awakening, the māra who is the son of the gods is present, he will not turn back from unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And he will not be destroyed by the māra of the Lord of Death.

Sons of good family, in this way the bodhisattva, the great being, is called one who applies himself with great diligence to the noble conduct. Sons of good family, why is it called "noble conduct"? It is called noble conduct because it is the conduct practiced by buddhas and bodhisattvas. Why are buddhas and bodhisattvas called noble ones (āryas)? Because they and those like them are endowed with noble qualities, and because they have realized that all phenomena are empty of essential nature. Therefore they are called noble ones. Furthermore, they are called noble ones because they are endowed with noble moral discipline. They are called noble ones because they are endowed with noble meditative absorption and wisdom. Furthermore, they are called noble ones because they are endowed with the seven noble wealths: the wealth of faith, moral discipline, inner restraint, decorum, learning, wisdom, and equanimity. Furthermore, they are called noble ones because they are endowed with the seven limbs of the noble path. Therefore it is called noble conduct.

Sons of good family, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, who practices noble conduct examines this body from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet, and sees it as filled with nothing but impurity and filth: hair of the head, nails, teeth, unclean foulness, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, bile, intestines, stomach, what has been digested and what has not, the two vessels for feces and urine both large and small, saliva, mucus, tears, the brain, the skull, pus, blood, blood-vessels, and so on — he sees it as filled with nothing but impurity.

When the bodhisattva examines this with a one-pointed mind in great detail, he inquires most carefully: "Who is this called 'self'? Where does it reside? Who is this called 'self'?" He then thinks: "Is the bone the self? Or does something other than the bone exist?" At that moment the bodhisattva sets aside skin and flesh and reflects solely upon the bare skeleton. He then thinks: "The colors of the bones too are various — blue, yellow, red, white, like the wings of a dove. Since this is so, the defining mark of bone is also not the self. Why? Because what is called 'self' is not something blue, yellow, red, white, or like the wings of a dove."

When the bodhisattva examines this with such a one-pointed mind in great detail, all attachment to form becomes pacified. He then thinks: "This skeleton too arises through dependent origination: the heel-bone supports the ankle-bone, the ankle-bone supports the shinbone, the shinbone supports the knee,

the knee-bone supports the thigh-bone, the thigh-bone supports the hip-bone, the hip-bone supports the bones of the waist, the bones of the waist support the bones of the spine, the bones of the spine support the bones of the ribs, and again the bones of the spine support the bones of the shoulder-blades, the bones of the shoulder-blades support the bones of the jaw, and the bones of the jaw support the teeth and the skull.

Furthermore, the collar-bone rests upon the bones of the shoulder, the bones of the shoulder rest upon the bones of the upper arm, the bones of the upper arm rest upon the bones of the elbow, the bones of the elbow rest upon the bones of the palm, and the bones of the palm rest upon the bones of the fingers.

In this way, all the bones rest upon and depend upon one another. As the bodhisattva, the great being, examines in this fashion, he comes to understand that all the bones of the body stand each in their own separate place. Upon understanding this so thoroughly, he entirely abandons the three kinds of attachment: attachment to visible form, attachment to what one possesses, and attachment to what is pleasant to the touch.

When the bodhisattva, the great being, contemplates the blue bones, he sees this entire great earth — south, north, east, west, the four intermediate directions, above, and below — as all blue. And just as when contemplating blue, so too with yellow, white, and the color of a dove's wings.

When the bodhisattva, the great being, contemplates in this way, from between his eyebrows rays of light stream forth — blue, yellow, red, white, and like the wings of a dove — and within each ray of that light the bodhisattva, the great being, sees buddhas dwelling. He then inquires and asks of them concerning the causes and conditions through dependent origination by which this impure body comes into being: "This body sits, stands, walks, stays still, bows down, stretches out, looks about, closes the eyes, breathes in and out, weeps, laughs, and comes to feel joy — if there is no master, who is it that moves it thus?" This is what he asks and inquires. And having asked these words, the buddhas who had been dwelling within the light then disappear from sight.

The Noble Great Sūtra of Complete Nirvāṇa, the sixteenth fascicle.

He then thinks: "But might that consciousness be the self? Why have the buddhas not shown me this?" He examines consciousness, and in examining consciousness he finds that consciousness arises and ceases moment by moment, like the current of a river — and so that too is not the self.

He then thinks: "This breath that moves inward and outward is wind, and the characteristic of wind belongs to the four great elements. Among the four great elements, what then is there to be called 'self'? The characteristic of earth is also not the self, and likewise the characteristics of water, fire, and wind are none of them to be called 'self.'"

He then thinks: "In this body there is altogether nothing to be called a 'self.' The various actions that manifest openly arise from the causes and conditions of the gathering and assembling of mind and breath — like something produced by the power of a spell, or like the work of a magician. Moreover, when one bows down, it is like a puppet moved by strings, and sound arises at will. Therefore this body is impure; it is accomplished entirely through depending on an assemblage of causes and conditions — what is there in it to be attached to? And if another were to revile or abuse it, what is there in it to give rise to aversion? This body of mine is wholly filled with thirty-six kinds of impurity — what basis is there for reviling and abusing it? When he hears abuse, he thinks to himself:

"By what sound could one be reviled?" When each and every component of that sound is examined one by one, no reviling is found to exist. As with one component, so too with many — they are just the same. Therefore aversion does not arise.

If the other person then strikes him, he thinks to himself: "From what does this blow arise?" Examining it, he sees that from the hand, the strength, the weapon, and the assemblage of his own body, what is called "a blow" has come about. Why then be angry at the other? It is because my body exists that I have experienced such a thing. Because this body of mine — this body of the five aggregates — exists, it has come to be like this. Just as an arrow comes when there is a target as its condition, my body is like that too: because the body exists, there are blows. If I do not bear this body with patience, the mind will be disturbed. If the mind is disturbed, correct mindfulness will be lost. If correct mindfulness is lost, one will not understand the meaning of virtue and non-virtue. If one does not understand the meaning of virtue and non-virtue, one will engage in blameworthy conduct. Having engaged in blameworthy conduct, one will fall into the hells, into animal births, and into the realm of hungry ghosts.

When the bodhisattva understands it in this way, he will at that time attain the four establishments of mindfulness. By attaining the four establishments of mindfulness, he will come to abide on the ground of supreme forbearance. When that bodhisattva, that great being, abides on that ground in this way, he is patient with attachment, aversion, and delusion. Moreover, he is patient with cold and heat, hunger and thirst, mosquitoes, flies, wind, unpleasant sensations of touch, and all manner of illness; he is patient with harsh words, reviling, abuse, blows, slashing, and cutting — in short, he is patient with everything that brings suffering to body and mind. Therefore this is called abiding on the ground of supreme forbearance.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, until a bodhisattva has come to abide on the immovable ground, when keeping moral discipline in a perfectly pure manner, are there causes and conditions by which the moral discipline might be damaged?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, there are. Until a bodhisattva has come to abide on the immovable ground, there are causes and conditions by which the moral discipline may be damaged."

Kāśyapa, filled with wonder, asked: "Blessed One, what are they?"

The Blessed One then spoke to Kāśyapa: "A bodhisattva, by a certain cause and condition, may damage his own moral discipline — namely, if other persons come to have faith in and cherish a sūtra of the Great Vehicle, holding to it with devotion; if other persons come to read it, recite it, understand it inwardly, write it in book form, and teach it extensively and expound it to others — so long as it reaches the point of establishing them as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening — for that purpose he damages his moral discipline. And at that time the bodhisattva thinks to himself: 'Even if I were to fall into the great unrelenting hell for a full eon, or for the waning of a full eon, that would be acceptable — so long as I can establish that other person as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.' It is for that cause, that condition, that the bodhisattva, the great being, comes to damage pure moral discipline."

At that time, the bodhisattva, the great being Mañjuśrī, youthful in appearance, addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Blessed One, if a bodhisattva damages moral discipline in order to protect and gather someone so that they will not turn back from the awakening mind, there is no occasion for that bodhisattva to fall into the unrelenting hell."

Then the Blessed One spoke to Mañjuśrī: "Excellent! Most excellent! It is just as you have said. I too, long ago in this Jambudvīpa, was born as a great king named Ṛṣi. With deep reverence I had great faith and devotion toward the sūtras of the Great Vehicle, and striving with a mind intent only on virtue, I avoided non-virtuous actions — the heedlessness of envy and miserliness. With speech I continually spoke pleasant words, taught and expounded virtuous Dharma. With body I made myself the support and refuge of the destitute, those without protection and without shelter, and I strove without interruption in generosity. At that time there was no buddha present in the world, no śrāvakas, and no pratyekabuddhas. It was because of my deep devotion to the widely-expounded sūtras of the Great Vehicle that I served a brahmin for twelve years, providing him with whatever requisites he desired.
