After giving him comfort for twelve years, I spoke to those teachers these words: 'O Teacher, you should arouse the mind aimed at unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.' The brahmin replied: 'Great King, the defining mark of awakening is the absence of any characteristic whatsoever, and the sūtras of the Great Vehicle are just the same — Great King, why should one call it "great"? One should say it is equal to space.' O son of good family, at that time, due to my intense devotion to the Great Vehicle, when I heard the brahmin speaking those words disparaging the extensive teaching, I killed that brahmin. O son of good family, because of that cause and that condition, I have not been born in the hells from that time until now. O son of good family, such is the immeasurable power and strength of protecting and guarding the sūtras of the Great Vehicle.

"Kāśyapa, there is also this: the noble practice is as follows — it is the Four Noble Truths. And what are they? Suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path — these are called the Four Noble Truths.

"Kāśyapa, what is called suffering has the defining mark of being exhausting and tormenting. The origin of suffering has the defining mark of arising and proliferating. Cessation has the defining mark of peaceful stopping. The path has the defining mark of the Great Vehicle.

"O son of good family, further: suffering has the defining mark of being manifest and apparent. The origin of suffering has the defining mark of transformation. Cessation has the defining mark of elimination. The path has the defining mark of transformation through elimination.

"O son of good family, further: suffering has three aspects — the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change. The origin of suffering is the twenty-five modes of existence. Cessation is the cessation of those twenty-five. The path is the cultivation of moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom.

"O son of good family, further: among defiled phenomena (āsrava) there are two kinds — those with cause and those with result. Among undefiled phenomena there are likewise two kinds — those with cause and those with result. Defiled phenomena with result are called suffering. Defiled phenomena with cause are called the origin. Undefiled phenomena with result are called cessation. Undefiled phenomena with cause are called the path.

"O son of good family, further: these eight kinds of defining marks are called suffering — namely, the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is desired, the suffering of encountering what is hated,"

the suffering of not obtaining what is desired, and the five aggregates — these are suffering. Whatever produces these eight kinds of suffering is called the origin. The absence of any abiding place of these phenomena is called cessation. The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, and great compassion — these are called the path.

O son of good family, what is called birth is the defining mark of arising, and it has five aspects: first arising, final cessation, growth and coming into being, birth from a womb, and birth from a lineage.

What is called aging has two aspects: aging moment by moment, and aging at the end. Again there are two aspects: aging through arising and growth, and aging through cessation and disintegration — these are called aging.

What is called illness? Illness arises from the unequal and toxic imbalance of the four great elements, and it has two aspects: illness of the body and illness of the mind. Illness of the body also has five aspects: illness arising from phlegm, illness arising from wind, illness arising from bile, illness arising from their combination, and illness arising from carelessness.

Illness arising from carelessness also has four aspects: acting beyond one's capacity while in a weakened state, falling into a precipice, being struck by stones, sticks, or weapons, and being seized by non-human beings.

Illness of the mind also has four aspects: illness arising from extreme joy, illness arising from fear and terror, illness arising from grief, and illness arising from delusion.

O son of good family, furthermore, illness of the body and illness of the mind each have three aspects: karmic maturation, failure to abandon the remedies for wrongdoing, and illness arising from the time and season. From these and other such causes, conditions, designations, and distinct kinds, illness arises in varied forms. Illness arising from causes and conditions consists of ailments such as disorders of wind and so forth. Designated illness refers to madness of mind, lung disease, shortness of breath, nausea, palpitations of the heart, and dysentery from fever. Illness of distinct kinds consists of illness of the head, illness of the eyes, and illness of the limbs and so forth — these are called illness.

What is called death? It is the separation from this very body that one has taken. Separation from the body one has taken also has two aspects: death through the exhaustion of one's lifespan, and death through external conditions.

Death through the exhaustion of one's lifespan also has three aspects: lifespan exhausted but merit not exhausted, merit exhausted but lifespan not exhausted, and both merit and lifespan exhausted together.

Death through external conditions also has three aspects: dying by taking one's own life through improper means, being killed by another adversary, and dying through a combination of both.

Furthermore, there are also three aspects of death: dying through heedlessness, dying through the breaking of moral discipline, and dying through the destruction of the faculty of life.

What is dying through heedlessness? Repudiating the vast Mahāyāna Perfection of Wisdom is called dying through heedlessness. What is dying through the breaking of moral discipline? Transgressing the moral discipline established by the buddhas of the past, the future, and those abiding in the present is called dying through the breaking of moral discipline. What is dying through the destruction of the faculty of life? Separation from the body of the five aggregates is called dying through the destruction of the faculty of life. These are called the great suffering of death.

What is the suffering of separation from what is desired? It is the breakdown, separation, or dispersal of that which is pleasing and desired, whether it be a faculty, a parting, or a scattering. Separation from pleasing and desired things also has two aspects: the dissolution of the five aggregates among humans, and the separation from the five aggregates among the gods. Thus, for gods and humans alike, the five aggregates of desire are, when analyzed, measureless. In brief, all of these are called the suffering of separation from what is desired.

What is the suffering of encountering what is hated? It is the coming together and meeting with that which is unpleasant and unwanted. Encountering what is unpleasant and unwanted has three aspects: rebirth in the hells, rebirth as a hungry ghost, and rebirth as an animal. Although these three lower destinies, when analyzed in detail, are measureless, in brief all of them are called the suffering of encountering what is hated.

What is the suffering of not obtaining what is desired? The suffering of not obtaining what is desired also has two aspects: not obtaining what is desired despite having grounds for hope, and performing great effort yet failing to accomplish the intended result. These are called the suffering of not obtaining what is desired.

What is the suffering of the five aggregates? The suffering of the five aggregates is: the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is desired, and the suffering of encountering what is hated. These are called the suffering of the five aggregates.

O Kāśyapa, for beings born into existence, there are thus seven kinds of suffering, from the suffering of aging through the suffering of the five aggregates. O Kāśyapa, decline and illness are not present in all beings — they are certainly not found in buddhas or among the gods, and even among humans they are not universal: some have them and some do not. O Kāśyapa, there is no being who has taken a body within the three realms who does not undergo birth; aging alone is not universal. Therefore, birth is the root of all of it. O Kāśyapa, because the sentient beings of the world are obscured by wrong views, they desire and are attached to birth, yet do not desire aging and death. O Kāśyapa, a bodhisattva is not like this: from the very moment of birth the bodhisattva recognizes it as a fault.

O Kāśyapa, consider this analogy. A beautiful woman arrives at someone's house — lovely in appearance, of graceful and pleasing manner, adorned with fine ornaments. The householder asks her, "Woman, what is your name?" The woman replies, "I am the auspicious Great Goddess (Śrī Mahādevī)." The householder asks again, "If you were to come to my house, what would you be able to bring?" The woman replies, "Wherever I go, I bring the householder gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl, coral, emerald, asmagarbha, musāgalbha, and many other kinds of precious things, as well as sheep, oxen, horses, chariots, male servants, female servants, and working people." Upon hearing these words, the householder is overcome with delight and joy, and he says, "By the ripening of our merit, O goddess, you have come to my house," and he worships her with incense and flowers, bowing to her with reverence and respect.

At that very gate, another woman also arrives — exceedingly ugly, wearing filthy, soiled clothing, with rough skin and a terrible complexion. The householder asks this woman, "What is your name?" The woman replies, "My name is Black Ears." He asks, "Why are you called Black Ears?" The woman replies, "Wherever I go, all the wealth, riches, and possessions in that household disappear — that is why I am called Black Ears." Upon hearing this, the householder seizes a sharp weapon and says to her, "Be gone at once! If you do not leave, I will kill you!" The woman replies, "You are extremely foolish and witless." The householder says, "Why am I foolish and witless?" The woman replies, "The one now residing in your house is my younger sister. Wherever either of us goes, the other must accompany her."

"If you wish to drive her away, then drive out the one who is presently inside your house as well." The man went back inside and said to the goddess Auspiciousness, "Is there a woman at the gate who claims to be the goddess's younger sister?" Auspiciousness replied, "She is indeed my younger sister. Wherever I go, she accompanies me — we have never been parted. Wherever I go, I delight in what is good and do good; I bring benefit. But my younger sister always delights in harm and does harm; she brings injury. If you desire me, you must desire her as well. If you show respect to me, you must show respect to her too." Upon hearing these words, the householder said, "If the two of you come as a pair — one good and one harmful — then neither of you is needed by me. Go now wherever you please." And so both women departed and left for elsewhere, and the householder was filled with utter joy and delight.

Then those two women went together to the home of a poor man, and the poor man was overjoyed to see them, and he said to both of them, "From this day forward, may you two always remain in my home." Auspiciousness replied, "We were driven away by another just now — so why do you ask us both to stay?" The poor man replied, "Please be gracious to me. I will attend to this one too for your sake — that is why I beg you both to stay."

The bodhisattva (bodhisattva), the great being, Kāśyapa, is likewise — he has no desire to be born among the gods. For birth is followed by old age, sickness, and death, and therefore he rejects both and has no desire for them. Childish and base people, not knowing the many faults of old age, sickness, death, and the like, become attached to both birth and death in their ignorance of these two failings.

Noble son, there is yet another analogy. A young brahmin boy, oppressed by hunger and on the verge of starvation, found a mango fruit inside a pile of vomit and took it. Wise and learned people who saw this rebuked him, saying, "You are of a very pure brahmin lineage — why are you taking a mango fruit from a pile of vomit?" The brahmin boy, ashamed, replied, "I certainly had no intention of eating it as it was — I meant to wash it and then throw it away." The wise man said, "You are utterly foolish. If you meant to throw it away, it was wrong to pick it up in the first place."

Noble son, the bodhisattva, the great being, is just the same — he neither takes up the side of birth nor rejects it, just as the wise man rebuked that boy. Base and childish folk desire birth but do not desire death — just like the boy who took the fruit and then threw it away.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another analogy. At a crossroads, a man was selling food in a fine vessel — food that was fragrant, cool, and of excellent color. A traveler who had come from a long distance, hungry, weary, and exhausted, drew near upon seeing this fragrant, cool, and beautifully colored food, and asked, "What is this?" The owner of the food replied, "This is the finest of foods — fragrant, cool, and of excellent color. Whoever eats it will gain both complexion and strength, hunger and thirst will be dispelled, and he will even come to behold the gods. There is, however, one single flaw: he will die." Upon hearing this, the man thought, "I do want the complexion and strength, but I do not want to see the gods and then die," and he said aloud, "If eating this food means I will die, what would be the point of buying and eating it?" The owner of the food replied, "No one with wisdom and discernment would buy it."

"The foolish and witless pay me a great price and buy it to eat. Son of good family, the great bodhisattva is just the same: he desires neither birth as a god, nor the fine complexion, strength, or sight of the gods that come with it. Why is that? Because one is not liberated from the multitude of sufferings. The foolish and low-born, not seeing the faults of aging, sickness, and death, become attached to every form of birth.

Son of good family, here is another illustration: a poisonous plant kills with its root, kills with its trunk, and kills with its bark, its leaves, its flowers, and its fruits as well. Son of good family, it is the same with taking up the five aggregates at birth in any of the twenty-five modes of existence: all of them lead to death.

Kāśyapa, here is another illustration: vomit is equally foul whether there is much of it or little. Son of good family, birth is just the same: whether one lives eighty thousand years or manages ten, it is all equally suffering.

Son of good family, here is yet another illustration: at the edge of a terrible and terrifying precipice, covered over with grass, there lies an abundance of ambrosia. Were one to eat it, one might live for a thousand divine years, and all one's diseases would be completely cured and one would dwell in bliss. Yet a foolish and low-born child, attached to the taste, does not know that beneath his very feet there lies a dreadful abyss. He reaches out to take it, slips a foot, falls into the chasm, and dies. The wise and discerning, knowing this, do not go there. Son of good family, the great bodhisattva is just the same: if he does not desire even the excellent divine food of the gods, what need is there to speak of human food? If the foolish and low-born can endure eating iron balls in the hells, what need is there to speak of the fine food of gods and humans?

Kāśyapa, through these illustrations and countless and immeasurable further analogies one should understand that this birth is great suffering.

Kāśyapa, thus it is that the great bodhisattva's understanding of the suffering of birth, from the Mahāyāna sūtra of the complete nirvāṇa (Skt. mahāparinirvāṇasūtra), is to be understood in this way.

Kāśyapa, how then does the great bodhisattva understand the suffering of aging from the Mahāyāna sūtra of the complete nirvāṇa? Aging is something repulsive and decaying; it robs one of valor and skill; it renders inappropriate all mindfulness, effort, retention, youthful bloom, perfect ease, pride, and proud bearing, and all enjoyment of pleasure at will; and in their place it brings indolence, great sluggishness, and contempt from others.

Kāśyapa, consider this illustration: a small pond full of lotuses in full bloom, their petals wide open, their vivid colors beautiful and pleasing to everyone's eye and desired by all — if hail falls, all are broken and made ugly. Son of good family, aging is just the same: it renders ugly the fine complexion of youth.

Kāśyapa, here is another illustration: a king has a wise and intelligent minister, skilled in the strategies of the enemy. A certain vassal king rebels against the king and will not listen. The king commands that minister, "Go and capture that vassal king," and the minister goes and brings him back. Aging is just the same: it seizes upon youth and delivers it to the king who is the Lord of Death.

Kāśyapa, here is another illustration: when the axle-beam of a chariot breaks, it can no longer be used. Aging is just the same: it renders one useless for anything whatsoever.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: in the home of a wealthy householder there is an abundance of gold, silver, lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya), coral, aśmagarbha, and musāragalva — and a thief, or..."

— many robbers arrive and plunder everything, leaving the house utterly empty. Noble son, it is just the same with the fine bloom of youth: the enemy that is aging perpetually steals it and carries it away.

Noble son, here is yet another illustration: a poor man longs for fine food and soft clothing, yet finds himself forever unable to obtain them. Noble son, old age is just the same: one may wish to enjoy at will the pleasures of the five desirable qualities, yet one is unable to do so.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: a tortoise sitting on dry ground thinks constantly of water. Noble son, it is just the same with a human being: withered and bent by old age, the mind dwells constantly on the remembered pleasures of the five desirable qualities of youth.

Noble son, here is yet another illustration: in the autumn, a fully opened lotus blossom is desired and delighted in by all; but once it has withered and turned yellow, no one desires it any longer. Noble son, it is just the same with the fine bloom of youth: while it is desired and cherished by all, once it has turned to old age it no longer pleases anyone, and no one desires it.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: the pressed-out stalk of sugarcane is utterly tasteless. Noble son, the fine bloom of youth is just the same: once it is covered over and ruined by the decay of old age, three flavors are lost — the flavor of going forth into renunciation, the flavor of study and recitation, and the flavor of meditative concentration. All three are gone.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: a full moon is exceedingly bright and clear by night, but not so by day. Noble son, it is just the same with a human being: in youth one is fair and beautiful, but in old age one is withered and haggard.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: suppose there is a king who governs his realm by righteous Dharma, who is free of deceit and trickery, who is endowed with compassion and generosity. He is attacked by the armies of another land and wanders, driven away to a foreign country. Everyone who encounters him feels affection and says, "This great king formerly governed his realm by righteous Dharma, and there was not a single one who was displeased. Why has he come to wander like this?" Noble son, it is just the same with a human being: weakened and diminished by the infirmity of old age, one longs for all that one did in the days of youth.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: the very essence of an oil lamp depends upon its oil; when the oil is exhausted, it does not last long. Noble son, it is just the same with a human being: one depends upon one's youth. When youth is spent, the essence of the infirmity of old age does not last long.

Noble son, here is yet another illustration: a dried-up riverbank is of no benefit to humans, to non-humans, to birds, to beasts of prey, or to any other creature. Noble son, it is just the same with a human being: once withered by old age, one becomes of no benefit whatsoever for any task.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: a tree growing on the edge of an eroded cliff, the moment a fierce wind rises, will inevitably fall. Noble son, it is just the same with a human being: the edge on which old age stands is close to the precipice, and when the wind of death arises, one does not remain long.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: when the main axle-beam of a chariot breaks, it cannot bear a heavy load. Noble son, old age is just the same: one is unable to hold fast to all virtuous qualities.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: a small seedling that has not yet grown strong is scorned by everyone. Noble son, old age is just the same: one is scorned by everyone.

Kāśyapa, these illustrations and...

Furthermore, through illustrations beyond measure and beyond counting, one should understand that old age is a great suffering. Kāśyapa, all of this is called "the understanding of the suffering of old age" when a great bodhisattva (bodhisattva mahāsattva) practices this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa.

Kāśyapa, how then does a great bodhisattva, in practicing this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa, understand the suffering of illness? Illness is that which destroys all things that are pleasant and agreeable. For example, when hail falls, it destroys all the crops and renders them worthless.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: if a person has a bitter enemy, he is forever in grief and in fear. Noble son, all sentient beings are just the same: they are forever in grief and in fear, terrified by the suffering of illness.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: there is a man of handsome and excellent appearance. A queen, overcome with desire, summons him and sleeps with him. When the king discovers this, he has the man seized, puts out one of his eyes, cuts off one of his ears, and cuts off one of his hands. From that moment on, the man's handsome appearance, which he had before, is destroyed, and no one wants him any longer. Noble son, a human being is just the same: though he may have limbs, eyes, and ears, once he is afflicted and tormented by the suffering of illness, no one wants him any longer.

Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: the plantain tree, the bamboo, the reed, and the mule — when they bear fruit or offspring, they die. Noble son, a human being is just the same: where there is illness, there is death.

Noble son, here is yet another illustration: a wheel-turning king (cakravartin) follows behind a minister who commands the armies, walking in the wake of one who has gone before. The king of fish, the king of bees, the king of conch-shells, the lord of the herd, and the caravan leader — the rest follow behind whoever has gone first, and they do not part from him. Noble son, the wheel-turning king of death is just the same: it forever follows behind illness as its minister and never parts from it. Just as the fish, the bees, the conch, the lord of the herd, and the caravan leader are followed by their retinues, so too does the wheel of death forever pursue in the wake of illness as its king, and never parts from it.

Kāśyapa, the causes and conditions of illness are these: suffering, disturbance, the grief of being exhausted, lamentation, and the causing of discomfort to body and mind. It is also called "being threatened by a merciless enemy," "the tearing apart of what had been bound together," "the destruction of the bridge," "the robbing of right-mindfulness," and furthermore "that which ruins the fair complexion, the strength, and the happiness of youth." It scorches and burns the body and mind, leaving behind neither shame nor decency. Through these illustrations and through countless other illustrations beyond measure and beyond counting, one should understand that the suffering of illness is a great suffering. Kāśyapa, this is called "the understanding of the suffering of illness" when a great bodhisattva practices this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa.

Kāśyapa, how then does a great bodhisattva, in practicing this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa, understand the suffering of death? It is as follows: death is that which severs and annihilates. Kāśyapa, it is like this: when the cosmic fire (kalpa-fire) arises, it burns up everything except the second meditative concentration.

Noble son, death annihilates the mind of all beings entirely — save those great bodhisattvas who abide in the power and strength of practicing this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa. Kāśyapa, consider this: when the cosmic water-flood arises, it washes away and annihilates everything — except the third meditative concentration. Noble son, the water of death is likewise: it washes away and annihilates all — except those bodhisattvas who abide in this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa. Kāśyapa, consider this: when the cosmic wind-storm arises, it scatters and annihilates everything — except the fourth meditative concentration. Noble son, the wind of death is likewise: it annihilates all — except those bodhisattvas who abide in this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One, saying: "For what reason is the fourth meditative concentration not destroyed by wind, not washed away by water, not burned by fire?"

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Noble son, it is because the fourth meditative concentration is free from all inner and outer faults. Noble son, in the first meditative concentration there is the inner fault of discursive thought, and therefore it is burned by the outer cosmic fire. In the second meditative concentration there is the inner fault of joy, and therefore it is washed away by the outer cosmic water. In the third meditative concentration there is the inner movement of breath, and therefore it is destroyed by the cosmic wind. Noble son, the fourth meditative concentration is free from all inner and outer faults, and therefore the cosmic catastrophes cannot touch it.

"Noble son, a great bodhisattva is likewise: when one abides comfortably in this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa, being free from all inner and outer faults, the king of death cannot touch one.

"Noble son, here is another illustration: the king of garuḍas (the great bird of prey) can devour nāgas, fish, gold, silver, and jewels, and these can be dissolved — but a vajra alone it cannot dissolve. Noble son, the king of the garuḍas of death is likewise: it can devour all sentient beings and dissolve them — but a great bodhisattva who abides in this sūtra of the great and complete nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle it cannot dissolve.

"Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: all the trees and grasses that grow on a riverbank are carried away by a flood and swept all the way to the ocean — except for the willow, because its roots are flexible. Noble son, likewise, all sentient beings flow down into the ocean of saṃsāra — except those great bodhisattvas who abide in this sūtra of the complete nirvāṇa.

"Kāśyapa, here is another illustration: a powerful wrestler can subdue all opponents — wrestlers and the like — but he cannot subdue a great storm-wind. Why? Because there is no antidote for it. Noble son, the powerful wrestler of death is likewise: it can subdue all sentient beings — but it cannot subdue a great bodhisattva who abides in this sūtra of the complete nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle. Why? Because there is no antidote for it.

"Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: enemies who bear hatred and a grudge may draw near through cunning, disguising themselves as if they were intimate friends, following like a shadow and seeking an opportunity to kill — yet if the other party has been forewarned and on guard from the start, they cannot be killed. Noble son, the enemy called death is likewise: it is always seeking an opportunity to kill all sentient beings — but it cannot kill a great bodhisattva who abides in this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa. Why?"

Because the bodhisattva is on guard.

"Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: when a vajra (diamond-thunderbolt) rainstorm falls, it can destroy everything — trees and forests, earth and sand, gravel, grass and rocks, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and all the rest — yet it cannot destroy a true and genuine vajra. Noble son, the rainstorm of death's vajra is likewise: it can annihilate all sentient beings, yet it cannot touch a bodhisattva, firm as a vajra, who abides in this complete nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle.

"Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: the garuḍa bird devours all nāgas, yet it cannot devour one who has gone for refuge to the Three Refuges. Noble son, the garuḍa of death is likewise: though it may devour countless, limitless sentient beings, it cannot touch one who abides in the three doors of liberation — emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

"Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: when one is seized by the deadly serpent called Malanā, even skilled mantra-healers and expert physicians can do nothing. Only one who knows the mantra called Akatasyā can save that person's life. Noble son, when one is seized by the deadly serpent of death, all forms of medical treatment are likewise utterly useless — except for a bodhisattva who abides in the mantra of this complete nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle.

"Kāśyapa, here is yet another illustration: if a person has incurred a king's hatred, that person may offer pleasant and gentle words and present the king with wealth, valuables, and precious things — and thereby win the king's favour. Noble son, but the king of death is not like that: even if one speaks pleasant and gentle words, even if one presents wealth, valuables, and precious things, one cannot escape from it.

"Noble son, a fool going to a great abyss is without a companion; going on an extremely long road is without a companion; travelling day and night, one does not know its end; one wanders in the most profound darkness; there is no illuminating lamp; there is no door through which to enter and yet there is a dwelling there; there is no visible remedy and no healing is possible; for those going there, there is no interruption and one arrives at a place from which there is no liberation; it is without firm ground; the mere sight of it causes grief; though it is not a harmful form, all tremble in fear at it; though it pervades the entire body, one does not feel or know it.

"Kāśyapa, through these and countless other illustrations it should be understood that death is a great suffering. Kāśyapa, these are what is called 'a great bodhisattva's comprehension of the suffering of death while practising this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa.'

"Kāśyapa, how is it that a great bodhisattva, abiding in this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa, comprehends the suffering of separation from what one desires? The suffering of separation from what one desires is the root of suffering for all sentient beings — and from verse too these words arise:

From desire as its condition grief arises.
From desire as its condition fear arises.
If all desire is entirely abandoned,
whence could grief and fear ever come?

From desire as its condition, the suffering of grief arises; and because it is the suffering of grief, sentient beings grow old and decay. The suffering of separation from what one desires is simply this: the exhaustion of one's life.

"Noble son, as a result of separation, many and various subtle forms of suffering also arise — and these I shall explain to you at length.

"Noble son, in a time long past, human lifespans were immeasurable. At that time there arose a king by the name of Established in Virtue."

At that time, the king served in the office of regent with his youthful body for eighty-four thousand years, after which he was consecrated to the royal throne and reigned as king for another eighty-four thousand years. During his reign, an exceedingly soft growth of flesh appeared upon the crown of the king's head — as soft as wool or fine cotton cloth. Though it grew ever larger with time, it caused no discomfort. When ten months had passed, it burst open, and from within there emerged a young boy of incomparable beauty and excellence, endowed with marks and complexion, altogether foremost among men. The great king was overjoyed and gave him the name Born-from-the-Crown. Then the king, Established in Virtue, having entrusted the entire royal dominion to Born-from-the-Crown, fully relinquished his palace, his queens, his sons, and all his retinue, and for a full eighty-four thousand years applied himself diligently to awakening.

Now, King Born-from-the-Crown, on the fifteenth day of the month, performed his ritual bathing, took up the royal throne, and was seated on a high upper terrace. From the eastern direction there appeared a golden wheel with a thousand spokes — not fashioned by any craftsman, but arisen of itself, spontaneously complete. At that moment, King Born-from-the-Crown reflected: "Long ago I heard from a sage possessing the five superknowledges that a king of noble lineage who, on the fifteenth day, performs his bathing, takes the royal empowerment, and while seated on a high upper terrace witnesses a golden wheel with a thousand spokes appear spontaneously — not made by a craftsman — will without doubt become a wheel-turning king. Calling that to mind, I shall now put it to the test." He took the wheel in his left hand, held a bowl in his right hand, planted his right knee on the ground, and spoke these words: "If this golden wheel is genuine, let it proceed according to the manner of the wheel-turning kings of the past." The moment he had spoken those words, the golden wheel soared up into the sky above, circled in all ten directions, and returned to his left hand.

King Born-from-the-Crown was filled with great delight and joy, and declared: "I am indeed a wheel-turning king!"

Not long after, there appeared of its own accord a precious jewel elephant of surpassing excellence, white as a white lotus, its seven limbs touching the ground. King Born-from-the-Crown saw it and thought: "Long ago I heard from a sage possessing the five superknowledges that if a wheel-turning king, on the fifteenth day, after bathing ascends to a high upper terrace and sits there, and there appears a precious jewel elephant of surpassing excellence, white as a white lotus, with its seven limbs touching the ground, then that king will without doubt become a wheel-turning king. Calling that to mind, I shall now put it to the test." He held the bowl, planted his right knee on the ground, and spoke these words: "If this precious jewel elephant is genuine, let it proceed according to the manner of the wheel-turning kings of the past." Having spoken, the precious jewel elephant circled from the morning until the evening through all eight directions to the very shore of the ocean, and then returned to his dwelling. King Born-from-the-Crown was supremely joyful and declared: "I am without doubt a wheel-turning king!"

Then, not long afterward, there spontaneously appeared a precious jewel horse with a coat of deep blue and a mane and tail of a color resembling gold. King Born-from-the-Crown saw it and thought:

"I once heard from a sage endowed with the five higher knowledges: 'If a wheel-turning king, on the fifteenth day of the month, having bathed and ascended to the highest upper story, sees a precious jewel horse appear, with a coat of deep blue and a mane and tail resembling the color of gold, then that king is without doubt a wheel-turning king.' Recalling this, King Born-from-the-Crown took up a golden bowl, placed his right knee upon the ground, and spoke these words: 'If this precious jewel horse of deep blue is genuine, let it proceed according to the manner of the wheel-turning kings of the past.' Having spoken, the precious jewel horse circled from the morning until the evening through all eight directions to the very shore of the ocean, and then returned to his dwelling. At that time, King Born-from-the-Crown was supremely joyful and declared: 'I am without doubt a wheel-turning king!'

Then, not long afterward, there appeared a precious jewel woman, supremely beautiful in form and appearance, of neither tall nor short stature, neither too fair nor too dark of complexion, from whose every hair-pore there breathed the fragrance of sandalwood incense, from whose mouth there breathed the fragrance of blue lotus blossoms, whose gaze could see clearly to a distance of one league, whose hearing and sense of smell were likewise sharp, whose tongue was very supple, long, and broad, whose complexion was smooth and lustrous like polished copper, who was keen of wisdom and great of mind, who always spoke gently to all sentient beings. By the mere touch of this woman's hand upon the king's garment, she knew both his illness and his wellbeing, and whatever he looked upon or thought. At that time, King Born-from-the-Crown thought to himself: 'A woman who knows the king's mind is indeed a precious jewel woman.'

Then, not long afterward, from within the king's palace there appeared a precious jewel gem resembling a great blue beryl (vaiḍūrya), as large as a man's thigh. This precious jewel gem illuminated the darkness all around to a distance of one league, and even should raindrops fall as thick as the axle-shaft of a chariot, by the power of that precious jewel gem a canopy would form all around to a distance of one league, and not a drop of rain would fall through. At that time, King Born-from-the-Crown thought: 'If a wheel-turning king obtains this precious jewel gem, he is without doubt a wheel-turning king.'

Then, not long afterward, there spontaneously appeared a minister who was lord over the treasury, with very many precious jewels, exceedingly wealthy, with measureless storehouses completely full, lacking nothing, never at a loss, who through the faculty of a meritorious eye could see all the treasure that existed beneath the earth, and who served the king's wishes exactly as desired. At that time, King Born-from-the-Crown, in order to test him, boarded a vessel and set out upon the great ocean. The king commanded him thus: 'I desire various kinds of precious jewels.' As soon as the minister heard those words, he reached both hands into the ocean and drew them out, and on his ten fingers there appeared ten treasuries of precious gems. He offered them to the king and said: 'Great King, take as much as you desire and cast what remains back into the ocean.' At that time, King Born-from-the-Crown was supremely joyful and declared: 'I am assuredly a wheel-turning king!'

Then, not long afterward, there appeared a minister who was lord over the army, exceedingly capable and courageous, supremely skilled in the stratagems of war, and highly expert in commanding the fourfold host of troops.

When advancing against other kings, he would make the army openly visible; when there was no adversary, he remained unseen. He was skilled in subduing those not yet subdued, and exceedingly capable of protecting by force those who had already been subdued.

At that time, King Born-from-the-Crown thought to himself: "A wheel-turning king possesses this precious minister of the army. I am assuredly a wheel-turning king." Then the wheel-turning King Born-from-the-Crown declared to his ministers: "Know this well. Here in this Jambudvīpa all has become supremely happy and prosperous, and I now possess the seven precious treasures and a thousand sons. What more is there to do?" The ministers replied: "It is so, Great King. Yet the eastern continent called Videha has not yet been subdued. If it will not heed the royal command, it should be brought under subjection." Then the wheel-turning king, together with the seven precious treasures, rose up into the sky with all his retinue and set out for the eastern continent of Videha. All the people of that continent, filled with joy, submitted to his command.

Then the king again declared to his ministers: "The southern Jambudvīpa and the eastern continent of Videha have become supremely prosperous, and all have submitted to my command. I possess the seven precious treasures and a thousand sons. What more is there yet to do?" The ministers replied: "It is so, Great King. Yet the western continent called Aparagodānīya has not yet been subdued." Then the king, together with the seven precious treasures, rose up into the sky with all his retinue and set out for the western continent of Aparagodānīya. No sooner had he arrived there than all the people dwelling there submitted to his command.

Again he declared to his ministers: "The people dwelling in the southern Jambudvīpa, the eastern Videha, and the western Aparagodānīya are all supremely prosperous and happy, and have submitted to my command. I possess the seven precious treasures and a thousand sons. What else is there yet to do?" The ministers replied: "It is so, Great King. Yet the northern continent called Uttarakuru has not yet been subdued." Then the king, together with the seven precious treasures, rose up high into the sky with all his retinue and set out for the northern Uttarakuru. No sooner had he arrived there than all the people dwelling there were filled with great joy and submitted to his command.

Then once more he declared to his ministers: "The people dwelling in all four continents are supremely joyful and content, and have submitted to my command. I possess the seven precious treasures and a thousand sons. What else is there yet to do?" The ministers replied: "It is so, Great King. Yet the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three are exceedingly long-lived and supremely happy. Their bodies are most excellent and incomparable. Their palaces for residing, their thrones for sitting, and their beds for sleeping are made exclusively of the seven precious gems. They are proud of their divine merit, and should they not heed the royal command, they too should be brought under subjection and subdued." Then the wheel-turning king, together with the seven precious treasures, rose up high into the sky with all his retinue and set out for the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. Upon arriving there, he saw a tree whose foliage was of a blue color, and he asked his ministers: "What is this thing of blue hue?" The ministers replied: "This is called the Pārijāta tree. The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three take their pleasure and delight beneath this tree during the three months of summer." He also saw something of a white color, resembling a white cloud, and he asked: "What is this?" The ministers replied:

"This is called the Assembly Hall of Goodly Dharma of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three gather here and speak of matters concerning gods and humans." At that time, Śakra (Indra, king of the gods) learned that the wheel-turning king had come, and went out to receive him. Taking him by the hand, he led him inside, and in the Assembly Hall of Goodly Dharma he spread out half his own seat and they sat together. When the two kings sat side by side, there was no difference between them in form, appearance, and marks; they differed only in the movement and blinking of their eyes. At that time the wheel-turning king thought to himself: "Should I overpower this king of the gods by force and make his domain my own?" Noble son, at that time and on that very occasion, Śakra was performing the work of holding, preserving, reading, reciting, and expounding to others the sūtras of the Great Vehicle — though without having penetrated to exhaustion the meaning of the profoundly deep. And it was by reason and condition of that — of holding, preserving, reading, reciting, and broadly expounding to others those Great Vehicle sūtras — that he had come to be endowed with such great majesty and splendor. Noble son, at that time, because the wheel-turning king had aroused malicious thoughts toward Śakra, he fell immediately back down to Jambudvīpa and was parted from both the gods of the desire realm and from humans, and great suffering arose in him. Then he was struck by illness and passed away. Noble son, he who was Śakra at that time and on that occasion is none other than the buddha Kāśyapa. And that wheel-turning king is none other than myself at the present time. Noble son, therefore you should understand that to be parted from desired things brings great suffering. Noble son, if a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa, recalls the suffering of separation experienced in times past, how much more will such a bodhisattva understand the suffering of separation from desired things in the present time.

Noble son, how then does a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa, understand the suffering of encountering what one hates and fears? Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, understands that in the hells, in the realms of birth among animals, in the world of the Lord of Death, and among humans and gods alike, there is what is called the suffering of encountering what one hates and fears. Just as a person imprisoned, seized, bound, placed in irons, put in a pillory, or locked in the stocks is seen to be in great suffering, so too does the bodhisattva, the great being, understand that all sentient beings throughout the five paths of wandering are in great suffering from encountering what they hate and fear. Noble son, consider further this example: a person who, out of fear of an enemy, of a pit, of irons, or of a pillory, abandons father and mother, wife, children, retinue, and all his precious belongings, and flees and escapes along a long road. Noble son, the bodhisattva, the great being, is likewise: fearing saṃsāra, he practices the six perfections to completion and enters into nirvāṇa. This, Kāśyapa, is called understanding the suffering of encountering what one hates and fears, on the part of a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa.

Noble son, how then does a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa, understand the suffering of not obtaining what one desires?

Desire is the desire for everything. And the desire for everything is of two kinds: the desire for virtuous phenomena and the desire for non-virtuous phenomena. Not obtaining virtuous phenomena is suffering, and not being free from non-virtuous phenomena is suffering. These are a brief account of the suffering of the five aggregates. Kāśyapa, these are called the truth of suffering.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Kāśyapa, addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, I do not think it correct that the Blessed One has declared the five aggregates to be suffering. Why is that? The Blessed One once said to the great Śākya chieftain: 'If form were suffering, it would be improper for all sentient beings to desire form; yet since they all desire it, it cannot be called suffering.' And the Blessed One also declared to the monks: 'Feeling has three kinds — pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and feeling that is neither pleasant nor painful.' Previously the Blessed One said to the monks: 'Whoever applies themselves diligently to virtuous phenomena will come to experience happiness.' And the Blessed One also said: 'Even through contact with the six sense objects of a virtuous continuum, happiness will be experienced — if the eye sees a beautiful form, that too is happiness; and likewise pleasant contact through the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind is also happiness.' And the Blessed One declared in verse:

One who holds moral discipline is happy
and does not experience the suffering of the body.
Even when lying down in sleep, one finds happiness,
and upon waking, the mind is filled with joy.

Whether receiving robes and alms,
or reading, meditating, and teaching,
or dwelling at last in a hermitage, a mountain, or a grove —
in these one attains supreme happiness.

Whoever, with compassion for the many
day and night and without ceasing,
does no harm to others —
by that very condition, is always happy.

Desiring little and knowing contentment — this is happiness.
Likewise, much learning is happiness.
The arhats who are free from attachment
are called supremely happy.

The bodhisattva, the great being,
who has reached the far shore of the perfections
and has completed all that is to be done —
that one is called supremely happy.

Blessed One, since this is what you have described as the characteristic of happiness in other sūtras, and if the Blessed One has said what has been said, can these meanings be consistent?"

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "Excellent! Most excellent! Noble son, it is good that you have asked the Tathāgata about these meanings. Noble son, all sentient beings forcibly perceive even the worst suffering as happiness. Therefore, explaining this characteristic of suffering is no different from what was said before."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, as the Blessed One has previously said, if one generates the perception of happiness even toward the worst suffering — then toward the worst birth, the worst aging, the worst illness, the worst death, the worst separation from what one desires, the worst not obtaining what one desires, the worst encounter with what one hates, and the worst of the five aggregates and so forth — in all these sufferings there can likewise be happiness. Blessed One, what is called 'the worst birth' refers to the three lower destinies. What is called 'middling birth' refers to birth among human beings. And what is called 'the best birth' refers to birth as a god in the higher realms. If then someone were to say: 'I perceive the worst happiness as suffering, the middling happiness as free of suffering and pleasant, and the best happiness as truly happy' — if someone were to ask that, what answer should one give?"

Blessed One, perceiving the worst suffering as happiness — for example, if someone is being flogged with a thousand strokes, and after the very first stroke has landed they were to perceive it as happiness, that perception of happiness would not be valid. So why would one perceive the worst suffering as happiness?

The Blessed One declared to Kāśyapa: "That is indeed so. That is indeed so. It is just as you have said. Seen in that light, there is no such thing as a perception of happiness. Why is that? For example, a man is being flogged with a thousand strokes. When one stroke lands and is let pass, at that moment a perception of happiness arises in him. Therefore, where there is no happiness, one forcefully generates a perception of happiness."

Kāśyapa said: "It is not that the man perceives happiness at the landing of that one stroke. Rather, he perceives happiness because he is delivered from more."

The Blessed One declared: "Kāśyapa, this is precisely why my earlier teaching that there is happiness in the five aggregates, given to the great Śākya clan, was perfectly true and not false. Kāśyapa, there are three kinds of feeling and three kinds of suffering. The three kinds of feeling are as follows: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant. The three kinds of suffering are the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change. Noble son, painful feeling is associated with all three sufferings — the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change. The remaining two feelings are associated with the suffering of formations and the suffering of change. Noble son, it is by reason of causes and conditions such as these that genuine pleasant feeling exists even within birth and death. The great bodhisattva, understanding that suffering and happiness are not in fact two different things, teaches that all is suffering. Noble son, within birth and death there is in truth no happiness; when buddhas and bodhisattvas say that there is happiness, they say so in accordance with worldly convention."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked the Blessed One: "When buddhas and bodhisattvas speak in conformity with the world and teach in that way, does that not become falsehood? According to what the Blessed One has taught, whoever performs virtuous deeds will experience the fruit of those deeds. By guarding ethical discipline one obtains physical well-being, is free from suffering, and all one's purposes are fulfilled — this becomes the highest happiness. And those passages in various sūtras and so forth that speak of experiencing happiness — would those too not then become falsehood? If they were to be falsehood, then consider: the Blessed One the Buddha, over the course of hundreds of thousands of immeasurable and incalculable aeons of pursuing awakening, thoroughly abandoned all false speech. How then is one to understand the meaning of such statements?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, the happiness spoken of in the verses quoted earlier is the root of the path to awakening — through it, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening itself arises. It was for this reason that the defining characteristic of happiness was described in that way in those sūtras. Noble son, for example, the enjoyment of worldly resources for one's needs becomes a cause of happiness and is accordingly called happiness. Such things include a fine wife, pleasing wine, the finest food, encounter with water when one is parched with thirst, encounter with fire in the cold, clothing, bodily adornments, woolen and silk fabrics, horses and chariots, male and female servants, hired laborers, gold, silver, lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya), coral, pearls, treasure-houses,

barley, rice, and the like are worldly necessities; because they become causes of happiness, they are accordingly called happiness. Noble son, those very same things and others like them also produce suffering. For instance, on account of women, men are caused to suffer, to grieve, to mourn, to beat their breasts, and even to have their lives cut short. From fine wine and food all the way to treasure-houses, great suffering too can arise. Therefore, all of it is suffering, and there is no defining characteristic of happiness in any of it.

Noble son, a great bodhisattva (bodhisattva mahāsattva) recognizes all eight kinds of suffering as suffering, and sees no happiness in them. Noble son, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and the like do not understand the causes of happiness, and it is for that reason that they declare there to be a defining characteristic of happiness in what is ultimately suffering. Only a bodhisattva who abides in the sūtra of the Great Vehicle, the Mahāparinirvāṇa, truly comprehends and understands both the causes of suffering and the causes of happiness.

Noble son, one may ask: in what way does a great bodhisattva who abides in the Mahāparinirvāṇa sūtra of the Great Vehicle come to comprehend the truth of the origin of suffering? Noble son, the great bodhisattva comprehends this truth of the origin as the cause and condition of the aggregates. What is called "origin" is craving (Skt. tṛṣṇā) for renewed existence, and craving is of two kinds: craving for one's own body, and craving for what one needs.

Again, there are two kinds: single-mindedly seeking after the five objects of desire that have not yet been obtained, and enduring with strong attachment once they have been found.

Again, there are three kinds: craving of the desire realm, craving of the form realm, and craving of the formless realm.

Again, there are three further kinds: craving for the cause and condition of karma, craving for the cause and condition of affliction, and craving for the cause and condition of suffering.

For those who have gone forth into renunciation, craving is of four kinds: craving for robes, craving for alms-food, craving for bedding and seats, and craving for medicine as a condition when ill.

Again, there are five kinds: through attachment to the five aggregates, one craves after everything in pursuit of what one needs. Conceptual elaboration is boundless and without end.

Noble son, craving too is of two kinds: craving for virtue, and craving for non-virtue. Only the foolish crave non-virtue. Bodhisattvas crave virtue. As for craving virtuous Dharma, that too is of two kinds, non-virtuous and virtuous: seeking either of the two lower vehicles is non-virtuous, while seeking the Great Vehicle is virtuous.

Noble son, the craving of childish, ignoble persons is called "origin" and is not a truth. The craving of bodhisattvas is called a truth and is not the origin. Why is that? Because they take birth for the sake of liberating sentient beings, not because they crave rebirth.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One and said: Blessed One, Bhagavān, in other sūtras you have taught that karma becomes a cause and condition for sentient beings; elsewhere you have taught that pride becomes a cause; elsewhere that the six tangible objects become a cause; and elsewhere that ignorance becomes the five aggregates and thereby becomes a cause and condition. Why then, of all the Four Noble Truths, did you teach that craving alone, defined as its characteristic, becomes the cause of the five aggregates?

The Blessed One declared to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: Excellent, excellent! Noble son, it is just as you have said. Other causes and conditions also do indeed become causes, but in brief, the cause of the five aggregates is none other than craving.

Noble son, here is an analogy. When a great king goes on a journey, his chief ministers and retinue follow after him. Craving is just the same: wherever craving moves, all the afflictions follow after it. Again, it is like cloth that has become oily — dust will cling wherever the oil has soaked. Craving is just the same: wherever craving acts through karma, the afflictions too take up their dwelling there.

Noble son, here is another analogy. Wherever the ground is moist, a sprout will grow. Craving is just the same: it causes all the sprouts of karmic affliction to arise.

Noble son, bodhisattvas (bodhisattvas), great beings who abide in the thorough passing beyond sorrow of the Great Vehicle, understand craving under nine aspects. They are: like a debt that keeps accumulating interest; like a wife who is a demoness; like a venomous serpent coiled around a beautiful flowering tree; like food that is unpleasant and unwanted yet forced down nonetheless; like a woman who sells snakes; like the fruit of the bāluká plant; like flesh healing over a wound; like a violent wind; and like a shooting star.

How is it like a debt that keeps accumulating interest? Noble son, consider a poor man who has fallen into debt and finds himself overwhelmed by it — grasped by the body at the end, he cannot get free. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are the same: because the residual traces of the habitual tendencies of craving remain, they cannot awaken to the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Thus it is called being like a debt that keeps accumulating interest.

Noble son, how is it like a wife who is a demoness? Noble son, consider a man who takes a demoness as his wife: the moment she gives birth to a child, she devours that child. When the child is gone, she devours the husband as well. Noble son, the demoness of craving is just the same: whatever roots of virtue sentient beings generate, she destroys the very moment they arise. Having exhausted their roots of virtue, she causes sentient beings to be born in the hells, in the realm of the animals, and in the world of Yama — with the sole exception of bodhisattvas. Thus it is called being like a wife who is a demoness.

Noble son, how is it like a venomous serpent coiled around a beautiful flowering tree? Consider someone who is fond of beautiful flowers, and not knowing that a venomous serpent lurks around the flowering tree, draws near and takes hold of a flower. The moment he takes hold of it, the serpent seizes him and he meets his death. All those of inferior character are likewise: attached to the flowers of the five objects of desire, and not knowing that there is danger in the form of the venomous serpent of craving, they reach out and take hold. Having grasped them, they are seized by the venom of craving, they die, and they fall into the three lower realms — with the sole exception of bodhisattvas. Thus it is called being like a venomous serpent coiled around a beautiful flowering tree.

Noble son, how is it like food that is unpleasant and forced down against one's will? Consider someone who forces down food that is unpleasant and repugnant: the moment he has eaten it, his stomach gives him pain; he vomits with fever and dies. The food of craving is just the same: sentient beings of the five paths who cling to craving compulsively, through that very cause and that very condition, fall into the three lower realms — with the sole exception of bodhisattvas. Thus it is called being like food that is unpleasant and forced down.

Noble son, how is it like a woman who sells snakes? Consider how foolish men are beguiled by a snake-selling woman, and by her seductions and various tricks she robs the man of all his wealth.

Once his wealth is exhausted, she drives him away. The snake-woman of craving is just the same: foolish men without wisdom who rely upon her have all their virtuous qualities stripped away by that very craving. Having exhausted all virtuous qualities, they are driven and cast into the three lower realms — with the sole exception of bodhisattvas. Thus it is called being like a woman who sells snakes.

Noble son, how is it like the fruit of the bāḷuka plant? Consider how when the fruit of the bāḷuka is eaten, the moment it is swallowed it comes back out, strikes the ground, is carried off by the wind, and reaches the foot of a tree; there it sprouts immediately, winds itself around that very tree, and causes it to stop growing — even a nyagrodha tree of great size — and to wither away entirely. The fruit of the bāḷuka of craving is just the same: whatever roots of virtue the foolish and ignoble possess are strangled and choked so that they neither grow nor flourish, until at last they are utterly exhausted and destroyed. Having been withered and destroyed, after death one falls into the three lower realms — with the sole exception of bodhisattvas. Thus it is called being like the fruit of the bāḷuka plant.

Noble son, how is it like flesh within a wound? Consider how when a person has been wounded and the flesh within the wound is raw, it must be treated and cannot simply be left alone. If it is left untreated, the wound festers and worms enter it, and through that very condition it can bring about the end of one's life. The fruit of the five sense pleasures for the childish and foolish is just the same: craving is like raw flesh within a wound, and so it must be treated with diligence. If the raw flesh of craving is not treated, the moment one passes from this life one falls into the three lower realms — with the sole exception of bodhisattvas.

Noble son, how is it like a violent storm? Consider how when a violent storm arises, it levels mountains, scatters boulders, and uproots trees from their very roots. The violent storm of craving is just the same: it stirs up malicious thoughts even toward one's own father and mother, and it uproots from their very foundation even the most firmly established roots of the unsurpassed awakening — the supreme summit of great wisdom — with the sole exception of bodhisattvas. Thus it is called being like a violent storm.

How is it like a comet? Consider how when a comet appears, famine, sickness, and strife arise in whatever land it appears over. The comet of craving is just the same: it severs the seeds of all roots of virtue, causing the foolish and ignoble to fall into poverty and destitution, to meet with famine, to fall prey to the sickness of afflictions, and to revolve in saṃsāra experiencing suffering in its many forms — with the sole exception of bodhisattvas. Thus it is called being like a comet.

Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in this sūtra of the Great Vehicle, the Mahāparinirvāṇa, understands the defilement of craving in precisely these nine aspects.

Noble son, therefore, the foolish and ignoble have suffering but they do not have the truth of suffering. The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have suffering and they also have the truth of suffering, but they do not have the genuine truth. Bodhisattvas know suffering and are free from suffering; therefore they do not have suffering as such, yet they do have the genuine truth.

The foolish and ignoble have the origin of suffering but do not have the truth. The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have the origin and also have the truth of the origin. Bodhisattvas know the origin and are free from the origin; therefore they do not have the origin as such, yet they do have the genuine truth.

The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have cessation, but it is not genuine. Bodhisattvas, the great beings, have cessation and they also have the genuine truth.

The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have the path, but it is not the genuine truth. Bodhisattvas, the great beings, have the path and they also have the genuine truth.

Sons of good family, how is it that when a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in the Mahāyāna sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, they see cessation and see the noble truth of cessation? It is as follows: the complete cutting off of all afflictions — this is called permanence. Because the fire of affliction has been extinguished, it is called perfect peace. Because the afflictions have been arrested, one comes to experience bliss. Because buddhas and bodhisattvas accept dependent origination, it is called complete purity. Because one does not take up again the twenty-five modes of existence, it is called transcendence of the world. Because one has transcended the world, it is called self. Because one does not grasp as a characteristic mark any of the following — form, sound, smell, taste, or touch; male or female; birth, abiding, or cessation; suffering, bliss, or that which is neither suffering nor bliss — it is called the genuine truth of perfect, supreme peace, the consummation. Sons of good family, in this way it is said that a bodhisattva abiding in the Mahāyāna sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa thoroughly understands the noble truth of cessation.

Sons of good family, how is it that when a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in the Mahāyāna Great Nirvāṇa, they understand the noble truth of the path? Sons of good family, it is like this: when a lamp is lit inside a dark chamber, everything within it, great and small, becomes visible. A bodhisattva, a great being, is just like that. Those who abide in the Mahāyāna sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa come to see all phenomena through the condition of the noble eightfold path — namely, the permanent and the impermanent, the conditioned and the unconditioned, sentient being and non-sentient being, existent thing and non-existent thing, bliss and suffering, self and no-self, purity and impurity, affliction and non-affliction, karma and non-karma, truth and non-truth, vehicle and non-vehicle, knowing and not-knowing, quality and non-quality, owner and non-owner, the seen and the unseen, form and formlessness, path and non-path, wisdom and non-wisdom.

Sons of good family, in this way it is said that a bodhisattva abiding in the Mahāyāna sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa thoroughly understands the noble truth of the path.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One and said: Blessed One, if the noble eightfold path is the noble truth, that does not seem consistent in its meaning. Why? Because the Tathāgata has on some occasions declared that faith of mind, for the sake of liberating those with defiled outflows, is the path. On some occasions he has declared that heedfulness is the path — and it has also been said that when the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, practice heedfulness they thereby fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, and so it is a component of the bodhisattva's path. On some occasions he has declared that diligence is the path — and in that connection he spoke to Ānanda:

"Ānanda, one who strenuously applies diligence will fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening." He also declared this.

On some occasions he declared that close application of mindfulness to the body, with the mind focused one-pointedly — that is, diligently attending to close application of mindfulness to the body — will bring one to full awakening in unsurpassable, perfect, complete enlightenment.

On some occasions he also declared that right meditative absorption is the path. In that connection, as he spoke to the great Kāśyapa: right meditative absorption is the path; he did not say that what is not right meditative absorption is the path. He further declared that one who has entered meditative absorption will be able to attend mentally to the arising and cessation of the five aggregates, whereas one who has not entered meditative absorption will not be capable of such mental attention.

On some occasions he declared: one who cultivates and diligently applies a single thing — that being the meditative absorption of recollection of the buddha — will completely purify all sentient beings of their anguish, suffering, and distress, and will attain the authentic Dharma.

On some occasions he also declared that meditation on impermanence is the path. In that connection he spoke to the monks: one who meditates extensively on impermanence will fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

On some occasions he also declared: dwelling alone at the very end of profound solitude and attending to it with the mind, one will swiftly fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

On some occasions he also declared that teaching the Dharma to others is the path — for by hearing the Dharma the net of doubt is cut through, and by cutting through the net of doubt one fully awakens to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

On some occasions he declared that guarding moral discipline is the path. In that connection he spoke to Ānanda: Ānanda, one who applies extreme diligence to guarding moral discipline will cross beyond the ocean of saṃsāra.

On some occasions he declared that relying upon a spiritual friend is the path. In that connection he spoke to Ānanda: one who relies upon a spiritual friend will come to have completely pure moral discipline; and any sentient being who pays homage to me will give rise to the awakening mind directed toward unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

On some occasions he also declared that cultivating loving-kindness is the path — for one who cultivates loving-kindness will sever all mental afflictions and attain a state of unshakeable stability.

On some occasions he declared that wisdom is the path. In that connection, the Blessed One formerly spoke to the nun, the mother of the people, calling her "sister," and declared that the śrāvakas too, with the weapon of wisdom, cut through the afflictions together with the defilements of existence.

On some occasions the Tathāgata also declared that generosity is the path. In that connection the buddha, the Blessed One, formerly spoke thus to the king Utterly-Vanquished-in-Battle: "Great King, know that it is because I practiced generosity extensively in the past, and through that cause and that condition, that I have awakened as a buddha to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening."

If this is so, Blessed One — if you have declared that the noble eightfold path is the truth of the path — do not the declarations in other sūtras of those things become false? And if what arises from those sūtras is not false, why did those sūtras also not say that the noble eightfold path is the truth of the path?

Since it was not declared in that way, what the Tathāgata declared in former times would likewise appear to be mistaken. Yet I am certain that the Blessed One, the Buddha, has been utterly free from error for a very long time.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, it is very fine that you have asked this, wishing to understand the profoundly deep meaning of the sūtra collections of the Great Vehicle for bodhisattvas. Son of good family, those sūtra collections, each and every one of them, do lead into the truth of the path. Son of good family, faith is the path. That is to say, faith is the path, for faith is the root and thereby becomes a companion on the path to awakening. Therefore in what I have declared there is no error.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata, being supremely skilled in means without limit, has spoken in just that way, in all those various aspects, for the sake of taming sentient beings. Son of good family, here is an analogy: a skilled physician, thoroughly expert in the many different kinds of illness that afflict sentient beings, prescribes medicine to each patient according to their condition. And when showing what is unsuitable as a remedy among medicines, there is nothing except water alone that is excluded. And that water takes such forms as bitter-gourd juice, sugarcane juice, black molasses juice, āmalaka juice, nīpāla juice, pārāhala juice, cold water, hot water, winter water, Nepali citrus water, and the like. Son of good family, even skilled physicians who are expert in the various kinds of illness, while having many remedies unsuitable as antidotes, do not exclude water from among them.

The Tathāgata is like that as well. Through his supreme skill in means, he expands and teaches, with this or that name and characteristic suited to each different kind of sentient being, one single defining mark of the Dharma. And sentient beings in turn take up the practice just as they have been taught. Having taken it up and applied themselves diligently, all their mental afflictions are purified — just as a patient, by following a physician's instruction, is cured of illness.

Son of good family, here is another analogy: a person skilled in every kind of language is sitting among a great crowd of people, and every single person in the crowd is tormented by thirst and cries out, 'I am thirsty! I want water!' That person then gives them, each according to their way, clean cold water — and each one names it differently: some say 'I want water,' others say 'pāṇi,' others say 'udi,' others say 'salema,' others say 'sali,' others say 'pana,' others say 'nectar,' others say 'milk.' In this way, that person speaks to the assembly using countless names for water.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata is like that as well. With one single noble path, he expands and teaches to the śrāvakas everything from the faculty of faith through to the noble eightfold path.

Son of good family, here is yet another analogy: a skilled goldsmith takes a single piece of gold and fashions from it all manner of bodily ornaments as he pleases — such as bangles, rings, earrings, crowns, armlets, and many other kinds besides. Though they differ from one another, they are nothing other than gold.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata is like that as well. From one single path, a buddha unfolds and teaches it to sentient beings in many different aspects, and at various junctures teaches it as a single aspect. Thus it is said: the awakening of all the buddhas is one — it is without duality. Yet it is also said to have two aspects: meditative absorption and wisdom. It is further said to have three aspects: view, gnosis, and wisdom. And it is said to have four aspects: the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, the path of no-more-learning, and"

the path of the buddhas. It is also said to have five aspects: the path of practice through faith, the path of practice through Dharma, the path of liberation through faith, the path of arriving through vision, and the path of realization through the body. It is further said to have six aspects: the path of stream-entry, the path of once-returning, the path of non-returning, the path of the arhat, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the buddhas. It is said to have seven aspects: the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of discernment of phenomena, the awakening factor of diligence, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of pliancy, the awakening factor of meditative absorption, and the awakening factor of equanimity. It is said to have eight aspects: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right meditative absorption. It is said to have nine aspects: the eight branches of the noble path, together with faith. It is said to have ten aspects: the ten powers. It is said to have eleven aspects: the ten powers and great loving-kindness. It is said to have twelve aspects: the ten powers, great loving-kindness, and great compassion. It is said to have thirteen aspects: the ten powers, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the meditative absorption of recollecting the buddhas. It is said to have sixteen aspects: the ten powers, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the meditative absorption of recollecting the buddhas, and the three foundations of mindfulness perfectly established by the buddhas. It is said to have twenty aspects: the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the meditative absorption of recollecting the buddhas, and the three foundations of mindfulness.

Son of good family, all these paths are one single thing. The Tathāgata has taught them in many different aspects for the sake of sentient beings of former times.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: fire, which is one single thing in its essence, gives rise to many fires from its burning. Thus it is named in many aspects: the fire of wood, the fire of grass, the fire of chaff, the fire of horse-dung, and the fire of cow-dung. Son of good family, the path of the buddhas is likewise one and without duality, yet for the sake of sentient beings it has been divided and taught in many different aspects.

Son of good family, consider this further analogy: from a single consciousness, six aspects are distinguished and taught. At the occasion of the eye it is named eye-consciousness, and so on up to mental consciousness — this should be understood in full in the same way.
