Son of good family, the path too is like that: one and without duality, yet the Tathāgata has divided and taught it in many different aspects in order to tame sentient beings.

Son of good family, consider this further analogy: a single thing — like form — is called form when seen by the eye; it is named sound when heard by the ear; it is called smell when encountered by the nose; it is called taste when experienced by the tongue; and it is named tangible object when felt by the body. Son of good family, the path too is like that: one and without duality, yet it has been divided and taught in many different aspects in order to tame sentient beings.

Son of good family, for this very reason, the eight branches of the noble path are also to be called the truth of the noble path.

Son of good family, the buddha, the Blessed One, taught the Four Noble Truths in sequence, and through that cause and those conditions, immeasurable numbers of sentient beings were liberated from cyclic existence.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, once in a former time you were dwelling in a grove called Śiśumāra on the bank of the Gaṅgā river. At that time the Tathāgata took up a single leaf with his hand and declared to the monks: 'Are the leaves now in my hand many, or are the leaves of all the grasses, trees, and other plants that grow upon the great earth many?' The monks replied: 'The leaves of the grasses and trees that grow upon the earth are exceedingly many — beyond reckoning. The leaves held in the Tathāgata's hand are extremely few — not worth mentioning.' The Blessed One then declared: 'Monks, all the phenomena I have realized are like the leaves of the grasses and trees that grow on the great earth. What I have taught to sentient beings is like the leaves held in my hand.'"

Kāśyapa continued: "Blessed One, when you spoke those words at that time, the Tathāgata had realized immeasurable phenomena. If all of these are included within the Four Noble Truths, then the Tathāgata had already taught them before. But if they are not included, then there would have to be a fifth truth."

Then the Blessed One declared to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, your asking this question was asked well, for the sake of the benefit and happiness of immeasurable sentient beings. Son of good family, all phenomena whatsoever are indeed included within the Four Noble Truths."

Kāśyapa asked again: "If all phenomena are included within the Four Noble Truths, why did the Tathāgata merely mention this rather than explain it in detail?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, although they are indeed included within it, one should not speak of it as having been taught and explained in full. Why is that? Son of good family, there are two kinds of wisdom in the realization of the Noble Truths: the middling and the superior. The middling is the wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. The superior is the gnosis of buddhas and bodhisattvas.

Son of good family, to understand the aggregates as suffering — that is called middling wisdom. To analyze the aggregates into innumerable defining characteristics and to know all of them as suffering in a way that lies beyond the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. Son of good family, these meanings were not taught by me even in the sūtras.

Son of good family, to know engagement is also called a gateway, and it is also called suffering — that is middling wisdom. To analyze it into its various defining characteristics and to know all of them as suffering in a way that lies beyond the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. These meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras.

Son of good family, to know the elements (dhātu) is also called a limb, and also a defining characteristic, and also suffering — that is middling wisdom. To analyze the elements into their innumerable defining characteristics and to know all of them as suffering in a way that lies beyond the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. Son of good family, these meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras.

Son of good family, to know form as having the defining characteristic of disintegration — that is called middling wisdom. To analyze form into its various defining characteristics and to know all of them as suffering in a way that lies beyond the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis.

These meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras. Son of good family, to know feeling as having the defining characteristic of feeling — that is called middling wisdom. To analyze feeling into its various defining characteristics in a way that lies beyond the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. Son of good family, these meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras. Son of good family, to know perception as having the defining characteristic of apprehension — that is called middling wisdom. To analyze perception into its various defining characteristics of apprehension in a way that lies beyond the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. These meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras. Son of good family, to know formations as having the defining characteristic of construction — that is called middling wisdom. To analyze formations into their various defining characteristics of construction in a way that does not lie within the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can come to know — that is called superior gnosis. Son of good family, these meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras. Son of good family, to know consciousness as having the defining characteristic of discrimination — that is called middling wisdom. To analyze consciousness into its various defining characteristics of knowing in a way that does not lie within the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. Son of good family, these meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras.

The noble Great Sūtra of the Parinirvāṇa, the eighteenth fascicle.

Son of good family, to know that the five aggregates arise through the condition of desire — that is called middling wisdom. To know all the various desires that arise in a single person — desires that even immeasurable and boundless śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know — and to know all the various desires that arise in all sentient beings — that is called superior gnosis. These meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras. Son of good family, to know that afflictions are ceased — that is called middling wisdom. To analyze afflictions, which are immeasurable, together with their cessations, which are likewise immeasurable, in a way that does not lie within the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. These meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras. Son of good family, to know that afflictions are abandoned by means of the defining characteristics of the path — that is called middling wisdom. Son of good family, to analyze the defining characteristics of the path, which are immeasurable and boundless, together with the afflictions to be abandoned, which are likewise immeasurable and boundless, in a way that does not lie within the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. These meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras. Son of good family, to know conventional truth — that is called middling wisdom. To analyze conventional truth, which is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable, in a way that does not lie within the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. These meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras. Son of good family, to know that all formations are impermanent, that all phenomena are without self, and that nirvāṇa is peace — knowing these as ultimate truth — that is called middling wisdom. To know ultimate truth in its immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable dimensions in a way that does not lie within the domain of what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know — that is called superior gnosis. These meanings too were not taught by me in those sūtras.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, Mañjuśrī the Ever-Youthful, addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, what is the meaning of what are called conventional truth and ultimate truth? Blessed One, does conventional truth exist within ultimate truth?

Mañjuśrī continued: Does ultimate truth exist within conventional truth? If it does, then truth would be one. If it does not, would not what the Tathāgata has taught be false?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, conventional truth itself is ultimate truth.

Mañjuśrī replied: Blessed One, in that case the two truths do not exist.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, it is through supreme skillful means, following along with sentient beings, that the two truths have been taught. Son of good family, in terms of verbal expression there are two aspects: worldly phenomena and transcendent phenomena. Son of good family, what is known by a person who has transcended the world is called ultimate truth. What is known by a worldly person is called conventional truth.

Son of good family, the word "self" is imputed on the basis of an assemblage of the five aggregates, and because uninstructed sentient beings follow after that imputation, it is called conventional truth. To know that there is no self in the aggregates, and to know that there is no self beyond the aggregates either — that is called transcendent. To know the defining marks just as they are is called ultimate truth.

Furthermore, son of good family, there are phenomena that have both a name and a result, and phenomena that have a name but no result. Son of good family, what has a name but no result is conventional truth. What has both a name and a result is ultimate truth.

Son of good family, just as it is with "self" — so too with "sentient being," "life-force," "consciousness," "one who sees," "one who lives," "the virile one," "lord of vitality," "feeling," "the one who acts," the mirage of heat in the summer season, the city of the gandharvas (celestial fragrance-eaters), the hair of a tortoise, the horn of a hare, the wheel formed by whirling a firebrand, as well as the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases — all of these are called conventional truth. Suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path are called ultimate truth.

Son of good family, worldly phenomena are of five kinds: the world of names, the world of words, the world of bindings, the world of conventions, and the world of attachments — five in all.

Son of good family, what is the world of names? Things such as man, woman, pot, cloth, chariot, and house — that is called the world of names.

What is the world of words? A single verse of four lines — verses such as these are called the world of words.

What is the world of bindings? Tying, joining, knotting cords, wrapping, binding, and pressing the palms together — these are called the world of bindings.

What is the world of conventions? When a wooden board is struck, the Saṅgha assembles; when a drum is struck, warriors gather; when a conch is blown, people know the time — that is called the world of conventions.

What is the world of attachments? For example, when from a great distance one sees a person wearing robes of varied colors, one forms the attachment: "That is a śramaṇa (a wandering renunciant), not a brahmin." When one sees someone carrying knotted cords and a scraper at the shoulder, one thinks: "That is a brahmin, not a śramaṇa." That is called the world of attachments.

Son of good family, these are the five kinds of worldly phenomena.

Son of good family, if an ordinary person understands these five kinds of worldly phenomena with a mind that is not inverted, knowing them just as they truly are, that is called ultimate truth.

Furthermore, son of good family, what is burnt, cut, broken, and destroyed is called conventional truth. What is not burnt, not cut, not broken, and not destroyed is called ultimate truth.

Furthermore, son of good family, suffering together with its eight defining marks is called conventional truth. No birth, no aging, no sickness, no death, no separation from what one loves, no meeting with what one hates, no failing to obtain what one desires, no five aggregates — this is called ultimate truth.

Furthermore, son of good family, consider the example of a person of many skills: when he is running, he is called a runner; when he is plowing a field, he is called a farmer; when he is stirring food, he is called a cook; when he is working wood, he is called a carpenter; when he is beating gold and silver, he is called a goldsmith. In this way, a single person may be designated by many names. The Dharma, likewise, is truly one, yet it is designated by many names. What is born from the union and coming together of father and mother is called conventional truth. What is born from the assembly of the twelve links of dependent origination is called ultimate truth.

The great bodhisattva, the youthful Mañjuśrī, then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, what is the meaning of what is called genuine truth?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, what is called genuine truth is what is genuinely the Dharma. Son of good family, whatever is not genuinely the Dharma is not genuine truth. Son of good family, what is called genuine truth is what is without inversion; what is without inversion is called genuine truth. Son of good family, genuine truth is that in which there is nothing false. Whatever contains falsity is not to be called genuine truth. Son of good family, genuine truth is the Great Vehicle; what is not the Great Vehicle is not to be called genuine truth. Son of good family, genuine truth is what is spoken by the buddhas; it is not what is spoken by māra. What is spoken by māra and is not spoken by the buddhas is not to be called genuine truth. Son of good family, what is called genuine truth is a single path of complete purity — there is no second. Son of good family, permanence, bliss, self, and complete purity — these are called the meaning of genuine truth."

The youthful Mañjuśrī then asked again: "Blessed One, if what is genuine is genuine truth, then genuine Dharma is the emptiness of the Tathāgata and the intrinsic nature of the pratyekabuddhas. If that is so, then the Tathāgata, space itself, and the intrinsic nature of the buddhas would be without distinction."

The Blessed One then declared to Mañjuśrī: "Where there is suffering, there is truth and there is what is genuine. Where there is the origin of suffering, there is truth and there is what is genuine. Where there is cessation, there is truth and there is what is genuine. Where there is the path, there is truth and there is what is genuine. Son of good family, the Tathāgata is not suffering, is not truth in that sense, and yet is what is genuine. Emptiness, too, is not suffering, is not truth in that sense, and yet is what is genuine. The intrinsic nature of the buddhas, too, is not suffering, is not truth in that sense, and yet is what is genuine. Mañjuśrī, what is called suffering has the defining mark of impermanence and the defining mark of being subject to cutting off — and therefore it is not to be called genuine truth. The Tathāgata itself is not suffering, is not impermanent, and is not subject to cutting off — and therefore it is called what is genuine. Space and the intrinsic nature of the buddhas should likewise be understood in the same way."

"Moreover, noble son, what is called the origin of suffering is that which assembles the five aggregates and causes them to arise — and therefore it is also called suffering, also called impermanence, and is subject to cutting off; it is not to be called genuine truth.

Noble son, the Tathāgata does not have the defining mark of being the origin of suffering, is not the cause of the aggregates, and does not have the defining mark of being subject to cutting off — and therefore it is called what is genuine. Space and the intrinsic nature of the buddhas should likewise be understood in the same way.

Noble son, what is called cessation is the cessation of mental afflictions — and it is both permanent and impermanent. What is attained by the two vehicles is to be called impermanent. What is attained by the buddhas is to be called permanent, and is also to be called the phenomenon self-known through one's own awareness — and therefore it is called genuine truth.

Noble son, the Tathāgata itself is not to be called cessation, nor is it to be called the cessation of mental afflictions; it is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is not self-known through one's own awareness. It abides permanently, is unchanging — and therefore it is called what is genuine. Space and the intrinsic nature of the buddhas should likewise be understood in the same way.

Noble son, what is called the path is that which cuts through mental afflictions. It is neither permanent nor impermanent, and because it is a phenomenon to be cultivated through meditation, it is called genuine truth. The Tathāgata is not something that cuts through mental afflictions by means of the path; it is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is not a phenomenon to be cultivated through meditation. It abides permanently, is unchanging and unshifting — and therefore it is called bliss. Space and the intrinsic nature of the buddhas should likewise be understood in the same way.

Moreover, noble son, what is called what is genuine is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata too is what is genuine. What is genuine is space, and space too is what is genuine. What is genuine is the intrinsic nature of the buddhas, and the intrinsic nature of the buddhas too is what is genuine.

Mañjuśrī, where there is suffering, there is the cause of suffering, the exhaustion of suffering, and the antidote to suffering. The Tathāgata is none of these — neither suffering nor anything up through the antidote — and therefore it is called what is genuine, not truth in that sense. Space and the intrinsic nature of the buddhas should likewise be understood.

Suffering is compounded, is defiled, and is unpleasant. The Tathāgata is not compounded and is not defiled — and because it is supremely blissful, it is what is genuine, not truth in that sense.

Then the youthful Mañjuśrī spoke these words to the Blessed One: "The Blessed One has declared that what is non-inverted is genuine truth. If that is so, are there four inversions with respect to the Four Truths? And if there are, why did the Blessed One declare that what is non-inverted is genuine truth? For all that is inverted is not genuine."

The Blessed One declared to Mañjuśrī: "All inversions belong within the truth of suffering. Just as, for example, a sentient being who possesses an inverted mind is called inverted, noble son, just so — consider the example of a person who does not listen to the words of his parents, his teachers, and his spiritual master, and does not act as instructed: that person is called inverted. And that inversion is not something other than suffering — it is suffering.

Mañjuśrī then asked again: "If, as the Blessed One has declared, what is non-false is genuine truth, then what is false would not be genuine truth — I take it, then, that what is false is not genuine truth."

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, all that is false and deceptive belongs within suffering. For example, consider a sentient being who, overpowered by another adversary —"

acts of deceit and fraud, then by that cause and through those conditions, the sentient being falls into the hells, into the births of animals, or into the realm of hungry ghosts. These are called what is false. And that falseness is not something other than suffering — it is suffering.

Because śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and fully awakened Blessed Ones have utterly abandoned and do not engage in such things, they are not called false. And because falseness is wholly removed by the buddhas and by the two vehicles, it is called genuine truth.

Mañjuśrī then asked again: "If, as the Blessed One has declared, the Great Vehicle is to be called genuine truth, then would not the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas turn out to be not genuine?"

The Blessed One declared to Mañjuśrī: "Both vehicles are genuine, and yet both are also not genuine. They are called genuine because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have cut through the afflictions. Yet they are not genuine because they are impermanent, unstable, subject to change and transition."

Mañjuśrī then asked again: "If, as the Blessed One has declared, something is to be called genuine, then surely what māra (the Tempter) says should not be genuine. Blessed One, could what māra says be understood as noble truth?"

The Blessed One declared to Mañjuśrī: "What māra says falls within the two truths called suffering and the origin of suffering. Whatever is not Dharma, whatever is not discipline, whatever does not become the benefit and happiness of others — even though it may be spoken incessantly at all times, it will never enable the other person to see suffering, to cut through its origin, to realize its cessation, or to cultivate the path. Therefore it is false, and that falseness is called what māra speaks."

Mañjuśrī then asked again: "If, as the Blessed One has declared, the path of purification is one and not two, then the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) also say exactly this: 'The path of purification is one and not two.' If that single path were genuine truth, what distinguishes you from the non-Buddhists? And if there is no distinction, then it is also not fitting that it should have been said that the path of purification is one."

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, non-Buddhists do have the truths of suffering and of the origin of suffering, but they do not have the truths of cessation and of the path. Therefore they perceive as cessation what is not cessation, they perceive as a path what is not a path, they perceive as a result what is not a result, and they perceive as a cause what is not a cause. Therefore for them there is no 'one path of purification, not two' to be spoken of."

Mañjuśrī then asked again: "If, as the Blessed One has declared, what is endowed with permanence, endowed with self, endowed with bliss, and endowed with purity is to be called genuine meaning — then surely non-Buddhists too would have genuine truth, and it would not be found in the Dharma of the buddhas. Why? Because the non-Buddhists also say the following: 'All formations are permanent.' How so? Because the karmic maturation of agreeable and disagreeable karma and so forth will not fail to occur. What is agreeable is the experience of the fruit of the ten virtues. What is disagreeable is the maturation of the ten non-virtues. Now, if all formations were impermanent, then when one who has performed an action passes away from here and is reborn elsewhere, who would experience the fruit of that maturation?

Therefore all formations are permanent; they are called permanent on account of the condition of taking life. Blessed One, if all formations were impermanent, then both the killer and the one killed would become impermanent. If they were impermanent, sentient beings would experience blameworthy karma in the hells. Yet if they were certainly to experience the karmic maturation of the hells, then formations would turn out not to be truly impermanent. Blessed One, a mind that is single-pointed and mindful — this too we call permanent. For example, one remembers something for ten years and then recalls it for a hundred years without forgetting; this too we call permanent. For if it were impermanent, who would remember things previously seen? Therefore all formations are not impermanent. Blessed One, all memory too we call permanent. For instance, when a person previously sees another person's hand, foot, head, shoulder, or the like, and later, upon seeing them again, immediately recognizes them. If memory were impermanent, it would be fitting that the earlier mark should have vanished without trace. Blessed One, all skills come about through long habituation; from the very beginning of training, after three or five years one becomes expert — therefore we call this permanent. Blessed One, in arithmetic one learns from one to two, from two to three, up to a hundred and a thousand. If it were impermanent, then even the first unit, the one, would not exist. If the first one did not exist, how could there be two? Thus the one is permanent and is not two. Since the one has not passed away into nonexistence, from two onward one arrives at a hundred, a thousand — therefore it is permanent. Blessed One, take the example of reading or reciting the Dharma: one recites one passage, then two passages, then three passages, then up to four. If it were impermanent, recitation would never reach as far as four. Because reading and recitation increase and arise, we call this permanent. Blessed One, a pot, clothing, a chariot, a debt incurred, and the defining marks of the great earth — mountains, water, forests, the leaves of trees, and the healing of the illnesses of sentient beings — all these are permanent; they are like that. Blessed One, all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) say this very thing: "All formations are permanent." And if all formations are permanent, that would constitute genuine truth. Blessed One, some non-Buddhists also say: "There is happiness." How is this known? Because agreeable fruits will be experienced. Blessed One, the experience of happiness is certainly real. For instance, the great king of Brahmā, the great sovereign lord, Śakra (Indra) the lord of the gods, the averter of harm, gods, humans, and so forth — therefore happiness is certainly real. Blessed One, some non-Buddhists also say: "There is happiness" — and for sentient beings, a mind of seeking arises again and again. For instance, the hungry seek food, the thirsty seek water, those who are cold seek warmth, those who are hot desire coolness, the weary desire rest, the sick desire recovery, and those with desires seek objects of form. If happiness did not exist, why would they seek these things? Since seeking exists, it is evident that happiness exists. Blessed One, some non-Buddhists also say the following: one who has given generosity becomes happy. People of the world give to monks or brahmins or the poor: robes, food, drink, bedding, medicine for illness, sheep, oxen, horses, vehicles, incense powder, flowers, houses, dwellings, lamps, and so forth. By giving such gifts, in the next life one will experience agreeable fruits.

Therefore, happiness certainly exists. Blessed One, some non-Buddhists also say this: happiness exists because of causes and conditions. The experience of happiness arises because causes and conditions are present — this is called "making contact with happiness." If happiness did not exist, how could its causes and conditions exist? Just as if a rabbit's horn did not exist, its causes and conditions would also not exist. Since the causes and conditions of happiness exist, happiness exists.

Blessed One, some non-Buddhists also say this: happiness exists because there are higher, middling, and lower degrees of it. The lowest experience of happiness belongs to Śakra (Indra), the lord of the gods. The middling experience of happiness belongs to Great Brahmā, the king of the gods. The highest experience of happiness belongs to the Great Sovereign. Since higher, middling, and lower degrees exist, happiness exists.

Blessed One, some non-Buddhists say this: purity exists. Why? Because if purity did not exist, it would be improper for desire to arise; yet since desire does arise, purity must exist. Others also say: gold, silver, beryl, crystal, asamāgarbha, musālagalva, coral, pearl, crystal cloth, garlands, waterfalls, springs, bathing pools, food, drink, robes, flowers, incense, incense powder, ointment, and illuminating lamps — all these things possess the quality of being thoroughly pure.

Furthermore, it is said: the five aggregates are a pure vessel, and they are filled also with a pure essence. Gods, humans, seers, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas — for this reason they are called "pure."

Blessed One, some non-Buddhists say: the self exists. They say that whatever perceives and acts is the self. Just as a person who goes to a potter's house, even without meeting the potter himself, upon seeing the clay and the wheel will certainly know it to be a potter's house — in the same way, as soon as the eye sees form, the self is certainly affirmed to exist. If the self did not exist, who would see form, who would hear sound — and so it continues through tactile objects and mental phenomena. Furthermore, the self exists and is known through signs. What are these signs? Breathing, looking with the eyes and smiling, the span of life, experiencing suffering and happiness, being angered through attachment — all these and similar phenomena are the signs of the self. Therefore, the self certainly exists.

Moreover, the existence of the self is discerned by the distinguishing of flavors. Just as when a person eats fruit and immediately seeks to identify what flavor it has, for this reason the self exists. Furthermore, the existence of the self is known through actions. When one holds something dry, one performs the action of grasping; when one holds an axe, one performs the action of cutting; when one holds a pot, one performs the action of drawing water; when one rides in a chariot, one performs the action of turning the wheel. All such actions are performed because they are taken up by what is called the self. Therefore, the self certainly exists. Furthermore, what makes clear that the self exists? Take the example of a newborn infant who immediately seeks to drink milk — this arises from prior habitual tendencies. Therefore, the self certainly exists.

Furthermore, there is what is called the self. What makes this evident? It is because an assembled and gathered collection becomes beneficial to other sentient beings. For example, a pot, a garment, a chariot, a field, a house, a mountain, a forest, a tree, an ox, a horse, cattle, sheep, and so on — these things become beneficial through their assembly. Similarly, the inner five aggregates (skandhas) are like this: when the sense faculties such as the eye faculty and the rest are assembled and gathered together, they become beneficial to what is called the self. Therefore, the self certainly exists. Furthermore, what makes clear that the self exists? It is because something can obstruct and block. When something exists, it can block and obstruct; when something does not exist, it cannot obstruct. Since obstructing and blocking do occur, the self is held to exist. Therefore, the self certainly exists. Furthermore, what makes clear that the self exists? It is because of companions and non-companions. Relatives and non-relatives do not become companions in the same way. Correct Dharma and incorrect Dharma do not become companions in the same way. Wisdom and non-wisdom do not become companions in the same way. Ascetics and non-ascetics do not become companions in the same way. Brahmins and non-brahmins, sons and non-sons, day and non-day, night and non-night, self and non-self — these phenomena stand as companions and non-companions. Therefore, the self certainly exists. Blessed One, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) likewise, through many and various approaches, assert that permanence, happiness, self, and complete purity exist, and they hold that what is called permanence, happiness, self, and complete purity certainly exists. Blessed One, it is for this reason that the non-Buddhists too declare that a true reality exists.

The Blessed One then spoke: Son of good family, any ascetic or brahmin who declares that permanence exists, or that happiness exists, or that complete purity exists, or that the self exists — that person is not a true ascetic, not a true brahmin. Why? Because they have strayed from saṃsāra, and because they have abandoned the great Teacher who is endowed with the gnosis of omniscience. Those ascetics and brahmins are deeply sunk in desire, and their virtuous qualities are meager. Those non-Buddhists are bound by attachment, aversion, and delusion, and yet they remain content in the pleasures of desire. Those non-Buddhists know that the fruits of karma are created by the self and experienced by the self, yet they are unable to abandon unwholesome qualities. Those non-Buddhists do not possess the true Dharma, nor do they live by a true livelihood. Why? Because they lack the fire of wisdom and cannot purify themselves. Those non-Buddhists cling to the finest of the five sense pleasures, yet because they apply no diligence and earnest effort, they are impoverished in virtuous qualities. Those non-Buddhists desire true liberation, yet lack the legs that are the guarding of ethical discipline. Those non-Buddhists desire happiness, yet cannot seek out the causes and conditions through which happiness arises. Those non-Buddhists desire not to suffer, yet do not abandon all conduct that becomes the cause of suffering. Those non-Buddhists are coiled by the four venomous serpents of the great elements, and yet move through life heedlessly. Those non-Buddhists, completely covered by ignorance, abandon virtuous spiritual friends, and because they are devoted to remaining in the three realms, they cannot be liberated from the great and fiercely blazing fire of impermanence.

Those non-Buddhists are struck down by the grave sickness of affliction, which is difficult to cure, and yet they do not seek out a physician endowed with skill and knowledge. Those non-Buddhists must travel the boundless, immeasurably long, and utterly desolate road of future time, and yet they do not know how to accumulate a gathering of wholesome Dharma that would become their own adornment. Those non-Buddhists are slain by the poison of attachment, and yet they cling to the five venomous she-asses of desire. Those non-Buddhists are consumed by the fiercely blazing fire of aversion, and yet they rely upon unwholesome spiritual friends. Those non-Buddhists are covered and overwhelmed by ignorance, and yet they seek out the wrong Dharma of perverted views. Those non-Buddhists are perpetually deceived by perverted views, and yet they cultivate the perception of those very views as virtuous spiritual friends. Those non-Buddhists hope for sweet fruit, and yet they plant seeds of bitter fruit. Those non-Buddhists have entered the dark house of affliction, and yet they abandon the great lamp of primordial wisdom. Those non-Buddhists are utterly tormented and parched with thirst by affliction, and yet they drink the salt water of desire. Those non-Buddhists are tossed about on the boundless ocean of saṃsāra, and yet they abandon the unsurpassed vessel. Those non-Buddhists are thoroughly corrupted by inverted views, and yet they declare that all formations are permanent. But there is no ground whatsoever for saying that all formations are permanent. Noble son, when I look at this, all formations are impermanent. And how is this known? It is known through the door of causes and conditions. All phenomena that arise from conditions must be recognized as impermanent. Therefore there is not a single one of all the doctrines of non-Buddhists that has not arisen from conditions.

Noble son, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of a buddha is unborn, unceasing, neither coming nor going, neither past nor future nor present, not made from a cause, not made from the absence of a cause, not unmade, not made, not signified, not without sign, not possessed of a name, not devoid of a name — it is not a name, not a form, not long, not short, not an aggregate, not an element, not belonging to the sense bases. Therefore it is called permanent. Noble son, the intrinsic nature of a pratyekabuddha is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is Dharma. Dharma is permanent. Noble son, what is called "permanent" is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha is permanent. For this reason, one should not say that all phenomena arising from conditions are permanent. And not a single one of the doctrines of those non-Buddhists has failed to arise from conditions.

Noble son, non-Buddhists do not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha, the Tathāgata, or the Dharma. Therefore everything those non-Buddhists say is false and without genuine truth. Foolish children of little cultivation: having previously seen a pot, or clothing, or a vehicle, or a house, or a town, or a river, or a mountain, or a forest, or a man, or a woman, or an ox, or a horse, or cattle, or sheep, and so forth, when they later see something similar to what they saw before, they declare it to be permanent. But in truth, it is not permanent. Noble son, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Space and the unconditioned are called permanent. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is unconditioned and therefore is called permanent. What is called "space" is the intrinsic nature of a buddha. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata is unconditioned. The unconditioned is permanent. The permanent is the Dharma. The Dharma is the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha is unconditioned. The unconditioned is permanent.

Noble son, conditioned phenomena, in brief, are of two kinds: material phenomena and immaterial phenomena. What are called immaterial phenomena are mind and mental factors arising from mind. What are called material phenomena are earth, water, fire, and wind.

Noble son, mind is called impermanent. Why is that? Because it has objects by its own intrinsic nature and is accompanied by conceptual thought. Noble son, the intrinsic nature of visual consciousness is distinct from the intrinsic nature of mental consciousness, and each is distinct from the others — therefore it is impermanent. Noble son, the domain of form and the domain of phenomena are likewise each distinct from the other — therefore impermanent. Noble son, what arises together with visual consciousness is distinct from what arises together with mental consciousness, and each is distinct — therefore impermanent.

Noble son, if mind were permanent, it would follow that visual consciousness alone could apprehend all phenomena whatsoever. Noble son, because visual consciousness is distinct from mental consciousness, and each in the series from one to the other is distinct, mind is known to be impermanent. Phenomena that are similar arise and cease moment by moment, and childish, lowly persons, seeing them in this way, grasp them as permanent.

Noble son, because the defining characteristic of causes and conditions is that they can be destroyed, it is called impermanent. For example, visual consciousness arises from the conditions of the eye faculty, visible form, light, and attention. And when ear consciousness arises, it does so from its own distinct conditions — not from the conditions of visual consciousness. Each consciousness up to mental consciousness should be understood in the same way, each arising from its own distinct conditions.

Furthermore, noble son, because the causes and conditions of formations are destroyed, mind is impermanent. The mind that cultivates meditation on impermanence is one thing, and the mind that cultivates meditation on suffering, on emptiness, and on selflessness is another. If mind were permanent, then by constantly meditating on impermanence one would never come to realize suffering, emptiness, and selflessness — let alone realize permanence, bliss, self, and purity. For this reason, what is permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure cannot be gathered into the Dharma of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Noble son, therefore the phenomena of mind are definitely impermanent.

Moreover, noble son, because the intrinsic nature of mind is various and distinct, it is impermanent. The intrinsic nature of the mind of a śrāvaka is its own; the intrinsic nature of the mind of a pratyekabuddha is its own; and the intrinsic nature of the mind of the buddhas is also its own. The minds of all non-Buddhists are of three kinds: the mind of one who has gone forth, the mind of one who dwells at home, and the mind of one who is secluded from the household life. The mind accompanied by seclusion is one thing; the mind accompanied by suffering is another; the mind accompanied by neither pleasure nor pain is another; the mind accompanied by attachment is another; the mind accompanied by aversion is another; the mind accompanied by delusion is yet another — and thus the characteristics of the mind of every non-Buddhist also differ from one another. Likewise, the mind accompanied by delusion is one thing, the mind accompanied by doubt is another, the mind accompanied by wrong views is another, and the mind of one who is going about and of one who is staying still are also distinct. Noble son, if mind were permanent, then with regard to blue color, yellow, red, white, and

purple color there would be no reason to make distinctions among them. Noble son, if mind were permanent, it would be unreasonable for all the phenomena that are to be remembered to be forgotten. Noble son, if mind were permanent, it would be unreasonable that the activities of reading and recitation should increase and arise. Noble son, if mind were permanent, it would be unreasonable to speak of what has been done, what is being done, and what is to be done — and yet because there is what has been done, what is being done, and what is to be done, the mind must be understood as definitely impermanent. Noble son, if mind were permanent, there would be neither aversion nor loving-kindness, and it would be neither aversion nor loving-kindness. If mind were permanent, it would be unreasonable to speak of "my property" and "another's property," or to say "he dies" and "he is born." If mind were permanent, it would be unreasonable that, even though an action has been performed, arising and increase should occur. Noble son, therefore, because the intrinsic nature of mind is distinct and differentiated, it must be recognized as impermanent.

Noble son, what I have explained here with respect to impermanence in the domain of non-material phenomena is this. And further, I shall explain to you that form is impermanent. Form is impermanent because it was not arisen from the beginning; and having arisen, it is subject to cessation. At the time of the embryo entering the womb and being in the gelatinous stage, it has not arisen from the beginning, and having arisen it is subject to change. External sprouts and trunks likewise have not arisen from the beginning, and having arisen they are subject to change. Therefore all phenomena of form are to be understood as impermanent.

Noble son, inner form changes with time: the gelatinous stage is one thing, the hardening stage is another, the stage of becoming solid is another, the time in the womb is another, the time of birth is another, the time of infancy is another, and the time of youth is another — and so it changes, all the way through to old age, each stage being different. All outer forms are the same: the time of the sprout is one thing, the time of the trunk is another, the time of the branches is another, the time of the leaves is another, the time of the flower is another, and the time of the fruit is another.

Noble son, further, the inner taste also differs from the gelatinous stage all the way through to old age, each being distinct and other. Outer taste is the same: from sprout to trunk, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit, each is distinct and other. The strength and vigor at the gelatinous stage is one thing, all the way through to old age the strength and vigor also differs, each being distinct and other. The appearance of form at the gelatinous stage is one thing, and through to old age the appearance also differs, each being distinct and other. The fruit of karmic maturation at the gelatinous stage is one thing, and through to old age the fruit of karmic maturation also differs, each being distinct and other. The name given at the gelatinous stage is one thing, and through to old age the name assigned also differs, each being distinct and other.

So it is that inner form, the very moment it disintegrates, gathers again — and so it is impermanent. Outer trees and plants, the very moment they disintegrate, also gather again — and so they are impermanent. Because they arise gradually, they are also impermanent. From the gelatinous stage through to old age, arising and changing occur gradually; and from sprout through to fruit, arising and changing occur gradually — therefore they are impermanent. Because all forms are destined to cease, they are impermanent: the cessation of the gelatinous stage is one thing, the cessation through to old age is another; the cessation of the sprout is one thing, and the cessation through to the fruit is another — and therefore they are impermanent. Children of low birth who are without wisdom, seeing birth and grasping at it as something they remember, cling to it as permanent. Therefore it is called impermanent. And if something is impermanent, that is suffering. And because it is suffering, it is impure.

Noble son, these matters were also asked earlier by Kāśyapa, and I explained them in detail.

Furthermore, noble son, in all formations (saṃskāra) there is no such thing as a self. Noble son, what is called "all phenomena" is, in brief, form and the formless. In form there is no such thing as a self. Why is that? Because form is subject to being broken, cut, and soiled, and because it arises and grows. What is called a self cannot be broken, cannot be cut, does not arise, and does not grow — and therefore form is not a self. Formless phenomena, too, are not a self. Why is that? Because they arise from causes and conditions.

Noble son, if the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) claim that through one-pointed recollection they know that a self exists, well, one-pointed recollection itself is not what is called a self. Moreover, if one were to say that one-pointed recollection is the self, then there is also forgetting of things past — and since there is forgetting, it is certain that there is no such thing as a self.

Noble son, if the non-Buddhists claim that because there is recollection a self exists, then since there is also the absence of recollection, there is no such thing as a self.

Noble son, consider the example of seeing a person with six fingers on a hand: one would ask, "Did we not meet before, long ago?" But if a self truly existed, it would not be fitting to ask at all — and from the fact that one does ask, it is certain that there is no such thing as a self.

Noble son, if the non-Buddhists claim that because something can be interrupted and obscured a self exists, then noble son, because there is obscuration, know that it is certain there is no such thing as a self. For example, when one utters the name "Devadatta," one does not say "not Devadatta." Likewise with the self: if it were truly and certainly a self, it would not become obscured under the name "self" — but since it does become obscured, it is certain there is no such thing as a self. And if one claims that because there is obscuration a self exists, then in the case where you are not obscured, it is certain there is no such thing as a self.

Noble son, if the non-Buddhists claim that from the existence of companions and non-companions they know that a self exists, then because there are things without a companion, there is no self — and it is proper to conclude that there is no such thing as a self. Companionless phenomena do exist, namely the Tathāgata, space, and the nature of buddhahood. What is called a self is likewise truly and perfectly without a companion — and therefore it is certain there is no such thing as a self.

Noble son, furthermore, if the non-Buddhists claim that from the attribution of names they know that a self exists, then even for selfless phenomena the name "selfless" is attributed. For example, a very poor person may be given the name "wealthy." Another example: one says "I die" — but if what is called the self dies, then the self would be killed by the self. Since what is called a self cannot truly be killed, it is merely a conventional designation to say "the self dies." This is like calling a short person "tall." Therefore, know with certainty that there is no such thing as a self.

Furthermore, noble son, if the non-Buddhists claim that because a newborn infant immediately seeks milk they know that a self exists — noble son, if a self truly existed, then it would not be fitting for all small infants to grasp at filth, vomit, fire, snakes, and poison. Therefore it is certain there is no such thing as a self.

Noble son, all sentient beings possess equally this threefold gnosis (jñāna): attachment (rāga), eating, and fear. And therefore there is no such thing as a self.

Furthermore, noble son, if the non-Buddhists claim that from signs and from form alone they know that a self exists — noble son, because signs exist there is no self, and because signs are absent there is also no self. For example, when a person has fallen asleep, there is going and coming and —

there is no going, no coming, no stretching out, no yawning, no looking — and there is no feeling of pleasure or of suffering. Therefore it is unreasonable to assert that a self exists. And if someone were to say that because there is going and coming, stretching out, yawning, and looking, one knows that a self exists — then by that same logic one should assert that a self exists in a mechanical man made of wood. Noble son, the Tathāgata is just like that: he does not go, he does not stay, he does not yawn, he does not stretch out, he does not look, he does not smile; he is not suffering, not pleasurable, not attachment, not aversion, not delusion, not conduct. And yet in this very way, the Tathāgata is said to possess a true self.

Furthermore, noble son, if the non-Buddhists were to say that when a person on the far bank eats sour fruit from a tree, one knows from the saliva that rises on the near bank that a self exists — noble son, the saliva arises because of memory from seeing, yet the saliva is not the self and the self is not the saliva. The saliva is not joy, not sorrow, not laughter, not excitement, not falling, not birth, not thirst, not satiation. Therefore one must certainly know that there is no self.

Noble son, those non-Buddhists are like a small blind infant that has never seen sunlight. Having no knowledge, no skillful means, no understanding, they do not know permanence or impermanence, suffering or pleasure, complete purity or impurity, self or no-self, what is feeling or what is not feeling, what is a sentient being or what is not, what is happiness or what is not, what exists or what does not exist. Having taken a mere fraction of the Dharma of the buddhas, they grasp at permanence, pleasure, self, and purity; yet they do not know what true permanence, pleasure, self, and purity actually are.

It is like a blind man who does not know the color of milk. When he asks another person what color milk is, and the other says it is like the color of a conch shell, the blind man takes the color of milk to be something like the sound of a conch shell. Then when he asks what the color of a conch shell is like, and is told it is like ground rice powder, the blind man takes the color of a conch shell to be something exceedingly soft. Then when he asks what the color of ground rice powder is like, and the other says it is like snow, the blind man takes the color of ground rice powder to be something cold. And when he asks what the color of snow is like, and is told it is like the wing of a goose — yet even after receiving these four analogies, that blind man still does not know what the true color of milk is actually like. Those non-Buddhists are just the same: they do not know permanence, pleasure, self, and purity. Noble son, therefore in the Dharma of the buddhas there is genuine truth, but among the non-Buddhists there is not.

The Noble Great Sūtra of the Complete Passing into Nirvāṇa. The nineteenth fascicle.

Mañjuśrī, the young prince, addressed the Blessed One with these words: "How wonderful! The Tathāgata, on the very occasion of passing into complete nirvāṇa, has turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and taught the genuine truth in its fullness."

The Blessed One declared to Mañjuśrī: "Do you perceive the Tathāgata as passing into nirvāṇa? Noble son, the Tathāgata in truth is permanent, stable, unchanging, and not passing into complete nirvāṇa.

Noble son, whoever grasps him as a self — that is called the buddha-self, and such a one will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. The word 'self' is Dharma, and Dharma belongs to the self. The self is the path, and the path belongs to the self. The self is the Blessed One, and the Blessed One belongs to the self. The self is the śrāvaka, and the śrāvaka belongs to the self."

The self teaches Dharma, and others listen to it. The self turns the wheel of Dharma, and others are incapable of doing so. The Tathāgata does not grasp things in that way; therefore the Tathāgata does not turn the wheel of Dharma.

Noble son, whoever grasps things in such a manner: the self is the eye, and the eye belongs to the self. And so too with the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind. The self is form, and form belongs to the self. In the same way, understand this to extend through all the remaining phenomena. The self is earth, and earth belongs to the self. Understand water, fire, and wind likewise.

Noble son, in this regard, whatever one calls "self" is faith, and faith belongs to the self. What is called "self" is extensive learning, and extensive learning belongs to the self. What is called "self" is the perfection of generosity, and the perfection of generosity belongs to the self. What is called "self" is the perfection of moral discipline, and the perfection of moral discipline belongs to the self. The self is the perfection of patience, and the perfection of patience belongs to the self. The self is the perfection of diligence, and the perfection of diligence belongs to the self. The self is the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of meditative concentration belongs to the self. The self is the Perfection of Wisdom, and the Perfection of Wisdom belongs to the self. The self is the four establishments of mindfulness, and the four establishments of mindfulness belong to the self. Understand likewise the four right abandonments, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven branches of awakening, and the noble eightfold path.

Noble son, because the Tathāgata does not grasp in that manner, the Tathāgata does not turn the wheel of Dharma. Noble son, one might ask: if the Tathāgata is permanent, stable, unchanging, and unshifting, then why is it said that the Tathāgata turned the wheel of Dharma? Therefore it is not fitting for you to say that the Tathāgata turned the wheel of Dharma.

Noble son, consider this analogy: from the coming together of the eye, light, and intention, visual consciousness arises. The eye does not think "I have produced visual consciousness," nor does intention think "I have produced visual consciousness," nor does visual consciousness itself think "I have produced myself." And yet, noble son, from their assembly and convergence, seeing comes about.

Noble son, the Tathāgata is just like that. From the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of awakening, the investigation of phenomena, and furthermore from the palate, the throat, the tongue, the teeth, the lips, and the sound of words spoken from the mouth — the first teaching of Dharma given to the venerable Kauṇḍinya is called "turning the wheel of Dharma." It is for that reason that one should not say the Tathāgata turned the wheel of Dharma.

Noble son, that which is not turned is called Dharma, and Dharma is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, consider this further analogy: from the coming together of the fire-stick, the hearthboard, the hands, and the effort of friction, fire arises. The fire-stick does not think "I have produced the fire," the hearthboard, the hands, and the friction do not think "we have produced the fire," and the fire does not think "I have produced myself."

The Tathāgata is similar in just this way. From the six perfections up through the venerable Kauṇḍinya, that which arises is called "turning the wheel of Dharma," yet the Tathāgata does not conceive "I have turned the wheel of Dharma." Noble son, that very absence of such conception is called the true turning of the wheel of Dharma, and that turning of the wheel of Dharma is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, consider this further analogy: butter arises from the coming together of curds, water, a vessel, a churn-stick, a rope, hands, and the act of churning. The curds do not think "I have produced the butter," nor do any of the others, from the curds down to the hands, think "I have produced the butter," and the butter itself does not think "I have produced the butter." Butter comes to be from the gathering of many conditions. The Tathāgata is similar in just this way: he does not conceive "I have turned the wheel of Dharma." That very absence of conception is called the true turning of the wheel of Dharma, and that turning of the wheel of Dharma is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, consider this further analogy: a sprout comes into being from a seed, soil, water, fire, wind, space, time, and the act of cultivation. The seed does not think "I have produced the sprout," nor do any of the others, from the seed down to the act of cultivation, think "I have produced the sprout," and the sprout itself does not think "I have produced the sprout." The Tathāgata is similar in just this way: he does not conceive "I have turned the wheel of Dharma." Noble son, that very absence of such conception is called the true turning of the wheel of Dharma, and that turning of the wheel of Dharma is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, consider this further analogy: sound arises from a drum through the coming together of the drumframe, the hide, a person's hands, and the act of striking. The drum does not think "I have produced the sound," nor do any of the others, from the striking to the sound itself, think "I have produced the sound." The Tathāgata is similar in just this way: he does not conceive "I have turned the wheel of Dharma." Noble son, that very absence of such conception is called the true turning of the wheel of Dharma.

Noble son, the turning of the wheel of Dharma is unconditioned. The unconditioned is the turning of the wheel of Dharma. The turning of the wheel of Dharma is the Tathāgata. Noble son, the turning of the wheel of Dharma is the domain of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Noble son, space is not arising, not arisen, not acting, not made, and is not a conditioned phenomenon. The Tathāgata is similar in just this way: not arising, not arisen, not acting, not made, and not a conditioned phenomenon. Just as the Tathāgata is, so too the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is the same: not arising, not arisen, not acting, not made, and not a conditioned phenomenon.

Noble son, the speech of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is of two kinds: worldly speech and transcendent speech. Noble son, the Tathāgata addresses śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in worldly speech, and addresses bodhisattvas in transcendent speech.

Noble son, the assembly of the retinue is likewise of two kinds: those who seek the lesser vehicle, and those who seek the Great Vehicle.

In the past, at Vārāṇasī, I turned the wheel of Dharma for the śrāvakas, and now, here in this city of Kuśinagara, I have turned the wheel of Dharma for the bodhisattvas, the great bodhisattvas.

Noble son, furthermore, persons are of two kinds: those of middling faculties and those of sharp faculties. For those of middling faculties, the wheel of Dharma was turned at Vārāṇasī. For those of sharp faculties — who are like the finest bulls among men, such as the bodhisattva Kāśyapa and others — the great wheel of Dharma has been turned here in this city of Kuśinagara. Noble son, for those of the lowest faculties, the Tathāgata does not turn the wheel of Dharma; those called "the lowest faculties" are those who hold wrong views.

Noble son, furthermore, those who seek the awakening of a buddha are also of two kinds: those of middling diligence and those of supreme diligence. At Vārāṇasī, the wheel of Dharma was turned for those of middling diligence. Here in this city of Kuśinagara, the great wheel of Dharma has been turned for those of supreme diligence.

Noble son, furthermore, when I previously turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī for the first time, some eighty thousand gods and humans attained the fruit of stream-entry. Now, here in this city of Kuśinagara, some eight hundred thousand gods and humans have become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Noble son, previously at Vārāṇasī, the great Brahmin king Brahmā prostrated before me and requested that I turn the wheel of Dharma. Here in this city of Kuśinagara, the bodhisattva Kāśyapa prostrated before me and requested that I turn the wheel of Dharma.

Noble son, furthermore, when I turned the wheel of Dharma previously at Vārāṇasī, I taught impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness. Now, in turning the wheel of Dharma here in this city of Kuśinagara, I have taught permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity.

Noble son, furthermore, when I previously turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī, the sound of my voice reached as far as the Brahma world. Now, in turning the wheel of Dharma here in this city of Kuśinagara, the sound of my voice has reached as far as the buddha-fields to the east, as numerous as twenty times the grains of sand of the Ganges River, and likewise to the south, the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below.

Noble son, furthermore, everything that the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, ever speak is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma. Noble son, consider the example of the wheel-turning king: his precious wheel subdues those not yet subdued and brings ease to those who have been subdued. Noble son, in exactly the same way, the teaching of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, subdues those not yet subdued amid measureless afflictions, and causes roots of virtue to arise in those who have been subdued.

Noble son, consider also this: the wheel-turning king, by means of his precious wheel, pacifies all enemies that rise against him. Likewise, the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dharma pacifies all the enemies of affliction.

Noble son, consider further: the precious wheel of the wheel-turning king moves at will from below to above. Likewise, the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dharma leads all sentient beings of the lower destinies, from rebirth as gods in the higher realms onward, all the way to the awakening of a buddha.

Noble son, therefore, do not say that the Tathāgata has turned the wheel of Dharma for the very first time only now.

Then the youthful Mañjuśrī once again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, I did not ask these questions for my own sake; I asked them for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings. Blessed One, I understand that the turning of the wheel of Dharma over so long a time belongs to the domain of activity of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and not to the domain of activity of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

Then the Blessed One addressed the bodhisattva Kāśyapa and declared: "Noble son, in this way, a bodhisattva who abides in this sūtra of the Great Vehicle, the Mahāparinirvāṇa, is said to engage in the conduct of the noble ones."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "Why, furthermore, is it called the conduct of the noble ones?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, the term 'noble' refers to the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Therefore it is called the conduct of the noble ones. Moreover, when śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas hear it and practice accordingly, that too is called the conduct of the noble ones, for the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, also rely upon this great Mahāparinirvāṇa and are thus designated noble by virtue of having analyzed and taught it in this way."

The Blessed One continued: "Noble son, when the great bodhisattvas, the great beings, abide in this conduct, they come to dwell on the ground of fearlessness. Noble son, when a bodhisattva dwells on the ground of fearlessness, that one is never afraid of attachment, aversion, or delusion; never afraid of birth, aging, sickness, or death; and is free from fear of falling into the hells, into the realm of animals, or into the realm of hungry ghosts. Noble son, non-virtue is of two kinds: that which arises among the asuras, and that which arises among human beings. Among human beings, non-virtue is of three kinds: holding wrong views, rejecting the extensive sūtras, and transgressing the four defeats. Noble son, those bodhisattvas who dwell on that ground are never afraid of falling into such places of non-virtue. Furthermore, they are not afraid of mendicants, brahmins, tīrthikas of wrong views, or the māra-son gods of sinful nature and the like. Furthermore, they are not afraid of the twenty-five realms of existence. Therefore this ground is called the ground of fearlessness.

Noble son, a great bodhisattva who dwells on the ground of fearlessness crushes the twenty-five realms of existence by means of attaining twenty-five meditative absorptions. Noble son, by attaining the immaculate meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence as a hell-being. By attaining the irreversible meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence as an animal. By attaining the meditative absorption of mental ease and bliss, one crushes the realm of existence as a hungry ghost. By attaining the meditative absorption of great joy, one crushes the realm of existence as an asura. By attaining the meditative absorption of solar rays, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth on the eastern continent Pūrvavideha. By attaining the meditative absorption of lunar rays, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth on the western continent Aparagodānīya. By attaining the meditative absorption of a blazing flame, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth on the northern continent Uttarakuru. By attaining the illusion-like meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth on the southern continent Jambudvīpa. By attaining the meditative absorption of the immovability of all phenomena, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the realm of the Four Great Kings."

By attaining the meditative absorption of the extremely difficult to tame, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth among the Thirty-Three Gods. By attaining the pleasing meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the Heaven Free from Conflict. By attaining the meditative absorption of all being blue, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven. By attaining the meditative absorption of all being yellow, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the Heaven of Delight in Magical Creation. By attaining the meditative absorption of all being red, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Creations. By attaining the meditative absorption of all being white, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the first dhyāna. By attaining the variegated meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the Great Brahma Heaven. By attaining the paired meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the second dhyāna. By attaining the meditative absorption of thunder, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the third dhyāna. By attaining the meditative absorption of falling rain, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the fourth dhyāna. By attaining the space-like meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth in the sphere of no-perception. By attaining the mirror-like meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence involving rebirth as a once-returner in the pure abodes. By attaining the non-attachment meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence resting upon the sense base of infinite space. By attaining the permanent meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence resting upon the sense base of infinite consciousness. By attaining the joyful meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence resting upon the sense base of nothingness. By attaining the self-possessing meditative absorption, one crushes the realm of existence resting upon the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Sons of good family, these are what are called the twenty-five meditative absorptions of the bodhisattva, the attainment of which crushes twenty-five realms of existence. Sons of good family, these twenty-five meditative absorptions are called the kings of meditative absorption.

Sons of good family, when a bodhisattva, a great being, enters these kings of meditative absorption, if he wishes to destroy Mount Meru, the king of mountains, it is destroyed just as he intends. If he wishes to know the thoughts of all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm, he comes to know them just as he wishes. If he wishes all the sentient beings dwelling in the great trichiliocosm to enter together into a single pore of his body, it comes to pass just as he wishes, and there is not the slightest feeling of constriction or discomfort. If he wishes to manifest innumerable emanations of sentient beings and fill the entire great trichiliocosm, it comes to pass just as he wishes. And if he wishes to multiply one body into many bodies, or to gather many bodies back into one, it comes to pass just as he wishes. Yet even as these things occur, his mind clings to nothing, just as a lotus is unstained.

Sons of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, who enters these kings of meditative absorption comes also to abide on the ground of mastery. A bodhisattva abiding on the ground of mastery, endowed with the power of mastery, is born wherever he wishes to be born, in each and every such place, just as he intends.

Sons of good family, consider the example of a wheel-turning king who wishes to travel to the four continents: he goes just as he wills, and there is nothing to obstruct him. A bodhisattva, a great being, is likewise: wherever he wishes to be born, in each and every such place, he is born just as he intends.

Sons of good family, if a bodhisattva, a great being, were to establish the sentient beings dwelling in the hells on the root of virtue, the bodhisattva is born there. Yet even though the bodhisattva is born there, it is not the fruit of former karma.

A bodhisattva, a great being, who dwells on the ground that has become the ground of mastery is born there by reason of that cause and that condition. Sons of good family, although a bodhisattva, a great being, dwells among the hell-beings, he does not experience the sufferings of being boiled and so forth in the hells.

Sons of good family, the spontaneously present qualities of a bodhisattva, a great being, are likewise immeasurable and incalculable — they could not be fully expressed even in the span of a hundred thousand myriads of aeons. How much less need one speak of expressing the qualities of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. At that moment, within that assembled retinue, there was a bodhisattva named Vimalagarbharāja, King of the Heart of Stainlessness, who was endowed with great majesty and with superknowledges, who had attained the great dhāraṇī, who was perfected in meditative absorption, and who had attained fearlessness. He rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Blessed One, as the Blessed One has declared, the qualities and gnosis of the buddhas and bodhisattvas are immeasurable and incalculable, and could not be fully expressed even in the span of a hundred thousand myriads of aeons. Yet when I reflect on this in my mind and set it alongside the sūtras of the Great Vehicle, it does not appear to be so. Why? Because the unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arises and is born from the power of the vast and extensive sūtras of the Great Vehicle."

Then the Blessed One responded with the words "Excellent! Excellent!" and said: "Son of good family, it is indeed so. It is indeed so. As you have said — the vast and extensive sūtras of the Great Vehicle are likewise possessed of immeasurable and boundless qualities. Yet those sūtras cannot serve even as a comparison for this sūtra. They do not measure up as a hundredth part of it, not a thousandth, not a hundred-thousandth — and so on through reckoning, enumeration, and analogy.

Sons of good family, consider this example: from a cow comes milk; from milk comes curds; from curds comes butter; from butter comes clarified butter; and from clarified butter comes the essence of butter. The essence of butter is supreme and most excellent: whoever drinks it is purified of all manner of disease, and it surpasses all medicines. Sons of good family, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are likewise. From the buddha come the twelve branches of the teaching. From the twelve branches of the teaching come the sūtras. From the sūtras come the vast and extensive sūtras. From the vast and extensive sūtras comes the Perfection of Wisdom. And from the Perfection of Wisdom comes the great nirvāṇa, which is like the essence of butter. The essence of butter is an analogy for the intrinsic nature of a buddha. And the intrinsic nature of a buddha is the Tathāgata. Therefore, sons of good family, the qualities of the Tathāgata are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, as the Tathāgata has declared, the sūtra of the great nirvāṇa is supreme and most excellent, like the essence of butter: whoever drinks it is purified of all manner of disease, and it surpasses all medicines. Hearing this declared, I have thought to myself: one who does not listen to and does not recite this sūtra is one of very great delusion, and I regard such a one as being without a virtuous mind."

"Blessed One, I would flay my own skin and use it as a writing surface, draw out my blood to use as ink, pull out my bones and split them to use as pens, and endure all this in order to copy down this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa. Having copied it, I would endure reading it, reciting it, taking it to heart, and also widely teaching and expounding it to others. Blessed One, if there were a sentient being attached to material possessions, I would first give that being material things and afterward encourage them to read this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa. If there were one endowed with great wealth, I would first speak pleasing words to delight the mind and afterward encourage that one to read this sūtra of the Mahāyāna great nirvāṇa. If there were one of low birth, I would compel them by force to read it. If there were one filled with pride, I would first wait upon them as a willing servant to their every wish, making them utterly pleased and gratified, and afterward introduce them to this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa. If there were one who disparaged the vast sūtras, I would subdue them by force and strength, and having subdued them, afterward lead them to read this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa. If there were one who had faith in and devotion to the Mahāyāna sūtras, I would come into their presence and, with the utmost reverence, offer service, honor, veneration, and praise."

Then the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Excellent! Excellent! It is well that you have such deep devotion to the Mahāyāna sūtras, such great joy in the Mahāyāna sūtras, such longing for the Mahāyāna sūtras, such delight in the taste of the Mahāyāna sūtras, such firm faith in the Mahāyāna, and that you offer reverence, honor, and veneration. Son of good family, by the cause and condition of this profoundly virtuous mind of yours, you will become far superior to immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas — great bodhisattvas exceeding in number the grains of sand in the river Ganges — and sooner than they, you will fully and completely awaken to unsurpassed and perfect awakening. Without long delay, you will teach and explain the essence of this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa — spoken by the Tathāgata with the intention of revealing the buddha-nature — to many vast assemblies.

Son of good family, in a time long past, before the sun of a buddha had risen, I was then born as a brahmin, and while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva I had fully mastered all the scriptures of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), was living in perfect serenity, possessed of virtuous conduct, with a mind utterly pure, so that outward conditions did not give rise to perceptions of desire within me. The fire of aversion was extinguished. I held in mind the qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and yet, though I searched in all directions for the Mahāyāna sūtras, I had not even heard the mere name of such a vast scripture.

At that time I was dwelling on a certain snow mountain. That mountain was extremely remote, filled throughout with springs, cascading streams, bathing pools, flowering trees, forests, and medicinal plants. Throughout that place pure springs flowed out from the cliffs, adorned completely with fragrant flowers, and there were beyond counting birds and wild animals. There as well were trees of many varieties bearing fruits of the most exquisite flavor beyond counting, and besides these, sweet lotus roots and fragrant roots of blue plants filled the place completely. At that time I dwelt there alone, eating nothing but the fruit of the trees."

After eating, I turned my mind one-pointedly to meditative absorption, and for measureless years I neither heard that a Tathāgata had appeared in the world, nor did I hear even the name of the sūtras of the Great Vehicle.

O son of good family, while I was practicing austerities in that way, Śakra (Indra, lord of the gods) and the sons of the gods were filled with the utmost wonder. Gathering together, each one thought to himself, and then spoke these verses one to another:

"On this pure snow mountain
dwells one who is utterly peaceful, who has abandoned attachment —
the king possessed of the eight qualities.
He has abandoned attachment, aversion, and pride;
he has wholly cut away delusion, guile, and deceit;
