and through the door of speech he does not utter
words that are coarse and hurtful."

At that time, among that assembly there was a son of the gods named Supremely Joyful, who then also spoke a verse:

"He who has thus abandoned attachment
and strives with wholesome and vigorous diligence —
does he seek Śakra's power and method,
or does he aspire to be reborn in the realm of the gods?"

Then another son of the gods named Ṛṣika also addressed Śakra in verse:

"O lord of the gods, Kauśika —
it is not fitting to give rise to such doubt.
Even a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) practising austerities
does not seek the power and methods of Śakra."

Having spoken that verse, he then said further: "Kauśika, great beings in the world practice immeasurable austerities of every variety not out of attachment to their own bodies, but for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, for the sake of their welfare and happiness. Such a being, seeing the many faults of saṃsāra, would not develop even the slightest attachment — no more than to saliva or nasal mucus — even were he to behold this great earth, its mountains, and its great oceans completely filled with precious jewels. In this way, that great being wholly abandons precious gems, wealth, wives, sons, head, eyes, brain, hands, feet, major and minor limbs, his dwelling house, yaks, oxen, horses, vehicles, male servants, female servants, and laborers — and he does not aspire to be reborn as a god in the higher realms. He applies himself solely to the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings. As I understand it, that great being, utterly pure, having wholly severed all afflictions, seeks nothing but unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening."

Śakra, the lord of the gods, then spoke thus: "Just as you have said, that great sage will become a refuge for the entire world together with its gods. Moreover, if a great tree of buddhahood were to arise in this world, it would dispel the venomous serpent of afflictions from all — the gods, humans, and asuras and all the rest who inhabit the world. For those beings who sit in the shade of the tree of buddhahood will have every venomous serpent of affliction completely expelled. If that great sage is to become a Sugata in a future time, then the immeasurable blazing afflictions of all of us and all others will be utterly pacified. Yet this is most difficult to trust in. Why? Because among the countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who arouse the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, many will turn back from that unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening through even slight conditions — just as the reflection of the moon in water, when the water is stirred, is likewise stirred."

Again, consider a likeness: an image painted in a picture is difficult to create yet easy to destroy. The awakening mind is just like that — difficult to arouse, yet easy to lose.

Great sage, consider further a likeness: a man fully armored and equipped for battle, who, upon reaching the field of combat and meeting the enemy, is immediately seized with fear and turns back. All sentient beings are likewise — armed with the armor of having aroused the awakening mind and setting out for awakening, the moment they behold the faults of saṃsāra they are overcome with fear and turn back.

For this reason, I went to examine that man, who was practicing austerities without affliction and distress, and whose conduct I could see was entirely pure — and yet I could not bring myself to trust in him. I drew near to him in order to examine whether that man is capable or not of bearing on his shoulders the heavy burden of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

Consider the likeness of a chariot: if it has two wheels, it can be used; and a bird: if it has two wings, it can fly. Ascetic practice is just the same. I could see that he was extremely disciplined in his vows and ethical conduct — and yet one must still examine whether or not the profoundly deep wisdom is present. If that profoundly deep wisdom is present, then he will be able to carry on his shoulders the heavy burden of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

Sage, consider the likeness of a great fish: it may carry exceedingly many young in its womb, yet only a few are born as actual offspring. Or consider the mango tree: though it puts forth flowers in great abundance, only a few ripen into fruit. Sentient beings who arouse the awakening mind are likewise immeasurable in number, yet in the end, only very few bring it to its fruit.

Great sage, let us go together to find where that man is and examine him.

Sage, consider the likeness of gold: even genuine gold, when tested by three methods, is recognized as genuine or not — namely, by burning, by striking, and by rubbing. Ascetic practice is just the same.

Having said this, at that moment Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, transformed his own body into a most terrifying rākṣasa form, descended upon the snowy mountain range, and sat down not very far from the ascetic. Then that rākṣasa, with a fearless mind and in a voice of great boldness yet spoken in a whisper, recited this half-verse spoken by the buddhas of the past:

Alas — all conditioned things are impermanent,
their nature is to arise and to cease.

Having recited this half-verse, he sat nearby, displaying his terrifying form, eyes wide open and gazing all around in the four directions.

At that moment, when the one engaged in austerities heard this half-verse, an exceedingly joyful mind arose in him — as when a merchant traveling by night through a most frightening ravine loses his companions, becomes terrified, and in searching for a companion suddenly meets one, and immeasurable gladness and delight arise the very instant of that meeting.

Or again, consider the likeness of one long afflicted by illness who meets a skilled physician and is healed by excellent medicine; or one who has fallen into the ocean and comes upon a boat; or one parched by intense thirst who comes upon cool water; or one who has escaped from being captured by enemies; or one who has been imprisoned for a long time and wins release; or a farmer struck by a great drought upon whom rain falls; or one escorting travelers who has gone on a long road and hears news of their return — in each case, exceedingly great joy arises.

Noble son, when he heard that half-verse, the joy that arose in him was just like all of those. He rose from where he was sitting, lifted his hair with his hands,

looked out in all four directions, and spoke these words: "Who is it that has spoken this verse?" Looking around, he saw no one else but a single rakṣasa, and he spoke again these words: "Who is it that opens this gate of complete liberation? Who is it that roars the thunder of the melodious speech of the buddhas? Who is it that awakens from the deep slumber of sleep in which one lies utterly sunk in saṃsāra?" And again he said: "Who is it that offers the taste of unsurpassable awakening to sentient beings tormented by the extreme famine of saṃsāra? Who is it that, with a great vessel, draws out the countless sentient beings who have sunk into the ocean of saṃsāra? Who is it that, for the many sentient beings severely afflicted by the sickness of mental afflictions, becomes a physician and a skilled healer of that sickness? This half-verse that has been spoken has stirred my mind, so that it has opened like a lotus opened by the crescent moon."

Noble son, at that moment and at that time, he could see no one else at all; and seeing only the rakṣasa, he thought: "This half-verse was not spoken by the rakṣasa." And he thought further: "It was not spoken by him — and why? Because one of such exceedingly ugly and terrifying form could not be like this. One who has heard this verse is of a kind that is free from all that is terrifying and hideous. How could one of such an appearance have spoken this verse? It is as impossible as a lotus being born from within fire, or cool water arising from the scorching rays of the sun." Noble son, at that time I also thought: "I am a person of very little discernment. Yet perhaps this rakṣasa has in the past encountered a buddha and heard this half-verse from that buddha — who can say? I should ask about the meaning of this half-verse." Having thought thus, I approached that rakṣasa and spoke these words: "Excellent! O great being, from whom did you hear this half-verse, spoken in the past by one free from fear? O great being, where did you find this precious half wish-fulfilling jewel? O great being, the meaning of this half-verse is the true path of all the buddhas and Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and those who abide in the present. The countless sentient beings who dwell in the world are perpetually enmeshed in the net of wrong views, and so they never hear this meaning of emptiness, which transcends the world, taught with great courage by one endowed with the ten powers, free from the doctrines of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas)."

Noble son, when I had asked him these words, he replied to me in turn with these words: "O great brahmin, do not ask me such things. And why? It has been many days since I found no food, and having searched everywhere without finding any, I am utterly consumed by hunger and thirst. What I said before was spoken as if in delirium — it was not spoken with mindfulness or introspective awareness. Even if by my own power I were to fly through the sky, travel to the land of the Uttarakurus in the north, and journey as far as the abodes of the gods, still, since I found no food, I spoke what I did in that condition."

Noble son, then at that time I spoke to the rakṣasa these words: "O great being, if you will recite this verse to me in full, I vow to be your disciple for one whole lifetime. O great being, what you have spoken is incomplete both in words and in meaning — why do you not speak it in full?"

The generosity of material things has a final limit, but the generosity of Dharma has no final limit. And even though it has no final limit, it is supremely beneficial for the sake of benefit and happiness. Having heard this incomplete verse, I was struck with wonder and doubt, and so I said: 'Recite this verse in full, and if you resolve my doubt, I vow to be your disciple for one whole lifetime.'

The rakṣasa said: 'Your understanding surpasses your situation, and so you grasp my purpose well — but think nothing of my own intention. I am tormented by extreme hunger and cannot bring myself to speak.'

Then I said to him: 'What do you eat as food?' The rakṣasa replied: 'Do not ask me that. If I were to tell you, many people would be terrified.' Then I said to him: 'In this deserted place there is no one at all, and I have no fear of you — so why will you not speak?' The rakṣasa then said: 'My food is the raw flesh of human beings, and I drink warm blood. I am of such little merit that even food such as this I cannot find anywhere. Though there are many people in the world, all of them are endowed with merit alone, and protected by the gods — therefore I have no power to kill and eat them.'

Noble son, then I said to him: 'Recite this verse in full, with its complete meaning, and I shall utterly surrender this body of mine to you. O great being, what need is there? This body of mine is extremely light and worthless. It will be eaten by tigers, wolves, foxes, vultures, hawks, crows, and the like, and not even a hair's breadth of merit will arise from that. But as for me — I seek unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and so may this body, which is without essence, become a body endowed with essence.'

The rakṣasa then said: 'You say you will surrender your body — and all for the sake of eight syllables. Who could believe such a thing?' Noble son, then I said to him once more: 'You do not truly understand. Consider how a person might be carrying a clay bowl and exchange it for a vessel of seven precious substances — just so, if through this essenceless body of mine I were to attain a body like a vajra, who would doubt what I have said? As my witnesses I have the Great Brahmā (Mahābrahmā), king of kings, Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, and the kings of the Four Great Kings, and others as witness. Furthermore, there are also as witnesses the bodhisattvas with their magical vision, who strive in the Great Vehicle for the benefit and happiness of limitless sentient beings and who are endowed with the six perfections. And beyond these, the blessed buddhas now dwelling in the world-realms of the ten directions, who even now live and care for the sake of sentient beings — these too are my witnesses. I shall surrender this body for the sake of these eight syllables.'

The rakṣasa then said: 'If you are truly able to surrender your body in this way, then listen well — I shall teach you this verse.' Noble son, when I heard these words, great joy arose in my mind. I removed the garment of skin and flesh that clothed my body and spread it as a seat for the rakṣasa, saying: 'I beseech the teacher to be seated.' Then, with palms pressed together and knees placed upon the ground, I spoke these words:

'Teacher, I beseech you to teach me this half-verse.' Having spoken thus, the rakṣasa then recited the half-verse:

What has been born will cease —
those things find peace and bliss in stilling.

When the rakṣasa had spoken that verse, he then said these words: 'Bodhisattva, great being, if you were to hear the verse in its complete meaning, your aspiration would now be wholly fulfilled. But if you are truly sincere in your purpose of acting for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, then now the time has come for you to offer me your body.' Noble son, at that moment I took this meaning deeply to heart. Then, in the time that followed, I inscribed this verse everywhere — on rocks, on the faces of walls, on trees, on every road — and so that my flesh would not be visible, I wrapped my body in the garment I wore and climbed up into the tree. At that moment the deity of that tree asked me: 'Excellent! Excellent! Great being, what is it you now intend to do?' Noble son, at that time I spoke these words to the deity: 'I intend to surrender this body completely in order to repay the kindness of having heard this verse.' The deity of the tree said: 'If you hear that verse, what benefit will there be?' The bodhisattva replied: 'This verse is the Dharma that opens up emptiness as it is known by all the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present. It is for the sake of this Dharma that I surrender my body completely — not out of desire for gain, or for renown, or for wealth, or for jewels, or to become a wheel-turning king, or king of the four great kings, or Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, or the great king Brahmā, or the happiness of gods and humans. It is for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings that I surrender this body.' Noble son, as I was surrendering this body, I also spoke these words: 'May those sentient beings who are held in the grip of miserliness, upon seeing me surrender my body in this way, come to abide in generosity. And may those who are attached to generosity yet seized by pride also see me surrender my body in this way.' Having made this aspiration, I then surrendered this body as one might discard spittle or a clod of earth and stone. As soon as the bodhisattva had spoken these words, he leapt down from the tree. At that very moment, many kinds of sounds arose from the sky above and resounded all the way up to the peak of existence. At that time, the one who had appeared as the rakṣasa transformed back into the body of Śakra, caught the bodhisattva before he could strike the ground, laid him gently down, and made him comfortable. Then Śakra, lord of the gods, together with the sons of the gods and the great king Brahmā, bowed their heads at the feet of the bodhisattva and spoke these words: 'Excellent! Excellent! Bodhisattva, you are true — one who will bring benefit and happiness to measureless sentient beings, who causes the great lamp of Dharma to shine in the vast darkness of ignorance. I who disturbed your mind and did you harm in order to guard and protect the great Dharma of the Tathāgata — I confess and acknowledge that wrongdoing with regret. When in future you attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, we too aspire to be liberated.' Then Śakra, lord of the gods, and the sons of the gods bowed to the bodhisattva and vanished from sight. Noble son, thus in former times I also surrendered my body completely for the sake of a half-verse,

Through that cause and those conditions, twelve aeons before Maitreya, he manifested complete and perfect awakening into unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Noble son, that I attained such boundless qualities was likewise through the power of making offerings to the authentic Dharma of the Tathāgata. Noble son, you too are like that — by having aroused the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, you are supremely elevated and exalted above bodhisattvas, great beings, boundless and limitless in number as the grains of sand in the river Ganges.

Noble son, it is therefore said that when a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in the Mahāyāna's complete nirvāṇa, practicing the noble conduct, it is called the practice of noble conduct. This is the sixth chapter, called "The Practice of Noble Conduct," from the Noble Sūtra of the Great Mahāyāna Complete Nirvāṇa.

The Noble Sūtra of the Great Complete Nirvāṇa. The twentieth fascicle.

Noble son, how then does a bodhisattva, a great being, practice the holy life (brahmacarya)? Noble son, when bodhisattvas, great beings, abide in the Mahāyāna's complete nirvāṇa, they are endowed with the holy life through these seven kinds of Dharma. What are the seven? They are: knowing the Dharma, knowing the meaning, knowing the time, knowing moderation, knowing oneself, knowing the assembly, and knowing those above and below.

Noble son, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, know the Dharma? Noble son, the bodhisattva, the great being, knows the twelve branches of scripture — namely, the sūtra branch, the prose-and-verse mixed branch (geya), the prophetic branch (vyākaraṇa), the verse branch (gāthā), the inspirational sayings branch (udāna), the narrative context branch (nidāna), the tales of spiritual realization branch (avadāna), the branch of accounts of related events, the birth-story branch (jātaka), the extensive teachings branch (vaipulya), the wondrous branch (adbhutadharma), and the branch of systematic analysis (upadeśa). This is knowing the Dharma.

Noble son, what is called the sūtra branch? From the utterance "Thus did I hear" up to "they rejoiced and followed approvingly" — that is called a sūtra.

What is called the prose-and-verse mixed branch? It is what the Blessed One declared to the monks: "We too were utterly foolish; lacking knowledge, we did not understand the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, and because of that we wandered through cyclic existence and sank into the great ocean of suffering. What are those four truths? Suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path." After the Blessed One had first taught the sūtra branch to the monks, those among the congregation who were sharp-faculties then arrived before the Buddha in order to hear the Dharma, and asked others, "What did the Blessed One teach here before?" The Blessed One, knowing this, took what had been taught previously as a sūtra and then spoke it again in verse, in these words:

I, formerly, was like you —
I did not see the four truths.
Because of that I wandered through cyclic existence
and fell into the great ocean of suffering.
Whoever realizes the four truths
will utterly sever cyclic existence.
When all becoming through birth is exhausted,
it is impossible to take on any further existence.

This is what is called the prose-and-verse mixed branch.

What is called the prophetic branch? It is that which, in a sūtra or in the Vinaya, the Tathāgata prophesied at certain times to gods and humans about attaining buddhahood — as in: "Ajita, in a future time a king called Śaṅkha will appear; at that time, in that age, he will fully awaken, and his name will be Maitreya." Such statements are called the prophetic branch.

What is called the verse branch? It is in sūtras and in —

the Vinaya — where the following four-line verse is spoken:

Abandon every evil deed.
Fulfil all that is wholesome.
Tame your own mind completely.
This is the teaching of the buddhas.

Statements such as these are called the verse branch.

What is called the deliberate utterance branch? At an evening time, the Blessed One entered into meditative absorption and taught the Dharma at length to the gods. Meanwhile, the monks, each on their own, were thinking: "What is the Tathāgata doing right now?" The following morning, the Tathāgata arose from his absorption, and, without having been asked by anyone, knowing through his primordial wisdom of the thoughts of others, he spoke thus: "Listen, monks, know it to be like this: all those born as gods have extremely long life-spans. Monks, it is excellent that you do not seek gain for the sake of others' approval. It is excellent to have few desires. It is excellent to be content with what one has. It is excellent to dwell in a charnel ground." Statements spoken deliberately in this way, without anyone having asked, are called the deliberate utterance branch.

What is called the narrative-occasion branch? It is that which, in a sūtra, arises from a narrative occasion and reveals a verse, the verse being distinguished and taught on the basis of that occasion. In such a case, in the land of Śrāvastī, a certain person seized a peacock by the neck, stuffed it into a cage, poured water over it mixed with rice, and then sent it away. The Blessed One, knowing through his wisdom the prior causes and conditions of this, took occasion from that event and spoke the following verse:

Do not scorn a small and minor evil deed,
thinking it will cause no harm.
Even dripping drops of water
will fill a great vessel to the brim.

Statements such as these are called the narrative-occasion branch.

What is called the inspired utterance branch? Those passages in the Vinaya that present illustrations and examples — these are called the inspired utterance branch.

What is called the thus-it-occurred branch? Among the words spoken by the Blessed One: those spoken when the Blessed One passed into the world and taught — such as the sūtra called "The Compendium of Elements"; those spoken when the Blessed One Bhadrapāla passed into the world — called "The Five Nectars"; those spoken when the buddha Vipaśyin passed into the world — called "The Mirror of Dharma"; and those spoken when the Blessed One Kāśyapa passed into the world — called "The Analysis of Emptiness." Statements such as these are called the thus-it-occurred branch.

What is called the birth-tale branch? These concern the Blessed One's practice of the bodhisattva conduct in former times and the hardships he underwent. "Monks, know this well: in times past I took on the body of a deer, the body of a bear, the body of a spotted deer, the body of a hare, the body of a king, the body of a wheel-turning king, the body of a nāga, the body of a garuda, and many such forms — and in those lives, while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, I had these experiences." Statements such as these are called the birth-tale branch.

What is called the extensive sūtra branch? The meaning of the extensive Mahāyāna sūtras is said to be extremely vast and wide, like the sky itself. Sūtras such as these are called the extensive sūtra branch.

What is called the wondrous occurrence branch? The bodhisattva, immediately upon being born for the first time, without anyone guiding him, walked seven steps; he emitted a great radiance of light; he gazed in all ten directions; a monkey-bee carried a vessel of honey and offered it to the Tathāgata; a white dog listened to the Dharma from the buddha; the māra (Skt. māra) of evil form transformed himself into a dark-blue ox and entered among many nuns' almsbowls that had been set out, knocking and jostling among them and yet not breaking a single one; and when the buddha, from the moment of his first birth, entered into a divine shrine, the gods rose and paid homage and the like. Statements such as these are called the wondrous occurrence branch.

What is called "the branch of establishing conclusions" is this: in whatever sūtras the Blessed One, the Buddha, taught, the degree to which a subject is definitively determined, its particular divisions made, and its defining marks explained — that is called the branch of establishing conclusions.

When a bodhisattva thus understands and knows the twelve branches of the sūtras, that is called knowing the Dharma.

Now, in what way does a great bodhisattva know the meaning? A great bodhisattva who knows in detail the meaning of everything expressed in letters and in words — that is called knowing the meaning.

In what way does a great bodhisattva know the time? Son of good family, a great bodhisattva knows the time: the time for dwelling in a charnel ground; the time for applying oneself with great diligence; the time for cultivating equanimity and meditative absorption; the time for making offerings to the buddhas; the time for attending upon one's teacher; and the time for applying oneself earnestly to generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Knowing these things is called knowing the time.

In what way does a great bodhisattva know contentment? Son of good family, a great bodhisattva's knowing contentment is this: with regard to food and drink, robes, medicine, coming and going, sitting, resting, sleeping, waking, and keeping silent — knowing the appropriate measure in all these is called knowing contentment.

Son of good family, in what way does a great bodhisattva know himself? That bodhisattva knows himself in this way: "I have such and such faith; such and such moral discipline; such and such learning; such and such equanimity; such and such wisdom; such and such manner of coming and going; such and such mindfulness; such and such practice of virtue; such and such manner of questioning; and such and such manner of answering." Knowing these things about oneself is called knowing oneself.

In what way does a great bodhisattva know his assembly? Son of good family, a bodhisattva knows his assembly in this way: "This is an assembly of the warrior class; this is an assembly of brahmins; this is an assembly of householders; this is an assembly of renunciants." And he knows how to conduct himself in each of those assemblies, how to sit among them, how to teach the Dharma among them, and how to question and respond among them. Knowing these things is called knowing the assembly.

Son of good family, in what way does a great bodhisattva know the superior and the inferior? Son of good family, in this regard there are two kinds: those with faith and those without faith. The bodhisattva should understand that those with faith tend toward virtue and those without faith tend toward non-virtue. Among those with faith, again there are two kinds: those who dwell in the Saṅgha's residence and those who do not. The bodhisattva should understand that those who dwell in the Saṅgha's residence act virtuously, while those who do not dwell there act non-virtuously. Among those who do dwell there, again there are two kinds: those who pay homage and those who do not. The bodhisattva should understand that those who pay homage act virtuously, while those who do not pay homage act non-virtuously. Among those who do pay homage, again there are two kinds: those who listen to the Dharma and those who do not. The bodhisattva should understand that those who listen to the Dharma act virtuously, while those who do not listen act non-virtuously. Among those who do listen to the Dharma, again there are two kinds: those who listen with one-pointed mind and those who do not. The bodhisattva should understand that those who listen with one-pointed mind act virtuously, while those who do not listen with one-pointed mind act non-virtuously. Among those who do listen with one-pointed mind, again there are two kinds: those who attend to the meaning and those who do not attend to the meaning.

The bodhisattva should understand that those who attend to the meaning act virtuously, while those who do not attend to the meaning act non-virtuously. Among those who do attend to the meaning, again there are two kinds: those who practice in accordance with what has been taught, and those who do not practice in accordance with what has been taught. The bodhisattva should understand that those who practice in accordance with what has been taught act virtuously, while those who do not practice in accordance with what has been taught act non-virtuously. Among those who do practice in accordance with what has been taught, again there are two kinds: those who seek through the vehicle of the śrāvakas and do not act for the benefit and happiness of all suffering sentient beings, and those who dedicate their practice to unsurpassed awakening and engage in it for the benefit and happiness of the many — these latter are bodhisattvas, and whoever acts for the benefit and happiness of the many is the most excellent of all.

Noble son, as an example: among precious gems, the wish-fulfilling jewel is supreme. Among all savors, ambrosia (amṛta) is supreme. Likewise, the bodhisattva too has arisen as the highest and most excellent among gods and humans, utterly beyond compare.

Noble son, these are what is called "dwelling in the seven wholesome qualities" for a bodhisattva, a great being who abides in the sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete passing beyond sorrow. When a bodhisattva is endowed with these seven qualities of Dharma, that is called the holy life (brahmacarya).

Noble son, furthermore, what is called the holy life is this: loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.

The bodhisattva, the great being Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, since the extensive cultivation of loving-kindness eliminates aversion, and since the mind of compassion also cuts through aversion, why speak of four immeasurables? In terms of their actual import, they are sufficiently covered by three."

The Blessed One replied: "Kāśyapa, loving-kindness has three kinds of focus: focus on sentient beings, focus on phenomena, and non-focus. Compassion, joy, and equanimity are likewise — in terms of actual import they are covered by three, and there is no fourth.

Focus on sentient beings means: focusing on the five aggregates and wishing them to be happy — this is called focus on sentient beings. Focus on phenomena means: focusing on sentient beings and giving them whatever they need — this is called focus on phenomena. Non-focus means: focusing on the Tathāgata — this is called non-focus.

What is called loving-kindness focuses on impoverished sentient beings. The Tathāgata, the Great Teacher, is utterly free from poverty and is perfectly at ease. If one focuses on sentient beings, that is not focusing on a buddha — and the same holds for phenomena. Therefore, focusing on the Tathāgata is called non-focus.

Blessed One, loving-kindness focuses on all sentient beings, just as one might focus on one's mother or father, spouse, child, or dear friend — therefore it is called focus on sentient beings. Focus on phenomena means: not regarding all things as mother, father, spouse, child, or dear friend, but viewing all phenomena as arising through dependent origination — this is called focus on phenomena. Non-focus means: not resting in characteristics with regard to phenomena, and not resting in characteristics with regard to sentient beings — this is called non-focus. Compassion, joy, and equanimity are likewise. Therefore they are covered by three, and there is no fourth.

Blessed One, persons are of two kinds: those who are motivated by what they see, and those who are motivated by what they love. Those who are motivated by what they see cultivate loving-kindness and compassion to a greater degree. Those who are motivated by what they love cultivate joy and equanimity to a greater degree. Therefore they are covered by three, and there is no fourth.

Blessed One, the reason these are called 'immeasurable' is that they are boundless —"

because they are boundless, they are called immeasurable. If they are immeasurable, then there can be three but not four. If there were four, they could not be called immeasurable. Therefore there are three and not four."

The Blessed One then declared to Kāśyapa: "Son of good family, a buddha, a Blessed One, teaches the Dharma for the sake of the many ordinary persons, and what is taught is taught with very deep intention. It is therefore difficult to understand and to know.

For some sentient beings he taught dependent origination as a single thing. What is that single dependent origination? It is this: all conditioned phenomena.

Son of good family, for some he taught it in two aspects: cause and result. For some he taught it in three aspects: affliction, karma, and suffering. For some he taught it in four aspects: ignorance, formations, birth, and aging-and-death. For some he taught it in five aspects: feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, and birth. For some he taught it in six aspects: cause and result across the three times. On some occasions he taught it in seven aspects: consciousness, name, form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, becoming, and grasping. For some he taught it in eight aspects: the remaining eight besides ignorance, formations, birth, and aging-and-death. For some he taught it in nine aspects: as explained in the sūtra called 'The City,' the remaining nine besides ignorance, formations, and consciousness. For some he taught it in eleven aspects: because of the objection of the naked ascetics (Nirgranthans) who say all things arise from birth, the remaining eleven aspects besides that one. And on some occasions he taught dependent origination in its complete twelve aspects — as he taught in full to Kāśyapa and others at Rājagṛha, from ignorance all the way through birth and aging-and-death, the twelve complete links.

Son of good family, this single dependent origination he taught in different aspects for the sake of different ordinary persons. The immeasurable minds are likewise.

Son of good family, therefore do not give rise to doubt about the domain of what the Tathāgata taught with deep intention.

Son of good family, the buddha, the Blessed One, is endowed with the most supreme skillful means. Thus he taught the impermanent as permanent, and the permanent as impermanent. He taught the pleasant as suffering, and the suffering as pleasant. He taught the impure as pure, and the pure as impure. He taught the self as selfless, and the selfless as self. He taught what is not a sentient being as a sentient being, and the sentient being as not a sentient being. He taught what is not a thing as a thing, and the thing as not a thing. He taught the untrue as true, and the true as untrue. He taught what is not an object as an object, and the object as not an object. He taught what is not birth as birth, and birth as not birth. And further: he taught ignorance as knowledge, and knowledge as ignorance. He taught form as not form, and not-form as form. He taught what is not the path as the path, and the path as not the path.

Son of good family, with immeasurable skillful means the Tathāgata spoke what appear to be falsehoods in order to tame sentient beings. Son of good family, if a certain sentient being is attached to enjoyments and riches, then I conjure an appearance for him as a wheel-turning king and for a measureless span of years give him every kind of thing in manifold variety that he could desire —

and thereafter established him at last in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. If a certain sentient being is attached to the five objects of desire, then for a measureless span of years I let him enjoy the finest and most excellent of the five kinds of desirable things, and thereafter established him at last in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. If a certain sentient being is proud of his lineage and arrogant by nature, then for a measureless span of years I made myself that person's servant and honored him with the utmost reverence, gladdening his mind, and thereafter established him at last in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. If a certain sentient being is by nature arrogant and requires that others counsel and correct him, then for hundreds and thousands of years I instructed and corrected him until his mind was tamed, and only then established him in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Son of good family, is it a falsehood that the Tathāgata, for a measureless span of years, through manifold skillful means, established many beings in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening? The buddha, the Blessed One, though dwelling amid the unwholesome, is not stained by the mud of faults, just as a lotus is unstained. Son of good family, the meaning of the four immeasurables is likewise to be understood in this way.

Son of good family, the mind of immeasurability is by nature fourfold, and whoever cultivates it earnestly will be reborn in the realm of Brahmā the Great. Son of good family, there are thus four qualities that serve as companions to the immeasurables, and that is why they are called four. Whoever cultivates the mind of loving-kindness will fully cut off attachment. Whoever cultivates the mind of compassion will fully abandon aversion. Whoever cultivates the mind of joy will fully abandon unhappiness. Whoever cultivates the mind of equanimity will fully abandon the minds of attachment and aversion.

Son of good family, for this reason they are fourfold — not one, not two, not three. Son of good family, do not say: "Just as you explain that the mind of loving-kindness abandons aversion, compassion is similar to it in that regard, and so three would be fitting." Why not? Son of good family, aversion is of two kinds: aversion that takes life, and aversion that strikes and injures. Cultivating loving-kindness abandons aversion that takes life. Cultivating compassion abandons aversion that strikes and injures.

Son of good family, for this reason, are not four immeasurables appropriate? Furthermore, aversion is of two kinds: aversion toward sentient beings, and aversion toward what is not sentient beings. Cultivating loving-kindness abandons aversion toward sentient beings. Cultivating compassion abandons aversion toward what is not sentient beings. Furthermore, aversion is of two kinds: aversion that has causes and conditions, and aversion that lacks causes and conditions. Cultivating loving-kindness abandons aversion that has causes and conditions. Cultivating compassion abandons aversion that lacks causes and conditions. Furthermore, aversion is of two kinds: aversion habituated from the past, and aversion habituated in the present moment. Cultivating loving-kindness abandons aversion habituated from the past. Cultivating compassion abandons aversion habituated in the present. Furthermore, aversion is of two kinds: aversion toward noble ones, and aversion toward the base and ignoble. Cultivating the mind of loving-kindness abandons aversion toward noble ones.

Cultivating compassion abandons aversion toward the base and ignoble. Furthermore, aversion is of two kinds: intense aversion and middling aversion. Cultivating loving-kindness abandons intense aversion. Cultivating compassion abandons middling aversion.

Noble son, for these reasons, it is not fitting to object by saying that, since four aspects are appropriate, they are exhausted in three and there cannot be four. Therefore, Kāśyapa, the way in which these immeasurable minds function as support and antidote has been taught by distinguishing them into four aspects.

Furthermore, four aspects are fitting on account of the vessel. If one possesses loving-kindness toward a particular vessel, that does not mean compassion, joy, and equanimity are also present toward that same being. For this reason, there is no way to reduce the four aspects. Noble son, from the particular perspective of conduct as well, four aspects are fitting. If, when one is practicing loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity are absent, then for that reason the four aspects are manifestly necessary.

Noble son, four aspects are also fitting on account of the immeasurable itself. Furthermore, the immeasurable is of four kinds. Some immeasurable minds have an object but are not masterful. Some minds of loving-kindness are masterful but have no object. Some minds of loving-kindness both have an object and are masterful. And some minds of loving-kindness neither have an object nor are masterful.

As for an immeasurable mind that has an object but is not masterful: some focus on limitless and boundless sentient beings as their object, yet have not attained mastery in meditative absorption, or else have attained it but with uncertainty, or have attained it but then declined. As for an immeasurable that is masterful but has no object: this is like focusing on one's parents, siblings, or friends and relatives with the aim of bringing them happiness — this is not a focus on the immeasurable. As for an immeasurable that both has an object and is masterful: this refers to buddhas and bodhisattvas. As for an immeasurable that neither has an object nor is masterful: this is like śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who are unable to focus broadly on limitless sentient beings, and in whom mastery does not arise.

Noble son, for these reasons, the immeasurable is of four kinds, and it is not something that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are capable of fully knowing — it is the domain of the blessed buddhas. Noble son, though these four entities may be called immeasurable even in relation to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is not fitting to say so without qualification. The blessed buddhas are to be called immeasurable and boundless.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One again: "It is so, Blessed One. It is so. Just as the Blessed One has declared, this is the domain of the blessed buddhas, and it does not fall within the patience of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Blessed One, would a bodhisattva who abides in the great nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle, and in whom minds of loving-kindness and compassion arise, declare that these are not great loving-kindness and great compassion?" The Blessed One replied: "Noble son, if a bodhisattva divides sentient beings into three groups — friends, enemies, and those who are neutral — and further divides friends into superior, middling, and lesser, and likewise divides enemies in the same way, then the bodhisattva, the great being, bestows the highest happiness on those who are the most beloved friends; bestows a moderately high happiness equally on the middling and lesser friends; bestows a somewhat lesser degree of happiness on the most intense enemies;

bestows a moderately high happiness on the middling enemy; and bestows the highest happiness on the least intense enemy. In the same progressive manner, the bodhisattva strives to bestow a moderately high happiness on the most intense enemy, and strives to bestow an equally highest happiness on both the middling and the least intense enemies. Or, progressively still, does the bodhisattva strive to bestow an equally highest happiness on the superior, the middling, and the least? If the bodhisattva strives to bestow the highest happiness on the most intense enemy, that is called possessing a mind of loving-kindness. At that point, even though the bodhisattva has no distinction whatsoever between father and mother on the one hand and the most intense enemy on the other, and the mind has become equanimous toward all, noble son, that is still called loving-kindness — it is not yet great loving-kindness.

The questioner asked: "Blessed One, why is it that even a bodhisattva endowed with such loving-kindness as this is not said to have great loving-kindness?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, because it is extremely difficult to sustain it fully, it is not called great loving-kindness. Why is that? Over a very long time, throughout immeasurable eons, one has accumulated many afflictions and has not cultivated wholesome phenomena — therefore the mind cannot be tamed in a mere single day or a single night. Noble son, consider this analogy: just as a needle cannot pierce a dry bean, in the same way, afflictions that are extremely hardened are like that — even if the mind becomes one-pointed and undistracted for a mere single day or night, they are still exceedingly difficult to tame.

Consider further: a dog is not frightened of people, but deer and the like are afraid of people and flee the moment they see one. Aversion, which is so difficult to abandon, is like a guard dog. The mind of loving-kindness, which is so easily disturbed, is like a deer. Therefore, because the mind is so very difficult to tame, this is not called great loving-kindness.

Noble son, consider yet another analogy: if one carves a design on stone, it lasts forever; if one draws a design on water, it is gone the very next moment and does not remain. Aversion is like a design carved on stone. Virtuous roots are like a design drawn on water. Therefore this mind is exceedingly difficult to tame.

Furthermore, consider: the light of a great mass of fire endures for a long time; the light of lightning is but a single instant and does not remain. Aversion is like the great mass of fire; loving-kindness is like the light of lightning. Therefore this mind is exceedingly difficult to tame — and for that reason, this is not called great loving-kindness.

Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides on the first ground (bhūmi) is said to have great loving-kindness. Why is that? Noble son, the most extreme among those who are guilty of wrongdoing are called the perversely craving. A bodhisattva who abides on the first ground and cultivates great loving-kindness makes no distinction even with regard to the perversely craving, and because no fault is perceived in them, no aversion arises. For that reason it is called great loving-kindness.

Noble son, completely removing whatever is harmful and sorrowful for all sentient beings is called great loving-kindness. Giving immeasurable benefit and happiness to many sentient beings is called great compassion. Arousing a mind of joy toward all sentient beings is called great joy. Being without weariness is called great equanimity. Not perceiving a self, a phenomenon, a defining characteristic, or one's own body, and viewing all phenomena as being in a state of equanimity — this is called great equanimity. Surrendering one's own happiness and giving it to others is called great equanimity.

Noble son, from the four immeasurables alone, the six perfections arise and are perfected — not through any other practice."

Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, first attains the four worldly immeasurables, and from that basis arouses the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Gradually, one will also attain transcendence of the world. Noble son, from the cause of the worldly immeasurables, the transcendent immeasurables are attained — and for this reason they are called the great immeasurables.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, eliminating everything that is harmful and painful, and merely thinking of bringing benefit and happiness — that is no more than a thought. It will not truly bring benefit or happiness. Blessed One, consider the example of a monk who, upon perceiving something impure, perceives the clothes worn on the body as skin — and yet they are not truly skin. The monk perceives food as worms — and yet it is not truly worms. The monk perceives bean soup as impure fluid — and yet it is not truly impure fluid. The monk perceives yogurt as feet or brains — and yet it is not truly brains. The monk perceives flour as ground bones — and yet it is not truly ground bones. The four immeasurables are just like this: they do not truly bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings. If one merely says with one's mouth, 'I am giving happiness to sentient beings,' and yet they do not truly become happy — is not such a thought a falsehood? Blessed One, if it is not a falsehood and is truly true, then why do the buddhas and bodhisattvas not, through their blessing, cause all sentient beings to experience happiness? If they do not truly become happy, then what of this teaching the Blessed One gave that I recall to mind now: that by doing no more than earnestly cultivating the single mind of loving-kindness, for an entire age this world-system is washed clean seven times, and one is not born in this world-system during that time — that when the world is forming one is born as a god in the Brahmā heaven, and when the world is dissolving one is born as a god in the Akaniṣṭha heaven? When born as a god in the Brahmā heaven, one is endowed with power and might, uneclipsed by others, and becomes supreme and foremost among a thousand Brahmā realms, being born as the great king Mahābrahmā, so that all sentient beings come to regard oneself as their lord and sovereign. Thirty-six times one is born as Śakra (Indra), the lord of the gods of the Thirty-Three Heaven, with sovereignty over the gods. For hundreds of thousands of births one is born as a wheel-turning king.' If this were not true, what credibility would there be in such a teaching? Since by cultivating the single mind of loving-kindness alone one attains the excellent resources and enjoyments of gods and humans — how could it be untrue?"

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, you are so very brave and endowed with fearlessness." Then the Blessed One spoke these verses to Kāśyapa:

Whoever, toward even a single sentient being,
does not give rise to a mind of aversion,
but wishes for that being's happiness —
this is called pure loving-kindness.

Whoever, toward all sentient beings,
arouses a mind of compassion —
such a one is called of noble lineage,
and will attain immeasurable merit.

Suppose a sage possessed of the five superknowledges
were to fill a great expanse of land,
and a powerful king were to give all manner of happiness —
horses, cattle, and various riches —
the merit obtained thereby
could not match even one-sixteenth
of the merit born of cultivating loving-kindness.

Son of good lineage, the loving-kindness that is cultivated is not false — it is true and authentic. The loving-kindness of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, however, is called false. If it is asked why the loving-kindness of buddhas and bodhisattvas is true and not false in its subtler sense, then know this: a great bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in great and complete nirvāṇa, sees even earth as gold, and gold as earth; sees earth as water, and water as earth; sees water as fire, and fire as water; sees earth as wind, and wind as earth. Because whatever is wished for is accomplished, there is no falsehood. One who is truly a sentient being may be seen as not a sentient being, and one who is not a sentient being may be truly seen as a sentient being. Because whatever is wished for is accomplished, there is no falsehood. Therefore, son of good lineage, the intention that arises from the four immeasurable minds of a bodhisattva is authentic.

Furthermore, son of good lineage, what then is meant by authentic intention? It is for the sake of completely purifying all mental afflictions. Son of good lineage, by cultivating the mind of loving-kindness, attachment and desire will be entirely abandoned. By cultivating the mind of compassion, aversion and anger will be entirely abandoned. By cultivating the mind of joy, unhappiness will be entirely abandoned. By cultivating the mind of equanimity, attachment, aversion, and the perception of beings as substantially real will be entirely abandoned. Therefore this is called authentic intention.

Furthermore, son of good lineage, the four immeasurable minds of a great bodhisattva, a great being, become the ground and root of all virtue. Son of good lineage, if a great bodhisattva, a great being, does not see sentient beings who are impoverished, there is no cause for loving-kindness to arise. If loving-kindness has not arisen, the mind that wishes to give in generosity will not emerge. When generosity is given, many sentient beings are brought to happiness through its power — through giving food and drink, conveyances, clothing, incense, flowers, cushioned seats, houses, and illuminating lamps, and so forth. When generosity is given in this way, the mind is not bound and attachment does not arise, and without any reservation it is dedicated unfailingly to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. At that time the mind clings to nothing; perception is cut off; one does not fear gain and fame; one does not seek the happiness of gods or humans; pride does not arise; one does not expect anything in return; one does not give in generosity in order to deceive others; one does not give out of desire for possessions; when generosity is given, one does not look upon the recipient; one does not distinguish between those of moral discipline and those of poor conduct, between a field of merit and what is not a field of merit, between a spiritual friend and one who is not a spiritual friend; when giving, one does not look upon the gift as fit or unfit as a vessel; one does not look at the day, the time, the place, or whether the place is suitable; one does not consider whether it is a time of famine or a time of great abundance; one does not look at cause and effect; one does not distinguish between sentient beings and non-sentient beings, or between merit and non-merit. Thus, while not looking upon the giver, the receiver, or the material object, nor upon interruptions along the way, nor upon the ripening of results, one nonetheless always practices generosity and does not interrupt its continual flow.

Son of good lineage, if a bodhisattva were to look upon those of moral discipline and those of poor conduct and to keep in view the ripening of the result, generosity would not be given. And if generosity were not given, the perfection of generosity would not be completely fulfilled.

And if the perfection of generosity is not completely fulfilled, unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening will not be accomplished.

Son of good lineage, consider this example: a man has been struck by a poisoned arrow. His relatives and friends seek out a skilled physician in order to draw out the poison and bring him relief. But as the physician moves to extract the poisoned arrow, the man says: "Wait — do not touch my body yet. First let me determine from which direction the arrow came, who shot it — whether a warrior, a brahmin, or someone of low caste — and from where it came. And the arrow itself — is it made of wood, bamboo, or cane? What kind of shaft was used? Of what bird's feathers is the fletching made — a vulture's or some other bird's? And the poison — where did it come from and who made it? Or did it arise of its own? Is it a humanly compounded poison, or the venom of a deadly snake?" And so, while the fool deliberates without arriving at any understanding, he dies on the spot.

Son of good lineage, the bodhisattva is like that very man. When practicing generosity, he makes distinctions and discriminates: "This is the giver; this is the receiver. This one guards moral discipline; this one is of poor conduct" — distinguishing in this way all the way to the ripening of results, he will never give. And if he does not give, the perfection of generosity will not be completely fulfilled. And if the perfection of generosity is not completely fulfilled, unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening will not be accomplished.

Son of good lineage, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices generosity, the loving mind he holds equally toward all sentient beings is like that of a parent toward an only child. Furthermore, when generosity is given, the arising of a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings is like that of parents nursing their only child through illness. The mind of deep joy that arises while practicing generosity is like that of parents seeing their child recover from illness. The equanimity that arises in the mind after giving is like that of parents who, having raised their only child to full growth and seen the child flourish and be well, are at rest.

And so, when the bodhisattva, the great being, gives the gift of food with a mind of loving-kindness, he makes this aspiration: "May this act of giving that I have performed become something shared in common with all sentient beings. By its causes and conditions, may all sentient beings obtain the nourishment of great wisdom, and may they be devoted to dedicating it to the unsurpassed Great Vehicle. May all sentient beings obtain the nourishment of virtuous wisdom, and may they not seek the nourishment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. May all sentient beings obtain the nourishment of the joy of Dharma, and may they not seek the nourishment of sensual pleasure. May all sentient beings obtain the nourishment of the Perfection of Wisdom, may everything be completely and perfectly fulfilled for them, and may they gather the supreme unobstructed roots of virtue. May all sentient beings realize the characteristic of emptiness, attain an unobstructed body, and become like the sky. May all sentient beings always be recipients of generosity, may they be filled with loving-kindness and tender affection for all, and may they become a field of merit for everyone." Thus he makes aspiration.

Son of good lineage, when the bodhisattva, the great being, gives the gift of food with a mind of loving-kindness, he should be utterly steadfast in generating those aspirations.

Son of good lineage, furthermore, when the bodhisattva, the great being, gives the gift of drink to those who are thirsty, with a mind of loving-kindness, he makes this aspiration: "May this act of giving that I have performed become something shared in common with all sentient beings.

By that cause and that condition, may all sentient beings enter the river of the Great Vehicle, drink water possessed of eight flavors, and swiftly travel the path to unsurpassed awakening. May they abandon the torment of the thirst of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, be insatiable in the vehicle of unsurpassed buddhahood, completely abandon the torment of afflictions, be insatiable in the taste of Dharma, relinquish the desires of saṃsāra, and aspire to the complete nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle. May they fully perfect the dharmakāya, attain the meditative absorptions, and enter the ocean of profoundly deep primordial wisdom. May all sentient beings taste the flavor of ambrosia, and having abandoned the desire for bodhisattvas to appear in the world, may they taste the flavor of supreme bliss. May all sentient beings come to possess the measureless hundreds and thousands of tastes of Dharma, and having come to possess the taste of Dharma, may they behold the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Having beheld the intrinsic nature of a buddha, may they pour down a rain of Dharma. Having poured down a rain of Dharma, may the intrinsic nature of a buddha cover everything like the sky, and may all immeasurable sentient beings attain the single taste of the Dharma of the Great Vehicle — not the taste of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. May all sentient beings attain the single sweet taste, not the taste that has become sixfold. May all sentient beings seek only the taste of Dharma, and practicing the Dharma of the buddhas without obstruction, may they never seek any taste other than that.

Son of good lineage, when the bodhisattva, the great being, gives the gift of drink to those who are thirsty with a mind of loving-kindness, he should be utterly steadfast in generating those aspirations.

Son of good lineage, furthermore, when the bodhisattva, the great being, gives the gift of a vehicle with a mind of loving-kindness, he makes this aspiration: "May this act of giving that I have performed become something shared in common with all sentient beings. By that cause and that condition, may all sentient beings be uplifted by a vehicle that is the perfection of the Great Vehicle, a vehicle that abides in the Great Vehicle, a vehicle of non-return, a vehicle that is unshakeable, a vehicle of the seat of awakening (Vajrāsana), a vehicle that does not seek śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, a vehicle that leads to the vehicle of the buddhas, a vehicle that cannot be stolen away, a vehicle that is not inferior, a vehicle that does not turn back, a vehicle that is unsurpassed, a vehicle of the ten powers, a vehicle of great qualities, a vehicle that is wondrous, a vehicle that is marvelous, a vehicle exceedingly hard to find, a vehicle that is boundless, a vehicle that is omniscient."

Son of good lineage, when the bodhisattva, the great being, gives the gift of a vehicle with a mind of loving-kindness, he should always be steadfast in generating those aspirations.

Son of good lineage, furthermore, when the bodhisattva, the great being, gives the gift of garments to be worn with a mind of loving-kindness, he makes this aspiration: "May this act of giving that I have performed become something shared in common with all sentient beings. By that cause and that condition, may all sentient beings be possessed of the garment of modesty and sense of shame, have their bodies covered by the dharmadhātu, and be stripped of the garments pierced through by many wrong views. May their clothing not touch their bodies even by a cubit's width. May they attain bodies of golden hue, with tactile sensations exceedingly soft, luminous and unobstructed, their complexion brilliant, their skin smooth, and their light always immeasurable. May they become formless and entirely free from form. May all sentient beings attain a formless body, transcend all form, and enter the great nirvāṇa of formlessness."

So goes the aspiration prayer. O son of good family, when a great bodhisattva gives the gift of clothing, one should remain steadfast in generating aspiration prayers such as these.

O son of good family, furthermore, when a great bodhisattva cultivates the mind of loving-kindness and gives the gift of flowers, incense, powdered incense, or perfumed unguents, one makes aspiration prayers in this manner: "May this act of giving that I have performed be shared in common with all sentient beings. Through its cause and by its conditions, may all sentient beings attain the meditative absorption of the buddha-flower samādhi, and may they bear upon their heads the crown of the seven limbs of awakening. May all sentient beings become like a form as luminous as the full moon reflected on water, and may all visible forms become supremely excellent. May all sentient beings be entirely adorned with a hundredfold merit bearing a single defining mark. May all sentient beings behold, according to their wish, whatever form is pleasing to the mind. May all sentient beings always encounter a virtuous spiritual friend and receive speech that is unobstructed, so that they may be freed from all that is impure. May all sentient beings be endowed with roots of virtue unsurpassed, like precious jewels. May all sentient beings, by the mere sight of one another, feel joy and affection, be free from the sorrow that leads to suffering, each be endowed with virtue, and do no harm to one another. May all sentient beings be endowed with the fragrant protection of moral discipline. May all sentient beings guard moral discipline without obstruction, and may the fragrant perfume of that discipline pervade and fill the ten directions entirely. May all sentient beings be endowed with moral discipline that is supremely stable, moral discipline free from remorse, moral discipline of omniscient wisdom, moral discipline that has utterly abandoned inferior ethical conduct, moral discipline that is without anything at all, moral discipline of what has never before arisen, moral discipline without a preceptor, moral discipline without activity, moral discipline without anguish, moral discipline without mental affliction, perfected moral discipline, equal moral discipline — and may they be without partiality between one who anoints their body with fragrant incense and one who pierces and wounds them with a weapon, loving both equally. May all sentient beings attain unsurpassed moral discipline, not the moral discipline of the lesser vehicle, but endowed with the moral discipline of the Great Vehicle. May all sentient beings be endowed with the perfection of moral discipline and with the spontaneously accomplished moral discipline of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. May all sentient beings grow familiar with generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. May all sentient beings be endowed with the sacred lotus of great nirvāṇa, and may the fragrant perfume of that lotus fill and pervade the ten directions entirely. May all sentient beings be endowed with the supreme unsurpassed nourishment of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa, carrying its fragrance — just as bees, without harming the color or the fragrance of a flower, take what they need. May all sentient beings be endowed with a body constituted from qualities beyond measure." So goes this aspiration prayer.

O son of good family, when a great bodhisattva gives the gift of flowers and incense with a mind of loving-kindness, one should remain steadfast always in setting forth aspiration prayers such as these.

O son of good family, furthermore, when a great bodhisattva with a mind of loving-kindness gives the gift of thrones and seats, one makes aspiration prayers in this manner: "May this act of giving that I have performed be shared in common with all sentient beings. Through its cause and by its conditions, may all sentient beings be endowed with the divine resting throne of the god above gods. May they be endowed with great wisdom and abide in the state of the four meditative concentrations,

may they rest upon the resting throne of a bodhisattva, may they not rest upon the resting thrones of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and may they thoroughly abandon the resting thrones upon which the wicked recline. May all sentient beings rest in perfect ease, and having thoroughly abandoned the resting throne of saṃsāra, may they be endowed with the lion's throne of complete nirvāṇa. May all sentient beings, even while seated upon that throne, manifest for the benefit of immeasurable other sentient beings the lion's sport of higher knowledge. May all sentient beings, dwelling in this great palace of the Great Vehicle, reveal to all sentient beings the nature of a buddha. May all sentient beings, seated upon the unsurpassed throne, not be swept away by the ways of the world. May all sentient beings, having obtained the throne of patience, be freed from the famine of hunger and cold in saṃsāra. May all sentient beings, having obtained the fearless throne, abandon all enemies that are mental afflictions. May all sentient beings, having obtained the utterly pure throne, strive for nothing other than unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. May all sentient beings, having obtained the throne that abides in virtue, be ever protected by virtuous spiritual friends. May all sentient beings, having obtained the throne upon which one rests on the right side, abide in the Dharma as performed by the buddhas." Thus one sets forth aspiration prayers.

O son of good family, when a great bodhisattva with a mind of loving-kindness gives the gift of thrones and seats in this manner, one should remain steadfast always in setting forth aspiration prayers such as these.

O son of good family, furthermore, when a great bodhisattva with a mind of loving-kindness gives the gift of a dwelling house, one sets forth aspiration prayers in this manner: "May this act of giving that I have performed be shared in common with all sentient beings. Through its cause and by its conditions, may all sentient beings dwell in the house of the Great Vehicle, diligently practicing under virtuous spiritual friends, diligently cultivating great compassion, diligently practicing the six perfections, engaging in the deeds of a perfectly complete buddha, treading the path traveled by all bodhisattvas, and practicing what is as boundless and vast as the sky. May all sentient beings be endowed with correct mindfulness and thoroughly abandon all erroneous thoughts. May all sentient beings abide in ease in permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity, and thoroughly abandon the four inversions. May all sentient beings retain the letters and syllables that transcend the world. May all sentient beings be definitively established as vessels for the unsurpassed gnosis of omniscience. May all sentient beings enter the house of nectar. May all sentient beings, with minds of beginning, middle, and end all together, always enter the house of complete nirvāṇa. May all sentient beings always dwell in the palace of the bodhisattvas in time to come." Thus one sets forth aspiration prayers.

O son of good family, when a great bodhisattva with a mind of loving-kindness gives the gift of a dwelling house, one should remain steadfast always in setting forth these aspiration prayers.

O son of good family, furthermore, when a great bodhisattva with a mind of loving-kindness gives the gift of lamplight, one sets forth aspiration prayers in this manner: "May this act of giving that I have performed be shared in common with all sentient beings. Through its cause and by its conditions, may all sentient beings be endowed with boundless radiance and abide in ease within the Dharma of the buddhas. May all sentient beings be always fully illuminated everywhere by light.

May all sentient beings be endowed with a sublime and excellent complexion, blazing with surpassing radiance. May all sentient beings be endowed with perfectly pure eyes and have the film of blindness cut away. May all sentient beings be endowed with the lamp of omniscient wisdom and become supremely skilled in the absence of self, the absence of a sentient being, the absence of a person, and the absence of a life-force. May all sentient beings see the utterly pure intrinsic nature of the buddhas, like open sky. May all sentient beings be endowed with perfectly pure eyes and clearly see world-realms in the ten directions as numerous as the grains of sand in the river Ganges. May all sentient beings be endowed with the light of the buddhas and shine in the ten directions. May all sentient beings be endowed with unobstructed eyes and all see the utterly pure intrinsic nature of the buddhas. May all sentient beings attain the radiance of great wisdom and vanquish all darkness and all wrong craving. May all sentient beings be endowed with boundless light and illuminate all the boundless buddha-fields. May all sentient beings raise up the lamp of the Great Vehicle and relinquish the lamps of the two lesser vehicles. May all sentient beings be endowed with the light of radiance and, dispelling the darkness of ignorance, be endowed with the quality of illuminating all things in a manner surpassing a thousand suns. May all sentient beings attain the radiance called the Jewel of Fiery Light and dispel all the darkness within the world-realm of the great trichiliocosm. May all sentient beings be endowed with the five eyes, comprehend the defining characteristics of phenomena, and know these for themselves without needing a teacher. May all sentient beings not look upon ignorance. May all sentient beings, through the rays of light of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa, truly reveal the intrinsic nature of buddhas to all sentient beings." These are the aspiration prayers one sets forth.

O son of good family, when a great bodhisattva with a mind of loving-kindness gives the gift of lamplight, one should remain steadfast always in generating these aspiration prayers.

The Noble Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, the twenty-first fascicle.

O son of good family, the foundation of the wholesome roots of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddha-bhagavāns is loving-kindness. O son of good family, when a great bodhisattva applies diligence to the mind of loving-kindness, these immeasurable wholesome roots are born. They are as follows: contemplation of the unattractive; counting the inward and outward flow of the breath; impermanence; arising; cessation; the four applications of mindfulness; the seven skillful means; the three bases of examination; the twelve links of dependent origination; contemplation of selflessness and the like; heat, peak, patience, and the supreme worldly dharma; the path of seeing; the path of cultivation; the four right abandonments; the four bases of miraculous power; the faculties; the powers; the seven limbs of awakening; the noble eightfold path; the four meditative concentrations; the four immeasurables; the eight liberations; the eight stations of mastery; the ten totalities; emptiness; the signless; the wishless; the meditative absorption of non-conflict; the wisdom of knowing others' minds; the superknowledges; the wisdom of knowing the primordial limit; the wisdom of śrāvakas; the wisdom of pratyekabuddhas; the wisdom of bodhisattvas; and

the wisdom of buddhas and all such qualities — the ground of all of these is loving-kindness (maitrī).

Therefore, noble son, loving-kindness is true and not false. Noble son, if someone were to ask, "What is the ground of all virtuous roots?" you should answer: "It is loving-kindness." And for that reason it is true and not false.

Noble son, what becomes wholesome is right thought. Right thought is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata. Loving-kindness is the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). The Great Vehicle is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is the path to awakening. The path to awakening is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is loving-kindness.

Noble son, loving-kindness is the great Brahmā (Mahābrahman). The great Brahmā is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is like a father and mother to all sentient beings. Father and mother are loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is inconceivable. The inconceivable is the domain of the buddhas. The domain of the buddhas is loving-kindness. Therefore, know that loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is the buddha-nature of sentient beings. And yet that buddha-nature, having been overpowered and obscured by afflictions since time without beginning, is not seen by sentient beings. Thus the buddha-nature is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is the great emptiness. The great emptiness is great loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is space. Space is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is permanence. Permanence is the Dharma. The Dharma is the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is happiness. Happiness is the Dharma. The Dharma is the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is utter purity. Utter purity is the Dharma. The Dharma is the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is called the self. The self is the Dharma. The Dharma is the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is the nectar of immortality (amṛta). The nectar of immortality is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the buddha-nature. The buddha-nature is the Dharma. The Dharma is the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is the unsurpassed awakening of all bodhisattvas. Awakening is loving-kindness. Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is the limitless domain of all blessed buddhas, the Bhagavāns. The limitless domain is loving-kindness. Therefore, know that this loving-kindness is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, loving-kindness is impermanent. Impermanence is loving-kindness. Know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, if loving-kindness is suffering, then suffering is loving-kindness. Therefore, know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, if loving-kindness is not utterly pure, that is impure loving-kindness. Therefore, know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, loving-kindness is selfless. Selflessness is loving-kindness. Therefore, this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, loving-kindness is not real. What is not real is loving-kindness. Therefore, know that this loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, the loving-kindness of śrāvakas does not constitute the perfection of generosity; it is not the loving-kindness of generosity. That loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas. And in the same way, know this to be so all the way through to the Perfection of Wisdom; understand this in full.

Noble son, any loving-kindness that brings no benefit to sentient beings — that loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, any loving-kindness that has not entered the path of the single defining mark — that loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, any loving-kindness by which all phenomena are not directly realized — know that loving-kindness to be the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, any loving-kindness by which the buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha) is not seen — that loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, any loving-kindness by which all phenomena are not seen as bearing the defining mark of existence — that loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, if loving-kindness is accompanied by defilement, then that defiled loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, if loving-kindness is accompanied by conditioned existence, then that conditioned loving-kindness is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, if loving-kindness does not abide in the first ground, it is not the loving-kindness of the first ground — know that it is the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, if loving-kindness is unable to attain the ten powers of a buddha and the four fearlessnesses, know that loving-kindness to be the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, the loving-kindness by which one would attain the fruits of the ascetic life — know that loving-kindness to be the loving-kindness of śrāvakas.

Noble son, that loving-kindness which is accompanied by existence, non-existence, and neither-existence-nor-non-existence is something that cannot be fathomed by all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those like them.
