Noble son, if loving-kindness is inconceivable, then the Dharma too is inconceivable, the intrinsic nature of the buddhas too is inconceivable, and the Tathāgata too is inconceivable.

Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in the complete nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle applies himself diligently to such loving-kindness as this. Even while resting in the ease of sleep, he always commences with diligent effort, so that sleep does not overwhelm him. Though he is ever wakeful, because there is no sleep, there is no waking either. Though the gods guard him thoroughly while he sleeps, because he commits no wrongdoing, there is no guarding either. Because he is utterly free from sleep, no bad dreams or anything unwholesome can arise. Though he may be born among the gods of the Brahmā realm, because he has come under their power, there is no birth either.

Noble son, whoever diligently applies himself to loving-kindness will come to possess qualities such as these — boundless and inconceivable. Noble son, this holy sūtra of complete nirvāṇa likewise possesses such qualities — boundless and inconceivable. The Blessed One, the Buddha, likewise possesses such qualities — boundless and limitless.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if everything that the bodhisattvas, the great beings, hold in mind is perfectly true, while what śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas hold to be true is not perfectly true, why do the bodhisattvas, the great beings, not employ their power and might to cause all sentient beings to experience happiness equally? Since all sentient beings do not experience true happiness in that way, what benefit is there in the bodhisattvas diligently applying themselves to the mind of loving-kindness?"

The Blessed One then declared:

"Son of good family, the loving-kindness of a bodhisattva is not without benefit. Son of good family, among sentient beings there are some who will certainly experience suffering, and there are some who will not certainly experience it. For those sentient beings who will certainly experience suffering — those who are possessed of wrong craving — the bodhisattva's loving-kindness brings no benefit. But for those whose experience of suffering is not certain, the bodhisattva's loving-kindness does bring benefit, and it causes those sentient beings to experience genuine happiness.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: if a person at some distance catches sight of lions, tigers, wolves, rākṣasas, hungry ghosts, and the like, fear and dread arise in him naturally. And if at night he sees a precipice, fear arises in him in just the same way. Son of good family, just as fear arises naturally in that person, so too any sentient being who sees one diligently applying loving-kindness will naturally experience happiness. Son of good family, for this reason, a bodhisattva who diligently applies himself to loving-kindness is engaged in what is truly meaningful — and it is not without benefit.

Son of good family, I have taught that loving-kindness has limitless aspects, namely the supernormal knowledges (abhijñā).

Son of good family, consider this: Devadatta showed King Ajātaśatru that the Tathāgata had been killed. At that time, when I had entered Rājagṛha to collect alms in sequence, King Ajātaśatru released enraged yak-bulls that guarded the treasury, and set them to kill me and my disciples. At that time those yak-bulls trampled and killed many hundreds and thousands of limitless sentient beings. Spattered by the blood of those slain beings, the bulls grew all the more frenzied. When my disciples clad in ochre robes were seen, the bulls — taking them for blood — turned and fled. All of my disciples who had not yet parted from desire fled in the four directions, none remaining except the venerable Ānanda. At that time, all the people dwelling in Rājagṛha wept together with one voice, and with tears streaming down their faces they said: 'Alas! The Tathāgata is no more! Why has the Tathāgata been destroyed so suddenly, in a single instant?' At that time Devadatta felt a wondrous joy and said: 'It is good that the ascetic Gautama is no more. From now on, what is true is no more, and things have come to pass just as I had hoped they would.'

Son of good family, at that time, in order to tame the treasury-guarding yak-bulls, I entered into the meditative absorption called Loving-Kindness, and I stretched out my hand in display, and upon my five fingers five lions appeared. The yak-bulls, seeing this, were so terrified that they lost control of their bowels and bladder, and their bodies fell flat on the ground, and they reverently prostrated at my feet. Son of good family, at that time, though in reality there were no lions on my five fingers, by the power of the virtuous root of cultivated loving-kindness those bulls were tamed. Son of good family, there is more: when I was departing to the city of Kuśinagara to pass into final nirvāṇa, some five hundred wrestlers were blocking and jostling along the road, waving cloth and making a clamor. On the road there was a great boulder; the wrestlers turned to it and, using all the strength and power they had, could not lift it or budge it. Then, out of compassion for those wrestlers, I gave rise to the mind of loving-kindness, and with the big toe of my foot I tossed that boulder up into the sky, caught it with my hand, and set it in the palm of my right hand. Then, merely by blowing upon it, I reduced it to fine dust, and then gathered it back together — and had the wrestlers see it thus blown apart."

Having thus calmed the pride and arrogance in the minds of those wrestlers, I taught them Dharma in all its variety, and caused them to give rise to the awakening mind aimed at unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Now, noble son, at that time the Tathāgata did not in truth toss that boulder into the sky with the big toe of his foot, nor set it in the palm of his right hand, nor grind it to fine dust, nor gather it back into a lump. Rather, noble son, you should understand that it was through the power of the wholesome root of loving-kindness that the wrestlers perceived those very things in just that way.

Noble son, furthermore, to the south, in the land of Vetāla, in a great city called Śupāra, there once lived, in a time gone by, a householder named Doḍa who had planted roots of virtue in the presence of immeasurable buddhas and had become a guide to many beings. Noble son, all the people who dwelt in that great city had turned to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and were servants of the naked ascetics. At that time, in order to tame that householder, the Blessed One set out from Rājagṛha toward that city. The distance was some sixty-five leagues, and in order to tame the sentient beings dwelling along the way, the Blessed One traveled slowly on foot with his retinue.

When the naked ascetics dwelling in the city of Śupāra heard, "He is coming," they thought among themselves: "If the śramaṇa Gautama comes here, all those who live here will abandon us and give us no more provisions; we shall be left destitute — how then shall we survive?" So the naked ascetics dispersed, each going separately to the people living in that city, and proclaimed the following: "Word has it that one called the śramaṇa Gautama is coming here. This śramaṇa has abandoned both father and mother and roams and wanders wherever he will; and in every place he passes through, crop failures and famines arise, diseases multiply, and deaths multiply — and there is no escape from it. That wretched śramaṇa Gautama is coming, leading a retinue of nothing but rākṣasas and hungry ghosts, all equally wretched. He has neither father nor mother, and he comes wanting a retinue out of sheer desperation. Whatever teaching and preaching he offers is nothing but lies, and wherever he goes there has never from the very beginning been happiness or well-being." Having heard these words proclaimed, the people were seized with great terror and alarm. They bowed their heads at the feet of the naked ascetics and replied: "Great teachers, what means can we take so that the śramaṇa Gautama will not come here?" The naked ascetics said: "The śramaṇa Gautama is by nature drawn to forests, springs, and streams; therefore every tree outside the city — without exception — must be cut down and cleared away. Every spring, well, and stream must be fouled with filth and vomit. Then return, bar the city gates tightly, array your weapons, guard the city, and do whatever you can to prevent him from entering. If he cannot enter this place, you yourselves will be safe from the start. And we too will perform whatever rituals we can to turn the śramaṇa Gautama back." So saying, the people listened and did as they were told: they cut down every tree, dried up every water source, arrayed their weapons, and guarded the city.

Noble son, when I arrived at that city, not a single forest or tree was to be seen, and I beheld many people sitting there bearing arms.

When I saw all of this, I was moved by the deepest compassion and aroused a mind of loving-kindness. Thereupon every forest and grove sprang back into being, and in addition to those, countless other trees grew up as well. Every spring, pond, well, and flowing stream became utterly clear and limpid, turning blue as lapis lazuli, brimming and overflowing in every direction, and covered all around with flowers of every variety. The very walls surrounding that city became like deep blue lapis lazuli, and all the people dwelling within that city could see me plainly, together with my retinue, as though looking through open space. The city gates opened of themselves without obstruction. The weapons all turned into flowers of many kinds. And the householder Supriya, at their head, came before the Blessed One with all the people and their retinues. I then taught them Dharma in many ways, and every one of them aroused the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening.

Noble son, at that time I did not literally cause forests and groves to grow, nor fill every spring and pond with pure water, nor turn the city walls into lapis lazuli, nor make the people there see me as if through open space, nor cause the city gates to open of themselves, nor turn the weapons into flowers. Noble son, know that all of this came about through the power of the wholesome root of loving-kindness: it was by that power that those people perceived all those things.

Noble son, here is another account. In Śrāvastī there was a brahmin woman named Vasitā who had a single child, beloved and cherished beyond measure, and that child fell ill and died. At that time, overcome and maddened by intense grief, she ran about naked without shame, weeping at every crossroads and calling out "Where is my child, where has my child gone?" and wandered throughout the city without weariness.

Noble son, because that woman had in times past cultivated wholesome roots in the presence of buddhas, I aroused a mind of loving-kindness toward her. At that moment, when she saw me, she conceived of me as her child. Instantly her mind came to itself; she took me into her arms and suckled me. Then and there I spoke to Ānanda and declared, "Give this robe to that woman." The robe was given to her, and Dharma was taught to her in many ways. Having heard the Dharma, that woman was filled with great joy and delight, and she aroused the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening.

Noble son, at that time that child was truly not me, nor was I her child; she had not truly taken me into her arms nor suckled me. Noble son, know that here too it was through the power of the wholesome root of loving-kindness that that woman perceived things in just that way.

Noble son, here is yet another account. In the city of Śrāvastī there was a laywoman named Mahāsinadata who in times past had cultivated wholesome roots in the presence of immeasurable buddhas. For the space of three months she invited the Saṅgha and offered medicinal remedies for their illnesses. Among that company of monastics there was one monk who had been struck by a very serious disease. A physician was summoned, made an examination, and declared, "This illness must be treated with flesh. Without flesh, life cannot be sustained for long." When the laywoman heard those words, she took gold and went to the market, calling out, "Is there anyone here who sells flesh? I will give gold equal in weight to the flesh." She searched the market from end to end but found no flesh. Then that laywoman took a knife, cut flesh from her own thigh, minced it,

prepared it with various seasonings, and gave it to that ailing monk. When the monk ate the flesh, his illness was cured.

At that time, the laywoman, from the wound where the flesh had been cut, experienced tremendous and unbearable suffering. And she cried out in this way: "Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Buddha!" At that time I was dwelling in Śrāvastī, and hearing that cry, great compassion arose in me for that woman, and she immediately beheld me. Then, as soon as her wound was anointed with medicine, it was restored just as it had been before. After that, I taught her various aspects of the Dharma and explained them to her, and she rejoiced with great delight and raised the awakening mind oriented toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Noble son, at that time I had not actually gone to the city of Śrāvastī, nor had I anointed the laywoman's wound with medicine. Noble son, know that through the power of the wholesome root of loving-kindness, the laywoman came to see such things.

Noble son, there is yet another example. About five hundred unruly bandits banded together in the land of Kośala, committing robberies and causing great harm. King Brahmadatta (Skt. Brahmadatta) sent an army against them, captured every one of them, had their eyes gouged out, and abandoned them in a dense forest.

At that time those unruly bandits had only previously cultivated wholesome roots before the buddhas. Thus, blinded and experiencing tremendous suffering, they cried out in this way: "Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Buddha!" and they wept aloud, lamenting: "We have no protector, no refuge, no ally."

At that time I was dwelling in the Jeta Grove of Prince Jeta, and hearing that cry, I aroused a mind of great loving-kindness. At that time, a very cool breeze filled their eyes with various nectar-like medicinal substances from the sandalwood mountains, and they recovered their sight. Those unruly bandits, the moment their eyes were opened in this way, beheld the Tathāgata. Then I taught them the sacred Dharma, and caused them to raise the awakening mind oriented toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Noble son, at that time I had not actually manifested as a wind, nor gathered medicinal substances from the sandalwood mountains, nor taught the Dharma in the presence of those men. Noble son, know that through the power of the wholesome root of loving-kindness, those unruly bandits came to see such things.

Noble son, there is yet another example. A regent named Vaidūrya, foolish and deluded, seized the king's power by force and installed himself upon the royal throne.

Out of an old grudge, he cut off the ears and noses of twelve thousand young women of the Śākya clan, hacked off their hands and feet, and threw them into a pit. At that moment those women, in tremendous suffering, made prostrations to the Buddha, saying, "We prostration to the Buddha! We bow to the Buddha! There is no one to be our protector and refuge!" And with that they cried out with a great wail.

Those women had previously generated wholesome roots before many buddhas. At that time I was dwelling in the Luminous Grove, and when I heard the sound of their cries I was filled with great compassion. The women then saw me coming to the city of Serkya, washing their wounds with pure water, and anointing them with medicine, and their pain subsided at once. All the ears and noses, and all the hands and feet that had been cut off grew back and were restored. I also taught them the sacred Dharma, and they all raised the awakening mind oriented toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and they all went forth before the great abbess, the mother of beings, and received full ordination.

Noble son, in truth the Tathāgata had neither actually gone to the city of Serkya, nor washed their wounds, nor applied medicine, nor stilled their suffering. Noble son, know that all of those things were seen by those women through the power of the wholesome root of loving-kindness. The same is true of compassion and of joy.

Noble son, therefore the cultivation of loving-kindness mind by a bodhisattva, a great being, is genuine and not false. Noble son, the immeasurables are inconceivable, the conduct of bodhisattvas is inconceivable, the deeds of the buddhas are inconceivable, and this sūtra of the Great Vehicle on the complete passing beyond sorrow is also inconceivable.

Noble son, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, who earnestly cultivates loving-kindness, great compassion, and joy will come to abide on the ground called Supreme Joy, which is like regard for an only child. Noble son, why is that ground called Supreme Joy, and also called Like an Only Child? Noble son, it is like this: just as a parent whose child is seen happy and at ease is filled with supreme joy in the mind, so too a bodhisattva, a great being, abiding on that ground is similar. When they see all sentient beings diligently applying themselves to virtue, viewing them with regard as if toward an only child, a mind of supreme joy arises, and therefore that ground is called Supreme Joy.

Noble son, it is like this: just as a parent who sees their child fall ill is filled with a mind of intense suffering and, out of compassion, is never parted even for a moment from a mind of grief, so too a bodhisattva, a great being, abiding on that ground is similar. Seeing ordinary persons tormented by the sickness of mental afflictions, they grieve out of loving concern for them as for their own child, and blood seeps from the pores of their body. Therefore this ground is also called Like an Only Child.

Noble son, consider as an example a tiny infant who has not yet grown teeth, who picks up dirt, gravel, bones, little sticks, or filthy rags and puts them in its mouth. The parents, seeing this, fear that harm will come, and with the left hand they press the child's cheek while with the right hand they draw the object out. A bodhisattva, a great being, abiding on that ground is similar:

When the bodhisattva sees sentient beings, whose dharma-body (dharmakāya) has not yet fully developed, practicing non-virtuous and sinful phenomena through the gates of body, speech, and mind, he draws them out from that with the hand of wisdom, unwilling that those beings should wander in saṃsāra and experience manifold suffering. Therefore this ground is also called Like an Only Child.

Noble son, consider as an example: when parents have a single child whom they love most dearly, and that child should die, the parents too desire to die along with it. A bodhisattva, a great being, is similar: if beings who hold wrong craving should fall into hell, he too desires to go to hell along with them. Why is this? Because when those beings who hold wrong craving are experiencing suffering, if even for a single moment a thought of remorse arises in them, he thinks, "I will teach and explain to them Dharma of many kinds, and in that single instant cause a root of virtue to be born." Therefore this ground is called Like an Only Child.

Noble son, consider as an example: when parents have a single child, whether that child is asleep or awake, whether walking, staying, sitting, or lying down, it is always held in mind. And if the child commits some misdeed, they instruct it with gentle words and correct it — not with harshness. A bodhisattva, a great being, is similar: whether ordinary beings are born in hell, in the animal realm, in the world of Yama, or born among gods and humans — always and without fail he keeps his mind on what virtuous or sinful acts they are committing. And if they should perform some non-virtuous and sinful action, no thought of aversion arises in him toward them. Therefore this ground is called Like an Only Child.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, since it is, as you have taught, exceedingly profound, and our own search for it is exceedingly limited, how are we to search for it? Surely, if bodhisattvas abiding on a ground such as that of the Only Child are as you describe, then why was it that the Tathāgata, when in a former life he was a king and was practicing the bodhisattva's conduct, took the lives of so many brahmins? If this ground had been attained, it was the disposition of one who protects and becomes an ally; if it had not been attained, why did he not fall into hell? And if he regards all sentient beings as he would his own son Rāhula, why did the Blessed One say to Devadatta those words — calling him a stupid, shameless man who licks a human's running sores? And upon hearing this, Devadatta held a grudge, gave rise to a non-virtuous thought, and drew blood from the body of the Buddha. And even after Devadatta had committed such a sin, the Tathāgata prophesied that he would fall into hell and experience suffering for the duration of a whole aeon. Blessed One, would not what you have just said contradict that meaning?

Blessed One, when the venerable Subhūti, who abides on the ground of emptiness, enters a village and goes on alms-round, he thoroughly examines the other person beforehand. And if the other person's mind turns to contempt or reproach, then no matter how intensely hungry he may be, he accepts no alms from them. Why is this? Because the venerable Subhūti always reflects and mindfully recalls this: "For one who would become a field of merit for others, the mere arising of a single non-virtuous thought, through that cause and that condition, brings about a fall into the great hell and the experience of tremendous suffering. So what if I am hungry? Better to go without even a little clean food."

"By others showing contempt and reproach toward me, I must not fall into hell and undergo suffering." With this in mind, he also thinks to himself: "If any sentient being were to reproach me while I am standing, I would not rise from where I am sitting in a clean place. If any sentient being were to reproach me while I am sitting, I would not stir from where I am standing in a clean place. Walking and lying down are the same."

In this way, when even the venerable Subhūti, out of concern for the minds of sentient beings, generates such a resolve, what need is there to speak of a bodhisattva, a great being? But if one who has attained a ground comparable to an only child were to act thus, why would the Tathāgata have spoken words so careless as to cause many sentient beings to give rise to deeply non-virtuous minds?

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, do not argue that the awakened Blessed One has acted as a cause for the afflictions of ordinary beings. Son of good family, it may be possible for the beak of a mosquito to drain the ocean to its depths, but the Tathāgata never acts as a cause for the afflictions of sentient beings. Son of good family, it may be possible for this great earth to become formless, for water to take on the characteristic of dryness, for fire to take on the characteristic of cold, for wind to take on the characteristic of stillness, for the Three Jewels, the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and space to take on the characteristic of impermanence — but the Tathāgata never acts as a cause for the afflictions of sentient beings. Son of good family, it may be possible for those who have transgressed the four root precepts of moral discipline, who hold wrong views, and who denigrate the sacred Dharma to attain with this very body the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the thirty-two major marks, and the eighty minor marks of excellence — but the Tathāgata never acts as a cause for the afflictions of sentient beings. Son of good family, it may be possible for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and the like to abide permanently and unchangingly — but the Tathāgata never acts as a cause for the afflictions of sentient beings. Son of good family, it may be possible for bodhisattvas abiding on the ten grounds to transgress the four root precepts of moral discipline, to fall into wrong views, and to denigrate the sacred Dharma — but the Tathāgata never acts as a cause for the afflictions of sentient beings. Son of good family, it may be possible for all immeasurable sentient beings to come to lack the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and it may be possible for the Tathāgata himself to pass completely into nirvāṇa at the very end — but the Tathāgata never acts as a cause for the afflictions of sentient beings. Son of good family, it may be possible to catch the wind with a lasso, to cut iron with a damp cloth, or to demolish Mount Meru with a fingernail — but the Tathāgata never acts as a cause for the afflictions of sentient beings. It would be better to dwell together with a venomous snake, to thrust one's hand into the mouth of a hungry lion, or to have one's body bathed in the ashes of a funeral pyre — than to say that the awakened Blessed One acts as a cause for the afflictions of sentient beings. Son of good family, the Tathāgata genuinely and completely severs the afflictions of sentient beings; he never acts as a cause for their afflictions."

Son of good family, as for what you said — that the Tathāgata once killed a brahmin — son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, would not even intentionally kill so much as a small ant when young, let alone kill a brahmin. What need is there even to speak of such a thing? The bodhisattva is always skilled in means: through manifold forms of skillful means he bestows upon sentient beings an immeasurable gift of life and sustenance.

Son of good family, giving food is called giving life. When a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the perfection of generosity, he constantly bestows immeasurable sustenance and life upon sentient beings.

Son of good family, by guarding the moral discipline of fully abandoning the taking of life, one comes to have long life. When a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the perfection of moral discipline, he gives to all sentient beings an immeasurable gift of sustaining life.

Son of good family, through being free from the fault of verbal wrongdoing, one comes to have long life. When a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the perfection of patience, he does not show resentment toward sentient beings: he attributes good qualities to others and accepts blame upon himself, and so there is no contention — and thus one comes to have long life. Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience, this is called giving sentient beings an immeasurable gift of life.

Son of good family, through applying diligence to virtue, one comes to have long life. When a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the perfection of diligence, he urges sentient beings to apply themselves earnestly to virtuous Dharma, and thereby causes ordinary beings, by acting in that same way, to obtain immeasurable length of life. Therefore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the perfection of diligence, this is called giving sentient beings immeasurable life.

Son of good family, earnest application to collecting the mind leads to long life. When a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the perfection of meditative concentration, he urges sentient beings to apply themselves earnestly to the mind of meditative equipoise, and sentient beings who practice accordingly come to have long life. Therefore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the perfection of meditative concentration, this is called giving sentient beings an immeasurable gift of life.

Son of good family, practicing with heedfulness in all things that lead to virtue brings long life. When a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom, he causes sentient beings to practice virtue with heedfulness, and ordinary beings who thus practice in that way come, by that cause and by that condition, to have long life. Therefore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom, this is called giving sentient beings immeasurable life.

Son of good family, for these reasons, a bodhisattva, a great being, has no quality of taking life from any sentient being whatsoever.

Son of good family, you asked me: "When you killed the brahmin at that time, did you thereby obtain that ground?" Son of good family, at that time I had obtained that ground, and it was out of regard for their welfare that I cut off that person's vital faculty — not out of malicious intent.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: parents who have only one child cherish that child with the utmost affection. If that child has committed some grave offense and comes to face judgment and trial, then out of fear and dread the parents may drive that child away or even put an end to his life — and yet if they do so, drive him away or put an end to his life, there is no malicious intent.

A great bodhisattva who guards and protects the holy Dharma is like this as well. If any sentient being should slander and disparage the Dharma of the Great Vehicle, that bodhisattva may restrain that being, afflict that being, harm that being, and, if necessary, even cut off that being's vital faculty — wishing that, in times to come, that being will apply diligence to wholesome Dharma.

The great bodhisattva always reflects in this way: "By what causes and conditions will sentient beings come to give rise to a mind of faith?" and then, whatever method is appropriate, that is what the bodhisattva puts into action.

Now, a great many brahmins, having passed from this life, were born in the interminable hell (avīci naraka). There they reflected on three things. First, they recognized where they had dwelt before coming to be born here, knowing they had come from a human lineage. Second, they considered what this place of birth was, and understood it to be the interminable hell. Third, they reflected on what karma and what conditions had caused them to be born here, and understood: "It was because of the causes and conditions of mocking, disparaging, and lacking faith in the vast and expansive sūtras of the Great Vehicle that a king had us killed, and thus we came to be born in this place."

Having reflected in this way, a mind of intense faith and reverence arose in them toward the vast and expansive sūtras of the Great Vehicle. Then, passing from that life, they were born in the world of the Tathāgata called Resounding Drum of the Refreshing Cool, and their lifespan was complete for a full ten aeons.

Son of good family, therefore, when I gave those men of old a life enduring for ten aeons, could that rightly be called killing? Son of good family, if someone digs the earth, plucks grass, cuts down trees, strikes a corpse with a weapon, beats, afflicts, or restrains — do those acts, by their causes and conditions, bring about a fall into the hells?

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, according to the meaning you have taught, it would indeed bring about a fall into the hells." "And why?" he continued. "For previously, when the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma to the hearers, you declared: 'O monks, do not give rise to malicious intent even toward a plough-yoke. Why? Because through giving rise to malicious intent, all sentient beings fall into the hells.'"

The Blessed One then said "Excellent! Excellent!" to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa, and spoke: "Hold well in mind what you have said, just as you have said it."

"Son of good family, the statement that one falls into the hells through malicious intent — there is no such thing as malicious intent in a bodhisattva. Why? Because a great bodhisattva, toward all sentient beings, down to the very smallest ant, gives rise to a mind of love, affection, care, and the wish to bring benefit and happiness. And why is this? It is because such a bodhisattva becomes a cause and condition and is skilled in skillful means. Through the power of skill in means, sentient beings come to give rise to roots of virtue.

Son of good family, for this reason, at that time, it was through the utmost skill in means that I took away those beings' vital faculties — and it was not through malicious intent.

Son of good family, by the Brahmanical law, if one kills a full ten cartloads of insects, it does not become a misdeed. As for beings such as bees, gnats, cats, lions, tigers, bears, foxes, and vicious predators that cause harm to sentient beings — if ten full cartloads of these were killed; or hungry ghosts (pretas), rākṣasas, piśācas, kaṭapūtanas, beings that cause forgetfulness, beings that cause madness —

— and those hungry ghosts that cause withering and the like, all beings that harm sentient beings: even killing them produces no blameworthy karmic maturation. If, however, an evil person among human beings is killed, there is blameworthy karmic maturation. If it is not confessed immediately after the killing, one will fall into the realm of hungry ghosts. But if one fasts without eating for three days, confessing and purging the sin, every last trace of the misdeed will be cleansed away. If one kills a teacher, or kills one's parents or a woman, or kills a wool-bearing ox, one will fall into hell for a thousand immeasurable eons — so they say.

Son of good family, for buddhas and bodhisattvas, killing with full awareness is of three kinds: the least, the middling, and the greatest. The least refers to ants and the like, and indeed to all births in the animal realm. Excepted from that category is what appears as bodhisattvas being born in an animal body. Son of good family, there are indeed bodhisattvas, great beings, who by the power of aspiration appear to be born in animal rebirths — and this is called the least category of killing. Even through the causes and conditions of this least category of killing, one falls into hell, into animal rebirths, and into the realm of hungry ghosts, and will experience the least degree of suffering. Why is this? Animals also possess some root of virtue, and if they are killed, one will experience blameworthy karmic maturation — and this is called the least category of killing.

What is called the middling category of killing ranges from ordinary persons of the lowest birth up to and including those who have entered the stream. Through the causes and conditions of that karma, one falls into hell, into animal rebirths, and into the realm of hungry ghosts, and will experience a middling degree of suffering. This is called the middling category of killing.

What is called the greatest category of killing ranges from killing one's parents up to and including killing an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, or a definitive bodhisattva. Through those causes and conditions, one falls into the great uninterrupted hell and will experience the greatest degree of suffering. This is called the greatest killing.

Son of good family, if someone kills one who holds wrong views, such killing does not fall into any of the three categories of killing. Son of good family, all those brahmins are to be called holders of wrong views. For example, just as tilling the soil, mowing grass, cutting wood, stabbing or striking a corpse with a weapon, or even kicking filth do not constitute blameworthy karmic maturation — so too killing a holder of wrong views is like that and produces no blameworthy karmic maturation. Why is this? Because those brahmins also lack faith and the rest up to and including the five spiritual faculties, and therefore killing them does not bring about a fall into hell.

The noble great sūtra of the complete passage beyond sorrow. The twenty-second fascicle.

Son of good family, it is not fitting that you should say, as you have said to the Tathāgata: "Why did you rebuke Devadatta, that idiot who drools?" — or words to that effect. Why is this? Every word that the blessed Buddha speaks is inconceivable in its depth. Son of good family, all people in the world desire one who speaks truthfully. Words that are untimely, contrary to the Dharma, and of no benefit or comfort are never spoken by him. Son of good family, some words are extremely harsh and coarse, and are also false — untimely, contrary to the Dharma, unwelcome to whoever hears them, and of no benefit or comfort. Such words I have never spoken.

Son of good family, some words are extremely harsh and coarse, and yet are also true — not false, timely, in accordance with the Dharma, beneficial and conducive to well-being for all sentient beings. Even if those who hear them are displeased, such words are nonetheless most certainly spoken. Why is this? Because the blessed Buddha is possessed of knowledge and is supremely endowed with skillful means.

Son of good family, I recall that once, long ago, as I was wandering and traveling through wilderness retreats, villages, cities, and forests, there was near a forest a hungry ghost called "Wilderness Hermitage." He ate flesh and drank blood, harming many sentient beings, and each day he would devour the people of that city one by one. Son of good family, at that time I taught the Dharma to that hungry ghost at length and in full, but he was filled with rage, fierce and brutish, devoid of understanding, and so he would not listen to my teaching. At that time I manifested as a hungry ghost of great power and shook his dwelling, making him profoundly uncomfortable. At that very moment the hungry ghost, along with his retinue, came out from his dwelling and charged at me to attack. The instant that hungry ghost saw me, he lost his composure and, overwhelmed with terror as if drunk, he fell to the ground in a faint, his breath cut off, lying there like a corpse.

Then I aroused a mind of loving kindness and compassion toward him, and stroking the top of his head with my hand, he immediately revived and spoke these words: "Today I have recovered both body and life. This great divine king is endowed with tremendous power and majesty, and out of a mind of loving kindness and compassion he has even become my refuge from my own wrongdoing." At that time, the hungry ghost gave rise to a mind of faith toward me, and so I then manifested once again in the form of a Tathāgata and taught him further the Dharma in its many aspects. That hungry ghost was thus brought to observe the precept of refraining from taking life.

Now at that time, in the city of that wilderness region, it fell to one particular householder's turn in the rotation, and the townspeople escorted him to the hungry ghost's dwelling. The hungry ghost took the householder and presented him to me. I in turn received him and gave that householder the name "Hands." At that time the hungry ghost addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, we, together with our retinue, have been seekers of flesh and blood. Now that we have taken the precept of refraining from taking life, how shall we survive?" To this I replied: "From this day forward, wherever my close disciples and hearers dwell, in all places where they are diligently practicing the Buddha's Dharma, I hereby declare that everyone shall give you food."

Son of good family, on account of this cause and these conditions, a rule was established that monks should always offer torma cakes to the hungry ghosts of the wilderness. Should those at dwelling places fail to offer the torma cakes, know that they are not my close disciples — they belong to the host and retinue of the divine māra. Son of good family, the Tathāgata, in order to tame sentient beings, teaches such skillful means of many kinds — it is not that he deliberately seeks to terrify them.

Son of good family, I once struck with a staff a hungry ghost called Dharma Guardian. Again, on another occasion, there was a hungry ghost called Ram's Head, and I hurled him from a cliff into a ravine. Yet again, from a tree I cast a hungry ghost called Monkey into an abyss; I caused a hungry ghost called Yak, Guardian of Wealth, to encounter five lions; I manifested in a vajra body and terrified the tīrthika (non-Buddhist) debater Omnispeaker; and

I pierced the hungry ghost Hairy One with a thorn of the sengdeng tree. And although I did all these things, none of those hungry ghosts were harmed by them. Rather, in order to establish them in the sacred Dharma, I demonstrated skillful means of many kinds.

Son of good family, at that time I did not truly revile Devadatta, nor was Devadatta himself made a fool, nor did he come to eat human spittle, nor will he be reborn in the lower destinies, nor will he experience suffering for a full aeon in the Avīci hell of unceasing torment, nor did he cause a schism in the Saṅgha, nor draw blood from the body of a buddha, nor did he incur the loss of the four roots of virtue, nor did he denigrate the sacred Dharma or the sūtras of the Great Vehicle, nor does he hold wrong views, nor is he a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Son of good family, one called Devadatta truly lies beyond the domain of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; he is known and seen by a buddha alone.

Son of good family, therefore do not ask why the Tathāgata would revile, reproach, or abuse Devadatta. It is unworthy of you to generate such doubt about the domain of activity of the buddhas.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One: "Just as sugarcane, when pressed again and again, yields many different flavors, so too have I, by hearing again and again from the Blessed One, obtained many flavors of the Dharma — namely, the flavor of becoming, the flavor of abandoning desire, the flavor of peace, and the flavor of awakening. And again, Blessed One, just as genuine gold, when repeatedly smelted and hammered, becomes refined gold — exceedingly bright, supple, radiant, and precious — and comes to be a treasure for gods and humans; so too the Tathāgata, Blessed One, is like that: when one inquires of him again and again, one comes to hear and see meanings of profound depth. Thus those who practice meditation on what is profound commit them to memory and apply themselves diligently. Countless beings will generate the mind aimed at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. And after that, gods, humans, and others will revere and honor them with worship."

Then the Blessed One said "Excellent! Excellent!" to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Kāśyapa, great bodhisattva, it is excellent that you, out of your wish for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, have asked about this profoundly deep meaning. Son of good family, in view of that purpose, I too, just as you have intended, have taught the profound meaning of the vast and expansive Great Vehicle — that is, the ground comparable to having an only child, the ground of Boundless Joy."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One: "If bodhisattvas, through diligent cultivation of loving-kindness, compassion, and joy, attain the ground comparable to having an only child, then when they diligently cultivate the mind of equanimity, what grounds do they attain?"

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent, most excellent! Son of good family, you are supremely skilled in timing. You have asked about precisely what I intended to explain. When a great bodhisattva diligently cultivates the mind of equanimity, they come to abide on the ground of the equanimity of emptiness, like Subhūti."

Son of good family, when a great bodhisattva abides on the ground of the equanimity of emptiness, they do not perceive with partiality between father and mother, brother and sister, child, friend or companion — and from that point, between the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases,

sentient beings, and living beings — they perceive none of them with partiality. Son of good family, just as in space there is no father or mother, no brother or sister, no wife or daughter, no sentient being or living being, so too all phenomena are empty of father and mother up through living beings. Son of good family, a great bodhisattva who views all phenomena with a mind of equanimity is like space. Why? Because they are supremely skilled in diligently cultivating the Dharma of emptiness.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then put a question to the Blessed One: "What, then, is that which is called emptiness?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, what is called emptiness is as follows: inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of the objectless, ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, and the great emptiness.

How does a great bodhisattva fully investigate inner emptiness? A great bodhisattva investigates inner phenomena as emptiness. Inner emptiness of phenomena is as follows: there is no father or mother, no love or hatred, no sentient being, no living being, no permanence, no happiness, no self, no purity; and equally, there is no Tathāgata, no Dharma, no Saṅgha, no substantial thing.

Although the intrinsic nature of a buddha does exist within inner phenomena, that intrinsic nature of a buddha is neither inside nor outside. Why? Because the intrinsic nature of a buddha is permanent, stable, unchanging, and unaltering. This is what is called a great bodhisattva's full investigation of inner emptiness.

Outer emptiness is likewise — inner phenomena are utterly absent from it. Inner-and-outer emptiness is likewise.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata, the buddhas, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha do not abide in these two kinds of emptiness. Why? Because these four qualities — permanence, happiness, self, and purity — are not to be called emptiness. Both inner and outer are to be called emptiness.

Son of good family, the emptiness of the conditioned: to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, all of them are emptiness. That is: inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, and the emptiness of permanence, happiness, self, and purity; and emptiness of sentient beings, of living beings, of the Tathāgata, of the Dharma, of the Saṅgha, and emptiness in an ultimate sense. As for this, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not a conditioned phenomenon; therefore, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not the emptiness of conditioned phenomena — and thus it is called the emptiness of the conditioned.

Son of good family, how does a great bodhisattva fully investigate the emptiness of the unconditioned? All unconditioned phenomena are emptiness. That is: impermanence, suffering, impurity, no-self, the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, the characteristics of sentient beings and living beings, the conditioned, the defiled, inner phenomena, and outer phenomena. As for the unconditioned phenomena: a buddha and so forth, and these four qualities — these are neither conditioned nor do they bear the characteristics of the unconditioned, and by reason of being wholesome they are not the unconditioned. By reason of being permanent and stable they are not the conditioned.

These are called the bodhisattva's thorough examination of the emptiness of the unconditioned. Now, how does a bodhisattva thoroughly examine beginningless emptiness? A bodhisattva, a great being, seeing that saṃsāra is without boundary, sees that all things are emptiness and utterly peaceful. That is to say: what is called emptiness is permanent, blissful, selfhood, and utterly pure — all things are at peace through emptiness. There is no change and no alteration. There are no sentient beings, no living beings, no Three Jewels, no intrinsic nature of a buddha, and no unconditioned phenomena. This is called the bodhisattva's thorough examination of beginningless emptiness.

Now, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, thoroughly examine the emptiness that has no reference point? Consider, for example, a person who, having no children, thinks his house is empty — yet at the end he deliberates without attachment or aversion. Or consider foolish, deluded people who say that a mere direction is empty. Or consider wretched paupers, of whom some say "all is emptiness" while others say "it is not emptiness." This is not how it is with the bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva thus thoroughly examines, he is unlike a poor person — he understands all things as emptiness. In this way, a bodhisattva, a great being, is said to thoroughly examine the emptiness that has no reference point.

Now, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, examine ultimate emptiness? Noble son, when a bodhisattva, a great being, thoroughly examines ultimate emptiness, the faculty of the eye, at the moment of its arising, has not come from anywhere; and at the last moment of its ceasing, it has not gone anywhere. From the beginning it was absent, then it is present, and from being present it becomes absent once more. When traced back in precisely this way to its actual reality, there is no eye, and there is no owner of it. Just as the eye has no intrinsic nature, so too all phenomena are the same. As for what is called ultimate emptiness with respect to phenomena and so forth: karma exists, karmic maturation exists, yet an agent who performs is not seen. These phenomena that are empty are called ultimate emptiness. In this way, a bodhisattva, a great being, is said to examine ultimate emptiness.

Now, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, examine the emptiness of emptiness? What is called the emptiness of emptiness is something that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the like may come to experience. Noble son, that which is neither existent nor nonexistent is called the emptiness of emptiness. That which is and yet is not is also called the emptiness of emptiness. Noble son, even a bodhisattva dwelling on the tenth ground would, in regard to this, come to examine only a tiny particle's fraction of one direction of it — what need is there to speak of others? Noble son, the emptiness of emptiness in this sense does not become shared in common with the meditative absorption on the emptiness of emptiness belonging to śrāvakas. This is called the bodhisattva's thorough examination of the emptiness of emptiness.

Noble son, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, thoroughly examine great emptiness? Noble son, great emptiness is this: it is the Perfection of Wisdom — this is what is called great emptiness. Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides on this ground, having attained the gateway of emptiness, will come to dwell on a ground of equanimity like the expanse of the sky.

Noble son, when I teach in this great maṇḍala of the assembly the meaning of emptiness and the like in such ways, bodhisattvas, great beings, numbering as many as the grains of sand in ten rivers like the Ganges, have come to dwell on a ground of equanimity like the expanse of the sky.

Noble son, bodhisattvas, great beings, abiding on that ground, are unimpeded with respect to all phenomena. There is no apprehension, and there is no arising of partiality. For that reason it is called the ground of equanimity like the sky.

Noble son, consider this example: just as the sky does not become attached to pleasing forms, and does not give rise to aversion toward unpleasing forms, so too a bodhisattva, a great being, abiding on this ground is similar: there is no mind of desire or aversion toward forms fair or foul.

Noble son, consider this example: just as the sky is wide and vast and without peer, able to contain all phenomena, so too a bodhisattva, a great being, abiding on that ground is likewise utterly vast, without peer, and able to contain all phenomena. For that reason it is called the ground of equanimity like the sky.

Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, abiding on this ground will come to see and understand all phenomena — whether their conduct, their objects of focus, their intrinsic nature, their defining characteristics, their causes and conditions, the minds of sentient beings, their faculties, their meditative concentrations, their vehicles, their spiritual teachers, their maintenance of moral discipline, their practice of generosity, and all such phenomena they will come to understand and see.

Noble son, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, abiding there does not see with awareness — what is it that is known but not seen? The following: the practices of self-mortification, leaping into water, leaping into fire, leaping from cliffs, standing on one leg, burning oneself with the five fires, smearing oneself with ash, lying upon earth and thorns and leaves and grass and filth, wearing coarse rough garments and shrouds, wearing garments discarded in charnel grounds and ragpiles, wearing bark and deerskin, wearing tree bark and grass, eating grass and fruits and lotus roots, eating oil sediment and cow dung, eating roots and fruits, and if one begs for food, not begging from more than one householder — and if one is told there is nothing, going away empty-handed and not returning even when called back — not tasting the five flavors that derive from salt, meat, and milk, constantly eating flat bread and drinking warm water, undertaking the ascetic practice of a cow, undertaking the ascetic practices of a dog, a bird, and a pig, smearing the body with ash, taking the keeping of matted hair as a distinguishing mark, sacrificing sheep to the gods and then slaughtering them beneath, going without food for four months, sustaining oneself on wind alone for seven days, worshipping the gods with hundreds and thousands of flowers — declaring that through such conditions all desires will be fulfilled — these and similar practices have no basis for becoming the cause of unsurpassed perfect liberation. These are what is to be known. Not seeing them means that the bodhisattva, the great being, not having seen even a single person become genuinely and perfectly liberated through performing these practices, does not see — and therefore it is called not seeing.

Noble son, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, also has that which is seen with awareness. What is that seeing? Seeing those practices that lead sentient beings astray, one certainly sees that beings who perform such practices will fall into the hells without fail. That is called seeing. And what is that knowing?

Those sentient beings, having been liberated from those hells and reborn as humans, if they then practice fully — from the perfection of generosity through to the other perfections — one knows with certainty that they will attain genuine and perfect liberation. That is called knowing.

Noble son, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, also has that which is seen and that which is known. What is that seeing? Seeing permanence and impermanence, suffering and happiness, complete purity and complete impurity, self and no-self — that is called seeing. And what is that knowing? Knowing that the Tathāgatas do not ultimately pass into nirvāṇa, and knowing that the bodies of the Tathāgatas are vajra-like — indestructible, not produced from afflictions, not bodies that are impure, foul-smelling, decaying, or putrid. And furthermore, knowing that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha — that is called knowing.

Noble son, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, also has that which is known and that which is seen. What is that knowing? Knowing which sentient beings are endowed with a mind of faith; which sentient beings seek the Great Vehicle; which persons follow after saṃsāra; which persons turn back from saṃsāra; which persons abide in what is genuine; and which sentient beings have thoroughly understood the perfections. Those who follow after saṃsāra are foolish ordinary beings. Those who turn back from saṃsāra are those who have attained the path from stream-entry up through the level of the pratyekabuddha. Those who abide in what is genuine are the bodhisattvas. Those who have thoroughly understood the perfections are the perfectly and completely awakened buddhas. These are what is called knowing.

And what is that seeing? A bodhisattva, a great being, dwelling in the sūtras of the Great Vehicle's perfect nirvāṇa, with a mind of pure conduct and with the divinely purified supernatural eye, sees ordinary beings who, through acts of the three non-virtues committed by body, speech, and mind, are born in the hells, in animal births, and in the realm of the hungry ghosts. And he sees ordinary beings who apply themselves diligently to virtuous deeds and, upon passing from this life, are born among the gods of the higher realms or as humans. And he sees further: some sentient beings go from darkness to darkness; some sentient beings go from darkness to light; some sentient beings go from light to darkness; and some sentient beings go from light to light. That is called seeing.

Noble son, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, also has that which is seen and that which is known. The bodhisattva, the great being, sees that some ordinary beings diligently cultivate the body, diligently maintain moral discipline, diligently train the mind, and diligently cultivate wisdom — and yet for such a person, in this very life, the karmic maturation of negative actions will ripen, and through the conditions of attachment, aversion, and delusion, the karmic result that leads to the hells will inevitably mature. And he knows that persons who diligently cultivate the body, moral discipline, the mind, and wisdom will, in this very life, experience only a light result and will not fall into the hells.

Now, which actions ripen swiftly in this very life? Confessing and disclosing whatever sinful and non-virtuous deeds one has committed, and resolving after such confession not to commit them again; because one possesses remorse and shame, making offerings to the Three Jewels; and because one reproaches and chastises oneself — for such a person, through the cause and condition of that virtuous deed, he will not fall into the hells. The experience in this very life is as follows: headache, eye pain, stomach pain, back pain, unpleasant sounds, approaching death, being scolded and reviled, being beaten,

being roused, bent and struck, seized, hungry, and tormented by thirst — suffering of that kind. To know that all these and similar things are experienced even in this very life is called "knowing."

As for seeing: a great bodhisattva (bodhisattva) sees that for a certain person who takes no care with the body, who takes no care with moral discipline, the mind, or wisdom, yet who commits only a minor sinful act, that karmic act will be experienced swiftly in this very life. If that person, having committed that small sin, clings to it and does not confess and disclose it, does not reproach and chastise himself, does not feel shame or embarrassment, and does not feel fear or dread — then through that, the karma will grow and increase, and that person will be seen to experience the hells. This is called "seeing."

There is also the case of knowing without seeing. As for knowing: one knows that the buddha-nature is present in all sentient beings, yet because it is overwhelmed and obscured by the afflictions it is not seen. This is called "knowing without seeing."

There is further the case of knowing and yet seeing only partially. The great bodhisattvas who dwell on the ten grounds know that the buddha-nature is present in all sentient beings, yet do not see it with clarity — just as the moon during the day is not clearly visible. This is called "knowing yet seeing only partially."

There is further still the case of seeing as well as knowing: it is the buddha, the Blessed One, who both sees and knows. This is called "having vision and knowledge."

There is also the case of seeing and knowing, and of not seeing and not knowing. As for seeing and knowing: these refer to knowing the written scripts of the world, the spoken languages, male and female, vehicles, pots, houses, cities, food and clothing, mountains and rivers, enclosures, and the lifespan of sentient beings. This is called "seeing and knowing."

As for not seeing and not knowing: the words spoken with special intent by the noble ones (āryā), and the absence of male, female, and all the rest up to and including enclosures — this is called "not seeing and not knowing."

There is further the case of knowing without seeing. As for knowing: knowing the field of generosity (dāna), knowing the field of offering, knowing the field of receiving, and knowing causes and effects — this is called "knowing."

As for not seeing in this context: not seeing the field of generosity, the field of offering, and the field of receiving; not seeing the karmic maturation of cause and effect — this is called "not seeing."

A great bodhisattva's knowing of these eight categories is called knowing the five kinds of vision of the Tathāgata.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, if a great bodhisattva were to arrive at such understanding and discernment, what benefits would he obtain?"

The Blessed One declared: "If a great bodhisattva arrives at such understanding and knowledge, he will attain the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid). These are: analytical knowledge of phenomena, analytical knowledge of meaning, analytical knowledge of language, and analytical knowledge of eloquence.

As for analytical knowledge of phenomena: it is the knowledge of all phenomena and their defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa). As for analytical knowledge of meaning: it is knowledge of all that is designated as the meaning of all phenomena — that is, everything that becomes meaning through the designation of names and terms following upon phenomena. As for analytical knowledge of language: it is mastery of the science of writing, mastery of the science of spoken languages, mastery of the science of grammar, and mastery of the worldly sciences. As for analytical knowledge of eloquence: it is as follows —

Analytical knowledge of eloquence is this: however much a great bodhisattva speaks in words, there is nothing that obstructs or interrupts it; it is never turned back, is free of fear, and cannot be overwhelmed.

Son of good family, it is said that a bodhisattva attains the four analytical knowledges simply by seeing and knowing in that way.

Son of good family, furthermore, analytical knowledge of phenomena for a great bodhisattva means thoroughly knowing the phenomena of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas. Analytical knowledge of meaning means that although there are three aspects of the vehicle, one knows that they converge into one, and that in that convergence there are no separately distinguishing characteristics. Analytical knowledge of language means that a great bodhisattva, having designated a single phenomenon by many different names, could explain it for measureless eons without exhausting it — whereas śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have no such capacity to explain in that way. Analytical knowledge of eloquence means that a great bodhisattva, teaching all phenomena to all sentient beings for measureless eons, expounding the various different names and meanings, reaches no end of exhaustion.

Son of good family, furthermore, analytical knowledge of phenomena means that although a great bodhisattva knows all phenomena in this way, there is no attachment to them. Analytical knowledge of meaning means that although one knows meanings, there is no attachment to them. Analytical knowledge of language means that although a great bodhisattva knows names and words, there is no attachment to them. Analytical knowledge of eloquence means that although a great bodhisattva knows that teaching and explaining in this way is supreme, there is no attachment to it.

Why is this? Son of good family, if there were attachment, one would not be called a bodhisattva.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if there were no attachment, one would not seek the Dharma. Whoever seeks the Dharma has attachment; and whoever seeks without attachment seeks nothing at all. Why then did the Tathāgata say that the Tathāgata is without attachment in seeking the Dharma?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, insofar as there is attachment, that is not unobstructed. It is non-attachment that is called unobstructed. Son of good family, therefore all bodhisattvas alike — if there is attachment, there is no freedom from obstruction. And if there is no freedom from obstruction, one should not be called a bodhisattva; know such a person to be an immature ordinary being. Why is the one who has attachment called an immature ordinary being? All immature ordinary beings are attached, from form through to consciousness. Through attachment to form, a mind of desire arises. Having aroused a mind of desire, one is bound by form — and likewise bound through to consciousness. Being thus bound and fettered, one is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, the great suffering of grief and lamentation, and all the afflictions. Therefore, whoever has attachment is called an immature ordinary being. For that reason, all immature ordinary beings lack the four analytical knowledges.

Son of good family, a great bodhisattva comes to know and see all phenomena for measureless, countless eons. By knowing and seeing in that way, one comes to know meanings as well. By knowing the defining characteristics of phenomena and knowing meanings in that way, one generates no attachment to forms — and likewise through to consciousness. Being thus without attachment, the bodhisattva generates no mind of attachment to form, nor any mind of attachment through to consciousness."

Being thus without attachment, one is not bound by form — and likewise through to consciousness. Being thus unbound by consciousness, one is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death, from grief accompanied by longing, from lamentation, from great suffering, and from all afflictions.

For that reason, all bodhisattvas attain the four analytical knowledges.

Son of good family, by that cause and that condition, those in my retinue who are bound by attachment even to the twelve branches of scripture are said to be bound by Māra. Whoever is without attachment is said to be liberated from bondage by Māra.

Here is an illustration: in the world, one who commits wrongdoing is bound by the king. One who has committed no wrongdoing is not bound by the king. A bodhisattva, a great being, is likewise: whoever is bound by attachment is said to be bound by Māra, and whoever is not bound by attachment is said to be not bound by Māra. Therefore a bodhisattva, a great being, has no attachment.

Son of good family, furthermore, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (Skt. dharmapratisaṃvid) is this: a bodhisattva, a great being, who is highly skilled in the dhāraṇī of letters does not forget. A dhāraṇī is like the earth, like a mountain, like the eye, like a cloud, like a human being, like a mother — and so it is with all phenomena.

The analytical knowledge of meaning (Skt. arthapratisaṃvid): a bodhisattva may know the names and words of all phenomena, yet not know the meaning. One who has attained the analytical knowledge of meaning knows the meanings as well. How does one know meaning? It is like grasping the earth — for just as the earth holds all sentient beings and non-sentient beings, it is therefore called "earth-like grasping."

Son of good family, as for mountain-like grasping: a bodhisattva, a great being, thinks thus about it. Why is it called grasping like a mountain? A mountain takes hold of the earth and, by being immovable, is called grasping. Why is it called grasping like an eye? Because the eye grasps appearances, it is called grasping. Why is it called grasping like a cloud? A cloud is the breath of the nāgas, and because the breath of the nāgas holds water, a cloud too is called grasping. Why is it called grasping like a human being? Because a human being is able to hold both what accords with Dharma and what does not accord with Dharma, a human being too is called grasping. Why is it called grasping like a mother? Because a mother holds her child, a mother too is called grasping.

In just this way does a bodhisattva, a great being, know the names, words, and meanings of all phenomena.

The analytical knowledge of language (Skt. niruktipratisaṃvid): a bodhisattva, a great being, through knowing words and knowing meaning, teaches and expounds a single meaning through expressions of many kinds, and yet that expounding is without reified content. Examples of such names are those of man and woman, house, vehicle, sentient being, and so forth. Why is it said to be without reified content? Son of good family, "without reified content" is the domain of bodhisattvas and buddhas. "Words" is the domain of immature ordinary beings. It is because one knows the meaning that one attains the analytical knowledge of language.

The analytical knowledge of confident eloquence (Skt. pratibhānapratisaṃvid): because a bodhisattva, a great being, knows words and knows meaning, the bodhisattva's exposition of words and meanings never becomes exhausted throughout measureless and countless eons — and for that reason it is called the analytical knowledge of confident eloquence.

Son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, has applied himself with the utmost diligence to conventional truth throughout measureless, boundless, and countless eons. Through having so diligently applied himself, he comes to fully realize the analytical knowledge of phenomena.

Furthermore, through having applied himself with the utmost diligence to ultimate truth throughout measureless and countless eons, he comes to fully realize the analytical knowledge of meaning.

Furthermore, through having applied himself with the utmost diligence to the literary arts throughout measureless and boundless eons, he comes to fully realize the analytical knowledge of words.

Furthermore, through having studied the worldly arts throughout measureless and countless eons, he comes to fully realize the analytical knowledge of confident eloquence.

Son of good family, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have no occasion to attain these four analytical knowledges. Son of good family, I have taught in the nine branches of scripture that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain the four analytical knowledges — but in truth they do not perfectly attain them. Why is that? It is because a bodhisattva, a great being, applies himself to the four analytical knowledges for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. Pratyekabuddhas and the like pursue a course that is exclusively oriented toward peace, and because they delight in dwelling alone, even if they do act for the benefit of sentient beings, they demonstrate only supernormal knowledge and then remain silent, saying nothing at all. Where there is no teaching and no exposition, how could the four analytical knowledges be present?

Why is there no teaching when one remains silent? Because when a pratyekabuddha teaches the Dharma, he cannot bring it about that others accomplish the benefit of sentient beings, nor that those on the other side attain the stages of warmth, the summit, the supreme mundane quality, stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship, nor that they attain buddhahood, nor that they become bodhisattvas, great beings; and he cannot bring it about that those on the other side generate the mind oriented toward unsurpassed, genuinely perfect awakening (Skt. anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi). Why is that? Son of good family, pratyekabuddhas do not possess the nine branches of scripture, both worldly and world-transcending. Therefore pratyekabuddhas do not possess the analytical knowledge of words nor the analytical knowledge of confident eloquence.

Son of good family, a pratyekabuddha may know words in general, but he does not possess the analytical knowledge of phenomena. Why is that? The analytical knowledge of phenomena is called knowledge of syllables; and while a pratyekabuddha may know syllables in general, he does not possess what is called the analytical knowledge of syllables in their individual specificity. And why is that? Because he does not know the two syllables called "permanent" and "abiding," a pratyekabuddha has not attained the analytical knowledge of words. And though he may know meaning, he does not possess the analytical knowledge of meaning in its individual specificity. To truly know meaning is to know that in all sentient beings the nature of a buddha (Skt. buddha-svabhāva) is present. The meaning of the nature of a buddha is what is called unsurpassed, genuinely perfect awakening. Therefore a pratyekabuddha has not attained the analytical knowledge of meaning, and thus a pratyekabuddha is entirely without the four analytical knowledges in all respects.

Why do śrāvakas also lack the four analytical knowledges? Because śrāvakas do not possess the three aspects of skillful means. What are those three? Giving the gift of Dharma with gentle and definitive words; giving the gift of Dharma with sharp and definitive words; and giving the gift of Dharma through what is neither gentle nor sharp. Because śrāvakas lack these three aspects, they do not possess the four analytical knowledges.

Furthermore, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have not reached the limit of knowledge of words and meanings; they do not possess the wisdom that takes command of the domain of objects; they possess neither the ten powers nor the four fearlessnesses; they have not arrived at the limit of the twelve links of dependent origination; they have not come to discern the differences of sharp and dull faculties among sentient beings; and they have not fully severed the mind that harbors doubt with respect to the two truths.

They have not become skilled in knowing upon what objects the minds of sentient beings are focused, nor have they become truly skilled in teaching ultimate emptiness. For these reasons, those of the two lesser vehicles do not attain the four analytical knowledges.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with a question: "Blessed One, if the four analytical knowledges are in every respect entirely absent in śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, why did the Tathāgata say: 'The venerable Śāriputra is the foremost in wisdom; the great Maudgalyāyana is the foremost in supernormal knowledge; the great Kauṣṭhila is the foremost in the four analytical knowledges'? If they do possess them, why did the Tathāgata speak thus?"

Then the Blessed One praised the bodhisattva Kāśyapa, saying: "Excellent! Most excellent!" And he continued: "Son of good family, consider this: the waters of the Ganges River are immeasurable, the waters of the Sindhu River are immeasurable, the waters of the Vakṣu River are immeasurable, the waters of the Sītā River are immeasurable, the waters of Lake Anavatapta are immeasurable, and the waters of the great ocean are immeasurable. Though these many bodies of water are each alike in being immeasurable, in truth they are by no means equal in their greater and lesser measure. The four analytical knowledges of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are likewise. Son of good family, there is no basis for saying they are the same. Son of good family, it is in relation to common, inferior beings that I declared the great Kauṣṭhila to be the foremost in the four analytical knowledges — this is the intent of your question. Son of good family, among those who follow the śrāvaka vehicle, some attain just one of them, some attain just two — there is absolutely no case of attaining all four completely."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with a question: "Blessed One, you have declared, as stated previously in the chapter on the holy life, that 'A bodhisattva attains the four analytical knowledges through knowledge and vision' — and yet you also declared 'There is no attainment in the bodhisattva through knowledge and vision, and since even mind is absent, there is no attainment.' Blessed One, a great bodhisattva in truth has no attainment whatsoever. Yet if a bodhisattva were to have a mind of attainment, you have declared that such a one is not a bodhisattva but a common, childish being. Why then did the Tathāgata say that the bodhisattva has attainment?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family — excellent! Your question is most excellent, and it accords with my own intention to explain this matter. Son of good family, a great bodhisattva in truth obtains nothing whatsoever — and this very obtaining of nothing whatsoever is what is called the four analytical knowledges. Son of good family, why is it that obtaining nothing whatsoever is called the four analytical knowledges? Because if there were something to be obtained, that would be called 'entanglement,' and to whatever extent there is entanglement, that is called the four inversions. Son of good family, because a great bodhisattva is free from the four inversions, the bodhisattva attains the four analytical knowledges. Therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever. Son of good family, furthermore, this obtaining of nothing whatsoever is what is called wisdom. Because a great bodhisattva obtains that wisdom, the bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever. Having something to obtain is called ignorance, and because a bodhisattva has utterly severed the darkness of ignorance, the bodhisattva is said to have no attainment — therefore a bodhisattva is said to have no attainment. Son of good family, furthermore, this having no attainment is also called great nirvāṇa."

A bodhisattva, a great being, dwelling in bliss in great nirvāṇa in this way, does not perceive the defining characteristics of phenomena, and therefore a bodhisattva is said to have no attainment. Whatever there is of having something to attain — that is called the twenty-five modes of existence. A bodhisattva thoroughly severs those twenty-five modes of existence and thereby attains great nirvāṇa; therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever.

Son of good family, furthermore, this obtaining of nothing whatsoever is what is called the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). Because a great bodhisattva does not abide in any phenomenon whatsoever, the bodhisattva will attain the Great Vehicle; therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever. Whatever there is of having attainment — that is called the awakening of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. A bodhisattva thoroughly severs the awakening of those two lesser vehicles and attains the awakening of a buddha; therefore a bodhisattva is said to have no attainment.

Son of good family, furthermore, this obtaining of nothing whatsoever is what is called the vast and extensive sūtras. Because a bodhisattva reads and recites these sūtras, the bodhisattva is said to attain great nirvāṇa; therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever. Whatever there is of having attainment — that is the eleven sūtras.
