A bodhisattva teaches and expounds only the vast and extensive sūtras of the Great Vehicle; therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever.

Son of good family, furthermore, this obtaining of nothing whatsoever is called being equal to space. Space is that in which no thing whatsoever exists in the world. Because a bodhisattva attains the meditative absorption that is like space, the bodhisattva does not see anything whatsoever; therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever. Whatever there is of having something to attain — that is the wheel that revolves in saṃsāra. All childish and ignoble beings have something to perceive because they revolve in saṃsāra. A bodhisattva thoroughly severs all saṃsāra; therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever.

Son of good family, furthermore, what a great bodhisattva obtains by obtaining nothing whatsoever is called permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity. Because a great bodhisattva perceives the intrinsic nature of a buddha, the bodhisattva is said to attain permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity; therefore a great bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever. Having something to attain means impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and utter impurity. Because a great bodhisattva thoroughly severs impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and utter impurity in this way, the bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever.

Son of good family, furthermore, this obtaining of nothing whatsoever is called ultimate emptiness. When a great bodhisattva surveys ultimate emptiness, the bodhisattva sees nothing whatsoever; therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever. Having something to attain is called the five views. A bodhisattva thoroughly severs the five views and attains ultimate emptiness; therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever.

The Noble Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, the twenty-third fascicle.

Son of good family, furthermore, this obtaining of nothing whatsoever is called unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening. Because a great bodhisattva attains unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening by obtaining nothing whatsoever, a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever.

Awakening that comes with something to attain is the awakening of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. A bodhisattva thoroughly severs the awakening of those two lesser vehicles; therefore a bodhisattva is said to obtain nothing whatsoever.

Son of good family, your question, too, has nothing to attain, and my answer, too, has nothing to attain. Whatever has something to attain belongs to the party of Māra and is not in my company.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then spoke to the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, when you taught me this obtaining of nothing whatsoever for a bodhisattva, immeasurable sentient beings abandoned the mind that clings to marks. Therefore, by my asking about the meaning of obtaining nothing whatsoever, those immeasurable sentient beings have been freed from falling into the retinue of Māra and have become close companions of the Buddha."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then spoke again to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, previously, when you dwelt beneath the śāla trees, you declared this verse to Cunda:

What once existed now is no more;
what once was not now has come to be.
All phenomena of the three times in conditioned existence
cannot remain as such forever.

What is the meaning of what the Blessed One has declared?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, I spoke those words for the sake of taming many sentient beings. I also spoke them for the sake of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. I also spoke them for the sake of Mañjuśrī in his youth. But I did not speak that verse solely for the sake of Cunda alone. At that time Mañjuśrī was on the verge of asking me exactly that. Knowing his intention, I spoke for his sake. Having so spoken, the youthful Mañjuśrī fully and directly realized the meaning."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa spoke again to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how many beings have directly realized the meaning as Mañjuśrī has? May the Tathāgata please teach it extensively to the assembly in the maṇḍala."

The Blessed One replied: "Listen with utmost care, and I shall explain it to you as well.

The phrase 'what once existed' means this: from the very beginning I possessed afflictions without measure, and because of those afflictions, the great nirvāṇa I have now did not then exist. The phrase 'what once was not' means: from the very beginning the Perfection of Wisdom did not exist; because the Perfection of Wisdom did not exist, the defilement that now exists was present.

If any śramaṇa, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or human whatsoever were to say that the Tathāgata has afflictions in the past, the future, or the present, that would not be well founded.

Son of good family, furthermore, the phrase 'what once existed' means: from the very beginning I possessed a body born from the union of father and mother; and because of that, the dharmakāya that is like a vajra I have now did not then exist. The phrase 'what once was not' means: from the very beginning my body did not possess the thirty-two major marks and the eighty excellent features; and because from the very beginning it did not possess the thirty-two major marks and the eighty excellent features, the full complement of the four hundred and four diseases existed.

If any śramaṇa, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, human, or any other being whatsoever were to say that the Tathāgata has the suffering of illness in the past, the future, or the present, that would not be well founded.

Son of good family, furthermore, the phrase 'what once existed' means: from the very beginning I possessed impermanence, no-self, the absence of bliss, and the absence of purity. Because of that impermanence, no-self, absence of bliss, and

absence of purity, the unsurpassed and perfect awakening of the present does not exist. The phrase 'what from the beginning did not exist' means: from the very beginning the nature of a buddha was not seen. Not having seen it thus, there was no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no purity. If any śramaṇa, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, human, or any other being whatsoever were to say that the Tathāgata in the past, the future, or the present is impermanent, or lacks bliss, self, or purity, that would not be well founded.

Son of good family, furthermore, the phrase 'what once existed' means: from the very beginning, with the mind of one who has practiced austerities in a base and ignoble way, I thought to attain the unsurpassed and perfect awakening. Because things were thus, the four māras have not yet been overcome in the present time. The phrase 'what from the beginning did not exist' means: from the very beginning the six perfections did not exist. Because the six perfections did not exist, there arose the thought of attaining unsurpassed and perfect awakening through the mind of one practicing base and ignoble austerities. If any śramaṇa, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, human, or any other being whatsoever were to say that the Tathāgata in the past, the future, or the present practiced austerities, that would not be well founded.

Son of good family, furthermore, the phrase 'what once existed' means: from the very beginning I possessed a body mixed with food. Because such a body mixed with food existed, the boundless body of the present does not exist. The phrase 'what from the beginning did not exist' means: from the very beginning the thirty-seven factors of awakening did not exist. Because the thirty-seven factors of awakening did not exist, the body mixed with food of the present does exist. If any śramaṇa, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, human, or any other being whatsoever were to say that the Tathāgata in the past, the future, or the present possessed a body mixed with food, that would not be well founded.

Son of good family, furthermore, the phrase 'what once existed' means: from the very beginning I took up all phenomena with a mind of attachment. Therefore the meditative absorption of utterly consummated emptiness does not exist at present. The phrase 'what from the beginning did not exist' means: from the very beginning the genuine meaning of the Middle Way did not exist. Because the genuine meaning of the Middle Way did not exist, there was no mind unattached to all phenomena. If any śramaṇa, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, human, or any other being whatsoever were to say that the Tathāgata in the past, the future, or the present has characteristics with respect to all phenomena, that would not be well founded.

Son of good family, furthermore, the phrase 'what once existed' means: when I first attained the unsurpassed and perfect awakening, there were those of dull faculties who had become attendants of śrāvakas. Because there were those of dull faculties who had become attendants of śrāvakas, the truth of the single vehicle does not exist. The phrase 'what from the beginning did not exist' means: from the very beginning there were no bodhisattvas like Kāśyapa, a king among yaks, among those of sharp faculties. Because there were no sharp-facultied ones like Kāśyapa, the teaching was divided into three vehicles and proclaimed by whatever skillful means were appropriate. If any śramaṇa, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, human, or any other being whatsoever were to say that the Tathāgata in the past, the future, or the present is ultimately one who has perfected the three vehicles, that would not be well founded.

Son of good family, furthermore, the phrase 'what once existed' means: I previously declared in these words: 'In three months' time I shall pass into complete nirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.'

Therefore, at present, this greatly extensive sūtra of the Great Vehicle on the passing into complete nirvāṇa will not be expounded.

The phrase 'from the beginning nonexistent' means: from the very beginning, Mañjuśrī and the other great bodhisattvas were absent. Because they were thus absent, the Tathāgata now speaks of impermanence. Concerning this, if any śramaṇa, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or human were to say that the Tathāgata in the past, the future, or the present is impermanent, that would not be well founded.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata, for the sake of all sentient beings, though knowing all phenomena, declares that he does not know them. Though seeing all phenomena, he declares that he does not see them. Concerning phenomena that possess characteristics, he declares that they have no characteristics. Concerning phenomena that have no characteristics, he declares that they do possess characteristics. What is truly impermanent he declares to be permanent. What is truly permanent he declares to be impermanent. And so too, self, bliss, and complete purity are to be understood in an equally extensive manner. The Dharma of the three vehicles he declares as the one vehicle, and the one vehicle he declares, as is appropriate, as three. The defining characteristic of a sūtra he declares as the defining characteristic of an extensive text, and the defining characteristic of an extensive text he also declares in brief. The four root defeats (pārājikas) he declares as grave offences, and grave offences he declares as the four root defeats. What is blameworthy he declares as not blameworthy, and what is not blameworthy he declares as blameworthy. A light transgression he declares as heavy, and a heavy one he declares as light. For what reason? Because the Tathāgata clearly sees the faculties of each individual sentient being.

Son of good family, even though the Tathāgata speaks in such ways, it is not falsehood. For what reason? To speak falsehood is to be at fault, and the Tathāgata is entirely free from every fault and defect — how could there be any speaking of falsehood? Son of good family, although there is no false speech in the Tathāgata, if it should come about that what takes the form of falsehood toward sentient beings will serve the purpose of benefiting them through the Dharma, he teaches and speaks to them by whatever skillful means are appropriate.

Son of good family, all conventional truth is, for the Tathāgata, ultimate truth. For what reason? The Blessed One, the Buddha, teaches conventional truth out of ultimate truth, so that otherwise ordinary beings might come to attain ultimate truth. If ordinary beings were not to attain ultimate truth, the Blessed One, the Buddha, would never teach conventional truth at all.

Son of good family, when the Tathāgata at certain times teaches conventional truth, sentient beings think: "The Tathāgata is teaching ultimate truth." At other times, when ultimate truth is taught, sentient beings think: "The Tathāgata is teaching conventional truth." This is the profound domain of conduct of the Blessed Buddhas; it is not something known by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Son of good family, therefore it is improper of you to challenge the great bodhisattvas by saying that they attain nothing whatsoever. If a bodhisattva is always endowed with ultimate truth, why would you challenge them by saying they attain nothing?

Kāśyapa then asked: Blessed One, ultimate truth is also called the path, it is also called awakening, and it is also called nirvāṇa. If a bodhisattva attains the path, awakening, and nirvāṇa, then these would be impermanent. For what reason? If they were permanent, it would not be fitting to attain them either.

Just as space is not proper for anyone to attain, so too it is with this.

Kāśyapa continued: Blessed One, if worldly things that did not exist from the beginning but exist now are called impermanent, then awakening is similar: if awakening were something attained, it would be called impermanent. But if a phenomenon were permanent, then there would be no attaining it and no arising of it. Just so, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is also such that there is no attaining it and no arising of it. Blessed One, the path is not form, nor is it formless; it is not long, nor is it short; it is not high, nor is it low; it does not arise, nor does it cease; it is not red, nor is it white, nor blue, nor yellow; it is not existent, nor is it non-existent. For what reason, then, did the Tathāgata declare it proper to attain it? Awakening and nirvāṇa are likewise the same.

The Blessed One declared: Just so, just so it is. Son of good family, the path has two aspects: permanent and impermanent. Awakening likewise has two aspects: permanent and impermanent. Nirvāṇa is the same. The path of the outer non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) is called impermanent. The inner path is called permanent. The awakening of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called impermanent. The awakening of bodhisattvas and buddhas is called permanent. The outer liberation is called impermanent. The inner liberation is called permanent. Son of good family, the path, awakening, and passing beyond sorrow are all called permanent.

All sentient beings are perpetually covered over by countless afflictions, and lacking the eye of wisdom they do not see. Ordinary persons, wishing to see, apply themselves diligently to moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom. By so applying themselves diligently, they come to see the path, awakening, and passing beyond sorrow. That is what is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the path, awakening, and passing beyond sorrow. The defining characteristic of the path is not something that truly arises or truly ceases; therefore it cannot be grasped. Son of good family, what is called "the path" has neither form nor shape, is not something to be seen, measured, or known — and yet in truth it has purpose.

Son of good family, consider this example: the mind of a sentient being, too, is not form; it is not long, not short, not thick, not fine, not bound, not free, not something visible — and yet it does not not exist. Therefore I have said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada that the mind is like the owner of a treasury of countless things. Householder, if the mind is not guarded, body and speech will not be guarded either; but if the mind is guarded, body and speech will also be guarded. If body and speech are not well guarded, one causes sentient beings to fall into the three lower destinies. If body and speech are guarded, sentient beings come to attain the nirvāṇa of gods and humans. An attainment of that kind may be called genuine; what is not attained cannot be called genuine.

Son of good family, the path, awakening, and passing beyond sorrow are likewise: they are not existent, and they are not permanent. If they were non-existent, how could all the afflictions be cut through? Because they do exist in this way, all bodhisattvas clearly see and know them by direct perception. Son of good family, seeing has two aspects: seeing by means of signs, and clearly seeing by direct perception. What does it mean to see by means of signs? It is like this: when from a distance one sees smoke, one says, "I see fire" — yet one does not truly see the fire. Though the fire is not seen, it is not a falsehood.

When one sees a water-bird, one says, "I see water" — yet one does not truly see the water. Though the water is not seen, it is not a falsehood. Or again, when one sees flowers and leaves, one says, "I see the roots" — yet one does not truly see the roots. Though the roots are not seen, that too is not a falsehood. Or again, when a person standing behind a fence sees a horn, one says, "I see an ox" — yet one does not truly see the ox itself. Though the ox is not seen, it is not a falsehood. Or again, when one sees a pregnant woman, one says, "I see her lying with a man" — yet one does not truly see the lying itself. Though the lying is not seen, it is not a falsehood. Or again, when one sees the leaves of a tree, one says, "I see water" — yet one does not truly see the water itself. Though the water is not seen, it is not a falsehood. Or again, when one sees clouds, one says, "I see rain" — yet one does not truly see the rain itself. Though the rain is not seen, it is not a falsehood. Or again, when one sees the actions of body and speech, one says, "I see the actions of mind" — yet one does not truly see the actions of mind. But to say so is not a falsehood. This is what is called seeing by means of signs.

Now, what does it mean to clearly see by direct perception? It is like seeing form with the eye. Son of good family, consider this: just as when a person whose faculty of sight is unimpaired and perfectly clear holds an āmra fruit in the palm of his hand, in just the same way a bodhisattva, a great being, clearly sees the path, awakening, and nirvāṇa by direct perception. And yet, though seeing in this way, from the very beginning there is no defining characteristic of seeing as such.

Son of good family, it is for this reason and on this occasion that I formerly said to Śāriputra the following words: "Śāriputra, whatever is not known, not seen, and not understood by all those of the world — the renunciants, the brahmins, the gods, the māras, the Great Brahma, and humans — all of that the Tathāgata knows, sees, and understands. Bodhisattvas are likewise." And: "Śāriputra, whatever is known, seen, and understood by those of the world — that too I and the bodhisattvas know, see, and understand. What all those of the world do not know, do not see, and do not understand — it is not that I do not know, see, or understand it; rather, I know it thus: these sentient beings of the world say, 'I know it thus, I see it thus, I understand it thus.'"

Śāriputra, though the Tathāgata knows and sees all, he does not say, "I know and see it thus." All bodhisattvas are likewise. Why? Because if the Tathāgata were to intend that he knows, sees, or understands in that way, he could not rightly be called a buddha, a Blessed One, or a bodhisattva — that would be childish and ignoble.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, what is the meaning of what you declared to Śāriputra: 'What the world knows, I know; and what the world does not know, I too know entirely'?"

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, all those of the world do not know, do not see, and do not understand the intrinsic nature of a buddha. If they did know, see, or understand it, they would not be called worldly beings but bodhisattvas. For worldly beings do not know, do not see, and do not understand the twelve categories of scripture, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four inversions, the Four Noble Truths, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening, or the great and complete nirvāṇa. If they did know, see, or understand these, they would not be called worldly beings but bodhisattvas.

These, son of good family, are what is called that which worldly beings do not know, do not see, and do not understand.

Now, in what way do worldly beings know, see, and understand? It is as follows: they speak of the god Brahmā, of Īśvara, of the eight-armed one, of primordial nature, of time, of atoms, of dharma and non-dharma, of the lord of loving-kindness, of a beginning and an end to the world, of the two views of eternalism and annihilation, and they declare that from the first meditative concentration up through the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception there is nirvāṇa. Son of good family, that is called the knowing, seeing, and understanding of worldly beings.

The bodhisattva, the great being, likewise knows and sees these very things. The bodhisattva knows, sees, and understands them in just that way; yet if such a one were to say "I do not know, do not see, and do not understand," that would be a lie. Insofar as one speaks falsely, one commits a fault; and by the power of that fault, one falls into hell.

Son of good family, whether a man, a woman, a renunciant, a brahmin, or anyone at all who says there is no path, no awakening, and no nirvāṇa — such a one is possessed of wrong craving, belongs to the camp of Māra, and is called one who denigrates the Dharma. Such denigration of the Dharma is likewise called denigration of the buddhas. Such a person should be called neither a worldly being nor a non-worldly being.

At that time, upon hearing these words spoken, Kāśyapa praised the Buddha with these verses:

You hold compassion for all sentient beings,
and I take refuge in you.
Because you draw out the dart of wickedness and harm,
you are renowned as the King of Physicians.

When a worldly physician effects a cure,
the patient recovers in a moment but may fall ill again.
When a Tathāgata effects a cure,
one never falls ill again.

The Blessed One dispenses the medicine of nectar
and gives it fully to all sentient beings.
Sentient beings who seek and receive it
are freed from death and freed from birth.

The Tathāgata, for our sake, has revealed
the passing into complete nirvāṇa.
Those sentient beings who receive these words
will attain the state beyond arising and cessation.

Having spoken these verses, the bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, as you have taught, all worldly beings do not know, do not see, and do not understand certain things, while a bodhisattva knows, sees, and understands them all. But if a bodhisattva is also a worldly being, then it is not fitting to say that what worldly beings do not know, do not see, and do not understand, the bodhisattva knows, sees, and understands. And if the bodhisattva is not a worldly being, then what difference is there?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, a bodhisattva is both a worldly being and not a worldly being. One who does not know, does not see, and does not understand is called a worldly being. One who knows, sees, and understands is not called a worldly being. And your question about what difference there is — I will explain that.

Son of good family, suppose any man or woman, upon hearing this sūtra of complete nirvāṇa, immediately gives rise to faith and generates the mind of unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. Such a one is called a worldly bodhisattva. In the way that all worldly beings do not know, do not see, and do not understand, this bodhisattva too, in conformity with worldly beings, does not know, does not see, and does not understand. Yet having heard this sūtra of complete nirvāṇa, the bodhisattva —

what worldly beings do not know, do not see, and do not understand, the bodhisattva knows, sees, and understands. Having thus come to know those things, the bodhisattva thinks to himself: "By what means, through what method, through what endeavor, shall I come to know, to see, and to understand?" And then he thinks: "These things will be attained through guarding moral discipline in perfect purity with a mind of deep faith."

Son of good family, at that time, through those causes and those conditions, that bodhisattva guards moral discipline in perfect purity in whatever future birth and in whatever place he is born. Son of good family, because the bodhisattva, the great being, guards moral discipline in perfect purity, in whatever birth and in whatever place he is born, pride, wrong views, and doubt find no occasion to seize him. At no time does he ever say that the Tathāgata has finally entered complete nirvāṇa. These things are called the bodhisattva's guarding of moral discipline in perfect purity.

Through guarding moral discipline in perfect purity, he then applies himself diligently to meditative absorption. Through applying himself diligently to meditative absorption, in whatever birth and in whatever place he is born, his right mindfulness does not decline — mindfulness such as this: that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature, that there are the twelve branches of scripture, that the awakened Blessed Ones are permanent, blissful, self, and perfectly pure, and that all bodhisattvas, through dwelling extensively in the great sūtra of complete nirvāṇa, do not utter a word about seeing the buddha-nature and such other things. Through diligent application to meditative absorption, he will also attain the eleven absorptions of emptiness. This is called the bodhisattva's diligent application to the pure perfection of meditative absorption.

Having thus come to be endowed with moral discipline and meditative absorption, he then applies himself diligently to wisdom in perfect purity. Through diligent application to wisdom, he no longer grasps from the very beginning either that a self exists within the body or that the body exists within a self; he no longer grasps that the body and the self are identical, nor that the self is something other than the body. This is called the bodhisattva's diligent application to wisdom in perfect purity.

Through this diligent application to wisdom, the very moral discipline he has guarded also becomes exceedingly firm. Son of good family, consider this analogy: Mount Meru cannot be moved by the four winds. Likewise the bodhisattva, the great being, cannot be moved by the four distortions. Son of good family, that bodhisattva then knows, sees, and understands that whatever moral discipline he has guarded cannot be moved by anything whatsoever. That is what is called the bodhisattva's knowing, seeing, and understanding — and it is not the knowing of a worldly being.

Son of good family, because the bodhisattva, the great being, sees the moral discipline he has guarded to be exceedingly firm and unshakeable, his mind is free of remorse. Being free of remorse, his mind becomes greatly joyful. Being greatly joyful, his mind becomes utterly content. Being utterly content, he becomes blissful. His mind becoming utterly blissful, he attains the meditative absorption of imperturbability. Attaining the meditative absorption of imperturbability, his knowing and his vision become right and true. His knowing and vision becoming right and true, he becomes weary of saṃsāra. Being weary of saṃsāra, he becomes fully liberated. Being fully liberated, he sees the buddha-nature with clarity. That is what is called the bodhisattva's knowing, seeing, and understanding — and it is not the knowing of a worldly being.

Son of good family, these are the things that worldly beings do not know, do not see, and do not understand, but which the bodhisattva knows, sees, and understands.

Kāśyapa asked again: How is it that a bodhisattva, through diligent application to perfectly pure moral discipline, comes to see the buddha-nature with clarity, from the arising of a mind free of remorse all the way through to that seeing?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the moral discipline of worldly beings is not to be called perfectly pure. Why is that? The moral discipline of worldly beings is accompanied by continued existence, is uncertain in its intrinsic nature, is not ultimate, and does not extend to the benefit of all sentient beings — therefore it is not to be called perfectly pure. Because it is not perfectly pure, it is accompanied by a mind of remorse. Because it is accompanied by a mind of remorse, there is no mind of joy. Without a mind of joy, there is no contentment. Without contentment, there is no happiness. Without happiness, there is no meditative absorption of imperturbability. Without the meditative absorption of imperturbability, there is no right knowing and right vision. Without right knowing and right vision, there is no weariness of saṃsāra. Without weariness of saṃsāra, one will not become fully liberated. Without being fully liberated, one does not see the buddha-nature. Without seeing the buddha-nature, one does not attain the great and perfect nirvāṇa. Such is what is called the moral discipline of worldly beings — it is not perfectly pure.

Son of good family, the perfectly pure moral discipline of the bodhisattva, the great being, is moral discipline that is at the same time not moral discipline, that is unaccompanied by continued existence, that is certain, that is ultimate, and that works for the benefit of sentient beings. That is what is called the perfectly pure moral discipline of the bodhisattva.

Son of good family, although the bodhisattva, the great being, does not deliberately generate a mind free of remorse with respect to perfectly pure moral discipline, a mind free of remorse arises of itself. Son of good family, consider this analogy: when a person holds up a mirror, although they make no deliberate effort to produce a reflection of their face, the reflection arises of itself. Or consider: when a farmer sows seed in well-tilled soil, although they make no deliberate effort to produce shoots, the shoots arise of themselves. Or consider: when a lamp is lit, although no deliberate effort is made to remove the darkness, the darkness is removed of itself. Son of good family, when the bodhisattva, the great being, guards and maintains perfectly pure moral discipline, it is just the same — a mind free of remorse arises of itself.

Through perfectly pure moral discipline, one comes to attain a mind of supreme joy. Son of good family, consider this analogy: a person who has a fine and beautiful face, upon seeing their own reflection, gives rise to a mind of supreme joy. Perfectly pure moral discipline is just the same. Son of good family, one whose moral discipline is corrupted, having moral discipline that is not perfectly pure, does not give rise to a mind of joy. It is just as when a person with an ugly face sees their own reflection — a mind of joy does not arise. One whose moral discipline is corrupted is just the same.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: two women, each carrying a pot — one carries a pot of curd, the other a pot of butter — and they travel together heading toward a market. Along the way they stumble and both pots break. One of them is glad, the other is not. One who possesses moral discipline and one whose moral discipline has deteriorated are just like these two. Perfectly pure moral discipline causes the mind to be supremely glad.

When the mind is supremely glad, it thinks to itself: The Blessed One, the fully enlightened buddha, declared after entering into perfect nirvāṇa that whoever guards moral discipline in perfect purity will pass beyond sorrow. If I too apply myself diligently to perfectly pure moral discipline, I will attain it. By that cause and that condition, the mind becomes supremely glad.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: Blessed One, what is the difference between what is called joy and what is called happiness?

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, a great bodhisattva is called joyful because he commits no wrongdoing that would bring reproach. The mind that guards moral discipline with utter delight is called happiness.

Noble son, a great bodhisattva is called joyful because he thoroughly comprehends saṃsāra. Attaining the great nirvāṇa is called happiness. The lesser is called joy; the supreme is called happiness. Completely abandoning qualities that are mixed up with the world is called joy. Attaining qualities unmixed with the world is called happiness.

Through perfectly pure moral discipline, the body becomes serviceable and the fault of coarse speech is absent. At that time, in all that the bodhisattva sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, and cognizes, there is nothing that brings reproach. Because there is nothing that brings reproach, the mind becomes supremely happy. Because the mind becomes supremely happy, he attains the peaceful meditative absorption. By attaining the peaceful meditative absorption, his knowing and his vision become correct. With correct knowing and vision, he becomes thoroughly disillusioned with saṃsāra. Through thorough disillusionment with saṃsāra, he becomes fully liberated. Through full liberation, he sees the nature of a buddha. By seeing the nature of a buddha, he attains the great nirvāṇa.

These are the marks of a bodhisattva's perfectly pure moral discipline, and they are not the moral discipline of the world. Why is that? Noble son, when a great bodhisattva guards moral discipline in perfect purity, five kinds of Dharma become his companions. What are the five? He is endowed with faith, endowed with a sense of personal shame, endowed with a sense of social shame, endowed with a spiritual friend, and he is one who respects moral discipline.

By completely abandoning the five obscurations, his view becomes perfectly pure. By completely abandoning the five wrong views, he becomes free of a doubting mind. Furthermore, he completely abandons the five doubts. What are the five? Doubt concerning the Buddha, doubt concerning the Dharma, doubt concerning the Saṅgha, doubt concerning moral discipline, and doubt concerning heedlessness.

At that time the bodhisattva also attains the five faculties. What are the five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of meditative absorption, and the faculty of wisdom. By attaining the five faculties, he also attains the five liberations. What are the five? Liberation of form through to liberation of consciousness. This is called the perfectly pure moral discipline of a bodhisattva, and it is not that of the world.

Noble son, these are things unknown, unseen, and uncomprehended by worldly beings, but they are known, seen, and comprehended by bodhisattvas.

Noble son, if any of my attendants who carry, retain, read, recite, or copy out the sūtras of the Great Vehicle on great nirvāṇa, or who teach and expound them, should let their moral discipline deteriorate, others will look down on them and reproach them, saying: If the great nirvāṇa sūtra, which is the essential intent of the Buddha, were truly a powerful scripture, why would someone who has taken it up let their moral discipline fall into ruin?

If one who carries and retains the nirvāṇa sūtra lets his moral discipline deteriorate, let it be understood that for him the sūtra has no power. And if it has no power, then even if he reads or recites it, it will be of no benefit. In this way, by disparaging and reviling the nirvāṇa sūtra, he causes sentient beings beyond measure and without limit to fall into the hells.

If one who carries and retains this very sūtra lets his moral discipline fall into ruin, then he is an evil spiritual friend to sentient beings. He is not an attendant of mine; he belongs to the retinue of Māra.

Such a person would do better not to carry, retain, or even listen to this sūtra — better not to have held it, grasped it, or practiced it at all — than to carry or retain it while his moral discipline has deteriorated.

Son of good family, those who are my attendants and who wish to carry, retain, read, recite, transcribe into a volume, teach, or expound this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa must do so with body and mind that are genuine and wholesome — not with laxity, restlessness, or distraction. What arises from the body is called laxity; what arises from the mind is called restlessness. A mind filled with searching and striving is called restlessness; physical actions performed with such striving are called laxity.

If my attendants carry searching and active striving along with them, they must not carry or hold this sūtra of the Great Vehicle's complete nirvāṇa. And if, in such a condition, someone does carry or retain this very sūtra, others will look down on them and reproach them, saying: If the nirvāṇa sūtra, which is the essential intent of the Buddha, were truly a powerful scripture, why would you go about filled with searching and active striving? If one who carries this sūtra is filled with searching and striving, they will say this sūtra has no power. And if it has no power, then even carrying or retaining it will be of no benefit. By thus disparaging the nirvāṇa sūtra, one causes sentient beings beyond measure and without limit to fall into the hells. One who carries and retains this sūtra while filled with searching and active striving is an unwholesome spiritual friend to sentient beings. He is not my attendant; he belongs to the ranks of Māra.

Furthermore, son of good family, those who are my attendants and who carry, retain, read, recite, transcribe into a volume, or teach this sūtra of the complete nirvāṇa must not teach it at the wrong time; must not teach it to someone who has not received the proper introduction; must not teach it to one who has not made a request; must not teach it with a contemptuous mind; must not explain it at all times and in all places indiscriminately; must not teach it for the sake of praising themselves; must not expound it for the sake of disparaging others; must not expound it in a way that would cause the Dharma of the Buddha to decline; and must not expound it for the sake of causing the ways of the world to flourish.

Son of good family, if those who carry and retain this sūtra and who are my attendants teach it from wrongful timing all the way to teaching it for the sake of causing the ways of the world to flourish, others will scrutinize and reproach them, saying: If this nirvāṇa sūtra, which the Buddha intended and taught as its essential meaning, were truly a powerful scripture, why would it be taught at the wrong time and all the way to being taught for the sake of causing the ways of the world to flourish? If those who hold this sūtra teach it in such a manner, people will regard this sūtra as having no power. And if it has no power, then even holding or retaining it will serve no purpose of benefit or happiness. Thus, by disparaging the nirvāṇa sūtra in this way, those without measure among sentient beings will fall into the hells. Those who carry and retain this sūtra and teach it from the wrong time all the way to teaching it for the sake of causing worldly ways to flourish —

Such a person is a negative spiritual friend (Skt. kalyāṇamitra) to sentient beings, not a companion of mine; they belong to the retinue of Māra. Son of good family, whoever carries, retains, teaches, or expounds this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa — teaching and explaining the nature of buddhahood, explaining the essence of what the Tathāgata intended and taught, teaching the Great Vehicle, teaching the extensive sūtras, teaching the vehicle of the śrāvakas, teaching the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, teaching liberation, and bringing those who see the nature of buddhahood to purify their bodies thoroughly from the very beginning — such a person, by purifying the body thoroughly, will give rise to no contempt or disparagement. And because there is no contempt or disparagement, measureless sentient beings will develop pure faith in the sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa. With faith arisen in their minds, they will pay homage and render honor to this sūtra. If even a single four-line verse, or a single line, or even a single word of it is heard, and this teaching causes one to arouse the mind set on unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, then such a person is a true and genuine virtuous spiritual friend to sentient beings, not a negative spiritual friend. They are a companion of mine, not of the retinue of Māra. They are to be called a bodhisattva, not a worldly person. Son of good family, these things are unknown, unseen, and uncomprehended by worldly people; they are known, seen, and comprehended by bodhisattvas.

Son of good family, further, in what way does the entire world not know, not see, and not comprehend what bodhisattvas do know, see, and comprehend? It is this: the six objects of recollection. What are the six? Recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of the precepts, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the gods.

The Noble Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, the twenty-fourth fascicle.

Son of good family, in what way does one recollect the Buddha? The Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and completely awakened — endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer and guide of beings, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One — is permanent, unchanging, unmoving, endowed with the ten powers and the four kinds of fearlessness, roaring the roar of the great lion, the great ascetic, the great brahmin, the great Brahmā, one who has reached the final end, perfected beyond the reach of others, whose crown no one can behold, without apprehension, without embarrassment, without wavering, alone without companion, self-knowing without being taught, swift wisdom, great wisdom, sharp wisdom, deep wisdom, wisdom of liberation, unshared wisdom, all-pervading wisdom, consummate wisdom, precious wisdom — like a supreme bull among humans, like a king of elephants among humans, like a king of nāgas among humans, a man among humans, like a lotus blossom among humans, like the puṇḍarīka lotus, a guide, a teacher of humans, a great lord of generosity, a teacher of the great Dharma: he teaches the great Dharma because he knows the Dharma, he teaches the great Dharma because he knows the meaning, he teaches the great Dharma because he knows the right time, he teaches the great Dharma because he knows what is fitting, he teaches the great Dharma because he knows himself, he teaches the great Dharma because he knows the great assembly, he teaches the great Dharma because he knows the various natures of sentient beings, he teaches the great Dharma because he knows whether their faculties are sharp, dull, or middling, and he teaches the great Dharma because he teaches the middle path. This is called recollection of the Buddha.

Now, in what sense is he called the Tathāgata, the "thus-gone"? He is called the Tathāgata because he does not deviate from what the buddhas of the past have declared. How does he not deviate? Just as the buddhas of the past taught the twelve branches of scripture for the liberation of sentient beings, the Tathāgata likewise does the same — and therefore he is called the Tathāgata. The blessed buddhas (Bhagavāns) departed by way of the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of awakening, and the eleven kinds of emptiness, and arrived at the great nirvāṇa. The Tathāgata is the same in this regard, and therefore he is called the Tathāgata. The Blessed One, through that very skillful means, taught the three vehicles for the sake of sentient beings, and the span of his life and body is boundless and immeasurable — the Tathāgata is the same in this regard, and therefore he is called the Tathāgata.

Now, in what sense is he called the arhat, the "foe-destroyer"? All phenomena of the world are called enemies, and because the Buddha has vanquished all those forms, he is called the arhat. The four māras are called the enemies of bodhisattvas, and the Blessed One, while acting as a bodhisattva, vanquished the four māras through the primordial wisdom of omniscience — therefore he is called the arhat. Moreover, arhat means "one who has completely abandoned," for during his time as a bodhisattva he completely abandoned immeasurable afflictions — therefore he is called the arhat. Furthermore, arhat means "the bliss of the buddhas of the past." When previously acting as a bodhisattva, throughout measureless and countless eons he endured many and various forms of suffering for the sake of sentient beings, yet was without discomfort — he was always at ease. The Tathāgata is the same in this regard, and therefore he is called the arhat. Moreover, arhat means one who is worshipped: all the gods and humans of this world together with the gods offer divine flowers and garlands, victory banners and pennants, and all manner of music in his honor — therefore he is called the arhat.

Now, in what sense is he called the "perfectly and fully awakened one"? "Correct" means unerring. "Complete" means that there is not a single one of the four inversions that he has not directly realized. Furthermore, "correct" refers to the practice of austerity, and "complete" means knowing for certain that by the condition of practicing suffering one will experience the fruit of suffering. Furthermore, "correct" means the middle way of the world, and "complete" means that one who assiduously pursues the middle path to its end will certainly come to know perfect and full awakening without superior. Furthermore, "correct" refers to what is countable, measurable, and calculable; "complete" refers to what is uncountable, unmeasurable, and incalculable — and therefore the Buddha is called the "perfectly and fully awakened one."

Son of good family, one might say that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are also "perfectly and fully awakened," but in fact they are not. Why is this? Perfect and full awakening means knowing the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements — śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas know these as well, and so they might be called "perfectly and fully awakened." But why are they not truly so? Son of good family, if even throughout measureless eons the two of the lesser vehicles were to contemplate the aggregate of form alone and still not know it completely, then for that reason śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot be called "perfectly and fully awakened."

Now, in what sense is he said to be "endowed with knowledge and conduct"? Knowledge means the attainment of immeasurable fruits of virtue.

"Endowed with conduct" means conduct itself. The fruit of virtue therein is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. "Conduct" means moral discipline and wisdom; because one arrives at unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening on the two feet of moral discipline and wisdom, he is said to be "endowed with knowledge and conduct."

Furthermore, "knowledge" means vidyā. "Endowed" means auspiciousness. "Conduct" means fruit. Son of good family, these are the benefit of the world. Vidyā means liberation. Auspiciousness means unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Fruit means the great nirvāṇa. Therefore he is said to be "endowed with knowledge and conduct."

Furthermore, "knowledge" means illumination. "Endowed" means action. "Conduct" means fruit. Son of good family, this too is the benefit of the world. Illumination means heedfulness. Action means the six perfections. Fruit means unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Furthermore, "knowledge" refers to three kinds of vidyā: the vidyā of awakening, the vidyā of buddhahood, and the vidyā of ignorance. Of these, the vidyā of awakening is the Perfection of Wisdom. The vidyā of buddhahood is the very nature of buddhahood itself. The vidyā of ignorance is the perfection of emptiness. "Endowed" means having cultivated many wholesome actions for the sake of sentient beings throughout countless eons. "Conduct" means clearly seeing the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. Therefore he is said to be "endowed with knowledge and conduct."

Now, in what sense is he called the Sugata (the Well-Gone)? "Well" means high. "Gone" means not high. Son of good family, this is the benefit of the world. "High" means unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. "Not high" means the mind of the Tathāgata. Son of good family, if the mind were high, one could not speak of a Tathāgata; therefore a Tathāgata is called the Sugata.

Furthermore, "well" means a spiritual friend. "Gone" means the fruit of a spiritual friend. Son of good family, this is the benefit of the world. A spiritual friend means the first arousal of the awakening mind. The fruit means the great nirvāṇa. Because a Tathāgata never abandons the awakening mind first aroused and thereby attains the great nirvāṇa, he is called the Sugata.

Furthermore, "well" means excellent. "Gone" means existing. Son of good family, this is the benefit of the world. "Excellent" means seeing the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. "Existing" means the great nirvāṇa. Son of good family, although the intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa does not truly exist as such, the Blessed One the buddha, accommodating to the world, has declared it to exist. Son of good family, it is just as when people of the world tell a childless person, "You have a child," or tell someone without a road, "There is a road." In the same way, the great nirvāṇa too has been declared to exist as an accommodation to the world. Because the great nirvāṇa is effortlessly accomplished by the blessed buddhas, they are called Sugatas.

Son of good family, in what sense is he called "knower of the world"? Son of good family, "the world" means the five aggregates. "Knowing" means understanding. Because the Blessed One the buddha is supremely skilled in the five aggregates, he is called the knower of the world.

Furthermore, "the world" means the five objects of desire. "Knowing" means non-attachment. Because he is completely unattached to the five objects of desire, he is also called the knower of the world.

Furthermore, "the world" means the immeasurable, countless world-realms of the eastern direction — realms that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas neither know, nor see, nor comprehend, but which the Blessed One the buddha knows, sees, and comprehends. Likewise, the world-realms of the south, the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, the zenith, and the nadir are all known in the same way. Therefore the Blessed One the buddha is called the knower of the world.

Furthermore, "the world" means all common, ignoble beings. "Knowing" means that noble beings understand the causes and fruits of virtue and non-virtue — something not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but known by the buddha alone. Therefore the Blessed One the buddha is called the knower of the world.

Furthermore, "the world" means a lotus. "Knowing" means being unstained. Son of good family, "the world" here refers to the lotus, and "the Tathāgata" is spoken of as unstained — because the Tathāgata is not stained by the eight worldly concerns, the Blessed One the buddha is called the knower of the world.

Furthermore, "knower of the world" is an epithet applied to buddhas and bodhisattvas. Why is that? Because buddhas and bodhisattvas behold the world, they are called knowers of the world. Son of good family, just as one who is sustained by food as its condition is called one who lives on food, so too buddhas and bodhisattvas, because they behold the world, are called knowers of the world.

Now, in what sense is he called "unsurpassed"? "Having a superior" means being subject to being cut down. Because there is nothing that can cut him down, he is unsurpassed. Because the Blessed One the buddha is entirely free from mental afflictions, there is nothing that can cut him down. Therefore the Blessed One the buddha is called unsurpassed.

Furthermore, "having a superior" means being attended by dispute. "Unsurpassed" means being free from dispute. Because the Tathāgata is free from dispute, the Blessed One the buddha is called unsurpassed.

Furthermore, "having a superior" means being susceptible to refutation by words. "Unsurpassed" means not being susceptible to refutation by words. Because what the Tathāgata has taught cannot be refuted by any sentient being whatsoever, the Blessed One the buddha is called unsurpassed.

Furthermore, "having a superior" means having something above. "Unsurpassed" means having nothing above. Because among all the buddhas of the three times there is nothing surpassing them, the Blessed One the buddha is called unsurpassed.

Furthermore, "having a superior" refers to what is new or old. Because the Blessed One the buddha has become of the very nature of complete nirvāṇa, there is in him no such thing as new or old. Therefore the Blessed One the buddha is called unsurpassed.

Son of good family, now in what sense is he called the tamer and guide of persons? Because he himself is a person, he also tames other persons. Son of good family, in ultimate truth the Tathāgata is neither a person nor a non-person; yet because he tames persons, the Tathāgata is spoken of as a person.

Son of good family, whether a man or a woman, whoever possesses these four qualities is called a person. What are the four? Seeking a spiritual friend, listening to the Dharma, taking its meaning to heart, and practicing in accordance with what has been taught. Son of good family, any man or woman who possesses these four qualities is called a person.

Son of good family, if someone is male yet does not possess these four qualities, he is not to be called a person. Why is that? He has the body of a man, but his conduct resembles that of an animal. Because the Tathāgata tames both men and women, he is called the tamer and guide of persons.

Furthermore, son of good family, consider this analogy: a horse-trainer has four ways of working. He touches the hair, he touches the hide, he touches the flesh, he touches the bone. Whichever of these he applies, the horse goes according to the trainer's will. The Tathāgata is just like that: he tames sentient beings by these four methods of Dharma.

What are they? Those who, upon having birth explained to them, act in accordance with the Buddha's word — they are like a horse that goes according to the trainer's will at the mere touch of hair. That is the first. Those who, upon having the teachings on birth and aging explained to them, act in accordance with the Buddha's word — they are like a horse that goes at the touch of hair and hide. That is the second. Those who, upon having birth, aging, and illness explained to them, act in accordance with the Buddha's word — they are like a horse that goes at the touch of hair, hide, and flesh. That is the third. Those who, upon having birth, aging, illness, and death explained to them, act in accordance with the Buddha's word — they are like a horse that can be guided at the touch of hair, hide, flesh, and bone. That is the fourth.

Son of good family, a horse-trainer is not infallible, but the Buddha Blessed One's taming of sentient beings is infallible and without deception. Therefore the Buddha Blessed One is called the tamer and guide of persons.

Now, in what way is he the Teacher of gods and humans? There are two kinds of teacher: one who teaches what is wholesome, and one who teaches what is harmful. Buddhas and bodhisattvas always teach sentient beings the wholesome qualities — wholesome through body, speech, and mind.

Buddhas and bodhisattvas teach sentient beings in this way: "O sons of good family, you must thoroughly abandon unwholesome actions of body. Why? Because if unwholesome actions of body are thoroughly abandoned, you will be liberated. Therefore we teach you these qualities. We do not teach you that by failing to abandon unwholesome actions you will attain liberation." As for the claim that sentient beings who thoroughly abandon harmful actions would fall into the three lower destinies — there is no such case. On the contrary, there is every reason to say that by thoroughly abandoning them one will attain unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening and attain the great nirvāṇa. Therefore buddhas and bodhisattvas always teach these very qualities to sentient beings. Know that the same applies equally to speech and mind. For this reason the Buddha Blessed One is the unsurpassable Teacher.

Furthermore, having himself attained what was not yet attained, he teaches what he has attained to sentient beings; having himself lived the holy life from the very beginning, he teaches that way of living to sentient beings; having himself vanquished ignorance, he vanquishes ignorance in sentient beings; having himself attained the fully purified eye, he clears away the cataract of blindness in sentient beings and enables them to attain the fully purified eye; having himself known the two truths, he teaches the two truths to sentient beings; having himself attained liberation, he teaches the Dharma of liberation to sentient beings; having himself crossed the boundless river of saṃsāra, he liberates all sentient beings from it as well; having himself become fearless, he teaches fearlessness to sentient beings;

having himself completely passed into nirvāṇa, he reveals great nirvāṇa to sentient beings. For this reason, the buddha, the Blessed One, is called the peerless Teacher.

Now, the word "god" (lha) means "day," for among the gods the days are long and the nights are short — thus they are called gods. Again, "god" means "free from sorrow," for they are always in a state of happiness — thus they are called gods. Again, "god" means "the lamp of light," for having overcome darkness they become great radiance — thus they are called gods. Again, having overcome the dark deeds of unwholesome karma and attained the white deeds of wholesome karma, one is born as a god — thus they are called gods. "God" also means "auspicious," and because of being auspicious they are called gods. Again, "god" means "the sun," for the sun possesses light, and therefore the sun too is called a god. For reasons such as these, the term "god" is used.

The word "human" (mi) means one who reflects deeply on meaning and purpose. Again, "human" means one whose body and speech are gentle and pleasing. Again, "human" means one who is accompanied by pride. And "human" also means one who has overcome pride.

Son of good family, although the buddha, the Blessed One, is the peerless Teacher of all sentient beings, the scriptures speak of him as "the Teacher of gods and humans." Why is this? Because among all sentient beings, it is only gods and humans who are able to arouse the awakening mind directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and who are able to practice the ten virtuous deeds, and thereby attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, and unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. For this reason, the buddha, the Blessed One, is called the Teacher of gods and humans.

Now, how is it that he is called a buddha? The word "buddha" carries the meaning of perception or discernment: he himself perceives, and he causes others to perceive as well. Son of good family, consider the example of a person in a house who perceives a thief approaching — the thief cannot take hold. Likewise, the bodhisattva, the great being, perceives all the immeasurable afflictions completely, and by perceiving them in this way, none of the afflictions can take hold of him. For this reason he is called a buddha. And because of that perception, he is not born, does not age, does not fall ill, and does not die. For this reason he is called a buddha.

Now, how is he called "the Blessed One"? The word "vanquished" (bcom pa) means to vanquish, and the word "possessed" (ldan pa) here refers to the afflictions. Because he has vanquished all afflictions, he is called the Blessed One. Again, because he is possessed of all virtuous dharmas, because he is supremely skilled in the meaning of all phenomena, because he is possessed of great qualities and is therefore unassailable by others, because his great fame is renowned in all ten directions, because he has bestowed gifts of many kinds, and because throughout countless and immeasurable aeons he cast aside the feminine faculties as though they were vomit — for all these reasons he is called the Blessed One.

Son of good family, if any man or woman cultivates recollection of the buddha in this manner — whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, in light or in darkness — they will never be separated from seeing the buddha, day and night, at all times.

Son of good family, why is it that from "Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly complete buddha" all the way through "Blessed One," he is endowed with such boundless qualities and such great renown? Son of good family, it is because the bodhisattva, the great being, throughout immeasurable, innumerable aeons in the past, served and honored his parents, preceptors, teachers, spiritual masters, and superiors; and throughout immeasurable, innumerable aeons, for the sake of sentient beings, he gave gifts, guarded moral discipline,

cultivated patience, applied diligence, rested in meditative concentration, attended carefully to wisdom, and devoted himself earnestly to great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity. It is for these reasons that he attained the thirty-two major marks, the eighty excellent minor marks, and a body like a vajra.

Furthermore, throughout immeasurable, innumerable aeons in the past, the bodhisattva diligently cultivated the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, meditative absorption, and wisdom, and served and honored his teachers and spiritual masters — and this was done solely for the sake of the Dharma, not out of desire for food or gain.

If a bodhisattva takes up the twelve branches of scripture and then recites or chants them, it is always for the sake of liberating all sentient beings completely and bringing them to perfect happiness, and not for his own sake. Why is this? Because the bodhisattva always cultivates a mind that has transcended the world, a mind of renunciation, an unconditioned mind, a mind free of contention, a mind free of defilement, a mind free of bondage, a mind free of attachment, a mind free of obscuration, a mind that withholds nothing from the teachings, a mind free of cyclic wandering, a mind free of the net of doubt, a mind free of desire, a mind free of aversion, a mind free of delusion, a mind free of pride, a mind free of turbidity, a mind free of mental affliction, a mind free of suffering, a mind that is immeasurable, a mind that is vast, a mind like space, a mind of nothingness, a mind that is not nothing either, a tamed mind, a mind that does not weary, a mind that conceals nothing, a mind that is not of the world, a mind in constant meditative absorption, a mind of constant diligent application, a mind of constant liberation, a mind free of expectation, a mind without aspiration, a mind utterly without longing, a mind that does not assert, a mind that is yielding and content, a mind that does not abide, a mind that exercises mastery, a mind free of defilements, a mind of ultimate truth, an irreversible mind, a mind of impermanence, a correct mind, a mind free of deceit and cunning, a virtuous mind, a mind with no surplus and no deficiency, a mind free of interruption, a mind that is not like an inflated vessel, a mind not like that of a śrāvaka, a mind not like that of a pratyekabuddha, a mind of thorough understanding, a mind that knows the elements, a mind that knows the arising of the elements, a mind that knows how to abide within the elements, and a mind that knows how to exercise mastery over the elements. Through diligent cultivation of such a mind, he attained the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, the meditative absorption of great compassion, and the qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity.

This is why he is designated from "Tathāgata" all the way through "Blessed One." And thus is what is called the mindful recollection of the buddha by the bodhisattva, the great being.

Now, how does the bodhisattva, the great being, practice the mindful recollection of the Dharma? Son of good family, the bodhisattva, the great being, attends in mind to the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, the buddha, in the following way. The Dharma taught by the Blessed One is supreme and most excellent, and through practicing in accordance with the Dharma, even ordinary beings come to directly attain its fruit. This sacred Dharma alone is timeless and beyond measure, for it is seen with the eye of Dharma —

not seen with the eye of flesh. It is incomparable and cannot be likened to any example or analogy. It is unborn, unarisen, non-abiding, unceasing, without beginning, without end, unconditioned, and incalculable. It is the abode of those who have no abode, the support of those who have no support, the light of those who have no light. It liberates those who have not yet reached the other shore. It is the fragrance where there is no fragrance. It is without obstruction. It is seen as something that cannot be gazed upon directly. It is unmoving and unchanging, neither far nor near. Though all happiness is cut away, it has reached the ultimate of supreme bliss. It is neither form, nor the cessation of form, nor yet form — and so too from form all the way through to consciousness: it is neither consciousness, nor the cessation of consciousness, nor anything up to and including consciousness. It is not karma, nor is it apart from the cessation of karma. It is not affliction, nor is it the non-severance of affliction, nor yet affliction. It is not a thing, nor the severance of a thing, nor yet a thing. It is not an element, nor the severance of an element, nor yet an element. It is not existence, nor the severance of existence, nor yet existence. It is not a sense base, nor the severance of a sense base, nor yet a sense base. It is not a cause, nor the severance of a cause, nor yet a cause. It is not a result, nor the severance of a result, nor yet a result. It is not the false, nor is it the severance of all falsity, nor yet the false. It is not the true, nor the severance of all truth, nor yet the true. It is not arising, not cessation, and with arising and cessation entirely cut away, it is not even cessation. It is not a sign, nor is it the absence of a sign; with all signs entirely cut away, it is not even a sign. It shows nothing, yet it does not refrain from showing; with all showing entirely cut away, it is not even showing. It is not fearful, not pleasant; with all fear entirely cut away, it is not even pleasant. It is not to be endured, not to be unendured; with all that cannot be endured entirely cut away, it is not even endurance. It is not calm abiding, nor is it the absence of calm abiding; with all calm abiding entirely cut away, it is not even calm abiding. It has arrived at the summit of all phenomena. It utterly severs all mental afflictions. It is completely pure, signless, and thoroughly liberated from signs. It has become the abode that reaches unto the limitless ends of all sentient beings. It extinguishes all the blazing fires of saṃsāra. It is the sphere in which buddhas take their sport. Such is the Dharma contemplated with a mind that is steady and unchanging. This is called the mindful recollection of the Dharma by the bodhisattva.

Now, how does the bodhisattva practice the mindful recollection of the Saṅgha? The noble Saṅgha of the buddhas abides in accordance with the Dharma, holds the authentic Dharma, practices in full accord with the path of yoga, cannot be gazed upon directly, cannot be grasped, cannot be destroyed, cannot be harmed, and is beyond all conceptual comprehension. It has become the field of merit for all sentient beings, and yet though it is a field of merit, there is nothing to be appropriated from it. It is completely pure, free from turbidity, free from defilement, unconditioned, vast, and boundless. The mind is thoroughly tamed, perfectly even, non-dual, without sorrow, steady, and unchanging. This is called the mindful recollection of the Saṅgha.

Now, how does the bodhisattva practice the mindful recollection of the training precepts? The bodhisattva, attending to the fact that there is moral discipline, is without fear, without fault, unimpaired, and unmixed. Though without form, it is supremely well-guarded. Though there is no tangible object, it is through most skillful means that full ordination is bestowed. It is free from the fault of transgression, praised and extolled by buddhas and bodhisattvas, most extensive, and the cause of great and complete nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, consider these examples: the great earth, a boat, an island, a great mountain, the ocean, a clay vessel, a house, a sword, a bridge, a skilled physician, and excellent medicine —

an ointment, a wish-fulfilling jewel, limbs, eyes, parents, and a shadow — these are things that can never be seized away. They cannot be harmed, cannot be burned by fire, cannot be swept away by water. They are like steps for climbing a great high mountain, and like the victory banner of the precious and supreme Dharma of the buddhas and bodhisattvas.

Abiding in that moral discipline, I would indeed have the fortune to attain the fruit of stream-entry, yet I do not wish for it. Why is that? Were I to attain the fruit of stream-entry, I would be unable to work extensively for the benefit of all sentient beings. However, I do have the fortune to attain unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening by abiding in moral discipline, and that I do wish for. Why is that? If unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening is attained, one will be able to teach the supreme Dharma extensively to all sentient beings and become a refuge and protector for them. This, then, is what is called the recollection of moral discipline by a bodhisattva, a great being.

Now, how is it that a bodhisattva recollects generosity? When a bodhisattva, a great being, examines carefully, generosity is the cause of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening. Since the buddhas and bodhisattvas apply themselves diligently and with great dedication to generosity, I too shall apply myself to it with great diligence and dedication. If generosity is not practiced, one will not enter into the stream of the fourfold retinue. By practicing generosity, even though the afflictions are not yet entirely severed, the afflictions of the present moment will be overcome. Through the cause and condition of having practiced generosity, all sentient beings throughout the immeasurable and boundless world-realms of the ten directions — as many as the grains of sand in countless Ganges rivers — will continuously praise and extol one. When a bodhisattva, a great being, gives food to sentient beings, it is giving them life; and as the fruit thereof, at the time of full awakening one will abide in a permanent, unchanging state. By giving happiness, at the time of full awakening one will attain supreme bliss. When a bodhisattva gives through generosity, whatever is obtained is obtained in accordance with the Dharma and causes no harm to others; therefore at the time of full awakening one will attain perfectly pure nirvāṇa. When a bodhisattva gives through generosity, what is obtained is obtained without being solicited by sentient beings; therefore at the time of full awakening one will attain what is called sovereign lordship. Through the condition of having given generously, adversaries become endowed with power; therefore at the time of full awakening one will attain the ten powers. Through the condition of having given generously, adversaries become endowed with eloquence in speech; therefore at the time of full awakening one will attain the four thorough analytical knowledges. Since the buddhas and bodhisattvas, by practicing generosity, make it the cause of complete nirvāṇa, I too shall strive diligently in generosity and make it the cause of nirvāṇa. This is explained in detail in the text called Assorted Flowers.

Now, how is it that one recollects the gods? There are realms extending from the abode of the gods of the four great kings up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. One who has faith in the gods of the four great kings has the fortune to be reborn there. Yet although I too, through learning, generosity, and wisdom, have the fortune to attain any state from the gods of the four great kings up through the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I do not wish for it. Why is that? All states from the gods of the four great kings up through the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are impermanent. Being impermanent, they involve birth, aging, sickness, and death. Therefore I do not wish for them.

It is like this. As an example, an illusion deceives foolish people, but the wise and discerning are neither attached to it nor deceived by it. An illusion is like the states ranging from the gods of the four great kings up through the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The foolish are like all childish and lowly beings. I myself am not like those foolish ordinary beings. For I have heard of old that the ultimate gods — buddhas and bodhisattvas — are permanent, unborn, unaging, unsick, and undying. For the sake of all sentient beings, I seek the ultimate gods. Why is that? The ultimate gods completely sever the afflictions of sentient beings, like a wish-fulfilling tree. If I possess everything from faith through wisdom, I will attain the ultimate gods, and I will also teach and expound the ultimate gods extensively to all sentient beings. These are called the recollection of gods by a bodhisattva, a great being.

Noble son, thus a bodhisattva, a great being, is not worldly; worldly beings do not know, do not see, and do not understand — it is the bodhisattva who knows, sees, and understands. Noble son, it would not be right to say that reciting, proclaiming, holding, retaining, and copying into a book the twelve branches of scripture from my attendant's collection, and teaching and expounding them extensively to others, is comparable to reciting, reading, holding, retaining, copying into a book, and teaching and expounding extensively to others this Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra. Why is that? Noble son, the Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra is the profound import of the intention of all buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Because it is the profound import of the intention of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, it is supremely excellent. Noble son, therefore the Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra is wondrous and extraordinary — inconceivable.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: I too think of this Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra as wondrous and extraordinary — inconceivable. I think that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are also inconceivable. I think that the awakening of a bodhisattva and the Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra are also inconceivable. Blessed One, for what reason did you say that a bodhisattva too is inconceivable?

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, without having been taught by anyone, generates the awakening mind on his own. Having thus generated it, practicing with the utmost diligence, even if a great fire were to engulf his body and head, he would sustain the recollection of Dharma and would not extinguish the fire. Why is that? The bodhisattva, the great being, always thinks thus: For immeasurable and incalculable eons I have cycled through the births of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, and among gods and humans, burning all the while in the fire of afflictions — and yet I have certainly not attained even a single Dharma of certainty. The Dharma of certainty means unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. For the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening I do not begrudge even slightly this body and this life. For the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, even if this body were to be ground to the finest dust, I will not give up practicing with diligence. Why is that?

The mind of diligence becomes the cause of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Noble child, it is thus: even before attaining unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, a bodhisattva does not begrudge body and life — so what need is there to speak of after attaining it? Therefore a bodhisattva is inconceivable.

Furthermore, what is called "inconceivable" is this: the great bodhisattva's seeing of the measureless faults of saṃsāra is something that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not realize. And yet, even though that bodhisattva sees the measureless faults of saṃsāra, for the sake of sentient beings he does not grow weary of fully experiencing suffering. Therefore he is called inconceivable. Even though the great bodhisattva experiences many sufferings in the hell realms for the sake of sentient beings, it is to him as the bliss of the third meditative concentration (dhyāna). Therefore he is inconceivable.

Noble child, consider this example: if a householder's home catches fire, he comes out from that house. But if his children are left inside and have not escaped the fire, then that householder, even knowing with certainty that he will be burned by the flames, will enter back into that house for the sake of rescuing his children. The great bodhisattva is just like that: even knowing that there are many defects and faults in saṃsāra, for the sake of sentient beings he does not grow weary of dwelling in saṃsāra. Therefore he is inconceivable.

Noble child, countless sentient beings arouse the awakening mind and yet, seeing the many faults of saṃsāra, turn back from that mind. Some become śrāvakas; some become pratyekabuddhas. But if a bodhisattva hears this sūtra, he will not turn back from the awakening mind; it is impossible for him to become a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. And so, even without having attained the first unshakeable ground (bhūmi), his mind becomes extremely stable. Because he does not turn back, he is called inconceivable.

Noble child, suppose a person were to say: "I am able to swim across this great ocean." Would those words be inconceivable? The Blessed One replied: those words are both conceivable and inconceivable. Why is that? If a person were to swim and actually reach the other shore, that would be inconceivable. But if an asura were to swim and reach the other shore, that would be conceivable. Noble child, in this context it applies only to a human being, not to an asura. Blessed One, among humans too there are both the inconceivable and the conceivable. Blessed One, among humans there are two kinds: noble ones (āryas) and foolish ordinary people.
