If one speaks of a foolish ordinary person, it is inconceivable. If one speaks of a noble one, it is conceivable. Noble child, in this context I am speaking of the foolish ordinary person, not of the noble one. Blessed One, why is it inconceivable when it concerns a foolish ordinary person? Noble child, because a foolish ordinary person cannot in reality swim and reach the far shore of a great ocean. But the great bodhisattva truly crosses to the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra. Therefore he is called inconceivable.

Noble child, suppose someone were to lift Mount Meru with the stalk of a lotus and hurl it into the sky — would that be inconceivable? The answer was: No, Blessed One, it would not be. The Blessed One then declared: Noble child, the great bodhisattva measuring and fathoming all of saṃsāra in a single instant and moment — that is what is called inconceivable.

Noble child, the great bodhisattva, for immeasurable and incalculable eons, recognizes saṃsāra to be impermanent, without self, without happiness, and impure — and yet he teaches and expounds to sentient beings permanence, happiness, the existence of self, and purity in abundant detail. And although he teaches and expounds in this way, because he does not thereby hold a wrong view, he is called inconceivable.

Noble child, suppose someone were to leap into water and yet not be carried away by it, or leap into a great fire and yet not be burned by it — that would be called inconceivable. In the same way, the great bodhisattva dwells within saṃsāra and yet is not harmed by saṃsāra; therefore he is called inconceivable.

Noble child, consider this: among human beings there are three kinds — the lowest, the middling, and the highest. Among humans, the lowest, while still in the womb, thinks to himself: "I am dwelling in a pit, or in a foul place, or among corpses, or upon a heap of thorns, or in darkness." And when he emerges from the womb, he likewise thinks: "Now I have come out of a pit, a foul place, or a place of great darkness." Among humans, the middling, while in the womb in his suffering, thinks to himself: "I am dwelling in a grove of trees, or in a clear stream, or in a fine house." And when he is born, he thinks the same. Among humans, the highest, even while dwelling in the womb, thinks: "I am riding upon a fine upper floor, or in a pleasure garden, or mounted on a horse, an ox, or an elephant, ascending a great mountain." And when he is born, he thinks the same.

The great bodhisattva, from the very first moment of entering the womb, knows that he is entering; while dwelling in the womb, he knows that he is dwelling there; and when he comes forth, he knows that he has come forth. And although thoughts of attachment and aversion never arise in him at all, he does not abide on the grounds — therefore he is called inconceivable.

Noble child, unsurpassed perfect awakening (Skt. anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi) has no adequate analogy. Noble child, even mind is not something that can easily be compared, illustrated by analogy, or expressed in words. The great bodhisattva has attained unsurpassed perfect awakening even without a teacher in the role of preceptor and a student in the role of disciple. Having heard these teachings, he teaches and expounds them perpetually to sentient beings with a mind free of fear — therefore he is called inconceivable.

Noble child, the great bodhisattva: there is one who thoroughly abandons with the body but not with speech; one who thoroughly abandons with speech but not with the body; and one who thoroughly abandons with neither body nor speech. What is called thoroughly abandoning with the body? Taking life, taking what is not given, and engaging in sexual misconduct — these are abandoned with the body, not with speech. What is thoroughly abandoning with speech? Lying, slander, harsh words, and idle chatter — these are abandoned with speech, not with the body. What is thoroughly abandoning with neither body nor speech? Attachment, aversion, and wrong view — this is the thorough abandonment that is neither bodily nor verbal. Noble child, this is called thoroughly abandoning what belongs neither to body nor to speech.

Noble child, the great bodhisattva does not regard the thorough abandonment of even a single thing as being accomplished through the body, through action, or through a possessing agent — and yet there is thorough abandonment. Therefore he is called inconceivable. The same should be understood regarding speech.

Noble child, the abandonment of bodily things through the body —

— speech abandoned through speech. But the thorough abandonment by wisdom is neither bodily nor verbal. Noble child, in truth, these wisdoms will not be abandoned by the bodhisattva. Why is that? Noble child, not even a single phenomenon is destroyed or fabricated, for it is the very nature of conditioned phenomena to arise through differentiation and to cease through differentiation. Therefore this wisdom will not be thoroughly abandoned.

Noble child, wisdom cannot be destroyed, cannot be burned by fire, cannot be soaked by water, cannot be carried off by wind, cannot be seized by earth, cannot be produced by birth, cannot be aged by aging, cannot be established by establishment, cannot be destroyed by destruction, cannot be desired by desire, cannot be stirred to anger by anger, cannot be deluded by delusion — for it arises by the nature of conditioned things and ceases through differentiation.

The great bodhisattva does not think to himself, "My wisdom has vanquished all afflictions." Yet he says, "I have vanquished all afflictions." Even though he speaks thus, he does not speak falsely. Therefore he is called inconceivable.

The Noble Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra, the twenty-fifth section.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, I have from this day forward, for the first time, come to seek the great bodhisattva's inconceivability, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, the sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa, the upholding of it, awakening, and the inconceivability of nirvāṇa. Blessed One, for how long do the Dharma-qualities of the unsurpassed buddha abide, and when will they decline?"

Noble child, there are five modes of conduct in relation to this sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa: namely, noble conduct, brahmic conduct, divine conduct, the conduct of the sick, and the conduct of a child.

If any among my attendants is able to uphold, recite, chant, copy, explain the meaning, and honor sentient beings with reverence, esteem, service, praise, and offerings of many kinds — then at that time you should know that the Dharma of the buddha has not declined.

Noble child, if this Parinirvāṇa sūtra spreads widely but at that time many of my attendants have broken their vows of moral discipline, commit many non-virtuous deeds, and have no faith in this sūtra — and because of that lack of faith do not uphold it, recite it, chant it, copy it, or explain its meaning; many people do not revere or honor it; and when they see one who upholds it they disparage him, saying, "You are one who follows the teaching of the six teachers, not a true attendant of the Buddha" — then at that time you should know that the Dharma of the buddha will swiftly decline without long delay.

Again the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, I heard the Blessed One directly declare that the Dharma of the buddha Kāśyapa abided in the world for seven days and then declined. Blessed One, did the Tathāgata Kāśyapa possess this sūtra or not? If he possessed it, why did you say it declined? And if he did not possess it, why did you say that the Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra is the secret essence of all the Tathāgatas?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, I have said before that this matter is understood by Mañjuśrī alone. I shall say it again — listen well, take it very much to heart, and examine it carefully.

Son of good family, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess Dharma of two kinds: conventional and ultimate. The conventional Dharma ceases. The ultimate Dharma neither perishes nor ceases. And this again is of two kinds: that which is impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and without purity; and that which is permanent, blissful, the self, and thoroughly pure. Of these, impermanence, selflessness, the absence of bliss, and the absence of purity are subject to perishing and cessation. Permanence, bliss, the self, and thorough purity are not subject to perishing or cessation.

Again, there are two kinds: what is held by the two vehicles, and what is held by the bodhisattvas. Of these, what is held by the two vehicles is subject to perishing and cessation. What is held by the bodhisattvas is not subject to perishing or cessation.

Again, there are two kinds: the inner and the outer. Of these, the outer Dharma is subject to perishing and cessation. The inner Dharma is not subject to perishing or cessation.

Again, there are two kinds: the conditioned and the unconditioned. Of these, the conditioned Dharma is subject to perishing and cessation. The unconditioned Dharma is not subject to perishing or cessation.

Again, there are two kinds: that which has an object of reference, and that which has no object of reference. Of these, the Dharma that has an object of reference is subject to perishing and cessation. The Dharma without an object of reference is not subject to perishing or cessation.

Again, there are two kinds: the Dharma that is mixed, and the Dharma that is unmixed. Of these, the mixed Dharma is subject to perishing and cessation. The unmixed Dharma is not subject to perishing or cessation.

Again, there are two kinds: that of the gods, and that of humans. Of these, the human is subject to perishing and cessation. That of the gods is not subject to perishing or cessation.

Again, there are two kinds: the eleven sūtra collections, and the vastly extensive sūtra collection. Of these, the eleven sūtra collections are subject to perishing and cessation. The vastly extensive sūtra collection is not subject to perishing or cessation.

Son of good family, if any attendant of mine holds, recites, proclaims, copies in writing, explains, and pays reverence, honor, and worship to this vastly extensive sūtra collection, then you should know that at that time the Dharma of the buddha has not declined.

Son of good family, you asked before whether the Tathāgata Kāśyapa possessed this sūtra. Son of good family, the Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra is the secret essence taught through the intention of all the Tathāgatas. Why is that? Although the Tathāgatas possessed the eleven sūtra collections, if through those collections the intrinsic nature of a buddha — the permanence, bliss, the self, and the thorough purity of the Tathāgata — were not proclaimed, then the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would never pass beyond sorrow into nirvāṇa at all. Therefore this sūtra is called the secret essence taught through the intention of the Tathāgatas. Because it is what is not proclaimed in the eleven sūtra collections, it is called the essence — just as, because the seven precious treasures are not used openly in the world, they are called a treasure. Son of good family, the person accumulates and hides them as a treasure for use in the future: for such future needs as a famine in grain, the arrival of enemies in one's land, encountering a wicked king and having one's life deceived away, meeting with distress while traveling abroad, or a time of scarcity of wealth — at that point one brings it forth and makes use of it.

Son of good family, the essence taught through the intention of the Tathāgatas is likewise similar. In the future, degenerate monks, bearing the implements of the holy life without proper examination —"

— teaching to the fourfold retinue that the Tathāgata passes utterly into nirvāṇa without remainder, reciting and proclaiming the worldly arts, showing disrespect toward the scriptures of the Buddha — when such evil things as these arise in the world, the Tathāgata, in order to put an end to those evils and to cause beings to abandon wrong livelihoods, wrong gains, and wrong renown, taught this sūtra.

If the essence taught through the intention of this sūtra should decline and disappear from sight, then understand that the Dharma of the Buddha will also have declined.

Son of good family, if the Great Sūtra of the Parinirvāṇa is permanent, unchanging, and unshifting, why then would one ask the Blessed One Kāśyapa whether this sūtra exists? Son of good family, the sentient beings of the age of the Blessed One Kāśyapa had thin attachment and were endowed with wisdom. They were peaceful, tamed, easy to discipline, and possessed of great dignity. Their unforgetting dhāraṇī was like the finest herd of a white bull elephant. Their world-realm was utterly pure. Since all sentient beings knew that the Tathāgata does not pass wholly into nirvāṇa without remainder at the final end but abides forever, unchanging and unshifting, there was no need to preach or explain this sūtra, even while it existed.

Son of good family, the sentient beings of the present age are numerous in afflictions and great in delusion; they are forgetful and without wisdom, filled with doubts, unable to maintain the root of faith, their world-realm impure. All sentient beings say this: "The Tathāgata is impermanent, subject to change and shift — he has passed utterly into nirvāṇa without remainder at the final end." For this reason the Tathāgata taught this sūtra.

Son of good family, the Dharma of the Buddha Kāśyapa has not truly declined. Why is that? Because it is permanent, unchanging, and unshifting.

Son of good family, suppose there are sentient beings who view that which has a self as having no self, or view that which has no self as having a self; who view the permanent as impermanent, or view the impermanent as permanent; who view happiness as suffering, or view suffering as happiness; who view the utterly pure as impure, or view the impure as utterly pure; who view the non-cessation as cessation, or view the cessation as non-cessation; who view the sinful as non-sinful, or view the non-sinful as sinful; who view a light sin as a heavy one, or view a heavy sin as a light one; who view what is a vehicle as not a vehicle, or view what is not a vehicle as a vehicle; who view what is a path as not a path, or view what is not a path as a path; who view true awakening as not awakening, or view what is not awakening as awakening; who view suffering as not suffering, or view what is not suffering as suffering; who view the origin of suffering as not being the origin, or view cessation as not being cessation; who view what is true as not true; who view the conventional as ultimate, or view the ultimate as merely conventional; who view going for refuge as not going for refuge, or view what is not going for refuge as going for refuge; who call the genuine word of the Buddha the word of Māra, or call the genuine word of Māra the word of the Buddha — it is at such a time as this that the Tathāgatas proclaim this sūtra of the Parinirvāṇa from the very beginning.

Noble son, it would be better to say that a mosquito's proboscis has reached, without exception, to the very bottom of the ocean, than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has declined. It would be better to say that a violent gale can be bound with a noose, than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has declined. It would be better to say that Mount Meru, king of mountains, can be shattered and scattered by the breath of one's mouth, than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has declined. It would be better to say that a lotus flower has grown inside a blazing fire, than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has declined. It would be better to say that the medicine agada has turned to poison, than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has declined. It would be better to say that the moon is hot and the sun is cool, than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has declined. It would be better to say that the four great elements have abandoned their respective natures, than to say that the Dharma of the Tathāgata has declined.

Noble son, if, from the very moment that a Tathāgata first appears and attains the unsurpassed, perfect awakening of an arhat — that is to say, fully and perfectly realized awakening — he passes into complete nirvāṇa without having attendants who understand the profound meaning, you should know that the Dharma will not abide long in the world. Furthermore, noble son, if from the very moment a Tathāgata first appears and attains that unsurpassed, perfectly realized awakening he does have attendants who understand the profound meaning, then even after the Tathāgata has passed into complete nirvāṇa, you should know that the Dharma will long remain in the world. Furthermore, noble son, even if there are such attendants who understand the profound meaning, yet if the Tathāgata passes into complete nirvāṇa without there being faithful laypeople — laymen (upāsakas) who honour the Dharma of the Buddha with reverence — you should know that the Dharma will not long remain in the world. Furthermore, noble son, if from the very moment a Tathāgata first appears and attains that awakening there are both attendants who understand the profound meaning and faithful laypeople, laymen who honour the Dharma of the Buddha with reverence, then even after the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, the Dharma will long remain in the world. Furthermore, noble son, if from the very moment a Tathāgata first appears and attains that awakening there are both attendants who understand the profound meaning and greatly faithful laypeople, laymen who honour the Dharma of the Buddha, yet those attendants teach and expound the profound sūtras not for the sake of nirvāṇa but for the sake of gain and renown, then after the Tathāgata has passed into complete nirvāṇa, you should know that the Dharma will not long remain in the world. Furthermore, noble son, if from the very moment a Tathāgata first appears and attains that awakening there are both attendants who understand the profound meaning and greatly faithful laypeople, laymen who honour the Dharma of the Buddha with reverence, and those attendants teach and explain not for the sake of gain and renown but for the sake of seeking nirvāṇa, then even after the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, you should know that the Dharma will long remain in the world. Furthermore, noble son, if from the very moment a Tathāgata first appears and attains that awakening there are attendants who understand the profound meaning and greatly faithful laypeople, laymen who honour the Dharma of the Buddha with reverence, yet those attendants disparage one another greatly and quarrel frequently —

then even after the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, you should know that the Dharma will not long remain in the world.

Furthermore, noble son, if from the very moment a Tathāgata first appears and attains unsurpassed, perfect awakening as an arhat there are attendants who understand the profound meaning and greatly faithful laypeople, laymen who honour the Dharma of the Buddha with reverence, and those attendants live in harmony, do not disparage one another, and show one another respect — then even after the Tathāgata has passed completely into nirvāṇa, you should know that the Dharma will long remain in the world.

Furthermore, noble son, if from the very moment a Tathāgata first appears and attains unsurpassed, perfect awakening as an arhat there are attendants who understand the profound meaning and greatly faithful laypeople, laymen who honour the Dharma of the Buddha with reverence, and those attendants teach the Dharma for the sake of great nirvāṇa and show one another reverence without quarrelling — yet they grasp at things that have not been properly examined, and moreover proclaim of themselves, "I have attained everything from the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship" — then when the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, you should know that the Dharma will not long remain in the world.

Furthermore, noble son, if from the very moment a Tathāgata first appears and attains unsurpassed, perfect awakening as an arhat there are attendants who understand the profound meaning and greatly faithful laypeople, householders who honour the Dharma of the Buddha with reverence, and those attendants too, for the sake of great nirvāṇa, teach the sūtras and the like, live in harmony, show one another reverence and respect, do not grasp at any things that have not been properly examined, and do not say "I myself have attained the fruit of stream-entry" or even "I have attained up to the fruit of arhatship" — then even though the Blessed One, the Buddha, has passed completely into nirvāṇa, you should know that the Dharma will long remain in the world.

Furthermore, noble son, if from the very moment a Tathāgata first appears and attains unsurpassed, perfect awakening as an arhat the attendants do not claim anything ranging from understanding the profound meaning to having attained arhatship, yet each on his own grasps a separate view and expounds various and sundry divergent positions — and moreover, the venerable ones, even though the Blessed One established everything from the four weighty rules up to the seven rules for settling disputes, along with vows and qualifying exceptions for the sake of sentient beings, and likewise the twelve branches of scriptural teaching — yet say, "I alone understand this matter, having heard it from the Blessed One; you do not understand it. I alone know the Vinaya; you do not know it. I alone know the sūtras; you do not know them" — then when the Blessed One, the Buddha, has passed completely into nirvāṇa, you should know that the Dharma will not long remain in the world.

Noble son, consider the analogy of a skilled physician who both prescribes and withholds milk for patients: for a patient with a bile disorder he prescribes milk, while for a patient with a phlegm disorder he withholds it. In the same way, the Tathāgata, perceiving the root of sentient beings' afflictions, both permits and prohibits. The venerable ones, having heard this matter from the Blessed One in the following way — and so various vows and qualifying exceptions exist for sentient beings, and likewise the twelve branches are similar in that regard — the Blessed One, knowing that the places and times differ and the faculties of sentient beings vary between sharp and dull, therefore in some cases the Tathāgata restricted, and in other cases permitted, and proclaimed both the weighty and the light.

Furthermore, son of good family, as soon as the Tathāgata had first appeared and attained the unsurpassed, perfect awakening of an arhat, the attendants would not say "I have attained stream-entry" through to "I have attained arhatship." And they would not say "The awakened ones, the Blessed Ones, for the sake of sentient beings, prohibited this and permitted that." But the venerable ones would say: "I have heard from the Blessed One this matter, this teaching, and this Vinaya in the following way; let the venerable ones uphold the twelve branches of the Tathāgata's sūtras. If this matter is indeed so, I shall accept it; if it is not so, I shall set it aside." Knowing this, one should understand that even after that awakened Blessed One has passed into nirvāṇa, the Dharma will remain in the world for a long time.

Son of good family, at the time when my Dharma is approaching its final decline, the attendants among the hearers will sometimes teach that consciousness exists, and sometimes that consciousness is empty. Sometimes they will teach that an intermediate state between death and rebirth exists, and sometimes that there is no such intermediate state. Sometimes they will teach that the three times exist, and sometimes that the three times do not exist. Sometimes they will teach that the three vehicles exist, and sometimes that the three vehicles do not exist. Sometimes they will teach that all things exist, and sometimes that nothing exists. Sometimes they will teach that sentient beings have a beginning and an end, and sometimes that sentient beings have no beginning and no end. Sometimes they will teach that the twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned phenomena, and sometimes that the twelve links of dependent origination are not conditioned phenomena. Sometimes they will teach that the Tathāgata is subject to the suffering of illness, and sometimes that the Tathāgata is not subject to the suffering of illness. Sometimes they will teach that the Tathāgata did not permit monks to eat ten kinds of meat. What are these ten? Human flesh, snake, wild bull, horse, donkey, dog, lion, pig, fox, and monkey — and that all other meats were permitted. And sometimes they will teach that none whatsoever were permitted. Sometimes they will teach that the Tathāgata did not permit monks to engage in trade in five kinds of things. What are these five? Persons, weapons, alcohol, curds, and grain oil — and that all other things were permitted. Sometimes they will teach that monks were not permitted to go to five kinds of places. What are these five? The butcher's quarter, the snake-seller's quarter, the wine-seller's quarter, the royal palace, and the household of low caste — and that going to other places was permitted. Sometimes they will teach that monks were not permitted to wear woollen robes of the type called kauśeya, while all other garments were permitted. Sometimes they will teach that the Tathāgata permitted monks to keep in store ten hundred thousand gold śrāṅg weight in cloth, food, and bedding, and sometimes that he did not permit this. Sometimes they will teach that nirvāṇa is permanent, blissful, a self, and utterly pure. And sometimes they will teach that nirvāṇa is not the exhaustion of all afflictions, but rather that no other phenomenon exists that can be called nirvāṇa — just as when threads are woven together it is called a garment, and when the garment wears away it is called "no garment," yet there is no separate phenomenon called "no garment" — and that the defining characteristic of nirvāṇa is likewise similar to this.

Son of good family, at that time and in that age, those among my attendants who teach correctly will be few, and those who teach incorrectly will be many. Those who hold to the true Dharma will be few, and those who hold to a false Dharma will be many. Those who hold to the word of the Buddha will be few, and those who hold to the word of Māra will be many.

Son of good family, at that time there will be in the land of Kauśāmbī two attendants: one will be an arhat, and one will be a monk whose moral discipline is broken. The following of the monk with broken discipline will number five hundred, and the following of the arhat will number one hundred.

The monk with broken discipline declared that the Tathāgata had passed fully into nirvāṇa. "I have heard this matter directly from the Blessed One: whether a Tathāgata has been ordained with the four root precepts or not, if they are broken there is no fault. Even I have now attained the fruit of arhatship and the four kinds of unobstructed wisdom, and yet this very arhat has broken those four root precepts." That an arhat should violate all four of those root principles of Dharma and commit such evil was a wholly unworthy thing for an arhat to say.

When the Tathāgata was present in the world, he declared: "Hold firmly to restraint." After his final passing into nirvāṇa, they say: "Abandon everything." Concerning this, the monks led by the arhat said: "Venerable ones, to say that the Tathāgata has finally passed into nirvāṇa is an unworthy thing to say. We know that the Tathāgata is permanent, unchanging, and unaltered. Whether the Tathāgata is present in the world or has passed into nirvāṇa, the evil of breaking the four root precepts is equally grave. Therefore it is not fitting to say that an arhat has broken the four roots. Why? If even a stream-enterer does not violate the vows, what need is there to speak of an arhat? If you, venerable ones, say that one has attained the fruit of arhatship, then an arhat does not give rise to the perception of 'I am an arhat.' An arhat teaches only what is virtuous and does not teach what is non-virtuous. Everything that you, venerable ones, have taught is nothing but non-Dharma. Anyone who sees all twelve classes of scripture will know with certainty that those venerable ones are not arhats."

At that time, the followers of the monk with broken discipline took the life of that arhat. And at that time, the evil māra stirred the two factions of the Saṅgha into anger and strife, and in that moment he sorely afflicted those six hundred monks. Then base and lowly people, speaking here and there, exclaimed with wonder: "The Dharma of the Buddha has declined and is finished!" But in truth, my holy Dharma has not declined. For at that time in that land, one hundred and twenty thousand great bodhisattvas were upholding my Dharma most steadfastly — how then could my Dharma be said to have declined?

Yet at that time, in that age, there was not a single monk in Jambudvīpa who had become my attendant, and so the evil māra with his great fire burned all the sūtras. Whatever remained was stolen by brahmins, who extracted it into summaries and presented it as their own scripture. Thus, before the arising of a new buddha, lesser bodhisattvas drew one another away and became devoted to and attached to the words of brahmins. The brahmins declared, "We possess the Vinaya (monastic discipline)," but in truth the Vinaya does not exist among non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Though the tīrthikas claim to possess a self, bliss, and complete purity, in truth they do not know the meaning of self, bliss, and purity. They took one syllable, two syllables, one word, two words from the Buddha's Dharma and, presenting them, said, "Our scriptures contain meanings such as these."

Then at that time, in the city of Kuśinagārī, at the foot of the śāla trees, a vast and immeasurable assembly heard these words being spoken, and all of them cried out: "The world is empty! The world is empty!"

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then spoke to that great assembly: "Venerable ones, do not weep and be disheartened. The world is not empty,

the Tathāgata does not change, does not shift, but abides forever; and so too with the Dharma and the Saṅgha, it is the same."

Then that great assembly, having heard these words spoken, cried out in lamentation and aroused the mind set upon the highest, perfect, and complete awakening.

At that time in Rājagṛha there was a king known as Ajātaśatru. By nature he was wrathful and fierce, delighting in taking the lives of sentient beings, committing in full the four non-virtuous deeds of speech, deeply given over to minds of attachment, aversion, and delusion, seeing only the present moment and blind to the future, relying upon a deeply corrupt retinue, and, clinging through attachment to the five objects of desire of the present, he slew his own father, a man without fault.

Having killed his father thus, remorse arose in his mind, and tormented by grief he cast off his bodily ornaments and his music. Wracked by that mind of remorse, great boils broke out all over his body. The boils were so painful that they were unbearable to the touch, and he thought to himself: "My karma will ripen before long, and the ripening of a hell-being's karma is not far off." Such was his thought.

Then all the physicians of King Ajātaśatru anointed him with medicines of every variety, yet the boils only spread further outward and brought no relief. The king said to his mother: "These boils have arisen from the intention of my mind, not from the four great elements; therefore, there is no remedy by which any being could cure them."

Now at that time a great minister named Sunīdha came to where the king was, and standing to one side spoke these words: "Great King, if your body and mind have become uncomfortable and distressed, tell me — why do you sit thus with a darkened expression, grieving?"

The king said: "How could there be any ease for my body and mind? I have slain my father who was without fault. I had previously heard from wise men that one who commits the five acts of immediate consequence (ānantarya) in the world has no time of liberation from the hell-beings — and having heard that, I have committed boundless, immeasurable, countless transgressions. Since there is no skilled physician who can heal my ailing body and mind, how can there be any ease for body or mind?"

The minister then spoke in verse to say: "Great King, do not give way to excessive grief."

One who dwells always in sorrow
will return again and again to sorrow.
Just as one who loves sleep greatly
will return to sleep ever more deeply,
so too know that attachment and craving,
and great love of drink, are the same.

"As the king has said, it is told that one who commits the five acts of immediate consequence in the world has no time of liberation from the hell-beings — but who has actually experienced and witnessed this, and then reported it as fact to the king? As for what is called 'hell-beings,' it is simply a great many knowledgeable people in the world who have spread that as a saying of their own devising. And as for the king's saying that there is no skilled physician in the world to heal body and mind — that is not appropriate. At this very moment there is a great physician named Kāśyapa Paripūraka, one who is omniscient, who sees all things, who has attained meditative absorption of sovereign mastery, who has reached the ultimate end of fully pure holy conduct, and who shows to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings the unsurpassable path to nirvāṇa. He is even now teaching the Dharma to those nearby in these words: 'There is no dark karma, and there is no ripening of dark karma; there is no purely white karma, and there is no ripening of purely white karma.

There is neither mixed white-and-dark karma nor a ripening of mixed white-and-dark karma; there is no karma that is supreme, and there is no karma that is inferior.' Such is the teaching of that master of the Dharma who is even now residing in Rājagṛha. Go to that great king's presence. That master will heal both body and mind."

The king spoke: "If the words you have spoken are true and he is truly able to cleanse me of wrongdoing in that way, then I shall go for refuge to him."

Then another minister, one named Essence-Attained, came before the king and spoke these words: "Great King, why has your face gone dark, your mouth dry, your body trembling as though an unprepared soldier who encounters an enemy quivers faintly, and your complexion utterly drained? What has brought you such distress? Is it an illness of the body, or has some affliction come upon the mind?"

The king replied: "What reason do I have not to be sick in body and mind? Benighted by ignorance, lacking the eye of wisdom, I took an unwholesome spiritual friend as my guide, followed in the wake of evil in the manner of one like Devadatta, heeded the words of the wicked, and slew my own father the king — a man innocent of any wrongdoing — though he lived by the true Dharma. I once heard a verse from a learned and wise man of former times, spoken thus:

Whoever, with a mind of ill will
toward their father, their mother,
the buddhas, or those who dwell near them,
performs an act that brings forth evil —
the ripening of that act
is birth in the hell without respite.

For this reason I am utterly terrified, tormented by great suffering, and there is no skilled physician who can heal me."

The minister spoke again: "Great King, do not grieve for the moment. The Dharma has two kinds: the going-forth, and the law of kings. Under the law of kings, slaying one's father may be called an act without respite within this royal domain, yet it does not become a blameworthy sin. For example, there are insects such as the kakala worm that burst through their mother's womb and emerge at birth — it is simply the nature of reality that they are born in this way; though they harm their mother's body, it does not become a sin. The young of deer and other animals are similar. The law of royal sovereignty is likewise by its very nature of this kind, and so a king who slays his father does not thereby incur sin. The law of the going-forth, however, is different: under that law even the killing of a tiny insect in childhood becomes a sin. Therefore, Great King, do not grieve for the moment. And why? Because:

One who constantly gives way to grief
will return again and again to grief.
Just as one who loves sleep
will again fall ever more deeply into sleep —
so too should one understand
great craving and attachment,
and a great fondness for strong drink.

It is not right to say, as the king has said, that there is no skilled physician to heal body and mind. At this very moment there is a great teacher, the son of the brahmin Puṣkarasārin, named Mākandika, who is omniscient, who sees all things, who cherishes all sentient beings as though they were his only child, who has completely abandoned all afflictions, who draws out the poisonous thorns of the three harms from all sentient beings, who alone knows, sees, and realizes all phenomena that all sentient beings do not know, do not see, and do not realize — and he is constantly teaching the Dharma to those nearby in these words: 'The body of every sentient being has seven constituent parts. What are the seven? Earth, water, fire, wind, suffering, pleasure, and the life-force. These seven phenomena are neither emanated nor artificially made, and so they cannot be destroyed. For example, the reed known as iśikā stands eternally and does not move.'"

Mount Meru, the king of mountains, has neither been sent forth nor made by anyone. Just as there is no dispute over whether milk or yogurt is suffering or pleasure, virtuous or non-virtuous, so too they are not harmed even by a sharp weapon. Why is this? Because the seven constituent elements are empty, they are unobstructed. Life, moreover, cannot be cut. Why is this? There is no killing, no dying, no doing, no experiencing, no explaining, no listening, no understanding, and no teaching.

Constantly proclaiming these teachings, and pacifying all the blameworthy sins of countless sentient beings, that great master currently resides in Rājagṛha. Great King, go to wherever the great master dwells. The mere sight of him will purify all sin.

The king said: If he can truly rid me of my sin in this way, then I shall take refuge in this teaching.

Then another minister, one called Satyadatta, came before the king and addressed him in verse:

Great King, why have you removed all the adornments from your body? Why is your hair upon your head disheveled and bound up so? And why has it come to be like this? Why is the king's body now ill at ease, trembling and shaking, like flowering trees struck violently by the wind?

O King, your face is so deeply clouded and darkened — it is like farmers who have sown their seeds and then grieve when the rains do not fall. But tell me, has this grief arisen in your body or in your mind?

The king said: How could my body and mind possibly be at ease?

Father, the king loved me with the greatest affection and tenderness, and there was no fault of wrongdoing on his part. Yet from the very beginning, when the astrologers were consulted, the astrologers said, "This son of yours, once born, will kill his father" — and though those words were heard, he was nevertheless kept and raised. Then from the wise and learned, I had previously heard it said: "Anyone who lies with his mother in unchaste conduct, or who lies with a nun in unchaste conduct, or who steals the property of the Saṅgha, or who kills one who has aroused the awakening mind aimed at unsurpassed awakening, or who kills his father — such a person will, without any doubt, fall into the avīci hell, the hell of uninterrupted torment." Having heard this, how can my body and mind possibly be at ease?

The great minister spoke: Great King, do not grieve for now. If the killing were of someone earnestly practicing the path of liberation, it would indeed be sinful. But if the killing was for the sake of the king's rule, it does not become a sin.

Great King, what is not Dharma is called "not Dharma." What is devoid of Dharma is also called "devoid of Dharma" — just as when one has no son, one says "I have no son," and yet when one has a bad son, one also says "I have no son." Thus, though one says "I have no son," in truth it is not the case that there is no son. Or again, just as when there is no salt in a dish, one says "there is no salt," and yet when the salt is not salty, one also says "there is no salt." Or just as when there is no water one says "there is no water," and yet when there is only a little water, one also says "there is no water." Or just as something that ceases from moment to moment is called impermanent, and yet even something that endures for an entire eon is also called impermanent. Or just as when a person experiences suffering one says "there is no happiness," and yet when a person experiences only a slight measure of joy, one also says "there is no happiness." Or just as when one has no power one says "there is no pride," and yet even when one has only a little power, one says "there is no pride." Or just as when night has fallen one says "there is no sun," and yet when the sun is cut off by clouds, one also says "there is no sun."

Great King, even where there exists only a small measure of Dharma, one says "there is no Dharma," and yet in truth it is not that there is no Dharma at all.

Great King, listen to these words I now address to you. In every sentient being there exists what is called residual karma, and through the power of karma they revolve again and again in cyclic existence. If, Great King, your father too possessed this thing called residual karma, then even if the King were to slay him, it would not become a sin.

Great King, for the moment, I pray you put your grief aside. Why is this? Consider:

One who grieves without cease
shall return, and grieve again.
Just as one who loves to sleep
shall return, and sleep the more.
So too with attachment and craving,
and with strong addiction to drink — know it to be the same.

As for what the King has said — that there exists in the world no physician skilled in healing the ailments of body and mind — that cannot rightly be maintained. For at this very moment there dwells in Rājagṛha a great Teacher by the name of Jīvaka, son of Berāta, who is omniscient and all-seeing, whose wisdom is as profound and vast as the ocean, endowed with great majesty, possessed of great higher knowledge, who draws all sentient beings out from the net of doubt, and who alone knows and sees all phenomena that all sentient beings do not know, do not see, and do not comprehend. He is there right now, residing in Rājagṛha, teaching the Dharma in these very words to his many attendants.

He teaches that among the great multitude of an assembly, if a king of sovereign power were to perform virtuous and sinful actions as he pleased, even if he committed many sins, those sins would not become blameworthy transgressions. For example, when something is consumed by a great fire, there is no question of it being pure or impure — and so too it is with a king. Or consider how the great earth serves as the ground for all things both pure and impure; yet for all that it does, it harbors neither aversion nor delight. So too, Great King, you are like the great earth — there is no such thing as aversion or delight in you. Or as clear water washes both the pure and the impure, and yet holds neither pleasure nor displeasure in doing so, so too, Great King, you are like the water. Or as the wind sweeps through both the pure and the impure, and yet for all it does holds neither pleasure nor displeasure, so too, Great King, you are like the wind. Or consider how when the trees of autumn are cut down, they grow back again in summer — just so, the cutting of those trees does not in truth become a sin. And all sentient beings are like this as well: they pass away from here and are born here again. And because they are born here again, it does not become a sin.

The ripening of the fruits of suffering and happiness for all sentient beings is beyond my control. The karmic ripening of the present moment depends upon causes of the past — there is no ripening in the present moment from a cause of the present moment, and in the future too there will be no ripening of fruit. It is the present fruit itself that is ripening. This is why ordinary people keep moral discipline and undertake diligent effort — it is to reverse the future fruit that would ripen as sin in the present time. Through the keeping of moral discipline one becomes free from defilement. Through freedom from defilement one becomes free from defiled karma. And through the exhaustion of karma, the many sufferings will also be exhausted. Through the exhaustion of the many sufferings, one will be fully liberated.

Go quickly now to that Teacher! Even the illness that causes suffering in body and mind he shall heal, and upon meeting him, your sins too will be completely purified.

The Great King then said: If my sins will indeed be purified in this way, then I shall go to him for refuge.

Then a great minister named Sarvaarthavitta — "Knower of All Matters" — came before the king and spoke these words: Great King, why do you appear downcast and pale like this, without color? You look like a king who has lost his realm, or like a spring that has run dry, or like a pond without lotuses, or like a tree without flowers and leaves, or like a monk who has broken his moral discipline — bereft of splendor. Has your body become afflicted with suffering, or has your mind?

The king replied: How could there be any relief from suffering in my body and mind right now? My father the king loved me with tender affection and was always bringing me every comfort and happiness. Without remembering the kindness of his love for me, I slew my father the king — who was without fault and had done me no wrong. I had previously heard from wise and learned men that if one kills one's father or mother, one will without any doubt experience tremendous suffering for immeasurable aeons. Thus I am certain that before long I shall fall into the Avīci hell — the hell of uninterrupted torment — and there is no refuge that can heal this sin of mine.

The minister replied: Great King, do not grieve for now. Has the king not heard? In former times, a king called Lāmpa killed his father and seized the royal power. And likewise King Bde, King Byilatsina, King Nāhosha, King Kateka, King Byishaka, King Moonlight, King Sunlight, King Luminous, and King Upholder of Many Beings — all of them too killed their fathers and seized royal power, yet not even one of them fell into a hell realm. And kings such as the present King Vaidūrya, King Otana, King Tumpa, King Bya-ba, King Padma, and others — they too killed their fathers and seized royal power, and not one of them grieves over it. Who has ever seen a hell realm, a hungry ghost realm, or a divine realm? Great King, the only two existences that are directly perceptible are the human and the animal. And even those two existences are not born through cause and condition, nor do they die through cause and condition. Since there is no cause and condition in this way, how could there be anything such as virtue and sin? Great King, do not grieve. Why? Consider this verse:

One who is always given to grief
will return again to grief and be reborn into it.
Just as one who is fond of sleep
will in return fall into ever greater sleep —
so too with attachment, craving, and desire,
and with one's fondness for drink: know it to be just the same.

Now, as for what you said, O King — that there is no skilled physician in this world who can heal the illness of body and mind — that is not so. There is at present a great Teacher, the son of Kātyāyana, named Nirgrantha, who is omniscient, who sees all, who is like the great earth, who makes no distinction between gold and mere soil, who holds on his right side a sandal-wood smeared cord and on his left side a stone club and weapons, and yet makes no distinction between the two, whose mind is equal toward both the beloved and the hostile — a true Teacher and skilled physician of the world. Whether he is walking, sitting, dwelling, or lying down, he always holds his mind in meditative absorption without disturbance. That great unperturbed Teacher is right now teaching the Dharma to many attendants in words such as these: Whether I myself have done it, or caused another to do it; whether I myself have killed, or caused another to kill; whether I myself have burned, or caused another to burn; whether I myself have harmed, or caused another to harm; whether I myself have stolen, or caused another to steal; whether I myself have engaged in sexual misconduct, or caused another to do so —

Whether I myself have spoken falsely, or caused another to speak falsely; whether I myself have drunk intoxicants, or caused another to drink intoxicants; whether I myself have killed the people of a single city, a single town, or a single region; whether I have killed all sentient beings with a wheel of swords — even if, on the one hand, one were to give gifts to all sentient beings on the southern banks of the Ganges, and on the other hand were to kill all sentient beings on the northern banks of the Ganges, neither of these two acts would produce sin or merit, for there is no generosity, no moral discipline, no meditative absorption.

This is what that Teacher is now teaching while residing in Rājagṛha. O great king, go at once to that great Teacher. If you meet with him, your sins will be completely purified.

The king said: If my sins would truly be purified in that way, then I shall go for refuge to him.

The Noble Great Sūtra of the Passing into Nirvāṇa. The twenty-sixth fascicle.

Then a minister named Auspicious addressed the great king with these words: O great king, why have you become thus downcast and pallid, like a lamp placed next to the sun, or the moon in daytime, or a king who has lost his kingdom, or one who has sunk into the earth? O great king, at present you have no adversaries opposing you from any of the four directions — why then are you grieving and oppressed by suffering? O great king, is it that your body is in pain, or is it your mind that suffers? The princes always think to themselves, "When will the day come that I become a sovereign king with power over all?" O great king, you have achieved just such an aspiration and have become the wheel-turning king of the central lands, and command many great treasuries of precious things. You enjoy happiness just as you wish — do not be thus overwhelmed by sorrow and suffering.

The king replied: How could I possibly find cause not to grieve? O great minister, consider: a fool who is ignorant, when seized by attachment to food, does not notice even a sharp weapon. He is like one who does not know that poison has been poured into the food. I too am just like that. Consider how a deer, when it sees grass, does not notice a snare. Consider how a mouse, when seized by attachment to food, does not notice a cat. I am just the same: seeing only the pleasures of the present moment, I do not see the ripening of the fruits of non-virtue in the future. Long ago I heard from a learned and wise one these words: Even if three hundred spears were thrust into one's body in a single day, it would be better to bear that than to produce even a moment of ill will toward one's father or mother. As for me, I am in close proximity to the blazing fires of the hells — how could there possibly be any cause for me not to grieve?

The minister spoke again: Who ever told the king that hells exist? That was a lie. Consider: who sharpened thorns, which are sharp by their very nature? Who made the yellow color on a bird's feathers? Water is wet by nature, stone is hard by nature, wind moves by nature, fire is hot by nature — all these things arise of themselves and perish of themselves. Who made them? What is called "hell" has likewise been fabricated by learned and eloquent men who are clever with words. What meaning does the word "hell" have? Tell me, minister.

The minister replied: The syllable "hell" means the place of torment. The syllable "being" means one who is broken.

Having destroyed hell, and since there is no karmic maturation of evil, it is called "the sentient being of hell." Furthermore, the syllable "hell" means "human," and the syllable "being" means "god." Because one who has slain one's father is reborn as a god and a human, the sage called "Basu" teaches it in this way: since by burning one's body one attains the happiness of gods and humans, it is called "hell-being." Furthermore, the syllable "hell" means "life," and the syllable "being" means "long." Thus, since by taking life one's own life becomes long, it is called "hell-being." Therefore, Great King, in truth there is no such thing as a sentient being of hell.

Great King, consider: when a seed of barley is planted, barley grows; when a seed of rice is planted, rice grows. Likewise, if one kills a hell-being, one will again attain birth as a hell-being, and if one kills a human, one will certainly again become a human. Great King, hear the words that I, a proponent of the self, speak. In truth there is no such thing as killing. If there were such a thing as a self, it could not be killed. If there is no self, there is likewise no killing. Why is this? If a self exists, it is permanent, unchanging, and immutable. Being permanent, unchanging, and immutable in this way, there is no killing it — it is fearless, unbreakable, unbound, without aversion, without joy, like space itself. How then could killing it ever become a sin? If, on the other hand, there is no such thing as a self, then all phenomena are impermanent, and being impermanent they perish and cease moment by moment. Since they cease moment by moment, killing and dying also cease moment by moment. If they cease moment by moment in this way, who is there to experience that sin?

Great King, consider: when fire burns wood, no sin accrues to the fire. When an axe cuts wood, no sin accrues to the axe. When a sickle cuts grass, no sin accrues to the sickle. When a sword kills a person, the sword is not a person — if no sin accrues to the sword, why should sin accrue to the person? When poison kills a person, the poison is not a person — if no sin accrues to the poison, why should there be sin for the person? Since all things are of that same nature, if there is in truth no killing, how could sin arise?

Great King, do not grieve. Why? Listen:

One who always gives way to grief
will be reborn again in grief.
Just as one who is fond of sleep
will in turn sleep all the more,
so too with attachment and craving —
and know that love of liquor grows likewise.

O King, just as you have said — the view that in this world there is no wise physician skilled in purifying one's sinful actions is mistaken. At this very moment, the great Teacher, the unconquered one with matted locks, who is omniscient, who sees all, who knows the three worlds, who in a single instant simultaneously perceives world-realms without limit or number — whose hearing is likewise unbounded — who perfectly purifies all the sinful faults of every sentient being, who, like the river Gaṅgā, is utterly free from the stain of fault both inwardly and outwardly, completely pure: this great Teacher, who removes all the sinful actions both inner and outer of every sentient being, is right now teaching the Dharma to his attendants in these words:

Whoever kills all sentient beings, yet has no mind of shame or conscience, will never fall into the hell of sentient beings — just as dust and water do not cling to the sky. But one who possesses shame and conscience will fall into the hell of sentient beings — just as great waters drench all the earth. All sentient beings, too, are fashioned by him who is called the Sovereign of Gods, the one called Śakra (Indra, lord of the gods): if the Sovereign of Gods is pleased, all sentient beings will be happy; if the Sovereign of Gods is displeased, all sentient beings will suffer.

"If the non-virtuous actions and the merit of all sentient beings are likewise made by him who is called the Sovereign of Gods, then why would there be anything that becomes non-virtuous or meritorious?" So they assert. Consider the example of a carpenter: though he makes a mechanical figure of wood that walks, stands, sits, and lies down, the wooden figure itself cannot speak. In the same way, all sentient beings have been fashioned by him called the Sovereign of Gods — the Sovereign of Gods being like the carpenter, and the bodies of all sentient beings being like the mechanical figure. How then, the questioner asks, could there be any action that becomes non-virtuous? The great Teacher who teaches this is presently residing in Rājagṛha. Go quickly to that great king, and if you meet him, all your sins will be completely purified."

The king said: "If it is truly so, that my non-virtuous actions will be purified, then I will go to him for refuge."

Then a minister named Fearless came to where the king was and addressed him thus: "Great king, in this world, foolish and bewildered people in a single day rejoice a hundred times, grow angry a hundred times, sleep a hundred times, awaken a hundred times, are frightened a hundred times, and weep a hundred times. But for one who is wise and possessed of discernment, there is no such heedlessness. Great king, why do you grieve so deeply? You are like a traveler who has lost his companion, or one who has sunk in a swamp with no refuge, or one tormented by thirst with no water to drink, or one led astray in a wilderness who has lost the path, or one gravely ill with no skilled physician to heal him, or one who has entered the ocean and whose ship has been wrecked, left without refuge. Great king, is your body now in discomfort, or is your mind in distress?"

The king said: "How could there be any relief for body or mind? Through my reliance on an evil companion, and through heedlessly speaking wrongly, I killed my own father the king. I will certainly fall into the hells, and I have no protector or refuge."

The minister said: "Great king, do not grieve in this way. The kingly lineage is the lineage of kings. If one commits an act of killing for the sake of the royal dominion, or for a monk, or for a brahmin, or for the well-being of many beings, there is no sin of non-virtue. Your father the king honored the ascetics but did not honor the brahmins, and because his mind was not at ease, because his mind was not at ease in this way, he was not truly of the kingly lineage. Great king, since you do honor the brahmins, even though you killed the former king, there is no non-virtuous action. Moreover, Great king, what is called 'killing' does not truly exist. What is called killing means severing the life-breath, and what is called the life-breath is the in-breath and out-breath. But since the breath cannot be cut or slain, how could the taking of a life be a sinful non-virtuous action? Great king, do not grieve. Why so? Consider:

One who always grieves
will return again and again to grief.
Just as one who loves sleep
will again and again sleep deeply,
so too with attachment and craving —
know that a fondness for wine is likewise so.

It is not right to say, as the king has said, that there is no skilled physician in the world. Right now the great Teacher, the naked sage (Nirgrantha) Jñātiputra, is omniscient, all-seeing, filled with loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, skilled in knowing the sharp and dull faculties of all beings, and one who fully comprehends whatever skillful means are appropriate. He is unstained by the eight worldly concerns, and his holy life is supremely pure.

That supremely serene one now teaches the Dharma to his attendants in these words: there is no generosity, there is no virtue, there is no father, there is no mother, there is no present, there is no past, there is no arhat, there is no meditation, and there is no path. All sentient beings, after a hundred thousand eons have passed, will of themselves be liberated from the wheel of birth and death. Those who have committed evil and those who have not — all are alike in this. As an analogy, consider the four great rivers: the Sindhu, the Gaṅgā, the Pakṣu, and the Sītā — all four flow into the great ocean without distinction. So too with all sentient beings: at the time of liberation, all are without distinction.

Such is the teaching of that great Teacher. He now dwells in Rājagṛha. Go quickly to that great king, and when you meet him, your misdeeds will be purified.

The king replied: If my misdeeds are truly to be purified in that way, then I shall go for refuge to him.

At that time the great physician named Jīvaka came before the great king and said to him: Great king, have you slept well?

And at that the king spoke these verses:

Those who are able to cut through completely
all afflictions that defile from every side,
who are unattached to the three worlds —
they will sleep in perfect ease.

One who teaches the profoundly deep meaning
of how to pass beyond sorrow —
that true brahmin
will sleep in supreme ease.

One who has no fault of body,
who has abandoned the four faults of speech,
in whose mind no doubt whatever stirs —
they will sleep in perfect ease.

When body and mind are free from torment,
dwelling in great serenity and bliss,
one will attain unsurpassed happiness
and sleep in supreme ease.

One whose mind is attached to nothing,
who has utterly abandoned resentment,
who is always peaceable and lives without quarrel —
that one will sleep in perfect ease.

One who commits no evil deed,
who possesses a mind of shame and conscientiousness,
and who trusts in karmic maturation —
that one will sleep in perfect ease.

One who honors father and mother,
who does not take the life of even a single sentient being,
and who harbors no thought of stealing another's wealth —
they will sleep in perfect ease.

One who thoroughly tames the sense faculties,
who relies upon a spiritual friend of virtue,
and who has vanquished the four kinds of māra —
they will sleep in perfect ease.

One who sees neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious,
neither happiness nor suffering,
and who, for the sake of the many ordinary beings
who wander on and on through the wandering of saṃsāra,
feels no weariness —
that one will sleep in supreme ease.

Who is it that sleeps in ease?
The Blessed One, the buddha —
having fully realized meditative absorption in emptiness,
his body and mind are utterly still.

Who is it that sleeps in ease?
One endowed with loving-kindness and compassion,
who strives ardently for the realization of no-self
and regards all beings as a parent regards a child.

Sentient beings shrouded in ignorance
do not see the fruit of their afflictions,
and so they forever commit evil deeds —
they will not sleep in ease.

If by one's own body,
or by the body and speech of another,
the ten non-virtuous deeds have been committed —
they will not sleep in ease.

One who, desiring happiness,
says that killing one's father is no fault,
and who turns toward evil companions —
that one will not sleep in ease.

One who has not learned moderation in food,
and who has gone beyond the proper measure of cold drink,
will give rise to the suffering of illness —
that one will not sleep in ease.

If one has deceived the king,
or has lain with another's wife,
or if those who go to remote forest hermitages —

that one will not sleep in ease.

A physician afflicted by illness himself,
who has been cheated and killed by a king who governs his realm justly —
even though all skilled physicians apply their treatments and their mantras and the like,
my own illness will not be cured.

Why is this? My own father was a king who governed his realm justly, without fault or flaw, yet I deceived him and had him killed. When a fish is pulled out onto dry land, where is the joy in that? When a deer is caught in a snare, there is no feeling of joy. Or it is like a person who knows they will die before long, or a king who has lost his kingdom and fled to a foreign land, or one who hears that a serious illness he has contracted cannot be cured, or one who has broken the law and hears that there is a blameworthy deed to be reckoned with. In just that way do I feel.

In times past I heard from learned and wise teachers that if the actions of body, speech, and mind are not entirely pure, that person will certainly fall into hell. Since I too will certainly fall into hell, how could there be any question of sleeping in ease? And now there is no unsurpassed great physician who dispenses the medicine of Dharma to heal the suffering of my illness.

Jīvaka the physician spoke: Excellent, Great King, excellent! Although the king has committed such a blameworthy deed, the arising of a mind of profound remorse is good. And it is good that you possess a sense of modesty and a sense of shame.

Great King, the awakened Blessed One always teaches as follows: two things that are pure white in nature become a refuge and protector for sentient beings. What are these two? Modesty and shame. Shame means that one does not commit blameworthy deeds oneself. Modesty means that one does not lead others to commit them. Shame means that one feels self-reproach. Modesty means that one confesses and repents before others. Shame means being embarrassed before people. Modesty means being embarrassed before the gods. These are called shame and modesty. One who has neither shame nor modesty cannot be called a human being — they are called an animal. Because one possesses shame and modesty, one shows respect to one's parents and teachers. Because one possesses modesty and shame, one speaks of having fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters. Great King, it is excellent to possess shame and modesty.

Great King, let me now recount what I heard from the awakened Blessed One. A wise person is of two kinds: one who does not commit wrongdoing, and one who, having committed it, feels remorse and confesses. A foolish and deluded person is likewise of two kinds: one who commits wrongdoing, and one who, having committed it, conceals it. Thus, even if one has previously committed wrongdoing, if one later feels remorse and confesses, and having confessed vows through shame and modesty not to commit it again, it is like placing a precious jewel in turbid water until the water becomes clear, or like the moon shining fully when unobscured by clouds and fog — one who commits wrongdoing and then feels remorse is like that.

If the king too feels remorse and confesses, and possesses shame and modesty, then his blameworthy faults will be purified and he will become entirely clean. Great King, there are two kinds of wealth: wealth in cattle, horses, and various kinds of livestock, and wealth in gold, silver, and material riches. However many horses and cattle one may have, they cannot compare to a single precious jewel. Great King, it is the same with sentient beings: there is wealth in wrongdoing and wealth in virtue — however much wrongdoing one has done, it cannot match a single act of virtue.

I have heard from the Blessed One, the buddha, that one who applies the mind with diligence to a single act of virtue will overcome a great multitude of wrongdoings. Great King, consider this: a small vajra (Skt. vajra) can pierce even Mount Meru; a tiny flame can burn everything; a small amount of poison can kill a sentient being. In just the same way, even a modest degree of virtue can overcome great wrongdoing. Though that virtue may be called small, in reality it is great. Why? Because it overcomes great wrongdoing.

Great King, as the Blessed One has taught: concealing wrongdoing is defiled; not concealing it is undefiled. Therefore, to feel remorse and confess is to be undefiled. Accordingly, when one has committed blameworthy actions, one should not conceal those wrongdoings. Not concealing one's wrongdoings causes blameworthy actions to become weakened. And when one confesses with shame and modesty, blameworthy actions will be entirely purified.

Great King, even a small number of drops of water, falling one by one, will fill a great vessel. In just the same way, even a virtuous mind will overcome great blameworthy actions. If blameworthy actions are concealed, those blameworthy actions will arise again and again. But if one feels remorse and confesses with shame and modesty, blameworthy actions will be entirely purified. Therefore, as the Blessed One, the buddha, has taught, those who are wise and possessed of wisdom do not conceal their blameworthy actions.

Great King, it is excellent indeed to have trust in causes, trust in results, and trust in the karmic maturation of actions. Great King, do not grieve. If a sentient being who has committed blameworthy actions conceals them, does not confess, has no sense of shame or modesty, does not see causes and results and the karmic maturation of actions, does not supplicate those who are wise and possessed of wisdom, and does not rely on a spiritual friend — such a person cannot be healed by any physician, however skilled. It is just as when someone has been struck by the disease called kanka: no physician in the world can cure it. Concealing blameworthy actions is like that as well.

Who is it that conceals blameworthy actions? It is a person of wrong craving. And who is a person of wrong craving? It is one who has no trust in causes and results, who has no shame or modesty, who at present has no trust in the karmic maturation of actions, who does not foresee the actions of the future, who does not rely on a spiritual friend, and who does not engage with the teaching of the Blessed One, the buddha. Such a person is called one of wrong craving, and even the Blessed One, the buddha, cannot heal them. Why? Just as no physician in the world can cure a corpse, so too one of wrong craving is like that — even the Blessed One, the buddha, cannot heal them.

Great King, since you are not a person of wrong craving, it is not right for you to say, "There is nothing that can cure my illness." Let the king know it thus: it is not fitting to say, as the king has said, "My illness cannot be cured." Great King, the son of the pure-food king Śuddhodana of the land of the Śākyas, he of the Gautama clan, whose name means "one whose aims are accomplished," who by himself, without being shown by anyone else, awakened through his own knowing and became perfectly and completely awakened in the unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening — whose body is entirely adorned with the thirty-two excellent major marks and the eighty excellent minor marks, who possesses the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, who is omniscient, who sees all, who is great in loving-kindness and compassion —

who regards all beings with the same loving care as a parent feels for a cherished child, like Rāhu does for his own son; who speaks in accordance with the right moment, knowing it through his knowledge of the capacities of beings endowed with virtue — like a mother cow who never abandons her calf — who does not speak at the wrong time; who speaks truthfully, speaks with complete purity, speaks with utter clarity, speaks meaningfully, and speaks in accordance with the Dharma; who speaks concisely and decisively, and thereby fully eradicates the afflictions of countless sentient beings; who is supremely skilled in the characteristics of the faculties and intentions of ordinary people; who is supremely skilled in whatever skillful means are appropriate; whose wisdom is lofty and steep like Mount Meru; whose breadth and depth are like the ocean; and who, that Blessed One the buddha, possesses vajra-like wisdom — there is simply no ground for saying that the evil karma of any ordinary person could vanquish him and leave him defeated, for he himself shatters all such evil karma.

That buddha is now residing, twelve leagues from here, in the city called Kuśinagara, between a pair of śāla trees. At this very moment he is teaching the Dharma in all its varieties to an immeasurable and countless assembly of bodhisattvas — teaching on that which exists and that which does not exist; the conditioned and the unconditioned; the defiled and the undefiled; the fruits of affliction; pure phenomena; form phenomena and formless phenomena; phenomena that are neither form nor formless; self and what is not self; what is neither self nor not-self; the permanent and the impermanent; what is neither permanent nor impermanent; the blissful and the unblissful; what is neither blissful nor unblissful; the marked and the unmarked; what is neither marked nor unmarked; annihilation and non-annihilation; what is neither annihilation nor non-annihilation; the mundane and the transcendent; what is neither mundane nor transcendent; vehicle and non-vehicle; what is neither vehicle nor non-vehicle; what is done by oneself and experienced by oneself; what is done by oneself and experienced by another; and what involves no action and no experience.

Great King, whoever hears from the Buddha about the absence of action and the absence of experience will be entirely purified of all their evil karma.

Great King, live on yet a while. When Śakra, the lord of the gods (Indra), is drawing near to the moment of death, five signs appear beforehand. What are they? Stains appear on his robes; the flowers on his crown wither; his body gives off an unpleasant smell; sweat breaks out from his armpits; and he no longer wishes to remain in his seat.

At such a time, if Śakra the lord of the gods, while in solitude, should see any śramaṇa or brahmin, he approaches them and generates the perception of them as a buddha. And when that śramaṇa or brahmin sees Śakra, he makes an aspiration and speaks these words: "Lord of the gods, we take refuge in you!" Hearing this, Śakra realizes the person is not a buddha, and he thinks to himself: "Since this is not a buddha, I myself am powerless to remove these five evil signs."

At that time, a minister named Matsyaśrī spoke to Śakra and said: "Lord of the gods, the king of the gandharvas (celestial musicians) is named Kapulo, and he has a daughter called Subartā. If you grant her to me, I will show you a way to pacify the king's evil signs."

Śakra replied: "The asura king Prahlāda's daughter, Mānoramā, is to become my wife —"

"If you are able to show me the way to pacify my evil signs, then I would give even Mānoramā to you — what need is there to speak of Subartā? Lord of the gods, the Blessed One, a buddha named Śākyamuni, is residing at present in Rājagṛha. Go to wherever he dwells and hear from him what you have not heard before, and the evil signs portending the hour of death will without fail be pacified."

"Son of good family, if the Blessed One, the buddha, is able to pacify them, then let us go to wherever he dwells." So saying, Śakra turned his heavenly vehicle around and went to Rājagṛha, to Vulture Peak Mountain, to the place where the Blessed One, the buddha, was staying. Bowing his head at the feet of the buddha, he took his seat to one side and addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Blessed One, what is it that binds and fetters gods and humans?"

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, it is miserliness, attachment, and envy."

He asked again: "From what do miserliness, attachment, and envy arise?"

The Blessed One declared: "They arise from ignorance."

He asked again: "From what does ignorance arise?"

The Blessed One declared: "It arises from heedlessness."

He asked again: "From what does heedlessness arise?"

The Blessed One declared: "It arises from inversion — from perceiving things contrary to their true nature."

He asked again: "From what does inversion arise?"

The Blessed One declared: "It arises from a mind of doubt."

"Blessed One, that the phenomenon of inversion arises from doubt — this is in accord with the word of the noble ones. And why is that? Because doubt arose in my mind, inversion was born: I formed the perception of a buddha and Blessed One regarding someone who was not a buddha and Blessed One. But now, having seen the Blessed One, the buddha, my mind of doubt has been cleansed. With doubt completely cleansed, inversion is exhausted. With inversion exhausted, there is no longer a mind of miserliness, nor indeed a mind of envy."

The Blessed One declared: "You say there is no mind of miserliness and envy — have you now attained the fruit of once-returning, or is the attainment of the fruit of once-returning something you desire? One who has attained the fruit of once-returning has no mind of desire. If there is no mind of desire, why then did you come to me out of concern for your life? A once-returner has no hope in life."

"Blessed One, one who perceives inversely does have hope in life. One who does not perceive inversely has no such hope. As for myself, in truth I have no hope in this life, but I do have hope in the dharmakāya of the Blessed One, the buddha, and in the primordial wisdom of a buddha."

"Kauśika, one who seeks the dharmakāya of a buddha and the primordial wisdom of a buddha will without fail attain them in a future time to come."

Then Śakra, the lord of gods, having heard these words from the Blessed One, found that those very evil signs portending the hour of death had been entirely cleansed. He rose from his seat, bowed his head in homage, circumambulated three times, and with respectful joined palms addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"I have recovered from death. I have recovered my life from its loss. Moreover, having received from the Blessed One, the buddha, the prophecy that I will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, that is what I call recovery and the gaining of life.

"Blessed One, how is it that gods and humans increase and flourish? And how is it that they decline and diminish?"

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, through the condition of conflict and strife, gods and humans decline and diminish. Through the condition of deep harmony and concord, they are born and increase."

"Blessed One, if it is through conflict and strife that one declines and is diminished, then from this day forward I will not quarrel with the asuras."

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Kauśika, patience is the supreme cause of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening for a buddha, a Blessed One."

With these words, Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, touching his crown to the ground, and departed for his abode.

That great king declared that the Tathāgata dispels all evil omens born of non-virtue, and that therefore a buddha is beyond conception.

Moreover, if even a king were to approach him, all blameworthy actions would be completely purified.

Great King, may you live long.

There was a brahmin's son named Ahiṃsaka — "Harmless One" — who, having slain countless sentient beings, was given the name Aṅgulimāla, "Garlanded with Fingers." When he set out to kill again and arose with murderous intent, his body trembled and shook.
