The trembling of body and mind was born of the condition of having committed the five acts of immediate retribution, and so he would without doubt fall into the hell realms. Yet when he encountered the Buddha, his body and mind trembled still, and again the intent to kill arose in him. The trembling of body and mind was stirred by the condition of having committed the five acts of immediate retribution, and those who commit the five acts of immediate retribution will without doubt fall into the hell realms. Yet the very moment that man encountered the Tathāgata, the great Teacher, the cause for falling into the hell realms was completely purified, and he aroused the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Therefore the Blessed One, the buddha, is called the unsurpassed physician — unlike the six teachers.

Great King, there was also a prince named Jīvaka. His father the king, enraged, cut off his hands and feet and threw him into a pit. The king's mother, moved by affection, drew him out of the pit and led him to where the Buddha was. The very moment he encountered the Buddha, his hands and feet were restored, and he aroused the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Great King, through meeting the Buddha in just this way, one attains visible and immediate results. Therefore the Blessed One, the buddha, is called the unsurpassed physician — unlike the six teachers.

Great King, on the banks of the Ganges there were five hundred hungry ghosts. For countless years they had not seen a drop of water. When they went to the river's edge, they saw before them a great mass of blazing fire. Tormented by thirst and hunger, they cried out with loud lamentation. At that time the Tathāgata was dwelling at the foot of an udumbara tree in a grove near that very river. Many of those hungry ghosts then came to where the Buddha was and addressed him thus: "We are tormented by hunger and thirst and cannot sustain our lives much longer."

The Blessed One declared: "Why do you not drink from the flowing waters of the Ganges?"

The hungry ghosts replied: "Though the Tathāgata sees it as water, we see it as a great blazing mass of fire."

The Blessed One declared: "The waters of the Ganges river are indeed pure blue and clear — there is truly no fire there. It is your evil karma that has caused your minds to become distorted, so that you perceive it as fire. Let your distorted perception be thoroughly cleared away, and see it as water."

Having so declared, the Blessed One then taught those many hungry ghosts about the faults of miserliness and attachment.

The many hungry ghosts then said: "We are tormented by hunger and thirst, and even though we hear many words of Dharma, we do not have the capacity to retain them."

The Blessed One declared: "Enter the waters of the Ganges river and drink from them as you wish." By the blessing of the Buddha, those hungry ghosts were able to drink the water. Having thus drunk their fill, the Tathāgata then taught them the Dharma in its many aspects. Having heard the Dharma, they gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and, casting off their bodies as hungry ghosts, they attained the body of a god.

"Great King, for this reason the buddha, the Blessed One, is called the unsurpassed physician — he is not like the six teachers. Great King, in the land of Śrāvastī there were five hundred men who were blinded and left sightless by the army of King Prasenajit. They had no opportunity to go to where the Buddha was. The buddha, the Blessed One, out of compassion, went to where those blinded men were and gladdened them, saying: 'Sons of good family, restrain your body and speech with great care, and from this time forward commit no evil.' The moment those many men heard the perfectly clear speech of the Tathāgata from the Buddha, their sight was restored. They joined their palms before the Buddha, paid homage, and addressed the Blessed One thus: 'Blessed One, we understand that the mind of loving-kindness of the buddha, the Blessed One, extends to all sentient beings — not only to gods and humans.' At that time the Blessed One taught them the Dharma, and having heard the Dharma, they gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. For this reason the Tathāgata is called the unsurpassed, true physician of the world — he is not like the six teachers.

"Great King, in the city of Śrāvastī there was a merchant's son named Māpham who committed adultery with his mother. By reason of that act and that condition, he also killed his father. Later, when he discovered that his mother was being intimate with another man, he killed his mother too. He befriended an arhat, and then out of shame killed the arhat as well. Having thus killed an arhat, he went to a monastery and requested from the community of monks to go forth from home into homelessness. The community of monks, knowing that he had committed three acts of immediate retribution, did not grant him ordination. Furious at being refused ordination, that very night he took a torch and set fire to the monks' dwelling. Afterward he went to Rājagṛha, came to where the Tathāgata was, and requested ordination from the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata ordained him, taught him the Dharma, and through that teaching all the heavy sins and misdeeds he had accumulated were purified, and he gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. For this reason the buddha, the Blessed One, is called the unsurpassed Teacher — he is not like the six teachers."

Great King, you are by nature wrathful and fierce, and you place your trust in evil companions. And so it was that at that time Devadatta released intoxicated woolly bulls and drove them to charge at the Buddha. Yet the moment those bulls caught sight of the Buddha, they became tame of their own accord. The Buddha, the Blessed One, then stretched out his hand and stroked the bulls on their heads, taught them the Dharma, and through that teaching they gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Great King, even those born in an animal existence — the moment they encountered the Buddha, even the karmic maturation of their animal birth was utterly overcome. How much more need be said for those born in a human lineage? Great King, understand this well: if one encounters the Buddha, even grave and blameworthy sins will be entirely purified.

Great King, before the Buddha, the Blessed One, had manifested unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, immeasurable and innumerable hosts of māras came into the presence of the bodhisattva. At that time, through the power of his patience, the bodhisattva thoroughly subdued the evil-minded māras, taught the Dharma to those māras, and caused them to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Such is the power and might of the Buddha, the Blessed One's great qualities.

Great King, in a wilderness hermitage there were many hungry ghosts who slaughtered sentient beings. The Tathāgata, for the sake of the merchant Nordzang, went to that wilderness hermitage where those hungry ghosts dwelled and taught them the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma proclaimed, those hungry ghosts of the wilderness hermitage were filled with delight and joy. The merchant Nordzang offered them to the Buddha, and they gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Great King, in the region of Sershya there was a butcher named Changyanné who each and every day slaughtered countless sheep. Having been seen by Śāriputra, he took the eight precepts for a single day. Through that cause and that condition, upon his death he was reborn as the son of Gömpé Ngalwasö, the Protector of the Northern Quarter.

If even the Tathāgata's attendants possess such great qualities, what need is there to speak of the Buddha, the Blessed One, himself?

Great King, to the north of the region of Khor there was a city called Segma, and there a king named Luwi Chakgya killed his own father in order to seize the kingdom. Having killed his father in this way, a mind of intense remorse arose in him. He renounced the kingdom, came to where the Tathāgata was, and requested ordination. The Blessed One said to him, "Excellent!" and he became a fully ordained monk. His blameworthy sins were entirely purified, and he gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Great King, therefore know that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable and incalculable great qualities.

Great King, the Tathāgata had a younger brother named Devadatta, who created a schism in the Saṅgha, maliciously drew blood from the Buddha's body, and killed the fully ordained nun named Padmā — thereby committing three acts of immediate retribution. To him also the Tathāgata taught the Dharma in its many forms, and his blameworthy sins were straightaway entirely purified. For this reason the Tathāgata is called the great physician — he is not like the six teachers.

Great King, if you take to heart what I have said, go quickly to where the Blessed One, the Buddha, resides. And even if you do not take it fully to heart, at least reflect on it well.

Great King, the great compassion of the Blessed One, the Buddha, pervades all without exception — he does not teach the sacred Dharma to only one or a few. Because his mind is impartial toward friend and foe alike, he establishes not merely a single person in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, but establishes all beings therein. The Tathāgata is not the teacher of only the fourfold retinue of renunciants — he is the teacher of all: gods, humans, nāgas, hungry ghosts, animals, hell-beings, and every living being throughout the world. For this reason, it is fitting that all sentient beings cultivate the perception of the Blessed One, the Buddha, as their mother and father.

Great King, the Tathāgata does not teach the Dharma exclusively to noble and venerable kings — he also teaches the Dharma to those of low and humble birth, such as Upāli. He did not receive food offerings only from Ubarta and Anayyate — he also accepted food from the poor man Sudarati. He does not teach the Dharma only to those of sharp faculties, such as Śāriputra — he also teaches the Dharma to those of dull faculties, such as Cūḍapanthaka. He did not grant the going forth only to Mahākāśyapa and those of his kind, who were by nature free of attachment — he also granted the going forth to Nandaka and those like him, who were possessed of strong desire. He did not grant the going forth only to Laṅgulīya Kāśyapa and those like him, whose afflictions were thin and mild — he also granted the going forth even to Sūta, the younger brother of King Ajātaśatru, who had committed blameworthy acts. He did not uproot aversion only through acts of veneration accompanied by respectful service to someone called Jāgama — he also provided refuge even to the Aṅgulimāla, who with malicious intent had caused harm. He does not teach the Dharma exclusively to men endowed with wisdom — he also teaches the Dharma to foolish women who are wanton, even those skilled in the ways of wantonness. It is not only the fourfold assembly of renunciants who attain the fruit of awakening — he also enabled householders to attain the three fruits. He does not teach the meaning of the Dharma only to those like Sūtana, who have completely abandoned bustle and whose minds have become one-pointed — he also teaches the meaning of the Dharma to kings like Rūpasāra and others who govern kingdoms. He does not teach the Dharma only to those who have entirely renounced intoxicants — he also teaches the Dharma to fierce householders utterly drunk on liquor. He does not teach the Dharma only to those like Lipa who are established in meditative absorption — he also teaches the Dharma to the brahmin woman Vāsitā, whose mind was disturbed by the death of her son. He does not teach the Dharma only to his own attendants — he also teaches the Dharma to naked tīrthika ascetics. He does not teach the Dharma only to those in the full bloom of youth at twenty-five years of age — he also teaches the Dharma to those who are bent with old age at eighty years. He does not teach the Dharma only to persons whose faculties are fully ripened — he also teaches the Dharma to those whose roots of virtue are not yet ripened. He does not teach the Dharma only to queens adorned with garlands — he also teaches the Dharma to the snake-seller Padmā. He did not accept only the finest food of eight flavors offered by King Ajātaśatru — he also accepted food mixed with poison offered by the householder Śrīgupta.

Great King, know it in this way: as for Śrīgupta — even though in times long past he had accumulated the karma of having committed acts of immediate retribution, upon meeting the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he gave rise to the awakening mind aimed at unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Great King, even if one were to give food and clothing for an entire month to all sentient beings, the merit of a single person who, for just one instant, recollects the Buddha would not be matched even by a sixteenth part of that giving.

Great King, even if one were to give a hundred chariots' worth of gold to another person rather than keeping it for oneself, that giving would not match the merit of one who generates the awakening mind and takes a single step in the direction of the Buddha.

Great King, even if one were to give a hundred chariots laden by great white oxen with all manner of precious things from a great realm, along with a hundred women adorned with necklaces and garlands — all that giving would not match the merit of one who generates the awakening mind and takes a single step in the direction of the place where a Buddha dwells. And let that pass for now: even if one were to give, by way of the four kinds of offering materials, to all the sentient beings of this great trichiliocosm of three thousand worlds, the merit of one who generates the awakening mind and takes a single step in the direction of a Buddha would be greater still. Let even that pass: even if a great king were to make gifts to innumerable sentient beings equal in number to the grains of sand in the Ganges river, that giving would not match the merit of one who, from the heart, goes before the Tathāgata between two śāla trees simply to hear the Dharma.

Then the Great King spoke to Jīvaka in these words: "The Blessed One, the Buddha, is by his very nature supremely tame, and so his retinue too is supremely tame — just as a sandalwood grove is surrounded only by sandalwood trees. The Tathāgata is utterly pure, and so his retinue too is utterly pure — just as a great nāga lord is encircled by a retinue of nāgas. The Tathāgata is perfectly peaceful, and so his retinue too is perfectly peaceful. The Tathāgata is free of attachment, and so his retinue too is free of attachment. Since the Buddha is without affliction, his retinue too is without affliction. Yet someone like me — a grievous sinner, deeply stained by disgraceful deeds, utterly soiled and defiled, belonging to the class of hell-beings — how could such a one go into the presence of the Tathāgata? Even if I did go, I fear he would not look upon me and would not deign to speak to me. Though you urge me to go before the Buddha, I am so utterly defiled that not even the slightest wish to go arises in me."

At that moment, from the sky above, this voice was heard:

The unsurpassed Dharma of the Buddha is drawing near its setting.
The river of profound teaching is close to running dry.
The great lamp of the Dharma will not long remain.
The mountain of Dharma is on the verge of toppling.
The boat of Dharma is near to breaking apart.
The bridge of Dharma is close to collapsing.
The palace of Dharma is about to crumble.
The victory banner of Dharma is on the point of falling.
The trunk of Dharma is near to shattering.
The spiritual friend is about to depart.
Great ruin is drawing near.
Sentient beings starved of Dharma will soon arise.
The plague of afflictions is about to break out.
The time of being overwhelmed by great darkness has arrived.
The time of poverty in Dharma is close at hand.
The king of māras rejoices greatly and has cast aside his armor.
The sun of the Buddha is close to setting behind the summit of the great mountain of parinirvāṇa.

Great King, if the Buddha passes away, no one else will be able to heal these disgraceful deeds of the Great King.

Great King, you have committed the shameful deed of the avīci hell, a heinous act without interval. By the force of that karma, you will without doubt fall there.

Great King, the syllable "a" means "without." The syllable "vi" means "interval." Since there is not even a little interval of ease, it is called "without interval."

Great King, if even a single person falls into that hell, their body fills the entire space of eighty thousand leagues, and they experience sufferings of every kind pressing in upon them on all sides without any gap within. If many people fall there, their bodies fill it just the same, each piercing into the others without hindrance.

Great King, in the cold hells, even a brief encounter with a warm breeze is called ease. In the hot hells, even a brief encounter with a cool breeze is called ease. In the hell of revival, merely hearing the words "die and revive" brings one back to life at once. But in the avīci hell, there is no such respite whatsoever.

Great King, the avīci hell has one gate on each of the four sides. Outside each of these gates there burns a great fire, blazing outward in all four directions, south, north, east, and west. The entire expanse of eighty thousand leagues is encircled by iron walls; above, an iron lattice covers it like a lid; and the ground itself is made of iron. The fire above blazes downward, and the fire below blazes upward, burning in all directions throughout. Great King, just as a fish placed on a hot pan is scorched, so too are those who dwell there.

Great King, if one has committed one act without interval, one experiences a single avīci. If one has committed two acts without interval, one experiences a double measure. If one has committed five acts without interval, one experiences a fivefold measure.

Great King, knowing that I myself will certainly not escape this shameful deed of the king, go quickly to where the Tathāgata dwells. Apart from the Buddha, the Blessed One, there is no other who can be your refuge. I urge you in these words out of affection for you.

At that time, upon hearing those resonant words, the Great King was seized with extreme terror and shuddered; his five limbs trembled like the wood of a water plant. Looking upward, he spoke these words: "There is no visible form — who is it that only a voice is heard?"

"Great King, I am your father, the inner essence, appearing in a form you cannot see. Hear these words that will preserve your life. These are not the words of the six teachers of wrong views."

The moment the king heard those resonant words, he fell unconscious to the ground. Boils broke out across his body, and he became even more fetid and foul-smelling than before. Though he was anointed with cooling medicines, the boils burned all the more fiercely, and there was no sign of life.

This is the twenty-seventh fascicle of the noble great sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa.

At that time, the Blessed One, the Teacher, in his great compassion for King Ajātaśatru (whose name means "he who has no enemy born"), entered the meditative absorption like the moon. Having entered that absorption, he sent forth great rays of light. Those great rays of light, supremely soothing, touched the king's body; the boils on his body healed, and the torment of the fever was entirely stilled. The king, feeling the boils healed and a coolness spreading through his limbs, spoke these words to the life-restorer:

"In former times, sages used to say: 'When an eon is drawing to its close, three moons appear at once, and at that time all the sickness and suffering of every sentient being is stilled.'"

"That time has not yet come, yet from where did this light arise that, upon touching my body, has cured the suffering of the boils and brought ease to my limbs?"

The life-restorer replied: "This is not the three moons appearing together when an eon is drawing to its close. It is not fire, nor the sun, nor the stars, nor medicine, nor a precious jewel, nor the light of a god."

The king spoke again: "If it is not the light of the three moons, nor of precious jewels and the like, then whose light is this?"

The life-restorer said: "O king, know that this is the light sent forth by the God of gods. This light has no root and no limit; it is neither hot nor cold; it is neither permanent nor cessation; it is neither form nor formless; it has no defining characteristic and lacks no defining characteristic; it is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white. Yet for the sake of liberating sentient beings, it can be seen; it can be described by its defining characteristics; it has a root, it has extent, it has warmth, it has coolness; and there is also blue, yellow, red, and white in it. Yet, great king, even so, in ultimate truth this light is beyond description — from being seen all the way to being blue, yellow, red, or white, none of these truly obtain."

The king then said to the life-restorer: "For what cause and on account of what condition did the God of gods send forth this light?"

The life-restorer replied: "Great king, this present omen of light appears to have been sent out of loving regard for the king. In former times the king declared: 'There is no physician in the world skilled enough to cure diseases of both body and mind.' It is on that account that this light was sent forth — first to heal the king's body, and then to heal the mind as well."

The king asked the life-restorer once more: "Does the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, hold me in such loving regard?"

The life-restorer replied: "Consider, for example, a man who has seven sons. If one among the seven is struck by illness, the parents are not indifferent to any of their children — and yet it is for the sick child that their concern is the greatest. Great king, the Tathāgata is like that. He is not without equal concern for all sentient beings; and yet for those who are sinful he has especial care. For the indolent the buddha cherishes them with compassion. For those who are not indolent he rests in equanimity. Now who are those who are not indolent? They are the bodhisattvas who abide on the sixth ground.

Great king, the buddha, the Blessed One, makes no distinction on account of a being's class, or whether they are old, young, or in their prime, or poor or rich, or by time, day, month, or star, or by craft, low birth, male servant, or female servant. He takes note only of whatever sentient being possesses a virtuous mind — discerning whether a virtuous mind is present — and if it is, he regards that being with a mind of loving-kindness.

Great king, know that this omen of light is the light that the Tathāgata sent forth upon entering the meditative absorption like the moon."

The king asked: "What is this meditative absorption called 'like the moon'?"

The life-restorer replied: "Consider how moonlight causes all the udpala (blue lotus) flowers to open and bloom in brightness. In the same way, the meditative absorption like the moon causes the virtuous mind of all sentient beings to open and bloom — and it is for that reason it is called the meditative absorption like the moon.

Great king, consider further how moonlight brings joy to all travelers. In the same way, the meditative absorption like the moon causes those who journey the path to nirvāṇa to give rise to a mind of joy — and it is for that reason it is called the meditative absorption like the moon."

"Great king, consider how moonlight, from the first day of the month through the fifteenth, gradually grows in shape and brightness, waxing until it is full. In the same way, the meditative absorption like the moon causes the wholesome roots planted at the first arising of the awakening mind to grow and expand gradually, and it brings them to complete fulfillment all the way through to the great nirvāṇa — and it is for that reason it is called the meditative absorption like the moon.

Great king, consider further how moonlight, from the sixteenth day of the month through the thirtieth, gradually diminishes in shape, color, brightness, and luminosity, waning until it is small. In the same way, wherever the light of the meditative absorption like the moon shines, all afflictions (kleśas) there gradually diminish and grow small — and it is for that reason it is called the meditative absorption like the moon.

Great king, consider how in the time of intense heat all sentient beings constantly long for moonlight, and when moonlight falls upon them the heat is gone. In the same way, the meditative absorption like the moon extinguishes all the torment that afflicts sentient beings through the afflictions of desire.

Great king, consider how the full moon is like a king among the many stars, and all sentient beings delight in it and are drawn to it as though to the taste of nectar. In the same way, the meditative absorption like the moon is exactly like that: it is the king of all virtuous qualities, like the taste of nectar, and all sentient beings delight in it and are drawn to it — and it is for that reason it is called the meditative absorption like the moon."

The king then spoke: "I have heard it said that the Tathāgata does not dwell together with, keep company with, or converse with those who are wicked — just as a corpse does not rest in the ocean for even a day, just as a vulture does not linger where there is no water to drink, just as Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), does not dwell together with hungry ghosts, and just as the kuśī bird does not sleep upon a withered branch. Having heard this, I wonder: if the Tathāgata is like that, how am I to see him? And if I were to see him, would my body sink into the earth? When I think about approaching him, it seems to me that the Tathāgata, rather than ever consorting with the wicked, would prefer even a maddened elephant, a lion, a tiger, a wolf, a wildfire, or a venomous snake. With what kind of mind, then, should I go before the Tathāgata?"

Jīvaka replied: "Great king, one who is tormented by thirst swiftly makes for a clean source of water. One who is hungry longs for food; one who is afraid longs for refuge; one who is sick longs for medicine; one who is hot longs for shade; one who is cold longs for fire. In just such a way, it is fitting that the king who longs for the Buddha act accordingly.

Great king, the Tathāgata teaches the sacred Dharma even to those of wrong craving. When that is so, great king, how much more does he look with compassion upon those who are without wrong craving and grant them protection?

The king then spoke: "Jīvaka, I previously heard this said: 'Those with wrong craving are those without faith, who do not listen, who do not take the meaning to heart, and who do not understand the meaning.' If that is so, why would the Tathāgata teach the Dharma at all?"

Jīvaka replied: "Great king, consider someone who is stricken with a severe illness. In a dream, he finds himself sitting in a single-pillared house, eating butter and oil and the like, smearing them on his body, lying in ashes and eating ashes, climbing a withered and rotting tree, mingling and sleeping with monkeys at intervals, sitting or lying with them, sinking in water, being swamped in muddy swamp, or perhaps on a rooftop or inside a house —

or falling from a high mountain, a tree-top, a yak, a horse, a cow, or a sheep; or wearing blue, yellow, red, or black garments and singing, dancing, and playing; or seeing a crow, a vulture, a fox, or the like; or having one's teeth and hair fall out; or lying naked, smeared with filth, on a heap of refuse, keeping company with a dog; or consorting and sitting with people who have long since died; or walking with arms entwined with them; or wandering over ground swarming with venomous snakes; or dreaming of lying together with a disheveled woman, embracing her with one's arms; or wearing palmyra leaves as garments; or riding a cart drawn by donkeys and traveling southward — having dreamed such dreams, one becomes deeply distressed, and the mind is tormented by misery.

Because one is tormented by such misery, the illness flares up and grows worse. Because the illness has worsened, the family members send for a physician. Now suppose that the messenger sent to fetch the physician is short of stature, has incomplete limbs, lacks the proper faculties, has dust on his head, wears tattered clothing, and brings along a broken-down cart, and says to the physician: 'Please mount this cart at once.' When the skilled physician sees such ill omens and inauspicious signs as these, he thinks: 'This patient will be very difficult to cure.' Yet he also thinks: 'These are indeed inauspicious omens, but let me look to the sun to see whether it may yet be possible or impossible to heal.'

If the patient fell ill on the fourth, sixth, eighth, twelfth, or fourteenth day of the lunar month, the physician thinks it will be difficult to cure. Yet he also thinks: 'Though the day is unfavorable, let me look to the stars to see whether healing is possible or not.' If the stars that are present are Fire, Gold, the Pleaides, Yama, the Tortoise, or the River — and the patient took ill under such stars — the physician thinks it will be difficult to cure. Yet he also thinks: 'The stars are unfavorable; let me look to the season and the time.' If the patient fell ill in autumn or winter, at sunset, at midnight, or at moonset, the physician thinks it will be difficult to cure.

Then he thinks: 'All these many omens are unfavorable. Yet it may still be possible to heal, or it may not. Let me examine the patient himself — if he has merit, healing is possible; if he has no merit, what use are good omens anyway?' Having reflected thus, the physician sets out along the road in the company of the messenger. As he travels, he thinks: 'If the patient has signs of long life, healing is possible; if signs of short life are encountered, healing is not possible.'

Then, as the two boys sent as his escort quarrel with each other on the road — pulling each other by the topknot, tearing out hair, and throwing clods, stones, weapons, and sticks at each other and striking one another — he may see a torch going out by itself, or see trees being cut, or see a person carrying a hide and walking along the road, or see goods left abandoned on the road, or see someone carrying empty vessels, or see a lone monk walking without a companion, or see a tiger, a wolf, a crow, a vulture, a fox, or the like. Seeing all such things, the physician thinks: 'From the moment the messenger was sent to me until now, everything I have seen along the way is inauspicious — this patient will certainly be extremely difficult to cure.'

Yet he also thinks: 'If I do not go, I will not be known as a skilled physician; but if I do go, healing may not be possible.' And he thinks further: 'Even though all these many omens are inauspicious, nonetheless I will go single-mindedly to attend to the patient.' And so he proceeds along the road. Yet upon hearing the following sounds, healing is not possible. What are they? The sounds of death, of loss, and —

— arising, breaking, shattering, crashing, hissing, falling, coming loose, being carried as a load, burning, and the cry "He will not recover!" — upon hearing these sounds, healing is not possible; there is no hope of refuge or rescue.

Furthermore, upon hearing from the southern direction the cries of birds such as these: a crow, a carrion bird, a heron — or the sounds of a dog, a rat, a fox, a rabbit, or a pig — upon hearing any of these sounds, the physician again thinks to himself: "This patient will be extremely difficult to cure."

Then, upon entering the patient's dwelling and examining the patient, he finds that at times the patient is cold, at times feverish, with all the joints aching severely; the eyes are red with tears streaming from them; there is ringing within the ears; the throat is blocked and painful; the tongue is cracked; the complexion has become extremely dark; the head cannot be held up; the body is wasted and covered in dust; urine and stool are obstructed; the body has suddenly become extremely discolored — now very pale, now very red — and the sound of the breathing is irregular and uneven, sometimes coarse and sometimes fine; the entire body has become mottled, and strangely the complexion has turned blue and yellow; the belly is swollen and distended, and speech has become unclear. Having observed these conditions, the physician asks the patient's attendant: "What change has come over this patient compared to how he was before?"

The attendant replies: "Great physician, this man, who formerly had faith in and venerated the Three Jewels and the gods, has now changed — his mind has lost all faith. Where before he delighted in generosity, he has now become miserly. Where before his appetite was small, it has now become great. Where before he was gentle and pleasant, he has now become irritable and filled with great aversion. Where before he was exceedingly respectful and paid wonderful reverence to his father and mother, he has now lost all thought of honoring his father and mother."

The physician, upon hearing these words, draws near and smells the patient. He detects a range of scents from the body: the fragrance of blue lotus, or of aloe-wood and various incenses, or the scents of kṛtaka, takkola, tamalā, saffron, and sandalwood — or the stench of burnt flesh, or the odor of fermenting wine and of bile, or a smell like that of burning bones, or the stench of fish, or the smell of vomit. Having detected whatever pleasant fragrance or foul odor the body gives off, he then examines it by touch: whether the body is soft and pliable as silk or as the petals of a lotus flower, or instead hard as stone, or cold as a damp cloth, or hot as fire, or rough as sand.

Thereupon that skilled physician, having perceived these various manifold signs and omens, knows without doubt that this patient will die. Nevertheless, he does not utter the definitive pronouncement "This person will die." Instead, he says to the attendant: "I have some business to attend to today — I will come tomorrow. Whatever the patient desires, do not withhold it from him." Having said this, he returns to his own home. Then, if he is called again and says to the patient's wife: "My work is not yet finished, and moreover the medicine has not yet been prepared" — when a wise and discerning physician says this, he knows without doubt that the patient will die.

Great King, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, is just the same. Fully knowing the faculties and the inherent natures of those with perverted craving, he nonetheless teaches the Dharma to them as well. Why so? Because if he did not teach the Dharma to them, all foolish and ignoble people would say: "The Tathāgata has no loving-kindness and no great compassion." And they would say: "One who possesses loving-kindness and great compassion is called omniscient — but if there is no loving-kindness and no compassion, how can one speak of omniscience?" It is for this reason that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma even to those with perverted craving.

Great King, the blessed buddha, the Blessed One, whenever he sees the sick, always gives the medicine of the Dharma. If the patient does not drink it, it is no fault of the Tathāgata.

Great King, those with perverted craving, when distinguished and analyzed, fall into two kinds.

Those with perverted craving who, in the present time, obtain a root of virtue, and those who will obtain a root of virtue in a future time — knowing which of them, among those with perverted craving, will obtain a root of virtue in the present time, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to such a one. And to those who will obtain it in a future time, he also teaches the Dharma. Even when it will bring no benefit in the present time, because it will serve as a cause for a future time, the Tathāgata teaches the way of the Dharma even to those with perverted craving.

Moreover, among those called persons with perverted craving there are also two kinds: those of sharp faculties and those of middling faculties. Those of sharp faculties obtain a root of virtue in the present time. Those of middling faculties will obtain it in a future time. The blessed buddha does not teach the Dharma purposelessly.

Great King, consider this example: a person who has fallen into filth, and a dear and close friend who sees him there, grabs him by the hair and pulls him out. In the same way, when the blessed buddha sees sentient beings falling into the three lower realms, he raises them up and pulls them free by means of skillful means. It is for this reason that the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to all those with perverted craving.

Then the King said to Jīvaka: "If it is truly the case that the Tathāgata is like that, then I shall look to see whether tomorrow the sun is auspicious and the stars are favorable, and then set out."

Jīvaka replied: "Great King, in what concerns the Dharma of the Tathāgata, there is no such thing as a good or bad sun or stars. Great King, consider this example: when someone is gravely ill, he does not look for a good or bad sun or stars or an auspicious time — a skilled physician is what he seeks. The King is like one struck by grave illness; it is therefore not proper to look for a good or bad sun or auspicious time when seeking that physician who is the Tathāgata. Great King, consider this further example: sandalwood fire and eraṇḍa fire are alike in the defining characteristic of burning — there is no difference between them. Good and bad suns are just the same. If one goes into the presence of the Buddha, all sins will be purified. Great King, I urge you to go quickly, this very day."

Then the King summoned the minister named Auspicious and spoke these words: "Know this: I am going today into the presence of the blessed Buddha. Swiftly prepare all the necessary articles and requisites for offering." The minister replied: "Great King, excellent, excellent! Whatever articles you wish are all present and ready."

Then King Ajātaśatru, together with his queen, set out with two thousand beautifully adorned chariots and fifty thousand fine, great draft oxen, each of them with three men mounted upon it carrying parasols, banners, flowers, incense, and musical instruments, with every variety of offering articles present and complete. One hundred and eighty thousand cavalry troops and five hundred and eighty thousand people dwelling throughout the middle of the realm also set out as attendants of the King. At that time, the great assembly that filled the space around the city of Kusumapura for twelve leagues all saw from afar King Ajātaśatru coming together with his retinue.

Then the Blessed One declared to the great assembly: "There is no passing beyond a spiritual friend who serves as a proximate cause for the unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening — the arhatship — of all sentient beings. And why is that? If King Ajātaśatru had not listened to the words of Jīvaka, then on the seventh day of the following month he would certainly have met his death and fallen without doubt into the avīci hell for those without respite. It is therefore the case that there is no passing beyond a spiritual friend when it comes to a proximate cause. When King Ajātaśatru set out along the road, he heard these words:"

In the city of Śrāvastī, a king called Vaidūrya had boarded a ship and was burned while out at sea. The monk Kukari fell alive into the earth and dropped into the avīci hell without respite. A person named Sunakṣata committed many kinds of non-virtue, then came into the presence of the Buddha — and upon hearing those words spoken, that all his sins were thereby purified, King Ajātaśatru spoke to Jīvaka: "Today I have indeed heard two such accounts, yet whether they are true or not I cannot be certain in my mind. Jīvaka, come here. I would be pleased to ride together with you on a single ox. If I should fall into the avīci hell, see to it that you keep me from falling." And why? "Before this, I heard it said: a person who has attained the path does not go to hell."

Then the Blessed One declared to the great assembly: "Great King Ajātaśatru still harbors a mind of doubt. That mind of his must without fail be resolved."

Then within that assembled retinue, a bodhisattva named Sarvadharmadhara addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, just as the Blessed One has taught, the defining characteristic of all phenomena is indeterminate. That is to say, form is of the nature of indeterminacy, and so on all the way to nirvāṇa — all are of the nature of indeterminacy. If that is so, why then did the Tathāgata determine the mind of King Ajātaśatru?"

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! I have now indeed determined the mind of King Ajātaśatru. And why is that? If the king's mind were something that could be shattered by doubt, then one should understand that all phenomena likewise have no fixed defining characteristic. Therefore, understand that this very act by which I determined the mind of King Ajātaśatru is itself without fixed determination. Noble son, if the mind of that king were something fixed, then the grave misconduct of his unrelenting transgressions could not be destroyed. Because it is without fixity, that misconduct can be destroyed. For this reason I have determined the mind of King Ajātaśatru."

Then the great king went to the presence of the Buddha at the foot of the śāla tree. Beholding the thirty-two major marks and the eighty excellent minor marks of the Tathāgata, he perceived him to be like a mountain of pure gold. The Blessed One then projected a voice of eight qualities and called out, "Great King!" At that moment, Ajātaśatru looked around and thought: "Among this great assembly, who is it that bears the name 'Great King'? I am burdened with heavy misdeeds and without virtue — it would be unfitting for the Tathāgata to address me as 'Great King.'" Then the Tathāgata called out once more: "Great King Ajātaśatru!"

When the king heard this, a mind of intense joy arose in him, and he thought: "The Tathāgata has called me today and spoken to me — surely the Tathāgata's great compassion for all sentient beings is perfectly equal and impartial toward all." He then addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, today not even a trace of doubt remains in my mind. I have understood most deeply that the Tathāgata is truly the unsurpassed Teacher of all sentient beings."

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the bodhisattva Sarvadharmadhara:

The Tathāgata had resolved the mind of King Ajātaśatru. Then King Ajātaśatru addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, even if I were today in the company of Brahmā or of Śakra (Indra, lord of the gods), and were paying homage to them together, I would feel no joy in that. But having met the Tathāgata and been spoken to by him with even a single word, I am filled with the greatest delight."

Then King Ajātaśatru made offerings with parasols, banners, flowers, incense, music, and other such things that had been prepared in advance. He prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and took his seat to one side.

The Blessed One then spoke to King Ajātaśatru: "Great King, I shall teach you the discourse of the noble Dharma. Listen with great attentiveness and reflection. Foolish, ignoble beings always contemplate this body, holding it to be a permanent thing, in twenty ways. These twenty are as follows: that this body of mine is like a storehouse of accumulations; that it is not without defilement; that roots of virtue are absent in it; that I have not been tamed in this wandering through saṃsāra; that I have fallen into a very deep abyss and am surrounded on all sides by fear; that by whatever means one might see the intrinsic nature of a buddha; that however one cultivates meditative absorption one sees the intrinsic nature of a buddha; that saṃsāra is always suffering, lacking permanence, happiness, self, and purity; that the eight unfree states are difficult to abandon; that one is severely tormented by enemies who harbor resentment; that there is not even a single factor that can turn one back from existence; that one has not been freed from the three lower realms; that one is possessed of various kinds of evil wrong views and non-virtuous conduct; that one has not accumulated the store that transcends the five acts of immediate consequence; that saṃsāra has no end and no ultimate conclusion; that if actions are not performed, results are not obtained; that results produced by one's own actions cannot be experienced by another; that if the cause of happiness is not created, the fruit of happiness does not arise; that even though actions are performed, their results are not lost; and that one is born from the cause of ignorance and dies through the cause of ignorance — along with always engaging in laziness in past, present, and future. These twenty are the objects of contemplation. Great King, it is with these twenty kinds of contemplation about this body that foolish, ignoble ordinary beings are always engaged. Having contemplated in this way, one will come to have no delight in saṃsāra. Through having no delight in saṃsāra, one will attain insight and calm abiding.

"Then, gradually, one contemplates the mind, the characteristics of arising, the characteristics of abiding, and the characteristics of cessation. Just as one contemplates the characteristics of the mind, arising, abiding, and cessation in sequence, so too with meditative absorption, wisdom, diligence, and moral discipline. Having understood arising, abiding, and cessation, if one thoroughly knows everything from the characteristics of mind through to the characteristics of moral discipline, one will never commit non-virtue and will have no fear of death nor fear of the three lower realms. If one does not contemplate those twenty things with one-pointed mind, laziness and pride will arise, and one will end up committing all manner of non-virtue."

King Ajātaśatru said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has taught, I formerly committed a great deal of non-virtue because I had not contemplated those twenty things. Having committed a great deal of non-virtue, fear of death and fear of the three lower realms have come upon me. Blessed One, I have deceived myself and committed such a grave wrong. I killed my royal father, who had committed no offense. Whether or not one understands those twenty things, one will inevitably fall into the hell of immediate consequence — this I know for certain."

The Blessed One then declared:

"Great King, since the intrinsic nature and defining characteristic of all phenomena is impermanence and indeterminacy, why do you say that you will certainly fall into the hells?"

King Ajātaśatru then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, if indeterminacy is indeed the defining characteristic of all phenomena, then is not the wrong I committed by killing also indeterminate? And if that killing were something determinate, then all phenomena would no longer be indeterminate."

The Blessed One declared: "Great King, excellent, excellent! The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have indeed taught that indeterminacy is the defining characteristic of all phenomena. And since the King himself now knows that the killing is indeterminate, know therefore that killing bears the defining characteristic of indeterminacy.

"Great King, as you yourself said, you killed your royal father even though he had committed no offense. But as to what is meant by 'father' in this case — what is called 'father' is merely a perception (saṃjñā) applied to the five aggregates of a sentient being, a label given by convention and nothing more. Among the twelve sense bases and the eighteen elements, what is there that is 'father'? If form is the father, then the other four aggregates are excluded. If the four aggregates are the father, then form is excluded. And if what is meant by father is something that arises from the combination of what is form and what is not form and then transcends them — that is simply not tenable. Why so? Because what is form and what is not form are by nature incompatible for combination.

"Great King, inferior beings form the wrong perception of 'father' in relation to the aggregate of form. Yet that very aggregate of form is not something that can be killed. Why so? Form has ten aspects, and among those ten aspects form alone can be looked at, grasped, sought, measured, led away, and bound — it can be looked at and bound in this way; yet by its intrinsic nature it does not abide. Because it does not so abide, it cannot be looked at, cannot be grasped, cannot be measured, cannot be led away, cannot be bound. Since the defining characteristic of form is such as this, how can it be killed?

"If form were the father, and if it could be killed and harmed and a sin thereby ripened, then the remaining nine aspects would be excluded. But if those nine are excluded, then there is no sinful wrong at all.

"Great King, form has three aspects: past, future, and present. The past and the present cannot be killed. Why so? The past has already passed. The present ceases moment by moment. It is said that killing is the prevention of what is yet to come. Thus, of the one category of form, some aspects may be killable and some may not. Because some are killable and some are not, there is no determinacy with respect to form. Since there is no determinacy with respect to form, killing too is without determinacy. Since killing is without determinacy, karmic maturation is likewise without determinacy. How then can it be said that one will certainly fall into the hells?

"Great King, the sinful deeds performed by all sentient beings are entirely of two kinds: light and heavy. Those committed through mind and speech are light. Those committed through body, speech, mind, and mentation together are heavy.

"Great King, if something is conceived in the mind, expressed in speech, but not carried out in body, then the karmic maturation of everything so done is light.

"Great King, you did not give the order 'Kill him at once.' You gave the order 'Cut off his feet.' And if, Great King, while standing you had ordered your minister 'Cut off the king's head,' but the minister had carried it out only after sitting down, then even so no sin would accrue. How much less, then, would sin accrue if the King had not given the order at all? If the King does in fact incur sin, then the Blessed One, the Buddha, would also incur sin. Why so? Because your father, King Bimbisāra, was always cultivating roots of virtue directed toward the Buddha, and through this the king attained his royal estate."

If the Blessed One, the Buddha, had not accepted those offerings, your father would never have become king. And if he had not become king, you would have had no kingdom or royal estate to kill him for. If it is sinful for you to have killed your father, then I and all the other Blessed Buddhas would likewise be fitting recipients of sin. But if no sin accrues to the Blessed Buddhas, why should sin accrue to you alone?

Great King, consider the story of King Bimbisāra. Long ago he was roaming in the mountains of Pūrvavideha, having set out in pursuit of a deer that had escaped, and after searching through every stretch of forest and wilderness he found nothing at all — until he came upon a single sage endowed with the five kinds of higher knowledge. Upon seeing this sage, a mind of aversion arose in him: "It is because of this man that the deer has escaped and I have found nothing today." With that thought he chased the sage off the mountain and ordered his attendants to kill him. At the moment of that sage's death, a mind of rage arose in him, and by that anger his supernatural powers were destroyed. Then the sage made this solemn vow: "Though I am without fault, you have killed me through your mind and speech, pressing me with intensity — so in a future time I too shall kill you in just this way, through mind and speech." When the king heard this, remorse arose in his mind, and he performed funeral rites for the sage's body. Yet because the king had acted as he did, sin accrued to him again and again, though not to the point of falling into the hells — how much less, then, would the ripening of a hell result for a king who did not act as he had? If the suffering that Bimbisāra underwent was the ripening of what he himself had done, how could the sin of killing now accrue to the king?

Just as it is said that King Bimbisāra's father was without fault — in what way is it appropriate to say there is no fault? One who is associated with sin will experience the ripening of that sin. One who performs virtuous actions will have no ripening of sinful karma. If your father the king was truly without sin, how could any karma ripen for him? Bimbisāra in the present age is receiving both the fruits of virtue and the fruits of non-virtue. Therefore the previous king is indeterminate. Being indeterminate, the killing too is indeterminate. And if the killing is indeterminate, why insist that he will certainly fall into the hells?

As for sentient beings, there are four types of intoxication and killing: intoxication by desire, intoxication by medicine, intoxication by mantra, and intoxication by the condition of past karma. Great King, even among my own attendants there are those afflicted by these four kinds of intoxication who have committed abundant non-virtue, yet scripture does not declare them to have broken their ethical discipline. Whatever they have done, they will not go to the three lower realms, and if they come back to their senses, one should not say their ethical discipline has been impaired.

As for the king — if he killed his father king out of desire for the kingdom and royal estate, acting from a mind intoxicated by desire, how could sin accrue? Great King, consider the analogy of a man who, intoxicated with ale, kills his mother. When he becomes sober and a mind of deep remorse arises in him, know that karma to be one that will not ripen in its full fruit. The king likewise acted out of intoxication by desire, not with full mindfulness. Since he did not act with full mindfulness, how could a blameworthy sin accrue to him?

Great King, consider further: a magician at a crossroads conjures all manner of illusory forms — men and women, yaks, horses, jewel-handled swords, fine garments and the like — and a foolish, deluded simpleton takes them to be genuine and real.

The wise and discerning one, however, understands that it is not real. Killing is likewise similar: foolish, deluded ordinary persons take it to be genuinely real, while the Blessed One, the buddha, understands it to be not real.

Great King, consider further: a fool mired in delusion takes the sound of an echo to be a genuine voice. The wise and discerning one understands it to be not real. Killing is likewise similar: foolish, deluded ordinary persons take it to be genuinely real, while the Blessed One, the buddha, understands it to be not real.

Great King, consider further: when an enemy approaches by stealth, a person mired in delusion takes him to be a genuine friend drawing near. The wise and discerning one knows him to be a deceiver. Killing is likewise similar: foolish ordinary persons take it to be genuinely real, while the Blessed One, the buddha, understands it to be not real.

Great King, just as when one's own face appears in a mirror, a person mired in delusion takes it to be a real face. The wise and discerning one, through clear understanding, knows it to be not real. Killing is likewise similar: foolish, deluded ordinary persons take it to be genuinely real, while the Blessed One, the buddha, understands it to be not real.

Great King, consider further: a person mired in delusion takes a mirage to be water. The wise and discerning one, through clear understanding, knows it is not water. Killing is likewise similar: foolish, deluded ordinary persons take it to be genuinely real, while the Blessed One, the buddha, understands it to be not real.

Great King, consider further: a foolish person mired in delusion takes a gandharva city to be real. The wise and discerning one, through clear understanding, knows it to be not real. Killing is likewise similar: foolish, deluded ordinary persons take it to be genuinely real, while the Blessed One, the buddha, understands it to be not real.

Great King, consider further: a person mired in delusion takes the experience of enjoyment of the five sense pleasures within a dream to be real. The wise and discerning one, through clear understanding, knows it to be not real. Killing is likewise similar: foolish, deluded ordinary persons take it to be genuinely real, while the Blessed One, the buddha, understands it to be not real.

Great King, I have clearly understood this: from the phenomenon of killing, through the act of killing, the killer, the fruit of killing, and on to liberation itself, there is no blameworthy karma whatsoever.

Great King, why then should sin accrue from the mere knowing of killing? Great King, consider: a person who brews ale — if he does not drink it, he will not become drunk. In the same way, one who draws near to fire will not be burned unless they touch it. The king is likewise in this regard: why should sin accrue from the mere knowing of killing?

Great King, there are some sentient beings who, when the sun rises, commit various kinds of blameworthy sins, and when the moon rises, they rob and steal. If the sun and moon did not rise, they would not commit those sins. Yet although sins are committed through the condition of the sun and moon, no sin truly attaches to the sun and moon themselves. Killing is likewise similar: although things have come to be thus through the king serving as a condition, no sin truly attaches to the king.

Great King, just as in the royal capital sheep are constantly caused to be slaughtered, yet a man who from the very beginning has no mind of fear — why should fear arise in him on account of his father alone?

Great King, just as there is a hierarchy of distinctions between humans and animals, yet in their clinging to life and their dread of losing it the two are no different — why then is it that for the sheep there is no frightened, uneasy mind, yet for his father the king there arises the grief of deep non-virtue?

Great King, worldly beings have become the servants of desire and have lost all freedom. Because they are driven by desire, they perform the act of killing. If there is karmic maturation of that act as its result, then it is desire that becomes the sin. Since the king acts without freedom, why should fault accrue to him?

Great King, consider this: nirvāṇa in its fullness is neither existent nor nonexistent, and yet it is existent. Killing is similar: it is neither existent nor nonexistent, and yet it does come to be existent. For one who possesses shame and moral conscience, it is not existent. For one who lacks shame and moral conscience, it is not nonexistent. The experience of karmic maturation as its result is what is called existent. For one who views things as empty, it is not existent; for one who views things as existent, it is not nonexistent; for one who views things as existent, it is called existent. Why is that? For one who holds the view that things exist, there is karmic maturation as a result. For one who does not hold that view, there is no karmic maturation as a result.

For one who holds the view of permanence, it is not existent; for one who holds the view of impermanence, it is not nonexistent; for one who holds the view that what is permanent is permanent, it is not nonexistent. Why is that? For one who views what is permanent as permanent, there is the result of non-virtuous karma — and therefore it would not be right to say that for one who views what is permanent as permanent it is nonexistent. Thus, while it is neither existent nor nonexistent, it is also not existent.

Great King, what is called a sentient being is the flowing of breath, inner and outer. To cut off that flowing of breath is called killing. Even the Tathāgatas speak of killing in a manner that accords with worldly convention.

Great King, form is impermanent, and what arises in dependence upon form is likewise impermanent. If it arises from an impermanent cause, how could form be permanent? Consciousness is impermanent, and all that arises in dependence upon consciousness, down to the last arising by dependent origination, is impermanent. If it arises from an impermanent cause, how could consciousness be permanent? Being thus impermanent, it is suffering. Being suffering, it is empty. Being empty, it is without self.

If things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, then what kills what? If the impermanent is slain, one attains the permanent nirvāṇa. If suffering is slain, one attains bliss. If the empty is slain, one attains what is true. If the selfless is slain, one attains the true self.

Great King, one who slays the impermanent, the suffering, the empty, and the selfless is like me. I too have slain the impermanent, the suffering, the empty, and the selfless — and if I did not fall into the hells on that account, why should you?

Then King Ajātaśatru, just as the Blessed One had instructed, examined form and contemplated all the way through to consciousness. Having understood it thus, he addressed the Blessed One in these words:

Blessed One, I have now come to understand, for the very first time, that from form to consciousness all is impermanent. Had I understood it thus before, I would not have committed that blameworthy sin.

Blessed One, I had previously heard it said that the awakened ones, the Blessed Buddhas, are always like father and mother to sentient beings. Though I heard those words, I did not understand them with certainty. Now, for the first time, I understand them with certainty.

Blessed One, I had also heard this: Mount Meru, king of mountains, is made of four precious substances, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Though I had heard it said that in whatever direction many birds gather together, they take on a color matching that place, I did not understand it with certainty. Today I have gone into the presence of the Tathāgata, who is Mount Meru, and I have become of matching color. And what is meant by "becoming of matching color"? It means becoming equal in understanding that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.

Blessed One, in this world I have seen a sandal tree growing from the seed of a sandal tree, but I have never seen a sandalwood tree growing from the seed of an eraṇḍa plant. Today, for the very first time, I have seen a sandalwood tree grown from an eraṇḍa seed. The eraṇḍa seed is my own body; the sandalwood tree is the rootless ground of faith in my mind. By "rootless" I mean this: that formerly I had no wish to pay reverence to the Tathāgata, and I had no faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha — that is what I call "rootless."

Blessed One, had I not encountered the buddha, the Blessed One, I would have experienced boundless suffering in the great hell for immeasurable and countless eons. Today I have come to behold the buddha, and by whatever merit I have gained through beholding the buddha, may all the afflictions and unwholesome minds of sentient beings be destroyed.

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent, excellent, great king! I know with certainty that today the unwholesome minds of sentient beings have been destroyed."

The king spoke again: "Blessed One, if through my reflection in this manner the unwholesome minds of sentient beings are destroyed, then even if I were to remain in hell forever and take on great suffering for the sake of sentient beings for immeasurable eons, I would not regard it as suffering."

Then at that time, countlessly many people of the Middle Country gave rise to the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening (bodhicitta). Because of their giving rise to it so fully, the heavy sin of King Ajātaśatru (the king whose enemy was born with him) became lighter. Then the king and the queen and the ministers and all the others simultaneously gave rise to the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

Thereupon King Ajātaśatru said to his physician Jīvaka: "Jīvaka, without my dying, I have obtained a divine body. Having abandoned a short life, I have come to have a long life. Having abandoned the impermanent body, I have obtained a permanent body. This is what it means to arouse in sentient beings the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. Now I have a divine body, long-lived and permanent; I am close to all the buddhas."

Having spoken these words, he made offerings to the Blessed One with victory banners of many kinds of precious substances, with pennants, parasols, incense, flowers, garlands, and excellent music, and then praised him with these verses:

That one possessed of utterly true and pure speech,
supremely skilled in word and meaning,
reveals even the essence of the profound and secret
with clarity to the multitudes.

Words vast and boundless beyond measure
he gathers and teaches in brief summary to the assembly.
Endowed with such speech as this,
he is skilled in healing the illness of sentient beings.

Whatever sentient being hears those words —
whether one of faith or one without faith —
comes to understand that it is the speech of a buddha.
The speech of a buddha is gentle,
yet he also speaks words that are rough to the assembly.
Both what is spoken gently and what is spoken roughly
are, in both cases, the ultimate truth.
Therefore I too, here today,
go for refuge to the Blessed One.

The speech of the Blessed One is of one taste,
just as the water of the great ocean is one.
It is called the supreme truth:
there is not a single word in it that is without meaning.

Today the Tathāgata has —

taught immeasurable phenomena,
so that men and women alike, upon hearing them,
may accordingly attain the ultimate truth.
Without cause there is no result;
there is no arising and no cessation.
That is nirvāṇa:
hearing it, one destroys karmic maturation.
The Tathāgata acts as the supremely loving
father and mother of all.
Know that ordinary sentient beings, each and every one,
are the children of the Tathāgata.
With a mind of loving compassion,
the Blessed One has undergone hardship for the sake of the many.
Just as one seized by an evil spirit
acts in many and varied ways while possessed,
so too all the virtue of the three gates of action
by which I today have seen the Blessed One —
whatever merit I have thereby obtained,
I dedicate to unsurpassed awakening.

Whatever merit I have generated today
by making offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
by that merit may the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha —
the Three Jewels — dwell in the world forever.

Whatever merit I have obtained here today in this very place,
by that merit may the four māras of all sentient beings
be utterly destroyed.

By my encounter with evil companions,
whatever wrongdoing I have committed in the three times —
all of it I confess here and now in your presence,
and from this day forward I shall commit no more evil.

May all ordinary sentient beings,
having aroused the mind of awakening,
hold in mind with one-pointed thought
all the Victors of the ten directions.

Further, may all sentient beings,
having thoroughly vanquished their many afflictions,
come to perceive the nature of a buddha
just as Mañjuśrī does.

Then the Blessed One said to King Ajātaśatru: "Excellent! Excellent!" Whoever arouses the mind of awakening is said to be completely adorned with the maṇḍala of a buddha.

"Great King, long ago you aroused the mind of awakening before the buddha Viśvabhū. From that time until my appearance in the world, you did not experience the suffering of falling into hell. Great King, know this: the awakening mind has immeasurable fruits of that very kind. Great King, from this day forward you must always strive in the awakening mind. And why is that? Because through that cause and that condition, immeasurable unwholesome actions are purified."

Then King Ajātaśatru rose from his seat amid the people of the region of Madhyāntika, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed for his palace.

The chapter on divine conduct is as explained in the sūtra called the Array of Various Flowers.

From the Noble Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, this is the seventh chapter, entitled "The Holy Life."

Noble son, what then is the conduct of an infant? Noble son, an infant cannot stand up, sit, come, go, or speak — such is what is called the conduct of an infant. The Tathāgata is similar to that. That the Tathāgata cannot stand up means that the Tathāgata does not rise from the defining marks of all phenomena. That he cannot sit means that the Tathāgata has no attachment to any phenomena. That he cannot come means that the bodily conduct of the Tathāgata is unmoving. That he cannot go means that the Tathāgata has perfected the completion of great nirvāṇa. That he cannot speak means that although the Tathāgata teaches phenomena to all sentient beings, in ultimate truth there is no teaching. And why is that? Whatever teaching there is belongs to conditioned phenomena; but the Blessed One, the Buddha, is unconditioned, and therefore he has no teaching. Furthermore, that he does not speak means: just as an infant, though it utters sounds, does not know how to articulate words clearly, so in ultimate truth there is no speaking. The Tathāgata is similar to this:

"Speaking unclearly" means that the Tathāgatas teach with intention and purpose. And even though they do teach, because sentient beings do not understand, it is said that they do not speak.

Again, "an infant" means that, not knowing words properly, it has not yet fixed upon a single name for a thing. And though it has not fixed upon a single name for a thing due to not knowing words properly, apart from that cause there is no other way by which knowledge of the thing could come about. The Tathāgata is similar to this: because all sentient beings belong to many different classes with different dispositions, words do not agree, yet by teaching each according to their capacity through skillful means, the Tathāgata causes all of them to understand.

Again, "an infant" means that it can only utter the one great syllable. The Tathāgata is likewise, for he teaches the one great syllable — namely, "bha-hva." In this, "hva" signifies the conditioned, and "bha" signifies the unconditioned. That is what is meant by "infant." "Hva" means: I am impermanent. "Bha" means: permanence. And because the Tathāgata teaches permanence, sentient beings who hear it, wishing to say that phenomena are permanent, cut off what is impermanent. That is the conduct of the infant.

Again, an infant does not know suffering and pleasure, day and night, or father and mother. The great bodhisattva (bodhisattva mahāsattva) is likewise: for the sake of sentient beings, seeing no distinction between pleasure and suffering, there is no such thing as day or night; and because one's mind is equal toward all sentient beings, there is no distinction of the characteristic marks of father, mother, or kin.

Again, an infant cannot perform great or minor deeds. The great bodhisattva is likewise: because the bodhisattva does not perform the deeds of cyclic existence, it is said that he does not act. As for "great deeds," these are the five acts of immediate consequence (pārājika), and the great bodhisattva never commits the heavy misdeeds of these five acts of immediate consequence. As for "minor deeds," these are thoughts of the two other vehicles, and the bodhisattva never turns away from the awakening mind and falls into the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, the conduct of a child is this: when an infant cries, the parents give it a yellow willow leaf, saying, "Child, do not cry, do not cry — I will give you gold," and upon seeing this, the infant develops the perception that it is real gold and stops crying. But that willow leaf is not real gold. If an infant sees carved wooden oxen, horses, men, and women, it develops the perception that they are actual men and women, and stops crying. Because it places the perception of men and women upon what are not men and women, it is called an infant.

The Tathāgata is likewise. When sentient beings commit many non-virtuous acts, the Tathāgata teaches that in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three there is permanence, bliss, selfhood, utter purity, beauty, and abundant enjoyment; that within magnificent palaces one enjoys the five objects of desire; and that all the counterparts to the six senses are nothing but bliss and joy. Hearing that such bliss exists, sentient beings give rise to a mind attached to bliss, abandon non-virtue, and strive in the virtuous deeds that lead to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. But this is genuine cyclic existence — it is impermanent, without bliss, without self, and not utterly pure. Yet in order to liberate sentient beings, through skillful means he teaches it as permanent, blissful, a self, and utterly pure.

Again, "an infant" means:

If there are sentient beings who feel profound weariness with cyclic existence, the Tathāgata teaches them the two vehicles. Even though, in ultimate truth, the two vehicles have no existence of their own, by reason of the two vehicles one comes to know the faults of cyclic existence and to see the bliss of nirvāṇa. Through seeing in this way, one comes to know for oneself what is to be cut off and what is not, what is true and what is not, what is to be practiced and what is not, what is attained and what is not.

Noble son, just as a toymaker gives rise to the perception of gold regarding something that is not gold, so too the Tathāgata, in a similar way, describes what is not utterly pure as utterly pure. In reality, the Tathāgata has no falsehood, because it is for the purpose of attaining the ultimate. Just as a toymaker perceives something that is neither a cow nor a horse as a cow or a horse, so too, if there are sentient beings who take what is not the path to be the genuine path, the Tathāgata likewise teaches what is not the path as the path. Although what is not the path is not genuinely the path, it is taught as the path because it is capable of generating at least some causes of the path. Just as a toymaker perceives wooden boys and girls as real boys and girls, so too the Tathāgata, in a similar way, though knowing that what is presented lacks the defining characteristics of a sentient being, nonetheless teaches the defining characteristics of sentient beings. In reality, there are no defining characteristics of a sentient being. If the Blessed One, the buddha, were to teach that sentient beings do not exist, all sentient beings would fall into the wrong view of nihilism. Therefore the Tathāgata has declared that sentient beings exist. To impose the perception of a sentient being upon what is a sentient being is to be unable to dissolve the defining characteristics of a sentient being. But whoever dissolves the defining characteristics of a sentient being from within what appears as a sentient being will attain great nirvāṇa. Having thus attained great nirvāṇa, one will no longer weep — and that is called the conduct of an infant.

Noble son, if any man or woman holds, maintains, recites, writes out, liberates others by, or teaches these five conducts, know that such a person will without doubt attain those five conducts. Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One and said: Blessed One, in accordance with my understanding of the meaning as taught by the Blessed One, I too have without doubt attained those five conducts. The Blessed One declared: Noble son, it is not you alone who have attained those five conducts — right now, within this very assembly, nine hundred and thirty thousand people have likewise attained those five conducts just as you have.

This concludes the eighth chapter of the Noble Sūtra of Great Nirvāṇa, called "The Conduct of a Young Infant."

The Noble Sūtra of Great Nirvāṇa. The twenty-eighth fascicle.

Then the Blessed One spoke thus to the great bodhisattva Sarvadarśī Uttamaśrīrāja: Noble son, if a great bodhisattva practices yoga on this Sūtra of Great Nirvāṇa, that bodhisattva will attain ten qualities — qualities not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, inconceivable, such that merely hearing them is a source of wonder and amazement. These qualities are neither inner nor outer, neither difficult nor easy, neither characterized nor uncharacterized, not of the world — they are free from marks and forms, and do not exist anywhere in the world.

What are the ten qualities? As for the first, it has five aspects. What are the five? First, one will come to hear what has not been heard. Second, having heard, it will become of benefit. Third, doubt and vacillation will be decisively cut through. Fourth, there will be no guile or deception in one's wisdom. Fifth, one will understand the profound meaning intended and expressed by the Tathāgata. Those are the five.

Now, what is meant by "one will come to hear what has not been heard"? It is this: the profoundly deep meaning intended and expressed by the Tathāgata — that buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha) is present in all sentient beings; that there is no difference between the buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; that the intrinsic nature of the Three Jewels is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity; that none of the blessed buddhas ever finally pass into nirvāṇa, for they are permanent, stable, unchanging, and unalterable — and that the Tathāgata's nirvāṇa is neither existent nor nonexistent, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither defiled nor undefiled, neither form nor formless, neither name nor nameless, neither characterized nor uncharacterized, neither existent nor nonexistent, neither thing nor no-thing, neither cause nor effect, neither relative nor independent, neither appearance nor darkness, neither arisen nor unarisen, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither annihilated nor unannihilated, neither a beginning nor an end, neither past nor future nor present, neither aggregate nor non-aggregate, neither sense base nor non-sense-base, neither element nor non-element, neither the twelve links of dependent origination nor other than the twelve links of dependent origination — these and all such profoundly deep matters, expressed with intent, one will come to hear for the first time, having never heard them before.

And furthermore, what else has not been heard before?
