The four orders of learning belonging to all the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), the learning of grammar, the learning of kingship, the learning of arithmetic and calculation, and so forth; mantras and incantations, medicine and medical analysis, the arts, the eclipse of the sun and moon by the planetary demon, the shifts and movements of the stars, drawing and writing, the learning of prophecy and divination, and all such writings — the hidden meaning of all that learning, which one had not heard before, will now come to be understood through this sūtra.

And furthermore, the profoundly deep meaning intended and expressed — which is absent from the other eleven sūtra collections apart from the very extensive sūtras — will also come to be understood through the occasion of this sūtra. O son of good family, that is what is meant by "one will come to hear what has not been heard."

As for "having heard, it will become of benefit": if one takes up and upholds this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, one will be able to know in full the entire savour of the profoundly deep meanings of the extensive Mahāyāna sūtras. Just as boys or girls see their appearance and form clearly reflected in a bright mirror, so too is this mirror of the Great Nirvāṇa: when a bodhisattva has heard it, the profoundly deep meanings of the Mahāyāna sūtra collections are seen with clarity. And furthermore, just as when someone brings a great lamp into a dark chamber all things become visible, so too is the lamp of the Great Nirvāṇa: when a bodhisattva holds it, even those profound and difficult-to-see meanings of the Great Vehicle become visible. And furthermore, just as when the sun rises with its thousand rays of light it illuminates the deepest darkness in every mountain valley, and all beings see things from a great distance, so too is the sun of the pure wisdom of the Great Nirvāṇa: it illuminates the most profound reaches of the Great Vehicle, and causes the awakening of a buddha to be seen from a far greater distance than the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. And why? Because one listens to and upholds this supreme sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa.

Noble son, whatever great bodhisattva listens to or upholds this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa in this way will come to understand all the synonyms of the Dharma. And if one writes it down, reads it, recites it, thoroughly absorbs it, expounds it in full to others, and reflects upon its meaning, one will come to understand the meaning of all phenomena in the proper way.

Noble son, one who merely listens to and upholds it will know only the synonyms, and will not realize the meaning itself. But one who writes it down, memorizes it, reads it, recites it, expounds it in full to others, and reflects upon its meaning will come to realize the meaning itself.

Furthermore, noble son, by merely listening to this sūtra one hears that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists, but is unable to see it. But one who writes it down and reads it, recites it, expounds it in full to others, and reflects upon its meaning will come to see it.

By merely listening to this sūtra one will attain generosity, but will not yet see the perfection of generosity. If one writes down this sūtra and recites it, reads it, expounds it in full to others, and reflects upon its meaning, one will come to see all the perfections from the perfection of generosity through to the Perfection of Wisdom.

Noble son, if a great bodhisattva listens to this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, one will come to know the Dharma and to know its meaning. When one is endowed with both of these kinds of individual perfect knowledge, one will have fearlessness before all — whether ascetics (śramaṇas), brahmins, gods, māras, Brahmā, or any others of the world — one will be without contradiction in distinguishing and teaching the meaning of the twelve branches of scripture, one will understand things through one's own insight without having heard them from others, and one will draw near to the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening.

Noble son, this is what is called "being benefited upon hearing." What is called "the cutting off of a doubting mind" has two aspects: doubting words, and doubting meaning. By listening to this sūtra, doubt about words is cut off. By reflecting upon its meaning, doubt about the meaning is cut off.

Furthermore, noble son, doubt has five aspects: doubting whether a buddha definitively passes into nirvāṇa; doubting whether a buddha abides permanently; doubting whether a buddha is truly real; doubting whether a buddha is truly perfectly pure; and doubting whether a buddha truly has a self. By listening to this sūtra, the doubt about whether a buddha passes into nirvāṇa will be completely resolved. By writing it down, reading it, reciting it, expounding it in full to others, and reflecting upon its meaning, the remaining four doubts will be completely resolved.

Noble son, furthermore, doubt has three aspects: doubting whether śrāvakas exist or do not exist; doubting whether pratyekabuddhas exist or do not exist; and doubting whether buddhas exist or do not exist. By merely listening to this sūtra, all three of these doubts will be eliminated without remainder. By writing it down, reading it, reciting it, expounding it in full to others, and reflecting upon its meaning, one will come to realize that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists in all sentient beings.

Noble son, if any sentient being has not heard this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, they will have many doubting thoughts such as these: whether things are permanent or impermanent, pleasant or unpleasant, perfectly pure or impure, whether there is a self or no self, whether there is a life-force or there is not, whether one is a sentient being or is not, whether things have an ultimate end or do not, whether there is a future time or

a past time, or whether things exist or do not exist, whether something is suffering or is not suffering, whether something is the origin of suffering or is not its origin, whether something is the path or is not the path, whether something is cessation or is not cessation, whether something is Dharma or is not Dharma, whether something is virtue or is not virtue, whether something is empty or is not empty. If one hears this sūtra, all such doubts will be completely resolved.

Furthermore, noble son, if one has not heard this sūtra, still more doubting thoughts will arise. For instance: Is form the self, or is feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness the self? Or does the eye see, or does the self see? And likewise, from the eye up through consciousness — can consciousness know, or does the self know? Does form experience karmic maturation, or does the self experience maturation? And likewise, from form through to consciousness — does consciousness experience karmic maturation, or does the self experience it? Does form pass on to the world beyond, or does the self pass on to the world beyond? And likewise with consciousness. Does saṃsāra have a beginning and an end, or does it have no beginning and no end? Such are the doubts that arise. If one hears this sūtra, all such doubts and the like will be completely resolved. This is what is called the resolving of doubt and uncertainty of mind.

What is called having no deceit or guile in wisdom? If there is doubt in the mind, all views will be wrong. If ordinary persons have not heard this precious sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, all their views will be wrong. And likewise, right through to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, all their views will be wrong.

In what way are childish ordinary persons said to hold wrong views? They regard defiled phenomena as permanent, pleasant, as a self, and as perfectly pure; and they regard the Tathāgata as impermanent, suffering, impure, and as lacking a self. They view sentient beings, life, a vital force, a seer, and a knower as existing. They grasp at the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as nirvāṇa. They view the great god who wields sovereignty over the devas as possessing the noble eightfold path. They hold to views of permanence and views of annihilation. All such views are called wrong views.

If a great bodhisattva hears this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa and practices the noble conduct, all those wrong views will be no more.

In what sense do śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also hold wrong views? When the bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita heaven, they hold that he rode a white elephant and entered the womb of his mother — whose father was Śuddhodana and whose mother was named Māyādevī — and that after ten full months in his mother's womb in the city of Kapilavastu he was born; and that at the time of birth, Śakra (Indra, king of the gods) held him above the ground so that he did not touch the earth, and that the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda then poured down water to bathe and cool his body;

and that Maṇibhadra, the great king of yakṣas, held aloft a precious jeweled parasol; and that the earth deity (Skt. pṛthivīdevatā) conjured forth lotus blossoms to support his feet; and that he took seven steps in each of the four directions; and that he went to the realm of the gods, where all the gods rose to welcome him; and that the sage Asita took him in his arms and examined his marks; and that after examining the marks Asita was overcome with great suffering, thinking to himself, "I shall die before my time and will not live to see the buddha come to full awakening" — and so was plunged into deep grief; and that he learned writing, arithmetic, archery, navigation, painting, prognostication, and the arts from his teachers; and that he dwelt in the palace, sporting and enjoying pleasures together with sixty thousand women and consorts; and that when he departed the palace and went for a walk, he saw at the gate of the city of Kapilavastu an old man, bent and decrepit; and that, just as he had seen that, he also saw a renunciant (Skt. śramaṇa) walking along, robed in the dharma-robe; and that after returning to the palace he saw the bodies and forms of the women and consorts as though they were mere skeletons; and that he saw the palace itself as no different from a charnel ground; and that, grown weary of the household, he departed the palace at the dead of night and went to the sages Uḍḍaka Rāmaputra, Ārāḍa Kālāma, and others, and from them he heard teachings on the sense base of infinite consciousness, and the sense bases of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and that, having heard this, he thoroughly investigated those sense bases and recognized them to be impermanent, suffering, utterly impure, and without self, and so abandoned them; and that he then practiced austerities under a tree for six years; and that even having practiced such austerities he did not attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; and that he then bathed in the river called Nairañjanā, received from a cowherd woman an offering of milk porridge mixed with ghee, accepted it, and proceeded to the seat of awakening, where he tamed the evil māra and attained unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; and that from there he went to Vārāṇasī and first turned the wheel of Dharma for the group of five monks, continuing up to his passage into great nirvāṇa here in the city of Kuśinagara — to hold such a view as this is called a wrong view on the part of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

O son of good family, if a bodhisattva, a great bodhisattva, hears, retains, recites, reads, thoroughly assimilates, expounds to others, and takes to heart the meaning of this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, all of those wrong views enumerated above will be entirely dispelled. Moreover, if one writes it down, reads it, recites it, thoroughly assimilates it, teaches it extensively to others, and applies its meaning to mind, one will obtain genuine wisdom and be freed from wrong views.

O son of good family, if a bodhisattva, a great bodhisattva, applies diligent effort to this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, then the realization — from the bodhisattva's descent from Tuṣita and birth from his mother's womb through to his passage into great nirvāṇa here in the city of Kuśinagara — that this occurred throughout measureless eons, is called the right view of a bodhisattva, a great bodhisattva.

"Knowing the profound meaning of what the Tathāgata taught with a specific intent" refers to this: in this Great Nirvāṇa it is taught that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature, and that by virtue of this they may confess the four root downfalls, dispel the mind that slanders the sacred Dharma, be entirely purged of the faults of the five acts of immediate retribution, and be freed from the mind of wrong craving — and that thereafter they will attain perfect, complete unsurpassed awakening. This is what is meant by "the profound meaning taught with a specific intent."

O son of good family, furthermore, in what sense is the meaning exceedingly profound?

This, then, is what is meant by "the profound meaning taught with a specific intent": one has confidence that, even though sentient beings are rightly understood to be without a self, the karmic fruits of future actions will not fail to ripen; one understands that although these very five aggregates will without remainder be brought to cessation, wholesome and unwholesome actions will not fail to exist; one understands that although there are many kinds of karma, no agent can be pinpointed; that although there is a destination reached, there is no one who goes; that although there is bondage, there is no bound one; and that although there is nirvāṇa, there is no cessation. This is what is called "the profound meaning taught with a specific intent."

Then the great bodhisattva (bodhisattva), the great being, Universally Illuminating King of Majestic Glory, addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, as I understand it, the meaning of the expression 'what was not heard shall come to be heard' that the Blessed One has used does not stand up. Why so? If something exists, it is necessarily a thing that exists. If something does not exist, it is necessarily a thing that does not exist. It is not fitting that what does not exist should arise, nor is it fitting that what does exist should be brought to cessation. In just the same way: what was heard is still called 'heard,' and what was not heard remains not heard. Why then did you say 'what was not heard shall come to be heard'? Blessed One, it is not fitting that what is not heard should come to be heard, and what was previously heard cannot become heard for the first time again. Why? Because it was heard before. Then why did you say 'what was not heard shall come to be heard'? Consider the analogy: if one has arrived, one does not travel; if one is traveling, one has not arrived. Furthermore: once one has been born, one is not being born; what is not being born will not come to be born. Once one has attained, one does not attain; what is not attained will not come to be attained. Likewise, once one has heard, one does not hear; what is not heard will not come to be heard.

"Blessed One, if what is not heard were to come to be heard, it would follow that all sentient beings, even those who have not attained awakening, would attain it; that those who have not attained nirvāṇa would attain it; and that those who have not seen the buddha-nature would see it. Why then did you say: 'A bodhisattva abiding on the tenth ground has seen the buddha-nature, yet it has not become fully manifest'? Blessed One, if what is not heard were to come to be heard, what did the Tathāgata listen to in former times? If he listened to something, why did you say that the Tathāgata has no teacher who instructs from scripture? And if it is by hearing what was not heard that the Tathāgata attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, then by the same token all sentient beings, by hearing what they had not heard, would also be fit to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Again, if the Tathāgata could behold the buddha-nature without having heard this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, then all sentient beings likewise, without having heard this sūtra, would be fit to behold the buddha-nature.

"Blessed One, some forms are seen and others are not seen. Sounds are the same: some are heard and others are not heard. But the Great Nirvāṇa is not a form and not a sound, so why did you say it is seen and heard? Blessed One, the past is ceased and therefore cannot be heard; the future has not yet arrived and therefore cannot be heard; and in the very moment of listening in the present, one does not yet call that 'hearing,' for once the sound has ceased after being heard, it has already passed beyond being heard. This Great Nirvāṇa belongs neither to the past, nor to the future, nor to the present — and if it does not belong to the three times, it is beyond all expression."

"If it is beyond expression, it cannot be heard either — so why did you say that a bodhisattva who applies himself diligently to this sūtra of Great Nirvāṇa will come to hear what he has not heard?"

Then the Blessed One addressed the bodhisattva, the great being, the All-Illuminating, Sublime, Glorious King, and declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, you have understood most profoundly that all phenomena are like a magical illusion, like a mirage, like the city of a gandharva, like a drawing made on water — and further, like a bubble on water, like foam, like a plantain trunk — hollow throughout, without essence, not alive, not a self, and free of suffering and pleasure. This is just as the bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten grounds know and see. Well done!

Then, in that very moment, in an instant, a great radiance appeared within that assembled retinue — not blue, yet seen as blue; not yellow, yet seen as yellow; not red, yet seen as red; not white, yet seen as white; not colored, yet seen as colored; not luminous, yet seen as luminous; not a seeing, yet seen — and this is what is called 'seeing.'

At that time, when that light touched the many members of the assembly, their bodies and minds became supremely blissful, just as when meditators enter the meditative absorption of the Lion King.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, Mañjuśrī asked the Blessed One: "From where have these rays of light come?" At that moment the Tathāgata said nothing — he did not reply.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked Mañjuśrī: "By what cause and condition does this light appear to the many in the assembly?" And Mañjuśrī likewise said nothing — he did not reply.

Then the bodhisattva Anantakāya asked the bodhisattva Kāśyapa: "Whose light is this?" The bodhisattva Kāśyapa said nothing — he did not reply.

The bodhisattva Vimalasthitarājakumāra asked the bodhisattva Anantakāya: "By what cause and condition does this light exist among the many in the assembly?" And the bodhisattva Anantakāya likewise said nothing — he did not reply.

In just the same way, the five hundred bodhisattvas questioned one another in this manner, yet not one of them gave any answer.

Then the Blessed One addressed Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, by what cause and condition has this light appeared among all these many in the assembly?"

Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, this light is primordial wisdom — and what is called primordial wisdom is something that abides permanently. What abides permanently has no cause and no condition. Why then, Blessed One, did you ask 'By what cause and condition has this light arisen?'

"This light is what is called Great Nirvāṇa — and what is called Great Nirvāṇa is something that abides permanently. What abides permanently did not arise from cause and condition. Why then, Blessed One, did you ask 'By what cause and condition does this light exist?'

"This light is what is called the Tathāgata — and what is called the Tathāgata is something that abides permanently. What abides permanently did not arise from cause and condition. Why then did the Tathāgata speak of cause and condition?

"This light is what is called loving-kindness and great compassion — and what is called loving-kindness and great compassion is something that abides permanently.

What abides permanently did not arise from cause and condition. Why then did the Tathāgata speak of cause and condition?

"This light is what is called recollection of the buddha. And what is called recollection of the buddha is something that abides permanently. What abides permanently did not arise from cause and condition. Why then did the Tathāgata speak of cause and condition?

"This light is what is called the path that is not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. And the path that is not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is something that abides permanently. What abides permanently did not arise from cause and condition. Why then did the Tathāgata speak of cause and condition?

"Blessed One, there is no such thing as cause and condition. It is by the cause and condition of ignorance ceasing that the lamp of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening blazes forth."

The Blessed One then declared: "Mañjuśrī, without entering into the ultimate — which is the extremely profound meaning of the defining marks of all phenomena — speak and explain in conventional terms."

Mañjuśrī replied: "Blessed One, to the east of here, beyond world-realms as numerous as the grains of sand in twenty Ganges rivers, there is a buddha-field called the Immovable. The extent of the dwelling place of the buddha who resides there is twenty thousand leagues in breadth. The ground of that realm is made entirely of the seven precious substances, with no earth or gravel — perfectly level and smooth, without ridge or furrow. The trees are made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and the four precious substances, and they perpetually abound with flowers and fruits. If any sentient being is touched by the fragrance of those flowers, the joy and ease of body and mind they experience is like that of monks who have entered the third meditative concentration.

"Surrounding that realm on all sides are three thousand great rivers, whose waters are pure and excellent, endowed with the eight qualities. If any sentient being bathes in those waters, the joy and bliss they attain is like that of monks who have entered the second meditative concentration.

"In those rivers there bloom many varieties of flowers of every kind: utpala, padma, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, fragrant flowers, greatly fragrant flowers, supremely fragrant flowers, the flower called Everlasting, and the flower called Unconquered-by-All-Beings — flowers of many forms and diverse kinds.

"Along the banks of those rivers too there bloom many varieties of flowers, namely: atimukta flowers, campaka flowers, pāṭala flowers, pāśika flowers, mārikā flowers, great mārikā flowers, simārikā flowers, sumanā flowers, yūthikā flowers, dandurikā flowers, Everlasting flowers, Unconquered-by-All-Beings flowers, and so forth.

"The bed of those rivers is spread with golden sand, and along their steps there stand terraces of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal of many diverse colors, upon which vast numbers of birds of every kind gather. And furthermore, there are immeasurable numbers of tigers, wolves, lions, and other fierce animals and birds, yet they regard one another as if they were their own young.

"In that buddha-field there are none who commit such misdeeds as breaking their root vows, disparaging the holy Dharma, holding wrong views, or committing the five acts of immediate consequence. In that field the temperature is always pleasant; no one is tormented by the suffering of hunger or thirst. There is no attachment, aversion, heedlessness, or jealousy. There is no sun, moon, day or night, or division of time.

Just as it is with the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the people of that realm too are possessed of radiant light. None among them harbor pride or arrogance. All of them are great bodhisattvas who have attained higher knowledge, endowed with great qualities: they direct their minds toward reverencing and respecting the holy Dharma; they are borne up by the Great Vehicle; they have faith in the Great Vehicle; they are devoted to the Great Vehicle; they guard the Great Vehicle; they are endowed with great wisdom; they have attained the great dhāraṇī; and toward all sentient beings they are invariably filled with heartfelt love and care.

The name of the Blessed One of that realm is Radiance of the Full Moon. He is a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly and fully awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide and charioteer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One — and wherever he teaches the Dharma, there is not a single sentient being in that buddha-field who fails to hear it. That buddha teaches this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa to the bodhisattva, the great being, called Lapis-Lazuli Radiance. The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, any bodhisattva, any great being, who applies himself diligently to this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa shall come to hear everything he has not yet heard." In precisely the same way that the bodhisattva, the great being, All-Illuminating King of Lofty and Glorious Majesty, addressed his question here — with no difference whatsoever — the bodhisattva, the great being, Lapis-Lazuli Radiance addressed his question to the buddha Radiance of the Full Moon. And the buddha Radiance of the Full Moon, having thus declared to the bodhisattva Lapis-Lazuli Radiance, "Son of good family, to the west of here, beyond a number of buddha-fields equal to the grains of sand of twenty Ganges rivers, there exists a world-system called Endurance."

In that world-system there are mountains, crags, ravines, valleys, thickets, and thorn-laden wildernesses filling every direction, and the beings there are perpetually tormented by the suffering of hunger, thirst, cold, and heat. The people of that land show no respect to renunciants (śramaṇas), brahmins, parents, teachers, or spiritual masters. They are attached to what is contrary to Dharma; they desire and cling to what is contrary to Dharma; they engage in conduct that is perverted and wrong; they have no trust in the holy Dharma; their lifespans are exceedingly short; those who commit misdeeds are cut down by the punishment of the king; and the kings, though surrounded by lands and dominions, know no contentment and do not know when enough is enough — they conceive the desire to seize the wealth of others, and through waging war, sudden deaths become many. Because the kings thus conduct themselves unrighteously, the gods of the Four Great Kings who are virtuous grow displeased, and as a result great pestilence arises, grain and crops fail to grow, disease among humans increases greatly, and beings are tormented by immeasurable and manifold sufferings.

In that world, the Blessed One called Śākyamuni — Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed one, guide and charioteer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, buddha, Blessed One — moved by his exceedingly great compassion, out of loving care for sentient beings, teaches this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa to a vast assembly gathered beneath the śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara.

Then the bodhisattva called All-Illuminating King of Lofty and Glorious Majesty likewise, beginning from that very point, addressed his question: "You are no different from him." And that Blessed One likewise declared: "You must go swiftly, and you shall hear it."

The Blessed One — upon the bodhisattva Lapis-Lazuli Light hearing of such matters — together with eighty-four thousand great bodhisattvas (Skt. mahāsattva), came here, and a foretoken appeared beforehand: it was through this cause and this condition that this light arose. Yet one may also call it "cause and condition" — and yet it is not cause and condition.

Then the bodhisattva Lapis-Lazuli Light, together with those eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, arranged a great many supremely excellent and varied offerings of banners, parasols, flowers, incense, garlands, and music, surpassing all that had come before. They all came to this grove of śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara and, each with their own offerings and ritual requisites, made offering to the Blessed One. They touched their foreheads to the feet of the Blessed One, joined their palms in reverence, and with devoted homage circumambulated him three times. Having made offering, they took their places to one side.

Then the Blessed One spoke to those bodhisattvas: "Noble sons, have you come here, or have you not come?"

The bodhisattva Lapis-Lazuli Light replied: "Blessed One, in coming there is no arrival, and in not coming there is also no arrival. Because I have realized the meaning of this, there is simply no arrival in any sense. Blessed One, if all formations (Skt. saṃskāra) were permanent, then coming would be without arrival; and since they are impermanent, coming is likewise without arrival. Ordinary persons who hold that there is a fixed, inherent nature of sentient beings — for them there is neither coming nor not coming. Since I myself do not perceive any inherent nature fixed in sentient beings, on what grounds would you ask whether I have come or not come?

Those who are filled with pride see no going or coming, yet in the absence of pride there is also no going or coming. Those who possess clinging see no going or coming, yet in the absence of clinging there is also no going or coming. Those who see the Tathāgata as passing into nirvāṇa ultimately and finally see going and coming as real; those who do not view the Tathāgata as having passed into nirvāṇa ultimately and finally see going and coming as unreal. Those who have not seen the intrinsic nature of a buddha see going and coming as real; those who have seen the intrinsic nature of a buddha see no going and coming. Those who see śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as having attained nirvāṇa see going and coming as real; those who do not see śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as having attained nirvāṇa see no going and coming. Those who view śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as possessing permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity see going and coming as real; those who do not view them thus see no going and coming. Those who view the Tathāgata as lacking permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity see going and coming as real; those who view the Tathāgata as possessing permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity see no going and coming.

Blessed One, let that matter rest for now. I humbly request that, out of loving care, you open the door and give me this opportunity to ask on one particular point."

The Blessed One replied: "Noble son, now the time has come — ask whatever you wish, and I shall expound the scripture pertaining to each matter and teach it. Why so? Because buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are exceedingly rare to encounter — just as the bloom of the udumbara flower. And the Dharma likewise is exceedingly rare to hear."

Among the twelve branches of scripture, hearing the vast expansive ones is exceedingly rare, and so one must listen with single-pointed mind.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Vaiḍūryaprabhā, knowing that an opportunity had been granted and that the teaching would be given, addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva, a great being, who cultivates this sūtra of Great Nirvāṇa, comes to hear what has not been heard before?"

The Blessed One then uttered the words "Excellent! Excellent!" and said: "Noble son, today you have resolved to traverse the entire ocean of the Great Vehicle's nirvāṇa without remainder — and I am meeting with a skilled teacher who has thoroughly taught and shown the way. So today I shall skillfully draw out all the nets of your doubts and all the thorns of your uncertainty whatsoever, acting as a great physician. You have not yet become clear about the nature of a buddha — let me cause the lamp of my wisdom to shine. If you wish to cross the great river of saṃsāra, let me become your guide. Generate toward me the perception of a father and mother, and I in turn regard you as I would my own child. You seek the precious treasure of the sacred Dharma, and since I have it in abundance, now that we have met, receive it as a gift. Listen attentively and examine it well, and I shall expound and teach it in full detail.

Noble son, if you wish to hear the Dharma, the time has now come. If upon hearing the Dharma you give rise to faith, listen with single-pointed mind, and show reverence and respect. Do not seek faults in the sacred Dharma. Do not let your mind dwell on attachment, aversion, or delusion. Do not scrutinize whether the words of the Dharma teacher are good or bad. After hearing the Dharma, do not give rise to pride. Do not do it for the sake of honor, gain, or renown — seek instead the nourishment and benefit of a Dharma that transcends the world. Likewise, do not think: 'Having heard the Dharma, I shall first liberate my own body and only then liberate others.' Do not think: 'I shall first free my own body and only then free others.' Do not think: 'I shall first cause my own body to touch happiness and only then bring happiness to others.' Do not think: 'I shall first pass into nirvāṇa and only then lead others beyond sorrow.' Instead, generate the perception of equality with regard to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Generate the perception that saṃsāra has the defining characteristic of great suffering. Generate the perception that Great Nirvāṇa has the defining characteristics of permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity. Accomplish the benefit of others first, and only afterward your own benefit — and this for the sake of the Great Vehicle, not for either of the two lesser vehicles. Do not grasp at the many defining marks of all phenomena, for all phenomena have no fixed abode. Rather than generating the perception of desire regarding all phenomena, always generate the perception of knowing and seeing the Dharma.

Noble son, if you listen to the Dharma with single-pointed mind in just this way, that is what is called 'coming to hear what has not been heard before.'

Noble son, there is hearing the unheard. There is not hearing the unheard. There is not hearing what has been heard. And there is hearing what has been heard.

Noble son, it is just as with the unborn being born, the unborn remaining unborn, the born remaining unborn, and the born being born; and just as with the unattained being attained, the unattained remaining unattained, the attained remaining unattained, and the attained being attained.

'Blessed One, how is it that the unborn is born?' Noble son, abiding on the conventional level, when one issues forth from the womb at the very beginning — that is called the unborn being born. 'How is it that the unborn remains unborn?' Noble son, Great Nirvāṇa has no defining characteristic of birth — that is called the unborn remaining unborn. 'How is it that the born remains unborn?' Noble son, conventionally, at the time of death, that is called the born remaining unborn. 'How is it that the born is born?'"

"Noble son, all ordinary beings are called 'the born being born.' Why is that? Because the continuum of birth is uninterrupted, and because all defiled phenomena arise moment by moment — that is called the born being born. A bodhisattva on the fourth ground is called 'the born remaining unborn.' Why is that? Because they have gained mastery over birth — that is called the born remaining unborn.

Noble son, these are inner phenomena. As for how outer phenomena are the unborn being born, the unborn remaining unborn, the born remaining unborn, and the born being born: Noble son, take the example of a seed — before a sprout has arisen, when the four great elements have assembled and gathered and have been made to function, only then does it come to birth. That is called the unborn being born. How is it that the unborn remains unborn? Take the example of a seed that has rotted, or has not met with the right conditions — something like that is called the unborn remaining unborn. How is it that the born remains unborn? Take the example of a sprout that has arisen but has not yet reached full maturity — one that has been born but not yet matured is called the born remaining unborn. How is it that the born is born? What has grown from a sprout to full maturity is like something already born — yet for what has been born but not yet matured, that maturation still lies ahead. In this way, all defiled outer phenomena are called 'the born being born.'"

Then the great bodhisattva Vaidūryaprabha addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, if birth exists within defiled phenomena, is that birth permanent or impermanent? If that birth is permanent, then birth would not exist within defiled phenomena. If that birth is impermanent, then those defiled phenomena would themselves become impermanent. Blessed One, if one were to say that birth itself produces birth, then birth would have no defining characteristic. If something else were capable of producing birth, then for what reason, through what cause and condition, do undefiled phenomena not arise? Blessed One, if before something is born there is no birth, then how can the very designation 'birth' be applied? If there is no birth before a thing is born, then why did you not say that birth occurs in empty space?"

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, the unborn being born is inexpressible. The born remaining unborn is inexpressible. The unborn remaining unborn is inexpressible. The born is inexpressible. The unborn is also inexpressible. And yet, in terms of causes and conditions, expression is appropriate.

How is it that the unborn being born is inexpressible? Whatever is said of 'birth' in regard to what has not been born — that too is a birth. Why? Because it also arises through birth. How is it that the born being born is inexpressible? Because it is born on account of birth having occurred, and yet because it is also unborn through that very occurrence of birth, it is inexpressible. How is it that the born remaining unborn is inexpressible? What is called 'having been born' is precisely birth itself — and since birth itself is not a birth, it is inexpressible. How is it that the unborn remaining unborn is also inexpressible? That which is unborn is called nirvāṇa, and nirvāṇa is inexpressible because it is without birth. Why? Because it is attained through cultivation of the path. The born is also inexpressible, because that very birth is without birth. How is it that the unborn is inexpressible? Because there is something to be attained. How is it that expression in terms of causes and conditions is nonetheless appropriate? The twelve phenomena of dependent origination have birth as their cause — and for that reason, expression is appropriate.

Noble son, do not enter too deeply into the meditative absorption of emptiness. Why? Because the faculties of many in the assembly are still untrained."

Noble son, birth in conditioned phenomena is also permanent. Mere duration within impermanence, birth too is impermanent. Duration is also not permanent, for since birth has arisen, duration too is impermanent. Differentiation is also not permanent, for since there is no permanence in phenomena, differentiation too is impermanent. Destruction is also permanent, for what did not exist from the beginning now exists, and hence destruction too is impermanent. Noble son, by reason of intrinsic nature, birth, duration, differentiation, and destruction are all permanent, yet since they cease moment by moment, they cannot rightly be called permanent. Great nirvāṇa is annihilation and cessation, and thus it is to be called impermanent. Noble son, defiled phenomena, not yet arisen, have the intrinsic nature of arising, and so when caused to arise, they do arise. Undefiled phenomena have had no intrinsic nature of arising from the very beginning, and so even when caused to arise, they are unable to arise. Just as fire, having the intrinsic nature of burning, blazes upon meeting its conditions, and just as the eye, having the intrinsic nature of seeing, sees form when the conditions of form, light, and consciousness come together, so too with the arising nature of sentient beings: having had that intrinsic nature from the very beginning, birth occurs from the causal conditions of karma and the union of father and mother.

Then the great bodhisattva Vaiḍūryaprabha and some eighty-four thousand great bodhisattvas, having heard these teachings, rose up into the sky above to the height of seven palm trees, joined their palms in reverence while hovering there, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, the Tathāgata has taught us again and again, and through this great nirvāṇa we have heard and realized what we had never heard before. All eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas have now utterly realized the non-arising, arising, and so on of all phenomena. Blessed One, I have realized everything, and the net of doubt has been severed. Yet in the midst of this assembly there is a bodhisattva named Abhaya who wishes to ask and inquire. May the Blessed One grant permission and give him opportunity." Then the Blessed One addressed the bodhisattva Abhaya: "Noble son, ask whatever you wish, and I shall prophesy and explain each matter accordingly."

Then the bodhisattva Abhaya, together with his accompanying sixty-four thousand bodhisattvas all seated together, rose from their seats, arranged their robes, placed their knees on the ground, joined their palms, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, what must the sentient beings of this world do in order to be reborn in the unmoving world-realm? And for what reason are the bodhisattvas of that realm endowed with wisdom, magnificent among human beings like a king of yaks, endowed with yogic practice, sharp and swift in wisdom, so that they realize immediately upon hearing?"

Then the Blessed One spoke in verse:

Those who do not cut the lives of sentient beings,
who thoroughly restrain themselves in ethical conduct and precepts,
and who follow the teachings of the sublime buddha
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who do not steal the wealth of others,
who constantly give to all,
and who provide lodging for the Saṅgha and for guests
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who do not seek the wives of others,
who are content with their own spouse,
and who guard the precepts of the bed
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who, for the sake of benefit to self or others,
do not falsify out of fear or ill intent,
who restrain their speech and do not speak lies
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who do not part from virtuous friends,

and who utterly abandon evil companions,
and always speak words of conciliation,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Just as a bodhisattva always abandons harsh words,
so that what is spoken is a delight to hear,
one who does so will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who, even in jest and play,
do not speak untimely words,
but speak only what is timely and fitting,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who, upon seeing another's gain and good fortune,
always give rise to a mind of rejoicing,
and do not bind themselves in the knot of envy,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who do not harm sentient beings,
who always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness,
and who through skillful means do not generate evil,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who do not give rise to the wrong view
that there is no giving, no mother or father,
no past and no future,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who dig wells and provide water along desolate roads,
who plant many food-bearing trees,
and who give food to those who beg,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who make an offering to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
even of a single stick of incense or a single lamp,
or even a single flower,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who, out of fear or in search of advantage,
or in order to seek merit and virtue,
copy out even a single verse of this sūtra,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who, for the sake of merit for the many
and for the benefit of all,
read this holy scriptural teaching for even a single day,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who, for the sake of the unsurpassable path,
uphold the eight precepts of moral discipline and restraint
for even the span of a single day and night,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who do not dwell together with one who has broken the root precepts of moral discipline
or who has rejected the extensive scriptural teachings,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who give even a single grain of fruit from a tree
to one who is afflicted with illness,
and who serve that person with a joyful mind,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who do not make use of the Saṅgha's wealth,
who carefully guard the property of the Buddha,
and who sweep the dwelling places of the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who always give rise to a joyful mind
and make even a thumbprint's worth of an image or representation of a buddha,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who, for the sake of this sūtra,
give their own body and precious riches
to a Dharma teacher,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Those who listen to the secret essences of the Blessed One,
or write them down in letters,
or hold them, recite them, or chant them aloud,
will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

Then the great bodhisattva Abhaya addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, from this day forward I have come to understand that by whatever causes and conditions one acts, one will be reborn in that unmoving realm.

The great bodhisattva Sarvaprakāśaśrīrāja had asked out of compassion for the many beings, and through the Tathāgata's thorough exposition and teaching, this came to be of benefit to all — to gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, and great serpents, and to all the rest.

Then the Blessed One declared to the great bodhisattva Sarvaprakāśaśrīrāja: Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, attend to this with great care and listen well. I shall explain and set forth for you the causes and conditions by which one who has not arrived does not arrive, by which one who has not arrived does arrive, by which one who has arrived does not arrive, and by which one who has arrived does arrive.

What are the causes and conditions by which one who has not arrived does not arrive? Son of good family, what is called "not having arrived" is great nirvāṇa.

Ordinary beings have not arrived because, possessed of attachment, aversion, and delusion, the actions of their body and speech are entirely impure; they cling to all things that have not been examined; they violate the four roots; they denigrate the extended sūtras; they perform the deeds of those who cling to wrong craving; and they commit the blameworthy acts of the five heinous crimes without interval. For these reasons this is called "not having arrived, and not arriving."

Son of good family, what then are the causes and conditions by which one who has not arrived does arrive? What is called "not having arrived" is great nirvāṇa. How is it that one arrives there? By utterly abandoning attachment, aversion, and delusion, by abandoning the evil conduct of body and speech, by not clinging to things that have not been examined, by not violating the four roots, by not denigrating the extended sūtras, by not performing the deeds of those who cling to wrong craving, and by not committing the blameworthy acts of the five heinous crimes without interval. For these reasons this is called "not having arrived, and yet arriving."

One who has entered the stream arrives after eighty thousand aeons. One who returns once arrives after sixty thousand aeons. One who is a non-returner arrives after forty thousand aeons. An arhat arrives after twenty thousand aeons. A pratyekabuddha arrives after ten thousand aeons. For these reasons this is called "not having arrived, and yet arriving."

Son of good family, what then are the causes and conditions by which one who has arrived does not arrive? What is called "having arrived" is the twenty-five realms of existence. All sentient beings are perpetually bound by immeasurable afflictions, thoroughly ensnared, and circle round again and again — just as a wheel turns — unable to cast it off. That cannot be called "having arrived." Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are called "not having arrived" because they have utterly abandoned those realms. Yet because they manifest and appear in these realms for the sake of taming sentient beings, they may also be called "having arrived."

Son of good family, what then are the causes and conditions by which one who has arrived does arrive? What is called "having arrived" is the twenty-five realms of existence. All base and ignoble ordinary beings, along with stream-enterers and those up to the level of once-returner, are called "having arrived, who arrive" on account of the conditions of affliction.

Son of good family, with regard to hearing what has not been heard, it is likewise: there is hearing what has not been heard, there is not hearing what has not been heard, there is not hearing what has been heard, and there is hearing what has been heard.

Now how is it that what has not been heard is heard? Son of good family, "not having been heard" refers to great nirvāṇa. Why is it called "not having been heard"? Because it is not conditioned, it is not a sound, and it is not expressible in words. How then is it heard? It is heard as a name in the following way: permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity. This is called "hearing what has not been heard."

Then the great bodhisattva Sarvaprakāśaśrīrāja addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, if, as the Blessed One has said, great nirvāṇa is not fit to be heard, why did you say that permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity are fit to be heard?

Blessed One, and why is this so? That which has had afflictions cut away is nirvāṇa. If one were not to call what is to be honored "nirvāṇa," then the intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa would have been absent from the beginning and would only now exist. But if, following the conventions of the world, something is absent at first and then comes to exist, it would have the character of impermanence. For example, things such as clay did not exist at first and then came to exist —

— and then ceases to exist; that is what is called impermanent. If nirvāṇa were like that, why did you say that it possesses permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity?

Furthermore, Blessed One, whatever comes into existence through assembled causes is called impermanent. If nirvāṇa were like that, then, since it is the right way of things for what is impermanent to be impermanent, by what cause and condition is it impermanent? It is as follows: the thirty-seven factors of awakening, the six perfections, the four immeasurables, meditation on the skeleton, mindful breathing, the six close placements of mindfulness, the six great dissolutions, and all things of that kind serve as the causes and conditions for accomplishing nirvāṇa, and so they are called impermanent.

Furthermore, Blessed One, conditioned existence is called impermanent. If nirvāṇa were conditioned existence, then it would be right for it to be impermanent as well. For the Blessed One previously declared in scripture: "Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas, the Blessed Ones, can achieve nirvāṇa." For that very reason, it would then be called impermanent.

Furthermore, Blessed One, all phenomena that are subject to investigation are impermanent. And the Blessed One previously declared: "Beholding nirvāṇa, all afflictions are cut through." For that very reason as well.

Furthermore, Blessed One, just as empty space is called permanent because it is equally unobstructed and unimpeded for all sentient beings, if nirvāṇa were equally permanent in that same way, why would it be that some sentient beings have attained it and others have not? If nirvāṇa were like that — not equal with respect to all sentient beings — then how could it be called permanent?

Blessed One, take for example: there are many hundreds of people, and there is one enemy among them. If that enemy were slain, all those many people would be at ease. But if nirvāṇa were a phenomenon of equality, then it would be right that if one person attains it, all the many people together would attain it. If one person's afflictions are cut through, then all the many people's afflictions together would be cut through. If it is not like that, why is it called permanent?

Take another example: when someone pays honor, makes offerings, performs ceremonies of reverence, and shows respect to a king, a prince, a father and mother, a teacher, and a master, they attain ease and happiness — yet that is not called permanent. If nirvāṇa were like that, it would not be called permanent either. And why is that? For the Blessed One previously declared this in scripture, speaking to Ānanda: "If someone pays reverence to nirvāṇa, all afflictions are cut through and immeasurable happiness is attained." For that very reason, it cannot be called permanent.

Blessed One, if nirvāṇa possesses the names "permanent," "blissful," "self," and "utterly pure," then it cannot be called permanent. But if it lacks them, how can it be properly described at all?

Thereupon the Blessed One declared to the bodhisattva, the great being, the king of glory, Samantaprabha Uttungaśrī:

Nirvāṇa itself is not something that was absent from the beginning and has only now come to exist. If nirvāṇa itself had been absent from the beginning and now existed, then it would not be a phenomenon of the undefiled that abides permanently. Whether buddhas arise or do not arise, its intrinsic nature and its characteristic marks abide forever. Because sentient beings are obscured by afflictions, they do not see nirvāṇa, and so they think it does not exist.

Bodhisattvas, great beings, who are practiced in moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom cut through the afflictions and come to see it. Therefore, nirvāṇa is something that abides permanently, and one should understand that it is not the case that it was absent before and now exists at present. For this reason it is called permanent.

Noble son, consider this example: inside a dark room there is a pit containing the seven precious substances in all their variety. People know that these are present, yet because of the dense darkness they cannot see them. A person of wisdom, skilled in means, takes up a great lamp and looks, and everything becomes visible. That person does not think: "The water and the seven precious substances were absent before and have only now come into being." Nirvāṇa is just like that. It has existed from the very beginning; it has not come to exist only now, at this moment. Sentient beings do not see it because they are covered by the darkness of the afflictions. But the Tathāgata, who possesses the primordial wisdom of omniscience, through supremely skilled means has lit the lamp of wisdom so that bodhisattvas may behold the permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity of nirvāṇa. Therefore a person of wisdom should never say of nirvāṇa that it "was absent before and has now come to exist."

Noble son, the argument you have set forth — that nirvāṇa, having been produced through causes, is impermanent — is not acceptable. Why? Because, noble son, the essential nature of nirvāṇa is not birth, not arising, not true, not false, not something born through being made by action, not a phenomenon that is defiled or conditioned, not heard, not seen, not a transgression, not a binding, not characterized by distinct defining marks, not characterized by a single defining mark, not coming, not going, not past, not future, not present, not one, not many, not long, not short, not round, not square, not tapering, not flat, not possessed of defining characteristics, not a perception, not a name, not form, not a cause, not a result, not self, and not belonging to a self.

Because this is so, the crossing beyond sorrow is permanent — it does not change or shift. Yet only when one has adorned oneself by practicing and cultivating wholesome qualities over countless, immeasurable eons does one finally come to see it.

Noble son, consider this example: below the ground there is water possessing the eight excellent qualities, yet it cannot be obtained by just any sentient being. It is only when a wise person performs the work of digging that one finally obtains it. Nirvāṇa is just like that.

Consider also the example of people who are blind: they cannot see the sun and moon. When a skilled physician applies medicine, the sun and moon become bright and visible to them. Yet the sun and moon are not something that was absent before and has now come to exist. Nirvāṇa is likewise: it has existed from the very beginning; it has not come to exist only now, at this moment.

Noble son, consider this example: those who have committed offenses are bound and cast into prison, and only after a long time do they at last obtain release and go forth, whereupon at home they once again meet their parents, brothers, sisters, children, wife, and relatives whom they had not seen all that while. Nirvāṇa is just like that.

Noble son, your claim that because nirvāṇa depends on dependent origination its phenomenon is also impermanent — that too is not the case. Why? Because, noble son, causes are of five kinds. What are those five? The cause of birth, the cause of assembly, the cause of abiding, the cause of arising and growth, and the cause of duration.

What is meant by the cause of birth? The cause of birth refers to karma, afflictions, and the like, and to the seeds of outer herbs and trees.

What is meant by the cause of assembly? Just as virtuous actions and virtuous intentions come together, and non-virtuous actions and non-virtuous intentions come together —

and non-virtuous actions and non-virtuous intentions come together — likewise, when actions without scriptural transmission and minds without scriptural transmission come together, that is called the cause of assembly.

What is the cause of abiding? Because a pillar stands below, a house does not fall; mountains, water, trees, and all forests abide because of the great earth; and sentient beings abide because there are within them the four great elements and afflictions beyond measure — this is called the cause of abiding.

What is the cause of arising and growth? Sentient beings arise and grow through conditions such as clothing, food, and the like. Just as seeds of the outer world, when not burned by fire and not eaten by insects, will arise and grow; just as śramaṇas, brahmins, and the like arise and grow by relying on teachers and spiritual friends; and just as children arise and grow through the substance of their parents — this is called the cause of arising and growth.

What is the cause of duration? For example, through the power of mantra one cannot be killed by demons or harmed by poison; by relying on a king, thieves cannot prevail. Just as a sprout depends on earth, water, fire, wind, and the like; just as water, a churning staff, and human labor serve as the cause of butter's duration; just as light and visible forms and the like serve as the cause of duration for consciousness; just as the white and dark reproductive substances of the parents serve as the cause of sentient beings' duration; and just as time and all such factors are likewise called the cause of duration.

Noble son, if the nature of great nirvāṇa is not produced by such five causes, how can it be called a cause of impermanence? Noble son, furthermore, there are two kinds of causes: the cause of production and the cause of manifestation. Just as a potter's wheel is called the cause of production, noble son, so too, just as a lamp and the like illuminate objects in the darkness — this is called the cause of manifestation. Noble son, great nirvāṇa is not produced by the cause of production; it is by the cause of manifestation alone. The cause of manifestation is this: the thirty-seven factors of awakening and the six perfections are called the cause of manifestation.

Noble son, giving is a cause of nirvāṇa, but it is not a cause of great nirvāṇa. The perfection of giving is called a cause of great nirvāṇa. The thirty-seven factors of awakening are a cause of nirvāṇa, but they are not a cause of great nirvāṇa. The limitless and numberless factors of the branches of awakening are called the cause of great nirvāṇa.

May there be auspiciousness.

Here begins the Sūtra section, volume Ta. The Noble Sūtra of Great Nirvāṇa. The twenty-ninth fascicle.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, Samantaprabhāsa, the Glorious King of Lofty Majesty, addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, if one gives generously in such a way that it cannot be called the perfection of giving, and, continuing in that same way through to wisdom, if one cultivates wisdom in such a way that it cannot be called the perfection of wisdom — and what would then be designated the perfection of wisdom — and further, what should be called nirvāṇa and what should be called great nirvāṇa?

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, when a bodhisattva, a great being, applies himself thoroughly and at great length to great nirvāṇa, he does not hear of giving, he does not see giving, he does not hear of the perfection of giving.

he does not see the perfection of giving, and continuing in that same way through to wisdom: he does not hear of wisdom, he does not see wisdom, he does not hear of the Perfection of Wisdom, he does not see the Perfection of Wisdom, he does not hear of nirvāṇa, he does not see nirvāṇa, he does not hear of great nirvāṇa, he does not see great nirvāṇa. For a bodhisattva, a great being, who applies himself thoroughly to great nirvāṇa, realizes and sees within the dharmadhātu, and fully attains the defining characteristic of what is perfectly real — empty, utterly without anything, uncompounded, without feeling or cognition — and realizes, as it truly is, the defining characteristic of being without defilement, the defining characteristic of being without activity, the defining characteristic of being like a magical illusion, the defining characteristic of being like a mirage, like a gandharva city, and the defining characteristic of being like space. When at that time a bodhisattva has attained such a defining characteristic, because he is free from attachment, aversion, and delusion, he neither hears nor sees. That is the perfectly real defining characteristic of a bodhisattva, a great being.

Bodhisattvas, great beings, who abide in the perfectly real defining characteristic fully understand: "This is giving, this is the perfection of giving" — and continuing in that way through wisdom — "this is wisdom, this is the Perfection of Wisdom, this is nirvāṇa, this is great nirvāṇa."

Noble son, as to how giving can be giving and yet not be the perfection of giving: when one gives only upon seeing a supplicant, that is called giving — it is not the perfection. When one gives of one's own accord even without a supplicant, that is called the perfection of giving. When one gives only occasionally, at certain times, that is called giving — it is not called the perfection. When one always gives without ceasing, that is called the perfection of giving. When one gives to another and afterwards a mind of regret arises, that is called giving — it is not called the perfection. When one gives without subsequent regret, that is called the perfection of giving.

When a bodhisattva, a great being, generates the four fears regarding wealth and material possessions — such as kings, thieves, water, and fire — and gives with great joy, that is called the perfection of giving. When one gives in hopes of receiving something in return, that is called giving — it is not called the perfection. When one gives with no expectation of return, that is called the perfection of giving.

When one gives out of fear, or for gain, or for fame, or for the sake of one's household, or to sustain one's clan, or to be reborn among the gods, or for the five objects of desire, or out of pride, or out of arrogance, or to cultivate a friend, or in hope of recompense — this is like one who engages in trade, or, noble son, like a person who plants trees in expectation of shade, flowers, fruit, timber, and the like: whoever gives in such a way, that is called giving — it is not the perfection.

A bodhisattva, a great being, who in this way applies himself thoroughly to great nirvāṇa does not see giving and receiving as real objects, does not see a time, does not see merit or non-merit, does not see a cause, does not see a condition, does not see a ripening result, does not see an agent, does not see a recipient, does not see much, does not see little, does not see purity, does not see impurity, does not disparage the recipient, the self, or material things, does not see what is seen, does not see what is unseen, does not grasp at self or other — and it is on account of the Dharma of always abiding in the vast and expansive great nirvāṇa that he gives, for the benefit of all sentient beings, and

and gives for the sake of happiness, and gives for the sake of completely severing the afflictions of all sentient beings, and he is diligent in giving so that all sentient beings may come to see neither giving, nor receiving, nor material things as real.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: if a man who has fallen into the ocean grasps hold of a corpse, he will be freed from the ocean. When a bodhisattva, a great being, is diligent in the great nirvāṇa, his practice of giving is just like that.

Son of good family, consider another analogy: if a man is placed in a very deep, tightly sealed pit of filth, there is no escape from any other direction, but there is one small opening through which waste flows out — and if he emerges through that, he arrives at a place free from obstruction. When a bodhisattva, a great being, is diligent in the great nirvāṇa, his giving is just like that.

Son of good family, consider another analogy: a woman of high brahmin lineage, seized with terror and having no protector or refuge, takes shelter in and goes for refuge to an outcaste of low birth. When a bodhisattva, a great being, is diligent in the great nirvāṇa, his giving is just like that.

Son of good family, consider another analogy: a sick person, in order to dispel the suffering of illness and attain well-being, eats something impure. When a bodhisattva, a great being, is diligent in the great nirvāṇa, his giving is just like that.

Son of good family, consider another analogy: a brahmin, for the sake of his very life when food is extremely scarce, eats dog flesh. When a bodhisattva, a great being, is diligent in the great nirvāṇa, his giving is just like that.

Son of good family, within the great nirvāṇa there are such things as: hearing, for immeasurable aeons, what had never been heard before; and the teaching from moral discipline and the perfection of moral discipline all the way through to wisdom and the Perfection of Wisdom — all of this is explained in detail just as in the sūtra known as "The Buddha, the Sūtra of Varied Flowers."

Son of good family, how does it come about that when a bodhisattva, a great being, is diligent in the great nirvāṇa, he hears what has never been heard before? It is through the occasion of this sūtra that the profoundly deep meaning of the twelve branches of scriptural teaching, never before heard, is heard completely and fully. That which previously existed in some slight measure and was heard only by name — now, from this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa, its actual meaning is heard for the very first time.

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, from the twelve branches of scriptural teaching, hear only the names but do not hear the meaning. Now, from this sūtra, they hear it in complete fullness — and this is called "hearing what was never before heard."

Son of good family, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, from sūtras that declare the buddha to be permanent, blissful, possessed of self, and utterly pure — not coming to an end — and from sūtras concerning the Three Jewels, and sūtras teaching that the buddha-nature has no distinctive defining characteristics, and sūtras concerning the falling away of the four roots, and sūtras denigrating the vast and expansive teaching, and sūtras teaching the misconduct of the five acts without interval, and sūtras teaching that even all those given to wrong craving possess the buddha-nature — from all of these, today, through this sūtra, they hear for the first time what was never before heard. And this is called "hearing what was never before heard."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, the King of Glorious Lofty Universal Illumination addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, if those who have broken the four roots, who have denigrated the vast and expansive scriptural teaching, who have committed the misconduct of the five acts without interval, and those given to wrong craving and the like — if all these possess the buddha-nature, why then should they still fall into the hells?"

"Blessed One, if those beings do indeed possess the buddha-nature, why then is it said that they lack permanence, bliss, self, and purity? Blessed One, if one who has completely severed the roots of virtue is called 'one given to wrong craving,' then at the time of severing the roots of virtue, why was the buddha-nature not severed along with them? And if the buddha-nature were severed, why would it then be called permanent, blissful, self, and pure? Yet if it was not severed, why apply the designation 'one given to wrong craving'? Blessed One, those who have broken the four roots are indeterminate. Those who have denigrated the vast and expansive scriptural teaching, those who have committed the misconduct of the five acts without interval, and those given to wrong craving — these too are indeterminate. But if they were determinate, how could they ever fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening? From stream-enterers to pratyekabuddhas, they too are indeterminate. And if those from stream-enterer through pratyekabuddha were determinate, it would be equally unreasonable for them to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Blessed One, if those who have broken the four roots are indeterminate, then so too are those from stream-enterer through pratyekabuddha indeterminate. And if all of these are indeterminate, then the Blessed One, the buddha, is also indeterminate. If the Blessed One, the buddha, is indeterminate, then the essential nature of nirvāṇa is also indeterminate — and so too are all phenomena, down to the last, indeterminate. How so? If those given to wrong craving were to awaken by abandoning the deeds of wrong craving, then the Blessed Ones, the buddhas, having fully passed into nirvāṇa, might equally return once more — which would mean they are the kind who do not enter final nirvāṇa. If things were so, then the nature of nirvāṇa itself would become indeterminate. Since it is indeterminate in that way, and since permanence, bliss, self, and purity are absent, why then would those given to wrong craving and the like attain nirvāṇa?"

Then the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva, the great being, the King of Glorious Lofty Universal Illumination: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, you have asked these questions well — out of love and compassion for the world, for the sake of benefit and happiness for measureless sentient beings, for the arousing of awakening mind, and in order that bodhisattvas may rise ever higher and higher. Noble son, you have in the past served and honored measureless Blessed Ones, the buddhas, and in dependence upon those buddhas you have generated the roots of virtue. For a very long time you have cultivated the qualities of awakening and, having defeated and shattered the hosts of Māra, you have worked for the welfare of measureless and boundless sentient beings and established them all in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. For a very long time you have understood this profoundly deep essential meaning, intended and taught by the Tathāgatas. Among all the past Blessed Ones, the buddhas, as countless as the sands of the Ganges River, measureless and boundless — I have not seen a single one to whom anyone in all the world, whether god or human, ascetic or brahmin, māra or Brahmā, has put these profound and ultimate questions to a Tathāgata as you have done. Now listen well and with great care and close attention, for I shall set it forth and explain it. Noble son, those given to wrong craving are not determinate."

If it were determinate, one given to wrong craving could never attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Because it is indeterminate, attainment is possible. Therefore, if the nature of a buddha has not been cut off, why speak of one as given to wrong craving? As for the cutting off of wholesome roots, noble son, wholesome roots are of two kinds: inner and outer. The nature of a buddha is neither inner nor outer; therefore the nature of a buddha is not cut off. Again, there are two kinds: defiled and undefiled. The nature of a buddha is neither defiled nor undefiled; therefore it is not cut off. Again, there are two kinds: permanent and impermanent. The nature of a buddha is neither permanent nor impermanent; therefore it is not cut off. If it were cut off, it would be fitting that it be regained. If it cannot be regained, it is called "not cut off." What is cut off and then regained — that belongs to one given to wrong craving. The falling away of the four roots is likewise indeterminate. If it were determinate, those who have fallen away from the four roots could never attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Rejecting the extensive scriptural collections is likewise indeterminate. If it were determinate, those who have rejected the sacred Dharma could never attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Committing the fault of the five acts of immediate consequence is likewise indeterminate. If it were determinate, those who have committed the five acts of immediate consequence could never attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Both form and the defining characteristic of form are indeterminate. From scent, taste, and the defining characteristic of tangibles, through the defining characteristic of birth, up to the defining characteristic of ignorance, and including the defining characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense sources, the twenty-five modes of existence, the four births, and all phenomena without exception — all are indeterminate.

Noble son, consider the following analogy. A magician conjures, before a great crowd, four kinds of assemblage: a host of chariots, footmen, oxen, and horses; an array of precious ornaments; and towns, cities, villages, mountains, forests, trees, springs, ponds, streams, and wells. Among that crowd, the foolish and ignorant see these illusions and take them all to be real. The wise and discerning know they are not real — they understand that the power of illusion deceives the human eye. Noble son, the same applies to ordinary beings all the way up through śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas — to all of them, every phenomenon appears to have a fixed, determinate defining characteristic. Buddhas and bodhisattvas, however, do not regard any phenomenon as having a fixed, determinate defining characteristic.

Noble son, consider another analogy. Foolish people see a summer mirage and think it is water. The wise and discerning do not take that mirage to truly be water — they know the mirage is not real water, that it is something that deceives the human eye, and that it is not in any genuine sense water. All ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are the same in how they see all phenomena — they take them all to be real and genuine. Buddhas and bodhisattvas do not look upon any phenomenon as having a fixed, determinate defining characteristic.

Noble son, here is yet another analogy. When a voice is raised near a cliff and the cliff returns an echo, the ignorant and foolish hear it and take the sound to be real. The wise and discerning know it is not genuinely what it seems — they understand that a mere semblance of sound deceives the ear-consciousness. Noble son, all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas look upon all phenomena as though they had such fixed, determinate defining characteristics.

Bodhisattvas, having thoroughly understood that all phenomena lack any fixed, determinate defining characteristic, see them under the characteristic of impermanence, under the characteristics of emptiness, peace, and so forth, and under the characteristic of being without arising and ceasing. Therefore bodhisattvas, great beings, see all phenomena under the characteristic of impermanence.

Noble son, yet there are also determinate defining characteristics. What are those determinate characteristics? They are: permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity. And where do these abide? In nirvāṇa.

Noble son, the fruit of stream-entry is also indeterminate. Because it is indeterminate in this way, one may attain the awakening mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening over the course of eighty aeons. The fruit of once-returning is likewise indeterminate. Because it is indeterminate in this way, one may attain the awakening mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening over the course of sixty aeons. The fruit of non-returning is likewise indeterminate. Because it is indeterminate in this way, one may attain the awakening mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening over the course of forty aeons. The fruit of arhatship is likewise indeterminate. Because it is indeterminate in this way, one may attain the awakening mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening over the course of twenty aeons. The awakening of a pratyekabuddha is also indeterminate. Because it is indeterminate in this way, one may attain the awakening mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening over the course of ten thousand aeons.

Noble son, now, here in this city of Kuśinagara, the Tathāgata reclines upon a lion throne between the śāla trees, drawing near to his passing into nirvāṇa. Many novices who have not yet attained the fruit of arhatship, together with the greatly powerful Vajrapāṇi and others, give rise to great grief. Gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas (scent-eaters), garuḍas, kinnaras (half-human beings), and great nāgas and others make lavish offerings and magnificent worship. Multitudes of people wrap the body in a thousand lengths of cloth, encase it in a casket of the seven precious substances, fill it with oil of essence, and pile fragrant woods around it; yet when it is lit and burns, neither of two things are consumed by fire. What are those two? Contact with the body itself, and the innermost layer of cloth nearest to it.
