It is shown that the relics are to be divided eightfold among all sentient beings. All the śrāvaka attendants declare, "The Tathāgata has passed into complete nirvāṇa." Yet one should understand that the Tathāgata has decidedly not passed into complete nirvāṇa. Why? Because the Tathāgata is permanently abiding, unchanging, and unshifting. Therefore the Tathāgata's nirvāṇa is also indeterminate. Noble son, one should understand the Tathāgata to be indeterminate. For in this way the Tathāgata is not an asura. Why? Because there are four kinds of god (deva): worldly gods, gods by birth, gods of purity, and gods by meaning. Those called worldly gods are like kings. Those called gods by birth are those born anywhere from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Those called gods of purity are those from stream-entrants up to pratyekabuddhas. Those called gods by meaning are those great beings who are bodhisattvas on the tenth ground. Why is a bodhisattva on the tenth ground called a god by meaning? Because such a one is supremely skilled in the meaning of all phenomena. And what is that meaning? It is seeing all phenomena in the meaning of emptiness.

Noble son, the Tathāgata is not a king.

The Tathāgata is not a king — not from the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and not from stream-entrants up to pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas on the tenth ground. Therefore the Tathāgata is not a god.

And yet sentient beings speak of the buddha as the god of gods. Therefore the Tathāgata is not a god, yet is also not a non-god; not a human, yet also not a non-human; not a rakṣasa, yet also not a non-rakṣasa; not a hell-being, not an animal, not a hungry ghost, yet also not a non-hell-being, non-animal, or non-hungry-ghost; not a sentient being, yet also not a non-sentient-being; not a phenomenon, yet also not a non-phenomenon; not form, yet also not non-form; not long, yet also not non-long; not short, yet also not non-short; not a characteristic, yet also not a non-characteristic; not mind, yet also not non-mind; not defiled, yet also not undefiled; not conditioned, yet also not unconditioned; not permanent, yet also not impermanent; not an illusion, yet also not a non-illusion; not a name, yet also not a non-name; not definite, yet also not non-definite; not existent, yet also not non-existent; not nonexistent, yet also not non-nonexistent; not expressible, yet also not inexpressible; not a Tathāgata, yet also not a non-Tathāgata. Therefore the Tathāgata is indefinable.

Noble son, why is the Tathāgata not designated a worldly god? Worldly gods are kings. Since the Tathāgata long ago, over measureless aeons, relinquished the ways of kingship, he is therefore not a king. And why is he not a non-king? Because the Tathāgata was born in the city of Kapilavastu in the household of King Śuddhodana; therefore he is not a non-king either.

Why is the Tathāgata not a god by birth? Because the Tathāgata, from long ago, separated himself from all states of existence; therefore he is not a god by birth. And why is he not a non-god-by-birth? Because he descended from the Tuṣita heaven to Jambudvīpa; therefore the Tathāgata is also not a non-god-by-birth.

Why is the Tathāgata not a god of purity? Because the Tathāgata is not a stream-entrant up to a pratyekabuddha; therefore he is not a god of purity. And why is he not a non-god-of-purity? Because he is unstained by the eight worldly concerns, just as a lotus is unstained by water and dust; therefore the Tathāgata is also not a non-god-of-purity.

Why is the Tathāgata not a god by meaning? Because the Tathāgata is not a bodhisattva on the tenth ground; therefore he is not a god by meaning. And why is he not a non-god-by-meaning? Because the Tathāgata always applies himself to the eighteen emptinesses; therefore the Tathāgata is also not a non-god-by-meaning.

Why is the Tathāgata not a human? Because the Tathāgata long ago, over measureless aeons, completely abandoned human existence; therefore he is not a human. And why is he not a non-human? Because he was born in the city of Kapilavastu; therefore he is also not a non-human.

Why is the Tathāgata not a rakṣasa? Because he harms no sentient being whatsoever; therefore he is not a rakṣasa. And why is he not a non-rakṣasa? Because he appears in emanated forms resembling a rakṣasa and tames sentient beings thereby; therefore he is also not a non-rakṣasa.

Then why is the Tathāgata not a hell-being, an animal, or a hungry ghost?

Because the Tathāgata long ago completely abandoned wrongful views, he is therefore not a hell-being, an animal, or a hungry ghost. And why is he also not a non-hell-being, non-animal, and non-hungry-ghost? Because the Tathāgata, in order to tame sentient beings, has actually appeared even in the three lower realms; therefore he is also not a non-hell-being, non-animal, and non-hungry-ghost.

Why is the Tathāgata not a sentient being? Because long ago he abandoned the intrinsic nature of a sentient being; therefore the Tathāgata is not a sentient being. And why is he also not a non-sentient-being? Because on various occasions he has spoken of sentient beings using their very characteristics; therefore the Tathāgata is also not a non-sentient-being.

Why is the Tathāgata not a phenomenon (dharma)? Because all phenomena have their own individually distinct characteristics, and the Tathāgata is not like that — he is exhausted in a single characteristic; therefore he is not a phenomenon. And why is he also not a non-phenomenon? Because the Tathāgata is the dharmadhātu, the basic space of phenomena; therefore he is also not a non-phenomenon.

Why is the Tathāgata not form? Because he is not included within the ten sense bases of form; therefore he is not form. And why is he also not a non-form? Because his body is adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty excellent minor marks; therefore he is also not a non-form.

Why is the Tathāgata not tall? Because he has completely transcended all form; therefore he is not tall. And why is he also not a non-tall? Because the whole world cannot perceive the mark at the crown of his head; therefore he is also not a non-tall.

Why is the Tathāgata not short? Because long ago he abandoned the affliction of conceit and arrogance; therefore he is not short. And why is he also not a non-short? Because he displayed to the householder Kuśila a body three cubits tall; therefore he is also not a non-short.

Why is the Tathāgata without characteristics? Because long ago he separated from all characteristics; therefore he is without characteristics. And why is he also not without characteristics? Because he is skilled in and has realised all characteristics; therefore he is also not without characteristics.

Why is the Tathāgata not mind? Because he has the characteristic of space; therefore he is not mind. And why is he also not a non-mind? Because he possesses the mind of Dharma endowed with the ten powers, and because he knows the minds of others as well; therefore he is also not a non-mind.

Why is the Tathāgata not a conditioned phenomenon? Because he is permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure; therefore he is not a conditioned phenomenon. And why is he also not an unconditioned phenomenon? Because there is coming and going, sitting and lying down, and because he has also demonstrated passing fully into nirvāṇa; therefore he is also not an unconditioned phenomenon.

Why is the Tathāgata not permanent? Because his body possesses limbs and members; therefore he is not permanent. And why is he also not impermanent? The reason is that he possesses awareness. A permanent thing has no awareness — just as space, for example, has none. Because the Tathāgata possesses awareness, he is therefore not permanent. But then how is he not impermanent? Because he possesses speech. A permanent thing has no speech — it is like space. Because the Tathāgata possesses speech, he is therefore not permanent. He is called impermanent because he has bones and a lineage. That which has no bones and no lineage is called permanent: space is permanent, and therefore has no bones. The Tathāgata has bones and belongs to a lineage — the lineage of Gautama — and therefore he is impermanent. He is called impermanent because he has father and mother. That which has no father and mother is designated permanent.

Space is permanent, and therefore has no father and mother. The Tathāgata has father and mother, and therefore he is impermanent. He is called impermanent because he possesses the four modes of deportment. That which lacks the four modes of deportment is called permanent: space is permanent, and therefore has no four modes of deportment. The Tathāgata possesses the four modes of deportment, and therefore he is impermanent. That which abides permanently has no fixed location and no fixed direction. Space is permanent, and therefore has no fixed location and no fixed direction. The Tathāgata, by contrast, arose in the eastern land, dwelt in Śrāvastī and at Rājagṛha, and therefore he is impermanent. For all these reasons, then, the Tathāgata is not permanent.

As for the statement that he is not impermanent — this is because birth has been completely severed. Whatever phenomenon is accompanied by birth is called impermanent; whatever phenomenon is without birth is called permanent. The Tathāgata too is without birth, and therefore he is permanent. A permanent phenomenon is without lineage, and whatever phenomenon is accompanied by a lineage is called impermanent. The Tathāgata is without birth and without lineage, and because he is without birth and without lineage, he is permanent. A permanent phenomenon pervades everything everywhere, just as space pervades every place without exception. The Tathāgata likewise pervades everywhere in the same way, and therefore he is permanent. An impermanent phenomenon is such that it exists in this location but not in others. The Tathāgata is not like that — it cannot be said of him that he exists here but not elsewhere — and therefore he is permanent. An impermanent phenomenon sometimes exists and sometimes does not. The Tathāgata is not like that: it is not the case that he sometimes exists and sometimes does not, and therefore he is permanent. A permanently abiding phenomenon has no name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Space is permanent, and therefore has no name-and-form. The Tathāgata likewise has no name-and-form, and therefore he is permanent. A permanently abiding phenomenon has no cause and no result. Space is permanent, and therefore has no cause and no result. The Tathāgata likewise has no cause and no result, and therefore he is permanent. A permanently abiding phenomenon does not fall within the three times. The Tathāgata likewise does not fall within the three times, and therefore he is permanent.

As for the statement that the Tathāgata is not an illusion — this is because all sentient beings of untruth have been completely severed, and therefore he is not an illusion. As for the statement that he is also not non-illusion — this is because the Tathāgata sometimes projects from this single body into bodies beyond measure, and sometimes gathers those measureless bodies back into one; sometimes he passes unobstructed through mountains and crags; sometimes he walks upon water as upon solid ground; sometimes he sinks into the earth as though into water; sometimes he walks through the sky as upon the earth; sometimes smoke billows from his body and great fires blaze, as from a mighty column of flame; sometimes he sends forth clouds and the sound of thunder, producing awe-inspiring roars; and sometimes he transforms into towns, cities, villages, houses, mountains, forests, and trees; sometimes he makes his body vast, and sometimes he makes it small; and sometimes he displays the form of a man, a woman, a boy, or a girl. For all these reasons the Tathāgata is also not non-illusion.

As for the statement that the Tathāgata is not definite — this is because the Tathāgata displayed passing into complete nirvāṇa beneath the śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, and therefore he is not definite. As for the statement that he is also not non-definite — this is because of his permanence, his bliss, his selfhood, and his utter purity, and therefore the Tathāgata is also not non-definite.

The statement that the Tathāgata is not defiled — this is because he has completely severed the three kinds of defilement (āsrava), and therefore he is not defiled. As for what is meant by the three defilements: all the afflictions of the desire realm, excepting ignorance, constitute the defilement of desire. All the afflictions of the form realm and the formless realm, excepting ignorance, constitute the defilement of existence. The ignorance of all three realms constitutes the defilement of ignorance. Because the Tathāgata has completely severed all of these, he is without defilement.

Furthermore, all ordinary beings who are childish and unrefined do not perceive the defilement of existence. Why is it that childish and unrefined ordinary beings do not perceive the defilement of existence? It is because all childish and unrefined ordinary beings are possessed of a mind of doubt regarding the future, of the following kind: Will a body be obtained in a future time, or will it not be obtained? In the past, did this body exist from the very beginning, or did it not exist from the very beginning? In the present, does this body exist, or does it not exist? If there is something called a self, is it form, or is it not form, or is it both form and not-form, or is it neither form nor not-form? Is it perception, or is it not perception, or is it both perception and not-perception, or is it neither perception nor not-perception? Is this body under another's control, or not under another's control, or both under another's control and yet not under another's control, or neither under another's control nor not under another's control? Is there a life-force but no body, or a body but no life-force, or both a body and a life-force, or neither a body nor a life-force? Are the body and life-force permanent, or impermanent, or both permanent and impermanent, or neither permanent nor impermanent? Were this body and life-force made by a sovereign power, or made by time, or made without a cause, or made by the inherent nature of the world, or made by atoms, or made by what is Dharma and what is not Dharma, or made by a person, or made by afflictions, or made by one's parents? Does the self reside in the mind, or does it reside in the eye, or does it pervade the body? Did it come from somewhere else? Where does it go? Who is it that is born? Who is it that dies? In the past, was the self of brahmin caste, or of royal caste, or of merchant caste, or of low caste? In the future, what sort of caste will one obtain? In former times, was this body of mine male, or female, or an animal? If I were to take a life, would there be a sinful transgression worthy of blame, or, ranging from there being no such blameworthy sin all the way to drinking the soup of the mad, would it be sinful, or would it be without sin? Was it done by oneself, or done by another? Have I experienced the maturation of the result, or will I experience the maturation of the karmic result? — With such a mass of doubt-ridden, view-laden afflictions, measureless beyond counting, the minds of sentient beings are obscured. Conditioned by views of doubt, six kinds of mind arise. What are they? The certainty that a self exists; the certainty that there is no self; the view of self; the view of self and what belongs to self; the absence of self and the view of no-self; and that which is self or made by self, experienced by self, or known by self — these are called wrong views. Because the Tathāgata has, in this way, uprooted from their very base the measureless defilements that accompany such views, he is therefore without defilement.

Son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the noble conduct drawn from the Great Nirvāṇa will utterly sever defilements of just that kind. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, because they always practice the noble conduct, are therefore without defilement.

Son of good family, an ill-bred youth, because he does not properly restrain the five sense faculties, will come to have three defilements, and, led on by non-virtue, will go to a state of non-virtue. Son of good family, consider the analogy of one who rides an unruly horse that is difficult to control: he is thrown into danger and goes over a precipice. One who cannot properly restrain the five sense faculties is just like that — utterly parted from the virtuous path of nirvāṇa, he goes on toward a state of non-virtue. Consider again the analogy of an intractable, untamed yak upon which someone tries to ride: it does not go as intended, but leaves the town behind and goes off to a desolate place. One who cannot restrain the five sense faculties is just like that — parted from the city of nirvāṇa, he is led into the vast wilderness of saṃsāra.

Son of good family, consider the analogy of a treacherous minister who shows his king nine kinds of evil. The five sense faculties when treacherous are just like that — they constantly display to sentient beings measureless quantities of evil and non-virtue. Son of good family, consider the analogy of an ill-bred youth who will not listen to the words taught by his teachers, his preceptors, and his parents, and who commits every kind of non-virtue. Untamed five sense faculties are just like that — they do not listen to the words taught so well by teachers and preceptors, and they bring about the full completion of wrongdoing.

Son of good family, an ill-bred youth, because he cannot restrain the five sense faculties, is constantly tormented by hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts. Others, like wicked men who harm the virtuous, afflict him in the same way. Son of good family, an ill-bred youth who cannot restrain the five sense faculties is scattered and distracted among the five sense objects. Just as herdsmen who do not properly tend their cattle allow them to stray into the fields, so too an ill-bred youth who does not restrain the five sense faculties constantly abides within the realms of conditioned existence and encounters suffering in great abundance.

Son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, who is diligent with respect to the Great Nirvāṇa and who practices the noble conduct — in order to attain all virtuous qualities of the Dharma — always tames the five sense faculties and is utterly fearful of attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, arrogance, and envy. Son of good family, whoever guards the five sense faculties very carefully will find that the mind becomes fully gathered and concentrated. Whoever gathers the mind will also gather the five sense faculties. Consider the analogy of one who protects the king: this is called protecting the kingdom. And whoever protects the kingdom is said to be protecting the king. A bodhisattva, a great being, is similarly like that — if he hears this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, he will attain wisdom. Having attained wisdom, he becomes single-pointed with respect to the five sense faculties, and even should mindfulness wander, it returns to right mindfulness. Why is this so? Because of the wisdom of mindfulness.

Son of good family, a skilled herdsman, if his cattle stray into the fields, drives them back and does not let them graze there. A bodhisattva, a great being, is just like that — by means of guarding and gathering the five sense faculties through the wisdom of mindfulness, he does not let them scatter in all directions.

A bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses the wisdom of mindfulness does not perceive the characteristics of a self, does not perceive the characteristics of self and what belongs to self, does not perceive sentient beings as such, and does not perceive objects of conduct as such. Instead, seeing all phenomena as conforming to the characteristic of the nature of reality, he gives rise to characteristics like those of earth, pebbles, and sand. Just as a house arises from many conditions —

— just as a house that has been severed and demolished has no intrinsic nature, so too sentient beings, when examined, arise from the four great elements and the five aggregates, and therefore have no fixed, definitive characteristic. Because they have no fixed, definitive characteristic, the bodhisattva does not give rise to attachment and clinging toward them. All foolish, ordinary people, seeing sentient beings as truly existent, are born into affliction. A bodhisattva, a great being, who is diligent in the great nirvāṇa sūtra, possessing the wisdom of mindfulness, does not give rise to attachment and clinging toward sentient beings. Furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, who is diligent in the sūtra teaching of the great nirvāṇa, does not become attached to the characteristics of sentient beings; rather, he works with the various characteristics of phenomena. Good son, take the example of a painter who, using many colors, paints images of boys and girls, cattle, horses, and many other forms. When foolish, unintelligent ordinary people see these, they give rise to the characteristics of boys, girls, and so forth. The painter, however, clearly understands that there are no actual boys or girls or any of the rest. A bodhisattva, a great being, is likewise: by understanding the varied characteristics of phenomena as a single characteristic, he does not give rise to the characteristics of sentient beings. Why is this? Because he possesses the wisdom of mindfulness. Bodhisattvas, great beings, who are diligent in the great nirvāṇa — even if they see a beautiful woman, they never give rise to a mind of desire and attachment. Why? Because they have thoroughly understood characteristics. Good son, a bodhisattva, a great being, understands that the five objects of desire hold no genuine pleasure, no real happiness; they are not stable even for a single moment. They are like a dog gnawing a bare bone, like a torch carried into the wind, like the vessel of a venomous serpent, like something found in a dream, like food set out at a crossroads that all are snatching at, like a piece of meat that every bird in the sky is tearing at, like a bubble on water, like a drawing made on water, like the thread of a loom when its material is exhausted, like a prisoner being led to execution, like a reflected image that does not last long. In these and many other ways, he understands that desire is laden with the most numerous faults. Furthermore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, examines sentient beings, he sees that through the causes and conditions of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, they have continuously experienced suffering throughout immeasurable, incalculable eons. The bones of each single sentient being, stacked up over the course of one eon, would form a pile greater than Mount Vipula near Rājagṛha. The milk each has drunk would exceed the waters of the ocean. The blood that has flowed from each one's body would exceed the waters of the four oceans. The tears wept by parents, siblings, spouses, children, and relatives at each one's death would likewise exceed the waters of the four oceans. Were one to make tokens four finger-breadths long from all the grasses and trees on this great earth and use them to count one's past parents, their number could not be known. For immeasurable eons, sentient beings have taken birth in hells, in the realms of animals, and as hungry ghosts, experiencing vast suffering beyond any telling or reckoning. It would be easier to reduce this entire great earth to balls the size of juniper berries and count them to their end than it would be to find an end to saṃsāra. When a bodhisattva, a great being, examines all sentient beings in this way, he understands that through the causes and conditions of desire they experience immeasurable suffering. Yet these sufferings — the sufferings of the conditioning factors of saṃsāra — do not cause the bodhisattva to let the wisdom of mindfulness decline. Good son, take this example: in the world, within a tract of land twenty-five leagues across, filled with a great multitude of people, a king sends one of his ministers carrying a bowl full of sesame oil,

and commanded him to pass through all that great multitude of people without spilling even a single drop of the oil. "If you spill even one drop," the king declared, "you will be put to death." A man was then sent behind him carrying a sword. The minister, having received the king's command and taken it deeply to heart, exerted himself with extreme care and walked throughout the midst of that vast assembly. Even though he saw the five objects of desire all around him, his mind constantly held this thought: "If I grow slack and become attached to those pleasures, I will spill this oil, and my life will be forfeit." It was through causes and conditions of fear such as these that he did not spill even a single drop. The bodhisattva, the great being, is likewise: moving through the midst of saṃsāra, he does not lose the wisdom of mindfulness, and because he does not lose it, even though he sees the five objects of desire, no mind of attachment arises in him. Even if he sees a beautiful form, he does not generate the characteristic mark of form as form; he understands it to the extent of the characteristic mark of suffering and the characteristic mark of consciousness. In the same way, he does not apprehend it under the characteristic mark of arising, does not apprehend it under the characteristic mark of cessation, does not apprehend it under the characteristic mark of a cause, but perceives it under the characteristic mark of what has arisen through conditions.

At that time the bodhisattva's five faculties are thoroughly purified. Because the five faculties are thoroughly purified, he is endowed with the guarding of the root of moral discipline. All base and ignoble persons, because their five faculties are not purified, are quite unable to guard it thoroughly — these faculties are called "defiled." The bodhisattva, through thorough severance, is without defilement. The Tathāgata has extracted it by the root and so is beyond defilement altogether. Good son, there is yet another way of fully abandoning defilement: the bodhisattva, the great being, fully abandons wicked defilement out of longing for the buddha-field of the unsurpassable ambrosia. And what is this abandoning? Whoever applies himself diligently to this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa — writing it down, holding it, reading it, reciting it, expounding and explaining it, taking its meaning to heart — this is called abandonment. Why is that? Good son, among the twelve branches of scripture I have not found any other teaching on the full abandonment of wicked defilement as extensive as this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa.

Good son, take this example: when a skilled master teaches his students, any student who listens to his instruction commits no fault. In the same way, the bodhisattva, the great being, who cultivates this supreme and excellent sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa likewise commits no fault.

Good son, take this example as well: in the world there is a noble spell of knowledge, and whoever hears it will not be harmed by any poison for seven years and will not be seized by snakes. Whoever recites it aloud will, for as long as they live, be free from evils of many kinds.

Good son, this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa is likewise: if any sentient being hears it even once, entering through the ear, they will not fall into the lower realms for seven eons to come. And if someone writes it down, reads it, recites it, expounds and explains it, or takes its meaning to heart, they will without fail attain unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening, and will perceive the perfectly pure intrinsic nature of a buddha — just as a wheel-turning king of magical power attains the taste of ambrosia. Good son, this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa possesses immeasurable qualities such as these.

Good son, if someone writes down this sūtra, reads it, recites it, expounds and explains it,

spreads it to others, teaches it, or takes its meaning to heart — that person is truly my close attendant, one who genuinely hears my scriptural transmission. Know that I look upon such a person and hold them in my intention, and understand that one so regarded by me will not pass beyond nirvāṇa without attaining it. Wherever that person resides — in a village, a city, a town, in the mountains, at the foot of a tree, in a hermitage, a dwelling, a house, an upper story, or a vast palace — I too remain there and go nowhere else. I constantly accept their offerings, appearing in emanation as a monk, a nun, a layman, a laywoman, a brahmin, a wandering mendicant, a poor person, a destitute person, or a beggar, and in that form I receive their gifts.

Noble Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, the thirtieth fascicle.

Now, how does the Tathāgata receive such offerings? Good son, if that person, dreaming in the night, sees the form of a buddha, the form of a god, the form of a renunciant, the form of a king or a wheel-turning king, the form of a lion king, a lotus, a flower of the udumbara tree, a great mountain, an ocean, the sun, the moon, a white bull, a white horse, or the forms of one's parents and the like; or if in the dream one finds flowers, fruit, gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, or other precious jewels; or if one dreams of obtaining the five flavors of cow's milk — at that very time and in that very moment, know that the Tathāgata has accepted the offerings of that person. Upon waking, one will be filled with great joy and happiness, will obtain various desired objects, will be free of ill will, and will become devoted to practicing virtuous qualities.

Good son, this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa is capable of accomplishing immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable stores of merit such as these. Good son, you should place your trust in my words. If any son or daughter of good family wishes to see me, or wishes to pay me homage, or wishes to see me in a way consonant with the nature of reality, or wishes to attain the meditative absorption of emptiness, or wishes to see the true defining marks, or wishes to cultivate the meditative absorption of courageous conduct and the meditative absorption of the lion king, or wishes to vanquish the eight māras — and the eight māras are: the four māras, together with impermanence, the absence of bliss, no-self, and the absence of perfect purity — or wishes to be born as a human being, or wishes the happiness of the gods: let such a person, upon seeing someone who upholds this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, who has written it down, reads it, recites it, expounds and explains it, or takes its meaning to heart — let them draw near to that person, approach them, take up residence with them, make supplications and requests, offer veneration, respect, and honor, wash their feet, prepare a seat and a cushion, make offerings with the four kinds of requisites, and do so without reluctance. If that person has come from a great distance, one should go out to meet them for up to ten leagues. For the sake of this sūtra, one should offer all precious wealth held dear. And if one has none, one should even sell one's own body. Why is this? Because this sūtra is as rare to encounter as the flower of the udumbara tree.

Good son, in times long past, through immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless eons beyond reckoning, there was in this world-system called Endurance the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, fully possessed of knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed one, the guide and master of persons to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans —

— a Blessed One, a buddha, arose and taught this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra to a vast assembly. At that time I heard from a spiritual friend that this buddha was teaching the Great Nirvāṇa to a vast assembly. When I heard this I was filled with great joy, and I thought to make an offering. But having thought to offer, I found I was utterly destitute and had nothing whatsoever. Having tried to sell my body, I found only a trifling sum — not enough to matter. So I turned back homeward, and on the road I met a man and said to him, "If I sell this body of mine, would you buy it?"

He replied, "I have a task that no one else is able to perform. If you are capable of doing it, I will buy you."

I asked him what it was that no one else could do, and he said, "I have a severe illness. Skilled physicians have examined it and say that if I eat three sers of human flesh every day, it will cure me. If you are able to cut three sers of flesh from your body each day and give it to me, I will give you five golden coins."

When I heard these words, my mind was filled with great joy, and I said to him, "Give me the coins and grant me seven days, and after I have done what I need to do, you may do with me as you please."

He replied, "Seven days is too long. If it is truly possible, grant me at least one day."

Good son, at that time I took the coins, went back to where the buddha was, bowed at his feet with my head, and offered and presented everything I had without remainder. Then, with a settled and composed mind, I listened to this sūtra. At that time, because my faculties were dull, though I heard this sūtra, I was able to retain only a single chapter of four lines. And this is what it was:

The passing beyond sorrow of the Tathāgata
is the utter severing of all cyclic existence.
Whoever listens to it with one-pointed mind
will forever obtain immeasurable bliss.

Having retained these verses, I went back to the sick man's house. Good son, at that time, each day I cut three sers of flesh, and yet through the power of meditating on these verses as cause and condition, I did not grow faint. Not for a single day was there any interruption; I gave in this way for a full month. Good son, through that cause and those conditions, the sick man recovered. My own body too became as it was before, free of any wound, without a scar. And when at that time I saw that my body was unharmed, I generated the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. If even a single verse has such power when one retains it fully, recites it, or proclaims it aloud — how much more need be said? Seeing that this sūtra has such benefit, I aroused an even greater aspiration than before and made this prayer: "May I in a future time attain the awakening of a buddha, and may my name be Śākyamuni."

Good son, through the cause and condition of the power of that single verse, I am today, within a great assembly, able to teach it fully and completely to gods and humans alike. Good son, therefore this Great Nirvāṇa is inconceivable. It is endowed with qualities that are boundless and without limit. This is the very essence spoken with deep intention by the Blessed One, the buddhas. Therefore whoever retains it will abandon and cut off all evil defilements.

As for "evil" — this refers to evil yaks, evil horses, evil cattle, dogs, places harboring vicious and harmful snakes, ground covered with sharp and wicked thorns, filth, precipices and chasms, desolate and dangerous places,

evil foxes and wolves, evil people, evil lands, evil towns, evil households, evil spiritual friends, and the like. If any of these become a cause for defilement, the bodhisattva abandons them. If they do not, he does not abandon them. If they generate defilement, he abandons them; if they do not generate defilement, he does not abandon them. If they lead to unwholesome Dharma, he completely abandons them; if they lead to virtue, he does not abandon them. How does he abandon them? He abandons them always through the method of a mind of solitude, unimpeded as a weapon. Therefore this is called abandonment through a mind of solitude. He abandons unwholesome Dharma in order to bring forth virtue.

The bodhisattva, the great being, understands this body to be like a disease, like a wound, like a swelling, like an enemy, like an arrow piercing the flesh, and understands that this great mass of suffering is the root of all virtue and non-virtue alike. Although this body is impure in this way, the bodhisattva nonetheless cares for it and tends to it. Why is that? Not out of attachment to the body, but for the sake of wholesome Dharma. It is for the sake of nirvāṇa, not for the sake of wandering in saṃsāra. It is for the sake of permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity — not for the sake of impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and impurity. It is for the sake of the path of awakening, not for the sake of the path of continued existence. It is for the sake of the one vehicle, not for the sake of the three vehicles. It is for the sake of the sacred body adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks — not for the sake of a body up to and including the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. It is for the sake of becoming a king who turns the wheel of Dharma, not for the sake of becoming a wheel-turning monarch.

Good son, the bodhisattva, the great being, must always guard the body. Why is that? If the body is not guarded, one will not be able to sustain life. If life is not sustained, one will be unable to transcribe, retain, read, recite, teach extensively to others, or contemplate the meaning of this sūtra. Therefore the bodhisattva must guard the body most carefully. For this very reason the bodhisattva has come to abandon all evil defilements.

Good son, consider these examples: one who crosses water guards his boat and raft with the greatest care; a traveler who has set out on the road tends most carefully to his good horse and other mounts; a farmer guards his oxen and the like with the greatest care; one who wishes to benefit from poison guards a venomous snake with the greatest care; one who possesses many goods guards against low-caste outcasts; one who goes to battle with enemies guards his fighting men with care; just as one guards fire against the cold; and just as lepers seek potent medicine — in just the same way, the bodhisattva, the great being, though seeing this body as possessed of measureless impurity and utterly filled with it, nonetheless guards and tends to it without neglect or abandonment, in order to uphold this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra as a dhāraṇī.

The bodhisattva, the great being, when he considers a vicious bull and an evil spiritual friend and the like, sees them as non-dual. Why is that? Because both bring destruction to the body. The bodhisattva, the great being, has no mind of fear and dread toward a vicious bull and the like. But toward an evil companion, he gives rise to a mind of the most intense fear and dread. Why is that? A vicious bull and the like can only destroy the body, but they cannot destroy the mind.

An evil companion can destroy both. A vicious bull and the like can destroy only the body, but an evil companion can destroy boundless virtuous bodies and boundless virtuous minds as well. A vicious bull and the like can destroy only this unclean body, but an evil companion can destroy a purified body and a purified mind. A vicious bull and the like can destroy only a body of flesh, but an evil companion can destroy the Dharma body. If one is killed by a vicious bull, one does not go to the three lower destinies, but if one is killed by an evil companion, one will without doubt go to the three lower destinies. A vicious bull and the like become an enemy of the body, but an evil companion becomes an enemy of virtuous Dharma. Therefore a bodhisattva must abandon evil companions from afar.

Defilements of this kind are not abandoned by base and ignoble people, and so defilements arise. The bodhisattva abandons them, and so defilements do not arise. If even a bodhisattva is thus free of such defilements, what need is there to speak of the Tathāgata? Therefore these are not defilements for him.

What then is meant by proximity to defilement? All base and ignoble people, for the sake of physical and mental comfort, accept robes, food, bedding, and medicines for illness and the like. Seeking such goods, they commit many kinds of evil and do not recognize their wrongdoing, and so they revolve through the three lower destinies. This is therefore called defilement.

The bodhisattva, the great being, seeing such faults, thoroughly abandons them. If he desires robes and accepts them, it is not for the sake of the body alone but solely for the sake of the Dharma. Not giving rise to pride or conceit, always maintaining a humble mind, it is not for the sake of ornament or wanting fine things, but for the sake of protection from shame, and from heat, cold, wind, driving rain, mosquitoes, gnats, and venomous creatures. When he accepts clothing and food, there is no mind of attachment, and it is not for the body's sake but always for the sake of the holy Dharma. It is not for the sake of weakness but for the sake of sentient beings. It is not for pride and conceit but for the sake of the body and its strength. It is not for the sake of animosity or enemies but to heal the wound of hunger. Even when excellent flavors are obtained, there is no mind of attachment to them. It is the same with accepting lodgings: he does not remain pervasively afflicted by attachment and pride, but makes them a place of awakening. He accepts lodgings in order to overcome the enemies of affliction and as shelter from strong winds and driving rain. In seeking medicine for illness too there is no mind of attachment; it is for the sake of the holy Dharma, not for the sake of sustaining life — rather it is to keep life going for as long as needed.

Son of good family, it is just as when someone afflicted with the disease of ulcers is rubbed with flour and butter, wrapped in cloth, and, because pus and blood have issued forth, medicine is applied to heal the ulcers and one enters a deep chamber to keep off the wind. In just the same way, the bodhisattva, the great being, regards the body as if it were a wound, covers it with cloth, and because pus oozes from the nine openings he seeks food; for shelter from strong winds and driving rain he accepts lodgings; and to counteract the four kinds of poison he seeks medicine. Thus the bodhisattva accepts the four requisites for the sake of the path to awakening and not for the sake of mere livelihood.

Why is that? The bodhisattva, the great being, thinks to himself: if I do not accept these four requisites, my body will lack support and become unstable. If it becomes unstable, suffering will become unbearable. If suffering becomes unbearable, I will not be able to practice all virtuous Dharmas fully and completely.

If one can endure suffering, one will cultivate virtuous Dharmas without measure. But if one cannot endure suffering, a mind of aversion will arise toward the experience of pain, and a mind of attachment will arise toward the experience of pleasure. If happiness is sought but not found, ignorance will arise. For these reasons, the foolish and ignoble ordinary person generates defilements from the four requisites. The bodhisattva, the great being, however, through thorough and clear discernment, does not generate defilements. Therefore, if even the bodhisattva is said to be without defilement, how much less can it be said that the Tathāgata possesses defilements — for the Tathāgata is without defilement.

Furthermore, noble son, all foolish and ignoble persons, even while guarding body and mind most carefully, give rise to three kinds of non-virtuous thought. Through these as cause and condition, the afflictions cut off entirely, yet even those reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception fall back into the three lower realms. Noble son, consider the example of a person who crosses an ocean and, just as the far shore draws near, drowns and dies in the water. The foolish and ignoble ordinary person is just like this: just as the three realms are about to be exhausted, he falls back again into the three lower realms. Why is that? Because virtuous thoughts are absent. And what are virtuous thoughts? They are the six applications of mindfulness. In the foolish and ignoble person, the virtuous mind is weak while the non-virtuous mind blazes fiercely. Because the virtuous mind is weak, the mind of wisdom becomes thin. Because the mind of wisdom is thin, all defilements arise and proliferate.

The bodhisattva, the great being, with the eye of wisdom wholly purified, sees the fault of these three kinds of thought. He understands that these three thoughts, together with their manifold faults, are at all times the enemy of sentient beings across the three vehicles. Through these three thoughts as cause and condition, measureless inferior sentient beings are prevented from seeing the nature of the buddhas, and throughout measureless eons they generate perverted minds of this sort: "The Blessed One, the Buddha, has no permanence, no bliss, no self — only purity exists. The Tathāgata has passed into final nirvāṇa, and as for all sentient beings, there is no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no purity" — and with minds of inversion they declare that permanence, bliss, self, and purity do exist. Again they say: "In reality, not even the three vehicles exist" — yet with perverted minds they declare that the three vehicles do exist. "The one path of truth is the truly true" — yet with perverted minds they declare that not even one truth exists. The three kinds of non-virtuous thought are always and utterly condemned by the buddhas and bodhisattvas. These three kinds of non-virtuous perverted thought always do great harm to oneself and others alike. Because these three thoughts are present, all non-virtues follow without cease, like a shadow that never parts. These same three thoughts become the three thorough afflictions, linking together the endless succession of sentient beings' bondage in saṃsāra.

The bodhisattva, the great being, always reflects thoroughly upon these three thoughts in this way. If, through some cause and condition, a thought of desire arises in the bodhisattva, he does not indulge it and says nothing.

Consider how a man of excellent and fastidious cleanliness will accept nothing that is soiled or impure. Consider how no one grasps a blazing fire with bare hands. By nature, a brahmin does not eat the flesh of cattle. Those who are full will not take inferior food. Just as a wheel-turning king (cakravartin) would not sit on the same seat as the lowest of outcaste birth, so too the bodhisattva, the great being, does not take up or experience the three perverted thoughts. Why is this so?

The bodhisattva reflects in this way: if all sentient beings regard me as a field of merit, how could I possibly engage in these non-virtuous phenomena? If I were to engage in such non-virtuous thoughts, I would be unworthy to be a field of merit for sentient beings. Even if I did not myself declare, "I am a field of merit," sentient beings would, seeing how I conduct myself, say that I am their field of merit. If I were to give rise to non-virtuous thoughts of that kind, I would be deceiving all sentient beings. I was deceived in precisely this way before, and so I wandered in saṃsāra for immeasurable aeons, falling into the three lower destinies. If I were to receive, with a non-virtuous mind, what a donor offered with faith, I would be condemned and reviled by all gods, humans, and sages endowed with the five higher knowledges. If I were to receive with non-virtuous thoughts what a donor offered with faith, the donor's fruit would become diminished, or the fruit would be rendered meaningless; and if I were to receive with a non-virtuous mind what the donor gave, I would become an enemy to that faithful donor. All donors regard me as they regard their only child. Why then should I deceive them and conceive of them as enemies? For if a donor fails to obtain the fruit, or the fruit becomes diminished, it would always be inappropriate for me even to be called "one who has gone forth" (pravrajita). One who has gone forth should not engage in non-virtue; it is unworthy of that status. If one produces non-virtue, one should not be called one who has gone forth. One who has gone forth is possessed of purity in body and in speech. If one lacks those qualities, one should not be called one who has gone forth.

I have abandoned my father and mother, brothers and sisters, my wife, my children, and all relatives and friends, and I have gone forth and am cultivating the path. This is the time for thoroughly cultivating wholesome thoughts, not a time for cultivating non-virtuous thoughts. It is like a person who enters the ocean to seek jewels and, rather than taking genuine jewels, takes only crystals instead. Or again, it is like someone who abandons sublime music and plays instead in a place of filth and impurity. It is like casting away a precious jewel of a daughter and sleeping with a slave woman. It is like setting aside a vessel of gold and using a clay bowl. It is like abandoning ambrosia and drinking poison instead. It is like abandoning a dear and skilled physician and receiving treatment and drinking medicine from a hostile, ill-natured physician who is one's enemy.

I am just the same: it is as though I have abandoned the taste of Dharma, which is like ambrosia, taught by the great Teacher, the buddha, the Blessed One, and instead am drinking the various kinds of non-virtuous thoughts of Māra.

A human body is exceedingly difficult to obtain, like the udumbara flower, and I have now obtained one. An encounter with a Tathāgata is exceedingly rare, like the udumbara flower, and I have now had that encounter.

To see and hear the pure jewel of Dharma is as rare as a blind tortoise finding a yoke floating upon the water, and I have now heard it. Human life does not linger — it is swifter than a deer on a steep cliff face; here today, it is not certain to remain tomorrow. Why then should I dwell with a scattered, distracted mind in non-virtuous things? Youth, too, does not linger — it is swifter even than a galloping horse. Why then be proud and arrogant on account of it? Just as a hungry ghost (preta) in a wretched state seeks any opportunity to harm a person, so too do the hungry ghosts of the four great elements always seek an occasion to cause me harm. Why, then, should I give rise to non-virtuous thoughts? Like a decaying house on the verge of collapse, my life is just the same — why, then, should I give rise to non-virtue?

I am called a renunciant (śramaṇa). The word "renunciant" means one who reflects upon virtuous thoughts. If I now give rise to non-virtuous thoughts, how can I rightly be called a renunciant? I am called one who has gone forth (pravrajita). The meaning of "gone forth" is one who cultivates the path of virtue. If I now engage in non-virtue, how can I rightly be called one who has gone forth? I am called a brahmin. The word "brahmin" means one who lives the holy life (brahmacarya). If I engage in the non-virtuous, impure thoughts of an unholy life, how can I rightly be called a brahmin? I am also called one of the great warrior-noble class (kṣatriya). "Warrior-noble" means one who has tamed the enemy. If I do not now tame the enemy of non-virtue, how can I rightly be called a warrior-noble? I am also called a monk (bhikṣu). "Monk" means one who conquers the afflictions. If today I have not conquered the afflictions through non-virtuous thoughts, how can I rightly be called a monk?

In this world, these six things are exceedingly difficult to encounter, and I have now encountered them. Why, then, should non-virtuous thoughts be allowed to dwell in the mind? What are the six? They are: the arising of a buddha in the world, which is hard to encounter; the hearing of the holy Dharma, which is difficult; the arising of a mind of urgency and spiritual fear, which is difficult; birth in a central land, which is difficult; obtaining a human body, which is difficult; and possessing all one's faculties intact, which is difficult. Such things, these six, which are so hard to obtain, I have now obtained. Therefore it is improper to give rise to non-virtuous thoughts — so he thought in his mind.

At that time, the bodhisattva who was diligently applying himself to this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa was perpetually and vigilantly examining whether diligence itself might be a form of non-virtuous mind. All those of base and ignoble character, not seeing the fault in such a non-virtuous mind, seize upon the three kinds of thought, and are therefore called defiled, possessed of outflows (āsrava). The bodhisattva, seeing this, does not seize upon them; without attachment, he utterly relinquishes and does not preserve them. Relying upon the noble eightfold path, he expels and utterly cuts them off. Therefore, if even a bodhisattva does not take up outflows, why would anyone say that the Tathāgata possesses outflows? For this very reason, the Tathāgata is not one who possesses outflows.

Son of good family, those of base and ignoble character, when tormented by suffering in body and mind, give rise to all manner of non-virtue. If the body or mind is sick and in pain, they perform all manner of non-virtuous deeds of body, speech, and mind. Having committed non-virtue, they cycle through the three lower destinies and come to experience suffering in its fullness. Why is this? Because those of base and ignoble character, lacking mindfulness and wisdom, give rise to all manner of outflows — and this is called the outflow of mindlessness.

The bodhisattva, the great being, always reflects thus: "In the past, over countless eons, on account of this body and mind, I have performed all manner of non-virtue. Through the causes and conditions of having done so, I have spun deep in cyclic existence, experienced abundant suffering in its fullness in the three lower destinies, and have kept myself far from the path of the three vehicles." Reflecting in this way, that bodhisattva, through those very causes and conditions, gives rise to a profound terror toward body and mind, thoroughly abandons the many forms of non-virtue, and enters earnestly upon the path of virtue.

Son of good family, consider this example. A certain king placed four venomous serpents inside a single vessel and commanded a man to guard them, to bathe them, to rouse them, to wash them, and to perform other such tasks. The king decreed: "If any one of these serpents becomes enraged, I shall have you put to death by the law before a great assembly of people." Upon hearing the king's command, the man was seized with great fear. He abandoned the vessel of serpents and fled. The king then dispatched five men of vile and outcast character, each bearing a sword, to pursue him from behind. The man glanced back, saw the five men coming from behind, and fled all the faster. Then the five men, by a deceitful stratagem, concealed their drawn swords and, feigning closeness and friendship, approached him. One of them said to him, "Come back!" But the man did not trust him, and in order to hide he went into a certain city. Having entered the city and looked into every house, he saw not a single person; and looking into the earthen jars and other vessels, he found them all empty, with nothing whatsoever inside. Having found neither person nor goods, he sat down on the ground, and from the empty sky a voice rang out: "Son of good family, in this empty city not a single person dwells, and tonight six hostile enemies will come. If you encounter them, you will not escape with your life — why then do you remain idle?" The man, now more terrified than before, rose from that place and set out, and along the road he came upon a great river. The river was extremely fierce, and there was neither boat nor raft; yet out of fear he gathered much grass and wood and fashioned a makeshift raft. He then thought: "If I remain here, I will be harmed by the four venomous serpents, the five vile outcasts, the one who feigned friendship, and the six hostile enemies. Yet if I try to cross this river, the raft may not hold firm and I shall sink into the water and die. But even so, it is better to drown and die than to be tormented by the serpents and enemies." With that thought he launched the grass raft into the water, seated himself upon it, paddled with his hands and kicked with his feet, cut across the current, and arrived safely at the far bank. His mind and heart became at ease, and he was free from fear and terror.

The bodhisattva, the great being, who hears and retains this great sūtra of the great nirvāṇa, should regard the body as like the vessel, should regard earth, water, fire, and wind as like the four venomous serpents — venomous through sight, venomous through touch, venomous through breath, and venomous through ingestion — for all sentient beings who come into contact with any one of those four forms of venom will meet their end. The four great serpents of sentient beings are likewise so: seeing causes one to commit non-virtue, touching causes one to commit non-virtue, associating causes one to commit non-virtue, and consuming causes one to commit non-virtue — and through those causes and conditions, one comes to abandon all virtue.

Furthermore, son of good family, the great bodhisattva contemplates that, just as the four venomous serpents fall into four kinds, so too there are four social classes: the warrior-noble class, the brahmin class, the merchant class, and the outcaste class. Likewise, the serpents of the four great elements have four distinct natures: the nature of solidity, the nature of moisture, the nature of heat, and the nature of movement. Therefore the bodhisattva regards the four great elements and the four venomous serpents as alike in nature.

Furthermore, son of good family, the bodhisattva regards the four great elements as being like the four venomous serpents. How so? The four venomous serpents are ever seeking an opportunity against a person, thinking: "When will I get to be seen? When will I get to be touched? When will my breath be inhaled? When will I get to be eaten?" In the very same way, the venomous serpents of the four great elements are always seeking out the faults and failings of sentient beings. If one is killed by the four venomous serpents, one will never go to the three lower realms. But if one is killed by the four great elements, one will certainly and without doubt go to the three lower realms — there is no question about it. The four venomous serpents, even when well tended and cared for, still think of killing a person. The four great elements are likewise: no matter how constantly one nourishes and serves them, they cause one to commit every kind of non-virtue without exception. If even one of the four venomous serpents becomes enraged, it is capable of killing a person. The nature of the four great elements is just the same: even a slight imbalance in a single great element is capable of killing a person. The four venomous serpents, though they dwell together, each has its own separate mind. The venomous serpents of the four great elements are likewise: though they abide together, each has its own distinct nature. Even if one shows respect to those four venomous serpents, they are hard to approach safely. The venomous serpents of the four great elements are just the same: even if one shows them respect, they are hard to approach safely. If one is seized by the four venomous serpents, a renunciant (śramaṇa) or brahmin or the like may be able to heal one with spells and medicine. But if one is killed by the four great elements, even if renunciants or brahmins and the like were to tend one with the finest spells and medicines, one would not recover. Even those who play with snakes, if struck by the smell of the four venomous serpents, will utterly flee. Buddhas and bodhisattvas are just the same: if they sense the smell of the four great elements, they utterly abandon them. At that moment the bodhisattva generates great fear of the venomous serpents of the four great elements, turns away from them, swiftly flees, and resolves: "I must meditate upon the noble eightfold path."

The "five vile clans" is an analogy for the five aggregates (skandhas). How does the bodhisattva regard the five aggregates as being like five vile clans? The so-called vile clan is one that is forever separated from those who are dear and beloved, and is instead delivered up to enemies and those who bear hatred. The five aggregates are just the same: they cause the great mass of beings to be attached to and to engage with unwholesome phenomena, and at the same time they cause one to be parted from every wholesome quality without exception.

Furthermore, son of good family, by way of example: the vile clan adorns itself with swords, clubs, bows and arrows, armor, spears, and weapons of every variety, and uses them to harm others. The five aggregates are just the same: thoroughly adorned with mental afflictions, they injure those who are under the sway of delusion and cause them to fall into the various states of conditioned existence. Son of good family, if a member of a vile clan encounters someone who has done wrong, he will kill them. The five aggregates are just the same: accompanied by the faults of complete affliction, they kill without cease. Therefore the bodhisattva fully understands the five aggregates to be like five vile clans.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva fully understands the five aggregates to be like a vile clan. A vile clan has no mind of loving-kindness or affection, and kills both enemies and friends alike. The five aggregates are just the same: lacking any mind of loving-kindness or affection, they kill both the virtuous and the non-virtuous alike. A vile clan harms every person. The five aggregates are just the same: through the mental afflictions, they constantly harm all sentient beings who wander in cyclic existence. Therefore the bodhisattva understands the five aggregates to be like a vile clan.

A vile clan is always accompanied by a mind intent on harm. The five aggregates are likewise always accompanied by a mind intent on harm, being thoroughly bound up with complete affliction. Just as a person on foot, without a sword or weapon and without a servant, will without question be killed by a vile clan, so too sentient beings who are without feet, without weapons, and without a servant will be killed by the five aggregates. Here, "feet" means moral discipline; "sword" means wisdom; and "servant" means a spiritual friend. Without these three, one will be harmed by the enemy that is the five aggregates. Therefore the bodhisattva understands the five aggregates to be like a vile clan.

Furthermore, son of good family, the bodhisattva, the great being, understands the five aggregates to be even worse than a vile clan. Why is that? If a sentient being is slain by a vile clan, that sentient being will not fall into the hells. But if one is slain by the five aggregates, one falls into the hells. For this reason the bodhisattva understands the five aggregates to be worse than a vile clan.

Having understood this, the bodhisattva makes this solemn pledge: "I would rather dwell together with a vile clan for an entire lifetime than associate with the five aggregates even for a single instant." A vile clan can only harm the foolish and simple-minded of the desire realm. But the enemy that is the five aggregates harms all the noble and ignoble, all the foolish throughout the three realms. A vile clan kills only those who have done wrong. But the enemy that is the five aggregates harms and thoroughly injures all sentient beings, whether they have done wrong or not. A vile clan does not harm the weak, the aged, women, or young children. But the enemy that is the five aggregates harms all sentient beings, whether old or young, whether male or female.

This is what is called the bodhisattva's understanding the aggregates to be worse than a vile clan. Therefore the bodhisattva makes this vow: "I would rather dwell together with a vile clan for an entire lifetime than approach or rely upon the five aggregates even for a single instant."

Furthermore, son of good family: a vile clan harms only others, not oneself. But the enemy that is the five aggregates harms both oneself and others, as well as those of the vile clan itself. From a vile clan one can escape by offering gentle words and precious wealth. But the five aggregates are not like that: even if one flatters them with gentle words and offers precious wealth and the like, there will be no escape. A vile clan does not kill continuously at every moment of the four periods of day and night. But the five aggregates are not like that: at every single instant, moment after moment, they kill sentient beings without ceasing. When a vile clan is spent in one place, there is room to slip away and flee. But the five aggregates are not like that: they pervade every place without exception, and there is nowhere to slip away and flee. A vile clan may kill a person, but once killed, it does not pursue them further. But the five aggregates are not like that: even after killing a sentient being, they pursue that being and never separate from it.

Therefore, a bodhisattva, even if they must dwell together with a vile clan for the whole of their life, would not draw close to the five aggregates even for a single instant. Those who possess wisdom will, through skillful means, gain liberation from the five aggregates. What is meant by skillful means? It is the noble eightfold path, the six perfections, and the four immeasurables. Through such means one becomes completely free, and neither body nor mind will be harmed by the aggregates. Why is this? Because the body is like a vajra, and the mind is like space — and for that reason it is exceedingly difficult to destroy body and mind. In light of this meaning, the bodhisattva, having understood that the five aggregates are endowed with many forms of non-virtuous phenomena, gives rise to tremendous, profound fear, and applies themselves earnestly to the noble eightfold path. This is like a person who, fearing four venomous snakes and a vile clan of five, enters the path without hindrance and departs.

One who acts like an enemy pretending to be a friend is one driven by attachment. The great bodhisattva, the bodhisattva of vast mind, fully recognizes that defilement arising from desire acts like an enemy feigning friendship. Whoever knows this in such a way cannot be overcome by anything. Whoever does not know it will without fail be harmed. Attachment is just like that. Those beings who, at that time, know its characteristic marks will not experience the suffering of wandering in cyclic existence. If they do not know it, they will revolve through the six classes of beings and experience all manner of suffering without remainder. Why is this? Because the sickness that arises from attachment is extremely difficult to abandon — just as it is difficult to abandon an enemy who feigns friendship. An enemy who feigns friendship is always seeking an opportunity: it separates one from what is dear and agreeable, and delivers one over to what is hated and hostile. Attachment is exactly the same: it keeps beings distant from all virtuous phenomena and draws them close to all non-virtuous phenomena.

In light of this, the great bodhisattva, the bodhisattva of vast mind, fully understands that attachment is like an enemy feigning friendship — for what was not seen comes to be seen, and what was not heard comes to be heard. Ordinary childlike beings may see the faults of cyclic existence, and though they possess wisdom, they are covered by delusion and so, in the end, fail to see. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are similar: though they see, it is as if they do not see; though they hear, it is as if they do not hear. Why is this? Because they are accompanied by the mind of desire. And how is that? Even though they see the faults of cyclic existence, they cannot swiftly proceed to unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. Therefore, the great bodhisattva, the bodhisattva of vast mind, fully recognizes that this affliction of desire and attachment is like an enemy feigning friendship.

What, then, are the characteristic marks of one who feigns friendship like an enemy? Consider: an enemy, while being untruthful, displays the marks of one who is truthful; while being unsuitable to draw near to or be intimate with, displays the marks of closeness; while being genuinely non-virtuous, displays the marks of virtue; and while being genuinely unlovely, displays the marks of loveliness. Why? Because such a one is always seeking an opportunity, wishing to cause harm. Desire is just like this: it perpetually deceives all sentient beings — presenting what is untrue as true, what is not close as close, what is non-virtuous as virtuous, and what is unlovely as lovely — and it perpetually deludes everyone and causes them to revolve in cyclic existence.

In light of this, the bodhisattva recognizes attachment as being like an enemy who feigns intimacy. One who feigns intimacy like an enemy — you see their actions of body and speech, but you do not see their mind, and for that reason you are deceived. Desire is just the same: it is nothing but false deception — there is no truth in it at all.

And so all sentient beings have been deceived. One who feigns intimacy like an enemy has a beginning and an end, and is therefore relatively easy to abandon. Attachment (rāga) is not like that: having neither beginning nor end, it is extremely difficult to abandon. One who feigns intimacy like an enemy is difficult to recognize from a distance, but easy to recognize when near. Desire is not like that either: even when near it is difficult to recognize — how much more so when far away. For these reasons, the bodhisattva understands attachment as something even worse than an enemy who feigns intimacy.

All sentient beings, through the complete affliction of attachment, have come to be far from great nirvāṇa and close to cyclic existence. They have come to be far from permanence, bliss, selfhood, and perfect purity, and close to impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and the impure.

Therefore, in all the sūtras, I have taught three kinds of stain. Because of ignorance, one does not see the faults and defects in present things, and so one is unable to abandon them. The feigned intimacy of the enemy of attachment can never harm one who is wise and endowed with wisdom. Therefore, the bodhisattva, having thoroughly understood this desire and given rise to great fear, applies earnest effort to the noble eightfold path — just as a person, frightened by one who feigns intimacy while harboring four venomous serpents and five wicked companions, sets out upon the road and does not turn back.

"The empty city" refers to the six sense bases (āyatanas). The bodhisattva, the great being, regards the six inner sense bases as empty, devoid of anything whatsoever — like an empty city. Just as a frightened person who enters an empty city sees not a single person and, looking into every pot and vessel, finds not a single substance — so too the bodhisattva, when he thoroughly examines the six sense bases, finds them empty and devoid of anything whatsoever, and does not find even one truly real substance belonging to a sentient being. Therefore the bodhisattva regards the six inner sense bases as empty, devoid of anything whatsoever, like that empty city.

Noble son, when enemies and thieves look upon that empty city from a distance, the perception of emptiness does not arise in them. Similarly, ordinary, foolish, worldly beings are like this: in regard to the city of the six sense bases, the perception of emptiness does not arise in them. Because the perception of emptiness does not arise, they revolve in cyclic existence and come to experience immeasurable suffering.

Noble son, just as enemies and thieves, upon actually entering that city, give rise from the outset to the perception of emptiness — so too is the bodhisattva: upon examining these six sense bases, the perception of emptiness always arises. Because the perception of emptiness has arisen, he does not revolve in cyclic existence and does not experience suffering. The bodhisattva, the great being, does not fall into error with regard to these six sense bases. Because he does not fall into error, he does not come to revolve in cyclic existence.

Furthermore, noble son, thieves who enter an empty city come to attain pleasure. The thieves of the afflictions are likewise: upon entering into those six sense bases, they come to attain pleasure. And just as thieves dwelling in an empty city have no mind of fear — so too the enemy-afflictions: dwelling within those six sense bases, they have no fear.

Just as that empty city is not harmed by lions, tigers, wolves, and...

just as an empty city is the dwelling place of all manner of fierce and harmful wild beasts, so too are these six inner sense bases: they are the dwelling place of all manner of fierce and harmful wild beasts — the afflictions. Therefore, the bodhisattva fully recognizes that the six sense bases, utterly devoid of anything real, are the dwelling place of all non-virtue.

Furthermore, noble son, the bodhisattva, the great being, recognizes that the six inner sense bases — utterly devoid of anything real — are like that empty city. Why is this? Because they are deceived by what is false: one perceives as existent what is utterly devoid of anything real, one perceives as pleasurable what is truly without pleasure, and one perceives a person where there is truly no person. The six inner sense bases are likewise: one perceives as existent what is utterly devoid of anything real, one perceives as pleasurable what is truly without pleasure, and one perceives a person where there is truly no person. Only the learned and wise are able to know this truly and as it is.

Furthermore, noble son, an empty city is at times inhabited and at times uninhabited. The six sense bases are not like that — they do not go to either extreme. Why is this? Because they are empty by essential nature. What the learned and wise know of this is not something seen with the eye.

Therefore, having understood that the six inner sense bases are filled with enemies and harms, the bodhisattva does not dwell there at ease but applies himself strenuously to the noble eightfold path — just as a person, fearing four venomous serpents, five villains, one who pretends to be a friend while plotting with treachery, and six thieves, enters upon the path of truth.

The six great enemies are the six outer sense objects. The bodhisattva, the great being, fully recognizes the six sense objects as being like six great enemies. Why is this? Because they plunder all virtuous qualities. Just as six enemies can seize all the wealth, possessions, and precious things of every person, so too the enemies of the six sense objects: they can seize all the wealth of virtue belonging to every sentient being. Just as, if six great enemies were to enter a person's home, they would not distinguish between good and poor goods but would seize everything present and reduce even the very wealthy to poverty — so too the enemies of the six sense objects: if they enter a person's sense faculties, they will plunder all virtuous qualities. Once those virtuous qualities are exhausted and one is impoverished, one commits even the deeds born of wrong craving. Therefore, the bodhisattva fully and correctly recognizes the six sense objects as being exactly like six great enemies.

Furthermore, noble son, when those six enemies set out to plunder, they need something on the inside to assist them. If there is nothing on the inside to assist them, they turn back from there on the spot. The enemies of the six sense objects are likewise: when they set out to plunder virtuous qualities, they need, on the inside, the perceiving and recognizing of sentient beings as real, and the perceiving and knowing of such signs as permanence, pleasure, self, purity, non-emptiness, and so forth. If there is no such grasping at signs as these on the inside, then the hostile enemies of the six sense objects cannot plunder all virtuous qualities. The learned and wise person has no such signs within. The foolish and base, however, do have such things within, and so the six sense objects continually come to seize the wealth of virtuous qualities. Because one has not guarded well, one is robbed. The guard is wisdom, and those who possess wisdom, having guarded well, are not robbed. Therefore, the bodhisattva understands, without distinction, that the six sense objects are exactly like six great enemies.

Thirty-first fascicle.

Furthermore, noble son, the six great enemies are able to afflict the bodies and minds of others with suffering.

The six sense-object enemies are likewise: they continually afflict the bodies and minds of sentient beings with the three kinds of suffering. The six great enemies can only rob the wealth of the present moment, but the six sense-object enemies always rob all the virtuous wealth of sentient beings across the three times. The six great enemies rejoice when the sun sets. The six hostile sense-object enemies are likewise: they rejoice when dwelling in the darkness of ignorance. The six great enemies can be brought down by kings. The six hostile sense-object enemies are likewise: they can be brought down by buddhas and bodhisattvas. When the six great enemies intend to plunder, they do not discriminate between the good and the well-born, the keen-faceted and the learned, the broadly educated and the young, the venerable and the poor, or the lowly. The six sense-object enemies are likewise: when they intend to rob virtuous qualities, they do not discriminate between anyone from the good and noble down to the poor and lowly. Even if kings were to cut off the limbs of the six great enemies, they could not thereby pacify those enemies' minds. The six hostile sense-object enemies are likewise: even if stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners were to sever their own limbs, they could not thereby rob virtuous qualities. Heroic persons can tame and bring down the six great enemies. Buddhas and bodhisattvas are likewise: they can tame and bring down the six great sense-object enemies. Just as nothing can be stolen from one who carries a large and heavy load, sentient beings are likewise: if they have a spiritual friend, the six hostile sense-object enemies cannot rob them. If the six great enemies happen to see a person's wealth, then and only then can they steal or plunder it. The six sense objects are not like that: by merely seeing, knowing, hearing, smelling, touching, or sensing, they can plunder. The six great enemies can only plunder the material wealth of human beings in the desire realm; they cannot plunder what belongs to the form realm and formless realm. The six hostile sense-object enemies are not like that: they can plunder all the precious virtuous wealth of beings in all three realms. Therefore, the bodhisattva understands the six sense objects as being even more to be scrutinized than the six enemies.
