Having understood this, one who applies oneself to the noble eightfold path without turning back in confusion is like one who, fearing four venomous serpents, five wicked men, one who feigns friendship while being treacherous, six great enemies, and an empty city, goes forth in fear and sets out on the road. What is called "encountering a great river along the way" is the afflictions. How does the bodhisattva understand the afflictions as being like a great river? Just as a powerful current can carry away and sweep aside even a powerful musk ox, the six currents of the afflictions are likewise: they can sweep away even a pratyekabuddha. Therefore, the bodhisattva understands the afflictions as being like a powerful current. It is called "a river" because it is profound and difficult to fathom its depths. It is called "great" because it has no end. Within it there are many varieties of harmful tangible objects and the like. The great river of the afflictions is likewise: it is called "exceedingly profound" because only buddhas and bodhisattvas can reach its depths. It is called "vast and great" because only buddhas and bodhisattvas can reach its far end. It is called "harmful tangible objects" because it always harms all sentient beings.

Therefore the bodhisattva understands the afflictions as being like a great body of water. The water of a great river can give rise to all grasses, trees, and forests. The water of the great river of the afflictions is likewise: it can give rise to the twenty-five states of existence of sentient beings. Therefore the bodhisattva understands the afflictions as being like a great river.

Consider the analogy: when a person falls into a great river, there is no shame or restraint. Sentient beings are likewise: when they fall into the waters of the afflictions, there is no shame or restraint. When one falls into a great body of water, one loses one's life before ever reaching the bottom. When one falls into the waters of the afflictions, it is the same: without ever touching the bottom, one revolves and revolves through the twenty-five states of existence. What is called "the bottom" here refers to the defining characteristic of emptiness. One should understand that whoever has not applied diligent effort to the defining characteristic of emptiness will never grow distant from the twenty-five states of existence. Because all sentient beings have not applied diligent effort to emptiness and signlessness, they are perpetually swept along by the fierce current of the afflictions.

A great body of water can scatter and destroy the body alone, yet it cannot scatter all virtuous qualities. The great water of the afflictions is not like that: it can destroy all virtuous qualities of both body and mind. A great fierce current can scatter and carry away only the humans of the desire realm, but the great water of the afflictions can scatter and carry away all gods and humans of the three realms. When a person strokes with the hands and kicks with the feet in a great worldly body of water, they can reach the far bank. In the great water of the afflictions, only a bodhisattva, through the boat of the six perfections, can reach the far shore. Just as a great body of water is extremely difficult to cross, the great water of the afflictions is likewise extremely difficult to cross. How is it said to be extremely difficult to cross? It is thus: even up to the bodhisattvas of the tenth ground have not yet crossed to its end — only buddhas have fully crossed to its end. Therefore it is called extremely difficult to cross.

Consider the analogy: when a person is swept away by a great body of water, they are unable to practise even a hair-tip's worth of virtuous qualities. Sentient beings are likewise: when swept away by the waters of the afflictions, they are unable to practise virtuous qualities. Just as people who have fallen into the water and are being carried away can be rescued by those who are powerful, those fallen into the waters of the afflictions who are possessed of wrong craving cannot be rescued even by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, nor even by the Tathāgatas. In the world, a great body of water, when the time of the aeon's end comes and the seven suns blaze, can be dried up. But the great river of the afflictions is not like that: even if śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate the seven branches of awakening, they cannot dry it up.

Therefore the bodhisattva understands the afflictions as being like a fierce torrent. It is as when a certain person, fearing four venomous serpents, five enemies of evil kind, one who feigns closeness while deceiving, and six great foes, abandons an empty city and sets off on the road, only to encounter a great body of water and gather grass to make a raft. The bodhisattva is likewise: fearing the venomous serpents of the four great elements, the evil kind of the five aggregates, the one who feigns closeness that is attachment (rāga), the empty city of the six sense bases, and the hostile enemies of the six objects — arriving at the bank of the waters of the afflictions — and with moral discipline, meditative absorption (samādhi), liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the six perfections,

and by cultivating the thirty-seven factors of awakening (bodhipakṣadharma), making of them a boat and a raft — relying on that raft to cross the waters of the afflictions — one reaches the far shore, the ultimate destination of nirvāṇa, which is permanent and blissful.

A bodhisattva who cultivates great nirvāṇa reflects in this way: "If I cannot endure such sufferings of body and of mind, I will be unable to liberate all sentient beings from the waters of the afflictions." Thinking thus, even while tormented by such sufferings of body and mind, the bodhisattva practices patience with full composure and acceptance. By taking up the practice of patience, no defilements (āsrava) will arise. If such a bodhisattva is already free of defilements, how much more need it be said that the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are entirely without defilement. Therefore, the Tathāgata must not be said to have defilements.

Then how is it that the Tathāgata is also said to be not entirely without defilements? The Tathāgata always enters into the company of those with defilements — for defilements are the twenty-five modes of existence — and therefore śrāvakas, childish common people, and those of lowly birth say that the Blessed One has defilements. In truth, the buddha Blessed Ones are entirely without defilement.

Good son, by that cause and that condition, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have no fixed defining characteristic. Good son, therefore, even one who breaks the four roots of moral discipline, who maligns the extensive sūtras, or who holds wrong views is not definitively condemned.

Then the great bodhisattva, the great being, the king of radiant and lofty glory, Universally Illuminating Splendid Royal Glory, addressed the Blessed One: "So it is, so it is, just as the Blessed One has declared — all phenomena likewise are without fixed determination. Because they are thus unfixed, one should understand that the Tathāgata has not finally passed into complete nirvāṇa."

"As the Blessed One previously declared, through cultivating great nirvāṇa, a bodhisattva, a great being, comes to understand — among things previously unheard — that there is nirvāṇa and great nirvāṇa. But what, may I ask, is nirvāṇa? And what is that called great nirvāṇa?"

Then the Blessed One said to the great bodhisattva, the great being, the king of radiant and lofty glory, Universally Illuminating Splendid Royal Glory: "Excellent! Excellent! Good son, only a bodhisattva who has attained the dhāraṇī of mindful retention would be able to ask as you have asked.

Good son, in the world, people speak of a lake and a great lake, a river and a great river, a mountain and a great mountain, a land and a great land, a city and a great city, a sentient being and a great sentient being, a king and a great king, a person and a great person, a god and a god among gods, a road and a great road. Nirvāṇa is similar to this: there is nirvāṇa and there is great nirvāṇa.

And what is nirvāṇa? Good son, just as one who is hungry and finds even a little food is said to be at ease — that ease is also called nirvāṇa. Just as a sick person who recovers from illness is said to be at ease — that ease too is called nirvāṇa. Just as one who is frightened and finds refuge and support is said to have attained ease — that ease too is called nirvāṇa. Just as a poor person who finds the seven precious substances is said to have attained ease — that ease too is called nirvāṇa."

Just as one who contemplates a skeleton and thereby finds that desire does not arise is said to have attained ease — that ease too is called nirvāṇa. Yet these nirvāṇas are not to be called great nirvāṇa. Why is that? Because they arise on account of hunger and thirst, illness, fear, and attachment — they are called nirvāṇa, but they are not great nirvāṇa.

Good son, if persons of inferior birth, śrāvakas, and so forth — whether on the level of conventional reality or through the condition of the noble path — sever the afflictions of the desire realm, they are said to have attained ease. That ease too is called nirvāṇa, yet it is not to be called great nirvāṇa. And the severance of afflictions beginning with the first meditative concentration, up through and including the severance of afflictions in the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception — that too constitutes the attainment of ease, and that ease too is called nirvāṇa, yet it is not to be called great nirvāṇa. Why? Because afflictions still arise, and because of the habitual tendencies of existence one is born again.

What then are the habitual tendencies of affliction? Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess habitual tendencies of affliction. This is what is meant: they say, "My body, my robes; I go, I come; I speak, I listen" — and further, they say: "The blessed buddhas are completely passed into nirvāṇa, and the nature of nirvāṇa is without self, without bliss, possessing only permanence and perfect purity." That is what is called the habitual tendency of affliction.

There is a difference in defining characteristics among the buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Yet some say that the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa forever, and that the nirvāṇa attained by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the blessed buddhas is equal — there is no difference. For that reason, what is attained by those of the two vehicles is not great nirvāṇa. Why? Because permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity are absent in it. It is great nirvāṇa that possesses permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity.

Good son, consider this example: a place that holds a vast quantity of water is called the ocean. In the same way, great nirvāṇa is called great nirvāṇa because it is the place entered by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the blessed buddhas. It gathers together immeasurable virtuous phenomena: the four meditative concentrations, the three meditative absorptions, the eight types of noble individuals, the eight sacred abodes, and the ten universal bases.

Good son, consider another example: a river that even the finest bull-elephant cannot ford is called a great river. Likewise, from śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas up to bodhisattvas of the tenth ground — those who do not see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood — that is called nirvāṇa, not great nirvāṇa. Whoever clearly sees the intrinsic nature of buddhahood — that is called great nirvāṇa. And this great nirvāṇa is fathomable only by the lord of the herd. The lord of the herd is none other than the Blessed One himself.

Good son, a great mountain is one that wrestlers such as the Mahānaga and the elder Dāla and others have long tried to scale and yet cannot ascend. Likewise, that which is not seen by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and wrestlers such as the Mahānaga — that is called great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, good son, a place where a minor king resides is called a minor city.

A place where a wheel-turning king resides is called a great city. A place where eighty thousand, sixty thousand, forty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas reside is called nirvāṇa. A place where the wheel-turning king who is the sovereign lord of the unsurpassable Dharma resides is called great and complete nirvāṇa. Therefore it is called great nirvāṇa.

Good son, consider this: a person who, upon seeing an army with its four divisions, feels no fear is called a great being. Likewise, if there is a sentient being who feels no fear at the afflicted evil karma that leads along the path of the three lower destinies, and who, in the midst of those destinies, liberates sentient beings in great numbers — know that such a one has attained great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, one who serves one's parents with reverence, shows respect to ascetics and brahmins, applies oneself diligently to virtuous qualities, speaks only truth, is free from falsehood and deceit, bears with wrongdoers patiently, and is able to give and be generous to the destitute — such a person is called a great being. A bodhisattva is likewise: cherishing all beings with loving-kindness and great compassion, becoming as a father and mother to sentient beings, liberating many beings from the river of cyclic existence, and showing all sentient beings the single path of truth — such a one is called great nirvāṇa.

Good son, what is called "great" is inconceivable. That which is inconceivable cannot be believed in by all sentient beings — therefore it is called great nirvāṇa. It is seen only by buddhas and bodhisattvas, and therefore it is called great nirvāṇa.

Now, why and for what cause and condition is it called "great"? Because its causes and conditions are immeasurable, it has from the very beginning been called great.

Good son, consider: in the world, something made by many causes and conditions is called great. Nirvāṇa is likewise — because it is attained through many causes and conditions, therefore it is called great.

Again, why is it called great? Because within nirvāṇa there exists a great self, it is called great nirvāṇa. In nirvāṇa, since it is without self yet has attained great sovereignty, it is called a great self. And how has it attained great sovereignty? It is the self that has attained the eight sovereignties.

What are the eight? The first is this: from one body manifesting many bodies, and filling with those bodies — as numerous as the finest atoms — the immeasurable world-systems of the ten directions. In reality the body of the Tathāgata is not composed of fine atoms, but by reason of sovereignty it displays bodies as numerous as the finest atoms. Such sovereignty is what is called the great self.

The second is this: filling the great trichiliocosm with a body no larger than the finest atom. In reality the body of the Tathāgata pervades the entire great trichiliocosm without limit, but by reason of this sovereignty it fills the great trichiliocosm in this way. Such sovereignty is what is called the great self.

The third is this: with a body that fills the entire great trichiliocosm, soaring through empty space and travelling beyond buddha-fields as numerous as the grains of sand of twelve Ganges rivers without any obstruction. In reality the body of the Tathāgata has neither heaviness nor lightness, but by reason of sovereignty it acts as if heavy or light. Such sovereignty is what is called the great self.

By reason of sovereignty, mastery is attained. What, one might ask, is that sovereignty? The Tathāgata abides in perfect one-pointed stillness: without moving, he displays forms and physical characteristics of measureless variety and, each by each, his mind pervades each being ripe for taming. By performing on occasion a single act, the Tathāgata accomplishes the individual purposes of each and every sentient being. Though the body of the Tathāgata always abides in one buddha-field, he causes beings in all other buddha-fields to behold it. Such sovereignty is what is called the great self.

The fourth is mastery through the faculties. What is it to have mastery through the faculties? Through a single faculty the Tathāgata sees form, hears sound, smells scent, tastes flavor, feels what is tangible, and knows phenomena; yet through the six faculties of the Tathāgata he does not see form, does not hear sound, does not smell scent, does not taste flavor, does not feel what is tangible, and does not know phenomena. By reason of sovereignty, he exercises mastery through the faculties. Such sovereignty is what is called the great self.

Through sovereignty, all phenomena are attained. In the mind of the Tathāgata there is no perception of having attained anything. Why is that? Because there is nothing that is being acquired. If there were something that existed and one spoke of acquiring it, how could one speak of acquiring what in truth is utterly nonexistent? If the Tathāgata possessed a perception of having attained something, the Tathāgata would not have passed into nirvāṇa. Since there is nothing being acquired, he is said to have passed into nirvāṇa. Through sovereignty, all phenomena are attained; and because all phenomena are attained, this is called the great self.

Through mastery over exposition, the Tathāgata might expound the meaning of a single verse throughout measureless eons and the meaning would never be exhausted. Whether he is teaching moral discipline, meditative absorption, generosity, or wisdom, the Tathāgata at that moment does not think "I am now expounding" or "the other beings are listening," and he does not even generate the perception of a single verse. In the world, what worldly people call a single verse consists of four lines, and so in conformity with convention he speaks of a single verse. In reality the essential nature of phenomena has never been expounded; yet through sovereignty the Tathāgata expounds it, and because he expounds it, this is called the great self.

The Tathāgata pervades all places, like empty space. The essential nature of space is that it is invisible. Similarly the Tathāgata, in ultimate reality, is equally invisible, yet through sovereignty he causes all to be seen. Such sovereignty is what is called the great self.

Such a great self is called the great nirvāṇa, and for that reason it is called the great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, noble son, consider a great treasury of jewels: because it contains wealth in vast quantity and of every variety, it is called a great treasury. The supremely profound treasure of the Tathāgata is just like this: it possesses what is wondrous and marvelous, and since it admits of no diminishment, it is called the great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, noble son, an inexhaustible store of riches is called a great treasury. Nirvāṇa likewise is called great because it is without limit.

Furthermore, noble son, because there is great bliss, it is called the great nirvāṇa — for nirvāṇa does not lack bliss. Because of four kinds of bliss, it is called the great nirvāṇa. What are the four? The first is because all sufferings have been cut. Whatever has not cut off suffering is called suffering; and that in which suffering exists cannot be called great bliss. Because suffering has been cut, there is no suffering.

The absence of both suffering and bliss is called great bliss. The intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa is free from both suffering and bliss; and therefore nirvāṇa is called great bliss. For this reason it is called the great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, noble son, bliss is of two kinds: that of the foolish common being, and that of the buddhas. The bliss of the foolish common being is impermanent and subject to destruction, and so it is not true bliss. The permanence and bliss of the Tathāgata are free from change and transition; therefore it is called the great nirvāṇa.

Noble son, furthermore, feeling is of three kinds. What are the three? Feeling felt as pleasant, feeling felt as painful, and feeling felt as neither pleasant nor painful. Even that feeling of neither pleasure nor pain is itself suffering. Nirvāṇa likewise resembles the feeling of neither pleasure nor pain, yet it is called great bliss. Because it is great bliss, it is called the great nirvāṇa.

It is called the great nirvāṇa because it is utterly tranquil. The intrinsic nature of nirvāṇa is utter tranquility. Why? Because it is utterly tranquil through being free from all conditioned phenomena, it is called the great nirvāṇa.

It is called great bliss because of knowing all things. What does not know all things cannot be called bliss. The Blessed One, the buddha, is omniscient, and therefore it is called great bliss. Because it is great bliss, it is called the great nirvāṇa.

It is called great bliss because the body is indestructible. What has a destructible body cannot be called bliss. The body of the Tathāgata is indestructible as a vajra; it is not a body born of affliction, it is not an impermanent body — and therefore it is called great bliss. Because it is great bliss, it is called the great nirvāṇa.

Noble son, among the names given in the world, some have causes and conditions, and some have no causes and conditions.

Those that have causes and conditions are, for example: the monk Śāriputra — because his mother bore the name Śārī, he was named Śāriputra on account of that condition. The nun named Tūlā was born in the region of Tūlā, and so she was named Tūlā after the name of that region. Maudgalyāna is a clan name, and because he was named after his clan, he is called Maudgalya. As for myself, I was born into the lineage of the Gautamas, and therefore I was given the name Gautama. The monk Biṣaka — Biṣaka is the name of a star, and having received his name from that star's name, he is called Biṣaka. Just as one who has six fingers is named Six-Fingers on account of having six fingers. Buddhādatta and Devadatta are named Buddhādatta and Devadatta by reason of the Buddha and of the gods respectively. One born from warmth and moisture is named Born-from-Warmth-and-Moisture by reason of that condition. Birds, for example, are named Kāka, Kukula, and Tsutsula after the sounds they make. Names such as these are names given on account of causes and conditions.

Names with no causes and conditions are like the following: lotus, earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Mandapa is called "a drinking hall" — yet even one who does not drink in a hall is called by this name. Sarvacchādana is called "a snake's hood" — yet in truth it is not a snake's hood, and so this is a name forcibly imposed without basis in fact. Just as the word Jilabāyi is said to mean "one who drinks butter" — yet in truth this person does not drink butter, and is still called "one who drinks butter"; this too is a name forcibly imposed without any real cause.

O son of noble family, this great nirvāṇa is likewise a name forcibly imposed without causes and conditions.

O son of noble family, consider this: space is not called "great" by virtue of some small measure of space. Nirvāṇa is the same: it is not called "great nirvāṇa" by virtue of some small measure of characteristic. O son of noble family, consider this: that which is immeasurable in Dharma and inconceivable is called "great." Nirvāṇa is likewise: because it is immeasurable and inconceivable in its complete transcendence, it is called "great nirvāṇa." Because it is solely and utterly pure, it is called "great nirvāṇa."

Now, why is it called solely and utterly pure? Utter purity has four aspects. In this regard, the twenty-five modes of existence are called "impure." By their complete severance, one speaks of "utter purity." This very purity is called nirvāṇa. Yet in relation to that nirvāṇa, what is called "existence" — nirvāṇa in truth is not existence at all. The Blessed One, the Buddha, spoke of nirvāṇa as though it were existence, following the ways of the world. Just as worldly people say "father" and "mother" of those who are not in truth father and mother, calling them father and mother even though in truth they are not — nirvāṇa is likewise: following the ways of the world, it was said that the Tathāgata possesses great nirvāṇa.

Purity of action: all those of base family are without nirvāṇa because their actions are impure. The Blessed One, the Buddha, because his activity is utterly pure, is called the utterly and greatly pure one. Because he is greatly and utterly pure, he is called one who has attained great nirvāṇa.

Purity of body: if a body is impermanent, it is impure. The body of the Tathāgata is permanent, and therefore it is called greatly and utterly pure. Because it is greatly and utterly pure, it is called great nirvāṇa.

Purity of mind: if the mind is accompanied by defilements, it is called impure. The Tathāgata is without defilements, and therefore is called greatly and utterly pure. Because he is greatly and utterly pure, he is called great nirvāṇa. These are the four.

O son of noble family, a son or daughter of noble family who has meditated upon this sūtra of great nirvāṇa is said to possess the first of its qualities.

Furthermore, O son of noble family, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, come to possess the second merit from diligently applying themselves to this sūtra of great nirvāṇa? O son of noble family, when a bodhisattva, a great being, diligently applies themselves to this sūtra of great nirvāṇa, they will attain what they had not previously attained, they will see what they had not previously seen, they will hear what they had not previously heard, they will reach what they had not previously reached, and they will know what they had not previously known.

Now, how will they attain what they had not previously attained? It is as follows: they will attain miraculous powers not previously attained. Miraculous powers are of two kinds: outer and inner. The outer kind is shared in common with tīrthikas, non-Buddhist adherents. The inner kind again has two aspects: that common to the two vehicles, and that of the bodhisattva. The miraculous powers attained by a bodhisattva diligently applying themselves to this sūtra of great nirvāṇa are not shared in common with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why are they not shared in common with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas? It is as follows: the miraculous powers and displays of transformation produced by the two vehicles involve but a single intention and a single act — they do not multiply into many.

A bodhisattva is not like that. With a single intention, the bodhisattva can display a body that is fully perfected across the five pathways of travel. Why is this? Because through the blessing of this sūtra of great nirvāṇa, the bodhisattva has gained power — this is called "attaining what was not previously attained."

And what does it mean to attain now what was not previously attained? It means attaining mastery over the body and mastery over the mind. What exactly does this entail? All ordinary, undisciplined beings lack mastery over body and mind: in some cases, the mind follows after the body, and in other cases, the body follows after the mind.

How is it that the mind follows after the body? Consider those who are drunk from alcohol — since the alcohol is within the body, when the body sways, the mind sways along with it. Likewise, when the body is fatigued, the mind too becomes fatigued. This is what is called the mind following after the body. Moreover, a person whose body is small has a small mind as well, and a great person whose body is large has a correspondingly large mind. Furthermore, there are those whose body is coarse, and on that account the mind constantly craves smoothness, softness, and pliability. This too is called the mind following after the body.

And how is it that the body follows after the mind? In this way: in going, in coming, in sitting, in lying down, in practicing generosity, in maintaining moral discipline, in cultivating patience, in applying diligence — whoever is overcome by grief has a face that is drawn and wan. Whoever is joyful has a body that is nourished and a complexion that is bright. Whoever is frightened has a body that trembles. Whoever listens to the Dharma with one-pointed attention has a body that is greatly at ease. Whoever beats their breast and weeps has tears and mucus flowing forth. This is what is called the body following after the mind.

A bodhisattva is not like that. Having attained mastery over both body and mind together, this is called "attaining now what was not previously attained."

Furthermore, noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, can display the faculty of the body as though it were a dust mote. With that body, no larger than a mote, the bodhisattva travels unobstructed through buddha-fields as numerous as the measureless and boundless grains of sand of the Gaṅgā river — and yet the mind remains ever still, unmoved from its former abode. This is called the mind not following after the body, and it may also be called "going where one has not gone before."

And what does it mean to go where one has not gone before? All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to go there. Because the bodhisattva goes there, it is called "going now where none has gone before." All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do indeed possess miraculous powers, but they are unable to emanate their bodies as though a dust mote and travel through buddha-fields as numerous as the measureless sands of the Gaṅgā. For śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, when the body moves, the mind moves along with it.

A bodhisattva is not like that. Though the mind does not stir, there is nowhere that the body has not reached. This is called a bodhisattva's mind not following after the body.

Furthermore, noble son, a bodhisattva can emanate this body so that it equals the world-system of a great trichiliocosm, and that vast body can enter into a single dust mote — yet the mind at that time does not become correspondingly small. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can indeed emanate their bodies to the size of a great trichiliocosm, but they cannot cause that enormous body to enter into a dust mote. If they cannot accomplish even such feats as these, how much less can they keep the mind unmoved! This is called a bodhisattva's mind not following after the body.

Furthermore, noble son, a great bodhisattva can, with a single sound, cause all sentient beings throughout the world-system of a great trichiliocosm to hear it in their ears — yet he does not think, "By this sound of mine, let beings throughout all world-systems hear what they had not heard before." Nor did the bodhisattva, from the very beginning, ever say, "By my own effort I will cause beings to hear what they have not heard." If a bodhisattva were to say, "Through my teaching of the Dharma, I will cause beings to hear what they have not heard," one should know that such a person will never attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Why is that? The thought "I have taught this so that beings who had not heard it may hear" is a thought rooted in saṃsāra, and all bodhisattvas have utterly exhausted that thought. For this reason, body and mind do not companion one another in the great bodhisattva. Noble son, all immature childish beings have body and mind companioning one another. The bodhisattva is not like that: though he may display a small body for the benefit of sentient beings, his mind does not become small. Why? Because the intrinsic nature of a bodhisattva's mind is always vast, so that even when a great body is displayed, the mind does not become great. How great is the great body? It is like the world-system of a great trichiliocosm. How small is the mind? It engages in the conduct of a small child. This is why the mind does not follow after the body.

Although a great bodhisattva may go without drinking alcohol for measureless hundreds of thousands of aeons, the mind may still be stirred. Though the mind knows no suffering or despair, tears may fall from the eyes. Though there is no genuine fear, the body may tremble violently. Therefore, it should be understood that the bodhisattva, having gained mastery over body and mind, is one in whom body and mind do not companion one another. When a great bodhisattva displays a single body, sentient beings each see it differently from their own vantage point.

Furthermore, noble son, what is it that the great bodhisattva hears — what had not been heard before — through diligent study of the sūtras of the great Mahāparinirvāṇa? The great bodhisattva's prior engagement with the characteristics of sound is as follows: the sounds of camels and oxen, the sounds of horses, the sounds of chariots, the sounds of human voices, the sounds of conch shells, the sounds of drums, the sounds of flies and insects, the sounds of flutes and other instruments, the sounds of song, and the sounds of weeping — all of these he meditates upon thoroughly. Through sustained and repeated meditation, he comes to hear all the sounds of the hell-beings throughout as many world-systems of a great trichiliocosm as are immeasurable and boundless. Through yet further repeated meditation, he attains a faculty of hearing that is distinct, a faculty of divine hearing that is different from the miraculous ear faculties of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why? Because attaining the superknowledge of the ear, purified by the second vehicle, depends upon the four great dhyānas of the first dhyāna: relying upon only the first dhyāna one hears only its range, and so it is from the second dhyāna through to the fourth dhyāna. Even hearing simultaneously all sounds that exist in the world-system of a great trichiliocosm, one is still unable to hear the sounds of as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, immeasurable and boundless. Therefore, the bodhisattva's hearing is distinct from the faculty of the ear of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Through this distinction, what was previously unheard now comes to be heard. Yet even as a sound is heard, the mind has from the very beginning no characteristic of hearing a sound — no characteristic of existence, no characteristic of permanence, no characteristic of bliss, no characteristic of self, no characteristic of purity, no characteristic of ownership, no characteristic of support, no characteristic of agency, no characteristic of being a cause, no characteristic of certainty, and no characteristic of being a result. It is for this reason that bodhisattvas have now heard what was previously unheard.

Then the great bodhisattva (bodhisattva mahāsattva) Universally Illuminating, Sublime King of Glory, spoke in petition: "What the Blessed One has declared — that sounds possess neither the characteristic of certainty nor the characteristic of result — does not appear to me to be so. Why? Because the Blessed One previously declared that if someone hears even a single verse or even a single syllable of this great sūtra of great nirvāṇa, they will without question attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Now, is the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening not itself the characteristic of certainty and the characteristic of result? Then why has the Blessed One declared that there is no certainty and no result? Again, when one hears an unpleasant sound, malice arises in the mind, and through that malice one falls into one of the three lower destinies. Is not that very falling into the three lower destinies itself the certain result? Then why has the Blessed One declared that there is no certainty and no result?"

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, it is good that you have had the boldness to ask in this way. If the Blessed One were to declare that sounds possess the characteristic of certainty and the characteristic of result, that would not be the characteristic of a buddha, a Blessed One — it would be the characteristic of the king of māras, the characteristic of saṃsāra, the characteristic of being far from nirvāṇa. Why? Because everything declared by the Blessed One, the buddha, is without the characteristic of certainty and without the characteristic of result. Noble son, take this example: when one looks at a human face reflected inside a sword blade, looking along the length of it the face appears long, and looking across it the face appears wide. Now if that appearance had the characteristic of certainty, why would the face appear long when looked at lengthwise and wide when looked at crosswise? For this reason, everything declared by the Blessed One, the buddha, is without the characteristic of certainty and without the characteristic of result. Noble son, nirvāṇa is not the result of a sound. If nirvāṇa were the result of a sound, you should understand that nirvāṇa would not be a permanent phenomenon. Noble son, take this example: in the world, phenomena that arise through dependent origination have a cause and therefore also have a result. Where there is no cause, there is likewise no result; and where the cause is impermanent, the result too is impermanent. Why? Because from the cause comes the result, and from the result comes the cause in turn. For this reason, all phenomena are without the characteristic of certainty. If the passing beyond sorrow were born from a cause, then since the cause itself is impermanent the result too would be impermanent. Therefore, the passing beyond sorrow is not born from a cause, and its essential nature is not a result — and for this reason it is permanent. Noble son, for this reason, the essential nature of the passing beyond sorrow has no certainty and no result. Noble son, the passing beyond sorrow may be spoken of as certainty, and it may also be spoken of as result. In what sense is it certainty? Because the nirvāṇa of all buddhas is permanent, blissful, self, and

because it is utterly pure — that is certainty. Because it has no birth, no aging, and no dissolution — that is certainty. Because those who have abandoned wrong craving, those who have broken the four root defeats, those who have slandered the vast sūtras, and those who have committed the five acts of immediate consequence will, when they relinquish their former mind, without question attain it — and for that reason it is certainty.

Noble son, as for what you said — that if someone hears even a single verse or a single syllable of this sūtra of the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow they will attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening — since you have not yet clearly understood the meaning of that statement, listen closely and reflect carefully, for I shall open it up and explain it.

Noble son, if a son or daughter of good family hears even a single syllable or a single verse from the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow, and upon hearing it does not grasp at the characteristic of a syllable, does not grasp at the characteristic of a verse, does not grasp at the characteristic of what has been heard, does not grasp at the characteristic of a buddha, and does not grasp at the characteristic of what has been taught — that is called the characteristic of non-characteristic. And through that characteristic of non-characteristic, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Noble son, as for what you said — that hearing a harsh sound causes one to go to one of the three lower destinies — that too is not the case. Why? Because it is not the harsh sound itself that causes one to go to the three lower destinies; rather, what causes that is a malicious mind. Why? Because if a son or daughter of good family hears a harsh sound yet does not give rise to a malicious mind, then the condition of the harsh sound does not cause that being to go to the three lower destinies. It is because sentient beings let malicious minds born of affliction spread and multiply that they are born in the three lower destinies — not because of a harsh sound as their condition. If sound possessed the defining characteristic of certainty, then everyone who heard it would be of the type to generate a malicious mind. But in some it arises and in others it does not; therefore you should understand that sound has no defining characteristic of certainty. And because it has no defining characteristic of certainty, even when sound serves as a condition, a malicious mind does not necessarily arise.

A question was put: Blessed One, if sound is not determinate, why would bodhisattvas come to hear what they had not heard before?

Noble son, it is precisely because sound has no defining characteristic of certainty that bodhisattvas who had not previously heard come to hear it now. That is why I said, "what was not previously heard is now heard."

Noble son, in what sense is "what was not previously seen now seen"? Noble son, for a great bodhisattva who applies himself diligently to this sūtra of the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow, engagement with the characteristics of what formerly appeared is as follows. Through long habituation to the light of the sun, the moon, stars, masses of fire, lamps, jewels, firelight, medicines, and the like, he attains a distinct faculty of the eye — distinct from that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

In what way distinct? One who has attained the pure celestial eye by means of the two vehicles, if they rely on the eye faculty of the four great kings of the desire realm, cannot see the first dhyāna. If they rely on the first dhyāna, they cannot see anything above it, and downward too they are unable to see as far as their own eye. Even if they see a great deal, they cannot see beyond the world-system of the great trichiliocosm.

But the great bodhisattva, even without having cultivated the celestial eye, sees all bodies possessed of fine form as having the characteristic of a skeleton. He sees as many world-systems as there are grains of sand along the Ganges River, perceiving the characteristics of form in all of them — yet he does not grasp at those appearances as a defining characteristic of form.

He does not grasp at it as the characteristic of permanence, as the characteristic of existence, as the characteristic of substantial reality, as the characteristic of name and letter, of cause and condition, or of seeing. Nor does he say, "This is the characteristic of the eye as something supreme and perfectly pure." Rather, he sees form with the characteristic of dependent origination, and sees it also with the characteristic of what is not dependently originated.

How is it dependently originated? Form is the condition for the eye. Were form not dependently arisen, it would follow that even the most foolish and base among men would not give rise to the perception of seeing form. Therefore form is said to be dependently originated. As for what is meant by "not dependently originated": even though the great bodhisattva perceives form, he does not generate the characteristic of form. Therefore it is said to be not dependently originated.

For this reason, the pure miraculous eye that a bodhisattva obtains differs from what is obtained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Because it differs in this way, he simultaneously sees all the buddhas presently dwelling in the world-systems of the ten directions — and this is called the bodhisattva's seeing what was not seen before. Because it differs in this way, he sees things as fine as the subtlest particles, which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot see. Because it differs in this way, although his own eye sees, it has no characteristic of seeing from the very beginning. He sees with the characteristic of impermanence, and he sees the body of any person as completely filled with the thirty-six impure substances, like a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of the hand. For this reason it is said that what was not seen before is now seen.

If, the very moment he sees the form and appearance of any sentient being, he recognizes whether that being belongs to the Great Vehicle or to the lesser vehicle — and even from a single touch of clothing he knows the distinguishing characteristic of that person's faculties of virtue and non-virtue — then for this reason what was not known before becomes known now. From a single glance alone, what was previously unknown becomes known. Because he knows in this way, what was not seen before is now seen.


The Thirty-Second Fascicle.

Furthermore, son of good family, how does a bodhisattva know what was previously unknown? The great bodhisattva, even while knowing the minds of attachment, aversion, and delusion in the most foolish and base of people, does not grasp at those minds from the very beginning as having the characteristic of mind or of what arises from mind. He does not grasp at them as having the characteristic of sentient being or of substantial reality, but applies himself diligently to the characteristic of the ultimate, which is empty to its very end. Why is this? Because all bodhisattvas are ever engaged in diligent application to the characteristic of emptiness. By this diligent application to emptiness, what was previously unknown becomes known.

How is it known? He knows the absence of self and the absence of what belongs to a self, and he knows that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature (Skt. tathāgatagarbha). Because they possess the buddha-nature, those who harbour wrong craving, if they abandon their former minds, will all come to fully manifest unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. These things śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to know, but a bodhisattva is able to know them — and for that reason it is said that what was previously unknown is now known.

Furthermore, son of good family, how does one come to know what was previously unknown? When the great bodhisattva applies himself diligently to the noble sūtra-text of the Great Nirvāṇa, he comes to know the birthplaces, family lines, fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters, wives, children, friends, and companions of all sentient beings in the time of the past —

by recalling enemies, one attains in a single instant a distinctive gnosis — a gnosis that surpasses the gnosis of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. How is it surpassing? The wisdom of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas recalls, regarding sentient beings of the past, their family lines, fathers and mothers, relatives, and enemies, and thereby produces the defining characteristics of family, kin, and enemy. A bodhisattva is not like this: although he too recalls past family lines, fathers and mothers, relatives, and enemies, he does not produce the defining characteristics of family, fathers and mothers, kin, enemies, and so forth. Instead, he constantly enters into the defining characteristic of Dharma and the defining characteristic of emptiness and peace. That is what is called the bodhisattva's knowing what was previously unknown.

Furthermore, son of good family, how else does one come to know what was previously unknown? The gnosis of knowing others' minds that the great bodhisattva obtains through applying himself diligently to the noble sūtra-text of the Great Nirvāṇa differs from that obtained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. How does it differ? When śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas know the minds of humans in a single instant, they do not at that same moment know the minds of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, or gods. A bodhisattva is not like this: in a single instant he knows the minds of all sentient beings throughout the six classes of beings. That is called the bodhisattva's knowing what was previously unknown.

Son of good family, there is yet another distinction in knowing. The great bodhisattva, in a single moment of intention, knows from the very first mind of one who has entered the stream, and knows in succession up to the sixteenth mind. For that reason it is called knowing what was previously unknown. These, then, are what is meant by the great bodhisattva's being endowed with the second quality through applying himself diligently to the Great Nirvāṇa.

Moreover, son of good family, how is it that the great bodhisattva is endowed with the third quality through applying himself diligently to the Great Nirvāṇa? Son of good family, the great bodhisattva who applies himself diligently to the Great Nirvāṇa: even if he relinquishes loving-kindness, he will attain loving-kindness. And the loving-kindness he attains is not conditioned by dependent origination. How is it that one attains loving-kindness even after relinquishing it? Son of good family, what is called loving-kindness is a conventional truth. The great bodhisattva relinquishes conventional loving-kindness and thereby attains ultimate loving-kindness. Ultimate loving-kindness is not attained through conditions.

Furthermore, how is it that one attains loving-kindness even after relinquishing it? If a loving-kindness is of the kind that can be relinquished, it is called the inferior loving-kindness of common folk. That loving-kindness which is of the kind that can be attained is called the bodhisattva's objectless loving-kindness.

If one relinquishes the loving-kindness of those given to wrong craving, the loving-kindness of those who have broken the four root vows, the loving-kindness of those who slander the extensively proclaimed teaching, and the loving-kindness of those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, one attains affectionate loving-kindness, the Tathāgata's loving-kindness, the Blessed One's loving-kindness, and loving-kindness free from cause and condition.

Furthermore, how is it that one attains loving-kindness even after relinquishing it? When one relinquishes the loving-kindness shown toward the sexually diminished, the sexually indeterminate, the genderless, the two-gendered, and women; toward those of low birth, butchers, hunters, and those who rear birds and pigs and so forth; and when one relinquishes the loving-kindness of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas — one attains the objectless loving-kindness of bodhisattvas, loving-kindness that does not regard anything as a self, loving-kindness that does not regard anything as other, loving-kindness that does not regard anyone as virtuous in ethical conduct, loving-kindness that does not regard anyone as poor in ethical conduct,

one attains compassion that, though perceived as dwelling within oneself, does not regard its object as a sentient being, and that, though there is feeling perceived as suffering, does not regard that suffering as something experienced. Why is this? Because one cultivates the ultimate meaning precisely as it is. This is called possessing the third quality of a bodhisattva, a great being, who is devoted to the great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, son of good family, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, who is devoted to the great nirvāṇa come to possess the fourth quality? Son of good family, when a bodhisattva, a great being, is devoted to the great nirvāṇa and possesses the fourth quality, there are ten aspects to that. What are the ten? They are as follows: being firmly rooted, grounded in a way that is hard to dislodge; generating the perception of being utterly certain of oneself; not discriminating between merit and non-merit; purifying buddha fields; removing what is residual; cutting off the cause of karma; cultivating a purified body; fully recognizing conditions; abandoning enemies; and cutting through the two extremes.

Now, how is one firmly rooted, grounded in a way that is hard to dislodge? In this context, the root is called heedfulness. What is the root of heedfulness? It is the root of unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. Son of good family, the roots of virtue of all buddhas are heedfulness. Because of heedfulness, other roots of virtue likewise grow and arise in ever-increasing measure. As roots of virtue grow and multiply, they become supreme and distinguished among all virtues.

Son of good family, just as among footprints, the footprint of the great ox is supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it becomes supreme and supremely distinguished among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among lights, the light of the sun is supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it becomes supreme and supremely distinguished among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among kings, the wheel-turning king is supreme and foremost, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it becomes supreme and foremost. Son of good family, just as among flowing waters, the four great rivers are supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it becomes supreme among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among mountains, Mount Meru, the king of mountains, is supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it becomes supreme among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among water-born lotuses, the blue lotus is most excellent, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it becomes supreme among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among flowers born on dry land, the campaka flower is supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it becomes supreme among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among beasts of prey, the lion is supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it becomes supreme and foremost among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among birds, the king of garuḍas is supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it is supreme and most excellent among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among great bodies, the asura king called Rāhu is supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it is supreme and most excellent among all virtuous qualities.

Son of good family, just as among beings — whether two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, or

footless — among all of them the Tathāgata is supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it is supreme among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among the many assemblies the Saṅgha of the buddhas is supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it is supreme among all virtuous qualities. Son of good family, just as among all the qualities of the buddhas the quality of great nirvāṇa is the most excellent and supreme, so too the quality of heedfulness is like that: it is the most excellent and supreme among all virtuous qualities.

Son of good family, therefore the root of heedfulness is deep and firm, and exceedingly difficult to uproot. Now, how is it that heedfulness grows and arises ever more and more? It is like this: through heedfulness, the root of faith, the root of moral discipline, the root of generosity, the root of wisdom, the root of patience, the root of learning, the root of diligence, the root of mindfulness, the root of meditative absorption, and the root of spiritual friendship — these and other such roots grow and arise ever more and more. Having thus grown and arisen, they become exceedingly deep and firm, and are most difficult to uproot. It is for this reason that it is said that, through a bodhisattva mahāsattva's earnest application to the great nirvāṇa, the root becomes deep and difficult to uproot.

Now, how does one enter into what is characterized as certainty with respect to the body? One generates a mind of certainty regarding one's own body, thinking thus: this very body of mine will, in the future, certainly and without doubt become a vessel for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening; and the mind too shall be correspondingly free from smallness and weakness, shall not shift and change, shall not be the mind of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, shall not be the mind of Māra, shall not be a mind seeking one's own happiness or inclined toward saṃsāra, but shall always seek a mind of loving-kindness and compassion for the sake of sentient beings. This is the thought the bodhisattva generates: through this very body of mine, I shall certainly and without doubt, in the future, become a vessel for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. It is therefore said that the bodhisattva mahāsattva, through earnest application to the great nirvāṇa, generates the perception of certainty regarding his own body.

Now, how is it that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not conceptually discriminate between a field of merit and what is not a field of merit? Here, what is called a field of merit extends from one who has entered into the austerities of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) all the way up to the buddhas — all of these are called fields of merit. If one thinks to oneself, "These are the true and genuine fields of merit," then one should understand that such a mind is weak and small. The bodhisattva mahāsattva does not regard even a single one among all immeasurable sentient beings as not being a field of merit. Why is that? Because one has thoroughly cultivated undivided mindfulness. One who possesses and has thoroughly cultivated undivided mindfulness sees all sentient beings without distinction as those who guard moral discipline or those who have broken moral discipline, and sees them all as obtaining the perfectly pure fruit of the four kinds of giving taught by the Blessed One, the buddhas. What are the four? They are these: the giver is pure but the recipient is impure; the giver is impure but the recipient is pure; both giver and recipient are pure; and both giver and recipient are impure. How is it that the giver is pure and the recipient is impure? It is like this:

The giver is endowed with moral discipline, extensive learning, and wisdom, and understands that giving exists and that the fruit of giving ripens. The recipient, however, has broken moral discipline, clings to wrong views, and regards giving as nonexistent and its fruit as nonexistent. This is called "the giver is pure and the recipient is impure."

How is it that the recipient is pure and the giver is impure? In that case, the giver has broken moral discipline, clings to wrong views, and regards giving and the ripening of the fruit of giving as nonexistent. The recipient, however, observes moral discipline, possesses extensive learning and wisdom, and understands that giving exists and that the fruit of giving ripens. This is called "the giver is impure and the recipient is pure."

How is it that both giver and recipient are pure? In that case, both giver and recipient observe moral discipline, possess extensive learning and wisdom, and understand that giving exists and that the fruit of giving ripens. This is called "both giver and recipient are pure."

How is it that both are impure? Both giver and recipient have broken moral discipline, hold wrong views, and regard giving and the ripening of the fruit of giving as nonexistent.

If that is so, why should such giving be called "obtaining a perfectly pure fruit"? In that case, since there is neither giving nor fruit, it is not to be called pure. Noble son, one who does not see giving or the fruit of giving is to be understood as not being someone who has broken moral discipline or clung to wrong views. If, like a śrāvaka, one does not see giving or the fruit of giving, that is called having broken moral discipline and clinging to wrong views. But one who does not see giving or the fruit of giving in the manner of a scripture of the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra is called guarding moral discipline and holding right view.

A great bodhisattva who possesses and has thoroughly cultivated undivided mindfulness does not see sentient beings as those who observe moral discipline or those who have broken it, does not see givers or recipients, and does not see the fruit of giving. Therefore it is designated "right view in keeping with moral discipline." For this reason, the great bodhisattva does not conceptually discriminate between a field of merit and what is not a field of merit.

As for how such a bodhisattva purifies a buddha-field: the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to this excellent sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, when liberating sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, utterly relinquishes any intention to take life. That root of virtue he then makes common to all sentient beings and makes this aspiration: "May all sentient beings obtain long life, strength, splendor, and great miraculous power." Through the force of that aspiration, when he attains buddhahood in a future time, all the sentient beings of that buddha-field, however many there may be, will all enjoy long life, be endowed with might and strength, and obtain great miraculous power.

Furthermore, noble son, when the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to the Great Nirvāṇa, liberates sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, he utterly relinquishes any intention to take what has not been given. That root of virtue he likewise makes common to all sentient beings and makes this aspiration: "May all the buddha-field grounds, however many there are, become nothing but the seven precious substances, and may sentient beings enjoy and make use of them for themselves and be wealthy and content."

By the power of that aspiration, when he attains complete awakening in the future, every buddha-field will be nothing but the seven precious substances, and all sentient beings will enjoy and make use of them for themselves and be wealthy and content.

Furthermore, noble son, when the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to the Great Nirvāṇa, liberates sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, he utterly relinquishes any intention toward sexual misconduct. That root of virtue he likewise makes common to all sentient beings and makes this aspiration: "May all sentient beings, however many there are in the buddha-fields, be free from minds of attachment, aversion, and delusion, and may they be free from the suffering of being tormented by hunger and thirst."

By the power of that aspiration, when he attains complete awakening in the future, all the sentient beings of that field will be free from minds of attachment, aversion, and delusion, and will be entirely free from all suffering caused by being tormented by hunger and thirst.

Furthermore, noble son, when the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to the Great Nirvāṇa, liberates sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, he utterly relinquishes any intention to speak falsely. That root of virtue he likewise makes common to all sentient beings and makes this aspiration: "May there always be flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, and fragrant trees in the buddha-fields, and may all the sentient beings there, however many they are, hear beautiful sounds and melodies."

By the power of that aspiration, when he attains complete awakening in the future, that field will have flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, and fragrant trees, and all the sentient beings there will fully and clearly receive the unsurpassed sweet sounds of melody.

Furthermore, noble son, when the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to the Great Nirvāṇa, liberates sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, he utterly relinquishes divisive speech. That root of virtue he likewise makes common to all sentient beings and makes this aspiration: "May all the sentient beings, however many there are in the buddha-fields, be in harmony and may they teach one another the sacred Dharma."

Likewise, by the power of that aspiration, when he attains complete awakening, all the sentient beings of that field, however many there are, will be in harmony and will speak words of Dharma.

Furthermore, noble son, when the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to the Great Nirvāṇa, liberates sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, he utterly relinquishes harsh speech. That root of virtue he likewise makes common to all sentient beings and makes this aspiration: "May the ground throughout the buddha-fields be as level as the palm of a hand, with no pebbles, no uneven terrain, no thorns of any kind, and may all sentient beings have an even and equanimous mind."

By the power of that aspiration, when he attains complete awakening in the future, the ground of that field will be level as the palm of a hand, with no pebbles, no uneven terrain, and no thorns, and all the sentient beings there, however many they are, will have an even and equanimous mind.

Furthermore, noble son, when the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to the Great Nirvāṇa, liberates sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, he utterly relinquishes idle chatter.

That root of virtue too is made common to all sentient beings, and the aspiration is made: "May every sentient being in the buddha-field, however many there are, be free from the suffering of afflictions." By the power of that aspiration, when he attains complete awakening in the future, every sentient being dwelling in that field will be free from the suffering of afflictions.

Furthermore, noble son, when the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to the Great Nirvāṇa, liberates sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, he utterly relinquishes the mind of jealousy born of desire. That root of virtue too is made common to all sentient beings, and the aspiration is made: "May all sentient beings in the buddha-field be free from the affliction of jealousy born of desire that brings harm, and free from wrong views." By the power of that aspiration, when he attains complete awakening in the future, all sentient beings in that field will be free from the harm of jealousy born of desire and free from wrong views.

Furthermore, noble son, when the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to the Great Nirvāṇa, liberates sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, he utterly relinquishes all harmfulness. That root of virtue too is made common to all sentient beings, and the aspiration is made: "May all sentient beings, however many there are in that buddha-field, cultivate loving-kindness and great compassion, and attain the ground of the only child." By the power of that aspiration, when he attains complete awakening in the future, all sentient beings, however many there are in that field, will cultivate loving-kindness and great compassion, and will attain the ground of the only child.

Furthermore, noble son, when the great bodhisattva, by diligently applying himself to the Great Nirvāṇa, liberates sentient beings for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, he utterly relinquishes wrong views. That root of virtue too is made common to all sentient beings, and the aspiration is made: "May all sentient beings, however many there are in the buddha-field, attain the Perfection of Wisdom." By the power of that aspiration, when he attains complete awakening in the future, all sentient beings, however many there are in that world-realm, will come to uphold and retain the Perfection of Wisdom. This is called the bodhisattva's purification of the buddha-field.

Now, how does the great bodhisattva remove what remains? There are three kinds of remainders: the remainder that is the fruit of afflictions, the remainder of karma, and the remainder of continued existence.

Noble son, what then is the remainder that is the fruit of afflictions? A sentient being who, through habitual tendencies of attachment, is intimate with those tendencies and thereby ripens that fruit, falls into the hell realms. When they have been released from the hell realms perhaps a hundred times, they are reborn in the abodes of animals — born, for instance, as a pigeon, a sparrow, a crow, a myna bird, a crane, a śārikā bird, a sparrow, a fish, a frog, a monkey, or a deer. Even if they obtain a human body, they are reborn as a dwarf, a person of indeterminate sex, a woman, a hermaphrodite, a person without sex characteristics, or a snake-charmer. If they go forth into renunciation, they will break the first root of moral discipline. This is called the remainder that is the fruit.

Furthermore, noble son, if a sentient being clings with an attached mind to habitual tendencies of aversion —

When the karma of aversion ripens, sentient beings fall into the hells. And when one in a hundred is freed from the hells, they are reborn in bodies such as these: a snake with four kinds of venom — venom in its gaze, venom in its touch, venom in its bite, and venom in its breath — or a lion, a tiger, a wolf, a bear, a brown bear, a rat, a hawk, and the like. If they obtain a human body, they are endowed with twelve kinds of bad conduct. If they go forth into renunciation, their faculties are dull and sluggish, and they will break from the first root of moral discipline up to as many as five of those roots. This is called the remainder that is the fruit.

Furthermore, noble son, one who performs actions of delusion — when that karma ripens, they fall into the hells. And when one in a hundred is freed from the hells, they are reborn in the abodes of animals — born, for instance, in the bodies of a woolly ox, a pig, a cow, a sheep, a buffalo, a donkey, a louse, a fly, or an ant, and the like. Even if they obtain a human body, they are deaf, blind, mute, hunched, their faculties are incomplete, and they cannot retain the Dharma. If they go forth into renunciation, their faculties are confused and dull, and from one root of moral discipline up to five of those roots will be broken. This is called the remainder that is the fruit.

Furthermore, noble son, one who performs actions of pride and arrogance — when the karma ripens, they fall into the hells. And when one in a hundred is freed from the hells, they are reborn in the abodes of animals — born, for instance, in the bodies of intestinal worms, a mule, a donkey, a dog, or a horse. Even if they are born as a human, they take the bodies of male servants, female servants, paupers, destitute persons, or beggars. If they go forth into renunciation, they will be utterly despised by all sentient beings, and they will break all four roots of moral discipline. This is called the remainder that is the fruit.

These are called the remainders of the karmic maturation of the afflictions.

Now, all these remainders of karmic maturation are entirely removed when the bodhisattva, the great being, applies earnest diligence to the great nirvāṇa.

As for what constitutes the remainder of karma: it is the karma of all those who belong to the lowly lineages, the karma of all śrāvakas, the karma of stream-enterers who take seven more existences, the karma of once-returners who take two more existences, and the karma of non-returners who take rebirth in the form realm. These are called the remainder of karma.

This remainder of karma, too, is entirely removed when the bodhisattva, the great being, applies earnest diligence to the great nirvāṇa.

As for what constitutes the remainder of existence: when an arhat attains the fruit of an arhat, and when a pratyekabuddha attains the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, though there is no more karma and no more affliction, there is still a twofold fruit that comes about — this is called the remainder of existence.

In this way, these three kinds of phenomena that have a remainder are entirely removed when the bodhisattva, the great being, applies earnest diligence to the sūtra collection of the Great Vehicle called the great nirvāṇa. This is what is called the bodhisattva, the great being, removing the remainder of existence.

Now, as for how the bodhisattva cultivates the body of perfect purity: the bodhisattva, the great being, in guarding the moral discipline of refraining from taking life, has five kinds of mind. What are they? The lowest, the middling, the superior, the most superior of the superior, and the superior of the middling. The same should be understood in full all the way up to right view. These fifty kinds of mind are called the first arousal of mind.

One comes to possess fifty minds of unshakeable certainty. Thus the hundred minds being perfectly complete is called possessing a hundred merits, and possessing a hundred merits results in a single major mark. In this way, gradually coming to possess the thirty-two major marks is called the body of perfect purity, and beyond that one accomplishes the eighty minor marks (Skt. anuvyañjana).

In the world, sentient beings speak of there being some eighty gods. What are the eighty? The twelve gods of the sun, the twelve great gods, the five great stars, the Seven Sisters, the god called the Horse, the god of travelers on the road, the god called Bharadvāja, the god of merit, the twenty-eight constellations, the god of the earth, the god of wind, the god of water, the god of fire, Brahmā, the god called Rudra, the god called Indra (Śakra), the god called Kumāra, the Hundred-Handed One, the god of great dominion, the god called Vaśala, the god of many sons, the god of the Four Protectors, the god of the unwritten, and the god called Vāsu — these are the eighty.

Having accomplished the eighty minor marks for the sake of sentient beings and being fully adorned with them, this is called the body of perfect purity of the bodhisattva. Why is this so? Because all sentient beings have faith in those eighty gods and follow them. Therefore, when the bodhisattva has accomplished the eighty minor marks, without moving the body, he causes each of those sentient beings to see him in just the form in which they have faith, each according to their own disposition. Having seen him, they develop even greater reverence, and each individually gives rise to the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

For this reason, the bodhisattva, the great being, purifies the body completely.

Noble son, consider this example: when a person is inviting a great king, they first adorn and cleanse the entire dwelling most thoroughly, prepare various kinds of fine food, and only then invite the king to come. In the same way, the bodhisattva, the great being, when inviting the king who turns the wheel of Dharma of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, should first purify the body most thoroughly, and then the unsurpassed king of Dharma will take up residence. For this reason, the bodhisattva, the great being, must accomplish the body of perfect purity.

Noble son, consider this example: when a person drinks ambrosia, the body is purified first. In the same way, the bodhisattva, the great being, when about to drink the ambrosia of the supreme Dharma, the Perfection of Wisdom, must first purify the body with the eighty minor marks.

Noble son, consider this example: when pure water is poured into a vessel of fine gold or silver, it is clear and pure both inside and out. In the same way, the body of the bodhisattva, the great being, being perfectly pure, is just like that: when the water of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening is poured in, it is pure both inside and out.

Noble son, consider this example: a cloth of Vārāṇasī, being very white, is easily dyed when boiled. Why is this? Because it is naturally white and clean. In the same way, because the body of the bodhisattva, the great being, is pure, one quickly attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Therefore the bodhisattva, the great being, accomplishes the perfectly pure body.

Now, in what way is the bodhisattva supremely skilled with regard to causes? The bodhisattva, the great being, does not perceive the defining characteristic of form, does not perceive the cause of form, does not perceive the intrinsic nature of form, and does not perceive the extraction of form.

One does not perceive the cessation of form, does not perceive a single defining characteristic, does not perceive distinct defining characteristics, does not perceive the act of seeing, and does not perceive form together with its aspects, nor does one perceive the taking up of form. Why is this? Because one thoroughly understands causes and conditions. Just as form is, so too are all phenomena like that. This is called the bodhisattva being supremely skilled with regard to causes.

Now, in what way does the bodhisattva abandon enemies? All mental afflictions are the enemies of the bodhisattva, and because the bodhisattva, the great being, constantly abandons them, the bodhisattva is called one who has overcome enemies. A bodhisattva at the fifth ground does not regard mental afflictions as enemies. Why is this? Because it is through the condition of mental afflictions that a bodhisattva has birth, and because one has birth, one goes from one to another benefiting sentient beings. For that reason, they are not to be called enemies. Then what is called an enemy? It is this: the denigration of the extensive sūtras. Although the bodhisattva enters into birth and does not fear the realms of hell-beings, the birthplaces of animals, or the hungry ghosts, the bodhisattva fears only the denigration of the extensive sūtras. For all bodhisattvas there are eight kinds of māra, and these become enemies. When those eight kinds of māra are abandoned, this is called the abandonment of enemies. This is what is meant by the bodhisattva abandoning enemies.

Now, in what way does the bodhisattva abandon the two extremes? What are called the two extremes are these: the twenty-five modes of existence and the afflictions of existence. The bodhisattva constantly abandons the twenty-five modes of existence and the afflictions of existence. This is called the bodhisattva abandoning the two extremes.

These, then, are the four qualities possessed by the bodhisattva, the great being, who has applied diligent effort to the great passing beyond sorrow.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, Sarvasamāgamaśrīrāja asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, as the Blessed One has declared — that those bodhisattvas who have diligently applied themselves to the great passing beyond sorrow require these ten essential qualities — why then did the Tathāgata cultivate only nine? Why did he not cultivate the thorough purification of the buddha-field?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, I too cultivated those ten essential qualities in former times. There is not a single bodhisattva, nor any other Tathāgata, who has not cultivated these ten essential qualities. If the world were so thoroughly filled with filth that there were no place where the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, could appear, then, son of good family, you should not hold the view that the Tathāgatas arise in a filthy world. Such a view is utterly feeble and small-minded. You should now understand it in this way: understand that the present arising is not truly in Jambudvīpa. For example, if someone were to say, 'The sun and moon exist only in this world; in other worlds there is no sun and moon,' those words would be without meaning or reason. In the same way, if a bodhisattva were to say, 'This buddha-field is foul, wretched, and impure, while other buddha-fields are thoroughly pure and beautifully arrayed,' that too is like this."

Noble son, to the west of this world-system of Endurance, past buddha-fields as numerous as the grains of sand of thirty-two Ganges rivers, there exists a world-system called the Invincible. Why is that field called the Invincible?
