Because all the objects arranged within it are equal and without distinction — just as the western world-system is called Sukhāvatī and the eastern world-system is called the Full Moon. I shall manifest in that world-system, and for the benefit of sentient beings I have shown the turning of the wheel of Dharma in this world-system of Jambudvīpa. It is not I alone who have shown the turning of the wheel of Dharma in this world-system; all Tathāgatas likewise have turned the wheel of Dharma in this world-system. Therefore, there is not a single buddha, a Blessed One, who has not cultivated those ten things.

Noble son, the bodhisattva Maitreya (Loving-kindness), by the power of his aspiration, will in a future time adorn this world-system and make it thoroughly pure. In light of this, no buddha-field of any buddha whatsoever is impure.

Furthermore, noble son, how is it that a bodhisattva, a great being, who diligently applies himself to this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa comes to possess five excellent qualities? Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, who diligently applies himself to this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa comes to possess five excellent qualities through five kinds of things. What are those five? Possessing the sense faculties intact; not being born in a border region; being regarded with esteem by the gods; being constantly honored by gods, māras, ascetics, the warrior caste, and brahmins and others; and remembering one's previous lives.

Through the power of the causes and conditions of this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, a bodhisattva will come to be endowed with these five excellent qualities.

The bodhisattva, the great being, Samantaprabhā Uttamaśrīrāja (Universally Radiant, King of Lofty Glory) asked: "As the Blessed One has said, if a noble son or noble daughter practices generosity, they will come to possess five excellent qualities — then why does the Blessed One say that through the condition of the Great Nirvāṇa one obtains these five qualities?"

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, these qualities are of different meanings, and I shall now distinguish them and explain them to you. The five qualities obtained through practicing generosity are uncertain, impermanent, impure, not supreme, not distinct, and not undefiled; they serve to establish all sentient beings in happiness, for their benefit and for the sake of affection. Whereas the five qualities obtained through reliance on this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa are certain, permanent, thoroughly pure, supreme, distinct, and undefiled; they serve to establish all sentient beings in happiness, for their benefit and for the sake of happiness.

Noble son, generosity removes hunger and thirst. This sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa frees all sentient beings from the illness of being thoroughly tormented by the twenty-five states of existence. Through the cause of generosity, the stream of cyclic existence is made uninterrupted. Through the Great Nirvāṇa sūtra, cyclic existence is severed and its stream is cut. Through the cause of generosity, low and inferior ordinary beings come to act according to the Dharma."

Through the cause of this Great Nirvāṇa sūtra, one becomes a bodhisattva. Through the cause of generosity, all those tormented by the suffering of poverty and destitution will be freed from it. The Great Nirvāṇa sūtra in its entirety can sever all poverty in wholesome qualities. Through the cause of generosity, the result is one that has a partial aspect. Through the cause of the Great Nirvāṇa sūtra, the attainment of the unsurpassed, genuinely perfect awakening is a result without any partial aspect whatsoever. This is what is called a bodhisattva, a great being, who is endowed with the five qualities by virtue of having applied diligent effort to this Great Nirvāṇa sūtra.

Noble son, how is it that a bodhisattva is endowed with six qualities by virtue of having applied diligent effort to this Great Nirvāṇa sūtra? When a bodhisattva, a great being, has applied diligent effort to the Great Nirvāṇa sūtra, he will attain the vajra-like meditative absorption (samādhi). Abiding in that absorption, he will see all phenomena as utterly disintegrating, seeing them to be: marked by impermanence and instability, to be causes of destruction and fear, to be seized by the suffering of illness, to be ceasing and perishing moment by moment, to be without genuine truth, to be entirely within the domain of māra, and to be without any fixed object of apprehension.

The bodhisattva, the great being, while abiding in that meditative absorption and practicing generosity toward sentient beings, does not truly perceive even a single sentient being. And in the same way, his striving from the perfection of moral discipline all the way through to the Perfection of Wisdom for the sake of sentient beings should be understood to be equally extensive. For if a bodhisattva were to apprehend even a single sentient being as truly existent, he would never fully perfect the perfections from generosity through to the Perfection of Wisdom.

Noble son, consider this example: wherever a vajra strikes, there is nothing that does not crack or shatter, yet the vajra itself never breaks or disintegrates. In the same way, there is nothing the vajra-like meditative absorption strikes that does not disintegrate, yet that very meditative absorption can never itself be destroyed.

Noble son, just as the vajra is supreme among all precious gems, so too the attainment of the vajra-like meditative absorption by a bodhisattva, a great being, is similar in this respect: it becomes the sovereign of all meditative absorptions. Why? Because when a bodhisattva, a great being, cultivates that meditative absorption, all other meditative absorptions are gathered into it.

Noble son, just as a wheel-turning king exercises sovereignty over all minor kings, so too the vajra-like meditative absorption exercises sovereignty over all meditative absorptions.

Noble son, consider this example: if a person becomes an enemy of an entire region, everyone will despise him. And if someone slays that enemy, all people of the world will sing his praises without exception. In the same way, the vajra-like meditative absorption is similar: when a bodhisattva cultivates it, he becomes capable of vanquishing the enemies of all sentient beings. Therefore it becomes the queen of all meditative absorptions.

Noble son, consider this example: a person of tremendous physical strength, beyond what anyone else can overcome, yet who is subdued by the strength of another — that other person will be praised by everyone without exception. In the same way, through the power of the vajra-like meditative absorption, even the most difficult-to-tame phenomena can be tamed. For this reason, all meditative absorptions are gathered into it.

Noble son, consider this example: if a person bathes in the ocean, know that that person has bathed in all the waters of rivers, springs, and ponds.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva, a great being, cultivates the vajra-like meditative absorption, know that this is the cultivation of all other meditative absorptions.

Noble son, consider this example: on a fragrant mountain there is a spring called "the unheated spring." The water of that spring is endowed with eight excellent qualities. If someone drinks from it, all the sufferings of illness are entirely removed. In the same way, the vajra-like meditative absorption is endowed with the eight limbs of the noble path, and when a bodhisattva cultivates it, the wounds and heavy ailments of the afflictions are cut away.

Noble son, consider this example: if someone makes an offering to a great sovereign lord, know that by doing so that person has made an offering to all the gods. In the same way, cultivating the vajra-like meditative absorption is to be understood as the cultivation of all meditative absorptions.

Noble son, if a bodhisattva who is perfectly established in the vajra-like meditative absorption looks upon all phenomena without obstruction — just as one would see a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of one's hand — even though a bodhisattva sees in this way, no perception of "I see all phenomena" arises.

Noble son, consider this example: if a person sits at a crossroads, that person will see sentient beings coming, going, sitting, and lying down. In the same way, through the vajra-like meditative absorption one sees all phenomena arising, ceasing, appearing, and passing away.

Noble son, consider this example: if a person ascends a high mountain and looks in every direction, everything is seen with clarity. In the same way, the vajra-like meditative absorption is like that mountain: when a bodhisattva ascends it and looks upon all phenomena, there is nothing that is not clearly seen.

Noble son, consider this example: the fine and beautiful droplets of summer rain leave no gap between them, and when a person of keen eyesight looks, everything is seen with clarity. In the same way, when a bodhisattva obtains the pure eye of the vajra-like meditative absorption, in every world-system in the eastern direction — however many there may be — all their destructions and completions are seen without obstruction and with full clarity; and the same is true of the ten directions likewise.

Noble son, consider this example: if seven suns were to rise simultaneously over Mount Yugaṃdhara, all the trees and forests of that mountain would be burned. In the same way, when a bodhisattva cultivates the vajra-like meditative absorption, all the dense thickets of afflictions are pacified.

Noble son, consider this example: the vajra can shatter all things that exist in the realm of existence, yet no perception arises in it of thinking "I have shattered this." The vajra-like meditative absorption is just the same: when a bodhisattva has cultivated it and has overcome all afflictions, no perception arises of thinking "I have now overcome all afflictions entirely."

Noble son, consider this example: the great earth bears all things that exist in the realm of existence, yet no perception arises in it of thinking "I have held these by my own power." Fire does not give rise to the perception "I have burned." Water does not give rise to the perception "I have performed the work of moistening." Wind does not give rise to the perception "I have performed the work of stirring." Space does not give rise to the perception "I have performed the work of containing." And nirvāṇa does not give rise to the perception "I have drawn sentient beings beyond sorrow." The vajra-like meditative absorption is just the same: though it removes all afflictions entirely, from the very beginning there is no mind that thinks "I have removed them."

If a bodhisattva abides in the vajra-like meditative absorption, in a single instant they emanate forms without number and without measure that resemble those of the Tathāgata, filling all the buddha-fields of the ten directions to the very number of grains of sand in the Ganges River. And yet, though that bodhisattva performs such manifest emanations, they have no mind of pride or arrogance. Why is that? The bodhisattva always thinks: "No other meditative absorption can display such miraculous powers — only the one who abides in the vajra-like meditative absorption is able to display them." It is with this thought that they remain.

When the great bodhisattva abides in that vajra-like meditative absorption, they have the power, in a single instant, to journey to buddha-fields in the ten directions to the very number of grains of sand in the Ganges River and then return to their dwelling place — yet they do not have the perception "I am capable of this." Why? Because of the cause and condition that is that meditative absorption.

When the great bodhisattva abides in the vajra-like meditative absorption, they are able, in a single instant, to sever all the afflictions of sentient beings in world-systems throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the grains of sand in the Ganges River — and yet they do not have the perception "I have severed the afflictions of sentient beings." Why? Because of the power of the cause and condition that is that meditative absorption.

Abiding in that vajra-like meditative absorption, a bodhisattva utters a single sound, and all sentient beings individually understand things just as they are. They display a single form, and all sentient beings individually perceive the marks of forms in their variety. They remain in a single place, their body utterly still, and sentient beings, wherever they may dwell in any direction, each see them present in their own direction. They teach a single Dharma — whether pertaining to an element (dhātu) or a sense base (āyatana) — and all sentient beings each hear it as though knowing it beforehand.

When a bodhisattva abides in such a meditative absorption, though they perceive sentient beings, from the very beginning there is no mind that grasps at sentient beings as a defining mark. Though they perceive men and women, there is no mind that grasps at maleness and femaleness. Though they perceive phenomena of form, there is no defining mark of form. And so too, through to consciousness: though they perceive consciousness, there is no defining mark of consciousness. Though they perceive day and night, there is no defining mark of day and night. Though they perceive all things, there is no defining mark of anything at all. Though they perceive all the afflictions that arise through involvement, there is no defining mark of any affliction. Though they perceive the noble eightfold path, there is no defining mark of the noble eightfold path. Though they perceive awakening, there is no defining mark of awakening. Though they perceive nirvāṇa, there is no defining mark of nirvāṇa. Why? Noble son, because all phenomena are, from the very beginning, without defining marks — and through the power of that meditative absorption, the bodhisattva sees all phenomena just as they are: without defining marks from the very beginning.

Why is it called the vajra-like meditative absorption? Noble son, consider: when a vajra is placed in sunlight, its color is not fixed as any single hue. In just the same way, when the vajra-like meditative absorption is placed within a great multitude, it cannot be determined as having a single, fixed character. It is for that reason that it is called the vajra-like meditative absorption.

Noble son, consider again: a vajra is beyond any price that all beings in the world might set upon it. In just the same way, whatever qualities the vajra-like meditative absorption possesses cannot be measured or gauged by all gods and humans together. It is for that reason that it is called the vajra-like meditative absorption.

Noble son, consider: if a poor man were to find a precious vajra-gem, it would relieve him of the sufferings of poverty and destitution, and —

he would be freed from all the harm of māras and wrong views. In just the same way, when a bodhisattva, a great being, attains that meditative absorption, he too is freed from the suffering of mental afflictions and from all the harm of māras and wrong views. It is for that reason that it is called the vajra-like meditative absorption. This, then, is what is meant when it is said that a bodhisattva who applies himself diligently to the great nirvāṇa possesses the sixth quality.

The Noble Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa, the thirty-third fascicle.

Furthermore, noble son, how is it that a bodhisattva, a great being, who applies himself diligently to this noble sūtra of the great nirvāṇa comes to possess seven qualities? Noble son, when a bodhisattva, a great being, applies himself diligently to this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa, he reflects: "What are the qualities of Dharma that serve as proximate causes for the great nirvāṇa?" He then understands that these four qualities of Dharma serve as proximate causes for the great nirvāṇa. It is not the case that practising all manner of austerities serves as the proximate cause for the great nirvāṇa. And why not? Beyond these four qualities of Dharma there is simply no ground on which one could transcend into nirvāṇa. What are the four? They are these: attending upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); listening to the Dharma with a one-pointed mind; applying oneself diligently to its meaning after having heard it; and practising exactly in accordance with what is true.

Noble son, consider the example of a person afflicted by bile, phlegm, and many diseases, or tormented by hunger. That sick person goes to a skilled physician, and the physician teaches him the proper treatment for the illness. The patient listens with a one-pointed mind and follows the prescribed treatment, taking the medicine correctly. His illness is cured and his body becomes well.

In this analogy, the sick person is like the bodhisattva. The skilled physician is like the spiritual friend. The physician's teaching of the proper treatment is like this extensive sūtra. Listening carefully to and retaining the physician's taught treatment is like applying oneself diligently to the meaning of this extensive sūtra. Administering the medicine in accordance with the treatment is like correctly practising the thirty-seven factors of awakening (bodhipākṣikadharma) exactly as they truly are. The curing of the illness is like the cessation of the mental afflictions. Attaining wellbeing is like attaining the permanence, bliss, selfhood, and utter purity of nirvāṇa.

Noble son, consider further the example of a king who, wishing to govern his realm according to the Dharma and to bring happiness to his subjects, asks his wise ministers what course of action would be best. The ministers then explain to him the principles of governance by which former kings had ruled their realms. The king hears this, and with a one-pointed mind places his trust in it. Governing his realm according to those very principles, his enemies are vanquished, and thereby his subjects attain happiness and are freed from harm.

In this analogy, the king is like the bodhisattva. The wise ministers are like the spiritual friend. The wise ministers' exposition to the king of the principles of governance is like the twelve branches of scripture (dvādaśāṅgadharma). The king's hearing this and with a one-pointed mind placing his trust in it and acting accordingly is like bodhisattvas, with one-pointed minds, reflecting upon and diligently applying themselves to the profound meaning of the twelve branches of scripture. The governing of the realm in accordance with the Dharma is like bodhisattvas diligently practising exactly and truly in accordance with the Dharma of the six perfections — and this they do for the sake of diligent application to the six perfections.

The elimination of enemies is like bodhisattvas utterly abandoning all the enemies of afflictive mental afflictions. The attainment of happiness is like bodhisattvas attaining the permanence, happiness, selfhood, and perfect purity of nirvāṇa.

O son of good family, consider this example: a man afflicted with a severe case of leprosy had a dear and close friend who said to him, "If you were to go to the foot of Mount Meru, all your diseases would be cured. Why? Because there is an excellent medicine there, like the nectar of immortality, and if it is drunk, there is no disease that cannot be healed." The man then placed his trust in this, went to the foot of that mountain, gathered the medicine that was like nectar, and ate it. His disease was cured and his body became well and comfortable.

The severe leprosy is like base and ignoble afflictions. The dear and close friend is like great bodhisattvas (bodhisattva-mahāsattvas). The wholeheartedness of faith is like the minds of the four immeasurables. Mount Meru is like the noble eightfold path. The taste of nectar is like the nature of buddha. The healing of the leprosy is like freedom from afflictions. The attainment of happiness is like attaining the permanence, happiness, selfhood, and perfect purity of nirvāṇa.

O son of good family, consider this further example: a teacher who has students of keen faculties teaches them day and night without ever growing weary. In the same way, bodhisattvas too, whether sentient beings have faith or do not have faith, teach without ceasing and without ever growing weary.

O son of good family, a spiritual friend (Skt. kalyāṇamitra) is one who has profound trust in buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas. Why is such a person called a spiritual friend? A spiritual friend is one who causes sentient beings to abandon the ten non-virtues and to practise the ten virtues — it is for that reason such a person is called a spiritual friend. Again, a spiritual friend is one who teaches the Dharma exactly as it is and who practises in accord with exactly what has been taught. How does one teach the Dharma as it is and practise in accord with what has been taught? It is like this: because one does not take life oneself, one teaches others not to take life; because one oneself diligently applies to right view, one leads others to diligently apply to right view — and so on up through the full range of virtues. One who acts in this way is called a genuine spiritual friend. Because one diligently applies oneself to awakening, one leads others to diligently apply themselves to awakening — it is for that reason such a person is called a spiritual friend. Because one cultivates faith, moral discipline, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom oneself, one leads others to cultivate faith, moral discipline, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom — it is for that reason such a person is called a spiritual friend. A spiritual friend is so called because of the presence of virtuous qualities. What are those virtuous qualities? It is this: whatever one does, one does not apply it to one's own benefit and comfort; rather, one is ever engaged in bringing sentient beings to happiness; and even upon seeing the faults of others, one does not speak of their failings but speaks only and always of virtuous qualities. It is for that reason such a person is called a spiritual friend.

O son of good family, consider the analogy of the moon: from the first day of the lunar month up through the fifteenth day it steadily and visibly waxes. In the same way, a spiritual friend likewise causes the students they guide to gradually grow distant from non-virtuous qualities and to give rise to virtuous qualities.

O son of good family, if anyone relies upon a spiritual friend, they will come to possess moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation — even those they did not have before.

Those not yet complete will arise and grow. Why is that? Because of drawing near to a spiritual friend. Through the condition of such nearness, one will come to understand even the very deep meaning of the twelve branches of scriptural teaching. Listening to the very deep meaning of those twelve branches of scriptural teaching is called listening to the Dharma. That very listening to the Dharma is called the extensive sūtras of the Great Vehicle. Listening to those extensive sūtras is called genuinely listening to the Dharma. Genuinely listening to the Dharma means listening to the sūtra of the great nirvāṇa, in which one hears that within the great nirvāṇa there exists the nature of the buddha, and that a Tathāgata does not pass beyond nirvāṇa finally and completely. Therefore it is called one-pointedly listening to the Dharma. One-pointedly listening to the Dharma is called the noble eightfold path, and by means of the noble eightfold path, attachment, aversion, and delusion are cut through. Therefore it is called listening to the Dharma. Listening to the Dharma is called the eleven emptinesses, and by those emptinesses one does not look upon any phenomenon as having a defining mark. Listening to the Dharma is called first arousing the mind: from the cause of first arousing the mind one will attain, step by step, the unsurpassed awakening mind of a perfect arhat — that is, the fully and perfectly enlightened awakening mind — all the way through to great nirvāṇa. Yet great nirvāṇa is not attained merely by hearing; it is attained through thorough cultivation in meditation.

O son of good family, consider the analogy of a sick person: merely by hearing the name of a physician's treatment and medicine, the illness will not be cured, but it will be cured by actually drinking the medicine. In the same way, merely by listening to the twelve profound factors of dependent origination, all afflictions will not be cut through; they will be cut through by applying the mind one-pointedly and exerting oneself earnestly. That is called earnest application of the mind.

Furthermore, why is it called earnest application of the mind? It is as follows: there are three kinds of meditative absorption — the meditative absorption of emptiness, the meditative absorption of signlessness, and the meditative absorption of wishlessness. Among these, emptiness means not seeing even a single truth in the twenty-five modes of existence. Wishlessness means not wishing for or seeking anything among the twenty-five modes of existence. Signlessness means freedom from ten signs: the sign of form, the sign of sound, the sign of smell, the sign of taste, the sign of touch, the sign of arising, the sign of abiding, the sign of cessation, the sign of the masculine, and the sign of the feminine. Thus, cultivating these three kinds of meditative absorption is what is called earnest application of the mind on the part of a bodhisattva.

Now, what does it mean to conduct oneself in accord with the Dharma? To conduct oneself in accord with the Dharma means to practise from the perfection of generosity through to the Perfection of Wisdom, to be skilled in the true defining marks of the five aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements, and to understand that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the blessed buddhas alike pass into nirvāṇa together in harmony along a single path. The word "Dharma" refers to that which is permanent, blissful, self, utterly pure, unborn, unaging, undiseased, undying, free from hunger, free from thirst, without suffering and affliction, undeclining, and unceasing.

O son of good family, to know the very deep meaning of the great nirvāṇa is to know that a blessed buddha does not pass away into final and complete nirvāṇa.

O son of good family, the true and genuine spiritual friend is none other than bodhisattvas and blessed buddhas. Why is that? Because they constantly guide others by means of three kinds of steering. What are the three? Always speaking gently, always being firm, and mixing gentleness with firmness together. For this reason, bodhisattvas and blessed buddhas are genuine spiritual friends.

Furthermore, O son of good family, buddhas and bodhisattvas are called spiritual friends because they are great physicians. Why? Because they know the illness and know the medicine, and they give medicine according to the nature of the illness. Consider, for example, a skilled physician expert in the eight branches of medical knowledge, who first examines the defining marks of disease. There are three such defining marks: wind, bile, and phlegm. For one afflicted with a wind disease, he gives butter. For one afflicted with a bile disease, he gives sugar. For one afflicted with a phlegm disease, he administers broth. In this way, knowing the defining marks of the illness and giving the appropriate medicine so that the patient recovers — this is what it means to be a skilled physician. Likewise, buddhas and bodhisattvas know that the foolish, immature ordinary beings of this world have three kinds of illness. What are the three? Attachment, aversion, and delusion. To those afflicted with the illness of attachment, they teach contemplation on the skeleton. To those afflicted with the illness of aversion, they teach contemplation on loving-kindness and compassion. To those afflicted with the illness of delusion, they teach contemplation on the twelve links of dependent origination. For this reason, buddhas and bodhisattvas are called spiritual friends.

O son of good family, just as a great vehicle is so called because it conveys beings to ease and liberation, so too buddhas and bodhisattvas liberate all sentient beings from the great conflagration of saṃsāra — and for this reason they are called spiritual friends.

Furthermore, O son of good family, through the condition of buddhas and bodhisattvas, all sentient beings come to fully complete the practice of the roots of virtuous Dharma. O son of good family, consider the snow mountain, which is the abode of many excellent and supreme medicinal herbs. Likewise, buddhas and bodhisattvas are the abode of all roots of virtue. For this reason they are called spiritual friends.

O son of good family, on the snow mountain there is a supreme fragrant herb called Vāha. If certain people see it, they gain immeasurable lifespan and are freed from the suffering of illness. The four malevolent ones cannot harm them. If someone touches it, they gain long life and complete one hundred and twenty years. If someone calls it to mind in recollection, they remember their former lives. Why is this? Because of the power and strength of that medicine. Likewise, whoever sees a buddha or a bodhisattva has all their afflictions utterly severed, and the four māras cannot disturb them. Whoever touches them does not die suddenly at an untimely moment. They are unborn, they do not die, they do not decline, they do not perish. "Touching" here means hearing the sublime Dharma from a buddha. Whoever calls them to mind in recollection attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Therefore buddhas and bodhisattvas are called spiritual friends.

O son of good family, consider the fragrant mountain lake called Anavatapta. From that lake flow four great rivers. What are the four? The Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Sītā, and the Vakṣu.

Worldly people say this: "Whoever has committed blameworthy deeds and bathes in those four great rivers will be purified of many blameworthy and sinful acts." Know that what they say is not true. Then what, one may ask, are the truths they have failed to understand? It is this: buddhas and bodhisattvas are the true ones. Why? Because whoever venerates and honors them will be purified of all their many blameworthy and sinful deeds. Therefore buddhas and bodhisattvas are called spiritual friends.

Furthermore, O son of good family, consider the great earth: all the medicinal herbs and forests, the crops, the sugarcane, the flowers, the fruits, and so forth that have grown upon it become withered and are on the verge of drying out. Then the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, moved by compassion for sentient beings, arise from the ocean and release a rain of nectar, whereupon all the medicinal herbs, forests, crops, and trees become moist and grow again. In the same way, when the wholesome roots of all sentient beings are on the verge of exhaustion, buddhas and bodhisattvas arouse great compassion and release a rain of nectar from the ocean of wisdom, endowing all sentient beings with the tenfold path of virtue. Therefore buddhas and bodhisattvas are called spiritual friends.

O son of good family, consider a skilled physician, expert in the eight branches of medicine. When he sees patients, he does not look to their family lineage, their good or bad qualities, their wealth, their jewels, or anything of that sort — he heals them all. And so he becomes renowned throughout the world as a great and skilled physician. In the same way, when buddhas and bodhisattvas see the disease of affliction in sentient beings, they do not look to family lineage, good or bad qualities, wealth, jewels, or anything of that sort. With minds of loving-kindness and compassion they teach the Dharma to all. When sentient beings hear it, the disease of their afflictions is purified. Therefore buddhas and bodhisattvas are called spiritual friends.

By relying on a spiritual friend in this way, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa, the thorough passing beyond sorrow. How, one may ask, does a bodhisattva draw near to the great nirvāṇa through the condition of hearing the Dharma? It is like this: for the sake of hearing the Dharma, all sentient beings come to be endowed with the faculty of faith. Having come to be endowed with the faculty of faith, they grow devoted to the practice of generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. They then attain a stream of results, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry up through the fruit of buddhahood. Therefore one should understand that it is through the power of hearing the Dharma as its cause that one comes to attain virtuous qualities.

O son of good family, consider a householder who has a single son. He sends that son off to trade in another land in search of what is needed, and after pointing out which roads along the way are safe and which are dangerous, he says to him: "If you meet a serpent-woman, do not draw close to her, do not become attached to her. If you draw close or become attached, you will lose both body and life, and your wealth and jewels and all the rest will be lost as well. Do not seek out evil and unruly companions." The son heeded his father's counsel, and as a result he was happy in body and mind and obtained wealth and jewels in great abundance. In the same way, the bodhisattva, the great being, when teaching the Dharma to sentient beings, shows to those sentient beings and the four kinds of retinue which paths are safe and which are dangerous.

The members of the retinue, having heard the Dharma, abandoned all non-virtue and came to be endowed with virtuous qualities. Thus, through the condition of hearing the Dharma, they drew near to the great nirvāṇa.

O son of good family, consider this example: when one looks into a clear mirror, no face fails to appear. In the same way, when someone looks into the clear mirror of hearing the Dharma, they see without any obscuring film both virtue and non-virtue with perfect clarity. Thus, through the condition of hearing the Dharma, they draw near to the great nirvāṇa.

O son of good family, consider this example: merchants setting out for an island of jewels do not know the way. One person shows them the road, and following the directions they were given, they reach the island of jewels and obtain jewels beyond counting. In the same way, all sentient beings, setting out for the virtuous realm to gather the jewel of awakening, do not know which roads lead to liberation and which do not. The bodhisattvas show the way, and the sentient beings, following as they were shown, arrive at the virtuous realm and obtain the jewel of the great, unsurpassed nirvāṇa. Thus, through the condition of hearing the Dharma, they draw near to the great nirvāṇa.

O son of good family, consider this example: a drunken bull elephant, wishing to kill many, is brought under control the moment an elephant trainer inserts a great iron hook into its temple — and from that instant it is tamed and no longer harbors the intention to harm. In the same way, all sentient beings, intoxicated by attachment, aversion, and delusion, engage in a great deal of non-virtue. The bodhisattvas insert the iron hook of hearing the Dharma and hold it firm, causing the intention to commit non-virtuous acts to cease arising. Thus, through the condition of hearing the Dharma, they draw near to the great nirvāṇa.

It is for this reason that throughout all the sūtra collections I have declared to my attendants that if with one-pointed mind they hear and hold the twelve branches of the sūtra collection, they will be free from the five obscurations and will cultivate the seven limbs of awakening. Through cultivating the seven limbs of awakening they will draw near to the great nirvāṇa. Through hearing the Dharma, those who have entered the stream will be freed from fears.

Why is this? Because the householder Śkyabmed (a man without refuge) was stricken by severe illness and his mind was overwhelmed with terror and misery. Śāriputra then set forth the four qualities of a stream-enterer and spoke of ten kinds of inspiration, and upon hearing this the man became free from fear. Thus, through the condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa.

Why is this? Because it is the Dharma-eye that is opened. In the world there are three kinds of people: those without eyes, those with one eye, and those with two eyes. Those without eyes are those who never hear the Dharma at all. Those with one eye are those who hear the Dharma for just a moment yet whose mind does not rest upon it. Those with two eyes are those who listen and retain with one-pointed mind and who act in accordance with what they have heard. It is by hearing the Dharma that one comes to know there are these three kinds of people in the world. Thus, through the condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa.

O son of good family, in former times when I was residing in the city of Kuśinagara, Śāriputra was stricken by illness. At that time I summoned the monk Ānanda and taught the Dharma in full. Then Śāriputra, having received such a gift, said to his four disciples: "Carry this seat of mine and let us go into the presence of the Buddha — I wish to hear the Dharma." His four disciples then carried him, and he went to where I was abiding and heard the Dharma.

Through the force of hearing the Dharma, suffering was purified and the body became at ease. Thus, through the condition of hearing the Dharma, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa.

How is it that through the condition of a bodhisattva's contemplation one draws near to the great nirvāṇa? It is like this: through the condition of such contemplative reflection, the mind is fully liberated. Why is that? It is because all sentient beings are perpetually bound by the five objects of desire and become liberated through reflection that draws the mind away from them. Thus, through the condition of contemplation, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, O son of good family, all sentient beings are perpetually misled by four aspects of phenomena — permanence, pleasurableness, self, and purity — and, through contemplating these, they perceive all phenomena as impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure. Having seen in this way, the four inverted views are severed. Thus, through the condition of contemplation, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, O son of good family, all phenomena have four characteristics (lakṣaṇa). What are those four? The characteristic of birth, the characteristic of aging, the characteristic of illness, and the characteristic of cessation. By these four characteristics, all ordinary persons of inferior lineage, up to and including stream-enterers (srotāpanna), are thoroughly afflicted. Yet one who contemplates with single-pointed mind does not give rise to affliction even when encountering those four aspects. Thus, through the condition of contemplation, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, O son of good family, none of the wholesome qualities are attained by others without contemplation. Why is that? Even if one were to listen to the Dharma with single-pointed mind for immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless eons, if one does not contemplate, one will never attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Thus, through the condition of reflection in the mind, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, O son of good family, if any sentient being places unwavering and unaltering faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and pays them honor and respect — that being too, through the condition of single-pointed mental engagement, should be understood to have severed all afflictions. Thus, through the condition of mental engagement, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa.

How does a bodhisattva cultivate in accordance with the Dharma? O son of good family, one who abandons all unwholesome phenomena and applies oneself diligently to wholesome phenomena — this is called a bodhisattva's cultivation in accordance with the Dharma.

Again, how does one cultivate in accordance with the Dharma? By seeing all phenomena as empty, objectless, impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure — and, because of seeing them in this way, never breaking one's vows of moral discipline even at the cost of body and life. This is called a bodhisattva's cultivation in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, how does one cultivate in accordance with the Dharma? Cultivation has two aspects: authentic and inauthentic. The inauthentic is this: not knowing the defining characteristics of nirvāṇa, the intrinsic nature of the buddhas, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, truth itself, and space — this is called inauthentic cultivation. The authentic is this: knowing the defining characteristics of nirvāṇa, the intrinsic nature of the buddhas, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, truth itself, and space — this is called authentic cultivation.

Now, how does one know the defining characteristics of nirvāṇa? The defining characteristics of nirvāṇa have eight aspects. What are those eight? Exhaustion, the characteristic of virtue, truth, authenticity, permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity — that is nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, there are another eight aspects. What are those eight? Liberation, an intrinsically virtuous nature, inauthenticity, untruth, impermanence, suffering, no-self, and utter impurity.

Furthermore, there are another six defining characteristics. What are those? Liberation, an intrinsically virtuous nature, untruth, inauthenticity, bliss, and utter purity.

Now, if any sentient being relies upon the conventional path and cuts through afflictions, the nirvāṇa that is the cutting of afflictions has eight aspects — yet that liberation is untrue. Why? Because it is impermanent. Being impermanent, it lacks truth. Lacking truth, it lacks authenticity, for even though the afflictions have been cut, they can arise again. Impermanence, no-self, suffering, and utter impurity — these are what are called the eight aspects of the liberation that is nirvāṇa.

Then, how are there six defining characteristics? Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, because they have cut through afflictions, are called liberated; yet because they do not attain unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening (bodhi), they are called untrue. Being untrue in this way, they are called inauthentic. Because in a future time they will come to attain unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, they are called impermanent. Because they have attained the noble eightfold path (Skt. āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), which is without defilement, they are called blissful and utterly pure.

O son of noble family, one who knows this in this way is said to know nirvāṇa, and is said to know the defining characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the buddhas, of the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, truth itself, and space.

Now, how does a bodhisattva know the intrinsic nature of the buddhas? The intrinsic nature of the buddhas has six aspects. What are those six? Permanence, utter purity, truth, virtue, being something that will be seen, and authenticity. Furthermore, there are seven aspects: the first is that it will be known, and the remaining six are as before. This is called a bodhisattva's knowing the intrinsic nature of the buddhas.

How does a bodhisattva know the defining characteristics of the Tathāgata? In this context, what is called "the Tathāgata" is: the characteristic of feeling, the characteristic of virtue, permanence, bliss, self, utter purity, liberation, truth, authenticity — one who is fit to show the path. This is called a bodhisattva's knowing the defining characteristics of the Tathāgata.

How does a bodhisattva know the defining characteristics of the Dharma? In this context, knowing the Dharma means knowing: virtue and non-virtue, permanence and impermanence, bliss and suffering, self and no-self, utter purity and utter impurity, knowing and not knowing, awareness and ignorance, truth and untruth, what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, what is a teacher and what is not a teacher, what is authentic and what is inauthentic. Knowing all these is called a bodhisattva's knowing the defining characteristics of the Dharma.

How does a bodhisattva know the defining characteristics of the Saṅgha? What is called the Saṅgha has the characteristics of permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity; it is fit to display the defining characteristic of one who is a learner; it is virtuous, authentic, and yet untrue. Why? Because all śrāvakas will attain the awakening of a buddha. What then is truth?

knowing the essential nature of phenomena. Knowing all of this is called a bodhisattva's knowing the defining characteristics of the Saṅgha.

How does a bodhisattva know the authentic defining characteristics? What are called the authentic defining characteristics are: permanence and impermanence, bliss and suffering, self and selflessness, utter purity and utter impurity, virtue and non-virtue, existence and non-existence, nirvāṇa and what is not nirvāṇa, liberation and non-liberation, knowing and not knowing, annihilation and non-annihilation, understanding and ignorance, cultivation and non-cultivation, seeing and not seeing — these are called the authentic defining characteristics. Nirvāṇa, the intrinsic nature of a buddha, the Tathāgata, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and space are not among them. For it is through the condition of cultivating the great nirvāṇa in just this way that a bodhisattva comes to understand the distinctions among the defining characteristics of nirvāṇa, the intrinsic nature of a buddha, the Tathāgata, the Dharma and the Saṅgha, the authentic, space, and so forth.

Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, who cultivates the sacred sūtra of the great, complete nirvāṇa does not see space. Why is that? Although buddhas and bodhisattvas possess five eyes, they do not see it with those; it is seen only with the eye of wisdom. And even what is seen with the eye of wisdom is called seeing by virtue of not seeing any phenomenon whatsoever. If space is said to be that in which no thing of any kind exists, then space would be something authentic. But if it were authentic, it would be permanently non-existent, and being permanently non-existent, it would also lack bliss and utter purity.

Noble son, the empty is a phenomenon of non-existence; it is called empty because it is a thing that has the character of non-existence. It is like calling something empty in the world when no thing whatsoever is present in it. In the same way, the intrinsic nature of space is also called space because no thing whatsoever is present in it. Noble son, both the intrinsic nature of sentient beings and the intrinsic nature of space are alike in having no authentic intrinsic nature. Why? Because some people say: if existing things were made absent, it would become empty. But space is not, in truth, something that can be made. Why? Because there is nothing there at all. And because there is nothing at all, one should understand that emptiness too is absent. If the intrinsic nature of space were something that could be made, it would be impermanent, and what is impermanent should not be called space.

Noble son, for example, worldly people say: space is without form, without obstruction, permanent, unchanging, and unaltering. That is why in the world space is spoken of as the fifth of the great elements. Noble son, but in truth space has no intrinsic nature; it is merely designated space because it appears, and in truth space does not exist. It is like conventional truth, which has no intrinsic nature of its own, yet has been taught as conventional truth for the sake of sentient beings.

Noble son, the essential nature of nirvāṇa is similar in this respect: although it has no fixed abode, it is called nirvāṇa because it is the abode in which all Tathāgatas sever the afflictions. Nirvāṇa itself is permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure. Nirvāṇa is bliss, yet it is not the experience of bliss in the ordinary sense; it is the supreme, peaceful, and sublime bliss. The Blessed One, the buddha, has two kinds of bliss: the bliss of complete peace and the bliss of full awareness. Within the intrinsic nature of the authentic defining characteristics, there are three kinds of bliss: the bliss of experience, the bliss of complete peace, and the bliss of full awareness.

The intrinsic nature of a buddha is a single bliss: the bliss of attaining the unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening.

Then the great bodhisattva Samantaprabha, Glorious King of the Lofty and Sublime, addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, it is not proper to call that abode in which the afflictions are severed nirvāṇa."

"Why is that?" he continued. "From the time the Tathāgata first became fully and completely awakened until he came to the banks of the river Hiraṇyavatī, at that very time the king of māras, together with his retinue, appeared before the Blessed One and said: 'Blessed One, the time has come to pass into nirvāṇa — why do you not pass into nirvāṇa?' The Blessed One replied to the king of māras: 'I will not pass into nirvāṇa, because as yet I have no attendants who are learned, who hold moral discipline and vows, whose faculties are clear and whose wisdom is keen, and who are capable of working for the benefit of sentient beings.'

"But if the very abode in which the afflictions are severed were nirvāṇa, then since bodhisattvas have severed the afflictions since immeasurable aeons, why would nirvāṇa not be attributed to them? Since both have that abode of severed afflictions, why does it apply to the blessed buddha but not to bodhisattvas?

"And if severing the afflictions is not nirvāṇa, then why did the Tathāgata formerly say to the brahmin Jyotiṣka: 'This very body of mine is nirvāṇa'?

"Furthermore, once when the Tathāgata was residing at Vaiśālī, māra again made this request: 'In former times, Tathāgata, you declared that you would not pass into nirvāṇa because you had no attendants who were learned, who upheld moral discipline, whose wisdom was clear and whose faculties were keen, and who were capable of working for the benefit of sentient beings. But now such persons do exist — so why do you say you will not pass into nirvāṇa?'

"At that time the Tathāgata replied to the king of māras: 'Do not form the perception of something obstructed by form. In three months from now, I will pass completely into nirvāṇa.'

"Blessed One, if the passing away of the body is not nirvāṇa, why did the Tathāgata say: 'In three months from now I will pass completely into nirvāṇa'?

"Blessed One, if the severing of afflictions itself were nirvāṇa, then since the Tathāgata first became fully and completely awakened in essence at the foot of the Bodhi tree and thereby overcame the afflictions — if that itself were nirvāṇa — why did he say: 'In three months from now I will pass completely into nirvāṇa'?

"And Blessed One, if he had already passed into nirvāṇa at that time, why did he say at the midnight hour to the śāla trees of the great forest in the city of Kuśinagara: 'I will now pass completely into nirvāṇa'?

"The Tathāgata is one who speaks truthfully — how then did he utter those words that appear untrue?"

Then the Blessed One replied to the great bodhisattva Samantaprabha, Glorious King of the Lofty and Sublime:

"Son of good family, because it has been said that the Tathāgata possesses a long and broad tongue, you should understand that from immeasurable aeons the Tathāgata has been free from untrue words. Everything whatsoever that is spoken by all buddhas and bodhisattvas is carefully considered speech — it is not untrue.

"Son of good family, just as you have said, it is true that the sinful māra formerly petitioned me to pass into nirvāṇa. But son of good family, the king of māras does not know the authentic and true defining characteristics of what nirvāṇa definitively is. Why is that?"

The sinful māra thinks in his mind: "If the Tathāgata sits in silence, speaking nothing and doing nothing for the benefit of sentient beings, that is nirvāṇa." Son of good family, consider this analogy: when worldly people see someone who is silent and doing nothing, they say, "That person is no different from a corpse." In the same way, the sinful māra thinks: "The very fact that the Tathāgata does nothing for the benefit of sentient beings and speaks nothing — that itself is the Tathāgata's nirvāṇa."

Son of good family, the Tathāgata has not taught the defining characteristics of the buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha as undifferentiated from one another. Rather, he has taught only that two qualities — abiding permanently and being completely pure — are undifferentiated among them. Son of good family, the Tathāgata has not taught a buddha, the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and nirvāṇa as sharing undifferentiated defining characteristics. Rather, he has taught only that being utterly lasting and permanent, changeless and immovable — these alone are undifferentiated among them.

Son of good family, at that time and on that occasion all my śrāvaka attendants will fall into dispute. Just as the monks of the region of Kauśāmbī who were of bad conduct acted contrary to my word, broke their vows of moral discipline, and took unstipulated goods — so they will seek gain and fame by praising themselves before householders, saying: "I have attained the undefiled. What have I attained, you ask? I have attained everything from the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship." And they will disparage others. They will show no respect for the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, moral discipline, or their preceptors. When you tell me, "Such-and-such an article the Buddha permitted to be held," or, "Such-and-such articles the Buddha did not permit to be held" — even if I myself should say, "Such-and-such articles I have not truly permitted," they will contradict my word and say, "Such-and-such articles were truly permitted by the Buddha." Those of bad conduct will not trust my word. Because of them, do not think to yourself that I bear a grudge against the sinful māra. I have declared: "In three months' time I shall pass fully into nirvāṇa."

Son of good family, because of those monks of bad conduct, the śrāvaka attendants who are engaged in the trainings will neither see my body nor hear my Dharma, and so they will say, "The Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa." But the bodhisattvas, seeing my body and constantly hearing Dharma from me, will not say that I have passed fully into nirvāṇa. Although the śrāvaka attendants say, "The Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa," I have not truly passed into nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, if among my śrāvaka attendants there is one who says, "The Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa," know that such a person is not truly my attendant. He is a companion of māra, one of wrong views, one who is evil, one who does not hold correct views. But whoever says, "The Tathāgata has not passed into nirvāṇa" — that person alone is my true attendant; know him to be no companion of māra, not one of wrong and evil views.

Son of good family, I have never once encountered any of my attendants saying that the Tathāgata, while dwelling without speaking and without acting for the benefit of sentient beings, has thereby passed fully into nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: a householder has many children. If that householder has gone away to another place and not yet returned, the children think their father has died —

yet the householder has not died — the children, deceived by a wrong perception, give rise to the perception of death. In just the same way, the śrāvaka attendants, not seeing me, think: "The Tathāgata has passed fully into nirvāṇa between the sal trees in the city of Kuśinagara." I have not truly passed fully into nirvāṇa, yet the śrāvaka attendants give rise to the perception of nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: when a bright lamp is covered by something, those who do not know think the lamp has died, and because they do not know that the glory of its light has not truly died, they give rise to the perception of death. In just the same way, the śrāvaka attendants are like that: though they possess the eye of wisdom, it is obscured by the afflictions, their minds have become inverted, and not seeing the true body they give rise to the perception of absence and of passing — yet I have not truly passed into nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: a blind person does not see the sun and moon. Because they do not see them, they do not know the marks of day and night, of light and darkness. Because they do not know them, they say, "The sun and the moon do not truly exist." Yet it is precisely because the blind person cannot see them that they exist — truly the sun and moon are there — and because they cannot be seen, a wrong perception arises and one says, "There is no sun or moon." In just the same way, the śrāvaka attendants are like that blind person: not seeing the Tathāgata, they think the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa — but the Tathāgata has not truly passed into nirvāṇa. With wrong perception they give rise to such a thought.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: when clouds and mist obscure the sun and moon, those who are foolish and do not understand say, "There is no sun or moon." The sun and moon truly exist, but because they are fully covered, sentient beings cannot see them. In just the same way, the śrāvaka attendants are like that: obscured by many afflictions, the eye of wisdom is veiled, and not seeing the Tathāgata they say, "The Tathāgata's life has ended."

Son of good family, consider this analogy: when the sun sets over Jambudvīpa, it is obscured by the dark mountains and sentient beings cannot see it — yet the sun's own nature has not truly set. Because sentient beings cannot see it, they give rise to the perception of setting. In just the same way, the śrāvaka attendants are like that: obscured by the mountain of the afflictions, they cannot see my body, and because they cannot see it they give rise to the perception that the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa. I have not truly passed into nirvāṇa.

Therefore, when I was in Vaiśālī, I declared to the evil māra: "From this day, in three months I shall pass fully into nirvāṇa." Son of good family, the Tathāgata had foreseen beforehand that three months hence the roots of virtue of the bodhisattva Kāśyapa would ripen, and that he would come forth from the fragrant mountain of Gandhamādana and appear in my presence. Therefore I declared to the evil māra: "From this day, in three months I shall pass fully into nirvāṇa."

Son of good family, furthermore, five hundred men of great power would, in three months, give rise to the mind set upon the unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening — and therefore I declared to the evil māra: "From this day, in three months I shall pass fully into nirvāṇa."

Son of good family, Cunda and the five hundred Licchavīs, and the maiden Ambā — in three months they too would give rise to the mind set upon the unsurpassable awakening,

and their roots of virtue would be fully ripened — and therefore I declared to the evil māra: "From this day, in three months I shall pass fully into nirvāṇa."

Son of good family, there was one called Sundaraka, a follower of the naked non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) and others. For twelve years I had taught him the Dharma, yet he had no faith in me and no trust. I knew that in three months the root of his wrong views would be severed — and therefore I declared to the evil māra: "From this day, in three months I shall pass fully into nirvāṇa."

Son of good family, why, and for what reason, had I previously declared to the evil māra on the banks of the Nairañjanā River: "Since I have no attendant of great learning, I shall not pass fully into nirvāṇa"? It was because at that time I was contemplating turning the wheel of Dharma for the group of five monks in Vārāṇasī. It was for those five monks, namely Yaśa, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāṃpati, and Subāhu. It was also for the fifty householders led by Drakpo. It was also for the countless gods and humans led by the king of Madhyadeśa named Rūpasāra. It was also for Uruvelā Kāśyapa together with his retinue of five hundred monks, and for Nadī Kāśyapa and Gayā Kāśyapa together with their five hundred kinsmen and attendants. And it was in order to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma for Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the twelve hundred and fifty monks and others — for all of these that I declared to the evil māra: "I shall not pass into nirvāṇa."

Son of good family, there is such a thing as nirvāṇa, but it is not great nirvāṇa. How is it that nirvāṇa is not great nirvāṇa? When one has severed the afflictions without having seen the intrinsic nature of a buddha, that is called nirvāṇa — but it is not great nirvāṇa. Because one has not seen the intrinsic nature of a buddha, permanence is absent and selflessness remains, though there is bliss and utter purity. Therefore, although the afflictions have been severed, it is not to be called great nirvāṇa. Whoever has seen the intrinsic nature of a buddha and has severed the afflictions — that is called great nirvāṇa. Because one has seen the intrinsic nature of a buddha, there is permanence, self, bliss, and utter purity. Therefore such a severing of the afflictions is called the great and complete nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, what is called the "sorrow" in nirvāṇa refers to what weaves and entangles. The meaning of not being woven and entangled is nirvāṇa. Again, "passing" refers to what covers and obscures. The meaning of not being covered and obscured is nirvāṇa. Again, "passing" refers to going and coming. The meaning of not going and not coming is nirvāṇa. Again, "passing" refers to grasping and taking up. The meaning of not grasping is nirvāṇa. Again, "passing" refers to uncertainty and indeterminacy. Certainly being free of all uncertainty is nirvāṇa. Again, "passing" refers to the new and the old. The meaning of there being no new and old is nirvāṇa. Again, "passing" refers to obscuration. The meaning of being free of obscuration is nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, the disciples of the school called Ūrukakabila say that "passing" means characteristic marks, and that the meaning of being without characteristic marks is nirvāṇa. Son of good family, "passing" refers to existence and being. The meaning of there being no such existence is nirvāṇa.

"Passing" refers to accumulation, and the meaning of there being no accumulation is nirvāṇa. "Passing" refers to suffering, and the meaning of there being no suffering is nirvāṇa. Son of good family, cutting off afflictions is not called nirvāṇa; rather, not giving rise to afflictions at all is what is called nirvāṇa. Son of good family, the Buddha, the Blessed One, does not give rise to afflictions, and therefore is called nirvāṇa.

One who possesses wisdom and is unobstructed with respect to all phenomena is called a Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is not a child of low birth, nor a śrāvaka, nor a pratyekabuddha, nor even a bodhisattva — the Tathāgata is called the intrinsic nature of a buddha. The wisdom of the Tathāgata's body, speech, and mind is unobstructed throughout all world-systems, immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless in extent, and therefore is called space. The Tathāgata abides permanently, neither changing nor shifting, and therefore is called the characteristic mark of what is true and real. It is for this reason that the Tathāgata does not ultimately pass into complete nirvāṇa. This is what is meant by possessing the seven qualities of a bodhisattva, a great being, who applies himself diligently to this noble sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, you ask how it is that a bodhisattva, a great being, who has applied himself diligently to this noble sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa comes to possess eight qualities. Son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, who applies himself diligently to the Great Nirvāṇa does so by: cutting off five things; abandoning five things; cultivating six things; thoroughly meditating on five things; carefully guarding one thing; drawing near to four things; having faith in and inclining toward one true thing; and attaining thorough liberation of mind and thorough liberation through wisdom.

Son of good family, how does a bodhisattva cut off five things? They are the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. What is meant by "aggregate"? The aggregates are that which perpetuates sentient beings' uninterrupted flow in cyclic existence, that from which one never separates — the heavy burden; they are that which disperses and accumulates, belonging to the three times, and yet however one examines them, they cannot be found as an object. These are called aggregates.

A bodhisattva, a great being, may perceive the aggregate of form, yet does not regard it as a characteristic mark. Why is that? Because even when the intrinsic nature of the ten aspects of form is examined, it cannot be found as an object. It is spoken of as "aggregate" only for the sake of the world. There are one hundred and eight feelings, and though one perceives the aggregate of feelings, from the very beginning there is no characteristic mark of feeling. Why is that? Because, although there are one hundred and eight feelings, they have no true or definitive meaning, and therefore a bodhisattva does not perceive a real aggregate of feeling. In the same way, perception, formations, and consciousness are also like this. A bodhisattva, a great being, thoroughly understands that the five aggregates are the root from which afflictions arise, and therefore cuts them off through skillful means.

Son of good family, how does a bodhisattva abandon five things? They are the five kinds of wrong view. What are the five? The view of the perishable collection (ātmagrāha, the view that the aggregates constitute a self), extreme views, wrong views, the conceit of moral discipline and conduct, and the conceit of views. Through these five kinds of wrong view as conditions, sixty-two views arise, and through those views as conditions one circles in cyclic existence without interruption.

Therefore the bodhisattva is heedful and does not draw near to them.

Now, how is a bodhisattva to be endowed with six things? They are the six recollections (anusmṛti) held close. What are the six? Recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of the gods, recollection of generosity, and recollection of moral discipline. These constitute the bodhisattva's endowment with six things.

How does a bodhisattva thoroughly cultivate five things? They are the five kinds of meditative absorption (samādhi). What are the five? The meditative absorption of knowing, the meditative absorption of peace, the meditative absorption of touching bodily and mental rapture, the meditative absorption without rapture, and the meditative absorption of courageous advance. When these five kinds of meditative absorption are cultivated, one draws near to the great nirvāṇa. Therefore a bodhisattva thoroughly cultivates them with a mind of diligent effort.

How does a bodhisattva guard one thing? It is the awakening mind. The bodhisattva, the great being, constantly guards the awakening mind with diligent effort. Just as a worldly person guards an only child, just as one guards the single eye that remains, just as a caravan leader guards those who travel through the great wilderness, so too does a bodhisattva guard the awakening mind. By guarding the awakening mind in this way, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. And having attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, one is endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity. That itself is the unsurpassed great nirvāṇa. Therefore the bodhisattva thoroughly guards this one thing.

How does a bodhisattva draw near to four things? They are the four immeasurable minds. What are the four? Great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity. Through these four minds one gives rise to the awakening mind for as many sentient beings as there are, boundless and without limit. Therefore the bodhisattva draws near to them with single-pointed mind.

What is the one right thing in which a bodhisattva places faith and toward which the bodhisattva inclines? Here the bodhisattva understands that all sentient beings travel by a single path. That single path is none other than the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). Buddhas and bodhisattvas have divided it into three aspects for the sake of sentient beings. Therefore the bodhisattva places faith, inclines toward it, and does not act contrary to it.

What is meant by the bodhisattva's mind being supremely liberated? Because the minds of attachment, aversion, and delusion have completely ceased, it is called the supreme liberation of the bodhisattva's mind.

What then is the supreme liberation of the bodhisattva's wisdom? Because the bodhisattva, the great being, is unobstructed with respect to all phenomena, it is called the supreme liberation of the bodhisattva's wisdom. Through the condition of this liberation of wisdom, what was not previously heard comes to be heard, what was not previously seen comes to be seen, and what was not previously reached comes to be reached.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, Sarvadarśī (Glorious King of Lofty Radiance) addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Blessed One, what the Blessed One has taught — calling it 'the supremely liberated mind' — that is not actually the case. Why so? Because from the very beginning the mind has never been bound. How is that? The intrinsic nature of mind is not one of attachment, aversion, or..."

delusion that the mind could be bound by affliction. If from the very beginning the mind has never been bound, why then did the Blessed One speak of 'the supremely liberated mind'?

"Blessed One, if the intrinsic nature of mind is not bound by the affliction of attachment, then by what cause and by what condition could it become bound? Consider the analogy of a horn: since from the very beginning it has not had the characteristic of milk, no matter how much effort one applies, milk cannot possibly come from it. The breast of a nursing mother is not like that — even with little effort, milk flows abundantly. In the same way, if from the very beginning the mind has no attachment, how could attachment exist in it now? And if attachment did not exist from the very beginning but arose only later, then buddhas and bodhisattvas, who likewise never had the characteristic of attachment from the very beginning, should also come to have it later. But that is untenable.

"Blessed One, consider another analogy: a barren woman has not had the characteristic of giving birth from the very beginning. No matter how much effort she makes, no matter how many causes and conditions she accumulates, it is impossible that she could give birth to a child. In the same way, if the mind has not had the characteristic of attachment from the very beginning, then even when it encounters many conditions, it is impossible for attachment to arise.

"Blessed One, just as green wet wood, no matter how it is rubbed, will not produce fire, so too the mind is like that: if no matter how it is rubbed attachment does not arise in it, how could the affliction of attachment bind the mind?

"Blessed One, just as sand, no matter how it is pressed, will yield no oil, so too the mind is like that: no matter how it is pressed, attachment does not arise in it. Therefore, since attachment and mind are distinct from each other, even if an affliction is present, how could it adhere to the mind?

"Blessed One, just as if one were to drive a peg into empty space there would be no surface for it to cling to, in the same way the implanting of attachment in the mind is like that: through causes and conditions of every kind, attachment cannot bind the mind.

"Blessed One, if one says the mind is 'liberated' because it is without attachment, why then do buddhas and bodhisattvas not remove thorns from the sky? Blessed One, the past mind is not called 'liberated,' and the future mind is likewise not liberated. The present mind does not co-arise with awakening. So in which moment's mind does one speak of obtaining liberation?

"Blessed One, just as a lamp that has already gone out cannot dispel darkness, and a lamp yet to be lit also cannot dispel darkness, and the present lamp too cannot dispel darkness — why so? Because light and darkness do not exist at the same time. In the same way, if the mind is also like that, why did the Blessed One speak of the mind as liberated?

"Blessed One, attachment does exist. If it did not exist, it would make no sense for attachment to arise upon seeing a woman. But if it does arise through the condition of seeing a woman, then one must recognize that attachment genuinely exists. Since attachment does exist, one falls into the stream of the three lower destinies.

"Blessed One, consider that some people, upon seeing even a painted image of a woman, give rise to attachment, and having given rise to attachment they incur various moral faults. If attachment did not exist from the very beginning, why should the mere sight of a painting give rise to attachment? And if the mind is without attachment, why did the Tathāgata teach that the bodhisattva attains liberation of mind? If the mind has no attachment, then why does attachment arise upon seeing a sign but not arise when no sign is seen?

"I see at present the karmic maturation of evil deeds ripening, and from this I affirm that attachment exists; and that aversion and delusion exist is likewise the same. Blessed One, consider that sentient beings possess a body and yet no self truly exists, yet foolish and ignoble people perceive a self. Now, even though the perception of clinging to a self exists, if one does not fall into the three lower destinies on account of it, then why should one who has attachment generate the perception of a woman upon encountering a woman's sign, and thereby fall into the three lower destinies?

"Blessed One, consider that fire arises through friction. If the intrinsic nature of fire does not exist within any of its causes, then from what cause and condition did it arise? Blessed One, attachment is just like that. Attachment does not exist within form; it does not exist within smell, taste, or tangible objects; nor does it exist within mental phenomena. If that is so, then why does attachment arise from form, smell, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena? If attachment does not exist within the many causes, then why does attachment arise in sentient beings alone, while it does not arise in buddhas and bodhisattvas?

"Blessed One, mind too is indeterminate. If mind were something determinate, there would be no attachment, aversion, or delusion. But if it is indeterminate, then the Tathāgata has taught that one can attain liberation of mind. Attachment is likewise indeterminate. But if it is indeterminate, why should it cause rebirth in the three lower destinies? Therefore both attachment and its object are indeterminate. Why is that? Because when one focuses on a single form, some develop attachment, some develop aversion, and some develop delusion. Therefore both attachment and its object are indeterminate.

"If both are indeterminate, then why did the Tathāgata teach that if a bodhisattva applies himself to great nirvāṇa, the mind will attain liberation?"

Then the Blessed One declared to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantaprabhāsaśrīrāja:

"Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, the mind is not bound by the total affliction of attachment; nor is it unbound; nor is it liberated; nor is it unliberated; it is not existent; it is not nonexistent; it is not present; it is not past; it is not future. Why is that? Son of good family, because all phenomena are without intrinsic nature.

"Son of good family, certain non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) say this: 'From the assembly of causes and conditions a result arises.' If the conditions had from the very beginning no intrinsic nature of arising, yet a result were still to arise from them, then space, which has never arisen, should likewise be capable of producing a result. But space does not arise because it is not a cause. It is because the conditions contain from the very beginning the intrinsic nature of the result that a result arises from their assembly.

"How is that? Consider this example. When Devadatta builds a wall, he employs clay and earth; he does not employ paint. When he paints a picture, he employs paint; he does not employ grass and wood. When he weaves cloth, he employs thread; he does not employ clay and wood. When he constructs a house, he employs clay and wood; he does not employ thread. From each of these assembled materials a particular result arises — and this shows that the intrinsic nature of each result is certainly already present within its cause. Since a result arises, the intrinsic nature is without doubt present within the cause.

"If intrinsic nature did not exist, it would follow that from any one thing all things whatsoever could arise and come forth. Moreover, since in such assemblies it is possible to add more and possible to remove some, there is without doubt a result present from the very beginning within those causes. If there were no result, then no one would assemble or separate them, and nothing would come forth."

Space, by contrast, neither assembles nor separates, and therefore all things are able to arise and come forth from it. Thus it is because a cause exists that the seed of the nyagrodha tree resides within the nyagrodha tree, that the essence of butter is present within milk, that cloth comes forth from thread, and that clay is present within a lump of earth. Noble son, all the benighted Vaiśeṣikas, blinded by ignorance, explain the matter in this way: "Attachment means fixation; the mind is of the nature of desire," they say.

They also say this: in the mind of a benighted Vaiśeṣika there is both a nature of attachment and a nature of liberation. When it meets with the condition of attachment, a mind of attachment arises; when it meets with the condition of liberation, a mind of liberation arises. So they say, but this is not the correct meaning.

Furthermore, some benighted Vaiśeṣikas say: there is no result within any cause at all. A cause has two aspects: subtle and gross. The subtle is permanent; the gross is impermanent. From the subtle cause comes the gross cause, and from that gross cause comes the result. Because the gross is impermanent, the result too is impermanent — so they explain.

Noble son, still other benighted Vaiśeṣikas say: the mind has no cause, and attachment too has no cause; it is through time that a mind of attachment arises. These and others like them do not know the causes and conditions of the mind, and so they circle through the six classes of beings, fully taking on birth and death again and again.
