Noble son, consider the example of a dog tethered on a leash to a pillar: it circles the pillar endlessly and cannot break free. In just the same way, all those benighted Vaiśeṣikas and all common individuals are like that dog — bound to the pillar of saṃsāra by the leash of ignorance, they circle through the twenty-five existences and cannot break free.

Noble son, consider further: just as someone who has fallen into a pit of filth climbs out and then goes back in again; just as a sick person, having recovered, returns to the very causes of illness; just as someone who has gone to a remote wilderness turns back from leaving saṃsāra; just as one who has been washed clean smears himself again with mud and excrement — all the benighted Vaiśeṣikas are likewise. They are liberated from the sense base of nothingness, yet because they are not liberated from the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, they return once again to the three lower destinies.

Why is this so? All the benighted Vaiśeṣikas attend only to results and give no thought to dependent origination. Just as a dog bites the stone rather than the one who threw it, so too all those benighted common individuals attend only to results and give no thought to causes and conditions. Because they give it no thought, they return from the state of non-perception and fall once more into the three lower destinies.

Noble son, buddhas and bodhisattvas do not teach in a one-sided, decisive way — asserting definitively that the result is present within the cause, or that it is not present, or that it is both present and not present, or that it is neither present nor absent. Whoever says, "The result is from the beginning definitively present within the cause," or "It is definitively absent," or "It is both present and absent," or "It is definitively neither present nor absent" — know that such a person is an ally of Māra, belongs to the faction of Māra, and is one in whom craving still exists. Such a being, existing in that state, cannot sever the bonds of saṃsāra, for they do not know the defining mark of the mind and the defining mark of attachment.

Noble son, buddhas and bodhisattvas teach the path of the Middle Way. Why? Because all phenomena are not existent —

— nor are they non-existent, yet neither is determinately the case. How so? Through the eye, form, appearance, mind, and the condition of mentation, consciousness arises. Yet that consciousness does not definitively reside in the eye, nor does it reside within form, appearance, mind, or mentation, nor does it reside in between. It is not existent, and it is not non-existent. Because it arises from dependent origination, it is said to be existent. Because it has no intrinsic nature, it is said to be non-existent. Therefore the Tathāgata teaches that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.

Noble son, buddhas and bodhisattvas will never declare that the mind definitively possesses a pure intrinsic nature, nor that the mind definitively lacks a pure intrinsic nature — because neither a pure mind nor an impure mind has fixed abiding. Because attachment arises from conditions, it is not non-existent. Because attachment has no intrinsic nature from the very beginning, it is not said to be existent.

Noble son, because of dependent origination, the mind of attachment arises, and because of dependent origination, the mind is liberated. Noble son, dependent origination has two aspects: that which follows the course of saṃsāra, and that which follows the course of nirvāṇa.

Noble son, because of dependent origination, the mind arises together with attachment — and there is also the cessation of that mind together with attachment. There is also the mind arising together with attachment without cessation together with attachment. There is also the cessation of attachment without the mind arising together with attachment. And there is also neither arising together with attachment nor cessation together with attachment.

How then does the mind arise together with attachment and also cease together with attachment? Noble son, if a foolish, undisciplined person applies effort to the mind of attachment without having cut off the mind of attachment, that is called the mind arising together with attachment and ceasing together with attachment. All sentient beings, having not cut off the mind of attachment, have the mind arising together with attachment, and the mind ceasing together with attachment. As an analogy, all sentient beings of the desire realm have the fortune of the first dhyāna. Whether they have cultivated it or not, they always possess it, and when they encounter the proper condition, they will attain it. The condition referred to here is the aeon of fire. In the same way, all foolish and undisciplined persons — whether they have cultivated it or not — have the mind arising together with attachment and ceasing together with attachment. Why? Because attachment has not been cut off.

How then does the mind arise together with attachment without ceasing together with attachment? The close-dwelling śrāvakas have the mind of attachment arise through cause and condition. Because they fear the mind of attachment, they cultivate the contemplation of the skeleton. That is called the mind arising together with attachment without ceasing together with attachment. Moreover, there is yet another case of the mind arising together with attachment without ceasing together with attachment. As an analogy, śrāvakas who have not yet attained the four fruits have the mind of attachment arise through cause and condition. When they attain the four fruits, the mind of attachment ceases. That is called the mind arising together with attachment without ceasing together with attachment. When a bodhisattva, a great being, attains the immovable ground, the mind arises together with attachment but does not cease together with attachment.

Now, how is it that the mind does not arise together with attachment and yet ceases together with attachment? If a bodhisattva, a great being, has cut off the mind of attachment, yet for the sake of sentient beings still displays the appearance of having attachment — and by so displaying it, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings are stirred to strive after wholesome Dharmas and bring them to complete fulfillment — that is called the mind not arising together with attachment yet ceasing together with attachment.

Now, how is it that the mind does not arise together with attachment and does not cease together with attachment? Apart from arhats, pratyekabuddhas, Tathāgatas, and bodhisattvas who have attained the immovable ground, all other bodhisattvas do not have the mind arise together with attachment, yet neither does the mind cease together with attachment.

Therefore, whether the intrinsic nature of mind is utterly pure or not utterly pure cannot be definitively settled for buddhas and bodhisattvas alike. O son of good family, mind is not connected with the thorough affliction of attachment; it is not connected with aversion, nor with delusion.

O son of good family, consider the following: the sun and moon are obscured by mist, dust, clouds, fog, the eclipse-demon (Rāhu), and so forth, and on account of this sentient beings cannot see them. Although they cannot be seen in that way, the intrinsic nature of the sun and moon is not connected with those five obscurations. Mind is similar: because, on account of certain causes and conditions, the thorough affliction of attachment arises, it is said that the mind of a sentient being is connected with attachment — yet the intrinsic nature of mind is not truly connected with it. That mind which is a mind of attachment has the intrinsic nature of attachment. That which is without attachment has the intrinsic nature of non-attachment. A mind without attachment does not become a mind with attachment, and a mind thoroughly afflicted by attachment does not become a mind without attachment. O son of good family, therefore the thorough affliction of attachment cannot penetrate or invade mind. Since buddhas and bodhisattvas have utterly destroyed the thorough affliction of attachment, it is said that they attain the liberation of mind. As for all ordinary, inferior sentient beings, through causes and conditions the thorough affliction of attachment arises, and through causes and conditions the mind becomes liberated.

O son of good family, consider this example: at a place on a steep rocky mountain, neither humans nor monkeys can go. At certain places, monkeys can go but humans cannot. At yet other places, both monkeys and humans can go.

O son of good family, at a place accessible to both humans and monkeys, hunters coat a flat board with pitch and catch monkeys in this way. The monkey, curious and not cautious, reaches out its hand and tastes the pitch. The hand touches it and becomes stuck. Wanting to free the hand, it kicks with its foot, and the foot too becomes stuck. Wanting to free the foot, it grabs with its teeth, and the mouth too becomes stuck. In this way all five limbs are trapped. The hunters then place it on a carrying pole, haul it away, and bring it home.

Likewise, the steep rocky mountain is an analogy for buddhas and bodhisattvas attaining the true path. The monkey is an analogy for foolish, inferior ordinary persons. The hunter is an analogy for the wicked māra (Māra). The pitch is an analogy for the thorough affliction of attachment. The fact that neither human nor monkey can escape from that place is an analogy for inferior ordinary persons and wicked Māra together having no escape. The monkey escaping while the human does not is an analogy for those tīrthikas (non-Buddhists) endowed with wisdom who cannot be bound even by the five objects of desire associated with wicked Māra and the like.

The fact that both the human and the monkey escape is an analogy for inferior ordinary persons and wicked Māra dwelling perpetually in cyclic existence and being unable to engage in earnest practice. The fact that inferior ordinary persons, being bound by the five objects of desire, are easily carried off by wicked Māra is an analogy for the hunter catching the monkey, loading it on his back, and returning home.

Noble son, consider this example: a king dwelling in his own realm finds both body and mind at ease. But if he were to go into another's territory, many sufferings would arise. In the same way, all sentient beings are like this: if they remain in their own domain, they are perfectly at ease; but if they dwell in another's domain, they will encounter wicked Māra and experience many sufferings. What is called "one's own domain" is the four foundations of mindfulness. What is called "another's domain" is the five objects of desire.

Now, in what way does one come to belong to the camp of Māra? Some sentient beings regard the impermanent as permanent, and the permanent as impermanent. They regard what is suffering as pleasurable, and what is pleasurable as suffering. They regard what is thoroughly pure as impure, and what is impure as thoroughly pure. They regard what is without self as having a self, and what has a self as being without self. They regard what is not true liberation as liberation, and what is true liberation as not liberation. They regard what is not a vehicle as being a vehicle, and what is a vehicle as not being a vehicle. Those who hold such views are said to be bound by Māra. To be bound by Māra is to have an untrained mind.

Furthermore, noble son, whoever regards all phenomena as truly existent and holds their individual defining characteristics to be fixed — when such a person sees form, they grasp at the defining characteristic of form; and so on up through consciousness, grasping at the defining characteristic of consciousness. They see a man and grasp at the defining characteristic of a man. They see a woman and grasp at the defining characteristic of a woman. They see the sun and grasp at the defining characteristic of the sun. They see the moon and grasp at the defining characteristic of the moon. They see a year and grasp at the defining characteristic of a year. They see the aggregates and grasp at the defining characteristics of the aggregates. They see the sense bases and grasp at the defining characteristics of the sense bases. They see the elements and grasp at the defining characteristics of the elements. Such a way of seeing is called being bound by Māra, and to be bound by Māra is to have an untrained mind.

Furthermore, noble son, whoever regards the self as form, regards the self as containing form and form as contained within the self, and regards form as belonging to the self — and continuing in this way through to consciousness, regards the self as consciousness, regards consciousness as containing the self and the self as containing consciousness, and regards consciousness as belonging to the self — such a view is being bound by Māra and belonging to the camp of Māra. Such a person is not my close attendant.

Noble son, those who are close attendants of my śrāvakas abandon the twelve branches of scripture and instead study the many texts and treatises of the tīrthikas. Without cultivating the peaceful path of renunciation, they pursue nothing but the worldly activities of householders. What does it mean to pursue the activities of a householder? It means keeping all manner of goods without discernment — that is, male servants and female servants, fields and houses, draft oxen and horses and carts, female buffaloes and donkeys, fowl and dogs and monkeys and pigs and sheep, and various grains and produce. They abandon their preceptors and the Saṅgha, rely on laypeople, act in contradiction to the noble Dharma, and say to those lay persons: "The Buddha permitted monks to keep all manner of goods without discernment." To say such a thing is to do nothing but the work of a householder.

Furthermore, some close attendants do not act for the sake of nirvāṇa, but rather —

for the sake of gain and renown, they may listen to the twelve branches of scripture, yet they treat the Saṅgha's common wealth, the Saṅgha's rosaries, and its requisites and food as though these were their own. They are envious and miserly toward others who receive gain and renown. They ingratiate themselves with kings and princes, making prophecies for them, reading auspicious and inauspicious omens, consulting the stars, performing divinations with owls, examining markings, playing dice, and engaging in amusements of every kind. They frequent nuns and the wives of others, support two novices, and constantly frequent the homes of butchers, hunters, and liquor-sellers, and the dwellings of low-caste outcastes. They engage in all manner of commercial deceit, process their own food by hand, travel as messengers to other regions, and go so far as to perform the work of message-carrying. Those who act in such ways should be understood to be the retinue of māra — they are not my true close attendants.

On account of those causes and those conditions, the mind arises together with attachment and ceases together with attachment; and from attachment onward, up to and including delusion, the mind arises together with these afflictions and ceases together with them.

O son of noble family, on account of those very causes and conditions, the intrinsic nature of mind is neither pure nor impure. That is why I have taught that the mind attains liberation.

One who does not take up or keep any goods without discernment, and who, for the sake of great nirvāṇa, upholds and preserves the twelve branches of scripture, reads them aloud, recites them, writes them down, expounds them, and explains them — such a person is truly my close attendant and will not fall within the domain of the sinful māra. Know that this is the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of awakening (bodhipākṣikadharma).

One who cultivates in this way does not arise together with attachment, and does not cease together with attachment. Such a person should be understood to be a bodhisattva possessed of eight qualities by virtue of diligently practicing this noble sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa of the complete liberation of bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, O son of noble family, in what way does a great bodhisattva who diligently practices this noble sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa come to be possessed of nine qualities? O son of noble family, a great bodhisattva who diligently practices this noble sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa need only generate five things at the outset, and all the rest will be accomplished. What are those five? They are as follows: faith, mental solitude, moral discipline, reliance on a spiritual friend, and extensive learning.

And what, in this context, is faith? A great bodhisattva trusts in the Three Jewels, trusts in the existence of the result of generosity, trusts in both kinds of solitude, and trusts that apart from the path of the single vehicle there is no other path — that buddhas and bodhisattvas have divided it into three aspects for the sake of enabling sentient beings to swiftly attain liberation. One also trusts in ultimate truth and trusts in skillful means. This is what is called faith. Faith of this kind cannot be destroyed by any ascetic or brahmin, any god, māra, Brahmā, or any sentient being whatsoever. Through the condition of that faith, one attains the noble nature. Whether one's giving is much or little, all of it becomes proximate to great nirvāṇa, and one does not fall back into saṃsāra. Likewise, moral discipline, extensive learning, and wisdom are similar in this regard. This is what is called faith.

Even though one possesses such faith, not perceiving things in the manner described is what is called a bodhisattva possessing the substance of cultivating the great nirvāṇa of bodhisattvas.

Now, what is meant by mental solitude? The bodhisattva, the great being, establishes a mind of straightforwardness toward all sentient beings. It is true that all sentient beings, when they encounter the right causes and conditions, give rise to deceit and cunning; but the bodhisattva is not like that. Why? Because he is supremely skilled in understanding that all phenomena arise through dependent origination.

Even though the bodhisattva, the great being, sees all the faults and defects in sentient beings, he does not speak of them. Why? Because he fears that afflictions may arise; and if afflictions do arise, one will fall into the lower realms. If the bodhisattva sees even a small virtue in sentient beings, he praises and extols it. What is that virtue? It is the very intrinsic nature of a buddha. By praising the intrinsic nature of a buddha, awakening mind toward unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening will arise in all sentient beings.

Thereupon, the bodhisattva, the great being, Samantaprabha Uttamatejaśrīrāja addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, as the Blessed One has said, by the bodhisattva, the great being, praising the intrinsic nature of a buddha, as many sentient beings as there are will generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening — I submit that the meaning intended cannot be quite as stated. Why? When the Tathāgata first opened the sūtra teachings of great nirvāṇa, he taught three kinds of sentient beings. What are they? There is the patient who swiftly recovers when he meets a skilled physician, good medicine, and a nursing attendant; the patient who, if those are absent, will never recover, and will also not recover whether he meets them or not; and the patient who will recover whether he meets them or not. These are the three kinds the Teacher taught. In the same way, if all sentient beings meet a spiritual friend and hear the sublime Dharma from a buddha or a bodhisattva, they will generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening. Those who will not generate it if they do not meet such a friend are the following: stream-enterers (srotāpannas), once-returners (sakṛdāgāmins), non-returners (anāgāmins), arhats, and pratyekabuddhas. Those who meet a spiritual friend and hear the sublime Dharma from a buddha or a bodhisattva, yet are still unable to generate awakening mind, and likewise are unable to generate it even without meeting such a friend, are those with wrong craving. And those who generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening whether they meet such a friend or not — these, the Teacher declared, are bodhisattvas. Since there are those who generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening whether they meet such conditions or not, I respectfully submit that the statement made by the Blessed One — that by the Tathāgata's praising the intrinsic nature of a buddha, sentient beings generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening; and that whether they meet a spiritual friend or not, and whether they hear the Dharma from a buddha or a bodhisattva or not, they will not generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening — that statement also seems not to be quite as intended. Why? Because all of them too are destined to attain unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening."

Those with wrong craving, too — whether they hear of the intrinsic nature of a buddha or not — all will attain unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening. Blessed One, in the same way that you have stated that those called "persons with wrong craving" have cut off the root of virtue — that statement also seems not to be quite as intended. Why? Because the intrinsic nature of a buddha has not been cut off. Since the intrinsic nature of a buddha is a phenomenon that cannot be cut, why then did the Blessed One declare that the root of virtue has been cut off?

Just as previously the Blessed One, in teaching the twelve branches of scripture, declared that virtue is of two kinds — permanent and impermanent — permanent virtue cannot be cut, and impermanent virtue can be cut. If, because impermanent virtue can be cut, sentient beings fall into hell, why then is permanent virtue, which cannot be cut, not also reversed? If, because the intrinsic nature of a buddha cannot be cut, one is not a person with wrong craving — then why did the Tathāgata speak of persons with wrong craving?

Blessed One, if the awakening mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening arises through the condition of the intrinsic nature of a buddha, then why did the Tathāgata teach sentient beings the twelve branches of scripture at length?

Blessed One, consider this analogy: the four great rivers all arise from the lake called Anavatapta (the Unheated Lake). There is no situation in which a human being, a god, or a fully awakened buddha could cause those great rivers not to flow into the ocean and instead to flow back to their place of origin. The awakening mind is similar. Because the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present, whether one hears the teaching or not, whether one keeps moral discipline or not, whether one practises generosity or not, whether one engages in conduct or not, whether gnosis is present or not — all will attain unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening.

Blessed One, consider also this analogy: from the mountain called Udayana, the sun rises and travels to its midpoint in the sky. There is no situation in which that sun would think, "I will not go to the west; I will turn back and go east again." The intrinsic nature of a buddha is similar. Even without hearing, without keeping moral discipline, without practising generosity, without engaging in conduct, without gnosis — there is no situation in which unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening would not be attained.

Blessed One, in the same way that the fully awakened Blessed One has stated that the intrinsic nature of cause and result is neither existent nor non-existent — that statement too seems not to be quite as intended. Why? Just as, if the intrinsic nature of yoghurt were not present within milk, yoghurt too would not be present; and if the intrinsic nature of a nyagrodha tree's (the banyan's) growth to five fathoms in height were not present within its seed, it would not grow into a tree five fathoms tall — in the same way, if the seed of the tree of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening were not present within the intrinsic nature of a buddha, how could the tree of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening ever grow? Therefore, how can the statement that cause and result are neither existent nor non-existent be taken as meaningful?

Then the Blessed One declared, "Excellent! Excellent!" and continued to teach:

Son of good family, in the world there are two kinds of people who are as extremely rare as the udumbara flower. Who are they? One who does not commit non-virtuous acts, and one who, having committed a blameworthy wrong, feels remorse — such people are extremely rare.

There are also two kinds of people: those who are ungrateful, and those who are grateful.

There are also two kinds of people: those who listen to Dharma they have not heard before, and those who do not forget what they have already heard.

There are also two kinds of people: those who are innovators and

those who preserve the old ways. There are also two kinds of people: those who delight in hearing the Dharma, and those who delight in teaching the Dharma. There are also two kinds of people: those who are skilled in questioning, and those who are skilled in answering. You are skilled in questioning, and the Tathāgata is skilled in answering. Son of good family, through the condition of skilled questioning, the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma is turned — and thereby the trunk of the twelve links of dependent origination is dried up, beings are freed from the vast and boundless river of cyclic existence, the armies of Māra, the king of evil, are overcome, and the victory banner raised by the evil one is brought low.

Son of good family, earlier I described three kinds of sick people. You asked what it means that a patient will recover whether or not he encounters a skilled physician, good medicine, and a nurse. This is to be understood as follows: what applies regardless of whether those conditions are present refers to a person whose lifespan has a definite measure. What does this mean? It means a person who, throughout innumerable lifetimes, has practiced the three kinds of virtue — superior, middling, and lesser. Because they have practiced these three kinds of virtue, their lifespan has become definite. Just as the people of the northern continent Uttarakuru, whose lifespan is a full thousand years, if they fall ill, will recover whether or not they encounter a skilled physician, good medicine, nurses, and so forth — this is because they have attained a definite lifespan.

Son of good family, as for the meaning of my earlier statement that a sick person who encounters a skilled physician, good medicine, and a nurse will recover, but if they do not encounter them will not recover — this applies to a person whose lifespan is not yet fixed. Though their life is not yet exhausted, they may suddenly meet death through any one of nine causes and conditions. What are these nine? Eating food one knows to be disagreeable; eating in excess; eating again before the previous meal has been digested; not evacuating the bowels and bladder at the proper time; not heeding the physician's instructions when ill; not following the nurse's directions; taking an emetic and then straining to suppress the vomiting; being struck in the night by a fierce possessing spirit; and engaging in sexual misconduct with carelessness. For someone who falls ill through such conditions, it is said that if they encounter a physician and medicine they will recover, and if they do not encounter them they will not.

Son of good family, as for the meaning of my earlier statement that a person will not recover whether they encounter medicine and the rest or not — this applies to a person whose life is exhausted. If a person's life is spent, they will not recover whether they encounter a physician and the rest or not. Why? Because their life is exhausted. For this reason I said that such a sick person will not recover whether or not they encounter medicine, a physician, and the rest.

Sentient beings are similar to this. One who has generated the awakening mind will meet a spiritual friend — a buddha or bodhisattvas — and will question and listen to this profound Dharma; yet even without meeting such a one, all will be accomplished. Why? Because the awakening mind has been generated — just as the people of Uttarakuru have a definite lifespan.

As I have taught, from the level of a stream-enterer all the way to that of a pratyekabuddha: if one hears profound Dharma from a spiritual friend — a buddha or bodhisattvas — the awakening mind oriented toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening will arise. But if one has not met buddhas and bodhisattvas and has not heard this profound Dharma, the awakening mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening will not arise.

Just as a sick person whose life will be cut short suddenly by a conjunction of nine causes and conditions will recover if they meet a physician, but will not recover if they do not — so too, I have said: if one meets buddhas and bodhisattvas and hears the profound Dharma, the awakening mind will arise; but if one does not meet them, it will not arise.

Now, as I stated above, one might ask: what is the meaning of the statement that the awakening mind may or may not arise whether or not one meets a spiritual friend — a buddha or bodhisattvas — and hears the profound Dharma? Noble son, those who hold wrong craving (log sred can), even if they meet a spiritual friend, a buddha or bodhisattvas, and hear the profound Dharma — or even if they do not hear it — will not abandon the mind of wrong craving. Why? Because they have severed the wholesome Dharma. Those who hold wrong craving will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Why? Because if they were to generate the awakening mind, they would not be called holders of wrong craving.

Noble son, it has been said that through certain causes and conditions even a holder of wrong craving may attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening — yet a holder of wrong craving will not truly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. It is just like one whose life-force is exhausted: even if they meet medicine, a skilled physician, and a nursing attendant, they will not recover. Why? Because their life is spent.

Noble son, the word wrong refers to faith, and the word craving refers to its absence. Because one has faith yet lacks it, one is called a holder of wrong craving. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is not faith, nor do sentient beings possess it; since they do not possess it in that way, how could it be severed?

The word wrong refers to skillful means, and the word craving refers to their absence. Because one has skillful means yet lacks them, one is called a holder of wrong craving. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is not the cultivation of skillful means, nor do sentient beings possess this; since they do not possess it in that way, how could it be severed?

The word wrong refers to diligence, and the word craving refers to its absence. Because one has diligence yet lacks it, one is called a holder of wrong craving. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is not diligence, nor do sentient beings possess it; since they do not possess it in that way, how could it be severed?

The word wrong refers to mindfulness, and the word craving refers to its absence. Because one has mindfulness yet lacks it, one is called a holder of wrong craving. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is not mindfulness, nor do sentient beings possess it; since they do not possess it in that way, how could it be severed?

The word wrong refers to meditative absorption (samādhi), and the word craving refers to its absence. Because one has meditative absorption yet lacks it, one is called a holder of wrong craving. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is not meditative absorption, nor do sentient beings possess it; since they do not possess it in that way, how could it be severed?

The word wrong refers to wisdom, and the word craving refers to its absence. Because one has wisdom yet lacks it, one is called a holder of wrong craving. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is not wisdom, nor do sentient beings possess it; since they do not possess it in that way, how could it be severed?

The word wrong refers to impermanent virtue, and the word craving refers to its absence. Because one has impermanent virtue yet lacks it, one is called a holder of wrong craving. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is neither impermanent nor virtue nor non-virtue. Why? Because wholesome Dharma is obtained through skillful means, whereas the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not obtained through skillful means; therefore it is not virtue. And why is it not non-virtue? Because it is the fruit obtained from virtue.

The fruit of virtue is unsurpassable perfect awakening. Furthermore, what is called wholesome Dharma is obtained upon taking birth. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is not obtained upon taking birth; therefore it is not virtue. Because the wholesome Dharma obtained at birth is severed, one is called a holder of wrong craving.

Noble son, you have said: "If those with wrong craving possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha, why are they not turned back from the misdeeds of the hells?" Noble son, whether or not those with wrong craving possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha — it is only through skillful means that it will first come to be seen. Because it is seen in that way, unsurpassable perfect awakening is attained.

If those with wrong craving do not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha, how could they be turned back from the misdeeds of the three lower destinies? Noble son, if those with wrong craving place their trust in the existence of the intrinsic nature of a buddha, they will not go to the three lower destinies — and know that they are no longer holders of wrong craving. It is precisely because they do not place their trust in the existence of the intrinsic nature of a buddha that they fall into the three lower destinies. Because they fall into the three lower destinies, they are called holders of wrong craving.

Noble son, to continue with what you said — that if milk lacks the intrinsic nature of yogurt, it would be unreasonable for yogurt to arise from it; and that if the seed of the nyagrodha tree lacks the intrinsic nature of a tree five fathoms tall, it would be unreasonable for a tree five fathoms tall to grow — such things are said only by the foolish. A wise and discerning person would never utter such words. Why? Because there is no intrinsic nature of that kind.

Noble son, if the intrinsic nature of yogurt were already present within milk, it would be reasonable that it should not depend on many causes and conditions. Noble son, if water and milk are mixed together and pressed, even after a month no yogurt will form. But if a single drop of the juice of the plant called śiṃbikā is added as a fermenting agent, yogurt will form at once. If the intrinsic nature of yogurt were present from the very beginning, why would it depend on so many causes and conditions?

In just the same way, the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings comes to be seen only through many causes and conditions, and through many causes and conditions it becomes unsurpassable perfect awakening. That which is attained in dependence on many causes and conditions has no intrinsic nature of its own. It is precisely because it has no intrinsic nature of its own that it becomes unsurpassable perfect awakening.

Therefore, son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, always praises the virtues of others and does not speak of their faults. This is called an upright mind.

Furthermore, son of good family, how does a bodhisattva have an upright mind? A bodhisattva, a great being, never commits a transgression. If a transgression does occur, that very moment he confesses and acknowledges it before an abbot or a teacher, concealing nothing. With a sense of moral shame and conscientious dread, he reproaches himself and vows not to do it again. He generates the perception that what is light is in fact heavy. If someone asks about it, he answers truthfully: "I have indeed transgressed." If asked whether that transgression is good or bad, he answers: "Bad." If asked whether it is virtuous or non-virtuous, he answers: "Non-virtuous." If asked whether that transgression bears the fruit of virtue or the fruit of non-virtue, he answers: "It is truly not the fruit of virtue." If asked who committed this transgression — was it committed by the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha? — he answers: "It was not committed by the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; I myself committed it, and moreover it was done through the accumulation of afflictions." Because his mind is thus upright, he has confidence that the buddha-nature exists. Because he has confidence that the buddha-nature exists, he should not be called one of wrong craving. Because his mind is thus upright, he is called a companion of the Buddha. Even if sentient beings offer him robes, food, lodging, bedding, and medicines for illness, he should not think "this is too much" even if he receives ten million of any one of these things. This is called the upright mind of a bodhisattva.

How then does a bodhisattva uphold moral discipline? A bodhisattva, a great being, does not maintain the vow of moral discipline for the sake of being reborn as a god, nor for the sake of destruction — nor has he undertaken it all the way down to the vow of dogs, the vow of birds, the vow of cattle, or the vow of peacocks. He does not break moral discipline, he does not degrade moral discipline, he does not hold moral discipline to be advantageous in a calculating way, he does not practice a mixed moral discipline, and he does not practice the moral discipline of śrāvakas. Rather, he receives and holds the moral discipline of a bodhisattva, a great being, and the discipline of the Perfection of moral discipline. The fact that, even after full ordination, neither pride nor arrogance arises in him — this is called the bodhisattva's possession of the three components of the discipline of the vow of great parinirvāṇa.

How then does a bodhisattva attend upon a spiritual friend? A bodhisattva, a great being, always shows sentient beings the path of virtue and does not show them the path of non-virtue, teaching that the path of non-virtue does not bear the fruit of virtue. Son of good family, I am the true spiritual friend of all sentient beings, and I am able to cut away all the evil views of the brahmin Pūraṇa Kāśyapa. Son of good family, if there is a sentient being who pays respect and homage to me, then even if the causes and conditions for falling into hell exist in that sentient being, he will be reborn as a god. Just as those such as the caterpillar and the like, who by their very nature are destined to fall into hell — because they catch sight of me, the causes and conditions for falling into hell are purified, and they are reborn as gods of the form realm. Even if one were like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana and their companions, one should not be called a true spiritual friend of sentient beings. Why is that? Because one produces the cause for wrong craving in the mind of sentient beings.

Son of good family, long ago when I was dwelling in the land of the yellow-robes, I had two attendants who served Śāriputra. One I set to contemplating a skeleton, and the other I set to contemplating the breath.

Yet even after many years had passed, neither of the two attained meditative absorption. Failing to attain it in this way, they gave rise to the wrong view that there was also no nirvāṇa, and also no undefiled phenomena. They reasoned: "If such things existed, we of all people would have attained them — for we hold and guard the scriptural transmission of the teaching most scrupulously."

When I saw that those two monks were generating minds of wrong view, I called out to Śāriputra and said these words: "You have not taught well. Why have you confused those two disciples and taught them the Dharma incorrectly? Your two disciples are of different kinds — one is a washerman and the other is a goldsmith. It is fitting to teach the goldsmith the contemplation of the breath, and it is fitting to teach the washerman the contemplation of the skeleton. Because you taught them incorrectly, wrong unwholesome thoughts arose in those two people." At that time I taught those two people exactly the right Dharma appropriate to each of them, and upon hearing it, both of them attained the fruit of arhatship.

Therefore I am a true spiritual friend of all sentient beings, whereas Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana and their companions are not. If there are sentient beings whose afflictions are extremely heavy, when they encounter me I cut through those afflictions by means of skillful means. Take my younger brother Nanda, for example, who was burdened with extremely heavy attachment — I severed it entirely through many varieties of supremely skillful means. Aṅgulimāla was burdened with extremely heavy aversion — by catching sight of me, his aversion was pacified. King Ajātaśatru was burdened with extremely heavy delusion — by catching sight of me, his deluded mind was removed. The householder Yikaskalpa had accumulated masses of afflictions over countless aeons — by catching sight of me, all of those were at once exhausted and stilled. Even if base and vicious people attend me and remain close to me, by the causes and conditions of that, all gods and humans come to honor and revere them. Śirikubata, whose wrong view was extremely virulent, caught sight of me and was freed from wrong view; and through the condition of seeing me, the causes for rebirth in hell were blocked and he was set instead on the causes for rebirth as a god. Just as someone known as a malicious breath-stealer was near to drawing his last breath at the moment of death, upon catching sight of me his life was lengthened once more. Take as another example Kauśika, whose mind had become confused and disturbed — through the condition of seeing me, his mind was restored to its former clarity. The vicious Gautama's son Kreka habitually performed unwholesome deeds — by catching sight of me, he abandoned those deeds. Both the monk Candanadāsa and the monk Tṛṇaknot, even when their bodies and lives were nearly spent because of seeing me, did not break their vows of moral discipline.

Seeing it in this light, it is said that a monk who teaches half of the holy life like Ānanda becomes a spiritual friend. But I do not teach it that way. It is rather said that one who perfectly fulfills the holy life in its entirety becomes a spiritual friend. Therefore, a bodhisattva who meditates on the great nirvāṇa is said to attend a spiritual friend.

Now, in what sense is a bodhisattva said to be endowed with great learning? A bodhisattva, a great being, who for the sake of the great nirvāṇa writes out, reads aloud, recites, analyzes, and teaches the twelve branches of scriptural teaching is called a bodhisattva endowed with great learning. But setting aside the other eleven branches of scripture, one who holds, reads aloud,

recites, analyzes, or teaches it is also called a bodhisattva endowed with great learning. Setting aside the other twelve branches of scripture, one who holds, writes out, recites, reads aloud, analyzes, or teaches this noble sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa is also called a bodhisattva endowed with great learning. Setting aside even this sūtra, one who holds even a single four-line verse is also called a bodhisattva endowed with great learning. And setting aside even that verse, if one holds the meaning that the Tathāgata abides forever, that his nature is unchanging and unwavering, that bodhisattva too is called one endowed with great learning. Setting aside even that, if one knows that the Tathāgata never truly teaches the Dharma in a conventional sense, that too is called being endowed with great learning as a bodhisattva. Why is that? Because the Dharma has no intrinsic nature. Even though the Tathāgata teaches all phenomena, he forever says nothing whatsoever. That is what is meant by a bodhisattva being endowed with great learning through meditating on the great nirvāṇa.

Noble son, if any noble son or noble daughter who seeks the great nirvāṇa is endowed with these five qualities, they will do what is difficult to do, endure what is difficult to endure, and give up what is difficult to give up.

How is it that a bodhisattva does what is difficult to do? If someone hears it said that by eating a single sesame seed one will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (Skt. anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi), and trusting in those words, one steadfastly eats just one sesame seed throughout immeasurable and boundless aeons, that is a bodhisattva doing what is difficult to do. If someone hears it said that by leaping into fire one will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and throughout immeasurable aeons one enters a mass of fiercely blazing fire in the Avīci hell, that is called a bodhisattva doing what is difficult to do.

How is it that a bodhisattva endures what is difficult to endure? If someone hears it said that by experiencing suffering of the kind caused by being struck with fists, clubs, swords, and stones, one will thereby attain the great nirvāṇa, and throughout immeasurable and boundless aeons one undergoes all such experiences without regarding them as suffering, that is called a bodhisattva enduring what is difficult to endure.

How is it that a bodhisattva gives up what is difficult to give up? If someone hears it said that by giving to others one's lands, cities, wife, children, head, eyes, feet, and brain one will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and throughout immeasurable and boundless aeons one gives away one's lands, cities, wife, children, head, eyes, feet, brain, and all other possessions, that is called a bodhisattva giving up what is difficult to give up. Yet even while doing what is difficult to do, enduring what is difficult to endure, and giving up what is difficult to give up, the bodhisattva does not entertain the perception of thinking: "I have done this."

Noble son, consider, for example, parents who have a single beloved child, greatly cherishing it, nourishing and caring for it in timely fashion with fine clothing and delicious food, making sure it lacks for nothing. Even if that child should develop a mind of contempt toward its parents and abuse them with harsh words, the parents, because of their love, do not give rise to anger or displeasure, and do not think: "I gave this child clothing and food." A bodhisattva, a great being, is just like that: he regards all sentient beings as he would his only child. If the child falls ill, the parents too fall ill, and with medicine and physician they strive with all their effort to heal the sickness. Once the child is healed, they do not think: "I have cured my child's illness." A bodhisattva is just like that.

Seeing that sentient beings are tormented by the sickness of affliction, he teaches the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness. Through hearing the Dharma, their afflictions are thoroughly severed. Yet having severed those afflictions, he does not think: "I have severed the afflictions of sentient beings." For if he were to think in that way, he would never attain unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening. Thus he holds no thought such as: "I have taught Dharma to even a single sentient being and severed their afflictions." A bodhisattva, a great being, neither resents nor cherishes sentient beings. Why is that? Because he thoroughly cultivates meditative absorption in emptiness. A bodhisattva who has cultivated meditative absorption in emptiness — toward whom would he generate aversion, and toward whom would he generate affection? Noble son, consider this example: if a forest is burned by fire, cut down by people, or swept away by water, the trees of that forest do not resent anyone, nor do they generate delight in anyone. A bodhisattva, a great being, is just the same: he has neither resentment toward nor delight in any sentient being. Why is that? Because he cultivates meditative absorption in emptiness.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, Vairocana (the Radiant, Sublime, Glorious King) addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, are all phenomena empty by their intrinsic nature, or do they become empty through the cultivation of emptiness? If they are empty by intrinsic nature, it would be unreasonable to say that one first sees emptiness through the cultivation of emptiness. Yet the Blessed One has declared that by cultivating emptiness one sees emptiness. On the other hand, if they are not empty by intrinsic nature, then no matter how much one cultivates emptiness, they would not become empty."

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, all phenomena are empty by their intrinsic nature. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is not to be apprehended as an object. Noble son, the intrinsic nature of form is not to be apprehended as an object. What then is the intrinsic nature of form? What is called 'form' is not earth, water, fire, or wind, nor is it something other than earth, water, fire, and wind. It is not blue, yellow, red, or white, nor is it something other than blue, yellow, red, and white. It is neither existent nor nonexistent. Why then does one speak of form as having an intrinsic nature? Because the intrinsic nature is not apprehensible as an object, it is said to be empty. All phenomena are likewise. Because of the unbroken continuity of their similar defining marks, the childish, stupid, and foolish, seeing this, declare that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is not empty and not at peace. A bodhisattva, a great being, because he is endowed with five qualities, sees the intrinsic nature of phenomena as primordially empty and at peace. Noble son, if any ascetic or brahmin sees the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as not empty, they are not true ascetics, not true brahmins; they will not attain the Perfection of Wisdom, they will not pass fully into nirvāṇa, and they will not see buddhas and bodhisattvas face to face. Know them to be members of Māra's following. Noble son, all phenomena are empty by their intrinsic nature, and a bodhisattva who cultivates emptiness sees all phenomena as empty. Noble son, because all phenomena are impermanent by their intrinsic nature, they will be ceased by cessation. If they were not impermanent, they would not be ceased by cessation. Conditioned phenomena have the defining mark of arising, and therefore they will arise through arising; they have the defining mark of ceasing, and therefore they will be ceased by cessation. Because all phenomena have the defining mark of suffering, they are made to suffer by suffering."

Noble son, consider the following examples. Salt has the defining mark of saltiness, and therefore it makes other things salty. Sugar cane has the defining mark of sweetness, and therefore it makes other things sweet. Fermented drink has the defining mark of sourness, and therefore it makes other things sour. Pepper has the defining mark of heat, and therefore it makes other things hot. The fruit āmalaka has the defining mark of astringency, and therefore it makes other things astringent. The fruit āmra has the defining mark of bitterness, and therefore it makes other things bitter. Poison has the defining mark of causing death, and therefore it makes other things deadly. But the antidote elixir has the defining mark of preventing death, and therefore, even when mixed with other things, it can prevent death. A bodhisattva who cultivates emptiness is just like this: because of having cultivated emptiness, he sees all phenomena as tranquilly empty by their intrinsic nature.

Then the bodhisattva and great being, the majestic king Kun-du Nangwa Tobtsün, spoke to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if cultivating the meditative absorption of emptiness were such that it causes what is not empty by nature to become empty, then that meditative absorption would not be virtuous and not be excellent — its very nature would be perverted. If the meditative absorption of emptiness sees only emptiness, and if emptiness is a non-existent phenomenon, then what and how could anything at all be seen?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, if that meditative absorption of emptiness sees phenomena that are not empty, then since emptiness has not been thoroughly pacified, it is not a perversion. Just as salt causes what is not salty to become salty, that meditative absorption of emptiness likewise causes what is not empty to be seen as empty.

Noble son, attachment has existence as its defining mark, not emptiness. If attachment were empty, it would be unreasonable for sentient beings to fall into hell through the condition of desire. And if sentient beings do fall into hell, how could the intrinsic nature of attachment be empty?

Noble son, form has existence as its intrinsic nature. And what is this intrinsic nature? It is none other than inversion — mistaken perception. Through inversion, attachment arises in sentient beings. If the defining mark of form were not a mistaken inversion, how could attachment arise in sentient beings? Because attachment does arise in this way, the intrinsic nature of form is not non-existent. Therefore, cultivating the meditative absorption of emptiness is not a perversion.

Noble son, all vulgar and debased people, when they see a woman, generate the defining mark of womanhood. A bodhisattva is not like that. Even when seeing a woman, the defining mark of womanhood does not arise in him. Since that defining mark of arising does not arise, attachment does not arise. Because attachment does not arise, it is not a perversion. Yet because worldly people see a woman there, the bodhisattva too, following along with them, will describe her as a woman. If, however, upon seeing a man one were to say 'that is a woman,' that would be a perversion. Therefore, as I have explained, the Blessed One spoke these words:

O brahmin, if you call the day 'night,' that is a perversion. If you call the night 'day,' that too is a perversion. Take the day to have the defining mark of day, and do not call the night's defining mark a perversion.

Noble son, all bodhisattvas who dwell on the nine grounds see phenomena as having an intrinsic nature. Because they see in this way, they do not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha. But if one sees the intrinsic nature of a buddha, why does one not see the intrinsic nature of all phenomena? It is because when one has cultivated the meditative absorption of emptiness, the intrinsic nature of phenomena is not seen. Because it is not seen in that way, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is seen. Buddhas and bodhisattvas have spoken of two modes: phenomena having intrinsic nature, and —"

phenomena having no intrinsic nature. For sentient beings, phenomena are said to have intrinsic nature; for noble ones (āryas), phenomena are said to have no intrinsic nature. Those who are not empty cultivate the meditative absorption of emptiness (samādhi) in order to see the empty nature of phenomena, and by doing so they come to see emptiness. And those who are already without intrinsic nature also become empty through cultivating emptiness. Therefore, through cultivating emptiness, one sees emptiness.

Noble son, you may ask: if what is seen as empty is a phenomenon that does not exist, then how can anything be seen at all, and what is there to see? Noble son, it is exactly so: a bodhisattva, a great being, does not in truth see anything at all. Not seeing anything at all means there is nothing whatsoever. That nothing whatsoever is all phenomena. A bodhisattva, a great being, who cultivates the great nirvāṇa does not see anything in all phenomena. Whoever has something that is seen does not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Such a one cannot fully cultivate the Perfection of Wisdom and cannot attain the great nirvāṇa. Therefore a bodhisattva sees all phenomena as having no intrinsic nature.

Noble son, a bodhisattva does not see emptiness by virtue of the condition of seeing a meditative absorption. Rather, the Perfection of Wisdom is empty, the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna) is empty, the perfection of diligence is empty, the perfection of patience is empty, the perfection of moral discipline is empty, the perfection of generosity is empty. Form is empty, the eye is empty, consciousness is empty, the Tathāgata is empty, nirvāṇa is empty. Therefore the bodhisattva sees all phenomena as utterly empty.

For this reason, when I was residing in the city of Kapilavastu, I said to Nanda: "Nanda, do not grieve, do not lament, do not wail." And Nanda replied: "Blessed One, if all my attendants and relatives have died, how am I not to grieve? The Tathāgata was born in this very city along with me, and all who belong to the Śākya clan are close kin to me. How is it that the Tathāgata alone does not grieve, and even appears with his complexion more radiant than before?"

Noble son, I then spoke to him in this way: "Nanda, you see the city of Kapilavastu as truly and really existing, whereas I see it as empty, peaceful, and utterly without anything. You see all the Śākya clan as your close kin, whereas I, through cultivating emptiness, see nothing whatsoever. It is for that cause and condition that grief and suffering arise in you, whereas my complexion has grown more radiant than before. Buddhas and bodhisattvas, because they have cultivated the meditative absorption of emptiness in this way, do not give rise to grief."

This constitutes the ninth quality belonging to a bodhisattva who diligently applies himself to the sūtra of the great nirvāṇa.

Noble son, you ask: in what way does a bodhisattva who diligently applies himself to this holy sūtra of the great nirvāṇa come to possess the tenth and last of the inner qualities? Noble son, a bodhisattva cultivates the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣika dharmas), enters into the great nirvāṇa's qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity, and for the sake of all sentient beings elucidates and teaches the sūtra of the great nirvāṇa, fully revealing the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Whether it be a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), a non-returner (anāgāmin), an arhat, a pratyekabuddha (solitary buddha), or —

— or bodhisattvas who place their trust in those words, all of them will enter into the great nirvāṇa. Whoever does not place their trust in them will continue to wander in saṃsāra.

Then the great bodhisattva, the mahasattva Samantabhadra (Samantaprabhā), the Glorious King on High, addressed the Blessed One in these words: "Blessed One, what of those sentient beings who show no respect for this sūtra?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, after my passing into nirvāṇa, there will be monks who are attendants — deluded, their moral discipline destroyed, fond of quarrelling, who have abandoned the twelve branches of scripture and recite and read the various scriptural works of non-Buddhist tīrthikas and worldly compositions and verses. Carrying without examination all manner of things, they will declare, 'The Buddha has permitted this.' Such people are like sandalwood being traded for inferior wood, like gold being traded for a leather bag, like silver being traded for weeds, like silk being traded for coarse woolen cloth, and like nectar being traded for poison.

How is it that sandalwood is traded for inferior wood? My attendants, for the sake of gain and fame, teach this nirvāṇa sūtra and the Dharma to householders, but the householders, swollen with pride, have no wish to listen. The monks seat the householders in a higher position and themselves sit below, and even when served with abundant and varied fine food and drink, still cannot get the householders to listen. This is what is called trading sandalwood for inferior wood.

How is it that gold is traded for a leather bag? The leather bag is a simile for form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Gold is a simile for moral discipline. My attendants, on account of attachment to form and the like, violate and break their moral discipline. This is what is called trading gold for a leather bag.

How is it that silver is traded for weeds? Silver is a simile for the ten virtues. Weeds are a simile for the ten non-virtues. My attendants abandon the ten virtues and practice the ten non-virtues. This is what is called trading silver for weeds.

How is it that silk is traded for coarse woolen cloth? Coarse woolen cloth is a simile for being without moral shame and without moral dread. Silk is a simile for possessing moral shame and moral dread. My attendants cast aside moral shame and moral dread and conduct themselves without moral shame or moral dread. This is what is called trading silk for coarse woolen cloth.

How is it that nectar is traded for poison? Poison is a simile for all manner of gain and fame. Nectar is a simile for the undefiled dharmas. My attendants, for the sake of gain and fame, extol themselves to householders, declaring, 'I have attained the undefiled.' This is what is called trading nectar for poison.

It is on account of such corrupt monks as these that this supreme sūtra of the great nirvāṇa has come to be widely disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa. Yet at that very time some attendants will write out this sūtra, preserve it, read it, recite it, explain it, and propagate it — and those corrupt monks will kill them. Those corrupt monks will then gather together and lay down these strict rules: 'If anyone writes out this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa, preserves it, reads it, recites it, opens it, or teaches it, none of us shall live together with that person, sit together with that person, or speak with that person. Why? Because this nirvāṇa sūtra was not spoken by a buddha — it was composed by those of wrong view. Wrong view has six teachers, and this is a sūtra of the six teachers, not a sūtra of a buddha.' How so? 'The buddhas teach that all phenomena are impermanent, selfless, without bliss, and without perfect purity.' They therefore claim that if one were to say that phenomena are permanent, blissful, possessed of self, and perfectly pure —

Why, then, should this be called a sūtra spoken by a buddha? The buddhas and bodhisattvas permit their attendants to carry all manner of various material goods, whereas the six teachers permit their attendants to carry no material goods at all. So why should this be called the authentic Dharma of a buddha? The buddhas and bodhisattvas have not prohibited their attendants from consuming the five kinds of choice dairy products derived from cow's milk, nor flesh, nor similar things. The six teachers, however, permit their followers to consume none of the five kinds of salty preparations, nor the five kinds of dairy flavors, nor oil, nor blood, nor the like. Since they prohibit the consumption of those things, it is not proper to call their teaching the true Dharma of a buddha.

Furthermore, the buddhas and bodhisattvas have taught the three vehicles, whereas this sūtra teaches only a single vehicle, that of great nirvāṇa. How, then, should this be called the authentic Dharma of a buddha? The buddhas have declared that they pass into nirvāṇa at the end, yet this sūtra teaches that the buddhas are permanent, blissful, possessed of self, and perfectly pure — and that they do not pass away into nirvāṇa. Therefore this sūtra does not fall within the category of the twelve branches of scripture; it was spoken by Māra, not spoken by a buddha.

Son of good family, those people are indeed my attendants, and yet they are unable to have faith in and inclination toward this sūtra of great nirvāṇa. Son of good family, if at that time any sentient being has faith and confidence in even half a verse of this sūtra, know that such a person is truly my genuine attendant. Through the condition of such faith, one perceives the nature of a buddha and passes into nirvāṇa. Through the condition of that faith, one perceives the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and just as the Blessed One has declared, one too will attain great nirvāṇa.

This is called a bodhisattva who is endowed with the ten qualities arising from earnest application to nirvāṇa and to this holy sūtra.

This is the tenth chapter, the chapter of thorough inquiry by the bodhisattva Samantaprabha Uttamaśrī Mahārāja, from the noble Sūtra of Great Nirvāṇa.

Then the Blessed One addressed the entire vast assembly and declared: Sons of good family, suppose someone were to question you thus: Is there a buddha or is there no buddha? Is there Dharma or is there no Dharma? Is there a Saṅgha or is there no Saṅgha? Is there suffering or is there no suffering? Is there an origin of suffering or is there no origin of suffering? Is there cessation or is there no cessation? Is there a path or is there no path? Is there truth or is there no truth? Is there a self or is there no self? Is there suffering or is there no suffering? Is there perfect purity or is there no perfect purity? Is there permanence or is there no permanence? Is there a vehicle or is there no vehicle? Is there an intrinsic nature or is there no intrinsic nature? Are there sentient beings or are there no sentient beings? Is there continued existence or is there no continued existence? Is there what is correct or is there nothing correct? Is there a cause or is there no cause? Is there a result or is there no result? Is there an agent or is there no agent? Is there karma or is there no karma?

Is there karmic maturation or is there no karmic maturation? If you are in doubt about any of these, ask me whatever you wish, and I will analyze each of those points and explain them to you. O noble son, whether a god, a human, a māra, a Brahmā, a monk, a brahmin, or anyone else asks me, there is nothing I cannot answer.

Then, from within that assembled retinue, a bodhisattva named Lion's Roar rose from his seat, arranged his robe, bowed his head to the feet of the Buddha, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Blessed One in these words: Blessed One, I too have been thinking that I would like to make a request, and it is wonderful that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, has opened this opportunity to ask.

Then the Blessed One declared to the great assembly: O noble sons, you should show this bodhisattva the highest honor, reverence, and respect, and offer him incense, flowers, music, garlands, parasols, victory banners, robes, food, drink, bedding, medicines for illness, and dwellings, and you should go out to welcome him and escort him on his way. Why is this? Because this one has planted roots of virtue before the buddhas of the past, and by virtue of that merit he now, before my very eyes, roars the lion's roar.

O noble sons, just as the lion king, knowing his own strength, the sharpness of his fangs and claws, plants his four paws firmly on the ground, and even while dwelling in his mountain cave, lashes his tail and lets out his roar — know that one endowed with such qualities is capable of roaring the lion's roar. The true lion king, early in the morning, emerges from his lair, stretches himself, surveys the four directions, and for eleven purposes roars his great roar. What are those eleven? They are: to destroy those who falsely pretend to be lions without truly being lions; to awaken his own power and prowess; to purify his domain; to let his cubs know their abode; to free the many animals from their state of fear; to awaken those who are sleeping; to rid all the lazy beasts of their laziness; to make the beasts circle around him and take refuge in him; to tame the great musk elephants; to instruct his cubs; and to adorn all his retinue — these are the eleven.

When all the beasts hear the lion's roar, those born of the water plunge to the depths; those who walk on dry land flee into their holes; those who fly fall to the ground; and even the great musk elephants lose control of themselves and flee.

O noble sons, even if a fox were to walk behind a lion for a hundred years, it still could not roar the lion's roar. But lion cubs who have reached three years of age are able to roar just as the lion king does.

O noble sons, likewise the Tathāgata, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, endowed with the fangs and claws of wisdom, the four legs of supernatural power (ṛddhi), the body in which the six perfections are fully complete, the ten powers of a hero's strength, the tail of great compassion, and dwelling in the perfectly purified lair of the four meditative concentrations, roars the lion's roar for the sake of sentient beings, utterly vanquishing the armies of Māra, revealing the ten powers to the great assembly, elucidating the domain of a buddha's activity, and acting as protector and refuge for those who hold wrong views. He arouses enthusiasm in those who are afraid of saṃsāra, awakens sentient beings who are oppressed by the sleep of ignorance,

causes those who practice non-virtuous phenomena to give rise to a mind of remorse. He causes sentient beings who hold wrong views to understand, through repeated and thorough teaching, that the teachings of the six teachers are not the lion's roar. He crushes the pride of Kāśyapa the Perfector and others like him. He causes those of the two vehicles to give rise to a mind of remorse. He causes bodhisattvas on the fifth ground and above to give rise to great power and great mind. And in order that the four assemblies of right view may be without fear before the four factions of wrong view, he emerges from the innermost lair of the domain of the noble ones, the domain of Brahmā, and the domain of the gods, stretches himself wide, and roars in order to crush the pride, arrogance, and related afflictions of all sentient beings. He gazes in all four directions in order to cause wholesome phenomena to arise in all sentient beings. He plants his four paws firmly on the ground in order that all sentient beings may attain the four discriminating knowledges (pratisaṃvid). He roars the lion's roar in order to establish all sentient beings in the perfection of moral discipline. To roar the lion's roar is to declare with certainty to all sentient beings that the buddha-nature exists within them, and that the Tathāgata abides permanently, unchanging and unaltering. Sons of good family, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even if they were to follow in the footsteps of the Blessed One the Buddha for hundreds and thousands of immeasurable and incalculable aeons, would still be incapable of roaring the lion's roar. Know that if a bodhisattva on the tenth ground applies himself diligently to all three aspects of conduct, that is what it means to roar the lion's roar. Sons of good family, the bodhisattva, the great being Lion's Roar, has now been considered to have proclaimed the great lion's roar. Therefore, honor him, serve him, and revere him with an elevated mind.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva, the great being Lion's Roar: "Son of good family, if you have questions, ask whatever you wish."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Lion's Roar, addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, what is the buddha-nature? What is meant by the term 'buddha-nature'? And what, further, is meant by 'permanence,' 'bliss,' 'self,' and 'perfect purity'? If the buddha-nature is present in all sentient beings, why is it not seen? In the presence of the buddha-nature in all sentient beings, in what Dharma does a bodhisattva on the tenth ground abide such that he does not see it clearly? And in what Dharma does a buddha abide such that he does see it clearly? With what kind of eye does a bodhisattva on the tenth ground fail to see it clearly? And with what kind of eye does a buddha see it clearly?"

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family! Whoever asks a question for the sake of the Dharma will come to possess both accumulations. What are the two? The accumulation of wisdom and the accumulation of merit. If a bodhisattva possesses both of those accumulations, he will know the buddha-nature. And from knowing what is meant by 'buddha-nature,' he will know all the way through to what kind of eye a bodhisattva on the tenth ground sees with, and with what kind of eye the Blessed Buddha sees."

The bodhisattva Lion's Roar then asked: "Blessed One, what is the accumulation of wisdom? What is the accumulation of merit?"

"Son of good family, the accumulation of wisdom is as follows:

from the first ground through to the tenth ground, that is called the accumulation of wisdom. The accumulation of merit is as follows: from the perfection of generosity through to, but not including, the Perfection of Wisdom. Furthermore, son of good family, the accumulation of wisdom refers to buddhas and bodhisattvas. The accumulation of merit refers to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas on the ninth ground. Furthermore, son of good family, the accumulation of merit is conditioned, defiled, bound up with existence, productive of results, obstructed, and impermanent — it is the characteristic of the immature and inferior. The accumulation of wisdom is unconditioned, undefiled, free from existence, without results, unobstructed, and permanently abiding.

Son of good family, it is because you possess these two kinds of accumulation that you became bold enough to ask about this profoundly deep matter. And it is because I too possess these two kinds of accumulation that I was able to answer when this matter was asked of me.

The great bodhisattva Lion's Roar then said: "Blessed One, if it is improper to ask of a bodhisattva who possesses these two accumulations whether things are one or two, then why did the Blessed One reply in terms of one and two?"

"Why do you ask?" responded Lion's Roar. "Because all phenomena are neither one nor two. Oneness and twoness are the defining characteristic of the immature and inferior."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, if a bodhisattva lacked these two accumulations, he would not know whether things are one or two. A bodhisattva who possesses these two accumulations does know whether things are one or two. Yet the point that there is no such thing as 'one' or 'two' with regard to phenomena is not quite right either. Why? If there were neither one nor two, how could one speak of all phenomena as being neither one nor two?

Son of good family, what is called 'oneness and twoness as the defining characteristic of the immature and inferior' — that refers to a bodhisattva on the tenth ground, and not to the immature and inferior. Why? Because 'one' is nirvāṇa, and 'two' is saṃsāra. Why is 'one' called nirvāṇa? Because it is permanent. Why is 'two' called saṃsāra? Because it is bound up with craving rooted in ignorance. Yet nirvāṇa, which is permanent, is not the defining characteristic of the immature and inferior, and saṃsāra is likewise not the defining characteristic of the immature and inferior. It is for this reason that possessing the two accumulations constitutes the asking and answering of the question.

Son of good family, listen carefully now to how the question of what is meant by 'the buddha's intrinsic nature' is to be examined, and I will analyze it and explain it to you.

Son of good family, what is called 'the buddha's intrinsic nature' is ultimate emptiness. Ultimate emptiness is what is called wisdom. With regard to this, 'emptiness' means seeing neither emptiness nor non-emptiness. One who possesses wisdom sees all of the following: empty and non-empty, permanent and impermanent, suffering and bliss, self and no-self. What is called 'empty' is all of saṃsāra. What is called 'non-empty' is complete nirvāṇa. Up through no-self is saṃsāra. What is called 'self' is complete nirvāṇa.

To see everything as empty while not seeing what is non-empty — that is not to be called the Middle Path. To see everything only up through no-self without seeing the self — that is not to be called the Middle Path. What is called the Middle Path is the buddha's intrinsic nature.

Because of that, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is permanent and without change. Yet because it is covered by ignorance, no sentient being has been able to see it. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas see everything as empty — they do not see the non-empty — and they see everything up through no-self, yet they do not see the self. Therefore they have not attained ultimate emptiness. Because they have not attained ultimate emptiness, they do not travel the Middle Path. Because they do not travel the Middle Path, they do not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Son of good family, there are three modes of seeing the Middle Path: practicing with definite bliss, practicing with definite suffering, and practicing with both definite suffering and bliss. What is called practicing with definite bliss is this: a great bodhisattva, out of compassion for all sentient beings, may dwell in the Avīci hell, yet experiences it as though touching the bliss of the third meditative concentration. What is called practicing with definite suffering refers to the ignorant and base. What is called practicing with both definite suffering and bliss refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas arouse the perception of the Middle Path with respect to both suffering and bliss — and for that reason, although the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists, they do not see it.

You have asked: "What sort of thing would you say the intrinsic nature of a buddha is?" Son of good family, what is called the intrinsic nature of a buddha is the seed of the Middle Path of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening of all buddhas — arhat, perfectly and completely awakened.

Furthermore, son of good family, the path has three grades: superior, middling, and inferior. What is called inferior is the Brahmā gods who, in error, view what is impermanent as permanent. What is called superior is to see saṃsāra, which is impermanent, as permanent in error, while improperly superimposing impermanence onto the Three Jewels, which are in fact permanent. Why is it called superior? Because it leads to the attainment of the supreme, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. What is called middling is ultimate emptiness — seeing the impermanent as permanent and seeing the permanent as impermanent. Ultimate emptiness should not be called inferior. Why? Because it is unseen by all the ignorant and base. Nor should it be called superior. Why? Because it is not the highest. The path traversed by all buddhas and bodhisattvas is neither superior nor inferior — and for that very reason it is called the Middle Path.

Furthermore, son of good family, the first extreme of saṃsāra has two aspects: ignorance and craving. Between these two arises the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death — and that is what is called the Middle Path. It is called the Middle Path because, by means of that Middle Path, saṃsāra will be utterly destroyed.
