Thus the Dharma of the Middle Path is called the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Therefore the intrinsic nature of a buddha is permanent, blissful, a self, and utterly pure. Because sentient beings do not see it, it appears to them as impermanent, as suffering, as no-self, and as not utterly pure. In truth, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not impermanence, not suffering, not no-self, and not absence of purity.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: in the house of a poor man there is a treasure of jewels, yet because he does not see it, by reason of that non-seeing he has no permanence, no bliss, no self, no complete purity. A spiritual friend comes to him and says: "In your house there is a treasure of gold and jewels — why then are you poor and afflicted, impermanent, without bliss, without self, and without purity?" And by skillful means that friend causes him to see it.

When he sees it, that man gains permanence, bliss, self, and complete purity. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is just like that: sentient beings do not see it. Because they do not see it in this way, there is no permanence, no bliss, no self, no complete purity. The spiritual friends who are buddhas and bodhisattvas teach it through various skillful means and cause it to be seen. Once sentient beings have thus come to see it, they attain permanence, bliss, self, and complete purity.

Furthermore, son of good family, there are two kinds of view that sentient beings give rise to: eternalism and annihilation. Those two views are not called the Middle Way path. The absence of both eternalism and annihilation — that is called the Middle Way path. Freedom from both eternalism and annihilation is the wisdom that realizes the twelve links of dependent origination. The wisdom that realizes in this way is called the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Although the two vehicles do realize dependent origination's twelve links, this is not called attaining the intrinsic nature of a buddha. One may indeed perceive the intrinsic nature of a buddha, yet because sentient beings are thoroughly covered over by ignorance they do not see it — just as a hare and a horse cannot cross the river of the twelve links of dependent origination. Why is that? Because they do not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Son of good family, the wisdom that realizes the twelve links of dependent origination is the seed of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. It is for this reason that the twelve links of dependent origination are called the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: ghee becomes the cause of bile disease. Why? Because it becomes a cause and condition for bile disease. The twelve links of dependent origination are similar to that. Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha has a cause, a cause of the cause, a result, and a result of the result. "Having a cause" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination. "The cause of the cause" refers to wisdom. "Having a result" refers to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. "The result of the result" refers to unsurpassed great nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: conditioned by ignorance, formations are the result; conditioned by formations, consciousness becomes the result. Thus the essential nature of ignorance is both a condition and a condition of the condition. Consciousness too is both a result and a result of the result. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is similar to that.

Son of good family, it is for this reason that the twelve links of dependent origination neither arise nor cease, are neither eternal nor annihilated, neither one nor two, neither coming nor going, neither cause nor result.

Son of good family, that which is a cause but not a result is like the intrinsic nature of a buddha. That which is a result but not a cause is like great nirvāṇa. That which is both a cause and a result is like the phenomena born from the twelve links of dependent origination. That which is neither cause nor result is called the intrinsic nature of a buddha — and because it is neither cause nor result, it is permanently unchanging and unmoving.

It is for this reason that I have declared in the sūtras that the twelve links of dependent origination have a profoundly deep meaning that is beyond knowing, beyond seeing, and beyond conceiving.

It is the domain of buddhas and bodhisattvas, and it is not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Why is it said that the meaning is profoundly deep? The profound depth lies in this: although the karma and conduct of sentient beings are neither permanent nor annihilated, the result nonetheless ripens; although karma ceases moment by moment, nothing is lost; although there is no agent, the karma that has been performed exists; although there is no experiencer, the ripening of results occurs; although there is no cessation of experience, the result neither perishes nor is lost; no one can think about the arising of all sentient beings and come to know it by inference; although it accompanies the twelve links of dependent origination, it is neither known nor seen; and because it is neither seen nor known, there is no beginning and no end. Even a bodhisattva on the tenth ground sees only the beginning but does not see the end, whereas a blessed buddha, a Bhagavān, sees both beginning and end. It is for this reason that the Tathāgatas clearly perceive the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

O son of good family, it is because all sentient beings do not see the twelve links of dependent origination that they revolve thoroughly in cyclic existence. O son of good family, just as a silkworm spins a cocoon, is born within it of itself, and dies within it of itself, so too all sentient beings are like this: because they do not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha, they perform afflicted karma of their own accord, and like one struck by a club they revolve thoroughly in cyclic existence.

O son of good family, it is therefore that I have declared in all the sūtras: if one sees the twelve links of dependent origination, one sees the Dharma; and if one sees the Dharma, one sees the buddha. The word "buddha" refers to the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Why so? Because that very intrinsic nature is the nature of all buddhas.

O son of good family, the investigative wisdom (Skt. vicārajñāna) that examines the twelve links of dependent origination has four levels: the least, the middling, the excellent, and the most excellent. The least investigative wisdom does not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha; because it does not see it, one attains the path of the śrāvakas. The middling investigative wisdom does not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha; because it does not see it, one attains the path of the pratyekabuddhas. The excellent investigative wisdom does not see it clearly; because it is not seen clearly, one abides on the ten grounds. The most excellent wisdom sees it clearly; through seeing it clearly, one attains the path of unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening.

It is therefore that the twelve links of dependent origination are called the intrinsic nature of a buddha. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is the emptiness of ultimate truth. The emptiness of ultimate truth is the middle path. The middle path is the buddha. And the buddha is called nirvāṇa.

The thirty-sixth fascicle.

Then the great bodhisattva, the great being Lion's Roar, addressed the Blessed One thus: Blessed One, if there is no difference between a buddha and the intrinsic nature of a buddha, what is the point of all sentient beings striving on the path?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, your question does not quite hit the mark. Although there is no difference between a buddha and the intrinsic nature of a buddha, sentient beings do not possess it. O son of good family, consider this example: suppose a person is killed not through malicious intent, yet after killing, remorse arises, and they perform virtuous deeds of the three paths — yet they are still called a hell-being. Why? Because that person will inevitably fall into hell. That person does not possess the aggregates, elements, or sense bases of a hell-being — and yet they are called a hell-being.

O son of good family, it is therefore that I have declared in all the sūtras: one who sees a being practicing virtuous Dharma is said to see a god.

One who sees a being practicing non-virtue is said to see a hell-being. Why? Because they will inevitably experience karmic maturation.

O son of good family, because all sentient beings will without fail attain unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening, it has been declared that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature. And yet all sentient beings do not actually possess the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks. It is for that reason that I have spoken these verses in this sūtra:

What has a beginning does not exist now.
What has no beginning exists now.
All phenomena of existence throughout the three times
have no fixed abode of such a kind.

O son of good family, what is called "existence" has three aspects: future existence, present existence, and past existence. With respect to these, because all sentient beings will possess unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening in the future, this is called the buddha-nature. Because all sentient beings presently have all-pervasive afflictions, they do not presently possess the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks. As for those sentient beings who, in past time, cut off their afflictions — they now behold the buddha-nature. It is for this reason that I have always declared that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature, extending even to those of wrong craving: even they possess the buddha-nature.

Even though those such as the wrongly craving lack virtuous phenomena, the buddha-nature itself is virtuous, since it will come to exist in the future. Therefore, even those with wrong craving and so forth possess the buddha-nature. Why? Because even those with wrong craving will without fail realize unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening.

O son of good family, consider this example: in someone's household there is milk and curds. Another person asks, "Do you have butter?" And the reply comes, "I do." Now, curds are not actually butter — and yet one says there is butter, because through skillful means it will without fail be obtained. Sentient beings are likewise: all have mind. Whoever has mind will without fail attain unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. It is for this reason that I have always declared that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature.

O son of good family, perfection has two kinds: the perfection of arrangement and the perfection of the ultimate. Furthermore, there is the worldly perfection and the supramundane perfection. Of these, the perfection of arrangement is the six perfections (pāramitās). The perfection of the ultimate is all sentient beings' attainment of the single vehicle. The single vehicle is what is called the buddha-nature. It is therefore that I have declared: all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature; all sentient beings possess the single vehicle — yet, obscured by ignorance, they do not see it.

O son of good family, consider this example: the ripened fruit experienced in the Thirty-Three Heaven is beyond the sight of these obscured sentient beings here in the northern continent of Unpleasant Sound. The buddha-nature is likewise: because it is obscured by the afflictions, sentient beings do not see it.

Furthermore, O son of good family, what is called the buddha-nature is the meditative absorption of heroic progress (śūraṃgama samādhi). In its intrinsic nature it resembles the essence of butter, and it is therefore the mother of all buddhas.

Through the power of the meditative absorption of heroic progress, the Tathāgatas have become permanent, blissful, possessed of self, and utterly pure. Although the meditative absorption of heroic progress is present in all sentient beings, they do not see it because they have not cultivated it, and therefore they have not attained unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

O son of good family, the meditative absorption of heroic progress has five names. It is called the meditative absorption of heroic progress; it is also called the Perfection of Wisdom; it is also called the vajra-like meditative absorption; it is also called the meditative absorption of the lion's roar; and it is also called the intrinsic nature of the buddhas. In each context, according to what qualities are present, the name is applied accordingly.

O son of good family, how is it that a single meditative absorption comes to receive so many different names? Consider: in the context of meditative concentration, it is called the four dhyānas; in the context of the faculties, it is called the faculty of meditative absorption; in the context of the powers, it is called the power of meditative absorption; in the context of the factors of awakening, it is called the factor of awakening that is meditative absorption; in the context of the noble path, it is called right meditative absorption; in the context of a person's eight contemplations, it is called the contemplation of meditative absorption. In just the same way, the meditative absorption of heroic progress is analogous to all of these.

O son of good family, all sentient beings are endowed with three grades of meditative absorption. What are the three? The superior, the middling, and the inferior. The superior is the intrinsic nature of the buddhas; therefore it is said that the intrinsic nature of the buddhas is present in all sentient beings. The middling is that all sentient beings are endowed with the first dhyāna: if the conditions are met, they will fully cultivate it; but if the conditions are not met, they will not fully cultivate it. The conditions are of two kinds: the aeon of fire, and the utter elimination of the afflictions of the desire realm. Therefore it is said that all sentient beings are endowed with the middling meditative absorption. The inferior meditative absorption is the mind-arisen meditative absorption of the ten great bodhisattva grounds; therefore it is said that all sentient beings are endowed with the inferior meditative absorption.

The intrinsic nature of the buddhas is present in all sentient beings, but because it is completely covered over by the afflictions, they are unable to see it. A bodhisattva on the tenth ground does see the one vehicle, yet does not know the Tathāgata as one who permanently abides. Therefore, although a bodhisattva on the tenth ground sees the intrinsic nature of the buddhas, it has not become fully clear to them.

O son of good family, the word heroic means having reached the end of all things. The word progress means to rely upon. Because one relies upon the end of all things, it is called heroic progress. Therefore the meditative absorption of heroic progress is called the intrinsic nature of the buddhas.

O son of good family, once upon a time I was dwelling on the bank of the Ganges river and I spoke to Ānanda, saying: "I am about to bathe. Please take my robe and rub in the washing powder, then set it out." When I entered the water, all beings who move through the sky, through water, or across the land came and looked upon me. At that time some five hundred wanderers gathered on the riverbank and came into my presence, saying to one another: "How did this one attain a body like vajra? If this Gautama does not teach the annihilationist view, we offer him our scriptures and our ethical precepts." O son of good family, at that time I, knowing the minds of those wanderers through the gnosis that perceives the minds of others, understood their intentions, and spoke to them thus:

"Why do you think I am teaching the annihilationist view?" The wanderers then asked: "Gautama, in all your sūtras you have declared that all sentient beings are without self. If you say they are without self, why is this not the annihilationist view? If there is no self, who would uphold moral discipline, and who would transgress it?"

The Blessed One declared: "I have never said that all sentient beings are without self. I have always said that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature. Is not that very buddha-nature itself a self? For that reason I do not teach the annihilationist view. Because all sentient beings do not see the buddha-nature, they lack permanence, lack selfhood, lack bliss, and lack perfect purity. Whoever speaks in those terms — that one is said to be teaching the annihilationist view."

Upon hearing at that moment that the buddha-nature itself is the self, all those wanderers aroused the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening, and right then, going forth into renunciation, they applied themselves diligently to the path of awakening. All beings moving through the sky, through water, and across the land likewise aroused the mind of unsurpassable awakening. Having thus aroused that mind, they at that same moment abandoned those very bodies.

O son of good family, the buddha-nature, in ultimate truth, is not a self; it is called "self" for the sake of sentient beings. O son of good family, because cause and condition exist, the Tathāgata has spoken of a self with respect to what is actually selfless — yet in ultimate truth there is no self. Though he speaks thus, it is not a falsehood. O son of good family, likewise, because cause and condition exist, what has a self is explained as selfless; and though in ultimate truth a self exists, it is spoken of as selfless for the sake of the world — yet that too is not a falsehood. The buddha-nature is indeed without self, and the Tathāgata's teaching of "selfless" with respect to it is because it is permanent. The Tathāgata is indeed a self, and teaching it as "selfless" is because sovereignty has been attained.

Then the great bodhisattva Siṃhaghoṣa asked: "Blessed One, if all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature, like a great vajra-force, why is it that all sentient beings do not see it?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, consider visible forms — blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, and various others. They exist and can be apprehended, yet a blind person does not see them. Because a blind person does not see them, it does not follow that these forms — blue, yellow, red, white, long and short in shape — do not exist. Why so? Because even though a blind person does not see them, someone with eyes does not fail to see them. The buddha-nature is just like that: even though all sentient beings do not see it, a bodhisattva of the tenth ground sees a portion of it, while the Tathāgata beholds it without remainder. What the bodhisattva of the tenth ground sees of the buddha-nature is like a form seen in darkness, while the Tathāgata beholds it as a form seen in full daylight.

"Son of good family, consider also one with cataracts, who cannot see forms clearly. When a skilled physician treats the eye, by the power of that medicine one comes to see clearly. The bodhisattva of the tenth ground is similar: though the buddha-nature is seen, it is not seen clearly. By the power of the meditative absorption called Heroic Advance (śūraṃgama-samādhi), one comes to see it fully and clearly.

"Son of good family, there are those who perceive all phenomena as lacking permanence, lacking selfhood, lacking bliss, and lacking purity, and who perceive all that is not the Dharma as lacking permanence, lacking selfhood, lacking bliss,

and lacking purity — those who see in this way do not see the buddha-nature. Here, "all phenomena" refers to saṃsāra. "What is not all phenomena" refers to the Three Jewels. The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas see all phenomena as lacking permanence, lacking selfhood, lacking bliss, and lacking purity, and they likewise see all that is not Dharma as lacking permanence, lacking selfhood, lacking bliss, and lacking purity. Because they see in this way, they do not see the buddha-nature.

The bodhisattva of the tenth ground sees all phenomena as lacking permanence, lacking selfhood, lacking bliss, and lacking purity, yet sees in all that is not Dharma only a partial glimpse of permanence, selfhood, bliss, and purity. Because of seeing in this partial way, it is said that such a one sees only one tenth of it.

The Blessed One, the buddha, sees all phenomena as lacking permanence, lacking selfhood, lacking bliss, and lacking purity, and sees in all that is not Dharma permanence, selfhood, bliss, and purity in full. Because of seeing in this way, the Blessed One sees the buddha-nature as clearly as a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of the hand. It is for this reason that the meditative absorption called Heroic Advance (śūraṃgama-samādhi) is said to be the ultimate.

Son of good family, consider the moon on the first day of the month: though one cannot see it, it is not right to say it does not exist. The buddha-nature is similar: though it is not seen by all who are foolish and undeveloped, it is not right to say that the buddha-nature does not exist in them.

Son of good family, the buddha-nature is as follows: the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness — all three of these aspects are present in every sentient being, yet they will first become visible only when the afflictions are thoroughly overcome. Those who have wrong craving will, only when that wrong craving is thoroughly overcome, come to attain the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness. It is for this reason that I have always declared that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature.

Son of good family, these twelve links of dependent origination are equally present in all sentient beings — both inner and outer. What are the twelve? The affliction of the past is ignorance. The karma of the past is formations. The consciousness at the very first moment of entering the womb in the present time is consciousness. Having entered the womb, while the five limbs and four faculties are not yet complete, that is name-and-form. While one possesses the four faculties but contact cannot yet be spoken of, that is the six sense sources. The inability to distinguish between suffering and pleasure is called contact. Attachment clinging to a single object is called feeling. Attachment to the five sense pleasures is called craving. Attachment-desire for inner and outer things is grasping. The production of bodily, verbal, and mental karma through inner and outer things is becoming. The consciousness of the present time is birth in the future. The name-and-form, the six sense sources, contact, and feeling of the present time are aging, sickness, and death in the future. These are called the twelve links of dependent origination.

Son of good family, although all these twelve links of dependent origination are present in every sentient being, when one is still in the embryonic state, not yet fully formed, at the time of death in that state the twelve links of dependent origination are not present. From the moment of birth until death and aging, one is possessed of all twelve. As for sentient beings in the form realm, although there is no threefold feeling, no threefold contact, no craving, no aging, and no death, they are nonetheless said to possess all twelve.

As for sentient beings in the formless realm, although form is absent and the links from form through to aging and death are lacking, they are nonetheless said to possess all twelve aspects. This is because they are certain to attain them. Therefore it is said that all sentient beings equally possess the twelve links of dependent origination.

Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is similar to this. Because all sentient beings are certain to attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, I have therefore declared that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Son of good family, in the Himalayas there is a certain grass called bzodpa. If cows eat it, the essence of butter arises. There is another grass such that if cows eat it, no essence of butter arises. Now although the essence of butter does not arise from the latter, it would be wrong to say that bzodpa grass does not exist in the Himalayas. In the same way, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is to be understood likewise. The Tathāgata is like the Himalayas. The great and complete nirvāṇa is like the bzodpa grass. The twelve divisions of scripture are like that other grass. Whatever sentient being hears, retains, or inquires into this complete nirvāṇa will behold the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Although one has not heard that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists from within the twelve divisions of scripture, it would still be wrong to say that the intrinsic nature of a buddha does not exist.

Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is form, and yet it is not form. It is not form, and yet it is not non-form either. It has characteristics, and yet it is without characteristics. It is without characteristics, and yet it is not without characteristics either. It is one, and yet it is not one. It is not one, and yet it is not non-one either. It is not permanent and it is not annihilated. It is not non-permanent, and it is not non-annihilated either. It exists, and yet it does not exist. It neither exists nor is it non-existent. It is exhausted, and yet it is not exhausted. It is neither exhausted nor non-exhausted. It is a cause, and yet it is also a result. It is neither a cause nor is it non-result. It is not a meaning, and being not a meaning it is not non-meaning either. It has letters, and yet it is without letters. It is without letters, and yet it is not without letters either.

Now, in what sense is it said to be form? It is the vajra-like body. In what sense is it not form? It is the eighteen unshared qualities, which are immaterial. In what sense is it neither form nor non-form? It is the absence of any fixed defining characteristic with respect to both form and non-form.

In what sense does it have characteristics? It has the thirty-two major marks. In what sense is it without characteristics? The marks are not manifest to any sentient being. In what sense is it neither with characteristics nor without characteristics? It is the state in which neither the marks nor their absence is determinate.

In what sense is it one? All sentient beings belong to a single vehicle. In what sense is it not one? Three vehicles have been taught. In what sense is it neither one nor non-one? It is the countless Dharma categories.

In what sense is it not permanent? It is seen to arise from conditions. In what sense is it not annihilated? It is free from the view of annihilation. In what sense is it neither non-permanent nor non-annihilated? It is the absence of any beginning or final extremity.

In what sense does it exist? All sentient beings exist. In what sense does it not exist? It is seen through skillful means. In what sense is it neither existent nor non-existent? It has the defining characteristic of space.

In what sense is it exhausted? It is the attainment of the power of the meditative absorption called the Heroic March (sūraṃgama). In what sense is it not exhausted? It is that which is not permanent. In what sense is it neither exhausted nor non-exhausted —

it has the defining characteristic of the exhaustion of all things, and is thus cut off. What is the cause? The cause is thorough understanding. What is the result? The result is that which becomes inescapable. What is that which is neither cause nor result? It is permanence. What is the meaning? The meaning is that it gathers all aims without obstruction. What is the non-meaning? It is that which cannot be expressed. What is that which is neither non-meaning nor not non-meaning? It becomes empty at the extreme end. What is called a syllable? It is that which has been designated by name. What is the non-syllable? It is that which has not been designated by name. What is that which is neither non-syllable nor not non-syllable? It is the cutting off of all syllables. What is that which is neither suffering nor happiness? It is the cutting off of all feeling (vedanā). What is the non-self? It is that which has not come to be endowed with the eight powers. What is that which is also not non-self? It is permanence. What is that which is neither non-self nor not non-self? It is that which is unmade and unexperienced. What is called emptiness? It is ultimate emptiness. What is the non-empty? It is permanence. What is that which is neither non-empty nor not non-empty? It is that which has become the fruit of virtuous phenomena.

Son of good family, know this: if anyone who has taken to heart and understood these meanings of the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra perceives the intrinsic nature of a buddha, that nature is inconceivable, and it is the domain of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones; it is not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not the aggregates, the elements, or the sense sources. It is not something that exists from a beginningless time up to the present. It is not something that, having come into existence, later ceases to be. It is seen by sentient beings through causes and conditions of virtue. Just as when black iron is burned in fire it turns red, and when removed and cooled it turns black again, and yet that black color is neither within nor without but has arisen from causes and conditions — so too is the intrinsic nature of a buddha: when the fire of the afflictions of all sentient beings is absent, it is seen and heard. Son of good family, just as when a seed has ceased a sprout arises, and the defining characteristic of that sprout is neither within nor without — and so it is likewise all the way up through the flower and the fruit — for they have come to exist from conditions. Son of good family, this sacred scriptural collection of the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra is endowed with immeasurable qualities, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha is likewise endowed with immeasurable and innumerable qualities.

Then the great bodhisattva Lion's Roar addressed the Blessed One: Blessed One, when a bodhisattva is endowed with the Dharma attributes, the seeing of the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not made clear. But when the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are endowed with those same Dharma attributes, they behold it with perfect clarity.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, when a bodhisattva is endowed with ten Dharma attributes, although he sees the intrinsic nature of a buddha, it is not clear. What are the ten? Wanting little, knowing contentment, being thoroughly pacified, diligence, right mindfulness, right meditative absorption (samādhi), right wisdom (prajñā), liberation, being praised on account of liberation, and ripening sentient beings through the Great Nirvāṇa.

The bodhisattva Lion's Roar asked: Blessed One, what is the difference between wanting little and knowing contentment?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, wanting little is not seeking and not taking.

Knowing contentment is this: even when one obtains little, one feels no distress, and the mind harbors no thoughts of harm toward those in one's company. Wanting little means having few desires. Knowing contentment means that, for the sake of the meaning of the Dharma, one's mind is free from being tormented by grief.

Son of good family, desire has three forms: base desire, great desire, and desire for desire.

As for base desire: if a monk gives rise to thoughts of desire such as these — "How might I become the leader over all my many followers, so that the entire Saṅgha of monks becomes my retinue? How might my retinue of four groups offer me worship, service, reverence, and praise? How might everyone who has previously heard me teach the Dharma to those four groups place their trust in my words and hold them fast? How might kings, ministers, and householders all pay me honor? How might I obtain in abundance robes, alms, bedding, medicines for illness, fine dwellings, and the like?" — this is samsaric desire, and it is called base desire.

What then is so-called great desire? If a monk, out of desire for gain and fame, thinks to himself that his four-group retinue will come to know that he has attained from the first bodhisattva ground up through the tenth ground, or that he has attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, or that he has attained the fruit of an arhat up through the fruit of a stream-enterer, or that he has attained from the four dhyānas up through unobstructed primordial wisdom — this is called great desire.

What then is so-called desire for desire? If a monk, out of desire for gain and fame, aspires to be reborn as a Brahmā deity, or in the ranks of Māra, or as a great lord, or as a wheel-turning king, or to be born into the warrior caste or the brahmin caste and thereby attain power — this is called desire for desire.

Not living by any of these three base desires is what is called wanting little.

Desire refers to the twenty-five modes of existence. The absence of those twenty-five modes of existence is called wanting little. Not seeking future objects of desire is wanting little; having obtained something and yet feeling no attachment to it is knowing contentment.

Not seeking gain and fame is wanting little. Having obtained something and yet not accumulating more is knowing contentment.

Son of good family, there are cases where one who wants little is nonetheless not said to know contentment, and cases where one who knows contentment is nonetheless not said to want little. There are those who both want little and know contentment, and there are those who know contentment in nothing and whose desire is abundant.

In this regard: the stream-enterer has wanting little. The pratyekabuddha knows contentment. The arhat both wants little and knows contentment. Bodhisattvas are those who neither truly want little nor know contentment.

Son of good family, wanting little and knowing contentment together have two aspects: wholesome and non-wholesome. The non-wholesome kind belongs to ordinary persons who are like empty vessels. The wholesome kind belongs to noble ones and bodhisattvas. All noble ones, even when they have attained the path and its fruit, do not say "I have attained it." Because they do not say so, their minds remain undisturbed — and that is called knowing contentment.

Son of good family, this being so, if a bodhisattva, a great being, wishes to cultivate the Mahāyāna sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa (parinirvāṇa) and to see the intrinsic nature of a buddha, he must apply himself diligently to wanting little and to knowing contentment.

Now, what is thorough pacification? Pacification has two aspects.

The two aspects are: pacification of mind and pacification of body. Pacification of body means never committing any of the three kinds of physical non-virtue. Pacification of mind means never committing any of the three kinds of mental non-virtue. That is what is called pacification of body and mind.

Again, pacification of body means not relying upon the four kinds of wrong retinue, and having no attachment to the objects and affairs that such a retinue brings about. Pacification of mind means never being stained by attachment, aversion, or delusion. That is what is called pacification of body and mind.

Among monks, some have a pacified body but an unquiet mind; some have a pacified mind but an unquiet body; some have both body and mind pacified; and some have neither body nor mind pacified.

One whose body is pacified but whose mind is not is a monk who perseveres in meditative concentration to the very end, and who has abandoned the four kinds of wrong retinue, yet whose mind is constantly occupied with attachment, aversion, and delusion — this is called having a pacified body but an unquiet mind.

One whose body is not pacified but whose mind is is a monk who, though he associates with and relies upon the four kinds of wrong retinue and upon kings and ministers, has utterly cut off attachment, aversion, and delusion — this is called having a pacified mind but an unquiet body.

Those who have both body and mind pacified are buddhas and bodhisattvas. Those who have neither body nor mind pacified are lowly, ignoble ordinary beings. Why so? Because such lowly, ignoble ordinary beings are utterly incapable of contemplating impermanence, the absence of happiness, selflessness, and the absence of purity. For that very reason, such lowly, ignoble ordinary beings are incapable of conducting themselves purely in the actions of body, speech, and mind. Those who hold wrong views, those who have broken the four root precepts, and those who have committed one of the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya) — such persons likewise cannot be called possessors of pacified body and mind.

Now, what is diligence? A monk who, wishing to purify the actions of body, speech, and mind entirely, abandons all non-virtuous actions and cultivates all virtuous actions — this is called diligence. Such diligence, moreover, abides in the six close applications of mindfulness. What are the six? They are: mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of ethical conduct, mindfulness of generosity, and mindfulness of the gods. This is what is called the right close application of mindfulness.

One who is endowed with the right close application of mindfulness and thereby attains meditative absorption — that is called right meditative absorption (samādhi). One who, having attained right meditative absorption, comprehends all phenomena as if they were like space — that is called right wisdom. One who, endowed with right wisdom, abandons all the afflictions — that is called liberation. And one who, having attained liberation, praises the qualities of liberation to all sentient beings and declares that liberation is permanent, unchanging, and unshifting — that is called praising the qualities of liberation. Liberation is the unsurpassed great nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, great nirvāṇa is that which extinguishes the fire of all afflictions. Again, nirvāṇa is also called a support and a resting place, because it gives shelter from the fierce winds and rains of affliction. Again, nirvāṇa is called a protector and a refuge, because it causes one to pass beyond all fears. Again, nirvāṇa is called an island, because the four great floods cannot sweep one away. What are the four floods? The flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. For this reason, nirvāṇa is called an island. Again, nirvāṇa is called the ultimate refuge.

Why is it called the ultimate refuge? Because through it one attains all lasting happiness.

Even when a bodhisattva, a great being, possesses these ten qualities of Dharma, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is still not seen clearly. Furthermore, O son of good family, there are four qualities by which one who has gone forth fails to attain the four fruits of the renunciant life. What are the four? They are four base desires: the desire for robes, the desire for food, the desire for bedding and seats, and the desire for existence. These are the four base desires, which are the sickness of one who has gone forth. A good medicine of four kinds is able to cure that sickness. What are they? Wearing robes of cast-off rags cures the base desire of a monk for robes. Living on alms cures the base desire for food. Dwelling at the foot of a tree cures the base desire for bedding and seats. Pacification of body and mind cures the base desire of a monk for existence. By these four medicines eliminating these four sicknesses, this is called the noble conduct. Thus the noble conduct is called having few desires and knowing contentment.

In peace there are four kinds of happiness. What are the four? The happiness of going forth, the happiness of peace, the happiness of cessation, and the happiness of complete fulfillment. Attaining these four kinds of happiness is called peace. Because one possesses the four diligences, it is called diligence. Because one possesses the four close applications of mindfulness, it is called right close application of mindfulness. Because one possesses the four meditative concentrations, it is called right meditative absorption. Because one sees the four noble truths, it is called right wisdom. Because all afflictions are utterly severed, it is called liberation. Because all the faults of affliction are condemned, it is called the praise of liberation.

O son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses these ten qualities of Dharma and abides in them does indeed see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, yet it has not become clear.

Furthermore, O son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, upon hearing this sūtra, draws near to it and applies himself diligently. Relinquishing all worldly possessions is called having few desires. After going forth, not giving rise to a mind of regret is called knowing contentment. Knowing contentment, dwelling in solitude and abandoning crowds is called peace. One who does not know contentment takes no delight in solitude. One who knows contentment always delights in solitude and peace, and while constantly dwelling in a place of solitude and peace, thinks to himself: all people of the world consider me to have attained the fruit of the renunciant life, yet I have not truly attained it — why then should I deceive others? Having thought thus, striving diligently to cultivate the fruit of the renunciant path is called diligence. Drawing near to and cultivating great nirvāṇa is called right close application of mindfulness. Inclining toward and engaging in divine conduct is called right meditative absorption. Abiding in that meditative absorption, seeing rightly and knowing rightly is called right wisdom. Through seeing and knowing rightly, becoming free from bondage to all afflictions is called liberation. A bodhisattva of the tenth ground proclaiming the qualities of nirvāṇa for the sake of sentient beings is called the praise of liberation.

O son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in and is endowed with those ten qualities of Dharma does indeed see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, yet it has not become clear.

Furthermore, O son of good family, having few desires means: whether a monk dwells in solitude sitting upright without lying down, or abides at the foot of a tree —

or dwells in a charnel ground, or dwells in an unsheltered place, or sits upon a mat of grass and goes on alms-round, being content with however much he receives; or who uses only one seat, or does not eat more than one meal, or possesses only the three robes, or carries nothing but rags gathered from charnel grounds — this is having few desires. When one who practices in such a way does not give rise to a mind of regret, that is contentment. Cultivating meditative absorption in solitude is peace. Not abandoning the awakening mind of unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening even after attaining the fourth fruit is diligence. Keeping the mind one-pointedly upon the Tathāgata as permanent, unchanging, and unmoving is the establishment of right mindfulness. Cultivating the eight liberations is right meditative absorption. Attaining the four thorough analytical knowledges is right wisdom. Being free from the seven underlying tendencies is liberation. Proclaiming the qualities of nirvāṇa by saying that great nirvāṇa is free from ten characteristics — that is the praise of liberation.

What are those ten characteristics? They are: birth, aging, illness, death, form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and impermanence. To be free from these ten characteristics is what is called great nirvāṇa.

O son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in and is endowed with those ten qualities of Dharma does indeed see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, yet it has not become clear.

Furthermore, O son of good family, having many desires for gain and fame means: attending upon kings, ministers, the warrior caste (kṣatriya), brahmins, the lowest caste, and the merchant caste, and saying, "I have attained everything from the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship." And for the sake of gain and fame, in all four modes of conduct, even down to the act of urinating and defecating, whenever one sees a donor one makes obeisance, goes forth to meet them, and flatters them. To overcome such base desires is having few desires. Although the afflictions have not yet been fully purified, to act in conformity with the deeds of the Tathāgata is contentment.

O son of good family, these two qualities of Dharma are the proximate cause and condition for mindfulness and meditative absorption. Those who share the same preceptors and masters will constantly praise them, and I too have always praised throughout all the sūtras the qualities of these two qualities of Dharma. Whoever is endowed with these two qualities of Dharma has drawn near to the gateway of great nirvāṇa and to the five kinds of well-being. This is peace. The restraint of moral discipline is diligence. Possessing conscience and shame is right mindfulness. Not perceiving the characteristics of mind is right meditative absorption. Not seeking the cause of the intrinsic nature and defining characteristics of phenomena is right wisdom. The thorough cutting off of afflictions through the absence of defining characteristics is liberation. Praising the sūtras of the complete parinirvāṇa is what is called the praise of liberation.

O son of good family, a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in those ten qualities of Dharma does indeed see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, yet it has not become clear.

O son of good family, you asked: with what kind of eye does a bodhisattva of the tenth ground see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood without it becoming clear, and with what kind of eye does the Blessed One, a buddha, see it with full clarity? O son of good family, seeing with the eye of wisdom is unclear. Seeing with the buddha-eye is clear. Practicing the conduct of awakening is unclear. The absence of any such conduct is clear. Because of abiding on the tenth ground, one sees, yet it is not clear. Because of neither abiding nor moving, it has become clear.

A bodhisattva, a great being, sees through the condition of wisdom, and that seeing is unclear. The Blessed One, a buddha, sees with full clarity by having severed cause and result, and omniscience is called the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. A bodhisattva of the tenth ground is not called omniscient, and therefore, though he sees, it has not become clear.

O son of good family, there are two kinds of seeing: seeing with the eye, and seeing through hearing. The Blessed One, a buddha, sees the intrinsic nature of buddhahood with the buddha-eye, as one sees an āmalaka fruit lying in the palm of one's hand. A bodhisattva of the tenth ground sees the intrinsic nature of buddhahood only through hearing, and therefore it has not become clear. A bodhisattva of the tenth ground knows with certainty that he himself will undoubtedly attain unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, yet he does not know that the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is present in all sentient beings.

O son of good family, furthermore, seeing with the eye means that the Blessed One, a buddha, and bodhisattvas of the tenth ground see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. And seeing through hearing means that all sentient beings and those up through the ninth ground see the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. If, upon hearing that the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is present in all sentient beings, a bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of faith, that is not called seeing through hearing.

O son of good family, if any son of good family or daughter of good family wishes to see the Tathāgata, they should uphold, memorize, read aloud, recite, transcribe, expound, and thoroughly contemplate the twelve branches of scripture.

The bodhisattva, the great being, Lion's Roar then asked: Blessed One, if all sentient beings do not seek the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's mind, how could they come to seek it through investigation?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, if all sentient beings, who do not truly know the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's mind, wish to realize and know it, they will come to know it through two kinds of causes and conditions. What are these? Seeing with the eye, and seeing through hearing.

Seeing all the bodily activities of the Tathāgata, however many there may be, is the Tathāgata — and that is called seeing with the eye. If one realizes the activities of the Tathāgata's speech, one should understand that to be the Tathāgata — and that is called seeing through hearing.

Seeing that his form and appearance are incomparable, unlike those of all sentient beings, one should understand that to be the Tathāgata — and that is seeing with the eye. Hearing his supremely exalted, most excellent voice, unlike the voices and tones of sentient beings, one should understand that to be the Tathāgata — and that is seeing through hearing.

Examining whether the Tathāgata performs miraculous deeds for the sake of sentient beings or for the sake of gain and fame, and seeing that he does so for the sake of sentient beings and not for gain and fame — one should understand that to be the Tathāgata, and that is seeing with the eye. When the Tathāgata, through the gnosis that knows the minds of others, attends to sentient beings, examining whether he teaches the Dharma for the sake of gain and fame or for the sake of sentient beings, and seeing that it is for the sake of sentient beings and not for gain and fame — one should understand that to be the Tathāgata, and that is seeing through hearing.

Examining how the Tathāgata came to possess this body, and for what reason he took on this body —

— and for whose sake he took on this body — is seeing with the eye. Understanding how the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, for what reason he teaches the Dharma, and to whom he teaches the Dharma — that is seeing through hearing.

When he is harmed by unwholesome acts of body yet does not become angry — one should understand that to be the Tathāgata, and that is seeing with the eye. When he is harmed by unwholesome acts of speech yet does not become angry — one should understand that to be the Tathāgata, and that is seeing through hearing.

He in whose case the bodhisattva, immediately after birth, took seven steps in each of the ten directions; in whose case the yakṣa kings Maṇibhadra and Pūrṇabhadra held parasols and banners in offering and roused countless and boundless world-systems, while a golden-hued radiance blazed and shimmered, filling the empty sky; in whose case the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda used their miraculous power to bathe the bodhisattva's body; in whose case the forms of the gods of the world came to receive him and make obeisance; in whose case the sage Asita joined his palms in reverence and paid homage; in whose case the desire for the pleasures of youth was abandoned like spittle; who was not deceived by worldly joys; who, having gone forth from home into homelessness, delighted at the end in cultivating the path; who, in order to demolish wrong views, practiced austerities for six years; who remained equal and even toward all sentient beings without duality; whose mind ever abided in meditative absorption, undisturbed from the very beginning, without distraction; whose body was beautifully adorned with the major and minor marks; in whose presence, wherever he went, the sounds of drums and cymbals arose in harmony of themselves; upon whose body, though clothing touched it with four fingers' breadth, it did not fall; who, when walking, gazed directly ahead and did not look to the right or left; who did not hastily swallow what was placed in his mouth; at whose seat, when he rose from where he had been sitting, the grass was neither stirred nor disturbed; and who, though he went to teach the Dharma in order to tame sentient beings, was seen to be utterly without pride — seeing all this is seeing with the eye.

Now, when the bodhisattva had taken those seven steps and then said, "This body of mine is the last of inner existences," and when the sage Asita joined his palms and spoke thus: "Great King, know this: the prince Siddhārtha will without any doubt attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening — he will not remain a householder and become a wheel-turning king. Why is that? Because the marks are clearly manifest. The marks of a wheel-turning king are not clearly manifest, whereas the marks of the prince Siddhārtha are supremely clear — therefore he will assuredly attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening." And when, having seen old age, sickness, and death, the prince then thought thus: "All sentient beings are deeply pitiable — they go about always accompanied by birth, aging, sickness, and death such as this, and through not understanding they endure suffering without end. I must put a stop to this." He then went to the sage Ālāra, who possessed the five superknowledges, trained in the meditative absorption of nothingness, and attained it — but afterwards saw its faults. Then again he went to the sage Udraka, trained in the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, attained it, but understood that this too was not nirvāṇa but a condition of cyclic existence. For six years he practiced austerities, yet obtained nothing at all, and then spoke thus: "Even having practiced these austerities, it is pointless — I have obtained nothing whatsoever. If there were something genuine, it would be fitting that I attain it. Since I have not attained anything, judging from the fact that I have obtained nothing, this is the path of wrong view, not the path of what is right." And having said this —

After attaining complete awakening, the Brahmā King made this request of the Tathāgata: would the Tathāgata be pleased to open wide the gates of Dharma for sentient beings with the unsurpassed elixir of his teaching? The Blessed One then spoke to the Brahmā King thus: "All sentient beings are perpetually veiled by the obscuration of affliction, and are therefore unable to take hold of the words of my sacred Dharma." The Brahmā King again implored: "Blessed One, among all sentient beings there are three kinds — those of sharp faculties, those of middling faculties, and those of dull faculties. Those of sharp faculties will be able to receive and hold what is taught and explained. May you please teach and expound." The Blessed One declared: "Great King, attend to this with very great care and listen well. I shall open the gates of the elixir for all sentient beings." Having said this, at the city of Vārāṇasī he turned the wheel of the sacred Dharma in full and taught the path of the Middle Way.

And what is that? The Middle Way is this: although all the afflictions of sentient beings have not been overcome, it is not the case that they cannot be overcome; yet neither have they been overcome, nor do they remain un-overcome — that is the Middle Way. No sentient being has yet been liberated, yet it is not that none will be liberated — that is the Middle Way. Not everything is accomplished, yet not everything is unaccomplished — that is the Middle Way. Whatever one teaches, one does not grasp oneself as the teacher nor grasp others as the students — that is the Middle Way. Teaching is not done for the sake of gain, yet it is not the case that no fruit will be obtained — that is the Middle Way. Words that are correct, words that are true, words that are timely, words that are straight, and words that say nothing meaningless — understanding such supreme and sacred Dharma as this is what is seen through hearing. Son of good family, the defining characteristic of the Tathāgata's mind is not something that is seen. If any son of good family or daughter of good family wishes to see the Tathāgata, they should abide in two things: cause and condition.

Then the great bodhisattva Siṃhaghoṣa again addressed the Blessed One thus: "Blessed One, you taught earlier that four types of persons are comparable to the fruit of the mango tree. Now, there are some persons whose conduct is refined but whose mind is not genuine; some whose mind is refined but whose conduct is not genuine; some whose mind is refined and whose conduct too is genuine; and some whose mind is not refined and whose conduct also is not genuine. How shall the first two types be known? Even if one abides in the two ways you, Blessed One, have described, one will not come to know them."

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, those two types of persons are indeed, in truth, as difficult to know as in the simile of the mango fruit. Because they are so difficult to know, I have taught in the sūtras that one should dwell together with them. If, even while dwelling together, one does not know, then one should associate with them for a long time. If, even after long association, one does not know, then one should examine with wisdom. If one still does not comprehend even through wisdom, then one should examine very thoroughly. Through thorough examination one will come to know whether they uphold moral discipline or whether their moral discipline is impaired. Son of good family, if one possesses these four qualities — dwelling together, long association, wisdom, and thorough examination — one will come to know whether a person upholds moral discipline or whether their moral discipline is impaired.

Son of good family, there are two kinds of moral discipline, and correspondingly two kinds of guarding it. What are they? Discipline that is perfected, and discipline that is not yet perfected. There are also cases of upholding discipline through cause and condition, and so the wise and discerning person should examine whether someone's vow of moral discipline is being upheld as perfected discipline for the sake of gain and fame."

Son of good family, the moral discipline of the Tathāgata is called perfected discipline because it is free from cause and condition. For this reason, even when unwholesome sentient beings harm and injure a bodhisattva, no mind arises in that bodhisattva that is obstructed by aversion. Therefore a Tathāgata is said to be endowed with the holding of perfected discipline.

Son of good family, once in a former time I was residing with five hundred attendants including Śāriputra in the city of Campā in the central land. A hawk seized a dove, and the dove, utterly terrified, took shelter in the shadow of Śāriputra and trembled like a tree in the wind. When it moved into my shadow, however, its body and mind became at ease and it became free of fear. Know therefore that because the shadow of a buddha, the Blessed One, possesses such power, one who abides in it is a holder of perfected discipline. Son of good family, if even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot be attained through discipline that is not yet perfected, what need is there to speak of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?

Furthermore, there are two kinds: discipline held for the sake of gain, and discipline held for the sake of the sacred Dharma. Know that one who holds discipline for the sake of gain does not, through that discipline, behold the intrinsic nature of a buddha and the Tathāgata. Though such a person hears the name of the intrinsic nature of a buddha and the Tathāgata, one should not say that hearing constitutes seeing. But know that one who holds discipline for the sake of the sacred Dharma does behold, through that discipline, the intrinsic nature of a buddha and the Tathāgata. That may be called seeing with the eye, and it may also be called seeing through hearing.

Furthermore, there are two kinds: that which is hard to dislodge because the root is deep, and that which is easy to shake because the root is shallow. Cultivating emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness in meditation is called hard to dislodge because the root is deep. If one does not apply oneself to these three kinds of meditative absorption, then even while practicing and cultivating, one will come to twenty-five existences — this is called easy to shake because the root is shallow.

The thirty-seventh fascicle.

Furthermore, there are two kinds: discipline practiced for one's own sake, and discipline practiced for the sake of sentient beings. One who practices for the sake of sentient beings beholds the intrinsic nature of a buddha and the Tathāgata.

As for the vow of moral discipline, there are also two kinds: discipline that is a restraint by intrinsic nature, and discipline that is a restraint through the condition of another. As for the former, one who has undertaken discipline without it ever being broken throughout immeasurable births — even if the country is in turmoil, even if one encounters an unwholesome spiritual friend, even if one encounters an evil age and hears perverse and corrupt teachings, or even if one dwells alongside wrong views — in that situation, though there be no ceremony of undertaking discipline, one is restrained just as one was at the very beginning of undertaking it, without impairment. This is called discipline that is a restraint by intrinsic nature. As for one who attains discipline through approaching a preceptor and the Saṅgha, making the request, and performing the fourfold act — that discipline, received through the condition of the preceptor, the master, fellow students, and the spiritual friend, who correct and instruct one, knowing what is to be done and what is not to be done through listening to the Dharma, through expounding it, and through knowledge of all proper conduct — this is called discipline that is a restraint through the condition of another.

Son of good family, one who is restrained by intrinsic nature beholds the intrinsic nature of a buddha and the Tathāgata with the eye; and this may also be called seeing through hearing.

As for moral discipline, there are also two kinds: the discipline of a śrāvaka, and the discipline of a bodhisattva.

From the first arousing of the awakening mind up to unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening, it is called the discipline of a bodhisattva. That which is attained from the contemplation of bare bones up to the fruit of arhatship is called the discipline of a śrāvaka. And here one should understand that whoever upholds the discipline of a śrāvaka does not behold the intrinsic nature of a buddha and the Tathāgata. Whoever upholds the discipline of a bodhisattva, one should understand, does attain unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening, and does behold the intrinsic nature of a buddha, the Tathāgata, and nirvāṇa.

The bodhisattva Siṃhasvara then asked: Blessed One, for what cause and by what condition does one take up and become bound by moral discipline?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, it is in order to have a mind free of regret. And why is there no regret? Because one experiences happiness. And why does one experience happiness? Because one has thoroughly abandoned. And why does one thoroughly abandon? Because one is supremely at ease. And why is one supremely at ease? Because one is a yogi engaged in meditative concentration. And why is one engaged in meditative concentration? Because one knows and sees correctly. And why does one know and see correctly? Because one sees the faults of saṃsāra. And why does one see the faults of saṃsāra? Because the mind is without attachment. And why is the mind without attachment? Because one attains liberation. And why liberation? Because one attains the great unsurpassed nirvāṇa. And why does one attain the great nirvāṇa? Because one attains permanence, happiness, self, and utter purity. And why permanence, happiness, self, and utter purity? Because one attains the state of neither arising nor ceasing. And why neither arising nor ceasing? Because one beholds the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Therefore the bodhisattva upholds moral discipline that is utterly pure and perfected through intrinsic nature.

Son of good family, monks who are bound by the discipline of moral precepts do not deliberately seek or aspire after a mind free of regret, yet they naturally attain a mind free of regret. Why is this? Because the nature of reality is such that it becomes so. Happiness, thorough abandonment, supreme ease, correct knowledge and vision, seeing the faults of saṃsāra, a mind without attachment, liberation, nirvāṇa, permanence, happiness, self, utter purity, neither arising nor ceasing, and beholding the intrinsic nature of a buddha — these they do not deliberately seek, yet they come to attain them spontaneously. Why is this? Because the nature of reality is such that it becomes so.

The bodhisattva Siṃhasvara then asked: Blessed One, if from the cause of moral discipline one attains the fruit of a mind free of regret, and from the cause of liberation one attains the fruit of nirvāṇa, then if there is no cause for moral discipline, there is likewise no fruit for nirvāṇa. That which has no cause is called permanent. If nirvāṇa has no cause, then surely it is impermanent. If it is so, then nirvāṇa would have come into existence from a state of prior non-existence. If something comes into existence from a state of prior non-existence, it would be impermanent — just like a butter lamp. And if nirvāṇa is like that, for what reason does one designate it as self, as happiness, and as utterly pure?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, excellent, excellent! Because you have planted roots of virtue before countless buddhas, you have the confidence to ask the Tathāgata about these profound matters. Son of good family, because you have not lost the memory of former times, you have posed this question in just this way.

I recall that in the past, an immeasurable number of eons ago, a Tathāgata named Suprāpta appeared in the world in the land of Śerakya. At that time, that Tathāgata taught this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa for thirty million years, and both you and I were gathered in that assembly. When I asked that Blessed One about these very matters, the Blessed One at that time entered into meditative absorption (samādhi) for the sake of sentient beings, and so did not explain this point.

Excellent, O great being! Recall that former situation well, hold it deeply in mind, and listen steadily — I shall explain it to you fully.

Moral discipline (śīla) also has a cause. What is that cause? It is the hearing of the holy Dharma. The hearing of the holy Dharma also has a cause. What is that cause? It is reliance upon a spiritual friend. Reliance upon a spiritual friend also has a cause, and that cause is a mind of faith. The mind of faith also has a cause. That cause has two aspects: the hearing of the Dharma and the contemplation of its meaning.

Son of good family, the mind of faith arises from the cause of hearing the Dharma, and the hearing of the Dharma also arises from the cause of a mind of faith. These two phenomena become cause and effect in mutual relation: each serves as cause, each serves as cause of a cause, each serves as result, and each serves as result of a result.

Son of good family, consider the analogy of a Nirgrantha (a Jain ascetic) who places a pot on a tripod of three sticks: each stick is the cause of the others, and the fruit of each is the others — they cannot be separated out individually.

Son of good family, just as ignorance is a condition for formations, and formations are in turn a condition for ignorance — so ignorance and formations become cause, and cause of cause, and result, and result of result — likewise, all the way through to birth, which is a condition for old age and death, and old age and death in turn a condition for birth. Birth and old age-and-death thus become cause, and cause of cause, and result, and result of result.

Son of good family, birth and the phenomena that are produced cannot arise of themselves. Because they do not arise of themselves, they arise through being generated by birth. Birth does not arise of itself; it arises through the power of what generates it. Therefore both births become cause, and cause of cause, and result, and result of result.

Son of good family, the mind of faith and the hearing of the Dharma are similar to this.

Son of good family, that which is result and yet is not cause — that is the Great Nirvāṇa. Why is it called a result? Because it is the unsurpassed result, the fruit of the ascetic and the brahmin. It is called a result because it severs cyclic existence (saṃsāra) and because it has overcome the afflictions. It is called a result because all afflictions have been utterly repudiated. The afflictions are spoken of as that which is defective.

Son of good family, nirvāṇa has no cause; its essential nature is simply result. Why is that? Because it is without arising and without cessation, without agency, neither compounded (saṃskṛta) nor uncompounded (asaṃskṛta), permanent and unchanging, without location, and without beginning or end.

Son of good family, if nirvāṇa had a cause, one could not call it nirvāṇa. The word "fully" (parinirvāṇa) refers to what pertains to a cause; the word "nirvāṇa" refers to the absence thereof. Because nirvāṇa has no cause, it is called "complete nirvāṇa" (parinirvāṇa).

The bodhisattva Siṃhanāda then posed this question: As the Blessed One has declared that nirvāṇa has no cause — that statement does not seem right to me. If one says "there is no," this meaning connects with six implications. What are those six? One says "there is no" in the sense that it does not exist by virtue of coming...

One says "there is no" in the sense that, just as all phenomena lack a self and what belongs to a self, so too there is an absence of anything in between — as when worldly people say of the ocean "there is no water" or "there is no sun or moon." One says "there is no" in the sense of scarcity — as when worldly people say of food that is not salty "there is no saltiness," or of a sweet liquid that has little sweetness "there is no sweetness." One says "there is no" in the sense of not having experienced something — as when a person of low birth has not experienced the Dharma of a brahmin and says "there is no brahmin Dharma." One says "there is no" in the sense of holding to bad and non-virtuous Dharma — as when worldly people who hold to sinful, non-virtuous Dharma are said not to be renunciants (śramaṇas) or brahmins, so people say "there are no renunciants or brahmins." One says "there is no" in the sense of the absence of a counterpart — as when, because white is absent, one says "it is black," or because light is absent, one says "there is no light." Nirvāṇa, O Blessed One, is similar to these: something does exist, yet because it has no cause, one speaks of "nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One then declared: Son of good family, you have spoken in six modes — yet to find an analogy for passing beyond sorrow among them, one should not take a simile for non-existence; rather, one should take the simile of the absence of something in between. Son of good family, the essential nature of nirvāṇa is indeed something that exists — like, for example, the absence of self and what belongs to self. Son of good family, worldly phenomena cannot rightly be compared to nirvāṇa, and therefore the similes of those six things are not fitting illustrations. Son of good family, all phenomena are without self, yet this nirvāṇa truly does have a self. It is for this reason that, although nirvāṇa has no cause, its essential nature is itself a fruit. What is a cause but not a fruit is called the intrinsic nature of a buddha, because it is not born from a cause. What is a cause but not a fruit is called "not a fruit" in the sense that it is not the fruit of a monk — that is why it is called "not a fruit." It is called "a cause" because it illuminates causes.

Son of good family, causes are of two kinds: the cause of arising and the cause of illumination. Of these, what brings phenomena into being is the cause of arising. What makes things manifest through the light of a lamp is called the cause of illumination. Thorough affliction is the cause of arising. The parents of sentient beings are the cause of illumination. Seeds and the like are the cause of arising. Earth, water, manure, and the like are the cause of illumination. Again, the cause of arising is this: through the six perfections one attains unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. The cause of illumination is this: through the intrinsic nature of a buddha one attains unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. Further, the cause of illumination is: the six perfections and the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Further, the cause of arising is: the meditative absorption called "the courageous advance" attaining unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. Again, the cause of illumination is: the noble eightfold path attaining unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. Again, the cause of arising is: the six perfections of a mind of faith.

The bodhisattva Siṃhanāda then posed this question: Blessed One, in accordance with what the Blessed One has taught — what is the meaning of "seeing the Tathāgata" and "seeing the intrinsic nature of a buddha"? Blessed One, the body of the Tathāgata has no marks or form. It is not long. It is not short. It is not white. It is not black. It has no directions or boundaries.

It does not abide in the three realms. It does not possess the characteristics of conditioned things. It is not known through visual consciousness. If the intrinsic nature of a buddha is likewise, how could it be seen?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the body of a buddha has two aspects: the permanent and the impermanent. Of these, the impermanent is what is called "seeing with the eye" — that is, the form manifested through skillful means in order to liberate all sentient beings. The permanent is also called "seeing with the eye" and "seeing through hearing" — that is, the Tathāgata's body of liberation.

The intrinsic nature of a buddha also has two aspects: what is seen and what is not seen. Of these, what is seen pertains to the tenth-ground bodhisattvas and to the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. What is not seen pertains to all sentient beings. "Seeing with the eye" means that the tenth-ground bodhisattvas and the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, behold with their vision the intrinsic nature of a buddha present in sentient beings. "Seeing through hearing" means that all sentient beings and the ninth-ground bodhisattvas hear that the intrinsic nature of a buddha and the body of the Tathāgata exist.

This too has two aspects: what has form and what is without form. Of these, what has form is the liberation body of the Tathāgata. What is without form is the Tathāgata's complete relinquishment of all form and characteristics.

The intrinsic nature of a buddha also has two aspects: what has form and what is without form. Of these, what has form is unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. What is without form arises from the most inferior worldly beings all the way up through the tenth-ground bodhisattvas — and it is called "without form" because it is not clearly seen even by the tenth-ground bodhisattvas.

Son of good family, again the intrinsic nature of a buddha has two aspects: what has form and what is without form. Of these, what has form pertains to buddhas and bodhisattvas. What is without form pertains to all sentient beings. What is seen with the eye is form. What is seen through hearing is without form. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is neither inner nor outer. Although it is neither inner nor outer, it is not nonexistent and it is not empty; therefore it is said that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

The bodhisattva Siṃhanāda then posed this question: Blessed One, as the Blessed One has taught — just as cream is present within milk, so in all sentient beings there is the intrinsic nature of a buddha, as mighty as a vajra, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha is like the pure essence of butter. If that is so, why has the Blessed One declared that the intrinsic nature of a buddha is neither outer nor inner?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, I did not say that cream exists within milk as such; rather, I said that cream exists because cream comes from milk. 

He asked: Blessed One, do all phenomena that are subject to birth exist separately at their own respective times?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, when milk exists there is no cream, nor butter, nor clarified butter, nor the essence of butter — and yet because all sentient beings cling to it as milk, I said that cream does not exist within milk. If something does exist, why would a skilled person not give it two names, as in the case of one who is called both a goldsmith and a blacksmith? Therefore, at the time of cream, neither milk nor butter nor clarified butter nor the essence of butter is present. So too, sentient beings hold that since cream is not milk, butter, clarified butter, and the essence of butter do not exist within it. One should understand it in that same way, extending the analysis all the way through to the essence of butter.

Son of good family, causes have two aspects: the true cause and —

the cause-as-condition. Of these, the true cause is illustrated by how cream arises from milk. The cause-as-condition means that because cream arises from milk through conditions such as warmth and impurity, one speaks of the intrinsic nature of cream as being present within milk.

The bodhisattva Lion's Roar asked: Blessed One, if the intrinsic nature of cream is not present within milk, that would seem to be like its not being present in a horn either — so why does cream not arise from a horn?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, cream does arise from a horn as well. Why is that? I have taught the cause-as-condition as having two aspects: impurity and warmth. The intrinsic nature of a horn, by reason of its impurity, is what causes it to become cream.

Lion's Roar said: Blessed One, if cream can arise from a horn, why is it that those who seek cream desire milk and do not desire a horn?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, that is precisely why I have explained the two kinds of cause: the true cause and the cause-as-condition.

Lion's Roar said: If the intrinsic nature of cream has never been present within milk from the beginning and is present now, then since a mango tree likewise has never been present within milk from the beginning, both are equally absent — so why does a mango fruit not arise from it?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, a mango tree too would grow from milk. If milk were poured at the base of a tree, within a single night five cubits of growth would arise. For that very reason I have taught the two kinds of cause.

Son of good family, if all phenomena arose from a single cause, one could equally object: why does a mango tree not arise from within milk?
