Son of good family, take the example of the four great elements: they are the cause and condition for all material form, yet they differ from and are incompatible with the defining characteristics of each individual material form — each is distinct and separate. For that very reason, a mango tree does not arise from milk.

Lion's Roar asked: Blessed One, just as the Blessed One has taught — the true cause and the cause-as-condition, these two kinds of cause — what is the cause for the intrinsic nature of buddhahood within sentient beings?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood within sentient beings also has two kinds of cause: the true cause and the cause-as-condition. Of these, the true cause is sentient beings themselves. The cause-as-condition is the six perfections (pāramitās).

The bodhisattva Lion's Roar said: Blessed One, I hold that the intrinsic nature of cream is definitely present within milk. Why do I say this? I observe that in the world, those who seek cream seek out milk and never seek out water — therefore I hold that the intrinsic nature of cream is present within milk.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, what you are asking is not quite the right way to put it. Why? Consider someone who wishes to see their own face reflected and so looks into a sword blade.

Lion's Roar said: Blessed One, by that reasoning, the intrinsic nature of cream must be present in milk — for if one's reflection were not present within the sword blade, why would one look into it?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if one's reflection were definitely and truly present within the sword blade, then why is it that when one holds the blade upright one sees a long face, and when one holds it sideways one sees a wide face? If it were truly one's own face, why would it appear elongated? And if it were some other face, why would one say "the reflection of my own face"? And if, through the condition of one's own face, one were seeing another's face, why does one not see the reflection of a horse's or a donkey's face?

Lion's Roar said: Blessed One, it is because the eye's light reaches there that one sees one's face elongated in the water.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the eye's light does not truly reach there. Why is that?

Because one sees both near and far simultaneously and all at once, yet between those two points one sees no object whatsoever. Son of good family, if it were the case that the eye's light travels there and thereby enables seeing, then when all sentient beings look, why do they not burn up? And if someone at a great distance sees a white object and is uncertain whether it is a goose, a flag, a person, or a tree, that would be unreasonable. If the eye's light truly travels there, then why does one see the contents inside a crystal, and the fish and stones inside a spring? And if seeing occurs without the light traveling there, then why does one see objects inside a crystal and yet fail to see forms on the other side of a wall? Therefore the idea that one sees at a distance because the eye's light travels there is not so.

Son of good family, just as you said: if yogurt already existed within milk, why would those who sell milk take only the price of milk and not the price of yogurt? Those who sell mares take only the price of the mare and not the price of the foal. Son of good family, people in the world take a wife because they have no son. If a wife becomes pregnant one would not say she has a daughter. And it is not right to say one takes a wife because a daughter already has the nature of a son. Why is that? If the nature of a son existed, it would follow that a brother also exists. If a brother exists, he would become a sibling. Why is that? Because they come from the same womb. Therefore I have taught that a daughter does not have the nature of a son.

If the nature of yogurt existed within milk, why would it not simultaneously possess all five tastes at once? If the defining characteristic of a nyagrodha tree growing to a span of five fathoms existed within the seed, why would the distinct shapes and forms of the sprout, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, fruit, and so forth not appear all at once simultaneously? Son of good family, when milk, at the stage of being milk, is distinct in form, distinct in taste, distinct in result — all the way through to the essence of butter — how can one say that the nature of yogurt exists within milk?

Son of good family, consider a person who says, "I shall drink butter tomorrow," and says even today, "I have already drunk it." Likewise, whoever says, "The nature of yogurt is definitely present in milk," is just the same.

Son of good family, consider a person who, using a pen, paper, ink, and so forth, produces written letters. There were originally no letters in the paper. Because they did not exist from the beginning, they come to be produced in dependence on conditions. If something existed from the beginning, many causes and conditions would be unnecessary. Consider blue and yellow pigments mixed together: they become green pigment. Neither of those two pigments originally had the nature of green. If it existed from the beginning, what would be the need to mix them?

Son of good family, consider that sentient beings are sustained by means of food. Truly, within food there is no life. If life were inherently existent therein, then even before the food is eaten, the food itself would be life.

Son of good family, because all phenomena are without inherent nature from the outset, contemplating that point he spoke these verses:

What has no beginning exists now.
What has a beginning does not exist now.
All phenomena of existence throughout the three times —
there is no fixed abiding of that kind.

Son of good family, all phenomena arise through causes and conditions and cease through causes and conditions.

Son of good family, if the nature of a buddha existed within sentient beings, it would follow that all sentient beings right now would possess the body of a buddha just as I do. The buddha-nature of sentient beings does not decay, does not deteriorate, cannot be seized, cannot be grasped, cannot be bound, cannot be designated —

just as empty space exists within sentient beings. Because it is unobstructed, empty space exists within all sentient beings, yet none of them individually sees their own empty space. If empty space did not exist within sentient beings, there would be no going and coming, no moving and staying, no sitting and lying down, and no birth or growth. For that reason I declared in the sūtras that the expanse of space exists within all sentient beings. That very expanse of space is what is called empty space. The intrinsic nature of a buddha within sentient beings is similar to this — just as a precious jewel, it is seen to a small degree by bodhisattvas of the tenth ground. Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha within sentient beings is the domain of the buddhas; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Because all sentient beings do not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha, they are perpetually seized upon by afflictions and wander in cyclic existence. Through seeing the intrinsic nature of a buddha, one is no longer bound by all-pervading afflictions; one is fully liberated from cyclic existence and attains the great nirvāṇa.

The bodhisattva Siṃhaghoṣa (Lion-Voice) then asked: Blessed One, the existence of the intrinsic nature of a buddha within all sentient beings is comparable to the existence of the intrinsic nature of yogurt within milk. If the intrinsic nature of yogurt did not exist within milk, then why did the Blessed One speak of two kinds of cause — the cause of reality and the conditioning cause? The conditioning cause consists of warmth and ferment. Space is without intrinsic nature, and so has no conditioning cause.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if the intrinsic nature of butter were definitively present within milk, what need would there be for conditioning causes?

The bodhisattva Siṃhaghoṣa replied: Blessed One, it is precisely because the intrinsic nature is present that a conditioning cause is sought. And why? In order to make it manifest. The conditioning cause is a cause of making visible. Blessed One, consider: when objects are already there in the darkness, one lights a lamp in order to see them. If they were not there from the beginning, what would the lamp illuminate? In the same way, because clay is present in the earth, a person, water, a wheel, a cord, and a stick are causes of making visible. The fruit of the banyan tree likewise has earth, water, and dung as causes of making visible. Similarly, in the case of milk, warmth and ferment become causes of making visible. Therefore, although the intrinsic nature is present from the very beginning, it depends on causes of making visible, and through them it becomes seen. For that reason it is evident that yogurt has been present in milk from the very beginning.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if there were definitely an intrinsic nature of yogurt present in milk, that very thing would become a cause of making visible. But if it were itself a cause of making visible, what need would there be to make it visible in the first place? Son of good family, if that cause of making visible were self-luminous by its very nature, it would be fitting that it always illuminated itself. And if it does not illuminate itself, it cannot illuminate others. To say that the cause of making visible has two natures — illuminating itself and illuminating others — is not the case. Why? How could what is one thing as a cause of making visible become two? If it became two, milk too would become two. And if milk does not have a twofold nature, why should that which is solely a cause of making visible become two?

Siṃhaghoṣa replied: Blessed One, just as worldly people speak of "self" and "other," so too the cause of making visible is of that same kind — it illuminates both self and other.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if the cause of making visible were as you say, it should not be called a cause of making visible at all. Why? Number counts forms of self and other, and so the word "eight" is used — that is the essential nature of form. Yet for the self there is no defining characteristic of a cause of making visible. Because there is no defining characteristic of illumination, it is by the power of the intrinsic nature of wisdom that self and other come to be counted. Therefore the cause of making visible cannot illuminate the self, and it cannot illuminate others either.

If the buddha-nature exists in all sentient beings, why would it be necessary to accumulate an immeasurable store of merit? If that accumulation were the cause of making visible, it would be comparable to the destruction of curds. And if one were to hold that the result is necessarily present in the cause, then moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom could not arise and grow. For I myself have seen that in the world, people who previously had no moral discipline, no meditative absorption, and no wisdom have received instruction from a preceptor and have, from the very beginning, arisen and grown directly. If what the preceptor teaches were the cause of making visible, then at the very moment of receiving instruction from the preceptor there would be no moral discipline, no meditative absorption, and no wisdom in the one being instructed. And if something were truly a matter of illumination — such that what does not yet exist would become illuminated — why should it be the case that moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom arise and grow only after illumination has occurred?

Siṃhaghoṣa asked: Blessed One, if there is no cause of making visible, why should the names "milk" and "curds" be assigned?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, there are three kinds of reply to an objection raised in debate. The first is a consequential reply: just as was said before — "What then is moral discipline? From the absence of remorse up to the attainment of great nirvāṇa." The second is a reply of silence: just as when a wanderer came to me and asked, "Is what is called 'self' permanent?" — at that time I said nothing. The third is a reply of doubt, such as the question posed here in this sūtra: "If the cause of making visible were to become two, why is there no duality in milk?" — these are the three.

Son of good family, I have now given a consequential reply: just as people in the world say, "If there is milk, without doubt curds exist, and therefore both milk and curds exist" — and they assign these names accordingly — so too with the buddha-nature: if there are sentient beings, there is buddha-nature, because it will be seen later.

Siṃhaghoṣa said: Blessed One, what the Blessed One has stated does not seem right to me. Why? The past has ceased, and the future has not yet arrived — so how can one speak of it as existing? If one says that what has not yet arrived exists, that too is untenable. It is like people in the world who, seeing that there is no child, say "There is no child." Since sentient beings do not possess the buddha-nature, why does the Blessed One say that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the past is to be called "existent." Consider, for example, a shoot that sprouts from the seed of a sour fruit-tree and brings forth fruit: the shoot too begins sweet, and yet from that point until the fruit appears it is just so — it ripens and becomes sour. Son of good family, the sour taste is not present in the seed, the shoot, or the period up to the fruit's arising; it arises from the color, form, and substance of the fruit. Thus that sour taste, though absent from the beginning, has now come into being.

In this way, though absent from the beginning, it comes to exist now — yet this does not mean it lacks a beginningless cause. In this way, too, the seed from the beginning is something past, and yet it is called "existent." For this reason, the past is also called "existent."

Now, in what way is the future called "existent"? Consider, for example, a person who ploughs a field of sesame, and another person asks, "Why are you ploughing this? What is the point?" The ploughman replies, "There is oil here." Truly, the oil is not yet there — and yet, once the sesame ripens, the grain is gathered, pressed, pounded, and squeezed, and only then does the oil appear for the first time. Therefore, one should understand that this man is not speaking falsely. For this reason, the future too is called "existent."

Furthermore, in what way is the past called "existent"? Son of good family, consider a man who secretly slandered the king, and many years passed. Then the king came to hear of it, and upon hearing it asked him, "Why did you slander me?" The man replied, "Great King, I did not slander you." "And why not?" "Because the slander that was spoken has already ceased." The king said, "Both I and the slander exist right now — why then do you say it has ceased?" And on account of that cause and condition, the man's body and life were destroyed. Son of good family, though those two things — the king and the slander — were no longer truly present, the result was nonetheless not absent. For this reason, the past too is called "existent."

And once more, in what way is the future called "existent"? Consider a man who went to a potter's place and asked, "Do you have any pots?" The potter replied, "I have pots." In truth, the potter has no pots at that very moment — but because the clay is there, he says, "I have pots," and one should understand that he is not speaking falsely in saying so. For this reason, just as curds exist within milk, so too does the nature of buddhahood exist within sentient beings. If one wishes to see the nature of buddhahood, one must examine with great care the time, the measure, the shape, and the form. Therefore, my saying that the nature of buddhahood exists in all sentient beings is not untrue.

Lion's Roar then asked: If the nature of buddhahood were not present in all sentient beings, how could they attain unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening? If sentient beings can attain unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening through the cause of truth, then the cause of truth is precisely this: the nature of buddhahood. Blessed One, if the nyagrodha tree were not present in the fruit of the nyagrodha, why would it be called the fruit of the nyagrodha and not the fruit of the khadira? Blessed One, consider how it is not fitting to designate the lineage of Gautama as the lineage of Ātreya, nor to designate the lineage of Ātreya as the lineage of Gautama. In the same way, it is not fitting to call the fruit of the nyagrodha the fruit of the khadira, nor the fruit of the khadira the fruit of the nyagrodha. Just as the Blessed One is none other than one of the lineage of Gautama, so too is the nature of buddhahood in sentient beings like that. Therefore, I hold that the nature of buddhahood is present in all sentient beings.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the meaning that "the nyagrodha is present in the fruit" is not appropriate. If it were truly present, why is it not seen?

Son of good family, consider: things of the world, owing to the presence of causes and conditions, appear as though absent. What are these causes and conditions? They are as follows: not being seen because of distance, as in the tracks of birds in the sky; not being seen because of proximity, as in the dirt in one's own eye; not being seen because of deterioration, as in a root that has rotted; not being seen because of distraction of perception, as in a mind that is not one-pointed; and not being seen because of subtlety —

as with subtle particles; not being seen because of being obscured, as when stars are covered by clouds; not being seen because of the multitude, as when sesame is inside a heap of grain; and not being seen because of intermixture, as when sesame is placed within a heap of sesame.

Now, the nyagrodha tree is unlike those eight types of causes and conditions. If it were truly present, why is it not seen? If one says it is not seen because of subtlety or because of being obscured — that account, too, is untenable. Why? Because the characteristic mark of a tree is that it is gross. If it were by nature subtle, how could it grow? And if it were not seen because it is obscured, then it would follow that it is never seen at all. Since a previously gross nature was absent and yet now it is seen to be gross, that grossness has never had inherent existence from the beginning. Since what was previously unseen lacked any inherent nature, and yet now comes to be seen, that seeing likewise has no original inherent existence. And the fruit is the same: from the beginning the tree was absent, and that it should come to exist now involves no fault.

The bodhisattva Siṃhaghoṣa asked: The Blessed One has taught two kinds of causes — a cause of truth and a cause of manifestation. In that regard, earth, water, and warmth are what function as the cause of manifestation for the nyagrodha fruit, and thus it grows from subtle to gross.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if it truly existed from the beginning, what need would there be for a cause of manifestation? And if it had no inherent existence from the beginning, what is there to manifest? Consider: if the nyagrodha has no inherent grossness from the beginning, and yet through a cause of manifestation it comes to arise as gross, then since both the seed and the tree seem equally absent, why does the khadira tree not grow from that seed?

Son of good family, if it were the case that the subtle is not seen but the gross is seen, then — just as a single particle is not seen but when many particles are gathered together they come to be seen — by the same logic, the gross fruit should be seen as well. And why? Because there is a sprout, a trunk, flowers, and fruit — and within each single fruit there are immeasurable seeds, and within each single seed there are immeasurable trees. It is for this reason that it is called "gross," and it is because it has thus become gross that it comes to be seen.

Son of good family, if the growth of the nyagrodha tree were due to an inherent nature of the nyagrodha seed truly present in the seed, then by eye one would see that seed being burned. And in that case, the nature of burning would likewise have existed from the very beginning. But if burning existed from the beginning, it would not be right for the tree to grow at all. Moreover, if all phenomena were arising and ceasing from the beginning, why would it be that one arose earlier and another ceases later — that they do not occur simultaneously? For these reasons, one should understand that there is no inherent nature.

The bodhisattva Siṃhaghoṣa asked: Blessed One, if, despite the nyagrodha fruit's having no inherent nature of a tree from the beginning, the tree comes to grow — and since both the tree and the seed seem equally absent — why does oil not come from that fruit?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, oil does in fact come from it. Though inherent nature is absent from the beginning, it comes to exist through causes and conditions.

Siṃhaghoṣa asked: Then why is it not called sesame oil?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, because it is not sesame. Son of good family, consider: through the condition of friction fire arises, and through the condition of water moisture arises — both arise from conditions, yet neither produces the other. The nyagrodha fruit and sesame oil are just the same: both arise from conditions, but the one does not produce the other. The nature of the nyagrodha fruit is beneficial for disorders of phlegm, while the nature of sesame oil is beneficial for disorders of wind.

Son of good family, consider: through the causes and conditions of the sugarcane plant, both sugar crystals and raw sugar arise. Thus from a single cause,

their colors and potencies are distinct. Sugar crystals are beneficial for disorders of bile, while raw sugar is beneficial for disorders of phlegm.

The bodhisattva Siṃhadhvaja then addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, just as milk has no intrinsic nature of curd, sesame has no intrinsic nature of oil, the nyagrodha fruit has no intrinsic nature of wood, and clay has no intrinsic nature of a vessel — in the same way, if all sentient beings lack an intrinsic nature of buddhahood, then the statement made previously by the Blessed One, that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of buddhahood and will therefore attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, is not tenable.

"Why so? Because gods and humans have no fixed intrinsic nature, and precisely because they lack such a fixed nature, a human can become a god and a god can become a human. Yet even that transformation occurs through the condition of karma, not through any intrinsic nature. Likewise, a bodhisattva, a great being, also attains unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening through the condition of karma.

"Furthermore, if all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, for what cause and through what condition do those of wrong craving (mithyātṛṣṇā), having severed the roots of virtue, fall into the hells? If the awakening mind were itself the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, it would follow that those of wrong craving could not cut it — which is reasonable. But if it could be cut, then it would be improper to call the intrinsic nature of buddhahood permanent. And if it is not permanent, one should not call it the intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

"Again, if all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, why do we speak of first arousing the mind of awakening, of those who fall back, and of those who are irreversible? One who falls back, it must be held, is a person who lacks the intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

"Blessed One, the way in which great bodhisattvas, noble great beings, arrive with single-minded resolve at unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is this: through great loving-kindness and great compassion, seeing the afflictive faults of birth, aging, and death, they contemplate the freedom from those very afflictions of birth, aging, and death in great nirvāṇa. Trusting in the Three Jewels and in the karmic maturation of the fruits of action, they take up moral discipline and the training in vow-keeping and other such Dharmas — it is this that we call the intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

"If, beyond such Dharma, there existed some intrinsic nature of buddhahood, what use would there be for causes and conditions? Blessed One, milk does not have the property of becoming curd and butter without conditions — what depends on causes and conditions requires, in the case of milk, the human effort, the water, the vessel, the churning stick, and the cord. The intrinsic nature of buddhahood in sentient beings is likewise similar: it is unreasonable to attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening apart from causes and conditions.

"If such a nature were definitively present, why would yogins (yogins), upon seeing the sufferings of birth, aging, sickness, death, and so forth, and the suffering of the three lower destinies, give rise to a mind of turning away from them? And it would follow that they need not cultivate the six perfections (pāramitās) in order to attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Milk does not become curd without conditions, and without the cause of the six perfections there can be no attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. For these reasons, sentient beings do not possess an intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

"Moreover, regarding what the Blessed One stated earlier: the Saṅgha Jewel is permanent. If it is permanent, it is not impermanent."

If it is not impermanent, how then can one attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening? And if the Saṅgha is permanent, why did you say that all sentient beings possess an intrinsic nature of buddhahood?

"Blessed One, if sentient beings have never from the beginning had the awakening mind, and have never from the beginning had the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and if these arise only afterward, then the intrinsic nature of buddhahood in sentient beings is likewise such: it would arise afterward from what was not present at the beginning. For this reason, all sentient beings do not possess an intrinsic nature of buddhahood."

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, you have long understood the meaning of the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, and now you have asked thus on behalf of sentient beings — well done. All sentient beings truly do possess an intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

"As for what you said — that if sentient beings possessed an intrinsic nature of buddhahood it would be unreasonable for the mind of awakening to have arisen at a first moment — son of good family, mind is not the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. Why? Because mind is impermanent, whereas the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is permanent.

"As for what you said — 'why is there a mind of turning away?' — there is in truth no turning away with respect to mind itself. If mind turned away from mind, one would never attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; it is called 'non-returning' because what is attained is offered up and does not turn back. The awakening mind is not in truth the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. Why? Because beings with wrong craving, having severed the root of virtue, fall into hell. If the awakening mind were the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, those with wrong craving would not be called beings with wrong craving. Nor can the awakening mind be called impermanent. Therefore, you should understand with certainty that the awakening mind is not in truth the intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

"Son of good family, as for what you said — that if the intrinsic nature of buddhahood exists, it must depend on conditions just as milk becomes curd — that too is not so. Why? Just as milk becomes butter through five kinds of cause, so too is it with the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. For example, in stone there is gold, there is silver, there is copper, there is iron; though these appear to abide alike in the four great elements, each arises from a single essence under a single name, and each requires many causes and conditions. These come to arise in the first instance from the merit of sentient beings and from the work done by human effort. Therefore one should understand that from the beginning there is no intrinsic nature of gold. The intrinsic nature of buddhahood in sentient beings is not called 'buddha'; it is only when the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is perceived through the assembly of many causes and conditions of merit that one will for the first time attain buddhahood.

"As for what you said — that if sentient beings possess an intrinsic nature of buddhahood why do they not attain it — that too is not so. Why? Because the causes and conditions have not yet assembled.

"Son of good family, for this reason I have taught two kinds of genuine cause: the cause of truth, which is the intrinsic nature of buddhahood itself, and the conditional cause, which is the arousal of the mind of awakening. By means of these two — cause and condition — one attains unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, just as gold comes forth from stone."

"Son of good family, you have said this: 'Since the Saṅgha is permanent, no sentient being lacks an intrinsic nature of buddhahood.' Son of good family, the word 'Saṅgha' means harmony, and harmony is of two kinds: conventional harmony and ultimate harmony. Conventional harmony is the Saṅgha of śrāvakas. Ultimate harmony is the Saṅgha of bodhisattvas. The conventional Saṅgha is impermanent, but the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is permanent. Just as the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is permanent, so too the ultimate Saṅgha is like it.

"Furthermore, there is this understanding of the Saṅgha: it is harmony with the Dharma. Harmony with the Dharma means the twelve branches of scriptural teaching. Because the twelve branches of scriptural teaching are permanent, I have therefore declared that the Dharma and the Saṅgha are permanent.

"Son of good family, the Saṅgha is called harmony, and that which is harmony is the twelve links of dependent origination. Because the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is present within the twelve links of dependent origination, just as the twelve links of dependent origination are permanent, so too the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is like them. For this reason I have declared that the Saṅgha possesses the intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

"Again, 'Saṅgha' means the harmony of all buddhas. For this reason too I have declared that the Saṅgha possesses the intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

"Son of good family, you have asked with great earnestness: 'If sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, why are there those who are reversible and those who are irreversible?' Listen carefully and well — I shall explain and set this forth in full.

"Son of good family, bodhisattvas, great beings, are made reversible from awakening by thirteen qualities. What are the thirteen? They are these: a mind of faithlessness; a mind that makes no effort; a mind of doubt; attachment to body and material possessions combined with miserliness; generating great fear toward great nirvāṇa, thinking 'How could sentient beings ever be fully liberated?'; the absence of a patient mind; an untamed mind; a mind tormented by grief; dishonesty; heedlessness; contempt for one's own body; the view that one is unable to uproot the afflictions; and lack of inclination to enter into the qualities of awakening. Son of good family, these thirteen qualities cause bodhisattvas to turn back from awakening.

"Furthermore, these six qualities destroy the mind of awakening. What are the six? They are: miserliness toward the Dharma; generating unwholesome thoughts toward sentient beings; relying on unwholesome spiritual friends; failing to undertake diligent effort; praising oneself and being arrogant; and engaging in worldly activities. These six qualities are what destroy the mind of awakening.

"Son of good family, some people, upon hearing that the buddha, the Blessed One, is the teacher of gods and humans, supreme among all sentient beings, incomparable, surpassing śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who with the eye of Dharma sees the Dharma clearly without obstruction, and who liberates all sentient beings from the ocean of afflictions — upon hearing this, they generate a great aspiration and solemn resolve, thinking: 'If such a being as this exists in the world, then I too shall attain this.' Moved by that cause and that condition, they arouse the mind aimed at unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Or others arouse the mind aimed at awakening because they have been shown the way by another. Or again, others hear that a bodhisattva, after practicing austerities for immeasurable eons, at last attains unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and —"

upon hearing this, one thinks: 'If I am unable to practice such austerities as these, how shall I ever attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?' And for that reason one turns back.

The thirty-eighth fascicle.

Noble son, there are also these five qualities of Dharma by which one turns back from the awakening mind. What are the five? They are: delight in going forth into the teachings of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); failure to cultivate the mind of great loving-kindness; delight in seeking faults in those who teach the Dharma; constant delight in cyclic existence; and, with regard to the twelve branches of scripture (sūtra-piṭaka) — receiving, reading, reciting, copying, expounding, and explaining them — having no inclination to do so. These are the five qualities leading to turning back from the awakening mind.

Furthermore, there are these two qualities of Dharma by which one turns back from the awakening mind. What are the two? They are: attachment to and fixation upon the five objects of desire, and failure to pay homage, reverence, and honor to the Three Jewels. Through these and many other conditions of this kind, one turns back from the awakening mind.

Now, what is meant by a mind that does not turn back? There are those who, upon hearing that a Tathāgata liberates sentient beings from birth, aging, illness, and death, and that through diligent effort that depends on no one else, one attains unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening — having heard this, they think: 'If there is a path to awakening to be obtained, then I too, by exerting myself with utmost diligence, shall without fail obtain it.' Moved by that cause and that condition, they arouse the mind set upon awakening, and then — whether the merit they have accumulated is great or small — they dedicate it all to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And they make this solemn aspiration: 'May I always pay reverent service to the buddhas and to the attendants of the buddhas. May I always hear the profound Dharma and be endowed with the five sense faculties. And even if I am tormented by suffering, may I never lose this mind.' They further aspire: 'May the buddhas and the attendants of the buddhas always hold me in their compassionate regard. May I be endowed with the five roots of virtue. And if sentient beings cut my body, or sever my limbs, hands, feet, head, eyes, or any part of my body, may I arouse toward them a mind of great loving-kindness, and may I rejoice, thinking: Those people have caused the causes of my awakening to arise and increase. If they had not done so, through what condition would I come to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?' And they make this great aspiration. They also aspire thus: 'May I not be born with indistinct or doubled marks, nor take on a woman's body. May I not be subject to another's dominion. May I not meet with an evil lord. May I not be dominated by an evil king. May I not be born in a bad land. Even if I obtain a fine and beautiful body, may I be of noble lineage and possess abundant wealth and precious things, yet not be made arrogant by possessing them. May I always hear the twelve branches of scripture, uphold them, read them, recite them, copy them, expound and explain them. And when I expound and explain them to sentient beings, may those who hear me have faith and receive my teaching, may they grow perfectly clear-minded and free of doubt, and may they never give rise to ill-will toward me. Even if I have heard little, may I come to know much. Even if I have heard much, may I not be without understanding of the meaning. May my mind incline to teach and not turn toward a mind that withholds teaching. May the actions of my body, speech, and mind not be mixed with wrongdoing and non-virtue. And may I bring happiness to all sentient beings.'

May the moral discipline of my body and the wisdom of my mind become as unshakeable as a mountain. May I never be timid about my body, my life, or my possessions for the sake of upholding the supreme holy Dharma. May I never perform meritorious deeds with goods that have not been properly examined. May I sustain myself by right livelihood and be free of any mind of deceit and guile. May I always be mindful of kindness shown to me, and may I repay even the smallest kindness generously. May I become skilled in the practical arts of the world. May I become skilled in the languages of sentient beings in every direction. When reading, reciting, or writing the twelve branches of the sūtra collections, may I never be lazy or negligent. If there are sentient beings who take no delight in hearing, may I bring it about that all of them delight in hearing. May my speech be gentle and tender, and may I never utter words of non-virtue. May I reconcile those who are in conflict. For those who are in grief and fear, may I dispel their grief and fear. In times of famine, may I become satisfaction and sufficiency. In times of illness and epidemic, may I become a king of physicians, freely supplying whatever medicines, wealth, and precious things are needed as conditions for curing illness, and may all diseases be removed. In an age of weapons, may I possess great power and strength, and may harm and violence be decisively cut off. May I cut away the many and varied fears of sentient beings — such as the fear of death, of imprisonment, of beatings, of water, of fire, of kings, of thieves, of poverty, of the breakdown of law, of ill-repute, of the lower rebirths, and all such fears as these — may I eliminate them entirely. May I show profound reverence to my parents, my preceptor, and my teachers. Toward those who harbor grudges and hatred toward me, may I give rise to a mind of great loving-kindness. May I always cultivate the six close placements of mindfulness, the various categories of meditative absorption on emptiness, the twelve links of dependent origination, insight into arising and cessation and the like, the counting of the in-breath and out-breath, the conduct of the gods, the conduct of Brahmā, the conduct of the noble ones, the vajra-like meditative absorption, and the heroic march meditative absorption and so forth.

In places where the Three Jewels are absent, may I myself attain a fully pacified mind, and even if my body and mind experience great afflictions, may I never lose the unsurpassed awakening mind, bodhicitta. May I never be content with the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. In places where the Three Jewels are absent, may I always go forth into the teachings of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), so as to demolish wrong views, and without becoming accustomed to their teachings, may I attain mastery over the Dharma and mastery over my mind. May I clearly see the faults of conditioned phenomena. Just as a living creature with its life at stake fears the abandonment of the body, may I feel that same fear regarding the fruits of the two paths — my own and the vehicle. Just as sentient beings are drawn by longing toward the pleasures of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, may I, for the sake of sentient beings, feel that same longing for the three lower rebirths. Even for the sake of a single sentient being, should I experience the sufferings of the hells for measureless eons, may I never give rise to a mind of regret. When I see others gaining possessions, may I not give rise to envy, but just as I rejoice when I myself attain happiness, may I always rejoice likewise. Should I encounter the Three Jewels, may I offer to them in full with food and drink, beverages, bedding, lodgings, medicines for illness, lamps, flowers, incense, music, parasols, banners, the seven kinds of precious things, and all manner of offerings.

Should you take up the moral discipline of a buddha, guard it with utmost firmness and never give rise to the characteristic of its decay. Should you hear of the arduous practices of bodhisattvas, rejoice in them wholeheartedly and never give rise to a mind of regret. Remembering the things of your former lives, never act through karma of attachment, aversion, or delusion. Do not accumulate causes and conditions in hope of a ripening result. Do not become attached to and fixated on present happiness. Such is the vow to be taken.

Son of good family, one who takes such a vow as this is also called a bodhisattva who never turns back from or loses the awakening mind. Such a one is also called one who has the six perfections — one who directly perceives the Tathāgata and the intrinsic nature of a buddha, who is skilled in taming sentient beings, who liberates from saṃsāra, and who holds and guards the supreme Dharma that is unsurpassed.

Son of good family, for this reason, the irreversible mind should not be called the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Son of good family, because you possess an irreversible mind, it would not be right to say that all sentient beings are without the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Take this as an example: two men hear that in another region there is a mountain of the seven precious things, and that there are fine springs upon it with delicious water. Whoever went there would be freed from poverty and want, and whoever drank of that water would live long, for a full thousand hundred years. Yet they also hear that the road is long and dangerous, with many obstacles. And so the two men, both contemplating whether to go, one of them made ready all the provisions for the journey and set out. The other set out with nothing whatsoever, empty-handed.

As they traveled along the road together, they met a man laden with many of the seven precious things. Both men then asked him: "Good sir, is there truly a mountain of the seven precious things in that land?" He replied: "It truly exists — I do not lie. I myself obtained precious things there and drank of the water. However, the road is dangerous and desolate, with bandits and robbers abroad; there are many hardships and thorns, little water and no grass. Of several hundred going out, very few actually arrive." Hearing him say this, one of the two felt regret and said: "The road is long, the obstacles are exceedingly many, and countless have set out but only one or two have ever arrived. How could I ever get there? My livelihood is adequate as it is. If I set out and fail to reach it, I will lose body and life. And if I lose body and life, where will that long life and happiness be?" And so he spoke. The other said: "Others have managed to arrive — if they can, so can I. If I reach the far side, I will gather precious things to my heart's content and drink of the fine spring. And if I do not escape, then I will pay for it with my life." And so he spoke.

Then the two men parted: one turned back in regret, and the other set forth and went. The one who set forth arrived at the mountain, took many precious things, drank his fill of the water as he wished, and returned with an abundance of precious things. He gave to his parents in full, and satisfied all his friends and companions with what remained. At that time, the one who had turned back in regret, seeing all these things, felt his mind deeply tormented. He thought: "Even he who went has returned — so why do I sit here?" And so he too set out and went.

In this simile, the mountain of the seven precious things is like the great nirvāṇa. The sweet water is like the intrinsic nature of a buddha. The two men are like two bodhisattvas who first gave rise to the mind of awakening.

The difficult road is like saṃsāra. The man met along the road is like the Blessed One, the buddha. The bandits and robbers are like the four māras. The grief and thorns are like the mental afflictions. The absence of water and grass is like not cultivating the path to awakening. The one who turned back is like a bodhisattva who turns back. The one who set out and went is to be understood as the simile for a bodhisattva who does not turn back.

O son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha within sentient beings abides permanently and does not change. Just as it would be wrong to say, on account of the difficulty of the road, that the road itself is impermanent because one turned back in regret, so too is the intrinsic nature of a buddha. O son of good family, there is no turning back on the path to awakening.

O son of good family, consider how the one who had turned back, upon seeing his companion having obtained many precious things, having gained dominion through power and strength, having cared for his parents, having given sufficiently to his friends and companions, and having enjoyed great happiness — felt his mind deeply tormented and, setting out to enter the road, not sparing his body or his life, enduring great hardship and many obstacles, arrived at the mountain of the seven precious things. The bodhisattva who does not turn back is just like that.

O son of good family, since all sentient beings will without fail attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, for that very reason I have declared across all the sūtras — from the five acts of immediate consequence (anantarya), through the four root defeats, and on up to those of perverted craving — that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Siṃhaghoṣa (Lion's Roar) then asked: Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva turns back and how is it that a bodhisattva does not turn back?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, a bodhisattva who accomplishes the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata — such a one is called one who does not turn back; such a one is also called a great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; such a one is called immovable and unchanging; such a one is called one who has affectionate love for all sentient beings; such a one is called one who is superior to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and such a one is called a non-returner.

O son of good family, a great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who is unwavering in the restraint of moral discipline, whose mind is steadfast in generosity, and who abides in words of truth like Mount Meru — through the karmic cause and that condition, such a one obtains the mark of flat, even soles on the feet, like a box with a flat lid. O son of good family, a great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who from childhood — even in lives as animals — honors and makes offerings to parents, preceptors, teachers, and spiritual mentors with material goods obtained in accordance with the Dharma — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of wheels on the soles of the feet, complete with a thousand spokes.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who does not take life, who does not take what is not given, and who always generates joy toward parents, preceptors, and spiritual mentors — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains three marks: slender and long fingers on the hands, long heels on the feet, and an upright body with four equal sides. These three marks share one karmic cause.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who gathers sentient beings by means of the four ways of gathering — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of webbed fingers, resembling the king of geese.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who personally takes up a cloth and washes the bodies of parents, preceptors, and spiritual mentors when they are afflicted by illness, and who massages the limbs of their body — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of soft hands and feet.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who upholds moral discipline, listens to the Dharma, and —

— who gives generously without growing weary: through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of joints and limbs that are proportionate and even, and bodily hairs that turn upward.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who listens to the Dharma with single-pointed mind and teaches the sacred Dharma — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of calves like those of the king of deer.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who never arouses a mind of harm toward any sentient being; who is content in food and drink and always delights in giving generously; and who tends to the sick and gives medicine — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of a body perfectly proportioned like the nyagrodha tree, and arms that, when standing, extend past the knees, along with the mark of a fleshy crown-protrusion and a crown-protrusion that is invisible when looked upon.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who, upon seeing those who are frightened, becomes their protector and refuge, and upon seeing those who are naked, gives them clothing — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of the male organ retracted within a sheath.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who keeps close company with those who are wise and relinquishes those who are deluded; who is skilled in asking questions and giving answers; who corrects the path of wayfarers and sweeps the road — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of skin that is fine and supple, and bodily hairs that coil to the right.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who always gives robes, food, bedding, medicines for illness, incense, flowers, and lamps — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of a body whose complexion is like gold, ever radiant and lustrous.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who gives generously, who is able to bestow an abundance of wealth without reservation, and who makes no distinction between those who are fields of merit and those who are not — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of the seven fully rounded prominences.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who, when giving generously, does not give rise to a mind of doubt — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of a beautiful, melodious voice.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who seeks in accordance with the Dharma and gives generously: through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of full and even collarbones, an upper body like that of a lion, and forearms and shoulders that are proportionate and long.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who thoroughly abandons divisive speech, harsh words, and a mind of aversion — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of forty teeth that are white and even, with fine rows of teeth.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who arouses loving-kindness and great compassion toward all sentient beings — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of possessing two canine teeth.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who makes the aspiration, "I shall give freely and according to the wishes of all those who come to beg, giving whatever they desire," and who always gives in this way to those who come seeking — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of lion-like cheeks.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who gives to sentient beings whatever food they desire, each according to their wish — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of possessing, among all tastes, the supreme taste.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who personally practices the ten virtuous actions and also teaches them to others — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of a tongue that is long and broad.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who does not speak of the faults of others and does not disparage the sacred Dharma — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of a voice like that of Brahmā.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who, upon seeing enemies and those who hate, arouses a mind of joy — through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of eyes that are deep blue, like collyrium.

A great being, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who does not conceal the good qualities of others but proclaims them everywhere —

through that karmic condition, such a one obtains the mark of a white curl of hair between the brows.

O son of good family, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thus accomplishes the karmic causes and conditions of the thirty-two marks, the awakening mind becomes irreversible.

O son of good family, all sentient beings are inconceivable, the domain of activity of the buddhas is inconceivable, the karmic result is inconceivable, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha is inconceivable. Why is this? Because these four things are permanent, and because they are permanent, they are inconceivable. Because all sentient beings are obscured by mental afflictions, they are called "permanent." When those permanent afflictions are cut, one is called "impermanent."

If all sentient beings are permanent, why must the noble eightfold path be cultivated? It is because many sufferings are cut. If many sufferings have been cut, that is called "impermanent." Whatever experiences happiness, that is called "permanent." Therefore I have taught that because all sentient beings are entirely obscured by mental afflictions, they do not see the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and not seeing it in that way, they do not pass beyond suffering.

Siṃhasvara then asked: O Blessed One, as the Blessed One has taught, all phenomena have two kinds of cause — a cause of truth and a cause of conditions. Through these two kinds of cause, there is neither bondage nor liberation. The five aggregates arise and cease moment by moment. If they arise and cease in this way, who would be bound or liberated? O Blessed One, the five aggregates of this present life give rise to the five aggregates of the next life. These aggregates do not pass over to become other aggregates, since these aggregates cease of themselves. Though they do not pass over, the arising of subsequent aggregates is possible — just as a sprout arises from a seed as its cause. The seed does not enter into the sprout, and yet, though it does not enter, the sprout arises. If sentient beings are likewise, how can there be bondage and liberation?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, attend carefully and reflect well upon this, and I shall explain and teach it to you.

O son of good family, consider a person who is experiencing the suffering of dying. Surrounded by relatives and friends, who are lamenting, that person, terrified, does not know what refuge or support there is. Though the five consciousnesses are present, nothing is perceived; every limb and joint trembles and stirs, yet there is no power to stir. As the whole body grows cold and the warmth is nearly exhausted, the characteristics of the karmic maturation of virtue and non-virtue practiced in the past come into view.

O son of good family, consider how, when the sun draws near to setting, all the shadows of mountains and mounds appear to the east — they have no nature of going westward. Just so, the karmic result of sentient beings is the same: when these aggregates cease, a continuity of another set of aggregates arises, just as when a lamp is lit, darkness ceases, and when a lamp is extinguished, darkness arises.

O son of good family, consider how, when a seal carved from wood is pressed onto clay, a design appears from the meeting of seal and clay. The design of the wooden seal has not transferred onto the clay, nor has the design arisen from within the clay itself, nor has it come from elsewhere — yet by the condition of the seal, the design has arisen. Just so, when the present aggregates have ceased, an intermediate-state being has not yet been born; the present aggregates do not themselves become the intermediate-state being, nor does the intermediate-state being arise on its own, nor does it come from elsewhere — rather, the intermediate-state being is born from the cause of the present aggregates.

Just as when a seal is pressed into wax, the instant the seal is removed the impression appears — the name is the same, yet the times are distinct — so too, I have declared that the intermediate-state being formed from the five aggregates is not seen with a fleshly eye but with a miraculous eye.

The intermediate-state being formed from the five aggregates is sustained by three kinds of nourishment: nourishment of intention, nourishment of contact, and nourishment of consciousness. This intermediate-state being formed from the five aggregates is of two kinds: the fruit of virtuous karma and the fruit of non-virtuous karma. One who bears the cause of virtuous karma inclines toward the virtuous. One who bears the cause of non-virtuous karma inclines toward the non-virtuous.

When father and mother meet and perform the act of union, one proceeds to a place of birth in accordance with whatever karma one has created. Toward the mother, desire arises; toward the father, aversion arises. When the father's semen appears, one grasps it as one's own, and seeing it, one becomes pleased and gives rise to great joy. It is in this way, through three causes and conditions of affliction, that the moment the intermediate-state aggregates dissolve, the subsequent aggregates arise — just as when a seal is pressed into wax, the instant the seal is lifted an impression appears.

At the time of birth, the sense faculties may be complete or incomplete. One whose sense faculties are complete sees form and desire arises. When that desire arises, it is called craving. The ignorance that produces desire through delusion is called ignorance. Through the two causes and conditions of attachment and ignorance, one sees all objects in an inverted manner: what is impermanent is seen as permanent, what is without self is seen as having a self, what is painful is seen as pleasurable, and what is utterly impure is seen as utterly pure. Because of these four inversions, one performs virtuous and non-virtuous actions. Affliction thus becomes karma, and karma in turn becomes affliction — and that is what is called bondage. It is by this process that the arising of the five aggregates is so called.

But if that person were to attend upon a buddha, or a close attendant of a buddha, or a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he or she would come to hear the twelve divisions of the scriptural collection. Having heard the Dharma in this way, one reflects upon the domain of virtue. Through reflecting upon the domain of virtue, one attains great wisdom. What is called great wisdom is right wisdom and right vision. Through attaining wisdom and vision, a mind of deep remorse toward saṃsāra arises. When that mind of remorse has arisen, delight and enthusiasm do not arise. Because delight and enthusiasm do not arise, the mind of attachment is destroyed. When the mind of attachment is destroyed, one cultivates the noble eightfold path. Through cultivating the noble eightfold path, saṃsāra comes to an end. When saṃsāra is no more, this is called attaining complete liberation — just as fire, when it meets no wood, is called ceased. Through the cessation of saṃsāra, this is called nirvāṇa. It is by this process that the cessation of the five aggregates is so called.

Siṃha asked: Without thorns, what is there to pick out of the sky? Without there being any bondage in the aggregates, by what is one bound?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the five aggregates are bound by the iron shackles of affliction. Beyond the five aggregates there is no other affliction, and beyond the afflictions there is no other thing called the five aggregates. Son of good family, just as pillars support a house — there are no pillars apart from the house, and no house apart from the pillars — so too the five aggregates of a sentient being are just like that: because afflictions exist, this is called bondage; because afflictions are absent, this is called liberation.

Son of good family, a fist, a palm, and a knot — and so forth, these three — arise and cease through coming together and coming apart. Apart from that, there is no other phenomenon.

The five aggregates of a sentient being are just like that: because afflictions exist, this is called bondage; because afflictions are absent, this is called liberation.

Son of good family, it has been taught that sentient beings are bound by name-and-form (nāmarūpa). If name-and-form were to cease, there would be no such thing as a sentient being. Beyond name-and-form there is no other sentient being, and beyond the sentient being there is no other thing called name-and-form. Name-and-form binds the sentient being, and the sentient being in turn is said to bind name-and-form.

Then Siṃhasvara spoke: Blessed One, just as an eye does not see itself, a finger does not point to itself, a sword does not cut itself, and a feeling does not feel itself — why then does the Blessed One say that name-and-form binds name-and-form?

The answer is this: what we call name-and-form is precisely the sentient being, and the sentient being is precisely name-and-form. If name-and-form binds the sentient being, then it is name-and-form that binds name-and-form.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, when two hands are clapped together, no other phenomenon apart from those two comes and joins in. Name-and-form is just like that. For this very reason I say that name-and-form binds the sentient being, and if name-and-form is abandoned, liberation is attained — and so I say that the sentient being is liberated.

Siṃhasvara asked: Blessed One, if bondage is said to consist in the presence of name-and-form, then since arhats have not abandoned name-and-form, are they still bound?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, liberation is of two kinds: the cutting of the seed, and the cutting of the fruit. The cutting of the seed means the cutting of the afflictions. Arhats have cut the afflictions; with the afflictions utterly purified and exhausted, they cannot be bound any further by affliction at the level of the seed. Yet because the fruit has not been cut, they are said to be bound by the fruit. Arhats do not see the buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha), and because they do not see it they do not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. For this reason it is appropriate to say that they are bound by the fruit, but not appropriate to say that they are bound by name-and-form.

Son of good family, consider a butter lamp: as long as the butter is not exhausted, the light will not go out, but if the butter is exhausted, it will certainly be extinguished. Son of good family, the butter is the analogy for the afflictions, and the butter lamp is the analogy for sentient beings. All sentient beings, sustained by the butter of affliction, do not pass into nirvāṇa. If that butter is exhausted, they pass into nirvāṇa.

Siṃhasvara said: Blessed One, a butter lamp and its butter have distinct defining characteristics — a sentient being and the afflictions are not like that. The sentient being itself is the affliction, and the affliction itself is the sentient being. The sentient being is the five aggregates, and the five aggregates are the sentient being. The five aggregates themselves are the afflictions, and the afflictions themselves are the five aggregates. If that is so, why does the Blessed One take the butter lamp as an analogy?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, analogies are of eight kinds: the analogy that is inclined toward the point, the analogy that is inverted, the analogy that is direct, the analogy that is not quite fitting, the earlier analogy, the later analogy, the analogy that spans earlier and later, and the all-encompassing analogy.

Of these, what is the inclined analogy? As is taught in a sūtra: when a great rain falls, every hollow vessel is filled; every small ditch is filled by the hollow vessels filling; every large channel is filled by the small ditches filling; every small spring is filled by the large channels filling; and every great spring is filled by the small springs filling.

Every great spring fills the small pond; every small pond fills the great pond; every great pond fills the small river; every small river fills the great river; every great river fills the great ocean. In just the same way, the rain of the Dharma of the Tathāgata completely fills the moral discipline of sentient beings. When moral discipline is completely filled, the mind free of regret is completely filled. When the mind free of regret is completely filled, great joy is completely filled. When great joy is completely filled, seclusion is completely filled. When seclusion is completely filled, ease and happiness are completely filled. When ease and happiness are completely filled, meditative absorption is completely filled. When meditative absorption is completely filled, right knowledge and vision are completely filled. When right knowledge and vision are completely filled, disenchantment is completely filled. When disenchantment is completely filled, utter revulsion is completely filled. When utter revulsion is completely filled, liberation is completely filled. When liberation is completely filled, nirvāṇa is completely filled. That is the inclined analogy.

Now, what is the inverted analogy? The source of the great ocean is the great river. The source of the great river is the small river. The source of the small river is the great lake. The source of the great lake is the small lake. The source of the small lake is the great spring. The source of the great spring is the small spring. The source of the small spring is the great channel. The source of the great channel is the small channel. The source of the small channel is the great hollow vessel. The source of the great hollow vessel is the great rain. The source of nirvāṇa is liberation. The source of liberation is utter revulsion. The source of utter revulsion is disenchantment. The source of disenchantment is right knowledge and vision. The source of right knowledge and vision is meditative absorption. The source of meditative absorption is ease and happiness. The source of ease and happiness is complete renunciation. The source of complete renunciation is the mind of joy. The source of the mind of joy is freedom from regret. The source of freedom from regret is the keeping of moral discipline. The source of the keeping of moral discipline is the rain of Dharma. That is the inverted analogy.

Now, what is the direct analogy? As it is taught in a sūtra: the nature of the mind of sentient beings is like a monkey. The nature of a monkey is to release one thing and grasp another. The nature of sentient beings is likewise: because of attachment to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, textures, and mental phenomena, there is not a single moment of remaining still. That is the direct analogy.

Now, what is the analogy that is not quite fitting? It is this: I formerly addressed King Prasenajit with these words: "Great King, trustworthy and close companions come to you from all four directions and say: 'Great King, from the four directions four great mountains are coming, threatening to crush and harm the king's people.' If such a thing were to come, what wisdom would you apply?" The king replied: "Blessed One, if such a thing were to occur, there would be no place of escape.

"With one-pointed mind I shall observe moral discipline and practice generosity alone." Having said this, I gave him the response: "Excellent!"

Great King, when I spoke of the four great mountains, I was referring precisely to birth, aging, sickness, and death among sentient beings. Since birth, aging, sickness, and death are always coming to harm and afflict sentient beings, why should the Great King not practice moral discipline and generosity? The king asked: "Blessed One, if one observes moral discipline and practices generosity, what fruit does one obtain?" I declared to him: "Great King, one will come to experience abundant pleasurable enjoyments among gods and humans." The king asked: "Blessed One, if the nyagrodha tree were to observe moral discipline and practice generosity, would it too experience the pleasurable enjoyments of gods and humans?" I declared to him: "Great King, the nyagrodha tree is not capable of observing moral discipline or practicing generosity. But if it were capable, then the happiness it would experience would likewise be no different."

That declaration is the analogy that is not quite fitting.

Now, how is the earlier analogy fitting? Throughout all the sūtras I have stated, for example, that when a certain person, seized by attachment to a beautiful flower, goes to pluck it, he is swept away by the current. Sentient beings are just like that: seized by attachment to the five objects of desire, they are swept away by the current of birth, aging, sickness, and death. That is the earlier analogy.

And how is the later analogy fitting? From the sūtra of Dharma-words, these verses were spoken:

Do not scorn a small and minor evil
thinking it cannot do harm.
Even drops of water dripping slowly
will fill a great vessel to the brim.

That is the later analogy.

And how is the analogy that fits both earlier and later? Consider, for example, a plantain tree that dies as soon as it has borne fruit, or a fool who has found a means of sustenance: in just the same way, a pregnant she-mule does not long survive. That is the analogy that fits both earlier and later.

And how is the all-pervasive analogy? From a sūtra I have stated: In the Heaven of the Thirty-Three there is a tree called Pāricittra. Its roots descend into the earth for some fifty leagues. Its height is one hundred leagues. Its branches and leaves spread out to cover some fifty leagues in the four directions. When its leaves ripen, they turn yellow, and the gods, upon seeing this, give rise to minds of joy. Before long, the leaves fall, and when they fall, great joy arises once more. Before long, the branches change color, and when the branches change color, joy arises again. Before long, after the change of color, buds appear, and when the buds appear, joy arises. Before long, from the buds, shoots grow, and upon seeing them, there is great joy. Before long, the shoots open into blossoms, and when they have opened, their fragrance spreads for some fifty leagues, and their radiance shines out for some eighty leagues. At that time, for the duration of three summer months, the gods take delight and enjoy themselves in perfect happiness beneath that tree.

Sons of good family, my attendants are just like that. The leaves turning yellow is like my attendants wishing to go forth into renunciation. The leaves falling is like my attendants shaving head and beard. The change of color is like my attendants requesting ordination, performing the fourfold act, and receiving full ordination. The appearing of buds is like my attendants generating the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. The arising of shoots is like the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds seeing the buddha-nature. And the opening of blossoms is like a bodhisattva attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

The fragrance of the blossoms is like the moral discipline and restraint of innumerable sentient beings in the ten directions. The radiant light is like the unobstructed marks of the Tathāgatas spreading throughout the ten directions. The three months of the rainy season are like the three meditative absorptions. The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three enjoying happiness is like the Tathāgatas attaining the permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity of great nirvāṇa. This is the example of all-pervasiveness.

O son of good family, the examples shown here are not exhaustive — they are taken up only in part, or in many, or if necessary all together. In this regard, the face of the Tathāgata being like the full moon is an example of taking a partial illustration.

O son of good family, take for example a person who has never seen milk before and asks another what milk is like. The other says it is like water, like honey, and like a conch shell — water for its characteristic of wetness, honey for its characteristic of sweetness, and the conch shell for its characteristic of color. Even so, although three examples have been given, the actual nature of milk remains unknown.

O son of good family, it is just the same with the examples I have given for sentient beings using the lamp. O son of good family, beyond the far bank of a river there is no river — and so it is with sentient beings. Beyond the relinquishment of the five aggregates, there are no other sentient beings. O son of good family, just as beyond the box, the rim, the axle, the hub, and the spokes there is no other chariot, so too it is with sentient beings.

O son of good family, if you wish to understand in accordance with the analogy of the lamp, listen and reflect carefully, and I shall explain it to you. In that analogy, the wick is the example for the twenty-five existences. The oil is the example for craving. The light is the example for wisdom. The dispelling of darkness is the example for the destruction of ignorance. The warmth is the example for the noble path. When the oil is exhausted, the light and the flame cease; and when a sentient being's existences are exhausted, the buddha-nature will be seen. At that point, name and form exist, yet they do not bind; one dwells within the twenty-five existences, yet the existences do not defile.

Lion's Roar asked: Blessed One, if the five aggregates of sentient beings are empty and utterly non-existent, who receives the transmission and who accumulates the provisions for awakening?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, in every sentient being there exists a mind of mindfulness, a mind of wisdom, a mind of arousal, a mind of undertaking diligent effort, a mind of faith, and a mind of meditative absorption. Minds such as these arise and cease moment by moment, but because each successive one of the same kind succeeds the one before without interruption, this is what is called accumulating the provisions for awakening.

Lion's Roar asked: Blessed One, if such phenomena as these cease moment by moment, and if it is by one continuous stream of similar moments succeeding one another — which are themselves ceasing moment by moment — that there is an uninterrupted continuity, how then can provisions be accumulated?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, just as the lamp ceases moment by moment and yet its light dispels darkness, so too with mindfulness and the other such phenomena — it is just the same. O son of good family, just as the food eaten by sentient beings ceases moment by moment and yet the hungry are satisfied, or just as excellent medicine ceases moment by moment and yet cures illness, or just as the light of the sun and moon ceases moment by moment and yet is able to grow all herbs, trees, and forests — so too it is with these.

O son of good family, you have asked: if cessation occurs moment by moment, how then can birth take place? Birth takes place because the mind-stream is unbroken.

O son of good family, just as those who recite texts cannot pronounce all the syllables of the recitation at once — the first syllable cannot travel to the middle, and the middle syllable cannot travel to the last — yet because names, letters, mind, and perception all cease moment by moment and yet have been practiced over a long time, everything comes to be known. O son of good family, just as a goldsmith who begins training from youth until old age proceeds through moment-by-moment cessation, and though the earlier and later moments do not intermingle, yet through long training he becomes ever more skilled in his craft — and so is called a skilled goldsmith — so too it is exactly the same with reading and recitation.

O son of good family, just as no one commands a seed, "You, produce a sprout!" — yet by the nature of reality a sprout arises of itself. And though no one commands a flower, "You, produce fruit!" — yet by the nature of reality fruit arises of itself — so too it is exactly the same with sentient beings accumulating the provisions for awakening.

O son of good family, just as the method of counting is such that one never passes to two as one, nor two passes to three as two — cessation occurs moment by moment — yet one can reach as far as a thousand and ten thousand. So too it is exactly the same with sentient beings accumulating the provisions for awakening.

O son of good family, just as a flame ceases moment by moment, and yet the earlier flame that ceases never says to the later flame, "I have gone out — you now arise and dispel the darkness." So too it is just the same.

O son of good family, just as a newborn calf suckles at the breast at once, and no one teaches it the understanding of how to suckle — cessation occurs moment by moment — yet from the initial hunger it comes to be satisfied. Therefore one should understand that it is improper to take an equal thing as one's objection. If they were identical, birth as something distinct would be unreasonable. And just so it is the same with sentient beings accumulating the provisions for awakening. From the very beginning there is no leaping progressively upward as such, yet because one cultivates over a long time, all afflictions come to be destroyed.

Lion's Roar then asked: O Blessed One, as the Blessed One has taught — those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (Skt. srotāpattiphala), even if born in a wretched realm, maintain moral discipline: they do not kill, they do not steal, they do not engage in sexual misconduct, they do not speak divisive speech or harsh words, and they do not drink alcohol. Now just as the aggregates of one who has entered the stream cease here and do not proceed to a wretched realm, should the accumulation of the provisions for awakening not also be the same — that is, should it not proceed to a wretched realm either? But if they are indeed alike, then why is such a person not born in a pure realm? And if the aggregates of the wretched realm are not the aggregates of the stream-enterer, then why is it that they do not commit evil deeds?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, a stream-enterer, even though born in a wretched realm, does not lose the name "stream-enterer."
