Because the aggregates are not identical, I gave the simile of the calf. A stream-enterer, though born in a wretched realm, does not commit evil deeds by virtue of the power of awakening.

O son of good family, just as on a fragrant mountain where the king of lions dwells, every bird that flies and every beast that roams the earth will not run onto that mountain — they cannot bear to be near it. And even if the king of lions goes to a snow mountain, every flying bird and every beast that dwells and moves there cannot bear its presence. So too is the stream-enterer: even though he may not be diligent with respect to awakening, by the power of awakening he commits no unwholesome deed whatsoever.

O son of good family, just as when a person drinks ambrosia —

that ambrosia ceases moment by moment, yet by its power the person lives long and becomes free from birth and death.

O son of good family, take the example of the excellent medicine on the king of mountains, Mount Meru, called Laṅkali. When someone takes it, it ceases moment by moment, yet by the power of that medicine one encounters no suffering of illness.

O son of good family, take the example of a wheel-turning king: in the place where he resides, even when the king is absent, no one can bear to draw near. Why is that? It is by the power and blessing of the king. The stream-enterer is likewise: even though he may be born in a bad realm and may not be diligent with respect to awakening, by the power of awakening he commits no unwholesome deed.

O son of good family, these aggregates of the stream-enterer cease here, and though one is born with other aggregates elsewhere, the aggregates of the stream-enterer are not lost. O son of good family, it is just as when people, wishing for trees, fruit, and crops, plant seeds with dung and do many things such as watering and so forth: before the fruit and crops are obtained, the seed rots away — yet through the power of the seed, the tree and its fruit are obtained. The aggregates of the stream-enterer are just the same.

O son of good family, take the example of a very wealthy man who has only one son. That son had a child of his own in a previous life, but that grandchild was living in another region. When the man died, his heir heard the news, returned, and gathered all the wealth and possessions. Those possessions had not been made by this heir himself, yet no one refused to hand them over when he came to collect and gather them. Why is that? It is because they are of one bloodline. The aggregates of the stream-enterer are just the same.

Siṃha asked: How should we understand the verse that the Blessed One taught, which says:

Whatever monk cultivates moral discipline,
meditative absorption, and wisdom,
know him to be one who will not turn back,
going ever closer to nirvāṇa.

Blessed One, how is one to cultivate moral discipline? How is one to cultivate meditative absorption? How is one to cultivate wisdom?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, if someone undertakes moral discipline and keeps it for their own benefit, or out of desire for the pleasures of gods and humans, and not for the sake of liberating all sentient beings or protecting the supreme Dharma — or if one keeps it merely for the sake of gain and fame, or out of fear of the three lower realms, or out of desire for long life, good complexion, strength, happiness, unobstructed confidence, or out of fear of kings, fear of ill repute, or for the sake of worldly affairs — that is not called cultivating moral discipline.

O son of good family, what then is genuine cultivation of moral discipline? It is when one undertakes moral discipline and keeps it for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, or for protecting the supreme Dharma, or to rescue those not yet rescued, to free those not yet freed, to give refuge to those without refuge, to bring those who have not passed beyond sorrow to complete nirvāṇa — and when keeping it in this way, one does not regard it as moral discipline, does not regard it as the defining characteristic of moral discipline, does not regard it as something to be grasped, does not regard it as bringing about the ripening of a result, and does not entertain thoughts of fear or of failure. O son of good family, keeping it in just that manner is called cultivating moral discipline.

As for how one is to cultivate meditative absorption: when cultivating meditative absorption, if one does so for one's own liberation or for the sake of gain and fame, and not for the sake of sentient beings or for protecting the Dharma — if one looks upon attachment, the faults of impure food and the like, upon men and women and so forth, upon the impurities that flow from the nine bodily openings, upon conflict and strife —

striking and beating one another, harming and killing one another — and cultivates meditative absorption on account of such things, that is not to be called the thorough cultivation of meditative absorption.

O son of good family, what then is it to cultivate meditative absorption rightly? If one cultivates meditative absorption thoroughly for the sake of sentient beings — whether in order to attain a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, or in order to cause sentient beings to attain the Dharma of non-regression, or in order to cause sentient beings to attain the noble Dharma, or in order to cause sentient beings to attain the Great Vehicle, or in order to guard and uphold the unsurpassable Dharma, or in order to ensure that sentient beings do not turn back from the awakening mind, or in order to cause sentient beings to attain the heroic stride samādhi, or in order to cause sentient beings to attain the vajra-like samādhi, or in order to cause sentient beings to attain dhāraṇī, or in order to cause sentient beings to attain the four analytical knowledges, or in order to cause sentient beings to behold the nature of buddha — and while practicing in that way one does not regard the meditative absorption as an object, does not regard the defining characteristics of meditative absorption as an object, does not regard the act of cultivating as an object, and does not regard the karmic maturation of its result as an object — O son of good family, one who cultivates in that manner is said to be thoroughly cultivating meditative absorption.

Now, as for how one is to cultivate wisdom: if one cultivates in the following manner — thinking, "If I were to cultivate wisdom, I would attain liberation and escape from the three lower realms; but then who would be capable of acting for the benefit of all sentient beings? Who would be able to liberate beings from saṃsāra? The arising of buddhas in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower. Therefore, right now I shall cut off all afflictions and shall diligently cultivate wisdom in order to attain the fruit of liberation; I shall swiftly sever the afflictions and swiftly attain liberation" — cultivating in that manner is not to be called cultivating wisdom.

Then what is true cultivation? The one endowed with wisdom, having closely examined sentient beings who are tormented by the suffering of birth, aging, and death, obscured by ignorance, not knowing how to cultivate the unsurpassable and perfectly correct path — makes this aspiration: may I, with this very body, become the surety (Skt. pratibhū) for those sentient beings in their experience of great suffering. And may all the deeds performed by sentient beings through minds steeped in poverty, in being the lowest of all, in the collapse of moral discipline — all the deeds done through attachment, aversion, and delusion — be gathered upon my own body. And may all sentient beings not take birth in the stream of desire, and may they not be bound by name and form, and may they not be ensnared. And may all sentient beings be swiftly liberated from saṃsāra, so that I alone remaining holds no sorrow for me. And may all sentient beings attain unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening — making such aspirations and cultivating in that way, one does not regard wisdom as an object, does not regard the defining characteristics of wisdom as an object, does not regard the act of cultivating as an object, and does not regard the karmic maturation of its result as an object. Cultivating in that manner is called thoroughly cultivating wisdom.

O son of good family, one who cultivates moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom in this way is called a bodhisattva. One who is unable to cultivate moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom in this way is called a śrāvaka.

The thirty-ninth section.

Furthermore, O son of good family, how is one to cultivate moral discipline?

One who is able to sever the sixteen corrupt modes of conduct of all sentient beings is said to be cultivating moral discipline. What are these sixteen? They are as follows: raising lambs to maturity and selling them to others for the sake of gain; buying them and slaughtering them for the sake of gain; raising piglets to maturity and selling them to others for the sake of gain; buying them and slaughtering them for the sake of gain; raising calves to maturity and selling them for the sake of gain; buying them and slaughtering them for the sake of gain; raising birds to maturity and selling them for the sake of gain; buying them and slaughtering them for the sake of gain; fishing; hunting; poaching; butchering; fowling; slander; serving as a keeper of prison stocks; and casting spells upon nāgas. Definitively cutting off these sixteen kinds of harmful actions of sentient beings is called cultivating moral discipline.

And how is one to cultivate meditative absorption? It is by cutting off all worldly meditative absorptions. The following are examples of such worldly absorptions: the bodiless meditative absorption, in which one arises in the mistaken notion that sentient beings who are in nirvāṇa have passed beyond existence; the meditative absorption of mind with infinite becoming; the meditative absorption of the aggregate of the world's purity; the meditative absorption of the world's end; the meditative absorption of the world's annihilation; the meditative absorption of the world's inherent nature; the meditative absorption of the world's person; and the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Absorptions such as these give rise to the mistaken notion that sentient beings are in nirvāṇa, that they have passed beyond sorrow. Definitively cutting off those meditative absorptions that give rise to such mistaken notions is called thoroughly cultivating meditative absorption.

And how is one to cultivate wisdom? It is by demolishing all the wrong views of the world. All sentient beings have wrong views. They are as follows. Some say: form is the self, and it also belongs to the self; the self exists within form, and form exists within the self — and in the same way they speak up through consciousness. Some say: the self is permanent; even when form ceases, the self still exists. Some say: form itself is the self, so when form ceases the self too ceases. And some say: there is an agent, which is the self, and feeling is form. And some say: the agent is form, and feeling is the self. And some say: there is neither agent nor feeling — things arise by themselves and cease by themselves, not through cause and condition. And some say: there is neither agent nor feeling — all is done by one called the Lord of All. And some say: there is neither agent nor feeling — all is done by time. And some say: there is neither agent nor feeling — sentient beings are simply a name for the five great elements such as earth and so forth. O son of good family, one who demolishes all these wrong views of all sentient beings is said to be cultivating wisdom.

O son of good family, through cultivating moral discipline the body becomes pacified. Through cultivating meditative absorption the mind becomes pacified. Through cultivating wisdom the mind of doubt is overcome. And when the mind of doubt is overcome, one comes to thoroughly cultivate awakening. Through cultivating awakening one comes to see the nature of a buddha. Through seeing the nature of a buddha one attains unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. Through attaining unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening one attains the supreme great nirvāṇa. Through attaining the supreme great nirvāṇa one severs all the afflictions of saṃsāra of all sentient beings, all existence, all realms, and all pleasures. Having severed from saṃsāra all the way through to severing pleasure, one attains permanence, bliss, self, and

purity — one attains the Dharma of complete purity.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: Blessed One, just as the Blessed One has taught that what neither arises nor ceases is called great nirvāṇa — birth, too, in the same way, neither arises nor ceases, so why is birth not also called nirvāṇa?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, it is just as you say. It is exactly so. Just as you have stated, birth neither arises nor ceases. Yet it has no beginning and no end.

Siṃhaghoṣa asked: Blessed One, the phenomena of saṃsāra also have no beginning and no end. If they have no beginning and no end, they would be permanent. And if something is permanent, it would be nirvāṇa. So why then is saṃsāra not designated as nirvāṇa?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, the phenomena of saṃsāra have cause and effect. Because they possess cause and effect, they are not designated as nirvāṇa. Why is that? Because in the essential nature of nirvāṇa there is no cause and no effect.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: Blessed One, even nirvāṇa, according to a verse the Blessed One himself has spoken, has cause and effect — namely:

From a cause one is born as a god in the higher realms.
From a cause one falls into the lower realms.
From a cause one attains nirvāṇa.
Therefore everything has a cause.

And furthermore, the Blessed One previously declared to the monks: I shall teach the path and the fruit of the śramaṇa life. The śramaṇa life means fully and perfectly practicing moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom. The path is the noble eightfold path. And the fruit of the śramaṇa life is nirvāṇa.

Blessed One, is not that nirvāṇa itself a fruit? Why then did you say that in the essential nature of nirvāṇa there is no cause and no effect?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, when I spoke of the cause of nirvāṇa, what I meant is this: the intrinsic nature of a buddha. The intrinsic nature of a buddha does not produce nirvāṇa by generating it from itself. Therefore I have said that nirvāṇa has no cause. It is called a great fruit because it vanquishes the afflictions. And it is said to have no fruit because it is not born from the path. Therefore nirvāṇa has neither cause nor fruit.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: Blessed One, does the intrinsic nature of a buddha that belongs to all sentient beings exist as something common to all, or does it exist in each individually? If it is common to all, then when one being attains unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening, all sentient beings should equally attain it as well. It is as if twenty persons shared a single enemy: if one of those persons eliminates that enemy, the remaining nineteen would equally be freed of that enemy. In the same way, if the intrinsic nature of a buddha is shared in common, when one attains it, all others should attain it too. But if it exists individually in each, then it would be impermanent. Why? Because it could then be counted and enumerated. The Blessed One has indeed taught that the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings is neither one nor many. If it existed individually in each, it would not be right to say that the Tathāgatas are equal to one another; nor would it be right to say that the intrinsic nature of a buddha is like space.

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings is neither one nor many, and yet the buddhas are equal to one another and like space — and it exists equally in all sentient beings.

If someone cultivates the noble eightfold path, they will come to see it clearly. Son of good family, there is a grass called "patience grass" in the Himalayas: if a cow eats it, it becomes the essence of butter. The intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings is like that.

Siṃhaghoṣa asked: Just as the Blessed One has spoken of "patience grass" — is it consumed by one cow or by many? If it is consumed by one, then when one seeking it has consumed it, it is exhausted. If it is many, then, as you have said, the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings is like that. Yet as the Blessed One has declared — that whoever cultivates the noble eightfold path will see the intrinsic nature of a buddha — that does not seem right. Why? If the path, too, is consumed by one, like patience grass it would seem to be used up; and if it were used up, then one person's cultivation of it would leave others without any share. If, on the other hand, the path were many things, how could one speak of perfectly cultivating it completely as the wisdom of omniscience?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, consider how all sentient beings travel without obstruction along a level and pleasant road. Along that road there is a shady tree, exceedingly cool in its shade. Travelers rest beneath it and take their ease; yet that shade of the tree remains always present — it does not change and perish, and no one can carry it away. The road in that simile stands for the noble path. The shade stands for the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Son of good family, consider a great city with a single gate: many beings pass in and out through it, and no one can interrupt them or demolish it and carry it away. Son of good family, consider a great bridge along which many people pass: no one can interrupt or block them, and no one can destroy it and carry it away. Son of good family, consider a skilled physician who heals all illnesses everywhere: no one can stop him and say, "Heal this one; abandon that one." In just the same way the noble path and the intrinsic nature of a buddha are like that.

Siṃhaghoṣa said: Blessed One, the similes you have given do not quite fit the point. Why? If someone who has not walked the road before is timid going forward, why should it be said that there is no obstruction? In the same way, others too experience timidity. If the noble path and the intrinsic nature of a buddha are like those things, then when one person cultivates the path, it would seem fitting that others would experience timidity.

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, when you say that what I have said lacks meaning, know that the simile of the road I used was only a partial simile — not a complete one. Son of good family, a worldly road can be interrupted and obstructed, and because near and far are distinct for it, it is not fully analogous. The undefiled path is not like that: it does not interrupt sentient beings, it is level and without duality, and there is no occasion for timidity in it — near and far are distinct for worldly roads but not for this. This genuine path is the cause of the illumination of the intrinsic nature of a buddha in all sentient beings, not the cause of its arising. This is like how the light of a lamp illuminates objects without creating them.

Son of good family, all sentient beings equally have formations conditioned by ignorance. Because ignorance conditions the formations of one person, one cannot block those formations and then say that others have none; all sentient beings have formations conditioned by ignorance. Therefore it is taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are present equally in all.

In the same way, when sentient beings cultivate the undefiled path, this equally severs all afflictions of sentient beings, all four modes of birth, all the elements, and all the routes of continued existence. It is for this reason that it is called "equal." Whoever fully absorbs this path knows and sees both this side and the further shore, and is without obscuration. Therefore it is called the wisdom of omniscience.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: Blessed One, sentient beings do not all have bodies of the same kind. Some have the bodies of gods, some have human bodies, some have the bodies of animals, hungry ghosts, or hell-beings. Since these bodies are distinct and not one, why do you teach that the intrinsic nature of a buddha is one and the same?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, consider an example. If someone were to put poison into milk, the poison would be present all the way through to the essence of butter. One does not call the milk butter, nor does one call the butter milk, yet from milk through to the essence of butter, each stage has its own name and characteristic mark, but the nature of the poison is never lost, and it pervades all five stages of flavor. Even without poison being added to the essence of butter, if one were to drink that essence of butter, it would still cause death. In the same way, the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings circulates through the five paths as they transmigrate, and although they assume bodies that are different from one another, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is one, permanent, and unchanging.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: Blessed One, among the sixteen great territories there are six great cities: Śrāvastī, the city of Kuśinagarī, the city of Campā, Vaiśālī, the city of Śrāvaka, and Rājagṛha. These six cities are the greatest in the world. Why then, passing those by, did the Tathāgata go to this city of Kuśinagara, which is at the very border of the territory, utterly poor and ugly, a place of destitution and misery, to pass into nirvāṇa?

The Blessed One declared: It is improper to say of this city of Kuśinagara that it is at the border of the territory, poor, and destitute. Rather, it is fitting to say that it is supremely adorned with the highest and most excellent qualities. Why so? Because it is the place where buddhas and bodhisattvas dwell. Son of good family, just as if a king were to visit even a humble house, that house becomes most beautifully adorned, is considered meritorious, and one must offer praise saying, "How wonderful that the king has come here!" Son of good family, just as a person afflicted by a severe illness might send for an inferior medicine, and if that medicine heals the disease, one would rejoice in it and call it supreme and excellent, praising it by saying, "This medicine has cured my illness!" Son of good family, just as someone who has boarded a vessel and entered the ocean, and whose boat breaks apart, leaving them without refuge or support, might grasp hold of a human corpse and reach the far shore, and would then rejoice greatly in it and offer praise, saying, "Through meeting you I have been brought to safety!" — in just the same way this city of Kuśinagara is the place where buddhas and bodhisattvas walk and dwell. Why then should one say it is a miserable border town, ugly, destitute, and wretched?

Son of good family, I call to mind the past. In ages gone by — as many as the sands of the Ganges rivers — in a kalpa called Excellent Wisdom, there was at that time a wheel-turning king of the lineage of Kauśika, possessed of the seven precious treasures and complete with a thousand sons. That king was the first to build this city. All around it, a moat of water twelve leagues in breadth surrounded it as a girdle, and it was beautifully adorned with the seven precious treasures.

At that time in that land there were very many rivers, and all their waters were exceedingly clear, gentle, and sweet. There were, for example, the river called Jīlanaśana, the river called Ilapatī, the river called Hilenaśana, the river called Iśomatī, the river called Bāviśana, and so on — some five hundred rivers in all. Along both the near and the far banks of those rivers the trees were exceedingly numerous, and they were filled with abundant blossoms and fruits. At that time the human lifespan was immeasurable. After a hundred years had passed, the wheel-turning king spoke and said these words: "Even as the Blessed One has taught — all phenomena are impermanent. Whoever practises the teaching of the ten virtues will cut through the great suffering of impermanence." Then, when all the people heard him speak those words, everyone took up the practice of the ten virtues. At that time I heard the name of the Buddha, and grasping the ten virtues as a dhāraṇī (a holding formula), I held them firmly in mind and cultivated them in meditation, and in that very moment the awakening mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening was born in me for the first time. Having aroused that mind, through those very teachings I showed to countless, immeasurable sentient beings that all phenomena are impermanent — arising and passing away, shifting and changing. Therefore, even now, in this very place, I continually teach: "All phenomena are impermanent — shifting and passing away; only the body of a buddha has the quality of permanence." From that time onward I have been proclaiming this, and bearing in mind the causes and conditions of my former conduct, it is for the sake of repaying the kindness of this very land that I am passing into nirvāṇa here today. It is for this reason that I have declared in all the sūtras that those included in my retinue are repaying a kindness.

Furthermore, son of good family, in the distant past, when the lifespan of sentient beings extended for incalculable kalpas, the city bore the name Kośavarī, and the moat encircling it on all sides was fifty leagues in breadth. At that time in Jambudvīpa this city was situated on its outskirts, so close to the edge that one could leap from rooftop to rooftop and pass from one part to another in a single bound. At that time there was a wheel-turning king called Magnificent Radiance, possessed of the seven precious treasures, complete with a thousand sons, and sovereign over the four continents. His regent son, having devoted his mind to the sublime Dharma, came to full realization as a pratyekabuddha. Then the wheel-turning king, seeing that his royal son and regent had achieved realization as a pratyekabuddha — his deportment supremely beautiful and his miraculous powers extraordinary — seeing such things, he cast aside the affairs of kingship as though spitting out saliva, went forth into homelessness, and here at the root of the śāla tree he cultivated the mind of loving-kindness for eighty thousand years. He likewise cultivated the minds of compassion, joy, and equanimity, each for eighty thousand years. Son of good family, do you think that the king called Magnificent Radiance at that time and in that age was someone other than myself? That was I. Therefore even now I rejoice always in resorting to those four qualities of Dharma. Those four qualities of Dharma are precisely what is called meditative absorption.

Son of good family, for this very reason, the body of a Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure. Son of good family, by that cause and through that condition I too, at the city of Kuśinagara, enter into meditative absorption at the root of the śāla tree. Son of good family, among those countless kalpas that I call to mind, at that time and in that age, this city was called Kapilavastu, and the king there was named Pure Food. That king's queen was called Celestial Beauty. The king's son was called Accomplished Goal. At that time, without having been taught by any teacher, through his own reflection that prince attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

There were two chief attendants: one was Śāriputra, and one was Mahāmaudgalyāyana. The personal attendant was named Ānanda. At that time, the Blessed One taught this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa at the root of the śāla tree, and I was among the assembly gathered there. At that time I heard it proclaimed that all sentient beings possess the nature of a buddha. Having heard such matters, I became irreversible from awakening and made this aspiration: "In the future, at the time when I myself attain complete and perfect awakening, may my parents, the name of my land, my chief attendants, my personal attendant, and the teacher who expounds the Dharma all be just as those of this present Blessed One." Having made that aspiration, by that cause and through that condition I too now teach and expound this sūtra of the great nirvāṇa here.

Son of good family, long ago, after I had gone forth but before I had attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, King Rūpasāra sent a messenger with these words: "Prince Accomplished Goal, if you were to become a wheel-turning king, I would serve you as your minister. But if you have no love for the household life and instead attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, then please come first to this royal city, teach the Dharma, liberate all sentient beings, and be pleased to accept my offerings." At that time I said nothing but granted his request.

Son of good family, after I first attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, I was traveling toward the land called Karka. At that time, on the bank of the river called Terrifying, there was a brahmin of the lineage of Kāśyapa who, together with five hundred disciples, was practicing the path to unsurpassed awakening on the bank of that river. I went there specifically to teach the Dharma for their sake, and Kāśyapa said to me this: "Gautama, I am old and have reached one hundred and twenty years of age. All the people of the central land of Campā, as well as King Rūpasāra and the rest, think that I have attained the fruit of arhathood. If people were to hear the Dharma from you, they would all develop wrong views and say that the venerable Kāśyapa is not an arhat. Gautama, please depart quickly to another place. If these people come to know that Gautama's qualities surpass mine, then we and those like us will no longer be able to obtain our livelihood."

I then said to them: "Kāśyapa, if you show me no respect and bear me no aversion, then stay for one night, and when you rise in the morning you may go before me." Kāśyapa replied: "Gautama, my mind harbors no other intention — I am indeed pleased with you — but in this place of mine there lives a nāga (nāga) that is extremely wrathful and fierce, and I fear it may do you harm." I replied: "Kāśyapa, among those that are poisonous, the most venomous are none other than the three poisons, and since I have cut those away, I have no fear of the world's poisons." Kāśyapa replied again: "Very well then, since you have no fear, please remain and we shall see."

Son of good family, at that time I displayed eighteen miracles for the sake of Kāśyapa, exactly as described in the sūtras. Then Kāśyapa, together with his five hundred attendants, having seen and heard such things, attained the fruit of arhathood. Kāśyapa had two younger brothers: one was called River Kāśyapa and one was called Lake-Reed Kāśyapa. Each of them likewise had about five hundred attendants, and they too all attained the fruit of arhathood.

At that time, upon hearing these things, the six teachers of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who were in Rājagṛha, together with their retinues, conceived great ill-will toward me. So that I might not go back on my promise, I went to Rājagṛha as the king had requested. Before I had even arrived, the king came out to meet me with a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands, and I taught the Dharma there. At that very moment, upon hearing the teaching, some eighty-six thousand gods of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) generated the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening. Of those who had gone as servants and attendants of King Bimbisāra, about one hundred and twenty thousand attained the fruit of stream-entry. Beyond that, immeasurable numbers of sentient beings came to possess minds of patience. Remaining within the city, I also sent forth two hundred and fifty people, together with their retinues, including Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, in the going-forth of renunciation (pravrajyā). Having relinquished their former minds, they came to train on the path. I stayed there at that time and accepted the king's offerings. The six non-Buddhist teachers then gathered their retinues and departed for the land of Śrāvastī.

Now, at that time, in that same region, a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada had come to Rājagṛha in order to obtain a bride. Having arrived at Rājagṛha, he was staying there at the house of a householder named Sañjaya. In the middle of the night, that householder rose and said to his attendants: "Come now, quickly, adorn the house and hang up banners, and prepare excellent food and drink." When Anāthapiṇḍada heard these words, he thought to himself: "Is this a wedding feast, a musical celebration, or perhaps a reception for King Bimbisāra, the ruler of the central lands?" Thinking this, he went over and asked: "Great householder, is this for a wedding feast, or for a musical celebration, or is it because you are receiving King Bimbisāra, the ruler of the central lands? Why all this bustle and urgent work?" The householder replied: "It is none of those things. Householder, tomorrow I am receiving a buddha, the unsurpassable King of Dharma." When Anāthapiṇḍada first heard the word "buddha," his entire body was suffused with a tingling rapture, and he asked again: "What is meant by the word 'buddha'?" The householder said: "Have you not heard? In the land of the yellow-robed ones, one of the Śākya clan, named Siddhartha, of the Gautama lineage, whose father is called Śuddhodana — though not long after his birth the astrologers declared without any doubt that he would certainly become a wheel-turning king, as clear as an āmra fruit resting in the palm of one's hand, he felt no inclination for that, and so went forth from home into homelessness, and through his own insight, without a teacher, attained unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening. He is one in whom attachment, aversion, and delusion are utterly exhausted; who abides always, unchanging, unshifting, unborn, and unceasing; who is free from grief and fear; whose mind is equal toward all sentient beings, as a parent gazes upon an only child; whose many bodies and minds are supreme above all; who, though surpassing all, has no conceit or arrogance; whose mind is non-dual with respect to anointing and censure; who comprehends all things through wisdom; who is unobstructed with regard to phenomena; and who is endowed with the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, the five wisdoms, meditative absorption, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness — it is for these reasons that he is called a 'buddha.' He is graciously coming tomorrow, and that is why I am so busy I have no time even to talk." Anāthapiṇḍada said: "Excellent!"

"Where does this great being, the buddha possessed of unsurpassed qualities, currently abide?" The householder replied: "At present he dwells in a great pavilion in the Kalandakanivāpa grove, here in Rājagṛha." Then Anāthapiṇḍada fixed his mind one-pointedly on the Buddha, recollecting and bearing in mind the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, the five wisdoms, meditative absorption, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, and all his qualities. As he recollected in this way, a great radiant light blazed and shone forth like the sun, and he set out in the direction from which the light had come. When he reached the city gate, by the blessing of the Blessed One the gate opened of itself.

Upon passing through the gate he came upon a shrine to a worldly deity standing along the road. Anāthapiṇḍada paid homage to it with reverence, but in a moment it disappeared entirely. A feeling of fear and dread arose in him and he turned back toward home, but when he reached the city gate again, a deity addressed Anāthapiṇḍada with these words: "O man, if you were to proceed into the presence of the Tathāgata, you would obtain abundant benefit and happiness." Anāthapiṇḍada said: "What do you mean by 'benefit and happiness'?" The deity replied: "Householder, suppose someone were to give to a single person a hundred fine horses adorned with genuine jewels, a hundred fragrant bulls, a hundred jewelled chariots, a hundred men cast in gold, a hundred beautiful young women wearing garlands and adorned with jewels, fine and excellent mansions and great pavilions with carved relief decoration, a hundred golden bowls filled with silver coins and a hundred silver bowls filled with golden coins — and were to give such gifts in like manner to every last person in Jambudvīpa. The merit thereby obtained would not equal even a single step taken by one who sets out to go into the presence of the Tathāgata."

Anāthapiṇḍada said: "Son of good family, who are you who speaks like this?" The deity replied: "Householder, I am the son of the brahmin Gyaltsen. In times past I was also your spiritual friend. Formerly, when I beheld Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana and joy arose in my mind, I followed in their wake and became the son of the guardian of the North, the Lord of Rest, and I constantly guard this city of Rājagṛha. Because joy arose in me toward Śāriputra and the others and I paid homage to them, through that cause and that condition I obtained such an excellent and noble body. What then need be said of beholding the Tathāgata, the great Teacher, and making offerings and paying homage to him?"

Householder Anāthapiṇḍada, upon hearing these words, turned back onto the road and came to where I was, and with the crown of his head he paid homage at my feet. I then taught him the Dharma as it is, and upon hearing it, the householder attained the fruit of stream-entry. Having attained that fruit, he further made this entreaty: "May the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, be pleased to accept a modest offering from me and proceed to Śrāvastī." At that time I asked the householder: "Is there a pavilion in your land of Śrāvastī large enough to accommodate me?" Anāthapiṇḍada replied: "If the Blessed One out of loving kindness will definitely consent to come, then I shall gather whatever I have and arrange a suitable dwelling." Son of good family, at that time I said nothing and consented to come.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, knowing that consent to come had been given, addressed me with these words: "I have never before done anything of this kind. Would the Tathāgata be pleased to send Śāriputra to show me what procedures I should follow?" I granted his request accordingly, and Śāriputra and Anāthapiṇḍada together boarded a single carriage and set out for Śrāvastī. By the power of my blessing they reached the place within a single day.

Then Anāthapiṇḍada said to Śāriputra: "Venerable one, outside this city there is a site that is neither too near nor too far away, with springs, pools, good shade trees, groves, flowering trees, and many fruit trees in great abundance — a thoroughly pure and secluded place. I ask you to examine it. I shall build a monastery there for the Buddha, the Blessed One, and the Saṅgha of monks."

Śāriputra replied: "This Jeta Grove is neither too near nor too far away; it is thoroughly pure and secluded, with springs, flowing streams, flowering trees, and many fruit trees — whatever is needed is there at hand. Examine this site and raise a monastery."

When Anāthapiṇḍada heard these words, the great householder went to where Prince Jeta was and spoke to him thus: "I am building a dwelling for the sake of the unsurpassed king of Dharma. Your grove has been selected. If I wish to purchase it from you, will you sell it to me?"

Jeta replied: "Even if you were to fill every inch of ground with nothing but gold, I would not sell it."

Anāthapiṇḍada said: "Excellent, Jeta! The ground itself shall be mine to dispose of — spread out the gold."

Jeta said: "I am not selling my grove — why then do you say 'spread out the gold'?"

Anāthapiṇḍada said: "If you are not satisfied with this, let us go before a judge to settle the matter."

The two householders went before a judge, and the judge ruled that the ground was under the authority of Anāthapiṇḍada, and that Jeta was to spread out the gold. Then carts and horses were loaded with gold, and it was laid out across the ground. By the end of one day, only a stretch of five hundred paces remained uncovered by gold.

Jeta said: "Householder, if you have any regret, you may withdraw."

Anāthapiṇḍada replied: "I am content to draw from the full treasury of gold. I have no regret in my heart."

Jeta then reflected: "The Tathāgata, the king of Dharma, teaches the perfectly unsurpassed and sublime Dharma — pure and completely free of attachment. And this man has spared no precious wealth for his sake." Thinking thus, he said to Anāthapiṇḍada: "The remaining portion that has not yet been covered — no gold is needed from you. I myself shall build a gatehouse for the Blessed One, so that the Tathāgata may always walk to and fro."

Then the householder Jeta built the gatehouse. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, within the span of seven days, built three hundred large dwelling halls, sixty-three meditation cells, warm winter quarters, cool summer quarters each in their number, bath-houses, foot-washing rooms, and the places for sweeping the grounds of both the larger and smaller latrines — every one of them fully equipped. When everything was done, he took up a golden vessel and, standing at a distance to one side toward Rājagṛha, proclaimed these words: "All the offerings have been arranged."

"O Tathāgata, compassionate one, please accept this dwelling for the sake of all sentient beings." Such were the words he spoke.

Now at that time, knowing the intention of that householder through his own mind, I set out with my retinue from Rājagṛha — in the time it takes a strong man to extend and draw back his arm — and arrived at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī, at the great dwelling hall of Anāthapiṇḍada. Having arrived, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada presented to me all the offerings he had arranged. I accepted them at that very time and remained there in that place.

Then the six teachers of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), their minds seized by jealousy, assembled together and went to the court of King Prasenajit, where they spoke these words:

"Great King, be pleased to understand this: the peace and happiness that prevail throughout your royal domain are due to our presence here as those who have truly gone forth. That is why we now reside here. The Great King governs by righteous Dharma and protects his subjects from harm. Yet this ascetic Gautama has spent only a short time here studying, and he knows nothing at all. Puffed up with pride in his royal lineage, he shows no respect to those who were established in this land before him, or to those of genuine merit. If he is of royal lineage, it would be fitting for one who has governed the affairs of subjects, even upon going forth, to show respect to elders. Great King, please listen well. The ascetic Gautama was not born of a true royal lineage. If the ascetic Gautama had a father and mother, why did he steal away the parents of others? Great King, in our scriptures it is said: 'After a thousand years have passed, there will appear a wicked omen full of deceit.' That very one is none other than this ascetic Gautama. The ascetic Gautama has no father and no mother. If he did have parents, why would he teach that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, selfless, empty, without agent, and without one who grasps? He is a deceiver and a fraud who misleads sentient beings. The deluded will believe him, but those with wisdom will reject him.

Great King, what is called a king is the father and mother of all subjects. He is like a scale, like the earth, like the wind, like fire, like a road, like a river, like a bridge, like a lamp, like the sun, like the moon — he judges in accordance with Dharma, impartially, free from love and hate.

This ascetic Gautama does not provide us with our livelihood; wherever we go, he follows on our heels and will not leave us be. Great King, allow us to compete with Gautama in displays of miraculous power. If he wins, we will submit to his authority; if we win, please place him under ours."

The king replied: "Venerable ones, you each have your own practices to follow and your own places to dwell. I know for certain that the Tathāgata does no harm to any of you."

The six teachers asked: "How does he do no harm? This ascetic Gautama bewilders people with his Dharma of illusions, so that brahmins and all the rest have gone to him for refuge, and all are exhausted. If the king permits a contest of miraculous power between us, the king's fair name will ring out in all eight directions. If you do not permit it, your name will everywhere be known as an ill one."

The king replied: "Venerable ones, it is because you do not know how very great the Tathāgata's miraculous power truly is that you wish to compete with him. If you truly understood, I suspect you would not dare attempt it."

He continued: "Great King, have you already been deceived by the ascetic? Great King, for the moment, be patient — and do not revile us."

"Better that it be accomplished than merely spoken of to no purpose." The king then said, "Very well! Excellent!" and with that, the six teachers departed together with their retinues, greatly pleased.

At that time, King Prasenajit, together with his retinue, came into my presence, and with full reverence bowed his head to the ground in homage, circumambulated me three times to the right, and stationed himself to one side. He then addressed me in these words: "Blessed One, the six teachers of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) came before me and requested permission to contest in miraculous power. Without deliberating carefully, I granted permission. Blessed One, please forgive me."

The Blessed One declared: "Well done, Great King! Well done! Have lodgings constructed in this other place as well. And why is that? If they are to contest with me in miraculous power, an even greater multitude will come streaming here from those assemblies, and this place will be too cramped to hold them." "Noble son, at that time, for the sake of the six teachers of the non-Buddhists, I displayed wondrous and extraordinary miracles and magical displays from the first day of the month through the fifteenth.

At that very time, immeasurable numbers of sentient beings generated the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Immeasurable numbers of sentient beings came to hold faith in the Three Jewels without any doubt. Immeasurable numbers from the retinues of the six teachers shattered their minds of wrong view and went forth into renunciation within the true Dharma. Immeasurable numbers of sentient beings attained a mind of non-return from awakening. Immeasurable numbers of sentient beings attained the various categories of dhāraṇī samādhi. Immeasurable numbers of sentient beings attained everything from the fruit of stream-entry through to the fruit of arhatship.

At that time the six non-Buddhist teachers were utterly mortified and ashamed. They all went together to a city called Cīta. Having arrived there, they taught perverse doctrines to all the people living there and won them over, and proclaimed abroad: 'The ascetic Gautama teaches nothing but emptiness.' Noble son, at that time I ascended to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three for the sake of my mother and, at the foot of the Pāricitra tree, entered into the proper posture and taught the Dharma. Then the six teachers, with minds full of delight, proclaimed: 'Excellent! That deceiver Gautama has now disappeared!' and drew yet further immeasurable, innumerable sentient beings into wrong view.

Thereupon, King Śuddhodana, King Prasenajit, the four-fold retinue (parṣad), and others addressed the son of Maudgala in these words: "Venerable one, wrong views are arising and spreading here in Jambudvīpa, and even those who have been a refuge of deep care for sentient beings are falling into great darkness. Venerable one, you must ascend to the heavens above and address the Blessed One thus: 'Blessed One, we reverently bow before you and say this: just as a newborn calf, before it has grown, will surely perish if it does not drink its mother's milk — we and all sentient beings are in just such a state. Out of compassion for all sentient beings, please, Tathāgata, be so gracious as to return here once more.'"

Then Maudgalyāputra, without uttering a word, ascended to the heavens above — as swiftly as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm — and came into the presence of the Blessed One and addressed him thus: "In Jambudvīpa, the four-fold assemblies long with thirst, as though parched, to hear the Dharma from the Tathāgata. King Śuddhodana,

King Senavardhana and the fourfold assembly and their retinues prostrated at his feet and spoke these words: "All the sentient beings that dwell in this Jambudvīpa have fallen into wrong views and those views are spreading and growing; they wander in deep confusion as though lost in darkness, and are greatly worthy of compassion. It is as with a newborn calf: if it has not long been born and does not drink its mother's milk, it will surely perish. We and all beings are in just that same condition. Therefore, Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings, please be so gracious as to return once more to Jambudvīpa."

The Blessed One declared: "Maudgalyāputra, go back to Jambudvīpa quickly and say this to the kings and to the fourfold assembly: 'In seven days from now I shall return. I go to the land of Citā on account of the six teachers.'" Then, when seven days had passed, he came to the land of Citā, surrounded by Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, by Brahmā, by the gods of Māra's realm, by immeasurable and countless divine sons, and by all the gods of Śuddha's retinue, and proclaimed these words with a great lion's roar: "It is only in my Dharma that there are ascetics and brahmins for whom all phenomena are impermanent, without self, nirvāṇa, and peace — free from every blemish and fault. In the Dharma of others there is no basis whatsoever for the claim that their ascetics and brahmins know permanence, self, or nirvāṇa."

At that time, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings aroused the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Then the six teachers of the non-Buddhists said to one another: "If our Dharma has no ascetics, brahmins, and the like, how will those who dwell in the world come to revere it?" And having said this, the six teachers went together to the city of Vaiśālī.

Noble son, there was a time when I was dwelling in the Āmra Grove of the city of Vaiśālī. A woman named Āmrapālī learned that I was dwelling there and thought to herself that she would go into my presence. At that time I spoke to the monks: "Monks, examine the establishment of mindfulness closely, cultivate wisdom, and do not be slothful in whatever you cultivate." Now, how does one examine the establishment of mindfulness? If a monk examines the inner body and does not find therein a self or what belongs to a self, examines the outer body and the body that is both inner and outer and does not find a self or what belongs to a self, and similarly examines feeling, mind, and phenomena — this is called the establishment of mindfulness. And how does one cultivate wisdom? If a monk sees suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path just as they actually are — this is called the cultivation of wisdom. And what is the mind free of sloth? If a monk recollects the Buddha, recollects the Dharma, recollects the Saṅgha, recollects moral discipline, recollects generosity, and recollects the gods — this is called a monk's mind free of sloth.

At that time, the woman Āmrapālī came into my presence, prostrated with her head at my feet, circumambulated three times to the right, made offerings, and sat to one side. Noble son, I then taught her the Dharma as it truly is. Having heard the Dharma, that woman aroused the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Then, at that same time, about five hundred young Licchavī men came into my presence, prostrated with their heads at my feet, circumambulated three times to the right, made offerings, and stood to one side. I then taught the Dharma to those young Licchavī men just as it truly is.

Noble sons, heedlessness ripens five kinds of fruit. What are the five? One has no power over one's own wealth; one's reputation becomes ill-famed; one takes no pleasure in giving to the poor; one does not wish to see the four kinds of retinue; and one does not attain the body of the gods.

Noble sons, from the cause of heedfulness, both worldly and supramundane Dharmas arise. Therefore, whoever desires unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening must strive in the qualities of heedfulness.

As for heedlessness, there are also thirteen further fruits that ripen from it. What are the thirteen? One is inclined to engage in worldly activities; one is inclined to speak meaningless words; one is inclined to sleep for a long time; one is inclined to talk about worldly things; one is constantly inclined to associate with unwholesome spiritual companions; one is lazy and inclined to idle behavior; one is always despised by others; whatever one hears, one immediately forgets it; one delights in dwelling in remote borderlands; one is unable to tame the sense faculties; one does not know moderation in food; one has no inclination toward truth; and one holds incorrect views. These are the thirteen.

Noble son, though a heedless person may be near a buddha and close to a buddha's presence, they should be called one who is utterly far away.

The Licchavīs then said: "We acknowledge that we have been heedless. And why? If we had not been heedless, the Tathāgata, the king of Dharma, would not have come to our land." At that moment, in the midst of the great assembly, a brahmin's son by the name of Ajita spoke to the Licchavīs and said: "Excellent! Excellent! Just as you have said. The king Rūpasāra obtained great benefit and happiness, and thus the Blessed One, the Buddha, came to that land. Just as the finest lotus born from a great lake, though born within the water, is not stained by the water — so too, young Licchavīs, though the Buddha came to that land, he is not stained by the phenomena of the world. The Blessed Buddhas have neither arising nor entering, yet for the sake of sentient beings they appear in the world and are not obscured by worldly phenomena. People deceive themselves: attached and clinging to the five desirable objects, not knowing to take refuge in the Tathāgata — such people are called heedless. But it is not right to say that the Buddha is heedless because he appears and dwells in the midst of the world. Why? Because the Blessed Buddhas are like the sun and moon: they do not appear in the world for the sake of one or two."

When those Licchavīs heard these words, they aroused the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening and said: "Excellent! Excellent! The young Ajita has spoken the sublime Dharma of the utterly unconquered."

Then those Licchavīs, each one removing an upper garment, offered it to Ajita. Ajita accepted them and then offered them to me, saying: "Blessed One, these garments I have received from the Licchavīs. May the Tathāgata, out of loving compassion for sentient beings, please accept this offering I present." At that time, I accepted them out of loving compassion for the young Ajita.

Then all the Licchavīs together, pressing their palms together, addressed me thus: "Tathāgata, you have come to this land at this time according to the proper way. Will you please accept a little of our offerings?" I said nothing at that time, and by my silence I granted the Licchavīs what they had requested.

Then, upon hearing what had befallen those six teachers, they — the teachers together with their retinues — departed for the town of Śerkya. I too then went to Śerkya and sat down on the bank of a river called Kluṅpa.

Now in Śerkya there lived a householder named Ratnakīrti who was extremely attached to and captivated by the five sensual pleasures, and who did not understand impermanence. When I went to him, by his own attainment of the teaching of reflection upon the skeleton, he came to see his house, his home, his wife, and all his possessions as skeletons. Terror arose in his mind, and as though confronted by a sword, a venomous snake, a thief, or fire, he rushed out of his house and came before me. Along the way, right there on the road, he spoke these words: "Ascetic Gautama, I am now gripped by terror, as though driven by an enemy. I pray that you grant me refuge." Then the Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are happiness itself — they hold no fear." The householder replied: "If the Three Jewels hold no fear, may I too attain that fearlessness." Having spoken thus, he petitioned me for the going forth, and I granted it.

At that time, the householder had fifty friends. Hearing that Ratnakīrti, overcome by weariness with desire, had gone forth, they too joined together and went forth. Upon hearing this, the six teachers went on to the great city of Campā. Then all the people of Campā made offerings and paid homage to the six teachers and their retinues, and they did not even hear the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Many people came to commit deeply non-virtuous deeds. At that time I traveled to the city of Campā for the sake of sentient beings.

In that city there lived a householder whose lineage was on the verge of dying out. Wishing for a son, he was making offerings to the six teachers. Later his wife became pregnant, and when the householder learned of it, he went to the six teachers and with a joyful heart asked them: "Is the child in my pregnant wife's womb a boy or a girl?" They looked and declared with certainty: "Without a doubt, a girl will be born." When the householder heard this, he was tormented by grief and became unhappy. Then a friend of his came to him and asked why he was so afflicted with sorrow. The householder replied: "My wife is pregnant, but I did not know whether it would be a boy or a girl, so I asked the six teachers. They looked and said that without a doubt, according to their reading of the signs, a girl would be born. Hearing that, I am distressed — I am an old man grown aged, with wealth beyond counting, and if there is no son to inherit it, there is no one to whom it can be entrusted. That is why I am unhappy." His friend replied: "You are ignorant! Have you not heard before? The two brothers of the river Kāśyapa — did they go to the Buddha or to the six teachers? If the six teachers were omniscient, why would Kāśyapa have left the six teachers and gone to the Buddha? Moreover, did not Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the like, and kings such as Bimbisāra and others, and royal queens, and householders from every land who distribute food to the unprotected — did not all of these go over to the Buddha's side rather than remain with the six teachers? And did not the Tathāgata tame even such beings as the hungry ghost of the remote hermitage, King Ajātaśatru, the maddened bull that guarded a treasure hoard, and Aṅgulimāla — he who had so intensely spread non-virtuous thoughts and was restrained before he could kill?"

"Householder, the Blessed One the Buddha is called 'buddha' because he knows and sees all phenomena without obstruction. He is called 'Tathāgata' because all his speech is free from duality. He is called 'arhat' because he has overcome all afflictions. What the Blessed One has declared is beyond duality. If the six teachers are not like this, how can one place trust in them? The Tathāgata is dwelling here right now. If you truly wish to understand, go into the presence of the Buddha." So the householder said.

Then that man accompanied the householder, came into my presence, bowed his head to my feet, circumambulated to the right three times, pressed his palms together, placed his knees upon the ground, and addressed me with these words: "Blessed One, you look upon all sentient beings with equanimity and without duality, seeing both enemy and friend with the same characteristic. Yet I am bound by the afflictions arising from craving, and so I have not become non-dual toward enemy and friend. Because of this, I had thought to petition the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, but shame and fear overcame me and I did not dare to ask. Blessed One, now concerning my pregnant wife — the six teachers looked at her and declared with certainty that a daughter would be born. How does that matter stand? What is the truth of it?"

The Blessed One declared: "Householder, the child that your wife carries in her womb is certainly a boy, and when he is born he will be endowed with immeasurable merit."

Then, upon hearing me speak those words, the householder was filled with great joy and returned home. At that moment the six teachers heard that I had prophesied with certainty that a meritorious son would be born to that householder's wife, and jealousy arose in their minds. They mixed poison into a mango fruit, came to the householder, and said to him: "Gautama has made a very fine prediction. For the birth of your wife's child, have her drink this medicine — if she takes this medicine, the child will be excellent, handsome, and free from illness." The householder, delighted, took the poison, gave it to his wife, and she drank it. The moment she drank it, she died.

Then the six teachers, rejoicing, proclaimed throughout every city and marketplace in a loud voice: "The ascetic Gautama prophesied that that householder's wife would certainly give birth to a boy endowed with incomparable merit — yet instead the child was not born and the mother has died!" So they announced.

Then that householder's faith in me was shaken, and following worldly custom, he placed her body in a coffin, carried it outside the city, piled up dry wood, and set it alight to burn.

I, seeing these events with my divine eye, commanded Ānanda: "Ānanda, put on my robe. We are going to crush a wrong view." Then I commanded the spirit-lord of hungry ghosts, whose name was Jewel Pātala (Ratnpātala), as follows: "The Tathāgata is now going to the charnel ground. Go quickly, level the ground, sweep it and wipe it clean with banners, set up a lion throne, and strew the earth thickly with flowers and fine incense."

Then the six teachers, seeing me coming from a distance, said to one another: "Is the ascetic Gautama going to the charnel ground to eat flesh, or what?"

At that time, those lay practitioners who had not yet obtained the Dharma eye were each filled with shame and embarrassment, and they said to me: "The householder's pregnant wife has passed away, Blessed One. Please do not go there."

Then Ānanda said to those people: "All of you wait a moment —"

"The Tathāgata will very soon open and reveal the vast domain of buddha conduct." So they spoke.

I then went there, took my seat upon the lion throne, and the householder addressed me with these words: "Since the Blessed One's speech is entirely without duality — when even the mother has died, how can a child be born?"

I then said this to that householder: "At that time you should not have asked about the length or shortness of the mother's life. You should have asked only this: is the child in the womb male or female?"

The Blessed One, whose speech is entirely without duality, declared: "Therefore, without any doubt, a son will be obtained."

At that moment a fire blazed up around the corpse, the belly split open, and from within it a child emerged — just as a newborn lotus rests upon the water, so too a child appeared there within the fire.

When the six teachers saw this, they said: "Gautama is a trickster, clever at illusions."

When the householder saw it, he was filled with joy, and he taunted the six teachers: "If this is illusion, why do you not do the same yourselves?"

Then I said to the midwife: "Go into the fire and bring that child out."

As the midwife was going into the fire, the six teachers seized her and said to her: "Ascetic Gautama's illusionists are not always capable — some times they can, and some times they cannot. If you go in, you will die. Do not trust those words."

The midwife replied: "Even if the Tathāgata were to say, 'Enter the smoldering fires of hell,' I would not be burned. What need is there to speak of ordinary fire?" And with those words she entered into the mass of flames.

Upon entering, as though stepping into cool water, she took the child in her arms, came back to my presence, and gave the child to me.

I received the child and then said this to the householder: "For all sentient beings the measure of life is not fixed — it is like a bubble on water. If a sentient being has the karmic fruit of very strong attachment to life, then fire cannot burn him and poison cannot kill him. This too is the karmic fruit of the child himself; it is not something I have done."

The householder then said: "Excellent. Blessed One, if this child is to live out his lifespan, may the Tathāgata please give him a name."

The Blessed One declared: "Householder, since this child was born from within the smoldering fire, his name shall be Śute — let him be called Śute."

Then, having witnessed my miraculous powers and emanations, immeasurable numbers of sentient beings in that entire assembly gave rise to the mind aimed at unsurpassed and perfect awakening.

At that time the six teachers, finding no place to reside in any of the six great cities, were utterly humiliated, and came — their heads bowed — to this city of Kuśinagara. Having arrived, they proclaimed: "Know this, all you common people: the ascetic Gautama is a great master of illusion who has deceived everyone and spread through the six great cities. He is like a conjuror who creates assemblies of chariots, assemblies of horses, assemblies of cattle, and assemblies of infantry. Moreover, just as a conjuror creates islands, cities, houses, rivers, lakes, trees, and the like, so too is Gautama the ascetic — he conjures by illusion the bodies of kings. Sometimes, for the sake of teaching the Dharma, he appears in a brahmin's body, sometimes in an ascetic's body, sometimes in the bodies of men and women, sometimes in a great body and sometimes in a small body, sometimes in the bodies of animals and hungry ghosts, and sometimes he expounds the absence of permanence."

Sometimes he expounds permanence, sometimes he expounds suffering, sometimes he expounds bliss, sometimes he expounds the existence of a self, sometimes he expounds selflessness, sometimes he expounds the existence of complete purity, sometimes he expounds the absence of complete purity, sometimes he expounds existence, and sometimes he expounds non-existence. Because none of these are true, they are to be called illusion.

Just as fruit is obtained from a seed as its cause, so too is Gautama the ascetic: he was born of the goddess Māyādevī. If the mother herself is an illusion, how could the son be otherwise? Gautama the ascetic has no genuine knowledge and no genuine vision. Brahmins who practice austerities for many years and maintain ethical conduct still have no genuine knowledge and genuine vision — so how then could Gautama, who trained for only a short time in youth and did not even practice austerities, have genuine knowledge and genuine vision? If even one who practices austerities for seven full years does not attain manifold vision, what need is there to speak of less than six years? Only the foolish and the ignorant believe what he says. Just as a great conjuror deceives the simple-minded, so too is Gautama the ascetic.

O son of good family, those six teachers thus aroused malicious views in sentient beings throughout this city. O son of good family, seeing this, I, with great compassion, gathered the bodhisattvas and great bodhisattvas of the ten directions, filled this grove for a full forty leagues, and today here I shall roar the great lion's roar.

O son of good family, though one may speak at length in an empty place, that is not called roaring the lion's roar. But when it is proclaimed in the midst of a great assembly of the wise and the discerning, that is what is called roaring the great lion's roar.

Now, roaring the lion's roar does not mean expounding that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and utterly impure. It means expounding only that the Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, a self, and utterly pure.

Then the six teachers spoke again, saying: "Gautama, if you have a self, then we too have a self. What is called 'self' is the self of what is seen. Gautama, just as one sees an object through an aperture, so too is the self — the seeing is like an eye, the seeing is like a self."

The Blessed One then declared to the six teachers: "To say that what is seen is the self — that is not the correct meaning. Why? Because in the analogy you have offered, that through an aperture one sees, when a person looks through a single aperture all six sense faculties function. If there were necessarily a self that sees by means of the eye-faculty as its condition, then why is it that through a single aperture all six sense objects are not cognized simultaneously? If a single sense faculty cannot see all six objects at the same time, then what is seen is devoid of self. Furthermore, in the analogy of the aperture, no matter how long one looks through it — even for a hundred years — what is seen remains undifferentiated and the same. If the eye-faculty were also like that, then even when one grows old and the faculties decline, what is seen should logically remain the same and undifferentiated. Moreover, because the eye and the aperture are distinct, inner and outer things are seen. If the eye-faculty is like that, then it should logically be possible to see both inner and outer simultaneously and all at once. If one cannot see both, can it be maintained that a self exists?"

The six teachers said: "Gautama, if there is no self, then who is it that sees?"

The Blessed One declared: "What is called 'seeing' is a convergence of four things: form, appearance, mind, and the eye and the other sense faculties. And in that, in ultimate reality, there is neither a seeing nor a grasping at seeing. It is sentient beings who are confused that speak of grasping at seeing.

Because of this, all sentient beings see in a distorted way. Buddhas and bodhisattvas, however, see correctly. As for the six teachers: if one were to assert that form is a self, that too is not the case. Why? Because form is not, in ultimate reality, a self. If form were the self, there would be no such thing as an unpleasant bodily appearance. And why should the four social classes be distinguished from one another rather than all being subsumed into a single brahmin caste? Why should one be subject to another's power and lack power of one's own? Why should the sense faculties deteriorate and become impaired? Why should one not simply take on a divine body, but instead take on the various kinds of bodies found among hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and the rest? Looking at the fact that things do not turn out as one wishes, one must inescapably recognize that there is no self.

Because there is no self, things are said to be impermanent. Because they are impermanent, they are suffering. Because they are suffering, they are empty. Because they are empty, they are distorted. And because they are distorted, all sentient beings revolve thoroughly in saṃsāra. The same applies equally to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

The Blessed One, the Buddha, has severed completely the bonds of form through to the bonds of consciousness, and therefore is called permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure. Furthermore, form is dependently originated, and whatever is dependently originated is said to be without self. Whatever is without self is said to be empty and suffering. The body of the Tathāgata does not arise through dependent origination. Because it is not dependently originated, it is said to possess a self. Whatever possesses a self is said to be permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure.

The six teachers then asked again: "Gautama, from form through to consciousness, none is a self; and what is called a self, being all-pervasive, is like empty space."

The Blessed One declared: "If there were something that existed as all-pervasive, it would be illogical to say 'I saw it before.' For if it was seen before, then that seeing was absent earlier and becomes apparent later. If it was absent earlier and present later, then it is called impermanent. And if it is impermanent, why call it all-pervasive? If it were all-pervasive, it would follow that it should be fully present in body throughout all five paths of rebirth. If it were present as a body in each of those, it would follow that karmic maturation should be experienced separately in each one. But if maturation is experienced separately, why do you say one becomes a god or a human? And this that you call 'all-pervasive' — is it one or many? If that self is one, then the very names of father, son, kinsman, and enemy would not exist. If that self is many, it would follow that the five sense faculties of all sentient beings are equal, and that karma and its results would likewise all be equal. If that were the case, why would one speak of any distinction between having complete sense faculties and incomplete ones, between virtuous and non-virtuous action, between the deluded and the wise?"

The six teachers replied: "Gautama, the self of sentient beings is boundless and limitless, while Dharma and non-Dharma admit of degrees. Sentient beings who practice Dharma obtain a good body, and those who practice non-Dharma obtain a poor body. For this reason the karmic fruits of sentient beings are not without distinction."

The Blessed One then declared to the six teachers: "If Dharma and non-Dharma are as you say, then that self is not all-pervasive. But if that self were all-pervasive, it would follow that it permeates everything entirely. If it permeates everything entirely, then even a person who practices virtue would have sin present,

and a person who commits sin would likewise have virtue present. If it is not so, why call it all-pervasive?"

The six teachers replied: "Gautama, consider this example: even if a hundred thousand oil lamps are placed inside a single room, each shines separately, and none obstructs the other. The self of sentient beings is just like that — those who practice virtue and those who commit sin do not intermingle with one another."

The Blessed One declared: "The meaning of your claim that the self is like an oil lamp is not so. Why? Because the light of an oil lamp arises from conditions: when the lamp is born, the light too is born. The self of sentient beings is not like that. The light arises from the oil lamp and dwells in a distinct location. The self of sentient beings, though it arises from the body, does not dwell in a distinct location. Furthermore, the light of an oil lamp coexists with darkness. Why? Consider this: if a single oil lamp is placed outside a dark room, the room does not become bright; but if the lamp is placed inside, it does become bright. If the first lamp had already dispelled the darkness, there would be no need for a second lamp. Yet if a second lamp is needed, it is evident that the prior light was coexisting with the darkness."

The six teachers asked: "Gautama, if there is no self, who then will perform virtue and non-virtue?"

The Blessed One declared: "If it is that self which acts, would it be appropriate to call it permanent? But if it is permanent, why does it sometimes perform virtue and sometimes perform non-virtue? If there are times of performing virtue and times of performing non-virtue, how can you say the self is boundless? If it is the self that acts, why does it engage in the phenomena of non-virtue? If that self truly acts and truly knows, why would doubt arise in sentient beings that there is no self? Therefore, in the teaching of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), there is assuredly no self. What is called 'self' is the Tathāgata. Why? Because his body is boundless and free from the net of doubt, and because he neither acts nor grasps, he is called permanent. Because he neither arises nor ceases, he is called bliss. Because he is free from the stain of mental afflictions, he is called utterly pure. Because he is free from the ten defining characteristics, he is called empty. Therefore the Tathāgata is permanent, bliss, self, utterly pure, empty, and without marks."

The non-Buddhists said: "If you, Gautama, teach that the Tathāgata is permanent, blissful, self, utterly pure, and without marks, then we recognize that the Dharma taught by Gautama too is not empty. Therefore we shall receive it with bowed heads and hold it as a dhāraṇī." Having said this, at that very moment countless non-Buddhists went forth into renunciation with minds of faith in the teaching of the Buddha.

"O son of noble family, it was for that cause and by that condition that I proclaimed here, at the foot of these sāla trees, a great lion's roar. That very proclamation of the lion's roar is what is called nirvāṇa.

O son of noble family, the pair of sāla trees to the east: by overcoming impermanence, they bring about the attainment of permanence. The pair of trees in the north: by overcoming that which is not utterly pure, they bring about the attainment of utter purity.

O son of noble family, the sentient beings dwelling here guard the sāla grove for the sake of the sāla trees, and do not allow outsiders to break off and cut branches, leaves, and the like. In the same way, I too am like that: for the sake of four qualities of Dharma, I have caused my attendants to guard the Buddha's Dharma. What are those four? Permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity."

These four pairs of trees are guarded by four kings, and it is in order that those four kings may guard and uphold my Dharma that I pass into final nirvāṇa here. O son of noble family, the sāla trees blossom and bear fruit at all times, and they bring benefit at all times to immeasurable sentient beings. I too am like that: I bring benefit to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. In this analogy, the flower stands for self, and the fruit stands for bliss. For this very reason I have entered the meditative absorption of complete peace here between the sāla trees. The meditative absorption of complete peace is nothing other than great nirvāṇa.

Siṃhanāda then asked: "Blessed One, why does the Blessed One pass into nirvāṇa in the middle month of spring?"

The Blessed One replied: "O son of noble family, the middle month of spring is called spring because in the spring months all living things grow and all seedlings take root, flowers and fruits blossom fully, all rivers flow freely, and the milk of all animals increases. At that time many sentient beings give rise to the perception of permanence. In order to dispel sentient beings' notion of permanence, all phenomena are taught to be impermanent, while the Tathāgata alone is taught to abide permanently, unchangingly.
