O son of noble family, among the six seasons, winter is when everything is dry and all is joyless, while summer is when all is lush and everything delights and clings. In order to dispel sentient beings' worldly bliss, permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity are taught. The Tathāgata is likewise: in order to dispel worldly notions of self and worldly notions of purity, the Tathāgata teaches true self and utter purity. In this analogy, the middle month of spring stands for the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata in its twofold aspect. The joylessness of winter stands for the sadness of the wise and discerning who take no delight in the Tathāgata passing into impermanence and final nirvāṇa. The joy of summer stands for the admiring faith of the wise and discerning in the Tathāgata as permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure. The seedlings stand for the example of all sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma, rejoice and thereby plant wholesome roots of virtue in their minds directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. The rivers stand for the example of the great bodhisattvas from all ten directions who gather in my presence to inquire about and uphold this sūtra of great nirvāṇa. The increase of milk in all animals stands for the example of my attendants giving rise to wholesome roots of virtue. The flowers stand for the example of the seven branches of awakening. The fruits stand for the example of the four fruits. For this very reason I pass into final nirvāṇa in the middle month of spring."

Siṃhanāda then asked: "From the Tathāgata's birth onward — through the going forth, the full awakening, and the turning of the wheel of Dharma — all of these were associated with the eighth day of the month. Why then is the final nirvāṇa alone associated with the fifteenth?"

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! O son of noble family, just as on the fifteenth day the moon rises full and without blemish, so too the buddha, the Blessed One, is like that: in the final nirvāṇa there is no decrease and no blemish. Therefore I pass into final nirvāṇa on the fifteenth. O son of noble family, on the night of the fifteenth day, when the moon is full, it serves eleven purposes. What are those eleven? It dispels darkness. It enables sentient beings to see the path and what is not the path. It enables sentient beings to see the wrong path and the right path. It dispels the torment of heat and brings about the attainment of cool comfort. It defeats the pride and arrogance of fireflies.

It calms the perception and the mind of all things that are containers. It dispels from sentient beings the fearful mind caused by ferocious wild beasts. It causes the blue lotus (utpala) to open. It closes the petals of the day-blooming lotus. It arouses in travelers the intention to set out on the road. And it causes sentient beings to take pleasure in the fivefold sense-enjoyments and to be touched by great ease.

O son of noble family, in just the same way, the moon of the Tathāgata is like that: it vanquishes the great darkness of ignorance; it reveals the right path and the wrong path; it shows the misery of the path of saṃsāra; it opens and reveals the bliss of the path of nirvāṇa; it abandons the torment of attachment, aversion, and delusion; it overcomes the ignorance of non-Buddhists; it vanquishes the thief of all-pervasive mental affliction; it dispels the mind obscured by the five fears; it opens the mind of sentient beings to generate roots of virtue; it covers over the minds of sentient beings stirred by the fivefold sense-desires; and it urges all sentient beings to enter into the great nirvāṇa, and causes them to delight in the conduct of complete liberation. For these reasons, I pass into final nirvāṇa on the fifteenth day — yet truly I do not pass into nirvāṇa.

My foolish and wicked attendants will think, "The Tathāgata has passed into final nirvāṇa." This is like a woman who has many children, and their mother, separated from her children, goes away to another land. While she has not yet returned, each of the children says, "My mother has died." Yet in truth the mother has not died.

The bodhisattva Lion's Roar then asked: "Blessed One, what kind of monks will adorn these śāla trees?"

The Blessed One replied: "O son of noble family, if a monk memorizes, recites, chants, corrects the written letters of, understands the profound meaning of, and then teaches to others the twelve branches of sūtra teaching — such a monk is virtuous at the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous at the end, and teaches the holy life for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings. Such a monk as this will greatly adorn the śāla trees.

The bodhisattva Lion's Roar asked: "Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, is it the monk Ānanda himself?"

"Just so, O son of noble family. And why is that? The monk Ānanda memorizes, recites, and chants the twelve branches of sūtra teaching, and he also reveals and teaches their excellent words and ultimate meaning to others. Just as water is poured from one vessel into another, so too is the monk Ānanda: just as he has heard it from the Buddha, so he teaches it to others."

"O son of noble family, if a monk, having obtained the pure divine eye, sees the entire billion-world great universe of the ten directions as clearly as a mango placed in the palm of one's hand — such a monk as this will also greatly adorn the śāla trees."

Lion's Roar asked: "Blessed One, if that is so, then it is the monk Anuruddha himself. And why is that? The monk Anuruddha, with his unobstructed divine eye, sees with complete clarity and without impediment all that exists within the billion-world great universe, even down to beings in the intermediate state between the five aggregates."

"O son of noble family, if a monk has few desires, is content, delights in ease, applies himself with great diligence, and cultivates mindfulness, meditative absorption, and wisdom — such a monk as this will also greatly adorn the śāla trees."

Lion's Roar said: "Blessed One, if that is so, then it is the monk Kāśyapa himself. And why is that? The monk Kāśyapa cultivates to the highest degree the qualities of having few desires, contentment, and so forth."

"O son of noble family, if a monk, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, with respect to gain and —

not for the sake of fame or reputation — the meditative absorption of non-contention, the conduct of the noble ones, and the practice of dwelling in emptiness: a monk of this kind will also greatly adorn the śāla trees."

Lion's Roar said: "Blessed One, if that is so, then it is none other than the monk Subhūti himself. And why is that? Subhūti is skilled in the meditative absorption of non-contention, the conduct of the noble ones, and the practice of dwelling in emptiness."

"O son of noble family, if a monk cultivates supernatural power and in a single instant displays various forms of miraculous transformation — and from a single mind and a single meditative absorption manifests the two fruits of water and fire — such a monk will also greatly adorn the śāla trees."

Lion's Roar said: "Blessed One, if that is so, then it is none other than the monk Mahāmaudgalyāyana himself. And why is that? Mahāmaudgalyāyana is skilled in displaying supernatural powers and miraculous transformations without limit."

"O son of noble family, if a monk cultivates great wisdom, sharp wisdom, swift wisdom, liberating wisdom, profoundly deep wisdom, vast wisdom, boundless wisdom, undefeated wisdom, and authentic wisdom — and is endowed with this supreme faculty of wisdom, and harbors no partial thoughts distinguishing between enemies and friends — and upon hearing that the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa and is impermanent, remains free of grief and abides steadily without passing away, and upon hearing that he will not pass beyond sorrow, feels no joy — such a monk will also greatly adorn the śāla trees."

Lion's Roar said: "Blessed One, if that is so, then it is none other than the monk Śāriputra himself. And why is that? Śāriputra is endowed with great wisdom in all its forms."

"O son of noble family, if a monk teaches that all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature — a body like a vajra, boundless and without limit, permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure — and that, with body and mind unobstructed, one attains the eight masteries: such a monk will also greatly adorn the śāla trees."

Lion's Roar said: "Blessed One, if that is so, then the Tathāgata alone is truly that. And why is that? The body of the Tathāgata is a body like a vajra — boundless, without limit, permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure. His body and mind are unobstructed, and he is endowed with the eight masteries. The Blessed One alone will adorn the śāla trees. If he were not to remain, they would not be beautiful. Therefore, out of great compassion, wishing to adorn them perfectly, I aspire that he always remain in this grove of śāla trees."

The Blessed One declared: "O son of noble family, the essential nature of all phenomena is such that there is no fixed place of abiding. Why then do you speak of wishing the Tathāgata to remain? O son of noble family, what is called 'abiding' is a characteristic of form, for it is called abiding because it arises from causes. That which is without cause and condition is called the abiding of non-abiding. Since the Tathāgata has severed all bonds of form, why do you speak of wishing the Tathāgata to remain? Understand that the same applies equally to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. O son of noble family, what is called 'abiding' is what is called pride — because of pride one is not liberated. Since one who is not liberated is said to abide, in whom does pride exist, and from where has it come?"

Therefore it is called the abiding of non-abiding. Since the Tathāgata has utterly severed all pride, why do you speak of wishing the Tathāgata to remain? Abiding is a conditioned phenomenon, and since the Tathāgata has utterly severed all conditioned phenomena, he does not abide. Abiding is a phenomenon of emptiness, and since the Tathāgata has utterly severed such phenomena of emptiness, he has attained permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity — so why do you speak of wishing the Tathāgata to remain? Abiding is the twenty-five existences, and since the Tathāgata has utterly severed the twenty-five existences, why do you speak of abiding? Abiding is all ordinary beings who are foolish and lowly. Noble ones have neither going, nor coming, nor abiding, and since the Tathāgata has utterly severed even the very characteristics of going, coming, and abiding, why do you speak of abiding?

Now, non-abiding is the body that is boundless. Since the body is boundless in just this way, why do you speak of wishing the Tathāgata to remain in the śāla grove? For if he were to remain in this grove, his body would become one that has limits; and if it had limits, it would become impermanent. Since the Tathāgata is permanent, why do you speak of abiding? Again, non-abiding is empty space. Since the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata is like empty space, why do you speak of abiding? Again, what is called non-abiding is the vajra-like meditative absorption (samādhi). The vajra-like meditative absorption destroys all stations of abiding, and since the Tathāgata himself is the vajra-like meditative absorption, why do you speak of abiding? Again, non-abiding is what is called illusion. Since the Tathāgata is like an illusion, why do you speak of abiding? Again, non-abiding is the absence of beginning and end. Since the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata likewise has no beginning and no end, why do you speak of abiding? Again, non-abiding is the boundless dharmadhātu, the basic space of phenomena. Since the Tathāgata is the very boundless dharmadhātu, why do you speak of abiding? Again, what is called non-abiding is the meditative absorption called the Courageous March. Through the meditative absorption of the Courageous March one knows all phenomena to be without attachment; and because there is no attachment, it is called the Courageous March. Since the Tathāgata is endowed with the meditative absorption of the Courageous March, why do you speak of abiding? Again, non-abiding is called the power of knowing what is possible and what is not possible. Since the Tathāgata is endowed with the power of knowing what is possible and what is not possible, why do you speak of abiding? Again, what is called non-abiding is called the perfection of generosity. If there were abiding in the perfection of generosity, one could not proceed all the way to the perfection of moral discipline and through to the Perfection of Wisdom. Therefore the perfection of generosity is called non-abiding, and since the Tathāgata likewise does not abide anywhere up to and through the Perfection of Wisdom, why do you speak of always wishing him to remain in the śāla grove? Again, non-abiding is called the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness. If the Tathāgata were to abide in the four foundations of mindfulness, he would be unable to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening — and therefore it is called the abiding of non-abiding. Again, non-abiding is called the boundless realm of sentient beings. Even though the Tathāgata reaches the boundless realm of all sentient beings, he does not abide. Again, what is called non-abiding is this: the absence of support and ground is called having nothing whatsoever. Having nothing whatsoever is called non-arising. Non-arising is called the absence of death. The absence of death is called the absence of marks. The absence of marks is called the absence of bondage. The absence of bondage is called the absence of attachment. The absence of attachment is called freedom from defilement.

Freedom from defilement is virtue. Virtue is the unconditioned. The unconditioned is the great nirvāṇa — permanent nirvāṇa. Permanence is the self. The self is perfect purity. Perfect purity is called bliss. Permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity — these are the Tathāgata.

Son of good family, consider this example: space does not abide in the east, the south, the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below. Likewise the Tathāgata does not abide in the east, the south, the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below.

Son of good family, there is no basis whatsoever for the claim that one who acts with non-virtue of body, speech, and mind could obtain the fruit of virtue. Equally, there is no basis for the claim that one who acts with virtue of body, speech, and mind could obtain the fruit of non-virtue. There is no basis for the claim that an ignoble person sees the nature of a buddha while a bodhisattva on the tenth ground does not. There is no basis for the claim that those who hold wrong craving, those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, those who have slandered the vast and expansive sūtras, or those who have broken the four root precepts could attain unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening. There is no basis for the claim that a bodhisattva, a great being, on the sixth ground could fall into the three lower realms through the causes and conditions of affliction. There is no basis for the claim that a bodhisattva, a great being, could truly attain unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening in a woman's body. There is no basis for the claim that one who holds wrong craving could say of the Three Jewels, which are permanent, "They are impermanent," while the Tathāgata dwells in the city of Kuśinagara.

Son of good family, they say the Tathāgata has today entered the profound sanctuary of great meditative absorption here in this city of Kuśinagara and has passed into complete nirvāṇa because sentient beings cannot see him.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: For what reason did the Tathāgata enter the profound sanctuary of meditative absorption?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, it was in order to liberate all sentient beings; in order to cause roots of virtue not yet generated to be generated; in order to cause roots of virtue already generated to grow and expand; in order to ripen wholesome fruits not yet ripened; in order to lead what has ripened into unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening; in order to engender reverence for the ripening of wholesome Dharma; in order to free the heedless from heedlessness; in order to preach the Dharma alongside those like Mañjuśrī the youthful, who are like great elephants scented with perfume; in order to inspire those who delight in reading and reciting to be deeply devoted to meditative absorption; in order to tame sentient beings through noble conduct, pure conduct, and divine conduct; in order to contemplate the profound essence of the unmixed Dharma; in order to chastise heedless attendants — for if the Tathāgata were ever at rest and delighting in meditative absorption, would you not grow heedless in your afflictions? — in order to chastise unsuitable monks who carry the eight types of unexamined possessions, who have many desires, and who know no contentment; and in order to engender reverence in sentient beings who have heard the Dharma of meditative absorption and the like. For these reasons and conditions did he enter the profound sanctuary of meditative absorption.

Siṃhaghoṣa then said: Blessed One, the meditative absorption free of characteristics is called the great nirvāṇa. Should it therefore be called nirvāṇa that is free of characteristics, or is it designated as free of characteristics for some other reason?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, it is because it is free of ten kinds of characteristics. What are the ten? They are as follows: the characteristic of form, the characteristic of sound, the characteristic of taste, the characteristic of smell, the characteristic of touch, birth, abiding,

decay, the characteristic of what is born, and the characteristic of femininity — these ten. To be free of such characteristics is what is called "free of characteristics."

Son of good family, whoever is attached to characteristics will give rise to delusion. Through delusion, craving arises. Through craving, bondage arises. Through bondage, one takes on birth. Through birth, one comes to death. Through death, one is impermanent. Whoever is not attached to characteristics does not give rise to delusion. Through the absence of delusion, there is no craving. Through the absence of craving, there is no bondage. Through the absence of bondage, one does not take on birth. Through not taking on birth, there is no death. Through the absence of death, one is called permanent. For this reason, nirvāṇa is permanent.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: Blessed One, by what means do monks sever these ten kinds of characteristics?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, if a monk repeatedly cultivates three kinds of characteristics, he will sever the ten kinds of characteristics. These are as follows: repeatedly cultivating the characteristic of meditative absorption, repeatedly cultivating the characteristic of wisdom, and repeatedly — at appropriate times — cultivating the characteristic of equanimity. These are called the three characteristics.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: Blessed One, what exactly are the characteristics of meditative absorption, wisdom, and equanimity? If what is called "the characteristic of meditative absorption" is simply meditative absorption itself, then since all sentient beings already possess meditative absorption, what would be the point of being told to cultivate it? And if meditative absorption means the mind being focused on a single object, and if focusing on a different object were also called meditative absorption, then if one had not entered into many absorptions, would one not be omniscient? And if one were not omniscient, why would it be called meditative absorption? On the other hand, if meditative absorption is attained by one mode of conduct, then another mode of conduct would not be meditative absorption. If it is not meditative absorption, then one is not omniscient. And if one is not omniscient, why call it meditative absorption? In just the same way, the two characteristics of wisdom and equanimity are equally problematic.

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, it is not as you say — that meditative absorption means the mind focusing on a single object, and that focusing on another object is therefore not meditative absorption. Why? Because another object of focus is also just a single object, and the same holds for formations. Likewise, it is also not the case that sentient beings possess meditative absorption from the very beginning and therefore have no need to cultivate it. Why? Because what is called meditative absorption refers to virtuous meditative absorption, and since it is not present in all sentient beings without qualification, how could one say there is no need to cultivate it?

Thus, resting in virtuous meditative absorption and then discerning all phenomena is called the characteristic of virtuous wisdom. Not perceiving the characteristics of meditative absorption and wisdom as distinct from one another is called the characteristic of equanimity.

Furthermore, son of good family, if one grasps form as a characteristic and does not discern it under the characteristics of permanence or impermanence, that is called meditative absorption. Discerning form under the characteristics of permanence and impermanence is called the characteristic of wisdom. Discerning all phenomena equally through meditative absorption and wisdom together is called the characteristic of equanimity.

Son of good family, just as a well-yoked chariot travels at a swift and proper pace — and traveling at that swift and proper pace is what is called the characteristic of equanimity —

So too is the bodhisattva: if meditative absorption predominates, let him cultivate wisdom; if wisdom predominates, let him cultivate meditative absorption. When meditative absorption and wisdom are equal in measure, that is called equanimity.

Son of good family, a bodhisattva on the tenth ground has the greater measure of the power of wisdom and a lesser measure of the power of meditative absorption; therefore the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not clearly seen. Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have the greater measure of the power of meditative absorption and a lesser measure of the power of wisdom; therefore the intrinsic nature of a buddha is not seen. The blessed buddhas, the Bhagavāns, have meditative absorption and wisdom in equal measure, and so they clearly behold the intrinsic nature of a buddha — just as an āmalaka fruit placed in the palm of the hand is plainly seen. Beholding the intrinsic nature of a buddha is called the characteristic of equanimity.

Calm abiding is also called restraint, because it restrains all afflictions entirely. Calm abiding is also called taming, because it tames the faculties from non-virtue. Calm abiding is also called pacification, because it pacifies the three doors of body, speech, and mind. Calm abiding is also called complete abandonment, because it completely abandons the five objects of desire for sentient beings. Calm abiding is also called purification, because it purifies attachment, aversion, and delusion. For these reasons it is called the characteristic of meditative absorption.

Insight is also called seeing correctly, and also called seeing directly, and also called being able to see, and also called seeing pervasively, and also called seeing progressively, and also called seeing characteristics as distinct — all of this is what is called wisdom. Equanimity is also called evenness, and also called non-contention, and also called non-conceptuality, and also called non-engagement — all of this is what is called equanimity.

Son of good family, calm abiding has two aspects: worldly and transcendent. Again, it has two aspects: accomplished and unaccomplished. Of these, the accomplished belongs to buddhas and bodhisattvas; the unaccomplished belongs to śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth. Again, there are three degrees: inferior, middling, and superior. Of these, the inferior belongs to those of low capacity and low conduct; the middling belongs to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the superior belongs to buddhas and bodhisattvas. Again, there are four aspects: erroneous, stationary, progressively ascending, and capable of benefiting others. Again, there are five aspects: these are the meditative absorptions of the five wisdoms. What are the five? The meditative absorption without food, the meditative absorption without fault, the meditative absorption of one-pointed mind with body and mind completely purified, the meditative absorption in which both cause and result are blissful, and the meditative absorption of continuous mindfulness.

Again, there are six aspects: the meditative absorption contemplating a skeleton, the meditative absorption of loving-kindness, the meditative absorption contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, the meditative absorption of counting the breath, the meditative absorption of subsequent recollection of what the mind has contemplated, and the meditative absorption contemplating arising and cessation.

Again, there are seven aspects: these are the seven branches of awakening — the branch of awakening that is mindfulness, the branch of awakening that is investigation of phenomena (Skt. dharmavicaya), the branch of awakening that is diligence, the branch of awakening that is joy, the branch of awakening that is pliancy, the branch of awakening that is meditative absorption, and the branch of awakening that is equanimity.

Again, there are seven aspects: the meditative absorption of the stream-enterer, the meditative absorption of the once-returner, the meditative absorption of the non-returner, the meditative absorption of the arhat,

the meditative absorption of the pratyekabuddha, the meditative absorption of the bodhisattva, and the meditative absorption of all the omniscient Tathāgatas.

Again, there are eight aspects, namely the eight liberations. They are as follows: the meditative absorption of liberation through perceiving forms by means of form; the meditative absorption of liberation through perceiving external forms while being without the characteristic of internal form; the meditative absorption of liberation through realization with the body; the meditative absorption of liberation through the sense base of infinite space; the meditative absorption of liberation through the sense base of infinite consciousness; the meditative absorption of liberation through the sense base of nothingness; the meditative absorption of liberation through the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and the meditative absorption of liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception.

Again, there are nine aspects: the nine successive absorptions, namely the four meditative concentrations, the four formless states, and the meditative absorption of the cessation of feeling and perception.

Again, there are ten aspects: the ten totality absorptions. They are as follows: the meditative absorption in which everything is earth; the meditative absorption in which everything is water; the meditative absorption in which everything is fire; the meditative absorption in which everything is wind; the meditative absorption in which everything is blue; the meditative absorption in which everything is yellow; the meditative absorption in which everything is red; the meditative absorption in which everything is white; the meditative absorption of infinite space; and the meditative absorption of infinite consciousness; and the meditative absorption of nothingness.

Furthermore, there are innumerable others, pertaining to the buddhas and bodhisattvas. Noble son, these are called the defining characteristics of meditative absorption.

Noble son, wisdom has two aspects: worldly and transcendent. Again, it has three aspects: wisdom, insight, and gnosis. What is called wisdom belongs to all sentient beings. What is called insight belongs to all noble ones. What is called gnosis belongs to the buddhas and bodhisattvas. Furthermore, wisdom has the defining characteristic of discrimination. Insight has the defining characteristic of the general. Gnosis has the defining characteristic of having overcome characteristics.

Again, there are four aspects: namely the four noble truths.

Noble son, for three reasons one cultivates calm abiding. What are the three? In order to eliminate heedlessness, in order to be established in great gnosis, and in order to attain mastery over the faculties.

Furthermore, for three reasons one cultivates insight. What are the three? In order to contemplate the ripening of non-virtuous karmic results in cyclic existence, in order to generate and increase the roots of virtue, and in order to overcome all afflictions.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: Blessed One, if, as it is taught in the sūtras, afflictions are overcome through insight, then what need is there to cultivate calm abiding?

The Blessed One declared: Noble son, your understanding of the statement that afflictions are overcome through insight is not what it actually means. Why? Because when wisdom is present there are no afflictions, and when afflictions are present there is no wisdom. If that is so, how can one say that insight overcomes afflictions? Noble son, take for example: when there is light there is no darkness, and when there is darkness there is no light. There is simply no situation in which one could say that light dispels darkness. Noble son, what then is wisdom and what are afflictions, such that one could say wisdom dispels afflictions? Since neither exists in that way, there is also nothing to overcome.

Noble son, to say that wisdom overcomes afflictions — does this mean that it overcomes them once it has gone somewhere,

or does it overcome them without having gone there? If it overcomes them without having gone there, then even foolish, common people of the lowest sort would qualify as having overcome them. If, on the other hand, it overcomes them after having gone there, then the preceding moment ought to be what overcomes them. If the preceding moment does not overcome them, then the subsequent moment does not overcome them either. If the moment just before arriving were to overcome them at the very instant of arriving, then that moment itself would still be one that has not yet arrived — so why say that wisdom overcomes them? And if one says they are overcome by both the arrived and the not-yet-arrived, that too is not how it is.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that insight overcomes afflictions — does insight overcome them alone, or does it overcome them with the aid of companions? If it can overcome them alone, why would a bodhisattva cultivate the noble eightfold path? If they are overcome with the aid of companions, then understand that they are not overcome by insight alone. And if insight alone cannot do it, then companions cannot do it either — just as when one blind person cannot see form, many blind people assisting one another still cannot see form; insight is the same as that.

Noble son, consider how earth's intrinsic nature is solidity, water's intrinsic nature is wetness, fire's intrinsic nature is heat, and wind's intrinsic nature is movement. In this way, from earth's intrinsic nature of solidity to wind's intrinsic nature of movement, none of these is produced by causes and conditions — by their intrinsic nature they are just so. Likewise the afflictions of the four great elements are the same: they are severed by their intrinsic nature. If they are severed in that way, why say that wisdom severs them?

For this reason, insight cannot definitively overcome afflictions. Noble son, take for example how the intrinsic nature of salt is saltiness and thereby makes other things different from itself salty as well, how the intrinsic nature of honey is sweetness and thereby makes other things different from itself sweet as well, and how the intrinsic nature of water is wetness and thereby makes other things different from itself wet as well. To say that wisdom, because it negates characteristics, causes phenomena to be negated — that is not how it is. Why? Because if phenomena have no negation in them, how can wisdom forcibly negate them? To say that wisdom negates other phenomena the way salt by its saltiness makes things different from itself salty — that too is not how it is. Why? Because the intrinsic nature of wisdom is to cease moment by moment. If it ceases moment by moment, why say that it negates other, distinct phenomena? For this reason, afflictions are not overcome by the intrinsic nature of wisdom.

Noble son, there are two kinds of cessation for all phenomena: cessation by intrinsic nature, and cessation at the end. Since cessation is by intrinsic nature, why say that wisdom brings about cessation?

If one says that wisdom can burn up afflictions, just as fire burns up material things — that too is not how it is. Why? When fire burns up material things, even ash remains. If wisdom were like that, what remains ought to be like ash. And when an axe cuts wood, the trace of the cut still appears. If wisdom were like that, what would be visibly manifest?

If wisdom could abandon afflictions, then those afflictions — like non-Buddhists who are not found in the six great cities yet appear to be in the village of Kuśāgra — would fittingly appear elsewhere. Since those afflictions do not appear elsewhere in that way, understand that wisdom cannot abandon them.

Noble son, all phenomena are individually empty by their intrinsic nature. No one can generate them and no one can negate them. Arising is one thing and ceasing is another, and neither has been made by anyone.

Noble son, whoever cultivates meditative absorption attains such correct knowledge and correct vision. For that reason, I declared in a sūtra: "If a monk cultivates meditative absorption, he sees the characteristic of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates."

Noble son, if one does not cultivate meditative absorption, one will not even know the things of the world — to say nothing of what transcends the world. If there is no meditative absorption, it is like falling into a chasm when walking on a smooth road. Even when the mind is focused on one thing, one speaks different words with the mouth and hears different things with the ears, and understands meanings that differ from what the mind intends. Even when one intends to write one letter, the hand writes a different one. Just as a foot steps elsewhere when one is walking in another direction — so it is without meditative absorption.

If one cultivates meditative absorption, everything from great benefit all the way to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening will be accomplished.

Noble son, a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses two qualities is able to accomplish great benefit. What are the two? Meditative absorption and wisdom.

Noble son, it is like this: just as a stiff rope snaps when pulled hard, so too does a bodhisattva, a great being, who cultivates these two qualities meet the same fate — that is, the opposing forces give way. Noble son, just as a hard tree is easier to uproot if it is first shaken and only then pulled out, so too with the bodhisattva's meditative absorption and wisdom: first meditative absorption shakes it loose, then wisdom pulls it out.

Just as when washing clothes one first scours them with ash and then rinses them with clean water so that they become clean — so too with the bodhisattva's wisdom and meditative absorption.

Noble son, just as one first reads and recites aloud, and then afterwards understands the meaning — so too with the bodhisattva's meditative absorption and wisdom.

Noble son, it is like a brave warrior who first dons armour and takes up weapons, and then meets the enemy on the battlefield and defeats them — so too with the bodhisattva's meditative absorption and wisdom.

Noble son, it is like a smith who pours gold into a mould and it melts just as desired — so too with the bodhisattva's meditative absorption and wisdom.

Noble son, it is like looking at the reflection of one's own face in a bright, clear mirror — so too with the bodhisattva's meditative absorption and wisdom.

Noble son, just as one first levels the ground and then sows the seed, and just as one first receives the scriptural transmission from a master and then reflects on the meaning — so too with the bodhisattva's meditative absorption and wisdom. For that reason, if a bodhisattva, a great being, cultivates these two qualities, great benefit will be obtained.

Noble son, if a bodhisattva, a great being, cultivates these two qualities, the five faculties become pliant and serviceable, and one becomes able to endure many forms of suffering: hunger, thirst, cold, heat, beating, burning, reviling, being eaten by fierce predators, being bitten by insects and stinging creatures, and all other such suffering. One always gathers the mind and maintains heedfulness. For the sake of gain and fame one does not engage in conduct contrary to the Dharma. One is not stained by sudden afflictions. One is not deceived by any distorted views. One always completely abandons all thoughts of non-virtue. And, in order to accomplish benefit for sentient beings without long delay, one will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

This is the forty-first fascicle.

Son of good family, when a great bodhisattva cultivates those two qualities, the fierce winds of the four perverted views cannot stir him — just as the four winds, even blowing together, cannot move Mount Meru, the king of mountains. Just as the victory banner of Śakra (Indra, king of the gods) cannot be moved, so too he cannot be moved by the teachers of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). He cannot be deceived by the various fraudulent tricks of the mistaken. He constantly enjoys the highest and most sublime happiness. He understands the profound meanings that the Tathāgata intended and taught. He neither delights in pleasure nor grieves over suffering. All gods and humans pay him reverence, honor, and praise. He sees clearly what is saṃsāra and what is not saṃsāra. He is skilled in the dharmadhātu and in the defining characteristics of phenomena. And he comes to know that within the body there exist phenomena of permanence, happiness, self, and perfect purity. This is called the happiness of complete nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, the defining characteristic of meditative absorption (samādhi) is called the meditative absorption of emptiness. The defining characteristic of wisdom is called the meditative absorption of wishlessness. The defining characteristic of equanimity is called the meditative absorption of signlessness.

Son of good family, if a great bodhisattva is skilled in knowing the right time and the wrong time for meditative absorption, for wisdom, and for equanimity, this is called a great bodhisattva practicing the path of awakening.

Siṃha (Lion) then asked: Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva seek out what is the right time and what is the wrong time?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if a great bodhisattva has generated great arrogance on account of experiencing happiness, or has generated arrogance on account of teaching the Dharma, or on account of beginning to apply diligence, or on account of being skilled in knowing the meaning and in asking and answering questions, or on account of associating with evil companions, or on account of giving precious wealth, or on account of being honored by people of great lineage and noble standing in the world — then at that time he should know not to cultivate wisdom, but to cultivate meditative absorption. This is called a bodhisattva knowing the right time and the wrong time.

If a bodhisattva, having undertaken diligent effort, has generated a mind of regret because he has not yet attained the nirvāṇa of benefit and happiness, or because his faculties are dull and he cannot tame the five faculties, or because the mass of defilements has grown thick and dense and he has come to doubt and to transgress in regard to moral discipline and the Vinaya — then at that time he should know not to cultivate meditative absorption, but to cultivate wisdom. This is called a bodhisattva knowing the right time and the wrong time.

If a bodhisattva finds that his portions of meditative absorption and wisdom are unequal, he should know that that is not the time to cultivate equanimity. If they are equal, then one should cultivate it. This is called a bodhisattva knowing the right time and the wrong time.

Son of good family, if a bodhisattva is cultivating meditative absorption and wisdom and afflictions arise at that time, he should not then cultivate equanimity. Instead he should know to read, recite, copy in writing, and teach to others the twelve branches of the scriptural collections, and to cultivate mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of moral discipline, mindfulness of the gods, and mindfulness of generosity. This is called cultivating equanimity.

Son of good family, when a bodhisattva cultivates those three defining characteristics of phenomena, he thereby attains nirvāṇa — the great passing beyond sorrow that is without defining marks.

Lion's Roar asked: Blessed One, because great nirvāṇa lacks ten defining marks, may it be called "nirvāṇa without defining marks"? And because of that, may it be said to be: unborn, unarisen, unconditioned, a support, an island, a protector, a refuge, supreme ease, cessation, nirvāṇa, peace, free from the suffering of illness, and free from existence?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, because it is without cause and condition, it is called unborn. Because it is unborn, it is called unarisen. Because nothing has been made or fabricated, it is also called unconditioned. Because it does not enter into the five views, it is called a support and a foundation. Because it is free from the four desires, it is called an island. Because it tames sentient beings, it is called a protector and a refuge. Because it has conquered the enemy of affliction, it is called ease. Because the fire of affliction has been extinguished, it is called cessation. Because it is free from conceptual thought, it is called nirvāṇa. Because busyness and agitation have been abandoned, it is called peace. Because death has been utterly cut off, it is called free from illness. Because all is absent, it is called free from existence.

Son of good family, if a bodhisattva — a great bodhisattva — reflects in that way, he will come to see clearly the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Lion's Roar asked: Blessed One, if a bodhisattva, a great bodhisattva, possesses the qualities of the Dharma, will he then see everything from nirvāṇa without defining marks all the way to the absence of existence?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if a bodhisattva, a great bodhisattva, possesses ten qualities of the Dharma, he will see everything from nirvāṇa without defining marks all the way to the absence of existence. What are the ten?

The first is possessing a mind of faith. How does one possess a mind of faith? One believes that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are permanent, and one believes that the buddhas of the ten directions too reveal this through skillful means, and one believes that all sentient beings — even those of wrong craving — possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Yet one does not believe that the Tathāgata is subject to birth, aging, illness, death, and ascetic hardship; that Devadatta truly caused a schism in the Saṅgha; that blood was drawn from the body of the Tathāgata; that the Tathāgata will ultimately pass beyond sorrow into final nirvāṇa; or that the sacred Dharma will entirely come to an end. This is called a bodhisattva possessing a mind of faith.

The second is possessing pure moral discipline. How does one possess pure moral discipline? Son of good family, if a bodhisattva claims that his own moral discipline is pure, yet when he sees a woman he speaks words of flattery or playful flirtation even without physical contact — that bodhisattva is one characterized by attachment, and he thereby impairs his pure moral discipline, disgraces his claim to celibate conduct, and blemishes his discipline. He is not to be called one possessing pure moral discipline.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva may claim that his moral discipline is pure and may refrain from touching a woman's body and from speaking words of flattery or play, yet while outside some retreat or shelter, if upon hearing the sounds of a woman's ornaments, garlands, and necklaces, and upon hearing various feminine voices, he gives rise to a mind of attachment — that bodhisattva too is one characterized by attachment.

He thereby impairs his pure moral discipline, disgraces his claim to celibate conduct, and blemishes his discipline. He is not to be called one possessing pure moral discipline.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva may claim that his moral discipline is pure and may refrain from touching a woman's body and from speaking words of flattery or play, and may not listen to sounds or voices — yet if upon seeing men following after women, or women following after men, he gives rise to attachment, that bodhisattva too is one characterized by attachment. He thereby impairs his pure moral discipline, disgraces his claim to celibate conduct, and blemishes his discipline. He is not to be called one possessing pure moral discipline.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva may claim that his moral discipline is pure, may not touch a woman, may not speak words of flattery or play, may not listen to sounds or voices, and may not look upon men and women keeping company with one another — yet if he is attached to and delights in the five objects of desire of the gods of the higher realms, that bodhisattva too is one characterized by attachment. He thereby impairs his pure moral discipline, disgraces his claim to celibate conduct, and blemishes his discipline. He is not to be called one possessing pure moral discipline.

O son of good family, a bodhisattva who holds pure moral discipline does so not for the sake of moral discipline itself, not for the sake of the perfection of moral discipline, not for the sake of sentient beings, not for the sake of benefit and happiness, not for the sake of being a bodhisattva, not for the sake of nirvāṇa, and not for the sake of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Rather, a bodhisattva who guards moral discipline solely for the sake of the unsurpassed and ultimate goal — he alone is to be called one possessing pure moral discipline.

He relies upon a spiritual friend. In this context, a spiritual friend is one who teaches faith, moral discipline, great learning, generosity, and wisdom, and by whom others will be led to practice — such a one is called a spiritual friend of a bodhisattva.

He delights in quietude. In this context, quietude means this: through the stilling of body and mind, to realize the profound dharmadhātu, the basic space of phenomena, of all dharmas — this is called quietude.

He is endowed with diligence. In this context, diligence means this: when, with one-pointed mind, one is contemplating the Four Noble Truths of the āryas, even if fire were blazing upon the crown of one's head, one does not abandon that contemplation — this is called diligence.

He is endowed with the close establishment of mindfulness. In this context, the close establishment of mindfulness means this: recollection following upon the Buddha, recollection following upon the Dharma, recollection following upon the Saṅgha, recollection following upon moral discipline, and recollection following upon generosity — these are called the close establishment of mindfulness.

He speaks gently. In this context, gentle speech means this: speaking words that are true, words that are excellent, words that are harmonious and pleasing, words that are timely, and words that are correct — this is called gentle speech.

He is endowed with the protection of the Dharma. In this context, protecting the Dharma means this: always delighting in and being devoted to teaching, reading, reciting, and writing down the sacred Dharma; taking its meaning to heart; and widely opening it up, teaching it, and causing others to assimilate it; and likewise, when one sees others copying it in writing, opening it up and explaining it, reading and reciting it, praising and extolling it, and taking its meaning to heart — then to provide them with the requisites of livelihood, namely, to offer robes, food, bedding, and medicines for illness and the like;

And not to begrudge one's body and life for the sake of protecting the Dharma — this is called protecting the Dharma.

When a bodhisattva, a great being, sees someone who shares the same training and the same moral discipline yet is in need and destitute, that bodhisattva takes from others an alms bowl, exchanges robes of a different color, acts as a nurse, and then gathering robes, food, bedding, and lodging and the like, gives them as gifts. Such a one is endowed with wisdom.

Now, what is called wisdom is this: to view the Tathāgata as permanent, blissful, possessed of self, and perfectly pure; to view all sentient beings as possessing the nature of a buddha; and to discern the twofold characteristic of phenomena — namely, to discern phenomena as: empty and not empty; permanent and impermanent; blissful and without bliss; self and selfless; perfectly pure and not perfectly pure; distinct phenomena that can be distinguished and distinct phenomena that cannot be distinguished; distinct phenomena that arise from conditions and distinct phenomena that are perceived as arising from conditions; distinct phenomena that have issued as a result from conditions, and distinct phenomena that have not issued as a result from conditions — one who discerns in this way is called endowed with wisdom.

O son of good family, a bodhisattva who possesses these ten qualities is called one who clearly sees the signless nirvāṇa.

Siṃhaghoṣa then asked: Blessed One, what is the meaning of what the Blessed One previously declared to Cunda: "You have seen the nature of a buddha; you will attain the great parinirvāṇa and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening"?

The Blessed One replied: It is taught in the sūtras that if one gives to an animal, one will obtain a hundredfold karmic maturation. If one gives to one who holds wrong views, one will obtain a thousandfold karmic maturation. If one gives to one who guards moral discipline, one will obtain karmic maturation on the order of a hundred thousand. If one gives to a non-Buddhist adherent (tīrthika) who has cut off afflictions beyond measure, one will obtain karmic maturation beyond measure. If one gives to those who have reached the four directions — that is, who have attained the four fruits — and to pratyekabuddhas, one will obtain karmic maturation beyond measure. The merit and the karmic maturation obtained from giving to non-regressing bodhisattvas, to great bodhisattvas who are obstructed by but one more life, and to the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is immeasurable, unbounded, inexpressible, and inconceivable.

Now, noble Cunda, if one were to experience such ripening of merit, one should not stop short of that ripening — for at some point in time one will attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Furthermore, Blessed One, it is taught in the sūtras that if someone performs virtuous and non-virtuous actions with a pure intention, the result will without fail ripen as a fruit — whether in the present life, or in future lives, or in this very life itself. Likewise, Cunda performed virtue from a pure intention, and that action will without fail ripen and be experienced as a fruit.

But if the fruit must certainly be experienced, how will unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening be attained? And how will one come to see the nature of a buddha?

The Blessed One replied: It is taught in the sūtras that if one gives to these three kinds of beings — the sick, one's parents, and the buddhas, the Blessed Ones — one experiences fruit that is inexhaustible.

And again, from the sūtras, the Blessed One declared to Ānanda: if all sentient beings were without karma in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, they would attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Again, the Blessed One spoke the following verse from the Sūtra of the Words of the Dharma:

Though one flee to the expanse of sky,
to the ocean, to mountains, or to cliffs,
to whatever region, wherever one may go,
one cannot escape from karma that has been done.

Then Ma-'aggapa asked further: Blessed One, I personally recall that through the gift of a single meal offered in a former life, I did not fall into any of the three lower destinies for eighty thousand eons. Blessed One, if even the gift of a single meal brings a karmic fruit of such ripening, what need is there to say that Cunda, having given with a mind of faith to a buddha, will come to possess the perfection of generosity? Blessed One, if one did not wish for the ripened fruit of virtuous karma to be exhausted, how would one exhaust the fault of disparaging the extensive sūtras, the transgression of the five acts of immediate consequence, the loss of the four root precepts, and the fault of perverse craving? And if it cannot be exhausted, one will behold the nature of a buddha and attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

The Blessed One declared: Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, by means of two things a person attains immeasurable and boundless qualities, beyond reckoning and beyond expression. He dries up the swamp of saṃsāra, tames māra and those who oppose the teaching, lays low the victory banner of māra, and turns the Tathāgata's unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. What are these two? Skill in asking questions and skill in giving answers.

Son of good family, among the ten powers of a buddha, the power of karma is supreme. Son of good family, the reason these words were spoken was to discipline those sentient beings who minimize the causes of karma and lack trust in it. Son of good family, among all karma that has been done, some is light and some is heavy. And within these two, light and heavy, each again has two kinds: determinate and indeterminate.

Son of good family, some say that non-virtuous karma has no fruit. But if the fruit of non-virtuous karma were certainly fixed, why did the one called "the Breath-stealer of Evil Lineage" take birth as a god in the higher realms and attain the fruit of liberation through an ornament on his finger? For this reason there are those who say: among karma that has been performed, there is karma that will certainly yield fruit and karma that will certainly not yield fruit. In order to cut off wrong views, the sūtras declare: there is no karma that has been performed which will fail to yield fruit.

Son of good family, karma that is heavy can also become light, and karma that is light can also become heavy. Yet this does not apply to all beings universally; it is to be distinguished between those who are foolish and those who are wise. Therefore not all karma will certainly yield its fruit; and although it is not certain, it is also not the case that fruit will not be obtained.

Son of good family, all sentient beings are of two kinds: those with wisdom and those possessed of delusion. One with wisdom, through the power of wisdom, can experience even the very heavy karma of a hell-being as something slight in this very life, and thereby be liberated. One possessed of delusion, through light karma in this very life, will experience heavy karma of a hell-being.

Siṃha asked: Blessed One, if that is so, then pure brahmacarya (the holy life of celibacy) and the fruit of liberation would also be undesirable.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if all karma were to yield its fruit with certainty, then it might be said that the holy life and liberation are unnecessary. But because it is indeterminate, one must cultivate the fruit through the holy life and through liberation. Son of good family, if one abandons all non-virtuous karma, one obtains the fruit of virtue. If one abandons virtuous karma, one obtains the fruit of non-virtue.

If all karma were to yield its fruit with certainty, there would be no need to cultivate the noble path. And if the noble path is not cultivated, liberation will not be attained. Therefore, noble ones cultivate the path in order to destroy determined karma and to interrupt its ripening, and in order to prevent the fruit of indeterminate karma from ripening at all. If all karma were to yield its fruit with certainty, the noble path would become unnecessary; and beyond abandoning the cultivation of the noble path, there would be no other way to attain liberation. Nor would it make sense to say that one could attain nirvāṇa without having attained liberation.

Son of good family, if all karma were to yield its fruit with certainty, then one who had performed only virtuous karma in a single lifetime would experience happiness forever, and one who had performed grave non-virtuous karma in a single lifetime would experience immense suffering forever. If the fruits of karma worked in that way, there would be no path to cultivate, no liberation, and no nirvāṇa. It would likewise follow that a person would always remain a person, and a brahmin would always remain a brahmin. And if that were so, there would be no high or low births, a person would always be reborn as a person, and a brahmin would always be reborn as a brahmin. Karma performed in youth would be experienced in youth — at the appropriate time — and it would make no sense for it to be experienced in old age. Non-virtuous acts performed in old age, which lead to falling into hell, could not reasonably be experienced through the body born immediately into hell; rather, it would follow that they should only be experienced from old age onward. Furthermore, if those who refrained from killing in old age did not experience that karma in their prime, how could they grow old at all? This is because karma does not become nonexistent. And if karma does not become nonexistent, then it follows that the cultivation of the path and nirvāṇa would not exist.

Son of good family, karma is of two kinds: determinate and indeterminate. Determinate karma is itself of two kinds: that which is certain as to its ripening, and that which is certain as to its time. Among these, some karma is certain as to its ripening but uncertain as to its time, and is experienced when the proper conditions are met. Some karma is experienced in any of the three times: experienced now in this present life, experienced in the future, or experienced later still.

Son of good family, when one performs virtuous or non-virtuous karma with a resolute mind, and having done so generates a mind of deep faith, rejoices, and vows, "May I always make offerings to the Three Jewels" — such karma is determinate.

Son of good family, the virtuous roots of a person of wisdom are deep and firm and difficult to disturb, and so even grave karma can be made lighter. For a person of delusion, non-virtue is deep and dense and solid, and so even light karma can ripen into a heavy result. For these reasons, one should not say that all karma is determinate.

Although a great bodhisattva has no karma that would lead to the hells, he makes aspirational prayers to be born in hell for the sake of sentient beings. Son of good family, in former times, when the lifespan of beings was a hundred years, I saw beings — as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges River — experiencing suffering in the hells. Upon seeing them, I aroused a great resolve and took birth in the form of a hell-being. Although the bodhisattva at that time truly had no such karma, for the sake of sentient beings he took on the ripening of hell. I then remained in hell for countless years, widely opening and teaching the twelve branches of scripture to sinful beings.

Having heard the teaching, those beings broke the karmic maturation of their non-virtue and emptied even the hells of sentient beings — all except those possessed of inverted craving. This is what is meant by saying that the great bodhisattva does not experience non-virtuous karma in the present, the future, or thereafter.

Furthermore, son of good family, in this Fortunate Aeon, I saw countless sentient beings — beyond all measure — who had been born in the animal realm and were experiencing the fruits of non-virtuous karma. Seeing them, I again aroused a great resolve in order to teach the Dharma to those beings and liberate them. And so, at various times, I took on the bodies of a deer, a stag, a bear, a vulture, a monkey, a nāga, a snake, a garuḍa, a fish, a frog, a fox, a rabbit, an ox, a horse, and other such forms. Son of good family, although the great bodhisattva truly had no such wicked animal karma, through the power of great resolve he took on those bodies for the sake of sentient beings. This is what is meant by saying that the great bodhisattva does not experience non-virtuous karma in the present, the future, or thereafter.

Furthermore, son of good family, in this Fortunate Aeon, countless and boundless sentient beings were born as hungry ghosts (pretas). Their food was vomit, grease, flesh, pus, blood, excrement, urine, saliva, and mucus; and for a lifespan lasting hundreds of thousands of immeasurable tens of thousands of years, they had never even heard the word for water, let alone seen it with their eyes or drunk it. If they perceived water from afar and tried to draw near, the moment they arrived it would turn to fire, or to pus and blood. And even if it did not transform, many men with swords and spears would stand guard and not allow them to approach. If rain fell upon their bodies it would turn to fire. Such is the karmic maturation of the fruit of non-virtue. Yet the great bodhisattva, although he truly had no such fruit of non-virtuous karma, aroused a great resolve and took on such bodies in order to bring sentient beings to liberation and to the attainment of liberation. This is what is meant by saying that the great bodhisattva does not experience non-virtuous karma in the present, the future, or thereafter.

Son of good family, in this Fortunate Aeon, I was born into the household of a butcher, killing birds, pigs, oxen, and sheep, scattering the implements of a hunter, wielding fishing nets and the like — born into the house of a debased family — and I acted as a thief and a brigand. Yet the bodhisattva truly had no such karma. Rather, through the power of great aspirational prayer, he took on such a body in order to liberate sentient beings and bring them to the attainment of liberation. This is what is meant by saying that the great bodhisattva does not experience non-virtuous karma in the present, the future, or thereafter.

Son of good family, in this Fortunate Aeon, I was also born in the remote borderlands, performing many acts of attachment, aversion, and delusion, engaging in conduct contrary to the Dharma, having no faith in the Three Jewels or in the karmic maturation of the fruits of future lives, and showing no respect to parents, relatives, elders, or teachers. Son of good family, although the bodhisattva at that time truly had no such karma, through the power of great aspirational prayer he took birth in such a place in order to liberate sentient beings. This is what is meant by saying that the great bodhisattva does not experience non-virtuous karma in the present, the future, or thereafter.

Son of good family, in this Fortunate Aeon, I also took on a female body, a degraded body, a body dominated by attachment, a body dominated by aversion, a body dominated by delusion, and

a body dominated by envy, a body dominated by fear, an illusory body, a deceitful body, a body that was loose and dissolute, and a body that was bound and constrained. Son of good family, although the bodhisattva at that time truly had no such karma, through the power of great aspirational prayer he took birth in such a place in order to liberate sentient beings. This is what is meant by saying that the great bodhisattva does not experience non-virtuous karma in the present, the future, or thereafter.

Son of good family, in this Fortunate Aeon I also experienced a body as a hermaphrodite, a body without sex, a body of uncertain between two sexes, and a body uncertain even as to a single sex. Son of good family, although the great bodhisattva truly had no such non-virtuous karma of the body, through the power of great aspirational prayer he took birth in such a place in order to liberate sentient beings. This is what is meant by saying that the great bodhisattva does not experience non-virtuous karma of the body in the present, the future, or thereafter.

Son of good family, in this Fortunate Aeon I also placed my trust in the doctrine of the naked tīrthikas, coming to hold a view in which there is no giving, no sacrifice, no fruit of giving and sacrifice, no virtuous and non-virtuous karma, no karmic maturation ripening from virtuous and non-virtuous karma, no present time and no future time, no this shore and no further shore, no noble ones, no emanation body, no path, and no nirvāṇa. Son of good family, although the bodhisattva truly had no such non-virtuous karma, through the power of great aspirational prayer he entered into that doctrine of wrong view in order to liberate sentient beings. This is what is meant by saying that the great bodhisattva does not experience non-virtuous karma in the present, the future, or thereafter.

Son of good family, I recall that in the past, when Devadatta and I were both merchants, each of us had a following of five hundred traders. Desiring to acquire wealth, they set out to sea to obtain precious jewels, and by the force of non-virtuous karma they were suddenly struck by a fierce storm. The ship was wrecked, and all our companions perished. At that time, Devadatta and I, through the fruit of our having refrained from taking life, were long-lived, and the wind carried us to dry land. Then Devadatta, stricken with longing and attachment to the wealth and jewels, was tormented by the great pain of grief and broke into loud weeping. At that point I said to him, "Do not weep." Devadatta replied to me with these words: "Listen well and consider. For example, suppose a poor and destitute man goes to a charnel ground and, grasping a corpse by the hand, says: 'Give me the ease of death; I will give you this life of poverty and destitution.' The corpse then rises, sits up, and says to the poor man: 'Son of good family, I have no wish for the life of poverty and destitution. I am supremely at ease right now, so I have no desire for a life of poverty and destitution in exchange for the ease of death.' I am in just that same situation — I have no ease of death to offer, and I am poor besides, so how could I not weep?" I too then roused my spirits and said: "Do not grieve. I have two jewels of immeasurable value; I will give you one." And so I gave him one, saying furthermore: "Whoever has the means and power may well obtain this jewel, but if one lacks that power, one will not obtain it." At that time I was exhausted, and I sat down to rest at the foot of a tree and fell asleep.

Devadatta, his mind overcome with craving for the other jewel, harbored ill will toward me. He gouged out my eyes, stole the jewel, and fled. At that moment, crying out in pain from my eyes, I wept and lamented. A young woman came up to me and asked: "Young man, why are you weeping like this?" I told her the whole story in detail. After hearing what I said, she asked me: "What is your name?" I replied: "My name is Truthspeaker." The young woman said: "Whether your name is truly Truthspeaker or not, how can that be known?" Then I made this oath: "If I harbor any ill will toward Devadatta, may my eyes remain forever blind just as they are now. If I do not, may my eyes be restored." The moment I said this, my eyes became just as they had been before.

Noble son, this is a teaching on the immediate karmic ripening of a bodhisattva, a great being, in the present time.

Noble son, I remember with direct recollection that in a time long past, I was born in the home of a brahmin in a city called Putana, in the southern land of Vetāla. At that time there was a king named Kalāpu — wrathful and fierce, seized by pride, in the full vigor of youth and handsome in appearance, attached to and infatuated with the five objects of desire. At that time I was dwelling outside that city, practicing yoga for the sake of liberating sentient beings. Then the king, during the summer season when the flowers were in bloom, went outside the city together with his retinue of consorts and princes, purifying himself with incense at the foot of a tree, sporting with the five pleasures. The royal daughters and princes left the king and went off to play, and they came to where I was. I was there teaching the Dharma to cut off their attachment to desire. The king came following after them, and seeing me, ill will arose in him, and he questioned me as follows: "Have you attained the fruit of arhatship?" I replied: "I have not." He asked again: "Have you attained the fruit of non-returning?" I replied: "I have not." He asked again: "If you have not attained those two fruits, and you possess desire and afflictions, why do you, in your negligence, gaze upon my consorts?" I said: "Great King, understand it thus: although I have not yet cut off the arising of afflictions from desire outwardly, inwardly my mind is genuinely free of attachment." The king said: "Fool! Even the forest sages who breathe air and eat only wild fruits — when they see many beautiful forms, desire arises in them. You are in the prime of youth, and desire has not been cut off in you — how much more would you not become attached upon seeing many beautiful forms?" I replied: "Great King, being free of attachment upon seeing forms does not depend on breathing air and eating fruit. It comes about through the power of one-pointed meditation focused on impermanence and impurity." The king said: "If one disparages and reviles others, can that be called purity of moral discipline?" I said: "Great King, one who speaks with a mind of envy reviles another. If I have no envy in my mind, why would I revile?" The king said: "Venerable one, what is moral discipline?" I replied: "Great King, patience is what is called moral discipline." The king said: "If patience is moral discipline, then if I cut off your ears and you endure it, I will know you to be one who guards moral discipline." Having said this, he cut off my ears. At that moment my complexion did not change. The king's ministers, seeing what had occurred, said to the king: "Your Majesty, it is not right to harm this noble person." The king said to his ministers: "How do you know this is a noble person?" The ministers replied: "We know it because, in experiencing suffering, his complexion did not change."

The king said again: "Whether the complexion changes or not must be put to the test." Having said that, he cut off the nose and all the hands and feet.

At that time the bodhisattva, having cultivated loving-kindness and compassion for countless and immeasurable lifetimes, and having generated a mind of tender affection for sentient beings in suffering, the four guardian kings, enraged at what had occurred, sent down a rain of stones and gravel from the sky. Seeing this, the king was seized with fear. He knelt upon the ground and, wishing to repent out of heartfelt concern, offered this entreaty.

I replied: "Great King, in my mind there is no anger, and there is no attachment either."

The king said: "How can you know that there is no anger in your mind?"

Then I uttered this aspiration: "If I am truly without anger, may this body of mine become as it was before." And at that very instant the body became as it was before.

This illustrates the immediate, visible fruition of karma within this very life for a great bodhisattva, a great being.

O son of good family, just as the result of virtuous karma ripens in the future, in a later time, so too should one understand non-virtuous karma in the same way. When a great bodhisattva, a great being, attains unsurpassed perfect and complete awakening, the results of all karma ripen and become directly manifest. As for the direct and visible ripening of evil non-virtuous karma: it is like a king who, on account of non-virtuous deeds, has stones and gravel fall from the sky, or like one who points out a she-bear to a hunter, or like one who points out a deer with the coloring of jewels to a hunter, and whose hand then falls off — this is what is called the directly manifest ripening of the result of non-virtuous karma.

Ripening in the future refers to one who holds wrong views and who has incurred the four defeats and committed the five actions of immediate retribution. Later ripening refers to how those of moral discipline aspire: "In the future, may I obtain a body endowed with such complete purity of moral discipline. If beings are able to live for one hundred and eighty years, may I then become a wheel-turning king and accomplish the welfare of sentient beings."

O son of good family, if all karma were to ripen with certainty right now, in direct and immediate manifestation, then there would be no future ripening and no subsequent ripening. The karma cultivated by a great bodhisattva, a great being, for the thirty-two marks of a great person does not ripen directly and immediately in the present. Karma that does not ripen in these three modes of ripening is called indeterminate.

O son of good family, if someone were to say that all karma certainly and without exception ripens, then there would be no holy life, no liberation, and no nirvāṇa. Know that such a person is not an intimate follower of mine, but belongs to the retinue of Māra.

As for this matter, there is karma that is determinate and karma that is indeterminate. The determinate is that which ripens in the present, ripens in the future, or ripens subsequently thereafter. The indeterminate is that which, upon meeting with a condition, is experienced, and which, upon not meeting with a condition, is not experienced. One who teaches this understanding is one for whom holy life, liberation, and nirvāṇa exist — therefore such a one is truly an intimate follower of mine and does not belong to the retinue of Māra.

O son of good family, for all sentient beings the paths of indeterminacy are many, while the paths of certainty are few. It is for this reason that there is value in applying oneself to the path. Because one applies oneself to the path, even weighty karma can be lightened.

The path of indeterminacy is not something experienced in a future time.

O son of good family, persons are of two kinds. What are they? There is the kind who causes what is indeterminate to ripen as determinate; who causes a ripening that is presently occurring to ripen instead in the future; who causes a light ripening to become heavy; and who causes what was fitting to be experienced in a human birth to be experienced instead in hell. And there is the kind who causes what is fully determinate to become indeterminate; who reverses what was fitting to ripen in the future and causes it to ripen in the present instead; who causes a heavy ripening to become light; and who causes what was fitting to be experienced in hell to be experienced in a human birth. Of these two kinds of person, one is possessed of delusion and one is possessed of wisdom. The one possessed of wisdom makes karma light; the one possessed of delusion makes it heavy.

O son of good family, consider as an example two people who have transgressed the law of a king. The one of high position and great connections, even if the offense committed is grave, will have it reduced. The one of low position and few connections, even if the offense is minor, will have it made greater. The one possessed of delusion and the one possessed of wisdom are just like this: for the one possessed of wisdom, because wholesome karma is abundant, even heavy karma becomes light; for the one possessed of delusion, because wholesome karma is scarce, even light karma becomes heavy.

O son of good family, consider as an example two people: one is highly skilled at swimming, and one is a poor swimmer with little skill. If both fall into a bog, the skilled one will emerge, while the unskilled one will sink.

O son of good family, consider as an example two people who have drunk poison. One possesses the power of mantras and the antidote of medicine; the other possesses neither. The one who has mantras and medicine is not overcome by the poison. The one who has neither mantras nor medicine dies the moment it is drunk.

O son of good family, consider as an example two people who have drunk a great deal of alcohol. One has a strong digestive fire, and one has a weak digestive fire. The one with strong digestive fire is able to digest it. The one with weak digestive fire falls ill.

O son of good family, consider as an example two people imprisoned by a king. One is possessed of wisdom and skillful means, and one is dull-witted and bad. The one possessed of wisdom and skillful means is freed immediately. The dull-witted and bad one has no time of liberation.

O son of good family, consider as an example two people traveling a dangerous road. One has eyes, and one is blind. The one with eyes passes through safely, while the blind one falls into an abyss.

O son of good family, consider as an example two people who have drunk alcohol. One has eaten a large meal beforehand, and one has eaten little. The one who ate little, even having drunk, comes to no harm. The one who ate a large meal falls ill after drinking.

O son of good family, consider as an example two people who have gone into battle. One is equipped with armor and weapons, and the other has nothing at all. The one equipped with armor and weapons will subdue the enemy, while the one with nothing cannot even save himself.

And again, consider two people whose clothes are soiled by something unclean. One washes immediately upon noticing it, and the other notices but does not wash. The garment of the one who washed is clean. For the one who did not wash, the defilement grows ever greater with time.

And again, consider two people who both ride a horse-drawn carriage. One has a srogśing and the other does not. The one with the srogśing travels at will, while the one without it cannot move from where it stands.

And again, consider two people who have gone into a vast wilderness. One has provisions and companions, and the other has none. The one with provisions and companions crosses through the wilderness, while the one who went empty-handed cannot cross. And again, consider two people who have been overcome by famine —

One has a treasure of jewels, and the other does not. The one who has the jewel-treasure, even when ruined, feels no sorrow, whereas the one without the treasure is consumed by grief.
