It is just the same with the one who is deluded and the one who is wise: the one who possesses the treasure of virtue experiences even heavy karma as something light, while the one who lacks that treasure experiences even light karma as heavy.

The bodhisattva Siṃhaghosa then asked: "Blessed One, you have declared that not all karma will necessarily yield its fruit, and that not all sentient beings will necessarily experience the result. Why, then, did the Blessed One say that sentient beings whose present ripening is light will experience the heavy ripening of the hells, while those whose ripening of the hells is heavy will experience it as light in this very life?"

The Blessed One replied: All sentient beings are of two kinds — the wise, who have wisdom, and the foolish, who are deluded. Those who cultivate body, moral discipline, mind, and wisdom are the wise. Those who do not cultivate body, moral discipline, mind, and wisdom are called the deluded.

How is it that one does not cultivate the body? Not gathering in the five sense faculties is not cultivating the body. Not upholding the seven aspects of pure moral discipline is not cultivating moral discipline. Not taming the mind is not cultivating the mind. Not engaging in the practice of the noble ones is not cultivating wisdom.

Furthermore, not cultivating the body means lacking the essential nature of pure moral discipline. Not cultivating moral discipline means carrying eight kinds of substance that have not been examined. Not cultivating the mind means being unable to cultivate the three kinds of defining marks. Not cultivating wisdom means not practicing the holy life.

Furthermore, not cultivating the body means: not reflecting on the body, not reflecting on form, not reflecting on the defining marks of form, not reflecting on the defining marks of the body, not knowing what arises from the body, not knowing how the body passes on from here to elsewhere, and grasping at what is not the body as bearing the marks of body, and grasping at what is not form as bearing the marks of form, while clinging to self, to body, and to what arises from the body — this is called not cultivating the body.

Not cultivating moral discipline means: taking up inferior moral discipline is not to be called cultivating moral discipline. Holding to peripheral ethical codes, to moral discipline that benefits only oneself, and to moral discipline merely for self-restraint — without benefiting all sentient beings, and not for the sake of guarding the supreme sacred Dharma — but rather in order to be born as a god in the higher realms and to enjoy the pleasures of the five desirable objects: this is not to be called cultivating moral discipline.

Not cultivating the mind means: when the mind is disturbed and distracted, being unable to protect one's own domain with single-pointed attention. What is meant by "one's own domain" is this: the four applications of mindfulness (smṛti). What is not one's own domain is this: the five objects of desire. Whoever is unable to cultivate the four applications of mindfulness is not to be called one who cultivates the mind. Whoever does not guard the mind against non-virtuous actions is not to be called one who cultivates wisdom.

Furthermore, not cultivating the body means being unable to clearly recognize that this body is impermanent, unstable, unreliable, disintegrating and ceasing moment by moment, and that it is the domain of Māra. Not cultivating moral discipline means lacking the perfection of moral discipline. Not cultivating the mind means lacking the perfection of meditative concentration.

Not cultivating wisdom means lacking the Perfection of Wisdom.

Furthermore, not cultivating the body means being attached to one's body, to what belongs to oneself, and to the idea that one's body is permanent and unchanging. Not cultivating moral discipline means committing the ten non-virtuous actions for the sake of one's body. Not cultivating the mind means being unable to withdraw the mind from non-virtuous actions. Not cultivating wisdom means that, because the mind is not withdrawn, one is unable to discern wholesome from unwholesome phenomena.

Furthermore, not cultivating the body means failing to cut through the view of self. Not cultivating moral discipline means failing to cut through conceit about one's moral discipline. Not cultivating the mind means acting out of attachment and aversion and thereby going to a hell realm.

Furthermore, not cultivating the body means being unable to examine sense objects clearly, and so treating everything as an enemy without cause.

Noble son, consider this analogy: if an enemy constantly follows a person and seeks an opportunity to strike, a wise person, perceiving this, always remains single-pointedly vigilant. If one is not vigilant, one will be harmed by that enemy. In just the same way, all sentient beings must constantly tend their bodies with drink, food, warmth, and cold in proper measure. If they do not so tend them and remain vigilant, the body will deteriorate and fall apart.

Noble son, consider further: a brahmin devoted to the fire god (Agni) may continually offer incense and flowers, sing praises, prostrate, and make offerings and acts of service for a hundred years, and yet the moment he touches the fire, his hand will be burned. However much he has worshipped that fire, it cannot repay even an instant's worth of gratitude for such veneration. All sentient beings are just like that. Though for many years one has nourished the body with incense, flowers, garlands, clothing, food, bedding, and medicines for illness, if it encounters causes of non-virtue from within or without, it will crumble and perish, without giving the slightest thought to the kindness of all the clothing and food with which it was sustained.

Noble son, consider this analogy: a king keeps four venomous serpents, places them in a single container, and assigns one person to tend them. If any one of those four venomous serpents becomes enraged, it will kill the person. Out of fear, that person constantly seeks food for them and feeds them at the proper times. The four great elements in the bodies of all sentient beings are just like this: if any one of the four great elements turns against the body, the body will be destroyed.

Noble son, consider this analogy: when a person falls ill, they earnestly seek medicine and a physician, and carry out the proper procedures for treating the illness. If the illness is not properly cured, death is certain. The bodies of all sentient beings are just the same: one must never be heedless in withdrawing and steadying the mind. If one is heedless, the body will disintegrate and perish.

Noble son, consider this analogy: an unfired clay vessel cannot withstand wind, rain, blows, being dropped, or being pressed upon. The bodies of all sentient beings are just the same: they cannot endure hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, rain, blows, binding, or abuse.

Noble son, consider this analogy: when an abscess swells, one must always be careful and not allow it to be touched. If it is touched even once, it causes tremendous pain and suffering. The bodies of all sentient beings are just the same.

Noble son, consider this analogy: when a she-monkey is pregnant, she becomes entirely preoccupied with her own body. Just so, when the bodies of all sentient beings are afflicted by disorders of wind and phlegm internally, they experience suffering.

Noble son, consider this analogy: when a fruit forms on a water-tree, it immediately begins to shrivel and dry. The bodies of all sentient beings are just the same.

Noble son, consider this analogy: just as a water-tree has no heartwood, the bodies of all sentient beings are just the same.

Noble son, consider this analogy: just as a snake and a mongoose always harbor harmful intentions toward one another, the four great elements of a sentient being's body are just the same.

Noble son, consider this analogy: just as the king of geese takes no delight in a charnel ground, a bodhisattva is just the same — holding no attachment or fondness for the charnel ground of the body.

Noble son, consider this analogy: just as one of base lineage who performs the deeds of a base lineage for seven generations in succession comes to be despised by all, the seed of the body is just the same — its seed arising from semen and blood, it is ultimately impure. Being thus impure, it is thoroughly censured by buddhas and bodhisattvas.

Noble son, this body is utterly unlike Mount Mālaya, for on it sandalwood, utpala flowers, pundarīka, campaka, mālikā, and pāriśāka do not grow. Through its nine openings it perpetually leaks blood, pus, and filth. It arose in a place rank with stench, it is repellent and fit to inspire dejection, and it dwells always in the company of worms.

Noble son, consider this analogy: just as a corpse placed within the enclosure of a fine, pure pleasure garden does not render that garden pure, and all people abandon it and no thought of attachment arises, so too the element of form is just the same — though pure and excellent in itself, because a body is present, buddhas and bodhisattvas utterly renounce it.

Noble son, one who cannot contemplate the body in this way should not be called one who cultivates meditation on the body.

As for not cultivating meditation on moral discipline: Noble son, whoever recognizes that moral discipline is the threshold of the stairway to all wholesome phenomena, and the very root of all wholesome phenomena — just as the great earth is the place from which all trees and forests grow — and that it goes first among all wholesome roots, just as a merchant goes first among all traders, should understand that moral discipline is the victory banner of all wholesome phenomena, like the raising of Śakra's victory banner. Moral discipline severs, once and for all, every unwholesome action and the actions leading to the three lower destinies. It heals the disease of non-virtue, like a medicinal tree. Moral discipline is like a provision of supplies for one traversing the rough road of saṃsāra. Moral discipline is the weapon and armor for vanquishing the enemy of affliction. Moral discipline is the mantra (vidyā) that renders the venomous serpent of affliction harmless. Moral discipline is like a bridge that liberates from the practice of unwholesome actions. One who cannot contemplate this should not be called one who cultivates meditation on moral discipline.

As for not cultivating meditation on the mind: the mind is distracted, agitated, changeable, difficult to grasp, and difficult to tame — wandering in all directions like an unruly dzo-bull. Moment to moment it is swift, like a flash of lightning. The mind is turbulent and will not stay still, like a monkey. The mind is like an illusion or a mirage, and is the root of all non-virtue. The five objects of desire are insatiable, like fire meeting wood. The mind is like an ocean, able to receive all rivers. The mind is like Mount Mālaya — a place where many grasses and trees grow — yet it cannot be contemplated and brings harm through attachment to the deceptions of false saṃsāra, just as fish are caught by a hook. That karma perpetually follows after whatever comes first is like the way that when a mother fish goes ahead, the young follow after her. Being attached to the five objects of desire and feeling no aspiration for nirvāṇa is like the way that when a bee has eaten honey it does not look toward the grass until it reaches the point of death. Attached to present pleasure and giving no thought to future harm —

Just as a calf is so attached to its mother cow that even when beaten with a stick it feels no fear, so does one circle and rush through the twenty-five modes of existence. That one is never satisfied in seeking what ought not be sought is like the way that foolish and stupid people seek fire that does not burn. That one always delights in saṃsāra and takes no delight in liberation is like the way the insect called the tree-clinging grub is attached to the crumbling of wood. That one craves and is attached to the foul-smelling stench of the deceptive wheel of existence is like the way prisoners delight in the warden's daughter, or like the way a pig is attached to filth. One who is unable to reflect in this way is said to be one who does not cultivate the mind.

As for not cultivating wisdom: to be unable to reflect that wisdom, with its great power and strength like that of Garuḍa flying through the sky, destroys all evil karma; that like sunlight it dispels the darkness of ignorance; that it tears out from the root the very roots of the tree of the aggregates, like the power of a violent river sweeping everything away; that it burns up wrong views like the power of a blazing fire; and that wisdom is the root of all virtuous phenomena and the mother and seed of all buddhas and bodhisattvas — such a one is not to be called one who cultivates wisdom.

Noble son, if in regard to the ultimate one views the body, the defining characteristics of the body, the cause of the body, the result of the body, the aggregates of the body, the first body, the second body, this body, the body of the other shore, the cessation of the body, the evenness of the body, and the cultivation of body by means of body — that is not to be called the cultivation of the body.

Noble son, whoever views moral discipline, the defining characteristics of moral discipline, the cause of moral discipline, the result of moral discipline, superior moral discipline, middling moral discipline, inferior moral discipline, the accumulation of moral discipline, the first moral discipline, the second moral discipline, this moral discipline, the moral discipline of the other shore, the cessation of moral discipline, the evenness of moral discipline, the cultivation of moral discipline by means of moral discipline, and the perfection of moral discipline — that is not to be called the cultivation of moral discipline.

Whoever views mind, the defining characteristics of mind, the cause of mind, the result of mind, the accumulation of mind, mind, what arises from mind, the first mind, the second mind, this mind, the mind of the other shore, the cessation of mind, the evenness of mind, the cultivation of mind by means of mind, superior mind, middling mind, inferior mind, the non-virtuous mind, and what is to be regarded as a non-virtuous mind — that is not to be called the cultivation of mind.

Noble son, whoever views wisdom, the defining characteristics of wisdom, the cause of wisdom, the result of wisdom, the accumulation of wisdom, the first wisdom, the second wisdom, this wisdom, the wisdom of the other shore, the cessation of wisdom, the evenness of wisdom, superior wisdom, middling wisdom, inferior wisdom, dull wisdom, sharp wisdom, and the cultivation of wisdom by means of wisdom — that is not to be called the cultivation of wisdom.

Noble son, one who does not cultivate body, moral discipline, mind, and wisdom will, even through a small non-virtuous action, arrive at a great karmic maturation of non-virtue. Out of fear of this, one should always think: "I, a sentient being, belong to hell and accordingly carry out the conduct of a hell-being." And even upon hearing a wise and discerning person teach the sufferings of the hells, one should always think: just as iron strikes iron, stone strikes stone, wood strikes wood, and insects that delight in fire resemble fire — in the same way the very body of a hell-being is commensurate with hell itself.

Thinking in this way — that a sentient being is commensurate with hell itself — one reflects: "What is there in the nature of things that is not suffering?" Just as a fly becomes stuck in mucus and cannot get free, so too it is the same for that being: one cannot get free even from a small non-virtue, and from the very beginning there is no mind of remorse. One cannot practice virtue, and having been tainted by faults, even the previously accumulated virtuous karma is stained by non-virtue. The karmic maturation that would fittingly be experienced in the present time is thereby altered, and the fruit of non-virtue in the hells becomes exceedingly heavy.

Noble son, just as when a small amount of salt is put into a small vessel with only a little water, the taste becomes so salty it is extremely difficult to drink — so too is the karma of that person's non-virtue.

Noble son, consider the example of a person who owes a single coin to another and, being unable to repay even that debt, is bound tightly and must endure great suffering — so too is the karma of that person's non-virtue.

The bodhisattva Lion's Roar (Siṃhanāda) asked: "Blessed One, for what reason does a karmic maturation that would fittingly be experienced in the present become experienced in the hells?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, when any sentient being possesses these five things, a present-life karmic maturation will come to be experienced in the hells instead. What are the five? Being deluded; having few roots of virtue; having heavy non-virtuous karma; having performed no complete remorse; and not engaging in one's former virtuous karma.

"Again, there are five more: engaging in non-virtuous actions; lacking the wealth of moral discipline; abandoning the roots of virtue; not cultivating body, moral discipline, mind, and wisdom; and relying on unwholesome spiritual friends. Noble son, for these reasons the ripened fruit of present-life karma comes to be experienced as the heavy karmic maturation of the hells.

Lion's Roar asked: "Blessed One, what persons are there who alter a heavy karmic maturation of the hells so that it is experienced lightly in the present life?"

The Blessed One declared: "Noble son, whoever cultivates body, moral discipline, mind, and wisdom, and — as explained above — realizes that all phenomena are like space: not regarding wisdom as wisdom, not regarding what possesses wisdom as possessing wisdom, not regarding delusion as delusion, not regarding what possesses delusion as possessing delusion, not regarding meditation as meditation, not regarding what is meditating as meditating — such a one is called a person of wisdom. Through cultivating body, moral discipline, mind, and wisdom, such a person experiences the heavy ripened fruit of the hells lightly in the present life. Even if such a person has performed deeply heavy non-virtuous karma, they think: 'My karma is very heavy, yet I need not think I am incapable of even a little virtuous action.' This is how it is:

Just as a hundred packs of cotton wool have no weight equivalent to even a single tola of pure gold; or just as a full bowl of salt poured into the river Ganges does not make it salty, and those who drink from it do not notice the salt; or just as a very wealthy person to whom another owes even hundreds of thousands of jewels cannot be bound tightly and made to suffer by anyone — or just as a great musk elephant, having snapped the iron hook used to guide it, is able to go wherever it pleases — so too is the person of wisdom. Such a person always thinks: 'My power of virtue is great, and since non-virtuous karma is weak, if I confess and acknowledge my misdeeds, the negativity will be purified; and if I cultivate wisdom, the power of wisdom will grow great and the power of ignorance will become small.' With this in mind, one relies upon a virtuous spiritual friend, becomes familiar with the correct view, and holds the twelve branches of the sūtras by heart.

One reads them, recites them, writes them down and teaches them to others; and when one sees others who are memorizing, reading, reciting, copying, or teaching them to others, one gives rise to a mind of reverence. One makes offerings of robes, food, lodging, bedding, medicine for illness, flowers, and incense, and renders homage and service. Wherever one goes, one speaks of the good qualities of that place and does not speak of its faults. One makes offerings to the Three Jewels, and through supreme confidence — drawn from the vast and extensive sūtra on nirvāṇa — that the Tathāgata is permanent, unchanging, and unaltering, and that the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present in all sentient beings, one now experiences, even in the present moment, the lightening of the heavy karmic maturation of the hell realms.

Noble son, for this reason not all karma necessarily bears fruit, and not all sentient beings necessarily experience it.

The bodhisattva Siṃhanāda then asked: Blessed One, if all karma necessarily comes to have a lighter result, and since all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha they will come to cultivate the noble eightfold path — then by what cause and condition have not all sentient beings already fully attained nirvāṇa? Blessed One, if all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha and will assuredly attain unsurpassed complete awakening, then what is the use of cultivating the noble eightfold path? Blessed One, this sūtra says that just as a sick person, if properly treated with medicine, a physician, a nurse, and care suited to the illness, will be cured of that sickness — so too it is with all sentient beings: by hearing the Dharma from śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, Tathāgatas, bodhisattvas, and virtuous spiritual friends, and by cultivating the noble path, or even if one does not encounter them, or has not heard it, or has not cultivated the path, one will still attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present. Blessed One, just as the sun and moon cannot be prevented from reaching a mountain range, just as the four great rivers cannot be stopped from reaching the ocean, and just as those with wrong craving cannot be prevented from going to the hell realms — so too with all sentient beings: there is no one who can prevent them from going toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Why is that? Because the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present. Blessed One, for this reason it seems that all sentient beings, without needing to cultivate the path, will attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening through the power of the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and are therefore not at all dependent on the power of cultivating the noble path. Blessed One, if even those with wrong craving, those who have broken the four defeats, and those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution cannot attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening — if one must cultivate the path — then since they are certain to attain it through the intrinsic nature of a buddha, it would not be that they attain it through cultivating the path. Blessed One, consider a magnet: though it is not close to iron, by its power it holds the iron. The intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings is just like that — and therefore there is no need to strive on the noble path.

The Blessed One declared: Excellent! Excellent! Noble son, consider this: seven kinds of people are bathing on the bank of the Ganges river, or they have entered the water out of fear of an enemy, or to gather flowers. Of these, one, the moment he enters the water, sinks.

Why is that? It is because such a person is weak, with no strength or skill, not having learned to swim. Of these seven, one enters the water and sinks, but having sunk, rises back up again — and having risen, sinks once more. Why is that? Because of great physical strength, he is able to sink and then rise; yet because he has not learned to swim, having risen he sinks once more. Of these, one sinks and then rises, and having risen, does not sink again. Why is that? Though his body is heavy so that he sinks, because of his great strength he rises back up; and because he has learned to swim, he does not sink again. Of these, one enters the water and sinks; having sunk, he rises back up; and having risen, he pauses and looks in all four directions. Why is that? Though his body is heavy so that he sinks, because of his great strength he comes back up; and because he has learned to swim, he stays there — yet not knowing the way out, he looks in all four directions. Of these, one enters the water and sinks; having sunk, he rises back up again; having risen, he pauses; and having paused, he looks in all four directions; and having looked, he sets off. Why is that? Out of fear. Of these, one enters the water and sets off; and when he reaches the bottom he stays there. Why is that? Because he is watching to see whether enemies are near or far. Of these, one reaches the far bank and climbs a high mountain; freed from enemies, he is without fear and becomes utterly at ease.

Noble son, the great river of saṃsāra is just like that, and there are seven kinds of people in it. They too, out of fear of the enemy that is mental affliction, think to cross the great river of saṃsāra, and so they go forth from home into homelessness. They shave their hair and beards and clothe their bodies in the Dharma robes. Having thus gone forth, they associate with companions in non-virtue, listen to their words, and take hold of these wrong teachings: the body of a sentient being is constituted by the five aggregates (skandhas), and the five aggregates are the five great elements; if a sentient being dies, the five great elements are permanently cut off; and if the five great elements are permanently cut off, why bother cultivating virtuous and non-virtuous actions? They therefore declare: understand that there is no virtue, no non-virtue, and no karmic maturation of the virtuous and the non-virtuous. One who holds such a view is called one of perverted craving. One of perverted craving is called one who severs all virtuous roots. Because the virtuous roots are severed, such a person sinks in the river of saṃsāra and cannot rise back out. Why is that? Because of the weight of non-virtuous karma and the absence of the power of faith — such a person is like the first of the people at the Ganges river.

Noble son, those of perverted craving, through six causes and conditions, sink into the three lower states and cannot rise back out. What are the six? They are as follows: a blazing mind of non-virtue; not seeing the next world; delighting in the pursuit of mental afflictions; abandoning the roots of virtue; being blocked and cut off by non-virtuous karma; and relying on companions in non-virtue.

Furthermore, through five kinds of actions, one sinks into the three lower states. What are the five? Acting improperly toward monks; acting improperly toward nuns; forcibly making use of the Saṅgha's property; acting improperly toward one's mother; and, with respect to a divided community of five members of the Saṅgha, generating the thought that what is not proper is proper and what is proper is not.

Furthermore, through five kinds of actions one falls into the three lower states. What are the five? Constantly teaching that virtuous and non-virtuous actions have no result; taking the life of a sentient being who has generated the awakening mind of bodhicitta; slandering one who teaches the Dharma; declaring that what is Dharma is not Dharma and what is not Dharma is Dharma; and listening to the Dharma for the purpose of finding fault with it.

Furthermore, through three kinds of actions one sinks into the three lower states. What are the three?

Saying that the Tathāgata is impermanent and therefore ceases, saying that the sacred Dharma is also impermanent and therefore changes and passes away, and saying that the Saṅgha Jewel will come to an end — on account of these three one constantly sinks into the three lower states.

That person, even while desiring to cross over the great river of saṃsāra, has cut off the roots of virtue and therefore, having sunk, cannot emerge. Now, what is meant by "emerging" is this: by attending upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) one attains a mind of faith. A mind of faith means: trusting in generosity and in the fruit of generosity; trusting in virtue and in the fruit of virtue; trusting in non-virtue and in the fruit of non-virtue; and trusting that saṃsāra is suffering, impermanent, and subject to destruction. That is what is called faith.

Because one possesses a mind of faith, one dwells in pure moral discipline and holds dhāraṇīs, reciting them, chanting them, writing them down, expounding and explaining them. One practises generosity constantly and cultivates wisdom. Yet, because one's faculties are dull, if one encounters a spiritual friend of unwholesome kind, one does not cultivate body, moral discipline, mind, and wisdom, and one takes hold of wrong teachings. Moreover, if in an evil age one is born in a bad region, the roots of virtue are cut. Because the roots of virtue are cut, one sinks continuously into saṃsāra. Such a person is like the second person on the river Gaṅgā.

Of those persons, the one who desires to cross the great river of saṃsāra, yet has cut the roots of virtue and therefore sunk — because that one attends upon a spiritual friend, this is called "emerging." The Tathāgata is omniscient; he does not change and does not become impermanent; for the sake of sentient beings he teaches the unsurpassed Dharma. All sentient beings possess buddha-nature. The Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha are not subject to cessation — having faith and confidence in this, one who still holds wrong cravings believes: "Unless I abandon these teachings, I shall never attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; but if I utterly relinquish them, I shall attain it from the very beginning." With such a mind of faith and confidence one cultivates pure moral discipline, and having cultivated pure moral discipline, one holds the twelve branches of scripture as dhāraṇīs, reciting, chanting, writing, and analyzing them, and teaches them extensively to all sentient beings. One delights in generosity and cultivates wisdom. In this way, because one's faculties are sharp, one comes to have faith and wisdom firmly established, and with a mind free from turning back — such a person is like the third person on the river Gaṅgā.

Of those persons, the one who desires to cross the great river of saṃsāra, yet has cut the roots of virtue and therefore sunk there — because that one attends upon a spiritual friend and possesses a mind of faith, this is called "emerging." Because one possesses a mind of faith, one holds the twelve branches of scripture as dhāraṇīs, reciting, chanting, writing, and analyzing them, and teaches them extensively to all sentient beings. One delights in generosity and cultivates wisdom. Thus, because one's faculties are sharp and one comes to rely on faith and wisdom, with a mind free from turning back one looks toward the four directions. What is meant by "looking toward the four directions" is the four fruits of the ascetic life — just as with the fourth person on the river Gaṅgā. Of those persons, the one who desires to cross that great river of saṃsāra, yet has cut the roots of virtue and therefore sunk there — because that one attends upon a spiritual friend and possesses a mind of faith, this is called "emerging." Because one possesses a mind of faith, one holds the twelve branches of scripture as dhāraṇīs, reciting, chanting, writing, and analyzing them, and teaches them extensively to all sentient beings.

One delights in generosity and cultivates wisdom. In this way, because the faculties have become sharp, faith and wisdom grow firm, and the mind of turning back is no more. Because there is no turning back, one leaps ever higher. That leaping ever higher is the pratyekabuddha. Although that one has liberated oneself, it is not so for all sentient beings — and therefore this is called "going." It is comparable to the fifth person on the river Gaṅgā. Of those persons, the one who desires to cross that great river of saṃsāra, yet has cut the roots of virtue and therefore sunk there — because that one attends upon a spiritual friend and comes to possess a mind of faith, this is called "emerging." Because one possesses a mind of faith, one holds the twelve branches of scripture as dhāraṇīs, reciting, chanting, writing, and analyzing them, and teaches them extensively to all sentient beings. One delights in generosity and cultivates wisdom. In this way, because the faculties have become sharp, faith and wisdom grow firm, and the mind of turning back is no more. Because there is no turning back, one leaps ever higher — advancing until one reaches the very bottom. Having reached the bottom, one remains there and does not move on. "Remaining there and not moving on" means this: the bodhisattva, in order to liberate sentient beings, deliberately engages with afflictions. This is comparable to the sixth person on the river Gaṅgā. Of those persons, the one who desires to cross that great river of saṃsāra, yet has cut the roots of virtue and sunk there — because that one attends upon a spiritual friend and comes to possess a mind of faith, this is called "emerging." Because one possesses a mind of faith, one holds the twelve branches of scripture as dhāraṇīs, reciting, chanting, writing, and analyzing them, and teaches them extensively to all sentient beings. One delights in generosity and cultivates wisdom. In this way, because the faculties have become sharp, faith and wisdom grow firm, and the mind of turning back is no more. Because there is no turning back, one leaps ever higher. By leaping ever higher, one arrives at the farther shore — ascending a great mountain, one abandons fearful enemies and comes to experience many joys. Noble son, "arriving at the farther shore" signifies the Tathāgata. "Experiencing joy" signifies the buddha's permanence. "Dwelling on the high mountain" is the simile for the great, complete nirvāṇa.

Noble son, just as all those persons on the river Gaṅgā possessed hands and feet yet were unable to cross, so too are all sentient beings. Although there truly exist the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha, and although the Tathāgata has taught the sūtra of all phenomena — the noble path with its eightfold branches — and great complete nirvāṇa, still sentient beings are unable to attain it. You should understand that this is not a fault of mine, nor a fault of the noble path; it is a fault arising from the flaws and afflictions of sentient beings themselves. It is for this reason that all sentient beings have not attained nirvāṇa.

Noble son, consider, for example, a skilled physician who, having understood the nature of a disease, prescribes medicine. If the patient does not drink it, the fault is not the physician's. Noble son, if a single patron were to give all his wealth to everyone, and some refused to accept it, the fault would not be the patron's. Noble son, consider the sun rising: even the deepest crevices are illumined, yet if a blind person does not see the path, the fault is not the sun's.

Noble son, consider, for example, how the waters of the Ganges river can satisfy the thirst of many. Yet if the thirsty do not drink, the fault is not the water's.

Noble son, consider, for example, how the great earth brings forth all fruits equally and without distinction. Yet if a farmer does not till the soil, the fault is not the earth's.

Noble son, in just the same way, the Tathāgata extensively expounds and teaches the twelve branches of scripture to all sentient beings without exception. If sentient beings do not take it up, the fault is not the Tathāgata's.

Noble son, whoever cultivates the path will attain the unsurpassed, utterly complete awakening of an arhat.

Noble son, your assertion that because all sentient beings possess the buddha-nature they will therefore attain the unsurpassed, utterly complete awakening — just as iron is drawn to a magnet — that much is excellent, well said. However, your further assertion that by the power of having the buddha-nature as their cause they will attain unsurpassed, utterly complete awakening and therefore need not cultivate the noble path — that meaning is not so.

Noble son, consider, for example, a person who, having gone to a solitary wilderness, is tormented by thirst and comes upon a well. The well is very deep, and though the water cannot be seen, one knows with certainty that it is there. Only after that person, by means and effort, has sought a vessel and a rope and lowered them does the water at last come into view. The buddha-nature is just like that: it is present in all sentient beings, yet only by cultivating the undefiled noble path does one at last come to see it.

Noble son, just as when sesame seeds are present, oil too will come to be seen — yet if the methods are abandoned, it will not be seen — so too with sugarcane, it is the same.

Noble son, consider, for example, how the gods of the Thirty-Three Heavens and the Dharma of Uttarakuru exist, yet without the power of virtuous karma or supernatural ability, one cannot see them. Just as the roots of grass beneath the ground and the water beneath the earth are hidden under the soil and cannot be seen, the buddha-nature in sentient beings is likewise: if the noble path is not cultivated, it will not be seen.

Noble son, consider how in the world a sick person might meet a good nurse, fine medicine, and a skilled physician, and medicine might be administered exactly according to the nature of the disease — or even if they do not meet such conditions, they may recover. Noble son, it is on that same point that I have taught these matters to bodhisattvas on the sixth ground.

Noble son, consider, for example, how space is neither inside all sentient beings nor outside them nor both inside and outside, and for that reason is without obstruction. The buddha-nature in sentient beings is just like that.

Noble son, consider, for example, how a person's wealth may reside somewhere else and not be at hand, yet that person has power to use it at will. And if someone were to ask whether it is truly theirs, the answer would be: "I have power over it" — and why? Because it is assuredly under their command. The buddha-nature in sentient beings is just like that: it is neither here nor there, and yet, because it is something they are certain to obtain, it is said to be present in all.

Noble son, consider, for example, how the virtuous and non-virtuous karma performed by sentient beings is neither inside nor outside. And in that way the intrinsic nature of karma neither simply exists nor simply does not exist; it is not something that has been present from beginningless time until now; it does not arise without cause; it is not the case that the one who acts experiences the result; nor is it the case that the one who acts causes another to experience it; nor does one person's act cause another person to experience its result; yet neither is there no acting nor no experiencing. Rather, when the right time and conditions have gathered, the result ripens —

The intrinsic nature of a buddha within sentient beings is likewise thus: it has no beginning, nor does it presently exist; it is not inside, it is not outside; it does not exist, it does not not-exist; it is not here, it is not elsewhere; it has not come from somewhere else; nor is it without cause; nor is it seen by all sentient beings. Bodhisattvas, however, will come to see it when the right time and conditions have gathered. As for what "the right time" means: it is this — when a bodhisattva, a great being on the tenth ground, is cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path and has attained a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, then and there that sight arises. Such a one is not to be called a child.

Good son, as for your saying "this is like a lodestone attracting iron" — that is not the right way to understand it. Why? Because the stone does not grasp the iron. And why is that? Because there is neither mind nor karma. Good son, because distinct phenomena exist, distinct phenomena arise; because distinct phenomena are absent, distinct phenomena cease. There is no one who creates and no one who destroys.

Good son, consider, for example, how a spark cannot burn wood all by itself, yet once fire has arisen and the wood has broken apart, it is called burning. Good son, consider how the sunflower turns to follow the sun: the sunflower has no intention to bow, no consciousness, no karma, yet by virtue of the characteristics of distinct phenomena, it naturally rotates and turns. Good son, consider how the trumpet tree grows when the sound of thunder is heard: that tree has no ears, no mind, no mental consciousness, yet because distinct phenomena exist, distinct phenomena arise, and when distinct phenomena are absent, distinct phenomena cease. Good son, consider how when a woman touches an Aśoka tree, flowers spring forth: that tree has no mind, no feeling of being touched, yet because distinct phenomena exist, distinct phenomena arise, and when distinct phenomena are absent, distinct phenomena cease. Good son, consider how a tamarind tree, when watered and fertilized with teeth-dust, bones, and scum, bears better and more abundant fruit: that tamarind tree has no mind and no sense of touch, yet because distinct phenomena exist, distinct phenomena arise, and when distinct phenomena are absent, distinct phenomena cease. Good son, a lodestone attracting iron is likewise: because distinct phenomena exist, distinct phenomena arise, and when distinct phenomena are absent, distinct phenomena cease. The intrinsic nature of a buddha within sentient beings is similarly so: it cannot take up unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening by means of grasping.

Good son, ignorance cannot take up the formations, nor can the formations take up consciousness, yet through the condition of ignorance arise the formations, and through the condition of the formations arises consciousness — this is how it is called. Whether or not a buddha is present, the dharmadhātu (basic space of phenomena) abides always.

Good son, if one says "the intrinsic nature of a buddha abides within sentient beings" — good son, a permanent phenomenon has no fixed abode; if it had a fixed abode, it would become impermanent. Good son, the twelve links of dependent origination have no fixed abode where they permanently reside. If there were a fixed abode where they reside, the twelve links of dependent origination could not be called impermanent. Likewise, the dharmakāya (truth body) of the Tathāgata has no fixed abode; nor do the dharmadhātu, the sense base of phenomena, the aggregate of phenomena,

space too has no fixed abode where it permanently resides. The intrinsic nature of a buddha likewise has no fixed abode where it permanently resides.

Good son, consider this example: the four great elements are equal in power. All share the same characteristics — solidity, heat, moisture, movement, lightness, heaviness, red, white, yellow, and black — yet the four great elements have no activity of their own. Just as, through the realm of distinct phenomena, they are individually distinct from one another, so too the intrinsic nature of a buddha is like that: through the realm of distinct phenomena, when the right time is encountered, it is seen for the very first time.

Good son, it is said that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha because they cannot turn back from it. Because they cannot turn back from it, because they will come to possess it, because they will certainly attain it, because they will certainly come to see it — for all these reasons, it is said that all sentient beings have the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Good son, here is an example. A certain king commanded one of his great ministers: "Bring a woolen ox and show it to the blind." The great minister, following the royal command, gathered the blind people together and displayed the woolen ox to them, and each of them felt it with their hands. The minister then reported back to the king, saying, "I have shown it to them." The king then summoned the blind people and asked each of them, "Did you see the woolen ox?" Each of the blind people replied, "I saw it." The king asked, "What does the woolen ox look like?" One blind person who had touched its teeth said, "The woolen ox is like mustard seed." One who had touched its ear said, "The woolen ox is like a sieve." One who had touched its head said, "The woolen ox is like a stone." One who had touched its nose said, "The woolen ox is like a plow beam." One who had touched its leg said, "The woolen ox's form is like a mortar." One who had touched its back said, "The woolen ox is like a throne." One who had touched its belly said, "The woolen ox is like a clay vessel." One who had touched its tail said, "The woolen ox's form is like a rope."

Good son, those blind people did not speak of the actual thing that a woolen ox is — yet neither did they speak of something other than it. If those things they described were not the woolen ox, then beyond what they set aside there would be no other woolen ox.

Good son, the king is an example for the Tathāgata, the omniscient one. The great minister is an example for the great Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, so vast and complete. The woolen ox is an example for the intrinsic nature of a buddha. The blind people are an example for sentient beings in their ignorance.

When those sentient beings hear what the Buddha has taught, some say this: "Form is the intrinsic nature of a buddha — why so? Because form, though it ceases, is one thing succeeding another without interruption, and through this the supreme form of the Tathāgata attains the thirty-two excellent marks, and the form of the Tathāgata is permanent and unceasing. Therefore form is the intrinsic nature of a buddha." They give this example: just as genuine gold, however it is fashioned, retains a color that is stable and unchanging — whether it is made into a bracelet, shaped like a snake, or beaten flat — the yellow color has not changed from the very beginning. Likewise, although the shape of the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings is impermanent, form itself is permanent; therefore they say, "Form is the intrinsic nature of a buddha."

Others say this: "Feeling (vedanā) is the intrinsic nature of a buddha — why so?"

Through the cause and condition of feeling, one attains the genuine bliss of the Tathāgata. The feeling of the Tathāgata is, in the end, feeling in the ultimate sense. Although the intrinsic nature of feeling in sentient beings is impermanent, each feeling succeeds the last in an unbroken stream, and through this continuity one attains the permanent feeling of the Tathāgata. The example given is this: the human bone called the kauśika — the human being is impermanent, yet the bone is permanent, remaining unchanged for a thousand eons. Likewise, the intrinsic nature of the buddha in sentient beings is similar to this; therefore they say, "Feeling is the intrinsic nature of a buddha."

Others say this: "Perception is the intrinsic nature of a buddha — why so?" Through the cause and condition of perception, the true perception of the Tathāgata is obtained. Now, the perception of the Tathāgata is a perception that is without perception. This perception-without-perception does not perceive sentient beings as sentient beings, does not perceive them as female or male, does not perceive form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness — it is not perception, it is the cessation of perception. Although the perceptions of sentient beings are impermanent, perception succeeds perception in sequence, one after another, in an unbroken stream, and through this continuity the everlasting and permanent perception of the Tathāgata is attained. Noble son, the example is this: it is like the twelve links of dependent origination of sentient beings — while sentient beings cease, the twelve links of dependent origination are as it were permanent. The intrinsic nature of the buddha in sentient beings is similar to this; therefore they say, "Perception is the intrinsic nature of a buddha."

Others say this: "Formations are the intrinsic nature of a buddha — why so?" Formations are what is called the life-breath of living beings, and through the cause and condition of this vital life-breath, the Tathāgata's bodily life comes to abide permanently. Although the vital life-breath of sentient beings is impermanent, the living life-breath succeeds the last in sequence, one after another, in an unbroken stream, and through this continuity the genuine and permanent bodily life of the Tathāgata is attained. Noble son, the example is this: just as listening to the twelve branches of scriptural teaching, and expounding them, and both together are impermanent, yet the sūtras themselves abide permanently, unchanged — the intrinsic nature of the buddha in sentient beings is similar to this; therefore they say, "Formations are the intrinsic nature of a buddha."

Others say this: "Consciousness is the intrinsic nature of a buddha — why so?" Through the cause and condition of consciousness, the equanimous mind of the Tathāgata is attained. Although the mental consciousness of sentient beings is impermanent, each consciousness succeeds the last in an unbroken stream, and through this continuity the genuine and permanent mind of the Tathāgata is attained. The example is this: it is like dyeing cloth with fire — although the fire is impermanent, the dyeing is not impermanent. The intrinsic nature of the buddha in sentient beings is similar to this; therefore they say, "Consciousness is the intrinsic nature of a buddha."

Others say this: "Apart from the aggregates there exists something called a self, and that self is the intrinsic nature of a buddha — why so?" Through the cause and condition of what is called the self, one attains the eight masteries of the Tathāgata. Certain non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) say that what goes, what comes, what sees, what hears, sorrow, joy, and speech — all of these are the self. Although the defining characteristics called the self in that sense are impermanent, the genuine self of the Tathāgata is permanent.

Son of good family, consider this example: the aggregates, the sense sources, and the elements are impermanent, yet the name applied to them is permanent — and the intrinsic nature of a buddha within sentient beings is similar to that. Son of good family, just as blind people, each one separately describing the form of an elephant, do not hit upon it directly, yet what they describe is not other than the elephant — so too with those who describe the intrinsic nature of a buddha: it is not the six phenomena, yet it is not other than the six phenomena either. Son of good family, therefore the intrinsic nature of a buddha within sentient beings has been taught thus: it is not form, nor is it other than form; and so on up through — it is not the self, nor is it other than the self.

Son of good family, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) do speak of a self existing, yet there is in truth no such thing as a self. What is called the self of sentient beings refers to the five aggregates themselves; beyond the aggregates there is no separate self to be found elsewhere. Son of good family, consider how a lotus comes into being from the assembly of stalk, leaves, petals, and stem — beyond those, once they are set aside, there is no other thing called a lotus. The self of sentient beings is similar to this. Son of good family, consider how from the assembly of walls, grass, and timber there comes to be what is called a house — beyond those, once they are set aside, there is no other thing called a house. Consider how from the assembly of acacia trees, palāśa trees, nyagrodha trees, udumbara trees, and the like there comes to be what is called a grove — beyond those, once they are set aside, there is no other thing called a grove. Consider how from the assembly of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry there comes to be what is called an army — beyond those, once they are set aside, there is no other thing called an army. Consider how from the assembly of five colors of Kashmiri silk there comes to be what is called a carpet — beyond those, once they are set aside, there is no other thing called a carpet. Consider how from the assembly of the four social classes there comes to be what is called a great assembly — beyond those, once they are set aside, there is no other thing called a great assembly. The self of sentient beings is similar to all of these: beyond the five aggregates, once they are set aside, there is no other thing called a self.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata abides permanently and is therefore called a self. The dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is boundless, unobstructed, neither arising nor ceasing, and has attained the eight masteries — and therefore is called a self. As for sentient beings, they do not in truth possess a self or what belongs to a self of that kind. Because they will ultimately and without fail attain ultimate emptiness, it is called the intrinsic nature of a buddha.

Son of good family, great loving-kindness (maitrī) and great compassion (karuṇā) are called the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Why is this? Because great loving-kindness and great compassion follow a bodhisattva always, like a shadow, and because all sentient beings will ultimately and without fail attain great loving-kindness and great compassion — therefore it is taught that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within all sentient beings. Great loving-kindness and great compassion are called the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha is what is called the Tathāgata.

In relation to this, great joy and great equanimity are also called the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Why is this? Because if a bodhisattva, a great being, does not abandon the twenty-five modes of existence, he cannot attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening — and because all sentient beings will ultimately attain these, it is taught that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within all sentient beings. Great joy and great equanimity are called the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha itself is what is called the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is called great faith of mind. Why is this?

Through the mind of faith, bodhisattvas, great beings, will perfectly complete the perfections from generosity (dāna) all the way through the Perfection of Wisdom. And because all sentient beings will ultimately and without fail attain the great mind of faith, it is taught that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within all sentient beings. The mind of faith itself is the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha itself is the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is called the ground of the only child. Why is this? Through the causes and conditions of the ground of the only child, a bodhisattva attains a mind of equality toward all sentient beings; and because all sentient beings will ultimately and without fail attain the ground of the only child, the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within all sentient beings. The ground of the only child is the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha itself is the Tathāgata — so it is taught.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is called the power of the fourth ground. Why is this? Through the causes and conditions of the power of the fourth ground, a bodhisattva comes to work for the benefit of all sentient beings; and because all sentient beings will ultimately and without fail attain the power of the fourth ground, the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within all sentient beings. The power of the fourth ground is the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha itself is the Tathāgata — so it is taught.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is the twelve links of dependent origination. Why is this? Because of the twelve links of dependent origination, the Tathāgata abides forever. And because all sentient beings will without fail attain those twelve links of dependent origination, the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within all sentient beings. The twelve links of dependent origination are the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha itself is the Tathāgata — so it is taught.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is called the four kinds of individual perfect knowledge. Why is this? Through the causes and conditions of the four kinds of individual perfect knowledge, one expounds words and meanings without obstruction. Because there is no obstruction with respect to words and meanings, one comes to work for the benefit of sentient beings. Therefore the four kinds of individual perfect knowledge are the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and the intrinsic nature of a buddha itself is the Tathāgata — so it is taught.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is called the crown-of-the-head meditative absorption (uṣṇīṣa samādhi). Why is this? When that absorption is cultivated, all buddha qualities become gathered together. Therefore the crown-of-the-head meditative absorption is the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Even a bodhisattva of the tenth ground, though cultivating this absorption, does not perfect it completely; they do perceive the intrinsic nature of a buddha, yet it does not become fully clear. And because all sentient beings will ultimately and without fail attain it, it is taught that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within all sentient beings.

O son of good family, just as all sentient beings will without fail attain the various kinds of qualities enumerated above, it is taught that the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within all sentient beings.

O son of good family, if I were to declare that form is the intrinsic nature of a buddha, sentient beings, the moment they heard it, would generate a mistaken view. On account of that mistaken view, at the end of their lives they would fall into the Avīci hell, the hell of uninterrupted torment. Because a Tathāgata's teaching of the Dharma is for the purpose of cutting off [rebirth in] the hells for sentient beings —

it is for that reason that he does not declare that form is the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and likewise down through consciousness he does not so declare.

O son of good family, if sentient beings were to understand the intrinsic nature of a buddha with perfect clarity, there would be no need to cultivate the path. A bodhisattva of the tenth ground, having meditated on the noble eightfold path, still sees the intrinsic nature of a buddha only slightly — what need is there to speak of seeing it without meditation? O son of good family, when bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī, having meditated on the noble path for immeasurable and boundless aeons, only then first see the intrinsic nature of a buddha, how could śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas see it?

If sentient beings wish to see the intrinsic nature of a buddha with complete clarity, they should, with single-pointed mind, hold fast to this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa (Skt. mahāparinirvāṇa), read it, recite it, write it out, copy it for distribution, explain it, make offerings to it, perform ritual service to it, and honor it. And if they see others holding it, reading it, and honoring it in all these ways, they should offer fine lodgings, clothing, bedding, and medicines for illness; they should praise such persons, prostrate to them, and speak well of them.

O son of good family, whoever in times past served and made offerings to buddhas as countless and boundless as there are — and thereby brought forth a great root of virtue — only then comes first to hear even the mere name of this sūtra. O son of good family, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is inconceivable; the Three Jewels — the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha — are likewise inconceivable. That the intrinsic nature of a buddha exists within all sentient beings, and yet that they are unable to know it, is also inconceivable. The qualities of the Tathāgata — permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity — are also inconceivable. And that all sentient beings should have faith in this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa is likewise inconceivable.

The bodhisattva Lion's Roar (Skt. Siṃhanāda) said: Blessed One, you have declared that it is inconceivable that all sentient beings should have faith in this sūtra. Yet in this very assembly there are eighty-five million sentient beings in whose minds no faith in this sūtra arises. How then can it be called inconceivable that there is faith in this sūtra?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, those very sentient beings too will in a future time come to have confidence in this sūtra, will see the intrinsic nature of a buddha, and will attain unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening.

The noble Great Sūtra of the Great Passing into Nirvāṇa (Skt. Mahāparinirvāṇamahāsūtra). The forty-third fascicle.

Lion's Roar asked: Blessed One, how will irreversible bodhisattvas know with certainty that they themselves truly possess the mind of irreversibility?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, bodhisattvas, great beings, can know this by examining themselves with the mind of one who practises austerities. That is to say: going without food, eating no more than one sesame seed per day, and continuing thus for seven days; then progressing through beans, or lentils, or hemp seeds, or white mustard seeds, each for seven days in turn, eating no more than one small grain per day — when, eating one small grain each day, one thinks, "This austerity is of no benefit, it serves no purpose," yet one further thinks, "Even though it serves no purpose, if I practise in this way and still do not act for the sake of benefit, what need is there to speak of it?" — and so, even knowing it serves no purpose, one perseveres in the practice and endures —

one will without fail attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. During all those days of practising austerities, the wasting and withering of the flesh and skin of the body is like freshly pressed sesame pulp left out in the sun. The sunken hollows of the eyes are like stars in a deep well. The body, all its flesh consumed, showing nothing but sinews and veins, is like a ruined thatched hut. The vertebrae of the spine standing out in plain view are like a knotted rope cast down. The place where one sits is like a horse's hoof-print, for when one sits one falls forward onto one's face, and when one rises one falls backward onto one's back. Yet even enduring such suffering that serves no beneficial purpose, one does not turn back from the awakening mind.

Good son, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, in order to destroy suffering and bestow happiness, gives away all outer and inner possessions, and surrenders body and life itself as freely as one would give away grass. That bodhisattva who places no value on body and life knows with certainty that he possesses a mind that will not turn back, and he understands with certainty that he will attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva, for the sake of the Dharma, lights a human lamp from his own body: he wraps his body in cloth, smears it with oil, and sets it alight. When the bodhisattva in that moment endures such great suffering, he speaks thus to reproach his own mind: "This suffering does not amount to even a hundredth or a thousandth part of the suffering of the hell-beings. You have already endured great suffering that serves no beneficial purpose throughout hundreds of thousands of incalculable aeons. If you cannot endure even this small suffering, how will you go to liberate the sentient beings who are suffering in the hells?" When the bodhisattva, the great being, reflects in this way, he feels no physical pain, and his mind neither turns back nor wavers nor is disturbed. At that moment the bodhisattva comes to understand with certainty that he will himself attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Good son, even though at that time the bodhisattva still has afflictions and has not yet cut through them, yet for the sake of the Dharma he gives to sentient beings the limbs of his body — his head, his hands, his feet, his eyes, his legs, his flesh, and his blood — driving iron nails into his body, leaping from cliffs, and leaping into fire. Though the bodhisattva at that time endures immeasurable suffering of this kind, if his mind does not turn back and does not waver or change, then that bodhisattva himself understands with certainty that he possesses a mind that will not turn back and that he will surely attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Good son, the bodhisattva, the great being, in order to destroy the suffering of all sentient beings, makes the aspiration to be born in the body of a very great animal, and gives that body's flesh and blood to sentient beings. When those sentient beings come to take from him, so that they may give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward them, the bodhisattva at that time does not breathe, making himself as if dead, so that there arises in him no thought of doubt as to whether those who take the flesh might be killed by his death. In this way, though the bodhisattva is born in an animal realm, he never engages in the actions of animal existence. Why is that?

Noble one, because the bodhisattva has attained the mind of non-regression, he never at any time performs the actions of the three lower realms. And though in future times the bodhisattva, the great being, is not destined to experience even the slightest fruit of a wretched rebirth, by the power of his great aspiration he experiences those things for the sake of sentient beings.

Here is an analogy. A sick person possessed by a hungry ghost becomes invisible to ordinary sight, yet through the power of a knowledge-mantra he becomes visible again, and at times speaks, at times rejoices, at times grows angry, at times scolds, at times strikes, at times weeps, at times laughs. In just the same way, the future actions of the three lower realms performed by the bodhisattva, the great being, are like that.

When the bodhisattva, the great being, has taken birth in the body of a bear, he always teaches the sacred Dharma to sentient beings. At times he takes birth in the body of a crow, a magpie, or a parrot, and teaches the sacred Dharma to sentient beings. In order to teach the sacred Dharma to sentient beings, he also takes birth as a cat, a deer, a rabbit, a yak, a sheep, a monkey, a white dove, a garuḍa bird, a nāga, and a snake. Thus, experiencing many animal bodies in this way, he never performs the deeds of the animal realm; rather, while always born in the animal realm, he teaches the Dharma to others, so that they may quickly be liberated from their animal bodies and come to hear the Dharma. Although the bodhisattva at that time experiences animal bodies in this way, since he does not perform the deeds of wretched rebirth, one should therefore understand with certainty that he possesses the mind of non-regression.

When the bodhisattva, the great being, sees sentient beings threatened by famine, he is born in the immeasurably vast body of a tortoise or a great fish, and makes this aspiration: "May all sentient beings cut and eat the flesh of my body; may it grow back again after being cut; and through the condition of having eaten my flesh, may they be freed from the suffering of hunger and thirst, and may all of them give rise to the awakening mind directed toward unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening." Furthermore, the bodhisattva makes this aspiration: "All those who, through the condition of having eaten my flesh, have been freed from hunger and thirst — may all of them in future lives, throughout twenty-five existences, be swiftly freed from every fault of hunger and thirst."

When the bodhisattva, the great being, thus experiences suffering, one should understand with certainty that his non-regressive mind will attain unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva witnesses a time of widespread sickness and sees beings tormented by disease, he thinks: "Just as a sick person who takes any part of the king of medicinal trees — whether root, trunk, branch, leaf, flower, fruit, or bark — is healed of illness, so too may my body become like that: may all those who hear my voice, touch my body, or eat my flesh and blood — down to eating my feet and my head — be cured of their sicknesses. May sentient beings who eat my flesh not give rise to malicious thoughts, but think of it as they would eating a child's flesh, and having been cured of their illnesses through me, may they receive the teaching of Dharma; and having heard it, may they have faith, retain it, and teach it to others as well." Thus does he make his aspiration.

Noble one, thus it is that the bodhisattva, though still accompanied by afflictions —

though the body experiences suffering, the mind does not turn back, waver, or change — one should know this to be a mind of definitive non-return, and that such a one will attain unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, noble one, should sentient beings be struck down by hungry ghosts and fall ill, the bodhisattva, upon seeing them, immediately makes this aspiration: "May I too become a body of hungry ghosts — a vast body, a body endowed with radiance, a body surrounded by a great retinue — so that, the instant those beings hear me, they may be healed of their sicknesses." Thus does he make his aspiration.

When the bodhisattva, the great being, practices austerity for the sake of sentient beings, though he is still accompanied by afflictions, his mind does not falter.

Noble one, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, though practicing the six perfections (pāramitās), does not place his hope in the fruits of the six perfections. When he applies himself diligently to the supreme six perfections, he makes this aspiration: "May I give the gift of the six perfections to each and every sentient being. And may each and every sentient being, having received my gift, all attain unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. May I myself become the six perfections, practicing austerity and experiencing many sufferings — and even when experiencing those sufferings, may I never turn back from the awakening mind." Noble one, when the bodhisattva, the great being, has come to bear such characteristics, this is called the characteristic mark of non-return from awakening.

Noble one, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, is called inconceivable. Why is that? The bodhisattva, the great being, knows full well that saṃsāra has exceedingly many faults and defects, and that great nirvāṇa has great qualities — and yet, for the sake of sentient beings, he remains in saṃsāra. Because his mind does not turn back from experiencing suffering in all its many forms, the bodhisattva is called inconceivable.

Noble one, the bodhisattva, the great being, does not arouse compassion and loving-kindness merely because he has been prompted by causes and conditions, nor does he seek gratitude for what he has done. He perpetually bestows benefit upon others. And even though he gives in this way, because he has no thought of expecting anything in return, he is called inconceivable.

Noble one, ordinary sentient beings practice austerity for the sake of benefit to themselves. The bodhisattva, the great being, practices austerity for the sake of benefit to others — and that is also of benefit to himself — and therefore he is also called inconceivable.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, though accompanied by afflictions, in order to dissolve the distinction between enemy and friend, experiences much suffering, yet applies himself diligently to a mind of equanimity. For that reason he is called inconceivable.

Furthermore, when the bodhisattva encounters sentient beings who are wicked and unwholesome, he may mock them, speak to them with gentle words, drive them away, or, at times, place them in equanimity. To one who is naturally given to anger, he shows even gentle speech. To one who is arrogant, he displays great arrogance openly — yet in truth, within his own mind there is no arrogance whatsoever. This is called the bodhisattva's inconceivable skillful means.

Furthermore, when the bodhisattva, the great being, though accompanied by afflictions, has neither material goods nor wealth, and though many come to beg of him, his mind is free of clinging — this too is called the bodhisattva's inconceivable quality.

Furthermore, when a buddha appears in the world, the bodhisattva, knowing the qualities of a buddha, takes birth for the sake of sentient beings in bodies on the outskirts where there is no buddha — experiencing a body such as that of one who is blind, or lame, or mute, or simple-minded. This too is called the bodhisattva's inconceivable quality.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva, fully comprehending whatever faults and defects sentient beings have, mingles with those beings in order to free them. Though he conducts himself in harmony with them in this way, he is not stained by the taint of their faults. This too is called the bodhisattva's inconceivable quality.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva understands and discerns that there is no defining mark of a sentient being, no affliction that takes hold, no striving on the path, no abandoning of afflictions, no striving toward awakening, no conduct of awakening, no spontaneously accomplished conduct of awakening, no experience of suffering, and no overcoming of suffering — yet, for the sake of sentient beings, he nevertheless overcomes suffering and engages in the conduct of awakening. This too is called inconceivable.

Furthermore, noble son, that the bodhisattva takes birth in the highest heaven of the desire realm, the Tuṣita heaven, as the inner and final rebirth of his body — this too is called the bodhisattva's inconceivable quality. Why is that? The Tuṣita heaven is the supreme abode within the desire realm. The gods of the lower heavenly levels conduct themselves heedlessly. The gods of the higher heavenly levels are subdued in their faculties; therefore the gods of Tuṣita are called the highest. Through the practice of generosity and moral discipline, one is reborn in the higher and lower heavens. Through cultivating meditative absorption together with generosity and moral discipline, one is reborn as a god in Tuṣita. All bodhisattvas utterly condemn conditioned existence, and though they have overcome conditioned existence and do not perform the deeds of a Tuṣita god, they are nonetheless reborn as gods in Tuṣita. Why is that? Because even if the bodhisattva is reborn into another existence, he will work for the benefit of sentient beings. Although he has no wish to be reborn in the desire realm, he is born into the desire realm. Therefore this is called inconceivable.

When the bodhisattva, the great being, is reborn as a god in Tuṣita, he becomes supreme in these three things: in length of life, in physical appearance, and in renown. Although the bodhisattva, the great being, harbors no expectation regarding length of life, physical appearance, or renown, he becomes supreme in these beyond all others. By the force of the bodhisattva's aspiration toward complete nirvāṇa, and through those very causes and conditions, he becomes supreme. Therefore this is called inconceivable.

Even though the bodhisattva, the great being, has thus become supreme among the gods in these three things, the sons of the gods do not give rise toward that bodhisattva any thought of aversion, any thought of envy, or any thought of pride; they always give rise to a mind of joy. And because the bodhisattva himself harbors no pride toward the gods, this is called inconceivable.

Although the bodhisattva, the great being, has not performed any deeds to secure length of life, by virtue of his lifespan reaching its full measure among those gods, his length of life is said to have become supreme. Although he has not performed any deeds to attain a beautiful form, he comes to dwell in a body of excellent appearance, and through the brilliance of his radiance shining everywhere, his form is said to have become supreme. The bodhisattva, the great being, though dwelling in the divine palace, is not attached to the five objects of desire; he engages only in the work of Dharma, and his renown spreads in all ten directions.

Therefore it is said to be supremely renowned, and that is what is called inconceivable.

When the bodhisattva, the great being, descends from Tuṣita Heaven, the great earth shakes in six ways — and that too is what is called inconceivable. Why is that? When the bodhisattva descends from the heavens, all the gods of the desire realm and the form realm pay him honor and escort him, and raising a great cry, they praise the bodhisattva with the utmost intensity — so that even the force of the breath from their mouths causes the earth to tremble. Furthermore, the bodhisattva is like a king of the finest herd among humans. The king of the finest herd among humans is called the king of the nāgas. When the king of the nāgas first enters the womb, certain nāga kings who dwell beneath the earth are gripped by fear, while others are filled with joy — and the great earth shakes in six ways. Therefore that too is called inconceivable.

The bodhisattva, the great being, knows the moment of entering the womb, the moment of dwelling therein, and the moment of emergence. He perceives his father and mother as utterly pure, completely unstained — beholding them as though they were the hair of Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, or a blue precious jewel. Therefore that too is called inconceivable.

O son of good family, this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa is likewise inconceivable. O son of good family, consider: the great ocean has eight inconceivable qualities. What are these eight? It shelves gradually; it is deep and its depths are vast; it has one single taste, the taste of salt; it does not transgress its shoreline boundary; it holds many precious things; it has become the dwelling place of many sentient beings; it does not retain a corpse; and though it receives all rivers and the rain of great clouds, it neither increases nor decreases. These are the eight.

O son of good family, as regards the quality of shelving gradually, there are three factors: the force of the merit of all sentient beings, the movement of wind in its direction, and the flow of rivers. And with respect to neither increasing nor decreasing as well, there are three such factors for each. In exactly the same way, this sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa also has eight inconceivable qualities.

What are they? Shelving gradually: this sūtra sets forth and teaches, from the five precepts of moral discipline, the ten precepts of moral discipline, the two hundred and fifty precepts of moral discipline, the moral discipline of the bodhisattva, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhathood, the fruit of the pratyekabuddha, the fruit of the bodhisattva, and up to the fruit of unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. These teachings are called gradual shelving — and therefore this sūtra is called the one that shelves gradually.
