Deep with vast depths: the Blessed One, the Buddha, is unborn and unceasing; there is no attaining of unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening; there is no turning of the wheel of Dharma; there is no receiving of alms; there is no act of generosity — and therefore there is permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity, and all sentient beings possess the nature of buddha. The nature of buddha is not form, nor is it other than form; it is not feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor is it other than consciousness. It is fit to be regarded as permanent; it is not a cause produced by conditions that generate illumination; from stream-entry all the way through to the pratyekabuddha, even upon attaining unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening, there is no affliction and there is no abiding.

Yet even though there is no affliction, one should not say "it is permanent" — therefore it is called profound.

Furthermore, what is "most profound" is this: throughout this sūtra, in various passages it teaches that there is a self, and in various passages it teaches that there is no self; in various passages it teaches permanence, and in various passages it teaches impermanence; in various passages it teaches utter purity, and in various passages it teaches that things are not utterly pure; in various passages it teaches bliss, and in various passages it teaches suffering; in various passages it teaches emptiness, and in various passages it teaches that things are not empty; in various passages it teaches that all things exist, and in various passages it teaches that all things do not exist; in various passages it teaches three vehicles, and in various passages it teaches a single vehicle; in various passages it teaches that the five aggregates themselves are the intrinsic nature of a buddha — referring to the vajra-like meditative absorption (samādhi), the meditative absorption of the middle path and courageous advance, the twelve links of dependent origination, ultimate emptiness, loving-kindness and compassion, joy, equanimity, the gnosis that crowns all sentient beings, faith of mind, faculties, powers, and the gnosis unobstructed with respect to all phenomena. Because the buddha-nature exists and yet has not been definitively taught, it is called "profound."

What is meant by "of one taste" is this: the buddha-nature exists in a way that is concordant for all sentient beings — concordant in that the vehicle is one, concordant in that liberation is singular, the cause is one, the fruit is one, and concordant in that the flavor is one. Because all will attain permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity, it is called "of one taste."

What is meant by "not transgressing the boundary of the grade" is this: from this sūtra, where it is prescribed as a rule that monks shall not retain eight unexamined things, any one who has become my attendant and who holds, grasps, reads, recites, copies in writing, expounds, and teaches this noble sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa — even should body and life be lost, that person will not let moral discipline deteriorate. This is what is meant by "not transgressing the boundary of the grade."

"Of many kinds of jewels" means that this very sūtra is a treasure of immeasurable jewels. "Treasure" here refers to: the four establishments of mindfulness, the four genuine abandonments, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven branches of awakening, the noble eightfold path, the conduct of an ordinary child, the conduct of a noble one, the conduct of Brahmā, the conduct of the gods, the means for many virtues, the buddha-nature of sentient beings, the qualities of bodhisattvas, the qualities of Tathāgatas, the qualities of śrāvakas, the qualities of pratyekabuddhas, the six perfections, immeasurable meditative absorptions, and immeasurable gnosis and wisdom — these constitute the treasure of jewels.

"The abode of great beings" — a great being is a buddha or a bodhisattva; they are called great beings because their gnosis and wisdom are great. Because the body is great, the mind is great; because the mind is great, the array is great; because the array is great, those to be tamed are many; because skillful means are great; because the teaching of Dharma is great; because might and power are great; because the maṇḍala of the retinue is great; because miraculous powers are great; because loving-kindness and compassion are great; because there is no change whatsoever; because there is no obstruction with respect to all sentient beings; and because all sentient beings can be accommodated — for all these reasons it is called "the abode of great beings."

As for "corpse" and "not remaining" — a corpse refers to one who harbors perverted craving, one whose four root defeats have deteriorated,

— who has committed any of the five acts of immediate retribution, who has reviled the vast sūtra collections, who has taught what is not the Dharma as if it were Dharma, who has taught the Dharma as if it were not the Dharma, who keeps eight things without proper examination, who acts according to their own pleasure with the property of the buddhas and the wealth of the Saṅgha, and who behaves improperly toward monks and nuns — such a one is what is called "a corpse." This sūtra of thorough nirvāṇa likewise does not keep company with a corpse, because it is thoroughly separated from all such things. That is what is meant by "not remaining."

As for "neither increasing nor decreasing" — it is so because it is boundless; because it has no beginning and no end; because it is without form; because it is not the product of effort; because it abides permanently; because it neither arises nor ceases; because it is equal and impartial toward all sentient beings; and because the defining marks of all things are consistent in being but a single mark. Therefore it neither increases nor decreases.

For all these reasons, this sūtra is like a great ocean, endowed with eight inconceivable qualities.

Lion's Roar then asked: Blessed One, if the Tathāgata is said to be profound because he neither arises nor ceases, then every ordinary person has four modes of birth: birth from an egg, birth from heat and moisture, birth from a womb, and miraculous birth. All four modes of birth are to be found even among human beings. For example, the monk Śāla, and Upaśīpala, and the laywoman Nīkalā's mother, and the laywoman Nikutā's mother, and the laywoman Phaṃśalā's mother — each of these had five hundred and five hundred children, and all were born from a single egg. Therefore there is also birth from an egg among humans. As for birth from heat and moisture, just as the Blessed One has taught — when the bodhisattva practised in former times, there was one called the king born from the crown of the head, and one called the king born from the arm; and just now you spoke of the maiden born from the mango tree, and the maiden born from the kabittha tree. Therefore birth from heat and moisture also exists among humans. When the cosmic age (kalpa) was first forming, all sentient beings were born miraculously. Since the Blessed One, the buddha, is endowed with the eight masteries, why was he not born miraculously?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, all sentient beings are born through four modes of birth. Having heard the noble Dharma, those who were formerly born from eggs and born from heat and moisture will no longer be so reborn. Son of good family, when the cosmic age was first forming, all sentient beings were born miraculously; yet at that time, no buddha had come into the world. Son of good family, if sentient beings are afflicted by illness, a physician and medicine are needed. When the cosmic age was first forming, all sentient beings were born miraculously; and though they had afflictions, the disease of those afflictions had not yet arisen — therefore the Tathāgata did not come into the world. Son of good family, the sentient beings of the first-formed cosmic age had not yet become suitable vessels, in body and mind, for the teaching — therefore the Tathāgata did not come into the world. Son of good family, the lineage of the Blessed One, the buddhas, together with his retinue and parents, is supremely noble, so that all who hear him teach the Dharma place their trust in him. Therefore the Tathāgata is not born miraculously. Son of good family, all sentient beings may perform in their role as children what belongs to a father, and may perform in their role as father what belongs to a child. If the Blessed One, the buddha, were born miraculously, he would have no parents. If he had no parents, how could he perform the many virtuous deeds for the sake of all ordinary persons? Therefore the Tathāgata is not born miraculously.

Son of good family, there are two kinds of guarding of the sacred Dharma taught by the buddha: inner and outer.

The inner guarding is moral discipline. The outer guarding is spiritual friends and one's retinue. If the Blessed One, the buddha, were born miraculously, there would be no outer guarding. Therefore the Tathāgata does not wish for a miraculously born body.

Son of good family, some persons, proud of their lineage, give rise to arrogance. In order to crush that arrogance of theirs, the Tathāgata is born into a noble lineage — he does not wish for a miraculously born body. Son of good family, the Blessed One, the buddha, truly has a father and a mother: his father is called Pure Rice and his mother is called Heavenly Beauty. Yet if one were to say that those sentient beings are illusions, how could a miraculously born body be desired? And if a miraculously born body were assumed, from what would the many relics arise? The Tathāgata, for the benefit of sentient beings, causes his body to be broken into fine relics so that all may make offerings to them. Therefore the Tathāgata does not wish for a miraculously born body. Since all buddhas do not wish for a miraculously born body, why should I alone assume one?

Then the bodhisattva Siṃhaghoṣa joined his palms together, knelt on his right knee, and praised the Blessed One with these verses:

The Tathāgata is a mass of virtues beyond all measure;
though I cannot set them forth in full,
for the sake of ordinary persons I shall speak of them in part —
out of love, I speak: may it please you to listen.

Ordinary persons wander in the darkness of ignorance
and come to experience suffering in its endless and manifold forms;
because the Blessed One has freed them from that,
throughout all the world he is renowned as the one of great compassion.

Because ordinary persons revolve around the causes of saṃsāra,
thoroughly corrupted by heedlessness, they are without happiness;
because the Tathāgata has fully bestowed happiness upon them,
the continuum of their revolving through saṃsāra has been utterly severed.

Because the Tathāgata has given happiness to all,
I myself feel no attachment to or longing for any happiness whatsoever.

Having practiced every hardship for the sake of ordinary persons,
he has come to be venerated by all the world with its gods.

When he sees others experiencing suffering, his body trembles —
yet even entering into hell with sentient beings, he feels no pain.
He has undergone great suffering for the sake of sentient beings;
thus he is victorious over all, and his measure surpasses reckoning.

The Tathāgata practiced austerities for the sake of sentient beings,
and fully perfected the six perfections (pāramitās).
His mind, though dwelling amid the winds of wrong views, is unmoved —
thus he is born as an utterly victorious person in the world.

Ordinary persons all desire happiness,
yet they do not know what it is that brings happiness about;
because the Tathāgata has taught it and they have come to meditate upon it,
it is as when parents cherish an only child.

The Blessed One, seeing sentient beings afflicted by the illness of mental afflictions,
is like a mother to a suffering, sick child;
ever intent on the means to eliminate the illness of the afflictions,
therefore this body of his has been placed under the power of others.

Although all sentient beings undergo manifold sufferings,
by a mind turned upside down they take those sufferings to be happiness.
The Tathāgata has spoken truly of both happiness and suffering —
thus everywhere he is renowned as the one of great compassion.

Though all the world dwells in the vestibule of ignorance,
the bill of the wisdom that lays it bare and destroys it has no mouth —

the beak of the Tathāgata's gnosis has broken all of it completely —
therefore he is the eldest son among those who are to become supreme.

Because the three worlds have neither seized nor gathered him in,
he has no name; there is no conventional designation assigned by those above.
Because he has accomplished and realized the aim of complete nirvāṇa,
the Blessed One is renowned as the One of Great Intelligence.

Though sentient beings are swept away and submerged by the river of conditioned existence,
and through the thorough blindness of ignorance do not know the path of escape —
the Tathāgata, himself liberated, liberates others;
therefore the Tathāgata is renowned as the Ferryman.

Because he knows all that becomes cause and effect,
he likewise realizes profoundly the work of exhaustion and cessation.
By dispensing medicine for sentient beings tormented by illness,
he is renowned throughout the world as the King of Physicians.

Non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who follow wrong views engage in austerities,
claiming that through such conditions the highest happiness is obtained.
What the Tathāgata has taught as true happiness
will most certainly be experienced as happiness by all sentient beings.

The Tathāgata has demolished the path of wrong going,
and excellently reveals to all sentient beings the path of true reality.
Those who travel that excellent path will find happiness —
therefore the Blessed One is renowned as the Caravan Leader.

It is not made by self, nor made by another,
nor made in common, nor made by cause and condition —
what the Tathāgata has taught concerning the experience of suffering
is supreme above all the assertions of the non-Buddhists.

From the complete perfection of moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom,
he teaches that very nature of phenomena to all ordinary persons.
When performing the gift of Dharma, there is no miserliness —
therefore the Blessed One is loving-kindness without object.

Since there is no loving-kindness and no cause and condition either,
one obtains a ripening that is without cause, condition, or fruit.
Therefore all the wise and discerning
call the Tathāgata the One Without Expectation.

Though he always dwells in the company of the heedless conduct of the world,
through heedlessness toward the body he is not at all defiled.
Therefore he is called the Inconceivable,
and is not defiled even by the eight worldly concerns.

The buddha, the Blessed One, is without attachment and without aversion —
therefore his mind is always perfectly equanimous.

May the one called Lion's Roar praise his great compassion
and may the measureless lion's roar resound!

This is the eleventh chapter, being the complete inquiry by the bodhisattva called Lion's Roar, from the noble Great Sūtra of Complete Nirvāṇa (Skt. Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra).

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One with these words: The Tathāgata is compassionate toward all sentient beings: those who are untamed he tames; those who are impure he purifies; those who have no protector or refuge, him he makes their protector and refuge; and those who are not fully liberated he liberates — and being thus endowed with eight qualities of mastery, he is like a great physician, a king of medicine. Yet, Blessed One, the monk called Auspicious Star was a son born in the time when you, the Blessed One, were acting as a bodhisattva. He went forth into renunciation, maintained, retained, recited, chanted, analyzed, expounded, and explained the twelve categories of scriptural teaching, overcame the afflictions of the desire realm, and attained the four meditative concentrations. Why then did the Tathāgata prophesy that the monk Auspicious Star is one of perverted craving, the very last of all, and that even though he dwells in the hells for an entire aeon he cannot be healed?

"Why then did the Tathāgata first teach the noble Dharma, yet not afterward cause Auspicious Star to become a bodhisattva? If the Buddha, the Blessed One, was not to become a refuge and protector for Auspicious Star, on what basis does one speak of his possessing great compassion and supreme skillful means?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, consider a father and mother who have three sons. The eldest serves and honors his parents, and with his sharp faculties, once he has undertaken any worldly task, he masters it swiftly. The middle son neither accords with his parents' wishes nor has any mind for service or respect, yet with his sharp faculties, once he undertakes worldly tasks, he masters them swiftly. The youngest acts contrary to his parents' wishes, has no mind for service or respect, is dull in his faculties, and lacks understanding. If the parents are to train and educate these children, they first send into training the son whom they had trained before, the one whom they love and hold dear."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, they would first train the one who does not act contrary to his parents' wishes, who serves and honors them, and who masters worldly tasks swiftly once he undertakes them. Then after him, the middle son and the youngest would also be taught. Though those two younger sons have no mind for service and respect, still, out of loving-kindness, they are enrolled among the students being taught."

"Son of good family, the Tathāgata is precisely like this. As for the three sons: within the category of sons, the eldest is an analogy for the bodhisattva; the middle son is an analogy for the śrāvaka; the youngest is an analogy for one of perverted craving. From among the twelve categories of scriptural teaching, I previously taught the very subtle and profound meanings to the bodhisattvas. The meanings that are less profound I taught to the śrāvakas. The worldly meanings I taught to those of perverted craving, and to those who commit the five crimes of immediate retribution, not for their immediate benefit in the present moment, but out of loving care, so that virtue may bear fruit for them in a future life.

"Son of good family, consider this: there are three kinds of field. A field where the soil is easy to work, and which has no rocks, gravel, weeds, or thorn-bushes, will yield a hundredfold. A field that has no sand, gravel, stones, weeds, or thorn-bushes, yet whose soil is difficult to work and which has not been properly irrigated, will yield only half a crop. A field where the soil is also difficult to work and which has many rocks, gravel, and thorn-bushes, so that weeds grow abundantly, will, if one plows it, yield no more than what was sown."

"Son of good family, when summer comes and it is time to plow, which field do the farmers plow first?"

The reply: "Blessed One, they first plow the excellent field, then afterward plow the other two kinds in order. Of these, the first is an analogy for the bodhisattva; the middle is an analogy for the śrāvaka; the last is an analogy for the one of perverted craving.

"Son of good family, consider this: a person has three vessels — one that is uncracked and intact, one that leaks, and one that is broken. If milk, curds, water, or butter are to be poured inside a vessel, into which one would one pour first?"

The reply: "Blessed One, one would first pour into the uncracked vessel, then into the leaking one, and then into the broken one as well. The uncracked and pure vessel is an analogy for the Saṅgha of bodhisattvas; the leaking vessel is an analogy for the Saṅgha of śrāvakas; the broken vessel is an analogy for one of perverted craving.

"Son of good family, consider this: three sick persons come before a physician. One is easy to heal; one is difficult to heal; one cannot be healed. Son of good family, among those three patients, which one does the physician treat first?"

The reply:

"Blessed One, one would first treat the one who is easy to heal, and after that, treat the other two as well. Why so? Out of love and affection. The one who is easy to heal is an analogy for the Saṅgha of bodhisattvas; the one who is difficult to heal is an analogy for the Saṅgha of śrāvakas; the one who cannot be healed is an analogy for one of perverted craving — for even if no virtuous fruit arises in the present moment, out of love and affection one plants the seed of virtue for the world to come.

"Son of good family, consider this: a great king has three horses. One is very well-trained and powerful. One is untrained yet powerful. One is neither trained nor untrained, but aged and without strength. If the king wishes to ride, which does he mount first?"

The reply: "Blessed One, he would first mount the one that is well-trained and powerful, and after that ride the other two as well. The well-trained and powerful one is an analogy for the Saṅgha of bodhisattvas; the untrained one is an analogy for the Saṅgha of śrāvakas; the untrained and aged one is an analogy for one of perverted craving — for even though it cannot serve any benefit in this present life, out of love and affection one plants the seed of future virtue for the world to come.

"Son of good family, consider this: a great patron resolves to give to three types of persons. One is of noble lineage, with sharp faculties, and endowed with moral discipline. One is of middling lineage, with dull faculties, yet endowed with moral discipline. One is of the lowest lineage, with dull faculties, and not endowed with moral discipline. Son of good family, to which of these three does the great patron give first?"

The reply: "Blessed One, one would first give to the one of noble lineage, with sharp faculties and endowed with moral discipline, and after that give to the other two as well. The first is an analogy for the Saṅgha of bodhisattvas; the next is an analogy for the Saṅgha of śrāvakas; the last is an analogy for one of perverted craving.

"Son of good family, just as the lion, king of beasts, when slaying a great musk elephant, brings to bear his full strength and power, and when slaying a rabbit does likewise — he does not use merely a small breath — so too the Blessed One the buddha is just like that: in teaching the Dharma to bodhisattvas and to those of perverted craving alike, his effort is without distinction between the two.

"Son of good family, once in former times, when I was residing in Rājagṛha, the monk Śubhakara (Legs pa'i skar ma) served as my attendant. At that time, in the first part of the night, I was teaching the holy Dharma to Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods. Since my attendant was obliged to inform me of the time, on that occasion I was detained at length, and the monk Śubhakara conceived ill will toward me. Now at that time in Rājagṛha, small children were crying, and could not be quieted. Their parents, wishing to frighten them into silence, threatened: 'If you do not stop crying, we will hand you over to the hungry ghost Bakula.' And with that threat the crying would cease. At that time the monk Śubhakara threatened me in just this way, saying: 'Please go quickly to your dwelling — the hungry ghost Bakula is coming!' I then declared to him: 'You utter fool — have you not heard that the Blessed One the buddha knows no fear?' At that, Śakra, lord of the gods, addressed me thus:"

"Blessed One, will a person such as this find a place within the buddhas' Dharma?" Having asked this, I declared to him: "Kauśika, this person too finds a place within the buddhas' Dharma, and because the nature of a buddha is present within him, he will attain the unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening."

Now, I taught the sacred Dharma to the monk Śubhakara, yet he had not the slightest mind of faith or receptivity toward it.

Noble son, once upon a time, when I was dwelling in the city called Śīpā in the land of Kāśī, the monk Śubhakara was serving as my attendant. At that time, as I was minded to go into that city for alms, an immeasurable number of sentient beings dwelling there longed to see me, burning with thirst as it were in their devotion. The monk Śubhakara, wishing to sweep behind me as I walked and to make me invisible to them, and being unable to make me invisible, caused many sentient beings to give rise to unwholesome thoughts.

At that time, as I entered the city, I saw before the door of a tavern a naked man who had stripped his body bare and was eating grass. The monk Śubhakara saw him too and said to me: "Blessed One, if there were an arhat in this world, this man would be the foremost among them. Why so? Because this man has no cause and no effect." I replied to him: "You fool — have you not heard that an arhat does not drink alcohol, does not harm others, does not deceive those around him, does not take what is not given, and does not engage in sexual misconduct? This man has even killed his own parents and eats grass — how could he be called an arhat? This man, immediately upon leaving the body, will without doubt fall into the avīci hell, the hell of uninterrupted torment. An arhat is one who has utterly cut off the three lower destinies — why do you call this man an arhat?"

Śubhakara then responded: "It is possible for the four great elements to change, yet there is no basis for saying that this man will fall into the avīci hell." I said to him: "You fool — have you not heard that the Blessed One, the buddha, speaks the truth without duality?" And so, though I taught the sacred Dharma to Śubhakara in this way, there was not the slightest mind of faith or receptivity in him toward it.

Noble son, I was also at one time dwelling in Rājagṛha together with the monk Śubhakara. At that time in Rājagṛha there was a naked ascetic called Duḥkhabhava — "Born-of-Suffering" — who constantly proclaimed: "The afflictions of sentient beings have no cause and no condition, and the liberation of sentient beings likewise has no cause and no condition." At that time the monk Śubhakara again said to me: "Blessed One, if there were an arhat in this world, this naked ascetic called Duḥkhabhava would be the foremost." I replied: "You fool — Duḥkhabhava the naked ascetic is not a true arhat, nor has he been liberated through the awakening of an arhat."

Śubhakara then said to me: "Why does an arhat harbor envy toward an arhat?" I replied: "You fool — I have no envy toward any arhat. It is you yourself who have given rise to a wicked wrong view that will bring you to ruin. Look at your claim that this naked ascetic is an arhat — within seven days he will be struck by an illness of indigestion and will die of it, his belly distended."

After death he would also be reborn as a hungry ghost that feeds on vomit. His corpse would be lifted by fellow students and carried off to the charnel ground.

At that time Śubhakara went to where Duḥkhabhava the naked ascetic was lying ill and said to him: "Venerable one, do you know? The ascetic Gautama has now prophesied that within seven days you will be struck by an illness of indigestion, that your belly will be distended, and that you will die of it; and that after death you will be reborn as a hungry ghost that feeds on vomit, and that your fellow students and your fellow disciples will lift your corpse and carry it off to the charnel ground."

Having heard this prophecy, the venerable one thought very carefully about every possible means to prevent it from coming true, and resolved by whatever means to make the ascetic Gautama out to be a liar. At that time, Duḥkhabhava, having heard Śubhakara speak those words, refused to eat, and from the first day through the sixth day ate absolutely nothing. When the seventh day had passed in full, he ate some raw sugar. After eating the raw sugar, he drank cold water. The moment he drank the cold water, his belly became distended and he died. After his death his fellow students lifted his corpse and carried it off to the charnel ground; and having become a hungry ghost that feeds on vomit, he remained beside the corpse.

The monk Śubhakara, having heard that things had turned out in this way, went to the charnel ground where the corpse lay. When he arrived there, he saw that the body of Duḥkhabhava had become the body of a hungry ghost that feeds on vomit and was crouching beside the corpse.

The Noble Great Sūtra of the Great Passing into Nirvāṇa. The forty-fourth fascicle.

Śubhakara said: "Are you dead?" Duḥkhabhava replied: "I am dead." He asked: "How did you die?" He replied: "I died of a distended belly." He asked: "Then who brought your corpse here?" He replied: "Fellow students brought it." He asked: "And where did they bring it?" He replied: "You fool — do you not know this is a charnel ground?" He asked: "And what kind of body have you obtained?" He replied: "I have become a body that feeds on vomit."

Duḥkhabhava continued: "Śubhakara, listen well. The Tathāgata speaks what is wholesome, speaks what is true, speaks at the proper time, speaks what is meaningful, speaks in accordance with the Dharma. Śubhakara — since the Tathāgata spoke in such a truthful way, why did you not believe it at the time? Any sentient being who does not believe what the Tathāgata has truthfully declared will experience a body like mine."

At that time Śubhakara came to where I was and addressed me thus: "Blessed One, the naked ascetic Duḥkhabhava has passed away and been reborn as a god among the thirty-three." I said to him: "You fool — an arhat has no place of rebirth; so why do you say that Duḥkhabhava has been reborn as a god among the thirty-three?" He replied: "It is just as the Blessed One said: the naked Duḥkhabhava was not truly reborn as a god among the thirty-three — he has become a hungry ghost that feeds on vomit." I said to him: "You fool — everything the Blessed Buddha has declared is without duality; there is no basis for saying that what the Tathāgata has declared admits of duality."

The Blessed One then declared: Śubhakara said: "Even though the Tathāgata spoke those words at that time, I myself did not have faith in them."

Noble son, I always taught the holy Dharma to the monk Śubhakara, and yet not even this much arose in him — a mind that had faith and took it to heart. Noble son, the monk Śubhakara, while reciting and intoning the twelve branches of scripture,

although he had attained the four meditative concentrations, he understood not even the meaning of a single verse, a single phrase, or a single syllable from his youth. By associating with a spiritual friend who was evil and unwholesome, he lost even the four meditative concentrations. When the concentrations were lost, he gave rise to wrong views, saying: "There is no buddha, there is no Dharma, there is no nirvāṇa. The ascetic Gautama was supremely skilled in the rites of astrology and sign-reading, and so he came to know the minds of others." At that time I declared to the monk Śubhakara the following: "The Dharma I have taught and proclaimed is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, of excellent meaning, of excellent wording, unmixed, complete and perfect, the conduct of purity, thoroughly pure." And yet the monk Śubhakara said to me: "Although the Tathāgata has taught the Dharma to me, in ultimate truth there is neither cause nor effect." Noble son, if you do not place trust in this matter as it has been described, then know that the monk Śubhakara is even now sitting on the bank of the river Nairañjanā — go there and ask him directly. Thereupon the Tathāgata, accompanied by Kāśyapa, went to where Śubhakara was. When the monk Śubhakara saw the Blessed One approaching from afar, he gave rise to an unwholesome state of mind. Having given rise to that unwholesome mind, right then and there he fell headlong into the avīci hell, the realm of uninterrupted torment.

Noble son, the monk Śubhakara entered the teaching of the Buddha and received incalculable heaps of precious jewels, and yet he obtained nothing at all. Because of his heedlessness, because of his association with an evil spiritual friend, from his youth he did not obtain even the slightest benefit of a single teaching. It is just like a man who enters the ocean and beholds many heaps of precious jewels, yet through the power of laziness fails to take any in hand. Or again, like one who enters the ocean and beholds heaps of precious jewels, yet dies or is slain by a vicious demon — so too was the monk Śubhakara. He entered the teaching of the Buddha, yet was slain by an evil spiritual friend, like a vicious demon. Noble son, for this reason the Tathāgata, out of compassionate love, declared that the monk Śubhakara was heedless.

Noble son, toward one who was formerly poor, one may feel a compassionate thought, yet that compassion does not reach its fullest depth. But toward one who formerly possessed wealth and resources, and later has lost them and fallen into poverty — toward such a one compassion is indeed most profound. So too it is with the monk Śubhakara: he upheld, preserved, recited, and read aloud the twelve branches of scripture, and had attained the four meditative concentrations — to have then fallen from those concentrations is cause for the deepest compassion. Thus I have declared that the monk Śubhakara is utterly heedless. Because of his heedlessness he completely severed all roots of virtue, and so whoever sees or hears of him as one who has become an object of fault in my presence — toward such a one, without exception, a mind of most profound compassionate love must arise, just as compassion arises upon seeing someone who once possessed wealth and resources later seen without them.

For many years I dwelt together with Śubhakara, and throughout that time he continuously gave rise to unwholesome states of mind toward me. Having given rise to those unwholesome minds, he never abandoned his wrong views.

Son of good family, if from the very beginning I saw not even a hair's tip of a root of virtue in Śubhakara, then he would be one holding a wrong view that has utterly severed all roots of virtue, and he would dwell in the hell realm for an entire aeon — this is what scripture teaches. Because he speaks declaring that there is no cause, no result, and no karmic action, he is one holding a wrong view that has utterly severed all roots of virtue, and scripture prophesies that he will dwell in the hell realm for an aeon.

Son of good family, consider this example: a man has fallen into a pit of filth, and a friend, thinking to draw him out, reaches down and grasps him by the hair. If he can take hold of the hair, he then pulls him out. But if he cannot grasp the hair and nothing appears to grip at all, his intention to pull the man out subsides. I am like this as well: having searched for whatever little root of virtue existed in Śubhakara and having found none whatsoever, had I then undertaken to rescue him, he would at all times have had not even a hair's tip of a root of virtue, and so he would not have been rescued from the hell realm.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, Tathāgata, for what reason did you prophesy that Śubhakara would fall into the Avīci hell realm?"

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, the monk Śubhakara had many spiritual friends and a large retinue. All of those followers of Śubhakara were arhats, and because they held him to be one who had attained the fruit of awakening, in order to destroy that wrong view they harbored toward him, it was prophesied that Śubhakara, through heedlessness, would fall into the hell realm.

Son of good family, you should know that what the Tathāgata has spoken is truly and without exception non-dual. Why? Because if the Tathāgata has prophesied that someone will fall into the hell realm, there is no instance of that person not falling into the hell realm. The prophecies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, on the other hand, are of two kinds: some are true, and some are false. For example, when Maudgalyāyana was dwelling in the central lands, he prophesied to all the people of that region, "In seven days rain will fall," but afterward no rain fell. He prophesied to a young pregnant woman, "A white calf will be born," but a spotted calf was born instead. He prophesied, "A boy will be born," but afterward a girl was born.

Son of good family, the monk Śubhakara constantly proclaimed to countless sentient beings in every respect: "There is no fruit of either virtue or evil." At that time, all roots of virtue were utterly severed, without so much as a hair's tip remaining. Son of good family, I knew from the beginning that the monk Śubhakara had no roots of virtue, and yet I dwelt together with him for a full twenty years and shared life in common with him. If I had completely abandoned him and not kept him near, left or right, then that Śubhakara would have led countless sentient beings into sinful and non-virtuous actions. This is what is meant by the Tathāgata possessing the power of omniscient knowledge.

Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, why is it said that one with wrong views lacks virtuous qualities?"

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, it is because one with wrong views has utterly severed all roots of virtue. While all sentient beings possess the five faculties beginning with faith, in one with wrong views these are entirely severed. Therefore, even killing a worm incurs a fault, yet killing one with wrong views incurs no fault of wrongdoing.

Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, is it because one with wrong views lacks virtuous qualities that they are called one with wrong views?"

The Blessed One declared: It is exactly so. It is exactly so.

Kāśyapa asked:

Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, virtue in all sentient beings has three aspects: past, future, and present. If one with wrong views has not severed the future virtuous Dharma, then why is it said that their virtuous Dharma is severed and they are called one with wrong views?"

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, severance has two aspects: being blocked in the present, and the future being obscured by the present obscuration. Because those with wrong views possess both kinds of severance, I have declared that they have utterly severed their roots of virtue.

Son of good family, consider this analogy: a person who has fallen into a cesspit is visible only up to a single hair-tip. Though a single hair-tip has not yet sunk, that single hair-tip is not enough to support the body. Those with wrong views are likewise. In the future there may exist a root of virtue, yet they will not be freed from the suffering of the hell-beings. Though they may be liberated at a future time, in the present there is nothing whatsoever to be done, and so they cannot be liberated now. They will, however, be liberated through the cause and condition of the intrinsic nature of the buddhas. The intrinsic nature of the buddhas is neither past, nor future, nor present; therefore the intrinsic nature of the buddhas cannot be severed. Just as no sprout can grow from a rotted seed, those with wrong views are similar in that respect.

Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, if those with wrong views have not severed the intrinsic nature of the buddhas, and if the intrinsic nature of the buddhas is itself virtuous, why then is it said that they have severed all virtue?"

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, any sentient being who presently possesses the intrinsic nature of the buddhas is not to be called one with wrong views — just as there is a conventional designation of a self applied to sentient beings in the world. If the intrinsic nature of the buddhas were permanent, it would be outside the three times; but if it fell within the three times, it would be called impermanent. Since the intrinsic nature of the buddhas will be seen at a future time, I have declared that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of the buddhas. Therefore it is seen to some small degree by a bodhisattva of the tenth ground who is endowed with the most excellent array of qualities.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, if the intrinsic nature of the buddhas is permanent, like the sky, why has the Tathāgata called it future?"

If the Tathāgata declares that those with wrong views lack virtuous Dharma, does not loving-kindness and affection arise in one who shares the training, or shares the teacher, or the father, or the mother, or friends and companions, or the wife, or the children of one with wrong views? And if it does arise, is that not itself virtue?

The Blessed One declared: Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, that was very well asked. The intrinsic nature of the buddhas is like the sky — it is neither past, nor future, nor present. All sentient beings also have a body of three aspects: past, future, and present. Since sentient beings will see the intrinsic nature of the buddhas in the future through karma of perfect purity and excellence of array, I have therefore spoken of the intrinsic nature of the buddhas as future.

Son of good family, for the sake of ordinary persons I have at certain times declared that the cause is the fruit, and at other times I have declared that the fruit is the cause. Therefore, in the sūtras it is said that food is life, and

seeing form is touch" — just so, because the body will become perfectly pure in the future, it is spoken of as the intrinsic nature of the buddhas.

The questioner asked: Blessed One, if the matter is as the Blessed One has declared, then why did you say that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of the buddhas?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, although the intrinsic nature of the buddhas is not present in sentient beings at this present time, it is not fitting to say it is absent. For example, although sky is not present in the present moment, it is not fitting to say it is absent. All sentient beings are impermanent, yet the intrinsic nature of the buddhas is permanent, unchanging, and unwavering. Therefore I have declared in this sūtra that the intrinsic nature of the buddhas in sentient beings is neither within nor without — like the sky, it is neither within nor without. If sky had an inside and an outside, it would not be fitting to call it one or permanent, nor would it be fitting to say it exists in all places. Sky is neither within nor without, and yet it is present in all sentient beings; the intrinsic nature of the buddhas in sentient beings is likewise the same.

As for what you say — that those with wrong craving possess virtuous phenomena — that is not the meaning. Why? Because for those with wrong craving, all actions of body, speech, and mind, actions of taking, actions of giving, actions of seeking, actions of knowing, and all other such actions are entirely wrong actions. Why is that? Because they hold no hope in cause and result.

Son of good family, consider this example: just as the āruṛa plant passes through sprout, leaf, trunk, branch, flower, and fruit — like the whiteness of snow throughout all of these — so too are the non-virtuous actions of those with wrong craving like that throughout.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata possesses the power of knowing the faculties of beings; therefore he knows with great precision the sharp, middling, and dull faculties of all sentient beings. He thoroughly understands which sentient beings will decline from middling to dull faculties, which will rise from middling to sharp, which will decline from sharp to middling, and which will fall from middling to dull. Therefore there is no certainty regarding the faculties of sentient beings. Because there is no certainty, some, having cut the root of virtue, will be reborn again. If the faculties of sentient beings were fixed, then from the very beginning there would be no cutting, and having cut they would not be reborn — yet it is declared that those with wrong craving fall into a hell realm for the duration of an entire eon, which would be contradictory.

Son of good family, therefore the Tathāgata has declared that all phenomena lack any defining characteristic that is fixed.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, the Tathāgata possesses the power of knowing the faculties. If he knew that the monk Suvarṇakāra had entirely severed the root of virtue, then why did he grant him the going forth?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, long ago when I myself went forth, I permitted my younger brothers Nanda, Upananda, Devadatta, and my son Rāhula, and all the others to go forth after me and to apply themselves diligently to the path. If I had not let Suvarṇakāra go forth, he would have gained a royal means and, being endowed with might and power, would have entirely destroyed the Dharma of the buddhas. For this cause, by this condition, I let him go forth and permitted him to apply himself diligently to the path. Son of good family, even if the monk Suvarṇakāra had not gone forth, he would still have cut the root of virtue and for incalculable lifetimes would have been deprived of benefit and happiness.

Now, having gone forth, even though he had cut the root of virtue, he would keep moral discipline, show reverence to elders, teachers, and those endowed with good qualities, and would cultivate the meditative concentrations, training in them from the first through to the fourth. This, too, is called a wholesome cause. And from that wholesome cause, wholesome phenomena would arise. When wholesome phenomena have arisen, he would apply himself diligently to awakening. And having applied himself diligently to awakening, he would attain the unsurpassable, perfect, and complete awakening. For this reason, I permitted the monk Suvarṇakāra to go forth. Son of good family, had I not permitted the monk Suvarṇakāra to go forth while keeping his moral discipline, it could not be said that the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers.

Son of good family, when a sentient being possesses roots of virtue yet is also endowed with unwholesome phenomena, and when that person is possessed of both, I understand that before long he will completely sever the root of virtue and come to be possessed of the root of non-virtue. Why is this? Because such a being does not rely on a spiritual friend, does not listen to the sacred Dharma, applies his mind to what is unwholesome, and does not apply his mind properly. For this cause, by this condition, he cuts the root of virtue and comes to be possessed of the root of non-virtue.

Son of good family, furthermore, the Tathāgata sees that if that same person, at the present time or in time to come, whether in youth, in the prime of life, or in old age, were to rely on a spiritual friend and were to hear and hold the sacred Dharma of suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path, then his root of virtue would arise again.

Son of good family, consider this example: near a town there is a sweet spring endowed with eight excellent qualities. If those who are thirsty and tormented by heat were to head toward that spring, then a wise and discerning person would have no doubt that those tormented by thirst would certainly reach the spring. Why? Because there is no other way. The Blessed One, the buddha, regards ordinary beings in exactly the same way. Therefore the Tathāgata is said to be endowed with the power of knowing the faculties.

Then the Blessed One took up a little handful of earth and placed it on his fingernail, and asked Kāśyapa: "Which is more, the earth of the world-realms of the ten directions, or the earth I have placed on my fingernail?"

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa replied: "Blessed One, the earth upon the fingernail is not to be compared with the earth of the world-realms of the ten directions."

Son of good family, obtaining a human body from a human body, leaving behind the bodies of the three lower destinies to obtain a human body with its faculties complete, being born in a central land, applying oneself diligently to awakening with genuine faith, and then, having applied oneself diligently to awakening, applying oneself diligently to the genuine path, and then, having applied oneself diligently to the genuine path, attaining liberation, and then, having attained liberation, passing beyond sorrow — this is comparable to the earth placed upon the fingernail.

Falling from a human body into the three lower destinies, passing from the three lower destinies into yet another body of the three lower destinies, having faculties that are incomplete, being born in a border region, placing one's trust in wrong and evil views, and applying oneself diligently to the path of evil views so that one does not attain liberation, the permanence and bliss of passing beyond sorrow — this is comparable to the earth of the world-realms of the ten directions.

Son of good family, keeping moral discipline in its full purity, being free of laziness through diligence, not transgressing the four root precepts,

not committing the five acts of immediate retribution, not misappropriating the property of the Saṅgha, not engaging in actions born of wrong craving, not cutting the roots of virtue, and placing one's trust in the sūtras of nirvāṇa and the like — this is comparable to the earth of the palm of the hand.

Allowing one's moral discipline to degenerate through laziness, transgressing the four root precepts, committing the offenses of the five acts of immediate retribution, freely misappropriating the property of the Saṅgha, engaging in actions born of wrong craving, cutting the roots of virtue, and not placing one's trust in these sūtras — this is comparable to the earth of the world-realms of the ten directions.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata is supremely skilled in understanding the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of all sentient beings. Therefore the Tathāgata is said to be possessed of the power of being skilled in the five faculties.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, since the Blessed One is possessed of the power of being skilled in the faculties, he knows fully all distinctions of superior, middling, inferior, sharp, and dull among the faculties of all sentient beings. He knows the faculties of sentient beings of the present time and also the faculties of sentient beings of the future. After the Blessed One has passed completely into nirvāṇa, those sentient beings will speak in the following ways.

Some will say that the Tathāgata has passed completely and finally into nirvāṇa. Some will say that he has not finally passed completely into nirvāṇa. Some will say that a self exists. Some will say that no self exists. Some will assert that the five aggregates exist. Some will assert that the five aggregates do not exist. Some will assert that there is return. Some will assert that there is no return. Some will say that the body of the Tathāgata is conditioned. Some will say that the body of the Tathāgata is unconditioned. Some will say that the twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned phenomena. Some will say that the twelve links of dependent origination are unconditioned. Some will say that mind is permanent. Some will say that mind is impermanent. Some will say that the pleasures of the five sense desires obstruct the noble path. Some will say that they do not obstruct it. Some will say that the supreme worldly dharma belongs to the desire realm alone. Some will say that it belongs to all three realms. Some will say that generosity is nothing but a mental action. Some will say that it is the five aggregates themselves. Some will assert that there are three unconditioned phenomena. Some will assert that there are no three unconditioned phenomena. Again, some will say that form is something made. Some will say that there is no made form. Some will assert that there is form that is not made. Some will assert that there is no form that is not made. Some will assert that mind-arisen phenomena exist. Some will assert that mind-arisen phenomena do not exist. Some will assert that there are five modes of existence. Some will assert that there are six modes of existence. Some will say that a lay practitioner can perfectly fulfil the eight precepts. Some will say that they can be fulfilled even without perfecting them. Some will say that even though a monk has broken the four root precepts, his monastic discipline still exists. Some will say that it does not exist. Some will say that stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats all attain manifest awakening. Some will say that they do not attain manifest awakening. Some will say that the nature of a buddha exists within sentient beings. Some will say that the nature of a buddha is other than sentient beings."

Some will say that the nature of a buddha exists in all beings without exception, including those who have broken the four root precepts, committed the five acts of immediate retribution, and fallen into wrong craving and the like. Some will say that it does not exist. Some will say that buddhas exist in the ten directions. Some will say that buddhas do not exist in the ten directions. If the Tathāgata possesses the power of knowing the faculties of beings, why then has he not spoken definitively on these matters?

Then the Blessed One declared to the bodhisattva Kāśyapaputra: Son of good family, this matter is not known through eye-consciousness, nor through any of the remaining forms of consciousness up to and including mind-consciousness. It can be known through wisdom. To one who is learned and possessed of wisdom, I have spoken without duality, and such a person understands that I have spoken without duality. To one without wisdom, I have spoken in an indefinite way, and that person without wisdom understands that I have spoken in an indefinite way.

Son of good family, all the virtuous teachings of the Tathāgata are spoken for the purpose of training sentient beings. Consider a skilled physician: every branch of his medical art and practice is directed toward healing all those who are afflicted with illness.

Son of good family, the Buddha, the Blessed One, expounds a single teaching in two aspects, and a single Dharma name in innumerable names, and a single meaning in innumerable names, and innumerable meanings in immeasurable names — for the sake of a given field of beings, for the sake of a given time, for the sake of those who speak to others, for the sake of showing it to non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), and for the sake of the varying capacities of beings.

As to how a single name is expounded in innumerable names: nirvāṇa, for example, is called nirvāṇa; it is also called birthlessness; it is also called non-arising; it is also called non-action; it is also called the unconditioned; it is also called the going for refuge; it is also called ground and support; it is also called complete liberation; it is also called luminous radiance; it is also called the lamp; it is also called the ultimate; it is also called fearlessness; it is also called the irreversible; it is also called the abode of bliss; it is also called peace; it is also called signlessness; it is also called non-duality; it is also called the single conduct; it is also called perfect coolness; it is also called the absence of darkness; it is also called unobstructedness; it is also called freedom from conflict; it is also called the great expanse; it is also called clarity and freshness; it is also called auspiciousness. This is how a single name is unfolded into innumerable names.

As to how a single referent is expounded in innumerable names: consider Śakra, the lord of the gods. He is called Śakra; he is also called Kauśika; he is also called Vāsava; he is also called Purandara; he is also called Maghavān; he is also called Indra; he is also called the Thousand-Eyed; he is also called the husband of Śacī; he is also called Vajra; he is also called the Crest Jewel; he is also called the Jewelled Victory Banner. This is what is meant by a single referent being expounded in innumerable names.

As to how innumerable referents are expounded in innumerable names: consider the Blessed One, the Buddha. He is called Tathāgata — a distinct meaning, a distinct name. He is also called arhat — a distinct meaning, a distinct name. He is also called the Perfectly and Fully Awakened One — a distinct meaning, a distinct name. He is also called the Ferryman; he is also called the Caravan Leader; he is also called Buddha, the Awakened One; he is also called One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct; he is also called the Lion King; he is also called the Wandering Ascetic (śramaṇa); he is also called the Brahmin; he is also called the Peaceful One; he is also called the Great Benefactor; he is also called the Perfected One; he is also called the Great King of Physicians;

He is also called the Great King of Bulls; he is also called the Great King of Nāgas; he is also called the Giver of Eyes; he is also called the Greatly Powerful One; he is also called the One of Great Fearlessness; he is also called the Assembly of Precious Ones; he is also called the Merchant; he is also called the One Who Has Attained Liberation; he is also called the Great Person; he is also called the Teacher of Gods and Humans; he is also called the Great White Lotus; he is also called the Solitary One Without Companions; he is also called the Great Field of Merit; he is also called the Ocean of Wisdom; he is also called the One Without Characteristics; he is also called the One Endowed with the Eight Gnoses — all of these are distinct meanings and distinct names. Noble son, this is called "the exposition of countless names from countless meanings."

Furthermore, there is also an exposition of countless names from a single meaning. What is that? For example, the aggregates (skandhas) are also called "aggregates"; they are also called "the inverted"; they are also called "the true"; they are also called "the four applications of mindfulness"; they are also called "the four defilements"; they are also called "the bases of the four consciousnesses"; they are also called "the conditioned"; they are also called "the path"; they are also called "time"; they are also called "sentient beings"; they are also called "conventional"; they are also called "ultimate"; they are also called "the cultivation of body, ethical conduct, and mind"; they are also called "cause and result"; they are also called "mental affliction"; they are also called "liberation"; they are also called "the twelve links of dependent origination"; they are also called "śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas"; they are also called "hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods"; they are also called "past, future, and present." This is the exposition of countless names from a single meaning.

Noble son, the Buddha, the Blessed One, for the sake of sentient beings teaches the extensive from the condensed, and teaches the extensive in condensed form. He teaches the ultimate as the conventional, and teaches the conventional phenomena as the ultimate.

How, then, does he teach the extensive from the condensed? For example, just as I have explained to the monks the twelve links of dependent origination — and what are those twelve links of dependent origination? They are, it was said, "cause and result."

How, then, does he teach the condensed in an extensive way? For example, just as I have explained to the monks today suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Therein, suffering is this: the immeasurable sufferings. The origin is this: the immeasurable mental afflictions. Cessation is this: the immeasurable liberations. The path is this: the immeasurable skillful means.

How, then, does he teach the ultimate as conventional? For example, just as he declared to the monks, "This body of mine is subject to aging, sickness, and death."

How, then, does he teach the conventional as ultimate? For example, just as when he said to Kauṇḍinya, "Because you have heard the meaning of the Dharma, you are named Kauṇḍinya" — since he knew the person as they were, the mind as it was, and the time as it was, the Tathāgata is therefore said to be endowed with the power of knowing the faculties.

Noble son, if I were to explain those meanings definitively and precisely in every case, then I could no longer be called a Tathāgata endowed with the power of knowing the faculties. Noble son, wise men know that a load of fragrant bull's wool is not something a donkey can carry. The modes of conduct of all sentient beings are without number, and therefore the Tathāgata has taught the Dharma in countless forms and varieties. Why is that? Because sentient beings have many kinds of mental afflictions. If the Tathāgata were to teach a single mode of conduct, then he could not be called the Tathāgata endowed with the power of knowing the faculties.

For this reason, in other sūtras I have explained that it is not fitting to teach five types of Dharma to five types of sentient being. To one who lacks faith, genuine faith is not to be praised. To one of poor moral discipline, restraint of ethical conduct is not to be praised. To one who is miserly, generosity is not to be praised. To one who is lazy, extensive learning is not to be praised. To one who is deluded, wisdom is not to be praised.

Why is that? If wise persons were to teach those five things to those five types of individual, such teaching would merit neither the name of being endowed with the power of knowing the faculties, nor the name of having compassion for sentient beings. Why? Because those five types of individual, upon hearing those five things, would give rise to minds of faithlessness, ill will, and anger. Through that cause and that condition, the fruit of suffering would ripen for them across countless lifetimes. Therefore one could not be called compassionate toward sentient beings or endowed with the power of knowing the faculties.

For this reason, in an earlier sūtra I said to Śāriputra: "Do not teach the Dharma at length to one of sharp faculties, and do not teach the Dharma in brief summary to one of dull faculties." Śāriputra then replied: "Blessed One, it is because of compassion that I taught it. It was not through being endowed with the power of knowing the faculties."

Noble son, teaching the Dharma in full detail or in brief summary belongs to the domain of a buddha. It is not something understood by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Noble son, what you said — that after the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, his close attendants will each explain things separately and in different ways — these are persons who, through wrong understanding, have not obtained the correct view. Therefore they are unable to benefit either themselves or others.

Noble son, those sentient beings are not uniform in their intrinsic nature, their conduct, their faculties, their objects of engagement, or their spiritual friends. Therefore the Tathāgata has taught them the Dharma in its many modes and varieties. It is for this cause and through this condition that the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the ten directions and the three times also open and teach the twelve branches of scriptural teaching for the sake of sentient beings. Noble son, the Tathāgata's teaching of these twelve branches of scripture was not for his own benefit but for the benefit of others. Therefore the fifth power of the Tathāgata is called the power of knowledge.

By reason of these two powers, the Tathāgata fully discerns: this one severs the roots of virtue in this life; this one severs the roots of virtue in a future life; this one attains liberation in this very life; and this one will attain liberation in a future life. Therefore the Tathāgata is called the great power unsurpassed by any.

Noble son, whoever says "The Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa forever" or "The Tathāgata never passes into nirvāṇa" — such a person says so because they do not understand the intention of the Tathāgata.

Noble son, in the fragrant sandalwood forest there dwelt thirty-eight thousand sages. All of them had, in times past, generated roots of virtue under the buddha Kāśyapa, yet they had not entered the correct path, paid homage to the buddhas, or listened to the sacred Dharma. For the sake of those sages, the Tathāgata declared to Ānanda: "Three months from now I shall pass completely into nirvāṇa." When the gods heard those words, the news spread from one to another and it became known throughout the fragrant sandalwood forest.

When the sages heard this, a mind of deep remorse arose in them and they said: "Why were we born as human beings yet failed to pay homage to a buddha? The arising of the blessed buddhas in this world is as rare as the udumbara flower. Let us go now into the presence of the Blessed One and listen to the sacred Dharma." And so they spoke.

Noble son, at that time thirty-eight thousand sages came into my presence, and I taught the Dharma to them just as it needed to be taught. "O great beings, form is impermanent. Why so? Because the causes and conditions of form are impermanent. If form arises from impermanent causes, can form possibly be called permanent?" The teaching should be understood to extend in the same way through to consciousness. Having heard those teachings, the sages attained the fruit of arhatship in that very instant.

Noble son, in the city of Kuśinagara there lived some thirty thousand wrestlers who were independent and ungoverned, and they were drunk with pride and arrogance over their bodies, their strength, their long lives, and their wealth. Noble son, in order to tame those wrestlers, I said to the son of Maudgala: "Subdue those wrestlers." Then, following my word, the son of Maudgala employed many and various skillful means for five years, yet not a single wrestler was tamed or persuaded to listen to the Dharma.

Then, for the sake of those wrestlers, I declared to Ānanda: "Three months from now I shall pass completely into nirvāṇa." Noble son, when those wrestlers heard these words they assembled and prepared the road. Three months passed, and at that time I traveled from Vaiśālī to the city of Kuśinagara. When I had gone about half the way, I saw from afar that the wrestlers had assembled, and I emanated the form of a monk, went in among all the wrestlers, and said: "Fellows, what are you doing?" When the wrestlers heard these words they were all enraged and said: "Monk, how dare you call us fellows?" I replied: "You are fellows indeed — some thirty thousand of you assembled, straining with all the strength you have, yet unable to move even this little stone. Is 'fellows' not the right word for you?" The wrestlers said: "If you call us fellows, then we know you must be a great man."

Noble son, at that point I lifted the stone with my two toes. When the wrestlers saw such a thing, they generated the perception of themselves as weak, inferior, and worthless, and then said again: "Monk, can you cast this stone to one side of the road?" I replied: "Fellows, why are you preparing this road?" The wrestlers said: "Monk, do you not know? The Tathāgata Śākyamuni is coming along this road on his way to pass completely into nirvāṇa in the sal grove — that is why and on that account we are preparing the road." Then I praised them: "Excellent! Excellent! Fellows, since you have thus generated a wholesome mind, I will make this stone disappear for your sake." Saying this, I took the stone in my hand and hurled it until it reached the pinnacle of existence.

Then, when the wrestlers saw the stone touch the sky, they were all filled with fear and terror and fled in the four directions, whereupon I said: "Wrestlers, do not generate a mind of fear and terror — do not scatter and run away." The wrestlers said: "Monk, if you would be our refuge, then we shall be at peace."

Then I took the stone and placed it in the palm of my right hand. The wrestlers, seeing this, felt joy arise in their minds and said: "Monk, is this stone permanent or impermanent?" Thereupon I blew on that stone with a single breath from my mouth and turned it to dust. When the wrestlers saw this, they said to the monk, "This stone is impermanent," and a mind of shame and deep regret arose in them, and they were struck with remorse, thinking: "Why did we take pride in our form, our strength, our lifespan, and our wealth, and generate minds of conceit and arrogance?" Knowing their minds, I sent forth a magical body, assumed an ordinary appearance, and taught the Dharma. When the wrestlers saw this, every one of them generated a mind of awakening.

Noble son, in the city of Kuśanagara there was a craftsman named Cunda who had made a great vow before the buddha Kāśyapa: "When the Tathāgata Śākyamuni passes into nirvāṇa, I will offer the last meal from within my household." For this reason, while I was in Vaiśālī, I summoned the monk Upavāna and declared: "Noble son, three months from now I shall pass into nirvāṇa at the foot of a tree in the city of Kuśanagara. See to it that Cunda is informed."

Noble son, in Rājagṛha there was a wandering ascetic (ṛṣi) of the five higher knowledges named Subhadra, one hundred and twenty years of age, who constantly proclaimed: "I am omniscient," and harbored great pride. In a former time he had planted roots of virtue before immeasurable buddhas. In order to tame him, I told Ānanda: "Three months from now I shall pass into nirvāṇa," and declared this aloud. When Subhadra heard this, he came to where I was and generated a mind of faith and reverence. I taught him the Dharma in its many aspects, and upon hearing it he attained the undefiled.

Noble son, Prince Ajātaśatru, son of King Bimbisāra, through conditions of evil influence from Devadatta, developed an evil mind and brought about the killing of his royal father — yet he found no opportunity to harm me. Devadatta, that wicked one, had also through the condition of his past karma generated an unwholesome mind toward me and, wishing to harm me, cultivated the five higher knowledges and quickly attained them. He then became an intimate friend and companion of Prince Ajātaśatru, and for the sake of the prince displayed all manner of miraculous powers — entering through solid walls and emerging through doors, entering through doors and emerging through solid walls, and at times appearing in the forms of elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, men, and women. When Prince Ajātaśatru saw all of this, a mind of faith, joy, and delight arose in him. On account of this he made offerings with many kinds of offering substances, and then said: "Noble teacher, I wish to see the Mandārava flowers." Thereupon Devadatta ascended to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and solicited flowers from those gods. But because Devadatta's merit was exhausted, not one of them gave him any. Having thus failed to obtain the flowers, he thought: "What fault would there be if I, with no one to give them to me, were to take the Mandārava tree for myself?" Drawing near and reaching out to take it, his supernatural powers instantly vanished. He found himself looking back to see his own body sitting in Rājagṛha, and a mind of shame and embarrassment arose, so that he was unable to face Prince Ajātaśatru. Then he thought: "Now let me go to where the Tathāgata is and muster a large retinue."

He thought: "If the Buddha grants this, I myself will be in charge of teaching the Dharma as I please to Śāriputra and the others." Then Devadatta came to where I was and said: "Tathāgata, entrust all these great multitudes to me. I will teach them the Dharma in many different ways and tame them."

I declared: "Fool! Śāriputra and the others are sharp in their faculties and endowed with great wisdom, and even though the whole world holds them in esteem, I would not entrust the great multitudes to them — what need is there to speak of entrusting them to you, a deluded wretch who eats filth?"

At that, Devadatta's mind grew worse toward me than before, and he said: "Gautama, you may be taming many followers now, but by the very nature of reality I see that before long you will be no more." Having said those words, the great earth shook in six ways, and right at Devadatta's feet the ground split open and a violent wind rushed out, swirling up dust and the like and covering him with it. When Devadatta saw such an evil omen, he said: "If this body of mine is inevitably destined to fall into the Avīci hell in this very life, then I must take revenge on my great enemy." So saying, he went to where King Ajātaśatru was.

The moment Ajātaśatru saw him, he asked: "Noble one, why do you look so pale and without any lustre?" Devadatta replied: "Am I not always like this? Do you not know?" Ajātaśatru said: "Tell me the cause and condition of what you have in mind." Devadatta said: "I am very close to you, and when the people of the land speak ill of you to me, I take it amiss. Is there any pleasant news for me to hear?"

Prince Ajātaśatru said: "What ill things do the people of the land say about me?" Devadatta replied: "The people of the land speak ill of you by calling you Ajātaśatru." Ajātaśatru said: "How did I come to be given the name Ajātaśatru?" Devadatta replied: "When you were born, all the astrologers said: 'Once this child is born, he will kill his royal father.' For that reason all the people of the land gave you the name Ajātaśatru. All the palace retinue call you Sudarśana in order to guard your feelings. When Queen Vaidehī heard this, the moment you were born she threw you from a great height, and one of your fingers was broken. Because of that cause and condition, people also gave you the name Bārāruce."

He went on: "When I heard them speak so, I felt displeasure arise, yet I was unable to say anything to you about it." Then Devadatta instructed him by various evil means to kill his royal father the king, saying: "If you kill your royal father, I too will kill the ascetic Gautama."

Prince Ajātaśatru went to the two great ministers known as Praśānta and asked them: "Great ministers, why have I been given the name Ajātaśatru?" The great ministers then gave the same account of how the name was given in former times as Devadatta had given. Upon hearing this, Prince Ajātaśatru conferred with the great ministers, seized his royal father, surrounded him with four armies outside the city, and set out.

When Queen Vaidehī heard of this, she went to where the king was, but the guards blocked her and would not let her see him. Then the queen's mind filled with anger and she scolded the guards.

This is the forty-fifth fascicle of the Noble Great Sūtra of Complete Nirvāṇa (Skt. Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra).

Then the guards went to the king and asked the queen's request to visit the royal father, and then asked the prince whether it was permitted or not.

When the prince heard this, he became even more enraged. He went to where his mother was, seized her by the hair, drew his sword, and was about to strike her down. At that point Jīvaka spoke up, saying: "Great King, even for the gravest offenses committed since the world began, no woman has ever been put to death by royal punishment — how much less your own royal mother?" Prince Ajātaśatru heard Jīvaka's words and refrained from killing her. But he cut off the royal father's clothing, bedding, food, and medicine for his illness, and after seven days had passed the royal father died.

When Ajātaśatru saw that his royal father had died, remorse arose in his mind. As he went to two of his great ministers, they spoke various perverse and unwholesome words, saying: "Great King, none of your actions are blameworthy. Why should you give rise to remorse today?" Jīvaka then spoke again: "Great King, please understand this: an action such as this carries two kinds of grievous wrongdoing — killing one's royal father, and killing a stream-enterer (Skt. srotāpanna). For a wrong of that kind, there is no one other than the Blessed One who has the power to purify such an action." Ajātaśatru said: "The Tathāgata is perfectly pure and without stain. I am a sinful person — how could he bear to look upon me?" Noble son, having known of this situation, I declared to Ānanda that I would pass into complete nirvāṇa after three months had elapsed.

When Ajātaśatru heard this, he came to where I was. I taught the Dharma, and his heavy wrongdoing became lighter, and he also attained irreversible faith. Noble son, my attendants, hearing me say this, did not understand my intention and said: "The Tathāgata has long since passed into nirvāṇa." Noble son, there are two kinds of bodhisattva: those who are genuine and endowed with real meaning, and those who bear the name only as a superficial designation. Among these, a bodhisattva who bears the name only as a superficial designation, upon hearing me say "I will pass into complete nirvāṇa in three months," gives rise to a mind of complete despondency and says: "If the Tathāgata himself is impermanent and does not abide, what should we do? Why, on account of such a state of affairs, must we go on experiencing for countless lifetimes the great suffering of affliction? Even the Blessed One, the Buddha, possessing immeasurable merit, could not defeat the māra of death — so how could we ever be capable of it?" Noble son, for that reason I told those bodhisattvas: "The Tathāgata is eternally abiding, unchanging, and unshifting." Noble son, my attendants, hearing me say this, did not understand my intention and declared with certainty: "The Tathāgata will ultimately never pass into nirvāṇa." Noble son, certain sentient beings, having produced a nihilistic view, say: "After the death of the body, there is nothing whatsoever that all sentient beings experience of virtuous or non-virtuous karma." For their sake I declared: "The ripened fruit of virtuous and non-virtuous karma is truly and genuinely experienced." How is its existence demonstrated? Noble son, in a past age there was in a city called Kuśāgranagara a king named Sudarśana. For eighty-four thousand years he lived as a youth, for eighty-four thousand years he served as regent, and for eighty-four thousand years he reigned as king. While dwelling in seclusion, he thought to himself: "Sentient beings, because of meager merit, have short lives in their rebirths, and

the four enemies are always following close behind, yet they neither know nor feel it, and go about in heedlessness. Therefore I shall go forth and cultivate the path to awakening, and cut these four enemies — birth, old age, sickness, and death — entirely away." With this thought in mind, he declared to his ministers: "Outside the city, build me a palace of the seven precious substances." When the palace was built, he declared to his ministers, his inner counselors, his princes, and his kinsmen: "Know this: I am thinking of going forth. Do you give your consent?" Then all the chief ministers, kinsmen, and the rest replied: "Excellent! Great King, now the time has come." Thereupon King Sudarśana, in the company of a single attendant, dwelt in that palace for eighty-four thousand years and cultivated the mind of loving-kindness (maitrī). Through that cause, for eighty-four thousand years he was successively made a wheel-turning king. After that, for thirty lifetimes he was made Śakra, lord of the gods.
