And for countless lifetimes he was made a petty king. Noble son, do not think that Sudarśana of that time and age was someone else: he was none other than myself as I am today. Noble son, when my attendants heard me speak in this way, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively declared that self and what belongs to self exist." Again, at another time I declared to sentient beings: "What is called 'self' is intrinsic nature — namely, the twelve inner and outer causes and conditions, dependent origination, the five aggregates of sentient beings, mind, the elements, the merit of the world, the power of karma, and the world governed by a divine sovereign — all of this is called 'self.'" When my attendants heard me speak in this way, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively declared that a self exists." Noble son, yet at another time a certain monk came to where I was and asked: "Blessed One, what is this thing called 'self'? Who or what is this 'self'? And by what condition is it called 'self'?" Then I declared to that monk: "Monk, self and what belongs to self do not exist. That which is said not to exist was not present from the very beginning, yet exists now. What exists will later come not to exist. Even at the first moment of birth it came from nowhere, and when it ceases later it goes nowhere. The fruit of karma exists, yet it was not made by anyone. There are no aggregates that are relinquished, and no aggregates that are taken up. The thing you asked about — 'what is this self?' — that is suchness itself. The thing you asked — 'who is this self?' — that is karma. The condition by which it is called 'self' is existence." "Monk, just as when two hands clap together a sound arises between them, so too is the self: through the connected cause of mind, karma, and existence, the three, it is called 'self.' Monk, the form of all sentient beings is not the self. The self is not found within form, nor is form found within the self — and so on likewise through to consciousness. Monk, even those who assert the existence of a self, such as the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), do not posit it as something other than the aggregates. There is no such ground as claiming that a self exists beyond the aggregates once the aggregates have been set aside. The formations of all sentient beings resemble a magical illusion and a mirage. Monk, the five aggregates are impermanent, devoid of happiness, selfless, and utterly impure."

Noble son, at that time an immeasurable number of monks attained the fruit of arhatship by realizing that these five aggregates are without self and without what belongs to a self.

Noble son, when my attendants heard those words, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively taught the absence of self."

Noble son, I also said in a sūtra: "This body was taken up from the conjunction of three things." That is to say, the body is taken up through the coming together of father, mother, and the intermediate-state aggregates.

I also said: "The person who is a once-returner will directly realize nirvāṇa — or, if the five aggregates of the intermediate state exist, will pass beyond sorrow in the intermediate state." This too means: having complete and clear faculties in the intermediate-state aggregates is the result of former karma, just as clarified butter is the essence of butter.

Noble son, I once said: "The intermediate-state aggregates of sinful sentient beings are like coarse chaff in the world. The intermediate-state aggregates of beings who are purely virtuous are like white fine cotton cloth from the land of the Śakas." When my attendants heard those words, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively taught that the intermediate-state aggregates exist."

Noble son, I also said to sentient beings who had committed the boundless misdeeds (Skt. ānantarya): "Having committed the five boundless misdeeds, such sentient beings fall into the hell of boundless retribution." I also said: "The monk called Kumārutsika, immediately upon leaving this body, fell without obstruction into the hell of boundless retribution." I also said to the wanderer Vatsīputra: "Wanderer, if the five aggregates of the intermediate state exist, then the six realms of existence also exist." I also said: "For sentient beings of the formless realm, there are no intermediate-state aggregates." When my attendants heard those words, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively taught that the intermediate-state aggregates do not exist."

Noble son, I have also taught in sūtras that regression exists. Why so? Because the immeasurable number of monks who are lazy and given to indolence do not apply themselves to awakening — and for their sake, five kinds of regression were taught: delight in many activities, fondness for worldly gossip, fondness for sleep, fondness for associating with householders, and fondness for wandering about. Through these causes and conditions, monks come to regress.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of conditions for regression: inner and outer. A person who is an arhat has abandoned the inner conditions, but has not abandoned the outer conditions; through outer conditions, afflictions arise. Because afflictions arise, regression and deterioration occur.

There was also the monk called Kuta, who regressed as many as six times; but each time he returned, he cultivated the mind of conscience and shame, and in the end, at the seventh time, he attained it. After attaining it, fearing that he might regress again, he drew a sword and took his own life.

I also spoke at various times of the occasion of liberation, and at other times of the six types of arhat and so forth. When my attendants heard those words, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively taught that regression exists."

Noble son, it is also said in a sūtra:

Just as burnt wood cannot become wood again, and just as a broken pot can no longer serve as a pot, so too with mental afflictions: once an arhat has completely severed them, they will not arise again. This is what was declared.

It is also taught that there are three causes for the arising of mental afflictions in sentient beings: afflictions that have not been severed, the causes and conditions of those afflictions that have not been severed, and unwholesome mental engagement. An arhat, however, has neither causes nor conditions, and because the afflictions have been severed, there is no unwholesome mental engagement either.

Noble son, when my attendants heard those words, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively taught that there is no regression."

Noble son, I also taught in a sūtra that the body of the Tathāgata is of two kinds: the birth body and the dharmakāya. Of these, the birth body is the body magically emanated through skillful means. Of that body, it is not right to say that there is birth, aging, illness, death, tallness, shortness, darkness, whiteness, this or that, one in training, or one beyond training. When my attendants heard me speak thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively taught that the body of a buddha is a conditioned phenomenon."

The dharmakāya, on the other hand, is permanent, blissful, a self, and perfectly pure, and is entirely without birth, aging, illness, and death. It is neither white nor black, neither tall nor short, neither this nor that, neither one in training nor one beyond training. Whether or not a buddha appears in the world, it abides always, changeless and unaltered. When my attendants heard those words, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively taught that the body of a buddha is an unconditioned phenomenon."

Noble son, I also taught in a sūtra the twelve links of dependent origination: from ignorance arise formations; from formations arises consciousness; from consciousness arise name-and-form; from name-and-form arise the six sense bases; from the six sense bases arises contact; from contact arises feeling; from feeling arises craving; from craving arises grasping; from grasping arises existence; from existence arises birth; and from birth arise aging-and-death, and the sorrow that follows in their wake.

When my attendants heard those words, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has definitively taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned phenomena."

I also spoke at one time to the monks, declaring: "Whether or not buddhas appear in the world, the twelve links of dependent origination are such that their intrinsic nature and defining characteristics abide always."

Noble son, among the twelve links of dependent origination, there are those that did not arise from conditions, those that arose from conditions yet are not themselves the twelve links of dependent origination, those that both arose from conditions and are the twelve links of dependent origination, and those that neither arose from conditions nor are the twelve links of dependent origination.

Of these, the twelve links of dependent origination that did not arise from conditions are the twelve links as they exist in the future. The twelve links that arose from conditions yet are not the twelve links of dependent origination are the five aggregates of an arhat.

Those that both arose from conditions and are the twelve links of dependent origination are as follows: the twelve links of dependent origination together with the five aggregates of foolish, common, ordinary beings. Those that neither arose from conditions nor are the twelve links of dependent origination are, as was declared, space and nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, when my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that the unconditioned is definitely to be included within the twelve links of dependent origination."

Son of good family, I declared in a sūtra: "When all sentient beings abandon this body formed by virtuous and non-virtuous karma, it dissolves and disperses into just those four great elements. One who has performed only virtue will have the mind's formations arise in their highest form. One who has performed only non-virtuous karma will have the mind's formations arise in their lowest form." Son of good family, when my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that mind is definitely permanent."

Son of good family, I once spoke these words to the great king Rūpasāranemi: "Great king, understand it thus: form is impermanent. Why is that? Because it arises from an impermanent cause. Since form arises from an impermanent cause, why would a wise and discerning person speak of it as permanent? If form were permanent, it would not disintegrate and cease, and it would make no sense for sufferings to arise. But we see this form disperse, cease, break apart, and disintegrate. Therefore, understand that form is impermanent. And likewise, up through consciousness, all are the same." Son of good family, when my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that mind is definitely subject to annihilation."

Son of good family, I declared in a sūtra: "Though my attendants hold eight categories of uninspected goods such as incense, flowers, gold, silver, precious jewels, wives, sons, male servants, female servants, and the like, they attain the path of truth. And having attained the path of truth, they do not give them up." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that if one indulges in the five sense pleasures, it will definitely not become an obstacle to the noble path."

Furthermore, at one time I declared: "There is no basis on which a householder can attain the path of truth." Son of good family, when my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that if one indulges in the five sense pleasures it will definitely become an obstacle to the path of truth."

Son of good family, I declared in a sūtra: "One who has abandoned the afflictions but has not yet attained liberation is comparable to one practicing the supreme worldly Dharma in the desire realm." Son of good family, when my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that the supreme worldly Dharma exists only in the desire realm."

And I also declared: "Heat, summit, forbearance, and the supreme worldly Dharma exist from the first meditative concentration up through the fourth meditative concentration."

Son of good family, when my attendants heard those words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that those phenomena exist in the form realm."

And I also declared: "Non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), having previously abandoned the afflictions of the fourth meditative concentration, then cultivate heat, summit, forbearance, and the supreme worldly Dharma, and thereby realize the Four Noble Truths and attain the fruit of non-returner." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that the supreme worldly Dharma exists in the formless realm."

Son of good family, I also declared in a sūtra: "Of the four kinds of generosity, three are pure. In this regard, the giver has faith in cause, result, and the act of giving, while the recipient has no such faith in cause, result, and the act of giving. Or the recipient has faith in cause, result, and the act of giving, while the giver has no such faith in cause, result, and the act of giving. Or both giver and recipient have faith. Or both giver and recipient have no faith. Of these four kinds of generosity, the first three are pure." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that generosity is mind alone."

Son of good family, I also declared at one time: "When giving is performed, five kinds of things are given: the gift of appearance, the gift of strength, the gift of happiness, the gift of life, and the gift of eloquence. Through this, the giver will obtain five kinds of karmic maturation as fruit." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Buddha has declared that generosity itself is the five aggregates (skandhas)."

Son of good family, I declared at one time: "Nirvāṇa is the complete and total exhaustion of the afflictions, ceased utterly without remainder — just as a fire, when it has died, has no nature of arising again, so too is nirvāṇa. What is called empty space is simply the absence of anything whatsoever. Just as in the world the absence of anything whatsoever is called empty space — and it is the absence of anything whatsoever, not a cessation brought about by the condition of wisdom — so if something existed, it would be fitting that causes and conditions also exist. If causes and conditions exist, it would be fitting that exhaustion and cessation exist. Since that is not the case, there is no exhaustion and no cessation." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Blessed One has declared that the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena do not exist."

Son of good family, I once addressed Maudgalyāyana with these words: "Maudgalyāyana, nirvāṇa is a verbal designation. It is the footprint of the path. It is the ultimate abode. It is fearlessness. It is the great Teacher. It is the great fruit. It is ultimate wisdom. It is great patience. It is unobstructed meditative absorption. It is the great dharmadhātu, the basic space of phenomena. It is a taste that is rare and wondrous to encounter. Maudgalyāyana, if it were said that nirvāṇa does not exist, why then have I declared that those who denigrate it fall into the hells?" When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that nirvāṇa exists."

And again at one time I addressed Maudgalyāyana with these words: "Maudgalyāyana, from the eye, which is without essence, through to the body — all are without essence."

"In this way, being empty of essence is called emptiness. Food and the like, which transform and are digested, as well as all sounds — these too are called empty." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Buddha has declared that space, which is empty, and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) certainly exist."

And again at one time I addressed Maudgalyāyana with these words: "Maudgalyāyana, understand this: when someone abides in forbearance without having attained the fruit of stream-entry, the immeasurable karmic maturations of the three lower destinies that have been cut off are not halted through the condition of wisdom (jñāna)." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Buddha has declared that these maturations are not halted through the condition of wisdom."

O son of good family, I also once explained the intermediate state to a monk named Barpa. I declared: "If a monk reflects on form as past or future or present, near or far, gross or subtle, form of such kinds is not a self and does not belong to a self. If a monk understands this, he is able to cut off existence in the form realm." The monk Barpa then asked: "What is meant by form and what by name?" I declared: "The four great elements are form. The four remaining aggregates are name." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that form is definitively the four great elements."

O son of good family, I also declared: "Just as a reflection appears through the condition of a mirror, form is similar: through the condition of the four great elements there appear, in this way, the gross and the subtle, the coarse and the smooth, the blue, the yellow, the red, the white, the long, the short, the square, the round, the tranquil, the light, the heavy, the cold, the hot, hunger, thirst, smoke, clouds, and concave forms as well — and this is conditioned form (saṃskṛta), and it is therefore like an echo." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that the four great elements are conditioned form, and that certain of the four great elements are without conditioned form."

O son of good family, long ago at one time the son of the king of the Awakening Tree said: "If a monk who holds the vow of moral discipline gives rise to a non-virtuous thought, at that moment his monastic moral discipline has become impaired." At that time I addressed the son of the king of the Awakening Tree and declared: "Moral discipline has seven aspects: there is form that is non-manifest (avijñapti), arising from body and speech. Even if, through the condition of non-manifest form, the mind abides in non-virtue or in what is doctrinally indeterminate, it is not to be said that the moral discipline is impaired — it is the guarding of moral discipline. For what cause and condition is non-manifest form called non-manifest? Because a distinct form, through the condition of another distinct form, does not become the cause and effect of yet another distinct form." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Buddha has declared that non-manifest form exists."

O son of good family, in other sūtras I have declared: "What is called moral discipline is the restraint of non-virtuous phenomena (dharmas).

If one does not commit non-virtue, that is the guarding of moral discipline." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that non-manifest form does not exist with certainty."

O son of good family, in other sūtras I have declared: "From the noble aggregate of form through to the aggregate of consciousness, these arise from the cause and condition of ignorance. All foolish and ignoble beings likewise arise through craving that springs from ignorance. One should understand that this very craving is ignorance. Because grasping arises from craving, one should understand that this very grasping is ignorance and craving. Because becoming arises from grasping, one should understand that this very becoming is ignorance, becoming, and grasping. Because feeling arises from becoming, one should understand that this very feeling is formations and becoming. From the cause of feeling there arise name-and-form, ignorance, craving, grasping, becoming, formations, feeling, contact, consciousness, and the six sense bases and so forth. Therefore feeling is the twelve links of dependent origination." When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that phenomena do not arise from mind."

O son of good family, in other sūtras I have declared: "From the eye, form, appearance, and defiled desire, eye-consciousness arises. What is called defiled desire is ignorance; when one seeks by the nature of desire, that is called craving. Through the condition of craving there is grasping; grasping is karma. Through the condition of karma there is consciousness; through the condition of consciousness, name-and-form; through the condition of name-and-form, the six sense bases; through the condition of the six sense bases, contact; and through the condition of contact, there arise perception, feeling, aspiration, faith, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Although these phenomena arise through the condition of feeling, they are not feeling." O son of good family, when my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that phenomena arising from mind do exist."

O son of good family, in some contexts I have declared that there is only one existence; in other contexts I have declared two existences, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten, up to twenty-five. When my attendants heard these words spoken thus, not understanding my intention, they said: "The Tathāgata has declared that there exist five cravings and six existences."

O son of good family, once in the past, when I was dwelling in the land of the Śākyas, in the Nyagrodha Grove, a man named Śākya Mingchen came to where I was and asked: "How does one become a lay practitioner?" I declared: "Whatever son or daughter of good family who is endowed with the sense faculties and has gone for refuge in the Three Jewels is called a lay practitioner." Śākya Mingchen then asked: "Blessed One, how is one called a one-sided lay practitioner?" I declared: "Śākya Mingchen, whoever has taken the three refuges and undertaken one precept is called a one-sided lay practitioner."

Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that the moral discipline of a layman is acceptable even without possessing all the precepts."

Son of good family, once I was dwelling on the bank of the Ganges, and at that time Kātyāyana came to where I was and said: "Blessed One, if one were to bestow upon a sentient being even a single canopy of the Dharma of the training's limbs — for a single day, a single moment, or even just an instant — would that being thereby receive a limb of the training?" I declared: "That monk would indeed obtain virtue, but one should not say that he has obtained a limb of the training."

Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that if one possesses the eight limbs of the training, then one has received the eight precepts of discipline."

Son of good family, I declared in a sūtra: "If a monk transgresses the four root precepts, he is no longer to be called a monk. He is called one who has broken the monk's vows, one who has lost and ruined the monkhood, one in whom the sprout of the fruit of virtue will not grow — just as a burned seed will not produce fruit, and just as a palmyra tree whose crown has been cut will not produce new growth. A monk who has transgressed the four root precepts is likewise."

Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that if monks transgress the four root precepts, their monastic discipline is thereby ruined."

Son of good family, I declared in a sūtra to Cunda: "There are four kinds of monks. What are they? One who has reached the culmination of awakening, one who teaches awakening, one who receives awakening, and one who defiles awakening. Among these, the one who defiles awakening is one who has transgressed the four root precepts."

Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that even if monks transgress the four root precepts, their discipline itself is not ruined."

Son of good family, I declared in a sūtra that monks have one vehicle, one path, one conduct, and one focus. From that single vehicle through to the single focus, by means of these they bring about great peace for sentient beings, cutting through all bondage, sorrow, suffering, and the causes of suffering, and they lead all sentient beings to pass through existence together as one.

Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that all of these, from stream-enterers to arhats, have fully and directly awakened."

Son of good family, I declared in a sūtra: "A stream-enterer is reborn at most seven times among gods and humans and then passes fully into nirvāṇa. A once-returner is born once more among gods and humans and then passes fully into nirvāṇa. As for the non-returner, there are five kinds, ranging from one who passes fully into nirvāṇa at an intermediate stage to one who does so at the final stage. As for the arhat, there are two kinds: the present and the future. The present arhat severs the five aggregates of affliction, and the future arhat also severs the five aggregates of affliction."

Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that from the stream-enterer through to the arhat, none of them obtain direct and complete awakening."

Son of good family, I declared in a sūtra: "The nature of a buddha is endowed with six qualities: permanence, authenticity, truth,

wholesomeness, purity, and vision." Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings exists somewhere apart from those sentient beings."

Son of good family, I then declared in another sūtra: "The intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings is like space. Space is not past, not future, not present; it is neither inner nor outer. Just as form, sound, smell, taste, and touch are all encompassed within it, so too the intrinsic nature of a buddha is like that." Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings exists somewhere apart from those sentient beings."

Son of good family, I then declared in yet another sūtra: "The intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings is comparable to a treasure of jewels in the house of a poor woman, to the precious wish-fulfilling jewel that is the immediate wealth of a powerful man, and to the spring of pure water belonging to a wheel-turning king." Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings exists somewhere apart from those sentient beings."

Son of good family, I then declared in yet another sūtra: "Even in those who have violated the four root precepts, who hold wrong views, who have rejected the extensive sūtras, and who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present. Whether or not those sentient beings possess wholesome phenomena, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is itself wholesome." Upon hearing these words spoken thus, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that the intrinsic nature of a buddha in sentient beings exists somewhere apart from those sentient beings."

Son of good family, I then declared: "Sentient beings themselves are the intrinsic nature of a buddha. Why is this? Because beyond and apart from sentient beings, there is no one who attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Therefore, just as I taught the example of the wool-bearing ram to King Conqueror-of-Armies, and just as when the blind describe the characteristics of a wool-bearing ram they do not grasp the ram itself, yet what they describe is not something other than the ram — in the same way, those who say that, throughout the range of sentient beings from form to consciousness, all of this is the intrinsic nature of a buddha are similar to those blind men. It is not the intrinsic nature of a buddha, yet it is not something other than the intrinsic nature of a buddha either. Just as I taught the nine similes of the garment to that king, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is like that."

Son of good family, upon hearing me declare this, my attendants, not understanding my intention, explain it in various ways. Like a blind man inquiring about milk, some explain that the intrinsic nature of a buddha is present in all — in those who have violated the four root precepts, who have rejected the extensive sūtras, who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, who hold wrong views, and so forth — each on account of its own particular causes and conditions. Others explain that it is not present in those beings.

Son of good family, in all the sūtra collections I have declared: "It never occurs that a single person arises in the world who brings benefit to many people and that two wheel-turning kings appear in one realm, or that two buddhas appear in a single world system. It never occurs that eight protectors exist in a single four-continent world, nor that two exist anywhere from that up through the realm of the gods who make use of others' emanations."

I have declared that in Jambudvīpa, the hell of unrelenting torment (avīci) reaches upward to the very summit of existence. Having heard me speak those words, my attendants, not understanding my intention, said: "The Tathāgata has declared that there are no buddhas in the ten directions." Yet in the sūtra collections of the Great Vehicle it is declared that buddhas do exist in the ten directions.

Son of good family, a dispute of this kind lies within the domain of the Blessed One's own experience; it is not something śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can know. Even if someone were to generate doubt regarding this matter, it would still be possible to eliminate afflictions beyond measure — afflictions as vast as Mount Meru. Yet if one generates certainty about it in an unquestioning way, that is what is called attachment and clinging.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, what is meant by 'attachment and clinging'?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, if a person, having heard something from another or having looked into the sūtras himself and seen something, or having followed what another has taught, is unable to let go of the objects to which he clings — that is called attachment and clinging."

Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, is such attachment and clinging wholesome?"

"It is not wholesome."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, such attachment and clinging should not be called wholesome. Why? Because it is incapable of cutting the net of doubt."

Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, if a person has had no doubt from the very beginning, why speak of being unable to cut the net of doubt?"

The Blessed One replied: "What is free of doubt — that is what is called doubt."

Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, when someone who has entered the stream declares, 'I will not fall into the three lower destinies' — is that also attachment and doubt?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, that is to be called certainty; it is not right to call it doubt. Why? Son of good family, consider the example of a person who has previously seen both a human being and a tree. Later, walking along at night, he sees a stump from a distance and thinks, 'Is that a person or a tree?' — and doubt arises.

Son of good family, just as someone who has previously seen both a monk and a wandering ascetic (parivrājaka), and later, at one moment, sees a monk from a distance on the road, thinks, 'Is that a monk or a wandering ascetic?' — and doubt arises.

Son of good family, in the same way, someone who has previously seen both a bull and a water buffalo, and later sees an animal from a distance, thinks, 'Is that a bull or a water buffalo?' — and doubt arises.

Son of good family, when all sentient beings have previously seen two different kinds of things, doubt arises afterward. Why? Because the mind has not understood them.

If I had spoken of a stream-entrant both falling into the three lower destinies and not falling into the three lower destinies, why would doubt arise in the mind? Since I have not said that, why would doubt arise?"

Kāśyapa said: "Blessed One, as the Blessed One has stated, it follows that seeing something beforehand leads to doubt afterward. Yet there is also something that gives rise to doubt without one having seen two different things — and what is that? It is nirvāṇa.

Blessed One, for example, if a person encounters a turbid stream in his path, he wonders from having seen water before, 'Is this water deep or shallow?' But if he has never seen it before, why would doubt arise?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, what is called nirvāṇa is the cutting off of suffering. What is not nirvāṇa is suffering. There are two ways in which all sentient beings see things: seeing them as suffering and seeing them as not-suffering.

What is meant by 'suffering' and 'not-suffering'? Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, joy, illness —"

— happiness, old age, youth, birth, death, bondage, freedom, separation from loved ones, encounter with enemies. Sentient beings see these things and sometimes wonder when they will be free from things afflicted by such suffering. Because of this, sentient beings give rise to doubt about nirvāṇa. Now, the meaning of your question — 'Why would that person who has never seen a turbid stream doubt it?' — is not quite as you supposed. Why is that? Because that person had previously seen such a thing in another place; therefore, even without having gone there before, doubt arises in him about it."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, just as you have said, doubt is attachment, and attachment is doubt — then what is to be done about that?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, it is to be applied to those who have cut the root of virtue."

Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, who are those who will cut the root of virtue?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, those who, though their wisdom is clear and their faculties are sharp, abandon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who is skilled in making distinctions, do not listen to the sacred Dharma, are of unwholesome intention, and do not abide properly — these are the ones who will cut the root of virtue. Having abandoned those four things, they think to themselves: 'As for generosity and material goods, there are none whatsoever.' Why? Because generosity means giving away wealth. If there were karmic maturation of a fruit from generosity, then the giver of generosity would always be destined to remain in poverty. Why? Because seed and fruit are alike; therefore they claim there is no cause and no fruit. To speak in this way of there being no cause and no fruit is what is called cutting the root of virtue.

Again, they think: 'The giver, the receiver, and the material gift — these three are impermanent; they do not abide, they do not remain. If they do not abide and do not remain, how can one say that this is giving, this is receiving, this is the material gift? If there is no receiving either, how could any fruit ripen?' Thinking in this way, they claim there is no cause and no fruit. Know that to speak in this way of there being no cause and no fruit is to cut the root of virtue.

Again, they think: 'When a gift is given, there are five aspects of the thing given. Even if the recipient then acts virtuously or acts non-virtuously, the karmic maturation of virtue or non-virtue will not ripen for the giver. Just as in worldly affairs a fruit arises from a seed and that fruit in turn becomes a seed again — the cause is the giver and the fruit is the recipient — even so, the recipient, through his virtuous or non-virtuous conduct, is not able to bring about the attainment of the giver.' Thinking in this way, they claim there is no cause and no fruit. Know that to speak in this way of there being no cause and no fruit is to cut the root of virtue.

Again, they think: 'The object of giving does not exist. Why? Because the object of giving is not taught in scripture. Since it is not taught in scripture, how could a virtuous fruit ripen? That for which there is no fruit of virtue or non-virtue is what is not taught in scripture. Since the object is not taught in scripture, one should understand that there is no ripening of a fruit of virtue or non-virtue.'"

"Therefore there is no giving, and there is no cause and no fruit" — so they think. Know that to speak in this way, after thinking in such a manner, of there being no cause and no fruit, is to cut the root of virtue.

Again, they think: "Giving is mind. If it is mind, it is invisible and without an equal and is therefore not a material phenomenon. If it is not a material phenomenon, what is there even in the act of giving? Therefore there is no giving, no cause, and no fruit." Know that whoever speaks in this way of there being no cause and no fruit has cut the root of virtue.

Again, the giver thinks: "If I give for the sake of an image of a buddha, or an image of a god, or for the span of a life, or for deceased parents, there is no one who receives. If there is no receiver, it follows that there is no karmic ripening of a fruit. If there is no karmic ripening of a fruit, there will be no cause. If there is no cause, there will be no fruit" — so they think. Know that to speak in this way, after thinking in such a manner, of there being no cause and no fruit, is to cut the root of virtue.

Again, they think: "There is no father and there is no mother. If one says that both parents are the cause of a sentient being and that a sentient being is born, then by that reasoning beings should be born continuously without interruption, without ever ceasing. Why? Because the cause is always present. Since birth does not occur continuously in that way, one should understand that parents do not exist" — so they think.

Again, they think: "There is no father and there is no mother. Why? Because if the body of a sentient being existed through the condition of its parents, it would follow that even in a single individual there would be the characteristics of both male and female. Since neither is the case in that way, one should understand that sentient beings do not arise through the condition of parents."

Again, they think: "Sentient beings do not arise through the condition of parents. Why? Because one sees sentient beings existing who are unlike their parents — unlike them in body, in form, in mind, in manner of conduct, in gait, and in posture. Therefore parents are not the cause of sentient beings" — so they think.

Again, they think: "Throughout the entire world there are four modes of non-existence. First, non-existence prior to birth — just as when clay is still a lump, pottery and the like do not yet exist. Second, non-existence after cessation — just as when pottery has shattered, it no longer exists. Third, mutual non-existence — just as an ox is not a horse, and a horse is not an ox. Fourth, absolute non-existence — just as the horn of a rabbit, or the hair of a tortoise. The parents of sentient beings are likewise non-existent, comparable to these four modes of non-existence. If one says that parents are the cause of sentient beings, then when the parents die, the children should also die. Therefore parents are not the cause of sentient beings" — so they think.

Again, they think: "If one says that parents are indeed the cause of sentient beings, then from the cause of parents sentient beings should always and invariably be born. Yet that is not so, for there are also beings who are born miraculously and beings who are born from warmth and moisture. Therefore one should understand that sentient beings do not arise from the cause of parents" — so they think.

Again, they think: "Sentient beings exist by their own intrinsic nature and do not arise from the cause of parents. For example, just as a peacock, upon hearing the sound of thunder, becomes pregnant in the womb, and just as the blue hummingbird becomes pregnant by drinking the tears of the male bird, and just as some birds become pregnant upon seeing the dance of the male bird — in the same way, sentient beings arise by their own nature" — so they think. Know that when one thinks in this way and has not met a spiritual friend (Skt. kalyāṇamitra), this too is the cutting of the root of virtue.

Again, they think: "Throughout the entire world there exist virtue and —"

there are no results of non-virtue — so they think. Why do they think so? Among sentient beings, some who practice the ten virtues and delight in giving, who strive earnestly after merit, are nonetheless tormented in the prime of their youth by illness and the like, their bodies afflicted, losing their lives or their wealth and possessions, and crushed by much grief and suffering. On the other hand, some who practice the ten non-virtues — who act from attachment, envy, and laziness, who are indolent and do not practice virtue — nonetheless enjoy physical comfort, are free from illness, live long lives, possess abundant wealth and precious goods, and are not crushed by grief and suffering. Therefore, they think: "We understand that there are no results of virtue or non-virtue."

Again, they think: "I have previously heard it said by noble ones (āryas) that some people, even though they have practiced virtue, fall into the three lower destinies after death, and there are many such cases; while some, even though they have practiced non-virtue, are reborn after death as gods in the higher realms or as humans." Having heard this, they think: "Therefore, we understand that there are no results of virtue or non-virtue."

Again, they think: "All noble ones speak in two contradictory ways. Some say that killing a living being ripens as the result of virtue; others say that killing a living being ripens as the result of non-virtue — they speak in two different ways. Therefore we understand that what the noble ones have said is not definitive. If even the noble ones have not spoken definitively, why should I speak definitively? Therefore we understand that there are no results of virtue or non-virtue" — so they think.

Again, they think: "There are no noble ones anywhere in the entire world. Why? If noble ones were to attain the true path, then while all sentient beings still possess afflictions, those who cultivate the true path would have both the true path and afflictions existing simultaneously and at the same time. But if they coexist simultaneously, the true path would be unable to uproot all the afflictions. On the other hand, if one cultivates the true path in the absence of afflictions, that true path would be unnecessary. Therefore, when afflictions are present, the path cannot destroy them; and when afflictions are absent, the path is not needed at all. Therefore we understand that there are no noble ones anywhere in the entire world" — so they think.

Again, they think: "The twelve links of dependent origination — from formations arising conditioned by ignorance, all the way through to old age and death arising conditioned by birth — exist equally and alike in all sentient beings. The noble eightfold path (Skt. āryāṣṭāṅgamārga) likewise, since its nature is equally the same, must be of a similar kind. If one person attains it, then all should attain it; and if one person cultivates it, all should be able to cease their suffering. Why? Because the afflictions are equally and uniformly present. Yet looking at those who do not attain it right now, we think: there is no true path" — so they think.

Again, they think: "Noble ones too have characteristics in common with the basest of ordinary people: eating food, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, feeling joy, laughing, feeling hunger and thirst, feeling cold and heat, feeling grief and fear. If noble ones equally share these things with the basest of ordinary folk, then they have not attained the noble path. And if they have attained the noble path, then all such characteristics should have been definitively cut off. Since those characteristics have not been cut off, we understand that there is no path" — so they think.

Again, they think: "Noble ones too have bodies, and they enjoy and indulge in the pleasures of the five desired objects; they feel proud; they even strike and beat others; they feel envy and arrogance toward others; they experience suffering and happiness; and they perform virtuous and non-virtuous actions. For these causes and conditions, we understand that there are no noble ones."

Again, they think: "One who possesses loving compassion is called a noble one. But what is the cause and condition for being called a noble one? One is called a noble one by reason of the path. If it were the intrinsic nature of the path to be compassionate, then by that very nature all sentient beings would become compassionate, and it would be unreasonable to make it depend on cultivation. If compassion is not intrinsically present, then why would noble ones become compassionate by reason of having attained the noble path? Therefore we understand that in this world there is no noble path" — so they think.

Again, they think: "The four great elements do not arise from conditions; they exist equally in all sentient beings. The intrinsic nature of the four great elements does not discriminate, thinking 'I will move into this sentient being but not into that one.' If the noble path existed and things were by nature as claimed, then since they are not presently so, we understand that in this world there are no noble ones" — so they think.

Again, they think: "If there were only one nirvāṇa for all noble ones, then we understand there are no noble ones. Why is that? Because it is without a referential object. A phenomenon that abides permanently is, by its very nature of reality (dharmatā), without a referential object, and is beyond acceptance or rejection. If noble ones were to transcend sorrow in great numbers, it would become impermanent. Why? Because it would be something that can serve as a referential object. If nirvāṇa were just one and completely exhausted, then when one person attained it, it would follow that everyone should attain it simultaneously. If nirvāṇa were many, it would be finite. If it were finite, how could one designate it as permanent? Now, if someone were to say: 'The essential nature of nirvāṇa is one, but liberation is many — just as under one umbrella there can be many spokes' — that too is not the case. Why? Because each person attains it individually, not all at once; therefore it is finite, and hence also impermanent. If it is impermanent, how can it be called nirvāṇa? If there is no nirvāṇa, who would become a noble one? Therefore we understand there are no noble ones" — so they think.

Again, they think: "The noble path is not attained through dependent origination. If the noble path were attained through dependent origination, why have not all beings become noble ones? If not all are noble ones, then we understand that noble ones and the noble path do not exist" — so they think.

Again, they think: "There are two causes and conditions for the right view that belongs to the noble path. What are they? Hearing the Dharma from another, and engaging in inner mental reflection oneself. If these two causes and conditions themselves arose from conditions, then what arises from conditions would itself also arise from conditions, and thus each giving rise to the next, one would fall into the fault of an infinite regress. If these two things did not arise from conditions, then why have not all sentient beings attained it?" — so they think. "Whoever conceives of it in that way cuts off the wholesome root at that very moment."

"Son of good family, if a sentient being views things in such a way — utterly denying cause and effect — that person cuts off the five roots beginning with faith. Son of good family, cutting off the wholesome root does not occur through being lowly, weak, or dull and confused of faculty; it does not occur through being born as a god or in one of the three lower realms. The same is true of one who creates a schism in the Saṅgha."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, at what time will the wholesome root of such a person grow back?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, for that person the wholesome root will grow back at the time of two moments:

the first being when one first falls into hell, and the second when one emerges from hell.

Son of good family, virtue has three aspects: past, present, and future. Of these, the past, by its very nature, has already ceased, so the cause has come to an end and is exhausted; yet the karmic ripening of its fruit has not yet matured. Therefore one does not say that the fruit of the past has been cut. What is called "cutting" is the cutting of the cause across all three times.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, if cutting the cause across all three times is what is called 'cutting the wholesome root,' then in one whose wholesome root has been cut, is there still the intrinsic nature of buddhahood? If there is, does that intrinsic nature of buddhahood belong to the past, the present, or the future, or does it pervade all three times? If it belongs to the past, how can it be called permanent? The intrinsic nature of buddhahood would have to be permanent, and therefore it cannot belong to the past. If it belongs to the future, again how can it be permanent? And yet the Blessed One has taught that all sentient beings will certainly attain it. If it is certainly to be attained, why speak of it as having been cut? If it belongs to the present, again how can it be called permanent? And why did the Blessed One say it will be seen with certainty? For the Tathāgata has also taught that the intrinsic nature of buddhahood has six aspects: permanence, authenticity, truth, virtue, purity, and being fit to be seen. If one whose wholesome root has been cut still possesses the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, it would be improper to speak of them as having their wholesome root cut. But if there is no intrinsic nature of buddhahood in them, why did the Blessed One teach that the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is present in all sentient beings? And if it is both present and yet can be cut, why did the Blessed One declare it to be permanent?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, a buddha, a Blessed One, answers questions asked for the sake of sentient beings in four ways. What are these four? A definitive answer, a differentiated answer, an answer given exactly in accordance with how the question was asked, and setting the question aside without answering it.

Son of good family, what then is a definitive answer? If one asks, 'Does a person who commits evil deeds obtain a virtuous fruit or a non-virtuous fruit?' the definitive reply is: 'They obtain a non-virtuous fruit.' Likewise for virtue in the same manner. If one asks, 'Does the Tathāgata possess the gnosis of omniscience, or not?' the definitive reply is: 'The Tathāgata is omniscient.' If one asks, 'By whom are the Dharma qualities of a buddha thoroughly purified?' the definitive reply is: 'They are thoroughly purified.' If one asks, 'Do the close attendants of a buddha abide in accordance with the Dharma?' the definitive reply is: 'They do indeed abide in accordance with the Dharma.' This is called a definitive answer.

What is a differentiated answer? It is as when I taught the Four Noble Truths. What are the four? Suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path. Of these, what is the truth of suffering? Because there are eight kinds of suffering, it is called the truth of suffering. What is the truth of the origin of suffering? Because there is a cause of the five aggregates, it is called the truth of the origin. What is the truth of cessation? The utter and complete cessation of attachment, aversion, and delusion without remainder is called the truth of cessation. What is the truth of the path?

The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening are the truth of the path — this is what is called a differentiated answer.

Now, what is an answer that corresponds exactly to the question asked? It is as when I taught that all phenomena are impermanent. When someone asks, "For the sake of what phenomenon did the Blessed One, the Buddha, teach impermanence?" the Tathāgata answers: "It is because of conditioned phenomena that I taught impermanence." The teaching of no-self is the same.

Again, as when I taught that all phenomena are ablaze: if another person asks, "For the sake of what did the Tathāgata teach that all phenomena are ablaze?" the Tathāgata answers: "It is because of attachment, aversion, and delusion that the Tathāgata taught that all phenomena are ablaze." This is what is called an answer that corresponds to the question.

Noble son, the ten powers of the Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, and the eighty thousand varieties of meditative absorption such as the absorption of courageous advance and the like; the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor excellent features; the thirty-five thousand varieties of meditative absorption such as the five mudrās of gnosis and the like; the four thousand five hundred varieties of meditative absorption such as the vajra-like absorption and the like; and the immeasurable and boundless varieties of meditative absorption of skillful means — these and all such phenomena are the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata's buddhahood.

Now, that intrinsic nature of buddhahood is endowed with seven qualities: permanence, selfhood, bliss, utter purity, authenticity, truth, and virtue. This is what is called a differentiated answer.

Noble son, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood of a bodhisattva who is bound by a single birth is endowed with six qualities: permanence, utter purity, authenticity, truth, virtue, and partial vision. This too is what is called a differentiated answer.

When the question was asked, "Does the intrinsic nature of buddhahood exist within one who has previously severed the roots of virtue?" — the answer is that the Tathāgata's intrinsic nature of buddhahood is indeed present, and the intrinsic nature of buddhahood of the bodhisattva bound by a single birth is also present. Because both of these intrinsic natures of buddhahood are obscured with respect to what is yet to come, they are said not to exist. Because they are ultimately and without fail to be attained, they are said to exist. This is what is called a differentiated answer.

The Tathāgata's intrinsic nature of buddhahood is neither past, nor present, nor future. The intrinsic nature of buddhahood of the bodhisattva bound by a single birth, because it is seen partially in the present and in the time to come, is called present; and because it is not seen completely, it is called future.

From before the Tathāgata's attainment of unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood may be called past, present, and future; but the fruit is not the same in this respect — for there is that which belongs to the three times, and there is that which does not belong to the three times. The causes of the intrinsic nature of buddhahood of the bodhisattva bound by a single birth are past, present, and future, and the fruit likewise corresponds to these. This is what is called a differentiated answer.

The intrinsic nature of buddhahood of a bodhisattva on the ninth ground is sixfold: permanence, virtue, authenticity, truth, utter purity, and visible presence. In this way, the causes of the intrinsic nature of buddhahood are past, present, and future, and the fruit is likewise — this too is what is called a differentiated answer.

The intrinsic nature of buddhahood of a bodhisattva from the eighth ground down to the sixth ground is fivefold: authenticity, truth, utter purity, virtue, and visible presence. Here too, because it serves as the cause of the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, it is past, present, and future, and the fruit likewise corresponds to these. This too is what is called a differentiated answer.

The intrinsic nature of buddhahood of a bodhisattva from the fifth ground down to and including the first ground is fivefold: authenticity, truth, utter purity, visible presence, virtue, and non-virtue.

Son of good family, that fifth intrinsic nature of buddhahood, the sixth intrinsic nature of buddhahood, and the seventh intrinsic nature of buddhahood exist because they are infallibly attained through roots of virtue not having been severed. This too is what is called a differentiated answer.

Now, if someone were to ask, "Does one who has severed roots of virtue definitely possess the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, or does one who has severed roots of virtue definitely not possess the intrinsic nature of buddhahood?" — to that question, one simply sets it aside and does not give an answer.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, as I have understood it, 'setting aside and not answering' means this: that the Tathāgata has set aside and not answered a question for which an answer was given — for what reason and by what condition has he done so?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, I did not say that I had 'set aside and not answered' what I set aside and did not answer. Son of good family, there are two kinds of setting-aside-without-answer: refutation and non-attachment. It is for that reason that it is called a setting-aside-without-answer."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, just as the Blessed One has explained — how is it that the cause is said to be past, present, and future, and likewise the fruit is past, present, and future, and yet also not past, present, and future?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, the five aggregates are of two kinds: as cause and as fruit. The five aggregates as cause are past, present, and future. The five aggregates as fruit are past, present, and future, and yet also not past, present, and future.

"Son of good family, all the afflictions arising from ignorance are the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. Why? Because they become the cause of the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. From the afflictions — ignorance, formations, and the rest — one attains the five aggregates of virtue, and therefore they are called the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. From the five aggregates of virtue one will attain unsurpassed, completely perfect awakening. That is why I previously taught in a sūtra that the intrinsic nature of buddhahood in sentient beings is like blood and milk mingled together. What is called 'blood' refers to the afflictions — ignorance, formations, and the rest. What is called 'milk' refers to the five aggregates of virtue. Thus I taught that from the afflictions and from the five aggregates of virtue, one attains unsurpassed, completely perfect awakening. Just as the body of a sentient being arises from semen and blood, so too is the intrinsic nature of buddhahood like that.

"The intrinsic nature of buddhahood of a stream-enterer (Skt. srotaāpanna) and a once-returner — who have cut off afflictions to a small degree — is comparable to milk. The intrinsic nature of buddhahood of a non-returner (Skt. anāgāmin) is comparable to yogurt. The intrinsic nature of buddhahood of an arhat is comparable to butter. The intrinsic nature of buddhahood from a pratyekabuddha up to a bodhisattva on the tenth ground is comparable to clarified butter."

The intrinsic nature of buddhahood of a Tathāgata is comparable to clarified butter's essence. Son of good family, it is not seen because it is obscured by present afflictions.

For example, there is a grass called "cattle-resistant" that grows on fragrant mountain slopes, and all cattle refuse to eat it. The intrinsic nature of buddhahood is likewise. This constitutes a detailed and well-answered reply.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, if the intrinsic nature of buddhahood has five, six, or seven aspects and something of it exists in the future — may it be said that a person whose roots of virtue have been severed also possesses the intrinsic nature of buddhahood?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, just as sentient beings have past karma, and due to that karma a result ripens for them in this present life, so too future karma, not yet having arisen, has not yet produced its result. There are present afflictions, and if those afflictions were absent, all sentient beings would straightaway perceive the intrinsic nature of buddhahood directly. Therefore, although a person whose roots of virtue have been severed has indeed had those roots severed by the condition of present-moment afflictions, through the power of the intrinsic nature of buddhahood that pertains to the future, the roots of virtue will arise again."

Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, how would the intrinsic nature of buddhahood of the future produce roots of virtue?"

"Son of good family, consider a lamp or the sun: even though they have not yet appeared, they are capable of illuminating darkness. In just the same way, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood of the future brings forth the intrinsic nature of buddhahood of the future within sentient beings. This constitutes a detailed and well-answered reply."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, if the five aggregates are the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, why did you say that the intrinsic nature of buddhahood of sentient beings is neither within nor without?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, why have you become confused in this way? Did I not previously say that the intrinsic nature of buddhahood of sentient beings is the Middle Way?"

Kāśyapa replied: "Blessed One, I myself am not confused. Yet sentient beings are unable to understand this Middle Way, and it is for their sake that I asked in this manner."

"Son of good family, what sentient beings do not understand is precisely the Middle Way. Regarding it, there is both understanding and non-understanding. Son of good family, in order to make what sentient beings do not understand into something they can understand, I have said that the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is neither within nor without. Why so? Because among sentient beings who are ordinary, childish persons, some say: 'The intrinsic nature of buddhahood abides within the five aggregates, just as fruit exists within a vessel.' Others say: 'It exists apart from the aggregates, like empty space.' It is for this reason that the Tathāgata has taught the Middle Way. The intrinsic nature of buddhahood of sentient beings is not the six inner sense bases, nor is it the six outer sense bases; what arises from the meeting of inner and outer is called the Middle Way. Therefore the Tathāgata has said: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood itself is the Middle Way."

That which is neither within nor without is called the Middle Way. This constitutes a detailed and well-answered reply.

"Furthermore, son of good family, how is it that it is neither within nor without? Son of good family, some say: 'The intrinsic nature of buddhahood itself is a tīrthika view.'"

Why is this so? Because a bodhisattva, a great being, cuts through the afflictions produced by tīrthika teachings over immeasurable eons, thoroughly tames the mind, acts for the benefit of sentient beings, and thereby attains the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. Therefore, they say, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is itself a tīrthika view.

Others say this: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is entry into the inner training. Why is this so? Because even if a bodhisattva were to practice tīrthika teachings for immeasurable eons, if the inner Dharma were abandoned, one could not attain unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. Therefore, they say, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood itself is entry into the inner training.

For this reason, in order to turn back from both extremes, the Tathāgata has declared: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is neither within nor without, and yet it is both inner and outer. That is called the Middle Way.

Furthermore, son of good family, some say this: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood itself is the vajra-like body of the Tathāgata, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor excellent features. Why? Because it is infallible. Others say this: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the three close mindfulnesses, the heroic march meditative absorption, and all other meditative absorptions. Why? Because from those absorptions there arises the vajra-like body adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor excellent features.

Therefore, in order to turn back from both extremes, the Tathāgata has declared: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is neither within nor without, and yet it is both inner and outer. That is called the Middle Way.

Furthermore, son of good family, some say this: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is profound mental engagement within. Why? Because without that profound inner mental engagement, one cannot attain unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. Therefore, they say, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is profound mental engagement within.

Others say this: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is hearing the Dharma from another. Why? Because it is through hearing the Dharma from another that profound inner mental engagement arises; if the Dharma were not heard, mental engagement would not arise. Therefore, they say, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is hearing the Dharma from another.

For this reason, in order to turn back from both extremes, the Tathāgata has declared: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is neither within nor without, and yet it is both inner and outer. That is called the Middle Way.

Furthermore, son of good family, some say this: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is outer — it is the perfection of generosity. Through the perfection of generosity, unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening is attained. Therefore, they say, the perfection of generosity is the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. Others say this: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is inner — it is the remaining five perfections. Why? Because one understands that apart from those five things, beyond them, there is nothing to be called the cause and result of the intrinsic nature of buddhahood. Therefore, they say, the five perfections are the intrinsic nature of buddhahood.

Therefore, in order to turn back from both extremes, the Tathāgata declared: "The intrinsic nature of buddhahood is neither inner nor outer, yet it is both inner and outer." This is called the Middle Path.

Furthermore, noble children, some say this: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood abides within, and is comparable to the precious jewel in the forehead of the mighty being Mahābala. Why is this? Because permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity are likened to a jewel. Therefore, they say, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood exists within.

Others say this: the intrinsic nature of buddhahood exists without, and is comparable to a treasure of jewels beneath the house of a poor man. Why is this? Because it is to be seen through skillful means. Likewise, they say, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood exists outside sentient beings and is to be seen through skillful means.

Therefore, in order to turn back from both extremes, the Tathāgata declared: "The intrinsic nature of buddhahood is neither inner nor outer, nor is it both inner and outer." This is called the Middle Path.

Noble children, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood in sentient beings is neither existent nor nonexistent. Why is this? The intrinsic nature of buddhahood does exist, yet it is not like empty space. Why? Because the empty space of the world cannot be apprehended as an object even by applying limitless skillful means, whereas the intrinsic nature of buddhahood can be apprehended as an object. Therefore, although it exists, it is not comparable to empty space.

The intrinsic nature of buddhahood does not exist in the way ordinary things do, yet it is not comparable to a rabbit's horn. Why? Because the hair of a tortoise and the horn of a rabbit cannot be brought into being even by limitless and manifold skillful means, whereas the intrinsic nature of buddhahood can be brought into being. Therefore, although it does not exist, it is not comparable to a rabbit's horn.

Therefore, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood is neither existent nor nonexistent, nor is it both existent and nonexistent.

In what sense is it existent? Because it is present in all beings and cannot be cut off or negated by sentient beings. Like the flame of a lamp, it will be attained, all the way up to the realization of unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening. Therefore it is called existent.

In what sense is it nonexistent? Because at this present time, in all sentient beings, permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity — all the qualities of buddhahood — are not yet present. Therefore it is called nonexistent.

The union of existence and nonexistence is called the Middle Way. Therefore the Blessed One declared: "The intrinsic nature of buddhahood in sentient beings is neither existent nor nonexistent."

Noble children, suppose someone were to ask: "Is the fruit present within the seed or not?" One should answer both yes and no. Why? Because apart from the seed, the fruit will not arise; therefore one says it is present. And because no sprout has yet emerged from the seed, one says it is not present. Thus one may say both that it exists and that it does not exist. Why? The two differ in time, but their essential nature is one.

In the same way, the intrinsic nature of buddhahood in sentient beings is like that. To say that the intrinsic nature of buddhahood exists somewhere other than in sentient beings is not tenable. Why? Because sentient beings themselves are the intrinsic nature of buddhahood, and the intrinsic nature of buddhahood itself is sentient beings. It is simply that, owing to the difference in time, there is what we call purified and what we call unpurified.

Son of good family, if someone were to ask, "Can a seed produce a fruit, or is the fruit unable to be produced?" one should reply: "It both is produced and is not produced."

A question was posed: Blessed One, what is the meaning of worldly people saying, "Cream is present in milk"?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, whoever says "Cream exists in milk" — that is attachment. Whoever says "Cream does not exist" — that is speaking falsely. Apart from those two positions, one may certainly say both that it exists and that it does not exist. Why say that it exists? Because cream arises from milk: milk is the cause, cream is the result — therefore one says it exists. How then does one say it does not exist? Because their shape and taste are different, and their manner of drinking and use is different. For a fever disease, milk is given; for a diarrheal disease, cream is given. Milk gives rise to disorders of cold; cream provokes disorders of heat.

Son of good family, if someone says "The intrinsic nature of cream exists within milk" — then milk itself would be cream, and cream itself would be milk, and their intrinsic nature would be one. In that case, by what cause and conditions would milk appear first and cream not appear first? If there are causes and conditions, why did not everyone in the world say so from the very beginning? And if there are no causes and conditions, why did cream not appear right from the start? Since cream did not appear at the very beginning, who established the sequence of milk, cream, butter, clarified butter, and the essence of butter? Therefore, one should understand that cream has no beginning yet exists now. But if something has no beginning yet exists now, it would become a thing belonging to the category of impermanence.

Son of good family, if someone says, "Cream arises from milk because the intrinsic nature of cream is present in milk, whereas cream does not arise from water and grass because the intrinsic nature of cream is not present in water and grass" — that too is not the case. Why? Because the intrinsic nature of milk and cream is also present in water and grass. In what sense? It is because milk and cream arise from water and grass. Whoever says "The intrinsic nature of cream is definitely present in milk, but not in water and grass" — that person is speaking falsely. Why is it called speaking falsely? Because the mind is not in accord with reality.

Son of good family, if someone says "Cream definitely exists within milk," then since it would follow that milk could likewise arise from within cream, by what cause and conditions does cream arise from milk but milk does not arise from cream? If there are no causes and conditions, then cream is to be understood as having no beginning yet existing now. Therefore the wise say: "The intrinsic nature of cream within milk is neither present nor absent."

Son of good family, for this reason, if the Tathāgata, in this sūtra, says "The intrinsic nature of buddhahood definitely exists in all sentient beings," that is attachment. If one says "It does not exist," that is speaking falsely. Those who are wise and endowed with wisdom should say: "The intrinsic nature of buddhahood is neither present nor absent."

Son of good family, from the assembly of four factors, visual consciousness arises. What are the four? The eye, form, light, and attention. The intrinsic nature of visual consciousness is not the eye, is not form, is not light, and is not attention — yet it arises from their assembly. In this way, visual consciousness has no beginning yet has come to exist now. Having existed, it will later cease to exist. Therefore one should understand that there is no such thing as a primordially existing intrinsic nature. In the same way, the intrinsic nature of cream within milk is like that as well.

If someone were to say, "Since the intrinsic nature of cream is absent in water, cream cannot arise from water — therefore the intrinsic nature of cream must certainly exist within milk," that too is not tenable. Why is that? Son of good family, all phenomena have different causes and different results. Not all results arise from a single cause, nor do all results come from a single cause. Son of good family, because visual consciousness arose from those four factors, it does not follow that auditory consciousness also arises from those same four factors. Son of good family, without the proper method, it is impossible for milk to become cream, or for butter to arise from cream. Seeing that this is impossible, skillful means are necessary. Son of good family, those who are skilled in means do not look, beyond the application of method, for milk having already become cream, nor do they look, all the way up to butter, for it having already become butter beyond the application of method. Son of good family, therefore I have taught in this sūtra that when a cause arises, a phenomenon exists, and when a cause ceases, a phenomenon does not exist.

Son of good family, consider the defining characteristic of salt: salt makes everything that is not salty become salty. If things that are not salty had the intrinsic nature of salt from the very beginning, why would people in the world go searching for salt? And if it were altogether absent from the beginning, then one would understand that what was absent from the beginning has come to exist now. Perhaps it is that through other conditions salt-tastiness comes about, and someone were to say, "All things that are not salty possess the intrinsic nature of salt — it is simply that, being present in too small a quantity, it is not perceived; and because that intrinsic nature exists in some measure, salt makes things salty. If there were no intrinsic nature from the beginning, then even when salt exists, things would not become salty — just as, because the seed itself possesses the four great elements, through the condition of the four outer great elements a sprout, a stalk, branches, and leaves arise; the intrinsic nature of salt is similar to that." If one were to say this, that too is not tenable. Why is that? If the intrinsic nature of salt existed from the beginning in things that are not salty, then logically those non-salty things should also possess a portion of non-saltiness. If salt were to have in that way two intrinsic natures, why would it be necessary to use non-salty things at all? Therefore one should understand that salt does not have two intrinsic natures from the very beginning, and that just as with salt, so too is everything that is non-salty.

If someone were to say, "Through the power of the outer four great elements, the inner four great elements arise," that too is not tenable. Why is that? This is not skillful means but rather a teaching given in sequential order. Just as no phenomenon — from milk becoming cream all the way to butter — comes to be accomplished without method, so too the four great elements are like that. If the outer four great elements arose, why is it not seen that from the inner four great elements the outer four great elements arise in turn? It is like the tree fruit called śirīṣa — though it is without density and without any solid core, when the Pleiades rise and the sky clears, a fruit of five finger-breadths grows. Yet that fruit did not truly arise from the outer four great elements alone.
