Son of good family, just as I have taught the twelve branches of scripture, some were taught in accordance with my own intent, some were taught in accordance with the intent of others, and some were taught in accordance with the intent of both myself and others. How is it that some were taught in accordance with my own intent? It is like the occasion when five hundred monks asked Śāriputra (Śāriputra, the foremost disciple in wisdom): "Venerable one, what did the Blessed One teach as the cause of the body?" Śāriputra replied —

"Venerable one, since you have each attained perfect liberation, why do you ask such a question out of knowledge of one's own kind?" Among those monks, some spoke thus: "Venerable one, before I had attained perfect liberation, I thought: 'Ignorance is the cause of the body.' Attending to it in that way, I attained the fruit of arhathood." Others spoke thus: "Venerable one, before I had attained perfect liberation, I thought: 'Craving and ignorance are the cause of the body.' Attending to it in that way, I attained the fruit of arhathood." Still others thought: "Formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, eating, sustaining, and the five objects of desire — these are the cause of the body."

Then those five hundred monks, each having spoken according to their own understanding, went to where the Blessed One was. They paid homage at the Blessed One's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having done so, stood to one side. Each of them presented to the Blessed One what they had understood. Then Śāriputra asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, which of these monks speaks correctly, and which does not?" The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, excellent! Excellent! Not a single one of the monks has spoken incorrectly." Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the Blessed One's intended meaning?" The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, I taught that parents are the cause of the body for the sake of sentient beings of the desire realm. That sūtra teaching was spoken in accordance with my own intent. Now, how is it that some teachings were spoken in accordance with the intent of others? For example, a householder named Pāla came to where I was and said: 'O Gautama, do you know illusion? If you know illusion, then illusion is something great. If you do not know illusion, then you do not possess the wisdom of omniscience.' I said: 'Householder, would you call someone who knows illusion an illusionist?' The householder replied: 'Excellent! Excellent! One who knows illusion is indeed called an illusionist.' The Blessed One declared: 'Householder, do you know that in Śrāvastī there is a king called Prasenajit (Prasenajit, the great king who fully defeats his enemies), and that there is one called Dūṣita (Breath-stealer of the base-born)?' The householder said: 'Gautama, I have known this from before.' The Blessed One declared: 'If you have known it from before, would it be fitting to call you base-born?' The householder said: 'Gautama, I know full well that he is base-born, yet this body of mine is not base-born.' The Blessed One declared: 'Householder, if, though knowing him to be base-born, you count yourself as not base-born, then why, when I know illusion, should I become an illusionist? Householder, in truth I know illusion; I know the cause of illusion; I know the karmic maturation of illusion; I know the craft of illusion; I know killing; I know the killer; I know the karmic maturation of killing; I know everything from liberation through killing down to wrong view; I know the person of wrong view; I know the karmic maturation of wrong view; and I know the liberation from wrong view. Householder, if I were to say of what is not illusion that it is illusion, or of what is not wrong view that it is wrong view, I would thereby incur measureless blame and sin.' The householder said:"

"Gautama, if what you have said is so, then I have incurred great wrongdoing. I offer you now everything I possess. And let not what I have just said be heard by King Prasenajit, the Conqueror of Armies."

The Blessed One declared: "Householder, because of that wrongdoing you will not merely lose your wealth — because of it you will fall into the three lower destinies."

At that, when the householder heard the name of the three lower destinies, a mind of terror and dread arose in him, and he addressed the Blessed One thus: "Noble one, if through losing my senses today I have incurred great sin, the noble one is omniscient, and since you thoroughly know how liberation is attained, how shall I be liberated from rebirth in the hells, among the hungry ghosts, and among the animals?"

Thereupon the teaching of the Four Noble Truths was given to him on that very occasion. Having heard it, the householder attained the fruit of stream-entry, and a mind of shame and conscience arose in him. He said: "Out of my confusion I called what is not illusion an illusion to the Blessed One. Today I confess and repent before the Blessed One, and I take refuge in the Three Jewels."

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent!" And he added: "This is called speaking in accordance with the minds of both oneself and others. Now, what is it to speak in accordance with the minds of both oneself and others? Just as I have taught, if the wise and learned of the entire world say that there are such things, I too say there are. If the wise and learned of the world say that the pleasures of the five objects of desire are impermanent, suffering, and selfless, and should be cut off, I too say that there are such things. If the wise and learned of the world say that in the pleasures of the five objects of desire there is no permanence, no happiness, no self, and no place of perfect purity, I too say that likewise there is no such place. This is called speaking in accordance with the minds of both oneself and others.

"Noble one, when I said that a bodhisattva on the tenth ground sees the intrinsic nature of a buddha only partially, that is called speaking in accordance with the minds of others. Why is it said that only a partial seeing occurs? It is because a bodhisattva on the tenth ground has attained three thousand categories of Dharma such as the meditative absorption called Courageous Progress and the like, and thus knows that I have actualized unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening — yet does not see that all sentient beings will without fail attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Therefore it is said that a bodhisattva on the tenth ground sees the intrinsic nature of a buddha only from one direction, and only partially.

"Noble one, when I constantly say that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha, that is called speaking in accordance with my own mind. That all sentient beings are not annihilated and not extinguished, and will attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening — this is spoken in accordance with my own mind. That all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha but do not see it because it is completely covered by afflictions — I too have said this very thing, and you too should teach this. This is called speaking in accordance with both one's own mind and the minds of others."

This is the forty-seventh fascicle of the noble Great Sūtra of the Passage into Nirvāṇa.

"Noble one, the Tathāgata has at certain times taught innumerable Dharmas with a single expression, just as it is said in the sūtras: 'The cause of all pure conduct is a spiritual friend.' Although the causes of all pure conduct are beyond count, all of them are included within the teaching on the spiritual friend."

Just as I have declared: "The cause of all non-virtue is wrong view" — although the causes of all non-virtuous conduct are beyond count, all of them are included within the teaching on wrong view.

Likewise, it has been declared: "The cause of unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening is a mind of faith" — although the causes that lead to awakening are beyond count, all of them are included within the teaching on a mind of faith.

Noble one, although the Tathāgata has declared the innumerable Dharmas he has taught to be the nature of a buddha, even so, they are none other than the aggregates, the elements, and the sense sources.

Noble one, in the Dharma that the Tathāgata has taught for the sake of sentient beings, there are seven kinds of expression: the causal expression, the resultant expression, the causal-and-resultant expression, the expression by simile, the expression of what is unreasonable to assert, the expression that is universally current in the world, and the wish-fulfilling expression.

What then is the causal expression? It is a statement of a future result on the basis of a present cause. For example, I have declared: "Noble one, do you see this? Know that any sentient being who takes delight in killing — up to and including one who takes delight in wrong view — is a being of the hells. And know that any sentient being who takes no delight in killing — up to and including one who takes no delight in wrong view — is a god or a human." That is the causal expression.

What then is the resultant expression? It is a statement of a past cause on the basis of a present result. Just as it is said in the sūtras: "Noble one, consider what you observe: a sentient being who is poverty-stricken, ugly in complexion, and lacking in radiance — know for certain that such a one has a mind tainted by the stain of broken moral discipline, a mind of aversion, and a mind devoid of a sense of personal shame and a sense of social conscience. And if a sentient being is wealthy and very prosperous, endowed with fine faculties, possessed of majesty and self-mastery — know for certain that such a one has moral discipline, generosity, and diligence, possesses a sense of personal shame and social conscience, and is free of jealousy and aversion." That is the resultant expression.

What then is the causal-and-resultant expression? It corresponds to what is stated in the sūtras: "Noble one, the six sense sources of sentient beings in the present, and what is felt by those sense sources, are the result of past karma — and the Tathāgata has also declared this to be karma." That karma, through its conditions, yields a future result. That is the causal-and-resultant expression.

What then is the expression by simile? Just as, for example, the lion, king of beasts, is taken as a simile for my body — so too are the following used as similes in the sūtra texts: the great king of wild yaks, the great king of nāgas, the citron tree, the heap of the seven precious substances, the ocean, Mount Meru, the great earth, the great rain, the ship's captain, the caravan leader, one who tames persons, the greatly powerful, the finest of horses, the brahmin, the ascetic, the great city, the palmyra tree, and simile sūtras of that kind. Those are expressions by simile.

What then is the expression of what is unreasonable to assert? In the sūtras I have said such things as: "Heaven and earth will come to collide; a mountain will come from the four directions to utterly defeat a king's army." And as has been said to the laywoman Khrisnaśāla's mother: "If this śāla tree were able to keep the eight precepts, it would experience the happiness of gods and humans." And also: "A bodhisattva on the tenth ground may still have a mind that turns back" — statements such as these are acceptable as figures of speech; but one should not say "The Tathāgata has two kinds of expression," just as one should not say "A stream-enterer (Skt. srotāpanna) falls into one of the three lower destinies" —

— the statement that "a bodhisattva on the tenth ground may still have a mind that turns back" is an expression that is wrong to say.

Now, what are expressions that extend worldly usage? As the Blessed One has taught: birth, woman, great, small, going, coming, sitting, lying down, a chariot, a vehicle, a residence, a house, a pot, a garment, a sentient being, permanence, happiness, self, complete purity, an army, a forest, a village, a city, the Saṅgha, an illusion, assembly, and dispersal — these are expressions that extend worldly usage.

What then are expressions of intentional meaning? As when I have reprimanded someone who has broken a vow, and through my remorse they have come to maintain their ethical vows; and as when, by praising a stream-enterer, ignoble persons have given rise to a virtuous mind; and as when, by praising a bodhisattva, sentient beings have given rise to the mind of awakening; and as when the suffering of the three lower destinies has been described in order to inspire the cultivation of virtuous qualities; and as when all conditioned phenomena have been described as "burning" on account of the nature of conditioned things; and as when — similar to no-self, in order to prevent all carelessness and heedlessness — it has been taught that all sentient beings possess the nature of a buddha: these are to be called expressions of intentional meaning.

Son of good family, there is further a mode of speech in which the Tathāgata speaks by associating his own intention with a statement. The nature of a buddha as a Tathāgata is twofold: what is present and what is absent.

What is present is as follows: the thirty-two major marks and eighty excellent minor marks, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the three foundations of mindfulness, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the meditative absorption known as the heroic march (sūraṃgama) and countless other absorptions, the vajra-like absorption and countless others, the absorption of skillful means and countless others, the absorption of the five gnoses and countless others — all of this is what is meant by "what is present."

What is absent is as follows: the Tathāgata's past virtuous actions and non-virtuous actions, the indeterminate, karma, cause, effect, karmic maturation, mental affliction, the five aggregates, and the twelve links of dependent origination — all of this is what is meant by "what is absent."

Son of good family, just as there are the categories of "what is present" and "what is absent," so too the Tathāgata speaks in terms of pairs: virtue and non-virtue, defiled and undefiled, worldly and supramundane, noble and ignoble, conditioned and unconditioned, correct and incorrect, peaceful and unpeaceful, contentious and non-contentious, being of the realm and not being of the realm, afflicted and unafflicted, grasped and ungrasped, prophesied and unprophesied, existent and non-existent, the three times and not the three times, time and non-time, permanent and impermanent, self and no-self, happiness and the absence of happiness, completely pure and incompletely pure; form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and what is not form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; inner sense bases and what are not inner sense bases, outer sense bases and what are not outer sense bases,

the twelve links of dependent origination, and what is not the twelve links of dependent origination — these are said to be the presence and absence of the intrinsic nature of a buddha in a Tathāgata. And it is the same, all the way through, for the presence and absence of the intrinsic nature of a buddha in one who holds wrong craving.

Son of good family, although I have declared that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha, sentient beings do not understand that this is a statement the Tathāgata made in accordance with his own intention. Son of good family, even a bodhisattva with only one more birth to go before awakening is unable to understand these words — how much less could those of the two vehicles or other bodhisattvas understand them?

Son of good family, once upon a time in the past I was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain, and when I engaged in a teaching on conventional truth with the bodhisattva Maitreya, even the five hundred hearers headed by Śāriputra were unable to know or comprehend those things. How much less could they comprehend the ultimate truth that transcends the world?

Son of good family, there are aspects of the intrinsic nature of a buddha that are present in those who hold wrong craving and absent in those who have roots of virtue. There are aspects of the intrinsic nature of a buddha that are present in those who have roots of virtue and absent in those who hold wrong craving. There are aspects of the intrinsic nature of a buddha that are present in both. And there are aspects of the intrinsic nature of a buddha that are absent in both.

Son of good family, among those who are my attendants, whoever understands the meaning of those four categories of statements should not be asked with certainty whether the intrinsic nature of a buddha is definitely present or definitely absent in one who holds wrong craving.

The statement that all sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha is a statement the Tathāgata made in accordance with his own intention. If even the Tathāgata made it in accordance with his own intention, why do sentient beings take it as a one-sided view?

Son of good family, consider the seven kinds of beings living in the waters of the Gaṅgā river: those that are always submerged, those that rise for a moment and then submerge again, those that rise and remain at the surface, those that rise and look in all four directions, those that look all around and then move on, those that move on and then rest, and those that travel both in water and on dry land.

Among these, those that are always submerged are the great fish who, through the maturation of great non-virtuous karma, have such heavy bodies that they remain in the depths of the water and therefore are always submerged. Those that rise for a moment and then submerge again are the great fish who, through the maturation of non-virtuous karma, have heavy bodies and dwell not far below the surface; for a brief instant they perceive the light of day, but on account of that flash of light they rise for only an instant, and because of the heaviness of their bodies they submerge once more. Those that rise and remain are the fish called Dvividya, who dwell in the shallower water and delight in seeing the light of day. Those that rise and look in all four directions are the fish called Tsakgu, who look in all four directions in search of food. Those that look all around and then move on are those fish called Tsakgu who, seeing whatever food appears in the distance, think "that is food" and swim swiftly toward it — that is what is meant by looking and then moving on. Those that move on and then rest are those fish that, having gone to that place, find something fit to eat and then stop — that is what is meant by moving on and then resting. Those that travel both in water and on dry land are tortoises.

Son of good family, within the great sacred river of the great, complete nirvāṇa there are likewise seven kinds of beings, from the always submerged to the seventh, and in between some are submerged and some emerge. Among these, the always submerged are those who, reading this sūtra of the great complete nirvāṇa, conclude that the Tathāgata abides permanently without change or alteration, and that therefore, being permanent, blissful, self, and completely pure, he will ultimately never pass into nirvāṇa. All sentient beings possess the intrinsic nature of a buddha, they say — including those who hold wrong craving, and

those who commit the grave offense of scorning the extensive sūtra, who commit the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya), and who violate the four root precepts — all of these, they declare, will without fail attain complete awakening. And hearing it taught that stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas will all without fail arrive at unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, no faith arises in their minds. Thinking to themselves, they speak these words: "This sūtra of the great complete nirvāṇa is a tīrthika text — it was not taught by the Buddha." Having said this, they part from their virtuous spiritual friends and do not hear the sacred Dharma. And even if they happen to hear it occasionally, they are unable to take it to heart. And even if they do take it to heart, they do not attend to it virtuously. Not attending to it virtuously, they come to dwell in non-virtuous phenomena.

Dwelling in non-virtuous phenomena has six aspects: non-virtue, the absence of virtue, the defiling of Dharma, the generation of further existence, being tormented by afflictions, and the experience of the results of non-virtue. This is called "submersion."

As for how one is submerged: having no virtuous mind, perpetually engaging in non-virtue, and not diligently applying the antidotes — this is called submersion.

Now, "non-virtue" means acting in ways that are condemned by noble ones, that give rise to a mind of fear, that are abandoned by virtuous spiritual friends, and that are of no benefit to sentient beings — for these reasons it is called non-virtue.

"The absence of virtue" means producing an incalculable quantity of the results of non-virtue, being perpetually overpowered by ignorance, associating with and befriending the wicked, having no means by which to apply diligence to virtue, and having a mind that has become thoroughly inverted and is forever in error — for these reasons it is called the absence of virtue.

"The defiling of Dharma" means perpetually defiling body and speech, defiling the purity of sentient beings, generating unwholesome karma, and abandoning virtuous phenomena — for these reasons it is called the defiling of Dharma.

"The generation of further existence" means that when one has fully accomplished the three qualities mentioned above, one is born in the hells, in the realm of animals, or among hungry ghosts; and not applying diligence to the qualities of liberation, one feels no weariness toward the actions of body, speech, and mind that perpetuate existence — this is called the generation of further existence.

"Being tormented by afflictions" means that when one has fully accomplished the four qualities mentioned above, body and mind become afflicted. It is called torment because one abandons peace. It is called torment because one experiences the karmic maturation of the hell realms. It is called torment because sentient beings are scorched. It is called torment because all virtuous phenomena are scorched. Noble son, the mind of faith is cool and satisfying — it is called torment because one is deprived of it.

"The experience of the results of non-virtue" means that when one has fully accomplished the five qualities mentioned above, at death one falls into the hells, into the realm of animals, or into the realm of hungry ghosts. Noble son, there is yet another way in which the experience of the results of non-virtue is described — through three aspects of non-virtuous things. What are the three? Afflictions that are non-virtuous, karma that is non-virtuous, and karmic maturation that is non-virtuous — this is called the experience of the matured result of non-virtue.

Noble son, when a person possesses the six qualities described above, they cut the roots of virtue. They commit the five acts of immediate retribution, they destroy the restraint of the four root precepts, they slander the Three Jewels, they use the wealth of the Saṅgha willfully for themselves,

they perform various non-Dharmic acts. Through those causes and those conditions, they sink into the Avīci hell — the hell of immediate retribution — and the body they experience there extends to some eighty-four thousand leagues in size. The karma of their body, speech, and mind is so heavily weighted that they are unable to arise from it. Why is that? Because the mind is unable to generate any virtuous Dharma. Even though countless Tathāgatas appear in the world, such beings neither see nor hear them. They are therefore compared to the great fish of the Ganges river that has sunk — this is called "sinking."

Noble son, I have said that those who possess false craving always sink. Yet there are also those who always sink but do not possess false craving. Who are they? Those who practice the virtue of generosity and keeping moral discipline for the sake of continued existence — they too are called "those who always sink."

Noble son, through these four kinds of virtuous acts, the fruit of non-virtue is obtained. What are the four? Reading and reciting sūtras and texts out of a wish to be considered superior to others; holding the vow of moral discipline for the sake of gain and renown; practicing generosity in order to exercise power over others; and focusing the mind one-pointedly for the sake of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Through these four virtuous things, the ripening of the fruit of non-virtue comes about. Those who act through these four kinds of things are said to rise up from sinking, only to sink again. Why do they sink? Because they are attached to the three realms of existence. Why do they rise? Because they see the light of appearance. The light of appearance is: learning, moral discipline, generosity, and meditative absorption. Why do they sink again? Because they harbor wrong views and cultivate pride. Therefore I have spoken these verses in the sūtra:

Whatever sentient being, attached to existence,
performs virtuous and non-virtuous karma through that existence —
such a one is led astray from the path of nirvāṇa,
arising for a moment, then sinking again.

Those who wander in the dark ocean of saṃsāra,
even if freed for a time, still bear afflictions with them;
and so they gather the fruit of non-virtue once more,
arising for a moment, then sinking again.

Noble son, just as the great fish, upon seeing the light of appearance, rises for a moment yet sinks again because of the heaviness of its body, so too are both the foregoing types of individuals.

Noble son, if anyone is attached to the three realms of existence, that is called "sinking." If, upon hearing this sūtra of great complete nirvāṇa, one generates a mind of faith, that is called "arising." By what cause and through what condition is it called "arising"? Having heard this sūtra, one abandons all non-virtuous phenomena and cultivates virtuous phenomena — this is called "arising." Yet although faith is present, one cannot be said to possess it fully. By what cause and through what condition is one said not to fully possess faith? Because that individual has faith that great complete nirvāṇa is permanent, blissful, self, and perfectly pure, yet claims that the body of the Tathāgata is impermanent, devoid of bliss, without self, and impure. Regarding the Tathāgata's nirvāṇa, there are two kinds: conditioned and unconditioned. The conditioned nirvāṇa lacks permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity. The unconditioned nirvāṇa possesses permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity. Such a person has confidence that buddha-nature exists in sentient beings, yet does not have certainty that it exists in all — therefore they are said not to fully possess faith.

Noble son, faith is of two kinds: faith and seeking.

That person possesses faith, yet is unable to seek and strive — nonetheless, they should not be called one who does not fully possess faith.

Again, there are two kinds: faith born from hearing, and faith born from reflection. If one's faith is born from hearing but not from reflection, one is said not to fully possess faith.

Again, there are two kinds: faith that awakening exists, and faith that attaining it is possible. If one's mind has faith that awakening exists yet does not have confidence that attaining it is possible, one is said not to fully possess faith.

Again, there are two kinds: faith in what is correct, and faith in what is wrong. One who says that cause and result exist, and that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha exist — that is faith in what is correct. One who says that cause and result do not exist, that the defining marks of the Three Jewels are different from one another, and who places confidence in wrong views such as those of Kāśyapa the Perfector and the like — that is called faith in what is wrong. If a person has faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, yet does not have confidence that the defining marks of the Three Jewels are one, and has faith that cause and result exist yet does not have confidence that attainment is possible — such a person is said not to fully possess faith. One who does not fully possess faith is likewise not one who fully possesses moral discipline.

If one asks by what cause and condition they are said not to fully possess it — it is because they lack the cause that they do not fully possess moral discipline.

And if one asks further why they are said not to fully possess it — moral discipline is of two kinds: the moral discipline of ritual observance, and the moral discipline that is genuine ethics. One who possesses only the moral discipline of ritual observance and does not possess the moral discipline that is genuine ethics is said not to fully possess moral discipline.

Again, there are two kinds: the moral discipline of commission and the moral discipline of refraining. One who possesses only the moral discipline of commission and does not possess the moral discipline of refraining is said not to fully possess moral discipline.

Again, there are two kinds: obtaining right livelihood through body and speech, and not obtaining right livelihood through body and speech. One who does not obtain right livelihood through body and speech is said not to fully possess moral discipline.

Again, there are two kinds: the moral discipline that seeks existence, and the moral discipline that relinquishes it. One who possesses only the moral discipline that seeks continued existence and does not possess the moral discipline that relinquishes it is said not to fully possess moral discipline.

Again, there are two kinds: the moral discipline oriented toward existence, and the moral discipline oriented toward awakening. One who possesses only the moral discipline oriented toward existence and does not possess the moral discipline oriented toward awakening is said not to fully possess moral discipline.

Moral discipline is again of two kinds: virtuous moral discipline and non-virtuous moral discipline. Virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind constitutes virtuous moral discipline. The vow of the cow and the vow of the dog constitute non-virtuous moral discipline. One who has confidence that those two disciplines yield virtuous results is said not to fully possess moral discipline.

Thus, one who does not fully possess these two things — the substance of faith and moral discipline — will also not be one who applies diligence to extensive learning. As for how one does not fully possess learning: among the twelve branches of scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, one who has faith in six branches but not in the other six is said not to fully possess learning. Likewise, even one who holds six scriptural branches yet is unable to read them, recite them, teach them to others, or render benefit — such a person is said not to fully possess learning. And further, even one who holds six scriptural branches yet does so for the sake of disputation —

— or who holds six scriptural branches in order to triumph over others, or for the sake of gain and fame, or who grasps, reads, recites, and expounds them for the sake of continued existence in the round of becoming — such a person is said not to fully possess learning.

Son of good family, I have now explained what it means to possess learning as described in the sūtras. What, then, does it mean to possess it? If a certain monk reveres, with body, speech, and mind, his preceptors, teachers, and those who are virtuous — if he pays them homage in this way — then those teachers will come to feel a mind of loving-kindness toward him, and through that condition they will teach him the sūtras and the Dharma. He in turn will hold them with one-pointed mind, reciting and familiarizing himself with them. Through holding, reciting, and growing familiar with them, he will attain wisdom. Having attained wisdom in this way, he will apply it with great diligence and will abide in accordance with the Dharma. Having applied it with great diligence and abided thus, he will attain the genuine meaning. Having attained the genuine meaning, his body and mind will become secluded. When body and mind have become secluded, a mind of joy will arise. Through the condition of that joyful mind, he will attain the mind of meditative absorption. Because he has attained the mind of meditative absorption, he will attain right knowledge and vision. Having attained right knowledge and vision, a mind of disenchantment with all states of becoming will arise. Through disenchantment with all states of becoming, he will attain complete liberation. One who lacks all such qualities as these is said not to fully possess attainment.

One who lacks all three of those qualities will likewise not fully possess generosity. Now, generosity is of two kinds: material generosity and the generosity of Dharma. Such a person may indeed practise material generosity, yet he seeks continued existence in the round of becoming. He may practise the generosity of Dharma, yet he will not possess it fully — and why is that? Fearing that others might surpass him, he withholds and does not teach everything: this is said to be not fully possessing generosity. Both material generosity and the generosity of Dharma each have two forms: noble and non-noble. The noble one, having given, places no hope in the ripening of a fruit as result. The non-noble one, having given, hopes for the ripening of a fruit as result. The noble one practises the generosity of Dharma in order to cause the Dharma to flourish. The non-noble one practises the generosity of Dharma in order to cause continued becoming to flourish — just as practising material generosity in order to cause material gain to increase, and practising the generosity of Dharma in order to cause the states of becoming to increase, is called not fully possessing generosity.

Furthermore, such a person holds six branches of scripture, and provides the needs of those who hold the Dharma, yet does not provide the needs of those who do not hold the Dharma — therefore this too is called not fully possessing generosity.

In this way, a person who lacks those four qualities described above will also not fully possess diligence in wisdom. The defining characteristic of wisdom is discernment by its intrinsic nature. Such a person fails to discern whether the Tathāgata is permanent or impermanent, and is unable to comprehend it. Moreover, in the sūtra of the Tathāgata's complete nirvāṇa it is declared: "The Tathāgata is complete liberation; complete liberation is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata himself is nirvāṇa; nirvāṇa itself is complete liberation." He neither discerns nor is able to comprehend the distinctions among these meanings. The perfectly pure life itself is the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata himself is loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, and joy. Loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, and joy are themselves complete liberation.

Complete liberation itself is complete nirvāṇa. Complete nirvāṇa itself is the four immeasurables." These meanings too — the inability to discern their distinctions — is what is called lacking wisdom.

Furthermore, what one is unable to distinguish is this: the intrinsic nature of a buddha is itself the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata himself is all the unmingled qualities. The unmingled qualities themselves are liberation. Liberation itself is complete nirvāṇa. Complete nirvāṇa itself is the unmingled qualities. These meanings too — the inability to discern their distinctions — is what is called lacking wisdom.

Yet another thing one is unable to distinguish is the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Because one does not discern the distinctions among the Four Noble Truths, one does not know the conduct of the noble ones. Not knowing the conduct of the noble ones, one does not know the Tathāgata. Not knowing the Tathāgata, one does not know the Tathāgata's liberation. Not knowing liberation, one does not know nirvāṇa. For these reasons one is called lacking wisdom.

Ordinary beings who lack the five things mentioned above do so for two reasons: they give rise to wholesome qualities, and they give rise to unwholesome qualities. How does one give rise to unwholesome qualities? Such a person, not seeing that the self is without inherent selfhood, generates a mind that clings to possessing a self. Within a community of those under equal training, one thinks, "I am the best." For that reason, one associates with companions of like mind who are unwholesome. Through such association, one will come to hear teachings that are further lacking. Having heard them, the mind becomes delighted and attached. One generates pride and arrogance and falls into widespread heedlessness. Through the condition of heedlessness, one becomes attached to associating with householders and to discussing and listening to the affairs of the household life, and one abandons the pure qualities of the renunciate life. Through that cause and that condition, unwholesome qualities are produced. Because unwholesome qualities are produced, one generates impure actions through the three doors of body, speech, and mind. Through the complete impurity of these three kinds of action, one produces rebirth in the hells, in the realm of animals, and in the realm of hungry ghosts. This is called: arising in a moment and then fading away.

As for the beings whose qualities are called "arising in a moment and then fading away," they are the following: the god Devadatta, the monk Kokālika, the monk Ānśu, the monk Supratiṣṭhita, the monk Tiśa, the monk Karmagupta, the nun Maitreyī, the nun Āraṇyikā, the nun Diśā, the nun Mānā, the householder Supariśuddha, the layman Bhavārthin, the Śākya Śāli, the householder Balendra, the laywoman Yaśomatī, the laywoman Ābhā, the laywoman Priyā, the laywoman Gaṇadāsā, and the laywoman Ghaṇṭā — these and others like them are called "arising in a moment and then fading away." It is like a great fish that rises up on seeing the light, but sinks back down because of the weight of its body.

By contrast, those of lesser station among such persons, recognizing that their own view and conduct are lacking, and recognizing that they are indeed lacking in this way, seek out and rely upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). By relying on a spiritual friend, they become eager to ask about what they have not yet heard. Having heard, they become eager to retain it. Having retained it, they take joy in reflecting upon it carefully. Having reflected carefully, they come to abide in accordance with the Dharma. Abiding in accordance with the Dharma, they cause wholesome qualities to increase.

Because wholesome qualities thus increase, they never decline. This is called abiding.

Who are those that abide in the Dharma of the buddhas? They are as follows: Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana; the five including Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya; the five monks including Yaśas; Anurāddha; young Kāśyapa; Mahākāśyapa; Kāśyapa of the Ten Powers; the nun Skye-dgu'i-bdag-mo; the nun Pāṭali-flower; the nun Damma; the nun Paramārtha; the nun Buddhi-mother; the nun Pāṭalā; the nun Purity; the nun Irreversible; King Bimbasāra; the householder Ugra; the householder Anāthapiṇḍada; the great Śākya-name; the poor Anātha-food-giver; the householder Son-of-Śreṣṭhin; the householder Yaśas; the householder Endowed-with-All; the minister Siṃha; the householder Upāli; the householder Sword; the laywoman Fearless; the laywoman Virtuous-Dweller; the laywoman Dharma-Devoted; the laywoman Courageous; the laywoman God-Given; the laywoman Well-Born; the laywoman Form-Endowed; the laywoman She-Who-Obtained-the-Best-of-Herds; the laywoman Solitary; and the laywoman Mahāsinā and others — these monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen are all called those who abide.

Why are they called those who abide? Because they are devoted to always beholding the luminous light of virtue. By that cause and that condition, whether a buddha has appeared in the world or has not appeared, those persons never commit evil deeds. Therefore they are called those who abide. Just as the fish called the nyadibid, out of its delight in beholding the light, neither sinks nor disappears, so too are they like that. For this reason I have spoken these verses from the sūtras:

One who is skilled in discerning the meaning,
who with one-pointed focus earnestly seeks the fruit of the ascetic life,
and who utterly scorns all conditioned existence —
such a one is called one who abides in accordance with the Dharma.

One who makes offerings to the boundless Blessed One
will, for countless births, cultivate the path.
If one enjoys the pleasures of the world yet remains heedful,
such a one is called one who abides in accordance with the Dharma.

One who relies on a spiritual friend and listens to the sacred Dharma,
who takes it to heart and abides in accordance with the Dharma,
who is devoted to beholding the rays of light and cultivates the path —
such a one will attain the blissful state of full liberation.

Noble child, for one who lacks wisdom there are five things. Once such a person recognizes this, he seeks out a spiritual friend. That spiritual friend in turn examines which is greatest among attachment, aversion, delusion, and conceptual thought. If attachment predominates, he teaches the Dharma of contemplating the impure. If aversion predominates, he teaches the Dharma of loving-kindness. If delusion predominates, he teaches dependent origination. If conceptual thought predominates, he teaches the counting of the breath. If attachment to the view of self predominates, he teaches the eighteen elements and so forth.

Having heard this, the student then grasps it with a one-pointed mind. Having grasped it with the mind, he applies himself diligently in accordance with the Dharma. Through diligent practice in accordance with the Dharma, he gradually attains the four close applications of mindfulness, and he comes to contemplate the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena. Having thus contemplated them, he gradually comes to investigate the twelve links of dependent origination. Having thus investigated them, he attains the quality of warmth.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, the quality of warmth is present in all sentient beings. Why is that? Just as the Blessed One has declared that a sentient being is so called because three phenomena have come together — vitality, warmth, and consciousness — therefore, since warmth has from the very beginning been present in all sentient beings, why has the Tathāgata taught that the quality of warmth arises through the condition of a spiritual friend?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, when you say that the quality of warmth exists, it exists in all beings, right up to and including those with wrong craving. But as for how I have taught the quality of warmth: it is first obtained through the condition of skillful means, and what has been without beginning now becomes presently possessed. Therefore, since it has not been there from the very beginning in all sentient beings, it is not fitting for you to say that all sentient beings possess the quality of warmth.

"Son of good family, moreover, this quality of warmth is a phenomenon of the form realm; it is not found in the desire realm. If you were to say it exists in all sentient beings, then it would follow that it also exists in the sentient beings of the desire realm — but seeing that it is absent in the desire realm, you should understand that it does not exist in all beings without exception.

"Son of good family, it exists in the form realm, yet not in all beings. Why? Because it is present in my attendants but not in non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Therefore it does not exist in all sentient beings.

"Son of good family, all non-Buddhists contemplate only six kinds of conduct. My attendants, however, possess sixteen kinds of conduct, and these sixteen kinds of conduct are not present in all sentient beings."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, regarding what you have called the quality of warmth — how is it to be understood as warmth? Is it warm by its own intrinsic nature, or does it become warm through the power of another?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, this quality of warmth is warm by its own intrinsic nature; it does not become warm through the power of another."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa said: "Blessed One, you have previously stated that the two — Aśvaka and Puṇarvasu — did not possess the quality of warmth. Why is that? Because they lacked a mind of faith in the Three Jewels, it is said they did not possess warmth. Therefore I would submit that faith itself is the quality of warmth."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, faith is not the quality of warmth. Why? Because warmth is subsequently obtained through the condition of a mind of faith.

"Son of good family, what is called the quality of warmth is wisdom. Why? Because it is the comprehension of the Four Noble Truths. This is why it is called the sixteen kinds of conduct — the conduct itself is wisdom.

"Son of good family, as to what cause and what condition make it called warmth: what is called warmth has the defining characteristic of the fire of the eight branches of the noble path, and therefore it is called warmth.

"Son of good family, consider this analogy: when fire is kindled by friction, warmth arises first, then fire appears, and afterwards smoke arises. The undefiled path is likewise: what is called warmth therein corresponds to the sixteen kinds of conduct; what is called fire corresponds to something like the fruit of stream-entry; and smoke corresponds to the cutting off of all afflictions through the cultivation of the path."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, this quality of warmth is indeed a phenomenon of existence, and it is also a conditioned phenomenon. Because its karmic maturation, through the condition of the form realm, results in the obtaining of the five aggregates — for this reason it is called a phenomenon of existence."

"And because of its cause and its condition it is also called 'conditioned.' If it is conditioned, how can it serve as the defining mark of the undefiled path?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, it is just so. It is just as you have said. Son of good family, although this quality of warmth is indeed a conditioned phenomenon and a phenomenon of existence, conditioned and existential phenomena are also capable of destruction — and it is for that reason that it comes to serve as the defining mark of the undefiled path. Son of good family, just as someone who rides a wild horse both loves it and yet bends it to his will, the mind of warmth is similar: it takes rebirth for the sake of existence, and for the sake of rebirth it comprehends the formations. Therefore, although it is a phenomenon of existence and is conditioned, it nonetheless also comes to serve as the defining mark of the true path.

The number of persons who have attained the quality of warmth is seventy-three. Of these, the desire realm comprises ten kinds: persons possessed of all afflictions who cut away one part, and so on up to those who cut away nine parts. From the first dhyāna up through the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is likewise. These are called the seventy-three kinds. Persons who have attained the quality of warmth will not cut off the root of virtue, will not commit any of the heinous acts without interval, and will not transgress the four root precepts of moral discipline.

There are, however, two varieties: those who have encountered a virtuous spiritual friend, and those who have encountered an unwholesome spiritual friend. Of these, encountering an unwholesome spiritual friend arises for an instant and then subsides once more. Encountering a virtuous spiritual friend is like looking out in all four directions. This looking in all four directions is called the summit quality (Skt. mūrdhāna). Although the intrinsic nature of the summit quality is not the five aggregates as such, it takes the Four Noble Truths as its object — and for that reason it is called looking out in all four directions. Having thus attained the summit quality, one then gradually attains patience. That patience too is similarly not the five aggregates as such in its intrinsic nature, yet it takes the Four Noble Truths as its object, and through it one gradually attains the highest worldly quality (Skt. laukikāgradharma). The intrinsic nature of that quality likewise is not the five aggregates, yet it takes the Four Noble Truths as its object, and through it one gradually attains the quality of patience toward suffering. The intrinsic nature of that patience is wisdom, and it takes a single truth as its object. In this way, through the quality of patience, one takes a single truth as its object and sees it; the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing are cut off, and thereby one attains the fruit of stream-entry. This is called looking out in all four directions, and here the four directions refer to the Four Noble Truths."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, in keeping with what the Blessed One previously taught — that the stream-enterer's complete severing of afflictions is like a lake four leagues wide and four leagues deep filled with water, while what remains is like a single drop of dew on the tip of a hair — why was it said that when these three, namely the view of self, the view of taking what is not a cause as a cause, and the defilement of doubt, are cut off, one has entered the stream? Blessed One, for what cause and through what condition does a stream-enterer come to look out in all four directions? And again, for what cause and through what condition is one called a stream-enterer? And again, for what cause and through what condition is a stream-enterer like what is called a small fish?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, although a stream-enterer has cut off immeasurable numbers of afflictions,

all the afflictions cut off by every stream-enterer are contained within these three aspects. Son of good family, consider the analogy of a great king who, when he walks or travels, is accompanied by an army of four divisions, yet people of the world say simply, 'The king has come,' or 'The king has gone.' Why? Because in the world he is to be honored. These three afflictions are just like that. And why are they called 'weighty'? They are called weighty because all sentient beings continually give rise to them, and because they are subtle and difficult to discern with wisdom. These three afflictions are extremely difficult to cut off because they become the cause of all afflictions, and because they become the cause, as their antidote, of moral discipline, meditative absorption, and wisdom.

Son of good family, when certain sentient beings hear it said that a stream-enterer has entirely cut off an immeasurable number of afflictions, a mind of turning back arises in them, and they say, 'How can a sentient being cut off such an immeasurable number of afflictions?' For that reason the Tathāgata, through skillful means, taught this in three aspects.

As for what you asked — for what cause and through what condition does a stream-enterer look out in all four directions — son of good family, a stream-enterer, having thoroughly examined the Four Noble Truths, attains four kinds of things. What are they? Abiding on the firm path, complete investigation, seeing correctly just as things are, and the ability to defeat the great enemy. Of these, the firm path is the stream-enterer itself. It is called abiding on the firm path because no one can dislodge one from the five faculties. Complete investigation means scrutinizing all internal and external afflictions. Seeing correctly just as things are is the wisdom of patient acceptance. Defeating the great enemy refers to the four inversions.

As for what you asked — for what cause and through what condition is one called a stream-enterer — son of good family, 'stream' refers to what is undefiled. 'Entered' means cultivated. Because one cultivates the undefiled, one is called a stream-enterer.

Son of good family, furthermore, 'stream-enterer' means 'one who flows.' There are two kinds of flowing: flowing downward and flowing upward. Because one flows upward, one is called a stream-enterer.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: "Blessed One, if that is the meaning, why are those who return once, those who never return, and arhats not also called stream-enterers?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, from stream-enterer all the way up to a buddha, all may also be called stream-enterers. For if there were no stream-entry in the progression from once-returner to buddha, how could a once-returner be designated all the way up to a buddha? For every sentient being, there are two kinds of name: the old name and the name newly assigned. In one's base and inferior time, there exists a worldly name. Having attained the path, a new name is assigned, and so one is called a stream-enterer. Because it was attained first, one is called a stream-enterer; because it is attained afterward, one is called a once-returner. That very same one may also be called a stream-enterer and also a once-returner, and so it is designated all the way to 'buddha.'

Son of good family, there are two aspects of a stream-enterer: liberation and nirvāṇa. Because all noble ones possess both of these two aspects, they may be called stream-enterers and

once-returner all the way through to buddha, it is the same. Son of good family, a bodhisattva too may be called a stream-enterer. Why is that? A bodhisattva possesses the gnosis of exhaustion and the gnosis of non-arising. Since a stream-enterer likewise seeks those two aspects of gnosis, it is fitting to designate a stream-enterer as a bodhisattva as well. It is also fitting to call a stream-enterer a buddha. Why is that? Because one genuinely sees the path and completely severs the afflictions; because one becomes a cause and result of perfect and complete awakening; and because one is in accord with the path of perfect and complete awakening, whether mixed or unmixed with it. From once-returner through to arhat, it is the same.

Son of good family, a stream-enterer has two aspects: sharp faculties and dull faculties. One with dull faculties goes back and forth between gods and humans up to seven times. Among those with dull faculties there are further five varieties: some go back and forth six times, some five, some four, some three, and some two. One with sharp faculties will, in the present life itself, attain everything from the fruit of stream-entry through to arhat.

Son of good family, you asked why the example taken for a stream-enterer is the fish called tsak-gu. It is because that fish has four qualities. What are they? It is light because its bones are fine; it is light because it has fins; it delight in seeing the light of luminosity; and it holds on firmly.

A stream-enterer likewise has four qualities. The fineness of bone is an example for the thinness of the afflictions. Having fins is an example for insight and calm abiding. Delight in seeing the light of luminosity is an example for seeing the path. Holding on firmly means this: having heard the Tathāgata teach impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and impurity, one holds steadfastly and does not abandon it. For example, when the king of māras conjured an appearance resembling the form of a buddha, the householder named Dragshul saw it and was struck with fear. The māra, seeing that the householder's mind was shaken, said to him: "What I taught before as the Four Truths was not correct. Now I will teach you, for the first time, five truths, six aggregates, thirteen sense bases, and nineteen elements." But the householder, having heard this, examined all the defining characteristics of the Dharma and found that such a meaning was absent there. Therefore, he held his mind unshaken and immovable. It is like that.

Here ends the forty-eighth fascicle of the noble Great Sūtra of the Parinirvāṇa.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One and said: Blessed One, is one called a stream-enterer because one previously attained the path, or is one called a stream-enterer because one attained the first fruit? If one is called a stream-enterer because one previously attained the path, then why is one who has attained the Dharma of patient acceptance of suffering not called a stream-enterer but rather called one who is approaching? And if one is called a stream-enterer because one attained the first fruit, then when a non-Buddhist has previously cut off the afflictions, gone to the sphere of nothingness, cultivated the undefiled path, and attained the fruit of non-return, why would that person not be called a stream-enterer?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, one is called a stream-enterer because one has attained the first fruit. As for your question — why should one who is a non-Buddhist and who has previously cut off the afflictions, gone to the sphere of nothingness, cultivated the undefiled path, and attained the fruit of non-return not be called a stream-enterer —

Son of good family, this is why one who has attained the first fruit is called a stream-enterer — for at that time such a person is possessed of eight wisdoms and sixteen modes of conduct. Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, one who has attained the fruit of non-return is likewise possessed of eight wisdoms and sixteen modes of conduct, so why is that person not called a stream-enterer?

Son of good family, the sixteen modes of defiled conduct are of two kinds: mixed and unmixed. The sixteen modes of undefiled conduct are likewise of two kinds: those oriented toward the fruit and those in which the fruit has been attained. The eight wisdoms are likewise of two kinds: those oriented toward the fruit and those in which the fruit has been attained. The stream-enterer has abandoned the sixteen mixed modes of conduct and attained the sixteen unmixed modes of conduct; has abandoned the eight wisdoms oriented toward the fruit and attained the eight fruits of wisdom. The non-returner is not like this. Therefore, one who has attained the first fruit is called a stream-enterer.

Son of good family, the stream-enterer focuses on the Four Noble Truths. The once-returner focuses on just the single truth of oneness. Therefore one who has attained the first fruit is called a stream-enterer. By virtue of that cause and that condition, the analogy of the fish is given. One who "goes about looking in every direction" is the once-returner. One who "diligently applies oneself to the path with single-pointed focus" does so in order to cut through attachment, aversion, delusion, and pride — just as a fish looks in every direction in search of food. "Remaining, having ceased from going about" is like the non-returner who, having found food, stays still.

Now, the non-returner is briefly of two kinds: one who attains the fruit of non-return in the present life and then, having applied even greater diligent effort, attains the fruit of arhatship; and one who, having become attached to the peaceful meditative absorption of the form realm and the formless realm, does not take up aggregates in the desire realm — and is therefore called a non-returner.

Furthermore, the non-returner is of five kinds: one who attains nirvāṇa in the intermediate state; one who attains nirvāṇa after taking a body; one who attains nirvāṇa through exertion; one who attains nirvāṇa without exertion; and one who attains nirvāṇa through the supreme stream.

Again, there are six kinds: one who attains nirvāṇa in the present life, and then the preceding five. Again, there are seven kinds: one who attains nirvāṇa in the formless realm, and then the preceding six.

As for those who attain nirvāṇa through exertion, there are two kinds: those who take two births and those who take four births. Of these, one who takes two births is of sharp faculties, and one who takes four births is of dull faculties.

Again, there are two kinds: those who have great diligence but lack the meditative absorption of mastery, and those who are lazy but possess the meditative absorption of mastery.

Again, there are two kinds: those who possess the meditative absorption of diligence, and those who possess neither of the two.

Son of good family, beings of the desire realm and the form realm have two kinds of karma: karma of activity and karma of birth-taking. One who attains nirvāṇa in the intermediate state has only karma of activity and lacks karma of birth-taking. Therefore that person is called one who attains nirvāṇa in the intermediate state — having cast off the aggregates of the desire realm, and because of sharp faculties, attaining nirvāṇa without having gone to the form realm. That is what is called attaining nirvāṇa in the intermediate state.

The non-returner has four kinds of intention: one who is neither in training nor beyond training; one who is in training; one who is beyond training; and one who attains nirvāṇa while being neither in training nor beyond training.

Now, how is it that one attains nirvāṇa in the intermediate state?

Son of good family, of the four types of intention of the non-returner, two attain nirvāṇa and two do not attain nirvāṇa. Therefore the latter are called those who attain nirvāṇa in the intermediate state. As for those who attain nirvāṇa having taken up the aggregates, there are two kinds: those with the karma of activity and those with the karma of rebirth. Such a person casts off the aggregates of the desire realm, takes up the aggregates of the form realm, and through diligent application to the path, attains nirvāṇa at the end of life.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, if one who has reached the end of life is said to attain nirvāṇa, then why did you say that one attains nirvāṇa having taken up the aggregates?

The Blessed One replied: Son of good family, having taken up the aggregates, that person cuts off the afflictions of all three realms from the very beginning. Therefore it is said that one attains nirvāṇa having taken up the aggregates.

Son of good family, one who attains nirvāṇa through conduct is one who applies diligence to the path continuously, who, through the force of conditioned meditative absorption, completely cuts off the afflictions and attains nirvāṇa — this is called attaining nirvāṇa through conduct.

One who attains nirvāṇa through boundless conduct is one who, knowing that nirvāṇa is certain to come, becomes complacent for that very reason. Yet that person too, through the force of conditioned meditative absorption, attains nirvāṇa at the end of life. Therefore this is called attaining nirvāṇa without conduct.

As for what is called attaining nirvāṇa through a continuous stream: one who has attained the fourth dhyāna arises in the mind of joy belonging to the first dhyāna, and through the condition of that, is reborn in the first dhyāna. The stream has two kinds: the stream of affliction and the stream of the path. Through the stream of the path, at the end of life, the mind of joy arises with respect to the second dhyāna, and through the condition of joy, one is reborn in the second dhyāna. Likewise it continues in the same way up through the fourth dhyāna.

Within the fourth dhyāna itself there are also two kinds: those who proceed to the formless realm, and those who proceed to the five pure abodes. Of these two likewise, one delights in meditative absorption and one delights in wisdom. One who delights in wisdom proceeds to the five pure abodes. One who delights in meditative absorption proceeds to the formless realm.

Of these two likewise, one cultivates the fourth dhyāna with five distinctions and one does not cultivate it. What are the five? The lowest, the middling, the superior, the middling-superior, and the supreme-superior. Of these, one who cultivates the supreme-superior dwells in the heaven of Akaniṣṭha. One who cultivates the middling-superior dwells in the heaven of Sudarśana. One who cultivates the superior dwells in the heaven of Sudṛśa. One who cultivates the middling dwells in the heaven of Atapa. One who cultivates the lowest dwells in the heaven of Avṛha.

Of these two likewise, one delights in discourse and one delights in stillness. One who delights in stillness proceeds to the formless realm. One who delights in discourse dwells in the five pure abodes.

Again there are two kinds: one who cultivates dhyāna through familiarity and one who does not cultivate through familiarity. One who cultivates dhyāna through familiarity proceeds to the five pure abodes. One who does not cultivate through familiarity is reborn in the formless realm, attains nirvāṇa at the end of life, and this is called attaining nirvāṇa through a continuous stream.

One who wishes to proceed to the formless realm is unable to cultivate the four dhyānas and the five distinctions. One who cultivates the four dhyānas and the five distinctions does not engage in the formless absorptions.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked:

"Blessed One, is one who attains nirvāṇa in the intermediate state a person of sharp faculties? If one is of sharp faculties, why does one not pass into nirvāṇa in the present time? And why does intermediate nirvāṇa exist in the desire realm but not in the form realm?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, in the present time such a person is unable to cultivate the path because the four great requisites are wanting. Monks, when those four great requisites — lodging, alms food, robes, bedding, and medical supplies and other necessities for illness — are lacking, one will not pass into nirvāṇa in the present time.

Son of good family, I shall tell you of a former time when I was dwelling in the great hall called An, in Śrāvastī. A monk came to where I was and said this: 'Blessed One, though I have constantly cultivated the path, I have not been able to attain any fruit from stream-entry up through the fruit of arhatship.' At that time I declared to Ānanda: 'You shall provide this monk with all his needs.'

Then Ānanda took that monk to the pleasure garden of Anāthapiṇḍada — the giver of food to the shelterless — and gave him a fine lodging. Then that monk said to Ānanda: 'Noble one, please have my lodging thoroughly purified and adorned with the seven precious substances, and have it decorated with silk crowns, banners, parasols, and the like.' Ānanda said: 'In the world a renunciant is called a pauper — where would I obtain all of that?' The monk replied: 'Noble one, if you will provide those things for me, good and well. If you will not provide them, I shall return to where the Blessed One is.'

Then Ānanda went to where the Blessed One was and spoke thus: 'Blessed One, that monk asks me for ornaments of the seven precious substances, crowns, banners, parasols, and various other such things. What am I to do?' At that time I again declared: 'Ānanda, go and provide that monk with all the necessary requisites according to his wish.'

Then Ānanda went back and provided all the requisites for that monk in full. Having received them, the monk cultivated with one-pointed concentration, and before long he attained every fruit from stream-entry up through the fruit of arhatship.

Son of good family, innumerable sentient beings fail to attain nirvāṇa because, being distracted and confused by the effort involved in fully attaining nirvāṇa, their minds become agitated. Son of good family, there are also sentient beings who, out of delight in performing many beneficial acts for beings, become so occupied that they do not attain meditative absorption, and thus have not attained nirvāṇa in the present time.

Son of good family, as for your question — why and through what causes and conditions intermediate nirvāṇa exists within the desire realm after abandoning the aggregates of the desire realm, but not in the form realm: son of good family, for that person the afflictions of the desire realm have two kinds of causes and conditions for conceptual elaboration — internal and external. In the form realm there are no external causes and conditions. In the desire realm there are two types of craving mind — craving for desire and craving for form. Having understood these two cravings, the mind condemns them with full concentration, and having condemned them thus, one passes fully into nirvāṇa. The way in which the gross afflictions of the desire realm are condemned is as follows: attachment, aversion, shamelessness, and lack of conscientiousness — through those causes and those conditions, one attains the passing into nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, the nature of the path of the desire realm is courageous. Why is that?"

It is for the sake of attaining the four fruits. Therefore, intermediate nirvāṇa exists in the desire realm but not in the form realm. O son of good family, concerning intermediate nirvāṇa, there are three types according to the sūtras: superior, middling, and inferior.

The superior is to pass fully into nirvāṇa while abandoning the aggregates (skandhas) and without having separated from the desire realm. The middling is to pass fully into nirvāṇa immediately upon separating from the desire realm, without having gone to the form realm. The inferior is to pass fully into nirvāṇa after separating from the desire realm and drawing close to the form realm at the very beginning — like a small fish that stays in place having obtained food; that person is similar to it. When asked how one stays in place: one stays because one has taken up the aggregates in the form realm and the formless realm. One stays because one does not take a body as a god or human of the desire realm, or as a hell-being, or in an animal birth, or as a hungry ghost. One stays because, having cut off all the immeasurable afflictions entirely, a small remainder is left behind.

Furthermore, when asked for what cause and by what condition one is said to stay in place: one stays because, though pressed, one does not perform deeds that accord with base conduct. One stays because, having no fear for oneself, one does not cause fear in others. One stays because one abandons the craving of both attachment and aversion.

O son of good family, having reached the further shore is an analogy for the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, the bodhisattva, and the buddhas — just as a turtle is able to go both in water and on dry land. When asked for what cause and by what condition the turtle is taken as an analogy: it is because the turtle is able to exercise the five limbs with great skill. Likewise, from arhats up through the buddhas, they take the turtle as an analogy because they too are able to exercise the five faculties with great skill. As for "water" and "dry land": water is an analogy for the world, and dry land is analogous to that which transcends the world. Those noble ones (āryas) likewise, having fully understood all the afflictions of sin and non-virtue and having gone to the further shore, are taken as examples from the ability to go both in water and on dry land.

O son of good family, just as in the great river Gaṅgā there are seven kinds of sentient beings — fish, turtles, and others each given their own separate names — yet none of them is other than water; likewise, within the great and sublime nirvāṇa, from those with distorted craving up through the buddhas, they are given their own separate names, yet none of them is other than the water of the buddha's intrinsic nature.

O son of good family, the virtue or non-virtue, the path of skillful means, the path of liberation, the path of gradual entry, the causes, or the fruits of those seven kinds of sentient beings — all of it is the intrinsic nature of a buddha. This is a statement that the Tathāgata spoke having applied it to his own mind.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: Blessed One, to whatever extent there is a cause, there will also be a fruit. If there is no cause, there is no fruit either. Nirvāṇa is called a fruit, yet for something permanent there is no cause. If there is no cause, how can it be called a fruit? That nirvāṇa itself is also called a śramaṇa (a contemplative), and it is also called the fruit of the śramaṇa. Then what is meant by "śramaṇa," and what is the fruit of the śramaṇa?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, throughout the entire world there are seven kinds of fruit. What are they? The fruit of skillful means, the fruit of repaying kindness, the fruit of rendering homage and service, the residual fruit, the fruit of equality,

the fruit of karmic maturation, and the fruit of abandonment. Now, as for the fruit of skillful means: just as people in the world speak of gathering many sheaves of grain together and say, "We have obtained, one from the other, the fruit of skillful means," what is called the fruit of skillful means is itself what is called the fruit produced by action. For that fruit there are two kinds of cause: the proximate cause and the distant cause. The proximate cause in this case is the seed. The distant cause is water, manure, and human labor. That is what is called the fruit of skillful means.

As for the fruit of repaying kindness: just as when worldly people make offerings to their parents, and the parents say, "We have received the repayment of the kindness of having raised this child," it is called the fruit because the child has repaid the kindness. For that fruit too there are two kinds of cause: the proximate cause and the distant cause. The proximate cause in this case is the virtuous karma previously performed by the parents. The distant cause is that a child possessed of dignity and grace is born. That is what is called the fruit of repaying kindness.

As for the fruit of rendering homage and service: for example, when someone renders homage and service to a spiritual friend, they will attain fruits ranging from the fruit of stream-entry all the way up to the fruit of the arhat. They then say, "I have obtained the fruit of having rendered homage and service." For that fruit too there are two kinds of cause: the proximate cause and the distant cause. The proximate cause in this case is a mind of faith. The distant cause is the spiritual friend. That is what is called the fruit of rendering homage and service.

As for the residual fruit: just as, through the cause of not taking life, one enjoys long life in the third rebirth — that is the residual fruit. For that fruit too there are two kinds of cause: the proximate cause and the distant cause. The proximate cause in this case is the purification of body, speech, and mind. The distant cause is the extension of the lifespan. That is what is called the residual fruit.

As for the fruit of equality: this refers to the world as a container vessel. For that fruit too there are two kinds of cause: the proximate cause and the distant cause. The proximate cause in this case is sentient beings conducting themselves in the ten virtuous actions. The distant cause is the third cosmic age. That is what is called the fruit of equality.

As for the fruit of karmic maturation: when an individual obtains a perfectly pure body, they perform perfectly pure actions of body, speech, and mind — this is comparable to one saying, "I have obtained the fruit of karmic maturation." For that fruit too there are two kinds of cause: the proximate cause and the distant cause. The proximate cause in this case is the present perfect purity of body, speech, and mind. The distant cause is the perfect purity of body, speech, and mind in the past. That is what is called the fruit of karmic maturation.

As for the fruit of abandonment: through complete nirvāṇa, the mental afflictions are abandoned. All virtuous karma is the cause of nirvāṇa. For that too there are two kinds of cause: the proximate cause and the distant cause. The proximate cause in this case is the three doors of liberation. The distant cause is the cultivation of virtuous phenomena across countless births. That is what is called the fruit of abandonment.

O son of good family, just as it is explained that for phenomena within the world there exists a cause of arising and also a cause of manifestation, so too it is explained that for phenomena which transcend the world there likewise exists a cause of arising and also a cause of manifestation.

O son of good family, the three doors of liberation and the thirty-seven factors of awakening (bodhipakṣadharma) are the cause for the non-arising of all afflictions, and they also serve as the cause of the manifestation of nirvāṇa. O son of good family, when the afflictions are abandoned, nirvāṇa is thereupon seen clearly and directly. Therefore, with regard to nirvāṇa, there exists only a cause of manifestation, and there is no cause of arising.

O son of good family, you ask: what is it that is called a śramaṇa, and what is it that is called the fruit of a śramaṇa? O son of good family, what is called a śramaṇa is the noble eightfold path. What is called the fruit of a śramaṇa is the complete cutting off of attachment, aversion, and delusion by means of the noble path. These, then, are what are called the śramaṇa and the fruit of the śramaṇa.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, for what cause and by what condition is the noble eightfold path called the path of a śramaṇa?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, worldly people call virtue something that does not satisfy, and they call the practice of refinement a path. Thus that path cuts through everything that does not satisfy and cuts through all false paths. For this reason, the eight branches of the noble path are called śramaṇa. And because the fruit is obtained from that path, it is called the fruit of the śramaṇa.

O son of good family, furthermore, just as one who in the world delights in solitude is called a śramaṇa, so too that path is similarly called śramaṇa because the yogins, having abandoned non-virtuous wrong livelihood and all such faults of body, speech, and mind, thereby attain delight in the peaceful solitude.

O son of good family, furthermore, just as in the world one who elevates the lowest among human beings to the highest among human beings is called a śramaṇa, so too that path is similarly called śramaṇa because it elevates the lowest among human beings to the highest among human beings.

O son of good family, an arhat who cultivates that path will attain the fruit of a śramaṇa, and for that reason is called one who has gone beyond, one who is perfected. What is called the fruit of an arhat is the state beyond training, which comprises five limbs of the dharmakāya: moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. By means of those five limbs one becomes fully perfected, and therefore this is called having gone beyond, having arrived at the far shore.
