Having thus gone beyond, one declares: "My births are exhausted. The holy life is fulfilled. What had to be done has been done. I will not take on another existence." O son of good family, that arhat declares "My births are exhausted" because the causes of birth in all three times have been completely severed. He declares "My births are exhausted" because the body of the five aggregates (skandhas) of the three realms has been cut off. He declares "The holy life is fulfilled" because the holy life has reached its final culmination. He also declares "The holy life is fulfilled" because he has relinquished the path of training. He declares "What had to be done has been done" because what was sought from the very beginning has now been obtained. He also declares "What had to be done has been done" because, having cultivated the path, the fruit has been obtained. He declares "I will not take on another existence" because, having obtained the wisdom of exhaustion and non-arising, he has purified without remainder all the afflictions bound up with existence. For these reasons, arhats are called those who have gone beyond, those who are perfected.

Just as an arhat is described in this way, so too is a pratyekabuddha. As for bodhisattvas and the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, they are called those who have gone beyond, those who are perfected, because they have fully completed the six perfections.

Buddhas and bodhisattvas are called those who have fully completed the six perfections because they have attained unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. Why is this? It is because they have obtained the fruit of the six perfections. Having thus obtained the fruit, they are called perfected.

O son of noble lineage, those seven types of sentient beings do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate moral discipline, do not cultivate mind, and do not cultivate wisdom. Because they are incapable of cultivating these four kinds of things, through the fault of the five acts of immediate retribution they sever the roots of virtue, they breach the four root precepts, and they denigrate the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. For these reasons they are said to be in perpetual decline.

O son of noble lineage, among those seven types of sentient beings, some possess all seven characteristics together, while others possess them one by one.

O son of noble lineage, whoever relies upon a spiritual friend, and with one-pointed mind listens to and receives the sacred Dharma of the Tathāgata, then deeply takes it to heart inwardly, abides in accordance with the Dharma, and strenuously applies himself to the cultivation of body, moral discipline, mind, and wisdom — such a one crosses the flood of saṃsāra and is said to have arrived at the farther shore.

If someone says that those with wrong craving have attained unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening, that is attachment and clinging. If someone says they cannot attain it, that is not correct either.

O son of noble lineage, among those seven types of persons, some are endowed with all seven together, and others with each one individually.

O son of noble lineage, if someone whose mind and speech are discordant says, "Those with wrong craving cannot attain unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening," know that this constitutes denigration of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. And if someone whose mind and speech are likewise discordant says, "Those with wrong craving cannot attain unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening," that too is denigration of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

O son of noble lineage, if someone says that the eight branches of the noble path can be attained by base and ignoble persons, that too is denigration of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

O son of noble lineage, if someone says definitively that all sentient beings certainly possess the buddha-nature (svabhāva), or says definitively that they certainly do not possess the buddha-nature, that too is denigration of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

O son of noble lineage, it is for this reason that it is said in the sūtras: "Two types of people commit denigration of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha." These two are: those without faith who have a mind of aversion, and those who have faith but do not understand the meaning.

O son of noble lineage, if someone has a faithful mind but lacks wisdom, they give rise to ignorance. If someone has wisdom but lacks a faithful mind, they give rise to wrong views.

O son of noble lineage, the faithless, whose mind is full of aversion, say "There is no Buddha, no Dharma, no Saṅgha — no Three Jewels." Those who have faith but lack wisdom misunderstand the meaning, and so they denigrate the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha when they hear the Dharma taught.

O son of noble lineage, it is for this reason that I have declared: those who are faithless and full of aversion, and those who have faith but lack wisdom, commit denigration of the Three Jewels — the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

O son of noble lineage, if someone says "Those with wrong craving have attained unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening without the arising of virtuous phenomena," that too is denigration of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. And if someone says "A person with wrong craving, having abandoned wrong craving, attains unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening with a different set of aggregates," that too is denigration of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

Yet there are those who say: "One with wrong craving is capable of generating wholesome roots; having generated those wholesome roots, and accumulating them one upon another in an unbroken stream, one with wrong craving thereby attains unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening." Know that such a statement does not constitute denigration of the Three Jewels.

O son of noble lineage, if someone says "All sentient beings certainly possess the buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha), and that nature is permanent, blissful, a self, and perfectly pure — it is simply that, without having engaged in practice, it does not arise; it is not seen because of the condition of afflictions" — that too is denigration of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

And if someone says "Sentient beings have no buddha-nature whatsoever — it is like a rabbit's horn. It has existed beginninglessly, arising through conditions, and having existed it will later cease to exist" — that too is denigration of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

And if someone says "The buddha-nature of sentient beings neither exists — being like space — nor does it not exist — being like a rabbit's horn. Why so? Because space is permanent, and a rabbit's horn is nonexistent. Therefore one may speak of it as existing, and one may also speak of it as not existing: as existing, it is not like a rabbit's horn; as not existing, it is not like space." A statement made in that way does not constitute denigration of the Three Jewels.

O son of noble lineage, what is called "buddha-nature" is not one phenomenon, not two phenomena, not ten phenomena, not a hundred phenomena, not a thousand phenomena, not ten thousand phenomena. When unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening has not yet been attained, everything without exception — the virtuous, the non-virtuous, and the ethically neutral — is called "buddha-nature." At certain times the Tathāgata taught cause from the perspective of result, and result from the perspective of cause. This is a statement the Tathāgata made in accordance with his own intention. Because he spoke a statement in accordance with his own intention, he is called Tathāgata. Because the Tathāgata spoke a statement in accordance with his own intention, he is called arhat. Because he spoke a statement in accordance with his own intention, he is called perfectly complete buddha.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: "Blessed One, just as you have declared that the buddha-nature of sentient beings is comparable to space — how exactly is it comparable to space?"

The Blessed One declared: O son of noble lineage, the intrinsic nature of space is not past, not future, and not present. The buddha-nature is exactly like that.

O son of noble lineage, space is not past. Why? Because it does not exist in the present. For if phenomena existed in the present, then one could also meaningfully speak of the past. Since it does not so exist, the past does not exist either.

Nor does it exist in the present. Why? Because the future does not exist. For if phenomena had a future, one could also meaningfully speak of the present. Since the future does not exist, the present does not exist either.

Nor does the future exist. Why? Because neither the present nor the past exists. For if the present and the past existed, the future too would exist. Since the past and the present do not exist, the future does not exist.

Therefore the intrinsic nature of space does not belong to any of the three times.

O son of noble lineage, space is without the three times because it is nonexistent — yet this is not to say that the three times are absent because it exists. It is comparable, for example, to a flower in the sky:

Just as a flower in the sky lacks the three times because it is nonexistent, so too space is without the three times because it is nonexistent. O son of noble lineage, "space" is the name given to that which is nothing whatsoever. The intrinsic nature of a buddha is exactly like that.

O son of noble lineage, space does not belong to any of the three times because it is nonexistent. Likewise, the intrinsic nature of a buddha does not belong to any of the three times because it is permanent. O son of noble lineage, since the Tathāgata has attained unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, the intrinsic nature of a buddha and all the qualities of a buddha are permanent — unchanging and unalterable. Therefore, like space, they are without the three times.

O son of noble lineage, space is neither inner nor outer because it is nonexistent. Likewise, the intrinsic nature of a buddha is neither inner nor outer because it is permanent. Therefore the intrinsic nature of a buddha is comparable to space — so it has been declared.

O son of noble lineage, just as what is designated in the world as "space" is the place that is unobstructed and unimpeded, so too the Tathāgata, having attained unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, is without obstruction with respect to all the qualities of all buddhas — and for that reason the intrinsic nature of a buddha is said to be comparable to space. It is on account of that cause and that condition that I have declared the intrinsic nature of a buddha to be like space.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Blessed One, saying: Blessed One, although the intrinsic nature of a buddha and nirvāṇa do not belong to the three times, they may still be said to exist. But if space likewise does not belong to the three times, why should it not also be said to exist?

The Blessed One declared: O son of noble lineage, what is not nirvāṇa is what is called "nirvāṇa." What is not a Tathāgata is what is called "Tathāgata." What is not the intrinsic nature of a buddha is what is called "the intrinsic nature of a buddha."

How then is something not nirvāṇa? It is this: all mental afflictions and all conditioned phenomena — because those conditioned afflictions have been destroyed, it is called "nirvāṇa."

And how is something not a Tathāgata? It is this: from one who has distorted craving all the way up to a pratyekabuddha — because all of those, from one who has distorted craving to a pratyekabuddha, have been destroyed, it is called "Tathāgata."

And what is not the intrinsic nature of a buddha? It is this: walls, enclosures, pillars, gravel, and all matter that lacks consciousness. The relinquishing of that matter which lacks consciousness — that is what is called "the intrinsic nature of a buddha."

O son of noble lineage, throughout the entire world there is nothing that is not space and yet becomes a synonym for space.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa said: Blessed One, in the world the four great elements do not exist as anything other than themselves, and yet there is nothing that becomes a synonym for the four great elements — yet the four great elements may still be said to exist. Since space has no synonym either, why should it not equally be said to exist?

The Blessed One declared: O son of noble lineage, to say that nirvāṇa does not belong to the three times and that space is therefore like nirvāṇa — that is not correct. Why? Because nirvāṇa does exist. It can be seen; it can be realized; it is a trace left by form; it is something expressible in words; it bears the defining marks of existence; it is an object of meditation; it is a place of refuge; it is the fruit of peaceful radiance and bliss. Therefore it does not belong to the three times.

The intrinsic nature of space has none of these qualities — and therefore it is said to be nonexistent.

If there were some other phenomenon beyond these that did not belong to them, then that phenomenon would belong to the three times. If space were indeed like that — a phenomenon possessing existence — then it would be wrong to say it does not belong to the three times.

O son of noble lineage, as worldly people speak of it, space is said to be formless, without a counteragent, and imperceptible. If it is without form, without a counteragent, and imperceptible, then it would become a phenomenon arisen from mind. If space accords with phenomena arisen from mind, then it would be wrong to say it does not belong to the three times. And if it does belong to the three times, it would be one of the four aggregates — and therefore, beyond the four aggregates, there is no such thing as "space."

Furthermore, O son of noble lineage, the non-Buddhist adherents (tīrthikas) say this: "Space is luminosity." If it is luminosity, it becomes a phenomenon of form, and if space is a phenomenon of form in that way, it would be impermanent. Being impermanent, it would belong to the three times — so why do the non-Buddhists say it does not belong to the three times? And if it did belong to the three times, it would not be space, and it would be wrong to call space permanent.

O son of noble lineage, some say this: "Space is a place for dwelling." To whatever extent a place for dwelling exists, to that extent it becomes a phenomenon of form. Every place where any phenomenon dwells is impermanent and belongs to the three times. Space is permanent and does not belong to the three times. If one asserts that a place of dwelling exists, then space must be understood to be nonexistent.

Others say: "Space is a series or sequence." If it were a series, it would become a countable phenomenon, and whatever is countable belongs to the three times. If it belongs to the three times, why call it permanent?

O son of noble lineage, if some say: "Space is the empty, the non-empty, and the empty-and-non-empty — it is inseparable from these three" — if one says it is empty, then space must be understood to be an impermanent phenomenon, because it is absent when things are non-empty. If one says it is non-empty, then space must likewise be understood to be impermanent, because it is absent when things are empty. If one says it is both empty and non-empty, then space must be understood not to be impermanent either, because it is absent in both states. Therefore space is to be called nonexistent.

O son of noble lineage, some also say: "Space is something that can be acted upon — just as when trees and buildings are removed, space has been made; or when something is leveled, it becomes space; or one covers space, or ascends into space, or draws the color of space as resembling the water of the ocean." If one says that space is therefore a phenomenon that can be acted upon, then every conditioned phenomenon is impermanent, like pottery. If space is like that, it would be impermanent.

O son of noble lineage, when worldly people say "whatever phenomenon is unobstructed with respect to everything is space" — does that unobstructedness exist completely within a single phenomenon, or only in part? If it exists completely, then space must be understood to be absent in other locations. If it exists only in part, it becomes a countable phenomenon — this one and that one — and whatever is countable must be understood to be impermanent.

O son of noble lineage, some say: "Space is unobstructed —

it will come to be connected with what exists." Others say: "Space exists within material substance, just as fruit placed inside a vessel." Both of these are false.

Why so? If something is said to be "connected," that connection takes three forms. First, connection through distinct functions — like birds gathering on a tree. Second, connection through shared experience of a common function — like two hands touching each other. Third, connection through a shared bond of relatedness — like two fingers clasped together. If it is claimed that things are connected through a shared common bond while being functionally distinct, then there are two aspects to that distinctness: the function of material substance, and the function of space. If the function of space were connected with material substance, space would not become impermanent. But if the function of material substance were connected with space, material substance would not become all-pervasive. And if it is not all-pervasive, then that too is impermanent.

If someone says: "Space is permanent, immovable by its own intrinsic nature, yet it comes to be connected with things that move" — that too is not the case. Why? If space is permanent, then material substance must be of the same category and also permanent. If material substance is impermanent, then space too is impermanent. And if someone says "space is both permanent and impermanent," that position has no ground to stand on.

If someone says space is connected through a shared common function — that too is not the case. Why? Because space is all-pervasive; if it were connected with function, then function too would have to be of the all-pervasive category. If it were all-pervasive, it would pervade everything everywhere. If it pervades everything everywhere, it would be wrong to say that among things of the kind that are connected with everything, there is some connection and some non-connection.

The claim that space is connected through a shared bond of relatedness — like two fingers clasped together — is also not the case. Why? Because what was not connected from the beginning would come to be connected later. And if something that did not exist at first comes to exist afterward, that too becomes a phenomenon possessing impermanence. Thus, just as in the case of worldly phenomena that are not present at first and then exist later, it is wrong to say that space is connected through a shared bond of relatedness.

If space were similar to impermanent material substance and like it in that way, then space too would become impermanent. Moreover, as for the claim that space exists within material substance just as fruit placed inside a vessel — that too is not so. Why? Before a vessel exists, where does space reside? If there is a place where it resides, then space would become multiple. If it is multiple, why is it called permanent, singular, and pervasive? If there were a place where that space resides beyond what is empty, then the substance of existence would likewise have to reside beyond space — and therefore it should be understood that space does not exist.

O son of noble lineage, as for the claim that the location in which one points a finger upward is space — that would make space a phenomenon that is impermanent. Why? Because a finger has four sides. If a finger has four sides, space too must be of the category of having four sides. All phenomena that are permanent have no sides. Therefore, because space has sides and spatial directions, space is impermanent.

If it is impermanent in this way, it is not connected with the five aggregates; and what lies beyond the five aggregates — beyond their absence — there is nothing to be called "existence." O son of noble lineage, if any phenomenon of existence abides in dependence upon dependent origination, it should be understood that that phenomenon is impermanent. O son of noble lineage, consider this example: all sentient beings, all trees, and all forests depend upon and abide on the earth. Because the earth itself is impermanent, the material substance that depends on the earth is also gradually impermanent.

O son of noble lineage, the earth depends upon water, and because water is impermanent, the earth too is impermanent. Water depends upon wind, and because wind is impermanent, water too is impermanent. Wind depends upon space, and because space is impermanent, wind too is impermanent. If things are impermanent in this way, why do some say that space is permanent and all-pervading? Because space does not exist, it is neither past, nor future, nor present. It is a substance that is non-existent, like a rabbit's horn, and therefore it is neither past, nor future, nor present. Hence, because the intrinsic nature of a buddha is permanent, it does not belong to the three times; and because space is non-existent, it likewise does not belong to the three times.

O son of noble lineage, I do not dispute with the world. Why is that? When the wise and discerning of the world say something exists, I too declare it exists. When the wise and discerning of the world say something does not exist, I too declare it does not exist.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: Blessed One, if a bodhisattva, a great being, possesses certain qualities of the Dharma, will that bodhisattva not dispute with the world and will not be tainted by the world's concerns?

The Blessed One declared: O son of noble lineage, if a bodhisattva, a great being, possesses ten qualities of the Dharma, that bodhisattva will not dispute with the world and will not be tainted by the world's concerns. What are the ten? They are as follows: faith; moral discipline; reliance upon a virtuous spiritual friend; inner mental engagement; being endowed with diligence; being endowed with correct mindfulness; being endowed with wisdom; being endowed with right speech; devotion to the holy Dharma; and loving affection toward sentient beings. O son of noble lineage, if a bodhisattva is endowed with these ten qualities of the Dharma, that bodhisattva will not dispute with worldly people, and, like the udumbara flower, will not be tainted by the world's concerns.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: Blessed One, just as the Blessed One has said — when the wise and discerning of the world say something exists, you too declare it exists; when the wise and discerning of the world say something does not exist, you too declare it does not exist — how, then, do the wise and discerning of the world speak of existence and non-existence?

The Blessed One declared: O son of noble lineage, when the wise and discerning of the world say of form that it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self — and say likewise of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness — O son of noble lineage, that is what the wise and discerning of the world call existence, and I too declare it exists. O son of noble lineage, when the wise and discerning of the world say of form that there is no permanence, no happiness, no self, and no purity — and say likewise of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness — O son of noble lineage, that is what the wise and discerning of the world call non-existence, and I too declare it does not exist.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then said: Blessed One, the wise and discerning of the world are buddhas, bodhisattvas, and all noble ones. If the noble ones declare that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, then why has the Blessed One declared that the form body of a buddha is permanent, stable, and unchanging? If the wise and discerning of the world declare that all phenomena are non-existent —

why did the Blessed One declare that it exists? And if the Buddha, the Blessed One, has spoken thus, how can it be said that he does not quarrel with the world and is not stained by worldly phenomena? For the Blessed One has taught that, through having thoroughly abandoned wrong perception, wrong mind, and wrong view — these three — the form body of a buddha is truly and properly impermanent; and he also declared, "I teach that it is permanent." How then can it be said that he has abandoned what is inverted and does not quarrel with the world?

The Blessed One declared: O son of noble lineage, the form of inferior worldly beings arises from affliction, and it is for this reason that the wise and discerning declare that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self. The form body of a Tathāgata, however, is utterly free from affliction, and it is for this reason that it has been taught to be permanent, stable, unchanging, and without alteration.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: Blessed One, in what way does form arise from affliction?

The Blessed One declared: O son of noble lineage, affliction has three aspects: the defilement of desire, the defilement of existence, and the defilement of ignorance. The wise and discerning must thoroughly understand the faults and flaws of these three defilements. Why so? Because it is only by knowing their faults and flaws that one will abandon them. It is like a physician who first examines the pulse of a sick person, comes to know the cause of the illness, and only then administers medicine.

O son of noble lineage, consider the example of a blind man who is led into a thorny thicket and then abandoned there. It would be extremely difficult for that blind man to find his way out, and even if he did manage to emerge, his entire body would be lacerated. In the same way, worldly beings of inferior stock are comparable to such a person: because they neither see nor understand the faults and flaws of the three defilements, they follow them wherever they lead. One who does see them will abandon them, and knowing their faults and flaws, both the actions performed and their karmic maturation will become progressively lighter and fewer.

O son of noble lineage, there are four types of persons. The first performs an action heavily but experiences its maturation lightly. The second performs an action lightly but experiences its maturation heavily. The third performs an action heavily and experiences its maturation heavily as well. The fourth performs an action lightly and experiences its maturation lightly as well. O son of noble lineage, the one who understands the faults of affliction finds that both the actions performed and the ripening of their fruits are light. O son of noble lineage, the wise and discerning person thinks: "I will abandon such defilements as these, and I will not commit sinful and non-virtuous deeds." Why so? Because he reflects: "I am not yet liberated from the karmic maturation of the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the destinies of gods and humans. If I apply myself diligently to practice, through its power all suffering will be thoroughly overcome." Having thus reflected, his attachment, aversion, and delusion will diminish. Seeing that his attachment, aversion, and delusion are diminishing, his mind will be filled with great joy, and he will think: "Even now, having come to be as I am through the power of diligent practice, I am separated from non-virtuous phenomena and have drawn near to virtuous phenomena. Therefore, I will rouse diligence and cultivate the authentic path so as to see it directly." And through the power of strenuously cultivating it in that way, immeasurable numbers of non-virtuous afflictions, along with the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and

the karmic maturation of human and divine results will be abandoned. For this reason, I have declared in the sūtras that one should examine the afflictions that are defilements of existence and the causes of those defilements of existence.

This is the forty-ninth fascicle of the Noble Great Sūtra of the Transcendence into Nirvāṇa.

And why is that? If the wise and discerning do not examine the defilements and do not investigate the causes of the defilements, all their afflictions will not be severed. Why is that? The wise and discerning, upon recognizing that defilements arise from their causes, reflect: "If I thoroughly cut off those causes, the defilements will not arise." So they reason.

O son of good family, just as a physician, when he has thoroughly eliminated the cause of an illness, ensures that the illness will not arise again, so too do the wise and discerning act in precisely the same way when they cut off the cause of afflictions. The wise and discerning first examine the cause, and thereafter examine the result. They come to understand deeply that from a virtuous cause a virtuous result arises, and from a non-virtuous cause a non-virtuous result arises. Having understood the result, they abandon the non-virtuous cause. Having examined the result in this way, they gradually discern which afflictions are subtle and which are gross. Having discerned the subtle and the gross, they first abandon the gross. And having abandoned the gross, the subtle too will naturally cease to exist.

O son of good family, when the wise and discerning have thus come to know the afflictions, the causes of the afflictions, the results of the afflictions, and the afflictions that are subtle and those that are gross, then, in order to suppress those very afflictions at that very time, they do not lag on the path of awakening. Without regret they strive strenuously, rely upon a spiritual friend, and with one-pointed mind listen to the Dharma.

O son of good family, consider, for instance, a sick person who, knowing that his illness is slight and that he will certainly recover, drinks a bitter medicine without regret. The wise and discerning are just like that: they are devoted to striving earnestly on the noble path, they do not grieve, they do not break off, and they do not regret.

O son of good family, whoever knows the afflictions, the causes of the afflictions, the karmic maturation of the results of the afflictions, and the afflictions that are subtle and gross, and strives earnestly in cultivating the noble path in order to remove those afflictions — for such a one, form does not arise from afflictions; and equally so up through feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

But if one does not know the afflictions, the causes of the afflictions, the karmic maturation of the results of the afflictions, and the afflictions that are subtle and gross, and does not strive on the noble path, then form does arise from afflictions; and equally so up through feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

O son of good family, whoever knows the afflictions, the causes of the afflictions, the karmic maturation of the results of the afflictions, and the afflictions that are subtle and gross, and strives earnestly toward awakening in order to sever those afflictions — such a one is a Tathāgata. Therefore the form of a Tathāgata is permanent, and so it is, permanent, all the way through consciousness.

O son of good family, whoever does not know the afflictions, the causes of the afflictions, the karmic maturation of the results of the afflictions, and the afflictions that are subtle and gross, and does not strive earnestly toward awakening — such a one is a foolish, ignoble, ordinary being. Therefore the form of a foolish, ignoble, ordinary being is impermanent, and equally so, impermanent, all the way through feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

O son of good family, worldly wise and discerning ones, and noble ones, and

bodhisattvas, and all the buddhas as well, have spoken of that matter in those two ways, and I too speak of it in those two ways. Therefore what I teach does not quarrel with the worldly wise, and is not tainted by the ways of the world.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, when the Blessed One teaches that the defilements of existence are of three kinds, how are we to understand the defilement of desire, the defilement of craving, and the defilement of ignorance?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, what is called the defilement of desire arises through conceptual thought directed inwardly toward the unwholesome, and through being stirred by external conditions. Therefore I previously, in the city of Rājagṛha, spoke to Ānanda in this manner: Ānanda, take up these verses spoken by this woman. These verses were spoken by the Tathāgatas of the past. Thus, internal conceptual thought directed toward the unwholesome, together with external conditions, is called desire, and that is the defilement of desire.

The defilement of craving consists of the unwholesome inner phenomena of the form realm and the formless realm, together with their external causes and conditions — that is, the external conditions of the desire realm, apart from the internal conceptual thought directed toward the unwholesome. These constitute the defilement of existence.

The defilement of ignorance is not knowing the self and what belongs to the self, and failing to distinguish between the inner and the outer. That is the defilement of ignorance.

O son of good family, ignorance is the root of all defilements. Why? Because all sentient beings, through the cause and condition of ignorance, perceive and conceptually fix upon the aggregates, the sense sources, and the elements, and because of that conceptual fixing they are called sentient beings. This consists of wrong perception, wrong thought, and wrong view, and through these as cause and condition all defilements are produced. Therefore I have taught in the twelve branches of scripture that ignorance is the cause of attachment, aversion, and delusion.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: Blessed One, if the Tathāgata previously taught in the twelve branches of scripture that through the cause and condition of conceptual thought directed toward the unwholesome, attachment, aversion, and delusion arise, why then did you also teach that they arise from ignorance?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, these two phenomena are each the cause of the other and each the result of the other; each one gives rise to the other. Conceptual thought directed toward the unwholesome produces ignorance, and through the condition of ignorance, unwholesome conceptual thought arises. O son of good family, whatever produces the afflictions itself becomes in turn a cause of the afflictions. Thus, the cause and the proximate cause of the afflictions are ignorance and unwholesome conceptual thought. Just as a sprout arises from a fruit — and the fruit is thereby a proximate cause — and just as the four great elements serve as a distant cause, the afflictions are similar in this regard.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, you have said that ignorance itself is a defilement, and yet you have also said that defilements arise through the condition of ignorance. Why do you say both?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, when I say that ignorance itself is a defilement, I am referring to inner ignorance. When I say that defilements arise from the cause of ignorance, I am referring to both inner and outer causes. That which is explained as ignorance itself being a defilement is what is called inner perversion — namely, not knowing impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness.

That which is explained as the cause of all afflictions is not knowing the outer self and what belongs to the self. That which is explained as ignorance itself being a defilement has neither beginning nor end. How so? Because from ignorance arise the aggregates, the sense bases, the elements, and so forth.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa (Ödsung) again addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, just as the Blessed One has said, the wise person endowed with discernment knows the causes of defilements. How then does one know the causes of defilements?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, the wise person endowed with discernment reflects in this way: From what cause and from what condition does this affliction arise? From what action performed does this affliction arise? At what time does this affliction arise? When dwelling together with whom does this affliction arise? Dwelling in what place does this affliction arise? By attending to what thing does this affliction arise? By accepting whose lodging, bedding, alms, robes, and medicines for illness and so forth does this affliction arise? From what cause and condition does what is minor become middling, and what is middling become great? And does what is great become middling, and what is middling become minor? Thus one thoroughly reflects.

When the bodhisattva, the great being, reflects in this way, he will thoroughly abandon the causes and conditions that give rise to defilements. Having understood in this way, those afflictions not yet arisen he blocks and does not allow to arise, and those afflictions already arisen he checks by means of skillful means. Therefore I have said in the sūtras that the wise person endowed with discernment should examine the causes of the arising of afflictions.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, how is it that many different kinds of affliction arise from a single body of a sentient being?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, take this example: just as when many different seeds are contained within a single vessel, and upon meeting water or rain they each grow separately, so too it is with sentient beings. Although there is but one vessel, through the causes and conditions of craving, many different kinds of affliction arise.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, how does the wise person endowed with discernment reflect on the ripening of results?

The Blessed One declared: O son of good family, the wise person endowed with discernment reflects thus: Through the causes and conditions of defilements, sentient beings will be reborn in the hells, in the realm of animals, and among the hungry ghosts. Through the causes and conditions free from defilements, one obtains a divine or human body — and yet even those are impermanent, marked by suffering, empty, and selfless. From this vessel of the body one obtains the three kinds of suffering and the three kinds of impermanence. Through the causes and conditions of these defilements, sentient beings commit the five acts of immediate retribution, experience the ripening of results in the lower realms, sever the roots of virtue, destroy the four foundations, and come to disparage the Three Jewels. Thus one thoroughly reflects. The wise person endowed with discernment thoroughly reflects: it is unworthy of me, having obtained this body, to generate afflictions and thereby reap the fruits of the lower realms.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again asked: Blessed One, you have also said that there are results that are free from defilements, and yet you have also said that the wise person endowed with discernment thoroughly severs the ripening of results. Does that which is free from defilements fall within what is thoroughly severed?

Since those who have attained awakening possess results that are free from defilements, and since the wise person endowed with discernment seeks results that are free from defilements, why did the Blessed One say that the wise person endowed with discernment should sever the ripening of karmic results? If such severing takes place, is it still fitting to say that noble ones exist at the present time?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the Tathāgata has spoken of certain things as results in relation to a cause, and certain things as causes in relation to a result. Just as worldly people say, "Clay itself is the pot," and "Thread itself is cloth" — these are cases where a result is described in terms of its cause. And as one says, "The cow itself is water and grass, and is also food for human beings" — this is a case where a cause is described in terms of its result. I too have spoken in this way, describing a result in terms of a cause. For example, in a sūtra spoken earlier, when I said, "I shall go in body and mind to the brahma-realm (brahmaloka)," that is describing a result in terms of its cause. And when I said, "These very six sense sources are the karma of previous lives," that is describing a cause in terms of its result.

Son of good family, in the ultimate sense there is no result that is free from defilements for any noble one. The result of what all noble ones have thoroughly cultivated is that no defilements arise — and for that very reason it is called a result free from defilements.

Son of good family, when the wise person endowed with discernment reflects in this way, the ripening of the results of afflictions will be completely exhausted. Son of good family, because the wise person endowed with discernment has thus completely severed the results of afflictions, he cultivates the noble path. The noble path consists of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. When those noble paths are cultivated, all results of afflictions will be completely exhausted.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, all sentient beings undergo the ripening of results through their afflictions, and afflictions are non-virtuous. The affliction that arises from non-virtuous afflictions is itself also called non-virtuous. Thus with regard to these afflictions there are two aspects: cause and result. Because the cause is non-virtuous, the result is non-virtuous; and because the result is non-virtuous, the seed is non-virtuous — just as the tree called the nimba, because its fruit is bitter, has a seed, flowers, trunk, and leaves that are all bitter. Just as the poisonous tree, owing to a poisonous seed, produces poisonous fruit, so too the cause is sentient beings and the result is sentient beings; the cause is afflictions and the result is afflictions. The very cause and result of afflictions are sentient beings, and sentient beings themselves are the cause and result of afflictions. If this is so, why did the Tathāgata say that on the snowy mountain there are both poisonous grasses and a sublime king of medicines? If afflictions are themselves sentient beings, and sentient beings are themselves afflictions, why did the Blessed One say that within the body of sentient beings there exists a sublime king of medicines?

The Blessed One declared: Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, countless sentient beings — as many as there are — harbor just such a doubt. Since you have asked in order to dispel this doubt, and since I am able to resolve it, listen attentively and reflect upon it carefully, and I shall explain and set it free.

Son of good family, "the snowy mountain" stands for sentient beings. "Poisonous grasses" stand for afflictions. "The sublime king of medicines" stands for the holy life (brahmacarya). Son of good family, whatever sentient being thus practices the holy life — within that being's body there exists a sublime king of medicines.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa again asked:

The Blessed One declared:

Son of good family, just as in the world a fruit is born from a seed, and some fruits in turn become seeds again while others do not — those that do become seeds again are called both fruit and seed, while those that do not are called simply fruit, not seed — in the same way, all sentient beings likewise have two kinds of causes. What are they? Some fruits of affliction become causes of affliction again, while some fruits of affliction do not become causes of affliction again. That which is the fruit of affliction yet does not become a cause of affliction — this is called the holy life (brahmacarya).

Son of good family, all sentient beings understand and know that feeling (vedanā) is the proximate cause of every defilement — namely, inner and outer defilements. Through the condition of feeling, one is unable to sever all defilements and thus unable to win freedom from the prison of the three realms. It is through the condition of feeling that sentient beings, clinging to self and what belongs to self, come to give rise to inverted mind, inverted perception, and inverted views. Therefore, sentient beings should first examine feeling.

Now, feeling is the proximate cause of all craving. Therefore, if a wise and discerning person wishes to sever craving, let that person first examine feeling.

Son of good family, all the virtuous and non-virtuous deeds that all sentient beings perform through the twelve links of dependent origination are done at the occasion of feeling. This is why I declared to Ānanda: "Ānanda, all the virtuous and non-virtuous deeds done by all sentient beings are done entirely at the occasion of feeling. Therefore a wise and discerning person should first examine feeling."

Having understood feeling, one should further examine: from what cause and from what condition does this feeling arise? If it arises from cause and condition, then what itself gave rise to that cause and condition? If there is no cause for arising, then why does the absence of a cause not itself produce an absence of feeling?

Moreover, this feeling does not arise from the cause of Īśvara, nor does it arise from a primordial person, nor from subtle particles, nor is it produced by time, nor does it arise from perception, nor from intrinsic nature, nor from self, nor from other, nor from both self and other, nor from no cause at all. Rather, feeling arises from the convergence of conditions, and that cause and condition is craving. Understanding that feeling is neither present in nor absent from that convergence of conditions, one therefore severs the convergence of conditions, thinking: because the convergence of conditions is severed, feeling will not arise.

Son of good family, when a wise and discerning person has understood causes, that person contemplates the karmic maturation of results: it is through the condition of feeling that sentient beings experience birth in the hells, in the animal realm, and in the bodies of hungry ghosts, thereby taking on immeasurable suffering throughout the three realms. Through the condition of feeling one takes hold of impermanent happiness. Through the condition of feeling one severs the root of happiness. And yet through the condition of feeling one may attain perfect liberation. Reflecting in this way, one no longer acts under the condition of feeling. How does one no longer act under the condition of feeling? One distinguishes which feelings lead to craving and which aspects of craving lead back to feeling.

Son of good family, when a sentient being has fully understood in this way the cause of existence and the cause of feeling, that being will completely sever the notions of self and what belongs to self.

Son of good family, one who has thus fully understood this knows from where feeling and craving, these two, are to be ceased. Seeing that there is a place where feeling and craving are partially ceased, and thereby knowing that their complete cessation also exists, at that moment faith in liberation arises. Having aroused a mind of faith, one reflects: through what cause shall the state of liberation be attained? Knowing that it is attained through the noble eightfold path, one then cultivates it thoroughly.

What is the noble eightfold path? When this path examines feeling, there are three characteristics: suffering, pleasure, and that which is neither suffering nor pleasure. All three are capable of producing body and mind. Through what cause and condition are they produced? Through the condition of contact. And from that contact there are also three kinds: the contact of ignorance, the contact of knowledge, and the contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance. Of these, what is called the contact of knowledge is the noble eightfold path. The remaining two kinds of contact produce body, mind, and the three kinds of feeling. Therefore I should sever the two kinds of cause of contact. When contact is severed, the three kinds of feeling will not arise.

Son of good family, feeling in this way is called both a cause and a result. One who is wise and possessed of wisdom examines it as both cause and result. How is it a cause? Because craving arises from the cause of feeling, it is called a cause. How is it a result? Because it arises from contact, it is called a result. Therefore feeling is both a cause and a result.

The wise one possessed of wisdom, having examined feeling in this way, gradually examines craving. The karmic maturation of feeling as result is called craving. The wise one possessed of wisdom, in examining craving, recognizes two kinds: that with various kinds of food, and that without food. Craving with various kinds of food becomes the cause of birth, old age, sickness, death, and all craving. Craving without food severs birth, old age, sickness, death, and all craving, for one longs for and is attached to action that is undefiled.

The wise one possessed of wisdom also reflects thus: if I generate craving with various kinds of food, I will be unable to sever birth, old age, sickness, and death. And though I may be attached to an undefiled path, if I do not sever the cause of feeling, I will not attain the fruit of the undefiled path. Therefore I should sever contact. Having severed contact, feeling too ceases of itself. When feeling has ceased, craving is completely extinguished. This is called the noble eightfold path.

Son of good family, if a sentient being understands it thus, although the body may be accompanied by affliction, there is nonetheless a supreme king of medicine. This is like a snow mountain having poisonous herbs yet also possessing excellent medicine.

Son of good family, in the same way sentient beings may have obtained a karmic maturation that arises from afflictions, yet they can prevent that maturation from becoming the cause of further afflictions. This is called pure conduct (brahmacarya).

Furthermore, son of good family, when the wise one possessed of wisdom examines from what cause feeling and craving, these two, arise, one comes to know that they arise from the cause of perception. Why is this? Even when a sentient being sees a visible form, desire does not arise. Nor does desire arise at the mere time of apprehending a feeling. But if one generates an inverted perception with regard to visible form, seeing form as permanent, pleasurable, self, and utterly pure, and seeing feeling as permanent, unchanging, and unshifting —

It is in this way that, on account of inverted perception, attachment, aversion, and delusion arise. Therefore, the wise one possessed of wisdom should examine perception.

Now, how is perception to be examined? One should think to oneself: all sentient beings, not having attained the noble path, have inverted perception. What is inverted perception? It is generating the perception of permanence regarding what is impermanent; generating the perception of pleasure regarding what is without pleasure; generating the perception of purity regarding what is impure; generating the perception of self regarding phenomena that are empty; and generating the perception of man, woman, great, small, day, night, year, month, clothing, dwelling, and bed-partner regarding what is not truly man, woman, or bed-partner. This perception is of three kinds: small, great, and boundless. By reason of smallness, a small perception arises; by reason of greatness, a great perception arises; by reason of boundlessness, a boundless perception arises.

Further, small perception is perception that has not entered meditative absorption. Great perception is perception that has entered meditative absorption. And boundless perception comprises the ten all-pervasive spheres. Again, small perception is the perception of the desire realm and so forth. Great perception is the perception of the form realm and so forth. Boundless perception is the perception of the formless realm and so forth.

When these three kinds of perception cease, feeling too ceases of itself. When perception and feeling have ceased, that is called liberation.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, if liberation is called the cessation of all phenomena, why then does the Tathāgata declare that when perception and feeling cease, that is liberation?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, the Tathāgata, at times, has taught the Dharma by way of the condition of sentient beings, so that whoever hears it comes to know the Dharma. At other times, by way of the condition of the Dharma, he has taught sentient beings, so that whoever hears it comes to know that sentient beings have been described. What does it mean to teach by way of the condition of sentient beings such that the hearer comes to know the Dharma? It is just as I formerly said to the great Kāśyapa: 'Kāśyapa, when sentient beings cease, wholesome phenomena too cease.' That is a teaching through the condition of sentient beings, whereby the hearer comes to know the Dharma. And what does it mean to teach by way of the condition of the Dharma such that the hearer comes to know that sentient beings have been described? It is just as I formerly said to Ānanda: 'I have not said to associate with all phenomena, nor have I said to dissociate from all phenomena. Whatever phenomenon is such that, through associating with it, wholesome phenomena decline and unwholesome phenomena flourish — with such a phenomenon one should not associate. Whatever phenomenon is such that, through associating with it, unwholesome phenomena decline and disappear while wholesome phenomena grow and increase — with such a phenomenon one should associate.' That is a teaching through the condition of the Dharma, whereby the hearer comes to know that sentient beings have been described.

Son of good family, although the Tathāgata has declared that perception and feeling, these two, are to be stopped, he has nonetheless declared that everything within them is to be stopped. The wise one possessed of wisdom, having examined perception in this way, gradually comes to understand that the cause of perception is not boundless perception. When one examines from what it arises, one comes to know that it arises from the cause of contact. Contact itself is of two kinds: contact arising from the cause of affliction, and contact arising from the cause of liberation.

That which arises from the cause of ignorance is called contact arising from affliction. That which arises from the cause of knowledge is called contact arising from liberation. From contact that arises from the cause of affliction, erroneous perception is born. From contact that arises from the cause of liberation, non-erroneous perception is born. Having thus understood the cause of perception in this way, one gradually comes to understand the karmic maturation of its fruit.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, if erroneous perception arises through the condition of afflicted perception, then all noble ones possess erroneous perception, yet they have no afflictions. What is the meaning of this?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, in what sense is it said that noble ones have erroneous perception?" The bodhisattva Kāśyapa replied: "Blessed One, all noble ones form the perception of a cow with respect to a cow and say 'This is a cow.' They form the perception of a horse with respect to a horse and say 'This is a horse.' And so on, likewise, with respect to men, women, the great, the small, houses, chariots, vehicles, those who have gone away, and those who have come — and this, I would call erroneous perception."

"Son of good family, all ordinary foolish beings possess two kinds of perception: worldly conventional perception and attachment perception. All noble ones possess only worldly conventional perception; they do not possess attachment perception. Because all ordinary foolish beings have non-virtuous conceptuality, they generate attachment perception with respect to worldly convention. Because noble ones have virtuous conceptuality, they do not generate attachment perception with respect to worldly convention. Therefore ordinary foolish beings are said to possess erroneous perception, whereas although noble ones perceive things, they are not said to have erroneous perception.

The wise one possessed of wisdom, having thus understood the causes of perception, gradually comes to understand the karmic maturation of its fruit. The fruit of non-virtuous perception is to experience rebirth in the hells, among hungry ghosts, in the animal realm, and among humans and gods. Since I have cut the cause of non-virtuous conceptuality, contact arising from ignorance is severed; therefore perception is cut off. Because perception is cut off, the karmic maturation of its fruit is also completely severed. The wise one possessed of wisdom, in order to sever those causes of perception, cultivates the noble eightfold path. Son of good family, this manner of reflection is called the complete purification of the holy life.

Son of good family, this is what is called the excellent king of medicines residing within the toxic body of sentient beings — just as on a snow mountain, even though there are poisonous plants, there are also excellent medicinal herbs.

Furthermore, son of good family, when the wise one possessed of wisdom examines desire, one recognizes that desire consists of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Son of good family, the Tathāgata has declared these as fruit arising from cause. From those five things desire arises, but in truth it is not desire itself. Son of good family, the deluded one, through attachment to feeling, generates erroneous perception with respect to form, and on through to tangible objects generates erroneous perception. Through the condition of erroneous perception, feeling arises. Therefore it is explained that through the cause of erroneous worldly perception, ten kinds of perception are born. Through the causes and conditions of desire, one comes to experience bad fruit in the world: with respect to one's father and mother, and —

— acting wrongly toward ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins, and deliberately doing so without the slightest concern for their bodies or their lives. Therefore, the wise one possessed of wisdom recognizes that through the causes and conditions of non-virtuous perception, a mind of desire is born. Having thus understood the cause of desire, the wise one possessed of wisdom then contemplates, in due order, the ripening of its fruit. The ripening of non-virtuous fruit from that desire consists in becoming a hell-being, or being born in an animal realm, or a hungry ghost, or among humans and gods and so forth. This is called the contemplation of karmic maturation of fruit.

If non-virtuous perception were to be brought to cessation, then at no time would that mind of desire arise. Because there is no mind of desire, one does not experience non-virtuous fruit. Because non-virtuous fruit is not experienced, non-virtuous fruit ceases to be. Therefore, one should first cut off non-virtuous perception. When non-virtuous perception is severed, those very phenomena will cease of themselves. Therefore, in order to eliminate non-virtuous perception, the wise one possessed of wisdom cultivates the noble eightfold path. This is also called the pure holy life (brahmacarya). It is like a mountain that harbors poisonous plants yet also contains excellent medicine — just so, within the body of sentient beings, which is itself like a poison, there is said to be the supreme king of medicines.

Furthermore, son of good family, having thus understood desire, the wise one possessed of wisdom then contemplates karma in due order. Why so? The wise one possessed of wisdom reflects thus: feeling, perception, contact, and desire are afflictions. Those afflictions create karma that produces birth, but they do not create karma that produces experience. Yet when those afflictions proceed together with karma, there are two kinds: karma that produces birth and karma that produces experience. Therefore, the wise one possessed of wisdom thoroughly examines karma.

Karma, moreover, is of three kinds: of body, speech, and mind. Son of good family, the two — bodily and verbal karma — may be called both karma and the fruit of karma. Mental karma alone is called karma; it is not called fruit. Thus, by reason of karma, it is called karma. Son of good family, the two — bodily and verbal karma — are also called outer karma, while the mind is called inner karma. These three types of karma, because they are accompanied by afflictions, become twofold: karma that produces birth and karma that produces experience.

Son of good family, true karma is mental karma. Temporal karma is bodily and verbal karma. Of these, what arises first is mental karma, and what arises from mental karma is bodily and verbal karma. Therefore mental karma is called true karma.

Having thus fully understood karma, the wise one possessed of wisdom then contemplates in due order the causes of karma. The causes of karma are ignorance and contact. Through the condition of ignorance and contact, sentient beings seek existence. The condition for seeking existence is craving. Through the condition of craving, the three kinds of karma — bodily, verbal, and mental — are enacted.

Son of good family, having thus understood the causes of karma, the wise one possessed of wisdom then contemplates in due order the ripening of fruit. Karmic maturation of fruit is of four kinds: the maturation of the darkest fruit from the darkest deeds; the maturation of the purest fruit from the purest deeds; the maturation of mixed fruit from mixed deeds; and the maturation of neither-dark-nor-bright fruit from deeds that are neither dark nor bright.

Of these, the maturation of the darkest fruit from the darkest deeds means that when karma is performed it is accompanied by defilement, and the maturation of its fruit is likewise accompanied by defilement. The maturation of the purest fruit from the purest deeds means that when karma is performed it is entirely pure, and

the maturation of its fruit is likewise entirely pure. The maturation of mixed fruit from mixed deeds means that when karma is performed it is mixed, and the maturation of its fruit is likewise mixed. The maturation of neither-dark-nor-bright fruit from deeds that are neither dark nor bright: this is what is called undefiled karma.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, you said earlier that where there is no defilement there is no maturation of fruit. Why, then, did you say there is a maturation of neither-dark-nor-bright fruit?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, in this matter there are two aspects: that which is a fruit and also a karmic maturation, and that which is merely a fruit but not a karmic maturation. The maturation of the darkest fruit from the darkest deeds is both called a fruit and called a karmic maturation. It is called a fruit because it arises from a dark cause, and it is called a karmic maturation because it in turn becomes a cause for further arising. The same applies to mixed deeds and entirely pure deeds. As for the fruit of undefiled karma: it is called a fruit because it arises from a defiled cause, but it is not called a karmic maturation because it does not in turn become a cause for anything further. Therefore it is called a fruit, but it is not called a karmic maturation."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then addressed the Blessed One once more: "Blessed One, if undefiled karma is not a dark phenomenon, why is it not called white?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, it is not called white because it lacks karmic maturation. It is called white because it is the antidote to darkness. In this context, I have spoken of dark and white in terms of experiencing the maturation of fruit. Undefiled karma does not experience karmic maturation, so it is not called white; it is called peaceful. In this way, there are definite destinations where the maturation of karma is experienced. For example, if one commits the ten non-virtues, one will certainly be reborn in hell, in the realm of animals, or among hungry ghosts. If one practises the ten virtues, one will certainly be reborn among gods or humans. Among the karma of the ten non-virtues there are three degrees: supreme, middling, and lesser. Those who commit them at the supreme degree experience a hell-being's body. Those who commit them at the middling degree experience an animal's body. Those who commit them at the lesser degree experience a hungry ghost's body. Among the ten virtues performed by human beings there are likewise four grades: lesser, middling, superior, and most superior. The lesser leads to rebirth in the northern continent of Unpleasant Sound. The middling leads to rebirth in the eastern continent of Videha. The superior leads to rebirth in the western continent of Godānīya. And the most superior leads to rebirth in Jambudvīpa.

A person who is wise and endowed with discernment, understanding this, reflects: 'How shall I put a stop to that maturation of fruit?' And further: 'The cause and condition of that karma are ignorance and contact. If I completely sever ignorance and contact, those fruits of karma will be arrested and will not arise.' For this reason, a person who is wise and endowed with discernment, in order to completely sever ignorance and contact, cultivates the noble eightfold path. That is what is called the entirely pure holy life.

Son of good family, in this way, for the afflicted body of sentient beings, there exists a supreme medicine-king — just as on the Himalayas, though poisonous plants are found, excellent medicines are also found there. Furthermore, son of good family, a person who is wise and endowed with discernment, having understood karma and the mental afflictions, examines in sequence the two maturations of fruit. Having understood that the maturation of fruit of both of these is suffering, and having understood it as suffering in this way, one abandons entirely every form of grasping at rebirth."

A person who is wise and endowed with discernment understands further that from the cause of affliction, affliction arises; from the cause of karma, affliction arises; and from the cause of affliction, karma arises. From the cause of karma, suffering arises; and from the cause of suffering, affliction arises. From the cause of affliction, existence arises; and from the cause of existence, suffering arises. From the cause of existence, existence arises; and from the cause of existence, karma arises. From the cause of karma, affliction arises; from the cause of affliction, suffering arises; and from the cause of suffering, suffering too arises — this is what one comes to understand.

Son of good family, know that when a person who is wise and endowed with discernment understands things in this way, that constitutes understanding the suffering of karma. Why is this so? Because those very reflections, as stated above, are the twelve causes and conditions of cyclic existence. Know, then, that whoever reflects thus upon those twelve causes and conditions of cyclic existence creates no new karma and destroys old karma.

Son of good family, when a person who is wise and endowed with discernment examines, one by one, the many and varied forms of suffering in each of the hells from the first hell all the way through to the one hundred and thirty-sixth, they come to understand that all of it is produced by the karma of affliction. Having thus understood the suffering of the hells, one proceeds in sequence to examine the suffering of hungry ghosts (pretas), animals, and the rest. Having understood all of that, one then examines all the suffering found among humans and gods, and comes to understand that all these many forms of suffering likewise arise from the karma of affliction.

Son of good family, there is nothing that afflicts the gods of the higher realms with great suffering — yet when the five omens appear to a god whose body is supple and tender, the great suffering that god experiences is comparable to the suffering of the hells: there is no difference whatsoever.

Son of good family, a person who is wise and endowed with discernment comes to understand most deeply that all the suffering of the three realms arises from the causes and conditions of the karma of affliction.

Son of good family, consider as an analogy: unfired clay pottery is extremely easy to break. The body taken up by a sentient being is similar — that body is a vessel for manifold suffering. Consider further: just as a great flowering and fruit-bearing tree is made unpleasant by many birds, so too the experience of a sentient being's body is made unpleasant by many sources of suffering. And just as a large heap of dry grass is burned up by even a small fire, so too the experience of a sentient being's body is destroyed by suffering.

Son of good family, know that when a person who is wise and endowed with discernment understands the eight kinds of suffering in the manner of noble practice (ārya), that person has thoroughly cut through suffering.

Son of good family, having thus deeply understood the eight kinds of suffering, a person who is wise and endowed with discernment proceeds in sequence to examine the causes of suffering. The causes of suffering are craving and ignorance. Craving and ignorance have two aspects: seeking a body and seeking material things. Both the seeking of a body and the seeking of material things are suffering. Therefore, know that craving and ignorance become the causes of suffering.

Son of good family, craving and ignorance have yet another two aspects: inner and outer. The inner causes the body to come into being. The outer causes growth and increase. Furthermore, while the inner causes the body to come into being, the outer causes the results of karma to come into being. Therefore, when inner craving is cut, karma is cut; and when outer craving is cut, the result is cut. Inner craving gives rise to the suffering of future time, while outer craving gives rise to the suffering of the present time.

Therefore, a wise and discerning person understands that craving becomes a cause of suffering. Having thus understood the cause of suffering, one gradually contemplates the karmic maturation of the fruit of suffering. What is called the fruit of suffering is grasping. What is called grasping is the fruit of craving. Through the causes and conditions of grasping, one comes to crave inner and outer things, and through that craving one experiences suffering. Son of good family, a wise and discerning person understands that through the condition of craving comes grasping, and through the condition of grasping comes becoming. Whoever cuts through these two things — craving and grasping — will not create karma, and will not come to experience manifold suffering. Therefore, a wise and discerning person applies diligence to the noble eightfold path in order to sever the suffering of craving.

Son of good family, whoever fully understands this as I have described — this is what I call the perfectly pure holy life. It is said that for the afflicted body of sentient beings there exists a supreme king of medicine, just as a snowy mountain, though it contains poison, also contains supreme medicine.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, what is meant by the perfectly pure holy life? The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, it is all phenomena. The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked again: Blessed One, the meaning of the expression "all phenomena" is indeterminate. Why so? Because the Tathāgata has at various times taught that virtue and non-virtue are so designated. At various times he has taught that careful establishment of the four foundations of mindfulness is so designated. At various times he has taught that the twelve sense bases are so designated. At various times he has taught that the spiritual friend is so designated. At various times he has taught that the twelve links of dependent origination are so designated. At various times he has taught that sentient beings are so designated. At various times he has taught that right view and wrong view are so designated. At various times he has taught that the twelve divisions of scripture are so designated. At various times he has taught that the two truths are so designated. And you yourself have now said that the perfectly pure holy life is all phenomena — so to what and to what else does the expression "all phenomena" refer?

The Blessed One declared: Excellent! Most excellent! Son of good family, this noble Dharma of the great sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa is called the precious treasury of all phenomena. Just as the ocean is the source of all precious things, so too this sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa is like that — it is the very heart of the intended meaning of all words. Son of good family, just as Mount Meru, the king of mountains, is the source of all the many medicines, so too this sūtra is like that — it is the source of the moral discipline of bodhisattvas. Son of good family, just as space is the abode of all things, so too this sūtra is like that — it is the abode of all virtuous phenomena. Son of good family, just as a fierce wind cannot be bound by anyone, so too all bodhisattvas who apply diligence to this sūtra are like that — they cannot be bound by any of the non-virtuous phenomena of the afflictions. Son of good family, just as nothing can withstand a vajra, so too this sūtra is like that — though the non-Buddhists with their many wrong views be numerous, they cannot demolish it. Son of good family, just as no one can count the grains of sand of the Gaṅgā river, so too the meaning of this sūtra is like that —

no one can count it. Son of good family, this sūtra will become the victory banner of the Dharma for bodhisattvas, just as the victory banner of Śakra (Indra), the lord of the gods, is like that. Son of good family, this sūtra is like a caravan leader guiding merchants to the great city of perfect nirvāṇa, just as a great caravan master leads many merchants and brings them out upon the great ocean. Son of good family, this sūtra will become the radiant light of the Dharma's illumination for bodhisattvas, just as in this world the sun and the moon dispel the darkness. Son of good family, this sūtra will become excellent medicine for sentient beings afflicted by illness, just as from the Himalayas (the mountain of medicinal herbs) arises the king of medicines, which pacifies the suffering of disease. Son of good family, this sūtra will become a staff for all those bent under the weight of wrong craving, just as all who are physically weakened rise up by its aid. Son of good family, this sūtra will become a bridge for all who are weighed down by evil and wrongdoing, just as in this world a bridge liberates all beings. Son of good family, this sūtra will become cool shade for those tormented by the afflictions in the twenty-five realms of existence, just as a worldly parasol or canopy screens out the blazing hot sun. Son of good family, this sūtra is a great fearless king that will vanquish all the wicked māras of the afflictions, just as the lion king subdues all the beasts of the wilderness. Son of good family, this sūtra is a great knowledge-mantra that will destroy all the wicked demonic spirits of the afflictions, just as in this world a mantra practitioner renders one free from harmful spirits. Son of good family, this sūtra is like an unsurpassed hailstorm that will shatter all the fruits of saṃsāric existence, just as in this world a hailstorm shatters all fruits. Son of good family, this sūtra will become like excellent medicine restoring the eyes of those whose moral discipline has become impaired, just as the medicine in this world called añjana benefits all who suffer from eye disease. Son of good family, this sūtra will become the source of all virtuous phenomena, just as in this world the earth becomes the abode of all things. Son of good family, this sūtra will become a clear mirror for sentient beings whose moral discipline has become impaired, just as a clear worldly mirror reveals all forms. Son of good family, this sūtra will become a garment for those who lack a sense of shame and moral restraint, just as in this world clothing covers and wraps the body. Son of good family, this sūtra will become a precious jewel-wealth for those who are impoverished in virtuous phenomena, just as the divine goddess Śrī (Lakṣmī) benefits all the poor. Son of good family, this sūtra will become a stream of ambrosia for all sentient beings who are parched with thirst for the Dharma, just as the water endowed with the eight qualities satisfies all who thirst. Son of good family, this sūtra will become a Dharma throne for all the afflictions, just as in this world when people encounter a comfortable seat. Son of good family, this sūtra adorns bodhisattvas from the first ground all the way through the tenth ground with garlands, incense, flowers, ointments, powders, and the purest and most excellent varieties of fragrant offerings — through a vehicle richly endowed in its kind, it causes them to abide in the six perfections. It causes them to experience supreme joy, just as the Pārijāta tree of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three is like that.

Son of good family, this sūtra is like a sharp blade of wisdom — it cuts down every tree of affliction. It is like a keen-edged weapon — it severs all habitual tendencies. It is like one who is supremely brave and bold — it vanquishes every māra that opposes and attacks. It is like the fire of wisdom — it burns away all afflictions. It is like the very heart of dependent origination — it is the birthplace of all pratyekabuddhas. It is like a treasury of learning — it is the birthplace of śrāvakas. It is like the eye of all the gods. It is the true path for all human beings. It is the foundation of refuge for all the animal realms. It is the place of liberation for all hungry ghosts. It is the supreme, unsurpassed excellence for hell-beings. It is the supreme, unsurpassed vessel for all sentient beings of the ten directions. It is the father and mother of all buddhas of the ten directions — those who have passed, those yet to come, and those who dwell in the present.

Son of good family, therefore this sūtra has gathered all Dharma together. I said before, as is well known, that this sūtra gathers all Dharma — and indeed I have declared that the holy life is the thirty-seven factors of awakening (bodhipākṣika dharmas).

The fiftieth fascicle of the noble great sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa.
