Son of good family, without the thirty-seven factors of awakening, no one will attain anything from the true fruit of the śrāvaka all the way through to the fruit of unsurpassed and perfectly complete awakening. Nor will they behold the nature of a buddha or the fruit of that nature. For that very reason, by that very cause and condition, the holy life is the thirty-seven factors of awakening. Why is this? Because the thirty-seven factors of awakening are not of the nature of error and inversion, they destroy error and inversion. Because they are not of the nature of wrong view, they destroy wrong view. Because they are not of the nature of decay and destruction, they bring decay and destruction to complete ruin. Because they are by nature wholly pure in their practice, they cause sentient beings ultimately to abide in the holy life of complete purity.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: Blessed One, if defiled phenomena can serve as a cause for undefiled phenomena, why did the Tathāgata not say that defiled things are the practice of the completely pure holy life?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, all defiled phenomena are characterized by inversion and error — therefore one should not call defiled phenomena the completely pure holy life.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, what is called the supreme worldly Dharma — is it defiled or is it undefiled?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, it is defiled.

Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, though it is defiled, if it is not by nature erroneous and inverted, why should it not be called the completely pure holy life?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the supreme worldly Dharma becomes a cause for the undefiled, and so it is comparable to the undefiled. Because it is oriented toward the undefiled, it should not be called inversion and error. Son of good family, from the moment one generates the mind of the completely pure holy life continuously, up to and including the supreme worldly Dharma, the mind is brought to one-pointed concentration, and

and for that reason it should not be called the completely pure holy life.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, the five consciousnesses of sentient beings are defiled, yet they are not inverted and they are not one-pointed. Why, then, should they not be called the completely pure holy life?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the five consciousnesses of sentient beings are indeed not one-pointed, yet they are defiled, and they are also inverted. They are called defiled because they give rise to defilements. They are not correct by essential nature, and they are called inverted because of attachment to perception. Now, how is it that they are not correct by essential nature, and are called inverted due to attachment to perception? Because one generates the perception of male and female toward what is neither male nor female — and in the same way, this should be understood expansively regarding a house, a vehicle, a pot, and cloth, all the way through to cloth. These are called inversions.

Son of good family, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipākṣikadharmas) are not by nature inverted, and therefore they are called the completely pure holy life.

Son of good family, whatever bodhisattva knows, with respect to the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the root, the cause, the gathering, the generation, the master, the guide, the victor, the correct, and the culmination — that bodhisattva is called one who practices the completely pure holy life.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, how should one understand knowing the root through knowing the culmination?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, excellent, excellent! There are two aspects of a matter regarding which a bodhisattva asks a question: that which one should understand oneself, and that which one causes others to understand. Although you yourself have realized and understood this, you ask about these matters for the sake of countless sentient beings who have not yet understood — and for that, I praise you, saying excellent, excellent!

Son of good family, the root of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening is aspiration. The cause is called luminous contact. The gathering is called feeling. The generation is called careful attention. The master is called mindfulness. The guide is called meditative absorption. The victor is called wisdom. The correct is called liberation. And the culmination is called the great nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, the most fervent aspiration is the root of all — from the initial generation of the mind of awakening all the way through to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Therefore aspiration is said to be the root.

Son of good family, consider these worldly examples: the root of all suffering is craving; the root of all illness is indigestion; the root of all litigation is dispute; the root of all non-virtue is falsehood. It is comparable to those.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked again: Blessed One, earlier in this very sūtra the Tathāgata declared that the root of all virtue is conscientiousness, yet now you say it is aspiration. What is the meaning of this?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if one speaks of the cause of arising, it is fervent aspiration. If one speaks of the cause of clarity, it is conscientiousness. Consider the worldly example: the cause of all fruits is said to be the seed, and furthermore the seed is said to be the cause of arising, while the soil is said to be the cause of clarity. The meaning here is comparable to that.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked:

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: In another sūtra the Tathāgata declared that the root of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening is the buddha. What is the meaning of that?

The Blessed One declared: The Tathāgata taught that for sentient beings who have no prior knowledge of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the buddha is the root. For one who understands through one's own discernment, fervent aspiration is the root.

Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, in what sense is contact said to be the cause of clarity?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the Tathāgata has spoken of clarity at various points as wisdom, and at various points as faith. Son of good family, through the cause and condition of faith, one draws near to a spiritual friend, and this is therefore called contact. Through the cause and condition of relying on a spiritual friend, one attains the sacred Dharma, and this too is called contact. Through the condition of hearing the sacred Dharma, the actions of body, speech, and mind become thoroughly pure, and this too is called contact. Through the condition of the actions of body, speech, and mind being thoroughly pure, one attains right livelihood, and this too is called contact. Through the condition of right livelihood, one attains fully purified ethical discipline. Through the condition of fully purified ethical discipline, one comes to delight in remote forest retreats. Through the condition of delighting in remote forest retreats, one applies the mind with great thoroughness. Through thorough application of the mind, one abides in accordance with the Dharma. Through the condition of abiding in accordance with the Dharma, one attains the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening and overcomes afflictions without number — and this is called contact.

Son of good family, feeling is called the gathering. When sentient beings experience feeling, they perform virtuous and non-virtuous actions, and therefore feeling is called the gathering. Son of good family, through the condition of feeling, many afflictions arise. And through the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, afflictions are overcome — therefore feeling is called the gathering.

Through the condition of thorough and excellent application of the mind, afflictions are overcome, and therefore this is called production. Why? Because through sustained diligence, one attains the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening. And for one who intends to overcome afflictions in that way, everything depends on mindfulness. Therefore mindfulness is called the master.

Just as in the world the four kinds of troops follow according to the will of their commander, so too the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening all follow after mindfulness, their master. Son of good family, one who has entered into meditative absorption comes to understand all the defining characteristics of the phenomena of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening — therefore meditative absorption is called the guide. Understanding the defining characteristics of the phenomena of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening becomes supreme wisdom — therefore wisdom is called the victor. In this way, wisdom comprehends the afflictions, and through the power of wisdom the afflictions are pacified. Just as in the world the defeat of an enemy by four kinds of troops may depend on a single warrior or two, so too with the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening — through the power of wisdom the afflictions are overcome, and therefore it is called the victory of wisdom.

Son of good family, through sustained application to the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening one attains the four meditative concentrations, higher knowledge, and bliss, yet even so this is not to be called perfect. Only when, having vanquished the afflictions, one attains complete liberation — that is called the true fulfilment.

Through arousing the mind and applying oneself diligently to the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, one may attain worldly happiness, transcendent happiness, the four fruits of the contemplative life, and liberation — yet even so, this is not to be called perfect. One who utterly cuts off the very substance of the practice of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening — that is called nirvāṇa. And therefore what is perfected I have called great nirvāṇa.

Son of good family, furthermore, the mind of intense aspiration is called conviction. Through intense aspiration one draws near to a spiritual friend — this too is called contact, and it is called cause. Through drawing near to a spiritual friend there is what is called feeling, and that is called gathering. Through drawing near to a spiritual friend, thorough mental engagement arises, and that is called production. Through the condition of these four kinds of phenomena, awakening is born — by conviction, mindfulness, meditative absorption, and wisdom. These are called the lord, the guide, and the victor. Through the condition of these three kinds of phenomena, two kinds of liberation are attained. By the complete cutting off of desire, the mind is liberated; by the complete cutting off of ignorance, wisdom is liberated — and this is called the genuine. Thus through these eight kinds of phenomena the ultimate fruit is attained, and this is called nirvāṇa — and it is also called perfection.

Son of good family, furthermore: conviction is the arousing of the awakening mind and the going forth into renunciation. Contact is the performance of the request and the four actions — and that is called cause. Taking hold is the embracing of the two kinds of moral discipline: the discipline of individual liberation and the discipline of thoroughly pure conduct — and that is called feeling and complete taking up. Production is the diligent application to the four meditative concentrations. The lord is the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of once-returning. The guide is the fruit of non-returning. The victor is the fruit of arhatship. The genuine is the fruit of the pratyekabuddha. And perfection is the fruit of unsurpassed, complete, perfect awakening.

Son of good family, furthermore: conviction is consciousness. Contact is the six sense bases. Gathering is feeling. Production is ignorance. The lord is name-and-form. The guide is desire. The victor is grasping. The genuine is becoming. And perfection is birth, aging, sickness, and death.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: Blessed One, what is the difference between root, cause, and production?

The Blessed One declared: What is called root refers to the very first arousing of the mind. What is called cause is the unbroken continuation of the similar. Production is the arising of the similar after the similar has ceased. Son of good family, furthermore: what is called root is the agent. What is called cause is the fruit. And what is called production is the purpose. Son of good family, although in the future the matured fruit exists, because it has not yet been experienced it is called cause. When it is about to be experienced, that is called production.

Son of good family, furthermore: what is called root is feeling. Attainment is cause. Purpose is production. Son of good family, in this sūtra what is called root is the path of seeing. What is called cause is the path of cultivation. And what is called production is the path of no-more-learning.

Son of good family, furthermore: what is called root is the authentic cause. What is called cause is skillful means — for through skill in means the fruit is attained. The attainment of the fruit is called production.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked again:

"Blessed One, if, as you have declared, one who has reached the end is said to have attained nirvāṇa, is it then possible to attain nirvāṇa?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, whatever bodhisattva, great being, monk, nun, layman, or laywoman applies themselves diligently to ten perceptions — know that such a one will attain nirvāṇa. What are the ten? They are as follows: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of selflessness, the perception of abandoning food, the perception of non-attachment to the entire world, the perception of death, the perception of the many faults and flaws, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of cessation, and the perception of absence of craving. Son of good family, whatever bodhisattva, great being, monk, nun, layman, or laywoman applies themselves diligently to these ten perceptions — such a one will, in the end, definitively attain nirvāṇa. And therefore, without depending on others, they will come to understand virtue, non-virtue, and so forth. Such a one is a true monk — and likewise, down to the true layman and the true laywoman."

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa then asked: "Blessed One, how is it that from a bodhisattva down to a laywoman, one applies diligent effort to the perception of impermanence?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, with regard to a bodhisattva there are two aspects: the initial arousing of the mind of awakening, and applying diligent effort toward awakening. The perception of impermanence likewise has two aspects: the coarse and the subtle. When a bodhisattva who has initially aroused the mind of awakening cultivates the perception of impermanence, this is the thought that arises in the mind: 'Things of the world have two aspects: inner and outer.' Thus one reflects that inner things are impermanent and subject to change. This body of mine passes through distinct times and stages — birth, youth, adolescence, old age and decline, and death — each different and separate from the others. Therefore one understands that inner things are impermanent; one knows them to be impermanent. Furthermore, one reflects: 'When I observe sentient beings, some are endowed with fine complexion and color, with power and strength, moving and coming and going without obstruction; others are tormented by illness and are utterly emaciated, lacking color and complexion, without power or strength, and unable to function freely. Some are endowed with great wealth and their storehouses overflow with abundance; others are so destitute they possess nothing at all. Some are seen to be endowed with excellent and abundant qualities; others are seen to be endowed with sinful and unwholesome phenomena.' And so one knows with certainty that inner phenomena are impermanent. Furthermore, with regard to outer phenomena: the times of seed, sprout, stem, leaf, flower, and fruit are each separate and distinct from one another. Thus among outer phenomena as well, some are endowed with excellence and abundance, others are not. One therefore reflects in the mind: 'I understand that all outer phenomena are likewise impermanent.' In this way, having understood all phenomena to be impermanent, one reflects upon all phenomena through the doorway of what one has heard, thinking as follows: 'When I listen, even the gods of the higher realms are endowed with supremely pleasant and abundant enjoyments, and though possessed of superknowledge and power, the five signs of decay appear, and therefore I understand them to be impermanent. Furthermore, I have heard that at the beginning of the cosmic age all sentient beings, each on their own, were endowed with supreme and excellent qualities, that the light of their own bodies illuminated everything and they had no need whatsoever of the light of sun or moon — yet by the force of impermanence even that light faded and those qualities were lost entirely.'

Furthermore, I have heard that even a wheel-turning king (cakravartin), sovereign over the four continents and possessed of the seven precious royal treasures and of great dominion, has yet been unable to overcome impermanence.

Furthermore, on this great earth in former times innumerable sentient beings dwelt at ease, and across every stretch of ground no larger than a chariot wheel there flourished in dense abundance all manner of excellent medicinal plants, forests, groves of edible trees, fruits, and the like. But now, because the merit of sentient beings has diminished, this great earth has lost its power and strength, so that even those things born from the soil are without flavour and have become bland and vapid. Therefore all phenomena, outer and inner, are impermanent. This is called coarse impermanence.

Having understood the coarse in this way, one then proceeds step by step to contemplate the subtle. What, then, is the subtle? A great bodhisattva contemplates all outer and inner phenomena as impermanent right down to their finest atomic particles at every future moment. Why so? Because such a bodhisattva is endowed with the complete destruction of signs.

If the form that exists in the next moment were not impermanent, it would be inappropriate to speak of there being these ten distinct temporal phases of form. What are the ten? They are: the phase of gestation, the phase of quickening, the phase of hardening, the phase of developing flesh and mass, the phase of growth of the limbs, the phase of early childhood, the phase of youth, the phase of young adulthood, the phase of full maturity, and the phase of old age.

If a bodhisattva were to regard form at the phase of gestation as not impermanent, it would never change into the phases from quickening through to young adulthood; and if those phases were regarded as not impermanent, old age would never arrive either. Thus if the many phases were not ceasing moment by moment, it would be inappropriate for old age to arise; rather, it would be fitting for everything to arise all at once, fully complete. But there is no such thing as arising all at once in finished form. Therefore one should understand with certainty that there is a subtle impermanence of cessation moment by moment.

Furthermore, we observe that certain persons who were once endowed with keen senses and radiant complexion later decline and deteriorate. This makes it evident that such persons are definitely impermanent, moment by moment.

Beyond this, one should also contemplate the four great elements and the four modes of conduct.

Furthermore, with respect to both outer and inner aspects, there are two causes of suffering in each: hunger and thirst, and cold and heat, are also to be contemplated.

Furthermore, one thinks: if those four aspects were not subtly impermanent moment by moment, it would be inappropriate to speak of four kinds of suffering. Any bodhisattva who contemplates in this way is said to be a bodhisattva who contemplates subtle impermanence.

Just as one understands outer and inner form, so too should one understand mental phenomena in the same way. Why? Because mind operates through the six sense bases (āyatanas). While operating through the six sense bases, at one moment a mind of joy arises, at another a mind of aversion arises, at another a mind of desire arises, and at another a mind of recollection arises — thus different minds arise in succession. Since they do not persist as a single unbroken continuity, one understands that all phenomena of form and of what is not form are impermanent.

O son of noble family, a bodhisattva who perceives the arising, cessation, and impermanence of all phenomena moment by moment is called a bodhisattva who possesses the perception of impermanence.

O son of noble family, one who is learned and endowed with wisdom, having applied themselves diligently to the perception of impermanence in this manner, should then contemplate the conceit of permanence, the inverted view of permanence, and —

— the inverted perception, and abandons it entirely, then applies themselves diligently to the perception of suffering. Contemplating thus — "By what cause and by what condition does one come to experience suffering in this way?" — one understands that suffering arises from the cause of impermanence. Through the condition of impermanence, one comes to experience birth, aging, sickness, and death; and because of the condition of birth, aging, sickness, and death, this is called impermanence. Through the condition of impermanence, one experiences the many outer and inner sufferings: the sufferings of hunger and thirst, of cold and heat, of being beaten and stabbed, of being reviled and verbally abused. In this way, the experience of so many sufferings also arises through the condition of impermanence.

Furthermore, one who is learned and endowed with wisdom understands that this very body is a vessel of impermanence. The vessel is suffering; and because the vessel is suffering, the essence it contains is likewise understood to be of the nature of suffering. Furthermore, O son of noble family, one who is learned and endowed with wisdom understands that arising itself is suffering and cessation itself is suffering. Because things arise and cease through suffering, they are impermanent; and so one applies oneself diligently to the perception of impermanence, free from the notion of self and what belongs to a self.

Furthermore, one who is learned and endowed with wisdom understands that suffering itself is impermanence, and impermanence itself is suffering. Since suffering is impermanence, why would one who is learned and endowed with wisdom assert that a self exists? Because there is no self in this way, impermanence too should be understood accordingly. Likewise, since the five aggregates (skandhas) are both suffering and impermanence, why do sentient beings assert that a self exists?

Furthermore, one understands that all phenomena arise from a diversity of assembled conditions, not from a single assembly; all phenomena do not arise from one assembly alone, nor is even a single phenomenon the fruit of all assemblies together. All assemblies have no nature of self, no nature of singularity, no nature of plurality, no nature of a thing, and no nature of anything under sovereign control. If those characteristics of intrinsic nature were indeed present in all phenomena, why would one who is learned and endowed with wisdom assert that a self exists?

Furthermore, one contemplates thus: in all phenomena there is not even a single agent. Even now there is not a single agent in even one phenomenon; in all phenomena, arising from assembly, there is likewise no agent. All phenomena do not arise or cease through their own intrinsic nature; they cease from assembly and arise from assembly. Having thus arisen, sentient beings generate an inverted perception, saying "they arise from assembly." Because sentient beings perceive invertedly, and because there is no genuine truth when one perceives in an inverted manner, why does one assert that a self truly exists? Therefore, one who is learned and endowed with wisdom understands there to be no self (anātman).

Furthermore, one contemplates: "By what cause and by what condition do sentient beings grasp at a self?" If that self were to exist, one asks whether it is singular or whether it exists in many forms. If that self were solely singular, why would there be the birth-states of kṣatriya, brahmin, merchant, outcaste, god, human, hell-being, hungry ghost (preta), and animal — why would there be great and small, young and old? Therefore, one understands that what is called "self" is not singular. If what is called "self" were multiple, why do people say that the self of all sentient beings is one — that it pervades everything and is without limit? Therefore, in neither the singular nor the plural does a self exist.

Having understood in this way that there is no self, one who is learned and endowed with wisdom then progressively cultivates the perception of complete disenchantment with food —

One might think: if all phenomena are indeed impermanent, suffering, and without self, then why do non-virtuous actions of body, speech, and mind arise for the sake of food? It is because sentient beings are attached to food that they commit non-virtuous actions of body, speech, and mind. And though material things that are obtained may be shared with others, when the karmic maturation of suffering is experienced, there is no sharing in that.

A son of good family who is learned and endowed with wisdom reflects further in this way: all sentient beings, for the sake of food, have caused their bodies and minds to suffer. Since food is obtained through the condition of so much suffering, he thinks, "Why should I give rise to a mind of attachment to that food?" — and so he does not allow a mind of attachment to food to arise.

Furthermore, when the learned one endowed with wisdom examines what the cause of the body is, he understands that it is through the condition of food that the body is born and grows. He reflects: "I have gone forth from home into homelessness and have taken up moral discipline — and I intend to completely relinquish this body. How then can I now be attached to food?" Having reflected thus, even while accepting food, he cultivates the perception of food as being like the flesh of a child, eaten by hungry ghosts on a desolate plain. He gives rise to a mind of complete disenchantment and does not become attached to it.

Having understood in this way that food has many faults, he then progressively cultivates the perception of contact-as-food in the following manner. He perceives it as like the skin of an ox, when flayed, utterly consumed by countless insects.

Then, progressing further, he cultivates the perception of volition-as-food in this way: he perceives it as like a great mass of fire.

As for consciousness-as-food, he perceives it as like being pierced by three hundred spears.

A son of good family who is learned and endowed with wisdom, having understood in this way the four kinds of food, will never again give rise to a mind of attachment or desire toward food. If such a mind should arise, he reflects thoroughly on impurity. Why so? In order to completely abandon attachment to food. He reflects very carefully that all food is impure. Having understood deeply that it is like something impure, whether he obtains good food or poor food, when he takes it he never gives rise to a mind of attachment or desire — regarding it as like applying medicine to a wound or a festering sore.

A son of good family who is learned and endowed with wisdom, if one understands it thus, is said to be endowed with the complete relinquishment of the perception of food.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when one learned and endowed with wisdom perceives food as impure in this way, does one perceive it truly, or merely as an illusion? If one perceives it truly, then that food being perceived would not actually be impure. If one perceives it merely as an illusion, then is that phenomenon being truly perceived?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, that perception is neither true nor illusory. Because it leads to the complete abandonment of attachment to food, it is called 'true.' Because one sees insects where there are no insects, it is called 'illusory.' Son of good family, all things that are defiled are illusory, and yet they can become true.

"Son of good family, if a monk sets out to go on his alms round and from the very outset thinks, 'May I obtain good food there and not poor food, may I obtain much and not little, may I obtain it quickly and without obstruction' — that monk has not attained the perception of complete relinquishment with regard to food.

virtuous qualities diminish day and night, while non-virtuous phenomena arise and increase.

Son of good family, when a monk sets out to go on his alms round and from the very outset makes this aspiration: 'May those who give me alms be satisfied with food,' and further thinks, 'May those who give me alms obtain immeasurable merit, may I sustain this body — which is afflicted and laden with impurity — through these alms, so that I may apply myself to virtuous qualities and bring about benefit and happiness for my donors' — in that monk, virtuous conduct arises and increases day and night, and non-virtuous phenomena are thoroughly purified. Son of good family, know that a monk who applies himself in this way is not one who receives the gifts of a single region alone.

Son of good family, one who is wise and endowed with wisdom (prajñā) thus applies himself to the non-attachment perception, being equipped with the four kinds of perception. He reflects: 'Throughout all the world, there is nowhere that is free from birth, aging, sickness, and death. There is nowhere in which this body of mine has not been born. If there is not a single place in the world that is free from birth, aging, sickness, and death, why should I be attached to the world? All worldly beings never ascend higher and higher without falling back — therefore the world is assuredly impermanent. If it is impermanent in this way, why would one who is wise and endowed with wisdom be attached to the world? Each and every sentient being has suffered everywhere throughout all the world, without exception. Even those born as Brahmā gods in the high heavens, and those born as gods of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception — the very moment their life departs, they fall into one of the three lower realms. Even those born as lords among the gods of the Four Great Kings, and those born as gods of the Heaven of Wielding Others' Emanations — the very moment their life departs, they are born in the realm of animals and arise as lions, tigers, wolves, yaks, horses, cattle, donkeys, and the like. Even a wheel-turning monarch who holds sovereignty over the four continents, possessed of enjoyments and power — when his merit is exhausted, he becomes destitute and must struggle greatly even to keep himself fed. One who is wise and endowed with wisdom, having understood this so thoroughly, gives rise to the perception of non-attachment to the world.

One who is wise and endowed with wisdom also reflects in this way: 'Worldly things — houses, clothing to wear, food, bedding, medicines for illness, flowers, incense, garlands, various kinds of music, material goods, jewels, and the like — may seem to be free from suffering, and yet these things are suffering by their very nature. How, then, can suffering be relinquished through suffering?' Son of good family, one who is wise and endowed with wisdom, having thus understood, does not give rise to attachment or the perception of pleasure with regard to any worldly thing whatsoever. Son of good family, consider this analogy: when a person is struck by grave illness, even if various kinds of music, flowers, incense, and many kinds of garlands are present, no thought of desire or attachment arises in him toward them. The understanding of one who is wise and endowed with wisdom is just the same.

Son of good family, one who is wise and endowed with wisdom understands that the entire world is not a refuge, not a place of liberation, not a place of perfect peace,

not a place of pleasurable dwelling, not a place where perfection is reached; and he carefully examines it as something devoid of permanence, happiness, self, and purity. He thinks: if I were to become attached to the world in that way, how could I ever fully abandon those phenomena? It is like a person who has no desire for darkness yet turns back from the light into the dark. Darkness is the world; light is the transcendence of the world. If I were to cling to the world and generate darkness, I would be utterly parted from the luminosity of light. Darkness is ignorance; light is wisdom. The cause of wisdom and light is the perception of non-attachment to the world. Desire is a form of bondage, yet I desire the luminosity of wisdom — I do not desire attachment to the world. One who is wise and endowed with wisdom examines things in this way, and having understood thus, should abide in the perception of non-attachment to the world.

Son of good family, one who is wise and endowed with wisdom, having applied himself diligently to the perception of non-attachment to the world, then progressively applies himself with diligence to the perception of death. Reflecting on this life and vital force: it is perpetually surrounded by countless hostile enemies who diminish it moment by moment and do not allow it to arise and grow. It is like a mountain torrent that does not stay still, or like dewdrops on a blade of grass that do not remain long, or like those led to slaughter who are close to death, or like a cow or sheep driven to the butcher's side.

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa asked: Blessed One, how does one who is wise and endowed with wisdom understand cessation moment by moment?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, consider this analogy: four skilled archers gather together and each deliberates, saying, "Let the four of us each shoot an arrow in a different direction, all released at once, and let them all fall to the ground at once." Now if someone were to say, "I will catch with my own hands, all at the same moment, all four arrows shot by those four men, before they fall to the ground" — son of good family, would not that person need to be extraordinarily swift?

The bodhisattva Kāśyapa replied: Blessed One, that is so.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, a hungry ghost (preta) that moves along the ground is swifter than that. A hungry ghost that moves through the sky is swifter than one that moves along the ground. The kings of the four great divine realms are swifter than the hungry ghosts that move through the sky. The gods of the sun and moon are swifter than the kings of the four great divine realms. The very swift gods are swifter than the gods of the sun and moon. And the life-span of sentient beings is swifter than even those very swift gods. Son of good family, in the single passage of a breath going in and out, there are four hundred arisings and cessations of the life-span by which a sentient being lives. Whoever understands life in this way is said to understand cessation moment by moment.

Son of good family, those who are wise and endowed with wisdom understand that this life and vital force are under the dominion of the king of death. They think: if I were to fully abandon the king of death, I would abandon impermanent life and vital force entirely. Furthermore, those who are wise and endowed with wisdom regard life and the vital force as like a great tree on a crumbling riverbank at the edge of a precipice. Furthermore, as a person who has committed a grave wrong is led away to be executed, left without a protector — or as a lion, the king of beasts, is extremely hungry — or as a venomous snake inhaling a great wind — or as a horse extremely parched with thirst and overcome with craving for water —

— or as a wrathful, extremely angry hungry ghost — so too does one regard the king of death over sentient beings in just that way. A son of good family who is wise and endowed with wisdom, understanding things clearly in this manner, is called one who is diligent in the perception of death.

A son of good family who is wise and endowed with wisdom thinks further to himself: even if, after going forth into renunciation, I cannot sustain life and vital force for more than seven days, still I shall rouse the utmost diligence, guard ethical conduct, benefit sentient beings, and teach the Dharma for their welfare and happiness — this is called the one who is wise and endowed with wisdom being diligent in the perception of death.

Let alone seven days — what need is there to say so much? Whether it be six days, or five, or four, or three, or two, or one, or from a single breath passing in and out to the duration of a single moment and instant — if during that time I apply diligent effort toward awakening, guard ethical conduct perfectly, benefit sentient beings, and teach the Dharma for their welfare and happiness — this too is called the one who is wise and endowed with wisdom being diligent in the perception of death.

One who is wise and endowed with wisdom, possessed of the six perceptions mentioned above, applies diligent effort to these seven causes of perception. What are the seven? They are: the perception that applies diligent effort to what is permanent; the perception that applies diligent effort to what is pleasurable; the perception free from aversion; the perception free from jealousy; the perception of virtue; the perception of aspiration; the perception free from pride; and the perception that has come under the dominion of meditative absorption.

A son of good family — a monk who possesses these seven perceptions is called a śramaṇa, a brahmin, one who is thoroughly pacified, one who is thoroughly pure, one who is completely liberated, one who is wise and endowed with wisdom, one of right view, one who has reached the far shore of perfection, a king of physicians, and a caravan leader. Such a one is supremely skilled in what the Tathāgata has intended and declared, and will completely resolve any doubt regarding the seven kinds of utterances that the Tathāgatas have spoken — contemplating, fully understanding, and seeing those seven kinds of utterances.

A son of good family — a person who possesses these six perceptions is one who utterly condemns the three worlds, who utterly abandons the three worlds, who utterly pacifies the three worlds, and who is unattached to the three worlds. Such a one is called the wise and wisdom-endowed one who possesses the ten perceptions.

A monk who possesses these ten is called one endowed with the marks of a śramaṇa.

Then the bodhisattva Kāśyapa praised the Blessed One before his presence with the following verses addressed to the buddha:

With compassion for the world and all it holds, you are the king of physicians —
in body and in wisdom both, you are completely stilled.
Since I am possessed of a self, while the phenomena of selflessness are certain,
for that reason I bow with reverence to you, the peerless Victor.

When the initial mind and the perfected mind are both examined,
the perfected mind takes supreme delight in the initial mind.
Though I myself am not yet liberated, I liberate others —
therefore I bow in homage to the initial mind.

The initial mind becomes the teacher of gods and humans,
far surpassing śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas alike.
One who has generated this mind has utterly transcended the three worlds —
therefore one may call the Victor "peerless beyond all excellence."

The protector of the world is fully obtained through accomplishment,
and the Tathāgata comes as protector without being implored.

Like a buddha departing from the world, and like a calf —
therefore it is said the Tathāgata is the supreme leader of the herd of great compassion.
The Tathāgata's qualities pervade all ten directions everywhere;
those of lesser understanding and without knowledge cannot offer praise.
I offer praise to the power of great compassion,
in order to repay the kindness of the deeds of body and speech.
The worlds perform acts that benefit me,
and the Tathāgata reveals those very activities.
Having severed the karmic maturation of many beings,
therefore I pay homage to the one who acts for the benefit of self and others alike.

The world together with its gods acts greatly for the benefit of those close to it,
yet in the Tathāgata's working of benefit there is no love or hatred.
The Tathāgata possesses no characteristics of the kind the world has —
therefore the mind is equal toward all, free from duality.
The world says one thing and does another;
in the Tathāgata there is no difference between what is spoken and what is done.
All those deeds of his sever every formation —
therefore the name "Tathāgata" has become renowned.

Having thoroughly understood all the faults of complete affliction,
and having demonstrated as well the remaining for the sake of sentient beings —
though liberated in this world for a long time,
out of loving concern the Tathāgata delights in remaining within saṃsāra.
Though appearing visibly in the body of a god or the body of a human,
through great compassion the Tathāgata follows after, as a cow follows its calf.

Since the Tathāgata is the mother of all sentient beings,
the very heart of great compassion is like the calf.
In consideration of sentient beings, the Tathāgata undergoes suffering;
yet when acting out of compassionate concern, no regret arises in the mind.
Being endowed with a mind of compassion, suffering is not felt as suffering —
therefore I pay homage to the one who fully liberates from suffering.

Although the Tathāgata performs limitless merit in every way,
the deeds of body, speech, and mind are utterly pure.
The work done for the sake of sentient beings is not done for one's own sake —
therefore I pay homage to the utterly pure deeds.

The Buddha undergoes suffering yet does not feel it as suffering,
just as those who see another experiencing suffering undergo it as if feeling it themselves.
Even entering the hells for the sake of sentient beings,
a mind of suffering and regret does not arise.
The many sufferings experienced by ordinary beings —
a single body of the Tathāgata takes them all on.
Having undergone them all, the mind becomes supremely stable —
therefore the Tathāgata strives most intently for unsurpassed awakening.

The Tathāgata, with a single flavor of great compassion,
regards every ordinary being as though they were an only child.
Not knowing that the Blessed One is a refuge, sentient beings
cast aspersions upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The worlds are thoroughly afflicted throughout,
and likewise are accompanied by boundless faults and flaws.
Yet whatever faults and flaws arising from thorough affliction there may be —
all were vanquished at the very moment the awakening mind was first generated.

Tathāgatas praise Tathāgatas;
none other than a Tathāgata is able to offer such praise.
Yet I today offer manifest praise by means of this one quality alone:
the Tathāgata has passed through the world with the mind of great compassion.

The aggregate of Dharma of the Tathāgata is loving-kindness (Skt. maitrī);
through the mind of loving-kindness, sentient beings will be fully liberated.
That is the unsurpassed liberation —
and that liberation is nirvāṇa.

This is the twelfth chapter, called "Comprehensively Questioned by Kāśyapa," from the noble great sūtra of complete nirvāṇa.

The fifty-first fascicle.

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the venerable Kauṇḍinya, who knows all:

Form is impermanent; yet through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that abides permanently. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise impermanent; yet through the condition of consciousness's cessation, one will attain a liberated consciousness that abides permanently.

Kauṇḍinya, form is suffering; yet through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is bliss. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are to be understood in the same way, and this should be known in full.

Kauṇḍinya, form is empty; yet through the condition of that empty form's cessation, one will attain a liberation of form that is not empty. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is without self; yet through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form possessed of a true self. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is impure; yet through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is utterly pure. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death; yet through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is free from birth, aging, sickness, and death. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form arises through ignorance; yet through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is free from ignorance. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is a cause of birth; yet through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is not a cause of birth. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is a cause of the four inversions; yet through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is not a cause of inversion. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is the cause of immeasurable non-virtuous phenomena — such as craving for the bodies of men and women and the like, craving for food, attachment to desire, aversion, delusion, miserliness, envy, unwholesome mind, the mind of dread, nutritive food, consciousness as nutriment, intentional food, contact as nutriment, birth from eggs, birth from a womb, birth from warmth and moisture, miraculous birth, the five objects of desire, and the five obscurations and so forth — all these phenomena arise from form. Yet through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated body free from that immeasurable multitude of faults and flaws. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is thoroughly bound by bondage; yet through the condition of that bound form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is free from bondage. Feeling, perception, formations, and

consciousness — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is a cause of the stream of rebirth. Through the condition of that form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is free from the stream. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is not a cause for going to refuge. Through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is a going to refuge. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is like a wound. Through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a liberated form that is free from wounds. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, form is not utterly pacified. Through the condition of form's cessation, one will attain a completely nirvāṇa-realized form that is utterly pacified. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as well — this should be known in full in the same way.

Kauṇḍinya, any person who knows things in this way is called a śramaṇa and a brahmin. One endowed with this understanding is said to possess the qualities of a śramaṇa, the Dharma of a śramaṇa, the qualities of a brahmin, and the Dharma of a brahmin.

Kauṇḍinya, apart from the Dharma of the buddhas, there is nowhere else a true śramaṇa, nowhere a true brahmin, and nowhere the Dharma of śramaṇas and brahmins. All the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are merely speakers of falsehood; not one of them has genuine conduct. They may adopt the outward appearance of those two, but they have no standing in those two. Why is that? Because without the Dharma of śramaṇas and brahmins, why would they claim there are śramaṇas and brahmins? I, for my part, always proclaim the lion's roar in this assembly, so you too should always sound the lion's roar in the great assemblies.

When the immeasurable multitude of non-Buddhists heard these words, they gave rise to minds of aversion and said: "The śramaṇa Gautama declares that among us there are neither śramaṇas nor brahmins, and neither the Dharma of śramaṇas nor the Dharma of brahmins. What are we to do?" And throughout that assembly one wandering ascetic spoke up and said: "Friends, the words of the śramaṇa Gautama are like the ravings of a madman — if they are not consistent, how can they be trusted? Even people who are not mad sometimes sing, sometimes dance, sometimes weep, sometimes laugh, sometimes revile, sometimes praise, unable to distinguish between friend and enemy. The śramaṇa Gautama is just like that: sometimes he proudly says he was born in a city of pure lineage, sometimes he says he was not born, sometimes he says that at birth he took seven steps, sometimes he says he went nowhere, sometimes he says he studied worldly arts in his youth, sometimes he says he is omniscient, sometimes he says he lived comfortably in the royal palace, enjoying pleasures and even fathering a son, sometimes he condemns all of that and says he wants none of it, sometimes he says he practiced austerities for six years, and sometimes he roundly denounces the ascetic practices of non-Buddhists."

Sometimes he says he heard teachings never heard before, such as the udumbara flower and the alalā and so on. Sometimes he says he attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening at the foot of the awakening tree. Sometimes he says, "I went to the foot of the awakening tree and attained nothing whatsoever." Sometimes he says, "This very body of mine is nirvāṇa." Sometimes he says, "When this body of mine ceases, that will be nirvāṇa." All that the ascetic Gautama says is like the raving of a madman — what is there to believe in, or to take pleasure in, regarding him?

The brahmins replied to him with these words: "O great man, how could there be any escape from grief for us now? The ascetic Gautama, after going forth long ago, taught impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so on. Our kinsmen heard this and became extremely frightened, and they did not trust his words — words saying that sentient beings are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure. But now the ascetic Gautama, here in this sal grove, has taught in the midst of a great assembly that there exist things that are permanent, blissful, possessed of self, and utterly pure. When our kinsmen heard him say this, they completely abandoned themselves and came to trust the words of the ascetic Gautama. It is on that account and by that condition that great grief has arisen."

At that time yet another brahmin spoke to them in these words: "Listen well, good people, listen well. The saying that the ascetic Gautama is compassionate is a lie — it is not true. If he were truly compassionate, why would it be that students of ours, who through our own doctrine had obtained the fruit of compassion, would have their minds turned to follow another, acting contrary to our intentions? For that reason, calling him compassionate is not fitting. Moreover, whoever says that the ascetic Gautama is unstained by the eight worldly concerns — that person too speaks falsely. For if the ascetic Gautama is said to be one of few desires and contentment, why does he go about plundering our gains and so forth? And if someone says that the ascetic Gautama is of noble lineage, that too is speaking falsely. Why? Because we have never heard or seen that the lion, the king of wild beasts, has ever killed a little mouse. If the ascetic Gautama were of noble lineage, why would he go about harming us and those like us? And if someone says that the ascetic Gautama is endowed with great power, that too is speaking falsely. Why? Because we have never heard or seen that the garuḍa, the king of birds, has ever fought with a little crow. If he were truly powerful, why would he quarrel with the likes of us? And if someone says that the ascetic Gautama is endowed with the wisdom that knows the minds of others, that too is speaking falsely. Why? If he possessed that wisdom, why does he not know the thoughts we have in our minds? O people, I have heard from wise elders of old that when a hundred years have passed, a magician who works illusions will appear, and it is to the ascetic Gautama that this refers. This creator of illusions will not tarry long — he will soon disappear from this sal grove, so you and the rest of you should not grieve."

At that time yet another naked ascetic spoke to them in these words: "O people, we do not grieve on account of our own bodies, or for the sake of our kinsmen, or for gains, or for reputation. Rather, it is because worldly beings have come to be covered by the darkness of delusion —

— that they do not know what is a field of merit and what is not a field of merit, and so they have abandoned the brahmins who were endowed with the wisdom of the ancient elders, and instead have come to honor those who are very young and without understanding. It is for this reason that we grieve.

"The ascetic Gautama is skilled in spells and incantations, and by the power of those spells he can multiply one body into bodies without number, and from those countless bodies can gather them back into one. With that same body he can take on the forms of men and women, of cattle, sheep, oxen, and horses. Yet by my own power I am able to neutralize the power of his spells. Once the power of the ascetic Gautama's spells has been nullified, we and the rest of us will gain offerings and renown and will enjoy great comfort."

At that time yet another brahmin spoke these words: "O people, the ascetic Gautama possesses immeasurable and fully perfect qualities. Therefore, do not any of you contend with him."

The retinue of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) said to him: "You fool, you deluded one — why do you say that the ascetic Gautama possesses immeasurable qualities? If a mother dies seven days after giving birth, is it fitting to say of the child that he possesses merit and qualities?"

The brahmin replied: "Even when the other party reviles him, he does not revile in return; even when the other party strikes him, he does not strike back. That is the very characteristic of one who possesses great qualities. He bears the thirty-two major marks on his body, the eighty excellent minor marks, and immeasurable miraculous powers. Therefore, know that he is endowed with immeasurable merit and qualities.

"Because he is free from a mind of arrogance, he spoke truthfully from the very first. His speech is gentle and measured, and there is no harshness in his words. Though he has come to the prime of youth, he is without anger and without fierceness. Though in a king's domain, with wealth and possessions in great abundance, he felt no attachment to them — he relinquished everything completely and went forth, abandoning it all as though spitting out a mouthful of phlegm. This is why I say that the ascetic Gautama is endowed with immeasurable and perfectly complete qualities."

Then the retinue spoke up: "Excellent! Great man, what you say is indeed true — the ascetic Gautama is endowed with immeasurable qualities and immeasurable miraculous powers arising from direct knowledge. We for our part cannot match him. The ascetic Gautama is gentle by nature, and having been born in Rājagṛha he has pursued no rigorous austerities and enrolled in no school of study. It may be fitting for him to speak softly, but he knows nothing of the arts, of letters, of traditional learning, and so forth. Let us debate with him on a limited selection of sacred texts. If the ascetic Gautama defeats us, we will enter his service; if we defeat him, he must enter ours."

Having said this, a countless number of non-Buddhists gathered together and went to the court of King Ajātaśatru in the capital.

The king, upon seeing them, spoke these words: "O people, where are you going? Each of you is diligently pursuing the noble path in your own tradition — having gone forth from home into homelessness, you have completely relinquished all household goods and possessions, and the people of the land honor and venerate you with reverence and service. If you have not taken offense at the honor and respectful attendance shown to you, then why have you all assembled and come here together?

"O people, each of you upholds your own doctrine, each of you has gone forth under your own code of moral discipline, and yet you are not in agreement with one another, each having gone forth under a different code of discipline and diligently practicing your respective paths —

"What is the cause and what are the conditions by which all of you have now assembled here with a single purpose? It is like leaves that have been stripped from their branches and then driven together by a fierce wind — so it is that all of you have come together here. As for myself, I am ever a refuge and protector for those who have gone forth; even in my youth I did not begrudge my body and life for their sake."

At that moment all the tīrthikas spoke these words in reply: "Long live the great king! The great king is like a mighty bridge of Dharma. He is like a great sieve of Dharma. He is like a great balance-scale of Dharma — a vessel for all good qualities, the very essential nature of all good qualities. He is like a road of the sacred Dharma. He is like a fertile field for all seeds. He is like a foundation for all territories and lands. He is like the reflected image in a mirror for all realms and regions. He is like a form visible to all the gods. He is like a father and mother to all the people of the land. Great king, the body of the king is a precious treasury of virtue for all world-realms everywhere. And why is he called a treasury of virtue? Because when a king passes judgment, he makes no distinction between friend and enemy but is impartial — like earth, like water, like fire, like wind. Therefore the king is called a treasury of virtue.

"Great king, though the lifespan of beings today is short, the virtues of the king are like the time of kings of old who lived long and dwelt in great happiness. Furthermore, the great king resembles such exemplary kings as Topknot-Born, Splendid Light, Patient One, Naho-zha, Yā-yā-de, Śi-phyi, or Pa-pa-i-tsa-gu and others, who were endowed with a full complement of virtuous qualities. So too is the great king like them. It is through the condition of the great king that all the people of the land have come to dwell in happiness and well-being. Therefore all of us who have gone forth are glad to reside in this country, and we uphold our moral discipline and apply ourselves diligently to the correct path.

"Great king, wherever persons who have gone forth from under our tradition reside, in whatever country that may be, they uphold moral discipline and apply themselves to the correct path — and this brings to the king as well the good fortune of practicing virtue. Great king, you have caused all thieves and bandits in the world to cease, so that all those who have gone forth live without fear. Yet you have not caused the one truly troublesome ascetic, Gautama, to cease — and so we are greatly afraid of him. Gautama, being proud of his birth-lineage and possessed of a fine physical complexion, and having obtained abundant gain through the merit of past generosity, has grown vastly arrogant on account of those possessions. He is further made arrogant through his mastery of mystic spells. Because of these causes and conditions, he is unable to practice austerities, and he indulges in exceedingly soft and comfortable clothing, bedding, and the like. Because of this, all disreputable persons in the world, out of desire for gain and fame, gather around him and assemble in his presence, and they too are unable to practice austerities. By the power of his mystic spells he has brought under his sway Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others like them. And now, in order to draw our own residents here into his circle as disciples in this grove of śāla trees, he proclaims that there exists a body that is permanent, blissful, a self, and utterly pure.

"Great king, we can accept it when the ascetic Gautama formerly taught impermanence, the absence of bliss, the absence of self, and the absence of purity. But now he declares that there is permanence, bliss, a self,

and a self, and that utter purity exists — and this we cannot endure.

"Great king, please listen carefully. What authority do you give us and the ascetic Gautama to establish opposing positions and enter into debate?"

The king then spoke: "Ah, good people, if someone has deceived you, then your minds have become utterly intoxicated and disturbed — like the surging waves of water, or a firebrand whirled in circles, or a monkey that has scrambled up into a tree. Even I would be embarrassed by this, and if a wise and discerning person were to hear it, he would feel deep pity; if a foolish and bewildered person were to hear it, he would mock and revile you. The words you have spoken are not the words of those who have gone forth from the household life. If you were afflicted by diseases of wind, bile, or phlegm, I have excellent medicine here that could heal you. And if you were seized by hungry ghosts (pretas), a physician skilled in healing mantras would cure you. What you are doing right now is like wishing to demolish Mount Meru with the nail of a finger, or to plant seeds in a thunderbolt. Noble sirs, it is like a foolish, bewildered person trying to rouse a lion — the king of beasts — from its hungry sleep, or thrusting a hand into the mouth of a venomous snake, or reaching with bare hands into a fire whose embers are covered with ash. You are doing exactly the same. Sons of good family, consider this further analogy: it is like a jackal trying to roar with the voice of a lion, or a tiny insect trying to race in speed against a garuḍa bird through the sky, or a hare trying to fathom the depths of the great ocean. You are doing exactly the same right now.

"Even if in a dream you were to see yourselves victorious over the monk Gautama, that dream would be false and unworthy of trust.

"Ah, good people, to conceive of such an intention is like walking into a mass of fire hidden beneath ash. Do not speak again in the way you have spoken. And the words of praise you used for me — saying I am equal to you as a scale — do not let others hear them."

At that moment the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) addressed the king again with these words: "Great king, have you been struck by the spells of the ascetic Gautama? Great king, do you distrust and doubt the words spoken by these noble ones? Great king, do not show such contempt toward these great beings. Great king, who is it that causes the moon to wane and to be born anew, that causes the vast ocean to be pervaded by the taste of salt, and the Himālaya and other mountains to arise? Was it not we — the brahmins and the rest — who did these things? Great king, have you not heard? For twelve years the sage Agata poured the waters of the river Gaṅgā into his ear. Have you not heard that the sage Gautama, endowed with great supernatural power, for twelve years transformed himself into the body of Śakra — Śakra whose body he then transformed into the body of a ewe with a thousand teats? Great king, have you not heard that the sage's gaze, in a single day, drank the waters of the four great oceans all at once and dried up the very earth? Great king, have you not heard that the sage Baśpu made the divine king of the gods — the lord of the three eyes — into a three-eyed one? Great king, have you not heard that the sage Alāla reduced a city like Alāla to dust? Great king, among the brahmins there are sages endowed with such great power, present and manifest right before your eyes — so why, great king, do you hold us in such utter contempt?"

The king replied: "Ah, good people, if you do not trust my words and wish to enter into contest, then the Tathāgata, the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha, is present at this very moment beneath the śāla trees. Go there, all of you, and question him as you please."

The Tathāgata, having analyzed the matter, will answer you as you wish."

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, together with the retinue of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), went to where the Buddha was. He bowed his head in homage, circumambulated to the right three times, and then, with due deference, took his seat to one side. He addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, these non-Buddhists wish to question and debate on such and such matters."

The Tathāgata was requested to give his reply to each point in turn. The Blessed One declared: "Great king, the Tathāgata knows the right moment — wait a little while."

Then, from within that assembly, a brahmin named Śateśana spoke these words: "Gautama, is what you call nirvāṇa a permanent phenomenon?"

The great brahmin replied: "It is so. Yes, it is indeed so."

The brahmin then spoke again: "Gautama, it is not fitting to call nirvāṇa permanent. Why? Because worldly phenomena are such that fruits arise from seeds in an unbroken continuum — just as clay pots arise from clay, and garments arise from thread. If Gautama has taught that one attains nirvāṇa by assiduously cultivating impermanence, then if the cause is not permanent, how can the result be called permanent?"

"Gautama, liberation from attachment is nirvāṇa. Liberation from attachment to form and liberation from attachment to the formless is nirvāṇa. When all afflictions — ignorance and the rest — are ceased, that is nirvāṇa, so you have taught. But all of these, from attachment through to the affliction of ignorance, are impermanent. If the cause is impermanent, then it follows that the attainment of nirvāṇa too would be impermanent."

"Gautama, you have taught that one is born as a god through the power of causes, that one falls into hell through the power of causes, and that one is liberated from causes. Therefore all phenomena arise from causes. If liberation were to occur through the power of causes, could it rightly be called permanent?"

"Gautama, you have taught that form, arising from conditions, is impermanent — and that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are likewise the same. If that liberation itself is form, then it is impermanent; and feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness would equally be impermanent. If there is some liberation beyond the five aggregates (skandhas), then that liberation would amount to nothing but empty space. But if it is empty space, it cannot rightly be said to arise from causes and conditions — because what is permanent and singular pervades everywhere."

"Gautama, you have further taught that whatever arises from causes is suffering. If that is so, why do you teach that liberation is bliss? You have further taught that what is impermanent is suffering, and what is suffering is selfless. If it is impermanent, suffering, and selfless, then it is impure. If all phenomena arising from causes are impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure, then why do you teach that nirvāṇa is permanent, blissful, self, and pure?"

"Gautama, if you have taught both permanence and impermanence, both suffering and bliss, both self and no-self, both pure and impure, does that not amount to teaching in contradictions? I have heard from wise and intelligent elders of old: if a buddha comes into the world, it is impossible that he would teach in contradictions. And yet now Gautama has taught in contradictions."

"Furthermore, what is the meaning of your saying 'I am what is called a buddha'?"

The Blessed One spoke to the brahmin: "As you have said, if I put a question to you, you must answer it accordingly."

The brahmin replied, "Excellent, Gautama."

The Blessed One then asked: "Is what you call intrinsic nature permanent or impermanent?"

The brahmin said: "What I call intrinsic nature is permanent."

"Does that intrinsic nature become the cause of all inner and outer phenomena?"

"It does."

The Blessed One asked: "Brahmin, how does it function as cause?"

The brahmin said: "Gautama, from intrinsic nature, the Great One arises. From the Great One, ego-pride arises. From ego-pride, the sixteen factors arise: namely, earth, water, fire, wind, and space — five; the five faculties of consciousness, which are the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body; the five faculties of action, which are the hands, feet, mouth, hair, and the faculty of male and female; and the faculty of the mind-in-equilibrium. These sixteen factors are born from the five sense objects: form, sound, smell, taste, and tangible objects. The root of these twenty-one factors is of three kinds: attachment, dust, and darkness. What is called attachment is desire. What is called dust is aversion. What is called darkness is ignorance. Gautama, all twenty-five factors arise from intrinsic nature."

The Blessed One asked: "Brahmin, are these factors — the Great One and the rest — permanent or impermanent?"

The brahmin said: "Gautama, the intrinsic nature of my Dharma is permanent, but all factors such as the Great One and the rest are impermanent."

"Brahmin, according to what you say, in your doctrine the cause is permanent and the result is impermanent. In my doctrine, the cause is impermanent, yet you ask what fault there is if the result is permanent. Brahmin, does your doctrine posit two kinds of cause?"

The brahmin said: "It does."

The Blessed One asked: "What are they?"

The brahmin said: "There are two: the cause of arising and the cause of manifestation."

The Blessed One asked: "What is the cause of arising and what is the cause of manifestation?"

The brahmin said: "What is called the cause of arising is like clay coming forth from the potter's wheel. What is called the cause of manifestation is like a lamp illuminating things."

The Blessed One declared: "The intrinsic nature of these two causes is one and the same. If they are one, would not the cause of arising also become the cause of manifestation, and the cause of manifestation also become the cause of arising?"

The brahmin said: "No."

The Blessed One said: "But if the cause of arising does not become the cause of manifestation, and the cause of manifestation does not become the cause of arising, can it be said that each is the cause of the other?"

The brahmin said: "Each does not become the cause of the other, and yet it is the case that each serves as a cause in relation to the other."

"Brahmin, does the cause of manifestation — that which causes illumination — accord with that illumination itself?"

The brahmin said: "No."

The Blessed One declared: "In my doctrine as well, although nirvāṇa is attained by way of impermanence, it is not itself impermanent. Brahmin, because it is attained by way of the cause of manifestation, it is permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure. Because it is attained by way of the cause of arising, it is impermanent, suffering, selfless, and not utterly pure. Therefore what the Tathāgata has taught also has two aspects, and although it is taught in two aspects, it is not in fact two."

Therefore the Tathāgata is said to teach without duality. You have said that you heard from the ancient sages of old that a buddha who comes into the world teaches without duality — that is very well said. All the buddhas who abide throughout the three times in all ten directions are without difference in what they teach. Therefore the Blessed One, the buddha, is said to teach without duality.

How is it that there is no difference? Whatever is taught as existent, that too is taught as existent; whatever is taught as non-existent, that too is taught as non-existent — this is called having one and the same meaning. Brahmin, the Blessed One, the buddha, by teaching in two aspects, clarifies what is taught as one. How does teaching in two aspects clarify what is taught as one? As an example: from the two terms "eye" and "form" there arises the single term "consciousness" — and in the same way, this is to be understood in full, up through "mind" and "phenomena."

The brahmin said: "Gautama, the meaning of what you have said is well expressed. We, however, did not understand how teaching in two aspects clarifies teaching as one."

Thereupon the Blessed One expounded to them the Four Noble Truths: namely, the truth of suffering is two, and yet is also one. In the same way, up through the truth of the path, each is two, and yet each is also one.

The brahmin said: "Blessed One, I understand."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, how do you understand it?"

The brahmin said: "Blessed One, what is called the truth of suffering is two for all childish, ignoble persons, and one for the noble ones. In the same way, I understand this up through the truth of the path."

The Blessed One declared: "You have understood well."

The brahmin said: "Blessed One, having heard this, I have attained right view. Now I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Out of your great compassion, please grant us the going forth."

Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya: "You, explain it and make the request. Shave hair and beard and go forth from home into homelessness."

At that time the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya, acting in accordance with the Blessed One's command, shaved hair and beard, and at that very moment two things fell away from him: hair and beard, and mental afflictions. Right there and then he attained the fruit of arhatship.

At that time another wanderer named Sīta spoke these words: "Is the nirvāṇa that Gautama teaches permanent?" "It is so." The wanderer Sīta asked: "Gautama, is what is free from afflictions called nirvāṇa?" "It is so." The wanderer Sīta said: "Gautama, there are four kinds of non-existence in the world. What are the four? There is that which is called non-existent because it has not arisen — as for example a clay vessel does not exist before it has been made. There is also that which is called non-existent because it has ceased and is gone — as for example a clay vessel that has broken and is no more. There is that which is called non-existent because one thing is absent in another — as for example a horse is not present in a cow, and a cow is not present in a horse. And there is that which is called non-existent because it is utterly non-existent — as for example the hair of a tortoise or the horn of a rabbit. Gautama, if nirvāṇa is called the passing beyond sorrow because afflictions are absent, then nirvāṇa is a non-existence. If it is a non-existence, why has it been taught as permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, nirvāṇa is not like that. It is not a non-existence in the sense of something that was not there before — like a clay vessel that does not yet exist. It is not a non-existence in the sense of something that was there and has broken apart — like a clay vessel that has shattered. It is not a non-existence in the sense of something utterly non-existent — like the hair of a tortoise or the horn of a rabbit. Rather, nirvāṇa accords with the sense of one thing being absent in another. Son of good family, you yourself have said that a horse is not present in a cow — yet it would not be right to say that the cow, too, is non-existent. And a cow is not present in a horse — yet it would not be right to say that the horse, too, is non-existent. Nirvāṇa is just the same: affliction is not present in nirvāṇa, and nirvāṇa is not present in affliction. Therefore, this is called 'the absence of one thing in another.'"

Vāsiṣṭha then asked: "Gautama, if nirvāṇa is called so in the sense that one thing is absent in another, then where one thing is absent in another there is no permanence, no bliss, no self, and no utter purity. Why then has Gautama taught that nirvāṇa is permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure?"

The Blessed One declared: "As you have put it, the absence of one thing in another is itself a threefold non-existence. A cow and a horse — before they come to be, they did not exist; this is called prior non-existence. Once they have existed, they cease to be; this is called non-existence through destruction. The absence of one thing in another, however, is not as you describe it. Son of good family, the three kinds of non-existence do not apply to nirvāṇa — only this third sense. Therefore, nirvāṇa is permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure.

"Consider, by way of analogy, the three diseases of the world: bile, wind, and phlegm. For these three diseases there are three medicines: for bile disease, butter cures it; for wind disease, sesame oil benefits it; for phlegm disease, honey benefits it. Thus the three medicines benefit the three diseases. Son of good family, sesame oil is not present within wind, and wind is not present within sesame oil; honey is not present within phlegm, and phlegm is not present within honey — yet healing occurs all the same.

"All sentient beings likewise have three diseases: attachment, aversion, and delusion. And for these three diseases there are three medicines: for the disease of attachment, one should cultivate the meditation on unattractiveness; for the disease of aversion, one should cultivate loving-kindness; for the disease of delusion, one should cultivate dependent origination. Son of good family, to remove attachment, one should cultivate what is free from attachment; to remove aversion, one should cultivate what is free from aversion; to remove delusion, one should cultivate what is free from delusion. The three medicines are not present within the three diseases, and the three diseases are not present within the three medicines.

"Son of good family, because the three medicines are not present within the three diseases, the diseases are impermanent, devoid of bliss, devoid of self, and devoid of utter purity. Because the three diseases are not present within the three medicines, the medicines are permanent, blissful, self, and utterly pure."
