Vāsiṣṭha then asked: "May the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, teach me about permanence and impermanence — which is permanence, and which is impermanence?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, form is impermanent, and so too with everything up through consciousness — all are impermanent. But liberated form is permanent, and liberated consciousness is likewise permanent."

"Son of good family, any son or daughter of good family who meditates correctly on impermanence — from form through to consciousness — should know that they have thereby attained the quality of permanence."

Vāsiṣṭha said: "Blessed One, I have understood the qualities of permanence and impermanence."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, how have you understood the qualities of permanence and impermanence?"

Vāsiṣṭha said: "Blessed One, I have understood that my own form is impermanent, and everything up through consciousness is impermanent, while liberation is permanent."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, you have repaid this body well."

Then the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Kauṇḍinya: "Vāsiṭha has attained arhatship. Give him the three Dharma robes and the alms bowl."

The venerable Kauṇḍinya did exactly as the Blessed One had instructed and gave him the robes and the alms bowl.

Then Vāsiṭha received the robes and the alms bowl, and said these words to Kauṇḍinya: "Through this wretched body I have obtained the fruit of virtue. Venerable one, without regard for the trouble it causes you, please go on my behalf before the Blessed One and say these words: 'A sinner such as I, having spoken of the Tathāgata's bones and having uttered words of disrespect toward you — I confess and openly acknowledge this fault. I do not wish to dwell long with this malignant body. I will pass into nirvāṇa.'"

Then the venerable Kauṇḍinya went to where the Buddha was, and upon arriving spoke these words to the Blessed One: "The monk Vāsiṭha, filled with deep shame and remorse, says: 'In my great foolishness I spoke of the Tathāgata's bones and uttered words of disrespect, and I have committed a fault. I confess my regret and repentance. I do not wish to keep company long with this body, which is like a venomous snake. I will pass into nirvāṇa.'"

The Blessed One said to the venerable Kauṇḍinya: "The monk Vāsiṭha, in former times, cultivated roots of virtue before immeasurable buddhas, and thus has come to abide here in accordance with the prophecy of the teaching. By so abiding in accordance with that prophecy, he has attained the true fruit. Therefore, you should pay homage to his body."

The Noble Sūtra of the Great Passing Beyond Sorrow. The fifty-second section.

Then Kauṇḍinya, having heard these words from the Blessed One, went back to where Vāsiṭha's body was and paid homage.

At the time of Vāsiṭha's cremation, various miraculous powers (ṛddhi) were displayed. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), seeing what had come to pass, cried out in a loud voice: "Vāsiṭha has obtained the mantras and conjuring arts of the ascetic Gautama, and before long he will certainly surpass even the ascetic Gautama!"

At that time, within that assembled gathering, there was one called Sāni who spoke these words: "Gautama, does there exist something called a 'self'?" The Tathāgata said nothing. "Gautama, then does there exist something called a 'non-self'?" The Tathāgata said nothing. Even when this question was put a second and a third time, the Tathāgata said nothing.

Then Sāni spoke again: "Gautama, if a self exists pervading all sentient beings, encompassing all of them, whether it be one or made — Gautama, why do you sit in silence?" The Blessed One said to Sāni: "Is what you call a 'self' something that pervades all?" Sāni said: "Gautama, it is not only I who say so. All the wise and learned say the same."

The Blessed One declared:

"Son of good family, if what is called a 'self' pervades everything, then births in the five streams of existence would all be experienced as ripening simultaneously. If that were so — if one born in the five streams were to experience simultaneous karmic ripening — then why would wanderers like yourself refrain from sinful and non-virtuous actions and practise virtuous Dharma in order to turn away from rebirth in the hells and aspire to experience birth in the body of a god in the higher realms?"

Sāni spoke: "Gautama, in our doctrine what we call the 'self' is of two kinds: the self of the fashioned body, and the self of the permanent body. It is on account of the self of the fashioned body that one abandons sinful and non-virtuous phenomena, so as not to go to the hells, and diligently applies oneself to virtuous Dharma and seeks rebirth as a god in the higher realms."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, you say that what is called a 'self' pervades everything. If this 'self' exists in the fashioned body, then it is impermanent. But if it does not exist in the fashioned body, is it fitting to say it pervades everything?"

Sāni spoke: "Gautama, the 'self' that I posit exists within the fashioned as well, and yet it is also called permanent. Gautama, consider the analogy: if a house catches fire and burns, the householder escapes. One does not say that because the house burns the householder burns. Our doctrine is similar: although this fashioned body is impermanent, at the time of the body's impermanence what is called the 'self' departs outward. Therefore what we call 'self' is both all-pervading and permanent."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, it is not fitting to say, as you maintain, that the 'self' is both all-pervading and permanent. Why? Because what pervades is of two kinds: permanent and impermanent. Furthermore, there are two further kinds: form and formless. Therefore, if, as you say, it exists in everything, it would be both permanent and impermanent, and both form and formless. Nor is it fitting to say, as you propose in your analogy, that although the house burns the householder has escaped and is therefore impermanent. Why? Because the house is not the householder and the householder is not the house. What burns is one thing; what escapes is another. Therefore what is called the 'self' is not that — for the self is form, and form is the self; the self is the formless, and the formless is the self. But if the self were formless, why do you say that when form is impermanent the self departs?

"Son of good family, consider this: if you think that what is called 'self' for all sentient beings is one and the same, that contradicts both worldly and supramundane Dharma. Why? In worldly convention there are such things as father, mother, son, and daughter. If the 'self' were one, then the father would also be the son, the son would also be the father, the mother would also be the daughter, and the daughter would also be the mother; the enemy would also be the friend, and the friend would also be the enemy; the far shore would also be the near shore, and the near shore would also be the far shore. Therefore to say that the 'self' of all sentient beings is one and the same contradicts both worldly and supramundane Dharma."

Sāni spoke: "I do not say that the 'self' of all sentient beings is one and the same. Rather, each and every individual person has their own individual self."

The Blessed One declared: "If you say that each individual person has their own individual self, then the 'self' becomes manifold — and that too is not fitting. Why? As you said before, the 'self' pervades everything. If it truly pervades everything, then the ripened fruits of all sentient beings would likewise have to be the same."

When Devadatta sees, Buddhadatta also sees; when Devadatta acts, Buddhadatta also acts; when Devadatta hears, Buddhadatta also hears — and all phenomena would become like that. Therefore, when Devadatta sees, it would not be the case that Buddhadatta does not see. For this reason, to say that what is called 'self' pervades everything is not fitting. But if it does not pervade everything, then it would become impermanent.

Sāni spoke: "Gautama, what I call 'self' does indeed pervade all sentient beings. Phenomena and non-phenomena, however, do not pervade everything. Therefore, what Buddhadatta has done is one thing, and what Devadatta has done is another."

"Therefore, Gautama, are you saying that when Buddhadatta sees, Devadatta also sees — or that when Buddhadatta hears, Devadatta also hears? That is not fitting."

The Blessed One declared: "Good man, are phenomena and non-phenomena produced by karma?"

Sāni spoke: "Gautama, they are indeed produced by karma."

The Blessed One declared: "Good man, if phenomena and non-phenomena are produced by karma, and if the very view that holds them to be congruent with one another is itself a phenomenon, then would it be fitting to call them distinct? Why? Because within the karma performed by Buddhadatta, there would also have to be the self of Devadatta; and likewise, within the karma performed by Devadatta, there would also have to be the self of Buddhadatta. Therefore, when Buddhadatta has acted, Devadatta would also have acted — and phenomena and non-phenomena would become similar in this way. Good man, if the phenomena and non-phenomena of all sentient beings are like that, then it would not be fitting for the karmic fruits to ripen differently either. Good man, from a seed comes a fruit, and that seed never thinks to itself: 'I shall produce only the fruit of a brahmin — I shall not produce the fruit of a kṣatriya, or of a vaiśya, or of a śūdra.' It makes no such distinction. Why? Because what ripens from a seed into a fruit does not cut across the four castes. Phenomena and non-phenomena are just the same: what is called 'self' does not make the distinction of thinking 'I shall become the fruit of Buddhadatta's actions and not the fruit of Devadatta's actions,' or 'I shall become the fruit of Devadatta and not the fruit of Buddhadatta.' It makes no such distinction. Why? Because karma is equal."

Sāni spoke: "Gautama, consider this analogy: if a hundred or a thousand butter-lamps are lit inside a single house, although the essences of the flames are distinct, there is no difference in the light they give. The distinctness of the flames' essences is the analogy for phenomena and non-phenomena. The absence of any difference in the illumination they produce is the analogy for what is called the 'self' of all sentient beings."

The Blessed One declared: "Good man, to say, as you do, that the light of butter-lamps is the analogy for what is called 'self' — that is not fitting. Why? The house is one thing and the butter-lamps are another, and the light of the butter-lamps would have to be present both in the essence of the flames themselves and also in the house. If what is called 'self' were like that, as you say, then 'self' would have to be present in both phenomena and non-phenomena alike; and likewise, within what is called 'self,' phenomena and non-phenomena would also have to be present."

But if what is called 'self' is absent in both phenomena and non-phenomena, then to say that it pervades everything would also be unfitting. And if it is present in both, can both the essence of the butter-lamp and its light serve together as the analogy?

Good man, if in your mind you truly regard the essence of the butter-lamp and its light as distinct and separate from one another, then why is it that when the essence of the butter-lamp is good the light too is bright, and when the essence of the butter-lamp is exhausted the light ceases to be? Therefore it is not fitting to take the essence of the butter-lamp as the analogy for phenomena and non-phenomena, and to take the light as an analogy for what is called 'self,' treating them as though there were no distinction between them. Why? Because phenomena, non-phenomena, and what is called 'self' would thereby become one and the same thing.

Sānu then said: "Gautama, the analogy you have drawn from the butter-lamp is not auspicious. Why? If drawing an analogy from the butter-lamp were auspicious, then what I stated before would stand. If it is not auspicious, why did you speak of it at all?"

The Blessed One declared: "Good man, I did not say that the analogy I gave was either auspicious or inauspicious. I gave it in relation to what is in your own mind — to illustrate whether the light exists beyond the essence of the butter-lamp, or whether the essence itself is the light. Because your mind was not at ease, you took the essence of the butter-lamp as the analogy for phenomena and non-phenomena, and the light as the analogy for what is called 'self.' And by doing so you end up asserting: that light arises from the essence; that light also exists beyond the essence; that self exists within phenomena; that phenomena exist within self; that what is not a phenomenon is self; and that self too is not a phenomenon. In affirming one extreme you cannot consistently reject the other, and this is unfitting. Therefore that analogy is not auspicious for you. And since I have shown you its implications in return, good man, that analogy is simply not a valid analogy. Because it is not valid, it is auspicious for me and inauspicious for you."

"Good man, according to what you say, since it is inauspicious for me, you should not think it is therefore also inauspicious for you. Why? Among the beings of the world, it happens that one person's own weapon harms oneself, and what one has done is enjoyed by an adversary. You who put forward this analogy are in just such a position — it is auspicious for me and not auspicious for you."

Sānu then said: "Gautama, you said earlier that I was not at ease; but now what you yourself say is also not at ease. Why? Gautama has claimed the auspicious for himself and cast the inauspicious upon me — and that too is not truly even-handed."

The Blessed One declared: "Good man, my very unevenness defeats your unevenness, so that you become even while I, through my unevenness, am auspicious. The reason my unevenness defeats your unevenness and renders you even is precisely that it is evened in accord with the noble ones (āryas)."

Sānu then said: "Gautama, if I am always even, why do you say you have defeated my unevenness? If what is called 'self' is present equally in all sentient beings, why do you say I was not at ease?"

"Good man, you yourself say that sentient beings fall into hell, fall into the birth-state of hungry ghosts, fall into the birth-state of animals, and become humans and gods. If what is called 'self' is something that pervades all five streams of existence, why do you say that the five streams are experienced? You also say that a child is born from the meeting of father and mother. If the child already existed before,

why do you say that a child comes to be from their meeting and joining? Therefore, a single person would have bodies in all five streams of existence. But if a body already existed before in all five streams, why would there be any need to act for the sake of a body? Therefore, this is not equanimity.

Good man, even the idea you hold in your mind that what is called 'self' is an agent — that too is untenable. Why is that? If what is called 'self' were an agent, why would suffering come about through its own doing, and why would ordinary people truly experience suffering? Therefore, you must understand that what is called 'self' is not an agent.

If you say that suffering was made by the self and yet was not born from a cause, then all phenomena would be the same — not born from a cause. In that case, why do you say the self is an agent? Good man, the suffering and happiness of sentient beings arise, in truth, from causes and conditions. Suffering and happiness, being such, give rise to grief and joy: at the time of grief there is no joy, and at the time of joy there is no grief. If sometimes there is joy and sometimes there is grief, why would a wise person endowed with wisdom say this is permanent?

Good man, if what you call 'self' is permanent, then why does it appear different and distinct across the ten phases of time? It is unreasonable for something with the characteristic of permanence to exist from the time of infancy all the way through to old age. Space has the characteristic of permanence — since there is not even one phase of time that applies to it, what need is there to speak of ten? Good man, if what is called 'self' is not in the time of infancy and is not in the time of old age — spanning all of that — why do you say it is inconsistent and distinct across the ten phases of time?

Good man, if what is called 'self' were an agent, then what is called 'self' would have times of flourishing and times of decline, and sentient beings too would have times of flourishing and times of decline. If what is called 'self' is like that, why would you call it permanent?

Good man, if what is called 'self' is an agent, why is it that among equally human beings there are those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties?

Good man, if what is called 'self' is an agent, then what is called 'self' would also perform bodily actions and verbal actions. But if verbal actions too were performed by what is called 'self,' why does the voice say 'there is no self,' and why does doubt arise as to whether it exists or not?

Good man, the idea you hold in your mind that there is a seer that exists beyond the eye — that too is untenable. Why? If there were some other seer existing beyond the eye, this eye here would become unnecessary; and it would be the same right up through the sense faculties of the body. And the idea that what is called 'self' sees, though by means of the eye as condition — that too is untenable. Why? Take the example of a man setting fire to a great city starting from a single flower. When asked how it burns, one would say "it burns by means of fire as the condition." Your saying that what is called 'self' sees is similar to that.

Seniya asked: Gautama, take the example of a person holding a sickle and cutting grass — in the same way, the self sees, hears, and touches by means of the five sense faculties as condition.

Good man, the sickle and the person are distinct — that is why there is someone who holds the sickle and acts. But if there is no other self beyond the sense faculties, why do you say that what is called 'self' acts by means of the sense faculties as condition?

Good man, are you saying in your mind that one holds a sickle and thereby cuts grass, and that what is called 'self' is like that?

Does what is called 'self' have hands, or does it have no hands? If it has hands, why does the self not grasp the sickle? If it has no hands, why do you say that what is called 'self' is the agent?

Good man, the blade of grass is the sickle — it is not the self, and it is not a person. If it is neither self nor person, then the sickle would not be needed at all.

Good man, a person has two kinds of action: grasping the grass and grasping the sickle. The one who grasps the sickle performs only the action of cutting. The seeing of phenomena by a sentient being is similar to that: even the seeing of form by the eye arises from an assembly and gathering of conditions. If seeing arises from the coming together of causes and conditions, why would one who is wise and possessed of wisdom say that a self exists?

Good man, is it your thinking that the body acts and thereby what is called 'self' experiences? That too is untenable. Why so? In the world, it is not seen that when Devadatta performs an action, Buddhadatta experiences its karmic maturation. If, on the other hand, you say that the body does not act and that what is called 'self' does not experience through the power of conditions — then why do you and others seek liberation from causes and conditions? If your body existed prior to all this and did not arise from causes and conditions, then even after liberation, without needing causes and conditions, the body would be born again. Whatever holds true of the body holds equally true of all the afflictions.

Seniya said: Gautama, what is called 'self' is of two kinds: one with consciousness and one without consciousness. The self without consciousness brings about the acquisition of a body. The self with consciousness brings about the relinquishing of a body. For example, when an unfired clay vessel is burned, its old color is destroyed and it cannot arise again. In the same way, the afflictions of one who is wise and possessed of wisdom, once they have been made nonexistent, can never arise again at any time.

The Blessed One declared: Good man, this thing called consciousness — is it known by gnosis, or is it known by what is called 'self'? If it is known by gnosis, why do you say 'I, the self, know'? If it is known by the self, why would one need to seek gnosis through skillful means? If you say in your mind that what is called 'self' knows by means of gnosis, that too is like an inappropriate simile about a flower.

Good man, take the example of a thorny tree: it pricks by its own nature — it is not fitting to say it takes hold of the tree's thorn and then pricks. Gnosis is similar: if gnosis knows by itself, why do you say the self takes hold of gnosis and thereby knows?

Good man, if you say that what is called 'self' is liberated from your own system's phenomena — is it attained by the self without consciousness, or attained by the self with consciousness? If it is attained by the self without consciousness, you should understand that it still has afflictions. If it is attained by the self with consciousness, you should understand that it still possesses the five sense faculties of consciousness. Why? Because there is no consciousness apart from the five sense faculties. If it comes together with the sense faculties, why would you call it liberation? And if you say that what is called 'self' is naturally pure and separate from the five sense faculties — then why do you say that the five paths and continuations pervade it, and why do you say one must be diligent in virtuous phenomena in order to attain liberation?

Good man, it is like a person shooting thorns into the sky. If what is called 'self' is pure, why do you say all the afflictions must be cut away? Is it your thinking that one is liberated from what is not a cause and not a condition? Then why are all the animals not liberated?

Seniya said: Gautama, if what is called 'self' does not exist, then who is it that remembers?

The Blessed One declared: If what is called 'self' exists, why would there be forgetting? Good man, if what is called 'self' is indeed what remembers, then why does one remember what is sinful yet not remember what one has not remembered, and why does one not remember what one does remember?

Seniya said: Gautama, if what is called 'self' does not exist, who is it that sees? Who is it that hears?

The Blessed One declared: Good man, there are the six inner faculties and the six outer objects. From the meeting of inner and outer, the six consciousnesses arise. The six consciousnesses are designated by name on the basis of dependent origination. Good man, take the example of fire, which is one and the same, yet receives distinct names based on its fuel: fire of wood is called wood-fire; based on grass, grass-fire; based on chaff, chaff-fire; based on dung, dung-fire. The mental consciousness of sentient beings is likewise: based on the eye, form, light, and desire, it is called eye-consciousness. Good man, in just this way, eye-consciousness does not exist within the eye, nor does it exist as far as desire — rather, from the meeting of the four conditions consciousness arises. Know that the same holds true as far as mental consciousness. Because they arise from gathering together through dependent origination, the wise and discerning do not speak of 'self' with respect to visual phenomena, and do not speak of 'self' even as far as tangible objects. Good man, therefore I have declared that all phenomena from eye-consciousness through mental consciousness are like a magical illusion. How are they like a magical illusion? What did not exist before comes to exist now, and having existed, it passes into non-existence.

Good man, take the following example: when butter, flour, honey, molasses, long pepper, rock salt, winter grain, Nepali citrus, coriander seeds, and such things are gathered together, the result is called a broth. Apart from those gathered ingredients, there is no broth to be found elsewhere. In the same way, what is called a sentient being, a self, a person, or an individual refers to the six inner and outer sense bases. Apart from those six inner and outer sense bases, there is no sentient being, no self, no person, and no individual to be found elsewhere.

Seniya said: Gautama, if there is no such thing as 'self,' why do people say, "I see," "I hear," "I suffer," "I am happy," "I rejoice," "I grieve"?

The Blessed One declared: Good man, if what is called 'self' is that which sees and hears, then why do you say, "I did not see," "I did not hear," when you have done something wrong in the world? Good man, take the example of four battalions assembled together — this is called an army. Yet those four battalions cannot rightly be called one single thing; nonetheless, one says "my army is brave" and "my army has defeated the enemy." The activity produced by the gathering of the inner and outer sense bases is likewise: though they are not one, one says, "I did it," "I experienced it," "I saw it," "I heard it," "I suffer," and "I am happy."

Seniya said: Gautama, according to what you say, when inner and outer are assembled, who is it that speaks, saying "I did it" and "I experienced it"?

The Blessed One declared: Through the condition of craving and ignorance, karma is born. From karma, craving is born. From craving, what arises from boundless mind is born. Mind generates conceptual thought. Conceptual thought generates wind. Wind, contacting the mind, and arising from the palate, tongue, lips, and the inverted perception of sentient beings, produces sound — and thus one says, "I did it," "I experienced it," "I saw it," and "I heard it."

"Son of good family, consider, for example, a bell hung at the top of a victory banner: by the power of the wind, sound arises. When the wind is great, the sound is great; when the wind is small, the sound is small — and yet there is no agent doing it. Son of good family, consider again: when heated iron is plunged into water, many different kinds of sound arise — yet in truth there is no agent doing so. Son of good family, ordinary worldlings conceptualize things of this kind and, because they do not distinguish them clearly, they say, 'I,' 'mine,' 'I did it,' and 'I experienced it.'"

Sānu then asked: "Gautama, if there is a self and what belongs to a self, why did you say that permanence, bliss, self, and purity are absent?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, I did not say that the six inner and outer sense bases and the six consciousnesses are permanence, bliss, self, and purity. What I said is this: it is the cessation of the six inner and outer sense bases and the six consciousnesses that is called permanence. Because it is permanent, it is called self. Because it is permanent and self, it is called bliss. Because it is permanent, self, and blissful, it is called purity. Son of good family, ordinary beings do not wish for suffering; having thoroughly severed and abandoned the causes of suffering, they come under the sway of relinquishment — and that is called self. Therefore I say there is permanence, bliss, self, and purity."

Sānu then asked: "Blessed One, out of great compassion, please teach me. What must I do to attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, everything that dwells in the world has, from beginningless time, been accompanied by great pride. In order to generate great pride, beings become causes of pride, and through pride they act. Thus the fruit of pride fully ripens, and because all mental afflictions have not been completely abandoned, permanence, bliss, self, and purity are not attained. Therefore, if ordinary beings wish to completely abandon all mental afflictions, they must completely abandon pride."

Sānu said: "Blessed One, it is so — it is exactly so. As the noble teaching says: since I had pride, by the power of pride I did not say 'Tathāgata' but said 'Gautama,' and I spoke of 'I' and 'you.' Now I have completely abandoned great pride, and so, seeking the Dharma with a sincere mind, how shall I attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, listen carefully and attend well to mind; I shall explain it to you in full. Son of good family, if it is neither self, nor other, nor a sentient being, then those very phenomena will be completely relinquished."

Sānu said: "Blessed One, I have understood, and I have also attained the genuine eye of Dharma."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, by knowing and understanding what, do you say you have attained the genuine eye of Dharma?"

He replied: "Blessed One, understanding that what is called form is neither other, nor self, nor a sentient being — and so on through consciousness — by understanding thus, I have attained the genuine eye of Dharma. Blessed One, if I am permitted to go forth and apply myself diligently to the path, please grant your assent."

The Blessed One said, "Welcome," and with that word he became a fully ordained monk, and right there he came to possess fully pure brahmic conduct and attained the fruit of arhatship.

At that time, among those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), there was one of the wandering ascetic class, of the Kāśyapa lineage, who spoke thus:

"Gautama, is the life-force identical with the body, or are the body and the life-force two separate things?" The Tathāgata remained seated in silence, saying nothing. The wanderer asked a second and then a third time, yet still the Tathāgata said nothing.

Then the wanderer Kunturu asked again: "Gautama, when a person has died and not yet taken up a new body, is it not said that the body is one thing and the life-force another? If they are indeed separate, why then does Gautama say nothing?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, I say that both body and life-force arise from dependent origination and not from what is not dependently originated. Just as it is with body and life-force, so too should all phenomena be understood in the same way."

Kunturu asked again: "Gautama, I see that certain phenomena in the world are not dependently originated."

The Blessed One declared: "What phenomena in the world do you see as not dependently originated?"

Kunturu replied: "When a great conflagration breaks out and the flames, fanned by wind, burn other places as well — that, I would say, is not dependently originated."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, even that fire arises from dependent origination, not from what is not dependently originated."

Kunturu asked: "Gautama, when a flame is cut off and extinguished, it comes neither from wood nor from fuel-fire — why then do you say it is dependently originated?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, although there is no wood and no fuel-fire, the flame is nonetheless cut off by the power of wind. Through wind as cause and condition, the flame does not simply cease to exist without cause."

Kunturu asked: "Gautama, when a person has died and not yet taken up a new body, what are the causes and conditions that make the taking up of life possible?"

The Blessed One declared: "Kunturu, ignorance and craving are the cause and condition for that. By the force of these two — ignorance and craving — as cause and condition, the continuation of life comes about. Son of good family, because of causes and conditions, the body itself is the life-force, and the life-force itself is the body. And again, because of causes and conditions, the body is one thing and the life-force is another. A wise and discerning person will not say simply and one-sidedly that the body and the life-force are categorically separate."

Kunturu said: "Blessed One, please explain and reveal this to me fully and make me comprehend cause and effect."

The Blessed One declared: "Kunturu, the cause is the five aggregates (skandhas), and the result is likewise the five aggregates. Son of good family, if sentient beings did not kindle fire, there would be no smoke."

Kunturu said: "Blessed One, I have sought and I have understood."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, what exactly is it that you know and understand?"

He replied: "Blessed One, what is called 'kindling fire' is affliction — it blazes intensely in the births of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, gods, and humans. What is called 'smoke' is the ripening of the fruit of affliction. Because it is impermanent, impure, and thoroughly foul, it is called smoke. For any sentient being who has not engaged in affliction, the ripened fruit of affliction will not arise for that being. Therefore the Tathāgata has said: 'If no fire is kindled, there is no smoke.'"

"Blessed One, since I now hold right view, I ask out of compassion: please grant me permission to go forth."

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to the venerable Kauṇḍinya, who knows all: "Grant this wanderer the going forth and confer upon him full ordination."

Then Kauṇḍinya, just as the Buddha had commanded, sought the faith of the Saṅgha of monks and went forth. When five days had passed after his full ordination, he attained the fruit of arhatship.

Among the retinue of the tīrthikas there was another wanderer, named Puṇa, who addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Gautama, because you perceive a permanent phenomenon in the world, do you declare it 'permanent'? Is that declaration true or false? Is it permanent or impermanent? Is it both permanent and impermanent? Is it neither permanent nor impermanent? Does it have a boundary or is it without boundary? Does it both have a boundary and lack a boundary? Does it have no boundary and also not lack a boundary? Are body and life-force the same? Or are body and life-force different? When the Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa, is it like going? Or is it not like going? Is it both like going and not like going? Is it neither like going nor not like going?"

The Blessed One replied: "Puṇa, I have not declared that in the world there is anything permanent, or true, or false, or impermanent, or permanent, or neither permanent nor impermanent, or that it has a boundary, or is without boundary, or both has a boundary and lacks a boundary, or neither has a boundary nor lacks a boundary, or that body and life-force are the same, or that body and life-force are different, or that when the Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa it is like going, or not like going, or both like going and not like going, or neither like going nor not like going."

Puṇa then asked: "Gautama, what fault do you see that you do not make such declarations?"

The Blessed One replied: "Whoever says, 'The world is permanent — this is true, all else is false,' that is a view. Through a view, looking upon the location of views as formations, one looks with a view, looks with attachment, looks with bondage, looks with suffering, looks with grasping, looks with destruction, looks with torment — or rather, one looks in a way that is thoroughly entangled. Puṇa, ordinary childish persons, being wholly enmeshed in views, are not freed from birth, old age, illness, and death; they revolve through the six classes of beings and experience immeasurable suffering. Up to and including 'neither like going nor not like going' — all of this is to be understood in the same way. Puṇa, because I see such faults in those views, I am not attached to them and I do not teach them to others."

Puṇa then asked: "Gautama, since you see such faults in those views, you are not attached and do not teach them — then, Gautama, to what are you now attached, and what do you teach?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, clinging to views is a phenomenon of saṃsāra. The Tathāgata, being free from the phenomena of saṃsāra, is called 'unattached.' Son of good family, the Tathāgata is called 'one who sees and one who teaches' — not 'one who is attached.' "

Puṇa asked: "Gautama, how does he see and how does he teach?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, I clearly see suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the path. Therefore I teach by fully opening up the Four Noble Truths. Because I see in this way, I have completely abandoned all views, all craving, all conflict, and all pride. Therefore I myself, endowed with thoroughly pure holy conduct, through the supreme and unsurpassed peace, have attained a permanent body. This permanent body belongs to no direction — neither east, nor west, nor south, nor north."

Puṇa then asked:

"By what cause and by what condition does this permanent body belong to no direction — neither east, nor west, nor south, nor north?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, whatever questions I put to you, answer them as they come to mind. Son of good family, what do you think? If a great fire were burning in front of you, would you know that it was ablaze?" "Just so, Gautama." "And when it goes out, would you know that it had gone out?" "Just so, Gautama." "Puṇa, if someone were to ask you: 'From where did this mass of fire come before it was burning, and where did it go when it went out?' — what would you say to that?"

Puṇa replied: "Gautama, if someone were to ask that, I would say this: fire burns in dependence upon many conditions. When the old conditions are exhausted and no new conditions are added, I would say that the fire has gone out. And if someone were further to ask, 'When the fire has gone out, in which direction did it go?' — what would be said to that?"

He replied: "Gautama, to that I would say: when the conditions are exhausted and the fire goes out, it has not gone in any direction."

"Son of good family, the Tathāgata is just like that. If there were impermanent form — and all the way up through impermanent consciousness — then it would blaze through the condition of craving. What is called 'blazing' is the experience of the twenty-five modes of existence. And so, while blazing, one may rightly say of this fire that it is in the eastern direction, or the western, or the southern, or the northern. But when present craving ceases and the ripened fruit of the twenty-five modes of existence no longer blazes, then of that one cannot speak of an eastern direction, or a southern, or a western, or a northern.

Son of good family, the Tathāgata has no impermanent form, and no impermanent consciousness — nothing up through impermanent consciousness. Therefore, the body is permanent. And if the body is permanent, it cannot be spoken of as eastern, or southern, or western, or northern."

Puṇa said: "If I might offer an analogy — would the Tathāgata be willing to hear it?"

The Blessed One replied: "Excellent! Excellent! Speak as you intend."

"Blessed One, it is like this. Outside a great city, within a grove of śāla trees, there stands a single tree that was the first to grow there, and it has reached a hundred years of age. The owner of the grove waters and tends it regularly. When the bark of that tree decays, the bark, the leaves, and all the branches fall to the ground, and only the heartwood within remains. The Tathāgata is like that tree: when everything that has decayed has been exhausted, the true Dharma alone remains.

Blessed One, I request that you grant me the going forth."

The Blessed One spoke the words "Welcome," and immediately he became a fully ordained monk, and, with his defilements exhausted, he attained the fruit of arhatship.

Then another, named Pariśuddha the Wanderer, spoke these words: "Gautama, what is the Dharma that ordinary beings fail to understand, which causes them to form views about the world as permanent, as impermanent, as both permanent and impermanent, as neither permanent nor impermanent — and all the way through to 'migrating,' 'not migrating,' and every such view?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, it is through not knowing form, and not knowing all the way up through consciousness, that they form views such as: the world is permanent — all the way through to 'it is like what migrates' and 'it is like what does not migrate.'"

The Wanderer asked: "Gautama, what is the Dharma that, when sentient beings understand it, they cease to form views such as: the world is permanent — all the way through to 'it is like what migrates' and 'it is like what does not migrate'?"

The Blessed One replied:

"Son of good family, when one knows form, and knows all the way up through consciousness, one will no longer form views such as: the world is permanent — all the way through to 'it is like what migrates' and 'it is like what does not migrate.'"

The Wanderer said: "Blessed One, please explain permanence and impermanence to me in full detail."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, whoever has abandoned what is old and does not create new karma — that person will understand permanence and impermanence."

The Wanderer said: "Blessed One, I have understood."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, what have you seen, and how have you understood?"

He replied: "Blessed One, the old is ignorance and craving. The new is clinging and becoming. Whoever thoroughly abandons ignorance and craving, and does not engage in clinging and becoming — that person correctly understands permanence and impermanence. As for myself, the eye of Dharma has arisen in me, purified with respect to the true Dharma, and I go for refuge to the Three Jewels. May the Tathāgata grant me the going forth."

The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Kauṇḍinya: "Give this wanderer the going forth and grant him full ordination."

Thereupon Kauṇḍinya, acting in accordance with the Blessed One's word, made the request and petition to the Saṅgha, and the going forth was given. Then, fifteen days later, all his defilements were exhausted and he attained the fruit of arhatship.

Now another wanderer, named Vatsā, spoke as follows: "Gautama, if I make a request, will it be granted?" The Tathāgata said nothing. In the same way this continued up to a second and a third time.

Vatsā spoke again: "Gautama, I am a friend of yours. Since our aims are not two but one, why do you remain silent and say nothing to what I ask?"

Then the Blessed One reflected in his mind: "This wanderer is gentle by nature, and because he is so very straightforward, his asking me as a friend is not for the purpose of finding fault. Whatever he asks, I should answer accordingly." Having thought this, he declared: "Come, Vatsā — excellent, excellent! Ask whatever you wish, and whatever it may be, I will give the answer."

Vatsā asked: "Gautama, is there virtue (kuśala) in the world?"

"There is."

"Gautama, is there non-virtue in the world?"

"There is."

The wanderer Vatsā then said: "Gautama, please teach and explain to us so that I may understand the Dharma of virtue and non-virtue."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, though I know those matters in full and could teach them at great length, I shall now explain just a portion to you. Son of good family, desire is non-virtue; desire directed toward liberation is virtue. Know that aversion and delusion are likewise to be understood in the same way. Taking life is non-virtue; the complete abandonment of taking life is virtue — and so on, expanded all the way through to wrong views. Son of good family, I have taught and explained to you both the threefold classification of virtuous and non-virtuous Dharmas, and also the tenfold classification of virtuous and non-virtuous Dharmas. If one who has become my attendant distinguishes and diligently practices these — from the threefold classification of virtuous and non-virtuous Dharmas all the way through to the tenfold — that person will become free of attachment, aversion, and delusion; all defilements will be exhausted; and all existence will be utterly cut off."

The Wanderer said: "Gautama, are there any monks at all in the Blessed One's teaching who are without attachment, aversion, and delusion —"

— who have exhausted all defilements and utterly cut off all existence?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, in the Buddha's teaching there are not merely one, two, three, five, or even a hundred monks who are without attachment, aversion, and delusion, who have exhausted all defilements and cut off all existence — monks of that kind are beyond counting."

The Wanderer asked: "Gautama, setting aside monks — are there even a few nuns in the Buddha's teaching who are without attachment, aversion, and delusion, who have exhausted all defilements and cut off all existence?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, in the Buddha's teaching there are not merely one, two, three, five, or even a hundred nuns who are without attachment, aversion, and delusion, who have exhausted all defilements and cut off all existence — nuns of that kind are beyond counting."

The Wanderer asked: "Gautama, setting aside monks and nuns — are there even a few laymen in the Buddha's teaching who are diligent in guarding moral discipline, who lead a life of pure celibacy, who have gone beyond doubt and cut the net of doubt?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, in the Buddha's teaching there are not merely one, two, three, five, or even a hundred laymen of that kind — laymen who are diligent in guarding moral discipline, who lead a life of pure celibacy, who have severed the last five fetters that bind through affliction, who have attained the state of non-return, who have gone beyond doubt and cut the net of doubt — laymen of that kind are beyond counting."

The Wanderer asked again: "Gautama, setting aside monks, nuns, and laymen — are there even a few laywomen in the Buddha's teaching who are diligent in guarding moral discipline, who lead a life of pure celibacy, who have gone beyond doubt and cut the net of doubt?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, in the Buddha's teaching there are not merely one, two, three, five, or even a hundred laywomen of that kind — laywomen who are diligent in guarding moral discipline, who lead a life of pure celibacy, who have severed the last five fetters that bind through affliction, who have attained the state of non-return, who have gone beyond doubt and cut the net of doubt — laywomen of that kind are beyond counting."

The Wanderer asked: "Setting aside those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen in the Buddha's teaching who are diligent in guarding moral discipline, who lead a life of pure celibacy, and who have cut the net of doubt — are there even a few laymen in the Buddha's teaching who do not indulge in the five objects of desire and who have cut the net of doubt?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, in the Buddha's teaching there are not merely one, two, three, five, or even a hundred laymen of that kind — laymen who have severed the three fetters that bind through affliction, who have attained stream-entry, who have thinned out attachment, aversion, and delusion, and who have attained the state of once-return — laymen of that kind are also beyond counting. And just as it is with laymen, so too should one understand it to be the case in full for laywomen."

The Wanderer said: "Blessed One, I wish to offer an analogy."

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent — speak just as you please."

"Blessed One, just as the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda cause a great rain to fall and spread everywhere, so too is the rain of Dharma from the Tathāgata — it falls equally upon laymen and laywomen alike."

The Wanderer continued:

"Blessed One, if members of non-Buddhist sects (tīrthikas) wish to go forth into the renunciant life, how long must the Tathāgata examine them?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, they must be examined for a period of four months; it is not fixed as one definite ruling."

"Blessed One, if it is not fixed, then out of your great compassion, may you please allow me to go forth."

The Blessed One then addressed the Venerable Kauṇḍinya: "Give this wandering colt his going forth and confer upon him full ordination."

Thereupon Kauṇḍinya, acting in accordance with the Buddha's word, made the formal motion and put the matter to the assembly of monks, and gave him the going forth. Fifteen days later, he attained the fruit of stream-entry.

Having attained that fruit, he then thought: "Whatever is to be attained through the wisdom that is gained by training — that I have attained. May I be granted an audience with the Buddha, to inform him of this." And so he went to where the Blessed One was, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, paid his respects, sat to one side, and addressed the Blessed One thus:

"Blessed One, I have attained whatever wisdom is to be attained through training. I beseech you now to teach me how to attain wisdom that goes beyond training."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, there are two things: devote yourself earnestly to calm abiding and insight. Son of good family, any monk who desires to attain the fruit of stream-entry should apply himself earnestly to these two things. Whoever desires to attain the fruit of once-return, the fruit of non-return, or the fruit of arhatship should likewise apply himself earnestly to these two things. Son of good family, any monk who desires to attain the four meditative concentrations (dhyānas), the four immeasurables, the six kinds of higher knowledge, the eight types of great beings, the eight stations of excellence, the wisdom free from dispute, the wisdom of universal scope, the wisdom of final perfection, the four kinds of analytical knowledge, vajra-like meditative absorption, the wisdom of exhaustion, and the wisdom of non-arising — should apply himself earnestly to those same two things. Son of good family, whoever desires to attain the ten grounds (bhūmis), the acceptance of dharmas as unborn, the acceptance of dharmas as without defining marks, the acceptance of dharmas as inconceivable, the conduct of a noble one, the conduct of holy life, the conduct of a god, the conduct of a bodhisattva, space-like meditative absorption, the meditative absorption of the wisdom seal, the meditative absorptions of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the earth-like meditative absorption, the absorption of non-return, the absorption of heroic advance, the vajra-like meditative absorption, unsurpassed perfect and complete awakening, and the conduct of a buddha — should apply himself earnestly to those same two things."

When the colt heard these words, he prostrated to the Blessed One, went out, and in the grove of śāla trees applied himself earnestly to those two things, and before long he attained the fruit of arhatship.

At that time, a great number of monks were on their way to where the Buddha was when they saw the colt and said: "Venerable one, where are you going?"

The monks said: "We are going into the presence of the Buddha."

The colt then said: "Venerables, when you go into the presence of the Buddha, please convey my words on my behalf: having applied myself earnestly to the two things, I have attained wisdom beyond training, and in gratitude for the Blessed One's kindness, I shall now pass into nirvāṇa."

At that time, those monks went to where the Buddha was and addressed the Blessed One, saying: "On behalf of the monk-colt: 'Having attained wisdom beyond training, and in gratitude for the Blessed One's kindness, I shall now pass into nirvāṇa.'"

The Blessed One declared: "The monk-colt has attained the fruit of arhatship. Go and pay homage to his body." At that time, the monks, in accordance with the Buddha's word, went to where the colt's remains lay and performed great acts of homage.

The Noble Sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa, the fifty-third fascicle.

At that time, the wanderer Śikhin of the needle-and-thread spoke again, saying: "Gautama, as you have said, throughout births beyond number one performs virtuous and non-virtuous deeds, and these will later, in the time to come, yield a virtuous or non-virtuous body — this position is untenable. Why? You say, Gautama, that a body is obtained through the cause of afflictions. If a body is obtained through the cause of afflictions, then which comes first: the body or the afflictions? If the afflictions come first, what do they rest in, and where do they abide? If the body comes first, would it then be fitting to say that from the cause of afflictions a body is obtained? Therefore it is not fitting to say the afflictions come first, nor is it fitting to say the body comes first. Nor is it fitting to say they are simultaneous. And to say that what comes earlier and later can be simultaneous is simply not coherent. Therefore I hold that all phenomena are exhausted in their intrinsic nature, and do not arise from causes and conditions.

"Furthermore, Gautama: solidity is the intrinsic nature of earth; moisture is the intrinsic nature of water; heat is the intrinsic nature of fire; movement is the intrinsic nature of wind; unobstructedness is the intrinsic nature of space. The intrinsic nature of the five great elements does not exist through causes and conditions. If even so much as a single phenomenon in the world exists not through causes and conditions, then the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is the same: they do not exist through causes and conditions. If, on the other hand, even one phenomenon does exist through causes and conditions, why do the intrinsic natures of the five great elements not arise from causes and conditions?

"Gautama, the liberation attained by sentient beings through virtuous or non-virtuous bodies is also intrinsic nature, not something from causes and conditions. Therefore I hold that all phenomena exist by intrinsic nature and not from causes and conditions.

"Furthermore, Gautama, worldly phenomena are fixed according to their place of function. For instance, a carpenter says: 'This wood is fit for a chariot and for a wheel,' and 'This wood is suitable for a door and a beam.' Likewise, when a goldsmith beats metal and attaches it to the neck, it is called a necklace; attached to the upper arm, it is called an armlet; placed on the finger, it is called a ring. Because it is determined by its place of function, one speaks of a determined intrinsic nature.

"Gautama, all sentient beings are the same: having a fivefold nature by continuum, they are hell-beings, hungry ghosts (pretas), animals, gods, or humans. If this is so, would it be fitting to say they change through causes and conditions?

"Furthermore, Gautama, all sentient beings each have their own separate intrinsic nature, and so all things are said to have intrinsic nature. For instance, a frog born on dry land still goes to water; a calf, the moment it is born, suckles; a fish naturally swallows things; a venomous snake, the moment it emerges, eats earth — and such behaviors, who taught them? As thorns are naturally sharp by intrinsic nature, and as the feathers of birds are naturally of distinct colors, so too are the beings of the world: with sharp faculties and —"

dull-witted and wealthy and poor and good and bad, those who attain liberation, and those who attain a final existence — therefore one should know that all phenomena each have their own separate intrinsic nature.

"Furthermore, Gautama, what you say — that attachment, aversion, and delusion arise from causes and conditions, and that the cause and condition of these three poisons are the five sense-objects — that too is untenable. Why? Take the example of a sentient being when it is asleep: the five sense-objects are not actively engaged, yet attachment, aversion, and delusion still arise. And a being dwelling in the womb, or one just emerged from the womb, cannot yet distinguish the good and bad of the five sense-objects, yet attachment, aversion, and delusion still arise. And noble sages dwelling in solitary places, though the five sense-objects are not actively engaged, still give rise to attachment, aversion, and delusion. And yet there are some who, through the operation of the six sense-faculties, do not develop attachment, do not develop aversion, and are not bewildered — therefore there is no certainty that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; they simply come down to intrinsic nature.

"Gautama, furthermore, in the world there are those who lack the five sense-faculties and yet possess great wealth and become powerful. And there are those who possess the five sense-faculties and yet are wretched, destitute, and powerless, serving as servants to others. If things arose from causes and conditions, why would it be so? Therefore the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is each distinct, and does not arise from causes and conditions.

"Gautama, furthermore, in the world there are infants of a million kinds who, though they cannot yet distinguish the five sense-objects, at one moment laugh and at another moment weep. When they laugh, they know joy; when they weep, they know unhappiness. Therefore all phenomena have their own distinct intrinsic nature.

"Gautama, furthermore, phenomena in the world are of two kinds: existent and non-existent. Space is an example of the existent; a rabbit's horn is an example of the non-existent. Both of these two phenomena — the existent is not from causes and conditions, and the non-existent is not from causes and conditions. Therefore all phenomena simply come down to intrinsic nature, and do not arise from causes and conditions."

The Blessed One then declared: "Son of good family, as you argue, that all phenomena are like the intrinsic nature of the five great elements — that cannot be right. Why? Son of good family, if your five great elements are permanent, then why do you say that all phenomena are not permanent? And if worldly things are impermanent, why would the intrinsic nature of the five great elements not be impermanent? If the five great elements are permanent, then worldly things should likewise be permanent by that reasoning. Therefore, since you claim that the intrinsic nature of the five great elements exists and is not from causes and conditions, to say that all phenomena are likewise like the five great elements — that cannot be right.

"Son of good family, as you argue, it is also untenable to say that intrinsic nature exists in a fixed locus of necessity. Why? Because names are acquired through causes and conditions. If from a cause a name is acquired, then the object too acquires its name through a cause. How does it acquire a name from a cause? Take, for example: when strung together they are called a garland; when hung around the neck they are called a necklace; when put on the wrist they are called a bracelet; when fixed to a chariot they are called a wheel; when wood and grass blaze they are called a fire of wood and grass. Son of good family, when a tree first grows, it has none of the intrinsic nature of an arrow or a spear — yet through causes and conditions it is fashioned into an arrow or a spear. Therefore it is unreasonable to say that all phenomena have intrinsic nature.

"Son of good family, as you argue, that a frog born on dry land goes to water by intrinsic nature, or that a calf suckles the very moment of its birth by intrinsic nature — that too is untenable. Why?

If going to water is not due to causes and conditions, and if both — going to water and going into fire — appear equally to be without causes and conditions, then why does the frog not go into fire? If a calf suckling the very moment of birth by intrinsic nature is not due to causes and conditions, and if both — suckling a mother and suckling a horn — appear equally to be without causes and conditions, then why does the calf not suckle a horn?

Son of good family, if someone were to say that all phenomena have intrinsic nature yet that teaching and training produce no development or transformation, that too is untenable. Why? Because it is plainly evident that development and transformation do arise from present teaching and training. Therefore one should understand that there is no such thing as intrinsic nature.

Son of good family, if all phenomena had intrinsic nature, then it would be right for all brahmins to slaughter sheep and make offerings to the gods as a means of performing right bodily action. But if purification could come from such offerings, one should understand that intrinsic nature, too, does not exist.

Son of good family, in the discourse of the worldly, phenomena are spoken of under three aspects: what is being done, what is being done by an agent, and what has been done. If all phenomena had intrinsic nature, why would they be designated in the world under these three aspects? From the very fact that they are designated under three aspects, it is evident that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.

Son of good family, if all phenomena had intrinsic nature, then all phenomena would have a fixed intrinsic nature, each distinctly its own. But if each thing had a single, fixed intrinsic nature of its own, why does sugarcane give rise to juice, to molasses, to sugar, to wine, and to vinegar? If its intrinsic nature were one and fixed, why would all these things come to be from it? And if such different things arise from a single entity, one should understand that it is impossible for all phenomena to have a single fixed intrinsic nature that is distinctly each thing's own.

Son of good family, if all phenomena were determined to have a single intrinsic nature, why is it that noble ones may drink the juice of the sugarcane tree, and molasses, and sugar, yet it is improper for them to drink it when it has become wine — and then again becomes proper to drink when it has turned to vinegar? Therefore one should understand that there is no fixed intrinsic nature. And if there is no fixed intrinsic nature, how could it be right to say that things do not arise from causes and conditions?

Son of good family, as for how you might give an example to demonstrate that all phenomena have intrinsic nature — if such an example can be stated, one should understand from that very example that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. For if intrinsic nature existed, there would be nothing that could serve as an example. It is the wise and discerning of the world who give examples; therefore one should understand that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are without any single fixed intrinsic nature.

Son of good family, your claim that the body comes first or that the afflictions come first is likewise untenable. Why? If I were to say the body comes first, you might either agree with me or counter that the body does not come first. Son of good family, the body and the afflictions of all sentient beings are both without prior or subsequent — they exist simultaneously. Though they exist simultaneously in this way, nevertheless the body arises from the causes of the afflictions; the afflictions do not arise from the causes of the body.

If it occurs to you to think that, just as a person's two eyes are obtained simultaneously and neither depends on the other — the right not depending on the left, the left not depending on the right — so too the afflictions and the body are similar in that way, that too is untenable. Why? Son of good family, in the world, when seen with the eye, the wick of a lamp and its light both exist simultaneously; yet the light arises because of the wick, and not the light from the absence of the wick.

Son of good family, if it occurs to you to think that because the body does not come first, it is without a cause — that too is untenable. Why? If one were to say that because the body comes first it is without cause and condition and therefore does not exist, then by that same reasoning you ought to say that all phenomena are without cause and condition. If you do not say so because they are not seen to be causeless, then since pots and so forth are presently perceived directly as having arisen from causes and conditions, why do you not say the same? Just as a pot is that way, so too should the causes and conditions of what precedes the body be understood in the same manner.

Son of good family, whether phenomena appear or do not appear, all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and have no intrinsic nature. Son of good family, if you were to say that all phenomena have intrinsic nature and are without cause and condition, then why do you say that the five great elements exist? The very intrinsic nature of the five great elements is itself cause and condition.

Son of good family, while it may be that the five great elements have causes and conditions in that way, it is unreasonable to say that all phenomena likewise conform to the causes and conditions of the five great elements. That would be like the worldly saying: "Since all those who have gone forth from home life are devoted to guarding moral discipline, therefore outcasts and the like are also devoted to guarding moral discipline."

Son of good family, when you say, as you maintain, that the five great elements have a fixed intrinsic nature — when I examine it, that so-called nature is changeable and is not fixed. Son of good family, in your system butter, fat, and plant resins are called "earth," but that designation of yours as earth is not definitive, for at certain times the same thing can serve as water, and at other times it can serve as earth. Therefore it is not correct to call it inherently solid.

Son of good family, in your system what is called "fire" with regard to red copper, bronze, copper, iron, gold, and silver — that has four intrinsic natures: when it flows, it is called water; when it moves, it is called wind; when it is hot, it is called fire; when it is solid, it is called earth. Why then designate it as necessarily of the nature of fire? Son of good family, the intrinsic nature of water is to flow. Even if water freezes, it should not be called earth — it is still called water. Why? Because when waves stir, that stirring is not called wind. Since movement is not called wind in that case, it is equally unreasonable to say that frozen water is not water.

In the same way, since both those substances arise from causes and conditions, why do you say that all phenomena do not arise from causes and conditions?

Son of good family, it is not tenable to say that the five sense faculties — seeing, hearing, feeling, knowing, and touching — are by intrinsic nature what they are and did not arise from causes and conditions. Why? Son of good family, if intrinsic nature were by its very nature something that does not change, then since the intrinsic nature of the eye is seeing, it would follow that one should always be seeing, and that there should be no distinction between times of seeing and times of not seeing. Therefore, know that seeing occurs through causes and conditions, and not from the absence of causes and conditions.

Son of good family, your assertion that the arising of attachment and liberation from it do not arise from the cause of the five sense objects — that too is untenable. Why? Son of good family, while it is the case that the arising of attachment and liberation from it do not arise from the cause of the five sense objects themselves, attachment arises through conceptuality directed toward what is non-virtuous, and liberation comes about through conceptuality directed toward what is virtuous. Son of good family, attachment arises and liberation occurs through inner causes and conditions, while through outer causes and conditions they arise and increase.

Therefore, your claim that all phenomena have an intrinsic nature of their own, and that attachment and liberation from it do not arise from the cause of the five sense objects — that too is untenable. Son of good family, according to what you say, those who possess their faculties intact are poor and without power, while those whose faculties are impaired and defective are wealthy and endowed with power. Viewed from that standpoint, the claim that there is an intrinsic nature independent of causes and conditions is untenable. Why? Because sentient beings undergo karmic maturation from their karma. That maturation of results is of three kinds: maturation that is apparent in this very life, maturation that occurs after birth, and maturation that occurs in a later life. Poverty and wealth, and possession or lack of intact faculties, are each distinct. If there were an intrinsic nature, those with intact faculties would naturally be wealthy, and the wealthy would naturally have intact faculties. Since this is not the case, it is certain that there is no intrinsic nature, and that things arise from causes and conditions.

Son of good family, according to what you say, in this world countless millions of infants, without distinguishing among the five sense objects, sometimes cry and sometimes laugh. The claim that all things therefore have an intrinsic nature is also untenable. Why? For if there were an intrinsic nature, one who laughs would always laugh and one who cries would always cry — it would be wholly unreasonable for them to sometimes laugh and sometimes cry. But precisely because they sometimes laugh and sometimes cry, one should understand that all things arise from causes and conditions. Therefore the claim that all phenomena have an intrinsic nature and do not arise from causes and conditions is unreasonable.

Sarvaśūra then asked: Blessed One, if all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, from what causes and conditions does this body arise?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, the causes and conditions of this body are afflictions and karma.

Sarvaśūra asked: Blessed One, if this very body has arisen from afflictions and karma, is it possible to sever afflictions and karma?

The Blessed One declared: It is so. Just so.

Sarvaśūra asked again: Blessed One, I beg you to explain and teach me in detail so that, having heard it, I may be decisively and unwaveringly established in this very understanding.

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, if one knows the two extremes and is unobstructed in the Middle Way, that person will completely sever afflictions and karma.

Sarvaśūra said: Blessed One, I have understood and realized this; the eye of Dharma has become pure and clear in regard to the sacred Dharma.

The Blessed One declared: In what way have you understood and realized it?

He replied: Blessed One, the two extremes are form and liberation from form. What is called the Middle Way is the noble eightfold path. The same elaboration applies in the same manner to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

The Blessed One declared: Excellent! Excellent! Son of good family, you have fully realized the two extremes and have completely severed afflictions and karma.

He said: Blessed One, I request the going forth and full ordination.

The Blessed One said, "Welcome," and he became a fully ordained monk. At that very moment all afflictions of the three realms were severed, and he attained the fruit of arhatship.

Then another brahmin, called Mahāvistara, also spoke these words: Gautama, do you know what I am thinking?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, nirvāṇa is permanent. Conditioned phenomena are impermanent.

"Crookedness is wrong view. Straightness is the noble path."

The brahmin asked: Gautama, for what reason and on what grounds did you say that?

The Blessed One declared: Son of good family, you were thinking: "Going on alms-round is permanent; being invited as a guest is impermanent; crookedness is base; straightness is the banner of victory." Therefore nirvāṇa is permanent, conditioned phenomena are impermanent, crookedness is wrong view, and straightness is the Noble Eightfold Path — it is not as you were thinking before.

The brahmin said: Gautama, you have truly known what I was thinking. Will all sentient beings be fully liberated by the Noble Eightfold Path?

At that moment the Blessed One said nothing and gave no reply.

The brahmin said: Gautama, if you know what I was thinking, why do you sit in silence without giving an answer to what I asked?

Then the venerable Kauṇḍinya spoke these words: Great brahmin, if one were to ask whether the world has an end or has no end, the Tathāgata, by the very nature of reality, says nothing and gives no reply. The Noble Eightfold Path is straightness. Passing beyond sorrow is permanence. If one applies oneself diligently to the Noble Eightfold Path, one will attain liberation. If one does not apply oneself diligently, one will not attain it. Great brahmin, consider this example: a great citadel has four walls with no opening or passage for escape — only a single gate. If the gatekeeper of that gate is wise and discerning, he will let pass those who should rightly pass, and he will not let pass those who should not pass. He may not know the exact number of all who travel through, yet he knows for certain that all who travel through must pass through that gate. Son of good family, the Tathāgata is just like this. The citadel is the analogy for passing beyond sorrow. The gate is the analogy for the Noble Eightfold Path. The gatekeeper is the analogy for the Tathāgata. Son of good family, although the Tathāgata has not declared whether it is exhaustible or inexhaustible, to whatever extent exhaustion occurs, that occurs through diligent application to the Noble Eightfold Path.

The brahmin said: Excellent! Excellent! Venerable Kauṇḍinya is supremely skilled in teaching the Tathāgata's sacred Dharma. I too have faith, knowing the citadel and the path and trusting one such as the gatekeeper.

Kauṇḍinya said: Excellent! Brahmin, it is excellent that you have aroused a vast and unsurpassed mind.

The Blessed One declared: Kauṇḍinya, do not say that. This brahmin has not aroused that mind for the first time just now. Kauṇḍinya, in a past age, incalculable eons ago, before a previous immeasurable number of Blessed Ones had passed, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, a fully and perfectly awakened one, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer and guide of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One, by the name of All-Pervasive Light. This brahmin, after arousing the awakening mind directed toward unsurpassed and perfect awakening in relation to that buddha, became fully awakened in this excellent aeon, thoroughly penetrating and realizing the defining marks of phenomena — and though he has done so for a long time, for the sake of sentient beings he appears as a non-Buddhist adherent and acts as though he does not know. Therefore, Kauṇḍinya, do not say "Excellent, excellent, you have aroused the unsurpassed mind."

At that time the Blessed One, though knowing already, asked the venerable Kauṇḍinya: Where is the monk Nanda now?

The venerable Kauṇḍinya replied: Blessed One, the monk Nanda is at this moment, twelve leagues beyond this Sāla grove, being fully assailed by sixty-four thousand māras.

Those māras, having emanated in the form of Tathāgatas, spoke various teachings. Some declared that all phenomena arise through dependent origination; others declared that all phenomena do not arise through dependent origination. Some declared that all phenomena arising through dependent origination are permanent; others declared that all phenomena arising through dependent origination are impermanent. Some declared that the five aggregates are real; others declared that they are illusions. And in the same way they taught at length concerning the sense bases and the elements. Some declared that dependent origination exists; others declared that only the four conditions exist. Some declared that all phenomena are like illusions, like emanations, like mirages. Some declared that the Dharma is attained through the cause of hearing; others declared that it is attained through the cause of reflection; others declared that it is attained through the cause of meditation. Some taught the Dharma of the thorough realization of the repulsive; others taught the Dharma of the movement of the breath, inward and outward. Some taught the thorough establishment of the four foundations of mindfulness and the perfect contemplation thereof. Some taught the three objectives of correct conduct and the seven skillful means. Some taught heat, the summit, patience, the supreme worldly dharma, the path of learning, the path of no more learning, and the ten bodhisattva grounds from the first through the tenth. Some taught emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Some taught the class of sūtras, the class of melodic utterances, the class of verses, the class of prophecies, the class of deliberate teachings, the class of present and past events, the class of birth stories, the class of origin narratives, the class of accounts of realization, the class of wondrous teachings, the class of extensive teachings, and the class of definitive teachings. Some taught the four foundations of mindfulness, the four perfect abandonments, the four bases of miraculous power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven limbs of awakening, and the eight limbs of the noble path. Some taught inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner and outer emptiness, emptiness of the conditioned, emptiness of the unconditioned, emptiness of beginninglessness and endlessness, emptiness of intrinsic nature, emptiness of non-discarding, emptiness of the unobjective, emptiness of intrinsic characteristics, emptiness of signlessness, emptiness of the aggregates, emptiness of the elements, emptiness of the sense bases, emptiness of virtue, emptiness of non-virtue, emptiness of the indeterminate, emptiness of awakening, emptiness of the path, emptiness of nirvāṇa, emptiness of conduct, emptiness of attainment, emptiness of the ultimate, emptiness of emptiness itself, and great emptiness. Some displayed the superknowledges (abhijñā): fire and water arising from the body — when water flows from the upper part of the body, fire blazes from the lower; when water flows from the lower part of the body, fire blazes from the upper; when the right armpit is lowered, water issues from the left; when the left armpit is lowered, water issues from the right; and from one armpit the sound of thunder rolls, while from the other armpit rain falls. Some displayed the many buddha-fields. Some displayed the bodhisattva first descending into the womb, being born, then taking seven steps in each direction; enjoying the five objects of desire in the palace; from the time of first going forth, performing austerities; proceeding to the foot of the tree of awakening and entering into meditative absorption.

Having routed the armies of Māra, turning the wheel of Dharma, and displaying great miraculous powers, some also demonstrated complete passing beyond sorrow into nirvāṇa.

The Blessed One's monk Ānanda, upon seeing such things as these, thought to himself: "Who has performed these miraculous feats, never seen before? Surely they must be the work of the Blessed One Śākyamuni?" Yet he could find no resolve as to whether he should rise, or speak, or what he should do.
