Now the monk Ānanda, seized by Māra's snare, was thinking to himself: "The teachings spoken by the blessed buddhas differ from one another — so what shall I now take hold of?" The Blessed One explained that the monk Ānanda had in this way been experiencing great suffering, and that even though he called the Tathāgata to mind, there was none to serve as a companion and ally; and so he was not present in this assembly circle.

At that moment the great bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, prince of Dharma, spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, within this assembly circle there are bodhisattvas who, having aroused the mind of awakening set toward unsurpassed perfect and complete awakening, have taken one more birth; and others who, having aroused the awakening mind, have taken birth innumerable times thereafter, honoring innumerable buddhas with offerings, and whose minds have become supremely steadfast. Beginning with the perfection of generosity (dāna) and completing every perfection through to the Perfection of Wisdom, endowed with qualities from long ago, having served innumerable buddhas and led a perfectly pure holy life, they are irreversible from the awakening mind; they have attained the patience of the irreversible, attained the dhāraṇī of the irreversible, attained patience with the Dharma, and attained the meditative absorption of courageous progress and innumerable other absorptions besides. With all of this, they never give rise to any doubt regarding the sūtras of the Great Vehicle; and they are supremely skilled in teaching and disclosing that the Three Jewels share a single defining characteristic, that they are permanent, abiding, and neither changing nor shifting. Even when they hear inconceivable phenomena, they feel no astonishment or wonder. Even upon hearing the many teachings on emptiness, their minds neither shrink back nor are frightened; and they directly realize the defining characteristics of all phenomena. They hold the twelve branches of scripture and are supremely skilled in their meaning. Moreover, if those who are not like this could yet hold the twelve branches of the scriptural word of innumerable buddhas — how much more should these be able to hold the synonyms of this Dharma of nirvāṇa?"

With this in mind, he addressed Kauṇḍinya, asking: "Where is the monk Ānanda?"

Then the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī: "Listen well, and take this deeply to heart. Son of good family, more than thirty years have passed since my perfect and complete awakening. While dwelling at Rājagṛha, at that time and on that occasion I spoke thus to the monks: 'O monks, which of you can hold the twelve branches of scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, serve as my attendant, and also be able to act for my benefit?' Within the assembly, the venerable Kauṇḍinya, he who knows all, spoke to me thus: 'I myself can hold the twelve branches of the scriptures spoken by the Tathāgata, and I can act both as attendant upon the Tathāgata and in my own benefit.' To this I replied: 'Kauṇḍinya, you yourself are old and bent — if an attendant is needed, how will you attend upon me?' Then Śāriputra said —"

Then Śāriputra said: "I myself can hold all the scriptures, serve as attendant for all activities, and also act for my own benefit." At that time I said to Śāriputra as well: "You yourself are old and bent — if an attendant is needed, how will you attend upon me?" And so it went, from that point through to the five hundred arhats, each offering to serve and each being refused by me — let this be understood in full detail in just the same way.

Now at that time Maudgalyāyana had gathered within that assembly, and he thought to himself: "If the Tathāgata has not appointed any among the five hundred monks as attendant, then in whom does the heart of the Blessed One delight?" He entered into meditative absorption, and perceived that the Tathāgata's heart was gladdened and delighted with Ānanda — just as when the sun first rises, its light falls upon the western wall. Rising from his absorption, he said to Kauṇḍinya: "Venerable one, I have examined this matter: the Tathāgata delights in Ānanda as his attendant." Thereupon Kauṇḍinya, together with the five hundred arhats, went to where Ānanda was and said to him: "Ānanda, you have been appointed as attendant upon the Tathāgata — please accept." Ānanda replied: "Venerable one, I do not presume to serve as attendant upon the Tathāgata. Why? The Tathāgata is majestic as a lion king, as a nāga, as fire — I am far too weak, and do not presume to serve as his attendant." The monks said: "Ānanda, do as we instruct and serve as attendant upon the Tathāgata — great benefit and happiness will come to you." This they urged upon him two and three times. Still Ānanda said: "Venerable ones, I do not seek even great benefit and happiness — I do not presume to serve as attendant upon the Tathāgata."

Then Maudgalyāyana said to Ānanda: "You do not understand." Ānanda replied: "Venerable one, please explain it to me." Maudgalyāyana said: "When the Tathāgata previously sought an attendant from within the Saṅgha, the five hundred arhats each offered to serve, yet the Tathāgata accepted none of them. I entered into meditative absorption and looked, and I perceived that the Tathāgata's heart is delighted with you — so why do you decline?" When Ānanda heard these words, he joined his palms together, knelt upon his knees, and spoke thus: "Venerable one, if that is truly so, then if the Tathāgata grants me three requests, I will, in accordance with the Saṅgha's instruction, serve as attendant upon the Tathāgata." Maudgalyāyana said: "What are your wishes?" Ānanda said: "My three wishes are these: if the Tathāgata permits me to decline whenever he offers me leftover food; if the Tathāgata goes to a donor's home and permits me not to go; and if the Tathāgata permits me to go anywhere at any time without restriction — then I will, in accordance with the Saṅgha's instruction, serve as attendant upon the Tathāgata."

Thereupon Kauṇḍinya and the five hundred monks returned to where I was and spoke to me thus: "When we instructed the monk Ānanda, he said: 'If three requests are granted, I will act in accordance with the Saṅgha's instruction.'" Mañjuśrī, at that time I said to Ānanda: "Excellent! Excellent!" For I had known from the outset that the monk Ānanda, being endowed with wisdom, would prove a worthy vessel. Why?

Because people would say, "You serve the Tathāgata for the sake of robes and food" — that is why I said I would not accept worn-out robes and would not go to his table as a guest.

Kauṇḍinya then said: "The monk Ānanda, endowed with wisdom — if he were to go about only at fixed times and measured intervals, he would be unable to accomplish extensively the benefit and welfare of the fourfold assembly. That is why he requested the freedom to come and go without restriction of time."

Kauṇḍinya then said: "I, for my part, have granted all three of the monk Ānanda's requests as asked." Thereupon Maudgalyāyana went to where the monk Ānanda was and said to him: "I presented your three requests, and the Tathāgata in his great compassion has granted them all."

Ānanda said: "Venerable one, if the Blessed One has granted this, then I shall serve as his attendant."

Mañjuśrī, Ānanda served as my attendant for more than twenty years, and he was endowed with eight inconceivable qualities. What are those eight?

First, though he served as my attendant for more than twenty years, he never went to a table as a guest in my place. Second, from the time he began serving as my attendant until just now, he never accepted worn-out robes. Third, when he came into my presence as my attendant, he never came at an improper time. Fourth, though he served as my attendant and, being possessed of afflictions, went in my train to royal palaces and to the residences of great noble families, even when he saw beautiful women, or daughters of gods, or daughters of nāgas, no thought of desire arose in him. Fifth, having served as my attendant, he would take up the twelve branches of scripture (sūtra and so forth) that I had taught, and having heard them even once, he never needed to ask again — just as when water is poured from one vessel into another vessel, not a drop is lost. The one exception was on the occasion when the regent Viḍūḍabha slaughtered the Śākya clan and razed the city of Kapilavastu. At that time Ānanda was utterly distressed and wept aloud, and he came to where I was and addressed me thus: "The Tathāgata was born in this city, and I too was born here; since we are alike in being of the Śākya lineage, why is it that the Tathāgata shines with brilliance and radiance while I have become dull and without lustre?" I then said to him: "Ānanda, I attend earnestly to the meditative absorption of emptiness (samādhi) — that is why I am different from you." Then, three years later, he came to me again and asked: "Blessed One, is it true or false that I previously, in Kapilavastu, requested the Tathāgata's instruction on the meditative absorption of emptiness?" I said to Ānanda: "It is true, it is true." Sixth, though he served as my attendant, he had not obtained the wisdom that knows the minds of others — yet he knew which meditative absorption the Tathāgata was dwelling in. Seventh, though he served as my attendant, he had not obtained the wisdom born of aspirational prayer — yet when any sentient being came into the Tathāgata's presence, he perceived directly which fruit of the contemplative life that being had already attained, which they would attain in the future, and by means of what kind of body — divine or human — the attainment would come. Eighth, having served as my attendant, he comprehended and realized all that the Tathāgata intended and taught.

Noble son, the monk Ānanda was thus endowed with these eight inconceivable qualities, and it is for this reason that the monk Ānanda is renowned as the treasury of one who has heard much. Noble son, the monk Ānanda, being endowed with eight qualities of Dharma, was able to hold and preserve the twelve branches of scripture taught by the Tathāgata. What are those eight qualities? They are as follows: a faculty of faith that is exceedingly stable, being extremely upright, being free of illness in body, being endowed with diligence, being endowed with mindfulness,

being free of pride, being endowed with meditative absorption and wisdom, and being endowed with the arising of wisdom from what has been heard. The attendant of Mañjuśrī, the buddha Viśāladarśin, named Anāmaya, was likewise endowed with these eight qualities of Dharma. The attendant of the Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣin, named Cāpaka; the attendant of the buddha Sarvasattvāpāyin, named Upaśānta; the attendant of the buddha Mithyāprasādavinodana, named Pati; the attendant of the buddha Suvarṇamuni Puṇyatrāṇa, named Sote; and the attendant of the buddha Kāśyapa, named Yābamita — all of these were likewise endowed with these eight qualities of Dharma. And so too, at this very time, my beloved one is endowed with these eight qualities. It is for this reason that the monk Ānanda is renowned as the treasury of one who has heard much.

Noble son, just as you have said, immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas have gathered here in this maṇḍala of the assembly. Yet those bodhisattvas, acting out of great loving-kindness and great compassion, do what is difficult to do, and so, through the power of their loving-kindness and compassion, each has their own activities — taming their respective retinues and performing the work of adorning their own bodies. Therefore, when I pass completely into nirvāṇa, they will not be able to proclaim the twelve branches of scripture in their full extent. And if bodhisattvas were to proclaim them here and there, others would not place their trust in it. Mañjuśrī, the monk Ānanda is my younger brother, and for over twenty years he served as my attendant, retaining everything he heard — just as water poured from one vessel into another vessel. It is for this reason that I summoned Ānanda, asking what his name was, in order to have him hold this sūtra of passing into complete nirvāṇa. The monk Ānanda will teach even those bodhisattvas who have not heard it, teaching it in full detail; and whatever Ānanda has heard, all of it will be thoroughly understood and realized.

Mañjuśrī, at this present time, twelve yojanas from here, in another place, the monk Ānanda is being harassed by sixty-four thousand māras. Go to him and call out loudly to those māras: "Listen well! Listen well! This is the great dhāraṇī (Skt. dhāraṇī) spoken by the Tathāgata." Announce this to gods (devas), nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, great mahoragas, humans, non-humans, mountain deities, tree deities, water deities, ocean deities, house deities, and all the rest — there is not a single deity among all these gods who, upon merely hearing the name of this dhāraṇī, would fail to pay reverence, or who would fail to hold the name of the dhāraṇī. This dhāraṇī was proclaimed by as many buddhas as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges rivers, and one who hears it will abandon a female body and will come to recall past lives. If someone practices the five modes — living in celibacy, abstaining from meat, abstaining from alcohol, abstaining from pungent root vegetables, and delighting in solitary places — and with a mind of faith reads this dhāraṇī aloud, or recites it, or copies it into a book, that person will surpass seventy-seven koṭis of sinful and non-virtuous actions.

Then the Blessed One declared the mantra:

Amale, vimale, nirmale, mugale, hemala-jagarbhe, samantabhadre, śavatha, sadanne, paramārthasādhane, manase, aśudghe, vilagi, amalete, balammi, balamba-svare, puṇye puṇye, manoladai.

At that moment, Mañjuśrī, the youthful one, having received that dhāraṇī from the Blessed One, went to where Ānanda was, and spoke these words to those māras: "Retinue of māras, listen well! I shall recite the dhāraṇī I have received from the Blessed One," — and so he spoke.

The moment the king of māras heard that dhāraṇī, he gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. He wholly abandoned the deeds of māras and released Ānanda. Mañjuśrī, the youthful one, accompanied by Ānanda, came back to where the Buddha was, and Ānanda bowed before the Buddha and sat to one side.

Then the Blessed One spoke these words to Ānanda: "Outside the grove of sāla trees there is a wandering ascetic called Śīntu Zangpo who is a hundred and twenty years of age, old and decrepit. Though he has attained the five kinds of higher knowledge, he has not relinquished his pride. He has attained the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and has grasped at it as if it were the gnosis of omniscience, thinking it to be nirvāṇa. Go to him and deliver this message: 'The arising of a Tathāgata in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower. This very night, at the middle hour of the night, he will pass into complete nirvāṇa. If there is something you need to do, now is the time — do it, lest regret arise in you later.' If you deliver the message, he will certainly listen. Why so? Because for five hundred past lives you were born as Śīntu Zangpo's son, and the habitual tendency of his affection and regard for you has not yet been exhausted. Therefore he will listen to words conveyed by you."

Then Ānanda, following the Buddha's command, went to where Śīntu Zangpo was and spoke these words: "Good sir, know this: the arising of a Tathāgata in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower. This very night, at the middle hour of the night, he will pass into complete nirvāṇa. Whatever there is to be done — now is the time. Do it without letting regret arise later."

Śīntu Zangpo replied: "Excellent! Ānanda, I shall go to where the Tathāgata is."

Then Ānanda accompanied Śīntu Zangpo and came to where the Buddha was. Śīntu Zangpo inquired after the Buddha's health and then addressed him thus: "Gautama, I have a question. Please answer it as I have thought to ask it."

The Blessed One declared: "Śīntu Zangpo, now is the time — ask whatever you wish, and I shall answer each question."

He said: "Gautama, there are ascetics (śramaṇas) and brahmins who say this: 'All the suffering and happiness that every sentient being experiences is entirely due to past karma. Therefore, if one strives to guard ethical discipline and the body and mind experience suffering, that suffering will exhaust past karma. When past karma is exhausted, suffering will be exhausted. When suffering is exhausted, one passes beyond sorrow.' What is the nature of what they are saying?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, if there are ascetics or brahmins who speak in such a way, then out of compassion for them you should go to them again and again and ask: 'Is what you say true?' And if such a one says, 'Yes, what I said is true — why? Because, Gautama, I directly perceive it myself: there are some sentient beings who commit sinful and unwholesome deeds and yet are prosperous and powerful; there are others who perform virtuous actions and yet are impoverished and without power; there are some who exert themselves in many ways and still do not obtain wealth, while others obtain it without any effort at all; there are some who possess a mind of loving-kindness and do not take life, yet their life is short; and there are others who delight in taking life and yet live to the end of their allotted span —'

there are some who are utterly pure in their celibate conduct, diligent in guarding their moral discipline, and yet some among them attain liberation while others do not.

Therefore, if you say that all the pleasure and pain experienced by sentient beings have their cause and condition in past karma, then I, in turn, would ask you this: Do you directly perceive past karma? If such karma exists, is it much or little? By practising austerities now, how much of it can be eliminated? Will that karma be exhausted, or will it not be exhausted? And if it will be exhausted, will it all be exhausted together?

If you were to tell me that you do not know, then I would offer you this analogy. Suppose a person is struck by a poisoned arrow. His friends and relatives find a surgeon skilled in removing arrows, and when the arrow is extracted, the person's body becomes thoroughly comfortable. Or even if ten years later that same surgeon extracts the arrow and treats the wound with medicine and it heals, one would clearly remember that this was a great relief. Now if you do not even know the past karma, how can you know that practising austerities in the present is able to eliminate past karma?

Suppose he were then to say this: "Gautama, you too have past karma — what fault, then, is there in my past karma alone? And besides, from the sūtras taught by Gautama himself it is said: 'When one sees someone who is wealthy, endowed with resources, and powerful, one thinks: this person made offerings in the past' — is that not past karma?" To this I would say: that is known through inference, not through direct and precise knowledge.

In my teaching, some understand effects from causes, and others understand causes from effects. In the teaching of the buddhas, there is both past karma and present karma. But yours is not like that — you hold that there is only past karma and no present karma. Your Dharma does not sever karma through skillful means and application, whereas my teaching is not like that — it does sever karma through skillful means and application. You say that when karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted. I say it is not like that — when afflictions are exhausted, both karma and suffering are exhausted. Therefore it is your past karma that I am criticising.

He might then say: "Gautama, I do not know. My teacher said such and such — I am not at fault." But to this I would reply: Who then is your teacher? He might say: "My teacher is Pūraṇa Kāśyapa." Then I would say to him: What harm is there in asking your teacher directly whether he knows past karma?

If your teacher says he does not know, why do you listen to his words? If he says he does know, then ask him this: Does a middling cause of suffering produce the greatest and intermediate degrees of suffering? Does an intermediate cause of suffering produce the greatest and lowest degrees of suffering? Does the greatest cause of suffering produce intermediate and lowest degrees of suffering? If he says it does not, then ask further: Teacher, why do you say that the pleasure and pain experienced by sentient beings come from past causes alone and not from present ones? And also ask: Is the suffering experienced right now the karma of a past time?

If it comes from past time, then all past karma has been exhausted. But if it has all been exhausted, why would it still be experienced in this present body? And if it does not exist from past time and exists only in the present moment, then why do you say that all the pleasure and pain of sentient beings are entirely past karma? If you claim that by practising austerities now, past karma will be eliminated —

— then why would the present practice of austerities cease to exist? And if it does not cease to exist, then suffering becomes permanent. But if suffering is permanent, why do you claim that one is fully liberated from suffering?

If it is some other practice that brings the austerities to an end, then — if what is past has already been exhausted — how can suffering still exist? Would a person who practises such austerities and has performed karma that yields pleasure end up experiencing a fruit of suffering? Or, having performed karma that yields suffering, would they end up experiencing a fruit of pleasure? Or would there be no experience of the karmic fruit at all, in the case of karma that yields neither suffering nor pleasure? Is it the case that a present karmic maturation gives rise to a future karmic maturation? Or that a future karmic maturation gives rise to a present karmic maturation? Or that from both these maturations a state without maturation arises? Or that from a fixed maturation a state without maturation arises? Or that from a state without maturation a fixed maturation arises? Ask all of this.

If they answer "None of that, Gautama," then I too shall say to them: If none of that holds, then why practise austerities at all?

Therefore there are certainly past phenomena, and there are also present causes and conditions. This is why it has been taught that karma arises through the condition of affliction, and that karmic maturation is experienced through the condition of karma. Accordingly, one should understand that all sentient beings have both prior past karma and present causes and conditions. Although karma from former times exists, there is still a need for present causes and conditions in the form of food and drink. If you, then, claim that the pleasure and pain experienced by ordinary people are entirely the cause and condition of past karma, that too is untenable. And why? Consider this example: if a person kills an enemy of the king, through that cause and condition he gains an abundance of wealth and precious things. Through gaining that wealth and those precious things, he experiences pleasure in the present time. He has created the cause for present pleasure, and so he experiences pleasure in the present. Consider another example: if a person kills a beloved son of the king, through that cause and condition he loses his body and his life. He has created the cause for present suffering, and so the maturation he experiences in the present is suffering.

Friend, the present causes for all sentient beings' experience of pleasure and suffering arise from the four great elements, from season, from measure, from soil, and from fire — and through these they experience suffering and pleasure. Therefore it is not at all certain that all sentient beings experience pleasure and suffering from past karma alone.

Friend, if liberation were to come about through the power of causes and conditions by simply cutting off karma, then all noble ones (āryas) would already be liberated — but they are not. Why? Because the past karma of all sentient beings is without beginning or end. This is why it has been taught that cultivating the noble path is what turns back karma that is without beginning or end. Friend, if the path were obtained by practising austerities, then all animals, too, would be fit to attain awakening. Therefore, it is the mind that is to be tamed first — not the body. This is why I have also declared in the sūtras: Cut the grove, but do not cut the tree. And why? Because fear arises from the grove, not from the tree.

If one wishes to tame the body, one should first tame the mind. The mind is the analogy of the grove, and the body is the analogy of the tree.

Subhavyūha submitted: "Blessed One, I have already tamed my mind."

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, in what way have you tamed your mind first?"

Subhavyūha submitted: "Blessed One, I attended with careful attention to desires as being impermanent, as being without pleasure, and as being impure. And I examined form as being permanent, as being pleasurable, as being self, and as being pure. Having understood this, the afflictions of the desire realm were severed, and I attained the sense base of the form realm. Therefore I had first tamed my mind. Then, examining form, I understood form to be impermanent — like a wound, like an ulcer, like something harmful, like a dart. And I saw the formless as being permanent, as being utterly pure, and as being supremely peaceful. Having understood this, with the afflictions of the form realm exhausted, I attained the sense base of the formless realm. Therefore I had first tamed my mind. Then, further examining perception, I understood it to be impermanent — like a wound, like an ulcer, like something harmful, like a dart. Having understood this, I attained meditative absorption at the level of the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. That meditative absorption at the level of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is omniscient wisdom — supremely peaceful, utterly pure, free from transgression, permanent and unchanging. Therefore I had tamed my mind."

This is from the fifty-fourth fascicle of the Noble Great Sūtra of the Passage Beyond All Sorrow (the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra).

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, in what way have you tamed your mind? What you have attained is meditative absorption at the level of neither-perception-nor-non-perception — and even that is still called 'perception.' If passing beyond sorrow were a state of having no perception, why would it be called 'attaining the passage beyond sorrow'? Son of good family, before, you criticized coarse perception — why do you now fail to recognize that you are attached to subtle perception and do not censure it? The level of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is likewise called 'perception' — like a wound, like an ulcer, like something harmful, like a dart. Son of good family, your own teacher Udraka (Skt. Udraka Rāmaputra), who had sharp faculties and a concentrated mind, venerated the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and as a result will experience evil karma. What need is there even to speak of others?"

Subhavyūha submitted: "Blessed One, how does one sever all becoming?"

The Blessed One declared: "Son of good family, if a person practises correct perception, that person will sever all becoming."

Subhavyūha submitted: "Blessed One, what is meant by 'correct perception'?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, the perception of non-perception is what is called correct perception."

He submitted: "Blessed One, how is there a perception of non-perception?"

The Blessed One replied: "Son of good family, all phenomena are without the characteristic of self, without the characteristic of other, without the characteristic of self-and-other, without the characteristic of causelessness, without the characteristic of having been made, without the characteristic of having passed, without the characteristic of an agent, without the characteristic of an experiencer, without the characteristic of being a dharma, without the characteristic of being a non-dharma, without the characteristic of male or female, without the characteristic of being a person, without the characteristic of subtle particles, without the characteristic of time and measure, without the characteristic of having been made by self, without the characteristic of having been made by other, without the characteristic of having been made by self-and-other, without the characteristic of existence, and without the characteristic of non-existence.

without the characteristic of having been born, without the characteristic of being produced, without the characteristic of cause, without the characteristic of passing from cause to cause, without the characteristic of result, without the characteristic of passing from result to result, without the characteristic of day and night, without the characteristic of light and darkness, without the characteristic of seeing, without the characteristic of that which causes seeing, without the characteristic of hearing, without the characteristic of that which causes hearing, without the characteristic of feeling and knowing, without the characteristic of that which causes feeling and knowing, without the characteristic of awakening, without the characteristic of that which causes awakening to be attained, without the characteristic of karma, without the characteristic of a master of karma, without the characteristic of affliction, and without the characteristic of a master of affliction.

Noble son, that in which all characteristics are ceased is called the true characteristic. Noble son, all phenomena are untrue. That in which they are ceased is called the true, is called true perception, is called the dharmadhātu, is called consummate wisdom, is called the ultimate, and is called ultimate emptiness.

Noble son, if one engages authentically with characteristic, with dharmadhātu, with consummate wisdom, with ultimate truth, and with ultimate emptiness through inferior wisdom, one will attain the awakening of a śrāvaka. If one engages authentically through middling wisdom, one will attain the awakening of a pratyekabuddha. If one engages authentically through supreme wisdom, one will attain unsurpassed awakening.

When this teaching was given, one hundred thousand bodhisattvas attained true perception (samādhi) that penetrates in a single lifetime. Seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the dharmadhātu in two lifetimes. Twenty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained consummate wisdom. Thirty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained ultimate truth. Ultimate truth may also be called ultimate emptiness and may also be called the meditative absorption of heroic advance. Forty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the meditative absorption like space. The meditative absorption like space may also be called the vast meditative absorption and may also be called the meditative absorption of the wisdom seal. Fifty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the irreversible patience (kṣānti). Irreversible patience may also be called the patience of Dharma and may also be called that which is like the dharmadhātu. Sixty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained dhāraṇī. That dhāraṇī may also be called the mind of great mindfulness and may also be called unobstructed wisdom. Seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the meditative absorption known as the lion's roar. The meditative absorption of the lion's roar may also be called the vajra-like meditative absorption and may also be called the meditative absorption of the wisdom seal. Eighty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the meditative absorption of equality. That meditative absorption of equality may also be called great loving-kindness and great compassion.

Sentient beings as innumerable as the grains of sand in the Ganges River generated the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Sentient beings as innumerable as the grains of sand in the Ganges River generated the mind directed toward pratyekabuddha awakening. Sentient beings as innumerable as the grains of sand in the Ganges River generated the mind directed toward the path of a śrāvaka. Some twenty thousand human beings and daughters of the gods directly manifested bodies born as male, having previously had female bodies. And the most excellent among them attained the fruit of arhatship.

At that time, Śīlavat (the Supremely Good One), having heard from the Blessed One the profoundly deep teaching of the great scripture on complete nirvāṇa, gained the perfectly pure eye of Dharma with respect to the Dharma. Having seen the purified Dharma and, out of longing for the sacred Dharma, having entirely abandoned wrong views, his faith in the teaching of the Buddha became exceedingly firm. He then requested going forth from the Tathāgata.

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent! Excellent! Śīlavat, welcome — you are a monk well-come. The noble ones too joyfully rejoice in this: you have entered well upon the awakening of a buddha."

Śīlavat was filled with immense joy and delight, and his devotion became boundless. At that very moment his hair and beard fell away of themselves, and he became a monk. By the power of dharmatā itself, the water of primordial wisdom saturated the vessel of mind, so that he was not bound by any bond, and with defilements exhausted and mind fully liberated, he became an arhat.

Having attained the fruit of arhatship, Śīlavat drew near to the Buddha and gazed upon the face of the Blessed One with unblinking eyes. He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, arranged his outer robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms together, and — grief and joy arising in him at one and the same time — repenting his former faults, he addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"For a very long time this malicious body of mine deceived me. For a very long time, sunk within what is like the darkness of vile ignorance, I wandered in cyclic existence through the three realms and was seized upon by the doctrines of the non-Buddhists. Alas, alas — from that great and grievous harm, I have now, by the kindness and grace of the Tathāgata, entered into the sacred Dharma. Blessed One, the great compassion of your ocean-like primordial wisdom is boundless; even across an eon I could not repay your kindness." So he thought in his mind.

Having spoken thus, Śīlavat shed tears. Then he addressed the Blessed One again with these words:

"Blessed One, I am old and decrepit. I am not yet liberated from suffering; I am utterly tormented by the suffering of formations. Out of compassion, Blessed One, please teach the precepts of ethical discipline and be my protector and refuge. Please remain for a while without passing into nirvāṇa."

At that time the Blessed One said nothing and did not grant the request. Since Śīlavat's plea had not been granted, his mind was afflicted with anguish, and he cried out with a great voice:

"Alas! Alas! The world is left empty! The world is left empty! Now a great terror draws near, and anguish has become manifest. Alas! Alas! By the exhaustion of the merit of sentient beings, the eye of true wisdom has gone blind!"

Saying this, he beat his breast in lamentation, wept until his voice gave out, and his body was drenched in blood. He cried out with a great voice, and then, casting his body to the ground before the Tathāgata, he fell unconscious. After a long while he revived, and weeping still, he again addressed the Blessed One with these words:

"Blessed One, I cannot bear to see the Tathāgata pass into nirvāṇa. My mind is deeply afflicted and I am stricken with grief. I myself, moreover, have no wish to continue in the company of this malicious body of mine — like an unfired pot — I am already gone ahead. May the Blessed One then pass into nirvāṇa later."

Having thus spoken, Śīlavat beat his breast in lamentation, and at that very moment entered into nirvāṇa himself.

At that time, bodhisattvas of the Great Vehicle as innumerable as the grains of sand in ineffably many Ganges Rivers, together with monks, nuns,

all the gods, humans, asuras, and every other being dwelling in the world cried out together with one voice, saying:

"Alas! Alas! The perfectly awakened buddha has abandoned us all at once. There is no dwelling, no refuge, no shelter, no protector — it is utterly terrible."

So they spoke, and every one of them wept. They embraced one another, beat their fists against their own breasts, fell unconscious, and collapsed in all directions. Even the great trichiliocosm — the vast world-system of three thousand great thousands of worlds — trembled.

At that time the Blessed One, with his voice endowed with the eight qualities, spoke these words to the great assembly:

"Do not weep as small children do. Each of you, let go of that weeping and do not disturb your minds. You who are in this ocean of saṃsāra, the suffering born of formations — you must be earnest in pure intention and must not forget the wisdom of recollection and mindfulness. Strive with true gnosis toward liberation from conditioned existence. To take birth in a body within the three realms is an endless wheel of suffering. Do not become servants and slaves whose bodies and minds are driven by the king of the māra of desire and the lord of ignorance. Focusing on the domain of objects of action, beings perform the karma of saṃsāra, and being tormented moment by moment by attachment, aversion, and delusion, they come to experience suffering for measureless eons — what wise and discerning person would not reflect on this?

You should understand it thus. From time immemorial I have entered into the great peace that is devoid of aggregates, elements, and sense bases; I have severed conditioned existence entirely and have attained permanence, bliss, self, and complete purity — like a treasure of precious vajra. Yet I am demonstrating, here and now, a passing into nirvāṇa that accords with the ways of the world, in order to reveal inconceivable skillful means — and this for the sake of causing ordinary beings to understand the body as being like a flash of lightning and to arouse a sense of reverence. The flood of saṃsāra's flow is extremely fierce and swift, and formations circle round and round in saṃsāra. Such is the nature of reality. The Tathāgata's passing into nirvāṇa is extremely profound and inconceivable; it belongs to the domain of experience of buddhas and bodhisattvas, and is not known to śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

The Blessed One then spoke again to the great assembly, saying:

"This Śīlavat, in former times, paid homage and rendered service to as many buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. Having thereby cultivated a vast root of virtue from those buddhas, and impelled by the force of his earlier aspirations, he continually went forth and lived according to the path of the naked non-Buddhist (tīrthika) ascetics, and through the wisdom of skillful means he brought sentient beings who had entered into wrong and evil views into the domain of true gnosis. Now, Śīlavat, driven by the force of those former aspirations, came to encounter me at this very passing into nirvāṇa and heard the sacred Dharma. Having heard the sacred Dharma, he attained the fruit of arhatship. Having attained the fruit of arhatship, he entered nirvāṇa. From the moment of my full awakening, the first person I ordained was the venerable Kauṇḍinya; and at the very last, at this passing into nirvāṇa, I tamed Śīlavat and thereby brought my work to completion. Having no more work to do, even though I were to remain long, there is no other work than this to be done."

At that time, having spoken these words, the Blessed One exclaimed with strong feeling: "Excellent! Excellent! Śīlavat has repaid the kindness of the buddha well. You should make offerings at his relics and build a stūpa for him."

At that time, the great assembly was deeply grieved, and with tears streaming down their faces, they carried out the word of the Blessed One: they cremated his bones with fragrant wood and butter. As the bones of the virtuous Śīlavat burned, a great radiance burst forth from within the fire, and eighteen kinds of miraculous display appeared openly. Water streamed from the upper part of his body while fire blazed from the lower; fire blazed from the right armpit while water streamed from the left. He transformed from small to great and from great to small, filling the entire sky completely. At that moment, countless members of the assembly, along with non-Buddhist beings holding wrong views, aroused the awakening mind and entered into right view. Having displayed these miracles openly, Śīlavat re-entered the fire. After the cremation, the great assembly gathered the relics, built a stūpa, and made offerings there.

This concludes the chapter on the venerable Kauṇḍinya from the Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa of the noble ones.

At that time, the Blessed One spoke these words to Ānanda and the great assembly: "After I have passed into nirvāṇa, you four assemblies should strive to uphold and preserve this teaching of the great nirvāṇa. I have accomplished this Dharma-text of nirvāṇa, which is supremely difficult to obtain, through countless immeasurable eons, and I am now setting it forth. You should understand it to be so. This Dharma-text of the great nirvāṇa is the imperishable vajra-treasury of precious jewels of all the buddhas dwelling in the ten directions throughout the three times; it is permanent, blissful, self, and perfectly pure — complete and undiminished. It is by passing into nirvāṇa by means of this that all buddhas pass into final nirvāṇa without remainder. All buddhas are said to 'pass into nirvāṇa' by relinquishing this present life. If you wish to repay the kindness of the buddhas in full, to swiftly attain awakening, to receive empowerment upon the crown of the head from the buddhas and to perfectly recall wherever you are born without forgetting, to have the buddhas of the ten directions come before you and protect you by day and by night, and to have all sentient beings attain the Dharma of transcending the world — then apply yourselves with diligence to this sūtra of nirvāṇa."

The Blessed One then spoke again to Ānanda: "Even before I had attained full awakening, I entered into the teaching of the non-Buddhist master Udraka Rāmaputra and studied the four meditative concentrations and the eight meditative absorptions, and I practised in accordance with his teaching. After I attained full awakening, I rejected his doctrine, and at the last I tamed Śīlavat and established him in the teaching of the Buddha. The great fire of the Tathāgata's primordial wisdom burned away the banner of wrong views — just as a dry leaf is placed into a great fire. Ānanda, I have profound affection for the Śākya clan, who are my own kindred. After I have passed into nirvāṇa, you should teach and expound the Dharma with diligence and excellence. Teach the noble Dharma to my attendants, so that they do not fall into frivolous and heedless conduct and activities, do not fall into practising doctrines of wrong view, and so that those who have not yet been liberated from the suffering of the three realms may swiftly be liberated. Generate profound fear toward the desire for the five polluted objects of sensual pleasure, and cultivate the perception of being without a protector. Reflect that a human body, once lost, is difficult to regain, that in this one life there must be care and vigilance, and that one should be fully liberated from the great demon of impermanence.

Generate compassion toward sentient beings, refrain from taking the life of any sentient being, and grant fearlessness even to the smallest creatures, down to insects. Through the complete purification of bodily karma, may you be born in a good world-realm; through the complete purification of verbal karma, may you become free from all the faults and flaws of wrongdoing. Do not eat flesh. Do not drink alcohol. Tame the snake of the mind and set it upon the path of awakening. Examine with great care the karmic actions of formations, knowing that the karmic maturation of virtue and non-virtue follows like a body's shadow. The fruits of the three times will not fail to come around in full cycle. Demonstrate and urge earnestly that squandering this life leads to regret afterward that is of no use. The time of my passing into nirvāṇa has come, and these are the instructions I give to you.

At that moment, upon hearing the words spoken by the Blessed One, Ānanda's body and mind trembled and shook; he was utterly overwhelmed, pierced through with grief, unable to utter a sound, and he fell into such a state of confusion that he became as if dead before the presence of the Tathāgata.

Then the one who had never ceased spoke, rousing Ānanda with encouragement, dispelling his grief, and said these words: Do not grieve in this way. The time has come for the Tathāgata to pass into nirvāṇa. Though he dwells today, he will not dwell tomorrow. Ask now the four petitions just as I have spoken them to you. After the buddha passes into nirvāṇa: how the six groups of monks are to be dealt with as they disturb the household life of those given to desire and wickedness; how one is to dwell and abide together with them in accordance with the teaching; since it is the Teacher, the buddha, who teaches while the Tathāgata remains in the world, who is to do the teaching after the Blessed One has passed into nirvāṇa; while the Tathāgata dwells in the world, those who rely and depend upon the Tathāgata — on whom are they to rely and depend after the passing into nirvāṇa; and after the Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa and the collection of the scriptural Dharma is compiled, what is to be placed at the head of all the sūtras — ask these things.

At that time, in Ānanda's dream, hearing the words of the one who had never ceased — words like "Ask the four petitions" — he awoke from his torpor, and he asked the four petitions of the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then spoke to Ānanda: Why are you so unhappy and so grieved? The buddha has performed all the deeds of taming. By the very nature of reality, the departure is thus. Excellent! Excellent! Ānanda, you have asked these four petitions as a final innermost request, and they will bring benefit and happiness to all who dwell in the world. Therefore listen well and hold them firmly in mind. It is so.

"Yes, Blessed One," said Ānanda, and he listened again to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One then spoke to Ānanda: You asked as follows: after the buddha passes into nirvāṇa, what of the six groups of monks and those given to desire and wickedness who disturb the household life, and how are they to dwell together and abide in the teaching? Ānanda, monks who are given to desire and unsuitable by nature will, after I have passed into nirvāṇa, discipline themselves and come to certainty, and they will also abandon their wicked minds. Ānanda, my younger brother Ānanda, though given to desire and unsuitable, was taught and corrected by the Tathāgata with skillful means, and the Tathāgata taught him the twelve links of dependent origination in accordance with the capacity of his faculties and wisdom. That is: conditioned by ignorance arise formations; conditioned by formations arises consciousness — and so on through aging and death, lamentation, and grief — all of it being the dense mass of ignorance and desire.

Through the suffering of formations one wanders in the three realms, cycling through the six classes of beings, and the root of all great suffering is ignorance. Thus, by examining with wisdom what is pure by its very nature, one cuts through the flaw of existence, which is ignorance. When the root is arrested, ignorance ceases. When ignorance ceases, formations cease — and so on through aging and death, lamentation, and grief, all of which cease as well.

Practicing in this correct way, the mind becomes settled and one enters meditative absorption (samādhi). By the power of meditative absorption one attains the first meditative concentration (dhyāna). Then, proceeding in sequence, one attains all four meditative concentrations and, sustaining that effort with a mind of correct and perfect mindfulness, one attains even the supreme fruit by oneself, and abandons entirely the suffering of the three realms.

Ānanda, at that time, if the monk Ānanda, with a thoroughly purified mind, applies diligent effort as I have taught, then without long delay he will attain the fruit of arhathood. Ānanda, after I have passed into nirvāṇa, you should teach what I have taught — in this very way — to the six groups of monks and to those given to desire, and those monks, with purified minds and relying on this pure and holy Dharma, will without long delay attain the supreme fruit.

Ānanda, therefore, from ignorance there has grown a great tree of wandering through the three realms. Carried by the wind of desire, tormented day and night for a long time by suffering, it revolves around the pillar of cyclic existence in the dark blackness, with the six branches of consciousness and the roots of distorted conceptuality, with waves of ignorance, and with mind and consciousness like boiling water running through the six sense-objects — seeds of suffering having been planted with no turning back. Just as a king is mighty and powerful, ignorance is like a lord and master that suppresses moment by moment, so that sentient beings, without feeling it, spin in cyclic existence and continue to revolve without end.

Ānanda, all sentient beings, under the power of this ignorance, fall into the afflictions of desire and, crushed by the view of self, are enslaved by the eighty-four thousand afflictions as though by so many lords and masters, so that not even a single body becomes its own master.

Ānanda, when the suffering of ignorance is extinguished and the three realms are exhausted, that is what is called transcending the world.

Ānanda, whoever understands that the twelve links of dependent origination are ultimately without self and enters into the domain of perfect purity — that one will wholly abandon the great fire of the three realms.

Ānanda, the Tathāgata speaks truly, and these words addressed to you with true speech — you should attend to them well and with care.

Ānanda, you have asked: if the buddha passes into nirvāṇa and is no longer present in the world, who will be the Teacher? Ānanda, moral discipline is your great Teacher. Abide in it and apply yourself diligently, and you will attain the meditative absorption and wisdom that transcend the world.

Ānanda, you have asked: after the buddha passes into nirvāṇa, on what shall one abide and rely? Ānanda, abide in the four close placements of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and, having adorned the mind, remain there. Examine the body in accordance with body — and if one understands it to be like empty space, that is called the close placement of mindfulness on body in accordance with body. Bring mindfulness to bear on feeling in accordance with feeling — and if one understands that feeling does not abide outside, does not abide inside, and does not abide anywhere in between, that is called the close placement of mindfulness on feeling in accordance with feeling. Examine the mind in accordance with mind — and if one understands that mind is exhausted in being a mere name, and that even the name itself is absent, that is called the close placement of mindfulness on mind in accordance with mind.

Examine phenomena in accordance with phenomena — and if one does not apprehend them as virtuous phenomena and does not apprehend them as non-virtuous phenomena, that is called the close placement of mindfulness on phenomena in accordance with phenomena.

Ānanda, you ask: after the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa and the treasury of Dharma has been compiled, what words are to be placed at the head of every sūtra? Ānanda, after the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa and the treasury of Dharma has been compiled, at the head of every sūtra place the words: "Thus did I hear. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in a certain place together with a fourfold retinue, and taught this sūtra."

Then Ānanda again addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Whether a buddha is present in the world or has passed into nirvāṇa, if a donor with faithful mind offers gold, silver, the seven precious substances, and many articles of enjoyment to the Tathāgata, how should such offerings be allocated?"

The Blessed One declared to Ānanda: "If the Buddha is present in person, everything offered to the Buddha should be entrusted to the Saṅgha. If the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa and a donor with faithful mind has dedicated and offered everything to the Buddha, all such offerings should be used to make images of the Buddha, garments for the Buddha, banners and parasols of the seven precious substances adorned with lamps, and jeweled flowers purchased as offerings to the Buddha. Apart from making offerings to the Buddha, they may not be used for anything else. If they are used otherwise, that constitutes the theft of what belongs to the Buddha."

Ānanda then asked: "Blessed One, when the Buddha is present — if a certain person with faithful mind, with reverence, pays homage and makes offerings, presenting gold, silver, the seven precious substances, a mansion, sons, a wife, servants, clothing, food, and every article of comfort — and then the Tathāgata passes into nirvāṇa, and another person with faithful mind, with reverence, pays homage and makes offerings by presenting gold, silver, the seven precious substances, sons, a wife, servants, clothing, food, and every article of comfort to an image of the Tathāgata — Blessed One, between these two persons who make offerings with faithful minds in this way, which one acquires the greater merit?"

The Blessed One declared to Ānanda: "Between these two persons who make offerings in this way with faithful minds, there is no difference in merit acquired. Why is that? Because even though the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, the dharmakāya is permanent; therefore, when offerings are made with faithful minds, the merit is equal and there is no difference."

Ānanda then asked: "Blessed One, if, while the Buddha is present in person, a certain person with faithful mind makes offerings with reverence in the manner described above — and after the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, another person with faithful mind and with reverence makes offerings to the bodily relics of the Buddha in the manner described above — Blessed One, which of these two persons acquires the greater merit?"

The Blessed One declared to Ānanda: "The merit of these two persons is equal and there is no difference. Their merit is immeasurable and incalculable in its breadth, and it is inexhaustible until the very end of suffering has been reached."

Ānanda then asked: "Blessed One, if, while the Buddha is present in person, a certain person with faithful mind makes offerings to the Tathāgata using all the aforementioned articles of offering — and after the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa —"

"If, however, a certain person were to make offerings with faithful mind and with reverence to half of the Tathāgata's relics after the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa — Blessed One, which of these two persons acquires the greater merit?" The Blessed One declared to Ānanda: "If these two persons make offerings with faithful mind, there is no difference in their merit; the accumulation of merit is immeasurable and incalculable.

"Ānanda, if a certain person with faithful mind, with reverence and with service, were to make offerings and praises to even a quarter of the Tathāgata's relics, or an eighth, or a sixteenth, or a hundredth part, or a thousandth part, or a ten-thousandth part, or even a portion as small as one grain of sand from the Ganges — down to something as tiny as a single mustard seed — worshipping with reverence and service; and if another person were to make offerings with reverence to the Buddha present in person — the merit of these two persons is, in every respect, equal and without distinction: immeasurable and incalculable.

"Ānanda, whether the Buddha is present in person or has passed into nirvāṇa — whoever bows with reverence and faithful mind, holds him as supreme, honors him, and praises him — it should be understood that the merit these two persons obtain is not twofold and not separate: it is without distinction.

"The Blessed One then declared to Ānanda and to the great assembly: 'After I have passed into nirvāṇa, if any sentient being in the heavens above or in the human world receives my relics in hand, and with grief and joy together bows in reverence and makes offerings with faithful mind, that person will obtain merit immeasurable and incalculable.

"'Ānanda, whoever sees the Tathāgata's relics — that person sees the Buddha. Whoever sees the Buddha sees the Dharma. Whoever sees the Dharma sees the Saṅgha. Whoever sees the Saṅgha sees nirvāṇa. Ānanda, for this reason it should be understood that the Three Jewels are permanent, stable, unchanging, and unaltering, and that they are the protector and refuge of all sentient beings.'"

Ānanda then asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, after you have passed into complete nirvāṇa, by what ritual procedure should we enter into the body of the Tathāgata and thereby obtain the relics, so that we may make offerings with faith?"

The Blessed One declared to Ānanda: "After I have passed into nirvāṇa, you should cremate the body according to the method used for a wheel-turning king (cakravartin)."

Ānanda then asked again: "What is the ritual procedure for cremating a wheel-turning king?"

The Blessed One declared to Ānanda: "When a wheel-turning king has died, the body is laid out for seven days, and then placed inside an iron casket. Once placed in the casket, the casket is filled with sesame oil and the lid is tightly sealed, and it is kept thus for another seven days. It is then removed from the casket and bathed with perfumed water. After bathing with perfumed water, it is honoured and fumigated with fragrant incense, and the whole body is wrapped in cotton wool. Over the wrapping of cotton wool, it is wrapped in layers of a thousand bolts of fine white cloth from end to end. Having been thus wrapped, the body is placed back into a casket filled with sesame oil — the royal remains are placed inside the casket once more, and the casket is tightly sealed. It is then carried upon a precious chariot of oiled and fragrant wood adorned with the seven precious substances, and the sides and base of the chariot are hung with decorative banners, and the chariot is further ornamented with various precious jewels. Countless flowers, pennants, parasols of the seven precious substances, victory banners, various fine incenses,"

accompanied by divine music, making offerings all around. Then the bones of the wheel-turning king are cremated upon fragrant wood adorned inside and out with painted designs, together with oil-soaked wood. After the cremation, the relics are gathered together. At the four cardinal points of a great city, a stūpa of the seven precious substances with four gateways is erected, and the relics are placed within it, so that all who dwell in the world may approach and behold it with rejoicing.

Ānanda, a wheel-turning king obtains the status of a king by virtue of a little merit, yet he is not free from cyclic existence. He is endowed with the five objects of desire. He has queens and palace retinues. He possesses evil views and the three poisons. He has not abandoned so much as a hair-tip of afflictions and utterly defiling tendencies. Yet when such a one dies and the world performs these funeral rites, erects a stūpa, and all rejoice and venerate it — how much more so, then, a Tathāgata. For throughout incalculable, boundless, immeasurable, and innumerable eons, he has completely relinquished queens and palace retinues and the five objects of desire; he has understood the dharmas of the world to be like hailstones or dew; he has sought out the most arduous austerities and practiced what is most difficult to practice; all bodhisattvas have practiced the transcendent austerities that go beyond the world; and he has accomplished without any omission the pure moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the wisdom of liberation as practiced by all buddhas dwelling in the ten directions throughout the three times. Moreover, he has brought to perfection the six perfections. And beyond this, he has accomplished the Tathāgata's ten powers, great compassion, the four fearlessnesses, the three gateways of liberation, the eighteen emptinesses, the six direct knowledges, the five eyes, the thirty-seven factors of awakening, the eighteen unshared qualities, the thirty-two major marks, the eighty excellent minor features, the lifespan of all buddhas, the complete purification of all buddha fields, the complete ripening of all sentient beings, all arduous practices, the moral discipline of gathering virtue, the moral discipline of benefiting sentient beings, the moral discipline of restraint, all excellent qualities, all wisdom, all adornments, all great aspirational prayers, all skillful means — and thus all inconceivable accumulations of merit and wisdom have been spontaneously and perfectly fulfilled. All non-virtue has been utterly severed. All afflictions have been utterly severed. All habitual tendencies of afflictions have been utterly severed. Deeply penetrating the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination, he subdued the four māras beneath the tree of awakening, and, having become the wisdom of omniscience, having thus striven diligently in all these supreme Dharmas, all buddhas declared with one voice "Excellent! Excellent!" and, in accord with the wisdom of the nature of reality, performed the consecration by pouring the water of the dharmakāya upon his crown, and proclaimed that he had fully and perfectly awakened to the utterly unsurpassable, true, and complete awakening.

Therefore I am now the Teacher of gods and humans, fully awakened in all ten directions, consummate, the Blessed One, peerless among gods and humans. Regarding all sentient beings as Rāhu regards the moon, the Tathāgata — perfectly and completely awakened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, the unsurpassed one, the tamer and guide of persons, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One — performing all acts of compassion for the world, when he passes into nirvāṇa for the sake of sentient beings,

just as a wheel-turning king (cakravartin) is venerated by all sentient beings in accordance with the ways of the world, so should you cause all sentient beings to render veneration. Ānanda, after I have passed into nirvāṇa, let my body rest for seven days, as would a wheel-turning king's, and first place it into an iron casket. Once it has been placed in the iron casket, fill it well with sesame oil and seal the lid tightly. Adorn and ornament the casket richly with the seven precious substances, and offer veneration all around the casket with victory banners of precious gems, with incense, and with flowers. Having venerated in this way for seven days, take the body out of the casket and wash it well with scented water. After thus bathing the Tathāgata's body with scented water, wrap it fully in cotton wool. Over that, wind it with a thousand bolts of priceless white cloth. Having wrapped it thus, place it again in the iron casket, fill it with sesame oil, and seal the lid tightly. Then, place it upon a carriage made of the seven precious substances, together with Goghīrṣa sandalwood, aloeswood, and all manner of fragrant woods. Adorned with every jewel, carry it to the place of cremation. Offer veneration with innumerable jeweled victory banners, innumerable jeweled parasols, innumerable jeweled garments, innumerable divine musical instruments, and innumerable flowers and incense filling the very sky, and weep. Let all the gods, humans, and the entire fourfold retinue weep and cremate my body with fragrant sandalwood, aloeswood, and sesame oil. After the cremation, let the gods, humans, and the fourfold retinue collect the relics and place them in vessels of the seven precious substances. At the four crossroads of the great city, build a stūpa of the seven precious substances. By venerating the relics, sentient beings will gain great merit, abandon the suffering of the three modes of existence, and attain the bliss of passing beyond sorrow into nirvāṇa. Ānanda, after the fourfold retinue has built a stūpa of the seven precious substances for the relics of the Buddha's body, they should also build three further stūpas. What are these? A stūpa for a pratyekabuddha, a stūpa for an arhat, and a stūpa for a wheel-turning king — so that all beings in the world, together with gods, may know the objects to which they may go for refuge.

Ānanda then asked: Blessed One, the Tathāgata came into the world out of compassion for sentient beings, proclaiming throughout the three realms the ten powers, great compassion, the four fearlessnesses, the twelve links of dependent origination, the Four Noble Truths, the three doors of liberation, and the eight tones of Brahmā's voice. Through the light of loving-kindness endowed with five colors, he caused the six pathways of transmigration to blaze with illumination. In accordance with the aspirations of sentient beings, some came to practice the four fruits and the two vehicles; some attained the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, undefiled and unconditioned; some were possessed and permeated by the awakening of the non-cessation and non-arising; some attained immeasurable dhāraṇīs; some attained the five divine eyes and the six kinds of higher knowledge; some were liberated from the three lower realms; some were freed from the eight unfree states; and some, whether gods or humans, were freed from the suffering of the three worlds. Through the utterly pure force of the Tathāgata's loving-kindness and the inconceivable principle of the Tathāgata's teaching of liberation, all beings in the world together with gods, up until their passing into nirvāṇa,

would build a stūpa of the seven precious substances and make offerings to the relics, thereby obtaining great merit. Ordinary persons would be liberated from the suffering of the three realms and would enter into true and complete liberation. Therefore, now that the buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, it is fitting that all in the world — gods, humans, and the fourfold retinue — should build a stūpa of the seven precious substances and make offerings to the relics, in order to honor the great kindness the buddha has shown and to follow in his wake of boundless loving-kindness. But, Blessed One, since you have built the three kinds of stūpas and thereby brought benefit to sentient beings, what further benefit is there in building stūpas and making offerings?" The Blessed One then declared to Ānanda: "A pratyekabuddha, having realized the profoundly deep Dharma of dependent origination, is fully liberated from all of existence; having shed every fault and flaw, he becomes a field of merit for gods and humans. Therefore, by building a stūpa and making offerings to it, one obtains merit. This is so because, second only to the Tathāgata, he causes many beings to attain the supreme fruit. Ānanda, an arhat has exhausted the tendency toward rebirth, will not take up a subsequent existence, and has completely fulfilled the holy life; he becomes a field of merit for the world. Therefore, by building a stūpa and making offerings to it, the merit obtained — ranking just below that for a pratyekabuddha — is also great, and he too leads beings to liberation. Ānanda, a wheel-turning king, though not yet fully liberated from the afflictions of the three realms, nonetheless, through the force of merit, holds dominion over the four continents; by establishing beings in existence through the ten virtuous actions, he is an object of veneration for those beings. Therefore, by the fourfold retinue building a stūpa and making offerings, they will obtain immeasurable merit."

Ānanda then asked: "Blessed One, after the buddha has passed into nirvāṇa and we, the fourfold retinue, have bathed and laid to rest the body of the Tathāgata, where shall we obtain the relics of the Tathāgata? May the Blessed One instruct us." The Blessed One declared to Ānanda: "After the buddha passes into nirvāṇa, if the fourfold retinue were to perform the cremation within the city of Kuśinagara, the people of that city would incur boundless royal penalties and disputes, and none would equally obtain the merit. Ānanda, if the fourfold retinue performs the cremation outside the city, then people of the world will equally obtain the merit."

Ānanda asked: "Blessed One, after the buddha has passed into nirvāṇa and the cremation has taken place, may the Blessed One instruct us: when the fourfold retinue has gathered the relics and placed them in a precious vessel, and a stūpa of the seven precious substances is erected wherever it may be, will all people generate faith and come to make offerings?" The Blessed One declared to Ānanda: "After the buddha passes into nirvāṇa and the cremation is complete, the fourfold retinue shall gather the relics, place them in a vessel of the seven precious substances, and within the city of Kuśinagara, at a crossroads, erect a stūpa of the seven precious substances with thirteen tiered levels, fitted with parasols, adorned and ornamented with all precious things, magnificently arrayed with victory banners to be exalted by all in the world, with steps on each of its four sides likewise fashioned of the seven precious substances, the whole supremely adorned with ornaments. That stūpa shall have one door opened on each of its four sides simultaneously; within the shaft of downward-falling light, a great precious vessel shall be set, and the fourfold retinue shall make offerings there. Ānanda, a pratyekabuddha's stūpa shall have eleven tiered levels and be adorned with various precious substances."

Ānanda, an arhat's stūpa shall have four tiered levels and shall likewise be adorned with various precious substances.

Ānanda, a wheel-turning king's stūpa shall be fashioned from the seven precious substances, yet without tiered levels. Why is that? Because he has not been liberated from the suffering of existence in the three realms.

At that time Māagalyāyana spoke to the Blessed One and said: "When the Buddha has entered nirvāṇa, how shall the relics of the Tathāgata be divided among gods, humans, and the fourfold retinue, so that all may make offerings?"

Then the Blessed One declared to Māagalyāyana: "After I have passed into nirvāṇa, gods, humans, and the rest shall gather the relics of the Buddha and, with a mind of perfect equanimity, distribute them throughout all three realms and all six classes of beings, so that offerings may be made."

At that time Śakra, Lord of the Gods (Indra, king of the gods), addressed the Blessed One and said: "Blessed One, I request half of the Tathāgata's relics from the Tathāgata."

The Blessed One declared to Śakra, Lord of the Gods: "The Tathāgata looks upon all sentient beings as a mother lion looks upon her cub. Therefore, do not say that you desire half of the relics. Why is that? Because he acts with impartiality for the benefit of all sentient beings."

The Blessed One then declared to Śakra, Lord of the Gods: "I shall give you one right-side canine tooth. You shall erect a stūpa in the divine world and make offerings there, and you shall thereby obtain merit that is inexhaustible and without end."

At that time all the gods and humans cried out with lamentation and wept.

Then the Blessed One declared to the fourfold retinue: "You gods, humans, and the rest — do not grieve at the passing of the Buddha into nirvāṇa. Why is that? Even though the Buddha passes fully into nirvāṇa, the relics are there always to be venerated. Moreover, the unsurpassed precious Dharma — the sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma — shall remain. Therefore the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths shall always abide in the world, and there shall be objects through which sentient beings of faith may make offerings. Why is that? To make offerings to the relics is to make offerings to the Buddha Jewel. One who sees the Buddha sees the dharmakāya. One who sees the Dharma sees the noble one. One who sees the noble one sees the Four Noble Truths. One who sees the Four Noble Truths sees the passing beyond sorrow. Therefore know that the Three Jewels are permanent, abiding, unchanging, and immutable — they are and shall remain the support and refuge of the world."

The Blessed One then declared to the great assembly: "Do not give way to great grief and torment yourselves with sorrow. I am about to pass into nirvāṇa. If any of you have doubt regarding moral discipline, or the place of practice, or permanence, or impermanence, or the Three Jewels, or the Four Noble Truths, or the six perfections, or the twelve links of dependent origination, ask now and quickly. This is the final opportunity to ask. After the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, let there be no regret." He declared this three times.

At that time the fourfold retinue and all the others were stricken with grief. They wailed aloud, and their hearts were overcome with despair and sorrow. Through the blessing of the Buddha they shed tears, yet they did not speak a word and asked nothing at all. Why was that? Because all those in the fourfold retinue had directly realized moral discipline, the place of practice, the Three Jewels, and the Four Noble Truths, and had become free from all doubt.

At that time, the Blessed One knew with his mind that the fourfold retinue had no doubt, and he declared: "Excellent! Most excellent! You of the fourfold retinue have thoroughly realized the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths and are free from all doubt — just as one who has been washed clean of stain by water and fragrance. Now you too must strive with diligence and attain the path of swift liberation. Do not grieve with mere faintness of heart."

At that time, the Blessed One, while seated upon the lion throne, took his golden-hued hand and, parting his robe, drew out the fringe of his lion's mane — radiant as refined gold — and displayed it to the great assembly. Then he declared to the many gods, humans, and all the gathered retinue: "Look upon my body, whose complexion is like refined gold."

This is the fifty-fifth fascicle of the Noble Great Discourse on Complete Nirvāṇa.

At that time all four assemblies of the retinue gazed upon the Tathāgata's body, whose complexion was like refined gold, looking with unblinking eyes. The bliss they experienced was like that of monks who have attained the third meditative concentration.

At that time the Blessed One, displaying his body of refined-gold complexion to the great assembly, emanated immeasurable, incalculable, boundless rays of light from his great nirvāṇa — eighty quadrillion in number — and illuminated all world-systems in the ten directions, so that even the light of the sun and moon was utterly eclipsed. Having thus spread his light, he declared to the great assembly:

"The Tathāgata, for your sake, over countless aeons practiced the most difficult of ascetic deeds, cutting off the very limbs of his body — his arms and his legs — and performing every kind of difficult practice. By the power of the aspirational prayer of great compassion, he appeared in this turbid world-realm and became fully and perfectly awakened in unsurpassable complete enlightenment. He attained this indestructible body, firm as vajra, of refined-gold complexion, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor marks of excellence, and he illuminated all directions with immeasurable rays of light. There is none who, merely upon being touched by those rays or upon beholding his form, has not been liberated."

The Blessed One then again declared to the great assembly: "For a buddha to appear in the world is exceedingly rare — like the udumbara flower, which is most rarely seen. You are now beholding my body for the last time. Do not let this pass without meaning. By the power of former aspirations I came to this turbid world-realm. Now, having completed the deeds of taming those to be tamed, I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — fix your gaze with single-pointed mind upon my body of refined-gold complexion. If you too apply yourselves with diligence to the most perfectly pure of actions, you will attain this same fruit."

At that time the Blessed One declared this again and again, three times in succession, and displayed his golden-hued body plainly and directly to the great assembly.

Then he rose from the lion throne of the seven precious substances and ascended into the sky above to the height of seven tāla trees, and again declared: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — look upon my body of refined-gold complexion." And so, gradually, ascending to the height of one further tāla tree at a time, he declared: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — with utterly pure intention, look upon my body of refined-gold complexion." He declared this seven times in all.

Then he descended from the sky and was seated once more upon the lion throne, and again declared to the great retinue: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — with utterly pure intention, look upon my body of refined-gold complexion."

Then the Blessed One rose again from the lion throne and ascended into the sky above to the height of one tāla tree, and declared to the great retinue: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — with pure intention, look upon my body of refined-gold complexion." And in the same way, ascending to the height of seven tāla trees, he declared seven times: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — look upon my body of refined-gold complexion."

Then he descended again from the sky, was seated upon the lion throne, and declared to the great retinue: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — with pure intention, look upon my body of refined-gold complexion."

Then the Blessed One rose once more from the lion throne, ascended into the sky above to the height of one tāla tree, and declared to the great retinue: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — with pure intention, look upon my body of refined-gold complexion." And again, ascending repeatedly to the height of seven tāla trees, he declared seven times: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — with pure intention, look upon my body of refined-gold complexion."

Then again he descended from the sky, was seated upon the lion throne, and declared once more to the great retinue: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa. You and all the gathered retinue — with pure intention, look upon my body of refined-gold complexion."
