At that time the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, displayed his body of refined-gold complexion, showing it directly and plainly to the great retinue. And so, in order to show it to the great retinue face to face, he ascended three times to the height of seven tāla trees in the sky above, and three times descended again from the sky to be seated on the lion throne. In this way, repeatedly, he declared to the great retinue twenty-four times in all: "I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa — look upon my body that is firm and indestructible as a vajra, of refined-gold complexion, imperishable. Know this well, you and all the gathered retinue: it is exceedingly rare to behold, like the udumbara flower. I am soon to pass into nirvāṇa — you and all the gathered retinue, with one-pointed mind, look intently upon my body of refined-gold complexion. Just as a person scorched by heat, intensely thirsty, who drinks cold water thinks of nothing else but being satisfied, so too are you and all the gathered retinue — with utterly pure intention, look intently upon me. This is the final time of seeing me within this life. After this seeing, there will be no further occasion to see me — therefore, you and all the gathered retinue, from this moment on, look your fill without regret."

Then the Blessed One again declared to the great retinue: "After I have passed into nirvāṇa, you and all the great retinue — in order to swiftly cross over the three existences, practice earnestly and extensively, and dwell in heedfulness without sloth."

At that time, in all world-realms, gods and humans and the fourfold retinue and all the rest were touched by the light of the passing into nirvāṇa, and all those who were gazing upon the Buddha were thereby entirely purified — without remainder — of the three lower destinies, the eight states without leisure, the afflictions of the gods and humans of the world, the four root downfalls, and all the blameworthy misdeeds of the five heinous acts, and they attained complete liberation.

At that time the Blessed One extended his body, resplendent as refined gold, and declared to the great retinue, "Behold it again and again." Then he drew the patchwork Dharma robe back over his body. This is the chapter on establishing the teaching, from the Great Sūtra of the Noble Complete Passing into Nirvāṇa.

The Blessed One then again declared to the great retinue: "My time has now come. All over my body there is pain and illness." Having so declared, he entered the first meditative concentration (dhyāna) and, surveying all world-realms with the light of passing into nirvāṇa, entered the meditative absorption of peaceful cessation.

At that moment, the instant the Blessed One had spoken, he entered the first meditative concentration. Arising from the first, he entered the second. Arising from the second, he entered the third. Arising from the third, he entered the fourth. Arising from the fourth, he entered the sense base of infinite space. Arising from the sense base of infinite space, he entered the sense base of infinite consciousness. Arising from the sense base of infinite consciousness, he entered the sense base of nothingness. Arising from the sense base of nothingness, he entered the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Arising from the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered the meditative absorption of cessation and exhaustion.

Arising from the meditative absorption of cessation and exhaustion, he once again entered the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Arising from the sense base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he once again entered the sense base of nothingness. Arising from the sense base of nothingness, he entered the sense base of infinite consciousness. Arising from the sense base of infinite consciousness, he entered the sense base of infinite space. Arising from the sense base of infinite space, he entered the fourth meditative concentration. Arising from the fourth, he entered the third. Arising from the third, he entered the second. Arising from the second, he entered the first.

At that time, having thus passed back and forth through the meditative concentrations, the Blessed One declared to the great retinue: "When I examine with my profoundly penetrating wisdom all sentient beings of the six classes throughout the three realms, and all living creatures dwelling in mountains, oceans, and the great earth, I find that these three realms are devoid of intrinsic nature, utterly at peace, and like space in their defining characteristic — they cannot be designated. There is no consciousness in them, all existence is completely severed, they are primordially equal, free of any perception of high or low, without seeing, without hearing, without feeling, without knowing, without bondage, without liberation, without sentient beings, without life, unborn, unarisen, inexhaustible, unceasing — neither the world nor what is not the world, with nirvāṇa and saṃsāra nowhere to be apprehended. Both extremes being equal is because all phenomena are equal. Abiding at the final limit, doing nothing at all, ultimately settled, with nothing whatsoever to be determined — performing the function of the defining characteristic of phenomena from among non-abiding phenomena, all marks completely severed and utterly without anything: these are the defining characteristics of phenomena. Whoever understands in this way is said to have passed beyond the world. Whoever does not understand in this way is called the beginning-edge of saṃsāra. Therefore, cut off ignorance completely — you and all the rest — and sever the beginning-edge of saṃsāra."

At that time, having so declared, the Blessed One again entered the soaring meditative concentration.

Rising from the first meditative concentration, he entered the third. Rising from the third, he entered the sphere of infinite space. Rising from the sphere of infinite space, he entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Rising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling. Rising from the meditative absorption of the cessation, he entered once more the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Rising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered the sphere of infinite consciousness. Rising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he entered the fourth meditative concentration. Rising from the fourth, he entered the third. Rising from the third, he entered the second. Rising from the second, he entered the first. Having thus entered the soaring meditative concentration, traversing up and down in this way, he again declared to the great assembly:

"When I examine, with great wisdom, all beings and all phenomena — animate and inanimate, persons and dharmas — dwelling throughout the three realms, I find them utterly consummated: without binding, without liberation, without owner, without abode, without anything to grasp; neither transcending the three realms nor entering into any form of existence; pure from the very beginning, stainless, unafflicted, equal to space, beyond equality and inequality alike; thought and conceptuality exhausted, all conceptual proliferation stilled. Such is the defining characteristic of phenomena, and it is called great nirvāṇa. To see this Dharma exactly as it truly is, is called liberation. Because ordinary, lowly beings do not see it, it is called ignorance."

Having so declared, he again entered the soaring meditative concentration, and from the first meditative concentration up through the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling, and from the meditative absorption of the cessation back down to the first meditative concentration, he traversed thus up and down throughout. Then he again declared to the great assembly:

"When I examine all phenomena of the three realms with the eye of a buddha, the beginning-edge of ignorance is, by its very nature, liberated: it cannot be found when sought in all ten directions, because it has no intrinsic nature. The branches and leaves that would serve as its cause are likewise liberated. Because ignorance is liberated, old age and death are liberated as well. Therefore, since I abide perpetually in the appearance of perfect peace, this is called great nirvāṇa."

At that time, Ānanda, stricken with grief and utterly overwhelmed, was beside himself and unaware — like one intoxicated with wine. He could not see or recognize the fourfold retinue, and he did not know or understand whether the Tathāgata had passed into nirvāṇa or had not passed into nirvāṇa.

At that time the Blessed One, having in this way entered the soaring meditative concentration three times and examined to the very depth of the dharmadhātu, taught the Dharma three times to the great assembly. In like manner, the Tathāgata entered into meditative concentration again and again, up to twenty-seven times in all. Ānanda, not understanding, each time the buddha entered concentration would ask once whether the buddha had passed into nirvāṇa or had not, and in this way he asked without ceasing up to twenty-seven times. And equally without ceasing, the Tathāgata, entering concentration, replied twenty-seven times that he had not passed into nirvāṇa. At that time all those in the assembly were utterly confused and bewildered.

They did not know or understand whether the Tathāgata had passed into nirvāṇa or had not. At that time the Blessed One, having entered meditative concentration three times in succession, taught the Dharma to the assembly three times in succession. Then he lay down on his right side upon a throne of seven precious substances, with his head pointing toward the north, his feet toward the south, his face turned to look toward the west, and his back toward the east. The throne of seven precious substances was adorned throughout with garlands of every variety.

There were four pairs of śāla trees, eight trees in all. The pair to the west stood before the Tathāgata; the pair to the east stood behind the Tathāgata; the pair to the north stood at the Tathāgata's head; and the pair to the south stood at the Tathāgata's feet.

At that time the Blessed One, lying upon the precious throne at the foot of the śāla trees, entered the fourth meditative concentration and, speaking not a word, passed completely into nirvāṇa at midnight.

After the Blessed One, the Bhagavān, had passed into nirvāṇa, the two pairs of śāla trees to the east and west merged into a single tree, and the two pairs to the south and north likewise merged into a single tree, forming together a canopy like a parasol over the precious throne. At that very moment those same trees turned white as the wings of a crane. Their branches, leaves, blossoms, and fruit all fell away; their bark peeled off; the wood itself cracked, and gradually withered until it broke apart entirely, leaving nothing behind.

At that time the innumerable world-realms in all ten directions, countless as the sands of the Ganges in number multiplied by ten million, shook with great violence, and a vast variety of mighty sounds arose. Among them came the cry of lamentation — "Alas! Alas! The world is empty!" — together with sounds of impermanence, of suffering, and of wailing grief.

At that time, throughout all the world-realms in the ten directions, every mountain — the minor surrounding ranges and the great surrounding ranges, the lesser encircling mountains and the great encircling mountains, Mount Meru, the fragrant mountains, the jeweled mountains, the vajra mountains, the black mountains, and all the mountains that rest upon the great earth — all, in a single moment, let out a great sound and crumbled together. The great sound that resounded through the world-realms was the cry, "Alas! Alas! In a single instant the world has been left without a protector! The sun of wisdom has set, and the great mountain of nirvāṇa has toppled!" And it was proclaimed: "The true father of loving-kindness for all sentient beings has departed; the deity worthy of worship and offering is no longer to be seen."

At that time all the great oceans in every world-realm in the ten directions churned and boiled and became turbid, and from the force of the great surging waves diverse sounds arose and resounded: "Alas! Alas! Now that the perfectly and fully awakened Buddha has passed away, the sins and the suffering of sentient beings, the unwholesome acts, will swirl and pour down into the vast ocean of existence. Having lost the true path, when shall liberation ever come?" — so it was proclaimed.

At that time all the rivers and streams, cascades and valleys, rivulets and springs, ponds and marshes and wells overflowed and then ran dry.

At that time the great earth and the expanse of the sky in all the world-realms of the ten directions became utterly dark, and the light of the sun and moon ceased to appear, so that all the world-realms were plunged into darkness. Immediately thereafter a black wind stirred and gave forth a great sound, churning up dust and sand.

At that time all the blossoms, fruits, leaves, and branches of every forest tree, grove, and herb-plant that grows from the great earth fell to the ground and broke apart, leaving not even a remnant behind.

Then, immediately thereafter, all the gods of the world-realms of the ten directions wept with profound grief in the expanse of the sky above. The great trichiliocosm shook violently, and divine flowers of many kinds along with divine incenses beyond count — hundreds and thousands of them — rained down and were heaped up in the great trichiliocosm to the height of Mount Meru (Sumeru), and thus an offering was made to the Tathāgata. Furthermore, in the sky above, countless divine victory banners, divine pennants, divine garlands, divine parasols, and divine precious jewels rained down in such abundance that the expanse of the sky was completely filled. They formed into a many-storied palace of jewels, its four sides beautifully adorned with garlands of the seven precious substances, radiant with the light of flowers, and thus an offering was made to the Tathāgata. In the sky above there also arose divine musical drums, and many forms of divine dance and song, and this cry rang out: "Alas, alas! The buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, and the world is emptied. Since the eyes of sentient beings are blind, the witch of affliction flourishes, and because the stream of the formations of suffering flows without ceasing, it is proclaimed that the wheel of cyclic existence turns on and on."

At that time Ānanda's mind was overwhelmed and he fell into a swoon, unable to comprehend whether the Tathāgata had passed into nirvāṇa or had not passed into nirvāṇa. Seeing only that the condition of the world-realm had changed from what it was before, he asked Aniruddha without pause: "Has the buddha passed into nirvāṇa?" Aniruddha replied: "The buddha, the Blessed One, has completely passed into nirvāṇa."

At that time, when Ānanda heard these words spoken, he fell to the ground in a faint, becoming like a corpse, his breath no longer moving, feeling nothing at all. Then Aniruddha sprinkled cold water on Ānanda's face and revived him. Then, with words of skillful means, arousing his courage, he again spoke to Ānanda thus: "Alas, alas, how sorrowful. Do not grieve greatly. The Tathāgata, having completed all the deeds of taming, and though besought by all the gods, humans, and the rest to remain, did not consent to do so. Do not let your mind be disturbed by excessive grief. Alas, alas, what is to be done? What is now to be done? In a single night, the Teacher of gods and humans reached the end of his work and did not consent to remain." Having aroused his spirit thus, he spoke further to Ānanda: "Although the buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, nonetheless the relics and the supreme precious Dharma Jewel remain forever in the world as a support and refuge for sentient beings. Therefore let us diligently present the precious Dharma of the buddha to sentient beings and liberate them from suffering — this is how we shall repay the kindness of the buddha." When Ānanda heard these words of encouragement, he recovered his breath with a sigh, shed a stream of tears, and was overcome by grief.

At that time, within the city of Kuśinagara, in the Śāla grove all around for a distance of twelve yojanas, gods and humans filled every space, so many sentient beings were present that not even the point of a needle could fit between them, yet not one was uncomfortable and none pressed upon another.

At that time countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of bodhisattvas and all the great assembly, their minds overwhelmed, fell into a faint. Not comprehending whether the Tathāgata had passed into nirvāṇa or not, but seeing only that the earth shook and trembled in a manner unlike anything before, they all asked Aniruddha: "Has the buddha passed into nirvāṇa?" Then Aniruddha, together with the great assembly,

announced to all the gods and humans of the world: "The buddha, the Blessed One, has passed utterly into nirvāṇa."

When the entire innumerable retinue heard those words, they all fainted and fell to the ground. Tormented by suffering so intense that no voice could leave their throats, some collapsed lifeless at the feet of the buddha. Some lost their minds. Some felt their bodies and minds burn as if on fire. Some clasped one another's hands and, barely able to cry out, wept with tears streaming down their faces. Some beat their chests with their fists and wailed aloud with great cries. Some struck their heads with their open palms and tore at their own hair. Some cried out: "Alas, alas, we are tormented by suffering!" Some said: "The Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa far, far too soon." Some said: "We have lost our god." Some said: "The world is empty — the eye of sentient beings is blinded." Some said: "The demoness of affliction has now come into the open." Some said: "The sprouts and seeds of virtue in sentient beings are cut off." Some said: "The hosts of Māra rejoice and have even shed their armor." Some lamented: "This body of mine is impermanent." Some, through the practice of righteous conduct, were thereby liberated. Some said: "We are now without protector or refuge." And some saw blood well up from their bodies and flow down to the ground.

At that time a great sound of many different cries shook every world-realm in all directions. Then the great Brahmā king (Skt. Brahmārāja), lord of the world-realm of Akaniṣṭha, understanding that the buddha had passed utterly into nirvāṇa, descended together with his divine retinue from the first dhyāna, wept with a great cry, fell into a faint before the Tathāgata, and collapsed upon the ground. After a long while he revived and, weeping in verse before the buddha, spoke thus:

By the power of former aspirations, the Blessed One
came to this world of Akaniṣṭha for our sake,
armed with the might to tame countless beings,
subduing wanderers who longed for Dharma yet were destitute.

With skillful means of wisdom he taught the Dharma as was fitting,
so that not a single sentient being came to grief.
He drew beings out from the suffering of the three existences
and set them on the path that leads at last to nirvāṇa.

The Blessed One was a loving mother to sentient beings,
pouring forth the milk of tender compassion upon them all.
Now, having abandoned everything at once,
you have left gods and humans destitute, without a protector.

Alas! The time when the rain of birth could fall
upon the sprouts of virtue in wandering beings is no more.
The sprouts of virtue, suddenly cut off —
gathered up by evil karma, they now proceed to lower rebirths.

The world is empty. What shall we do now?
Sentient beings are blinded, their eye of true wisdom gone.
Wandering, confused in the darkness of ignorance,
they fall and circle through the three existences.

Wretched sentient beings, without protector — what shall we do?
May they find liberation through reliance upon the relics!
Through the power of compassion in our prayer to the Tathāgata,
may they find refuge, freed from suffering!

Alas, how could you, the Blessed One, abandon us
and pass into nirvāṇa in this base and wretched world?

Then Śakra (Indra), lord of the gods, descended together with his retinue from the sky above, raised a great cry of "Alas, alas!", wept with tears flowing down his face, fell into a faint before the Tathāgata, and collapsed upon the ground. After a long while he too revived at last, and with his mind tormented by grief, wept before the buddha in these verses:

Blessed One, the hardships you undertook across eons
were for the sake of us and all living beings.
Having attained unsurpassable awakening,
you nurtured every being as though each were your only child.

The gift of Dharma is the highest among all medicines;
the healer who cures disease is the greatest of physicians.
Sheltering all beneath the cloud of your great compassion,
you rained down the nectar of wisdom upon every one.

The sunlight of wisdom dispelled the darkness of ignorance,
and beings in ignorance beheld the noble path.
With the radiance of noble loving-kindness you illumined the six classes of beings,
and those touched by that light were wholly freed from the three realms of existence.

For what reason have you turned away your great and loving heart
and passed into nirvāṇa — how are we to bear not seeing you?
Where now is the great compassion of your former vow?
You have abandoned sentient beings as though they were mere spittle.

We and all sentient beings without exception —
like calves certain to die when forsaken by their mother —
each of the four assemblies clinging to one another's hands,
beat their breasts, and the sound of their weeping shook the three worlds.

Alas, alas! All of this, the entirety of cyclic existence,
has all at once been left without a refuge.
How sad we are, we whose merit is exhausted —
there is no longer a time of moisture to revive the tender shoot of virtue.

May the radiance of the sacred Dharma Jewel and the relics
illumine all and liberate beings from the three realms of existence!

Alas, how unbearable for us —
when will we ever see the Tathāgata again?

At that time Māgha (Indra's attendant) too, his mind tormented by grief, wept until his very body trembled, and then, kneeling before the buddha, offered praise in these verses:

The buddha, king of Dharma, has nurtured us well,
quenched our thirst for Dharma, and brought forth in us the dharmakāya.
Yet the dharmakāya of sentient beings is not yet fully realized,
and the assembly of those sustained by wisdom has not yet fully gathered.

You who proclaimed with a voice endowed with eight qualities,
causing those in your retinue who heard it to realize awakening —
you who ever radiate the light of great loving-kindness in five colors,
may those in your retinue, touched by that light, be wholly liberated!

Why, having fully passed into nirvāṇa, have you departed,
leaving sentient beings caught in suffering — what are they to do?
Alas, the Blessed One has relinquished great loving-kindness;
we have no protector, and we shall surely perish.

Though we would wish the Blessed One to teach us skillful means,
there is no remedy by which we can cease our grief.
The four assemblies are intoxicated, distraught, fallen senseless, their minds lost;
the sound of their weeping stirs the heavens, the earth, and the three worlds.

O Blessed One, while you rest in great bliss as the sole one,
what is to become of the great suffering of the many beings?
Blessed One, in times gone by, for our sake,
across many eons you gave up your head, your hands, and your feet.
Having manifestly awakened to unsurpassable enlightenment,
you did not remain long but departed into nirvāṇa.

Because we four assemblies abide in the dense darkness of ignorance,
the king of māras rejoices and discards his armor in delight.

Alas, O Blessed One, through your great compassion,
may the loving light of the relics protect us!
For the sake of the four assemblies, out of your Blessed One's loving care,
may the sacred Dharma Jewel's benefit be inexhaustible!
May we not die right away —
yet with only this much of life remaining, what can we accomplish?

Alas, the suffering is utterly unbearable.
From this time forward, there will be no occasion to see the Blessed One again.

At that time, Nanda, having recovered from his faint —

slapped his palms against his head, struck his chest with his fists, cried out, and wept with a body that could scarcely bear the suffering. Then he knelt before the Blessed One and offered these verses of lamentation:

"In former times, by the power of a single shared aspiration with the Blessed One,
I was born in harmony into the Śākya clan.
After the Tathāgata had fully awakened to perfect awakening,
I served him as an attendant for more than twenty years.
While my heart was still unsated in serving with faith,
abandoning me in a single moment, he passes into perfect nirvāṇa.
Alas! Alas! I am tormented by great suffering.
For a long time this suffering will utterly wring my mind.
My own body is not yet free from the net of conditioned existence.
I have not yet emerged from the pit of the gateway of ignorance.
Without the Blessed One having broken open for me the gateway pit of ignorance,
why does he pass into perfect nirvāṇa?
I am like a newborn child,
and if the mother abandons it, it will surely die.
Why has the Blessed One utterly forsaken me,
crossing alone beyond the three realms, abiding in bliss?
What I now confess with remorse before the Blessed One is this:
in the twenty years of serving at his feet,
I fell under the power of laziness in the four modes of conduct,
and acted contrary to the noble mind, failing to bring him delight.
May the fully and perfectly awakened Buddha, through his great compassion,
grant me the nectar of ambrosia and bring me to happiness.
May I, through all the aeons of future time to the very end,
always remain in the presence of the Blessed One.
May the Blessed One, through the rays of his great compassion,
protect me in every world-realm throughout all things.
Alas! Alas! Words cannot express it.
Even a voice to speak of the noble one's kindness falls short."

At that time, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sand grains of countless Ganges rivers, and all the gods and humans of the world, grasping one another's hands, wept deeply and cried out in lamentation. Then, rallying their spirits one by one as best they could, they offered up before the Blessed One countless divine incenses, divine flowers — mandārava flowers, great mandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, and great mañjūṣaka flowers — and sandalwood from the shores of the ocean of the worlds of gods and humans beyond counting, and agaru, and compounded incenses of a hundredfold and thousandfold variety, and countless anointing perfumes, perfumed waters, jeweled parasols, jeweled victory banners, jeweled streamers, pearl garlands, and necklaces filling the entire expanse of the sky, presenting all of these as offerings before the Blessed One.

At that time all the men, women, boys, and girls of the city of Kuśinagara wept deeply, and one by one, mustering far more than before, prepared countless flowers, incenses, victory banners, parasols, and the like, and offered them before the Tathāgata.

At that time the four guardian lords of the four directions, together with their divine retinues, wept deeply, and each one prepared offerings of flowers, incenses, and all manner of offering substances — three times as many as before — and while still weeping approached before the Tathāgata and made offerings.

The gods of the five heavens of the desire realm likewise prepared offerings far surpassing those of before. The gods of the form realm and the formless realm also prepared offering substances far surpassing those of before and made offerings.

At that time the men and women dwelling in the city of Kuśinagara, with tears streaming down their faces, wept and —

not knowing how the funeral had been arranged before, they said this to Ānanda: "When the Tathāgata has passed into nirvāṇa, how are we to conduct the funeral?" Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra, king of heaven), said, as the Blessed One had declared before: "It should be done in the manner of a funeral for a wheel-turning king."

At that time all the people of the city of Kuśinagara wept, entered the city, and fashioned a casket of iron adorned with the seven precious substances. They also laid out a thousand bolts of fine, precious white cloth and countless lengths of exceedingly soft cotton. Beyond that, they set out countless pieces of sandalwood and aloe wood, together with offerings of compounded incense numbering up to a hundred thousand myriads, incense powders, liquid incense, parasols, banners, flowers, and the like — filling the sky like clouds, piled as high as Mount Meru — and having arranged all these things, with tears streaming down their faces they set them before the Tathāgata and, their hearts stricken with grief, made offerings.

At that time all the people of the city of Kuśinagara and the entire great assembly, their tears flowing as they wept, set out in the sky like clouds countless incenses, flowers, victory banners, parasols, and all manner of offering substances without measure, took hold of one another's hands, beat their chests with their fists, and their cries of lamentation caused even the great thousand-fold universe to tremble. They set these things before the Tathāgata and made offerings with all those offering substances.

At that time the great assembly wept, sobbing aloud, and then — wishing to pay the highest reverence — each person took fine white cloth stretchers and, lifting the Tathāgata's body, placed it within the iron casket. They filled the casket with melted butter until it was full, and sealed the lid.

Then all the men and women of the city of Kuśinagara, wishing for merit and wishing to partake in the Tathāgata's virtues, would not allow the Tathāgata's bier-casket to be borne by the gods or men or the great assembly alone; they deliberated together and had it lifted by four champions of unequalled and mighty strength. These four champions removed their garments and ornaments and came into the city to lift the Tathāgata's bier-casket, and after making offerings they strove with all their strength — but could not lift it.

Then eight great champions of that city attempted to lift the bier-casket, each removing their own garments and ornaments and making offerings, and they strained with all their strength — yet still could not lift it.

Then sixteen champions of that city attempted to lift it, and after removing their garments and ornaments they too strained with all the strength they had to lift the buddha's casket, but it could not be lifted.

At that time Mahākāśyapa said this to the champions: "Even if every man, woman, boy, and girl within this city were to try with all their effort to bear the Tathāgata's bier-casket into the city, they could not lift it — how much less could you alone? I ask that you join the strength of the great assembly and the gods together, and if you then lift the casket you will be able to carry it into the city."

The moment Mahākāśyapa finished speaking, Śakra, lord of the gods, arrayed a superb parasol of the seven precious substances along with countless flowers, incenses, victory banners, pennants, and divine music, and together with his divine retinue, weeping profusely, rose up from the sky and made offerings at the noble bier-casket. The gods of the six heavens of the desire realm and the gods of the form realm likewise made offerings at the bier-casket, just as Śakra, lord of the gods, had done.

At that time, the Blessed One, pervading all with his compassion and acting so that all those within the world might equally share in merit without distinction, caused the bier-casket to rise up from the sal grove into the sky above, to the height of a single tāla tree, and then to pass on. Yet all the people of the city of Kuśinagara, and all the gods, humans, and the entire retinue within the world, were unable to lift the buddha's casket.

At that time, Śakra, lord of the gods, together with his divine retinue, fashioned a great parasol of the seven precious substances, adorned on its four sides with garlands of the seven precious substances, and furnished with four jeweled pillars. Covering the Tathāgata's casket with it from the sky above, they made offerings of countless incenses, flowers, victory banners, pennants, garlands, divine music, and many kinds of silk streamers up in the sky. The gods of the six heavens and the gods of the form realm likewise arrayed their offering implements in surpassing fashion, exceeding even what Śakra had done, and made offerings to the Tathāgata's bier-casket.

At that time, when all the people of the city of Kuśinagara saw the Tathāgata's bier-casket rise up into the sky above, they beat their chests, gave out great cries, and wept.

At that time, all the gods and humans, wishing to make offerings to the Tathāgata's bier-casket, filled the entire expanse of the sky until it was completely packed, like clouds, with the seven precious substances, pearls, flowers, incense, garlands, and many kinds of silk streamers. Weeping bitterly, they made offerings to the Tathāgata's bier-casket of the seven precious substances, and all together with one voice they cried out: "Woe! Woe! Because we lack merit, we were unable to lift the Tathāgata's bier-casket. We have no protector, no refuge. We have no share in the root of virtue."

At that time, the Blessed One's golden bier-casket glided softly through the sky above the sal grove and entered through the western gate of the city of Kuśinagara.

At that time, all the laywomen residing in the city of Kuśinagara, together with countless bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, humans, and a great retinue, filling both the sky above and the ground below, followed along behind the Tathāgata's bier-casket. Grasping one another by the hand, they raised great cries, wept, beat their fists upon their chests, and each from their own place arrayed countless flowers, incenses, jeweled victory banners, pennants, and parasols until both the ground and the sky were completely filled, making offerings to the Tathāgata's bier-casket. Each side of the city of Kuśinagara measured forty-eight yojanas.

At that time, the Tathāgata's bier-casket of the seven precious substances glided softly through the sky above, passed out through the eastern gate of the city of Kuśinagara, and circling to the right, entered through the southern gate of the city. From there it glided gently through the sky, circled to the right from the northern gate, and entered through the western gate. In this same manner it circled three times, then glided softly through the sky above, entered again through the western gate, came out through the eastern gate, circled to the right, and entered through the northern gate. From there again it glided gently through the sky, came out through the southern gate, circled to the right, entered through the northern gate, and circled four times. In this way it circled the city of Kuśinagara seven times in all, always to the right.

When the jeweled casket of seven precious substances entered the city, all the vast assembly wept, tears streaming down their faces, and each one took up countless fragrant sandalwood logs and precious incense-logs adorned with patterns and fragrance that filled every world-realm with their scent. They also arranged countless jeweled victory banners, pennants, parasols, incense, flowers, and garlands, and made offerings at the place where the Tathāgata's remains were laid.

At that time the four Great Protectors of the directions, together with their divine retinues, wept and came to the place where the remains were enshrined, bringing with them divine sandalwood and agaru wood whose fragrance pervaded inside and out, wholly and completely saturating all with their scent — five hundred logs each as thick as a chariot wheel — along with other precious incenses, jeweled victory banners, noble jeweled parasols, garlands of flowers, and the like, all arranged as offerings. The gods of the second heaven arrayed one thousand logs; the gods of the third heaven arrayed two thousand logs; the gods of the fourth heaven arrayed three thousand logs; the gods of the fifth heaven arrayed four thousand logs; the gods of the sixth heaven arrayed fully five thousand logs. Each of them, holding pennants and flowers and the like, came weeping to the place where the remains were enshrined, in order to make offerings.

At that time the gods of the form realm (rūpadhātu) and the gods of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) came to the place where the remains were enshrined carrying only incense and flowers, and there made their offerings.

Then the many beings of the world, each and every one, came weeping to the place where the remains lay, carrying fragrant sandalwood wood, agaru wood, flowers, incense, pennants, parasols, and the like, to make their offerings.

At that time, with eyes unceasingly brimming with tears, weeping intensely, the gods and humans raised up fully six thousand logs of sandalwood and agaru wood — all adorned with patterns and fragrance, utterly and completely saturated with scent — and placed them at the place of the remains.

Now, the cool lake Anavatapta has four sides, each two hundred leagues in breadth, and four great rivers flow down from it. At the time when the Blessed One first became perfectly and fully awakened, a sandalwood tree sprang up on the northern bank of the Ganges, its girth as thick as a chariot wheel, reaching into the sky to the height of seven tāla palms, and its fragrance — supremely rich and penetrating — served as an offering to the Tathāgata. The deity of that tree was born at the same moment as the tree itself and constantly made offering to all buddhas with that fragrance. When the Buddha passed into nirvāṇa, the sandalwood tree shed its leaves and bark, withered, and dried up, and the tree deity also died there. Then the other gods took that tree, carried it to the place where the remains lay, and made offerings with it.

That very place on the ground is the site of the remains of all buddhas of the three times, and the Buddha Blessed One, through the power of his former aspirations, had arranged to pass into nirvāṇa in that very place. There, too, are to be found countless jeweled reliquary stupas of the buddhas of former times. That place is indestructible and supremely firm, like a vajra.

Then the Tathāgata's casket glided gently through the sky and arrived at the place of the remains, and by degrees it descended lower and lower, coming to rest upon a throne of the seven precious substances adorned all round with cascading silk streamers and garlands. From then until that moment seven days had passed.

At that time all the men and women of the city of Kuśinagara, together with countless bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and all the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, their hearts tormented by grief, wept profusely —

— holding banners, parasols, jeweled victory banners, incense, flowers, and the like, and following behind the Buddha's casket for seven days. Yet by the blessing of the Buddha, not one of the gods or humans felt any sense of thirst or hunger; they had no thought of food, but wept without ceasing, remembering the Tathāgata.

When seven days had passed since the Tathāgata's remains had been thus laid to rest, and the body was raised up out of the casket, all the men and women of the city of Kuśinagara, together with the countless multitudes of the retinue, wept with such cries that even the world-realm was shaken. And further, with flowers, incense, divine victory banners, parasols, and countless divine musical offerings, they wept and made offerings to the Buddha's remains. At that time the great assembly, weeping, their tears flowing, wrapped their hands in fine soft white cloth and, with hearts full of reverence, gently lifted from the jeweled casket the body of the Tathāgata — adorned with the color of refined gold, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks, indestructible in nature like a vajra — and placed it upon a throne of the seven precious substances. Then the great assembly wept so deeply that all the world-realms of the ten directions were shaken. And further they made offerings with incense, flowers, parasols, and music, and wept.

Then the great assembly, weeping, their tears streaming, each brought fragrant water and countless measures of perfumed unguent, and with these bathed from head to foot the body of the Tathāgata — endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks, bearing immeasurable accumulations of merit and wisdom, indestructible like a vajra, and golden in hue like refined gold. After that, the jeweled casket too was cleansed and purified. Then the great assembly, weeping profusely, their tears flowing, scattered divine incense and flowers of the seven precious substances, and filled the entire expanse of the sky with countless jeweled victory banners, parasols, and streamers in offering, and wept.

Then the great assembly, still weeping, took up countless layers of cotton wadding and wound them around the body of the Tathāgata, golden like refined gold. Over those wrappings of cotton wadding they then wound the body of the Tathāgata in a thousand bolts of priceless fine white cloth. Having wrapped it thus, the great assembly wept until they nearly fainted, and further made offerings with jeweled flowers, incense, jeweled victory banners, jeweled parasols, and divine music, and wept. Then the great assembly, weeping still, each brought strips of fine white cloth and together lifted the body of the Tathāgata and placed it within the jeweled casket; they filled it with butter oil and sealed the lid of the casket. Then the weeping of the great assembly resounded throughout every world-realm, and further they made offerings to the jeweled casket with flowers, incense, streamers, parasols, and music, and wept.

Then the entire great assembly heaped up the fragrant, supremely fragrant sandalwood and incense-wood they had gathered until it rose like Mount Meru, and fashioning it into a tiered pyre like a multi-storied hall of incense, adorned on four sides with the seven precious substances and ornamented with parasols, victory banners, streamers, incense, flowers, garlands, and billowing silken pennants that filled the entire expanse of the sky like clouds, they made offering with divine music.

This is the Noble Sūtra of the Great Passing into Nirvāṇa.

This is the fifty-sixth and final fascicle.

Then the gods, humans, and all the members of the retinue lifted the funeral casket and, as they placed it upon the tiered incense-wood pyre, they gave forth a great cry, beat their breasts, and wept with such a mighty sound of lamentation that it resounded and shook throughout a great thousandfold world system. Then, making further offering with precious victory banners, parasols, incense, flowers, and divine music, they wept.

After that, coming from every direction to pay their respects, they lifted the Tathāgata's funeral casket in white linen stretchers and set it upon the ornately adorned incense wood. There they recited the funeral rites and fell into a swoon. When they revived, they cried out: "Alas, alas — the world is left without a protector and without refuge!" And having said this, with tears streaming down their faces, they made offering with flowers, incense, precious victory banners, streamers, parasols, and divine music.

Then when the Tathāgata's funeral casket had been placed upon the incense wood and fire was applied, the entire vast multitude of the retinue wept intensely, and the sound resounded throughout a great thousandfold world system. Having wept, they made offering to the Tathāgata's funeral casket.

Then the great multitude of the retinue wept, and illuminating the world system with incense-lamp torches of the seven precious substances, each the size of a chariot wheel, they all cried out together with one great voice, causing the entire great thousandfold world system to tremble. They made complete offering with flowers and incense.

At that time, as soon as those precious lamp torches arrived at the place where the incense wood had been stacked, they went out of themselves. Then all the gods, bearing supreme torches of the seven precious substances, illuminated everything with the light of their flames, and weeping as they approached the place where the incense wood had been stacked, those torches too went out of themselves as soon as they arrived. Then all the gods of the ocean, bearing fires from within the ocean — torch-lights of the seven precious substances endowed with countless rays — burned them at the stacked incense wood, and those fires too went out of themselves.

At that time the great multitude of the retinue wept bitterly and made every kind of offering, yet they could not understand why, despite exhausting every rite that had been performed for the Tathāgata, the fire had failed to catch on the incense wood.

At that time the Blessed One, out of great compassion pervading all, settled his attention upon the retinue of Kāśyapa and entered into absorption with the purity of the original ground. At that time Mahākāśyapa, together with five hundred companions, was stationed on Gṛdhrakūṭa — the Mountain of the Vulture's Heap. That mountain lies fifty leagues from the excellent city of Kuśinagara. There, while dwelling in a meditative absorption in which body and mind are supremely at peace, he was startled; his body too trembled and shook.

He then arose from that absorption and, looking out, saw the earth and mountains everywhere shaking violently. Knowing thereby that the Tathāgata had passed into nirvāṇa, he spoke these words to the retinue: "Seven days have now passed since my great Teacher passed completely into nirvāṇa. He has been placed within the casket. Alas, alas — let us go quickly to where the Tathāgata is! If we delay and go late, we shall not be able to behold the Tathāgata's body adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty excellent minor features in their full purity."

Having said this, Kāśyapa, in order to pay his respects to the Blessed One, did not travel through the sky by means of supernatural power but instead took to the road together with his retinue, and went weeping rapidly toward the place where the Tathāgata lay. After seven days he arrived at the excellent city of Kuśinagara. At the eastern gate of the city he encountered a brahmin who was coming along carrying a divine flower. Kāśyapa asked him: "Friend, from where have you come?"

The brahmin replied:

"I have come from the place where the Buddha entered nirvāṇa and was revered."

Kāśyapa asked him: "Where did you find these flowers?"

The brahmin replied: "I found these divine flowers at the place where the Buddha entered nirvāṇa and was revered."

Kāśyapa said: "Give those flowers to me."

The brahmin replied: "That would not be right. I am going to visit my relatives and offer them in worship at home."

Kāśyapa said: "Just let me look at them for a moment." He took them in his hands, and the very instant he placed them upon his head he fainted and fell to the ground. After a long while he revived, and weeping he said: "The Tathāgata's form, adorned with the eighty excellent minor features, like the color of refined gold — from this day forward I shall see it no more." Then, together with his retinue, he entered the northern gate of the excellent city of Kuśinagara, and going inside the city he came to a place where monks were staying, and he saw monks assembled there and gathered together. Those monks said to Kāśyapa: "You have come from a long road — you must be wearied and uncomfortable. Please sit at ease and take your meal here."

Kāśyapa replied: "My great Teacher has passed into nirvāṇa. What eagerness is there in me to sit at ease and remain for alms? Is that at all fitting?"

The monks said: "Who is your Teacher?"

Kāśyapa replied: "Do you not know? Alas! My Teacher is the Blessed One, the Buddha — and now he has passed fully into nirvāṇa."

Upon hearing these words, the monks each said among themselves: "Excellent! Excellent! When the Tathāgata dwelt in the world, we could not endure his strict moral discipline and were unable to practice accordingly. Now that he has passed into nirvāṇa, the restraint of our discipline will become relaxed. For now, in the short term, sit and remain for alms."

By the blessing of the Buddha, the gods and the members of Kāśyapa's retinue had their ears blocked so that they did not hear the words spoken by those corrupt monks — only Kāśyapa alone heard them. Then Kāśyapa, together with his retinue, weeping bitterly, went swiftly to where the Buddha lay.

At that time Kāśyapa and his retinue thought to themselves: "How shall we find offerings and worship the Buddha?" Kāśyapa said: "I was born in this city, and I believe that if I solicit offerings I will find them." So together with his retinue he went through that city soliciting, one by one. Having done so, he found a thousand bolts of fine white cloth, and beyond that he found countless bolts of cotton, immeasurable precious flowers, ointments, scented water, scented oil, victory banners of jewels, jeweled parasols, pennants, musical instruments, ornaments of various kinds, silk streamers, and the like.

Then Kāśyapa and his retinue, carrying all the offering articles they had found, swiftly came out through the western gate of the city. There Kāśyapa heard, from the place where the Buddha lay in nirvāṇa, the sound of the entire vast retinue weeping and wailing intensely, and heard everyone asking Śakra (Indra), the Mighty One, "Now that we are making offerings, from where shall we find fire to light the funeral pyre?" — and heard Śakra saying to the great assembly: "For now, you must wait for Kāśyapa." No sooner had he heard Śakra speak those words to the great assembly than the great Kāśyapa arrived there with his retinue, still weeping. The circles of the assembly parted to make way, and when Kāśyapa from a distance saw the coffin of the Buddha, he and his retinue prostrated, wept bitterly, cried out in lamentation, and fell unconscious.

After a long while he regained consciousness, drew close, and approached the coffin. He then spoke these words to the great assembly: "How am I to open the noble one's coffin?" The retinue replied: "It has now been three times seven days since the Blessed One passed into nirvāṇa. Surely by now the body has deteriorated — how could the coffin be opened?" Kāśyapa said: "The body of the Tathāgata is hard as a vajra, firm, permanent, blissful, utterly pure, and indestructible — it is like a mountain of sandalwood, wholly unlike the bodies of ordinary beings steeped in qualities of a contrary kind." Having said this, he wept bitterly and drew close to the Tathāgata's coffin.

At that moment, through the Tathāgata's great compassion equally pervading all beings, the lid of the coffin opened of itself for the sake of Kāśyapa, and the thousand layers of white cloth and cotton in which the body had been wrapped fell open of their own accord. The body, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and the eighty excellent features, with a complexion like refined gold, firm and steadfast, was revealed openly to Kāśyapa.

When Kāśyapa and his retinue saw this, they wept bitterly, fell unconscious, and collapsed to the ground. After a long while they came back to consciousness, and with eyes full of tears, Kāśyapa and his retinue climbed the pyre of fragrant wood that had been built up and drew very close to the coffin. They cried out in lamentation, then made offerings of flowers, incense, victory banners, parasols, pennants, garlands, music, and the like. They bathed the Tathāgata's body — radiant as refined gold — with ointment and scented water, fumigated it with incense, scattered flowers over it, wept, and performed the rites of veneration.

Having bathed it in this way, Kāśyapa and his retinue wrapped the Tathāgata's body in fresh cotton cloth that could be found, then over that wrapped it in old cotton cloth, then over that wrapped it in a thousand lengths of new white cloth that had been prepared, and over that wrapped it again in a thousand lengths of old cloth. Having thus wrapped the Tathāgata's body in many successive layers, they closed the lid of the coffin and adorned it magnificently with the seven kinds of precious substances.

Then Kāśyapa, weeping bitterly, together with his retinue, circumambulated to the right seven times, and with eyes brimming with tears, joined his palms together, placed his right knee on the ground, and spoke these verses:

Alas, alas — O noble Blessed One!
I am plunged in the depths of suffering.
Why, with your great compassion unconcerned for me,
did you so swiftly pass into nirvāṇa?

When I entered absorption on the Vulture Peak,
I looked in every direction but could not see the Tathāgata.
Looking, I saw that the Blessed One had passed into nirvāṇa,
and I trembled violently, my mind seized with terror.

The world-realm fell into darkness,
mountains and the great earth shook and heaved.
Understanding that the Blessed One had passed away there,
I came swiftly, yet did not see the Blessed One.

Because the Blessed One's compassion did not reach out to me,
I have not seen the buddha pass into nirvāṇa.
Since you left me no single word of teaching,
if I have no protector, what is there to rely on?

Blessed One, I am tormented by suffering,
my mind is bewildered and utterly lost.
Shall I bow at the Blessed One's head?
Or shall I bow at the Blessed One's sacred topknot?
Or bow at the noble hands?
Or bow at the Blessed One's waist?
Or bow at the Tathāgata's feet?
Or bow at the Blessed One's navel?

Alas, O Blessed One — I cannot see you, for you have passed into nirvāṇa!

Please show me the place where I should bow.
When the Blessed One dwells among us, all in the retinue are at ease.
Now that you have passed into nirvāṇa, suffering presses down on everyone.
Alas, alas — I am pierced through with grief!
O great compassion, please show me the place of your hands where I may bow.

The moment Kāśyapa had spoken those verses and wept, the Blessed One, out of great compassion, caused both his feet — bearing the wheel mark adorned with a thousand spokes — to appear beyond the walls of the funerary shrine. From those wheels with their thousand spokes, a thousand rays of light streamed forth, illuminating all the world-realms in the ten directions.

Then Kāśyapa, together with the retinue, beheld the Blessed One's feet. All of them prostrated themselves, wept, and fell into a faint. After a long while they revived, and together with the retinue, weeping deeply, they circumambulated to the right seven times. They bowed before the Buddha, and their cries of grief shook even the fabric of the world-realm. Then, at the feet of the Buddha, they spoke these verses:

The Sugata (well-gone one), perfected, endowed with great compassion,
whose light of serene loving-kindness is utterly without duality —
wherever sentient beings are ripe, there he appears.
I behold both feet bearing the wheel mark adorned with a thousand spokes.
With a mind of pure devotion I reverently bow —
before those two feet adorned with the mark of the wheel.

From the mark of the wheel a thousand rays of light stream forth,
illuminating all the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
With the crown of my head I reverently bow as well —
before the rays of light from those feet adorned with the wheel mark.

Beings touched by that light are wholly freed.
They cast aside the suffering of the three lower realms and a hundred obstacles.
With the crown of my head I reverently bow —
before the one whose wheel's light liberates beings from the lower realms.

In former times, O Blessed One, through countless ages,
you practiced austerities of the greatest difficulty on our behalf.
Through that power you obtained a body like a vajra,
and even from beneath your feet a thousand rays of light spread out.
Seeking refuge, I bow with the crown of my head in reverence —
before the wheel that brings happiness to sentient beings.

Having gathered all merit for the sake of all,
beneath the bodhi tree you subdued the four māras in their fourfold form.
Having subdued the four māras, you brought down the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) as well,
and through this, sentient beings came to hold the right view.
With the crown of my head I reverently bow —
before the feet whose rays of light lead sentient beings to the right view.

Equal to the loving father of all buddhas,
the light of those feet equally liberates all sentient beings.
Seeking refuge, I reverently bow —
before the wheel of those feet that removes suffering.

Having seen the light of the wheel of those feet,
I am deeply tormented, caught between joy and sorrow.
Lamenting and prostrating myself,
I bow before the mark of the wheel adorned with a thousand spokes.

Seeking refuge, I bow before the light of the wheel of those feet.
By the perfected vehicle, may beings transcend the three worlds.
Reverently bowing, I — a god and human being — come seeking refuge.
The wheel's light reveals the suffering of existence in the three realms.

Those beings not yet freed from the gateway of suffering —
may they too take refuge in the light of the wheel of those feet.
We who are not yet wholly freed from saṃsāra —
may the wheel of those feet bring us complete liberation.

Alas, how pitiful — ordinary beings one and all:
for so long they do not see the light of the wheel of those feet.
I confess it: the light of the feet with the thousand-spoked wheel
belongs to the Blessed One of great compassion.
Alas, that today we behold the mark of the wheel —
there will be no time hereafter when we shall see it again.

Then Kāśyapa, together with the retinue, having spoken those verses, fainted once more and fell to the ground. After a long while they revived, and their grief was soothed.

Then the two feet of the Blessed One, bearing the mark of the wheel with a thousand spokes, also withdrew back into the golden casket and disappeared from sight.

At that time, all the men and women, gods and people of that city, seeing that the great Kāśyapa had become thus, beat their chests once more and let out great cries of lamentation, weeping until the sound of their laments resounded throughout immeasurable world-systems of the great thousandfold universe. Each in turn made further offerings with their offering articles.

At that time, four great mighty warriors dwelling in the city of Kuśinagara came, their bodies fully adorned, each bearing a torch the size of a chariot wheel, made of the seven precious substances, which they ignited with fragrant wood — yet the fire died of itself. Thereupon Kāśyapa spoke these words: "If the fire of the three realms combined cannot burn the precious golden casket of the great noble one, then how much less can your fire burn it? Speak no more of that." In that same city, another eight great mighty warriors took up large fires made of the seven precious substances and placed them beside the casket — yet those fires too died of themselves. Then sixteen great mighty warriors took up large fires of the seven precious substances and ignited fragrant wood, yet those fires also died of themselves. Then thirty-six great mighty warriors took up large fires of the seven precious substances and kindled them — yet those fires too died of themselves.

At that time, the great Kāśyapa spoke these words to the warriors and the great assembly gathered there: "Understand it thus: if all the fires of gods, humans, and the rest cannot burn the Tathāgata's golden casket, do not labor in vain as though you could." At that time all the men and women, gods, humans, and the many assembled retinues of that city wept greatly and made offerings with all their offering articles, and at the same moment they paid homage and circumambulated seven times, their cries of grief resounding throughout the world-systems of the threefold thousandfold universe.

At that time, from the power of the Tathāgata's great compassion, fire blazed forth from his breast, spread outward beyond the casket, and, fanned by the wind, caught the fragrant wood that had been heaped up. Seven days passed, and then the fire died out.

During those seven days, all the men and women, gods, humans, and the many assembled retinues of that city wept without ceasing and made continuous offerings.

At that time, the four guardian lords of the four directions thought to themselves: "Let us extinguish the fire with fragrant water, swiftly retrieve the sacred relics, and make offerings to them in the world of the gods." Thinking thus, each of them took up golden vases adorned with the seven precious substances and filled completely with fragrant water. Moreover, on the four sides of Mount Meru, great trees dripping with ambrosial milk stood, their girths a thousand fathoms in circumference and their heights reaching a hundred yojanas. Together with the four guardian lords, they entered those trees and came to the place where the trees leaned, and then poured both the tree's milky sap and the fragrant water simultaneously onto the fire — yet the fire blazed even greater than before and did not die.

At that time, the divine nāga king of the ocean, Sāgaranāgarāja, together with the gods of the rivers and the gods of the streams, seeing that the fire had not died, each of them thought: "Let us take fragrant water and extinguish the fire —"

— thinking "Let us quickly gather the bodily relics and honor them at our own abode" — and each of them, bearing jeweled vases filled with immeasurable quantities of fragrant water, entered at once and arrived at the place where the pyre leaned. They poured water upon it, yet the fire did not die; and so they departed.

At that time the one who had not been extinguished spoke to the four great guardian lords and to the gods of the ocean and the rest, saying: "Is it not that you have taken fragrant water in order to extinguish the fire out of desire for the bodily relics?" They replied: "It is so." Then the one who had not been extinguished said to the four great guardian lords: "Your desire is very great indeed. You dwell in the divine realm high in the sky. If all the relics were sent to the divine realm as you wish, would the human beings who dwell on the earth be able to go there to make offerings?" To the gods of the ocean he also spoke in this way: "You dwell within the ocean and within the rivers. If the Tathāgata's relics were sent wholesale to your domain, how would the human beings who dwell on the earth be able to make offerings to them there?" 

Then the four guardian lords of the four directions confessed their fault and departed back to their divine abodes. At that time the gods of the ocean and the gods of the rivers likewise confessed their fault and said: "We will do as you, the noble one, have said," and they departed back to their own abodes.

At that time Śakra (Indra), the lord of the gods, arrived at the place where the pyre leaned, bearing a vase of the seven precious materials and implements of offering, and the moment he arrived the fire also died of itself.

Then, as Śakra opened the jeweled reliquary casket and was about to lift out the Tathāgata's tooth-relic, the one who had not been extinguished said to Śakra: "What are you doing?" Śakra replied: "I intend to honor the Tathāgata's tooth-relic in the divine world." The one who had not been extinguished said: "It is not right for you alone to have taken it out beforehand like that. Let the retinue assemble, and let it be shared from the very beginning." Śakra said: "The Blessed One long ago granted me a single tooth-relic. The moment I arrived, the fire also died of itself." Saying this, he opened the jeweled reliquary casket, invited forth the single upper tooth-relic from the right side of the buddha's jaw, conveyed it to the divine world, built a stūpa over it, and made offerings.

At that time, two rākṣasas of exceptional swiftness concealed themselves so that their bodies were invisible, followed behind Śakra, and stole two of the buddha's tooth-relics — and no one among the great multitude of the retinue perceived it.

At that time all the men and women and the great retinue of that city, pressing forward to seize the relics, were addressed by the one who had not been extinguished in these words: "Wait a moment. Let them be distributed properly, in accordance with the scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, and then let offerings be made." At that time those among the men and women and the great retinue of that city who had not heard what the one who had not been extinguished said came, each from their own place, bearing many weapons — spears, bows and arrows, swords, lassos, and the like — and pressed forward to seize the relics.

Then, when the people of that city opened the Tathāgata's reliquary casket, the retinue saw that the cotton-tree fibers and the white cloth had not been burned at all, and they were struck with overwhelming grief; their eyes filled with tears and they wept. And weeping, they made offerings and prostrated; then, setting their knees upon the ground, they spoke these verses:

By the great commanding power of the Tathāgata,
who exercises sovereignty over all the world entire,
through great compassion and the aspirations of the past —

they liberate sentient beings entirely from the ocean of existence;
through the power of their boundless primordial wisdom and supernatural knowledge,
they enter into cyclic existence without obstruction.
From one body they manifest many bodies;
from many bodies, likewise, one — and without limit.
Those to be trained perceive them through the power of blessing.
They show the passing beyond sorrow without cause.

Our merit has been exhausted; thus, without cause,
the Tathāgata has passed away beyond us.
The precious jeweled casket of the Tathāgata:
all the strongmen together tried to lift it — it would not move.
By the force of great compassion, this noble one
could soar as high as a single palm tree into the sky above,
and passing through the sky, he circled the city of Kuśinagara,
encircling it seven times over the course of seven days.
After circling thus in that manner, he descended and returned to his resting place.
This miraculous display, pure and unmingled,
no one among gods and humans together could fathom.

The Blessed One's passage into nirvāṇa —
the vajra-like, indestructible, sovereign power —
was not consumed by fire at all.
From within his heart a fire of loving-kindness arose,
and for seven full days it showed how the cremation took place.
No one among gods and humans could ignite it,
but the Blessed One, through the force of his great compassion,
demonstrated this power — and the moment Śakra arrived, the fire went out.

The fine cotton-tree fibers that had wrapped the body of the Buddha
were not burned or scorched even by the great blazing fire.
The white cloth placed inside the precious jeweled casket
was likewise not scorched in the midst of the flames.
By this we understand the sovereign power of the Tathāgata.

We prostrate to you, sovereign of the Dharma, king of Dharma —
we prostrate, O Compassionate One, protector of the world.
We prostrate among the nobles, without fear, homage to you.
We prostrate to the strength of great compassion present everywhere.
We prostrate to the one who rules by blessing.

From this time forth we are separated from the Blessed One;
though we sink into suffering, we have no protector, no refuge.
Alas, alas! Noble Blessed One —
we are parted from you forever, and the time to see you again does not come.

Having spoken these verses, the great retinue wept most bitterly, and each took up offerings and made offerings.

At that time, Aniruddha (the unobstructed one, son of the śākyan clan), together with the gods, humans, and the great retinue, and all the people of that city, drew near to the reliquary casket, and looking upon the body wrapped in cloth and cotton-tree fibers, they found that the two outermost pieces — the thousand lengths of white cloth in which Kāśyapa had wrapped the body, and the thousand lengths of white cloth offered by the people of the city — and the cotton-tree fibers had not been burned; but all the rest had been burned by the fire.

Then Aniruddha cut the white cloths and the cotton-tree fibers into pieces and distributed them among the great retinue, and out of them made precious jeweled stūpas and made offerings. Aniruddha also divided separately the charred remnants of the other burned cloth, made precious jeweled stūpas of them, and made offerings. The remaining ashes he gathered separately, where it was not possible to distribute them further, and made stūpas and offered.

The people of that city had already had a goldsmith fashion eight golden caskets raised on lion thrones, each fully adorned with the seven precious substances. Each of the eight precious caskets held the capacity of half a khala, and they were placed upon thrones of lion seats made of the seven precious substances. Each of those eight lion thrones of the seven precious substances was lifted by thirty-two strongmen adorned with ornaments of the seven precious substances, their bodies wrapped in cloths of many colors. Upon each of those lion thrones, eight maidens each fully adorned with precious ornaments held the caskets of the seven precious substances.

Upon each of those thrones, eight more maidens fully adorned with the seven precious substances held parasols of the seven precious substances and used them to cover the golden caskets completely. Upon each of those thrones, yet another group of eight maidens each fully adorned in ornaments held swords of the seven precious substances and stood guard over the caskets of the seven precious substances. Upon each of those thrones, still another eight fully adorned maidens each held ritual vases and stood facing the four sides of the caskets.

Around each of those thrones, a countless multitude of people each held, in their own station, divine musical instruments, victory banners, pennants, precious parasols, incense, flowers, and garlands, and circumambulated them while making offerings. Around each of those thrones, yet another countless multitude each held bows and arrows, spears, lassoes, iron hooks, and a full complement of weapons, and surrounded them as a guard escort, proceeding from the city of Kuśinagara to the place where the Blessed One had entered into final cessation.

Following in the wake of the eight lion thrones of the seven precious substances, the people of that city each took up countless incense sticks and vessels of scented water. They walked behind the strongmen, anointing with incense sticks the road from the city all the way to the place of final cessation, purifying the path entirely with fragrant scent and making it very wide. Along both sides of that road, countless precious victory banners, pennants, parasols, incense, flowers, pearls, garlands, silk streamers, musical instruments, songs and dances, and all such things adorned the left and right of the way, as the relics of the Blessed One made their return journey.

Then the strongmen lifted the eight lion thrones of the seven precious substances and carried them to the place of final cessation. There, all of them weeping and lamenting in one voice, the sound of their lament resounded throughout the great thousandfold world-system, and each made offerings with a mind of faith.

At that moment, by the power of the Blessed One's great compassion, his vajra-like body dissolved into fine relics, while the four canine teeth remained whole and intact. When the great assembly saw that the bodily remains had thus become fine fragments, they were all the more tormented in their grief and wept, making offerings. Then the people of the city and those who had not yet dispersed, their eyes filled with tears, gathered up the relics, poured them into the caskets of the seven precious substances placed upon the lion thrones, and the eight caskets were filled to the full with the bodily remains.

At that time, when all the gods and humans of the world saw the bodily remains of the Blessed One laid to rest within the golden caskets, they were all the more tormented in their grief and wept, making offerings. At that time, the strongmen of that city, along with men and women, as the caskets of the relics of the Blessed One made their way back toward the city of Kuśinagara, the great assembly wept most bitterly, their tears streaming down, and made offerings. Then the strongmen, weeping deeply together with all their retinue, lifted the eight lion thrones of the seven precious substances and proceeded along the road that had been anointed with incense sticks, heading straight to the city of Kuśinagara.

Then the gods, humans, and the great assembly, weeping deeply, their lament resounding throughout every world-system, each made offerings to the bodily remains of the Tathāgata with whatever offerings they had to hand, and then placed them at the crossroads in the middle of the city.

At that time, the people dwelling in the city of Kuśinagara marshalled a countless host of soldiers, fully equipped with armor and weapons of every kind, and stationed them in countless rows around all four sides of the city. Yet this was done solely out of fear that the relics might be seized by others — it was a guard, not an army assembled with any intent to fight.

Moreover, around five hundred great masters of mantra were set to guard the four gates of the city, so that no obstructors might enter. And at the four corners of the city, victory banners of precious substances, pennants, parasols, ornaments of every variety, and vessels filled with flowers and the like were erected as offering-banners.

Then all the many men and women, gods, humans, and the great retinue of that city wept in a continuous great outpouring, and with minds of faith made offerings with whatever offering materials they had to hand. Each of the eight lion thrones of the seven precious substances was also guarded by five hundred masters of mantra, out of fear that gods, nāgas, yakṣas, hungry ghosts, rākṣasas, and the like might seize them.

In this way, a full day passed. The king of Kapilavastu, of the Śākya lineage — the land where the Tathāgata had formerly been born — together with his Śākya retinue, by the blessing of the Blessed One, had not perceived that the Buddha had passed completely into nirvāṇa. It was only after twenty-one days following the Buddha's passing that they first became aware of it. The king of Kapilavastu, together with the Śākya clan, wept deeply and then journeyed swiftly to where the city of Kuśinagara lay. There they saw the city surrounded by a countless army, and at the four corners of the city the precious victory banners and pennants had been erected, and at the four gates of the city many masters of mantra were stationed. Then the king and the Śākyas said: "The Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa."

The masters of mantra said: "The Buddha passed into nirvāṇa twenty-eight days ago. He has been washed and bathed, and the relics are now being laid out."

The king said: "We are kinsmen of the Blessed One. If, by the blessing of the Blessed One, we did not perceive the Tathāgata's passing into nirvāṇa — now, as we have come to pay our respects to the bodily remains of the Tathāgata, open the road and the gates without obstruction."

When the masters of mantra and the soldiers heard these words, they admitted the king and the Śākyas inside. They beheld the bodily remains of the Blessed One, and with a single cry broke into lamentation. Circumambulating to the right seven times, they wiped away their tears and spoke these words: "Please grant us even a single portion of the Tathāgata's relics as an object of worship for us."

The great assembly replied: "You are of the Śākya lineage, and you may be known as kinsmen — yet the Buddha Blessed One gave nothing to you. These relics, moreover, each have their own custodians; you have no claim to them. Turn back now."

At that, the king and the Śākyas, having obtained no share of the relics, were overwhelmed with grief, and weeping, they fell to the ground in a swoon. After a long while they revived, and disconsolate, they spoke thus to the great assembly: "The Buddha Blessed One was of our own Śākya lineage, and it was out of affection for you that he passed into nirvāṇa here among you — why then will you not give us even the slightest portion of the relics?" Having said this, they prostrated before the relics, circumambulated seven times, and then, weeping and yet furious, departed.

At that time, the king of the central land of Magadha, Ajātaśatru — who had slain his own father and was consumed with intense remorse — had broken out in malignant sores across his body. A ray of light belonging to the Blessed One, called "Moonbeam," touched his body, and by its power the sores healed and he recovered. He then came before the Blessed One, made full confession, and through the Blessed One's great compassion was cleansed by the medicine of the Dharma, that nectar-like antidote to wrongdoing. He departed back to his palace, purified of the stain of his grave offense, yet entirely unaware that the Tathāgata had passed completely into nirvāṇa.

On the very night of the Blessed One's passing into nirvāṇa, the king dreamed these dreams: the moon fell to the earth, and from the earth the sun arose, while stars rained down upon the clouds like falling rain; smoke rose up from the ground, and the seven planetary stars blazed openly in the sky; and a great mass of fire blazed in the heavens, manifestly burning in the sky, then fell all at once to the earth. He dreamed all this, and waking immediately in great fright, he assembled his ministers and declared: "I have had such dreams — what is to be made of them?"

The ministers replied: "These are omens of the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa. Since the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, the afflictions will rise up throughout all sentient beings in all three realms and along the six destinies, and it is as a great fire falling from the sky that this appeared. Since the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, the light of his compassion — like the moon — and his wisdom that pervades all equally will fade; thus the moon fell to the earth. The falling of the stars to the earth signifies that, since the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, all people will transgress the eighty thousand modes of conduct and every precept of moral discipline; rather than acting in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, they will practice wrong Dharma, and sentient beings will fall into the hells. The sun falling to the earth signifies that, since the Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, the mass of suffering of the three lower realms will rise like a sun in the world. Such are the meanings of these dreams."

When the king heard these words, in the middle of the night, accompanied by his retinue of ministers, he arrived near the city of Kuśinagara.
