He saw innumerable fourfold armies surrounding the city of Kuśinagara in countless ranks, and at the four gates he saw mantra masters (dhāraṇī-holders) and others keeping guard. He addressed one of the mantra masters, saying: "Has the Buddha passed completely into nirvāṇa?" The mantra master replied: "The Buddha passed into nirvāṇa twenty-eight days ago. The great assembly is at this moment still preparing the relics of his body." The king said: "I had not heard of the Buddha's passing. I saw ill omens in a dream, and when my ministers told me they were signs of the Tathāgata's nirvāṇa, we came here. Let the path be opened so that we may go and pay homage to the vajra-like body relics of the Tathāgata." The mantra masters admitted the king into the city.

At the crossroads of the main road, the relics had been placed in a golden casket upon a lion throne, and he saw the entire great assembly making offerings while weeping. The king and his retinue paid homage and wept, circumambulated seven times from the right side, and made offerings. The king then asked the great assembly whether they might grant him a portion of the Tathāgata's relics. The assembly replied: "Great King, you have come too late. The Lord previously declared to whom the Tathāgata's body relics were to be distributed, and the king has no allotted share — depart now." King Ajātaśatru, hearing these words, was displeased and aggrieved that his request had not been granted, yet he nonetheless paid homage to the relics and departed.

At that time, the king of Vaiśālī, learning only on the twenty-first day after the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa —

— arrived together with his retinue at the city of Kuśinagara. He saw that the city of Kuśinagara was surrounded by a countless host of soldiers in countless ranks. At that time, the king of the land of Akaleka also learned only on the twenty-first day after the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa, and swiftly came to the city of Kuśinagara, where he likewise saw the city surrounded by a countless host of soldiers in countless ranks. At that time, the king of the land of Byinuti, named Fearless, also learned of it only on the twenty-first day after the Buddha's complete passing into nirvāṇa. At that time, the king of the land of Cālaka likewise learned of it only on the twenty-first day after the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa. At that time, the king named Śikana likewise learned of it only on the twenty-first day after the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa. At that time, the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) king of Paśala likewise learned of it only on the twenty-first day after the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa, and came to the city of Kuśinagara together with a retinue of ministers. He saw the city of Kuśinagara encircled and guarded by a countless host of soldiers, and at all four gates he saw gatekeepers who were mantra-masters. He addressed a mantra-master and said: "Has the Buddha passed completely into nirvāṇa?" The mantra-master replied: "Twenty-one days have passed since the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa, and now a great assembly is engaged in the work of dividing the body relics. We ourselves did not learn of the Buddha's complete passing into nirvāṇa until later. If you wish to go and pay homage to the Tathāgata's relics, let us open the way for you." The mantra-master sent the king into the city, and at the crossroads in the heart of the city the king saw the relics residing in a golden casket adorned with seven kinds of jewels, set upon a lion throne. All of them at once prostrated themselves, wept, circumambulated to the right seven times, and made offerings with whatever was available. The king said: "Since we had not learned of the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa beforehand, might we be granted a portion of the Tathāgata's body relics as a support for worship?" The assembly replied: "The rite of distributing the body relics was declared beforehand. The king has no allotted share — depart now." The king, together with his retinue, his mind afflicted by sorrow at not having received the body relics, paid homage to the relics and departed in tears.

The noble sūtra of the Great Complete Passing into Nirvāṇa is concluded.

This sūtra of the Great Passing into Nirvāṇa, translated from Chinese, was translated, revised, and definitively established by the Chinese abbot Wang Faxun, the Dharma-keeper Géwé Lodrö, and the translator Gyatso Dé.

The volume designated Tha of the Sūtra section is contained herein.

This concludes the translation. The following are translator's notes.

The river name Hiraṇyavatī is reconstructed from the Tibetan phonetic rendering. The Tibetan phrase for "as a mother lioness regards her cub" (sgra can 'dzin) literally means "like Rāhu" which is a name for the lion constellation or, in some contexts, the eclipse-demon — here the comparison is clearly to a lioness protecting her young, a standard simile in this sūtra tradition, and has been rendered accordingly. The passage ends mid-sentence as the Tibetan input itself ends at the introduction of the senior monks.  The nun's names — Śrībhadrā, Priyadarśanā, and Sāgaramatī — are reconstructed from the Tibetan dpal bzang, bsnyen dga' ma, and rgya mtsho'i blo gros respectively; these reconstructions are plausible but not confirmed by a parallel Sanskrit witness in this passage.

The phrase rendered "like nāgas among human beings, having thoroughly entered the ten grounds" reflects the idiom that likens bodhisattvas on the tenth ground (daśabhūmi) to the nāga king — a standard comparison in Mahāyāna sūtra literature. The phrase "displaying the body of a woman" for bodhisattvas who are nuns reflects the Mahāyāna teaching that advanced bodhisattvas assume whatever form is most beneficial, including a female form, without being bound by it.  The phrase rendered "flushing blood" describes the body becoming suffused or reddened — a physical manifestation of overwhelming devotion and emotion classically compared in the text itself to the reddish flesh visible within a lotus flower. This is an unusual simile whose precise doctrinal valence is primarily devotional-aesthetic rather than technical.

The paired opposites listed as "antidotal teachings" — suffering and happiness, permanence and impermanence, and so on — represent a standard contemplative enumeration of Dharma themes taken as objects of analytical meditation (vipaśyanā); the Tibetan term rendered "antidotal" refers to teachings functioning as antidotes to false views.  The phrase "Ki hud! Ki hud! The worlds are emptied!" renders the exclamation "ཀྱི་ཧུད་ཀྱི་ཧུད་འཇིག་རྟེན་སྟོངས་སོ།" This is a ritual or apocalyptic cry; "ki hud" is a Tibetan interjection of alarm or lamentation. The sense "the worlds are emptied" likely refers to the miraculous evacuation of worlds as an auspicious sign in the sūtra's narrative context. The specific significance would depend on the surrounding sūtra; rendered phonetically since it functions here as a quasi-onomatopoeic sacred utterance.

The "nine-stringed lute" (དགུ་པོ་རྒྱུད་མངས) is a tentative rendering; the instrument referenced may be a vīṇā-type multi-stringed instrument. The exact identity of སེའུ and ཤིར among the musical instruments listed is not fully certain; rendered here as "cymbals" and "bells" respectively following standard lexicographical convention.  The phrase rendered as "inner offering" for "nang gi" in context most likely means the last personal or intimate offering, framed as something heartfelt and final rather than the technical tantric "inner offering." This reading is consistent with the narrative context.

The names of the laywomen at the close follow a reconstruction from the Tibetan: "Tsowo yon ten" is read as a name meaning something like "Jīvana-qualities" or "Jīvanaśrī," and "dpal gyi phreng ba" as "Śrīmālā" (garland of glory). These are standard figures in sūtra literature. If the Tibetan here is a translation of a specific Sanskrit name-list, some names may vary in other recensions.  The term rendered "eraṇḍa plant" preserves the Sanskrit botanical name (eraṇḍa, the castor-oil plant, Ricinus communis), a stock image of insubstantiality in Buddhist literature. The Tibetan ཨེ་རཎྜ is a direct phonetic transcription.

The phrase "the hollow of a hoof-print" renders བ་རྨིག་གི་ནང (literally "inside a hoof-print"), a classical Indian simile for a tiny vessel utterly inadequate to contain something vast; the meaning is that even the ocean's water poured into so small a space is more conceivable than a complete enumeration of the body's faults.

The three practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness correspond to the three gateways to liberation (vimokṣamukha): śūnyatā, ānimitta, and apraṇihita.  The three named Licchavi youths — Pure Stainless Essence, Mindfully Purified, and Ever Stainless Pure Virtue — are rendered from their Tibetan epithets rather than from recoverable Sanskrit originals; these appear to be stock epithet-names and no reliable Sanskrit back-formation is certain enough to include.

The phrase rendered "woolen oxen" (bal glang) literally means oxen or yaks covered or laden with wool bales — a standard image of wealth-bearing animals in offering processions; "woolen oxen" preserves the term's flavor without over-interpreting.  The merchant names Sunlight, Protector of the World, and Protector of the Dharma are translations of the Tibetan epithets Nyi ma'i 'od, 'Jig rten skyong, and Chos skyong respectively, rendered into English since no Sanskrit equivalents are given in the text.

The phrase rendered "their coming was subdued entirely, as hail falls upon grass and trees" is contextually difficult. The Tibetan compares their subdual or humbling to hail falling on grass and trees, likely meaning that those who had disparaged the Dharma were thoroughly chastened by the power of these Mahāyāna devotees. This interpretation follows the most natural reading of the passage.  The phrase rendered "led on" for ཐོག་མར་དྲངས་སོ is a continuation of the framing from the preceding passage, where these consorts appear in female form to tame beings; the verb means they were brought forward or led in procession, with the named consorts heading the group.

The measurements given — leagues (dpag tshad, Skt. yojana) — are treated as literal cosmological hyperbole appropriate to the sūtra genre and are not normalized.  The passage presents a sequence of three groups — divine daughters, nāga kings, and yakṣa kings — but the Tibetan text gives these groups slightly out of order, with the yakṣa king passage appearing after the nāga kings despite being introduced earlier. The translation follows the sequence as it appears in the Tibetan, preserving the textual order even where it may reflect a scribal displacement. The nāga king names Jokpo, Gawos, and Nyegawos are retained as transliterations of Tibetan names without attested Sanskrit equivalents in the immediate context.  The terms "tānapā" and "prabhāsana" render Tibetan ཏ་ན་པ and མདངས་ཟ་བ respectively. The former is likely a transliteration of an unidentified Sanskrit category; the latter literally means "those who consume radiance or luster" and may correspond to a class of beings in the Sanskrit original that is not immediately identifiable from the Tibetan alone.

The name "Lāhu" renders Tibetan ལ་ཧུ, which appears to be a phonetic transcription of an underlying Sanskrit or possibly Prakrit name for the lead bull king.  The phrase rendered "last inner offering" translates "mchod pa nang gi tha ma," which the commentarial tradition reads as the final personal or bodily offering — i.e., the sages' last act of homage before the Buddha's parinirvāṇa. The Tathāgata's silence is a standard narrative device indicating that acceptance would prolong his stay, contrary to his resolve to pass into nirvāṇa.

The river name "Hiraṇyavatī" is a standard Sanskrit reconstruction for the Tibetan "klung ha ri ba ti," the river near Kuśinagara beside which the Buddha is said to have passed into nirvāṇa.

"Uttarakuru" here glosses the Tibetan "byang gi sgra mi snyan," literally "the northern Unpleasant Sound" — one of the four continents — but in context the passage appears to be comparing the spontaneously appearing grove to the celestial pleasure grove of the Thirty-Three gods; the parallel phrasing is somewhat compressed and the exact referent is slightly ambiguous in the Tibetan.  The long sequence of flower names — māndārava, kacilika, mañjūṣaka, santānika, and the rest — are Sanskrit celestial flower names transliterated into Tibetan. Their Tibetan glosses (pleasing, all-good, timely, fragrant city, and so on) are rendered literally as given in the text, representing either actual Sanskrit meanings or traditional Tibetan explanations. There is some uncertainty about several of these identifications in the botanical and textual literature, but the translations given follow the literal Tibetan readings.

The phrase rendered "Victor of Immeasurable Mansions" reflects the Tibetan "gzhal med khang rgyal bar 'gyur ba," which could also mean "the palace that surpasses all immeasurable mansions." The reading adopted here follows the most natural sense of the compound.  The title "Māra pāpīyas" rendered as "Māra the Evil One" follows standard convention; the Tibetan བདུད་སྡིག་ཏོ་ཅན / བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན literally means "the sinful, evil māra," the standard rendering of the Sanskrit epithet pāpīyas.

The cosmological term སྟོང་འབྲིང་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས, rendered "a middling thousandfold world system," refers to the second tier of the standard three-tier Buddhist cosmological scheme: the small thousand, the middling (twice-thousand), and the great (trice-thousand) world systems.  The mantra syllables (cyog kye, ta ta la cyog kye, lo ha le, ma hā lo ha le, ala cala tala svāhā) are transliterated as they appear in the Tibetan, which represents a phonetic rendering of a Sanskrit or hybrid Sanskrit dhāraṇī. No normative Sanskrit reconstruction can be given with confidence, so the Tibetan phonetics are rendered as-is.

The phrase rendered "the last of our inner offerings" translates མཆོད་པ་ནང་གི་ཐ་མ, which is somewhat ambiguous — it may mean "the innermost and final offering" or "this last of the inner offerings." The same phrase recurs when Śakra's retinue speaks, confirming it is a set expression in this context.  The ten epithets of a buddha appear twice in this passage in their standard Tibetan form. The rendering follows the traditional enumeration: Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly and fully awakened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed, tamer and guide of persons, teacher of gods and humans, blessed buddha. The Tibetan "མཁྱེན་པ་དང་ཞབས་སུ་ལྡན་པ" literally means "endowed with knowledge and feet," a standard rendering of vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, meaning one perfected in knowledge and conduct, rendered here accordingly.  The phrase rendered "Palace of Joy called Sudharmā in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three" is an interpretive rendering: the Tibetan reads literally "the Thirty-Three Heaven's pleasure grove of supreme happiness." The Sudharmā is the assembly hall rather than a grove, so the translation keeps the literal "pleasure grove" of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three rather than importing that specific name.

The exclamation "ཀྱི་ཧུད་ཀྱི་ཧུད" is an untranslatable cry of alarm or dismay; it is rendered idiomatically as "in alarm" with the semantic content preserved in the reported speech.  The phrase rendered "fragrant food" translates a compound meaning literally "food with fragrance" or "food endowed with scent," functioning as a supernaturally purifying substance — a recognized tantric and sūtric motif.

The two named exceptions to the gathering — Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda — are given in a construction that most naturally reads as an exclusion from the general assembly, consistent with narrative context in parinirvāṇa sūtra literature where these two figures play distinct roles and are sometimes depicted as absent or delayed.

The "sixteen classes of wicked actions" is a specific doctrinal enumeration whose precise contents are not elaborated here; the number sixteen is given explicitly in the Tibetan. The passage is from the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, the section where the Buddha corrects the monks' understanding of the four perceptions (suffering, impermanence, emptiness, no-self) by revealing their inverted application: ordinary beings wrongly perceive the Buddha's own qualities — self, permanence, bliss, purity — as their opposites. The passage contains the key doctrinal assertion of the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra that the four qualities — permanence, bliss, self, and purity — are the true attributes of the Tathāgata and nirvāṇa, in deliberate inversion of the standard four marks of conditioned existence. The passage presents a sustained inversion of the standard three marks of existence. The Tibetan reads "grags 'dzin," meaning "one who holds to fame or reputation," interpreted as a pejorative epithet for Yaśodharā (sometimes rendered in Tibetan sources as a name equivalent to Yaśodharā, "she who holds fame"). The point of Kāśyapa's objection is that if the Tathāgata had truly transcended all afflictions long before his renunciation, why did he father a child with Yaśodharā? This is a standard doctrinal puzzle addressed in Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra literature: the Tathāgata's pre-awakening conduct is explained as the display of a being who had in truth long since crossed beyond afflictions but manifested the appearance of a householder as skillful means.

The phrase rendered "branches of awakening" translates byang chub kyi yan lag, the standard term for the seven factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga, Skt. saptabodhyaṅga). The phrase rendered "crowd one another nor feel crowded" translates the Tibetan "གཅིག་ལ་གཅིག་གཟེར་ཅིང་དོག་པ," which literally means something like "pressing upon one another and being cramped." The chosen rendering conveys the sense of spatial constriction intended by the context.

The sūtra referred to as "Going Heroically" is the Śūraṃgamasamādhi-sūtra, which is the standard identification for this reference in the tradition. The Tibetan "དཔའ་བར་འགྲོ་བའི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་མདོ" is a direct rendering of that title.

Rāhula is the name of the Buddha Śākyamuni's son in the biographical tradition; the passage addresses a potential misunderstanding that the Tathāgata fathered Rāhula out of ordinary desire. The phrase rendered "carrying a load on the head, on the back, on the side" translates a sequence of physical discomforts or bodily conditions: གླད་པ་ན་བ, ལྟོ་ན་བ, རྒྱབ་ན་བ, which literally mean aching at the temples, aching in the belly, and aching in the back. This is a meaningful doctrinal point: the list enumerates ordinary bodily ailments that the Buddha displays for the sake of ordinary beings, though in reality his body — being the fruit of merit — is entirely free of them.  The phrase rendered "the four lower states of existence along the path of karma" translates "lam rgyud bzhi," literally "the four streams of the path." The verse about the bird in flight is a well-known image in early Buddhist literature for the tracklessness of the liberated being; the Blessed One's subsequent reinterpretation of it in terms of wealth and the Saṅgha is the text's own exegesis and is rendered faithfully without harmonizing it with other traditions. The phrase rendered "those of wrong craving" translates a term literally meaning one who craves wrongly or perverts craving — likely corresponding to Sanskrit mithyātṛṣṇika or a related formation. The gods of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" render the standard formless realm deity class corresponding to the Sanskrit naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana; the discussion of whether they are "with form or without form" reflects a doctrinal point specific to the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's analysis of liberation that goes beyond standard Abhidharma. The phrase rendered "craving for Dharma" translates chos kyi 'dod pa, which in context denotes the Tathāgata's compassion-driven wish to teach and benefit beings — a deliberate contrast with the deluded craving of hungry ghosts. The pāśika flower — rendered here from the Tibetan "me tog pa shi ka" — is likely the Sanskrit pāṭalā or a related fragrant flower; the simile turns on the paradox that the fragrance is nowhere locatable in any individual petal, illustrating that liberation cannot be pinned down in any particular locus. The phrase rendered "moistens all births" is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan; it may mean liberation, like water, nurtures and sustains all living beings across their rebirths, bringing them toward growth and eventually release.  The passage distinguishes two senses of "emptiness": a spurious emptiness attributed to non-Buddhist renunciants who have nothing (mere material destitution mistaken for liberation), and the genuine "non-empty emptiness" of Buddhist liberation. The statement that "the view of self is the nature of a buddha" is a deliberate doctrinal provocation characteristic of tathāgatagarbha texts. It does not endorse an ordinary ātman but indicates that the buddha's mode of being transcends both the reifying "self" view and the nihilistic "no-self" view, and that what liberation cuts is only clinging and grasping, not the buddha's own self-awareness or self-possession. This should be understood within that tradition's technical framework. The phrase rendered "certainty" for "གདོན་མི་ཟ་བ" literally means "what cannot be otherwise" or "what is infallible / beyond doubt." The phrase "action without interval" renders the technical term for the five heinous acts (ānantarya-karma), deeds so grave that their karmic result follows immediately without any intervening rebirth. The passage makes the subtle doctrinal point that while the intention produces this heinous karma, the Tathāgata's body — being the nature of reality itself — cannot actually be harmed.  The phrase rendered as "the pile of grain-sacks" translates a term meaning a stack or heap of grain measures; the precise form of storage is contextually inferred but does not affect the doctrinal meaning of the example.

The description of the stream-enterer as one who "has transcended the ordinary world while still bearing the defining marks of affliction" is a technically precise formulation: the stream-enterer has crossed the threshold of the noble path and thus is no longer a worldling, yet has not eliminated all afflictions. This is consistent with Abhidharma classification.  The list of "eight great beings" with qualities beginning from "having few desires" and "having many desires" is unusual and likely refers to a specific enumeration from the source sūtra that is not a standard canonical list; the text appears to be making a technical distinction between these eight and ordinary persons, though the full enumeration is not given here and context from surrounding passages would be needed to identify it precisely.

The passage's attribution of the ten bodhisattva grounds to the arhat is doctrinally striking from a standard Mahāyāna perspective, suggesting this text may be using "arhat" in an elevated, Mahāyāna sense equivalent to a very advanced bodhisattva or even a buddha-level being, rather than the Foundational Vehicle sense of one who has attained personal liberation. This is a genuinely significant doctrinal point that readers should note.  The phrase rendered "the eye of miraculous vision" translates the Tibetan for a supernormal power of sight, contrasted with the ordinary "eye of flesh." The passage's doctrinal point — that a Great Vehicle practitioner with merely physical eyesight surpasses a śrāvaka with supernormal vision — is a standard Mahāyāna polemical argument about the superiority of the bodhisattva path and is preserved as such.

The term "Kuśīla" here is used as the name of a householder interlocutor in an earlier sūtra cited within the text, distinct from the more common use of kuśīla as a term meaning a morally inferior monk. The phrase rendered "this teaching will sink beneath the earth" after forty years follows a standard eschatological motif in this sūtra concerning the gradual disappearance of the Dharma; "sinking beneath the earth" is the literal Tibetan expression and is kept as such. The temporal framework of forty years and eighty years refers to a doctrinal schema in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition concerning the periods of flourishing and decline of the Dharma after the Buddha's passing; the text implies that the final eighty years before total decline are excluded from the forty-year period of wide propagation.  The passage presents a graduated schema of merit and corresponding capacity, measured in multiples of Gaṅgā-sands buddhas, from one through eight rivers. The phrase rendered "the Tathāgata is endowed with the quality of permanently abiding — unchanging, ultimately blissful" reflects key buddha-nature doctrinal vocabulary, echoing the tathāgatagarbha teaching that the Tathāgata's nature is permanent, immovable, and of the nature of bliss, as in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition.  The phrase rendered "like a tattered banner on a stick" translates a simile comparing a worn-out robe to a tattered pennant or flag on a wooden pole — an image of something that retains the outer form of its purpose while being entirely useless. The section on the four great beings refers to an established category in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra: the four types of persons — roughly, those who uphold, propagate, defend, or embody the Dharma — who are accorded the status of cosmic supports. The Tibetan sūtra citation about honoring a Dharma-knower "as the gods worship their sovereign lord" echoes language used for Śakra (Indra) as king of the gods; the gloss has been absorbed naturally into the verse rendering. The apparent tension that Kāśyapa raises at the close — between honoring anyone with Dharma-knowledge regardless of discipline versus the rule that a monastically junior person should bow to a senior and that a morally deteriorated person falls outside the Dharma — is a genuine doctrinal crux that the subsequent passage in the sūtra will resolve; it is deliberately left open here as Kāśyapa's question.  The phrase rendered "consecrates me by pouring empowerment upon my head" translates the rite of royal consecration by water-sprinkling over the crown, the abhiṣeka ceremony. The passage refers to "eight unsolicited requisites" (ma brtags pa'i dngos po rnam pa brgyad). This is a specific Vinaya category of items a monk may not normally keep without prior invitation or request from a lay donor. The bodhisattva's carrying of these on behalf of the compromised monk is the doctrinal crux: even this technical infraction is justified by the overriding goal of purifying the Saṅgha, exactly as the young brahmin's elaborate deception was justified by expelling the unworthy king. The parallel is deliberate and close.  The passage contains a verse rendering Śakra as "the Mighty Lord" translating དབང་ཕྱུག — this is a divine epithet meaning "lord of power" or "the powerful one," applied here to Śakra (Indra), king of the thirty-three gods. The final paragraph on the "harmonious Saṅgha" is a polemical voice being cited. The argument is that even the notion of a "harmonious" or "concordant" Saṅgha implies some kind of substantial basis, which when analysed turns out to be empty — hence there is no Saṅgha established in consciousness. The text cites this position approvingly to reinforce abiding in wisdom rather than in consciousness.  The passage identifies four things: Dharma, meaning, primordial wisdom, and definitive meaning, and then gives a compressed doctrinal gloss on each. The final gloss — "meaning means the Tathāgata, who is permanent and unchanging" — reflects the tathāgatagarbha doctrinal matrix of this text, likely the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra or a closely related scripture, where the permanence of the Tathāgata is a central thesis. This is not an error in the translation but a deliberate doctrinal claim of the source text.

The term rendered "lay attendant" translates a word that literally means "attendant" or "close attendant" and could refer to a monastic attendant rather than a lay person; in context the contrast with the fully endowed patron suggests the person in question is a monastic whose donor-support has lapsed, making "lay attendant" slightly loose. The translation preserves the general sense without introducing a technical distortion of consequence.  The passage contains a key doctrinal distinction drawn from Mahāyāna sūtra literature: the claim that the Buddha was born as an ordinary human, underwent austerities, and thereby attained buddhahood is here branded as "māra's teaching," whereas the view that the Tathāgata had in fact awakened long ago and merely displayed birth, austerities, and awakening as skillful means is affirmed as the Buddha's own teaching. This reflects the doctrine of the eternal or primordially awakened Buddha found prominently in the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra and the Lotus Sūtra tradition, and the passage's polemical force should be understood in that context.

This is the Vinaya category of falsely claiming superhuman attainments (uttarimanuṣyadharma), which constitutes the fourth root defeat (pārājika) for a monk. The rendering preserves this technical sense.

The palmyra palm image refers to the Vinaya principle that certain root defeats, like a felled palmyra that never regrows, are irrecoverable — here the text is making a counter-argument that a collective or notional defeat does not equal an individual one.  The phrase rendered "living a pure and holy life" translates brahmacarya, and the context specifies that the monk's conduct is genuine, which is the doctrinal basis for the absence of a pārājika fault — the monk has not actually made a false claim of superhuman attainment with intent to deceive, since the broader teaching on buddha-nature and the king's proclamation situate the statement differently. This is a nuanced Vinaya discussion concerning the boundary of the fourth pārājika.

The phrase "wrong craving" renders log sred, literally "perverted craving" or "wrong thirst," which in context refers to the most gravely obstructive form of craving or perhaps specifically to the craving for continued existence in forms contrary to liberation; the exact doctrinal referent here is somewhat context-dependent but "wrong craving" captures the sense clearly.  The passage lists specific numbers from the Vinaya code — four defeats (pārājika), thirteen remainders (saṃghāvaśeṣa), two indeterminate rules (aniyata), thirty forfeiture rules (niḥsargika-pāyantika), ninety-one transgressions (pāyantika), four rules of individual confession (pratideśanīya), and seven rules for settling disputes (adhikaraṇaśamatha) — rendered by their numerical descriptions to preserve the technical enumeration without interrupting the prose flow. The "eight hundred billion years reckoned by the days and months and years of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three" renders a passage computing time by the divine calendar of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, which measures years differently from human reckoning. The final sentence about "nine branches of sūtra scripture" refers to the traditional ninefold classification of Buddhist scripture (nava-aṅga), and the statement that none is more extensive than the "sūtra" category (mdo sde, sūtra proper) within it is a specific claim that may relate to the text's own self-positioning.  The passage contains an important doctrinal tension being navigated carefully: the text distinguishes between (a) the claim that buddha-nature exists not being found in the nine branches, which incurs no offense if denied out of ignorance, and (b) the claim that one has already fully awakened on the basis of possessing buddha-nature, which does constitute a defeat. This distinction is central to the passage's argument and has been preserved closely.

The passage contains a reference to the Tathāgatagarbha sūtra cited in the first person as scriptural warrant for buddha-nature, which is a notable doctrinal move — the monk is portrayed as appealing directly to that sūtra's teaching that all beings possess the tathāgatagarbha as the basis for proclaiming universal buddhahood. This is distinguished from the condemned behaviour described earlier: the bodhisattva motivation redeems what might superficially resemble the same outward conduct.

The phrase rendered "the Heaven of the Thirty-Three" reflects the Tibetan counting system based on the thirty-three gods (Trāyastriṃśa heaven, Indra's realm), whose year-length determines the duration of the hell-punishment described — a standard cosmological calculation in Indian Buddhist texts.  The term rendered "one of double marks" and "one of indeterminate sex" translates two technical Vinaya categories for persons of ambiguous or dual sexual characteristics (Skt. ubhatobyañjanaka and paṇḍaka respectively); the third term, translated "one of degenerate faculties," is a distinct sub-category. The word "mahāliṅga" in the final paragraph is an unusual term for a type of garment or cloth; its exact identity is uncertain, but the context makes clear it is an example of something falsely attributed as a permitted allowance, included here as a specimen of māra's false teachings.

The translation faithfully renders the text's own standpoint without smoothing these polemical edges.

The passage on the caterpillar simile presents a somewhat elliptical argument. The phrase rendered "the secret essence of the Tathāgata" throughout corresponds to the tathāgatagarbha doctrine, here expressed as the buddha's intrinsic nature that is permanent, unchanging, and unshifting — a central doctrinal claim of this sūtra.

The section distinguishing how different audiences misapprehend the same teaching reflects the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's characteristic hermeneutical concern: identical formulations lead to opposite errors depending on the capacity and disposition of the listener, which is why the Tathāgata employs skillful means rather than a single fixed formulation.  The phrase rendered "bear it on the crown of your head" translates a standard Tibetan expression of highest reverence for a teaching, meaning to receive it with the utmost honour.

The passage presents a descending hierarchy of Vinaya offenses: the four root defeats (pārājika), the remaining rules of the Saṅgha (likely the saṃghāvaśeṣa and related categories), the grave offenses, the transgressions requiring abandonment (pāyattika), the ninety transgressions (the standard ninety pāyattika rules of the prātimokṣa), and finally the acts of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta, the lightest class of Vinaya offense). The phrase rendered "flavor of going forth into renunciation, the flavor of study and recitation, and the flavor of meditative concentration" translates a threefold schema. The first term refers to the experiential richness of monastic life after ordination; the second to the joy of learning and oral recitation of texts; the third to the joy of meditation. The triple schema is a conventional pedagogical list in this text.

The phrase "non-humans" in the dried riverbank illustration renders a term that can mean supernatural beings but here, in the context of a list alongside humans, birds, and beasts, most naturally means beings other than humans in a general physical sense. The point is simply universal uselessness.  The passage lists "the king of fish, the king of bees, the king of conch-shells, the lord of the herd, and the caravan leader" as figures whose followers trail behind them inseparably. The Tibetan term rendered "king of conch-shells" (དུང་གི་རྒྱལ་པོ) is less common; it may refer to a legendary aquatic being or simply to the lead conch-shell in a formation — the sense of "leader followed by others" is clear in context and the doctrinal point is unaffected.

The final reference to the "second meditative concentration" (བསམ་གཏན་གཉིས་པ) reflects the standard Abhidharma cosmology in which the cosmic end-fire destroys the lower realms up to and including the first dhyāna heaven, but the second dhyāna and above are spared.  The final sentence ends mid-passage with an unanswered question, "Why?" This is not an error in the translation; the Tibetan itself breaks off at that point, and the answer follows in the next passage.

The term rendered "king of garuḍas" translates the Tibetan for garuḍa-king literally. The garuḍa is a mythic great bird, enemy of nāgas, well established in Indo-Tibetan cosmology; no further gloss is needed for informed listeners, but the parenthetical "great bird of prey" is offered for general audiences.  The serpent name "Malanā" and the mantra name "Akatasyā" are transliterations of Sanskrit terms obscured by the Tibetan phonetic rendering. The identification of these terms with known Sanskrit sources is uncertain, and the transliterations given here are approximate. The mantra name may reflect "akatasyā" (related to "akataś," meaning "unprevented" or "free"), but this is speculative.

The passage describing death as "without firm ground" renders a term that could also be read as "without a place of rest" or "without a ground of destruction," and the precise nuance is somewhat ambiguous in context.  The phrase "seven limbs touching the ground" refers to the traditional iconographic description of the auspicious royal elephant: all four feet, both tusks, and the trunk touch the earth simultaneously, signifying perfect, stable power. This is a recognized mark of the precious elephant treasure of a wheel-turning king.

The "five superknowledges" refers to the five mundane superknowledges or higher powers cultivated by accomplished sages: the ability to perform miracles, clairvoyance, clairaudience, knowledge of others' minds, and recollection of past lives.  The phrase translated as "the faculty of a meritorious eye" renders a compound meaning an eye-faculty produced by merit, understood in the tradition as a kind of clairvoyant vision arising from accumulated good karma. This is a standard feature in descriptions of the precious minister in wheel-turning king narratives.

The "fourfold host" refers to the classical Indian division of an army into infantry, cavalry, war elephants, and chariots.  The text here contains a chapter or section colophon marker indicating this is the seventeenth fascicle of the Noble Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra, embedded within the narrative flow. It has been omitted from the translation body as it interrupts the narrative and is a scribal/editorial insertion rather than part of the sūtra text itself.  The name འོད་སྲུང, rendered "Kāśyapa" in the final vocative, is the Tibetan translation of the buddha Kāśyapa (one of the past seven buddhas), not the disciple Mahākāśyapa. The text uses it both as a narrative identification earlier and as a direct address to the interlocutor at the close, which is consistent with Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra discourse structure where the interlocutor is identified with that buddha's lineage.  The phrase rendered "great Śākya chieftain" translates Śākya ming chen, which likely refers to a prominent Śākya householder or chieftain. Some editions read this as a reference to a specific named individual; the identity is not certain from the Tibetan alone, but it does not affect the doctrinal point.

The verse section's final stanza refers to the bodhisattva having "completed all that is to be done," a standard phrase echoing the arhat formula but here applied in a Mahāyāna context to the bodhisattva who has fulfilled all the perfections.  The term rendered "great Śākya clan" translates Śākya ming chen, literally "the great name Śākya" or "the great Śākya designation." The exact referent is slightly ambiguous — it may mean the Buddha speaking to the Śākya community specifically, or may simply be an epithet referring to the Buddha himself as the great one of the Śākyas. The translation follows the most natural reading in context.

The passage ends mid-sentence with the list of worldly goods, as the supplied Tibetan breaks off there.  The passage lists four requisites for the renunciant as robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicine — the standard four monastic requisites (Skt. catvāraḥ pratyayāḥ). The Tibetan term for "craving" here rendered throughout is "འདོད་པ" (lit. "desire/wanting"), used in this context specifically in the doctrinal sense of tṛṣṇā, the second Noble Truth, rather than the more neutral "wish." This choice is deliberate and consistent with the passage's explicit identification of it as the truth of origin (samudaya).  The phrase rendered "like the fruit of the bāluká plant" refers to a tree or plant known in Sanskrit as bāluka or a similar term, identified in some commentarial traditions as a tree whose fruit appears attractive but is poisonous or worthless inside. The Tibetan 'ba lu ka is a transliteration of a Sanskrit botanical name; exact botanical identification is uncertain but the doctrinal point — attractive appearance concealing harm — is clear from context.

The passage ends mid-analogy in the source text as given; the snake-seller simile is introduced but its explanation is cut off.  The bāḷuka plant is an Indian plant whose fruit or seed was proverbially known for its invasive, strangling growth habit. The nyagrodha is the banyan tree, famed for its vast canopy and lateral roots, making its suppression by the bāḷuka a vivid image of craving overwhelming even the greatest spiritual endowment.

The distinction drawn at the close between the three categories — the foolish and ignoble, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas — reflects a characteristic Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra doctrinal position: only bodhisattvas apprehend the Four Noble Truths in their full and genuine depth, because they simultaneously perceive suffering without being subject to it, origin without being bound by it, and cessation in its ultimate rather than partial form.  The phrase "twenty-five modes of existence" refers to a standard Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra enumeration of the states of conditioned rebirth in the three realms; the count varies by recension but the term is rendered literally.

The address "sons of good family" renders the standard vocative used throughout for the audience of noble lineage.

The translation breaks mid-sentence at the end because the Tibetan passage itself breaks off mid-quotation with the words addressed to Ānanda; the continuation presumably follows in the next passage.  The king named in Tibetan as "Sde rab tu pham byed" means something like "Utterly-Vanquished-in-Battle" or "He Who Utterly Defeats Armies." This appears to be a Tibetan rendering of a Sanskrit royal name; the exact Sanskrit original is uncertain, but the translation renders the meaning transparently.

The passage describing the nun as "mother of the people" likely refers to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Buddha's aunt and the first nun, though the text identifies her only by the epithet rendered here. This is not flagged in the body.  The list of water names in various languages appears to record vernacular or regional terms current in the text's milieu. "Pāṇi" is the standard Sanskrit and many Indo-Aryan vernacular word for water; "udi" may reflect a Dravidian or Prakrit form; "salema," "sali," "pana," "nectar," and "milk" are either regional synonyms or hyperbolic folk-names for water. The terms are rendered as transliterations since their precise linguistic identification is uncertain and does not affect the doctrinal point.

The plant and medicinal juice names — bitter gourd, sugarcane, black molasses, āmalaka, nīpāla, pārāhala — include both well-known Ayurvedic ingredients and less certain botanical identifications. "Nīpāla" and "pārāhala" are uncertain; they are retained as transliterations.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the supplied Tibetan, breaking off at the enumeration of the four paths.  The five-aspect classification of the path uses terms that correspond to traditional categories found in Abhidharma and early Mahāyāna sources. The "path of realization through the body" renders lus kyis rig pa'i lam, which likely refers to the direct, bodily or experiential realization attained in deep meditative absorption, as distinct from liberation through faith or through vision alone. This is an uncommon formulation and the precise technical referent may vary across commentarial traditions.

The "three foundations of mindfulness perfectly established by the buddhas" renders sangs rgyas kyis brnyes pa'i yang dag pa'i dran pa nye bar gzhag pa gsum, a set of three traditional qualities attributed to a buddha describing equanimity in the face of disciples who do and do not attend to the teaching.  The grove name "Śiśumāra" is a back-reconstruction from the Tibetan "shi shu." Some editions read this as a grove associated with the Śiṃśapā tree, which is the more famous parallel passage found in the Saṃyutta Nikāya and its Sanskrit parallels, where the Buddha takes up Śiṃśapā leaves. The Tibetan here may be a phonetic rendering of a different toponym or tree name; the reading is uncertain but does not affect the doctrinal sense.

The term rendered "engagement" for འཇུག་པ refers contextually to the sense bases (āyatana) as the locus of cognitive engagement with objects. The passage is treating aggregates, sense bases, and elements as the three categories of phenomenal analysis standard in Abhidharma, and showing that each can be understood at a middling or superior level of insight.  The colophon-style line marking the eighteenth fascicle of the Parinirvāṇa Sūtra appears mid-passage in the Tibetan, likely a scribal section marker inserted into the continuous text; it is rendered plainly as a sentence without imposing chapter-break formatting, in keeping with the TTS requirement.  The list of terms for "self" and related concepts — sentient being, life-force, consciousness, one who sees, one who lives, the virile one, lord of vitality, feeling, the one who acts — corresponds to a standard Indic enumeration of ātman-synonyms (Sanskrit: jīva, sattva, pudgala, draṣṭṛ, etc.) found in Abhidharma and Madhyamaka polemical literature. The translation renders their sense in English rather than attempting Sanskrit back-formations for each.

The phrase rendered "world of conventions" for ཆོས་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ is literally "world of Dharma" or "world of dharmic signs," but the illustrative examples given — drum, board, conch as social signals — make clear this refers to conventional signal-codes or socially established signs rather than the Dharma as Buddhist teaching. "Conventions" captures this functional sense accurately.  The passage's doctrinal logic turns on a careful distinction between "genuine truth" (yang dag pa'i bden pa), the Four Noble Truths as truths bearing the mark of suffering and impermanence, and the Tathāgata together with emptiness and buddha-nature, which are "genuine" (yang dag pa) but not "truths" in the sense of conditioned, suffering-bearing phenomena. The four qualities attributed to genuine truth — permanence, bliss, self, and purity — are the classical four transcendent qualities (guṇas) of nirvāṇa or the tathāgatagarbha, familiar from texts such as the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, and their appearance here is doctrinally significant. The phrase rendered "not truth in that sense" represents yang dag pa ma yin te, which in this context contrasts the Tathāgata with conditioned truths, not asserting the Tathāgata is untrue; the rendering reflects that nuance.  The passage contains a philosophically significant distinction running throughout: the Four Noble Truths, as conventionally understood, are characterized by impermanence and conditionality and are therefore described as "truth" in the ordinary sense but not as "what is genuine" in the ultimate sense. The Tathāgata, space, and the intrinsic nature of the buddhas transcend these categories entirely and are therefore called "genuine" but not "truth" in that same conventional sense. This is a characteristically Tathāgatagarbha doctrinal move, and the translation preserves this deliberately paradoxical formulation.

The phrase rendered "self-known through one's own awareness" translates rang gis rig pa, literally "cognized by oneself," a term pointing to the non-inferential, self-certifying quality of the buddha's realization — distinct from the cessation attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

The passage ends mid-sentence; the translation faithfully breaks off at that point.  The passage's argument about the non-Buddhists' claim to permanence runs directly into the classical Buddhist rebuttals about karmic continuity. The tīrthika position quoted here — that formations must be permanent in order to ensure karmic retribution across rebirths — is a standard opponent's argument addressed in Abhidharma and Madhyamaka literature; the passage leaves the Blessed One's response to continue in the next section.  The term rendered "the averter of harm" translates the Tibetan "'jug sel," which is an obscure epithet in this list of divine beings. It may refer to a specific deity who removes obstacles or harm; the exact Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain. This is noted here rather than glossed in the body, as the identity is not firmly established.  The list of precious substances includes "asamāgarbha" and "musālagalva," which are Sanskrit loanwords for semi-precious gems. Their precise identification in gemological terms is uncertain in the scholarly literature, but they are standard members of jewel lists in Sanskrit Buddhist texts. The rendering preserves the Sanskrit rather than inventing English equivalents.

The "Great Sovereign" (Tibetan: dbang sgyur chen po) in the hierarchy of happiness-experiencers may refer to Maheśvara or a supreme world-ruler figure; in context it denotes the highest rank above Great Brahmā and Śakra in a non-Buddhist cosmological scheme, so it is left as "the Great Sovereign" rather than identified with a specific deity, since the text does not name him explicitly here.  The passage presents a non-Buddhist interlocutor offering several arguments for the existence of the self, followed by the Blessed One's refutation. The four attributes listed — permanence, happiness, self, and complete purity — are the classical four inverted views (viparyāsa) that the Buddha's teaching on the four noble truths and the three marks of existence is meant to correct; the non-Buddhists are here accused of mistaking saṃsāric phenomena for their opposites.

The phrase rendered "the four venomous serpents of the great elements" refers to the four physical elements — earth, water, fire, and wind — understood in this context as the basis of the body that binds beings to cyclic existence.  The passage sets up a paradox common in tathāgatagarbha literature: conditioned phenomena are impermanent, including the doctrines of non-Buddhists, which all arise dependently; yet the buddha-nature, being unconditioned, is affirmed as permanent. The equation of buddha-nature, Tathāgata, Dharma, Saṅgha, and space as synonyms for the permanent unconditioned is characteristic of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition. The phrase rendered "five venomous she-asses of desire" follows the unusual Tibetan image literally; the "she-asses" represent the five objects of sensory desire traditionally depicted as beguiling yet harmful.  The phrase rendered "permanent, bliss, self, and utterly pure" refers to the four qualities of nirvāṇa as understood in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition — the four transcendent attributes that distinguish true nirvāṇa from ordinary conditioned states. The argument being made is that if mind were a permanent, unchanging entity it could not successfully meditate on impermanence and thereby reach the realization of these deeper truths, nor could non-Buddhist systems that posit a permanent self ever genuinely encompass these qualities. The passage breaks off mid-sentence, which is faithful to the source as given.  The phrase rendered "gelatinous stage" translates nur nur po, a technical embryological term in Indo-Tibetan tradition referring to the first stage of fetal development, sometimes called the "kalala" stage in Sanskrit (Pali: kalala), denoting the initial jelly-like or gelatinous phase of the embryo. The sequence nur nur po, mer mer po, mkhrags pa corresponds to the classical three early embryonic stages: gelatinous, thickening, and hardening or solid.

The final sentence naming Kāśyapa (rendered here as Kāśyapa) refers to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa who appears as an interlocutor in texts such as the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, where discussions of impermanence, suffering, and impurity in relation to the body occur at length. The Tibetan 'od srung is the standard rendering of Kāśyapa.  The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end ("For example, when a person has fallen asleep, there is going and coming and —"), exactly as the Tibetan source does; the translation faithfully follows the incomplete clause. The next passage in the text will continue this simile.

The "threefold gnosis" of attachment, eating, and fear is a somewhat unusual formulation. The Tibetan reads "rnam pa 'di gsum gyi ye shes mnyam par yod," meaning all beings equally possess awareness of these three drives. This is likely an argument that these instinctual drives operate without a presiding self, demonstrating selflessness. The term ye shes here carries a sense of innate or reflexive awareness rather than exalted primordial wisdom, but the house glossary term "gnosis" is retained with the qualification "threefold" to flag its specialized use in this context.  The phrase rendered "mechanical man made of wood" translates a Tibetan compound for an automaton or puppet. The point is that mechanical motion does not entail a self, and neither does the observed behavior of a sleeping person.

The passage on the "true self" of the Tathāgata and the final sequence equating self with Dharma, path, Blessed One, and śrāvaka reflects the distinctive mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra doctrine that the four marks of nirvāṇa — permanence, bliss, self, and purity — are positively affirmed of the Tathāgata in deliberate inversion of the usual no-self teaching. This is not a contradiction but a specialized doctrinal usage that the text itself is carefully developing throughout.  The passage's central philosophical move is important: "turning the wheel of Dharma" is said not to apply to the Tathāgata precisely because the Tathāgata is identified with the unchanging Dharma itself. The turning is a conventional description of dependent arising — the teaching arises from a convergence of conditions — whereas the Tathāgata-as-Dharma is beyond activity and motion. This is consistent with the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's tathāgatagarbha doctrine, in which the Tathāgata's buddha-self is identified with the eternal, unconditioned nature of reality.

The term rendered "hearthboard" is the lower board used in fire-by-friction, and "fire-stick" the upper spindle; "effort of friction" renders the idea of the drilling or churning action. The list of articulatory organs (palate, throat, tongue, teeth, lips) is a traditional enumeration of the places of articulation for speech production, used here to emphasize that speech — and thus the "turning" of the Dharma — is itself a conditioned convergence.  The term rendered "space" near the end is ākāśa in the tradition's technical vocabulary, the paradigmatic example of an unconditioned phenomenon in Abhidharma analysis; the text is making a direct parallel between ākāśa and the Tathāgata as equally unconditioned, which is doctrinally significant and somewhat bolder than Abhidharma orthodoxy, pointing toward Mahāyāna tathāgatagarbha discourse.

The list of conditions for the sprout includes "རྨེད" which most likely renders Sanskrit "ākāśa" (space), listed among the causal factors for growth; this six-factor analysis of plant growth is a classical Indian botanical-philosophical schema.  The city name rendered throughout as "Kuśinagara" translates the Tibetan "རྩྭ་མཆོག་གི་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་," which literally means "the city of supreme grass" — a calque of the Sanskrit Kuśinagara (kuśa = auspicious grass). This is the standard identification and is universally accepted in the scholarly tradition.

The bodhisattva "འོད་སྲུང་" is Kāśyapa — not Mahākāśyapa the śrāvaka-disciple, but a bodhisattva Kāśyapa who appears in this sūtra (the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra) as a principal interlocutor. This distinction is doctrinally significant.

The four qualities taught at Kuśinagara — permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity — are the famous four transcendent attributes (the "four pāramitās of nirvāṇa") taught in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra in direct contrast to the four marks taught at Vārāṇasī. The use of "self" (bdag, ātman) here is intentional and doctrinally charged: it refers to the buddha-nature teaching, not to the ordinary self denied by earlier doctrine.  The twenty-five realms of existence and their corresponding twenty-five meditative absorptions are a standard enumeration in the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra literature; the full list continues beyond this passage. The four continents named here follow the standard Buddhist cosmological schema. "Irreversible meditative absorption" renders a term that in this context denotes an absorption from which one does not turn back toward lower states, rather than the standard technical usage of "irreversibility" in the sense of non-regression from the path. The name Kāśyapa here refers to the bodhisattva Kāśyapa, not the elder monk Mahākāśyapa, as is clear from the narrative context.  The phrase rendered "sphere of no-perception" for འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པའི་སྲིད་པ refers to the heaven of non-apercipient beings (asaṃjñisattva), a specific god-realm within the fourth dhyāna, distinct from the formless sphere. The context places it between the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms, which is doctrinally consistent.

The phrase གཙང་མའི་རིས་ལན་ཅིག་ཕྱིར་ལྡོག་པའི་སྲིད་པ literally means "the realm of existence of the once-returner of the pure abodes class," which is an unusual formulation. It has been rendered interpretively as "a once-returner in the pure abodes," though some uncertainty attaches to exactly which class of beings is meant.  The "twelve branches of the teaching" refers to the standard Buddhist classification of scripture by literary form — the dvādaśāṅga, comprising sūtras, verses, prophecies, verses in verse, intentional utterances, introductory narratives, stories of past events, stories of past lives, extensive teachings, marvelous events, established doctrines, and doctrinal discussions. This progression from buddha through the twelve branches down to the Perfection of Wisdom and then to the great nirvāṇa mirrors a standard Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra argument for the supremacy of that text.

The bodhisattva name Vimalagarbharāja is a reconstruction from the Tibetan dri ma med pa'i snying po'i rgyal po; it is rendered here in Sanskrit form rather than by translation, as it functions as a proper name.  The fourfold quality set "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" refers to the four attributes of nirvāṇa in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition: nitya, sukha, ātman, and śuddha. The occurrence of ātman here is doctrinally deliberate and not a simple affirmation of a self; the sūtra uses it as a positive predicate of the buddha-nature, which is a significant and characteristic teaching of this text.  The epithet "Kauśika" is one of Śakra's (Indra's) well-known names, derived from his clan lineage; it is rendered in plain transliteration throughout as the text uses it consistently as a proper name in direct address.

The phrase rendered "the king possessed of the eight qualities" translates a Tibetan expression referring to the eight qualities or excellences traditionally attributed to a great ascetic or noble being; the precise enumeration of these eight is not specified in this passage.  The passage contains the celebrated "half-verse" episode (ardha-gāthā story), which in the Sanskrit tradition is the story of the bodhisattva Mahāsattva who gives his life to a rākṣasa to obtain the second half of a Dharma verse. The Tibetan here follows that narrative. The phrase rendered "lifting his hair with his hands" likely refers to the gesture of removing or loosening the ascetic's matted hair or topknot in reverence — a standard gesture of supplication — though the sentence breaks off mid-action and the continuation would clarify this.  The "crescent moon" opening a lotus is a reversal of the more common image of the full moon opening night-blooming lotuses; the text is deliberate here, using "ཟླ་བ་ཕྱེད་པོ" (half-moon) to mirror the "half-verse" motif running throughout the passage.

The rakṣasa explains that he spoke the half-verse involuntarily, in a state resembling delirium from starvation — a key narrative detail establishing that the verse arose not from his own understanding but from some prior encounter with the Dharma.  The phrase rendered "a body like a vajra" refers to the indestructible, adamantine body of a fully awakened buddha, a standard Mahāyāna trope contrasting the fragile ordinary body with the perfected buddha-body. The "seven precious substances" (rin po che sna bdun) are the traditional set of seven gems (gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, ruby, emerald, and agate in various canonical enumerations), serving here as a simile for the buddha-body obtained in exchange for the ordinary body. The image of spreading one's own skin as a seat for the teacher is a hyperbolic gesture of extreme reverence, consistent with the jātaka narrative register of the passage.  The phrase rendered "peak of existence" translates a standard Abhidharma cosmological term referring to the highest level of the formless realm, the apex of conditioned existence. The verse itself — "What has been born will cease, those things find peace and bliss in stilling" — is the famous second half of the Snow Demon verse (the full verse being a celebrated teaching on impermanence and nirvāṇa), well attested in multiple versions of this story across the canon. The first half of the verse, given in the preceding passage, is not retranslated here per instructions.  The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as this is a continuous passage. The list of twelve branches of scripture corresponds to the standard Mahāyāna dvādaśāṅga classification; the Sanskrit equivalents given parenthetically are the standard scholarly reconstructions. The name "Ajita" (rendered here from the Tibetan "Ma pham pa," literally "the Undefeated") is a common epithet for Maitreya before his buddhahood; it has been rendered by its meaning in the vocative address to make the prophecy clear in context. The figure "Śaṅkha" is a king prophesied to appear in the age of Maitreya's buddhahood.  The four-line verse rendered here is the well-known "Ovāda-Pātimokkha" stanza, appearing frequently across canonical collections. The standard rendering follows traditional commentarial consensus.

The figure "Bhadrapāla" appears here as one of the buddhas of the past under whose teaching a text called "The Five Nectars" was delivered. This identification is somewhat unusual in the canonical reckoning of past buddhas and may reflect a variant textual tradition; it is not flagged in the body.

The term rendered "thus-it-occurred branch" (Tibetan: "de lta bu byung ba") refers to the āvadāna-style category in some reckonings but here functions as a category of historically-situated utterances delivered at the occasions of past buddhas' appearances. The Tibetan term is closer to "itivṛttaka" in some schemas.

The "monkey-bee" offering honey is an allusion to the famous episode at Vaiśālī where a monkey offered honey to the Buddha; the Tibetan here uses a compound that may indicate a bee or monkey, and the episode as described follows the traditional account of the monkey offering.  The phrase rendered "knowing the superior and the inferior" translates a term that literally means knowing the "upper and lower," referring to gradations of spiritual quality among individuals. The context makes clear this is a progressive taxonomy of qualities, proceeding through increasingly refined levels of virtue, which the bodhisattva should be able to discern in those around him. The passage ends mid-sentence and will presumably continue with the same graduated pattern.  The term rendered "non-focus" for mi dmigs pa deserves brief comment. The Tibetan literally means "non-apprehension" or "without reference point," often translated as "objectless." In context it is used in a specifically paradoxical way: focusing on the Tathāgata counts as non-focus because the Tathāgata is beyond the ordinary subject-object relation that characterizes the other two modes. This is a standard Mahāyāna doctrinal usage.

The passage ends mid-sentence with "they are boundless," indicating the text continues beyond what was provided here.  The passage enumerating dependent origination in seven aspects lists eight items in the Tibetan as written (consciousness, name, form, six sense bases, contact, feeling, becoming, grasping). This apparent discrepancy between the stated "seven" and the number of items listed is present in the source text itself and likely reflects a variant enumeration in which "name-and-form" counts as one unit and "becoming and grasping" counts as one unit, or there is a textual irregularity. The translation renders the Tibetan as given without smoothing the count.

The sūtra called "The City" is most likely the Nagaropama-sūtra or a related text; the identification is reasonably certain in context but the precise canonical reference is not specified in the passage.

The phrase rendered "what appear to be falsehoods" translates a term that literally means something like "a little something false" or "a semblance of untruth" — the point being that the Tathāgata's apparently contradictory teachings are not deceptions but skillful adaptations, as the immediately following context makes clear.  The phrase rendered "aversion that takes life" and "aversion that strikes and injures" translates སྲོག་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཞེ་སྡང་ and རྡེག་འཚོག་བྱེད་པའི་ཞེ་སྡང་ literally: the first is "aversion that separates from life" (i.e., murderous hatred) and the second "aversion that beats and tramples." These renderings preserve the doctrinal distinction between lethal violence and non-lethal physical harm.

The passage on "aversion toward what is not sentient beings" is unusual doctrinally — it likely refers to aversion toward inanimate things, circumstances, or one's environment, a reading supported by the parallel structure. No emendation is warranted.  The passage shifts mid-paragraph from speaking in third person about "the immeasurable mind" to enumerating four sub-types in what reads as a slightly irregular structure in the Tibetan, likely due to the text conflating "immeasurable mind" generally with "mind of loving-kindness" specifically in the enumeration. The translation preserves this feature faithfully rather than smoothing it over, as it appears to be a genuine feature of the original rather than a scribal error.

The final sentence is deliberately left open, as the Tibetan breaks off mid-thought, continuing into the next passage.  The phrase rendered "perversely craving" translates a compound that literally means "possessing wrong craving" or "wrongly attached" — a technical category denoting those whose strong negative karmic propensities make them the most challenging objects of compassionate concern. The context makes clear it refers to those who are, by ordinary reckoning, the least deserving of loving-kindness.

The triple definition of great equanimity near the end — freedom from perceiving self and phenomena, viewing all phenomena as equanimous, and surrendering one's own happiness — represents three distinct formulations of the same term, all presented as valid characterizations rather than a hierarchy. This threefold structure is preserved faithfully.  The phrase rendered "washed clean seven times" translates a Tibetan expression describing a cosmic purification of the world-system over an aeon, likely reflecting a known canonical topos about the power of loving-kindness meditation; the exact imagery may echo passages found in Pāli and Sanskrit parallels where the world is said to be "flooded" or "pervaded" rather than "washed," but the Tibetan clearly uses the washing metaphor here.

The verse section on the sage and the king is a standard merit-comparison gāthā; the sixteen-fold comparison is a well-attested formula in this genre.  The passage describing the great bodhisattva who abides in great nirvāṇa and perceives earth as gold, water as fire, and so on is a statement of the bodhisattva's sovereign, wish-fulfilling mastery over phenomena — a standard feature of the mahāparinirvāṇa or "great complete nirvāṇa" as understood in texts such as the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, where this state confers the power to transform appearances at will. The phrase translated as "perception is cut off" renders the Tibetan term for cutting through or severing discriminatory conceptual perception, indicating non-attachment to the marks of giving.  The poisoned-arrow simile is a well-known motif in Buddhist literature, most famously found in the Cūḷamāluṅkya-sutta of the Pāli canon, though here it is deployed in a Mahāyāna context to warn against analytical hesitation that prevents generous action rather than, as in the Pāli source, against metaphysical speculation.

The phrase rendered "nourishment of great wisdom" and subsequent parallel phrases use "food" or "nourishment" as a sustained metaphor: just as physical food sustains the body, wisdom, Dharma-joy, and the Perfection of Wisdom are presented as the true sustenance of sentient beings. The Tibetan term translated "field of merit" carries the technical connotation of those beings or objects whose presence generates merit for those who make offerings or give generously to them.  The "eight flavors" of water is a classical Indian enumeration of water's qualities such as coolness, clarity, sweetness, and so forth; no doctrinal uncertainty attaches to this, though the list varies by source.

The phrase rendered "the taste that has become sixfold" refers to the six sense-object flavors or taste-varieties experienced through the six sense bases, contrasted with the single unified taste of Dharma. The exact referent is contextually clear within this rhetorical series but the precise doctrinal category being invoked is not elaborated in the text itself.

The "garment not touching the body even by a cubit's width" is an image for the subtle, light-body quality of advanced bodhisattvas or beings in the higher realms, where physical garments rest effortlessly without contact. This is a conventional literary image in this genre of aspiration literature.  The phrase rendered "the meditative absorption of the buddha-flower samādhi" translates "sangs rgyas ku su ma'i ting nge 'dzin," where "ku su ma" is a transliteration of the Sanskrit kusuma meaning "flower." This appears to be a specific named samādhi from the text's tradition; no attempt has been made to translate "kusuma" further since it functions as a proper name for the samādhi.

The phrase rendered "a hundredfold merit bearing a single defining mark" translates "mtshan nyid gcig pa'i bsod nams brgyas," which is elliptical. The sense appears to be that all sentient beings share a single unifying characteristic mark and are adorned with a multiplied hundredfold merit; the exact doctrinal referent may be text-specific.  The phrase rendered "rest on the right side" refers to the lion's posture of lying on the right side, the way buddhas and great beings are said to recline — a standard Indic iconographic convention preserved here in aspirational form.

The phrase "permanence, bliss, self, and perfect purity" refers to the four qualities of nirvāṇa as articulated in tathāgatagarbha literature — the four perfections that invert the four marks of conditioned existence. The "four inversions" are their mundane counterparts mistakenly superimposed on conditioned phenomena.

The phrase "letters and syllables that transcend the world" likely refers to dhāraṇī formulas or the sacred alphabet contemplations found in certain Mahāyāna sūtras; no single interpretation can be fixed with certainty.  The phrase rendered "wrong craving" translates a term literally meaning "craving for wrong views" or "perverted craving," indicating craving rooted in mistaken views; the rendering captures the doctrinal sense. The "five eyes" refers to the classical set: the physical eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the buddha eye. The list of meditative and path-related categories beginning with "heat, peak, patience, and the supreme worldly dharma" refers to the four preparatory stages of the path of preparation in the Abhidharma scheme. The passage ends mid-sentence in the Tibetan, indicating a continuation in the following fascicle.  The passage identifies loving-kindness with permanence, happiness, purity, and selfhood — the four qualities of nirvāṇa in the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra tradition (nitya, sukha, śuddha, ātman). The use of "self" here is deliberate and doctrinal, not a slip: the text is asserting that loving-kindness, as the buddha-nature, possesses the ātman quality of nirvāṇa. This is a characteristic move of the tathāgatagarbha literature and should not be smoothed over.

The final section distinguishes a deficient, śrāvaka-level loving-kindness — one still characterized by impermanence, suffering, impurity, and selflessness — from the transcendent loving-kindness identified with the Tathāgata throughout the passage.  The phrase "the path of the single defining mark" renders "mtshan nyid gcig pa'i lam," which likely refers to the non-dual path in which all phenomena share the single mark of emptiness or dharmatā; this is a somewhat compressed technical expression and the rendering follows the most plausible doctrinal reading.

The passage "loving-kindness accompanied by existence, non-existence, and neither-existence-nor-non-existence" describes a form of loving-kindness that transcends the four extremes of metaphysical predication, beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to measure — this appears to be the loving-kindness of the Great Vehicle that is contrasted throughout with the śrāvaka loving-kindness.

The sentence about being born among the Brahmā gods yet having "no birth" because "he has come under their power" is syntactically and doctrinally elliptical in the Tibetan. The most plausible reading is that such a bodhisattva, though capable of being reborn in the Brahmā realms through the power of loving-kindness (as is classically taught), transcends even that birth because he is no longer governed by compulsive rebirth. The Tibetan "dbang du gyur pa" could also read as "having brought them under his power," which would alter the sense; this alternative is noted here but not placed in the body.  The "yak-bulls" rendering deserves a note: the Tibetan reads "bal glang," which literally means wool-bulls or yak-bulls. In the parallel accounts of the Devadatta episode in Buddhist literature the animals are typically described as intoxicated or maddened elephants, not yak-bulls. The Tibetan here is unambiguous as written, but this divergence from the standard canonical account is worth flagging; it may reflect a variant textual tradition or a translation peculiarity in the Tibetan rendering of the underlying Sanskrit.

The name "Devadatta" is rendered from the Tibetan "lha sbyin," its standard equivalent.

The phrase rendered as "blocking and jostling along the road, waving cloth and making a clamor" is an attempt to render the wrestlers' activity idiomatically; the Tibetan describes them blocking the road, waving banners or cloths, and making noise in a festive or competitive display.  The householder's name rendered as "Doḍa" follows the Tibetan "འདོད་པ་" read as a proper name in this narrative context; it could alternatively be read as a descriptive epithet meaning "the desirous one." The city name Śupāra is a known ancient Indian port city (Sanskrit Śūrpāraka), and Vetāla as a southern region name is consistent with the geography found in related narrative literature. The householder named here appears to be Supriya, consistent with the broader sūtra context, though the Tibetan at this point uses only the phrase "the householder Supriya" implied by the preceding narrative; the term rendered "householder Supriya" follows the continuity established in the passage.

The woman's name Vasitā is a transliteration of the Tibetan Ba si ta; the Sanskrit original may be Vasiṭā or a related form, but the reading is not fully certain.

The name Mahāsinadata renders Tibetan Ma hā si na dar ta; the Sanskrit Mahāsenadattā is a plausible reconstruction but is not certain.  The king's name given in the Tibetan is "རྒྱལ་པོ་སྡེ་རབ་ཏུ་ཕམ་བྱེད" which reads literally as "King Brahmadatta" (a standard royal name in Buddhist narratives rendered as a Tibetan calque), but the syllables could also be read as a descriptive epithet meaning "utterly defeating the army."
