The sandalwood mountain reference (རི་བསུང་ཅན) literally means "fragrant mountain," a conventional term for sandalwood-bearing Himalayan peaks; "sandalwood mountains" conveys this clearly for the listener.  The city name rendered here as "Serkya" is a Tibetan place name appearing in the text; its precise identification is uncertain, but it appears consistently in this narrative episode and is treated as a proper noun.

The passage identifies the first bodhisattva ground as "Supreme Joy," corresponding to the Sanskrit Pramuditā, the first of the ten bodhisattva grounds, and offers an unusual etymological explanation linking it to parental joy and grief, which is a distinctive feature of this Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra passage rather than the standard Daśabhūmika account.  The phrase rendered "beings whose dharma-body has not yet fully developed" translates chos kyi sku'i shed ma rdzogs pa, literally "whose power or vitality of the dharmakāya is not complete." This is an unusual usage; in context it refers to sentient beings who have not yet fully actualized or ripened their potential for the dharmakāya, and the translation reflects that developmental sense.

The name lha sbyin is the Tibetan rendering of Devadatta throughout; rendered consistently as Devadatta.

The phrase sras sgra gcan 'dzin dang 'dra bar dgongs na, "if he regards all sentient beings as his son Rāhula," takes sgra gcan 'dzin as Rāhula, the Buddha's son, whose name in Tibetan literally means "seized by Rāhu." This is the standard identification.

The closing image of Subhūti refusing alms from someone who harbors contempt, lest he cause that person to generate non-virtue, is a well-attested motif in the prajñāpāramitā literature; the translation follows the plain sense of the text without alteration.  The phrase rendered "words so careless" translates an expression suggesting speech that was inattentive or heedless, implying the hypothetical objector is claiming the Tathāgata spoke without due care. The precise nuance of the underlying idiom is slightly compressed in translation but the doctrinal thrust is preserved.

The passage "a ground comparable to an only child" is a Mahāyāna technical usage in which the first bodhisattva ground is likened to an only child, indicating one who has just entered the irreversible path. The comparison here underlines that even a highly advanced practitioner like Subhūti exercises such care, making the implied standard for a bodhisattva all the higher.  The phrase "cut off that person's vital faculty" renders the Tibetan idiom for killing in a doctrinal register: the bodhisattva, having attained the relevant bodhisattva ground (bhūmi), acted from great compassion with the skill-in-means specific to that level of realization, not from affliction. The text is making the classical Mahāyāna point that a bodhisattva of high realization may perform what externally resembles killing while being entirely free of the unwholesome mental factor that constitutes the karma of killing. The bracketed question about which ground is intended is left unresolved by the text itself at this point.  The Tathāgata's name rendered here as "Resounding Drum of the Refreshing Cool" is a tentative rendering of the Tibetan epithet. The exact Sanskrit original is uncertain.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence in the source text, listing categories of malevolent beings; the translation follows the Tibetan exactly up to the point of truncation.

"Kaṭapūtana" is a class of demonic being in Indian Buddhist cosmology, often associated with foul odors; the Tibetan transliteration is retained as the Sanskrit is the clearest form for scholarly listeners.  The passage on killing holders of wrong views is doctrinally sensitive and depends on the text's identification of those brahmins as entirely lacking the five spiritual faculties (faith, diligence, mindfulness, meditative absorption, and wisdom), thereby placing them outside the moral calculus that governs ordinary killing. This is the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's own framing and is rendered as the text presents it, without softening.

The term rendered "one who holds wrong views" translates log sred can, literally "one who has wrong craving or wrong attachment," a term used in this sūtra for those who hold fundamentally mistaken views and lack any seed of virtue or spiritual faculty. It is broader than the usual "wrong view" (log lta) and specifically characterizes those deemed irredeemable within this passage's ethical scheme.  The torma cake offering rule described here appears to be the narrative etiology of a Vinaya custom. The phrase rendered "in a rotation" reflects the sense that the townspeople took turns providing the ghost's victim, a detail common in such narrative contexts.

The final sentence is left grammatically open because the Tibetan itself is an unfinished list — the passage continues in the next section and this translation ends at the same point where the Tibetan breaks off.  The name "sengdeng" refers to a thorny acacia tree, likely Mimosa or Acacia species used in classical Indian Buddhist literature. It is left as a transliteration since no standard English botanical identification is certain enough to use in place of the proper name.

The passage refers to Devadatta — the Buddha's cousin, notorious in Buddhist tradition for schism, attempted murder of the Buddha, and consignment to Avīci hell. The text is ironically asserting, from a Mahāyāna perspective, that none of the standard accusations against Devadatta literally apply to him, as his true nature is known only to a buddha. This is a classical Mahāyāna revaluation of Devadatta as a secret bodhisattva.

The ground "comparable to having an only child" corresponds to the Sanskrit ekaputrabhūmi, a Mahāyāna bodhisattva ground defined by impartial compassion for all beings as if they were one's only child. The phrase "Boundless Joy" renders "Rab tu dga' ba," the first bodhisattva ground, Pramuditā-bhūmi; its appearance here is contextually as an example or parallel term, not a conflation.  The passage presents an unusual doctrinal move: the four qualities of permanence, happiness, self, and purity — normally associated in Mahāyāna with buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha) — are explicitly excluded from being labeled "emptiness," while simultaneously the intrinsic nature of a buddha is said to be neither conditioned nor unconditioned. This reflects a tathāgatagarbha-inflected discourse that is navigating the tension between the emptiness teaching and the affirmative qualities of the dharmakāya. The text is likely drawing on a tradition related to the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra or a closely allied source.  The passage on beginningless emptiness lists "permanent, blissful, selfhood, and utterly pure" as attributes of emptiness — an apparent echo of the four qualities of the dharmakāya (nitya, sukha, ātman, śuddha) found in tathāgatagarbha literature. This is doctrinally significant: emptiness here is not the mere absence of inherent existence but is identified with the buddha-nature's positive qualities, reflecting a distinct strand of Indian and Tibetan Mahāyāna thought.

The phrase rendered "that which is and yet is not" for the second definition of the emptiness of emptiness is genuinely elliptical in the Tibetan and may reflect a dialectical formulation beyond standard tetralemma usage; the rendering preserves the logical paradox of the original.  The long catalogue of non-Buddhist (tīrthika) ascetic practices is a standard polemical list found across Indian Buddhist literature. The phrase rendered "sustaining oneself on wind alone for seven days" translates literally "seven days eating wind," a recognized ascetic claim. The "five fires" refers to the practice of sitting surrounded by four fires with the sun as the fifth. The expression "seeing without clearly seeing" in the ten-grounds bodhisattva passage renders a deliberate doctrinal grading of vision (mthong ba) into partial and complete, culminating in the buddha's perfect gnosis; the moon-in-daytime simile is a standard Tathāgatagarbha analogy.

The phrase rendered "field of receiving" (len pa'i gnas) refers in the commentarial tradition to those who receive gifts — i.e., the recipients of generosity — as a locus of merit, completing the triad: giver, offering, and recipient.

The phrase rendered "immature ordinary being" translates a compound meaning literally "childish, of low birth" — a standard pejorative for ordinary worldlings (Sanskrit bālapṛthagjana). The rendering captures both the doctrinal sense (one who lacks the realizations of the noble ones) and the connotation of spiritual immaturity.

The three aspects of the vehicle in the analytical knowledge of meaning section refer to the vehicles of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, which the bodhisattva understands as ultimately converging into the single vehicle — a standard Mahāyāna doctrinal position (ekayāna).  The passage explains the four analytical knowledges using a series of etymological wordplays in classical Tibetan that trace why certain things are called "grasping" or "holding": earth, mountain, eye, cloud, human being, and mother. These are likely calqued from Sanskrit etymological glosses (probably on terms like dhāraṇa or dhāraṇī) playing on the root dhṛ, "to hold." The Tibetan is doing scholastic etymology; the translation conveys the logic plainly rather than reproducing the Tibetan puns, which would be opaque in English.

The phrase rendered "without reified content" translates don med pa, literally "without meaning/object." In context, the point is that the bodhisattva's analytical knowledge of language recognizes that words like "man," "woman," or "vehicle" do not correspond to inherently existing referents; this is the domain of bodhisattvas and buddhas, while ordinary beings take words to have fixed referents. The rendering "without reified content" is a doctrinal judgment; a more literal rendering would be "without [ultimately real] object."  The phrase rendered "literary arts" for གཙུག་ལག་བེའི་ཀ་ར་ན (second paragraph) is a Tibetan transliteration of Sanskrit; the underlying term appears to be a form related to "karaṇa" in the context of the śāstric or literary arts tradition. The exact Sanskrit source is not fully recoverable from the transliteration alone, but the contextual meaning — bodies of learning or literary/scholarly texts — is clear from context.

The passage's claim that the analytical knowledge of phenomena amounts to knowing the two syllables "permanent" and "abiding" is an allusion to the tathāgatagarbha doctrine: the buddha-nature is permanent and abiding, and this knowledge is what distinguishes a bodhisattva's analytical knowledge from that of a pratyekabuddha.  The four rivers named — Ganges, Sindhu, Vakṣu, and Sītā — along with Lake Anavatapta are the classical Indian cosmological set of the four great rivers flowing from the Himalayan lake, a standard reference in Buddhist literature.

The phrase rendered "common, inferior beings" for བུས་པ་མ་རབས translates a Tibetan expression meaning literally "low, ordinary persons," contextually referring to practitioners below the bodhisattva level relative to whom Kauṣṭhila's distinction is valid.  The "twenty-five modes of existence" refers to a standard Abhidharma enumeration of the planes or states of conditioned existence in saṃsāra across the three realms. The "eleven sūtras" is a reference to a specific canonical list; the exact contents vary by tradition and may refer to eleven sūtra categories associated with the Foundational Vehicle, here implicitly contrasted with the Great Vehicle sūtras.

The four qualities — permanence, bliss, self, and utter purity — are the four transcendent qualities (Sanskrit: nitya, sukha, ātman, śuddha) ascribed specifically to the dharmakāya or buddha-nature in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition. This is a doctrinally significant and intentional reversal of the ordinary three marks of existence, and the translation preserves it without softening. The verse spoken beneath the śāla trees is addressed to Cunda (the smith who offered the Buddha his last meal), rendered here as a proper name. This is consistent with the preceding context of the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra.

The phrase rendered "close companions of the Buddha" translates སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཉེ་གནས, literally "near-dwelling of the Buddha," a term parallel to the earlier ངའི་ཉེ་གནས ("in my company") and carrying the sense of being within the Buddha's circle rather than Māra's.  The term rendered "base and ignoble" translates a phrase meaning literally "a son of low and inferior birth" used adjectivally to describe the quality of the austerities being practiced. The passage presents a dialectical structure throughout: what "once existed" (as a deficiency or limitation) entails the absence of something positive in the present, and vice versa. This is part of a larger argument, likely from the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, demonstrating that such limitations cannot be predicated of the Tathāgata in any of the three times, establishing the buddha's permanent, blissful, self-possessing, and pure nature against misconceptions.

The bodhisattva compared to "a king among yaks" renders the Tibetan term for the yak-bull, an image of strength and noble bearing used to describe a great bodhisattva, here likely referring to Mahākāśyapa.  The passage plays on a classical paradox concerning the two truths: conventional truth, when spoken by the Tathāgata from within ultimate truth and for the purpose of leading beings to it, is itself an expression of ultimate truth. This is a standard Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra doctrinal move and is rendered as such, without smoothing the apparent tension.

The final exchange introduces the classic philosophical problem of whether nirvāṇa and awakening, if permanent, can be "attained," since attainment implies coming-to-be, which implies impermanence. Kāśyapa's challenge sets up a likely further response by the Blessed One.  The householder reference — rendered here as "the householder Anāthapiṇḍada" — translates the Tibetan khyim bdag skyabs med zas sbyin, which is a Tibetan calque of the name Anāthapiṇḍada (literally, "the householder who gives food to the shelterless"). This is the standard identification in the commentarial tradition and the rendering is secure.  The passage has a rapid series of analogical examples used to illustrate "seeing by means of signs" as distinct from direct perception. The āmra fruit placed in the palm is a classical Indian philosophical illustration of vivid, unmediated perception; it recurs across Buddhist epistemological literature. The statement that "from the very beginning there is no defining characteristic of seeing" is doctrinally significant: even direct bodhisattva perception of the path, awakening, and nirvāṇa is free from reified conceptual marks. The closing distinction between what worldly beings know and what the Tathāgata and bodhisattvas know draws on a theme found in several Mahāyāna sūtras, where omniscience is understood not as a claim asserted in ordinary linguistic terms but as a mode of knowing that transcends the subject-object framework within which ordinary cognition operates.  The "eight-armed one" refers to Śiva in his eight-armed form, one of several non-Buddhist divine figures enumerated here as objects of worldly belief. The list that follows is a catalogue of tīrthika cosmological and soteriological positions: primordial nature (Skt. prakṛti, the Sāṃkhya first principle), time (kāla, the Vaiśeṣika / Ājīvika position), atoms (paramāṇu, the Vaiśeṣika view), the lord of loving-kindness (likely Maitreya as conceived by certain groups, or possibly a non-Buddhist deity), and the declaration that the highest meditative attainment — the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception — constitutes nirvāṇa (a position attributed to brahmanical and certain proto-Buddhist schools). The passage ends mid-sentence in the source; the translation accurately reflects this break.  The phrase rendered "the twelve branches of scripture" refers to the twelve-fold classification of the Buddhist canon by literary form, a standard Indic doctrinal category. The Tibetan here is མདོ་སྡེ་བཅུ་གཉིས, literally "the twelve sūtra-collections," but in context it denotes the twelve aṅgas or limbs of scripture.

The "eleven absorptions of emptiness" is a specific technical enumeration found in the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra tradition; the number eleven is striking and differs from other canonical lists of emptiness-absorptions, but the Tibetan is unambiguous.

The "four distortions" are the standard four viparyāsas: mistaking the impermanent for permanent, suffering for pleasure, the selfless for self, and the impure for pure.  The analogy of the two women with pots requires a small note: the one carrying curd is glad when both pots break because curd is relatively easy to replace, whereas the one carrying butter is not glad, butter being of greater value. The Tibetan does not spell this out, but this is the standard reading of the passage in the commentarial tradition. The contrast maps onto the person with deteriorated discipline, who has something precious to lose, versus the person with pure discipline, who has nothing to regret.

The phrase rendered "moral discipline that is at the same time not moral discipline" reflects the paradoxical formulation in the Tibetan: the bodhisattva's pure discipline transcends the conventional category of discipline itself, being non-fabricated and non-conceptual in character. This is a standard Mahāyāna doctrinal point and is preserved in the translation without smoothing.  The "five liberations" listed as running from "liberation of form through to liberation of consciousness" correspond to a set of five emancipations tied to the five aggregates, a less common enumeration that may reflect a variant doctrinal scheme in this sūtra's recension rather than the standard set of eight liberations. This is worth noting as a genuinely distinctive usage.

The phrase rendered "doubt concerning heedlessness" translates a Tibetan term meaning literally "doubt concerning negligence or carelessness." The passage employs a recurring paired term rendered here as "searching and active striving" (Tib. tsol ba dang bcas / byed pa dang bcas). The first element refers to a driven, seeking quality of mind; the second to effortful, purposeful activity of body or speech. The text itself defines laxity and restlessness as their bodily and mental counterparts respectively, which the translation preserves in the order given. The list of buddha-epithets "endowed with knowledge and conduct" renders the standard Tibetan equivalent of the Sanskrit vidyācaraṇasampanna; it is one of the ten traditional epithets of a buddha and is standard. The phrase "whose crown no one can behold" refers to the classical attribute of the uṣṇīṣa being of immeasurable height, invisible to any being — a recognized mark of a fully awakened one. The "great brahmin" and "great Brahmā" are distinct epithets in the Indian Buddhist tradition: the former recasts the brahmanical ideal in Buddhist terms, and the latter draws an analogy to the god Brahmā's purity and exaltation; both are standard epithets in this and related sūtras.  The phrase rendered as "eleven kinds of emptiness" follows the Tibetan numeral directly. Standard Madhyamaka enumerations give sixteen or eighteen kinds of emptiness; eleven is an unusual count found in certain early Mahāyāna sūtra contexts and likely reflects the particular doctrinal framework of the source text rather than a scribal error.

The clause about "correct" meaning "the practice of austerity" and "complete" meaning knowing that practicing suffering yields the fruit of suffering is a somewhat unexpected gloss, possibly reflecting a polemical or comparative doctrinal context distinguishing the Buddha's path from non-Buddhist austerity practices. The Tibetan is clear and has been rendered faithfully.  The phrase rendered "the vidyā of ignorance" translates ma rig pa'i rig pa, a deliberately paradoxical expression meaning the vidyā or clear knowledge that penetrates ignorance itself, here glossed as "the perfection of emptiness." The apparent contradiction is intentional and is part of the text's rhetorical structure.

The passage on nirvāṇa "not truly existing" yet being declared to exist is a classic instance of the two-truths teaching applied to nirvāṇa: ultimately it is beyond existence and non-existence, but conventionally the Buddha affirms it to encourage practitioners. The analogy of telling a childless person they have a child is an unusual simile worth noting — it may reflect a specific source passage.  The passage plays extensively on the Tibetan epithet "knower of the world" and "unsurpassed," offering a series of etymological glosses that are standard in this genre of buddha-epithet exegesis. The interpretation of "unsurpassed" as "not subject to being cut down" reflects a Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit anuttara parsed through the lens of utta meaning something like "that which cuts" — a non-standard but traditional commentarial move worth noting for scholarly readers.

The phrase rendered "eight worldly concerns" translates the standard list of the eight mundane dharmas: gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and infamy.  The horse-taming analogy here draws on a well-known canonical simile also found in Pāli sources, where progressively deeper physical contact corresponds to progressively more intensive Dharma instruction needed to subdue different types of practitioners. The four teachings — birth alone; birth and aging; birth, aging, and illness; birth, aging, illness, and death — mirror the progressive contemplation of the marks of impermanence and suffering.

The phrase rendered "the three lower destinies" translates a term referring to the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source; the translation reflects this open continuation faithfully.  The extended etymology of "lha" (god) in this passage is a scholastic wordplay typical of indigenous Tibetan or Chinese-translated Buddhist treatises rather than classical Indian Sanskrit etymological analysis, suggesting this text may derive from a Chinese Buddhist source rendered into Tibetan. The etymologies given are mnemonic and didactic rather than philologically rigorous, and the translation renders each in the spirit intended.

The phrase casting aside "the feminine faculties" (bud med kyi dbang po skyugs pa lta bur bor ba) is a somewhat striking formulation. It refers to the bodhisattva's renunciation of female rebirth or feminine characteristics over countless lifetimes as part of accumulating merit toward buddhahood — a doctrinal motif found in certain sūtras. The translation renders it literally as the text requires.  The list of mental qualities contains two consecutive terms rendered "a mind of nothingness" and "a mind that is not nothing either," reflecting the classical pair drawn from the formless absorptions: the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The passage applies these as qualifiers of the bodhisattva's mind rather than as meditative states per se, which is somewhat unusual; the rendering follows the Tibetan literally.

The closing line is syntactically incomplete in the source passage as given, ending mid-sentence with "for it is seen with the eye of Dharma." This reflects the passage breaking off at that point; the continuation belongs to the next segment.  The phrase rendered "cannot be gazed upon directly" translates the Tibetan literally meaning something like "not fitting to be looked at," which in Buddhist technical usage indicates transcendence of ordinary perception, not unsightliness. The same phrase recurs in the Saṅgha passage and is rendered consistently.

The sequence of negations following the five aggregates employs a triple-negation pattern throughout: neither the thing, nor the severing of the thing, nor yet the thing. The middle member in each triad is slightly variable in the Tibetan and may indicate either "the cutting off of" or "what is beyond." The translation follows the most internally consistent reading throughout.  The phrase rendered "stream of the fourfold retinue" translates a term referring to the four assemblies of the Buddhist community — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — and the idea is that without generosity one will not draw such a community around oneself. The phrase "adversaries become endowed with power" and "adversaries become endowed with eloquence" is an unusual formulation in which opponents or rivals (pha rol po) benefit from one's generosity and thereby develop strength and eloquence; the karmic fruit then ripens as the giver's own attainment of the ten powers and four analytical knowledges at awakening. This is doctrinally deliberate and has been preserved as given in the text.  The phrase rendered "the ultimate gods" translates "don dam pa'i lha," literally "ultimate-truth gods" or "gods of the ultimate." In context this clearly refers to buddhas and bodhisattvas as a category of divine beings surpassing all mundane gods — a doctrinal category somewhat unusual in standard Mahāyāna literature. The passage appears to be drawing a contrast between mundane devas (impermanent) and these "ultimate gods" (permanent, unborn, etc.), which are identified explicitly as buddhas and bodhisattvas. This usage is characteristic of certain buddha-nature sūtra literature, including the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition.

The "twelve branches of scripture" refers to the traditional twelve-fold classification of the Buddha's teachings (dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana), a standard canonical category.  The dialogue near the end shifts in voice between an interlocutor and the Blessed One in a way typical of sūtra question-and-answer format. The exchange about the ocean swimmer distinguishes what is "inconceivable" from what is merely extraordinary, hinging on the contrast between a foolish ordinary person's boast and the bodhisattva's actual accomplishment, which is the genuinely inconceivable act. The phrase rendered "measuring and fathoming all of saṃsāra in a single instant" translates a compound meaning to measure out or traverse the full extent of saṃsāra; the image implies comprehensive mastery rather than mere traversal.  The teaching on permanence, happiness, self, and purity taught to beings stands in deliberate tension with the bodhisattva's own recognition of impermanence, no-self, suffering, and impurity. This is the classical fourfold "pure inversion" doctrine found in tathāgatagarbha literature, where these four are attributes of buddha-nature rather than affirmations of the ordinary self, and the bodhisattva teaches them without falling into a view of substantialist permanence. The text does not make this explicit here, so it is left to the doctrinal note rather than inserted into the translation.

The phrase rendered "he does not abide on the grounds" translates sa la gnas pa ma yin pa — literally "he is not one who abides on a ground." This likely means he is not a bodhisattva abiding on any of the ten bodhisattva grounds in the ordinary sense, or possibly that he is beyond those stages. This is a genuinely ambiguous phrase in context.  The "six teachers" mentioned are the six famous non-Buddhist masters of the Buddha's era, a standard reference in Indian Buddhist literature. The text's structure shifts here from the thematic discussion of abandonment into a new sūtra section marker and then dialogue; the section heading "twenty-fifth section" is part of the canonical text itself. The phrase rendered "the conduct of the sick" and "the conduct of a child" reflect categories whose full elaboration presumably follows in the next passage; no uncertainty is intended by the rendering, which follows the literal Tibetan.  The phrase rendered "having one's life deceived away" translates the Tibetan srog slu ba, literally "the life being cheated or defrauded," meaning to be robbed of one's livelihood or endangered. The exact nuance is somewhat ambiguous; it may mean being cheated of one's sustenance or literally having one's life put at risk by treachery.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end ("degenerate monks, bearing the implements of the holy life without proper examination"), as the Tibetan input ends there; this is a continuity cut, not a textual problem.  The phrase rendered "without remainder at the final end" translates མཐའ་ཡུན་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ, which carries the nuance of a final, complete, and permanent nirvāṇa — the precise doctrinal point of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra being that the Tathāgata does not in fact disappear into such a nirvāṇa but abides permanently. The contrast between the erroneous view (that the Tathāgata is impermanent and perishes finally) and the sūtra's own teaching (permanent, unchanging, unshifting presence) is the central argument of this passage.

The white bull elephant (བལ་གླང་གི་ཁྱུ་མཆོག) is a standard Indian simile for an extraordinarily powerful and reliable memory; the dhāraṇī of Kāśyapa's age beings is praised as comparably faultless.  The term rendered "attendants who understand the profound meaning" translates ཉེ་གནས་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་ཤེས་པ, literally "attendants knowing the profound meaning." These are the close disciples capable of grasping and transmitting the deep Dharma; the rendering is intentionally kept close to the Tibetan rather than smoothed into "learned companions," as the doctrinal emphasis on comprehension of depth is important here.

The medicine name agada is a Sanskrit loanword (Skt. agada) preserved in the Tibetan transliteration; it refers to a renowned antidote or panacea in Indian medical literature.  The passage enumerating "the four weighty rules up to the seven rules for settling disputes" refers to standard Vinaya categories: the four pārājika rules, and the seven principles for resolving disputes found in the Vinaya. The phrase "twelve branches of scriptural teaching" refers to the standard dvādaśāṅga classification of the Buddhist canon.

The self-proclamation passage is slightly syntactically compressed in the Tibetan: the text presents attendants who neither make proper attainment claims nor avoid divergent personal views, then shifts into the boastful speech ("I alone understand…") as the fourth scenario's marker of decline. The rendering reflects this structure as accurately as possible while remaining fluent for listening.  The passage on nirvāṇa contains a reductionist or Sarvāstivāda-inflected view being attributed to those in the age of decline, using the textile analogy: nirvāṇa is not a positive cessation but merely the label applied when afflictions are gone, like "no garment" when a garment disintegrates. This is presented as a mistaken or partial teaching, not the text's own affirmation.

The term rendered "woollen robes of the type called kauśeya" translates a Tibetan phonetic approximation of Sanskrit kauśeya, a type of silk or fine cloth; the precise identification of this garment type is uncertain in context, though kauśeya normally refers to silk rather than wool.  The passage contains a reference to "གྲོང་ཁྱེར་རྩྭ་མཆོག་སཱ་ལའི་ཤིང་དྲུང་" which literally means "the city of Supreme Grass, at the foot of the śāla trees." This is a standard epithet or descriptive name for Kuśinagārī, the site of the Buddha's final passing, characterized by its grove of śāla trees. The translation renders it as Kuśinagārī for clarity.

The phrase rendered as "one hundred and twenty thousand great bodhisattvas" translates "ཁྲི་ཕྲག་བཅུ་གཉིས" (twelve groups of ten thousand), which equals one hundred and twenty thousand. This is consistent with standard Buddhist enumeration.  The minister's name is rendered as Sunīdha following the standard Sanskrit correlate of this Tibetan name as it appears in the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra context; the Tibetan gives only the phonetic rendering Nyī-zla grags-pa ("Renowned as Sun and Moon"), which may be a different textual tradition's form of the name. This is worth noting as a genuinely uncertain identification.

The great physician named here in Tibetan as Kāśyapa Paripūraka (ཨོད་སྲུང་རྫོགས་བྱེད) is a stock epithet in the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra tradition for the Buddha himself, framed as the supreme physician; the passage is setting up the minister's counsel that the king should go to the Buddha for healing of his remorse.  The minister's argument that regicide is not sinful "by the nature of royal law" is a deliberate dramatic and doctrinal provocation within the text — it represents the counsel of a bad friend that the narrative will go on to refute. The translator has rendered it faithfully without endorsement.

The name rendered "Mākandika" (Tib. ཕྱུགས་ལྷས་ཀྱི་བུ་མས་ཀ་རི) is a compound: ཕྱུགས་ལྷས་ཀྱི་བུ approximates "son of Puṣkarasārin" (the brahmin whose name means "he of the cattle god") and མས་ཀ་རི corresponds to Maskarin, referring to the tīrthika teacher Maskarin Gośālīputra. The text appears to name a different heterodox teacher here than the Kāśyapa Paripūraka of the preceding passage; Maskarin Gośālīputra is one of the six famous non-Buddhist teachers of the time of the Buddha. The rendering preserves the dramatic irony: the minister is recommending a heterodox teacher as a substitute for a true physician of souls.

The iśikā reed as an example of an eternal, indestructible element reflects the Ājīvika or similar non-Buddhist doctrine of eternal, uncreated substances — a doctrine the sūtra will go on to refute.  The phrase rendered "the avīci hell, the hell of uninterrupted torment" corresponds to མཚམས་མེད་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དམྱལ་བ, literally the "hell of beings without interval," the standard Tibetan rendering of Avīci, the lowest and most severe hell realm. The literal Tibetan compounds the word for hell with the term for the five heinous crimes (ānantarya), but the meaning is clearly Avīci and the rendering reflects this.

The passage from the minister Satyadatta contains a series of analogical arguments that appear to be setting up a sophistic justification for parricide on the grounds that the father, being wicked or being killed for political rather than personal reasons, does not truly count as a "father" in the morally relevant sense. This is a well-known narrative device in this text — the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra — where false reasoning is presented and subsequently refuted.  The name rendered here as "Jīvaka, son of Berāta" follows the Tibetan བེ་ར་ཏའི་བུ་ཀུན་རྒྱལ — "Kun-rgyal, son of Berāta." The Tibetan personal name ཀུན་རྒྱལ (Kun-rgyal, "All-Victorious") does not straightforwardly correspond to the famous physician Jīvaka, though the context — a physician residing in Rājagṛha — clearly points to that figure. The Sanskrit Vorlage likely had "Jīvaka" here, with ཀུན་རྒྱལ as a semantic rendering of a related form. The translation renders the name as "Jīvaka" in keeping with the doctrinal and narrative context, a choice noted here for transparency. The patronymic "Berāta" is a transliteration of the Tibetan and does not match the standard biographical tradition; it may reflect a variant or corrupt transmission.  The list of kings' names in the middle of the passage — Lāmpa, Bde, Byilatsina, Nāhosha, Kateka, Byishaka, Moonlight, Sunlight, Luminous, Upholder of Many Beings, Vaidūrya, Otana, Tumpa, Bya-ba, Padma — are transcriptions of Indic names whose exact Sanskrit originals are uncertain in several cases. The Tibetan renderings for some of them (e.g. Moonlight for Zla 'od, Sunlight for Nyi 'od, Luminous for 'Od ldan, Upholder of Many Beings for 'Gro ba mang po 'dzin) have been translated by sense; the others are left as transliterated approximations. This is a passage reflecting the nihilist (Ājīvika or similar) view being voiced by the minister, not the text's own doctrinal position.

The description of the Teacher as "the son of Kātyāyana, named Nirgrantha" refers not to the Buddha but to a non-Buddhist teacher — most likely Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta (Mahāvīra, the Jain founder) or a figure associated with the Ājīvika or related tradition. The Tibetan reads Kā-tyā'i bu Nag-can, which may render "Nirgrantha, son of Kātyāyana." The minister is presenting this non-Buddhist teacher to the king as an alternative to the Buddha, in a context that will presumably be refuted later in the text.  The phrase rendered "wheel-turning king of the central lands" translates a compressed Tibetan expression for a chakravartin or universal monarch, here specifically described as ruler of the middle country. The precise political geography implied may be symbolic rather than literal.

The minister's final etymological gloss on "hell-being" is a folk etymology playing on the syllables of the Tibetan word "dMyalba," breaking it into "dMyal" (torment) and "ba" (broken/destroyed). This is not linguistically rigorous but is a standard rhetorical device in the text's argumentative context, where the nihilist minister is denying the reality of hell by exposing the word as a mere human construction.

The nihilist speech attributed to "that Teacher" in the opening paragraph reflects the views of Makkhali Gosāla and the Ājīvika school as represented in Buddhist polemical literature, not the Buddha's own teaching.  The passage presents a series of heterodox philosophical arguments — specifically those of a materialist or Ājīvika-type interlocutor who denies karmic retribution, argues from both eternalist and nihilist premises that killing entails no sin, and offers fanciful etymologies of "hell-being." The subsequent paragraph shifts abruptly to a Buddhist rejoinder, introducing the "great Teacher" who is described with standard buddha epithets and who teaches the opposite. The transition is dramatically significant: the minister's nihilist speech is being presented as the wrong view, which the true Teacher now corrects.

The phrase rendered "the unconquered one with matted locks" translates a proper name or epithet in the Tibetan: "mi pham skra'i la bzhes bya ba," which appears to be a description of a specific teacher or deity with matted or plaited hair — possibly Śiva or a non-Buddhist sage used rhetorically. However, from context, the Buddhist "great Teacher" who is omniscient and sees all three worlds is clearly the Buddha Śākyamuni. This tension in the passage may reflect a textual conflation or a polemical framing. Given genuine uncertainty about this epithet's referent, I flag it here rather than in the body.

The verse section is metrically loose in the Tibetan but has a clear gnomic structure; it is rendered as verse accordingly.  The "great Teacher, the naked sage Jñātiputra" refers to Mahāvīra, the Jain tīrthankara, here identified by his epithet Nirgrantha ("unbound") and his clan name Jñātiputra ("son of the Jñāta clan"). The passage is presenting a Jain interlocutor making arguments against karmic responsibility — a standard polemical framing in Buddhist sūtra literature. The Tibetan reads "གཅེར་བུ་པ་གཉེན་གྱི་བུ" which literally means "the naked one, son of the Jñāta clan," confirming the identification with Mahāvīra rather than the Buddha.

The argument put into the minister's mouth — that killing one's father incurs no sin because "the life-breath cannot truly be cut" — is presented as a sophistic Jain or materialist position the text intends to refute, not as the author's own doctrine.  The four great rivers listed here correspond to the Indus (Sindhu), Ganges (Gaṅgā), Vakṣu (rendered Pakṣu in the Tibetan, likely a scribal variant for Vakṣu, the Oxus), and Sītā, a mythological Himalayan river — the standard Buddhist cosmological set of four rivers flowing from Lake Anavatapta. The slight textual irregularity "Pakṣu" for the expected "Vakṣu" is noted but not corrected in the body.

The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the source text itself is cut off.

The teaching attributed here to Jñātiputra (Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, the Jain leader Mahāvīra) — denying generosity, virtue, parents, present and past, arhat, meditation, and path — is the standard Buddhist polemical summary of Jain fatalist doctrine (niyativāda), according to which liberation comes automatically after a fixed span of transmigration, regardless of moral action. This is presented here as a foil to the Buddhist teaching that follows.  The physician Jīvaka is speaking with a king who has committed patricide, a narrative context familiar from the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition. The two terms translated throughout as "shame" and "modesty" correspond to the classical Pali and Sanskrit pair hrī and apatrāpya: here rendered as shame (the inner self-reproach, Tib. khrel ba) and modesty (the regard for social and cosmic witness, Tib. 'dzem pa). Some translators reverse the assignment; the definitions given in the text itself have been followed here for doctrinal precision. The phrase rendered "pure white in nature" (rnam par dkar ba'i chos) is a standard Abhidharma idiom for virtuous or wholesome qualities.  The disease name "kanka" (Tib. ནད་ཀམ་པ་ལ) is uncertain in its precise identification. It appears to refer to a fatal or incurable condition used as an analogy; the transliteration is approximate and the Sanskrit equivalent is not firmly established.

The text ends mid-sentence, apparently continuing into the next passage with a description of the Blessed One's qualities leading into a further teaching or narrative.  The list of doctrinal categories taught by the Buddha near the beginning is a formal Abhidharmic-style enumeration of paired and transcended extremes (tetralemma-style), rendered serially as in the Tibetan. No single received Sanskrit reconstruction is certain for this particular list, so it has been translated by meaning.

The name "Matsyaśrī" is a reconstruction of བན་ཙ་ཤྲཱི based on the phonetic Tibetan rendering; it is plausible but the original Sanskrit is uncertain.

The name "Kapulo" is transliterated from ཀ་པུ་ལོ; the underlying Sanskrit is unclear. "Subartā" likewise renders སུ་བར་ཏ་, and "Mānoramā" renders ཡིད་འོང་མ in its Sanskrit equivalent (meaning "the delightful / charming one").

The phrase rendered "like Rāhu does for his own son" (སྲས་སྒྲ་གཅན་འཛིན་དང་འདྲ་བར) is notable: Rāhu is here used as an example of parental tenderness rather than in his usual role as a malevolent being — a slightly unexpected usage, but it is what the Tibetan says.  The phrase rendered "deep harmony and concord" translates a term meaning something like "being very much at peace or in agreement" — the contrast with "conflict and strife" is clear, though the precise nuance of the Tibetan compound (ཤིན་ཏུ་དུམ་པ) carries a sense of thorough reconciliation or unity.

The dialogue on the fruit of once-returning is a reference to the second of the four stages of stream-entry in the śrāvaka path, where a practitioner has sufficiently attenuated desire, aversion, and delusion to be reborn only once more before final liberation. The Blessed One's pointed question — why Śakra came seeking to preserve his life if he truly possessed no desire — reflects a standard doctrinal test of attainment.  The name Aṅgulimāla is well attested; the text gives Ahiṃsaka as his birth name and explains the nickname "Garlanded with Fingers." The five acts of immediate retribution are the five ānantarya-karmas: killing one's mother, killing one's father, killing an arhat, wounding a buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṅgha. The "six teachers" are the six rival religious teachers of the Buddha's time, a stock reference in early Buddhist literature. The prince "Jīvaka" here is not the well-known physician of that name but a figure in the narrative whose name the text gives as Sivikā in Tibetan; the identity and story are likely a distinct episode. Genuine uncertainty attaches to this name: the Tibetan སི་བྱི་ལ is not a straightforward phonetic rendering of any widely attested Sanskrit name in this narrative context; "Jīvaka" is an approximation offered for readability.  The "six teachers" referred to throughout are the six famous non-Buddhist teachers of the Buddha's time, well-known figures in early Buddhist literature such as Makkhali Gosāla, Pūraṇa Kassapa, and others; the text contrasts the Buddha's healing and salvific power with theirs. The three "acts of immediate retribution" are three of the five ānantarya-karmas: matricide, patricide, and killing an arhat. The Tibetan name rendered here as "Māpham" is a transliteration of a Sanskrit name; the manuscript tradition may vary slightly. "King Prasenajit's army" is the most natural reading of the Tibetan, though the syntax could also be read as a rival king defeating Prasenajit's forces; given the narrative context the rendering chosen is preferable.  The "Protector of the Northern Quarter" is Vaiśravaṇa (Skt. Vaiśravaṇa), the guardian deity of the north, also known as Kubera. The Tibetan renders his name Gömpé Ngalwasö somewhat obscurely; this passage appears to indicate that the butcher was reborn as the son of this deity, which is a notable karmic elevation from a single day of precept-keeping and is preserved as-is per the source.

The three acts of immediate retribution (Skt. ānantarya-karma) attributed to Devadatta here number three rather than the canonical five; this is as the Tibetan reads and is not emended.  Several proper names in this passage are either hapax or difficult to identify with certainty in the standard Pāli and Sanskrit sources. Ubarta and Anayyate are not clearly attested elsewhere and the Tibetan may represent garbled transliterations of Indian names now difficult to recover. Sudarati is likely a Tibetan rendering of Sudatta or a similar name. Lipa is similarly obscure. Vāsitā for the brahmin woman whose son died may correspond to Vāsiṣṭhī or a related figure. The phrase rendered "the younger brother of King Ajātaśatru" for Sūta follows the most natural reading of rgyal po sde rab tu pham byed kyi nu bo, where sde rab tu pham byed is a standard epithet-translation of Ajātaśatru. The "three fruits" available to householders refers to the first three of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path — stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning — the fourth, arhatship, being in principle also attainable by a householder though rarely so described in this literature; the passage likely intends the first three.  The phrase rendered "a hundred chariots laden by great white oxen" translates "bal glang," literally "woolen" or "load-bearing oxen," likely referring to large draft oxen; the image is of a caravan of heavily loaded wagons, which is the standard reading in this context.

The "four kinds of offering materials" is a shorthand for the four requisites traditionally given in such lists: food, clothing, bedding, and medicine.

The voice from the sky shifts into verse, rendered here as verse lines for clarity in narration. The Tibetan does not mark these formally as verse but the parallel structure and elevated register make the verse rendering appropriate.  The phrase rendered "the life-restorer" refers back to the speaking presence, the spirit of the king's deceased father, who has been addressing him. The Tibetan འཚོ་བྱེད translates literally as "life-giver" or "life-restorer" and functions here as an appellative for that presence.

The syllable-by-syllable gloss of "avīci" in the text is the Tibetan author's own folk etymology explaining the name of the hell: "a" equals "without" and "vi" (rendered in Tibetan as བྱི, byi) equals "interval." This is a doctrinal etymology standard in Indian and Tibetan Buddhist literature, and the translation preserves it as given.  The description of the light as simultaneously possessing and lacking color, root, limit, heat, and cold is a classic apophatic-then-cataphatic dialectic found in Mahāyāna sūtra literature, affirming that the light is ultimately beyond predication yet conventionally describable. The translation preserves both movements without collapsing them.

The "udpala" flower is the blue water-lily or blue lotus, left in Sanskrit here as the text uses it as a named botanical reference whose color is part of the point.  The phrase rendered "wrong craving" translates "log sred can," literally "one possessing wrong craving or wrong thirst." Some commentators gloss this as wrong views combined with craving; the rendering preserves the literal sense. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the Tibetan source itself is incomplete at this point. The bird name "kuśī" (bya ku shi) is an unidentified species in the Tibetan; it is retained as a transliteration since its identity is uncertain. The simile of the Tathāgata preferring dangerous animals over the wicked is a well-known trope in Indian Buddhist literature illustrating the Buddha's scrupulous avoidance of immoral company while simultaneously underscoring the king's anxiety about his own unworthiness.  The passage is a continuous medical-omen narrative. The stars listed — Fire, Gold, the Pleaides, Yama, the Tortoise, and the River — are Tibetan renderings of Indian lunar mansions or nakṣatras; their precise Sanskrit equivalents in this textual tradition are uncertain, and the Tibetan terms have been rendered descriptively rather than forcing a Sanskrit identification that cannot be verified from context alone.  The list of sounds at the opening continues directly from the preceding passage's enumeration of inauspicious omens. The Tibetan terms for several aromatic substances in the smell-examination passage — kṛtaka (byi-yi-ka / spos-byid-ka), takkola (ta-ka-ra), and tamalā (ta-ma-la) — are transliterations of Sanskrit botanical names whose precise botanical identities are debated in the tradition; the renderings here follow standard Indological conventions for these spice-and-incense terms.  The phrase rendered "unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening — the arhatship" is a slightly unusual collocation in the Tibetan, joining "arhat" with "perfectly complete awakening." This likely reflects the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra's deliberately inclusive framing, embracing both the arhat ideal and the bodhisattva ideal under a single description of the spiritual friend's role; no emendation has been made to the text.

The city name rendered "Kusumapura" (Tibetan: rTsa mchog gi grong khyer) is literally "City of the Best Grass" or "City of Supreme Grass" in Tibetan; this corresponds to the Sanskrit Kuśāgrapura, the old name for Rājagṛha, and has been rendered accordingly as a city name in context.  The name rendered as Sarvadharmadhara — literally "holder of all phenomena" — is a restoration from the Tibetan "ཐམས་ཅད་འཛིན་པ." The preceding passage contains "Vaidūrya" as a royal name in Śrāvastī and "Sunakṣata" (Su-na-ka-ta), both of which appear in parallel Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra contexts; these identifications are probable but the textual tradition has variant spellings.  The list of twenty contemplations is structurally unusual: several items read as indirect questions or dependent clauses rather than simple nominal propositions, suggesting the Tibetan itself may preserve an awkward or compressed transmission of an underlying list. The translation renders them faithfully in their received form rather than attempting to reconstruct a smoother original. The final sentence of Ajātaśatru's speech — "whether or not one understands those twenty things, one will inevitably fall into the hell of immediate consequence" — is a self-referential confession: he acknowledges that regardless of understanding, his patricide constitutes an act of immediate consequence (ānantarya), and his fall is certain. This is doctrinally significant and is preserved precisely.  The passage's argument about form having "ten aspects" draws on an Abhidharma-style enumeration of form's modes of appearance and apprehension. The precise list of ten is not spelled out here, and the argument proceeds structurally rather than enumerating them explicitly; this is reflected in the translation.

The final sentence is doctrinally provocative: the Buddha argues that since Bimbisāra's devotion to the Buddha was the cause of his attaining kingship, and the king's death followed from that kingship, the Buddha would bear causal responsibility if Ajātaśatru truly bore karmic guilt for the killing. This reductio ad absurdum is left as stated in the text.

The name Bimbisāra is supplied from context; the Tibetan here reads "King Rūpasāra" (གཟུགས་ཅན་སྙིང་པོ, literally "Form-essence"), which is a Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit Bimbisāra.  The geography "ཕྱི་བོ་ལའི་རི་" refers to the mountains of Pūrvavideha, the eastern continent in Buddhist cosmology. The passage uses this as the setting for Bimbisāra's former-life story, which is a narrative known in Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra literature to illustrate how past karma and states of intoxication mitigate culpability. The logic of the argument — that Ajātaśatru killed in a state of "intoxication by desire" and therefore without full mindfulness — is the key doctrinal point being developed here; the translation preserves this carefully.  The passage is a series of epistemological analogies arguing that killing, like an illusion, an echo, a mirage, a dream, a mirror-reflection, or a gandharva city, has no ultimate reality, and that the Blessed One perceives this truth while ordinary beings do not. The rhetorical conclusion drawn — that neither the king nor even the act of killing carries genuine karmic fault — is a strongly antinomian argument whose doctrinal provenance and context within the larger text should be borne in mind; the translation renders it faithfully rather than softening it.

The final sentence about the royal capital, sheep-slaughter, and fear is syntactically compressed and somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan. The reading offered follows the most natural grammatical parsing, but the exact point of the analogy at that juncture is not fully transparent without the surrounding narrative context.  The passage contains a sustained and philosophically intricate discussion of the ontological status of killing, using a fourfold schema that is neither simply existent nor nonexistent. The argument turns on whether the agent holds the view of existence or non-existence, permanence or impermanence, and whether shame and conscience are present. This is consistent with a tathāgatagarbha doctrinal context in which the "true self" obtained by slaying the selfless alludes to the buddha-nature teaching of texts such as the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, from which this passage appears to derive. The rendering "what is permanent is permanent" for the doubled phrase is intentional, reflecting the text's deliberate redundancy as a technical formulation distinguishing the correct view of permanence from incorrect eternalism.  The eraṇḍa plant (Sanskrit: eraṇḍa) is a castor-oil plant, traditionally used in Indian literature as an image of something coarse, low, or valueless, in contrast to the noble sandalwood tree. The image here is deliberate and striking: a precious sandalwood tree arising from a worthless eraṇḍa seed symbolizes the arising of true faith and bodhicitta from an impure, sinful body and mind.

The passage ends mid-sentence with "Today the Tathāgata has —" reflecting that the Tibetan source text provided breaks off here in the middle of a verse. This is not an error in translation but a boundary of the supplied text.  The phrase rendered "evil companions" translates a term that literally means "a friend of non-virtue," indicating an unwholesome spiritual companion or negative associate. The doctrinal point is the danger of association with those who encourage wrongdoing.

The name "Viśvabhū" (Tibetan: rnam par gzigs, "All-Seeing") refers to one of the past seven buddhas in canonical enumeration. The passage asserts that Ajātaśatru's roots of connection to the awakening mind extend back to that buddha's time.

"The region of Madhyāntika" renders yul dbus 'gyur 'chang, a toponym that is slightly unusual; it may refer to a specific locality or possibly be a scribal variant. The meaning of the sentence is clear regardless.  The five acts of immediate consequence (Tib. mtshams med pa lnga) are the five heinous deeds in Buddhist ethics — matricide, patricide, killing an arhat, wounding a buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṅgha — which lead directly to rebirth in the lowest hell without interval. The text uses "great deeds" for these and "minor deeds" for mental lapses into the Hīnayāna orientation, which is a somewhat unusual but doctrinally coherent use of magnitude here.

The syllable "bha-hva" appears to be a transliteration of a Sanskrit or proto-Sanskrit pedagogical syllable whose precise original form is uncertain; the text's own gloss (hva equals conditioned, bha equals unconditioned and permanent) is followed faithfully here without further emendation.  The bodhisattva named in the final section is given in Tibetan as Kun tu snang ba mtho btsun dpal gyi rgyal po. This appears to be a rendering of a Sanskrit name meaning something like "King of Glory, Supremely Venerable, All-Illuminating" — possibly corresponding to Sarvadarśī Uttamaśrīrāja or a similar compound. The exact Sanskrit original is uncertain; the translation renders the components by their sense.

The phrase rendered "liberates others by" translates a term that in Vinaya contexts means reciting a text for the liberation or benefit of another — here used in the sense of expounding or reciting the text to free others from suffering.  The term rendered "the planetary demon" eclipsing the sun and moon refers to Rāhu, the eclipse-demon of Indian cosmology; the Tibetan phrase is a standard idiomatic expression for this and no technical gloss was inserted to keep the prose flowing, but listeners should be aware this is a proper mythological figure.

The passage's extended cataphatic-then-apophatic description of the Tathāgata's nirvāṇa — "neither existent nor nonexistent… neither permanent nor impermanent" and so on — is a deliberate doctrinal strategy characteristic of tathāgatagarbha literature (here most likely the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra), asserting that the final nirvāṇa of a Tathāgata transcends all conceptual pairs without being reducible to simple negation.  The passage ends mid-sentence in the source material provided, breaking off at "whether there is a future time or" — this is not an error in translation but reflects where the supplied Tibetan text ends.

The term rendered "individual perfect knowledge" translates སོ་སོ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཤེས་པ (Sanskrit: pratisaṃvid), the four analytical knowledges or discriminating awarenesses. The dual form here refers specifically to knowledge of the Dharma (its words and categories) and knowledge of its meaning — the first two of the four pratisaṃvids. This is a technical term whose full doctrinal resonance may not be immediately apparent to a general listener.

The five doubts about the buddha — concerning nirvāṇa, permanence, truth, purity, and self — directly mirror the four qualities (permanence, bliss, self, purity) taught in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra as the true attributes of nirvāṇa, a distinctively Mahāyāna doctrinal position.  The text lists a series of classic metaphysical doubts that mirror the Buddha's "undeclared questions" (avyākṛtavastu) in the Pali and Sanskrit traditions, and the passage is building toward a contrast between wrong views held by ordinary people, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas on one side, and the correct understanding available through the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra on the other.

The phrase rendered "the great god who wields sovereignty over the devas" translates Tibetan lha dbang sgyur, literally "the god who controls or rules," which is a standard epithet of Śiva (Maheśvara). The text is criticizing the tīrthika view that Śiva possesses the noble eightfold path, listing it among wrong views.

The names rendered "Nanda and Upananda" (Tibetan dga' bo and bsnyen dga' bo) are the standard pair of nāga kings who appear at the birth of the Buddha in many canonical accounts.  The passage lists meditation teachers as Uḍḍaka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma, rendered from the Tibetan phonetic spellings. The Tibetan here gives "Utaka" and "Alācala," which correspond to the standard Sanskrit names of the two teachers the bodhisattva sought out before his awakening.

The phrase rendered "the four root downfalls" translates a term literally meaning "the four defeats" (pārājika offenses in the Vinaya context), but in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra these are recast in terms of the buddha-nature teaching and the capacity for confession and purification — a point of significant doctrinal importance in this text.  The bodhisattva's name — here rendered "Universally Illuminating King of Majestic Glory" — is a compound of Kun tu snang ba (Samantaprabha or similar) and mTho btsun dpal gyi rgyal po; it may be a single honorific name or two compounded epithets. The rendering follows the most natural reading of the Tibetan as a single name.

The argument about "hearing what was not heard" is a sophisticated philosophical challenge: the bodhisattva raises a series of logical antinomies (existence and non-existence, motion and rest, birth and non-birth) to press the Blessed One on the paradoxical formulation used earlier, and ultimately concludes that the Great Nirvāṇa, being atemporal, is inexpressible — a key Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra doctrinal point.  The bodhisattva names in this passage require care. "All-Illuminating, Sublime, Glorious King" renders Kun tu snang ba mtha' btsun dpal gyi rgyal po, a bodhisattva figure addressed at the passage's opening. "Anantakāya" is the standard Sanskrit reconstruction of Lus dpag tu med pa, "Immeasurable Body." "Vimalasthitarājakumāra" renders Rnam dag gnas pa'i rgyal bu, "Prince Dwelling in Purity," though the Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain; a general listener will follow from context. The phrase "not blue, yet seen as blue" and its sequence renders a carefully paradoxical formulation in the Tibetan describing the light's transcendence of all color-categories while still being perceived within them — this is a deliberate doctrinal point about the nature of the Tathāgata's light as beyond phenomenal characteristics.  The flower names — atimukta, campaka, pāṭala, pāśika, mārikā, simārikā, sumanā, yūthikā, dandurikā — are rendered directly from the Tibetan transliterations of Sanskrit botanical names, which are standard in Buddhist cosmological descriptions of pure lands. The identifications are conventional; not all can be matched with certainty to specific species.

The phrase rendered "steps" in "terraces along their steps" reflects a Tibetan term for the graduated banks or stairs of the rivers, a standard feature of pure land descriptions.  The epithet "All-Illuminating King of Lofty and Glorious Majesty" renders the Tibetan name Kun tu snang ba mtho btsun dpal gyi rgyal po, a bodhisattva character internal to this narrative frame. The passage is part of a mirroring structure in which the scene described in the distant western buddha-field precisely recapitulates the scene in which this sūtra is being taught — a literary device signaling the universality and simultaneity of the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra's proclamation. The phrase "Endurance" renders Mi mje, the standard Tibetan equivalent of the Sanskrit Sahā, the name of our world-system; it is sometimes rendered "the Endurable" or "the World of Forbearance." The city named is Kuśinagara, rendered from grong khyer rtswa mchog tu, literally "the city of supreme grass," which is a standard Tibetan rendering of Kuśinagara.  The passage contains a deliberate paradox in the opening lines: the light's arising is described as having "cause and condition" and then immediately qualified as "not cause and condition." This is a standard Mahāyāna rhetorical device pointing beyond dependent origination to the ultimate non-arising of phenomena, preserved faithfully here.

The phrase rendered "utter purity" translates the Tibetan term for the fourth of the four qualities of nirvāṇa according to the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra — permanence, bliss, self, and purity — which are here affirmed of the Tathāgata but denied of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, a key doctrinal distinction of this text.  The fourfold schema of hearing — "hearing the unheard," "not hearing the unheard," "not hearing the heard," and "hearing the heard" — parallels the fourfold schema of birth and attainment that follows. The doctrinal point is that "hearing" here is not merely auditory reception but a quality of understanding and transformation: one can be exposed to a teaching and yet truly "hear" nothing, or one can encounter what is ostensibly familiar and hear it as if for the first time. This is a standard Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra pedagogical device. The fourth member of the birth series is left as an open question in the Tibetan text at this point, indicating that the sūtra continues with the Blessed One's answer in the next passage.  The final injunction not to enter "too deeply" into the samādhi of emptiness is a standard sūtra device: the teaching is being delivered to a mixed assembly, and a display of profound absorption by a senior bodhisattva would be lost on or harmful to those of weaker faculties. The phrase rendered "gained mastery over birth" for the fourth bodhisattva ground reflects the traditional identification of the fourth bhūmi with the perfection of diligence and a particular kind of sovereign command over conditioned arising.  The passage contains a philosophically dense opening section on the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena, namely birth, duration, differentiation, and destruction, and their paradoxical relationship to permanence and impermanence. The text appears to be from the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. The argument is subtle: birth is called "permanent" in one sense by intrinsic nature, yet "impermanent" in another sense by its moment-to-moment cessation. This antinomy is characteristic of the sūtra's dialectical style and has been rendered as faithfully as possible without smoothing over the tension.

The phrase rendered "king of yaks" translates a simile comparing the bodhisattvas to a supreme bull yak, which is a standard Indian and Tibetan image of majesty and power among one's peers.  The bodhisattva names rendered in this passage require comment. The name of the questioner rendered as "Abhaya" corresponds to Tibetan "Jigspa medpa" meaning "the fearless one," used here as a bodhisattva's name rather than a common epithet. The longer name "Sarvaprakāśaśrīrāja" is a reconstruction from the Tibetan "Kun tu snang ba mtho btsun dpal gyi rgyal po," meaning approximately "King of Glory, Sublime and All-Illuminating." These Sanskrit reconstructions are approximate, as no Sanskrit original of this passage has been verified for comparison.

The fourfold formula near the end — "not arrived does not arrive," "not arrived does arrive," "arrived does not arrive," and "arrived does arrive" — is a scholastic schema likely referring to degrees of approach toward and attainment of nirvāṇa. The final line identifying "not having arrived" with great nirvāṇa is the beginning of a doctrinal exposition that continues beyond this passage.  The "four roots" is a reference to the four root precepts or foundations whose violation constitutes the gravest transgressions in the monastic code; the precise list may vary by context, but this is the standard rendering. The text's argument about nirvāṇa's naming is a subtle philosophical point: if nirvāṇa's nature came into being only upon the cutting of afflictions, it would be conditioned and therefore impermanent like a clay vessel; the bodhisattva is pressing the Blessed One on this apparent tension.  The bodhisattva addressed as "Samantaprabha Uttungaśrī" renders the Tibetan name Kun tu snang ba mtho btsun dpal gyi rgyal po, literally "King of Glory, High and Venerable, All-Illuminating." This is a bodhisattva interlocutor in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra; the name is here rendered from Tibetan since no single standard Sanskrit equivalent is universally adopted in English scholarship.

The phrase "six close placements of mindfulness" renders dran pa nye bar gzhag pa drug, which normally refers to the four foundations of mindfulness but here appears in an expanded enumeration of six, consistent with certain Mahāyāna classificatory lists.

The "six great dissolutions" (chen po drug 'jig pa) is a less common enumeration; it likely refers to a group of six meditative contemplations on the dissolution or impermanence of composite things, contextually paralleled elsewhere in Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra literature.  The four qualities of nirvāṇa listed — permanence, bliss, self, and purity — are the celebrated four attributes of the Buddha-nature as expounded in the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra tradition, standing deliberately in contrast to the four marks of conditioned existence (impermanence, suffering, no-self, and impurity). The presence of "self" here is doctrinally significant and intentional in this text.

The passage ends mid-sentence in the Tibetan provided; the translation reflects this natural break.  The bodhisattva name rendered here in English as Samantaprabhāsa the Glorious King of Lofty Majesty reflects the Tibetan Kun tu snang ba mTho btsun dpal gyi rgyal po, a compound epithet-name; no extant Sanskrit original has been checked against this passage, so the reconstruction is tentative.

The phrase translated as "actions without scriptural transmission and minds without scriptural transmission" renders lung mi ston pa, literally "not showing scripture" or "not transmitting teaching." The precise doctrinal nuance in the context of the cause of assembly is unusual; it likely refers to worldly or uninstructed actions and mental states, in contrast to the virtuous and non-virtuous instructed ones mentioned just before.  The phrase rendered "gandharva city" refers to the classical Indian image of a city of gandharvas (celestial musicians), an apparition seen in the sky, used throughout Buddhist literature as a simile for illusion and insubstantiality.

The four fears regarding wealth — kings, thieves, water, and fire — are a standard list in Indian Buddhist literature of dangers that can destroy or confiscate one's property, used to motivate giving before such loss occurs.  The simile of the man grasping a corpse to cross the ocean is a classical image; the corpse serves as a makeshift float. The point is that even an impure or seemingly inauspicious support enables liberation when nirvāṇa is one's aim.

The "sūtra known as The Buddha, the Sūtra of Varied Flowers" renders the Tibetan title སངས་རྒྱས་མེ་ཏོག་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་མདོ, which appears to be a cross-reference to another sūtra within the Mahāparinirvāṇa corpus or a related text; the exact Sanskrit title is not established with certainty.

The "four roots" refers to the four root downfalls, the pārājika offenses entailing defeat and expulsion from the monastic order.

The "five acts without interval" are the five heinous acts (pañcānantarya-karma) whose retribution arises without any intervening lifetime: patricide, matricide, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and wounding a buddha with intent to harm.  The bodhisattva's argument is a reductio ad absurdum structured in several interlocking steps: if the wrongdoer's buddha-nature was not cut when the roots of virtue were cut, the wrongdoer cannot be definitively condemned; if no being is determinate in their spiritual status, then even buddhahood and nirvāṇa lose their fixity; and if wrong cravings can simply be abandoned to produce buddhahood, then buddhas who have passed into nirvāṇa might equally "return," which would undermine the permanence of nirvāṇa itself. The Blessed One's final pronouncement — "those given to wrong craving are not determinate" — resolves the tension by affirming indeterminacy as the doctrinally correct position, consistent with the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's teaching that buddha-nature is universal and indestructible.  The passage lists "the four roots" falling away as an obstacle to awakening. In context these are the four wholesome roots of faith, diligence, mindfulness, and wisdom, or alternatively the standard set of positive root-virtues; the text does not specify, and any standard commentarial gloss would supply the referent.

The phrase rendered "twenty-five modes of existence" translates a standard Abhidharma list that enumerates the realms of sentient existence across the three realms. The precise enumeration varies by tradition, but twenty-five is the standard figure found in this textual context.  The phrase rendered "the Tathāgata is not an asura" is unusual; the Tibetan reads "the Tathāgata is lha ma yin no" which literally means "the Tathāgata is not a god (lha)," but given the immediate context — which proceeds to enumerate four types of lha and implicitly asks which category the Tathāgata belongs to — the sentence likely means "the Tathāgata does not fit under the ordinary category of lha," serving as a pivot into the fourfold classification. The translation follows the natural logic of the passage.

The innermost layer of cloth not being consumed by fire is a well-known detail of the Buddha's cremation narrative in Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra literature; the two things unconsumed are the cloth touching the body directly and the outermost layer. The Tibetan here specifies the body-contact cloth and "the inner outer layer," which may reflect a variant reading; this has been rendered according to the most coherent sense without overcorrection.  The phrase rendered "eighteen emptinesses" translates stong pa rnam pa bco brgyad, a standard Mahāyāna doctrinal list (the eighteen kinds of śūnyatā); the number is textually given and is a recognized enumeration in Prajñāpāramitā literature.

The text ends mid-sentence with the question about hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, which is answered in the continuation of the passage.  The passage's argument that the Tathāgata "is not permanent" on the grounds of having awareness, speech, bones, a clan, and parents is a deliberate dialectical structure: each attribute that ordinarily marks an impermanent being is applied to the Tathāgata to deny his being simply permanent, while the subsequent denial of impermanence is maintained on other grounds. The text is building toward a transcendence of both extremes.

The householder "Kuśila" is an otherwise obscure figure; the name is retained as given in the Tibetan. The three-cubit measurement renders the Tibetan "sku mtho gsum pa," literally "a body of three heights," understood in context as three forearm-lengths or cubits.

The phrase rendered "exhausted in a single characteristic" translates "mtshan nyid gcig tu zad pa," meaning that the Tathāgata's defining mark is singular and absolute, unlike individual phenomena which each bear their own distinct characteristics — a point distinguishing him from the multiplicity of conditioned dharmas.  The four modes of deportment refer to the classical fourfold bodily comportment: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. This is standard throughout the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra literature and requires no special flag.

The phrase rendered "city of Kuśinagara" translates the Tibetan term for that city literally as "the city of supreme grass," which is a standard Tibetan rendering of Kuśinagara. The Sanskrit toponym is supplied for clarity.

The passage's dialectical structure — affirming and then negating each predicate in turn — is a hallmark of the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra's treatment of the Tathāgata's nature, systematically transcending every binary opposition.  The enumeration of the six kinds of mind arising from doubt-views is rendered straightforwardly, but the list in the Tibetan is not neatly sixfold in the usual sense — it reads as a series of paired or related cognitive stances rather than six cleanly distinct items. The translation preserves the text's own listing without forcing an artificial symmetry.

The phrase rendered "drinking the soup of the mad" is a Tibetan idiom for a form of minor, ambiguous transgression; its precise referent in the original Indian context is uncertain, but it functions here as the far end of a spectrum of moral ambiguity.  The closing sentence is syntactically incomplete in the passage as given, ending mid-analogy.
