The phrase rendered "the sage's gaze, in a single day, drank the waters of the four great oceans" translates a passage describing a ṛṣi's supernatural visual power consuming the oceans — the syntax is terse and the referent of "sage" here shifts; the Tibetan has "sage Baśpu" introducing a new figure immediately after, suggesting the ocean-drinking feat may belong to an unnamed or differently named sage; the translation follows the most natural reading of the Tibetan word order.

The name "Agata" and "Alāla" are transliterated from the Tibetan; the Sanskrit originals of these proper names are uncertain and no standard Sanskrit equivalents are established.  The brahmin's name rendered as Śateśana follows the Tibetan phonetic spelling. The Sanskrit original is uncertain; it may correspond to Śatasena or a similar form. This is not consequential to the doctrinal argument.

The extended speech beginning "Gautama, liberation from attachment is nirvāṇa..." through to the end is presented as a single continuous argument by the brahmin Śateśana, building a cumulative dialectical challenge. The Tibetan structure is somewhat compressed in places, and the transitions between sub-arguments have been clarified slightly for readability without altering the logical sequence.  The Sāṃkhya cosmological scheme is being described here: intrinsic nature (Sanskrit: prakṛti) generates the Great One (Sanskrit: mahat), which generates ego-pride (Sanskrit: ahaṃkāra), which generates the twenty-five tattvas. The Tibetan list of sixteen factors and the final count of twenty-five follows classical Sāṃkhya enumeration closely, though the specific groupings given here are somewhat compressed or variant. The Blessed One's dialectical move — distinguishing a cause of manifestation from a cause of arising, and mapping these onto the two aspects of his own teaching — is the doctrinal crux of this passage, establishing that impermanence is the instrumental condition for realizing nirvāṇa without nirvāṇa itself being impermanent.  The name "Sīta" for the wanderer is the Tibetan transliteration of a Sanskrit name that cannot be recovered with certainty from this form alone; it may represent Śīta or another name close in sound. This is not doctrinally consequential but is noted for philological completeness.

The passage on the four kinds of non-existence is a classical Indian philosophical taxonomy of absence and negation, here put in the mouth of the wanderer as a challenge to the Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra's positive characterization of nirvāṇa as permanent, blissful, self, and pure. The translation preserves the logical structure of each category and its illustrative analogy faithfully.  The text lists three kinds of non-existence in the Blessed One's reply but then enumerates only two explicitly before turning to the "one thing absent in another" type. The Tibetan appears to present the standard three as a framework, noting that the third type — the mutual absence of cow and horse in each other — is the operative one for nirvāṇa. This is consistent with the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's standard argumentation on this point.

"Liberated form" and "liberated consciousness" render rnam par grol ba'i gzugs and rnam par grol ba'i rnam par shes pa respectively. These refer to form and consciousness as they exist in the state of liberation or nirvāṇa — a distinctive Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra teaching that the aggregates, when purified and liberated, partake of permanence, in contrast to the ordinary defiled aggregates which are impermanent.  The phrase translated as "you have repaid this body well" renders a somewhat compressed Tibetan idiom meaning Vāsiṭha has made good use of his physical existence by attaining the fruit of practice. The sense is that the body has been put to its proper purpose.

The name "Sāni" renders the Tibetan "ས་ནི" (sa ni), which appears to be a Tibetan phonetic rendering of an Indian name; the exact Sanskrit original is uncertain, though it may be Sāni or a similar form.

The term rendered "bones" in the phrase "spoken of the Tathāgata's bones" is the literal sense of གདུང་རུས, which can also carry a meaning related to lineage or descent; here in context it seems to refer to disparaging the Tathāgata's physical person or remains, though the precise nature of the offense is not entirely clear from the passage alone.

The closing section, where the Blessed One begins a response to Sāni but the passage breaks off, reflects the fact that the translation ends mid-declaration, as the Tibetan text provided concludes there.  The phrase "born in the five streams of existence" renders "rgyud lnga," which literally means "the five streams or continuums" and here refers to the five destinies of rebirth (gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings). The argument being made is that if a single all-pervading self were shared across all beings, all would experience karmic maturation simultaneously and identically, which is absurd.

The final sentence is abruptly truncated in the supplied passage; the argument continues beyond what has been provided.  The four social classes mentioned follow the standard Indian varṇa scheme: brahmin (priestly class), kṣatriya (royal and warrior class), vaiśya (merchant class), and śūdra (servant class). The Tibetan renders them as bram ze, rgyal rigs, rje'u rigs, and dmangs rigs respectively. The argument from the seed is that karma, like a seed, ripens impartially without designating whose fruit it shall be — undermining Sāni's claim that phenomena and non-phenomena, though sharing a universal self, can still produce distinct individual results.  The figure addressed as "Sānu" (Tibetan: ས་ནིས) appears to be the interlocutor engaging the Blessed One throughout this dialogue. The name may correspond to a Sanskrit proper noun not fully recoverable from this passage alone; it is treated here as a proper name.

The phrase "five streams" renders "rgyud lnga," literally "five continuums" or "five streams," referring to the five destinies or modes of existence: hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. The translation "five streams of existence" is used to preserve the interlocutor's own framing, since the point is that a supposedly all-pervading self would have no basis for experiencing distinct destinies.  The phrase "ten phases of time" renders a standard Indic scheme of ten temporal divisions of a life span or of time more broadly. The argument is that genuine permanence, like space, admits no temporal phases at all, so a self said to be permanent cannot coherently vary across ten such phases.  The names "Devadatta" and "Buddhadatta" appear in the source as "Lha sbyin" and "Sangs rgyas sbyin" respectively — standard Tibetan renderings of the Sanskrit names. The example illustrates that one agent cannot experience the karmic fruit of another's action.

The phrase rendered "the five paths and continuations pervade it" reflects the Tibetan "lam rgyud lnga yang khyab bo" — the expression is somewhat compressed; it may refer to the five sense streams or five path-continuums being coextensive with the self. This is a genuinely ambiguous construction and the reading is provisional.  The list of ingredients in the broth simile contains several items whose precise identification is uncertain. The rendering "Nepali citrus" for bal po se'u and "rock salt" for na le sham are reasonable contextual guesses based on Tibetan medical and culinary usage, but the exact referents of some of these terms remain debated in the literature. The doctrinal point — that the composite has no existence beyond its components — is unaffected by these uncertainties.

The passage on wind generating speech is consistent with classical Abhidharma and early sūtra physiology of speech production, in which the wind element mediates between the mind's conceptual activity and the physical articulation of sound through the vocal organs.  The phrase rendered "wandering ascetic" translates "kun tu rgyu," literally "one who roams everywhere," a standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit parivrājaka, a wandering renunciant. The figure is identified as being of the Kāśyapa lineage, likely a Jaṭila or brahmanical wanderer, distinct from the Buddhist Kāśyapas. The text breaks off mid-sentence at the close of the passage.  The question of whether body and life-force are identical or distinct is a classical Indian philosophical debate, and the Tathāgata's silence in response to it is consistent with the canonical treatment of the "undeclared questions" (avyākata) — questions to which the Buddha declines to give a one-sided answer because they rest on a false presupposition. The Blessed One's subsequent teaching reframes the question entirely through the lens of dependent origination, which is the standard doctrinal move in such contexts.

The fire-and-smoke analogy here functions on two levels: literally, as a case study in dependent origination; and metaphorically, with affliction as the fire and karmic maturation as the smoke — an interpretive gloss that Kunturu himself supplies and that the Blessed One implicitly endorses by his silence.  The phrase rendered "like going" and "not like going" translates the Tibetan expression for the stock tetralemma applied to the Tathāgata's post-nirvāṇa status. The underlying Sanskrit would be "gacchati-sādṛśa" or similar; this is one of the fourteen unexplained questions (avyākṛta) of classical Buddhist discourse.

The phrase "permanent body" (rtag pa'i sku) is doctrinally significant: in this sūtra's context it refers to the dharmakāya of the Buddha conceived as the eternal, direction-transcending body of reality, not to a metaphysical eternal self. This connects to the tathāgatagarbha discourse and may reflect Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra influence.  The phrase "twenty-five modes of existence" refers to a traditional enumeration of the forms of conditioned existence in saṃsāra, a standard doctrinal category in this text's tradition. The number twenty-five is not the more common "thirty-one realms" scheme; this reflects an older or variant Āgama-style enumeration that the text preserves consistently.

The name "Pariśuddha the Wanderer" renders "Kun du rgyu rnam par dag pa," literally "the completely pure wanderer." "Kun du rgyu" is the standard Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit parivrājaka, a wandering mendicant, and "rnam par dag pa" means "completely pure" — taken here as a personal name or epithet.  The passage about Vatsā's request being met with silence, and the Buddha's internal reflection on his sincerity, is rendered following the plain sense of the Tibetan; the construction is standard in dialogue sūtras of this type. The name "Vatsā" (Tib. be'u) refers to the wanderer Vacchagotta, well known from the Pāli canon; the Tibetan name be'u is a calque of Sanskrit vatsa, "calf," and I have rendered it as Vatsā for consistency with the Sanskrit convention, though the Pāli form Vacchagotta could equally be used.  The "last five fetters" and "three fetters" refer to the standard Abhidharma enumeration of the ten fetters binding beings to cyclic existence. The last five higher fetters severed at non-return are: attachment to the form realm, attachment to the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. The three lower fetters severed at stream-entry are: the view of a self, doubt, and adherence to mere rules and vows. The text explicitly glosses the attainments (stream-entry, once-return, non-return) through these fetter-cuttings, so the rendering follows the doctrinal sequence precisely.

The nāga kings named here are Nanda and Upananda, a standard paired epithet in Indian Buddhist literature for rain-bringing nāga kings; "Nanda" means "joy" and "Upananda" means "near-joy" or "great joy."  The phrase rendered "the eight types of great beings" and "the eight stations of excellence" translates སྐྱེས་བུ་བརྒྱད and མཆོག་གི་གནས་བརྒྱད respectively. The first is a technical term referring to the eight individuals on the four paths and their fruits (the classic śrāvaka schema); the second refers to the eight bases of mastery or the eight stations of superiority (abhibhvāyatana). Both are standard Abhidharma lists and have been rendered by their most common English equivalents in the tradition.

The "wisdom of universal scope" renders སྤྱི་བོའི་ཡེ་ཤེས, literally "crown wisdom" or "wisdom at the crown," which in context likely refers to a specific meditative attainment; it has been rendered descriptively.  The wanderer's name is rendered from the Tibetan as "Śikhin of the needle-and-thread" (kun tu rgyu tshem bu can), meaning a wandering ascetic who carries a needle and thread as a distinguishing mark of his sect. This is a well-known figure in the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra debates, sometimes identified with the Ājīvika or a related determinist school; his argument here is a classic statement of svabhāvavāda, the doctrine that all things exist and act by intrinsic nature alone, without causes and conditions.

The phrase "wisdom beyond training" renders bslab pa ma mchis pa'i shes rab, literally the wisdom of one who is beyond training, a standard epithet for the arhat's attainment.

The fifty-third fascicle heading appears within the passage, marking a canonical division of the Tibetan translation of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra; it is rendered plainly in the translation as it appears in the source.  The phrase rendered "a final existence" translates "srid pa tha ma thob pa," meaning attainment of the last existence before liberation, a technical term in certain Abhidharmic and sūtra contexts referring to the final rebirth of one about to achieve nirvāṇa.

The list opening this passage ("dull-witted and wealthy and poor...") is a continuation of the tīrthika interlocutor's argument that variation in the conditions of beings proves intrinsic nature rather than causally conditioned arising.  The phrase rendered "development or transformation" translates a compound meaning "arising and flourishing" or "growth and increase," referring to the progressive improvement that teaching and training produce in a practitioner — the argument being that if phenomena had fixed intrinsic natures, no such improvement through instruction would be possible.

The brahmin sacrifice passage is a reductio ad absurdum: if intrinsic nature existed and bodily ritual action had its own fixed efficacy, then brahminic animal sacrifice should be a valid means of purification. The implicit conclusion is that since it manifestly is not, fixed intrinsic nature cannot be what grounds action.  The five great elements referred to throughout are earth, water, fire, wind, and space — the standard classical Indian enumeration — here being invoked against an opponent (likely a Sāṃkhya or Vaiśeṣika interlocutor) who posits that phenomena possess fixed intrinsic natures independent of causes and conditions.

The phrase rendered "red copper, bronze, copper, iron, gold, and silver" covers six metals listed in the Tibetan; "ཚོན་མོ་སྟེངས" is somewhat unusual and may refer to a reddish alloy or pigmented metal — the list is illustrative rather than technically precise, and the argument turns on the point that the same substance can exhibit all four elemental properties depending on conditions.  The name "Sarvaśūra" (Tibetan: Kun tu rgyu) is rendered consistently with the preceding passage. The name "Mahāvistara" (Tibetan: shin tu rgyas pa, "greatly extensive") is the brahmin's name here rendered into Sanskrit equivalently; it is also possible this is simply a descriptive epithet meaning "the highly learned" or "very expansive brahmin," but treating it as a proper name is the most natural reading in context.  The passage says the Blessed One "appeared as a non-Buddhist adherent and acted as though he did not know" — this refers to a bodhisattva's skillful means of taking birth in non-Buddhist guises for the benefit of beings, a motif well attested in sūtra literature. The subject shifts subtly: after stating that this brahmin aroused bodhicitta long ago before the buddha All-Pervasive Light, the text implies it is that same buddha (now the Blessed One Śākyamuni) who, long having realized reality, yet appears in various forms including as a non-Buddhist for beings' sake — a reading consistent with the broader narrative logic.  The long enumeration of emptiness types follows a well-attested Perfection of Wisdom schema; twenty-or-so varieties of emptiness are standard in large Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, and the rendering here follows that canonical sequence. The phrase rendered "emptiness of the indeterminate" translates a term literally meaning "emptiness of what is not shown by scripture," which in context refers to the category of dharmas that are neither explicitly virtuous nor non-virtuous. The display of fire and water from the body is a standard description of the twin miracle (yamaka-prātihārya) associated with the Buddha, here performed by the māras in disguise as Tathāgatas.  The phrase rendered "patience with the Dharma" translates the term that in Mahāyāna literature typically denotes a specific level of realization — the acceptance or patient endurance of the truth that phenomena do not arise, sometimes called the "tolerance of the non-arising of phenomena." The present context lists it among a series of attainments without further specification, so the literal rendering is retained.

The description of the Three Jewels as sharing "a single defining characteristic" and being "permanent, abiding, and neither changing nor shifting" is a doctrinal marker characteristic of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra's teaching that nirvāṇa and the buddha are, against the common śrāvaka understanding, permanent rather than impermanent.  The three conditions Ānanda sets are a well-known episode in Buddhist narrative tradition. They establish that Ānanda would not benefit personally from robes or food offered to the Buddha, would not be compelled to accompany the Buddha on all visits, and would have free access to the Buddha at any time — conditions that protected his integrity as attendant. These three points are sometimes enumerated slightly differently across traditions; the Tibetan here gives a clear threefold formulation.  The regent Viḍūḍabha's massacre of the Śākya clan is a well-attested narrative in Buddhist tradition. The Tibetan gives the regent's name as Be ro (likely a phonetic rendering of Viḍūḍabha or Virūḍhaka); the identification is firm and the event is rendered accordingly without marking it in the body.

The simile of pouring water from vessel to vessel denotes that Ānanda retained everything without spilling a word — except in the one instance noted. The exception (the single "question" he did ask) refers to his emotional reaction upon the destruction of Kapilavastu, not a failure of memory, and this passage clarifies that the exchange he sought was one of consolation, not doctrinal retrieval.

The final sentence is incomplete in the source passage as given; the translation faithfully renders what is present without supplying the missing enumeration.  The names of the attendant monks and their respective buddhas appear to be transcriptions of Sanskrit names rendered phonetically into Tibetan, with no surviving Sanskrit originals that can be reconstructed with certainty. The renderings given here follow the phonetic Tibetan as closely as possible. Cāpaka, Upaśānta, Pati, Sote, and Yābamita are best treated as transliterations rather than translations.

The mantra syllables are rendered as they appear in the Tibetan phonetic transcription. The underlying Sanskrit text may differ in orthography across witnesses; the rendering here is a best approximation.  The name rendered here as "Śīntu Zangpo" (Tib. ཤིན་ཏུ་བཟང་པོ) is a Tibetan common adjective meaning "very good" or "excellent," and almost certainly translates a Sanskrit proper name such as Sudarśana or Suprabha; however, since no Sanskrit manuscript is available for comparison, I have retained the Tibetan as a transliterated proper name throughout rather than guessing a Sanskrit equivalent. Readers should be aware this is likely a rendering of a Sanskrit name meaning something like "the Very Good One."

The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, breaking off at Śīntu Zangpo's list of empirical observations. This is a continuity break in the input; the translation faithfully reflects it.  The name rendered as "Pūraṇa Kāśyapa" for འོད་སྲུང་རྫོགས་བྱེད is a plausible identification: འོད་སྲུང = Kāśyapa (lit. "light-protector") and རྫོགས་བྱེད = Pūraṇa (lit. "fulfiller/completer"). Pūraṇa Kāśyapa was one of the six famous non-Buddhist teachers contemporary with the Buddha and is known in the Pāli sources as an akriyāvādin, one who denies the efficacy of action — fitting the doctrinal context here, which concerns whether karma has present efficacy or only past causation. The identification is contextually secure.  The closing image of "grove" versus "tree" is a quotation from a sūtra, likely paralleling the Pali Dhammapada verse 283 or a Sanskrit equivalent, where "grove" stands for the thicket of mental defilements and "tree" for a single object of attachment. The Tibetan text presents it as a direct scriptural citation. The doctrinal point is that the grove of mental proliferations is to be cleared, not the individual sensory or physical basis, reinforcing the argument that taming the mind, not mortifying the body through austerities, is the true path to liberation.  The name rendered here as "Subhavyūha" renders the Tibetan honorific form "Shin tu bzang po," which corresponds to the Sanskrit Subhavyūha or Supriya, a disciple figure in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra. The identity of this interlocutor is confirmed by context.

The teacher named "Udraka" renders Tibetan "Ur to lam pa," clearly a phonetic transcription of Udraka Rāmaputra, the well-known non-Buddhist teacher of the historical Śākyamuni who had attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. The passage's critique is that even this highest non-Buddhist absorption is still a form of perception and constitutes bondage rather than liberation.  The phrase "passing from cause to cause" and "passing from result to result" renders a somewhat unusual formulation suggesting the chain of causal continuity, i.e., one cause giving rise to another cause, and one result to another result, rather than the more familiar cause-to-result sequence. This is intentional and reflects the Tibetan precisely.

The term "heroic advance" for "dpa' bar 'gro ba'i ting nge 'dzin" renders the absorption known in Sanskrit as the Śūraṃgama-samādhi, a well-attested meditative absorption associated with bodhisattva heroism; its identification here as a synonym of ultimate emptiness is a notable doctrinal claim worth flagging.  The name rendered "Śīlavat" translates the Tibetan "Shin tu bzang po" (Supremely Good), which is likely the Tibetan rendering of the Sanskrit name Śīlavat or possibly Supriya or a similar epithet. The text uses it consistently as a personal name throughout. I retain Śīlavat as a working Sanskrit reconstruction while acknowledging uncertainty; an alternative reading could be "Supriya" or simply "the Supremely Good One" as a descriptive epithet rather than a proper name.

The phrase rendered "the water of primordial wisdom saturated the vessel of mind" is a figurative expression describing the arhat's realization; the Tibetan is somewhat condensed and this rendering follows the natural doctrinal sense.

The expression "like an unfired pot" refers to the fragility of the unprotected being — a common simile in Indian Buddhist literature for the body's vulnerability without spiritual refuge.  The four qualities attributed to the nirvāṇa the Tathāgata declares he has long since attained — permanence, bliss, self, and complete purity — are the four pāramitās of the Tathāgata's dharmakāya as taught in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra tradition. The use of "self" here is the Mahāyāna positive re-appropriation of the term, referring to the buddha's sovereign, indestructible selfhood, not to the ātman rejected by the anātman doctrine — an important doctrinal distinction that the text itself presupposes.

The phrase rendered "the king of the māra of desire and the lord of ignorance" follows the Tibetan closely: the māra of desire is identified as a king, and ignorance is his overlord, a standard Mahāyāna formulation of the dual bondage of beings.  The passage uses "self" as one of the four qualities of nirvāṇa — permanent, blissful, self, and pure — which is the technical Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra doctrine of the four pāramitās of nirvāṇa. This is an intentional doctrinal claim of the text, not a translation error; "self" here renders bdag in its positive, ultimate sense as a quality of nirvāṇa, distinct from the ātman rejected in ordinary usage.

"Udraka Rāmaputra" is the standard Sanskrit reconstruction for the Tibetan reference to the non-Buddhist master. The Tibetan here renders his name partly phonetically.

The phrase rendered "five polluted objects" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure as contaminated or defiled objects; "polluted" renders rnyog ma lnga, literally "the five turbid or murky ones," a common epithet for the five sense pleasures in this literature.  The phrase rendered "the one who had never ceased" translates a Tibetan epithet meaning one who is unceasing or uninterrupted. In context it appears to refer to a divine being or a being present in the assembly who speaks to Ānanda to rouse him; the identity is not entirely explicit in this passage alone, and a full understanding would require the broader narrative context.

The expression rendered "six groups of monks" refers to the well-known group of six wayward monks who appear frequently in Vinaya narratives as exemplars of problematic conduct.

The phrase "my younger brother Ānanda" is notable: the text has the Blessed One refer to Ānanda as his younger brother, which is consistent with the tradition that Ānanda was a cousin and in some accounts a younger kinsman of the Buddha.  The phrase rendered "the six groups of monks" refers to the six classes of the Saṅgha, the standard Vinaya grouping of the fourfold or sixfold assembly, here likely meaning the six divisions of practitioners including monks, nuns, novices, and lay followers. Some editions may parse this differently; the Tibetan "drug sde" most naturally means "six divisions" or "six classes."

The description of the four close placements of mindfulness here departs from the standard Pāli and Sanskrit Ābhidharma formulations and reflects a Mahāyāna reinterpretation that emphasizes the ultimate non-locatability and name-only nature of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena — consistent with a sūtra of the Great Vehicle register.  The "fourfold retinue" refers to the standard assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. This is standard but left unglossed in the body since it is a conventional term that does not interrupt the flow.

The phrase rendered "treasury of Dharma has been compiled" refers to the First Council's compilation of the Buddhist canon after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, a historically significant event that the passage is clearly alluding to.  The passage's description of the cremation rite for a wheel-turning king is a well-attested element of early Buddhist narrative, paralleled in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. The phrase rendered "enters into the body of the Tathāgata" reflects the Tibetan literally; the intended meaning is that the body is to be respectfully handled and prepared, not that one mystically enters it — this awkwardness may be a condensed or slightly elliptical passage in the Tibetan.  The phrase rendered "as Rāhu regards the moon" refers to the Vedic demon Rāhu who eclipses the moon — the Tibetan reads "like Rāhu" and the simile conveys that the Tathāgata watches over sentient beings with the same total, unwavering attention that Rāhu fixes upon the moon. This is a traditional simile for one-pointed care or gaze directed toward an object, here meaning the Buddha looks upon all beings with unceasing compassion.

The "four māras" are: the māra of the aggregates, the māra of afflictions, the māra of the Lord of Death, and the Divine Māra (Devaputramāra).  The phrase rendered as "the light of loving-kindness endowed with five colors" refers to the five-colored rays traditionally associated with a buddha's aura; this is a standard iconographic and doctrinal motif in this genre of sūtra literature.

The expression "awakening of the non-cessation and non-arising" translates a technical term pointing to the bodhisattva realization of the non-arising of phenomena as its object — equivalent to the anutpattikadharmakṣānti, the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, a hallmark of high bodhisattva attainment.  The phrase rendered "shaft of downward-falling light" translates a term that literally refers to a light-well or skylight aperture through which light descends perpendicularly. The architectural details here reflect classical stūpa typology in Buddhist canonical literature, and the specific number of tiers (thirteen for a buddha's stūpa, eleven for a pratyekabuddha's) corresponds to the standard hierarchy found in parallel Vinaya and sūtra sources. The city name translated as Kuśinagara renders the Tibetan "city of the finest grass," a literal gloss of the Sanskrit Kuśinagara; the Sanskrit form is used in the translation for clarity.  The phrase rendered "mother lion looks upon her cub" translates a Tibetan expression meaning the Tathāgata regards all beings as equal and as dear as a lioness her only cub — a standard classical simile for impartial compassion. The interlocutor who raises the question about dividing the relics is identified in the Tibetan only by context and the name Māagalyāyana is supplied by the preceding narrative convention; the Tibetan here reads "Ma 'gags pa," a name meaning "Unceasing" or "Akhaṇḍa" — this appears to be a distinct character, not Maudgalyāyana. The name has been rendered literally as Māagalyāyana for consistency with narrative flow, but readers should note the Tibetan name is literally "Unceasing" (མ་འགགས་པ), a named interlocutor who is not the well-known disciple Maudgalyāyana.  The phrase rendered "eighty quadrillion" translates a large Tibetan numerical expression used conventionally to indicate a virtually incalculable quantity of light-rays; the specific figure is formulaic rather than meant as a precise count.

The "lion's mane fringe" passage is textually compressed and somewhat unusual. The image appears to describe the Blessed One parting his robe to reveal the lustrous golden skin of his body, with the "lion's throne fringe" functioning as a visual emblem. Some manuscript traditions differ slightly here; the rendering follows the most natural reading of the Tibetan as it stands.  The phrase rendered "the light of the passing into nirvāṇa" translates mya ngan las 'da' ba'i 'od, literally "the light of the transcendence of sorrow," referring to a miraculous radiance emanating at the moment of the Buddha's parinirvāṇa that purifies those it touches. The doctrinal claim that this light extinguishes even the five heinous acts (mtshams med pa lnga) is consistent with this genre of buddha-biography literature, where the parinirvāṇa event is portrayed as a final, uniquely powerful purificatory occasion. The "four root downfalls" (rtsa ba bzhi) here most naturally refers to the four pārājikas of monastic discipline, though in other contexts the number and content of root downfalls varies by vehicle and vow-system.  The closing absorption is rendered "soaring meditative concentration" for "yang 'phar ba'i bsam gtan," a term referring to the leaping or ascending samādhi associated with the final moments before parinirvāṇa; the precise Sanskrit correlate is uncertain but this rendering preserves the sense of an upward progression.

The long descriptive catalogue of the nature of the three realms follows the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra's characteristic negative-theology style, listing attributes that deny all conceptual handles. The rendering preserves the list form as in the original rather than smoothing it into discursive prose, since the cumulative rhetorical impact is part of the doctrinal content.
